en: Oṃ, obeisances to the illustrious Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
Here begins the third book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Oṃ, obeisances to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
Now begins the first chapter: The Dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava.
Śrī Śuka said:
Indeed, in this very manner, the venerable Maitreya was formerly questioned by Kṣattra,
who had abandoned his prosperous home and entered the forest.

Regarding Madhva: "At the time of war, however, Vidura, although he had gone on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, remained mostly in Gajapura out of concern for the Pāṇḍavas," so it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. (1)
Śrīdhara: Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Homage to Śrī Gopāla Kṛṣṇa.
In the third book, the description of creation is given in thirty-three chapters:
through the agitation of the *guṇas* by the glance of the Lord, creation arises from Brahmā.
In that [work], however, in the first chapter, the conversation of Kṣattṛ (Vidura) with Uddhava— who had departed after abandoning his kinsmen whose lifespans had ended— is first described.
That which was previously described in brief as proclaimed by the Lord Brahmā,
he [Śukadeva] then spoke again in detail as the Bhāgavata, as proclaimed by Śeṣa.

Indeed, the transmission of the Śrīmadbhāgavata tradition proceeds in two ways: on the one hand, in brief, through Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Nārada, and others; on the other hand, in detail, through Śeṣa, Sanatkumāra, Sāṃkhyāyana, and others. Regarding the second [of these]:

The *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam* was first presented in brief through the dialogue between Śrī Nārāyaṇa and Brahmā in the four verses beginning with "I alone existed," and so forth. That same work was then described somewhat more extensively as having ten characteristics (*daśalakṣaṇa*) in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada. Finally, that very same work was expounded by Śeṣa in extreme detail.
The commencement of the third [book] and those following is for the purpose of narration.

Therein, in the third book, first comes the meeting of Kṣattṛ and Maitreya in four chapters; then follows the detailed account of creation (*sargaprapañca*) with its dissolution (*savisarga*) in eight chapters. Then, by way of introducing the theme of dissolution (*visarga*),...

The incarnation as Varāha [is described] by seven [chapters]; then, by one, the collection of the creation; and in connection with that, by four, the incarnation as Kapila; then, by nine, the narrative of Kapila. Thus, the third book proceeds with thirty-three chapters. Therein:
At the end of the second book:
"The measurement of time, characterized by the form of the Kalpas, I shall explain later; now, listen to the Pādma-kalpa. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.10.47]

Thus, in order to explain in detail the matter thus promised, the venerable Śuka introduces a historical narrative with two verses beginning with "evam" (thus). [The city was] possessed of supernatural power and filled with all kinds of prosperity. ||1||
The Third *Krama-sandarbha*: Homage to the illustrious Śrī Śrī Kṛṣṇacaitanyacandra!
By whose instruction this collection of *sandarbhas* is being composed in the third *Krama-sandarbha*, he is my refuge, for I have no other resort.
Viśvanātha:
Having bowed again to the venerable Guru, I take refuge in that Śrī Śuka, the Lord of the World, the eye of the universe, who is the ocean of compassion for all beings.
To Him who is dearer than life to the cowherd women and exceedingly powerful,
and who is the beloved servant of her [the Gopī's] heart, I offer myself and my own.
In the third book, consisting of thirty-three chapters,
the creation of the totality of the principles (*tattvas*) from *pradhāna* as observed by *puruṣa* is described.
Having been demonstrated by the Blessed One, Brahmā, Nārada, and others,
the state of *saraṇabhāva* is now shown by Śeṣa, Kumāra, and the rest.
The dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava consists of four chapters;
the account of creation, including its dissolution, consists of eight; and the description of the boar incarnation consists of seven.
Then follows the summary of the third book: the withdrawal of the emission with one [verse], the arising of Kapila with four, and [the rest] with nine.
There, at first, the charioteer, having heard of the undesirable [news], went away leaving his elder brother;
there, he met Uddhava and questioned him.

In the eighth chapter of the first book (*pūrvaskandha*), after providing answers to two or three of the many questions posed by the kings, the Great Sage reflected in his mind: "Just as I have been questioned by these kings now, so too was Maitreya questioned by Vidura in the past. And then:
Having resolved, "I shall provide the answer to all the King's questions by means of this very introduction," he said: "Thus. "Possessing prosperity" means full of all perfections. ||1||
Or rather, this Lord, the creator of mantras and sovereign of all,
having abandoned the palace of the lord of the Pauravas, entered that which he had made his own.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he says that this is highly praiseworthy and not unworthy of being given away: "That which is indeed well-known as your home, O Pāṇḍavas"—referring to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who acted as the envoy and the author of the counsel;
the designation "this one" is used because of his presence in their intellects—"the home of that lord of the Pauravas, Duryodhana."

Having abandoned [everything], he entered uninvited. The reason for this is that [the house] was made his own, taken as belonging to him; this is the sequence of the composition. Regarding the phrase "yad vā ayam," Citsukha and Viśvanātha read "yadāśrayam. Furthermore, that house of his was [superior] to those sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) which he desired to visit.
It was the most excellent of all things and not fit to be abandoned; yet he abandoned it solely through the grief caused by his brother’s gift.

He says this with the word "yat" (which): "vai" means certainly. That house which belongs to you, the Pāṇḍavas—this [house] was made illustrious by him acting as a messenger and a counselor; the designation "this" is used because of his presence in the mind.
Then Duryodhana, the lord of the Pauravas, entered even though uninvited. The reason for this was that [the city] had been made his own, having been accepted as his property. ||2||
The King said:
"O Lord, where did the meeting between the steward Vidura and the venerable Maitreya take place? Or when did their conversation occur? Describe this to us."
Śrīdhara: Where did that meeting take place? ||3||

The sequence of the composition: In that regard, like Śaunaka, the King also asks about her with particular longing for her story—"Where? Where and when did their meeting take place, or their conversation?
There, "where" is understood to mean in what place or concerning what subject. "This"—that is, these three.
This is the meaning. ||3||
Viśvanātha: He was; he existed. ||3||
For there is no small gain for that Vidura of pure soul;
his question regarding that most excellent one is augmented by the acclaim of the virtuous.

Śrīdhara: *Varīyasi* means in the most excellent [state]. It does not become such that there is the arising of only a small amount of merit. It is *upabṛṃhitaḥ*, meaning increased or nourished by the *sādhuvādaḥ*, the approval of the virtuous. Alternatively, the meaning is that it was praised by the *vādaḥ*, the reply, of the virtuous Maitreya. ||4||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: In the most excellent (*varīyasi*); it does not become such that there is the arising of only a small matter from it;
it is nourished and increased by the acclaim and approval of you all. That which...
Or rather, the meaning is that he was praised by the reply of the virtuous Maitreya. ||4||
Sūta said: Thus questioned by King Parīkṣit, this most excellent of sages,
possessing vast knowledge and a joyful soul, replied to him, "Listen!"
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Śuka said:
"But when the king [beheld] his own sons who were unrighteous..."
Fostering his own ruin through unrighteousness, he whose vision was destroyed caused the sons of his younger brother— though they were without kinsmen—
to enter the lacquer house and set it on fire.
Regarding *madhvaḥ*: whenever he says [this], then the touching of the hair (*keśābhimarśa*) is obtained; thus, the word *yadā* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
For it is stated in the *Abhidhāna* that "whenever... then" is expressed both in the sense of a reason and in the sense of time (*kāla*). ||6||

Śrīdhara: He describes the offenses of the Kauravas as the cause for abandoning the home, even though it was not fit to be abandoned, in eleven verses beginning with "yadā. And the connection of the action occurs in the eleventh verse: "Then that Kṣattṛ departed from them. [He described the offenses] of Yaviṣṭha, the youngest Pāṇḍu, who was without kinsmen, being deprived of his father.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: This has not been explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The connection of the words beginning with "yadā" is with the verb situated in the eleventh [verse], "tadā sa kṣattā ayāt" (then that charioteer went).
"Vinaṣṭadṛṣṭiḥ" means one whose sight—the eyes as well as knowledge—is destroyed. Of the youngest (*yaviṣṭhasya*).
Of the youngest Pāṇḍu; those who were without kinsmen and fatherless. ||6||
When, in the assembly, the king did not restrain his son from the despicable act of seizing the hair of the godlike lady, the daughter-in-law of the Kurus.
As she steals the saffron from her breasts with her own weapons...

Śrīdhara [comments]: [This refers to Kṛṣṇa] who, with his own tears—the tears shed by King Yudhiṣṭhira (the son of Kuru), Queen Draupadī, and himself—wipes away the saffron from his own breasts, or rather, wipes away the saffron from the breasts of the wives of his enemies, who had been taken away by the slaughter of their husbands. ||7||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [The verse describes] her who, by slaying their husbands, steals the saffron from the breasts of the wives of her enemies—or perhaps from those of the gods of the Kurus, namely Draupadī; this is a fourth type of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).
And poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is also suggested. ||7||
But when that virtuous man, who had relied on truth, was defeated unrighteously at dice and had gone to the forest,
he did not give his portion as requested according to the agreement.
When he, delighting in darkness, [approached] the son of Ajātaśatru.

Śrīdhara: When he—who had returned from the forest relying upon truth and taking refuge in truth—begged for his inheritance, that portion previously promised by agreement, at whatever time [the father] did not give it, then, indulging in *tamas* (delusion)—[meaning either serving his son or resorting to lack of discrimination]—he acted thus. ||8||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: When he, having returned from the forest, was requesting his share—that is, his portion—according to the previously established agreement. ||8||
And when Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the world, spoke those words sent by Pārtha in the assembly,
they were not merely sources of nectar for men.
The king thought that his small remnant of merit had been destroyed.

Śrīdhara: Those words of Bhīṣma and the others, which were sources of nectar and flowed with nectar for men, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra or Duryodhana did not value greatly (*uru mene*). He was one whose small remnant of merit (*puṇya-leśa*) was wounded and destroyed; they were not a cause for happiness, fame, or righteousness, but rather a cause merely for the acquisition of the kingdom.
There was merely a tiny fragment of merit; because even that had perished, he disregarded [the teaching]—this is the meaning. ||9||
The sequence of the composition: where [the text] says "yadā," [Citsukha reads] "amṛtāyanāni" as "amṛtāvahāni";
and where [the text] says "kṣata," Citsukha reads it as "hṛta. ||9||

Viśvanātha: [The word] *viśva* means "of men"; for Bhīṣma and the others, it produced that state [of hostility]. King Dhṛtarāṣṭra or Duryodhana did not consider it to be great or much. The reason for this is given by the word *kṣata*:
it does not produce happiness, fame, merit, and so forth; rather, it was merely a small fragment of merit (*puṇyaleśa*) that had secured the kingdom.
The meaning is that because even that has perished. ||9||
When, having been summoned, he entered the palace and was asked for counsel by his elder brother,
then that most excellent among the seers of mantras spoke.
That which the ministers call "the lapis lazuli."

Śrīdhara: Now, with six verses beginning with "yadā," he demonstrates the very humiliation suffered by Vidura. When he was summoned for counsel by his elder brother Dhṛtarāṣṭra, entered the inner chamber, and being asked for advice, he then spoke as follows.
Why do the ministers still speak that which is known as the "Vaidūrika," the words of Vidura? [This] sequence of composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Now, with six verses, he shows the very defeat of Vidura brought about by him (Duryodhana).
Immediately thereafter, Vidura said: "Do the ministers still speak that which is known as the 'Vaidurika,' the words of Vidura? ||10||
Bestow the inheritance upon Ajātaśatru, who has endured your unbearable offense;
for there, Vṛkodara is like a serpent accompanied by his younger brothers.
Since you are breathing with rage, you fear enough.

Śrīdhara says: He states that very point with three verses beginning with "ajātaśatroḥ. Grant—that is, give—the inheritance to him who is enduring your offense (*āga*). In this offense, the serpent in the form of Vṛkodara, remaining together with his younger brothers, exists while hissing with rage; for you are *alam*, meaning exceedingly [capable].
You are afraid. ||11||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha says the same thing: "Ajāta..."—that is, when there is some offense (*āgas*) against which the serpent Vṛkodara exists, hissing with anger; because of which you fear exceedingly. (11)
But the blessed Lord Mukunda, the god of gods upon the earth, took the sons of Pṛthā under his protection;
that god of the Yadus now dwells in his own city.
He who has completely conquered all men, gods, and deities.

Śrīdhara: [The Lord] says, "Do not be proud, thinking, 'I have many such sons,' for Mukunda has accepted the Pārthas as his own. Moreover, he is a god, and even there he is the Blessed Lord, not an ordinary being. Furthermore, together with the *kṣitidevas* (brahmins) and the gods—"
He exists together with Indra and the others; for in that very place, O brahmins, are the gods—this is the meaning.

And he dwells happily in his own city alone, having not gone elsewhere. Furthermore, he is the god of the Yadu-gods, the one worthy of worship; for in that very place are all the kings. Therefore, [he shall receive] the inheritance of the Pārthas.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, saying "Listen to another marvel regarding their great excess of strength," he says, "But the sons of Pṛthā... [He] took them as his own; and that god, even there...

The Blessed One was accompanied by the earth-gods, the brahmins, and the gods—the implication being that the brahmins and gods were on his side. Even there, he remained in his own city and did not go elsewhere;
for he was one from whom the Yadu-gods, the preeminent Yadu-gods, were most powerful. Wherever he was, right there [they remained].
The meaning is "by whom the heroes of the Yadus [were conquered]. Furthermore, he says, "Hear of his very strength":

by him all the god-like kings (nṛdevas), such as Kaṃsa and Jarāsaṃdha, were utterly defeated; and from childhood itself, the gods, such as Brahmā, Indra, Varuṇa, and Rudra, were likewise subdued by him. Therefore, if you [intend to give] the inheritance to the sons of Pṛthā, then give it.
The sense is: "You desire welfare for yourself. ||12||
This very fault, hostile to men, dwells within your house, which you nourish through excessive devotion to offspring; yet, turned away from Kṛṣṇa, you have lost your prosperity.
Abandon this lack of faith for the sake of the welfare of your lineage.

Śrīdhara: If it is argued that Duryodhana does not accept this, then he says: "This very one, who is a personified fault, remains having entered the house. The reason for his being a fault is that he is *puruṣadviṭ*, a hater of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Who is he? He whom you nourish with the delusion that he is your offspring, yet he is no offspring; he does not fall [into the category of a true son].

For they say that offspring is [derived] "from this" (*asmāt*); thus one reviles him, saying, "You are he from whom prosperity has departed. Therefore, quickly abandon this inauspicious and non-Śaiva state. To the question of how a son may be abandoned, he says: for the welfare of the family. For the maxim is: "One should sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family. (13)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: If it is argued that my son Duryodhana will object to this, he says in response: "This very one" (*sa eṣa*). The meaning is: he is the fruit resulting from the evil deeds committed by you over ten million births.

Since the defect (*doṣa*), being material, hates the Supreme Lord who is the Person (*puruṣa*), it has indeed entered even there— your external and internal houses, consisting of mind, intellect, and so forth— and remains there; moreover, you nourish it, even there, under the delusion that it is "offspring" (*apatya*), for it does not fall away from this [state].
This is according to the etymology of the word *apatya* (offspring). For this very reason, you are not inferred to be one who has turned away from Kṛṣṇa or one whose fortune has departed;

rather, know that Lakṣmī has departed, having emerged from your houses. Now, if that is so, what is the remedy here? To this he says: quickly, immediately, abandon this inauspicious *aśaivya*. By me, your father.

He says regarding the abandonment of his son: "In my family, there would be a stain upon the abandonment of a son. To this he replies: "One should abandon an individual for the sake of the family, according to the maxim that one should sacrifice one for the welfare and prosperity of the lineage. Otherwise, the implication is that your entire family would perish. ||13||
Having spoken thus there, he whose character was envied by the virtuous was treated with contempt by Suyodhana, whose lower lip quivered with mounting rage.
The steward, together with Karṇa, his younger brother, and Saubala.

Śrīdhara says: Having spoken thus, that Vidura—the steward whose character was envied by the virtuous—was treated with disrespect and insulted by Duryodhana, together with Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni. (14)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Having spoken thus, [he said]: Vidura was treated with disrespect—that is, insulted—by Suyodhana, who was accompanied by Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni. ||14||
Who has offered him here as a libation— this crooked son of a slave-girl, nourished only by his own strength— who remains hostile toward him, intent on the work of another?
Let him be banished quickly from the city while he still breathes.
Śrīdhara says: He expresses contempt with the word "ka" (who?). For a son of a slave-girl is unworthy of being addressed here; he is also "jihma," meaning crooked.

He explains this crookedness: he is nourished by the food of the powerful one, yet he acts in opposition and hostility toward that very person for the sake of others. Therefore, let him be banished from the city. [He is] "śvasānaḥ" (snorting/snubbing).
The meaning is that he is merely left with his breath. In an alternative reading, the sequence of composition is as inauspicious as a cremation ground; it has not been explained [by others].
Viśvanātha says: He expresses contempt itself—“Who summoned him here to the assembly of the Great King?”

The sense is that he is unworthy of being summoned. The reason for this is: "the son of a slave-girl," meaning he is corrupt by birth alone. He describes his crookedness through his actions as well: "he who, nourished by the food given by the powerful one, is hostile—that is, adverse—toward that very master of his own, and intent on the affairs of others, namely his enemies."

He is engaged in this task; therefore, the implication is that while staying here, he will strive to destroy our entire family. "Let him be banished" means let him be expelled from here by whoever among my people is present;
the sense is that this should be done immediately, without delay, and even today—this very day.
The meaning is that he is left with nothing but his breath, having been struck many times with canes. Regarding the reading "in the cremation ground" (śmaśāne):

"This man is as inauspicious as a cremation ground; by whom has he been brought into the middle of our house—he who speaks such inauspicious things to me? Therefore, let him be expelled immediately, otherwise this royal city will become a cremation ground."
The meaning is that he will act in this very way. ||15||
Having himself placed his bow at the gate, even though he was struck in his vital organs by the illusions of his brother before him with such exceedingly fierce ear-arrows, he—
Free from distress, he went forth, showing great honor.

Śrīdhara: Although struck in his vital organs by harsh words—which entered his ears like arrows and were exceedingly piercing—he remained free from pain. The reason for this was that he held Māyā in high esteem, thinking, "Oh, how great is the majesty of Māyā! Considering her alone to be the cause, prior to her expulsion, he...

He himself went out on foot. Having done what? Having placed his bow at the gate, thinking, "What is the use of a bow? Surely these will die. Or rather, he placed the bow there so that [the enemy] would not suspect, "He will fight with us after joining forces with Bhīma and the others. (16)
Regarding the sequence of composition: at the point where [the text] says "himself" (*svayam*), Citsukha reads "smiling" (*smayan*). ||16||
Viśvanātha: Thus, with exceedingly harsh words that entered his ears like arrows, he was struck in his vital spots as if by shafts piercing the ears.
Moreover, this occurred even before his brother, who had not even said, "O enemy, why do you speak thus? Furthermore—
"Though struck, I am free from pain. O Duryodhana, you are fortunate; you are fortunate!

For by you all my distress has been extinguished—since I shall be cast out from here and remain somewhere far away at sacred fords and such, having abandoned all attachment to your father, what pain can I have?"

The sense is that he lamented within his mind. "From here" means he went out by himself; the implication is that since he was driven out by the wicked, it is auspicious that he departed on his own accord. "Having placed his bow at the door" means that having now abandoned everything, including his own home and so forth, he sat down in some secluded spot and [addressed] Kṛṣṇa.

The thought is: "What use will he have for this bow marked with such ill omens? Or rather, the bow was set aside so that this wicked man might not suspect that we shall fight him in alliance with Bhīma and the others. Leading [him] toward the illusory thigh, or honoring it, he was blinded by that very illusion before his eyes.

Even though Kṛṣṇa was present, he did not see him. Or rather, oh, how great is the power of the illusory energy (māyā) of the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, that in this manner He caused me, His own devotee, to be driven away from here, thinking, "Without a doubt, these men will kill him along with Bhīma and the others. ||16||
Having departed from Hastināpura, he who had acquired merit through his Kuru lineage and whose feet were worthy of sacred fords set out upon the earth,
desiring to perform meritorious deeds.
He who possesses a thousand forms has presided over them.
Śrīdhara: Then, with eight verses beginning with "sa," he describes the manner in which [the king] departed and traveled to holy places (*tīrtha*).

Having departed from Hastināpura, he visited—that is, he reached—the sacred sites (*padāni*) of Hari, whose feet are the source of all *tīrthas*, out of a desire to perform meritorious deeds. These were obtained through the merit of the Kauravas.

It is indicated that their very fortune had taken on that form. The meaning is that he, possessing a thousand forms upon the earth—namely the many forms such as Brahmā, Rudra, and others—went to each and every one of those holy places (tīrtha) and bathing-grounds (pādya) where he remained presiding. ||17||

The sequence of the composition: *anvākramat* means he reached [them] in due order. Out of a desire to perform meritorious acts—that is, with the wish for atonement for that evil association—he considered himself tainted; thus, the sense is that he did not go even to see Śrī Kṛṣṇa immediately. ||17||

Viśvanātha: By the phrase "obtained through the merit of Kuru and his descendants," it is indicated that their very fortune has taken on that form. By the expression "of Hari, whose feet are the *tīrtha*," it is indicated that such people have a desire to see the sacred site (*tīrtha*) only by perceiving it as His feet. The word *padāni* refers to sacred precincts (*kṣetrāṇi*).
Being of a thousand forms, with many manifestations such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others, he remains presiding over whatever [beings or objects] there may be. ||17||
In pure, merit-bestowing groves and mountain thickets,
and in rivers and lakes whose waters are free from mud,
all beautifully adorned with infinite lingas.
He wandered through sacred fords and shrines with undivided devotion.
Śrīdhara: In those meritorious groves and the like, "kuñja" refers to a place hidden by creepers and so forth;
and in those rivers, lakes, and sacred fords (tīrtha) whose waters are free from mud, as well as in shrines (āyatana) and sacred fields (kṣetra).
Of what kind are they? They are perfectly adorned with the lingas and images (mūrti) of Ananta. "Ananya" means alone.

The sequence of the composition: In those renowned cities where there is no *paṅka*—meaning no sin—in those waters that destroy evil, he is *ananya*, having his gaze fixed solely on Śrī Kṛṣṇa everywhere. ||18||
Viśvanātha: He is non-dual and alone. ||18||
Wandering through the land, subsisting on pure and solitary food, always bathed, sleeping on the ground, and free from worldly ties—
an Avadhūta unrecognizable by his own choice, clad in the garb of an Avadhūta.
He observed vows for the propitiation of Hari.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, while wandering the earth, he observed—that is, practiced—vows. His livelihood was pure, holy, secluded, and unmixed. He was constantly bathed, having performed ablutions at every sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
His bed was upon the ground. He was an *avadhūta*, one whose body is unadorned and who wears the garb of a renunciant.
Wearing bark garments and the like, he was for that very reason unobserved by others. ||19||
The composition of the sequence: distinctness is the state of being unmixed with other functions. ||19||

Viśvanātha: He whose livelihood (*vṛtti*) is pure (*medhyā*), that is, sacred (*pavitrā*), secluded (*viviktā*), and unmixed with other modes of subsistence within his conduct; who is "always bathed" (*sadāpluta*), meaning he has bathed at every sacred ford (*pratitīrtha*)—by this, purity through ritual bathing is indicated. Following such bathing, even if there should ever be contact with the untouchable (*aspṛśya*), [he remains pure].

"He bathes" means that, for the sake of constantly remembering the mantra of the Lord and so forth, he remains perpetually pure; "the Avadhūta" refers to one whose body is unadorned by worldly refinement, who wears the garb of an Avadhūta such as bark garments, and is therefore unrecognizable by his own [people]. ||19||
Traveling in this manner through the land of Bhārata alone,
by the time he reached Prabhāsa,
he had ruled the earth as a sole sovereign.
Pārtha [ruled] with the single umbrella [of sovereignty] over the unconquered [earth].

Śrīdhara: [He went] to that [city] which had but a single army, namely the discus, and which possessed but a single royal insignia, namely the white parasol; with Ajita, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as his companion. ||20||

The sequential arrangement: According to the Viṣṇupurāṇa, since it cannot be reached elsewhere, the Kumārikākhaṇḍa situated in the very middle of Bhārata-varṣa itself is to be understood [as the subject]. ||20||

Viśvanātha: [He describes] that [city] in which there was but a single army, namely the *cakra* (the discus), and in which there was but a single royal insignia, namely the white umbrella (*śvetātapatra*). With the invincible Śrī Kṛṣṇa as his ally and cause, Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira [conquered it]. ||20||
Then, there he heard of the destruction of his friends,
who were like a forest consumed by a fire born from bamboo,
having been burnt by their own rivalry; and so he grieved for them.
He went silently back toward Sarasvatī.

Śrīdhara: There at Prabhāsa, he heard of the destruction—the ruin—of his friends, the Kauravas, caused by their mutual rivalry. As for the illustration regarding their mutual destruction: just as a forest that takes refuge in the fire born of its own bamboo is consumed by it, so it was. Pratyag-...
Facing upward. ||21||

The sequence of events: "the destruction of his friends" should be understood as the destruction of the Yādavas themselves, because Uddhava met him immediately after that [destruction] and was not delayed for long. ||21||

Viśvanātha: Regarding that, some explain it as follows: "the destruction (vinaṣṭiṃ), that is, the annihilation (vināśam), of his friends, the Kauravas"—because of the lack of affection for Duryodhana and the others—and "of his friends, the Yādavas," because of the meeting with Uddhava before long; the grammatical construction is: "as the forest becomes burnt."
"Pratyak" means flowing towards the west, that is, flowing westward. ||21||
In that [river] are the bathing places of Trita, Uśanas, Manu,
Pṛthu, Agni, Asita, Vāyu,
Sudās, Go, and Guha.
That which the god of faith (Śrāddhadeva) practiced.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha visited the eleven sacred fords (tīrthas) of Trita and the others, which are well known by their respective names. ||22||
The sequence of composition has not been explained.
Furthermore, there are other various shrines of Viṣṇu here established by the twice-born gods of gods.
Upon seeing their temples marked with the principal limbs [of the deity], people remember Kṛṣṇa.

"Madhva is Viṣṇu, the foremost among those who possess the *pratyaṅka*; Brahmā is Viṣṇu, the possessor of the *pratyaṅka*, most excellently endowed with all characteristics"—thus it is stated in the *Tantramālā*. (23)

Śrīdhara: [These are] the temples constructed by the twice-born, the gods, the sages, and the deities; "pratyaṅgāni" refers to the weapons that are applied to each individual limb, among which the discus is preeminent—the temples marked with it, that is, inscribed upon the golden jars on their summits, wherein those various [images] of Viṣṇu [reside].
He visited sacred sites, fields, and holy fords, by the sight of which—those places possessing temples marked with the wheel-sign—there arises the remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (23)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Pratyaṅga" refers to those [weapons] which exist limb by limb (*aṅgaṃ prati*) with the twice-born gods, the sages, and the deities;
these are the weapons. Among them, the primary one is the discus (*cakra*); the temples marked by that [discus] are those in which...
Those [are] ||23||
Then, having passed beyond the prosperous Surāṣṭra,
as well as Sauvīra, Matsya, and Kurujāṅgala,
he eventually reached the Yamunā in due course.
There he beheld Uddhava, the devotee of the Lord.
Śrīdhara: Having gone beyond—that is, having passed over—just as Uddhava arrived, he himself also approached the Yamunā. ||24||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The word *tāvat* is used as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*) or to express urgency (*sambhrama*). ||24||
Having embraced with deep affection that well-known son of Bṛhaspati, who was a follower of Vāsudeva and possessed of tranquility, he wished him prosperity.
He questioned his own venerable subjects.

Śrīdhara: He is Vidura. [He asked] about his former disciple (*prāktanaya*) in the science of ethics (*nītiśāstra*). According to an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*), it means "one by whom ethics (*naya*) has been acquired. *Pratīta* means renowned.
He inquired after the welfare (*bhadra*) of his own kinsmen (*svānām*, i.e., *jñātīnām*). The reason for this inquiry was [his concern for] the Lord’s subjects.
Of those who are to be supported. ||25||

The sequence of the composition: although he had heard of the destruction of his friends, he asked after the welfare of his own people; this is the nature of one overcome by grief. "His own" refers to those who are most dear to him. ||25||

Viśvanātha: [He addressed] his former son, his previous disciple, in the science of ethics (*nītiśāstra*). Alternatively, there is the reading *prāptanayam*. "Renowned" (*pratīta*) means famous. In that regard, even though Vidura was performing an embrace, Uddhava’s lack of formal salutation is to be understood as being due solely to the swoon of divine love (*premamūrchā*). ||25||
I trust that the two ancient persons,
having descended here indeed by following the lotus from their own navel,
remain after having ensured the welfare of the earth.
Having found the opportunity, they were well in the house of Śūra.
"In the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa]: 'Madhva is designated as Brahmā, and Padmā is also called Śrī.

In the *Pādma* [Purāṇa]: 'The well-being of the Lord is inquired about with respect to his being the creator of happiness for the worlds; why is that very same thing inquired about because of his constant bliss? (26)

Śrīdhara: First, he inquires after the welfare of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. "Kaccit" is used for the purpose of inquiry. "Svanābhyaḥ" means born from His own navel; that is, Brahmā, who is lotus-born. By his "anu-vṛtti"—that is, by his request—they have descended here and remain in good health. They are "kṛtakṣaṇau," meaning they have granted the opportunity.

Or, "Have they both celebrated the festival? Even though the two of them are always virtuous, the question is: "Are they perhaps staying at the house of Śūrasena, distinguished by the aforementioned attributes? ||26||

The sequential composition [of the commentary] begins with the words "svanābhyeti. The term *svanābhya* is explained as "that which exists at the navel (*nābhi*) of one's own (*sva*) [Lord], who resides within the *garbhoda* ocean," just as in the expression *nijaśāsanārhaṇam* (the worship of one's own teaching). It is used so that there may be *kuśalam*, meaning the auspiciousness or welfare of the worlds. ||26||

Viśvanātha: Thinking that the welfare of His progeny depends solely upon the Lord’s manifest presence, he inquires after the Lord’s state of happiness with the words "Kaccit" (I hope...). Regarding the question: although Brahmā, who dwells in Your own navel (*svanābhya*), namely the lotus-born one, has found leisure—that is, his festival has begun—and although they both are eternally well, [he asks for their news].
An inquiry after one's welfare should be understood as arising solely from affection. ||26||
I trust that Bhāma Śauri, our supreme friend of the Kurus, dwells in happiness, O dear one—
he who indeed provides for his sisters' sons like a father.
The generous one grants boons through the most excellent gratification.
Through the most excellent satisfaction with honeyed wine, that is, through the satisfaction of her husband. ||27||

Śrīdhara [comments]: With nine verses, he inquires after the welfare of the Yadus. Bhāma is venerable; Śauri is Vasudeva. Alternatively, Bhāma is the husband of a sister (bhaginī). Kuntī was the sister of Vasudeva; therefore, according to worldly convention, Devakī is the sister of Pāṇḍu. [He asks for] excellent objects; he is *vadānya*, meaning exceedingly generous.
Together with the satiation and nourishment of the boons and their lords.
The sequence of the composition: Bhāma is the husband of his sister (bhaginī), because he is the husband of Rohiṇī, who is a daughter of Puru (pauravī).
The term "sisters" (svasṝṇām) is used with the intention of expressing Kuntī’s affection. ||27||

Viśvanātha: *Bhāma* means a sister’s husband. Since Pauravī, the wife of Vasudeva, was the sister of Vidura and others, *Śauri* refers to Vasudeva. By the phrase "of his sisters," the excess of affection felt by Kuntī is suggested (*dhvanyate*), as such a state is not observed toward other sisters. *Varān* means desired objects.
Together with the gratification and satisfaction of those lords of excellent objects. ||27||
I trust that Pradyumna, the heroic lord of the Yādavas and protector of their forces, dwells in happiness,
O dear one— he whom Rukmiṇī obtained from the Blessed Lord.
Having propitiated the brahmins at the beginning of creation, he remembered [the past].
Regarding the term *madhvaḥ*, Śrīdhara states in his commentary on the *Abhidhāna* that "the mind, the protector (*varūtha*), and the self (*ātman*) are called one's own.

[In this context,] the commander of the army is the lord of the protectors (*varūthādhipati*). At the beginning of creation, in her previous birth, she obtained—that is, she gained—as her son the existing Smara, the god of love. (28)
The sequential arrangement: [He refers to] Smara, who is the form of the manifestation (vyūha) of the Blessed Lord; for this has been determined and explained in the *Śrīkṛṣṇasandarbha*. ||28||
Viśvanātha: In this question, due to extreme agitation, he did not follow the proper sequence.

*Varūthādhipati* means the commander-in-chief. Regarding the phrase "Smara" (the god of love) in the context of the primordial creation (*ādisarga*) or previous birth: since Kandarpa is divine and Pradyumna is human, such a designation serves to highlight his excellence.

In reality, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), Kandarpa is indeed a specific manifestation (*vibhūti*) of Him. Likewise, even further on, His partial manifestations (*aṃśavibhūtayaḥ*) are everywhere described in the accounts of His pastimes as being identical with Him.
For example, even Devakī and Vasudeva were spoken of by the Lord Himself as the sons of Pṛśni and Tapaḥ: "You..."
In passages such as, "Thus you were Pṛśni in the previous creation during the time of Svāyambhuva" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.3.32),
it should be understood everywhere that the cause is indeed the wonder produced by the nourishment of His pastimes as a human; as in this very instance,
"having propitiated the brāhmaṇas," and "Jāmbavatī, rich in vows" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.1.30), and Rukmiṇī.
Even for Jāmbavatī and the others, who are the very forms and powers of the Blessed One, there is likewise the respective means for each respective purpose. ||28||
I hope that lord of the Sātvatas, Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas, and Dāśārhas dwells in happiness—
he whom the lotus-eyed one consecrated.
Having abandoned the hope for the royal throne from afar.
Śrīdhara: Ugrasena is the lord of the Sātvatas and others; Śrī Kṛṣṇa has lotus-like eyes.

The meaning is that, having abandoned the hope for the royal throne—that is, the desire for sovereignty—he stands at a distance out of fear for his life; this is the sequence of the composition. [The phrase] "having abandoned even the direction of the royal throne" refers to this.
Or rather, the creator is indeed the one with eyes like a hundred-petaled lotus. ||29||

Viśvanātha: Ugrasena is the sovereign. The meaning is that he remained far away out of fear for his life, having abandoned his desire for the royal throne—that is, his longing for the kingdom. Śatapatranetra is Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||29||
O gentle one, I trust that Hari’s son Sāmba, the leader of chariot-warriors, remains well—
he whom the vow-observant Jāmbavatī brought forth.
The god Guha, who was held first by Ambikā.

Śrīdhara: O gentle one! Hari’s son, being like him—that is, similar to him—dwells happily. Guha is Svāmikārttikeya; he is the one who was held in the womb of Bhavānī in a previous birth, namely, in the former life. ||30||
The sequence of composition: Sāmba’s status as Guha is exactly like that of Pradyumna. ||30||

Viśvanātha: *Sadṛkṣaḥ* means similar. Regarding Guha, that is Kārttikeya. Because of the identity between the part and the whole (*aṃśāṃśinoḥ aikyāt*), and because Rudra is a partial incarnation (*aṃśa*) of the Blessed Lord, it should be understood through reasoning that Kārttikeya, his son, is likewise a partial incarnation of the son of the Blessed Lord. Alternatively, the Lord of the high and the low (*parāvareśaḥ*) is joined with the portion of the Great Principle (*mahadaṃśayukta*).
By such reasoning as will be stated hereafter, when Śrī Kṛṣṇa entered Nārāyaṇa at the time of His descent,

there arose the perception that Nārāyaṇa Himself had descended in the house of Vasudeva; likewise, because Samba entered Guha, Pradyumna entered Kāma, and Uddhava and others entered the Vasus and so forth, they were described in those respective ways.
It is not untenable. ||30||
Is Yuyudhāna,
who obtained the secret of the bow from Phālguna and swiftly attained [mastery] through service alone to Adhokṣaja, dwelling in safety?
His state, which is difficult for ascetics to attain.
Śrīdhara: Yuyudhāna is Sātyaki. Is he well? He is one by whom the secret of the bow was obtained from Phālguna, that is, Arjuna. "His" refers to that which pertains to Adhokṣaja. (31)
The sequential arrangement: [he perceives] her most intimate movement. ||31||
Viśvanātha: Yuyudhāna is Sātyaki. From Phālguna, that is, from Arjuna. ||31||
I trust that the wise son of Śvaphalka, who has taken refuge in the Blessed One, dwells in well-being and freedom from ailment—
he who [finds joy] in the dust of the path marked by Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
His fortitude shattered by love, he became motionless.

Śrīdhara: Akrūra was the son of Śvaphalka. He was wise and learned; therefore, he took refuge in and followed the Blessed One. For this very reason, he was *anamīva*, meaning free from sin. This is a mark of devotion. He who "strove" (*aceṣṭata*) means he rolled about [on the ground]. He is one whose fortitude was shattered and rent asunder by love. *Svasti* means well-being or security.
He remains. ||32||
The sequence of composition: Although Akrūra was always possessed of supreme devotion, it is appropriate that he should call out "Kṛṣṇa!
because of the extraordinary wonder produced by the specific qualities of time, place, and other factors. ||32||
Viśvanātha: Free from disease and sin, Akrūra, the son of Śvaphalka, moved forward and rolled about upon entering the village of Nanda. (32)
Is all well with Śivā, the daughter of Devaka and the mother of Viṣṇu, who, like the Mother of the Gods,
bore the Lord within her own womb?
Just as the three Vedas serve the purpose of supporting the sacrifice.
Śrīdhara: Of Devakī, the daughter of that Bhoja named Devaka; [of her] whose offspring was Viṣṇu, as if she were Aditi, the mother of the gods. Is all well?
Just as the triple Veda (trayī) sustains the purpose consisting of the expansion of sacrifice by means of its illuminating power, so did she sustain it.
The sequential arrangement [is as follows]: "Like the mother of a god" is given as an illustration because of the absence of anything else [to serve as a comparison]. ||33||
Viśvanātha: [He was born] from Devakī, the daughter of that Bhoja named Devaka; she whose offspring was Viṣṇu, just like Aditi, the mother of the gods. ||33||
Is the Blessed One well,
he who is Aniruddha, the wish-fulfilling cow for the Sātvatas,
whom they indeed declare to be the source of all speech?
The mind-made [body] is the reality of the fourth state of being.
Śrīdhara: He is the "milk-cow of desires" (kāmadugha) because he milks—that is, fulfills—the desires of the Sātvatas, the devotees.
The reason for his being the Blessed Lord (Bhagavat) is as follows: the Vedas declare him to be the source, that is, the cause, of the Word, which is the scripture.
Why so? Because he is "consisting of mind" (manomaya), meaning he is the impeller of the mind. And why is that? [Because...]

The fourth reality, the fourth [state], is the presiding deity of the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Indeed, Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are, respectively, the presiding deities of the distinctions of the internal organ—namely, *citta*, *ahaṅkāra*, *buddhi*, and *manas*. And of the *manas*...

The fact that sound is the source [of the Veda] is well known: "The mind is its prior form; speech is its subsequent form. Likewise, having introduced [the passage], "There is another inner self consisting of mind," the scripture continues: "The Yajus is indeed its head; the Ṛk is its right wing; the Sāman is its left wing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), and so forth. And thus:
Regarding the training:
"The self, having come together with the intellect, joins the mind to objects through the desire to speak;
the mind strikes the fire of the body, which impels the vital air."
"The wind moving within the chest produces a deep tone," and so forth. (34)

The sequence of the composition: Thus, he states the evidence for Aniruddha’s direct status as the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) with the words "api svid" and so on. "The source of sound" refers to the collection of Vedas manifested by his breath, according to the passage: "Verily, O Maitreyī, this great Being breathes forth this Rigveda... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10).
Because of the scriptural statement beginning with "ādi" (and so forth). "Consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) means it is to be meditated upon in the mind, like Vāsudeva.
"Sattva" refers to the Blessed Lord in the form of Śrī Vāsudeva and others, whose nature is pure *sattva*; therein lies His fourth form.
Therefore, in the battle with Bāṇa and other instances, acts such as feigning bondage are merely pastimes (*līlā*) consisting of His own will.
Like Śrī Rāmacandra and others. These are the names from the *Māhātmya* section of the *Padma Purāṇa’s Bṛhatsahasranāma*:
Aniruddha, Bṛhadbrahma, Prādyumni, Viśvamohana.
He is fourfold in nature, consisting of the four castes, and the ordainer of the four ages.
"The one whose self is the universe with its fourfold divisions, who is the source of millions of most excellent portions, whose nature is the substratum...
Thus, because he is Mahāniruddha by virtue of being the manifestation of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa-vyūha, this is indeed a specific mode of his manifestation.

The Puruṣa is to be known as having his abode in the ocean of dissolution and other states. For this very reason, it is stated in such passages as *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 1.3.1, "Therefore, the Blessed Lord assumed the form of Puruṣa without distinction," that the three other states—Saṃkarṣaṇa and so forth—are manifested as Puruṣa precisely through the portions beginning with Mūla-Saṃkarṣaṇa. In the same way, without distinction...
This is also stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. Therein, the inquiry of Śrīvajra is as follows:
"Who is this one who, in the form of a child, is seen by you again and again at the ends of the kalpas, yet remains unknown? In this matter, I have a great curiosity."
And further, in the *Śrīmārkaṇḍeya-uttara*:
"Again and again that Lord of the World was seen by me; indeed, He was recognized at the end of the kalpa by me, who was deluded by His māyā."
"When the dissolution of the eon has passed,
I recognize that Lord Aniruddha, the Grandfather, as your father, the Lord of the Universe"—
thus [is stated] in the Bhīṣmaparvan, within the instruction of Bhīṣma to Duryodhana, at the beginning of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s incarnation.
Then, as the boy beheld in his mind the manifestation of Brahmā who had arrived at Gandhamādana, he spoke these words:
"Having created the god Saṃkarṣaṇa by himself from his own self..."
O Kṛṣṇa, you yourself brought forth Pradyumna, who was born from your own self.
From Pradyumna you [produced] Aniruddha, whom they know as the imperishable Viṣṇu;
and Aniruddha indeed created me, Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds.
"I am that very Vāsudeva, created by you alone" (Mahābhārata 6.61.65–67).

For this very reason, in the passage "And for that same purpose, he formerly assumed a human form" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.3.1), Śrī Kṛṣṇa's inclusion within the Aniruddha incarnation was not explained; hence, there is a distinction.

In the *Kṛṣṇasandarbha* [Śrī Kṛṣṇasandarbha 89], Viśvanātha comments: "The cause of the devotion (*bhāva*) of the Sātvatas, a specific class of Yādavas; the source of sound (*śabdayoni*), which is the collection of Vedas manifested from His breath—thus it is said:
'Verily, O Maitreyī, this great Being breathed forth the Vedas... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10).

This is because of such scriptural passages as, "That which is the Rigveda... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10). It is called *manomaya* because it is made of mind; that is, it is the activator of the mind. Likewise, it is the fourth (*turīya*) principle of the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) whose nature is pure *sattva*; and that too [is present] for him in battles with arrows and the like.

Imprisonment and the like are merely His play (*līlā*), consisting of His own inconceivable will, just as in the case of Śrī Rāmacandra and others. Regarding His fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) here, the authority is found in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, in the *Vajrapraśna* section, as Mārkaṇḍeya’s reply,
as follows:
Again and again that Lord, the Master of the World, was seen by me; indeed, he was recognized at the end of the kalpa by me who was deluded by his illusory power.
"When the dissolution of the eon has passed, I recognize that Lord Aniruddha, the Lord of the Universe, as your father from my great-grandfather," thus [it is said] in the Bhīṣmaparvan,
in the instruction of Bhīṣma to Duryodhana, at the commencement of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s incarnation.
Then, as Brahmā arrived at Gandhamādana, perceiving in his mind that manifestation [of Viṣṇu] and offering praise, he spoke these words of the Veda:
"Having created the god Saṃkarṣaṇa by himself, through his own self..."
O Kṛṣṇa, you yourself brought forth Pradyumna, who was born from your own self.
From Pradyumna you [produced] Aniruddha, whom they know as the imperishable Viṣṇu;
indeed, it was Aniruddha who created me, Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds.
"I am that very Vāsudeva, created by you alone. Thus,
are there not others as well who, with undivided devotion, have followed their own self as their deity?
O gentle one, Hṛdīka, Satyā’s son Cārudeṣṇa, Gada, and the others are doing well.

Śrīdhara: "Api svit" means "what indeed? Others also practice for their own welfare. Those who have properly followed—that is, devoted themselves to—the divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa, their own self which is distinct from the body and so forth, with the state of exclusive and single-minded devotion; [such as] Hṛdīka.
And those whose leaders were Satyabhāmā’s son Cārudeṣṇa and Gada, they too [were present]. ||35||
The sequential composition: "His own" refers to one's own self; "the divine" refers to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||35||
Viśvanātha: They are those who have properly followed, that is, pursued, Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who is their own very self, their manifest destiny, as it were. ||35||
Moreover, through his own two arms— Vijaya and Achyuta—
Dharma protects the bridge of righteousness according to dharma;
that Duryodhana was tormented in the assembly hall [is because of this].
By means of the imperial fortune that follows upon victory.

Śrīdhara: Now he asks about the Kurus with six verses. "Api" means "whether. Does Yudhiṣṭhira, who is Dharma himself, protect the bridge—the boundary of righteousness—by means of the path of dharma, through Vijaya and Acyuta, namely Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa, who act like his own two arms? Of him...
"In the assembly" means by following victory, that is, by a succession of triumphs, or by the service of Arjuna;
the meaning is that his sovereignty is of such a nature. ||36||
The sequence of composition: The passage beginning with "api svadorbhyām" [is placed here] because their manifestation would be impossible following the disappearance of the Blessed Lord. ||36||

Viśvanātha: Now he asks about the Kurus with six verses. "Api" means "whether. By the two arms equal [to those of] Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa, did Dharma—Yudhiṣṭhira—[cross] the bridge, that is, the boundary of dharma? And by what kind of sovereignty? That in which there was the persistence of victory, meaning universal preeminence. (36)
Or rather, did Bhīma, exceedingly intolerant of offenses committed against him, release his most long-lasting wrath like a serpent,
such that the field of battle could not endure the falling of his feet?
He followed the diverse path of her who moves with a mace.
Madhva cast off his sin; having abandoned the thought of further transgression, he remains [in purity]. ||37||

Śrīdhara: Did Bhīma—who is as intolerant as a serpent—release his own long-cherished, most grievous sin against the Kurus who had committed offenses, while he was moving in various and wonderful ways with his mace; or did he not? [37]

The sequence of composition: *agham* refers to the calamity born of anger. According to Amara, "the word *agham* is used for sin, suffering, and calamity. This was stated by inference from the phrase "whose feet... (yasyāṅghri...). [37]

Viśvanātha: Did they not release upon the Kurus—who had committed offenses—the sin of their own doing, which was like poison, the cause of their destruction, and which they had contemplated for a long time? Or did they not? ||37||
I trust that Yaśodhā remains unharmed by the leaders of chariot-divisions,
while the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow— his enemies having been quelled—
remains unobserved, hidden within a mass of arrows?
Giriśa was pleased with Māyākirāta.

Śrīdhara: He who bestows glory (*yaśodhāḥ*) and maintains fame (*kīrtidhārī*) among the leaders of chariot-divisions; or rather, he who grants fame to his own [followers], from whom enemies have ceased (*uparata-arayaḥ*), and who is concealed (*gūḍha*)—that is, covered—by a mass (*kūṭa*) of arrows (*śara*), a multitude of shafts. ||38||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He who is the bearer of glory (*yaśodhāḥ*), the possessor of fame, remains among the leaders of the chariot-divisions (*rathayūthapānām*) with his enemies destroyed (*uparatiḥ*); he is hidden and covered by the multitude of his arrows (*yaccharasamūhena*). ||38||
Or perhaps the two sons of Pṛthā,
like the twin Yamās, are surrounded by the Pārthas as eyes are by eyelashes; having risen up in battle, they rejoice in their own inheritance.
Like two fair-winged birds from the mouth of the wielder of the thunderbolt.

Śrīdhara: Or rather, what indeed? The twins, Nakula and Sahadeva—meaning they sported and played. Even though they were the sons of Mādrī, they were surrounded by the sons of Pṛthā; like two *suparṇa* birds, they sported. Having done what? [Having taken] their own inheritance from the enemy Duryodhana.
Having seized the kingdom from Uddāyin, [they took] their own inheritance, the nectar, from the mouth of Vajrin—that is, from the mouth of Indra—just as Garuḍa [did].
Or rather, "like two Suparṇas": if two Garuḍas were to bring the nectar, then it would be like that. [The form] "akṣiṇīva" is a sandhi [resulting] because it belongs to the *maṇīvādi* group. ||39||
The sequential composition: Or rather, the performers of this [song] are indeed the Pārthas. For it is thus:

while being protected by the Pārthas, they two took delight like two *suparṇa* birds, sporting according to their own will. Having done what? Having taken (*ūddāya*) their own inheritance from the other. From what [did they take it], as it were?

“From the mouth of the Vajrī, as if from the hand of the Vajra-wielder”—this is an *abhūtopamā* (an impossible simile). Regarding the word “uddāya,” there is an alternative reading in the Puṇyāraṇya manuscript: “uddhṛtya. ||39||

Viśvanātha: Nakula and Sahadeva, the twin sons of Mādrī, were likewise protected by the eyelashes of Pṛthā as if they were her very eyes, and were surrounded by the sons of Pṛthā (the Pārthas). [The compound] "akṣiṇī-iva" belongs to the *maṇīvādi* class. From their enemy, the adversary Duryodhana, they wrested back their own inheritance—the kingdom—in the conflict of battle.

They sported. Why? Having snatched what? Like what? Having snatched the nectar—their inheritance—from the mouth of the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra), like two *suparṇa* birds. The agents of this act were either the Uddāyakas or the Pārthas. For it is thus: they sported while being surrounded and protected by the Pārthas. Having done what?

"Having taken his own inheritance from his father, as if from the mouth of the wielder of the thunderbolt who holds the vajra in his hand"—this is an impossible simile (*abhūtopamā*), like that of two *suparṇa* birds. (39)
Oh, even Pṛthā still lives for the sake of her children, despite being without that best of royal sages— he who,
as a peerless hero, conquered Adhiratha!
The bow is the second; there are four directions.

Śrīdhara: What indeed can I ask regarding Pṛthā’s welfare, since her mere maintenance of life without Pāṇḍu is itself a marvel? Thus he says, "Aho! (Oh!). She is maintained—that is, she lives. And this is not at all a great marvel, because she maintains herself for the sake of her children, not for the sake of enjoyment. Nevertheless...
He says, "It is indeed a marvel"—that is, without such a person as him. He explains that very point with the words "But he who..."—he whose second companion was the bow itself. (40)
The sequence of the composition: questioning all of them simultaneously, he grieves for Kuntī as well, exclaiming "Alas!

The meaning is: "for the sake of those very children who possess supreme and excellent qualities. And thus, the intention is: "Speak only that by which there may be welfare for them, and through that, welfare for her as well."

Viśvanātha: Oh, what a marvel! Even though she was asked about her welfare here, Pṛthā still remains [in distress]; the sense is that you should also inquire after her welfare. Now, why do you speak thus?
To this he replies: even without her husband, the eminent royal sage Pāṇḍu, for the sake of her children...

The sense is that she remained solely for the sake of protecting the children, Yudhiṣṭhira and the others; had those children, Yudhiṣṭhira and his brothers, not existed, then she surely would have perished. He who was Pāṇḍu—alone and without assistance—a hero whose only companion was his bow. ||40||
Gentle one, mourn for him as he falls downward— he who committed an offense against his deceased brother,
by whom his own friend was driven out from his city.
I [shall act] with complete devotion toward my own sons.

Śrīdhara: It is indeed appropriate that Pṛthā lives for the sake of her children; thus he says: "O gentle one, I grieve for that Dhṛtarāṣṭra while he is still alive. Why so? Because he is falling downward. The reason for this is that he committed an act of malice (*vidudruhe*)—that is, he harbored enmity—toward his deceased brother, the Pāṇḍava, by betraying his sons.
Furthermore, he says that even while his brother was still alive, he wronged him: "By whom I, a friend and a brother, have been driven forth and exiled from my own city. (41)

The sequence of the composition: Thus, I do not grieve for the deceased Pāṇḍu because he was worthy of a good rebirth; however, I do indeed grieve for Dhṛtarāṣṭra even though he is alive, because of the opposite being the case for him. Viśvanātha says: "O gentle one," [I do] not inquire after the welfare of the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, but rather him...

O gentle Uddhava, lament for him who is falling downward—he who, out of malice toward his deceased brother's son, committed an offense against me, and likewise committed an offense against his other brother who was still alive; he says: "He was sent away," though he was a friend and a well-wisher to him. 41.
Thus, by the grace of Hari— who, through his imitation of a mortal, captivates the eyes of men and the Creator alike— I am not to be perceived by others on my path.
I wander here, beholding and free from wonder.

Śrīdhara: "Aha! Indeed, it is truly astonishing that even though he knew of such wicked conduct, you, though a saintly person, were made to suffer. To this, he says: "I, having seen the path and the majesty of Hari through His grace, am now free from astonishment; remaining hidden here on the surface of the earth, I am not perceived by others."
I wander in happiness. Of what nature am I? One who, through a human imitation—a semblance of humanity that conceals my sovereignty—moves and bewilders the eyes and mental dispositions of men. ||42||

The sequence of the composition: "But even though I am associated with him, by the grace of the Blessed One I do not possess such ignorance. Therefore, having abandoned that association and becoming weary even of hearing news of him, I wander through the worlds concealing myself," he says with the words "so I am. His wonder has departed.

His doubts have vanished. Now, although Vidura was the supreme refuge of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, it appears that even his lifelong departure to a distant land—undertaken merely from the perspective of worldly convention by abandoning Śrī Kṛṣṇa—was brought about by Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself. And that...

This was for the purpose of causing Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others to abandon their absorption in worldly affairs and to induce in them remorse for their own solitary attire; therefore, it should be understood that even the intention of Vidura previously explained arose solely by her will. ||42||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, he says "So I am," meaning that his malice toward me did not cause me harm; on the contrary, it was indeed a supreme favor. [He does so] by means of the mockery—that is, the deception—of mortals such as Dhṛtarāṣṭra and others who have taken refuge in His grace, and by extension, of other men similar to them.
By the grace of Hari, who agitates and bewilders the mental faculties of ordinary eyes,
he beheld both the path of the Lord’s footsteps and His feet; thus,
his wonder vanished as he thought, "How great is this marvel of the Blessed One, who is so affectionate toward His devotees?"
Because this secret has not been disclosed anywhere, I am recognized by him and wander here among these very sacred fords.
At this very time, the Blessed One appeared before Vidura—who had been cast out by Duryodhana and was submerged in an ocean of grief—and spoke thus: "O my supreme devotee!"

"Vidura! Why do you grieve thus, remembering my separation? It is inferred from the boon granted by the Blessed One that wherever you desire to go, you shall travel seeing me moving ahead of you at that very sacred ford (tīrtha), as if we have already entered into conversation together; therefore—"

Even after the slaying of Duryodhana and Yudhiṣṭhira’s attainment of the kingdom, Vidura did not come, being instead absorbed in the bliss of the vision of the Blessed Lord; otherwise, he certainly would have come. Furthermore, at the conclusion of the Mausala-līlā, as the Blessed Lord was vanishing from the sight of Vidura’s eyes...
He had even vanished; for this very reason, Vidura remained in a state of agitation from that time until he beheld Uddhava. ||42||

Surely even the Lord, desiring to remove the suffering of those who have sought refuge, [acted] for the sake of slaying kings who were on the path of the three-fold pride and who repeatedly shook the earth with their armies.
The Blessed One overlooked the transgression of the Kurus.

Śrīdhara: But surely, why does Hari act with such sportiveness (līlā), whereby his own devotees undergo hardships such as dwelling in the forest, and he himself suffers humiliation such as the attempt at imprisonment during his mission as a messenger?
It would be better for him to kill them immediately after their offense rather than neglecting that offense. To this [he replies]:

He said: "Surely, it is certain that for the sake of slaying those who had gone astray and were arrogant due to the three types of pride, and out of a desire to remove the suffering of those who had sought refuge, the Lord—though capable of killing them even at the very moment of their sin—overlooked the transgression of the Kurus.
For had He killed them at that very time, there would not have been the slaughter of all those wicked kings."
The meaning is "with this intention.

"Pride of learning, pride of wealth, and likewise pride of noble birth—these are the intoxications of those blinded by intoxication, yet they alone are the self-restraints of the virtuous. Thus are the three intoxications. (43)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might ask: why does the Lord engage in such play (*līlā*) that his own devotees undergo hardships such as dwelling in the forest, and he himself suffers humiliation through efforts like being bound while acting as a messenger?

Since their slaughter occurred immediately after that offense and was not due to an indifference toward the crime, he says "surely" (nūnam): because of the destruction of those who have gone astray and follow evil conduct through the three intoxications, the Lord, desiring to remove the suffering of those who have sought refuge, is indeed capable of slaying the Kurus at the time of their transgression, yet [he does not do so].
He overlooked the offense; that is to say, he did so with the intention that by killing them at that very moment, there would not be a slaughter of all the wicked kṣatriyas.
[The causes of pride are: pride of learning, pride of wealth, and likewise pride of noble birth.
"These are the intoxications of those blinded by intoxication; for these very same things are the self-restraint of the virtuous. Thus are the three intoxications. 43.
Surely, the birth of the Unborn is for the destruction of the wrong path, and the actions of the Non-agent are for the sake of the perception [of truth] by men;
otherwise, who indeed would deserve union with a body?
The supreme [state] transcends the system of qualities and actions.
"Indeed, for Viṣṇu, birth is not a bodily union; birth is known as manifestation," so it is said in the Āgneya Purāṇa.
"Hari is called both the agent and the non-agent because of the absence of [worldly] fruit. (44)

Śrīdhara: By the logic of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so"), he states that the birth and activities of the Blessed One are solely for the purpose of destroying all forms of wicked conduct and not otherwise: "The birth of the unborn, and the actions of the non-agent, are for the sake of seizing men and for their engagement in [righteous] deeds; otherwise, if it were not so, then [there would be no purpose for the Blessed One’s appearance]."

Let alone the stories of his birth and so forth; for who else, even one superior to others, could be beyond all qualities (guṇa) and yet still be subject to bodily union or the expansion of karma? ||44||
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] is as follows: "The birth of the unborn" means that it is merely a manifestation.

"The actions of the non-agent" means they are his spontaneous pastimes (*svairalīlā*). [He acts] for the sake of attracting the minds of all men toward Himself. As it is said in the fifth [chapter]: "The lion [performs] His pastime..."
"I took up the faultless ones to win over the hearts of my own kin, O one of noble prowess" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.25.10).

Therefore, "the connection with a body" means merely the manifestation within bodies that are being accepted as His own through the status of fatherhood. Who is superior to the modes? Even the attendants (*pārṣada*) and others. ||44||

Viśvanātha: But surely, for the Blessed One, whose nature is the density of consciousness and bliss, why is there such concern with the good, bad, and neutral states of the worldly realm? True; the two reasons for this are His affection (*vātsalya*) toward His own devotees and His desire for the welfare of all others everywhere. Thus it is said: [text follows].

He said: Although He is unborn and free from modifications such as birth because He is dependent on *māyā* like the individual soul (*jīva*), His "birth" occurs through *yogamāyā* due to His dependence on the love of His devotees; it is a display of birth and so forth for the sake of destroying the wicked who obstruct the path of the righteous, by means of their own destruction brought about by Him.

For the sake of granting liberation, even for one who is a non-doer— as stated in the direction that there is no birth or other states resulting from his own karma— he possesses actions such as the lifting of Govardhana, which consist of consciousness and bliss, despite being devoid of agency based on the qualities of *sattva* and the rest; [these acts are performed] everywhere for the sake of his own devotees, the persons.
It is for the sake of attracting—even those who are detached from the pleasures of heaven, liberation, and so forth—for their acceptance through its quality of being delectable;

or rather, for the sake of attracting and drawing toward Himself those living beings (jīvas), whether they be liberated, seekers of liberation, or worldly, by means of [the hymns] sung by those whose thirst has ceased, and so on. It is not otherwise for living beings.

The meaning is that while birth is indeed dependent solely upon one's own past actions (*karma*), action is not so [dependent]. If he possessed a body whose birth and activity were dependent on *karma*, his connection with that body would likewise be dependent on *karma*.

Yet even for a living being who has attained perfection through devotion that transcends the material qualities (*guṇātīta-bhakti-siddha-jīva*), such conjunction with a body does not exist; how much less so, then, for him directly?

Regarding that Supreme Lord, he says: "Who indeed, even though being distinct from the qualities (guṇas) and beyond the qualities, would deserve union with a body that is subject to karma—that is, dependent on karma? Indeed, no one. Here, when it is said that he does not deserve union with a body subject to karma, [it implies] that which is not subject to karma.

The meaning obtained is that [the Lord] is worthy of union with a body; however, since union with *māyā* is impossible for that Supreme Lord, the fact that His body consists of a mass of consciousness and bliss follows by its very nature. ||44||
For him— the unborn one who had taken birth among the Yadus for the sake of those world-protectors who had surrendered and remained under his own command— [the earth trembled].
O friend, relate the news of that one whose glory is the sacred fords.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, he says "relate the story" of Him whose pastimes consist of such inconceivable *māyā*. [The phrase] "born among the Yadus for the sake of those who have surrendered to Him—the world-protectors and others—and for the sake of those established in His own command," refers to Him whose fame is a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) that carries one across the ocean of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).

The sequence of the composition: Alas, alas! That evil news was heard by me even then at Prabhāsa; for even though you gave no reply, whatever was touched limb by limb was indeed nothing but lamentation.
Therefore, he says—"of him"—expressing his desire to hear the very play of his birth and so forth in order to forget that [suffering].

Viśvanātha: Therefore, with the intention of describing his births and deeds, which consist of the essence of pure consciousness and bliss, he says: "For the sake (*arthāya*)—that is, for the purpose—of those guardians of all the worlds who have taken refuge in him, as well as others who abide by his own command; [he is] the *tīrtha*, the supremely purifying [source]."

The sense is: "I have effectively performed my ablutions in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) whose fame carries one across the ocean of *saṃsāra*. Now, having secured their fruitfulness, please immerse me in the nectar of the sacred ford that is Kṛṣṇa’s fame. (45)
Thus ends the first chapter of the third [section] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, and which is perfectly consistent with the wise.
Thus, in the glorious Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras,
in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā pertaining to the state of the Paramahaṃsas, in the third book, in the dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava.
First Chapter;
now begins the second chapter, in the dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus questioned by the Kṣatriya regarding the news concerning his beloved,
the devotee of the Lord was unable to reply, for he was overwhelmed with longing as the Lord was brought to mind.
Śrīdhara:
In the second [canto], having lamented due to his separation from Kṛṣṇa, Nandoddhava,
sighing deeply, described the childhood deeds of Kṛṣṇa to Vidura.

Thus, with six verses beginning with "iti," [the author] describes Uddhava’s inability to reply, due to being overwhelmed by the longing of separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa when questioned about pleasant news; he was one whose Lord had been reminded [of him]. ||1||
The sequence of composition: the word "smāritā" (made remembered) indicates a specific kind of recollection. ||1||
Viśvanātha: In the second [chapter], Uddhava, his face bathed in tears from the agitation of love,
described the pastimes of Vraja in brief, ending with the Rāsa dance.

Describing the state of Uddhava—who was swooning from the intensification of his love due to separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa—and his inability to offer a reply, [the author] shows a certain condition: he is one for whom the Lord has been recalled by the breaking of his swoon through the loud questions of Vidura. ||1||
When he was five years old, he was asked by his mother for breakfast;
yet, performing service for her with the playfulness of a child, he did not desire it.

Śrīdhara: He elaborates on this very point through the logic of *kaimutya* (the "how much more so" argument) with the two verses beginning with "yaḥ": "He who, though only five years old, having imagined Kṛṣṇa as some [ordinary] child through mere childhood play, performed service using only imagined means—even when requested by his mother for the sake of breakfast in the morning... [he did not eat].
He did not desire food. ||2||
The sequential arrangement: "He" constitutes a pair of verses (yugmaka). ||2||

Viśvanātha: He demonstrates his former devotion [as follows]: "While playing with dolls in childhood play," even while playing with dolls, imagining one particular doll to be Kṛṣṇa and performing service to him with only imagined offerings, he was entreated by his mother for his morning meal.
"Even now, my service to the Blessed One has not been fully accomplished," he thought; thus he did not wish for that food.
How could he, having grown old in time through his service to him, answer when questioned about news, while remembering the feet of his master?
Śrīdhara: He has gone to, that is, attained, old age, which is the state of being aged. ||3||

The sequential composition [of the verse]: "Of that puppet-form, 'old age' (jarasam) means having been served for a long time; this is because there is a contradiction with the statement, 'Even those of advanced age were young men of exceeding strength and vigor. (3)

Viśvanātha: By means of his service—that is, by the power of service—he did not undergo old age even with the passage of time. Alternatively, "by service at the proper time" means by that service which is appropriate for the particular time. The interpretation of *kālena* as having the third case ending (*tṛtīyānta*) is, however, inconsistent.
In that regard, there is a contradiction [in the text] with the statement: "There were even those who were advanced in years, yet they were young and possessed of exceeding strength and vigor. (3)
For a moment he remained silent, deeply immersed by the intense yoga of devotion in the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, and was perfectly at peace.
Śrīdhara: He is perfectly satisfied by the nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet, and he is deeply immersed in that very yoga of devotion, which is intense and brings about a state of total surrender. ||4||
The sequence of the composition: If so, how did He reply?
It is said that He replied by consoling him through a vision within His own mind during His eternal pastimes; this is stated in three verses beginning with "He" (saḥ). ||4||

Viśvanātha explains the remembrance of the feet with the words "He... and so forth. When Uddhava’s fainting fit was dispelled by Vidura’s questions, he cried out, "Alas, alas! I am separated from that Lord!
and through the remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet, there occurred a direct vision; by means of the nectar of beauty obtained therein—
Savoring this for a moment, he remained silent for the duration of two *ghaṭikās*; thereafter,

immersed in that very nectar through an intense practice of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*)— augmented by the pain of separation from Kṛṣṇa and overflowing with the abundance of his relish— he forgot the suffering of separation from Kṛṣṇa and became truly composed.
Thus, he became extinguished. ||4||
With all his limbs bristling with horripilation and shedding tears with closed eyes,
he was perceived by him as one whose purpose was fulfilled and who was immersed in a surging tide of affection.
Śrīdhara: He whose every limb was blossomed and expanded with horripilation;
shedding tears of grief with his closing eyes; by that Vidura, he (the Lord) was perceived as one whose purpose was fulfilled and whose aim accomplished;
for he was immersed in the overflowing flood of that affection which exists toward the Blessed One.
Immersed. ||5||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: He demonstrates the ensuant emotion (anubhāva) of bliss—since all limbs have "sprouted" (udbhida), meaning they are covered with horripilation (pulaka), the state of being like trees, shrubs, and so forth, is indicated, and thus paralysis (stambha) is manifested.
As Vidura closed his eyes and shed tears of grief, he was perceived by Kṛṣṇa as one whose purpose was fulfilled— that is, as one who had attained his goal—
by means of his outward manifestations, which led to the inference of his love. This is because, due to that very love for the Lord,
his affection and the melting of his heart had overflowed and were submerged in Him before him.
The meaning is that first he was immersed in *prema*, and then he became immersed in *sneha* at its second stage. ||5||
Gradually returning from the worlds of the Blessed One back to the world of men,
Uddhava wiped his eyes and spoke affectionately to Vidura with a smile.

Śrīdhara: The Blessed Lord himself is the world; therefore, "the world of men" (nṛloka) refers to the identification with the body. "Smiling" means experiencing wonder by recollecting the Lord’s skillfulness in the destruction of the Yadu clan and other such acts. [From] the "world of the Blessed One," known as Dvārakā which consists of eternal pastimes, [to] the "world of men."
Having come to the world of men, which consists of the external visible world and so forth, he remained connected with it;
the meaning is that he was greatly delighted by the experience of that [world], smiling with joy. ||6||
