Viśvanātha: And then, having returned from the world of the Lord—drawn back to the human world from that place called Dvārakā, which consists of eternal pastimes, by the intensity of his own love, while being pulled by the love of Vidura—the meaning is that this occurred when the second fainting fit had broken; "smiling slightly" (utsmayan).

Or rather, O Uddhava! Remembering His skill in removing the burden of the earth and so forth, He was filled with wonder; or else, consoling Vidura with a reply and bidding him return here, He broke into a sublime smile at the Lord’s reassurance. (6)
Uddhava said:
When the sun-gem Kṛṣṇa has set and we have been swallowed by the serpent of Time,
what welfare can I possibly speak of for our homes whose splendor has departed?

Śrīdhara: Tormented by separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he replies: When Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself—the sun—is setting, and when [the world] has been swallowed by the great serpent of Time (Ajagara), what indeed can I say regarding the welfare of your kinsmen who have been devoured? ||7||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: In order to console Vidura, who was overwhelmed with grief, [the Lord], stating the final conclusion right at the outset, [describes] his own external activity, the torment of separation from him, and the miserable state of the worlds.

He reports: "When the sun, the jewel of the sky, has set, and our homes have been swallowed by the great serpent of the darkness of grief in the form of a massive snake, what welfare can I speak of for our kinsmen who inquire after you? In this circle of lights—"

Just as for the sun, which remains stationary yet is distinguished by its retinue of horses, chariot, and charioteer, in whichever continent its setting is observed, at that very same time its rising, forenoon, midday, and so forth are observed in other continents; in exactly the same way [it is with the Lord].

At the very moment that the disappearance of Kṛṣṇa— who resides in Gokula, Mathurā, and Dvārakā with His retinue, and who has immersed the people of the world in the nectar of His respective pastimes—
is perceived in one cosmic egg, it occurs simultaneously in other cosmic eggs as well.
The pastimes, such as the festival of His birth, the festival of the Rāsa dance, the slaying of Kaṃsa, and the marriage festivals with Rukmiṇī and others, are perceived;
yet they are unreal because, within the sphere of light, the sunrise, forenoon, and so forth are merely appearances.
However, the distinction is that for Kṛṣṇa, the birth and other events are indeed real, because they are eternal in their respective places.

The eternality of all divine pastimes (*līlā*) has been shown in the First Canto, and it will be demonstrated once again with supporting evidence in the Tenth Canto. For example, in the year associated with the setting of the sun,
when [the world] is being swallowed by darkness, the lotuses wither and the *cakravāka* birds lament.
Thieves, bandits, rākṣasas, pretas, and others rejoice; likewise,

when the universe associated with the disappearance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is seized by the python of suffering, the saintly languish, the devotees of Kṛṣṇa lament, the bridges of dharma are broken, and the unrighteous [rejoice].
That those who are turned away from the Blessed One rejoice was indicated by Uddhava in the verse beginning with "gīrṇeṣu" (when [the Lord] has swallowed [the worlds]). ||7||
Alas, unfortunate indeed is this world, and the Yadavas even more so, who, though living together with Hari, do not know Him, just as fish do not perceive the moon.

Śrīdhara says, lamenting: "Unfortunate" means devoid of good fortune; those who, even while living together with Him, do not recognize, "This is Śrī Hari. Just as when the moon was born in the Ocean of Milk, the fish dwelling there at that time recognized it merely as some beautiful aquatic creature, and not [as the moon].

"Like that which consists of nectar," and so on; or rather, the sequence of the composition is "just as the moon reflected in water. "Unfortunate" (*durbhaga*) means devoid of fortune. This world residing in Dvārakā, throbbing within my heart—those who dwell together with him, even while living together, do not know [him].
The sense is: "It is no wonder that they know [Him], while I, being devoid of the fortune of living in His company, do not know Him.

Furthermore, it should be understood that in this context, if there had been no companionship at that time, he would have simply said, "They did not know Him. Moreover, although Hari is known for captivating everyone's minds, they did not recognize Him; yet He Himself...
They do not recognize him as the Blessed Lord. Regarding this, there is an illustration: "like fish [regarding] the moon.

Just as fish, for the sake of increasing their own strength, know the moon submerged in the ocean at Prabhāsa solely by its sweetness and brilliance, and not as the supreme deity—such is the meaning. ||8||

Viśvanātha: Having thus shown the miserable state of those supreme worlds inseparable from Him, and perceiving within himself a sudden flash of knowledge regarding His great sovereignty arising from the intensity of separation from them, [he reflects] upon those who are inseparable from Him— the attendants of His divine play.

Observing such a manifestation of great sovereignty, he censures them with a certain peculiar charm of amorous confusion, saying "unfortunate": "This world residing in Dvārakā, who is manifesting within my heart, is unfortunate (durbhaga), devoid of good fortune; and even among them, those Yādavas..."
Those who are in extremely close proximity are most unfortunate;
for even while dwelling together with Him—who captivates their minds with His own sweetness—they do not perceive, they do not know, Hari.
The implication is that I, however, being devoid of the fortune of living with Him, am exceedingly unfortunate, even though I have known Him. As it is said:
Just as the fish dwelling in the Ocean of Milk know only that the moon born therein is merely some exceedingly beautiful aquatic creature of theirs, and do not recognize him as the deity,
the nectar-rayed Lord of the Night, in the same way, the Yadavas know only the sweetness of Kṛṣṇa, and not [his divine nature].

The sense is that I call those [devotees] truly unfortunate because of their suffering regarding what they perceive as "sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*). In reality, however, he is one whose fortune—that is, his majesty—is difficult to comprehend; for it will be explained in the tenth chapter that those established in the knowledge of sweetness (*mādhurya*) are superior even to those established in the knowledge of sovereignty. Therefore, [the term *durbhaga*] does not apply here [in its literal sense].

By using the present tense in the word "vidura," it is intended to inform the residents of Dvārakā and the Yādavas of the Lord’s eternal non-attachment. [The meaning is: "O Vidura! Those Yādavas and others about whose welfare you inquired are currently sporting happily together with the Blessed Lord. Only—"

The sense is: "You were the questioner and I was the one questioned; thus, we two alone lament. It should be understood that had they not been in conversation with Kṛṣṇa at that time, he would have said simply, "Those who dwell [there] did not know. (8)
Skilled in reading gestures, highly mature, and finding delight in the one alone, all the Sātvatas regarded the Bull among the Sātvatas as the abode of all beings.
Śrīdhara: [The Lord] says that they do not know only because of their lack of fortune, and not due to a deficiency in the means of knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*):

"they know the *iṅgita*, that which resides in the mind. Likewise, they are *puru*—exceedingly mature and skillful—and thus they "delight in one and the same place. Even being such as these, [they do not know] the abode of all beings.
They regarded him as the Lord, the bull among the Sātvatas, the best of the Sātvatas. ||9||

The sequential composition (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, one might object, "Since they do not know even now, how do you know? Anticipating this doubt, he states his own ancient experience as the reason for his knowledge: "They are knowers of gestures. [He refers to] the Lord himself, the abode of all beings, who exists as the eternal head of the family (*nityakulapati*) and the bull (*ṛṣabha*) among his own people, the Sātvatas.

They must have considered him to be the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) who is a portion (aṃśa) of Him, because of the scriptural texts such as "One God" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11) ending with "the abode of all beings," which refer to the Inner Controller; and it is also stated [in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.43.17] that he is "the supreme deity of the Vṛṣṇis. ||9||

Viśvanātha: But surely the residents of Dvārakā, like those of Gokula, enjoy the singular sweetness of pure love; they are certainly not devoid of knowledge of His sovereignty. So why do you say that they do not know? To this he replies: "They are knowers of His gestures," meaning they understand even that which resides within His heart.

How much more, then, do they know the beauty, charm, and other qualities residing within the body? The reason for this is that they are *puru-prauḍhāḥ*, meaning those of mature and extremely subtle intellect. Furthermore, he describes their lack of knowledge regarding divine sovereignty (*aiśvarya*): they take delight in only a single seat, bed, and so forth. [They regard] the Bull among the Sātvatas as their own.

They regarded Kṛṣṇa— who exists as the eternal Lord of the family— as the abode of all beings, dwelling within all beings as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), because of the scriptural texts concerning the Inner Controller such as "The one God" and so forth, ending with "the abode of all beings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11). They did not regard him, however, as the Blessed Lord himself, as Nārāyaṇa directly.

"Because they do not know Hari as the possessor of parts (aṃśin), I alone have said here in this world that those who know what is appropriate and those who do not know it are not to be censured; rather, those situated between them are censured—this is the sense, meaning 'let them know at least half and half. ||9||
The intellect of those who are touched by the illusory power (māyā) of the Lord, and who rely on other false doctrines, is not deluded by their words, for their self is planted within Hari.

Śrīdhara: Those Yādavas who, touched and pervaded by the Lord’s māyā, say, "This Yādava is our kinsman," and those such as Śiśupāla and others who, resorting to false enmity, revile him— by their words, for one like me whose mind is offered to Hari and whose soul is fixed upon Him...
Their intellect is not deluded, nor do they fall into confusion; the meaning is that others, however, are indeed deluded. ||10||

The sequence of the composition: "Of the Lord" (devasya). And those others besides the Yādavas who are highly learned—according to the manner described in such passages as *bhā.pu. 10.43.17*, "the Virāṭ is for the ignorant"—they think that this other [entity], namely the most excellent material body, is the Supreme; such is the meaning. ||10||

Viśvanātha: Thus, those virtuous ones dwelling in the mortal world who suffer from the pain of separation from Him, and those such as the Yādavas who are His constant companions and enjoy the bliss of union—they alone, by virtue of possessing devotion, are truly fortunate. Others, however, being devoid of devotion, are merely inhabitants of hell; so he says: "Of the Lord..."

O learned one, by the words of those who are touched by illusion and consider themselves wise— even among them, those who have resorted to other, most wicked, demonic views such as the Piṣṭa-Sāṅkhya and the doctrine of cause— it is claimed that Kṛṣṇa abandoned his body and went to Vaikuṇṭha; likewise [is it said] of Kṛṣṇa.

The intellect of a devotee who has offered his mind to Hari, the Supreme Self— having heard the censure that the entire lineage was thus destroyed by a Brahmin’s curse arising from the act of treachery against great monarchs such as Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Jarāsaṃdha— does not waver.
However, he sinks into that very sweetness; the sense is: "Enough with those deluded ones who are like hell-beings. ||10||
Having displayed himself to men whose eyes were unsatiated and who had not yet performed sufficient austerity,
he withdrew his own form— the eye of the world— and placed it within.

Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry, "Who is this Hari?", he says: "Having shown... and so forth. Having displayed his own form—the beautiful embodiment—for such a long time to those whose eyes remained unsatiated because they had not performed penance, and who then vanished, taking away and severing the vision of the world—to another such [person].
Because of the non-existence of anything to be observed. ||11||

The sequential composition: nevertheless, he says "having shown" (*pradarśya*) to indicate that its very nature is the attraction of all things, according to the direction stated in the scripture: "The eye of the eye" (*cakṣuṣaś cakṣuḥ*, *Kena Upaniṣad* 1.2).
Having taken—that is, having grasped—his own reflection, his own form, which consists of the eyes of the world; as it was said in the *Mausala*:
At the time of the *parvan*:
"Having brought about the removal of the earth's burden, the large-eyed Kṛṣṇa, having cast off his body, has reached his own supreme abode. [Mbh. 16.9.29] Thus.
In this context, "having caused to be released" means having caused [them] to abandon [the burden] by removing it, and not in the sense of having liberated them. ||11||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, for devotees, only that which is their own [vision] can be real. To the question "What is that?", he says: "Having shown," etc. The genitive case in "of men whose eyes are not yet satiated" (*avitṛptadṛśām*) is used in a sense of disregard.
He who, having shown his own reflection—his own glorious form (*śrīvigraha*)—[reveals] its sweetness...

As soon as he began to relish them, [the sage], disregarding those [beings] whose eyes were unsatiated, took back his own reflection, snatched it away from their eyes, and having led it away, quickly vanished and disappeared. In this instance, because the word *yat* pertains to the meaning of the subsequent sentence, there is no requirement for the word *tat*. [As in: "O Moon, well done!"...

Just as in the verse, "The lotuses closed themselves because [the moon] was more beautiful," the poetic suggestion (*dhvani*) of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is implied: that they did so out of the very thought, "If we do not conceal ourselves, those excessively greedy ones will enjoy us once again to their heart's content."

"Is it not then the case that he was a stealer of what had been given? To this he replies: His own form was given to men only to steal away their eyes—that is, the eyes which reside within them; yet that was not a gift to him in the ultimate sense, but rather like that of a thief. This is yet another poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*). And thus, by Kṛṣṇa...
Having descended to the earth, he has blinded all people by stealing away their sight; thus, it is a "disguised praise" (*vyājastuti*) to say that they have not been protected.
[Objection: But surely, since the sweetness of his own form is infinite, what loss could there be even in drinking it for a long time?

Would it have been so? In that case, what fault is there on the part of that ocean of compassion? Rather, he says it is simply the lack of fortune on the part of the people—this is stated according to worldly convention. In reality, however, the meaning is: "for those who have not performed penance" (ataptatapasaḥ), yet who have actually obtained the full weight of His grace. For such [a thing] does not [occur otherwise].

The primary purpose is indeed the production of *anurāga* (passionate attachment), as suggested by the statement in the *Ujjvalanīlamaṇi* (14.79): "When this has arisen, one is never satiated with seeing and so forth. In this context, the state of having unsatiated eyes should be understood either as a characteristic of affection (*sneha*) or, due to an excess of longing, as a characteristic of *anurāga*.
In that same manner, having taken his own form, he vanished;

thus, those who argue for the abandonment [of the body]—namely, the proponents of the relinquishment of the physical body—are refuted. Likewise, regarding the passage "that which was for the sake of the means of mortal play" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.12), and that which pertains to the Son of Dharma... [Bhāgavata Purāṇa...]

[3.2.13] Thus, because the subsequent verses provide specific epithets for his own *bimba* (reflection/form) alone, those who attempt to explain the text as contradictory— claiming that he went away having abandoned his human *bimba* and taken up a divine *svabimba* (his own reflection)— are refuted.
Likewise, [the phrase] "having thus shown" (*pradarśya*) means "he disappeared" (*antaradhāt*), and not "he was looking" (*paśyati sma*) at the time of the showing.
Furthermore, since His disappearance depends solely upon His will, even those who dispute that He is subject to karma are refuted.

Therefore, this speech must be accepted as authoritative—it belongs to Uddhava himself, who proceeded to refute the views of the "unreal" ones mentioned in the preceding verse, beginning with: "Touched by the Māyā of the Lord" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.10). It is not [the word of others].

However, this statement—"even tens of millions of statements contrary to this"—should be understood as being exactly like the statement "but the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa himself" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.3.28); such is the natural flavor of this scripture that must be savored. ||11||
He assumed that power of His own yoga-māyā which is appropriate for the pastimes among mortals,
thereby causing wonder at the abundance of His own auspicious fortune.
The supreme state, whose limbs are adorned by ornaments.

Śrīdhara: He describes that very form with three verses. That which is *aupayika*—that is, suitable—for the divine sports (*martyalīlā*) among mortals; which produces wonder even in Himself; and because it is the supreme state (*paraṃ padam*), the ultimate limit (*parā kāṣṭhā*) of the abundance of good fortune (*saubhagarddhi*), the excellence of auspiciousness; and whose limbs are the ornaments of ornaments.
In which ||12||
The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Here, he states the conviction of those whose souls are absorbed in Hari: "Since [she is] mortal... and so forth.

"The power of her own *yogamāyā*" refers to the potency of her own consciousness-power (*cit-śakti*). By revealing that this Blessed Lady is the very illuminator even of such good fortune, it has been made manifest.
The meaning is that it is intended to cause amazement to the assembly of those who know all of its own majesty. It is not merely this much;

for even in another form of His, such [majesty] is not experienced. Even there, because of a manifestation that is ever-new at every moment, it causes amazement even to Himself, since it is the supreme state of the abundance of auspiciousness (*saubhagarddhi*).
The supreme foundation.
One might ask: "Does He not indeed possess ornaments as a cause of His auspiciousness? To this he says: "ornaments," etc. Of what kind?
The meaning is: "serving as a means for His play in the mortal world" (martyalīlaupāyikam), that is to say, having a human form. Therefore, what was said is all the more appropriate.

Also by the Lord of Śrī Mahākālapura: "The sons of the twice-born were brought by me, desiring to show them to you two" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.89.58), and so forth; and by the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the Śrī Harivaṃśa:
"Those children were carried away by that great-souled one for the sake of seeing me" (Harivaṃśa 2.114.8).
Viśvanātha: [Prītisaṃdarbha, 80] Now, one might ask: having made his own form disappear, did he lead [the Lord] directly to Vaikuṇṭha?
To that he replies: "That form which was appropriate (aupayika)—meaning suitable—for the pastimes in the mortal world, how could that [form] go to Vaikuṇṭha?"
The sense is: "Let it go. Therefore, even now, that very same [manifestation] exists in Dvārakā exactly as before;

the only distinction is that because of the absence of His will, the people here do not see it. Furthermore, one should not consider it to be inferior on account of its being suited for the display of human-like play (*martyalīlā*).

On the contrary, He is of supreme excellence even compared to the very nature of the pastimes of Vaikuṇṭha; thus he says: "By one who is displaying the full power—the complete capacity—of His own *yogamāyā*, which is His own essential spiritual energy (*cicchakti*), [there is] no [lack] whatsoever of either majesty (*aiśvarya*) or sweetness (*mādhurya*)."
It was not merely set aside after being concealed; rather, His entire self was deposited here in this image.

The sense is that even in Vaikuṇṭha, such power was never displayed. Regarding the word "gr̥hītam" (taken up), in the context of the verse "māyayā guṇā gr̥hītā vibhoḥ" (the qualities were taken up by the Lord's Māyā during maintenance, creation, and dissolution), it is the *guṇas* that were taken up by Māyā.

Thus, even though there is no difference, there is a statement of difference; for according to the maxim that "the divine intellect indeed produces a distinction even where there is no distinction. The context is that [the form] was grasped and manifested.
Or rather, by showing the original object (*bimba*), he displayed his own power of *yogamāyā*, which had been grasped.

This is well known from events such as the marriage of the royal consort; it demonstrates his very power and causes even one who resides in Vaikuṇṭha in the form of Śrī Nārāyaṇa to be struck with wonder. "Oh, what beauty! Oh, what excellence!"—it brings about such amazement for those who have witnessed the forms, qualities, and other attributes of his other incarnations.

The sense is: what can be said of the attendants (*pārṣada*) and others of Vaikuṇṭha? For this very reason, she is the supreme station, the ultimate limit of the abundance of good fortune (*saubhagarddhi*).
Therefore, even the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha feels a desire to see her; [so too does my daughter, the daughter of a brahmin, feel it toward you two].
From such passages as "desiring to see" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.89.58), it is stated that his limbs are the very ornaments of ornaments, signifying supreme beauty. ||12||
Alas, that which the three worlds beheld as the auspicious sight for their eyes at the Rājasūya sacrifice of the Son of Dharma has today been seen here in its entirety by the Creator.
He considered skill to lie in directing [the senses] toward the objects of the present world.
Regarding *madhvaḥ*: "The vow is ignorance of the three worlds;
even having seen the world as consisting of bliss, one considers it merely a pearl-necklace and the form of Viṣṇu—oh, how great is this pervasive delusion! Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. (13)

Śrīdhara: [He is] the supreme source of well-being for the eyes, bringing about the highest bliss. Every living being whatsoever dwelling in the three worlds—herein, in this very form—has now, in this downward course, that is, in the creation of the present cycle of existence or the creation of human beings, reached the full extent of its skill and proficiency; it has been exhausted.
He thought that there was no skill beyond this for him; thus, although the Creator lacks the state of being a created object, this worldly perspective has been described.
Regarding the sequence of the composition, he speaks of those touched by divine illusion: "That which is dharma... (verse 13).

Viśvanātha: He reminds [the reader] that you too have personally witnessed his abundance of fortune with the words "yaddharma" (whose nature...). Even the world residing in the three worlds—the world of Brahmā, Indra, and the rest—thought thus: what? That today, in this world, during the creation subsequent to that of the Creator (Brahmā)...
All that skill in creating this diverse and ever-renewing cycle of worldly existence has vanished and been exhausted upon seeing the beauty of her limbs;
for when her face is beheld, there arises a sense of loathing for the blue lotus petals, crushed collyrium, sapphire gems, and rain clouds created by the Creator.
Thus, there is even contempt for the moon and the lotus. ||13||
The women of Vraja, having regained their pride through his playful glances— glances filled with the rasa of laughter overflowing with passion— followed after him with their eyes.
Indeed, his thoughts remained occupied with the remaining tasks to be performed.

Śrīdhara: Those [gopīs] whose pride was regained after their own laughter and so forth [were witnessed by Him], through that passion-filled (*anurāga-pluta*)—meaning pervaded by—laughter, *rāsa*-dance, diversion, and playful glances; those whose intellects followed along with their eyes, meaning they moved following Him as He went; those for whom there remained nothing further to be done.
They remained there, their tasks still unaccomplished. ||14||

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, he describes the supreme excellence of love and its manifestations, beginning with the words "yasya" (of whom). Viśvanātha notes that since the pronouns *yat* appear at the end of the preceding sentences in these verses, they do not require connection with what precedes them. Furthermore, [he asks] from among those who are thus devoted, residing in the three worlds...

The women of Vraja possess a greater intensity of love even than that of Brahmā, Rudra, and others; for although Kṛṣṇa was thus honored by them, he honored only those women in such a manner, and not them [the gods] in the same way.
This is expressed by the phrase "with smiles overflowing—that is, pervaded—by love. A *rāsa* is a collection of aesthetic flavors (*rasa*); that which is characterized by such a *rāsa* is...

They stood there at that very moment, rendered speechless by the onset of a certain stupor; they were those whose glances had just received honor and respect from Līlā for her own act of bestowing such honor upon them, and whose minds likewise followed him as he departed, having accompanied him with those very eyes.
The meaning is that they were not able to move. Consequently, regarding their duties—such as sweeping, smearing, churning curd, and serving food—they were those whose tasks remained unfinished;
for, having encountered his sight unexpectedly right in the midst of those various activities, they were unable to complete them.

The meaning is that they became [so]. By this, the sense is that his capacity to cause wonder throughout all worlds extending to his own self, and furthermore his power to enchant the women of Vraja, occurred solely through the abundance of his love.
Thus, by elaborating upon how that form was suitable for the pastimes in the mortal realm...

The eternal presence [of the Lord] specifically in Gokula, Mathurā, and Dvārakā within the mortal world, as well as the distinction consisting merely of being seen or not seen, is illustrated by the analogy of the sun. ||14||
While his own peaceful forms were being oppressed by other forms, the Lord of the high and the low, whose nature is compassion, joined with a portion of Mahat.
For although the Blessed One is unborn, he is born just like fire.

Śrīdhara: He states the cause for seeing the image in such a state: "His own forms, both peaceful and unpeaceful. Among those, he is one whose self is compassionate—that is, who has shown compassion—toward the peaceful forms when they are being oppressed by others. Although unborn (*aja*), he is born, meaning he has manifested in the form of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Fire is eternally established, yet it manifests within pieces of wood; in the same way, the cause for the birth of the Unborn is that which is joined with the "great portion"—that is, the unmanifest whose portion is the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*), its subtle causal aspect. ||15||

The sequence of the composition: He speaks of compassion in the words "by his own tranquil [forms]. The meaning is: by other forms that are not tranquil, which have arisen from that very nature. And that occurs at birth only by taking up various portions of himself; thus he says, "endowed with portions of the Great One" (*mahadaṃśayuktaḥ*), meaning endowed with portions of his own Great Self, the pervasive Lord.

This is because of such scriptural passages as "the Self" (KaU 2.1.4), and because of the well-known logical principle expressed in "and like the great one" (VeSū 1.4.8). Alternatively, the term may mean "endowed with those parts which are the great beings, such as Puruṣa," just as in the expression "the great being, the Lord of the World"; thus there is no deviation regarding the Self. Or, it may mean "with the great lineages."
Or, [the word] "yukta" means "joined. ||15||

Viśvanātha: But surely, from your own mouth it has been heard that sometimes the Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa) descended into the house of Vasudeva after coming from Vaikuṇṭha as Nārāyaṇa himself, with white and black hair; sometimes as the Lord of the Ocean of Milk (Kṣīrodanātha);
sometimes as Nara and Nārāyaṇa; and sometimes as Upendra.
It is heard that He who resides in sacred abodes such as Dvārakā, manifesting for the purpose of mortal pastimes, is the most excellent of all.

What is the certainty regarding this? To this he says: "By His own peaceful [form]"—when His own devotees of peaceful nature are being afflicted by other forms that are terrible or deluded, He is moved by compassion.

He whose mind and self are filled with compassion; He who is the Lord of those who are beyond material nature—namely Nārāyaṇa and others in their essential forms—as well as of those who are lower, such as Brahmā and the rest; the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself, who is endowed with a portion of Mahat-tattva; the Great One (Mahān), the Puruṣa who creates Mahat; the Great, all-pervading Self.

According to such scriptural passages as [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.1.4], although He is unborn— being the ultimate cause, or being devoid of any natural birth— He has been "born," that is, manifested, while being endowed with His portions (aṃśas) such as the Fish, the Tortoise, the Man-lion, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Vāmana, and others.

Fire is eternally established in the form of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), just as it manifests from the friction of gemstones; likewise, the Lord resides eternally within His own abode in Mathurā and other places, yet He appears among His devotees in Mathurā, such as Vasudeva and Ugrasena, when they have encountered extreme hardship.
The analogy of fire is that He became visible, having manifested through the friction of the power of His compassion. Likewise,
having risen on the mountain of Mathurā’s dawn in the eastern direction, He arose from Devakī and, having destroyed the most wicked darkness,
satisfied the lotuses of the virtuous and the devoted cakravāka birds who were oppressed by it.
Having established the boundaries of dharma, the Radiant One has set upon the mountain of sunset; thus,
the analogy of the sun is mutually consistent, for He, while remaining in His own abode,
has become manifest and clearly declares Himself to be so, yet the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha has not departed from Vaikuṇṭha to anywhere else.

From the Ocean of Milk, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as Upendra and the others, having arrived from their respective abodes, descend; for it is well known that they occupy their respective places according to the qualification "endowed with a great portion" (mahadaṃśayukta),
and thus at the time of manifestation, those lords of Vaikuṇṭha and the rest arrive before the Lord of the high and the low.
"Because of meeting with Kṛṣṇa, it is through excellent association alone"—thus all the words of the sage are authoritative. ||15||
This birth of the Unborn in the house of Vasudeva, and his own dwelling in Vraja as if out of fear of enemies, causes me distress as a mere pretense.
Since he of infinite prowess has taken up residence within the city.

Śrīdhara: But how can he be the Lord of all things high and low, given that his dependence [on others] is perceived? To this, he says in two verses. Even this—which is difficult to conceive and difficult to reconcile—causes me distress;
he states that very point: "The mockery, the mere imitation, of that birth which occurred in the prison-house in the home of Vasudeva, and not..."

His sudden manifestation was like that of the Man-Lion (Nṛsiṃha). Like one hiding out of fear of Kaṃsa, he dwelt in Vraja; and as if out of fear of enemies such as Kālayavana, he fled and departed from the city of Mathurā. ||16||

The Sequence of Composition: Oh, behold this vine-like play of the world, which bestows happiness upon its own kin through the supreme gentleness of that one, despite his such greatness, and because of which our grief at separation from him exceeds all else; thus he says with the two verses beginning with "mām. (16)

Viśvanātha: Thus, all the reasons for Sāṅkhya have been revealed to you according to the awakening of my own self; however, regarding that which is difficult even for those like me to understand—the reality not attained even after questioning the learned—I previously felt only distress, as he says with the words "of the unborn" (*ajasya*).

"How can the state of being unborn and the state of possessing birth belong to one and the same [being]? Furthermore, since the possession of birth here is unreal by virtue of being merely a manifestation (*ābhāsana-mātratvena*), there would be no cause for distress; therefore, it should be understood that Uddhava’s intended meaning is that both states are indeed real. Likewise, in the house of Vasudeva...
That birth in the prison of Kaṃsa—which previously caused me distress—now causes me distress;

the present tense is used here because the past action is close to the present (*vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavat*). Since this was merely a mockery and a humiliation, for him that "sport" of birth was indeed [for the sake of] his mother, father, kinsmen, and other devotees.
It ought to have been a state of supreme festival for Him who is the most independent; why then was it not made so? Furthermore, His residence in Vraja is natural and consists of supreme bliss;
how then is the cause of fear from enemies proclaimed there? Even with the word "iva" (as if), [it is implied that] from Kaṃsa in Vraja...
Though established in fearlessness, He likewise formerly departed from Mathurā;

despite possessing immeasurable strength, He fled out of fear of enemies such as Kālayavana. For it was said even by Śrī Bhīṣma: "O King, no man ever knows His intended purpose," yet [He did so] in secret.
The sense is that, having been awakened by the Blessed Lord himself upon my back, my weariness has vanished this very moment. ||16||
This burns my heart as I remember what he said after bowing at the feet of his parents: "O father,
O mother, for those of us who were greatly terrified of Kaṃsa..."
Be gracious to us, who have not yet performed atonement.

Śrīdhara: And this deed of Hari causes my mind—which has become the object of that memory—to burn and suffer. He demonstrates that very point by saying: "O father, O mother, may you both be gracious; may you show favor. [This refers to those] by whom no service (śuśrūṣaṇa) was performed as an act of atonement (niṣkṛti).
The plural number in "no 'smākam" (of us), however, refers to Rāma and the others. ||17||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that my mind, being the object of the action, was pained as it remembered this very life-story of his. As for what he said, he was asking his parents to forgive his transgression: "O Father..."

"O Mother, be gracious toward us (the genitive case used in the sense of the accusative). Here, if the statement "of those who are greatly apprehensive of Kaṃsa" is true, there is a contradiction with his being the Lord;
if it is false, how can the word of the Lord be false? Thus, as before, there is distress. Even for one who is the Supreme Lord of all, it is thus.

"How can I forget that discipline, which nourishes such extreme sweetness according to worldly custom?"—thus did those various deeds become like thorns in my heart; such is Uddhava’s lamentation. ||17||
Or what man, having smelled the pollen of his lotus-feet, would be able to forget it—
that pollen which, by means of his quivering creeper-like eyebrows, [uprooted] the earth?
He surpassed the burden set by Kṛtānta.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "In that case, why could he not simply be a non-god (anīśvara)? For you, this is merely a matter of faith. To this, he replies with three verses: Who indeed, even while smelling the dust of the two lotus feet and serving it, would be able to forget it? Even one who is capable [of forgetting] would not be able to do so. [The Lord's] creeper-like eyebrows are quivering like a forest of trees.
That very thing is the end; by that [it is so]. ||18||

The sequential composition: Furthermore, he states "Who indeed... to show that its sweetness (*mādhurya*) attracts everyone, even though it possesses supreme power. Regarding sweetness, there is an implied comparison (*kaimutya*) in the word "feet" (*aṅghri*); the meaning is "even its dust. He describes what kind [of tree] it is with the words "which" (*yaḥ*). *Viṭapa* refers to a sprout, a shoot, or an extension.
"Regarding 'stamba' and 'śākhā', [this is] the Viśvaprakāśa. ||18||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: Well then, why might he not simply be a non-god (anīśvara)? To this, he replies with three verses, for you [the opponent] have nothing but mere faith in that regard. "By him whose leaf-like eyebrows were quivering—that very [quivering] was the God of Death (kṛtānta).
Regarding the word *viṭapa*, the *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *viṭapa* refers to a sprout, a peak, expansion, a trunk, and a branch. (18)
Indeed, you have witnessed at the Rājasūya sacrifice the success of the King of Cedi, even though he was an enemy of Kṛṣṇa—
a success which yogis rightly yearn for.
Who could endure separation from that through yoga?

Śrīdhara: Nor is his status as the Lord (Īśvara) to be established [by inference], since it is already perceived even by you; thus he says: "perceived" (dṛṣṭa). That perfection which they desire to attain through perfect yoga. ||19||
The sequence of the composition: He states the extreme boundlessness of compassion in the verse beginning with "seen" (dṛṣṭa). ||19||
Viśvanātha: To whom has the manifestation of his state as the Supreme Lord not been directly perceived?
He says: "They have seen... By the word "enemies," he indicates that even his compassion is boundless, [directed] toward whomever and for whatever purpose. (19)
In the same way, other heroes of the world of men,
drinking in with their eyes the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa, which is so pleasing to the sight, [remained] in the midst of battle.
Purified by the weapon of Pārtha, they attained his state.
Śrīdhara: Purified by the weapons of Pārtha—that is, having become free from sin—in the battle, i.e., in the combat. ||20||

The sequential arrangement [of the argument] is as follows: "In the same way" serves here as the reason for the truth of seeing the lotus-face of that [Arjuna], which was purified by the weapon of Pārtha. This very point has been established, as in the verse beginning with "as if placing the weight upon her eyebrows. (20)

Viśvanātha: Having described the compassion that bestows liberation upon those who harbor hatred, he now speaks of the compassion that bestows love even upon others who are indifferent—beginning with "In the same way" and "drinking with their eyes. He says: "They alone are blessed; we are unblessed, for we have been deprived of both drinking that sweetness and attaining His state."
The sound of lamentation. ||20||
But he himself, the Lord of the Three Worlds, who is beyond equal or superior, whose every desire is fulfilled by the splendor of his own sovereignty,
[is attended] by the long-enduring world-protectors who bring him tribute.
The pedestal of his feet was rubbed by the tips of [the gods'] crowns.

Śrīdhara: Thus, even though such supreme sovereignty exists, the fact that He remains subservient to Ugrasena causes us extreme distress; this is what he says. The connection with the following verse is as follows: "The service rendered by Him—who is Himself of such a nature—to him [Ugrasena] causes us weariness. He is one for whom there is neither equality nor superiority.
The meaning is: that in relation to which there exists neither equality nor superiority. The reasons for this are as follows:

he is the *tryadhīśa*, the lord of the three—either of the three persons (*puruṣas*), the three worlds, or the three qualities (*guṇas*). By the very splendor of his self-sovereignty (*svārājya-lakṣmī*), which is the attainment of the perfection of the nature of supreme bliss, he has obtained all enjoyments. [He receives] tribute (*bali*), that is, tax.

His footstool was praised—that is, lauded—by the tips of the crowns of the world-protectors (Lokapālas) who, having arrived after a long time, were presenting their offerings; the sound produced by the clashing of the crowns of those bowing down is itself poetically imagined as being the praise itself. (21)

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Furthermore, regarding His transcendental pastimes (*alaukikalīlā*), He speaks of the quality of supreme humility with the following two verses beginning with "But He Himself" (*svayaṃ tu*). "The Sovereign" (*adhīśaḥ*) means the Lord of the three creators of the great [universe], who are the lords of all beings situated within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). As for Viṣṇu, there are three forms, and so forth.
"He was surrounded on all sides by the ten guardians of the directions, who were of the form of Manu and were extraordinary guardians of the world"—thus from the *Brahmasaṃhitā*. (21)

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, with two verses he laments: "How can I ever forget the sweetness of His being subject to His devotees—whether it be His sovereignty over Brahmā and the other primal beings, or His service toward Ugrasena? There is no equality [with Him]; what excellence could possibly surpass Him?"
"Of whom he is": the meaning is that in comparison with him, there is no equality for anything else, much less any superiority.

The reasons for this are: he is the Lord (īśa) of the three—the Great One (mahat), the Creator (sraṣṭṛ), and the other Puruṣas; and of the three powers (śaktis)—the power of consciousness (cicchakti), the power of the individual soul (jīvaśakti), and the power of māyā (māyāśakti). [He is the Lord] by means of his own portions (aṃśas), which are the devotees (bhaktas) and the powers (śaktis).
He shines by means of his divine sports (*līlā*), sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*), and sweetnesses (*mādhurya*); thus, his state is *svārājya*.

That itself is *lakṣmī*, and by that as a cause, he is one in whom all desires have been attained. [He is worshipped] by world-protectors who have existed for a long time, and by Brahmās who are creating and protecting within infinite millions of universes.

He whose footstool is praised—that is, lauded—by the crowns of Viṣṇus as they withdraw [the world], by Rudras as they maintain it, and by Śeṣas; the very sound of the clashing of the crowns of those bowing down is here poetically imagined (utprekṣyate) as being the praise itself. ||21||
O dear one, that service of his— standing while Ugrasena sits upon the throne of the Supreme Lord— is enough to weary us who are already burdened.
He awakened him, saying, "O God, hold [it] steady!"
Śrīdhara: O dear Vidura! [He addressed] the supported servants. Regarding that very state of servitude toward Ugrasena, he says:

"To him who was seated—that is, sitting—upon the royal throne, which is the abode of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), he himself stood and informed him, saying, 'O Lord, please attend to this; take heed. ||22||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: O dear Vidura! "Bhṛtān" means servants. Regarding that very state of servitude toward Ugrasena, he says: [he saw him] seated—that is, sitting—upon the throne of the Great King, which is the abode of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), while he himself...
Standing there, assisting someone, he informed and made [the king] understand: "O Lord, Sovereign of Great Kings! Please determine the course of action for this local ruler within your domain.
Alas, Bakī, who [offered] that deadly poison from her breast—
Even though that unvirtuous woman caused [the child] to drink [poison] with the intent to kill,
she obtained the destiny appropriate for a nurse; to what other compassionate one, then, shall we go for refuge?

Śrīdhara: Indicating that such compliance was due solely to compassion, and demonstrating His merciful nature even toward those who have done harm, he says: "Oh, how wonderful is the mercy! Even though she desired to kill Him, Bakī—the unrighteous Pūtanā—made Him drink the Kālakūṭa poison gathered in her breasts."

Even though she was wicked, Yaśodā attained the destiny appropriate for a nurse; the meaning is that He granted her a good state merely because of her appearance as a devotee. Who else, then, should we worship? ||23||

The sequential arrangement: Oh, Bakī! At the beginning of this passage, there is once again the extreme lack of restraint in His grace during His worldly pastimes (*laukika-līlā*), as this is not seen elsewhere, such as in His descents (*avatāra*). In that regard, according to the verse, "What are these but our mothers? (*bhā.pu. 10.6.38*), He is the one to whom the nurses give the nectar of breast milk.
For some, that is their destination. ||23||
Viśvanātha, recollecting the sweetness of His compassion even toward those who commit great offenses from the very moment of His descent, laments:

"Oh, what a marvel! Even though Pūtanā was known as 'Bakī' and her maternal nature was artificial, He nevertheless made her drink the *kālakūṭa* poison, even while she intended to kill Him. From her..."

"Fit for a nurse"—Ambikā and Kilimbā were the two nurses (*dhātrī*) who gave breast milk to Kṛṣṇa; she attained the destination appropriate for them in Goloka. Even by merely wearing the dress of a devotee, one attains the delight appropriate for a devotee; in this regard, the Blessed One has cited Pūtanā, though she was His enemy, as an example. Thus...
It has been stated that even for enemies there shall be liberation and devotion; this is the extraordinary characteristic of Kṛṣṇa’s incarnation. ||23||
I consider the Asuras to be devotees of the Lord of the Three Worlds, whose minds were intent upon the path of fury when they beheld the son of Tārkṣya in battle.
The weapon with a beautiful nave fell upon his shoulder.
Even those Asuras who look upon Viṣṇu, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace,
with devotion should be known as Bhāgavatas.
But those who hate Viṣṇu, even if they are the sons of sages, should clearly be known as asuras; they always go to darkness.
Due to the conjunction of two life-forces (jīva), others have faces like those of golden [beings];
they may also be possessed of devotion or hatred, and their destiny follows their own nature.
For Kaṃsa, Pūtanā, and the others were accompanied by their kinsmen and so forth;
through the union of two lives, they sought to conquer two destinies.
"Liberation is said to come from devotion in every way, while darkness results from hatred;
this is the rule for these two. Any other statement would lead to constant delusion. Thus it is said in the Brāhma [Purāṇa]. 24.
Śrīdhara: Now, it is well known that the Blessed Lord bestows grace only upon the devotees (bhāgavatas); this is true.

However, I consider even the demons (asuras) to be indeed devotees, because like the devotees, they too perceive the Blessed Lord directly through their intense absorption in meditation upon Him; thus he says: "With fury... (saṃrambhaḥ).

Those whose minds were possessed by a fit of anger and were thus intent upon that path; for this very reason, they beheld—that is, saw—in battle Tārkṣya Kaśyapa’s son Garuḍa upon the shoulder (skandha) of him who had Sunābha as his weapon and the discus (cakra) as his enemy. Therefore, it is fitting to show them favor as well.
This is the meaning. And he will say: "Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.1.30). ||24||

The sequence of the composition: the word "I think" (*manye*) implies that although the reality of the Lord does not actually exist within them, one nevertheless imagines it to be so; and consequently, due to one's own outward-turned state of mind, one thinks, "I shall not obtain the vision of Him at the final moment."
This was stated for the purpose of self-reproach. ||24||

Viśvanātha: "I consider them" is merely an expression of lamentation, not a logical inference based on Sāṅkhya principles. By the two signs—the direct perception of the Lord and the attainment of the Lord’s state at the final moment—he considers those like us to be turned away from the Divine at the time of death. At the final moment...

This is implied by the phrase "due to the absence of seeing him and the absence of attaining him. *Saṃrambha* means an outburst of anger. *Tārkṣya* is Kaśyapa; they did not see (*acakṣata*) his son Garuḍa. Of what sort was he?
He upon whose shoulder (*aṃse skandhe*) rested the weapon with the beautiful nave—the discus-weapon—and who was rushing toward them (*āpatantam*), facing them.
Coming toward [him]. ||24||
Born of Devakī in the prison of the lord of the Bhojas, the Blessed One was born from Vasudeva,
having been entreated by Aja to bring about her welfare.

Śrīdhara: Now, in order to describe the manner of his disappearance, he relates his life story in brief, beginning from the outset. He was born of the wife of Vasudeva in the prison of Kaṃsa, the lord of the Bhojas; desiring himself to bring about the welfare and happiness of this earth.
Being entreated by Aja and Brahmā as well. ||25||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Since the *mauṣala-līlā* (the pastimes of the club) must necessarily be told for the purpose of answering Vidura’s questions, [the author], desiring to speak of that sorrowful pastime by joining it with the joyful pastimes, says:
He said: "Of Vasudeva," that is, in the prison of the lord of the Bhojas. "For this earth" means for the welfare and happiness of this world, by means of Aja, who is Brahmā. ||25||
Then, fearing Kaṃsa, his father sent him from here to Nandavraja;
there, for eleven years, he dwelt with Balarāma, his radiance concealed.
Śrīdhara: With his father acting as the cause, he went from here to Nanda’s cowherd settlement; for years, he remained there with his radiance concealed and his splendor hidden. (26)

The sequential arrangement: "Eleven" means that because they possess full youth (*kaishora*) by that time alone, it is so stated in passages such as, "In a short time, O royal sage... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8.26).

In some places, they are described as "two youths with exceedingly delicate limbs who have not yet reached full adolescence," and so forth; thus there are the stages of childhood (*bālya*), early boyhood (*paugaṇḍa*), and youth (*kaishora*).
[This is known] from such [scriptural passages] as "He became [manifest] through his two sons. Regarding the term *gūḍhārciḥ*:

just as a fire with hidden flames (*gūḍhārciḥ*) burns whatever fuel it encounters wherever it may be found, so too, while possessing a hidden power during His pastimes as a cowherd, He burns every host of demons He encounters—this is the meaning.

The interpretation that [the fire] has hidden flames up to the eleventh day and manifest flames thereafter up to the fifteenth— requiring the insertion of words not present in the text— is untenable, because the respective powers [of those days] arise intermittently within that interval; by that much alone [the matter is explained].
It was stated thus because his youth was full. ||26||

Viśvanātha: For the sake of his father, he departed from here and dwelt there for eleven years—that is, throughout eleven years. Within that very time, having completed the playful stages of childhood, boyhood, and youth, his true nature remained unperceived by ordinary people such as Kaṃsa and others, as his splendor was concealed; this was due to the intensity of his sweetness.
Or, [the Lord is called] "one whose sovereignty is hidden. ||26||
Surrounded by calves and tending the young cows,
the Lord wandered through the groves on the banks of the Yamunā, where the trees were filled with the warbling of birds.
Śrīdhara: He played; [the place] in which the trees were crowded—that is, pervaded—by warbling birds (dvijas). ||27||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: In that place where the trees were crowded—that is, pervaded—by warbling birds, [Kṛṣṇa] displayed the delightful movements of the residents of Vraja characteristic of childhood.
As if weeping while laughing, with the charming gaze of a young lion.

Śrīdhara: The word "iva" (as if) in the phrase "rudann iva" (as if weeping) is connected with every [subsequent term] as appropriate. He is one whose gaze is like that of a lion which is both charming and young. (28)

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] on the word *kaumārīm* is as follows: because of his extreme childhood, this previous play of his while tending the calves was recited out of order due to an onset of grief; thus, the phrase "he was surrounded in such a manner" and so forth should be applied there, wherein his childhood nature is shown by his acting as if weeping and as if laughing. (28)

Viśvanātha: "As if weeping" means that just as children display the act of weeping even without the physical signs of crying—using their tears as a weapon—so too, before their mothers, one acts as if weeping due to the forceful demand for desirable objects that ought not to be given. At that very moment...

Upon attaining that state, he laughs. Furthermore, even a child who is bewildered by the approach of terrifying demons and the like fears a fierce creature, yet like a lion, he merely displays his own prowess through his gaze—one whose very look is like that of such a lion. [He looks upon] his parents and others, who are supremely affectionate.
It causes agitation. ||28||
He himself, tending the wealth of cattle— the abode of Lakṣmī— along with white bulls,
delighted his followers and cowherds while his flute resounded.

Śrīdhara: He, having reached an advanced age, was tending the cattle-wealth (*godhana*). What kind of cattle-wealth? It was the abode (*niketana*) of *lakṣmī*, that is, of beauty and other forms of prosperity. In which there was a herd of cows of various colors, including white bulls (*sitā govṛṣāḥ*). He whose flute (*veṇu*) was making a resonant sound (*raṇan*); he delighted (*arīramat*), that is, caused them to rejoice.
He sat. ||29||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He himself, having grown slightly older, finished tending the calves and [tended] the wealth of cattle, which was the abode of Lakṣmī’s splendor in white, blue, green, yellow, and smoky colors.
While herding the white bulls, he delighted the cowherds there. ||29||
The boy effortlessly dispelled those various sorcerers sent by King Bhoja— who could assume any form at will— just as one might cast aside playthings.
Śrīdhara: *vyanudaj* means he struck down. He [struck] the playthings made of grass and so forth, such as lions; the sequence of the composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: *vyanudaj* means he struck down. [He struck] the playthings made of leaves and so forth, like lions and other animals.
Having subdued the lord of serpents who had caused the ruin through the drinking of poison,
he raised up the cows and made them drink that water which had returned to its natural state.
Śrīdhara: Having raised up the perished and dead cowherds as well as the cows, that very water became restored to its natural state and free from poison. ||31||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Having raised up the cowherds and the cows who had fainted from drinking the poisoned water, [he restored them] to their natural state, free from poison. (31)
Desiring to make a virtuous expenditure of his vast wealth, the lord caused the king of the Gopas to perform the Gosava sacrifice with the most excellent of the twice-born.
Śrīdhara: By means of the very worship of the cows—which was performed by subverting the worship of Indra—the *gosava* sacrifice was accomplished;

[he thus honored] Nanda, the king of cowherds. And by the word "of wealth" (*vittasya*), the particle "ca" (and) implies that he was performing the humiliation of Indra while possessing great abundance and immense burden. (32)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By means of the worship of cows initiated following the breaking of Indra’s sacrifice by Govardhana;
and by the word "ca" (and), [he refers to] the shattering of Indra’s pride and the excessive burden on his thighs. 32.
While Indra was raining down [torrents] out of anger and the cow-pen was utterly overwhelmed by its shattered pride,
it was protected by Bhadra, who compassionately held up the playful sunshade of his own herd.
Śrīdhara: He rains out of anger. "Gotra" refers to a mountain itself, which serves as his playful parasol; O noble one! (33)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: While it rains out of anger; "gotra" is a mountain itself, which serves as a playful parasol (līlātapatra);
O auspicious one! ||33||
Honoring the onset of night, which was polished by the rays of the autumnal moon,
he— the ornament of the circle of women— delighted while singing in sweet-toned phrases.
Śrīdhara: "Mṛṣṭa" means brilliant. He is so called because he adorns the circle of women. ||34||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The face of the night, that is, the evening—at which time the autumnal moon, acting as the hero, has been polished by the friction of his palms and made radiant by the removal of perspiration and other impurities by the Night.

Honoring and gladdening the face of the heroine whose husband is under her own control, and thinking "I too shall act in this very way," He adorns the circle of women following the pastimes of the rāsa-union; thus it is said in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for the hearts of devotees.
The second chapter of the third [section] is well-connected, well-connected for the virtuous.
Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras,
in the Vaiyāsikī collection known as the Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā, in the third book, in the dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava.
The Second Chapter;
now begins the Third Chapter:
The Dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava.
Uddhava said:
Then, desiring to bring about the welfare of his parents, he returned to the city accompanied by Śrī Baladeva.
Having cast down the leader of the enemy host from the height, he dragged the lifeless body across the earth with great force.
Śrīdhara:
In the third [canto], he described that which was performed by Kṛṣṇa after coming from Vraja to Mathurā— the slaying of Kaṃsa and so forth— as well as what was done in Dvārakā.
*Śam* is an indeclinable [expressing auspiciousness]. The meaning is: "with the desire to bring about the happiness of his parents. From the lofty royal throne (*tuṅga-rājamañca*).
To Kaṃsa, the lord of the hosts of enemies. Even the dragging away of one who was already ruined was for the sake of his parents' happiness;
such is the sequence of the composition. "Uddhava said" marks the beginning of the description of the *rāsa-līlā*.

The conclusion of the chapter occurs due to being overwhelmed by love; it should be understood that this happens after some effort in searching for her outside. "Then" (tataḥ) refers to the drawing away [of the senses] because [the objects] such as the beloved cause pain to the person dear to one, and because [objects] such as the gods are objects of attachment. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the third [canto], the pastimes such as the slaying of Kaṃsa at Mathurā and Dvāravatī, as well as the destruction of the Kurus, are described in brief.

The indeclinable *śam* denotes happiness; thus, the meaning is "with the desire to bring about the happiness of his parents. From the high platform (*tuṅgāt mañcāt*). He dragged out even one who was struck (*hatam*), having met with injury, and consequently deprived of life (*vyasum*, i.e., having met death)—[he did so] for the sake of his parents and others who were terrified, fearing that his death might occur.
This is for the purpose of dispelling the notion that [the self] exists in a state of unconsciousness. ||1||
Having studied the Veda in its entirety after it was taught only once by Sāndīpani, he gave him a boon:
his deceased son from the belly of Pañcajana.

Śrīdhara: *Brahma* means the Veda; *savistaram* means together with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and so forth. The meaning is: "having brought forth a son by means of tearing open the belly of Pañcajana. ||2||
The sequential arrangement is as follows: it should be understood that [the Lord], having reached the belly of Pañcajana and brought forth the deceased from the world of Yama, gave him [back]. ||2||
Viśvanātha: "Brahma" refers to the Veda along with its extensive details, including the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

The phrase "having torn open the belly of Pañcajana" uses the ablative case by ellipsis of the suffix *-lyap* (implying "having come from"); the remainder of the sense is "having brought [it] from the realm of Yama.
Those who were summoned by the daughter of Bhīṣmaka—

With a splendor like that of Śrī, he desired to surpass them; while they looked on, he took his own portion by the Gāndharva method, just as Suparṇa, placing his foot upon their heads, seized his share.
The Madhvas were summoned merely by their own caste name for the sake of Bhīṣmaka’s daughter.
The Lord conceived the idea of summoning them with the desire to seize their splendor.
"Suparṇa [is so called] because of his supreme bliss (suparānanda), and Kākutstha because he is established in speech (vāci saṃsthitiḥ)," thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa. (3)

Śrīdhara: Those kings who were summoned by Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka—the short vowel [in "samāhūtāḥ"] is an archaic usage (ārṣa). In the reading "samāhṛtāḥ," the meaning is "attracted. By what means?
By a complexion (savarṇena) equal to Śrī, that is, Lakṣmī; for although she [Rukmiṇī] [summoned] Śrī-Kṛṣṇa alone...

Although not all were invited in that manner, nevertheless, because her beauty was the cause of their arrival, it is said that they were invited by her alone. While they looked on with eyes wide open, she placed her foot upon their heads; and through the *gāndharva* mode—characterized by a mutual agreement—and through the desire to exist (*bubhūṣayā*), she sought to become one with them.

He carried away. Of what nature was she? Her own portion (*svabhāga*), because she was the very essence of Lakṣmī and because she had been offered by her to his own self. "Suparṇa" means one who flies well; or else, like Suparṇa [Garuḍa], he took his own portion, namely the nectar (*sudhā*); or else, she was equal to Śrī, that is, Rukmiṇī.

He whose name consists of two syllables is Rukmin, who is of the same color (varṇa) as Śrī; by him Śiśupāla and others were summoned. For what purpose? With the desire for prosperity (*bubhūṣayā*)—that is, with the wish that "prosperity (*bhūti*) may come to them"—along with the daughter of Bhīṣmaka. Among them, the summoning of Śiśupāla was due to the desire for prosperity regarding [his obtaining] the bridegroomhood.
For Jarāsandha and the others, it was due to that festival of their wedding; the rest is as before. ||3||

The sequential composition: by that which was the desire of Bhīṣmaka’s daughter, two instrumental case-endings in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa) took away their own portion, which was the form of Śrī Rukmiṇī. ||3||

Viśvanātha: The word "bhīṣmakakanyayā" (by the daughter of Bhīṣmaka) is used in the sense of the genitive case. Of the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, Rukmiṇī—who is Śrī, the goddess Lakṣmī herself—the two syllables "ruk-mī" are the expressive name of her brother Rukmin;
by him (tena), those kings were brought together (*samāhṛtāḥ*). The short vowel [in *samāhṛtāḥ*] is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣam*).

In the reading "samāhṛtā," the meaning is "brought together. Placing his foot upon the heads of these kings, Suparṇa Garuḍa carried off Rukmiṇī as his own portion, like nectar (sudhā). Of what sort were they? By the conduct [expected] in the Gāndharva form of marriage, Śiśupāla was the suitor, while for the others—

The meaning is: "by that choosing which takes the form of a bridal procession. With the desire to become [the groom], thinking "I am the bridegroom" and "we are the bridal party," while they were looking about with apprehension here and there—fearing that Kṛṣṇa might suddenly arrive and carry off the girl—the [gopīs] watched. ||3||
Having subdued the proud Kakudmin at his own choice-marriage, he married Nāgnajitī;
yet even those whose pride was thus shattered remained greedy through ignorance.
Unwounded himself, he struck down those who bore weapons with his own weapons.

Śrīdhara [comments]: "Of the humped bulls" means those with pierced noses; or, having made them with pierced noses. By means of those bulls and by that subduing, their pride was broken; yet he saw them still desiring—that is, longing for—those very kings who were ignorant and wielders of weapons, and he remained unhurt by their weapons.
He struck. ||4||

The sequential composition [of the commentary] is as follows: he slew his own [disciples], such as Arjuna and others, with weapons; the meaning is that, through the infusion of his own divine power (*prabhāva*), he himself slew them. This is explained in accordance with the dialogue in the *Śrī-daśama* (the tenth book of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*) which states, "The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow brought them to their end. ||4||

Viśvanātha: Having subdued only those horned bulls whose noses had not been pierced, he struck down with his own weapons those ignorant kings who were still coveting—that is, desiring—the maiden, their pride having been shattered by being defeated by those very bulls; and [he killed them] with their own weapons.
Though filled, full, and covered, it remains uninjured. ||4||
Desiring to do what was pleasing to his beloved, as if she were a rustic woman, the Lord went to fetch the celestial tree for her sake;
Indra, blinded by rage, rushed toward it with his host.
Surely this is a pet deer for the young women.

Śrīdhara: When the Ādityas went to heaven to give him earrings, the Lord—though independent—desiring to do what was pleasing to his beloved Satyabhāmā, as if he were a common man dependent on a woman, brought back the celestial Pārijāta tree;
for whose sake, that is, for which purpose, he did so.

Impelled by a woman, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrī) pursued Kṛṣṇa to fight him. [The author] states that his exertion for battle was entirely improper against one who accomplishes his own purpose, saying: "Like a pet deer. This refers to Vajrī. (5)

The sequence of composition: Although appearing like a vulgar lover, [Indra] was in fact desirous of performing that which was dear to his beloved—the one possessed of love—and for that purpose he approached the tree of the sacrifice (*dyutaru*); however, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrī*), perceiving him otherwise according to his own nature, pursued him with such a contrary perception.
Thus he said: "This Kṛṣṇa is surely a pet deer for those amorous women who were accepted by him solely out of greed for their beauty, being under the sway of lust. (5)

Viśvanātha: Like a rustic lover who, though appearing so, actually desires to bestow love upon his beloved—the one possessed of affection—by means of being under the sway of love, he seized (ārcchat) the celestial tree, the Pārijāta;
for whose sake the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra), accompanied by the Vajra itself, rushed toward him (tam ādravat) just slightly to fight.
He arrived there. The reason for this is that he was blind. Furthermore, the reason for that is that he was like a pet deer to his wives, Śacī and the others.

The meaning is that, according to the maxim "one considers the world as possessing a self," he ran toward him while censuring him, thinking, "This one is a pet deer to his wives, Satyabhāmā and the others. ||5||
Having heard that the sky was being swallowed by his form in battle and seeing it crushed by the Earth,
he addressed the remainder [of his speech] to his son.
Having given it, he entered that inner apartment.

Śrīdhara: Having been uprooted by the discus with its beautiful nave, and having seen his son Bhauma, he was entreated and requested by the Earth—the mother of that [son]—and so, having given the remainder of the kingdom to her son Bhagadatta, [he departed]. ||6||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha [comments]: Having seen that his son, the demon Naraka, had been crushed—that is, killed—by Sunābha, he was addressed and informed by the Earth (Dharitrī) of this matter to her son, Bhagadatta. Here...
Even though he was born of pure parents, his evil intellect arose solely from association with the demon Bāṇa;
thus, the story from another Purāṇa regarding the power of associating with the wicked should be understood here. 6.
There, seeing Hari— the kinsman of the distressed— Kujā beheld those princesses of kings who had been brought there;
rising immediately, they seized him with great joy.
With glances sent forth out of both bashfulness and passion.

Śrīdhara: There, in the inner apartments, those women who had been brought by Kujā (Bhauma), with glances sent forth—impelled—by great joy, bashfulness, and passion, accepted [him], having taken him as their own. ||7||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: There, in the inner apartments, by Kujā [or] Naraka-Asura; and by those glances sent forth—impelled—by joy, shame, and passion, they seized [him], thinking, "This one is mine."
"Excellent! they each accepted [the boon]. ||7||
In a single moment, he who was worthy of them took the hands of these women in their various dwellings into his presence by means of his own illusory power.
Śrīdhara: Being in accordance with each of them, he [held] the hands of these women in their proximity, in a manner appropriate for marriage. ||8||
The sequential composition: by his own *māyā*, that is, by his inconceivable power of consciousness (*acintyacicchakti*), [he created] the holy forest along with Brahmā. ||8||
Viśvanātha: Accompanied by his own *māyā*—that is, by *yogamāyā*, which is truly free from deceit (*amāyā*)—and together with the methods appropriate for a wedding. ||8||
Upon them he begot offspring equal to himself in every respect— ten upon each— one desiring to manifest the manifold nature of Prakṛti.

Regarding the word *madhvaḥ*: Śrīdhara states in the *Āgneya-purāṇa* that "some slight similarity with the highest [beings] is proclaimed in every respect. "In every respect" means equal to them in all qualities. "The manifold becoming (*bhavana*) of *prakṛti*"—that is, the expansion of *māyā*—occurs by His will; or alternatively, it is for the sake of the welfare of *prakṛti*, so that she may become manifold.
By will. ||9||
The sequence of the composition: In the present context, by the desire for the majesty of the very *svarūpa* (essential nature), the term *prakṛti* is used;

for Amarasimha states, "Prakṛti, *svarūpa*, and *svabhāva* [are synonyms]. And this has been explained by the commentators on the verse *bhajasva prakṛtim* [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.1.19], where they state that *prakṛti* means *svarūpa*. ||9||

Viśvanātha: Out of the desire for manifestation—the wish to manifest—their own nature (*prakṛti*), as indicated by the statement "equal to himself"; for Amara states that *prakṛti*, *svarūpa*, and *svabhāva* are synonyms.
[He besieged] the city with his armies against Kāla, Māgadha, Śālva, and others.
He himself did not strike him down, but rather directed his own divine splendor toward his men.

Śrīdhara: Kāla refers to Kālayavana. "Of him who was obstructing" means of him who was blocking [the path]. By means of Mucukunda, Bhīma, and others acting merely as instruments, He Himself slew him (ghātitavān). And by that act, He bestowed upon His own devotees splendor, power, and fame. ||10||
The sequence of composition: "by himself" means directly; however, in some instances, it means by means of immersion (āveśa) here and there. ||10||

Viśvanātha: Kāla and Kālayavana were obstructing or surrounding [him] with their armies. By means of Mucukunda, Bhīma, and others acting merely as instruments, He Himself slew them. And by that act, He bestowed upon those men their own splendor, power, and fame. ||10||
He slew Śambara, Dvivida, Bāṇa, Mura, and Balvala,
as well as others such as Dantavakra, and had some of them killed by his subordinates.

Śrīdhara: He caused Śambara, Dvivida, Balvala, and certain others to be killed by Pradyumna, Rāma, and the rest; or rather, the reading is "ghātayan" (causing to kill). He himself slew Dantavakra and others. ||11||
The sequential composition: "Śambara" constitutes a pair of verses. It should be applied accordingly that he caused Śambara and others to be slain, and Bāṇa and others were killed. ||11||

Viśvanātha: Now, immediately thereafter, which kings did he cause to be slain? The absence of the augment *a* (in *ghātayat*) is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). In the reading "ghātayan," the word "became" (*babhūva*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. ||11||
Then, as those kings who had fallen on the sides of his brothers' sons rushed toward Kurukṣetra with their forces, the earth trembled.

Śrīdhara: The phrase "causing kings to fall" is to be supplied [to the verse]. Of what nature were they? They were those who were approaching or going toward Kurukṣetra, by whose forces and armies the entire earth trembled and shook.
Regarding the sequence of the words: "fallen" refers to some [kings] because they themselves had become a burden to the earth.
And by "falling into their faction," the meaning is that some have fallen away from those who ought to be protected. ||12||

Viśvanātha: Whom—those who had fallen into the two factions of your brothers' sons, Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, and Duryodhana and the others—and of what sort were they? [He describes them as] those who rushed toward Kurukṣetra, arriving with whose armies the entire earth trembled and shook. (12)
He beheld Suyodhana lying there with his followers, his fortune and life destroyed by the ripening of the evil counsel of Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Saubala.
Seeing his thighs broken upon the earth, he did not rejoice.
Śrīdhara: He is Kṛṣṇa. Although he saw him lying on the earth—him whose fortune and life had been destroyed and whose thighs were broken—he did not rejoice; he found no satisfaction. ||13||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: That Kṛṣṇa, even though looking [at her], did not rejoice. ||13||
How much has this earth been relieved of its heavy burden by these eighteen akṣauhiṇīs of my own forces, which had Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Arjuna, and Bhīma as their leaders?
The invincible strength of the Yadus remains.

Śrīdhara says: He explains the manner of his lack of appreciation with the words "How much? (*kiyān*). By means of Droṇa and others as the primary causes (*mūlaiḥ kāraṇabhūtaiḥ*), that which was joined by eighteen *akṣauhiṇīs*—the short vowel being an archaic usage (*ārṣam*)—that burden of the earth which was destroyed, how much is this? The meaning is: it is very little. Because...
By means of my own portions, such as Pradyumna and others acting as causes, an invincible power resides [within me]. ||14||

The sequence of the composition: the meaning of the statement "strength remains" is as follows. The burden of the earth would not arise from a mere multiplicity of individuals, for mountains, oceans, and the like abound therein.
Rather, the burden there would exist solely due to an abundance of unrighteous persons. Let that matter rest for now.

In passages such as, "How did the curse of the Brahmins befall the Vṛṣṇis, who were devoted to Brahman, generous, exceedingly righteous, always serving their elders, and whose minds were fixed on Kṛṣṇa?"— it is stated that even those partial incarnations beginning with Pradyumna, who possessed only a fraction of [Kṛṣṇa's] power, were supremely virtuous.

"In sleeping, sitting, walking, conversing, playing, bathing, eating, and so forth, the Vṛṣṇis— whose minds are fixed on Kṛṣṇa— do not perceive their own selves as existing," and so on. Therefore, when "Bhāratva" (the state of being a descendant of Bharata) is mentioned here as being difficult to endure, it refers indeed to my disappearance while leaving them behind, causing those [Vṛṣṇis] to be afflicted by the pain of separation from me.
It is understood that this earth would be crushed by contact with a number of [worlds] reaching as far as a parārdha. ||14||

Viśvanātha: The reason for this is expressed by the word "how much" (kiyān). Since the burden of the earth was diminished by Droṇa and others—who were the primary causes—by means of eighteen akṣauhiṇīs, such that the burden became great; the meaning is that this [remaining burden] is "how much," i.e., extremely small. The *sandhi* is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). This is the explanation of the compound.

One must tolerate this lack of consideration for the portion to be enjoined; for by my own portions, such as Pradyumna and others, acting as causes, there exists a power that is difficult to withstand.
Now, it might be argued that the burden of the earth would not be excessive due to the multiplicity of individual beings, since mountains, oceans, and so forth also exist therein.
However, due to their abundance—specifically because of the abundance of the unrighteous among them—they were withdrawn by the Lord;
yet it should not be said that the Yadu clan was unrighteous, for they were the very retinue of the Lord.
How could a curse from the Brahmins have befallen those who were devoted to Brahmanas, generous, and ever-attending upon their elders?

And from such statements as: "Of the Vṛṣṇis whose minds are fixed on Kṛṣṇa; in their lying down, sitting, walking, conversation, play, bathing, eating, and so forth, the Vṛṣṇis, with their hearts on Kṛṣṇa, do not perceive their own selves as existing," and others. To this it is replied: Indeed, a burden is of two kinds—that which consists of suffering and that which consists of happiness. The first...
The first is difficult to endure, while the second is indeed easy to bear, such as the burden of one's own lover for a young woman;

or like the burden of an infant held in the lap by a compassionate mother; or like the burden of one's own wealth carried upon the head by a merchant. Furthermore, what can a person of little strength do?
