Even that which is exceedingly abundant and of the nature of happiness cannot be borne as a burden by oneself; just as the earth was burdened even by Dhruva, the supremely righteous and great devotee, when he manifested the excess of his power through austerity. As it has been said:
When that prince stood on one foot, the earth, pressed by his big toe,
sank down halfway there, as if occupied by a lordly elephant.
"...as if at every step, from one side to the other" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.8.79).

And when even the Blessed One manifests His own power, then even He, whose nature is supreme bliss, cannot bear the burden; as in the hymn of Bhīṣma, he approached with his chariot wheels turned back.

As it is said: "The earth trembled" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.9.37), and regarding the manifestation of Nṛsiṃha: "The earth, pressed down by his feet, surged upward" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.8.34). Therefore, although the burden of the Yadu clan was not perceived as a burden upon the earth—as it would be for a delicate woman—[the earth nevertheless shook].

Just as the burden of ornaments consisting of much gold, jewels, and so forth is removed from her limbs by her loving husband during festivals and the like— removing only those adventitious ornaments while retaining those that are always useful— in the same way, it occurs at the time of partial descent (*aṃśāvataraṇa*).
Those portions consisting of gods and others who had entered into the Yādavas and others—who were His eternal retinue—were led out from Dvārakā and withdrawn at Prabhāsa. ||14||
When there shall arise mutual dispute among these whose eyes are copper-red from intoxication with honey-wine,
this will be the means for their destruction; there is no other such way.
When I raised [my weapon], they vanished of their own accord.

Śrīdhara: No other means is effective here; rather, when a dispute arises among these men with copper-hued eyes due to that intoxication which spreads everywhere through honey, this alone shall be their means of destruction—there is no other. For even though they are of one mind, once I have exerted myself, they will [perish] of their own accord.
The meaning is that they would disappear through dispute. ||15||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: There, unlike others, a dissolution (*saṃhāra*) of these is not possible; rather, it occurs in a different manner. He says this to himself: "Mutually" (*mithaḥ*). That which is thoroughly intoxicated (*āsamadam*) by honey (*madhunā*)...
Therefore, even then, for those with copper-colored eyes, this dispute shall not take the form of killing;

rather, it shall be something other than killing—meaning it will not be actual slaughter. Thus, the meaning is that people will, in reality, perceive their mutual conflict as non-killing. This is the truth.
In fact, he states this clearly: "While I am intent on withdrawing these [beings], they themselves indeed disappear; that is, they will vanish," such is the certainty. ||15||
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One established the son of Dharma in his own kingdom and gladdened his friends, showing them the path of the virtuous.

Śrīdhara: Having thus reflected in sequence upon what was stated in these two verses, and having established [the lineage] in his own kingdom, the *kramasaṃdarbha*—which was previously held and established—is again held and protected. ||16||
Viśvanātha: Having established, that is, having caused [the deity] to be established. ||16||
The lineage of Puru was sustained by Uttara through the virtuous Abhimanyu;
that very lineage, scorched by the weapon of Aśvatthāman, was again sustained by the Blessed One.
Śrīdhara: "Dhṛta" means protected. ||17||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: *Dhṛta* means placed; *dhṛta* also means protected. ||17||
The powerful lord caused the son of Dharma to perform three horse-sacrifices;
he too, protecting the earth with his younger brothers, took delight in following Kṛṣṇa.
Śrīdhara: Together with his younger brothers. ||18||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He took delight and shone forth. ||18||
The Blessed One, the soul of the universe, following the paths of both the world and the Vedas, resided in Dvārāvatī; though established in Sāṅkhya and unattached, he indulged in desires.
Madhva says: "Sāṅkhya" is designated as the knowledge of the Lord alone; Śrīdhara says, regarding the inner self: "Sāṅkhya is the discrimination between Prakṛti and Puruṣa. (19)

The sequential arrangement: the meaning is that when the Blessed One had also attained the state of having accomplished all that was to be done, the pastime of detachment (*vairāgya-līlā*) was manifested. ||19||
Viśvanātha: In the fifth and sixth [verses], the Blessed Lord also illuminates sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

Like the inner ruler (*antaryāmī*) of the universe, yet unattached, he enjoyed—that is, partook of—the very desires that are not prohibited by worldly or Vedic law, which are of the nature of happiness and were sent to him as offerings by Indra and the other gods. Here, [the word] "unattached" (*asakta*)...
Thus is detachment; it is to be known as Sāṅkhya. ||19||
By his affectionate smile and gaze, by his speech which was like nectar,
by his faultless conduct, and by his own self which was the abode of splendor;
Delighting both this world and the next, he took great pleasure in the Yadus;
for him, who was devoted to the sight of his wife, every moment was granted by the goddess Kṣaṇadā (the Night).

Śrīdhara: By that look which is affectionate and accompanied by a smile; by [that speech] which is like nectar, equal to ambrosia—or according to another reading, in the form of a stream of ambrosia; by himself, that is, by his body. ||20||

By "kṣaṇadā" (giver of moments) is meant the night; he is one who possesses friendship (*sauhṛda*) for even a moment (*kṣaṇam*) toward those women to whom a moment—meaning an opportunity, a leisure time, or a festival (*utsava*)—has been granted. ||21||
The sequence of composition: therein, he states the sequence in three [verses]. The pair beginning with "snigdha" [is verse 20].
He whose friendship with women, granted an opportunity by the night, takes the form of a festival for a moment. ||21||

Viśvanātha: He states that his lack of attachment is solely due to the play of the power of *māyā*, whereas his attachment is indeed due to the play of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)—thus he says "Siddha... etc. By means of the four kinds of sweetness (*mādhurya*) consisting of glance, speech, play, and form, [he protects] this world—the devotee of his own situated in the mortal realm—and that [world] situated in the divine realm.
Even among them, he took delight especially in the Yadus; and even among the Yadus, he delighted in women.

Thus, his attachment was excessive. He was one whose friendship was formed in a moment—by means of the festival of love—with those women who had been granted a "moment" (an opportunity) by the night, the giver of moments. [This refers to] the principal queens.

Because it constitutes its very nature, it is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). This is seen in the *Skanda-Purāṇa*, in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*, within the dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī concerning the majesty of the Gopīs and others:
"Sixteen thousand Gopīs assembled there."
"One hundred and sixty thousand—these, O beloved, are the sons of Kṛṣṇa. Having begun thus, [it continues]:
"Kṛṣṇa is considered to be Haṃsa himself, the Supreme Self, Janārdana.
These sixteen, O Goddess, are proclaimed to be his very powers (śaktis)."
"Kṛṣṇa is considered to be the form of the moon, while they are remembered as being the forms of its digits.
A detailed explanation of this point will be elaborated upon in the tenth [chapter]. ||2021||
As he was thus enjoying himself for many groups of years,
a dispassion toward household life and worldly attachments arose within him.
"Even though Madhva was always detached, he manifested himself as if possessing detachment;
how could he have had it only occasionally? It is intended for the purpose of instructing the world," so it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
By him, too, detachment has been demonstrated. (22)

Śrīdhara: Among householders—that is, among the duties of a householder—and among yogas—that is, among the means for the enjoyment of desires—dispassion, meaning indifference, has arisen; such is the meaning. ||22||
The sequential composition: detachment, that is, indifference, toward householders' duties—the performance of religious practices appropriate for the householder stage of life. ||22||

Viśvanātha: In household duties, in yogic practices, on the paths of action characterized by the quality of *rajas*, and in the objects of enjoyment presented by those engaged in such actions, a complete detachment and indifference arose; indeed, he had always been so, but at that time—

The meaning is that it became exceedingly clear. Since non-attachment to the *guṇas* is the definition of *vairāgya*, one should not explain *vairāgya* here as being directed toward the amorous pastimes of Rukmiṇī and others, who are beyond the *guṇas* and composed of pure *sattva*. ||22||
When desires are dependent on fate and the person himself is dependent on fate,
who— devoted through yoga to the Lord of Yoga— could place his trust [in them]?
O Madhva! Who else but you could place such trust in this? ||23||

Śrīdhara: When even toward those things under His own control the Blessed One feels detachment, then who could place reliance, trust, or affection in that which is dependent on fate? [This is so] if one follows Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, through yoga. (23)
The sequence of the composition:

Viśvanātha says that she [the Goddess] spoke this in the form of a play of detachment (*vairāgya-līlā*) in order to make this known—he says, "When even toward things dependent on herself the Lord feels detachment, then who would place trust, confidence, or affection in things dependent on fate? (*daiva*).
If he should perform [this] through yoga, he would become a devoted follower of the Blessed One, the Lord of Yoga. ||23||
Once, while playing in the city, the princes of the Yadu and Bhoja clans provoked the sages who were experts in the doctrines of the Blessed One, and those sages cursed them.

Śrīdhara: They uttered a curse; they were experts, that is, well-acquainted with the intention of the Lord. Regarding the sequence of the composition: the intention of the Lord was previously stated in the passage beginning with "When, under the pretext of the Brahmins' curse, there arose among them... and so forth. Deva refers to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||24||
Viśvanātha: By stating that [the sages] are "experts in the intention" (abhiprāya) of the Blessed One, the fault attributed to the sages has been removed.
Furthermore, the reason why the Blessed One also held such an intention will be explained in the eleventh [chapter]. ||24||
Then, after some months, the Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas, Andhakas, and others,
delighted and enchanted by the gods, went to Prabhāsa by means of their chariots.

"Madhva says: 'That which is yet to come is certainly spoken of as having passed away, either because of a wheel-like revolution or for the purpose of deluding the wicked. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. (25)
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.

Viśvanātha: Only the Vṛṣṇis and others who were deluded by the Lord departed; however, those who were eternally present remained in Dvārakā itself, remaining invisible to the people of the phenomenal world. Alternatively, it may mean "the gods" and "those who were deluded. (25)
Having bathed there and satiated the ancestors, gods, and sages with that water,
they then gave many excellent cows to the brahmins.
Śrīdhara: Those cows which are endowed with many qualities such as youthfulness and good character. ||26||
The sequential arrangement: "Therein" constitutes a couplet (yugmaka). ||26||
Viśvanātha: "Gāvaḥ" means cows; "gāḥ" means those possessing many qualities, such as milk, character, and so forth. ||26||
Gold, silver, a bed, garments, skins, and woolen blankets;
vehicles, chariots, elephants, maidens, and even land that provides a livelihood.
Śrīdhara says: "And girls" means those who provide a livelihood, sufficient for their subsistence. ||27||

The sequence of the composition: by the phrase "the life-force for the sake of cows and Brahmins," his supreme righteousness is indeed reinforced; thereby it is suggested that such a state of mind was merely adventitious, occurring solely through the will of the Blessed Lord.
Consequently, the punishment meted out here and there is intended only to strike terror into the world, and not [for the sake of personal gain].
And it has been shown that this is the reality. ||27||
Viśvanātha: [He gave her] a livelihood-providing [gift], sufficient for her maintenance. ||27||
Having given them food of excellent flavor, offered to the Blessed One,
those heroes— whose very lives were dedicated to the cause of cows and Brahmins— bowed their heads to the ground.
Śrīdhara: [The phrase] "bhagavadarpaṇam" means "in such a way that there is offering to the Lord. [The phrase] "yeṣām asavo goviprārthāḥ" has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: That in which there is offering to the Lord—let it be so; [the phrase] "for the sake of cows and Brahmins" refers to those whose lives are for the sake of cows and Brahmins.
By stating "those for whom [the arrows] are *asavas* (deadly)," their righteousness is established,

thereby manifesting that their destruction is dependent upon the will of the Blessed One. Furthermore, the will of the Blessed One— that Brahmins must not be provoked to anger— is the principle governing the world, directed toward the Yādavas who are eternal beings.
The distribution of portions of the gods and others, by means of which they attain their respective positions and their own sixth-fold sovereignty is manifested;
yet this occurs through the concealment of the greatness of His own devotees, the abodes, the pastimes, the associates, and so forth.
These include the deluding of people who look outward and the spreading of affection among one's own devoted followers, and so forth. ||28||

Thus ends the third chapter, appropriately joined to the third [section], in this *Harṣiṇī* commentary that reveals the essential meaning for the hearts of devotees, composed for the sake of the virtuous.

Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā pertaining to the Pāramahaṃsyas, in the third book, in the dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava.
The Third Chapter.
The Fourth Chapter: The Dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava.
Uddhava said:
Then, permitted by him, they ate and drank the liquor;
their understanding being clouded by it, they pierced his vital points with harsh words.
Śrīdhara:
Having heard of the death of his kinsmen in the fourth [canto], he approached Maitreya for instruction from Uddhava in order to attain self-knowledge.
Permitted by those Brahmins, [he drank] the *vāruṇī* liquor made from flour. ||1||
The sequential composition: those whose knowledge has been destroyed by the Blessed One himself, using that [ignorance] as a mere indicator. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
Having heard from Uddhava about the non-manifestation of Hari and sighing for the sake of his own lineage,
Vidura followed Maitreya in the fourth [skandha] for the purpose of receiving instruction.
Permitted by those Brahmins or by that Kṛṣṇa, they [struck] each other at the vital points; this is the ellipsis. ||1||
As the sun was setting, those whose minds were deranged by the vice of liquor met with a slaughter like that of bamboos.
Śrīdhara: *Maireya* is indeed a type of *vāruṇī*; when it sets—that is, when it goes down due to its defect—there is "crushing," meaning slaughter. ||2||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: When the sun sets—that is, goes to its disappearance—due to the fault of that very *maireya* liquor, which is indeed *vāruṇī*, there is "crushing," meaning destruction. ||2||
Having observed that course of his own self-illusion, the Blessed One touched the waters of the Sarasvatī and sat down at the foot of a tree.
Having previously observed the course of Madhu’s own *māyā*— that is, his own power—
and having known [the future] through the perfection of his knowledge many years ago, Janārdana said: "O Uddhava, lead Maushala to Badarī."
Having spread that knowledge there, Uddhava returned again to Dvāravatī;
for although he had already been instructed in knowledge by Hari previously, [he now taught it further].
At the time of his ascent to heaven, he questioned Keśava once more;
having heard [the answer] again, he dwelt at Badarī for three years.
"Having established his consciousness and subsequently departed for heaven by his own will," thus [says] Śrīdhara in the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*;
having approached the Sarasvatī river and performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*). ||3||

The sequential composition: Viśvanātha [states] that the *mauṣala* pastimes were manifested by the Lord’s own *māyā*, like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*). Now, one might ask: how could the Blessed One—who is an ocean of compassion and who has previously performed the supreme protection of his sons, grandsons, and others—personally witness the slaughter of Pradyumna and the rest?

He says that he "saw" this by using the word "the Blessed One. Regarding the course or activity of Māyā—that the Yādavas, beginning with Pradyumna, met their immediate destruction through mutual slaughter—he says "in his own self," meaning that his own Māyā could not have deluded even him. This is intended to convince all the world.

Because illusion (*māyā*) has as its inherent nature not to delude its own substratum; and therefore, the Blessed One perceived that the eternal attendants of his divine play, such as Pradyumna and the other Yādavas, remained right there in Dvārakā,
while the gods who had entered those various bodies were separated from those respective limbs.

Having appeared in those respective forms, and having eaten and drunk according to their own desires, they went happily to heaven. Therefore, in the previous verse, the true meaning is simply that, permitted by Him, they went to heaven. In this regard, since Rāma, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha constitute the manifestation (*vyūha*) of the Lord, these indeed—

"O beautiful lady, all the Yādavas are indeed my own attendants; O Goddess, they are always dear to me and possess qualities equal to mine—just as Saumitri and Bharata, and just as Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others.
In that very same way, they are born from their own world by my will," and so forth, according to the statement in the *Padma Purāṇa*. And regarding the gods:

Furthermore, as stated by Akrūra in the *Harivaṃśa*: "We have attained this human state for the sake of [the Lord's] welfare. Since the Yādavas are eternal associates in His pastimes, even though Guha and others—who had entered among them through the scriptures and so forth—were actually gods, they were not subject to destruction within that very context of qualification; therefore, this *mauṣala-līlā* (the pastime of the pestle) is merely illusory (*māyikī*). Even though it is illusory...

Even though there is an absence of any creation consisting of illusion (*māyika*), it should be understood as eternal because it exists within the pastimes (*līlā*) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and is favored by inconceivable *yogamāyā*. ||3||
And I was told by the Blessed One, the remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge, as he desired to withdraw his own family: "Go to Badarī."
Śrīdhara said: "And I was told [this] previously in Dvārakā."
The sequential arrangement: "Go to Badarī. Regarding this, he will state the reason later: "When he has departed from this world" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.4.30), and so forth. ||4||

Viśvanātha: I was already addressed previously at Dvārakā with the words "I too," where the word "and" (*ca*) was employed by Sarasvatī to indicate that I, Uddhava, was protected within His own embrace through a distinction of manifestation (*prakāśabheda*). The reason for this is that, in the first case, [She spoke thus] regarding the distress of me, who have surrendered.

By that [name], he is one who removes the pain of separation from Himself; thus, according to the reasoning to be stated later— that "in the second [kalpa], He has passed away from this world"— He [relieved] the distress of His own partial incarnations (aṃśa), such as Nara-Nārāyaṇa and others, who were residents of Badarikāśrama and had taken refuge [in Him], through His own deeds.
He is so called because he removes [the world] by means of devotion, knowledge, detachment, and the like, which take the form of an intense longing for hearing [the teachings]. ||4||
Nevertheless, O subduer of enemies, knowing his intention,
I followed behind my lord, unable to bear the separation from his feet.
Śrīdhara: That refers to the intended destruction of the lineage and so forth. ||5||

Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "intended by him" means either that the Lord, even while saying "Go," will likely not abandon me, or it refers to the destruction of the Kula and so forth. ||5||
While searching for my beloved husband, I saw him sitting alone on the banks of the Sarasvatī— the abode of Śrī, who has made his home there, yet remains without a fixed dwelling.
Śrīdhara: *Kṛtakeṭam* means having made a dwelling; *aketanam* means without a refuge. ||6||
The sequential arrangement: "I saw"—this is the triad. ||68||
Viśvanātha: [He is] one for whom no abode (ketana) or support exists;
the sense is that, in reality, all material and non-material entities are supported by Him. ||6||
Dark-complexioned yet radiant, stainless, with peaceful reddish eyes,
he is known by his four arms and his yellow silk garments.
Śrīdhara: *Virajam* means free from passion; *virajasam* means consisting of pure *sattva*. *Viditam* means perceived or characterized.
*Kauśam* means silk (*kauśeya*). ||7||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*, Viśvanātha: [This portion] has not been commented upon.
Having placed the right lotus-foot upon the left thigh, he rests his body like a young *aśvattha* tree that has abandoned its coarse *pippala* fruits.

Śrīdhara: Having placed it upon [the fire] means having set it above. "Supported by" (apāśrita) means one who has leaned against from behind. "By whom the tender *aśvattha* tree—the child—is held" refers to Him. "By whom the *pippala*—the pleasure of sense objects—is abandoned," yet even so, He is "not emaciated," meaning full of bliss. ||8||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Having placed it upon [the fire], that is, having set it above; "supported from behind" means held from the back; "that by which the falling of the *aśvattha* [tree] occurs"—it is called *aśvattha* because it does not stand still (*na śvas tiṣṭhati*).

The manifestation of the worlds beginning with Bhūr is unstable and illusory; having cast that behind me, with the intention that "may the worlds that expand [this] henceforth not see me," the term *arbhaka* (small) indicates the extreme minuteness of this particular cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) among all cosmic eggs. It has been abandoned.
The word "pippala" refers to this entire manifestation of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), because the Veda uses the term "pippala" to denote the pleasure derived from sense objects. (8)
While wandering through the worlds as a perfected being, the illustrious friend and companion of Dvaipāyana happened upon him by chance.
Śrīdhara: He whose friend and companion is Dvaipāyana—meaning Maitreya, who is the disciple of Parāśara because he is the son of his own guru. ||9||
The sequence of composition: "by chance"—that is, by some rise in fortune.
In the term *dvaipāyanasuhṛtsakha*, the absence of the suffix *ṭac* is an archaic (Vedic) usage. ||9||
Viśvanātha: Dvaipāyana Vyāsa was his friend and companion because he was the son of his own guru;
Maitreya, that is to say, was the disciple of Parāśara. By chance—that is, quite unexpectedly—Mukunda [appeared] before that sage who was thus devoted to him.
As he listened to me with his neck bent in a state of joy, resting his gaze upon a smile of affection, he spoke to me as if to soothe me.

Śrīdhara: He whose neck was bent with a feeling of joy (*pramoda*); in another reading, by the weight of that joy. With that gaze, which possessed laughter along with passion (*anurāga*), he was causing [the Lord] to rest, making him free from fatigue. ||10||
The sequential composition: even though he was not hearing, he spoke to me alone as if I were present;

by this, too, his own state of being a fit recipient of grace (*anugrāhyatva*) is indicated. And so it will be stated by the Lord himself in two verses beginning with, "When I have departed from this world" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.4.30). For this very reason, the genitive case is used. For this very reason...
By the phrase "while he was not listening," a certain seal of concealment (*gopanāmudrā*) has been shown in that statement. ||10||

Viśvanātha: By saying "he spoke to me alone," even though she was distinguished by such qualifiers as "one who is enamored of him" and so forth, her own status as the preeminent object of his love is suggested; for this very reason, the genitive case is used.
[She looked] with a glance characterized by an "enraptured smile"—that is, a smile manifesting her passion—or, alternatively, by means of a glance endowed with both passion and a smile.
Or perhaps, by resting me, he will cause the exhaustion of my separation to vanish. ||10||
The Blessed Lord said:
"I know what is desired within your mind;
I shall grant that which is difficult for others to attain."
O Vasu, in former times at the sacrifice of the Vasus, the creators of the universe,
you were worshipped by them with the desire for their own perfection.

Śrīdhara: O Uddhava, I, who abide within, know—that is, I am aware of—the desire in your heart. The reason for this [knowledge] is: "In the sacrificial session (*satra*) of the Vasus, the creators of the universe, when they were assembled. O *Vasu*, in a former birth you were a Vasu; at that time, desiring to attain Me, you worshipped Me.

Therefore, I shall give—that is, I will bestow—this means of attainment, which is difficult to obtain for others who are turned away from me; for this very reason, even though they are eternal attendants, it was commanded that their status as Vasus be manifested through a single portion [of my power]. ||11||

Viśvanātha: I know; I understand. I shall grant that which is difficult for others to obtain. The reason for this granting is as follows: at the sacrificial session (*satra*) of the creators of the universe and the Vasus gathered together, you were called "Vasu" because in your previous birth you were a Vasu; at that time, desiring to attain me, you worshipped me.

Because Vasu entered into Uddhava, who is an eternal associate of the eternal pastimes, the Lord made it known to Maitreya that even Uddhava, though eternally perfected, attained perfection through spiritual practice (*sādhana-siddha*).
This was for the purpose of preserving the secrecy of the eternal pastimes; however, some maintain that Uddhava, as an associate of the pastimes, remained in Dvārakā itself.
They said, "This Uddhava stands here in the form of Vasu. ||11||
O virtuous one, this final existence among births has been attained by you through my grace,
since you have abandoned me here in the world of men in secret.
By good fortune, having seen [him] through clear and constant devotion.

Śrīdhara: He celebrates his good fortune. This very birth of yours is the last among all your births, provided that my grace has been attained and obtained in this one. Furthermore, that you have seen me in private and solitude through clear devotion—through exclusive attachment—is this [the result].
"By good fortune, a blessing has arisen"—this is the meaning. "The worlds of men": by the word *nṛ* (man), living beings are meant;
he was leaving their worlds, that is, going to Vaikuṇṭha—this is the meaning. ||12||

The sequence of the composition: The meaning is that he is the final among the many incarnations—such as those in the forms of Vasu and others—which [the Lord assumes] for the sake of the welfare of the world, having reached the ultimate pinnacle; he is one who has attained the nature of a portion of Him.
By means of clear persistence, by following with a state of pure devotion, that which you have seen—that is indeed a blessing, by good fortune!
Thus it was done. ||12||

Viśvanātha consoles him: "He... and so forth. Among all your births (*bhava*), this birth is the final one, the last. That [birth] in which You have been attained—that is, reached—and furthermore, that You have beheld me in private, in solitude, with clear devotion and exclusive attachment (*ekāntabhakti*)—by this good fortune, it is auspicious.
The meaning is "born. By the word *nṛ*, living beings (*jīva*) are meant; the meaning is that he goes to that Vaikuṇṭha, having abandoned the worlds of those living beings. ||12||
Formerly, at the time of my first creation, I proclaimed to Brahmā, who was seated upon the lotus in my navel,
the supreme knowledge that illuminates my own majesty.
That which the wise call the Bhāgavata.

Śrīdhara: He points out that very thing which was stated as "I give. "In the past," meaning in the previous Pādma Kalpa; "at the beginning of creation," meaning at the commencement of the cosmic manifestation. That by which my majesty is manifested through divine play—that is the sequence of the composition: "In the past, by me. "In the past" refers to the Brāhma Kalpa, in the second book (Skandha).
Because of the description of the Brahma-kalpa; "supreme knowledge" refers to that which takes the form of the *Catuḥślokī*.
By the phrase "the manifestation of my own majesty," it is not accepted that this [text] establishes a [Brahman] devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*). ||13||

Viśvanātha: He points out what was promised with the words "I shall give"—"In the beginning," that is, in the Brāhma-kalpa. Regarding the phrase "by which my greatness is manifested as sport," the venerable teachers (Svāmicaraṇaḥ) say it refers to that [text], while others say "greatness" means majesty. It is the Bhāgavata in the form of four verses. ||13||
Thus addressed by the Supreme Person,
I, a recipient of His grace at every moment, with my hair standing on end from affection and my words faltering, [spoke to Him].
Releasing tears, with palms joined in reverence, he spoke.

Śrīdhara: Thus addressed by him with such respect, I waited; for his compassionate glance alone was a favor, and I became its recipient—that is, its worthy vessel. According to another reading, "at every moment [I was] a vessel of his favor. Shedding tears of grief, you spoke. ||14||
The sequential arrangement: for this very reason he says "iti" and so forth. [The speech of Śrī Uddhava begins with "iti" and ends with "lokabhāvanā. ||14||]

Viśvanātha says: Thus I was addressed with respect. "Waiting" refers to the anticipation regarding mantras and so forth—that no one knows this except Uddhava; "let him come, and then this will happen," and so on. In the short-middling recension, it is read as *pratikṣaṇam*, meaning at every moment.
The tears of grief are the worthy recipients of his favor.
O Lord, what indeed is difficult for those who partake of Your lotus feet to obtain among even the four goals of human existence?
Nevertheless, O All-pervading One, I do not choose them.
Eager for the service of your lotus feet.

Śrīdhara: Indeed, I do not desire merely the cessation of my own ignorance; rather, being eager to serve you, I am bewildered upon seeing what appears to be inconsistent conduct on your part. Therefore, he says "Who indeed... in order to pray that you grant him knowledge of reality. [This refers to] among the four goals, beginning with dharma.
Nevertheless, O Infinite One! I am eager to serve Your lotus feet; I do not choose those [other paths].
At that very moment, the sequence of verses informs us: "Who indeed... (15).

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "O Blessed Lord, Master! If you wish to reveal your own knowledge in order to liberate me, your servant, from *saṃsāra*, or to cause me to attain [liberation] such as *sārūpya* and so forth, then enough of that! To this he says: "Who indeed...
Among the four goals of life beginning with *dharma*, what indeed is difficult to obtain for those who worship Your lotus feet?

The sense is this: even for those possessed of desire, the attainment of fruits such as liberation may occur through the mere worship of His feet, even without knowledge. Yet, I do not choose those goals even though they have come to me spontaneously. The reason for this is "bhavat" (because You exist). Therefore, the sense is: what need have I for knowledge?
Though you are devoid of effort and beyond existence, your actions consist of taking refuge in a fortress and fleeing from the fear of enemies;
yet, as the soul of Time, your dwelling is with young women.
The intellect of the wise here becomes distressed by its delight in its own self.
Śrīdhara: He demonstrates an impossible course of action. Actions [are attributed] to one who is effortless, desireless, or inactive;

to one who is without becoming, that is, without birth—yet for you, whose very nature is Time, there is "becoming," which is birth. Furthermore, fleeing for refuge to a fortress out of fear of enemies, and delighting in women, are attributed to one whose pleasure is in the Self. How could these be possible? For you, who possess many wives...

Regarding this matter of the householder’s stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*), even the intellects of the learned are distressed by doubt concerning its sequential arrangement: "If this is so, then how can anything desired to be known exist?"—for that which I have manifested is precisely what you longed for within your heart: "I know that which is desired within your mind" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.4.11).

Is this so? True; however, it is not for my own sake—for you already know that the pastime about which you ask consists of the majesty of His grace toward His devotees. Nevertheless, I desire to do so only to properly convince others through those words witnessed by Maitreya.

Making his request, he says with three verses beginning with "The deeds": "Even for such knowers as these, who are omniscient, the Lord of the Universe [is the goal]; for us, His servants, however, it is precisely His form, qualities, and pastimes that are the cause of supreme bliss through seeing, remembering, and so forth—and even for those [pastimes], there is an intense longing born of knowledge. As for that which...

Because there is some degree of knowledge [in him], yet knowledge in its totality is impossible; however, certain of his pastimes (*līlā*) appear contradictory when analyzed through logic, and it is precisely regarding those that my desire to know (*jijñāsita*) exists—thus he says in two verses: "The deeds of the effortless and inactive one," such as the lifting of Govardhana and so forth, but not...
The creation of the universe and so forth—since these are produced by the qualities of *māyā* and are superimposed upon You, they lack the nature of Yours in their own right;

therefore, there is no contradiction with Your actionlessness as described in the Śruti: "partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, and stainless. This applies even to such acts as the lifting of Govardhana.

My doubt is this: since you have performed actions in their very own nature, there is indeed a contradiction because those [actions] are devoid of activity. Or rather, if you, the Supreme Brahman in human form, possess a human form, you must possess infinite non-material (aprākṛta) actions; whereas if you are Brahman, you must be devoid of both material and non-material actions.

For it is precisely there that the term "Brahman" is established by convention. Nor should it be argued that this distinction is maintained because of a difference in essential nature—namely, that Brahman is an undifferentiated essence while the Blessed Lord is a differentiated essence—for as stated in the sixth [chapter], there is no duality of essential nature; since such a claim is thus made, doubt remains.

The birth of the unborn and non-existent You; Your flight from the fear of enemies such as Jarāsaṃdha and Your taking refuge in the fortress of the ocean, though You are the very self of Time; and even for You, whose delight is in Yourself alone, the life of a householder consisting of ten thousand women, involving the ritual service of gods, ancestors, and others—[all these are Your pastimes].

Your delight is in being self-content; however, in sporting with women such as Rukmiṇī and others, Your state of self-contentment would not depart, because they are Your very own Self—I know this well. For this very reason, I employed the word "hermitage" (āśrama). In this matter of apparent contradiction, even the intellect of the wise (*vidām*) falters.
One becomes weary because no such composure is observed.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the truth belongs solely to qualities such as being inactive, insentient, temporal, and delighting in the self,
while qualities such as being active, possessing birth, being afraid, and belonging to the householder's stage of life are merely imitative.

This must be said: if that were the case, it would not have been stated that "the intellect of the wise is distressed here," for if one knows that activity and so forth are merely imitations and not real, how could there be distress?
In the same way, by means of non-activity and so forth, only worldly activities and the like are negated, but not—
Why should there be distress regarding the knowledge that [the Lord] possesses non-ordinary actions and so forth? In the same way,

those who declare that through His very nature as Brahman and Bhagavān, qualities such as being actionless and being active are merely imitations, explain that "being actionless" means having non-ordinary action, and "being unborn" means having a non-ordinary birth.

The implication is that those who speak thus, asserting a distinction between non-activity and activity based solely on the states of being Brahman and being the Blessed Lord, are indeed ignorant, their intellects being unawakened. As it was said by the Blessed Lord himself: "Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin" (Gītā 10.2).
The meaning there is that even the hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā, and even the great sages beginning with Vyāsa, do not know my supreme birth. Bhīṣma also said:
"O King, no man indeed ever knows His intended purpose."
"Indeed, even sages are bewildered when intent on desiring to know that [Brahman]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.9.16). Thus [it is said].
16. "When You, whose self-awareness is eternally unimpeded and indivisible, having been invoked by me within the mantras..."
"O Lord, you should ask him while remaining vigilant as if you were bewildered;
O God, this [conduct] of yours seems to bewilder our minds."

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, when the mantras were being recited and the ritual proceedings were underway, you called out to me; indeed, you did not ask what you ought to have asked. [I am one] whose unimpeded, uninterrupted, and constant consciousness—unbroken by time and other factors, ever-abiding, and free from doubt—is the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*). [You spoke] like one who is deluded, as if ignorant.
Being heedful and attentive. ||17||
The sequence of composition: "It deludes" [is said] because, in reality, there is an absence of delusion in itself. ||17||

Viśvanātha: When the mantras concerning the slaying of Jarāsandha, the journey for the sake of the Rājasūya sacrifice, and other such matters were being discussed, you summoned me with certainty and asked: "O Uddhava, tell me what must be done here. You are unimpeded and undivided by means of your arts and other qualities.
He is one whose self-awareness, the power of consciousness (*saṃvit-śakti*), is always and eternally complete.

The meaning is that he asks just as any other person who is bewildered would ask. Furthermore, the sense is that he is "heedless" (*apramatta*) because he is free even from engagement with other duties. That [is] yours simultaneously.

In this way, [the verse] "maugdhyam sārvajñyam ca mohayati" (childlike simplicity and omniscience both delude) indeed deludes; it is as if it deludes. In this context, there is no logical consistency in the interpretation that "you are like one who is deluded, but not actually deluded," or "it is as if it deludes, but it does not actually delude. Therefore, its introduction amidst these coherent statements would be futile.
Therefore, it should not be explained in that manner. ||17||
To whom did the Blessed One fully proclaim that supreme knowledge, the secret illumination of one's own self? O Lord,
is it even possible for us to grasp it?
Speak directly so that we may cross over our distress.

Śrīdhara: O Lord, Master, tell us that secret—the reality of your own self—which reveals that [reality], if it is fit to be grasped even by us, for whom [it is meant]—the use of "whom" (*kasmai*) is an archaic Vedic form of the pronoun. Tell it, from which [knowledge] the sorrow of saṃsāra arises.
We shall cross over easily and without effort. ||18||

The sequential composition [of the verse] is as follows: "Therefore, knowledge is supreme. The sense is this: even for those who possess learning, their own suffering arises from doubt regarding You; however, for us—who are eager to serve Your lotus feet—there is no touch of any other suffering. [Regarding the phrase *svātmarahaḥprakāśām*...]
This should be understood according to the words, as seen in the twenty-fifth verse at the beginning and the forty-ninth verse of the twelfth chapter. ||18||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, wishing to dispel these initial doubts, he says "knowledge" (jñānam), meaning: that knowledge in which there is the revelation of that secret—which is your own self, inaccessible to all others, and which is what I desire to know—and not that which was promised by you to be given.
The meaning is: "the manifestation of its majesty. If you would tell me, for whom did you speak it?

Or rather, for whom did the Blessed One speak it—meaning, for no one at all? Even so, if you have such compassion for me, then, O Lord, speak it; and that [teaching] shall be sufficient for our comprehension.

The sense is: "If it were worthy for those who possess pure servitude to receive [it], or even if it were worthy, if it were possible—then speak; otherwise, do not speak. For from knowledge, the aforementioned evil (vṛjina), which is what I desire to know, has now presented itself.
And the destruction of the Yadu clan, the disappearance of your body, and so forth—[all these constitute] an ocean of suffering.
To me, whose heart had thus been made known, that supreme Lord,
the lotus-eyed one, instructed me regarding his own supreme state of being.
Śrīdhara: To him by whom the heart-felt intention residing within the heart has been made known. ||19||

The sequential composition [describes] the supreme state declared in the four verses; even while possessing such a form, it consists of the play characterized by the power of love known as the secret [mystery]. 19.

Viśvanātha: The meaning is that [this was told] to me, and not even to Maitreya. He described His own state (*sthiti*), His established condition (*vyavasthiti*), the limits of His divine play (*līlā-maryādā*), and His eternal residence in abodes such as Dvārakā; however, that state which was not fully realized by Śukadeva, nor by Uddhava, nor by Vidura, nor by anyone else—[that he described].

Because no specific reason for the Sāṅkhya position can be found here, some say that qualities such as being inactive (*niṣkriyatva*) and being active (*sakriyatva*) are established solely by means of inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*). As it is stated in the *Bhāgavatāmṛta*, concerning the verse beginning with "the actions of the effortless one" (*karmāṇy anīhasya*): [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.4.16].
"If that which appears were not real, then it would simply not be knowledge; rather, it would be a delusion of the intellect.
Therefore, inconceivable power alone is the cause in these divine sports.
Thus, from him whose feet and holy waters had been thus propitiated...
Having mastered the path to awakening the true nature of the self,
I have circumambulated the God and bowed at his feet; now, with a soul distressed by separation, I have come here.

Śrīdhara: He whose feet have been propitiated is the Blessed One himself; he is the sacred ford and the guru. From him I have studied and mastered the path of the awakening to the self of reality, which is the knowledge of the supreme self. Having circumambulated—that is, having performed a clockwise circumambulation of—the Lord [he speaks]. (20)

The sequence of the composition: He by whom the path to the knowledge of the Self as desired—which consists of the four verses—has been studied and understood in its true essence and according to reality;
and because that [path] establishes the state of being under the sway of divine love, I have come here as if my very self were distressed by separation.
And by this very [statement], his commitment to a harsh form of knowledge is refuted of its own accord. ||20||
Viśvanātha: I am that Uddhava who has worshipped the feet of the Blessed One; He alone is the sacred ford and the Guru.
Therefore, he is one by whom the path of knowledge—consisting of the awakening of the Self through which the true nature of reality is learned—has been attained.
Having circumambulated and departed from there, I did not see what was done by the Blessed One thereafter.
Such is the intended meaning. ||20||
Therefore, O Lord, filled with both the joy of beholding him and the pain of separation from him,
I shall go to his beloved hermitage of Badarī.
Śrīdhara: "From seeing him comes joy, and from separation comes pain; possessed of both these, I shall go to the site of Badarikāśrama. (21)

The sequence of the composition: If your soul is distressed by separation, then how are you able to move or speak? To this he replies: "I am that one," according to the passage, "The joy of seeing [the Lord] slowly [returns] from the world of the Blessed One.
But as for being joined with the pain of separation, it is according to the passage, "Having returned again to the world of men. Then...
Even during our separation, being unable to realize Him directly from time to time, the meaning is that I shall go even to Badarikāśrama, which he desired to send me to as his beloved. ||21||
Viśvanātha: [Objection: But how do you live even with the pain of separation from Him?
To this he replies: "At every moment, joined with joy through the sight of Him and with distress through separation from Him.
[The phrase] "to Badarikāśrama" indicates that he went there specifically because of the Lord's command. (21)
There, the divine Nārāyaṇa and the venerable seer Nara,
the creators of the world, performed mild and intense austerities for a long time.

Śrīdhara: "Mṛdu" means free from causing distress to others; "tīvra" means difficult to perform; "dīrgha" means until the end of the kalpa. The meaning is that they performed penance, i.e., practiced austerity. Regarding "lokabhāvanau," it means those who bestow grace upon the worlds; the sequence of the composition has not been explained [further].
Viśvanātha: He states that in that very place resides Nārāyaṇa himself as a partial incarnation (tadaṃśa)—beginning with "yatra.

"Mṛdu" means bestowing happiness upon all the worlds; "tīvra" means difficult for all the worlds to practice; "dīrgha" means extending over a long period of time; and "lokānām bhāvanau" means the two who are the progenitors or protectors of the worlds. ||22||
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus heard from Uddhava about the unbearable slaughter of his friends,
the wise Vidura allayed the grief that had arisen through spiritual knowledge.
Śrīdhara: By means of knowledge, that is, by means of discrimination. ||23||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "He heard from Uddhava such news as the slaughter of his friends, which was difficult to endure. [This refers to the passage beginning with] "By knowledge, when the sun Kṛṣṇa has set," and so forth.
[This is] produced by the thorough reflection on the intended meaning of Uddhava’s speech. ||23||
As that great devotee of the Lord was departing, the bull among the Kauravas,
out of confidence, spoke this foremost matter regarding the acceptance of Kṛṣṇa.
Śrīdhara: "From *viśrambhāt* means from trust (*viśvāsāt*). [24]"
The composition of the sequence: "from confidence and from affection. Amara states: "visrambhaḥ also means affection. ||24||

Viśvanātha: Out of *viśrambha*—that is, from confidence—even one who is naturally very junior (*ati-kaniṣṭha*) [is considered] "principal" (*mukhya*) in the acceptance of Kṛṣṇa; that is, in order to accept or subjugate Kṛṣṇa, he is superior by nature. Therefore, even those who are junior, if they possess an abundance of devotion, should be treated as elders (*guru*) by those who are senior; this is the point here.
It has been demonstrated that the words of Vidura alone are authoritative. ||24||
Vidura said: "The Supreme Lord, the Master of Yoga, has taught you that supreme knowledge which is the secret illumination of one's own self."
Indeed, you ought to tell us how the servants of Viṣṇu move about, performing the welfare of their own servants.

Śrīdhara: Because the servants of Viṣṇu wander about accomplishing the purposes of their own servants; for there is no other duty remaining for those who have already achieved their own ends—this is the meaning. ||25||

The sequential arrangement: that which is knowledge itself is the unique purpose of the servant (*bhṛtyārtha*). According to the statement, "One who is eager for service at Your lotus feet" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.4.15), the servants of Viṣṇu—those who perform that service consisting of worship—move about and carry out their duties; such is the nature of that knowledge.

The state of being composed of devotion (*bhaktimayatva*) is evident. For this very reason, in this statement as well as in the previously cited words of Śrī Uddhava, the word *rahaḥ* is indicated as having the same meaning as the word *rahasya* (secret/essence) recited in the *Catuḥślokī*.
Therefore, in the words of the Blessed Lord: "the manifestation of my majesty" (*manmahimāvabhāsam*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.4.13).

Thus, even the word *mahiman* (magnificence) has its purport only in reaching that [state]. Therefore, the Blessed Lord has established the conclusion: "Even though I am of such a nature, being under the sway of love alone, I become thus and thus possessed [by those states] in the human pastimes and so forth," because the word *paramasthiti* (the supreme state) also has its purport in this very [love]. ||25||
Viśvanātha: For us—here, by the rule *asmado dvayoś ca*, the plural form is used for both the singular and the dual;
that is, because you Vaiṣṇavas, the servants of Viṣṇu, acting for the sake of your own servants by providing instruction in devotion, have out of compassion become the very gurus of ignorant people.
They wander [in saṃsāra]. Therefore, the meaning is: "Teach me, who am proud of being their servant, the knowledge of the Blessed One. ||25||
Uddhava said: Indeed, the sage Kauṣārava, who is to be propitiated through the realization of truth,
has been personally directed by you to your presence as you desire to leave the world of mortals.

Śrīdhara: "Having propitiated for the sake of the truth"—this is the sense: by the Lord alone, through mere remembrance, the truth has already been virtually taught even to you. Now, merely for the removal of doubts such as incredulity (*asambhāvanā*), some person possessing knowledge (*jñānin*) must be propitiated; and that person to be propitiated by you is Maitreya.
But it is not I; for that [instruction] was prescribed by you to him in my very presence. ||26||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Speaking to himself, "How can I make this venerable person my disciple?", he says:
"O noble one, that which has been understood from the mouth of the Blessed One..."

I have already stated that for him and his followers, such as the Yādavas, there was no departure from their own abodes except through the casting off of the body. However, if you desire to know the specific details of his birth, deeds, and all other particulars, then the sage Maitreya alone must be made your teacher; thus he says: "Nanu... (Indeed...). Indeed.

This is indeed certain. His "state" (bhāva) is his true nature; by means of that—that is, by his being one who has performed service for his own master and by his gravity—Maitreya alone, and not I, has propitiated [the Lord].
For it was he alone whom the Blessed One directly instructed in my presence for the purpose of giving instruction to you. ||26||
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, together with Vidura, his great distress was washed away by the nectar of the discourse on the qualities of the Universal Form.
Having stayed that night on the bank of Yamunā’s sister as if for a mere moment, the son of Upagu then departed.
Śrīdhara: Not explained.

Kramasaṃdarbha: Because He, whose form is the universe, manifests as if directly present everywhere, therefore [the verse says] "even in separation, by the narration of His qualities," and so forth. ||27||
Viśvanātha: Having spent that night as if it were a mere moment, Aupagavi—the descendant of Upagu, namely Uddhava—departed from there at dawn. ||27||
The king said:
"When the Vṛṣṇis and Bhojas— the foremost among the leaders of the hosts of chariot-warriors— have met their death,"
But how was Uddhava left behind,
since even Hari, the Lord of the three worlds, abandoned his physical form?
The form of the honey is the earth. Form is the body, the physical frame; "ku" means the earth, the great one—such is the definition. ||28||
Śrīdhara: Since even Hari, the Lord of the three beginning with Brahmā, abandoned his form—the human shape—when they met their end through the curse of Brahmā. ||28||

The sequence of the composition: *Nidhana* is that which is essentially the ultimate wealth, the eternal abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes. [It remains] "near" (*upa*), meaning without any separation, for those who have departed. But how is He alone remaining? He alone remains in this phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Because of these three...

Hari, the supreme lord of Brahmā and others—or of Mahat, the creator, and so forth—abandoned his form, that is, his *vīraḍ* (cosmic) shape. This is because it accords with the preceding and following context: "by one desiring to leave the mortal world" (*bhā.pu.* 3.4.26) and "having departed from this world" (*bhā.pu.* 3.4.28). ||28||

Viśvanātha: The literal meaning is that because of him [Kṛṣṇa], even Hari—the lord of the three worlds—attained *nidhana*, which is destruction; that is, he completely (*ā*) abandoned his activity (*kṛti*), his effort, and his pastimes (*līlā*), bringing them to an end. But in reality, *nidhana* means "the ultimate wealth," namely Kṛṣṇa himself, who has become invisible to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
When the Vṛṣṇis and others had approached and arrived nearby, how was Uddhava alone left behind?

The sense is that it would have been improper for him to remain manifest even in part, as he would have experienced the heat of separation from Him. Nor should he be considered unknown among the Vṛṣṇis and others, since [he is called] Adhirathi...
[The word] "etcetera" [is used].
Now, how could one act otherwise than as commanded by the Lord, saying, "Go to Badarī"?
To this he says: for him, Hari—the Lord who removes all suffering—even [observes] his outward form and even his slightest gesture.

He abandoned [her]. According to Amara, *ākāra*, *iṅga*, and *iṅgita* are synonyms for facial expression or gesture. Had he made even the slightest gesture at the time of issuing the command—such as that found in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.29.22: "O Vraja-devis, depart! Do not delay; serve your husbands and remain chaste"—then this man of great intelligence [would have acted differently].
The meaning is that if Uddhava had not come to Badarikāśrama, he would have remained in his very presence. ||28||
Śrī Śuka said: Under the pretext of a Brahmin’s curse, Kāla, whose desires are never in vain,
having withdrawn his own flourishing lineage, reflected as he was about to cast off his body.
For Madhva, the abandonment of the earthly world and the abandonment of the body are considered the remembrance of Hari;
because his nature is eternal bliss, nothing else whatsoever is perceived.
"He may display a form resembling a corpse for the delusion of people;
the Lord Viṣṇu himself is the embodiment of supreme knowledge, like a juggler. Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O King, the embodied beings [perceive] the activity of birth and dissolution of the Supreme as His own."
"Know that illusion is a deception, like that of an actor. Thus [it is said]. (29)

Śrīdhara: By that Time, which has the curse of Brahmā as its pretext or guise—that is, whose very form is its own power—and whose desire is unfailing; for here the curse is not the master, but rather the will of the Blessed Lord alone—this is the meaning. ||29||

The sequential arrangement: it should also be understood that "thus, about to cast off the body" refers to the body in the form of Virāṭ, because of the reasons previously stated. This is to be investigated by looking at the ninety-third section of the *Śrīkṛṣṇasandarbha*. For instance: "Thus, although in this way..."

Once it has been thoroughly established that the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the Self-Born Lord (Svayaṃbhagavān), his eternal abiding in that very form is also established by itself. Nevertheless, this is explained for the sake of removing the delusions of those of dull intellect. In that regard, first of all, that [eternal abiding] is established by the very statement concerning worship (*ārādhanā*).
It is established that [the injunction] is not valid; for in the absence of one to be propitiated, the exhortation to propitiate would result in being produced by a desire to deceive.

And that is impossible in the case of a scripture from a supreme authority (*paramāpta*). Should it be possible, there would be no human goal (*puruṣārtha*) to be attained, and thus the scripture would be purposeless.
Furthermore, superimposition (āropa) is conceived only upon an object that possesses a delimited nature of qualities, not upon one whose nature consists of infinite qualities.

This very point was also affirmed by the venerable Śrī Svāmipāda in the eleventh book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa], at the end of the section on the eleven [qualities], in the verse "The auspiciousness of concentration and meditation" (Bhā.
Pu. 11.31.6), where he states that the auspiciousness (maṅgala) of concentration (dhāraṇā) and meditation (dhyāna) is their excellence (śobhana).

Otherwise, those two would be devoid of an object; yet even today, the direct realization and the attainment of its fruit are seen among their practitioners—this is the sense. Furthermore, it is heard thus in the *Pañcama* [Tantra] regarding the worship of various incarnations over nine years, as it has been said: "In all nine..."

"In the Varṣas, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Great Person, even today remains present through his own manifestation as the essence of the self (ātmatattvavyūha) for the sake of bestowing grace upon men" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.17.14).
And this presence is manifest, because the graceful movements and other qualities [of the Lord] are described as being present directly in Śrī Pradyumna and others;

and in that regard, it has been stated that He is by His very self. Likewise, only if there is eternality can the distinction between Narasiṃha and other forms in the Śālagrāma stones and so forth be logically consistent.

Indeed, the distinction between these various forms arises solely from the proximity of their respective incarnations. Likewise, regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa, it is sung at the beginning of the *Śrī Kṛṣṇa-sahasranāma* in the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Viṣṇu, surrounded by the cowherd women, was delighted in his heart by that praise."
"He showed his form, dark as the *tāpiñcha* flower, with a peacock feather as his crest-ornament.
And later, his words were:
"Know me, O illustrious one, best among those who know their duties, to be Kṛṣṇa."
"I have been honored by your devotion; may your desires be fulfilled.

Likewise, in the *Nirmāṇakhaṇḍa* of the *Padma Purāṇa*, after the words of the Blessed Lord—"Behold, I shall show you my true form, which has been hidden from the Vedas"—there follows the speech of Brahmā:
Then, O King, I beheld a cowherd boy with the luster of a dark rain-cloud,
surrounded by cowherd girls and laughing with the cowherd boys.
"Sitting at the foot of a kadamba tree, wearing yellow garments, wondrous,
in the forest named Vṛndāvana adorned with fresh sprouts," and so forth.
In the *Trailokyasaṃmohana-tantra*, in the context of the recitation of the glorious eighteen-syllable mantra:

"The mantra-practitioner who, with a restrained mind, recites [the mantra] day and night, beholds Hari wearing the guise of a cowherd; of this there is no doubt. And in the *Gautamīya*, in the context of right conduct (*sadācāra*):
"Day and night, the practitioner of mantra, with a restrained mind, should recite the mantra;
he will behold Hari wearing the guise of a cowherd, of this there is no doubt.
And so says the Śrī Gopālatāpanī Upaniṣad: "Then he said: 'This [mantra] of Brahmā, which is constantly present for me...'"

When meditated upon and praised, that Supreme Lord awakened at the end of a *parārdha*; "A person dressed as a cowherd appeared before me" (Goṭā Upaniṣad 1.29). Thus, even a statement by a perfected being (*siddha*) is heard, such as:
"I bow to Him who dwells in Vṛndāvana, the temple of bliss for Indirā" (Nārada Purāṇa 1.1.1).
The auspicious invocation at the beginning of the Bṛhannāradīya:
"O leader of the Daityas, that house becomes established [in merit] wherein the greatness arising from Dvārakā and the presence of Keśava are found."
Accompanied by Rukmiṇī, Kṛṣṇa dwells eternally in his home.

Thus, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the *Dvārakāmāhātmya*, are the words of Śrī Prahlāda addressed to Bali: "O destroyer of the lords of the Danujas, accept this *arghya* offered by me, which has been given according to the prescribed rite by me, a practitioner of vows who has bathed in the month of Kārttika. [Padma Purāṇa 6.93.24]
Thus ends the mantra for the morning bath and the *arghya* offering from the *Kārttikamāhātmya* of the *Padmapurāṇa*.

Furthermore, mantras such as the illustrious eighteen-syllable one (*aṣṭādaśākṣara*) and others establish them as accomplished instructions precisely by virtue of their being worshipped as distinguished by their respective retinues and attributes.
And there are also mantras for the worship of the coverings (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth. Why say more?
It is likewise heard even in the *Karmavipāka-prāyaścitta-śāstra*. As Bodhāyana says: "Then, for the pleasure of Govinda, the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed as before," and so on.
Immediately thereafter—
O Govinda, Lord beloved by the gopīs,
slayer of the demon Kaṃsa, worshipped by the king of the gods!
"O compassionate one, who has destroyed the host of enemies, satisfy me with the gift of a cow; grant me the destruction of my portion.
And elsewhere, as follows:
O Govinda, Lord of the beloved of the cowherd women, destroyer of Kaṃsa, worshipped by the lord of the gods,
you who held up Govardhana and other mountains with a single hand!

"O you who have protected all cattle and are skilled in their care, O destroyer of the bamboo-staffed leader of the herd, quickly dispel this abundant and fierce blindness as well as this darkness. Thus [he said].

And that very nature is clearly stated in the Śrīgopālatāpanī Upaniṣad: "I, together with the hosts of Maruts, constantly gratify Govinda, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, as He sits beneath the trees of the divine forest of Vṛndāvana" (Goṭā.U. 1.37).
Therefore, it was said: "I have been honored by your devotion. Enough, then, with this elaborate collection of such proofs;
for the same applies to his retinue and other attendants, as they too are manifested solely by the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
In the second section, it is established that there are only appearances and disappearances due to His eternal abiding;

however, origination and destruction are refuted in every respect. This applies not only to His incarnations, but even more so to the Blessed Lord Himself. Thus it has been explained: "He assumed a human form... [etc.]
Regarding the passage "rūpam" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.3.1], the teachers of the doctrine of reality (tattvavāda) accepted it with reference to the individual manifestation (*vyakti*).
And so it is said in the *Tantrabhāgavata*: "That form which is eternal and immutable is neither to be abandoned nor to be acquired."
That very Janārdana manifests as the very manifestation of those things whose forms are relative.
"He took up and he cast off bodies such as those of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa"—
thus the Blessed Lord is described with respect to the perspectives of those of deluded intellect.
For when the Lord is enveloped by darkness, that drinking of darkness which occurs is declared to be the "grasping" (grahaṇa) of his form as the Person (puruṣa).
"Regarding forms such as Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, this is in view of their manifestation in the world.

In the very same way, in the first book, the twelfth chapter, the Master (Śrīdhara Svāmī) also explained the verse beginning with *vidhūya* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.12.11): "He vanished right where he was seen, and not elsewhere."
He has gone, because the Lord is all-pervading; such is this [scriptural statement].
Likewise, there is a Śruti passage authenticated by the Mādhva Bhāṣya: "Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, I, the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf, Rāma, Rāma..."

"Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki, I myself—I am a hundredfold, I am a thousandfold; I am here, I am infinite. Indeed, these are not born, nor do they die. For them there is neither bondage through ignorance nor liberation. For all these are indeed complete, undecaying, immortal, supreme, and of supreme bliss."
In the *Caturvedaśikhā*,
and likewise in the *Śrīnṛsiṃhapurāṇa*: "In every age, Viṣṇu, assuming his beginningless form, protects the universe as the slayer of the wicked."
And so it has been explained by the authors of its commentary in the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanī*:
"This form of Nṛsiṃha is eternal. And this is the Śruti: "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Person whose form is that of the Man-Lion" (*Nṛsiṃhatāpanī Upaniṣad* 1.6).

And thus, in the *Brahma-pādma-uttara-khaṇḍa* and other texts, separate worlds such as Vaikuṇṭha for the illustrious Matsyadeva and others are also heard of. In this very way, the statement in the *Nārāyaṇa-varma* and other sources— "May the form of the Fish protect me in the waters"— is also consistent.

Therefore, even regarding the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the cause of any contrary misconception is solely the distraction caused by beginningless sin. Having this in mind, and seeking to enlighten even those of wicked intellect, he declares his own status as the object of worship, saying: "He is the Lord and the Goal of the Andhakas, Vṛṣṇis, and Sātvatas."

"May the Blessed Lord, the Master of the virtuous, be gracious unto me" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.4.20]. If there is a desire for specific inquiry regarding this, the Śrīkṛṣṇasandarbha (p. 93) should be consulted. ||29||

Viśvanātha provides the reply: "The pretext of Brahmā’s curse was a mere guise for withdrawing the universe from his range of perception; by that means, having withdrawn his own creation, he reflected. He was one whose desire (icchā)—that which is sought—was such that it could not be rendered fruitless even by Time, being unfailing. It was 'sphīta,' meaning expanded beyond its own natural limits."

As he was about to cast off his body, he reflected: "Although this body is all-pervasive by virtue of its nature as existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), its 'expansion' consists solely in its becoming an object of perception for the eyes of worldly people, which is dependent upon its own [limited] form. For in that case, injunctions and prohibitions apply to the qualified entity, and thus they necessarily extend to the qualification."

According to the maxim *sati viśeṣyabādhe* (when there is a contradiction regarding the substantive), the action of relinquishing connects only with the qualifier and not with the substantive, as in: "Caitra becomes a king," "He made his body stout," or "This virtuous woman perished. In these cases, there is a contradiction in connecting the action of relinquishing with the body.

Because the body of the Blessed One is eternal, being of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss. For it is said in the Mahāvārāha Purāṇa: "All the bodies of the Supreme Self are eternal and everlasting."
Devoid of both abandonment and acquisition, they are never born of primordial nature (prakṛti).
"Masses of supreme bliss and pure consciousness on all sides.
Likewise, there is the Śruti cited as authority in the Mādhva Bhāṣya: "Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, I [the Self], the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Rāma..."

"Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki, I myself—I am a hundredfold, I am a thousandfold, I am from this [world], I am infinite. These are not born, nor do they die; for them there is neither bondage through ignorance nor liberation. For all these are indeed complete, undecaying, immortal, supreme, and filled with supreme bliss."

"I, together with the hosts of Maruts, constantly propitiate Govinda, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, seated at the foot of a divine tree in Vṛndāvana"— thus says the *Gopālatāpanī*. "The Truth, the Reality,
the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, whose form is that of the Man-Lion"— thus says the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanī*.
And likewise in this very same place: "When the sun had set, O Kṛṣṇa... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.7);

and "Having taken up his own form, which is the eye of the world, he vanished" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.11); and "Increasing the god of love within the women of Vraja and the city... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.90.48).
Many such scriptural and traditional (smṛti) passages are to be seen.
Here, by interpreting the passage as referring to the abandonment of the body— thereby failing to notice the contradiction with the preceding and following statements—
those of demoniac nature alone have been deprived of the nectar of loving devotion.
Because it has been explained and will be further explained that the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* possesses the quality of enchantment (*mohanī*). Regarding the reading "nūnam" (surely):

[He] separated from his own body [the portion] named Nārāyaṇa, who was his own partial incarnation (*svāṃśarūpa*) and had come from Vaikuṇṭha to join him at the time of his descent; now, in order to send him back to Vaikuṇṭha, he divided him from his own body.
"Intending to abandon"—meaning intending to give it away for the sake of protection to Brahmā and the others who have arrived; for the root *tyaj* has the sense of giving (*dāna*).
"The body in the form of Virāj, [which is] the earth"—this is the context. (29)
When I have passed away from this world,
Uddhava alone— truly the best among those who have realized the Self— is worthy of receiving the knowledge centered upon Me.
Śrīdhara: When I have ceased [to exist], he becomes worthy of knowledge; that is, he becomes fit for knowledge. ||30||

The sequence of the composition: It has also been stated that knowledge possesses a specific distinction, namely that its locus is I, who am Śrī Kṛṣṇa. He is the best among those "possessors of the Self" (ātmavatām), for whom the Self—namely, I alone—is known as the supreme human goal. ||30||

Viśvanātha: When He has ceased from this worldly realm—that is, when He has desisted from the showers of the sweetness of His own form, qualities, and pastimes—then "He whose refuge is I alone" means that Uddhava is also capable of knowing that which I know. [This is said] for those who desire to see Me.

The sense is that [the Lord spoke] from his own mouth so that he might cause the sages dwelling at Badarikāśrama, who desire knowledge, to grasp wisdom by means of his own image. He is the best—the most excellent—among those self-possessed ones (ātmavat) for whom I alone exist as their sovereign. ||30||
Since Uddhava is not deficient by even an atom in his qualities and has not been distressed by the Lord,
let him remain here, teaching the world my secret doctrine.

Śrīdhara: He does not become even slightly inferior to me, provided he is not agitated by the qualities [of nature] or by sense objects. Teaching the knowledge concerning me—that is, knowledge regarding my domain—to the world:
this is the sequence of the composition. Because, due to the reason of being not at all inferior to me, he is [not agitated] by the qualities...

"Unafflicted" means not tormented by the *guṇas* and so forth; the meaning is that he has transcended the *guṇas*. "Since he is the Lord" means he is capable of accomplishing all purposes. "Causing them to grasp my wisdom"—that is, knowledge concerning me—means even toward those various great sages who had gone to Badarikāśrama. This is as follows:

The grasping is clearly to be understood even if it is not explicitly stated, because it is impossible for the Lord’s resolve to be otherwise; as it has been said: "His desires are unfailing" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.4.29). ||31||

Viśvanātha: He speaks of Uddhava’s fitness for being His own image: "Not even slightly" (*aṇv api*)—not even a little less than Me—because of his qualities (*guṇaiḥ*), such as *sattva* and the rest. Now, one might object: "In this world, there are thousands upon thousands of *jīvanmuktas* who have transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*) and are indeed untouched by the qualities. To that he says: "By that... [and so on].

What is their similarity to the Blessed One? Truly, it should be explained thus: he is not afflicted by non-material qualities such as strength, intellect, knowledge, and dispassion. Here, "not being afflicted" by them should be understood as the very capacity to restrain their force, just as there is the capacity to restrain the force of desire and so forth.
In this way, His freedom from the evils of desire and so forth is described. For Uddhava is said to be the foremost among the leaders of the Adhiratha clan;
yet, even he never displayed such extraordinary power (*aprākṛta-bala*).
Thus, the restraint of the force of strength is to be understood as applying likewise to the force of the intellect and the other faculties.
Thus is its uniqueness. "The Lord" means one who has brought Māyā under control, just as I have. "My *vayunam*" means my knowledge. ||31||
Thus instructed by the Teacher of the Three Worlds, whose source is the Word,
he reached Badarikāśrama and worshipped Hari through meditative absorption.
"Whether it be superiority, equality, or even victory over those who are superior,
it is spoken of [as such] for the sake of deluding the lowly, or out of indifference,
or following worldly precedent, or sometimes because a fool perceives some semblance of equality"— thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*. (32)
Śrīdhara: Thus, with this intention, he who has the Veda as his source—that is, the author of the Vedas—performed worship (*īje*, i.e., *pūjayāmāsa*).

The sequence of the composition is as follows: the intention is that this was an instruction from the Blessed Lord to go toward Badarikāśrama, because it is impossible for him to remain in this region which consists of the pastimes of the Blessed Lord.

With *samādhi*, that is, with a mental state focused on nothing else, he "served" him as if in person. This, however, should be understood as occurring immediately after his reception [of the teachings], due to his being accompanied by Maitreya;
thus, the cause of his steadfastness is shown. ||32||
Viśvanātha: In this manner, by the Guru [Kṛṣṇa], for the sake of some remaining inhabitants of the three worlds dwelling at Badarikāśrama— meaning even through Uddhava—
for the purpose of meeting Śrutadeva and others, for the purpose of conquering Bāṇa and other asuras, and for the purpose of bringing back the Pārijāta tree and so forth.
Furthermore, for the purpose of bringing back the son of Devakī and others,
he travels— though primarily to Mithilā— to all places on earth such as Vaikuṇṭha, Sutala, and so forth; there,
by his very appearance and by imparting the knowledge of his own glorious mouth, he fulfills the aspirations of those residing there.
The Blessed One, remembering the longing even of the sages residing there since his departure from Badarikāśrama, dispatched Uddhava; indeed, in a certain kalpa, Badarikāśrama itself was sent.
The meaning is that he was charged with this message: "Deliver this message to Nara and Nārāyaṇa."

And that [knowledge] is not lacking even in the slightest degree in Uddhava—this verse implies that since He is the source (*yoni*), the origin of words characterized by the Vedas, which are themselves the source of all speech, the Lord knows that knowledge which is unperceived even within the Vedas;
this is the primary suggestion (*dhvani*). Furthermore, the secondary suggestion (*anudhvani*) is that such knowledge has been entrusted to Uddhava. [This is conveyed] through the mouth of Uddhava.
The echo of the sound [of the divine names] is that Nara and Nārāyaṇa will attain that very state. And this is the message-letter:
"Hail! To the illustrious Nara and Nārāyaṇa, this is my petition:
may the pastimes manifest through my appearance last for exactly one hundred and twenty-five years."
And that is its limit. Having now completed his worldly career, I am withdrawing from Dvārakā along with my retinue;
and having gone to Prabhāsa, after sending back the gods and other authorized devotees to their respective abodes, I shall remain in Vaikuṇṭha with one portion of myself as requested by Brahmā.
It is perceived as being endowed with a portion of Arjuna, yet it proceeds toward your own state. Moreover,
for your sake— who are longing for a vision of my complete essential nature— I have bestowed upon this Uddhava, the foremost of my dear attendants, both my own form and my virtues.

"Since Uddhava is not deficient by even an atom in his qualities and is not oppressed by the Lord, let him remain here in this Badarikāśrama, teaching the world my secret doctrine. Thus [he spoke]. Here, at Badarikāśrama. (32)
Vidura also, having heard from Uddhava the deeds of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, who had assumed a body for the sake of divine play, as well as his praises, [was filled with wonder].
Thus, the placement of the body (dehanyāsa) for that very [purpose] increases the fortitude of the steadfast;
for others—those of animal-like nature whose minds are agitated—it is even more difficult to perform.
