O best of the Kurus, as the devotee departed, he meditated upon himself as envisioned by Kṛṣṇa in his mind and wept, overwhelmed with love.
Śrīdhara: "Of others" means those who are like animals; "of those with distressed souls" means those whose minds are lacking in fortitude.
That which is desired by the mind is what is intended. ||3335||

The sequential arrangement: "Vidura" constitutes a triad. Here, "upādāna" (taking up) means manifestation, for the purpose of bringing [the soul] into the proximity of worldly devotees. ||33|| "Dehanyāsa" (renunciation of the body): the meaning is the placing or entry of one's own form into the abode that provides space for the unmanifest pastimes.

For the wise, whose minds have dissolved into that [state], there is an increase in fortitude because the determination of that state occurs precisely through its very nature. For others, however, who possess contrary notions due to ignorance of reality, it is difficult to discern—this is the meaning. ||3435||

Viśvanātha: The meaning is that for him whose body is taken up—that is, seized—excessively by the agency of mere play (*krīḍā*), that body is entirely dependent upon his power of sport (*līlā-śakti*); it is manifested and made to disappear by that very power alone. Thus, in this manner, for those wise ones...

Having heard of the casting off of the bodies of even the Yadavas and others at the door of the inner chamber (Dvārakā) in the unmanifest light, and furthermore their abandonment at Prabhāsa—what kind of increase in fortitude is there? The meaning is that upon hearing this very thing, Vidura fixed his fortitude in his heart. Or rather, even that...

It cuts through fortitude at the cutting of the neck. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is exceedingly difficult even for other non-devoted yogins. The meaning is that it is difficult for yogins because [the body] disappears in one place while being manifested as having been abandoned in another place. For the bound souls (paśus)...
The meaning is: "thus, due to a lack of devotion"; [it is] for those of a weak nature, whose minds are thus distracted, that one [should act] toward oneself. ||3335||
O bull of the Bharatas, after how many days did he reach the celestial river from the Kālindī, where the sage, the son of Mitrā, resided?
Śrīdhara: Having already attained perfection through Kālindī, Vidura reached—the word *prāpadyata* meaning "he arrived at"—the celestial river Gaṅgā after a few days. ||36||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: When [the task] was accomplished (*siddhe*) after some days from the presence of the Yamunā (*kālindyāḥ sakāśāt*);
the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). The meaning is: "when several days had passed. [He went to] the celestial river, the Gaṅgā.
He entered; he had arrived. ||36||
Thus, in this *Harṣiṇī* commentary, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
the fourth [chapter] has been appropriately joined to the third for the sake of the virtuous.

Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā pertaining to the Pāramahaṃsyas, in the third book, in the dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava.
The Fourth Chapter.
The Fifth Chapter.
Śrī Śuka said:
At the gate of the celestial river, Kṣattṛ, having attained perfection through his devotion to Acyuta, approached Maitreya— the bull among the Kurus, seated there with unfathomable wisdom.
Satiated by his virtues of good character, he questioned him.
Śrīdhara:
The meeting of Vidura and Maitreya has been described in four chapters;
now their dialogue is being narrated in two sections (skandhas).

He was seated at the gateway of the celestial river Gaṅgā, at Haridvāra, and not preoccupied with ritual action. The reason for this is that his realization (bodha) was unfathomable and unlimited. He was fully satisfied by Maitreya’s good character—such as uprightness—and his virtues, such as compassion; or, according to another reading, [satisfied] by Vidura’s good character and so forth.
Maitreya was fully satisfied and contented. ||2||

The sequence of the composition: *Sauśīlya* means good character, that is, a virtuous nature; he was satisfied by those qualities which have that as their primary feature, being free from the desire for honor and the like.
In an alternative reading, it refers to Maitreya, who was fully satisfied and contented by the good character and other virtues of the *kṣattṛ*. ||2||
Viśvanātha: In the fifth [chapter], Maitreya, having been questioned by Kṣattra regarding the creation and so forth of the world, as well as its states of pleasure and pain,
replied concerning the creation through the principles (tattvas) and the praise of Hari.
Having explained by way of a stylistic device the existence of the primary substratum through four chapters,
its emanation (sarga), although already mentioned among its constituent parts, is now being described in detail.

Seated at the gateway of the celestial river Gaṅgā, that is, at Haridvāra, and not distracted by worldly affairs—in the reading with the nominative case, this refers to Maitreya’s quality of virtuous conduct;
in the reading with the accusative case, it refers to Vidura. ||1||
Vidura said:
People perform actions for the sake of happiness, yet through them they find neither happiness nor any other cessation from toil.
One might find even greater suffering than that very thing;
may the Blessed One tell us what is appropriate in this matter.

Śrīdhara says: He states the questions themselves with fifteen verses beginning with "for happiness" (*sukhāya*). [The meaning is: by those actions; or happiness for another, or the cessation of suffering—for this is the sense. Or else, one might not find anything else. In response to the expectation of what that [anything else] might be, there is the specific mention of that very thing: "or cessation" (*upāramam*). Therefore, by those [actions].

Through one's actions, one would experience only suffering again and again. In this very kind of saṃsāra, may the omniscient Blessed One speak of—that is, determine—whatever is proper and fit for us to do; such is the sequence of the composition. In that regard, although Vidura desired to hear the knowledge favored by the Blessed Lord,

Having previously desired and inquired [about this] from the illustrious Uddhava, and having been instructed by the illustrious Uddhava to inquire from the illustrious Maitreya in accordance with the command of the Blessed Lord, he nevertheless inquired about that very matter from him (Maitreya). Indeed, that is so.
Following the questions concerning the illustrious Uddhava, [the Lord spoke] out of a sense of humility that had arisen;

this humility arose from his own perception of his lack of sufficient qualification, due to the Blessed Lord’s failure to instruct him directly through Uddhava, who was His very representative. But the Blessed Lord, from the illustrious Uddhava...

Having understood, through the *Catuḥślokī*, the absence of mental illumination as well as many other points that ought to be questioned, he—disillusioned by those [earlier] dialogues—did not instruct him; rather, he did so for Maitreya alone, who was fit for it. Therefore, he [acted] solely as a means to bring about the fitness for that knowledge within Ātman.

He offers [this] for the sake of happiness by means of three [verses]. Among these, the first is for the common welfare of oneself; the second is for the wretchedness of the world at large, which lacks any other refuge in the absence of such [a protector];
and the third is to be understood as the prayer for what is desired. ||2||
Viśvanātha: Here, having received from Uddhava the secret knowledge taught by the Blessed Lord, Vidura—perceiving his own unfitness for it and being utterly despondent—reflected within his mind:
"To that devoted sage, whose neck is bowed by the weight of supreme joy, and who is listening to me, Mukuṇda [will speak]."

From Uddhava’s statement, "He spoke while resting [him] with a look of affectionate laughter," it appears that the Blessed One taught the secret of His own knowledge only to Uddhava—the crest-jewel among His most intimate devotees—and not even to those who were listening. This is not so; therefore, I [shall explain].

Not knowing this, I would not have first requested this great-souled one for the sake of that knowledge; rather, I shall ask whatever it is I desire to know myself. And if he knows that, then, O Vidura, I was commanded by the Blessed One for your sake regarding what has been spoken by the Blessed One.
He himself will say, "Grasp this most secret knowledge which resolves the contradictions such as its being unborn and yet possessing birth";

therefore, he says "for the sake of happiness," and so forth. By means of those actions, one would not find either happiness, or else the cessation of suffering, or the cessation that is dispassion (*vairāgya*).
But from those very actions performed again and again, there is only suffering. Regarding this question, may your lordship tell us the answer that is appropriate. (2)
Truly, they wander here for the sake of favoring those people who, by fate, have turned away from Kṛṣṇa, who are unrighteous in character, and who are deeply distressed.
All beings that have been and all that are to be belong to Janārdana.
Śrīdhara: By destiny—that is, due to past karma acting as the cause—people have become averse to Kṛṣṇa;

consequently, they are unrighteous and deeply distressed. For the sake of favoring such people, auspicious beings move about performing blessings. The meaning is that you all possess a nature solely devoted to the welfare of others.

The sequence of the composition: "of the person" (janasya). By "fate," meaning due to the cause of past karma, [it means] because of being possessed by that [karma], namely, one who is of unrighteous character, that is to say, devoid of the dharma of the Blessed One. ||3||

Viśvanātha: Only those like you, the great devotees (mahābhāgavatas) who show favor to all beings, know the truth; thus he says—"bhavyāni" refers to beings who are auspicious by nature, namely, the devotees. ||3||

Therefore, O best of the virtuous, point out the path that leads to our welfare— that path by which the Blessed One, when propitiated, dwells in the hearts of men purified by devotion and grants his grace.
Knowledge is the ancient realization of true reality.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, O best of virtuous men, point out—that is, tell us—the path that is auspicious, which is of the nature of bliss. By which path, being fully propitiated and abiding within the heart, [one attains] the realization of the true reality (satattva-adhigama), accompanied by the direct perception (aparokṣya) of the Self, which is ancient and has the beginningless Veda as its authority. ||4||

The sequential arrangement: That is excellent; thus, in that which is purified by devotion and stainless with love, there arises the manifestation of *sattva*, knowledge, and that which is the Brahman, the Bhagavat, and the Paramātman. ||4||
Viśvanātha: O Śaṃ, whose nature is bliss, instruct us in the path—that is, the way of devotion.

He is the renowned Blessed Lord. From whom comes the realization of the *tattva*—the essential nature of Brahman, the Supreme Self, and the Blessed Lord, as stated in the verse: "Those who know the truth speak of that... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.11).
It bestows that knowledge which was stated:
"The sages, endowed with faith and joined with wisdom and detachment,
perceive the Self within themselves through devotion acquired by hearing [the scriptures]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.12).
It is ancient and primordial, not a modern work such as the Mīmāṃsā and so forth. ||4||

Having entered into action, the Blessed One, the Lord of the three worlds who is self-dependent, performs those deeds which he performed at the beginning, even though he is himself devoid of personal exertion.
Having established the livelihood of the world, he ordains its existence.

Śrīdhara: In the fifth verse, beginning with "He performs actions," there is a connection to the verb "describe. Just as [it was said], in whatever manner He has taken incarnation in the form of a person, He is the Lord of the three worlds—the controller of the *māyā* of the three *guṇas*—and therefore He is indeed independent; such are the actions [which He performs].

He performs [actions]. He asks specifically about actions with the words beginning "as," and so forth. "Free from exertion" (*nirīha*) means inactive or desireless; "having established" (*saṃsthāpya*) means having made well-settled. "Livelihood" (*vṛtti*) refers to one's means of subsistence. ||5||

The sequential arrangement: therein, while many means exist, he declares what is dear to his own heart by means of the words "he performs" (*karoti*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by [the words] 'just as' (*yathā*) etc. in the commentary: because the word *yathā* connects with both instances, it has been applied even previously. ||5||
Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "He performs actions" (*karoti karmāṇi*) and so forth is syntactically connected with the word "describe" (*varṇaya*) found in the fifth verse.
Tryadhīśa is Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the three Puruṣas; his "actions" (*karmāṇi*) refer to the lifting of Govardhana and other such deeds.
And Mahāviṣṇu, the presiding deity over the *māyā* consisting of the three *guṇas*, is like this, as previously [stated] at the end of the great kalpa.

Having established and then withdrawn this [universe], he created it again at the beginning of the great aeon; and having created it, he ordained its *vṛtti*, meaning its livelihood or means of sustenance. ||5||

Furthermore, just as he, having withdrawn his functions and being the sole sovereign lord of the masters of yoga, rests in the cave of the heart after placing this [universe] within his own void; so too does this [Self].
He entered in many ways, just as he had been.

Śrīdhara: Having placed [the mind] in its own, individual space of the heart (hṛdayākāśa), he established it there. One whose mental fluctuations (vṛttayaḥ) have ceased [is meant]. In the cave, that is, within the Yogamāyā. "In many ways" means in the forms of Brahmā and others. ||6||

The sequential composition [of the verse] is as follows: having established—that is, having dissolved—the "kha" (the void) within its own nature, which is the "kha" of Brahman according to the maxim beginning with "ākāśas talliṅgāt," one abides in identity with that [Brahman] in the "guhā" (cave), meaning in some region inaccessible to all; the remainder is that this is the "Great Creator-Puruṣa."
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, having placed [the self] within one's own heart-space—that is, having established it in the "cave" (guhā), meaning in the Virajā river which is inaccessible to all;
with the functions of the qualities of Māyā ceased; and furthermore, having created this world, He entered into it in manifold ways.

The repetition of questions regarding creation and so forth—such as "In what manner did he exist in the form of gods, humans, and others?"—is due to the desire to know whether the pastimes of creation and so forth occurring throughout the great kalpas (mahākalpa) are uniform or diverse in form. ||6||
Playing about, he performs deeds through various incarnations for the welfare of the twice-born, cows, and gods;
yet our minds are not satiated even as we listen.
The nectars of the life-story of Suślokamauli.
Śrīdhara: While sporting through the various incarnations such as the Fish and others, He performs certain actions;

he now manifests a desire to ask for further particulars with the words "the mind" (*manaḥ*). "Suślokāḥ" means those of holy fame; "of Him" refers to Him who shines preeminently above them like their crown.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By means of the various incarnations, such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and so forth. ||7||
By means of those various categories of reality, the Lord of the World caused all beings—
including the worlds, the non-worlds, and the world-protectors—
to perceive that wherein [all things] truly abide.
The division of the schools (nikāyabheda) has been introduced and is well known.

Śrīdhara: Adhilokanātha means the sovereign lord of the worlds. He fashioned (acīkl̥pat), that is, he arranged, the *alokas*—the regions outside the Lokāloka mountain. In those [regions], whatever beings there are, their classes (*nikāya*) are distinguished according to the specific authority of their respective karmas, or rather, they are based upon it.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: By means of the distinctions of the principles (tattva-bheda), such as the Vairāja-pāda and others, [the Lord] fashioned (acīklṛpat) the worlds (loka), beginning with Pātāla, and the non-worlds (aloka), which are the regions outside the Lokāloka mountain, by means of the elements beginning with earth (pṛthivī).
In which [scriptures] and for whomsoever the distinction and manifold variety of all classes of living beings is intended,
such that one may become qualified for devotion, knowledge, yoga, action, and so forth; by which [scripture] the self and the actions of creatures are recognized, renowned, and uncontradicted.
And he brought about the differentiation of those things designated as "form";
O best of brahmins, describe this to us— how Nārāyaṇa, the creator of the universe, was born from his own self.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, in whatever manner he created the distinction among the individual selves (*jīva*), their natures (*ātman*), their inherent dispositions (*svabhāva*), the actions performed by them, their forms produced thereby, and the names assigned to them—he who is the creator of the universe, himself self-born and self-established—[has done so]. (9)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, in whatever manner the self (ātman) is the nature of living beings, karma follows that [nature], form follows karma, and names follow form; [he explains] their differentiation.
He performed [this]; the meaning is that Nārāyaṇa himself, being Brahmā—the source of the self—for the sake of the creation of the universe, was the creator of the world. ||9||
O Blessed One, I have repeatedly heard from the mouth of Vyāsa the vows of those who are high and low;
yet I was not satiated by those which bring only trivial happiness.
Except for the flood of the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s stories, they have none.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: [it means] "in the understanding of the intent," because of the root *ṛ* in the sense of "going"; for it is indeed a flood of the death-struggles of Kṛṣṇa when that intent is understood. ||10||

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But surely you have already heard everything in the Mahābhārata; what is the use of further questions? To this he replies: "The *pare* are those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), and the *avare* are the Śūdras and others; their *vratāni* are their religious duties (*dharma*). *Me* means by me. *Abhīkṣṇam* means again and again. By hearing them, we were not satiated—we remained unsatiated. Of them..."

Because it brings only trivial pleasure; however, apart from that flood of the nectar of the "Black" narrative (*kṛṣṇakathā*) which has been indicated therein, there is no sense of sufficiency—this is the meaning. ||10||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, you have surely heard all this in the *Mahābhārata*; to that he says: "The higher ones are the gods and so forth, and the lower ones are the animals and so forth; their vows are their respective natures; by means of those [vows], we were not satiated—that is, we were satisfied."
The genitive case here is used in the sense of "never enough," as in the expression "fire is never satiated with wood. "Kṣulla" means insignificant or trivial;
however, the meaning is that, except for that flood of Kṛṣṇa’s agonizing death, whatever I ask you about must all be told by you as being permeated precisely by Kṛṣṇa’s agonizing death. ||10||
Who could ever be satiated by that which is called the "source of sacred waters" (tīrthapada), which is praised by the wise in sacrificial sessions,
and which has entered the auditory canal of a person?
He cuts through attachment to the home, which bestows continued existence.

Śrīdhara: The reason for this is stated as "Who? [referring to] Kṛṣṇa, whose feet are the source of all sacred sites (tīrthapada). It is from the flood of the nectar of his narrations (abhidhāna), at the sacrificial assemblies (satra) or gatherings, by the wise ones (sūri) such as Nārada and others. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, you have heard the stories of Kṛṣṇa many times; to this he replies with the word "Who" (*ka*).
Is it merely by name (*abhidhānāt*), let alone from the stories themselves? Or rather, "by name" (*abhidhānāt*)...
This is a fifth case ending used after a word meaning "merely by telling," where the verbal suffix *lyap* has been elided.
The Sage Kṛṣṇa, though he is your friend, spoke the Bhārata, desiring to proclaim the virtues of the Blessed One—
in which [work], through descriptions of worldly pleasures for men...
Has your mind now been taken up with the discourse of Hari?

Śrīdhara says that the ultimate purport (*tātparya*) of the *Mahābhārata* as well lies in this very point: the sage Kṛṣṇa Vedavyāsa, desiring to speak of the qualities of the Lord in the narrative known as the *Nārāyaṇīya* at the conclusion of the *Mokṣadharma*,
[introduced] the description of wealth, desire, and so forth solely for the purpose of engaging the intellect in the stories of Hari.

He said: "In which... The minds of men have certainly been captured and led toward the narrations of Hari by means of accounts of vulgar pleasures that serve as gateways. As it is said in the *Itihāsasamuccaya*:
"One who describes sensual desires for those who lust, and describes greed for the greedy..."
What fruit does a man obtain by casting [them] into a well like a blind man?
Having described those two here for the purpose of winning over the minds of the world,
he has now censured them right here again with sacred narratives.
"Otherwise, how could that wise and greatly compassionate Sage have described those two as the causes of the terrible bondage of cyclic existence for people? (12)

The sequence of the composition: "The sage, desiring to speak... refers to that narrative concerning the Kauravas and others which consists mostly of descriptions of vulgar pleasures, yet follows the narrative of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
This hearing of it by Vidura from Śrī Vyāsa should be understood as having occurred precisely at the time of his pilgrimage. (12)
Viśvanātha states that even the *Mahābhārata* has its ultimate purport in that very same [Bhagavadgītā]:

"The sage Kṛṣṇa Vedavyāsa"—the genitive case in the word *guṇānām* is used in the sense of the accusative (*dvitīyā*). Alternatively, the word "excellence" (*utkarṣam*) is to be understood through ellipsis; [he composed it] in that *Bhārata* by means of descriptions of vulgar pleasures.

It is implied by way of objection: why did Vyāsa— who had already captured the minds of men greedy for sense objects through repeated discourses on wealth and pleasure— bring them under his own control and lead them into the stories of Hari, such as the Bhagavadgītā and the Nārāyaṇīya-upākhyāna?
Otherwise, not hearing of the supreme hardship, they would never have exerted themselves to go near him. As it is said in the *Itihāsasamuccaya*:
"Describing desires to those who lust after them, and describing greed to the greedy..."
What fruit does a man obtain by casting [it] into a well, like one throwing a blind man?
Having described those two here for the purpose of introducing the minds of worldly people,
he has now censured them right here again by means of purifying historical narratives.
"Otherwise, how could that wise and most compassionate Sage have described those two as the causes of the terrible bondage of cyclic existence for people? (12)
For a person of faith who is satisfied by the constant remembrance of Hari's feet, that [faith], as it increases, produces detachment from everything else.
It swiftly brings about the dissolution of all suffering.
Madhvaḥ: The intellect that increases in the narration of Hari’s stories. ||13||

Śrīdhara: He states the fruit of entering the intellect into the narration of Śrī Hari’s stories: "That [intellect] or that speech"—where else?—not in vulgar pleasure. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of Hari" (verse 13).
The sequential arrangement is this: that very narrative of Hari. The meaning of "entirely" is by means of the direct perception of Śrī Hari. ||13||

Viśvanātha: He states the fruit of entering the intellect into the narrative of Hari according to the distinction of qualified aspirants: "That narrative of Hari" refers to the pure devotee who has faith—that is, one who trusts in the narrative of Hari alone with the conviction that it is the supreme human goal—and who does not [trust] in other things, namely dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

[Objection: But how can there be liberation, or how can there be bliss and the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra, if one develops detachment even toward liberation? To this he says: for a person who is satisfied by that very experience of sweetness—the constant remembrance of the feet of Hari—and who has thus attained supreme bliss.

Even for that cycle of existence which consists of all suffering, there is an end— its destruction— and therein, indeed quickly and immediately, one should lament for those who are themselves not to be pitied: the ignorant ones who, through their own sin, are averse to the narrations of Hari.
The unblinking god consumes the lifespan of those whose speech, conduct, and mindfulness are in vain.

Śrīdhara: He laments those who do not take delight in such a narrative as this—those who are themselves objects of pity, and even more pitiable than they. Among them, those who are ignorant of the purport of the *Bhārata* are to be pitied;
but those who, despite knowing it, are averse to the narrative of Hari, they are to be considered even more pitiable than the former—thus the connection should be made.
Time is unblinking as it consumes their lifespan; the reason for this is that their activities of speech, body, and mind—consisting of talk, movement, and memory—are entirely in vain. (14)

The Sequence of Arrangement: Here, only three kinds of people are observed: some who listen to the narrations of Hari with spiritual absorption (āveśa), some without absorption, and some who are indeed averse.
Among them, those without absorption are objects of pity for those who possess absorption; however, the averse ones are objects of pity even for those without absorption.
Having reflected, he says: "Those" (tān). This is quite clear. ||14||

Viśvanātha: In this regard, regarding the narrative of Hari, three types of people are possible—the faithful, the faithless, and those who are averse. In the Śrīmad Bhāgavata system, those who place their trust in devotion as the supreme human goal are called the faithful (śraddadhāna).
"One should perform ritual actions as long as one does not become weary,
or as long as faith in hearing my stories and so forth has not arisen" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.20.9);
likewise, "one whose faith has arisen in my stories" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.20.27), and so on.

Because [the truth] is about to be established; those who believe only that it is a means for achieving human goals, yet lack faith; and those who, desiring to achieve human goals even without devotion, are turned away—having spoken with praise regarding the first group, and having bypassed the second, [he addresses] the third.

"I grieve"—I grieve even for those who are worthy of being pitied by pure devotees, namely those intent on the means for attaining heaven, liberation, and so forth, yet devoid of devotion, though they possess the yoga of ritual action and knowledge. The reason for this is:
"ignorant," meaning those who, despite having studied and studied the scriptures again and again, do not know their true purport; for [the scripture says], "of Hari," and so on.
The meaning is: "by means of sin" refers specifically to the cause of great transgressions committed both in the past and the present. "Animiṣaḥ" (the unblinking one) refers to Time.

Now, one might object: even they [the opponents] are eloquent in the assembly, possessing various doctrines for establishing their own respective systems, various arguments, various conclusions, and various traditional codes (smṛtis). To this, he replies with contempt: "In vain," and so forth. ||14||
Therefore, O Kauṣārava, friend of the distressed, having extracted from among all stories the very essence of the narrative of Hari, the bestower of peace,
for this man.
For our welfare, proclaim the glory of the Tīrtha-kīrti.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, O Kauṣārava! For the welfare of this world, extract only the story of Hari—the very essence within all stories—and narrate it to us, just as a bee extracts honey from flowers. 15.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Therefore, for that reason, O Kauśārava! ||15||
Having descended for the sake of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, and having assumed his powers,
he performed deeds that surpassed even those of the Great Puruṣa.
Proclaim those which Īśvara [has bestowed] upon me.
Śrīdhara: With the intention that the stories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa should be told in particular, he says "He" (saḥ).

He who previously assumed his powers for the sake of the creation of the universe and so forth—he, having taken an incarnation among men, performed deeds that transcend ordinary human actions; speak of those in detail. 16.

The Sequence of Events: Here, although she is specifically devoted to the stories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, she asks only in general terms out of fear that the pain of separation might increase—saying, "He who... It should be understood that for this very reason, the venerable Maitreya did not introduce those specific stories. Why? Because at present...

One should construe the verse as follows: Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is the descent (avatāra) by which [the Lord acts], having assumed the three potencies for the purpose of His birth and other activities, performed those deeds which are described. ||16||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, in accordance with the maxim that "having briefly stated the answers to my questions—which possess the characteristics already mentioned—in order to ensure they are free of further expectancy, one should conclude with sweetness," it must be proclaimed that the very narrative of the descent of the Śṛṅkhalā is to be expanded; thus he says: *sa* (He). He is the one by whom the incarnations, beginning with Puruṣa, were previously performed.
To cause me to have faith in me. ||16||
Śrī Śuka said: Thus questioned by the Kṣatriya for the sake of the supreme welfare of men, the sage Kauṣārava, the venerable one, spoke to him with great respect.
Śrīdhara: "By him for whom the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*) alone is the goal (*artha*), the purpose (*prayojana*). For that reason he was questioned.

Regarding the sequence of the composition: "by him for whom the *artha*, the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), is that very auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) consisting of devotion (*bhakti*), which is the ultimate good for all men whatsoever. (17)

Viśvanātha: By what kind of person? By one for whom the welfare (*niḥśreyasa*)—meaning liberation itself—is the sole purpose of men who will be born in the Kali age; the sense is that this is because he has already achieved his life's goal by being an attendant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||17||
Maitreya said: Well asked by you, O virtuous one, who out of kindness for the world and to spread the fame of yourself— whose nature is that of Adhokṣaja— have questioned me thus.

Śrīdhara says: He expresses great respect with five verses beginning with "Well done" (sādhu). By him who, while incidentally spreading his own fame, has fixed his very self and mind (ātman) upon Adhokṣaja. ||18||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He whose very self and mind are Adhokṣaja himself. ||18||
This is not surprising in you, O Kṣattṛ, born from the prowess of Bādarāyaṇa,
that Lord Hari has been grasped by you with undivided devotion.
Śrīdhara: That Hari was taken up is not surprising. Why?
Because Dhṛtarāṣṭra is also born from the seed of Bādarāyaṇa; that is true, but there is a distinction between him and you, as he says: "was taken up. (19)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: This is not surprising for you, since you were born from the seed of Bādarāyaṇa and since [the Veda] was received by you, and so forth. (19)
Due to the curse of Māṇḍavya, the blessed Yama, the restrainer of creatures,
was born from the son of Satyavatī in the wife of his brother who had been made a slave.
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "In that case, how is it that he has the status of a Śūdra? And how is it that he is a benefactor of the world?

To this, he says: "Due to the curse of Māṇḍavya. You were born as Yama himself in the field—that is, in the womb—of a maidservant (bhujiṣyā), who was accepted as a wife through the field-relationship (kṣetra) of his brother Vicitravīrya. ||20||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: [He says] "You are not an ordinary person; I indeed recognize you"—namely, "Māṇḍavya... [referring to the fact that she was] accepted as a field (*kṣetra*) in the field (*kṣetra*) of her brother Vicitravīrya.
In the case of a maidservant who is at her own disposal. ||20||
You were always highly esteemed by the Blessed One and his followers;
it was for your sake that the Blessed One, while traveling, instructed me to give you the teaching of knowledge.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, [the word] "you" (bhavān) [is used]. Why? Because he commanded me for the purpose of instructing you in knowledge. By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that he himself also instructed [me] through memory alone. ||21||

The sequence of the composition: "That the Lord, the Unborn, has commanded me here for the sake of imparting knowledge along with its followers"—this is the reading that expresses the relationship [of the work]. ||21||

Viśvanātha: You are not merely a favored devotee by virtue of your sense of "mine-ness," but you also exist as an eternal attendant of the Lord in another capacity; thus he says: "Bhavān" (You). "Mām" means me, as I am departing for Vaikuṇṭha. ||21||
Now, I shall describe in due order those divine sports of the Blessed One, augmented by the power of yoga, which have as their purpose the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of the universe.
Śrīdhara: Those [powers] whose objects are the purposes such as the maintenance of the universe and so forth. ||22||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding that, first, as an answer to the question, "How did He create this at the beginning, being devoid of effort?", he says—"Yogamāyā"—stating, "I shall describe the pastimes of the descent of the Person."

Those [energies] whose objects (viṣaya) are the purposes (artha)—namely, the maintenance of the universe and so forth—which are augmented by that specific manifestation of the power of essential nature (svarūpa-śakti-vṛtti-viśeṣa) and expanded through their own portion, Māyā;
for it is observed in the Nāradapañcarātra that the power of Māyā constitutes a portion of Yogamāyā. ||22||
The Blessed One, the all-pervading Lord, is the singular foremost Self among all selves;
he is the Self who follows his own will, characterized by manifold mental states.
Madhva is the sovereign lord of the individual souls. 23.
Śrīdhara: In order to describe the play of creation therein, he first states the prior state:

"Before this universe was created, the Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord, existed as one alone; He is the Self of the selves (the individual souls), the all-pervading, and the Master. There was nothing else consisting of subject and object."

It existed; for although it exists as the essence of the cause, there is no separate perception of it—thus he says: "not characterized by diversity," meaning that it is not perceived through various notions such as the seer and the seen. Alternatively, this meaning is obtained even without eliding the letter *a*: that which, in the process of creation, [is not perceived] by diverse notions.

It is observed that at that time he was indeed alone. Why? Because when there is dissolution following the will of the Self—that is, Māyā—or rather, because his desire to abide in the state of aloneness persists. ||23||
The sequential arrangement: Now, while narrating the story of the pastimes requested by him,

he explains the knowledge of the four verses commanded by the venerable Lord Śrīmad-Bhagavān, beginning with the words "The Blessed One" and ending with the passage "He effects the pacification of all afflictions" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.7.14).
Now, in accordance with the sequence of the narrative, the four meanings must be stated in reverse order.

Therein, he demonstrates the meaning of the half-verse, "I alone existed in the beginning, nothing else, whether being or non-being, nor anything beyond" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 2.9.32), by means of the commencement of the sport of creation, in two verses beginning with "The Blessed One": this...

The meaning is that at that time, the entire universe—from the *puruṣa* down to the earthly realm—became one with the Blessed One who remained alone. Furthermore, the Self (*ātman*) of even the pure individual souls (*jīvas*), which occupy the position of rays, is the Supreme Essential Nature (*paramasvarūpa*), which occupies the position of the orb; and there is nothing else beyond that.

The meaning is that the Self (*ātman*) is self-established by its very nature. Thus, in that context, it is shown that even its own parts possess the state of being "possessors of parts" (*aṃśitva*), as well as non-difference from Brahman. When? The meaning is: when the Self’s will—that is, its will for creation and so forth—is in a state of "conformity," which means in a state of dissolution (*līnatā*). But [an objection may be raised]: nanu...

Even though there exist many glories such as Vaikuṇṭha and others, how was it that He alone existed? To this he says: even though there are various names such as Vaikuṇṭha and so forth, He alone is indicated [as the reality], just as one says "the king is marching" even when he is accompanied by an army. (23)

Viśvanātha: In order to describe the play of creation (*sṛṣṭilīlā*), he first describes the prior state: "Before this universe, at the time prior to creation, the Blessed One (*bhagavān*)—endowed with the sixfold sovereignty—was alone.
According to some, this is because the Blessed One is the causal substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-kāraṇa*) by virtue of [the world] being dissolved within Him.

Others say it is because He is the effect of the Blessed One's power. Alternatively, by reading "idam agre" as a single compound, the meaning is "prior to this creation. Likewise, when worshipped through the path of yoga, He is the Self of selves—the inner controller of individual souls (jīvas); likewise, when worshipped through the path of knowledge, He is the all-pervading one.

The meaning is "Brahman. Thus, He is characterized by various perspectives according to the different opinions of His devotees, yogis of devotion, and men of knowledge. Similarly, the Śrutis also state: "In the beginning, this was indeed Vāsudeva; there was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara"; "Nārāyaṇa alone existed, not... [and so forth].
"Brahmā was not, nor Īśāna"; "The Self alone existed in the beginning"; "Being alone existed"—these and others [are such statements].

Now, in response to the inquiry as to from what time even prior to creation that One existed, he says: when there is dissolution (*laya*), following upon the selves—that is, the individual souls (*jīvas*)—as well as their will and desire to create.
The meaning is: "starting from the previous natural dissolution. ||23||
Then indeed, that sole sovereign seer no longer perceived the object of sight;
with his power of action dormant though his vision remained awake, he considered himself as if non-existent.

"Madhva [says]: 'The Supreme Self (paramātman) considered the individual soul (jīva) to be non-existent due to its lack of power; therefore, that [soul] is eternally non-existent, whereas Hari is Truth and Knowledge. Thus it is said in the Āgneya-purāṇa.
Because they are capable, the powers (śaktayaḥ) are the wives; 'power' (śakti) is said to mean capability (sāmarthya). Thus it is said in the Brahma-tarka."
"Sleep, however, is declared to be the supreme delight in the Blessed One, characterized by a lack of interest in anything else; O dear one, it is called the closing of the eyes toward Viṣṇu.
Thus it is stated in the Vyomasaṃhitā. 24.

Śrīdhara: Regarding this, he explains the manner in which Māyā arises first with two verses. Although he was indeed the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), he did not perceive the object of sight (*dṛśya*). Because he was the sole sovereign (*ekarāj*), he alone shone forth at that time. He considered himself as if non-existent, since in the absence of an object of sight, the state of being a seer is absent. Thus it is said: "Māyā and the others were dormant."

He is one whose powers exist; he did not consider them to be non-existent, because his power of vision (*dṛk*), which is consciousness (*cit*), was unslumbering. The sequence of the composition is as follows: he did not see the universe as an object of sight, precisely because of the absence of such seeing.
The meaning is that [the Lord] was absorbed. Likewise, he regarded even the Self—the Puruṣa who is a portion of the Self—as if non-existent;

the meaning is that he did not perceive it as distinct. Śakti is Māyā. Dṛk is the power of consciousness (cicchakti), meaning the internal power that constitutes his very nature. Ekarāṭ means the sovereign ruler of all.

Viśvanātha: That Puruṣa is indeed certainly the seer, the one who performs the act of looking at Prakṛti; then, at the time of the commencement of creation, he did not see the Pradhāna, which is the object to be seen for the purpose of creation.
Consequently, he regarded himself—though shining by his own nature—as if non-existent, like a householder without a wife.

This is according to the poetic convention (*kāvyarīti*) expressed by the word "iva" (as if). Alternatively, the sense is that he regarded his own self—the collective Virāj who was about to come into being—as non-existent, even though it existed within him in a subtle form; for its manifestation is impossible without the observation of *prakṛti* (primordial nature).

But surely, that beloved Māyā was an object of enjoyment for him through his very vision; what then was her state at that time? To this he replies: "He whose power, Māyā, is *suptā* (asleep). The implication is that a beloved who is asleep cannot be enjoyed. Furthermore, for his sake, there were many other beautiful beloveds who were awake.
He says that they exist in this way: "He is the one whose powers of consciousness, such as Lakṣmī and others, function as unslumbering perceptions.
The sense is that even then, for the purpose of creating the universe and so forth, that power of Māyā—which is external and unfortunate—must nevertheless be relied upon. ||24||
O illustrious one, that power of this Perceiver, which consists of both being and non-being, is called Māyā, by which the All-pervading Lord fashioned this universe.

Śrīdhara: That [māyā] indeed consists of the synthesis of the seer and the seen; it is of the nature of both the existent and the non-existent, and of the nature of both effect and cause. Alternatively, "existent" refers to the visible, and "non-existent" refers to the invisible; its essence (ātmā) is that which has those two as its own nature (svarūpa), because its form is the synthesis of both. ||25||

The sequential arrangement: subsequently, while explaining the meaning of the words "then I [thought] 'let this be'," he mentions another external power (*bahir-aṅga-śakti*) necessary for creation. By its nature as *śakti*, its character as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) is indicated; and by its being both existent and non-existent (*sadasad-ātmaka*), its character as the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) is partially manifested.

Viśvanātha: And then, by His will, that power of illusion (māyā-śakti) brought forth the world; thus he says: "She," the well-known one, "indeed" (vai), "certainly" (niścitaṃ), consisting of both being and non-being, having the nature of cause and effect—"this" universe—the all-pervading Supreme Lord [brought it forth]. ||25||
But by the operation of time, the powerful Adhokṣaja infused his seed into Māyā, who consists of the qualities (guṇas), through the Self-born Puruṣa.

Śrīdhara: By means of the operation of time—that is, by the power of time consisting of the *guṇas* which have become agitated—the Transcendent (Adhokṣaja), the Supreme Self, infused his seed, which is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), through the Person who is a portion of himself and exists as the presiding controller of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). "Possessing vigor" (*vīryavān*) means being endowed with the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). ||26||

The sequence of composition: He speaks of creation with the words "by the operation of time" (*kālavṛttyā*). From what was previously stated—"the Lord alone existed this [universe]" (*bhā.pu.* 3.5.23)—it follows that "Adhokṣaja, the Blessed One. By means of *māyā*, which has as its operation (*vṛtti*) time, [time] being mediated by the Person (*puruṣa*), who is the seer of *prakṛti* and His own partial manifestation (*svāṃśa*) acting as a door.
Through Māyā, who serves as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), He deposited His potency—known as the individual soul (*jīva*)—into the unmanifest (*avyakta*), which consists of the *guṇas*.
This is according to the Vedic revelation beginning with, "O, let these three deities... [Paramātmasandarbha 58].
Viśvanātha: Even the Lord of Mahāvaikuṇṭha is a partial manifestation (*aṃśin*) of the Primordial Person (*ādipuruṣa*), the Lord of Māyā.

Demonstrating that the Blessed One alone is the cause of all causes and the reality that is the substratum, he describes the commencement of creation: by the primary function of Time— that is, by the first glance of the exhalation of the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa)— Adhokṣaja [acted].

The Blessed Lord, the Master of Mahāvaikuṇṭha, through his own self-manifested partial expansion— the Primordial Person who presides over the Mother— placed into Māyā, which had been rendered fit for enjoyment by His mere glance,
the seed known as the reflection of consciousness, the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), according to the words: "My womb is the Great Brahman."

In the verse, "In that [womb] I place the embryo" (Gītā 14.2), the meaning is: "I place the embryo," which is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). At the time of creation, I join with the field of experience (kṣetra) the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who was merged in Me during the dissolution and who possesses the latent tendencies of ignorance, desire, and karma.

The venerable teacher Madhusūdana Sarasvatī states that the world arises precisely through the union of the power of *māyā* and the power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*). This is because of the Vaiṣṇava teaching that "I am that power of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña-śakti*) which exists in varying degrees," whereby the power of the individual soul enters into the power of *māyā*.

The meaning of the sentence is that He created the individual soul-power (jīva-śakti) as dependent upon His power of illusion (māyā-śakti). Furthermore, because His powers are infinite, there exist infinite individual souls who have not entered into Māyā; these are eternally established, appearing under names such as Viṣvaksena, and they are both manifest and unmanifest. This he states by the word "the powerful one" (vīryavān), [referring to those] deposited within the woman.
Since it is well known even in the worlds that energy (vīrya) remains in a man as something of a superior measure,
from that [energy], impelled by time, the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) arose from the Unmanifest;
it dispels darkness and manifests the universe residing within the bodies of the conscious selves.

Śrīdhara: [It arises] from the unmanifest (avyakta), which is impelled by Time, from Māyā. Having set aside the state of the [lower] principles (tattva), this is the definition of the Great One (mahat); hence the masculine designation "the conscious self" (vijñānātman). Because of its predominance of the quality of goodness (sattva), it manifests the universe residing within its own body, just as a tree manifests the form of sprouts and so forth contained within a swelling seed.
"Manifesting" means making manifest. He is called "the dispeller of darkness" (*tamonuda*) because he drives away darkness. As it is stated in the *Sāttvata-tantra*:
"The wise know that Viṣṇu indeed has three forms, which are designated as 'Puruṣa'."
"The first is the creator of the Great One (mahat); the second is situated within the egg;
the third resides in all beings—knowing these, one is liberated. Thus [ends verse 27].

The sequence of composition: That—meaning the category consisting of consciousness—also came into being; that very thing is called by the name "the Great Principle" (mahat-tattva). The dispeller of darkness is the agent who destroys the ignorance pertaining to dissolution. [Paramātma-sandarbha 58]

Viśvanātha: Regarding Māyā, which has acquired consciousness through the presiding presence of Puruṣa, he describes the birth of the first principle, Mahat-tattva, among its twenty-three constituent parts that are to arise in the relationship of cause and effect, starting with the words "From that" (tataḥ). From what kind of Unmanifest (avyakta)? From Māyā, impelled by Time (kāla).

Regarding that which has undergone transformation upon reaching the time appropriate for its arising: setting aside the term "Reality" (*tattva*), he states the definition of the Great One (*mahat*): "The Great One is the self of consciousness (*vijñānātman*)," meaning that, by virtue of the predominance of the *sattva* constituent, its nature is distinguished knowledge; it exists in all bodies as a portion in the form of the mind (*citta*).

The meaning is as follows: Since he is the dispeller of darkness—the destroyer of ignorance residing in the state of dissolution—he manifests and illuminates the universe situated within his own body, like a tree appearing from a sprout contained within a swelling seed;
therefore, when the quality of *rajas* predominates, there arises a differentiation of the principle of *mahat* through the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
It should also be understood that the reality of the Sūtra has thus come to be. ||27||
He too, whose nature consists of portions, qualities, and time, and who is within the range of the Lord's vision,
divided himself out of a desire to create this universe.
The *madhva-aṃśa* is the individual soul (*jīva*).
The four-faced Brahmā is the presiding deity (*abhimānin*) over time, the individual soul, the qualities (*guṇas*), and so forth.
Because he presides over all individual souls, he is indeed called an *aṃśa*. Thus it is stated in the *Brāhma-purāṇa*. (28)

Śrīdhara: He describes the origin of the ego (ahaṅkāra) with two and a half verses, beginning with "so 'pi" (he too). Here, the "part" (aṃśa)—the reflection of consciousness—is the instrumental cause; the "qualities" (guṇas) are the material cause; and "time" is the agitator. Dependent upon those [causes]—that is, subject to them—the Blessed Lord, the supervisor of all, being within the range of their vision, Himself manifested Himself as a different form.
He led [them]. ||28||

The sequential composition: "He too... [refers to] the Lord. That the Puruṣa, who is a portion of Him, is the Self—the very self of consciousness—[acts] out of a desire to create, is merely figurative, like saying "the riverbank wishes to fall. (28)

Viśvanātha: When the aspect of *tamas* predominates, he describes the arising of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*): "He too"—referring to the Great Principle (*mahat*)—is that which has as its essence those very causes: the *puruṣa*, the *vīrya* (the power of the individual soul), the *guṇas* (the aspects of *prakṛti* such as *sattva* and the rest), and *kāla* (time), which is conducive to its production. [This is] from the Lord...
The vision (dṛṣṭi), having become the object of that desire, differentiates itself—that is, it leads itself into another form.

Of what nature is it? It is the self (ātman), the substratum of this universe yet to be born. This occurs through the desire to create (sisṛkṣā), that is, the desire to emit the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra). ||28||
From the principle of Mahat, undergoing transformation, the principle of Ahaṃkāra was born;
it consists of the nature of the effect, the cause, and the agent, and is composed of the elements, the senses, and the mind.

Śrīdhara says: He states the definition of egoism (ahaṅkāra): the effect is the objective sphere (adhibhūta), the cause is the subjective sphere (adhyātma), and the agent is the divine sphere (adhidaiva); their self (ātman) is the substratum. The reason for this is that it consists of the elements, the senses, and the mind, and possesses their modifications. The mention of "mind" is also indicative of the deities. (29)
The sequential arrangement: [the portion] beginning with "from the principle of Mahat" constitutes half a verse. ||29||

Viśvanātha: From that which undergoes transformation (*vikurvāṇāt*), i.e., from that which is being modified. He states the definition of *ahaṅkāra*: the effect is the objective sphere (*adhibhūta*), the cause is the subjective sphere (*adhyātma*), and the agent is the divine sphere (*adhidaiva*); its self is their substratum. The reason for this is that it consists of the elements, the senses, and the mind; "mind" refers to that which possesses those modifications, and this is also an elliptical expression for the deities.
I am threefold: the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *tāmasa*.
From the principle of ego (*ahaṃtattva*) undergoing transformation, the mind (*manas*) arose from the *vaikārika* [ego].
And those gods who are *vaikārika* are so called because they manifest objects.
Śrīdhara elaborates on this very point through its divisions, beginning with the words "the vaikārika," and so forth.

*Vaikārika* means *sāttvika*; *taijasa* means *rājasa*. And the gods are *vaikārika*, meaning they are the effects produced by the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*). For from those [deities] who are the presiding deities of the sense organs...
For the sake of the gods, the manifestation of meaning arises from the cause, which is the illumination of sound and so forth. ||30||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: In order to explain this very point in detail, he says: *Vaikārika* is *sāttvika*; *Taijasa* is *rājasa*.
Those gods who are the beginning and end of the directions and so forth are *vaikārika*, meaning they are born from the *vaikārika*; for from whom [they arise]...

From the gods who preside over the sense organs comes the manifestation of objects, which is the illumination of sound and so forth; the sense organs themselves are composed of light (tejas) and consist of both knowledge and action.
The subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) and so on belong to the quality of darkness (tamas), from which arises the ether (kha), the subtle body (liṅga) of the self.

Śrīdhara: The grammatical connection is "only luminous" (*taijasāny eva*). The particle *eva* is used so that there may be no suspicion that those consisting of knowledge (*jñānamaya*) are of the nature of *sattva*. The *tāmasa* [element] is the primary cause of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-bhūta-sūkṣma*). From that sound, space (*kha*, i.e., *ākāśa*) arises. It is the mark (*liṅga*) of the Self, manifesting itself in the form of its own quality, sound.

Or [it is so] by virtue of being the space of the heart. Alternatively, according to the sequence of the textual arrangement based on the Śruti, "The subtle body (liṅga) is the body of space; Brahman is the body of space," they are "fiery" (taijasa). Of the Self—that is, the Supreme Self—its "indicator" (liṅga) is that which makes it known, as per this Śruti: "From this very Self, space was produced."
Because it sublates that [other cognition] by means of that [sublation]. ||31||

Viśvanātha: The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that the sense organs are indeed *taijasa* (fiery). The particle *eva* (indeed) is used to prevent the doubt that the organs of cognition, being composed of knowledge, might be considered *sāttvika*. [The element] *tāmasa* is the primary cause (*ādi*) of the subtle element of sound (*śabda*). From that sound, space (*kha*), which is the ether (*ākāśa*), arises.

The *liṅga* of the Supreme Lord, the Self, is that which manifests through its own qualities in the form of sound; or else, because it is an effect of the Self according to the Vedic revelation, "From this very Self, space was produced," it makes the Self known. (31) (3132)
Through the conjunction of time, illusion, and latent dispositions, the sky beheld by the Blessed One underwent transformation;
following from the sky, it modified its touch and fashioned the wind.

Śrīdhara: [The ether] transforms the touch that has issued forth from itself and produced it, leading it to another state of form—namely, the wind or air. In this very manner, it should be understood that the production of the elements occurs everywhere through the medium of the subtle elements (tanmātras). ||32||
The sequence of composition: "Touch" means the wind, which consists of touch and is the subtle form of the element; the same applies to what follows. ||32||

Viśvanātha: Space, as the agent, transforming the touch that had emerged from and followed upon itself—that is, bringing it to another state—created air. In this manner, it should be understood that the production of the gross elements occurs everywhere through the medium of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). ||32|| (33)
The wind also, undergoing transformation and endowed with the vast power of space,
produced the subtle element of form— light, the eye of the world.
Śrīdhara: Together with the sky (nabhas), he himself is endowed with great strength; from that arises light (jyotis), which is splendor (tejas) and the illuminating eye. ||33||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Accompanied by *nabhas* (space), he himself was endowed with great strength; from the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*), light (*jyotis*) arose, which is the eye of the world, its illuminator. (33) (34)
The light, joined with the wind and undergoing transformation while being observed by the Supreme,
produced water consisting of essence through the conjunction of time, māyā, and the constituent parts (aṃśas).
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].

Viśvanātha: He infused—that is, created—the essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasamaya*) within it, which possesses the quality of *rasa*. (34) (35) Water, conjoined with light, undergoing transformation when beheld by Brahmā, [became the egg].
He bestowed upon the earth the quality of fragrance through the conjunction of time, illusion, and latent impressions.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: *Saṃsṛṣṭa* means joined together.
(36) Whatever among the elements, beginning with ether (*nabhas*), is superior or inferior...
Through their association with others, they are known for their qualities according to their respective numbers.

Śrīdhara: O fortunate Vidura! (In an alternative reading, *bhāvya* means "that which is to be done. Whatever lower and lower task there may be, they know that through the successive association with other causes, those tasks possess increasingly superior qualities in their respective order. For instance, in the case of space (*nabhas*), there is only sound.

A quality [belongs to an element] because of the absence of connection with another; however, for air, there is touch, and sound due to its connection with space. Likewise, for fire, there are those two (touch and sound) and form. For water, there are those (the three preceding) and taste. For earth, all [five qualities]. (36)

The sequential composition: Thus, the meaning of the first three quarters has been shown; as for that which remains—namely, "I am He"—that has already been demonstrated by the Lord Himself through the verse, "He alone entered this" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.5.23).
Having thus shown the knowledge of the meaning of the first verse, [he now presents] the realization of the meaning of the second verse.

By stating "these gods" and so forth, up to the end of the passage beginning with "of those own powers," he demonstrates the meaning of the third and fourth verses— which reveal the secret means for attaining that [state]— namely, that even one who is higher than the highest, having abandoned [all else] because of what is about to be taught, becomes subject to devotion (*bhakti*). [This is the portion concerning] the portions (*kalā*) of Viṣṇu.
Those for whom the manifestations such as Time (kālādi) and the subtle body (liṅga) exist as their assistants—therefore, with palms joined in reverence (prāñjali), they spoke. ||36||
Viśvanātha: "Saṃsṛṣṭa" means conjoined. ||36||
The gods said: O Lord, we bow to your lotus feet, which are a parasol that extinguishes the heat of distress for those who have sought refuge.
By means of which, as their root-banner, ascetics quickly cast the great suffering of saṃsāra outside.

The Madhvas [hold that] those who possess the marks of Time (kāla), Māyā, and Aṃśa have bodies caused by them; thus, Hiraṇyagarbha alone has a twofold form: the presiding deity of Time and the presiding deity of the individual soul (jīva). "The four-faced one possesses a pair of forms as the presiding deities of Time and the individual soul," so it is stated in the Pādma Purāṇa. (38)

Śrīdhara: Competing with one another, unable to meet the gods face-to-face, and finding themselves powerless before Viśvakarman, they became despondent and praised Hari, saying, "We bow down. This is for the alleviation of the suffering of those who have surrendered. "Ātapatra" means a parasol or umbrella. The reason for this is that they take refuge at the base—the very foundation—of His lotus feet.
They cast off and abandon the suffering of saṃsāra far away from themselves, just as travelers, having reached their own homes, leave behind the fatigue of the road. (38)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: An *ātapatra* is a parasol. Those ascetics whose very root, base, crest, and refuge is that lotus-foot—none other than such as these—swiftly and completely [uprooted it].
In this way, having forcibly extracted the suffering of saṃsāra clinging to their own bodies like a leech, they cast it far away outside, so that it never returns to them again; here,
by the words *añjasā* (directly), *uru* (far), *bahiḥ* (outside), and *utkṣipanti* (they cast up), it is shown that those ascetics who have not taken refuge [in the Lord] do so only with great delay.
Nor was it with their very roots; they cast them out in such a way that it is understood that saṃsāra would swallow them again.

Although at that time there were no ascetics (yatayas), nevertheless, because they possessed knowledge of the causes of Sāṅkhya as found in all the scriptures, those knowers of reality were likewise knowers of the three times.
It should be understood that they say:
"O Creator, O Lord, since living beings in this world are struck by the threefold suffering, they find no peace. (39)
O Blessed One, they obtain the shadow of Your feet along with true knowledge; therefore, let us take refuge in it.
"Madhu is the knowledge of Brahman, the shadow of Hari; for he is indeed a portion of Him even among the gods.
All knowledge is declared to be the highest good, and the four-faced Brahmā is His primary portion. Thus it is stated in the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa]. (39)

Śrīdhara: Expressing their exhaustion, they say: "O Creator, O Father! Since, in this worldly existence (*bhava*), within the self (*ātman*)—or as an address—" *śarma* means happiness. In the reading "without" (*ṛte*) "that" (*yat*), it means that they do not obtain happiness without the worship of Your feet. [Objection: But surely [happiness comes] from knowledge, not from that which is produced by ignorance...
Suffering ceases; what need is there for taking refuge in the shade of my feet? To this they reply:
the meaning is that taking refuge in that [the Lord] alone, accompanied by knowledge (*vidyā*), is what brings about the attainment of knowledge. ||39||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: "Since the suffering of saṃsāra is rooted in ignorance, it should be pacified by knowledge alone; what then is the use of devotion for those who possess knowledge? To this they reply with the word "without" (*ṛte*). Without the worship of whose feet in this world...
In this worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), they do not find peace within themselves (*ātman*)—or rather, [O Lord,] they do not find peace in You.

The reason for this is that their knowledge (*vidyā*) exists together with ignorance (*avidyā*). Knowledge resides only in the shadow of Your feet and nowhere else; thus, without devotion, even knowledge itself cannot be perfected.
The meaning is: "of those possessing false knowledge.
(39) (40) That which the sages seek in solitude with the eagles of the Vedic meters, whose nests are the lotuses of their mouths—
Those who have taken refuge at every step of that best of rivers, the Aghamarṣaṇā, which consists of the footsteps of the Lord of Holy Places (Tīrthapada).
The honey [flows] from the celestial river and from the earth. ||40||
Śrīdhara: Since it is impossible to take refuge in that which is unknown, they state the means for knowing it:

"We have taken refuge in Your foot, the *tīrthapada*, which they seek—that is, they search for it—with what? With the *chandaḥ-suparṇas*, the birds of the Vedas; for Your very lotus-face is their nest."

Of those [who seek You]: just as birds, having flown out from their nest, wander here and there and then enter back into that very same place, so too the Vedas, having emerged from You, find their ultimate rest in You alone.
Therefore, relying upon the Vedas, they search for Your state. In a secluded and unattached mind—what?

And [the word] *ca* [is used]. The term *aghamaṛṣam* means that which wipes away sin; *udam* means water. Among those rivers whose waters [possess this quality], the "place" (*padam*) refers to the source of the most excellent Gaṅgā. Therefore, the meaning is that even those who follow and serve the Gaṅgā reach Your foot, which is her source. ||40||

The sequential composition (*kramasaṃdarbha*): "Those who seek"—that is, those who seek whatever station belongs to whom—[should be construed as follows]: "To that [person] and to that station we have gone for refuge. The sense is that even those seeking a nest resort only to the foot of the tree, which stands in the place of a station. ||40||

Viśvanātha: Now, one might object: "Since the suffering of saṃsāra is rooted in ignorance, it should be pacified by knowledge alone; what then is the use of devotion for the wise? To this they reply with the word "ṛte" (without). Without the worship of whose feet, O Soul—this being an address to oneself—one does not obtain *śarma* (bliss) in this *bhava* (existence), that is, in *saṃsāra*. In that regard...

The cause is that which exists together with knowledge (*vidyā*). The meaning is that knowledge resides only in the shade of your feet and nowhere else; thus, since knowledge itself cannot be accomplished without devotion, they are people of false knowledge. ||40|| (41)
Having fixed it in the heart being cleansed by faith, learning, and devotion,
the wise [attain it] through knowledge and the power of dispassion.
Let us go to that lotus-throne of your feet.
Śrīdhara: But how can those whose minds are drawn toward sense objects seek that [Self]?

To this they say: by fixing it in the heart—that is, by meditating upon it—and by means of that knowledge which has dispassion as its strength, they become wise (dhīra). For how can there be meditation at all when the mind is full of passion? To this they say: through faith (śraddhayā).
And being cleansed and purified by devotion preceded by hearing. ||41||
The sequence of composition: [it is achieved] through faith and attentive listening. ||41||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, they say that even among those [devotees], those who rely solely on pure devotion (bhakti) are superior: "By that devotion, through which your state—which has been heard and taught by the mouth of the Guru—is pursued as the path of worship, having fixed it within one's own heart and experienced it, [one attains liberation] through the knowledge thus obtained."

By what kind of power of detachment (*vairāgya*), which consists of the tasting of that sweetness and through which the wise become steadfast because they are free from thirst for everything— by the maxim, "If one finds honey in one's own lap, why should one go to the mountain?"— do they no longer undergo the labor of searching through the Vedas and other scriptures as they did before?
O Lord, let us all go for refuge to Your lotus feet, which You have manifested for the sake of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe.
When remembered, she bestows fearlessness upon her own people.
Śrīdhara: Remembering the grace shown to devotees, they say: "Of the universe," etc. (42)
The sequence of composition: It is remembered that [the Lord] bestows fearlessness upon others who are dependent on the "sky-men" (the Siddhas).
Viśvanātha: For the sake of making such devotion easy to attain, they speak of His grace toward devotees, beginning with the words "of the universe" (viśvasya). ||42|| (43)
For those men who, despite dwelling far away from their bodies and homes— which are devoid of continuity— maintain the stubborn insistence of "I" and "mine," [there is no liberation].
O Blessed One, may we worship that lotus of your feet.

Śrīdhara: Anticipating the objection that traveling is useless since [the Lord] is eternally present as the inner controller (antaryāmin), they say: "yat... [verse 43]. "Sānubandhe" means together with its consequences; "sopakaraṇe" means together with its instruments. "Asati" means in that which is worthless.
Even though He dwells within one's own body in the city [of the heart], He is "sudūram," meaning difficult to reach.

Regarding the sequence of the composition: Viśvanātha says that "that which [is near] is, for others, though close, very far away. He further states that devotion is difficult to attain for those who live poorly—this is what he means by "that which. Even though [the Lord] always dwells in the city, such as Mathurā or Dvārakā, through both manifest and unmanifest appearances;
Or [He exists] within the body in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin).
O Supreme Lord, those whose inner minds have been carried away by others through their eyes of unwholesome conduct— [may You protect them].
Moreover, O Wide-strider, they surely do not see those who are marked by the playful grace of Your footsteps.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "If the lotus feet of Him who dwells within the heart are so far away for some, then they must be likewise for others as well, since there is no distinction [between them]. Anticipating this doubt, they say: "Those..."—the mind, though situated within, is carried away (parāhṛta), that is, drawn far off, by the eyes and other senses (indriya) which are turned outward and engaged in improper activities (asadvṛtti).

Those for whom [that exists]; therefore, they surely do not see them—this is well known (*vai*). But how could there be any contact with them for those [who do not see them]? Whom? Those who possess the beauty (*lakṣmī*) of the grace (*vilāsa*), that is, the charm (*vibhrama*) of the movement of your footsteps; [those who possess it] through the stories of your pastimes (*līlā*) and so forth.

The meaning is "those who shine as your devotees. Regarding the readings *patha* and *lakṣyā*, the sense is: those for whom the playful grace of your footsteps (*tvat-padanyāsa-vilāsa*) is the object of perception (*lakṣya*). Alternatively, the meaning is that they do not perceive the paths (*pathaḥ*) which have become your own way, or the existing paths such as hearing and so forth (*śravaṇādi*). Or rather, those who are of such a nature...
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Those devotees of the Lord surely do not see those madmen at all.

The underlying sentiment is that due to the absence of association with the virtuous, they lack the opportunity to hear the stories of Hari; consequently, although [the truth] resides within their hearts, it remains very far away from them. ||44||

The sequence of the argument: Therefore, [the Lord] would be an object of remembrance only for those upon whom He has bestowed His grace; and that grace does not exist everywhere. Thus, even in cases where association with the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) is not perceived—whether it be contemporary, ancient, or traditional—[it must be inferred].

Or rather, it must indeed be inferred. In that regard, even for deities such as Śrī Nārada and others who have attained their status through [their own] actions, no attainment of such a state is heard of in the case of Śrī Nalakūbara and others; therefore, it must be analyzed in this way.
Even if the presence of an offense exists in a person, then by that fault, when [the conditions] are present...
For those who are disrespectful and hold common views such as those of the munis and others, in order to pacify those defects,

the assistance of His grace is required when the company of the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) serves as the cause for being in the presence of the Blessed One. However, for those whose supreme and most excellent vision has arisen through the company of the virtuous alone while remaining free from offense, [the result follows] in relation to them.

Even in the absence of focused attention, mere association with the virtuous (satsaṅga) is the cause [of liberation]. Therefore, it was said with reference specifically to those who have committed offenses—"those" (tān).
The meaning is: those devotees who belong to the beauty of the playful grace of Your footsteps. They...

The meaning is that they certainly do not see them, nor do they bring them within the range of their compassionate gaze. Which ones? Those whose inner minds have been repelled by eyes—that is, by the senses—characterized by improper conduct and offending actions; those whose mental states have been turned away from the interior and directed toward the exterior, being thus extroverted.
The commentary on this point should also be considered here. In this context, "residing in what is non-existent" (asadvṛttitva) is not understood as residing in that which is absolutely non-existent;

for prior to His grace, everyone is already in such a state. This would refer to the subject matter of such verses as, "For people who are averse to Kṛṣṇa by fate... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.5.3). Therefore...

Compassion certainly arises toward those who possess faultless and virtuous conduct. Even if compassion does not arise due to the absence of any offense whatsoever, their noble-mindedness would still be present through mere association.
However, as for one toward whom they exercise compassion even when he is at fault, out of their own spontaneous grace, it is that person alone who truly possesses that noble-mindedness.
It is not common to others like Nalakūbara and so forth, nor is it like that of a deity who is shared by all.

However, when they show compassion even toward one who has committed an offense solely out of their own free will, that [compassion] should belong to Him alone, and not to another, as is the case with Nalakūbara and others, or with a deity who is common to all. ||44||

Viśvanātha: Now, one might object: since there are many saintly persons (*sādhu*) wandering here and there in this world, why do you not attain pure devotion—which is easily obtained through their grace—by associating with them?

Regarding this, they say: "Those [who do not see]. Those whose internal mind (*manas*) has been carried away—that is, far stolen away—by the outward-turned senses through improper conduct; therefore, for that very reason, they certainly do not see You. How could there be association with You for them? Who are "those"? They are those for whom Your footsteps [are the goal].

His gait is grace (*vilāsa*), his movement is charm (*vibhrama*), and his splendor is prosperity (*sampatti*). Those who are related to that [splendor]—meaning those who are fulfilled and have attained their supreme purpose through the remembrance, recitation, and so forth of the graces of the stories of Your pastimes—are, for You, non-devotees; this is the meaning. In the reading *patha* (on the path) instead of *lakṣmyāḥ* (of Lakṣmī), the sense remains the same.

The meaning is that they do not see those holy men (*sādhus*) who constitute the paths—the paths upon which the playful placement of Your feet by Lakṣmī leaves its mark. Alternatively, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: those devotees (*bhāgavatas*) who are thus characterized do not at all look upon those [others] as if they were madmen or offenders. ||44||
O Lord, those whose hearts have been purified by the growth of devotion through drinking the nectar of Your stories,
having attained awakening whose essence is dispassion—
So that they might proceed directly to the unimpeded abode.

Śrīdhara: They clarify this very point with the two verses beginning with "By drinking" (pānena). Having obtained that awakening whose essence and strength is dispassion (vairāgya), they would follow after—that is, they would reach—the world of Vaikuṇṭha, which is the unimpeded abode (akuṇṭhadhiṣṇya). ||45||

The sequential arrangement: when that narrative exists, they say that the attainment of the supreme fruit occurs through the sequence [of stages]—beginning with "by drinking" (pānena). The commentary states: those of pure intent, who have cast off all hypocrisy, for whom service alone is the sole human goal, reach the world of Vaikuṇṭha, whose abode is unimpeded. ||45||

Viśvanātha: Just as devotees (*bhakta*) are supremely happy from the very beginning of the stage of practice (*sādhanadaśā*), so too are the men of knowledge (*jñānin*); yet, [the latter] are supremely miserable from the very beginning of the stage of practice. Thus, they say in two verses that this much alone is the difference between devotion and knowledge. [The first verse begins with] "By drinking..."—this is the essence of the distinction.

Because there is even greater power beyond union with Brahmā, having attained such awakening—arising from increased devotion and consisting of the experience of the Lord’s sweetness—one reaches Vaikuṇṭhaloka, the realm of unimpeded splendor; thus say the venerable teachers. (46)
