Likewise, others, having conquered the most powerful Prakṛti through the power of yoga consisting of self-concentration,
enter into you alone as the Wise Puruṣa.
Their effort would be in vain, for they do not attain it through service.
In the Dattātreya-yoga it is said: "The victory of Madhu and Vāyu, who are by nature Viṣṇu, comes through devotion alone and not otherwise. (46)

Śrīdhara: Concentration on the Self is the steadiness of the mind; that itself is the yoga, the means, by the power of which liberation is attained. Through the path of knowledge (jñānayoga), liberation comes through exertion, whereas through association with the virtuous and such acts as hearing Your stories, it comes without effort at all. The implication is that for those possessed by the notions of "I" and "mine," liberation does not occur by any means whatsoever. ||46||

The sequence of the composition: Regarding those who are devoted to the *jñānin*s, he states that for them, both the means (*sādhana*) and the goal (*sādhya*) are inferior—thus [he says] "likewise" (*tathā*). Others, desiring only liberation, would undergo exertion even for that singular human goal; however, for those whose sole human goal is service (*sevā*), there would be no exertion through such service.
The meaning is that for those who always experience the supreme bliss of service, liberation shall also occur as a natural consequence. ||46||
Viśvanātha: Samādhi within the self is the steadiness of the mind; that itself is the yoga, the means.

By its power—that is, by way of the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga)—is the meaning. Alternatively, it means that through the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga), they enter You as the Puruṣa, attaining union (sāyujya) with You. However, there would be exertion for them.

Regarding their lack of devotion, as stated in passages such as, "O Lord, having cast aside devotion, the path to the highest good, they suffer" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.4), and "In this world, O Infinite One, though there have been many yogins...
(Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.5), without devotion even genuine knowledge cannot arise; how much less so [liberation]?
Those who speak of "liberation" are indeed the most miserable of people. As it has been said:
"For them, only the husk of affliction remains, and nothing else, like those who thresh coarse chaff" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.4).

However, when accompanied by devotion as an auxiliary to knowledge (*jñāna*), they certainly attain union (*sāyujya*); yet, during the stage of practice (*sādhana-daśā*), effort is clearly required in seeking and performing the means for the sake of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*).
But in the stage of realization (*sādhya-daśā*), Your devotees, attaining love which is the cause of Your subjugation, [attain You].

The extraction of the meaning is simply this: for one who has renounced everything, the taking up of your entry [into the world] is itself the very thing to be extracted. And since that is indeed suffering, according to the view of the devotees, even you are thus subject to suffering; such is the sense.
Now, it may be argued that the exhaustion of the devotees is also inferred from their service and so forth; to this they reply: "But not by means of service."

Regarding the word "te" (they): here, those very experiencers are the authority. Just as for a man and woman who are both weary, there is no fatigue [from the act of union] because fatigue has not been reached, yet it is called "fatigue" precisely because of that non-attainment; so too, for Your devotees, on the contrary, through service, a great fatigue in the form of mental anguish arises precisely from the divine non-attainment. This is the intended meaning. Here—

It should not be understood that they enter You through service, because this would contradict what was stated previously—that they follow after one whose abode (dhiṣṇya) is unimpeded (akuṇṭha). Nor should it be explained there as "they follow after You, whose abode is impeded (kuṇṭha)," for in that case the qualifying attribute would be redundant. [The word] "anvīyuḥ" [is used].
The employment of a word whose meaning is already implied is also redundant. ||46||
Therefore, at this time, being impelled by you for the sake of creating the worlds, we three selves have all been separated from our own sphere of activity.
We are not able to counteract that of yours.
Madhva [is characterized] by three aspects: the portions of time, māyā, and the self. ||47||
Śrīdhara: Having thus offered praise, they pray with four verses. Therefore, O Primordial One, we are yours, for we have been created by you in succession through your desire to emit the worlds;
[we are composed] of three selves, that is, the natures of *sattva* and so forth, and it is precisely because of this that our natures are contradictory.

"Though we are separated [from you], for whatever purpose we were created—that universe, which is the system of our own abode and the instrument of your play—we are unable to hand it back to you, to restore it to you; therefore, O Three, bestow upon us your own eye. Thus [they spoke].
The connection [of this] is with the fourth verse. ||47||
The sequential arrangement: since, in this way, the superiority of all [beings] depends solely upon you, therefore... ||47||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, the sense is that we are indeed your servants, yet we suffer even without having obtained service. They explain the lack of attainment of service: "We were created—that is, produced in succession—by you through the desire to emit the worlds; by means of the three selves, namely the natures of *sattva* and so forth. Thus...

Thus, because they possess mutually contradictory natures, even though they are distinct from one another, we are unable to offer back—that is, to restore or surrender—to you the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*), which was created for that purpose: namely, as the system of your own abode and the instrument for your play. ||47||
As long as we bring you offerings at the proper time,
and as long as we eat our food where [it is found], so indeed shall these worlds belong to both of us.
Bringing the offering, they eat the food without hesitation.
Śrīdhara: To elaborate further upon their incapacity, they state the extreme variety of the task:
"O Unborn One! At the proper time, on each respective occasion, we shall bring and offer to you *bali*—that is, enjoyment—in its entirety;
and in such a manner that we may eat—that is, consume—mere food. By this, it is indicated that [we cannot even provide] mere food alone.

And it has been said that while we possess sovereignty, the enjoyment belongs to you alone. "Of both," meaning of both you and us, "staying where"—these living beings are without hesitation (*anūhā*), without obstruction, and free from impediment. Alternatively, "without hesitation" means without deliberation, i.e., free from doubt. And so says the Śruti: "They said to him..."
"Discern for us the sphere wherein we are established, so that we may eat food. ||48||
The sequential arrangement: therein they offer their refuge, which consists of service to their own duty, beginning with the words "as much as...
Whatever food has been given by the Lord for their respective livelihoods. ||48||

Viśvanātha said: "In that case, tell me what you desire; I shall fulfill it. They replied: "O Unborn One! At the proper time, when the occasion is right, we shall bring you the entire offering (*bali*), the sacrificial gift.

[We offer] the multitude of worldly instruments for Your play, consisting of both the collective and individual aspects of the phenomenal world, crowded with various cities such as those of gods and humans."

The meaning is: just as we have fashioned [this] for you and offered it to you, and just as we, acting through the operation of your power of māyā, have given food; just as the carpenters and builders commanded by the king obtain food for their respective bellies as wages.
And just as these worlds— the gods, animals, and so forth— subsist by the power and activity of Your life-force (*jīva-śakti*),
because they are dependent upon it and because they are dependent upon the power of Your *māyā*, they bring offerings (*bali*) to both You and us,
performing worship in the form of various sacrifices, yoga, knowledge, and the like, [offering] food.

"They eat" means they experience the fruits of their respective actions; "without deliberation" (*anūhā*) and "without reflection" (*avitarkāḥ*) means they are devoid of such deliberations as "Will the Lord give us the fruit of our actions, or will He not?"—the sense being, "May He fulfill this very desire of ours. And thus says the Śruti: "They said to Him..."
"Discern for us the abode wherein established we may offer food. ||48||
Among us gods and their progeny, you are the primordial, ancient Puruṣa, the immutable one; O Lord,
you [are born] from Śakti, the source of the qualities and actions.
He placed the seer within the goat as seed with skill.

Śrīdhara says: "And you must necessarily provide a means of subsistence for us and for these living beings who are conditioned by their tasks, because you are their progenitor. He explains: "For us, together with our lineage and our activities"—or alternatively, *anvaya* means that which follows along; you alone are the primary cause for those accompanied by that cause. In this regard:
The reasons are as follows: [He is] the immutable and changeless, the Puruṣa who is the presiding controller, the Ancient One (purāṇaḥ) meaning the primordial.

They establish this with the word "Thou" (tvam): O Lord! Thou art indeed unborn, yet at the very beginning, in Māyā—the power which is the womb, the causal source of the qualities such as Sattva and the rest, as well as of actions such as birth and so forth—[Thou art present].
"I have deposited the seed"—the meaning is that you have placed it. Of what kind? A seer (*kavi*), omniscient, and the nature of the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*). ||49||
The sequential arrangement: the poet is the collective individual soul (samaṣṭijīva). ||49||

Viśvanātha explains the relationship characterized by the served and the server: "Of us, who possess lineage (*anvaya*), that which follows along is *anvaya*, meaning the cause; together with that [cause], the primordial Person (*puruṣa*) is the ancient, primeval presiding deity, who, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), is the unchanging and immutable cause."

The meaning is that [the Self] is "empty from the beginning. For this reason, O Lord, since You are the father of us living beings, You alone cast Your seed—which is the collective totality of individual souls (samaṣṭijīva)—into the womb of Śakti, who is the primordial source wherein exist the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, and wherein resides the activity of the *guṇas* such as Mahat and the rest; [this seed is] the Seer (*kavi*) and the Knower (*vijña*).
The sense is that he is to be served. ||49||
Therefore, O Self, what can we do for you, we who exist for your sake with me at our head?
Grant us your own eye according to your power.
O Lord, that which pertains to the purpose of action among those [means] of favor.
*Madhvaḥ*: those headed by me, such as Mahat and the others. ||50||
Śrīdhara: "O Lord, O Soul! For what purpose have we—the Great Principle (Mahat) and the rest, headed by Sat—come into being? What work of Yours shall we perform? If You say 'creation,' they reply:
'In that case, grant us Your own eye, which is Your own knowledge, along with Your power.'"
Grant [this], for we are those whose favor comes from you alone (*tvad-anugrahāḥ*).
Or, as a single compound: *kriyārthe-iyān-evaitāvan-anugraho-yeṣām*, meaning "those for whom such and only such an extent of favor exists for the sake of action.
The sense is: "By your powers of knowledge and action alone are we capable of creation, and not otherwise."

The sequence of composition: Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then), it should be understood that in this context, according to the analogy of the earth [element], the Lord himself previously fashioned the bodies of these presiding deities of the *tattvas* because they were his devotees; however, for others, it will occur only through their own prayer. ||50||

Viśvanātha: "O Ātman, we—the Mahat and the rest, headed by me—what shall we do for you? Shall we perform the creation? To this they reply: "Then grant us your own eye along with its power; that is to say, grant us the knowledge and the power for the construction of the Virāj."
The sense is: "Only through Your powers of knowledge and action are we capable of creation, and not otherwise.
O Lord, such a favor alone is appropriate for You to grant toward our purpose, which consists of action:
that we may perform with ease the service ordained by You; this much alone is our desire.

The meaning is that it is not otherwise. In this context, because the deities presiding over the principles (tattvas) are devotees, the Lord himself fashions their bodies, whereas for others, there is merely the act of petitioning him; such is the purport of the passage. ||50||
Thus, in this *Harṣiṇī* commentary that reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
the twenty-first [chapter] has been appropriately joined here in the tenth [book] for the sake of the virtuous.

Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Origination of Mahat and the Other [Tattvas]" in the Third Book of the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsya, which is the Commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa.
Fifth Chapter.
The Sage said:
Thus, having failed to assemble those of his own powers, who were virtuous wives...
Having observed the course of those whose worldly systems were fast asleep, the Lord [acted].

"Because they are capable [of being designated as] 'powers' (madhvaḥ), the powers of Viṣṇu—beginning with Mahat—as well as Ramā, are his essential power (svarūpaśakti); for she is a power by virtue of being a power, since she is the primary power. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmatarka*.
That by which the effect is extended— whether [the causes] are assembled or unassembled, whether the world-process is dormant or the power of world-creation has not yet manifested—
is called *tantra*, the means of accomplishment.
"Or rather, the inherent power of causes is the primary means [of creation], because of that," so it is stated in the *Brahmatarka*. (1)
Śrīdhara:
In the sixth [chapter], he describes the creation of the Virāṭ body by those possessed by the Lord,
as well as the distinctions of the presiding deities (adhidaiva) and so forth therein, which were established by the Blessed One.

Having seen the state and condition of His own powers—the *mahat* and so forth—which, though existing, had not yet come together or met, and whose world-structure (the creation of the universe) was dormant; or rather, having seen the movement and stationing of those instruments of the sleeping living beings, He entered [them]—this is to be connected with what follows. ||1||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*:
In the sixth [chapter], Virāṭ arose through the entry of the Antaryāmin (the Inner Controller) by means of the *tattvas*.
The division of that [Self] into the objective world (adhibhūta) and so forth has been explained in detail with respect to the body.

Because they are effects of their own respective potencies, [he] beheld with his vision the course of those potencies— beginning with Mahat— which, while remaining ununited and unmixed, had the world-process, the act of universal creation, lying dormant within them. ||1||
Then the far-striding Lord, assuming the goddess Kālasaṃjñā as his power (śakti),
simultaneously entered the group of twenty-three principles.

The group of twenty-three consists of the objects of the senses beginning with sound and those beginning with the ether, the sense organs joined with the mind, as well as the ego and the Great Principle (mahat).
Because the deity and the sense organ are one, they are not counted separately;
thus, Prakṛti consists of twenty-four principles, while Hari himself is the twenty-fifth.
"When the individual soul (jīva) accepts the insentient portion, it becomes the twenty-fifth;
Mahāviṣṇu is the twenty-sixth, or with Śrī, the twenty-seventh"—thus it is stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya*.
[The Lord] entered the twenty-three principles along with Ramā.
Viṣṇu himself, by means of that which is called Time, exists in the form of power because it is capable [of such action].
And it is said: "By his own power, in the form of all-encompassing activity, Keśava joined together those divided principles (tattvas) by means of their respective portions. (2)

Śrīdhara: *Kālasaṃjñā* refers to that whose consciousness is awakened by time (*kāla*), or alternatively, that which impels (*kālayati*) and agitates its own effects; thus, it is *prakṛti*, that power. It is said that there are twenty-three principles because of the entry [of the Lord] together with *prakṛti*. He entered as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). ||2||

The composition of the sequence: *Kāla* (Time) is so called because it "drives" (*kālayati*) and gathers together everything; it is a specific mode of functioning. [The term refers to] her whose name is Time itself. Regarding the phrase "of the twenty-three principles": this is because only the principles beginning with *mahat* (the Great One) combine with one another, whereas *prakṛti* (primordial nature) pervades all of them. ||2||

Viśvanātha: *Kālasaṃjñā* refers to that *prakṛti* whose various designations, such as "the Great One" (*mahat*) and so forth, are due to time alone; bearing her, he entered. The meaning is that he first entered by means of the power that effects the initial integration, and subsequently, at the end of a thousand years, by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). This is because he entered together with *prakṛti*.

It is said that there are twenty-three: the Great Principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the five subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements (mahābhūtas), and the eleven organs; thus, they constitute twenty-three. As it has been stated:
"The root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great Principle, are both natures and modifications."
"The group of sixteen, however, is a modification; the Puruṣa is neither a primal nature nor a modification.
This is because of the Vedic revelation: "Having emitted that, he entered into it. (2)
Having entered that assembly in a visible form,
the Blessed One united those who were divided, awakening their dormant karma.
Of the honeyed [Soma], by measures, that is, by portions. ||3||
Śrīdhara: By way of activity, that is, through the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). "Karma" refers either to the actions of those living beings or their unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). ||3||
The sequential arrangement [is as follows]: by means of that which was previously described as activity (*ceṣṭā*), namely the very cause called Time (*kāla*).
For it has been said: "O friend of the Unmanifest (*avyaktabandhu*), they call this Time Your activity. (3)

Viśvanātha: By means of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) in the form of activity, [He perceives] their *karman*—that is, the action of those living beings—or their unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). ||3||
The group of twenty-three principles, consisting of awakened karma and destiny,
being impelled by the Supreme Person, produced that Adhipuruṣa through their own respective measures.
Of the honeyed [Soma], by its measures, that is, by its portions. ||4||

Śrīdhara: He whose awakened action is the power of agency—that group of twenty-three [tattvas]—is impelled by the divine Lord. By means of the *mātrās*, which are the constituent parts; toward the *adhipūruṣa*, the body of Virāj. ||4||

The sequential composition: [He is] the Supreme Person, whose form is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), as stated in such passages as: "Where am I, [composed of] darkness, the Great Principle (mahat), ego (ahaṅkāra), ether, air, fire, water, and earth? ||4||
Viśvanātha: He whose awakened action is the power of agency (*kriyā-śakti*). By "divine" (*daiva*), he means by the Lord (*īśvara*).
"By the measures" (*mātrābhiḥ*) means by the parts (*aṃśaiḥ*). "The presiding person" (*adhipūruṣam*) refers to the body of the Virāj. ||4||
When the host of world-creators entered into himself by a measure of twentyfold,
they were agitated upon encountering one another, within whom abide all worlds, both moving and unmoving.

Śrīdhara says: He describes the very act of birth—by the Supreme Lord, the creator of the universe, the host of beings was agitated by a portion [of his power], not in its entirety; that in which the worlds abide. (5)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He describes the manner of birth—the group of principles (*tattva*) that create the universe, having encountered one another while the Supreme Lord, the Transcendent, enters into them by means of His own measure (*mātrā*), that is, His partial aspect (*aṃśa*).
Having attained the state of being both primary and subordinate, it was agitated and became transformed into the form of an embryo. ||5||
That golden Puruṣa dwelt for a thousand years within the shell of the cosmic egg amidst the waters, nourished by all living beings.

Śrīdhara: That person is called the Supreme Person (adhipuruṣa). Within the "egg-shell" (āṇḍakośa), that is, in the midst of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), he is accompanied by all beings, including the latent souls (anuśāyin) and individual living entities (jīva). ||6||
The sequential composition: The golden egg is the cosmic universe; within it resides Hiraṇyagarbha, because it was previously filled internally with water. ||6||
Viśvanātha: He is the golden Virāṭ, the universal aggregate, consisting of the fourteen worlds within the cosmic egg;

[He dwells] in those waters which are the waters of the womb (garbhodaka). Or rather, in that cosmic egg which exists within the waters, He is expanded and pervaded by all sentient beings, the individual souls (jīvas) who lie latent within Him. ||6||
He, indeed, the embryo of the creators of the universe, possessing the power of divine action and the self,
divided himself by himself into one way, ten ways, and three ways.
And [it is said]: "Madhva is the Lord, designated as the deity because he possesses sovereignty over everything. Furthermore, *prakṛti* is the power (*śakti*) of the Self. ||7||

Śrīdhara: The embryo is the Virāṭ, whose nature is the effect (*kārya*). Divine power (*deva-śakti*) is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*); by that, [the Virāṭ] is one-fold in the form of consciousness delimited by the heart (*hṛdayāvacchinna-caitanya-rūpa*). Action-power (*karma-śakti*) is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); by that, [the Virāṭ] is ten-fold in the form of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). These are the five beginning with *prāṇa*: *nāga*, *kūrma*, *kṛkala*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya*.

Thus, these are the five. In this way, through the distinction of their functions, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is tenfold. The power of the Self (*ātma-śakti*), which is the power of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-śakti*), divided itself threefold according to the internal (*adhyātma*) and other distinctions. ||7||

The sequence of composition: regarding the phrase "sa vai," [it means] "endowed with divine power, the power of action, and the power of the self"; that is to say, he is joined with divine power (daiva-śakti), the power of action (karma-śakti), and the power of the self (ātma-śakti). ||7||

Viśvanātha: Now, in order to establish the limbs beginning with the face, he first states his threefold power (*triśaktitva*): He is the womb (*garbha*) of the creators of the universe, such as Mahat and the rest; he possesses the powers of destiny (*daiva*), action (*karman*), and the self (*ātman*); and he is endowed with the powers of the individual soul (*jīva*), vital breath (*prāṇa*), the spiritual self (*adhyātman*), and so forth. By means of himself alone, he [manifests] the self...

He divided—that is, he made it partitioned—into one way by the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), ten ways by the power of the vital breath (prāṇa-śakti), and three ways by the powers of the intellect and so forth (adhyātma-ādi-śakti). ||7||

For he is the portion of the Supreme Self that constitutes the very essence of all beings without exception; he is the primordial incarnation in whom this entire collection of living beings is manifested.

Regarding the phrase "by Madhva through the person who is his own self," it is said that he who created the cosmic egg is indeed he himself. The first incarnation of Viṣṇu is celebrated by the name Puruṣa;
he created the principle of Mahat and entered into its very end.
And it is said: "Because it resides in the heart of Brahman, it is also celebrated as the Heart. (8)

Śrīdhara: Thus, in order to demonstrate his excellence for the sake of [establishing] his capacity for division, he says "For this... He is the Self (ātman) of all beings, that is, of all living creatures, because individual entities (vyaṣṭi) are parts of him. The individual soul (jīva) is a part.
The statement regarding his being an incarnation (avatāra) is intended to show that Nārāyaṇa has manifested within him. (8)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states that for those who worship the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), this very one must first be worshipped for the sake of purifying the mind—beginning with "For he... He is the Self (*ātman*) of all beings (*sattva*, i.e., living creatures), because the individual selves (*vyaṣṭi*) are portions of Him.

"Descent" (avatāra) refers to the host of beings—the collection of gods, humans, and so forth—[attaining] oneness with that [Supreme Being] through the yogi's meditation on identity with Him as their inner controller. ||8||
The Virāj is threefold—as pertaining to the self (sādhyātma), as pertaining to the divine (sādhidaiva), and as pertaining to the elemental (sādhibhūta);
it is tenfold as the vital breaths (prāṇa), and also singlefold by way of the heart.

"Madhva consists of the pentad beginning with Prāṇa and likewise the pentad beginning with Nāga—namely, Sanāga, Kūrma, Kṛkala, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya. Thus the Prāṇa is tenfold; all of it is threefold according to its internal (adhyātma) and other aspects. So it is stated in the Vyomasaṃhitā.
"Prāṇa is the first-born, who is declared to be the primary Vāyu;

the skin, the self (ātman), and so forth are his sons, and [the principle] is said to be twofold. Thus Śrīdhara, in the *Tattvanirṇaya*, explains the meaning of the preceding verse. "Sādhyātmaḥ" refers to the internal organs (*adhyātmāni*), that is, the senses (*indriyāṇi*).
Accompanied; "Virāj" applies everywhere. ||9||
The sequential composition: here, the conscious power (cicchakti) of the Lord, which is the nature of the individual soul (jīva), exists as one with that [power] residing in the heart. ||9||

Viśvanātha: He explains in reverse order what was stated in the previous verse as "in one way, ten ways, and three ways"—namely, *ādhyātmam* (the internal self), which refers to the sense organs together with the self; *adhidaivam*, the deities presiding over the sense organs; and *adhibhūtam*, the physical bases and their respective objects.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkala, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.

Thus, by way of the distinction of functions (*vṛtti*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is tenfold; the meaning is that through these ten types, the Virāj itself is tenfold. Among them, *prāṇa* is the upward-moving [breath] residing at the tip of the nose; *apāna* is the downward-moving [breath] residing in the anus and other locations; *samāna* is that which equalizes the food and drink consumed.

The *udāna* resides in the middle of the body and functions as the upward-moving breath; it is located in the throat. *Nāga* causes vomiting. *Kūrma* causes the opening [of the eyes]. *Kṛkara* causes hunger. *Devadatta* causes yawning.
*Dhanañjaya* causes nourishment. [This is] by means of the heart—that is, by that which is delimited by the heart.
By means of the conscious living soul. ||9||
Remembering what had been requested by the creators of the universe, the Lord Adhokṣaja heated Virāj with his own splendor for the sake of their manifestation.

Śrīdhara: In order to elaborate upon the distinctions such as the "inner self" (*adhyātma*), he says, "remembering" (*smaran*). This refers to the passage beginning with, "O Unborn One, we shall bring you the tribute (*bali*) as requested" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.5.48). By his own splendor—that is, by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)—he "tormented," meaning he reflected, "I shall act in this manner. For his austerity consists of knowledge (*jñānamayaṃ tapaḥ*).
Thus, according to the sacred scripture (śruti). "For the sake of unfolding" means for the attainment of various functions (vividhavṛtti). ||10||

The sequence of the composition: Now, if the Virāṭ Puruṣa possesses such power, what is the purpose of the entry of the Lord? To this he says, "Remembering" (smaran). The Puruṣa is a portion of Adhokṣaja. The sense is that the power of the effect arises only through the grace of the cause. Therefore, immediately after this, he indeed...

The passage beginning with "of the creators of the universe" (viśvasṛjām) should be understood as previously stated. "He heated" (atapat) means he desired to illuminate by means of his own splendor. ||10||

Viśvanātha: In order to elaborate upon the distinctions such as the *adhyātma* (internal), he describes a certain activity of the Lord who has entered [the world] in the form of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), beginning with the words "remembering" (*smaran*). This refers to passages such as: "O Unborn One, we shall bring you the tribute (*bali*) as requested" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.5.48). "By his own splendor" (*svena tejasā*) means by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

He shone forth and illuminated [the world]. This is for the sake of the manifestation of these creators of the universe—that is, for their acquisition of various functions—according to the Vedic revelation: "The eye of the eye, the ear of the ear," and so on. The sense is that the causal power itself emerges within the effects. ||10||
Then, as he was thus tormented, how many abodes of the gods indeed burst forth? Listen as I declare them to you.
Śrīdhara: Listen to me. 11.

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: The abodes—the distinct locations—of that Virāj, who is the aggregate [of all beings], were pierced apart; that is, they became separate, once he had been heated by the Supreme Lord and illuminated by him. Me.
From me. ||11||
Agni, the guardian of the world, entered his mouth which had been split open as a place;
he entered with a portion of his own speech, by which that [speech] is uttered.

Śrīdhara says: He describes the abodes themselves with fourteen verses beginning with "Of him, fire... His mouth was split open, meaning it became distinct. "Place" means its own location. It entered together with speech, which is its own part or its own power. "This one" refers to the individual soul (jīva). "He attains that which is to be spoken"—the meaning is that he utters sound.

In every case, that which is expressed [by the first case ending] is the *adhiṣṭhāna* (the presiding locus). That which begins with "fire" (*agni*) and ends with the nominative case is the *adhidaiva* (the divine). The sense organs such as speech (*vāk*) and so forth are the *adhyātma* (the internal). That which ends with the instrumental case is the *adhibhūta* (the elemental), which is to be understood [as the object]. ||12||

Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Agni entered the mouth—the word *āsya* meaning the place [of speech] or the site—which had been opened (i.e., separated), together with speech, that is, the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*), by means of his own portion, his own single part; by that very speech, he [Agni] [entered].

The individual soul (*jīva*), being the *virāṭ*, attains what is to be expressed; the meaning is that it utters sound. Thus, in every case, that which is pierced and ends in the accusative case is the *adhibhūta* (the objective basis), while that which begins with "fire" (*agni*) and so forth and ends in the nominative case is the *adhidaiva* (the divine basis); and that which begins with "speech" (*vāk*) and so forth and ends in the instrumental case is [the *adhyātma* (the subjective basis)].

That which ends in the second case (accusative) is the internal; furthermore, that which ends in the sixth case (genitive) in some instances is the objective element (*adhibhūta*), namely the sense object. ||12||
Varuṇa, the guardian of the world, entered the palate of Hari, which had been split open;
and with a portion of his tongue, he is that by which [Hari] perceives taste.
Śrīdhara: [This refers to] Virāja, the manifestation of Hari. ||13||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Of Hari, who is to be meditated upon as the green one (haritvena), that is, Virāj. ||13||
When the nostrils were split open, the Aśvins entered the station of Viṣṇu;
for it is through the portion consisting of the nose that the perception of odor occurs.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: From which [organ], namely the nose. ||14||
When the two eyes were split open, Tvaṣṭṛ, the guardian of the world, entered into the Lord;
for it is by a portion of his eye that the perception of forms occurs.
Śrīdhara: Tvaṣṭṛ is Āditya. ||15||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Tvaṣṭṛ is the Sun. ||15||
The Wind, the guardian of the world, entered his split skin;
by means of that portion which is breath, he attains the sense of touch.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: "By the vital breath" (prāṇena) means by the sense of touch which pervades the body like the vital breath. ||16||

Regarding the *Kramasaṃdarbha*: the commentary on the second book states that "skins" (*carmāṇi*) means the skin as characterized by its leather-like nature. However, here [in this context], the meaning is "by means of the sense organ of touch (*tvagrūpeṇa*). (16)
His two ears were pierced through, and they entered their own abode, the quarters of space;
by means of which portion of the ear, one attains the perception of sound.
Śrīdhara: The accomplishment of sound is knowledge. ||17||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Siddhi means knowledge. ||17||
The plants entered his pierced skin, the seat of sensation,
by means of their portions in the form of body hairs, through which he experiences itching.

Śrīdhara: *Tvacam* means skin; *oṣadhīḥ* means medicinal herbs. Itching and touch are the two objects of the sense of touch (*tvag-indriya*) according to the difference in their locations. In this regard, both the distinction in names and the distinction in presiding deities have been explained in the Second Book (*dvitīyaskandha*) itself. (18)

The sequential arrangement: "the skin. Even though there is only one grasper of touch, this twofold division must be postulated: externally, there is the locus consisting of the hide, the sense organ, and the deities of the body hair, who are the presiding deities of the plants; this is one [division]. Internally and externally, however, there is also the sense organ of the skin (*tvagindriya*).
Furthermore, there is another distinction: the sense-organ of touch and its presiding deity, Vāyu, are distinct from one another. ||18||

Viśvanātha: *Oṣadhīḥ* means medicinal herbs. Here, upon the substrate of the skin (*tvac*), there are the skin, the body hairs, and two sense organs. Among them, for the sense organ of the skin, the presiding deity is Anila (the Wind), and its object is touch (*sparśa*).
For the sense organ of the body hairs, the presiding deities are the medicinal herbs (*oṣadhyaḥ*), and its object is itching (*kaṇḍu*). ||18||
His penis was split open; what [organ] entered its own seat, by means of which he experiences bliss through a portion of the semen?
Śrīdhara: Who is Prajāpati? ||19||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Who is Prajāpati? The meaning is: by means of the *retas*, that is, by means of the generative organ (*upastha*) characterized by semen (*retas*). ||19||
When the anus was split open from the man, Mitra, the Lord of the World,
entered it with the portion that is the anus, by which he effects the act of emission.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "Visarga" means the voiding of feces and urine. ||20||
His two hands were split apart; Indra, the lord of heaven, entered them with a portion of his vital energy, by which a person adopts a means of livelihood.
Śrīdhara: Svarpati means the lord of heaven. By means of *vārtā*—that is, by the power of buying, selling, and so forth—he [obtained] a livelihood, a means of subsistence. ||21||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By "news" (*vārtā*) is meant the power of buying, selling, and so forth; "news" refers to that which is denoted by the words "strength," "craft," and so on, [which is] the spiritual self (*adhyātma*). "Livelihood" (*vṛtti*) means the means of subsistence (*jīvikā*). ||21||
Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, entered his two feet—
the movement by which the Puruṣa, through his own portion, attains that which is to be reached.
It was not explained by anyone.
Then Vāgīśa entered his abode, having discerned his intellect,
so that through a portion of awakening there might arise the realization of that which is to be known.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha: "Intellect" (*buddhi*) refers to the physical seat of the intellect, the sphere located in a specific part of the heart. "Lord of Speech" (*vāgīśa*) refers to Brahmā; [the phrase "by means of awakening"] means by means of the intellect. This verse is not accepted by everyone. (23)
His heart was pierced, and the moon entered his abode—
that portion of the mind by which he undergoes transformation.
Śrīdhara: "Vikriyām" means modification in the form of volition and so forth. ||24||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Vikriyā means [mental] modification in the form of volition and so forth. ||24||
And as his own self was pierced through, pride entered its place—
that [pride] by which, through a portion of his actions, he undertakes what is to be done.

Śrīdhara: "The self" (ātmānaṃ) refers to the ego (ahaṅkāram). Rudra is called "the conceited one" (abhimānaḥ) because he conceives [of himself] by means of this; [he conceives] through action (karmaṇā), that is, through his function (vṛttyā), [thinking] "it must be done," which is activity (kriyām). ||25||
The sequence of composition: Viśvanātha [interprets] "self" as the locus of the sense of "I," and "by means of action" as by means of the organ of the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*).
Viśvanātha [also interprets] "self" as the locus of the *ahaṅkāra*, namely the "orb" (*golaka*), which is a specific part of the heart.
"Abhimāna" (the conceited one) is Rudra, so called because he "conceives through this. "By means of action" refers to the *ahaṅkāra* as the instrument of what is to be done.
That which is to be mentally conceived. ||25||
His *sattva* was fully manifested, and he entered the great abode by means of that portion of the mind through which he attains consciousness.

Śrīdhara: "Sattva" is a designation for both intellect (*buddhi*) and mind (*citta*) without distinction. "The Great One" (*mahān*) refers to Brahmā. [It is] by means of the mind, that is, by means of consciousness (*cetanā*). ||26||

The sequential arrangement: *sattvam* is the locus of the mind (*citta*), the physical sphere (*golaka*). Through the mind and the sense organ, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is to be known in a general sense; and this is also an indication for the intellect (*buddhi*). In some places, however, there exists a separate verse following [the mention of] "his feet," such as "and his intellect" (*buddhim cāsya*), and so forth. ||26||
Viśvanātha: *Sattvam* is the locus of the mind, the physical sphere (*golaka*), a specific part of the heart; *mahān viṣṇuḥ* is consciousness (*vijñāna*), that is, sentience (*cetanā*). ||26||
From his head arose the sky, from his feet the earth, and from his navel the ether;
within these are perceived the functions of the qualities (guṇas), such as the gods and others.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha state the origin of the three worlds: "From the head," etc. The *vṛttayaḥ* are transformations (*pariṇāmāḥ*). ||27||
The sequence of composition: "From the head" means from the head of this Virāj, which is a portion of the cause of the heavenly world (dyuloka).
In the same way, it should be understood elsewhere; [the reference is to] the earthly world (bhūrloka). ||27||
By their supreme essence the gods attained heaven;
by their nature of passion the *paṇis* and those who followed them attained the earth.

Śrīdhara: He elaborates on this very point with two verses. With "intense" (*ūrjitena*) means "absolute" (*ātyantikena*). Regarding the root *paṇ* in the sense of "transaction": humans are called *paṇayaḥ* because they transact through sacrifices and other such acts;
those cattle and other animals which serve as their instruments also reached the earth. (28)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By means of the ultimate and intense [power]. "Paṇayas" are humans who "transact," meaning they deal through sacrifice and so forth; those who follow them are those who have become their instruments.
Even those [beings] such as cows attained the earth. ||28||
O Blessed One, those hosts of Rudra’s attendants who dwell in the space between the two [worlds] have taken refuge in the third nature.

Śrīdhara: The third [layer] is darkness (tamas), belonging to that which is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). The space between both heaven and earth—the intermediate region (vyoman) or atmosphere—is the very navel of the Blessed One; resting upon that are the hosts of Rudra’s attendants (pārṣada), such as the Bhūtas and others. ||29||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The third [quality] is *tamas*; the meaning is "by his own *tāmasa* [nature]. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that those hosts of Rudra’s attendants, such as the *bhūtas* and so forth, have resorted to the navel of the Lord Virāj. *Nābhiḥ*...
What is that? To this he says: the space (vyoman) or atmosphere (ākāśa), the intermediate region between both heaven and earth, namely the Bhuvarloka. ||29||
From the mouth of the Puruṣa, O best of the Kurus, issued the Brahman;
because he was turned upward, he became the foremost of the castes, the Brāhmaṇa, the teacher.
Bhṛgu, the presiding deity of the Brahman, was born from the mouth of Brahmā;
Manu, the presiding deity of the Kṣatra, was born from the arms of Brahmā.
The one who presides over the thighs is Viḍabhimānin, and Vāstu likewise from the feet;
these were born first from Hari, and after that from Brahmā, as well as from Rudra and Vāyu, because Hari resides within them. Thus [it is stated] in the *Ṣāḍguṇya*. (30)

Śrīdhara: *Avartata* means it proceeded. *Brahma* means the Veda. That which, because the social classes (*varṇas*) originate from its mouth and because it is the source of their excellence, was the foremost, like a face, and the primary teacher—it too, by way of ellipsis, "proceeded from the mouth. For a Brāhmaṇa, the Veda is his livelihood through teaching and other such means; by that [livelihood], [he subsisted].
The meaning is that the Brāhmaṇa was born from the mouth together with his function (vṛtti). In the same way, this should be understood for the other three castes as well. ||30||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states the origin of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*). "Brahman" means the Veda. Because the Puruṣa is one with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), it proceeded from, or arose from, his mouth; for he was turned upward (*unmukhatvāt*).
Because he was oriented toward the Vedas, that Brāhmaṇa became the foremost of the social classes and the preeminent teacher;
the phrase "he also proceeded from the mouth" is to be supplied as a continuation. ||30||
From his two arms arose the Kṣatra, and the Kṣatriya followed that [duty]:
he who, being born of manly strength, protects the social orders from injury by thorns.
Therefore, it protects and guards one from calamities. ||31||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: *Kṣatra* is the power of protection; one devoted to that, i.e., oriented toward it, even a Kṣatriya arose from the arms—this is the meaning. Regarding *kaṇṭaka*s, such as thieves and the like, from them... [the protection arises].

"Kṣata" means affliction; therefore, he "trāyate," meaning he protects or guards from it. Since it belongs to a person (puruṣasyāyam), the meaning is that it is "pauruṣam" because of his capacity for protection. ||31||
From the thighs of that all-pervading Lord, the Viśas came forth, who provide the means of livelihood for the world;
from them arose the Vaiśyas, who established the economic activity of men.
Śrīdhara: The *viśas* (the Vaiśyas) are those whose occupations consist of agriculture and the like; they are the providers of livelihood for the world, the causes of its subsistence.

They proceeded from the thighs of that All-pervading Lord. He who, born from them—or "born from the thighs" (*ūruja*)—has accomplished his livelihood through his own occupation, [is called] *vārtā*. ||32||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Viś" refers to occupations such as agriculture and the like. From the thighs (*ūrvos* = from the two thighs) [came] those who provide the livelihoods (*vṛttikarīr*)—the means of subsistence—for the worlds. The Vaiśya also originates from that; he is "thigh-born. [He provides] *vārtā* (economics/agriculture).
He who established his livelihood by means of his own occupation, having accomplished it. ||32||
From the feet of the Blessed One was born Service (Śuśrūṣā) for the sake of the accomplishment of Dharma;
from her was formerly born the Śūdra, by whose mode of livelihood Hari is pleased.
Śrīdhara: With that [devotion] serving as the cause; by whose practice Hari himself is truly pleased. ||33||

The sequential arrangement is as follows: regarding the phrase "with the feet," the greatness of that disposition—consisting of service—is demonstrated by the fact that Hari is pleased not only by one's own duty, but by everyone, including Brāhmaṇas and others, when they practice such service toward Him.
This is shown in passages such as, "Having abandoned one's own duty... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.17), where it is indicated that He is pleased not merely by one's own specific duty alone.
Because the Blessed One did not accept [the objection] regarding the *toṣa* [of the opponent]. ||33||
Viśvanātha: Service (*śuśrūṣā*) is for the sake of accomplishing the duties of one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), which consist of attendance and ritual action.

Since the accomplishment of mere ritual action does not occur without service, although that service is the livelihood of a Śūdra, the underlying sense is that it actually pertains to all castes; thus, the Śūdra is born for that purpose.

The word "with the feet" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. By the phrase "by which conduct Hari is pleased," it is indicated that service (śuśrūṣā) is superior even to the Vedas and other such means. ||33||
These castes, by means of their own specific duty, worship Hari, their own Guru,
with faith for the sake of self-purification, according to the births they have received along with their respective vocations.

Śrīdhara: Since all these [beings] born at the beginning conceived their respective duties (*svadharma*) solely as the form of worshiping Hari, he says "these" (*ete*) with the intention of highlighting the excellence of those people of that time. Regarding the word "that" (*yat*) here: it is from the power of Hari alone that the power of Virāj [proceeds].
Therefore, the intended meaning of the statement regarding non-difference from Him lies precisely in the worship of Hari. ||34||

The sequential arrangement: because they are born from Him, due to His being their Guru, their progenitor, and their provider of livelihood, the worship of Hari is their supreme duty; this is the meaning. ||34||
Viśvanātha: "Together with their livelihoods" means that one should not worry about the means of subsistence during the sacrifice to Hari; this is the intended sense. ||34||
O Kṣattṛ, who could believe that this manifestation of the power of Yoga-māyā belongs to the Blessed One, whose nature consists of both the divine and the human?

"Madhva": because of his superiority; since the word *deva* (god) is supreme among the deities. Hari is the divine source of action, and thus he is called *kṛti* (the creator). Furthermore, he is called *ātman* because of his perfection, and *Mādhava* because he is the Lord of Śrī. Thus it is said. (35)

Śrīdhara: O Steward, who would believe— or even desire— to fully describe or comprehend this cosmic form (virāḍ-rūpa) manifested by the power of the Lord’s yogic illusion (yogamāyā), which consists of the nature of divine action and the self, and possesses the powers of time, karma, and inherent nature?
The meaning is that even desire is impossible to define, let alone [the object of desire]. ||35||
The sequential arrangement: here, *yogamāyā* is the power for the creation of the universe and so forth. ||35||

Viśvanātha: Time, karma, and inherent nature—consisting of destiny, action, and the self—are the forms of Him who possesses them, by virtue of being His own powers. Who could believe, or even desire, to describe this entire universe in its totality—that which has arisen through the power of *yogamāyā*? Even the desire is impossible; how much more so the description!
The meaning is "from afar indeed. ||35||

Nevertheless, O dear one, I shall proclaim the glory of Hari according to my understanding and as I have heard it, in order to honor my own speech which has been rendered false by the mention of others.

Śrīdhara: Friend Vidura, nevertheless, I shall proclaim the glory of Hari, just as I have heard it from the mouth of my guru. Yet even that not entirely, but according to my own intellect—that is, in accordance with my own understanding.
By "other designations" (anyābhidhā), meaning the naming of objects other than Hari, I [purify] my own speech which was otherwise untruthful and defiled.
To honor and to purify. ||36||
The composition of the sequence: *kīrtim* refers to speech or the organ of speech, consisting of descriptions such as that of the creation of the Virāṭ; ||36||

Viśvanātha: "Just as heard from the mouth of the guru" means exactly what was grasped by one's own intellect according to one's capacity, and not necessarily everything that was heard. [He says this] in order to honor his own speech—which might otherwise be considered "untrue" or defiled—by means of discourse other than that concerning Hari.
In order to purify. ||36||
They say that for men, the exclusive gain of speech is the praise of the virtues of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Suślokamauli),
when they are brought forth by the learned from the sacred revelation (Śruti).
The application [of this] in the nectar of stories.
Śrīdhara says: Even for one who recites or hears [this] according to their own understanding, even without full knowledge, liberation is certain;

thus he states: "They say there is a gain that is absolutely certain" regarding the hearing—that is, the ear—when it has been "rendered ready," meaning when it has been directed toward [the teaching]. This refers to its application in close proximity [to the object]. (37)
*Commentary on the Sequence (Kramasaṃdarbha):* "In solitude," etc. The sense is that this surpasses even the bliss of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
*Viśvanātha:* Because the ocean of Hari’s hardships and deaths is boundless, no one possesses knowledge of it in its entirety;
therefore, by merely hearing the recitation of whatever little is known of it, people attain their life's purpose and [glorify] Him.

He says that they attain [this]: they declare that "praise of qualities" (guṇavāda)—that is, the mere glorification of qualities—is exclusively a gain; the meaning is that everything else is merely a diminution of speech. Even for the ear—that is, for the listener—when [the praise] has been brought near, i.e., when it has been proclaimed, there is "application," which means its presentation in close proximity. ||37||
O child, the greatness of the Self has been determined by the ancient seer through his intellect ripened by yoga at the end of a thousand years.
Śrīdhara: One should not insist excessively upon knowledge, for even Brahman is difficult to know;

thus he says: "Has the majesty of the Self, Hari, been fully determined—that is, known—even by the Primordial Poet Brahmā, whose intellect was ripened through yoga, at the end of a thousand years? No, it has not.
By this intonation (*kākūkti*), it is stated that [the extent] is not known at all as being merely this much. ||38||

The sequential arrangement: "Of the Self" (referring to the verse beginning with *ātmanaḥ*) means that the majesty of the Supreme Self—consisting of inconceivable sovereignty and so forth—is realized at the end of a thousand years by the intellect alone when it has been matured through yoga; it is ascertained precisely as having inconceivable power. ||38||
Viśvanātha: One should not insist excessively upon knowledge, for even Brahman is difficult to know;

thus he says: "Has the majesty of Hari, the Self, been fully determined (avasita)—that is, known—even by the Primordial Poet Brahmā at the end of a thousand years, when his yoga has reached maturity? By this rhetorical question (kākūkti), it is implied that it is not [known] as being "this much."

The meaning is that [the greatness] is indeed known. Alternatively, because it is difficult to know due to its inconceivability and infinity, it is determined that the greatness [of the Lord] exists only at the end of a thousand years; the point is that this very knowledge of the Lord's greatness—knowledge in the form "this is so much" and "it is thus"—is precisely that [true] knowledge. And so:
The Śruti says: "The opinion of one who does not know it is as if it were the sixth of those who do not strive. (38)
Therefore, the illusory power of the Blessed One deludes even the masters of illusion;
for if the Self itself does not know its own path, how much less others?

"Brahmā does not know the Self of Madhu; I am Rudra. Because of the fullness of qualities, the word 'Self' refers to Brahmā, while because of his deficiency, it refers to Hara. Nevertheless, even these two do not know Hari, the Supreme. Thus it is said in the Brāhma [Purāṇa].

The illusion of the Blessed One, the majesty of the Blessed One. For it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Illusion (*māyā*) is declared to be majesty (*mahimā*), because the suffix *-mayaṭ* is used in the sense of abundance. The path of the Self is the state of the Supreme Self. (39)
Śrīdhara: Because even Hari himself, the Self, does not know this path of the Self—the course of His own Māyā—to be merely this much, owing to its infinity. ||39||

The sequence of the composition: Therefore, for those who determine [the Lord] as being merely an object of thought, the deluding *māyā* of the Blessed One becomes a source of delusion even for other masters of illusion (*māyin*). This is the meaning. For this reason, the connection with the half-verse is that "her *māyā* deludes even the masters of illusion. [This refers to] "of the Blessed One."

In this context, there is a reading "bhagavatī" in some places. He demonstrates the very nature of its inconceivability with the verse beginning "yad" (line 17), consisting of one and a half verses: because even he himself—the Self—does not know the sovereignty of the nature of the path, nor does he fully comprehend it even with omniscience due to its infinity; therefore, to him, there is only salutation.
The meaning. ||39||

Viśvanātha: Now, many philosophers are indeed seen who, knowing the reality of the Self, also cause others to know it; regarding them, he says—"Therefore" (ataḥ). For this reason, even among those [philosophers] who, being masters of illusion, impart only their own illusion to their disciples whom they intend to instruct, there is certainly a deluding power.

The sense is that she is *mohinī* (the deluder), intended to cast one down repeatedly into the cycles of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). For since even the Supreme Lord himself, though he is the Self, does not know his own path—that is, his own true nature—how much less could other wretched beings know it? ||39||
Since speech, together with the mind, turned back without reaching him—
as did I and these other gods— homage be to that Blessed One!

Śrīdhara: Therefore, because he is difficult to know, [the author] offers a simple salutation with the words "yataḥ" (from whom). Even the words, along with the mind, having set out for the sake of knowing him, returned without reaching him due to his difficulty to know.
Not only speech and mind, but I too—Rudra, the presiding deity of the ego (ahaṅkāra)—and these...
The deities who preside over the sense-faculties and others as well. ||40||
The sequence of the composition: he qualifies that very [reality] with the words "that from which," while some read "they turn back.

Viśvanātha: thus, establishing its very inscrutability, he offers salutation. "Without reaching the end"—meaning without having attained it—"from which" all [speech], both collective and individual, turns back.

The organs of speech along with the mind, as well as the minds themselves; or rather, all the Vedas that issued from the mouth of Brahman are "vācaḥ" (speeches), together with his very mind—[I am] Rudra, the presiding deity of ego (ahaṅkāra);
and these gods, Bṛhaspati and the others, turn back from there. Why? Because they have not reached it.

The meaning is: because of the inability to correctly grasp the sweetness of name, form, conduct, and so forth, and because of the capacity to reach the limit of those which are otherwise boundless. Scripture also declares: "From whence words return, together with the mind, not having attained it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1). Here, in this indication of the ablative case...
It should be understood that while there is indeed a cessation of speech and mind that indicates their union, it cannot be measured as something infinite;
however, one must not explain the Self as being entirely inaccessible to speech and the other senses, for it is said:
"And by all the Vedas, I alone am to be known" (Gītā 15.15).

For this would result in a contradiction with such scriptural passages as: "This immeasurable, eternal [reality] is to be perceived by the mind alone; the wise always behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.14). ||40||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, appropriately joined to the others, in this *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord; it is well-received by the virtuous.
Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras,
in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas, in the third book, in the dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava.
The Sixth Chapter.
The Seventh Chapter.
Śrī Śuka said:
To Maitreya who was speaking thus, the wise Vidura, son of Dvaipāyana,
replied with words that seemed to delight him.
Śrīdhara:
In the seventh [chapter], having rejoiced at the sage’s words which cut through doubt,
various questions were again properly posed by Kṣattrā.

Then, by means of the words beginning with "Now those [activities] of the Blessed One are augmented by *yogamāyā*" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.5.22), [the author]— as if pleasing Maitreya, who was speaking thus that the Blessed One performs creation and so forth through play (*līlā*) by means of the qualities of *māyā*— [proceeds] by way of an objection arising from a lack of understanding of the intended meaning. ||1||
The arrangement of the sequence: the word "iva" is used as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*). ||1||
Viśvanātha:

In the seventh [chapter], the cutting away of doubts regarding the Lord and the individual soul is presented; furthermore, other questions of Vidura, arising from a desire for devotion and inquiry, are proclaimed.
Thus:
"O fortunate one, that power of this observer, which consists of both being and non-being and is called Māyā, is by means of it that the Lord fashions this universe."

"O Brahmin, by speaking thus— beginning with the words, 'But through the operation of time, the powerful Adhokṣaja infused his seed into Māyā, which consists of the guṇas, by means of the Puruṣa who is his own self'— I have indeed been lifted out of the well of *saṃsāra* by you, O Bhāratī."
The meaning is that, because Vidura’s mental agitation was suddenly perceived by Maitreya as if [Kṛṣṇa] were pleasing him with sweet words, Kṛṣṇa was unable to please Maitreya. ||1||
Vidura said: O Brahmin, how could the qualities and actions of the Blessed One— who is pure consciousness alone, changeless, and devoid of attributes— even through sport, ever be joined with Him?

Śrīdhara: [The question is: "How can there be activity for one who is changeless, and qualities for one who is devoid of qualities? The statement that it is "by way of sport" (līlayā) removes the objection regarding the absence of a purpose, but it does not remove the contradiction regarding the nature of reality; this is the intended meaning. ||2||

The Sequence of Composition: Now, it has been stated that the Supreme Lord performs the creation and so forth of the universe through His inherent power of *māyā*, and that the individual soul (*jīva*) becomes deluded therein. He dispels the doubt regarding this matter by means of questions and answers, beginning with the word "O Brahman": "O Brahman! etc. O Brahman!

How [is this possible] for the Blessed One, who is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), by virtue of His own essential power (*svarūpaśakti*), and who is endowed with such sovereignty and other attributes residing in the glorious Vaikuṇṭha and other realms; who is therefore devoid of material qualities (*nirguṇa*) and untouched by the qualities of primordial nature (*prākṛtaguṇa*); and who, for that very reason, is immutable (*avikārin*)?

Since even infinite actions, which are the playful manifestations of such a nature and power, are eternally established within that ever-arising light of infinite variety, there is no occurrence of change for that which is changeless, just as there is no change for the agent who brings forth those various actions. Thus, it is "changeless" (*nirvikāra*).

How could qualities such as passion (*sattva*) and the rest, which belong to primordial nature (*prakṛti*), or how could activities such as establishing [the world], which have attachment to those qualities as their cause, be appropriate? Consequently, because they would contradict the reality that is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), neither those qualities nor those activities are tenable. Furthermore, even if he were the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*), they would not be tenable even through his own spontaneous activity.

Thus he says: "Or as a sport. Here, the opponent has raised the objection while accepting both [the Lord's] being pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*) and his being the Blessed One (*bhagavattva*), together with his changelessness (*avikāritva*) and freedom from qualities (*nirguṇatva*). ||2||
Viśvanātha: How can qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, as well as activities such as creation and so forth, belong to pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)?
In this regard, instead of employing terms such as "of the form of consciousness" (*cidrūpa*) or "consisting of consciousness" (*cinmaya*), he uses the term "of pure consciousness" (*cinmātrasya*).
By the use of the word *mātra* (merely), which expresses restriction, even the slightest trace of insentience (*acid-gandha*) is indicated as being absent therein;
consequently, because the phrase "she indeed belongs to him" describes Māyā— composed of the qualities of *sattva* and so forth—
as the power (*śakti*) of the Blessed Lord, and because it is impossible for a power to be distinct from its possessor, [she is] in reality...
One objection is this: "The qualities belong to Him alone. If He is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), how can He possess the inert qualities of *sattva* and so forth?

And if He possesses the inert qualities of *sattva* and so forth, how can He be pure consciousness? Furthermore, since modification is caused by time and is indeed a property of the qualities, if He is pure consciousness, He must be changeless. Thus there is a contradiction.
The second [objection] is: "How can there be the possession of activity that manifests transformation, and if there is the possession of activity, how can there be immutability? [To this we reply:
Indeed, even though qualities and activities are thus impossible for Him, they exist because of His playful freedom (*svairalīlatvāt*).

Could they possibly exist? To this he replies: "Or by way of sport" (*līlayā vā*). The point is that the contradiction cannot be resolved merely by saying "by way of sport," because if such an act were truly sport for Him, the possession of attributes (*guṇavattva*) would be difficult to avoid.
Here, the substantive "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavataḥ*) refers to the Blessed One as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone, and not to "fortune" (*bhaga*).
This must be stated, because even Bhaga’s status as Bhagavat— that is, his transcendence of the ordinary— is seen in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa,
as follows: "Knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor in their entirety..."
"Those things denoted by the word *bhagavat* are devoid of qualities (*guṇa*) and the like that are to be abandoned" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.5.79).

For this very reason, it has been stated that "this distinction between body and embodied being does not exist anywhere in the Lord. Therefore, even the sixfold sovereign powers denoted by the word *bhaga* are nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), and not—
The state of being the Blessed One (*bhagavattva*)—defined as the transformation of qualities such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth—is indeed the essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*).
Those who explain that the state of being the Blessed One is a non-essential definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) because it is illusory (*māyika*) are surely mistaken.
For when it is said, "This is Indra's illusion," or "By means of illusion, Indra becomes a bull," [it refers to] Indra's...

Just as the state of being a bull is perceived as something produced by His own *māyā* and not His actual nature as Indra, so too this *māyā* of the Blessed One is such that, by the statement "the Blessed One Himself becomes the universe through *māyā*," it follows logically that the Blessed One's possession of the universal form (*viśvarūpatva*) alone would be illusory, and not His status as the Blessed One.
The exertion of a child in play arises from desire, namely the wish to play;
but how could there be such exertion for one who is self-satisfied and eternally withdrawn from all else?

Śrīdhara: Even play is not appropriate for a child because of the resulting inequality; thus he says: "Udyama" means that which causes one to exert effort or engage in activity. In the case of a child's play, there exists desire (*kāma*) as the cause for engaging in it;
however, in other cases, his desire to play arises from another object or by being prompted by another child.

[The objection is: "How can there be desire for the Lord who is inherently satisfied? And how can there be a wish to sport with others for Him who is eternally withdrawn from anything else, detached, and non-dual? This is the meaning. ||3||
The sequential composition [of the argument] is as follows: Consequently, let there be the state of being the Blessed Lord (*bhagavattva*) for that whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*);

we have no doubt regarding that alone. However, the question is asked: "How is the acceptance of other qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth by that [consciousness] tenable? This is the meaning of the sentence. And thus, regarding its being pure consciousness...
Furthermore, if he were merely the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān), insubstantial qualities and actions would simply not be possible;

thus the question is raised with double force: "How could they even be joined [to him] as mere sport? He clarifies this with the words "In play," referring to a child who lacks those various excellences such as authority and so forth.

Desire takes the form of a wish to play; it serves as the cause for the exertion of another in play. But how could such desire arise from another in the case of the Blessed Lord, who is satisfied by the majesty of His own essential nature and is therefore eternally turned away from anything else? (3) [Paramātmasandarbha 85]

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, let it not be that the contradiction is resolved merely by the statement "by way of sport" (*līlayā*); rather, he states—with an illustration—that sport itself is not possible in the case of the Lord due to the absence of a cause, beginning with the words "In play" (*krīḍāyām*).
"Exertion" (*udyama*) means that which impels or initiates action; for a child, desire alone is the natural impulse toward play.
There is a cause for activity. Likewise, even the impelling of another fool [toward activity] on the part of the Supreme Lord is due to a desire to play (*cikrīḍiṣā*);

yet, since He delights in Himself (*ātmārāmatvāt*), how can there be desire, given the absence of another Lord? And how can there be a desire to play with another? To this he says: "Of Him who is self-satisfied," and so forth. [This refers to one] who has desisted from others.
Of that which is devoid of anything else. ||3||
The Blessed One created the universe by means of his own illusory power (māyā), which consists of the qualities (guṇas);
by that same power he maintains it, and he will again dissolve it.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding what was stated in the passage beginning with "Remembering the request made to Adhokṣaja by the Lord of the creators of the universe" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.6.1)— namely, that the Lord performs creation and so forth for the sake of the experience of the individual soul (jīva) who has ignorance as its limiting adjunct (upādhi)— he restates that very point in order to refute it:

Regarding the phrase "He created": by means of that *māyā* which consists of the three *guṇas* and which produces the delusion of agency, enjoyership, and so forth in the individual soul (*jīva*), He brought [the world] forth. This was stated in the first [chapter]:
"By which the *jīva* is deluded, [perceiving] himself as consisting of the three *guṇas*..."
"Even another person considers it an evil, and he accepts what was done by him" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.7.5), and so forth;

and here [it is said], "Therefore, the Māyā of the Blessed One deludes even the masters of illusion" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.6.39). He establishes and protects [the world]; and He will conceal it—that is, He will cause it to disappear—in the reverse order.
In another reading, he will maintain [the mantra] within himself in reverse order on all sides. ||4||

The sequence of the composition: Nor can it be denied that those qualities and those actions do not exist in Him, because they are well-known as being so; thus he says, "He created" (*asrākṣīt*). By means of *māyā*—which consists of the qualities (*guṇamayi*), which manifests the threefold nature (*traiguṇya*), and which is dependent upon the Self (*ātmāśritā*)—He establishes and protects [the world].
It will cover over, that is, it will render invisible by means of its contrary action. ||4||

Viśvanātha: Nor can it be denied that His qualities and actions are real, for they are well-established as such; thus he says, "He created," and so forth. He will conceal them again by way of reversal.
He will cause it to disappear. ||4||
How could that whose nature is unimpaired awareness— whether in terms of place, time, state, itself, or another— be joined with the Unconquered (Ajā)?

Regarding "madhvaḥ": since it resides within a body characterized by misfortune and suffering, it too ought to possess that [nature]. Yet, that is not tenable. This is indeed the Māyā of the Blessed One; for this is the greatness of the Blessed One.
What was stated—that miserliness, bondage, and so forth are not tenable for Him—is entirely correct. [This applies to] misfortune and the like.
The meaning is that even while residing within the body, his greatness consists precisely in being untouched by its defects.
How could the Lord, who is beyond the body, be tainted by those bonds?
How could he not be free from suffering? For if he were subject to suffering, how could he be the Sovereign?
This is the greatness of the Supreme: that though abiding in the body, he is not afflicted;
that though suffering, he is not the Lord—this is called "greatness" by way of illusion (māyā).
"They say that *maya* is the *pradhāna*; because of its predominance, it possesses the nature of *maya*. Thus says the Bhāllaveya Śruti.
Because his nature as consciousness is never lost, he does not possess a body made of *prakṛti*.
Creation and so forth are not his delusion; for those who speak of such delusions are indeed *dānavas*.
Therefore, no connection with delusion and the like is possible for this [Self] anywhere.
Through the knowledge of the Lord, the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (*jīva*)—which arises from delusion—is dissolved.
Delusion, which is the identification with the body and so forth, perishes through the knowledge of the Lord. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. (5)

Śrīdhara: And this would be possible if the individual soul (*jīva*) were the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*), but that is not possible; thus he says, "In terms of space" (*deśataḥ*). That Self which is the individual soul (*jīva*), whose consciousness is unobstructed by space and other such factors, is of the very nature of Brahman. How could it be joined with *ajayā* (the Unborn), i.e., ignorance? In that regard, [first] in terms of space...

There is no loss of it, as in the case of the light of a lamp, because it is all-pervading; nor is there loss from time, because it is eternal like lightning; nor is there loss from state, because it is changeless like memory; nor is there loss from itself, because it is real like a dream; nor is there loss from another, because it is non-dual like a jar or other objects. Thus, for whomsoever there is no such cognition [of these losses], [he is liberated].

If it is destroyed, how could it be joined with the unborn (*ajā*)? Furthermore, in this context, "the unborn" refers specifically to ignorance (*avidyā*), not to *māyā*, because there is no contradiction between [the destruction of ignorance] and its comprehension. ||5||

The sequence of the argument: How can the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) being deluded by *māyā* be logically consistent? To address this further objection, he says: "By way of space" (*deśataḥ*). How can that Self, which is the individual soul whose consciousness is unobstructed by space and other such factors, be joined with the unconquered ignorance (*avidyā*)? In that regard, [it might be argued] that it is due to spatial separation or due to defects inherent in space.

Or like the light of the eye, like lightning in terms of time, like memory in terms of state, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell in terms of its own nature, or like objects such as a jar in terms of something else—its realization is not lost; the meaning is that this is because it rests upon a knowledge whose very nature is unimpeded. ||5||

[Paramātma-sandarbha 87] Viśvanātha: He states another objection—beginning with "deśataḥ"—as to how it could be possible for the individual soul (jīva) to be deluded by *māyā*: "That Self, whose consciousness is never obscured by space and other such factors because of its eternal nature of knowledge..."

The meaning is: how could that *jīva* be joined with the unborn *avidyā*, and how could there be a loss of its awakening arising from union with the unborn? In this regard, [the relationship] is like a seed sown in a saline place spatially;
like lightning temporally; like memory in terms of state; like a dream intrinsically; and like a jar or other objects extrinsically.
The meaning is: how can he whose awakening cannot possibly be lost due to his being the very substance of consciousness be made to have his awareness eclipsed by ignorance? ||5||
The Blessed One is indeed one, abiding in all fields;
how could there be misfortune or affliction for him due to karmic actions?

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he raises an objection that because the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the very nature of Brahman, even its transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) does not exist; for although it is the experiencer residing in all fields (*kṣetra*), in reality it is the Lord alone, since there is no distinction from Him due to its being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). This being so, of this individual soul...
Misfortune, the loss of bliss and so forth, or affliction resulting from karma acting as a cause—how could these exist?
Because there is no connection with karma. Otherwise, such a consequence would apply to the Lord as well; this is the intended meaning.
This is the sequence of the composition. In that very context, the Blessed One states "He alone" to point out another contradiction: "This one..."

In this way, the Blessed One, though the Supreme Self, is present in all fields— that is, in the bodies of every individual soul. Given that this is so, how can there be misfortune for this very soul, which— just like the Blessed One— is characterized by the possession of knowledge that constitutes its essential nature as consciousness and is never subject to deviation?

The meaning is this: how could there be no loss of the knowledge and other qualities that constitute its very nature, nor any affliction caused by karma? For it is not logical that, when two things reside in the same water or similar medium, one is actually in contact with it while the other is not. 6.

Viśvanātha: Nor is this injustice—as if between a kingless realm and a dual monarchy—to be imagined, namely that the Unborn (Ajā) might overcome the innocent individual soul (jīva); thus he says: "In the fields, that is, the bodies, of all individual souls..."

The Blessed One alone is established as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*); he himself remains present, and not like a king who rules his kingdoms through the agency of his own representatives—this is the meaning. By saying "the one alone," even the suspicion of a dual sovereignty (*dvairājya*) is dispelled. Therefore, in that Blessed One, who protects all, [all things abide].
Even while remaining right here, how could there be misfortune for this living being, or the loss of bliss and other qualities, or suffering caused by actions rooted in ignorance? ||6||
O learned one, my mind is distressed by this crisis of ignorance;
