therefore, O All-pervading Lord, dispel this great mental dejection of ours.
Śrīdhara: Ignorance itself is the narrow and difficult pass; dispel—that is, cast away—that mental impurity which is delusion. (7)

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Ignorance itself is the narrow and difficult pass; dispel, drive away, that delusion therein—“naḥ” (us) is used in the plural according to the rule “when two [or more] are meant, the plural is used for *asmad*. ||7||
Śrī Śuka said: Thus urged by the Kṣatriya who desired to know the truth, the sage,
whose mind was fixed on the Blessed Lord and who was free from pride, replied as if smiling.
Śrīdhara: [The Lord] was urged—that is, challenged—and as if smiling, as if manifesting maturity; yet in reality, he was free from pride. ||8||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that the sage, thinking "How shall I resolve this matter regarding the mind of the Blessed One?", became intent on reflection and thus remembered the Blessed One; and immediately thereafter, he attained the realization of the truth.

The meaning is that, as if smiling and expressing outward astonishment, thinking, "Oh, how difficult it is to resolve these objections," he remains actually free from wonder, for these [objections] are indeed very easy to resolve. ||8||
Maitreya said:
This is indeed the illusory power (māyā) of the Blessed One, by which even that which is contradictory to logic is possible:
how could there be wretchedness or bondage for the Lord who is eternally liberated?

Śrīdhara: As for the claim that this *māyā* of the Lord, who possesses inconceivable power, is contradicted by logic (*tarka*), he restates that very contradiction through reasoning: "For a person who is already liberated, there is the bondage of ignorance and wretchedness. (9)

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Since even in the individual soul (*jīva*) pure consciousness alone is not possible, the state of being the Lord (*bhagavattva*) must indeed be accepted. Thus Śrī Maitreya said: "This [power]...
That by which the creation of the universe and so forth occurs, this is the power of the Lord known as *māyā*, whose nature is inconceivable.

The meaning is that *śakti* (power), which contradicts logic (*naya*) and reasoning (*tarka*) by virtue of being beyond reasoning (*tarkātīta*), is also "inconceivable" (*acintya*). Although both are thus inconceivable, nevertheless, because it is designated as the "māyā of the Blessed One," and because the essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*) is internal while *māyā* is external, [the former is primary].

The meaning is that he is not touched by the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, nor by their effects such as the [four] postures (*sthāpanā*) and so on. And this meaning is expressed through *tantra* (metonymy): that which, in whatever manner, is not in contradiction with the Blessed One is not made an object of contradiction by him. That which, by whomsoever, [is not contradicted] by the Blessed One...
"It is contradicted [by scripture], yet it is not rendered entirely devoid of an object. Likewise, in the sixth chapter, the ninth section:
"This yoga of yours appears difficult to comprehend, in that you, being without a refuge and without a body, [perceive] this..."
"Disregarding our conjunction, You, who are Yourself unchanging, being devoid of qualities, create, protect, and withdraw that which possesses qualities"—
this prose passage contradicts His being the agent of creation with qualities; yet, again—

Now, in this matter, we truly do not know whether Your Honor, like Devadatta, has fallen into the discharge of the modes of nature and, through dependence on others, reaps the fruit of your own good and evil deeds; or rather, whether you, delighting in the Self, tranquil by nature, and possessing correct vision, remain indifferent. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.9.35]

Thus, by means of this prose passage, having conceived the possibility of the Lord’s connection with the state of being an enjoyer— just like the individual soul (jīva)— due to His being the inner controller (antaryāmin) and His falling within the sphere of the manifestation of qualities (guṇavisarga),
[the author states]: "Indeed, there is no contradiction in both [states] existing in the Blessed One, who possesses an immeasurable multitude of qualities."

In the Lord, whose majesty is unfathomable, there is no occasion for dispute among those who rely on internal organs clouded by modern conceptualizations, conjectures, deliberations, fallacious proofs, sophistry, and sectarian scriptures—disputants who are difficult to restrain.

For when He, in whom all that consists of *māyā* has ceased, remains alone after withdrawing His own *māyā*, what purpose could possibly be "difficult to accomplish," since there is no duality of nature? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.9.36)

Thus, by means of this prose passage, it is established in various instances that the power [of Śiva] is indeed inconceivable (avitarkya) according to the Siddhānta; in each respective Siddhānta, it is joined with the quality of being an inconceivable power. Among these, the inconceivability of the power of essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*) is indicated by such qualifiers as "the Blessed One" (*bhagavatī*), while that of Māyā is likewise shown.

This is demonstrated by the passage ending with "ātmamāyam. In that context, because there is an absence of two distinct natures (*svarūpa*), the meaning is that even so, through inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*), neither the agency for various acts nor subordination thereto exists. Furthermore, as for the prose passage beginning with "samaviṣamamatīnām" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.9.37), even so—
It should be understood that you manifest in various ways according to the diverse levels of intellect among beings for the sake of their realization.

Regarding the phrase "as if difficult to comprehend" in the preceding prose section, "bodiless" (aśarīra) means without bodily movement, and "without refuge" (aśaraṇa) means without support such as the earth.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha tatra" and so forth, the phrase "svakṛta" (created by itself) should also be applied to that [Māyā] as its causal agency;

therefore, here too, the predominance of the power of its own nature (*svarūpa-śakti*) alone is demonstrated. For this very reason, in passages such as "That which is perceived apart from the object" (*ṛte 'rthaṃ yat pratīyeta*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.9.33), Māyā is shown to occupy the position of a mere appearance (*ābhāsa*).

Thus, the untouchability of the Blessed One has been demonstrated. This is made known by such passages as "You are the primordial Person directly" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.7.23) and by the statement "having cast aside Māyā through His power of consciousness" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.7.40). Furthermore, it is indicated by the verse: "And when He was facing her, Māyā became ashamed" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.7.47).

And thus, having resolved that contradiction regarding the Blessed Lord, he reconciles the connection of ignorance with the individual soul (*jīva*) by showing it to be inconceivable; he does so by means of the Lord's very *māyā*. As for the word "that" (*yat*):...

This very [term] is connected here by virtue of the sense, and is transformed into the instrumental case; that is, just as for the Lord— who is capable through His essential nature, knowledge, and so forth— and who is therefore liberated, there is "miserliness" (kārpaṇya),
which is the manifestation and concealment of this or that [power], so too is there "bondage."
And one enters the net consisting of qualities that has been displayed. Thus it is said:

"His sovereignty was destroyed by association with her" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.5.15). Having intended all this, the Śrutis also say: "He who, through Ajā, [united with] the Unborn" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.87.38).

And also: "In the beginning, devoid of fortune. Here, in this root verse, by the phrase "the Māyā of the Blessed One" (bhagavato māyā), it follows that the state of being the Blessed One (bhagavattva) is illusory (māyika). Just as in the case of "the Māyā of Indra," where his status as Indra is understood, so too should it be understood in the preceding instance. [Paramātma-sandarbha 25, 91]

Viśvanātha: This well-known Māyā of the Blessed One, whose sovereignty is inconceivable, is that which is contradicted by logic (*nyāya*) and reasoning (*tarka*); the meaning is that it is "unthinkable" (*atarkyā*). Although she herself is of the nature of the non-conscious (*acid-rūpā*), she is a power (*śakti*) precisely because [the Lord] is pure consciousness (*cin-mātra*); therefore, even her qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are indeed the qualities of the Blessed One himself.

It is said: even that [the world] is, in its essential nature, devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) according to the Blessed One. Just as for the sun, which is pure light, clouds, darkness, frost, and so forth—though they are contrary to light—belong to that very sun;

as it is said immediately following [the verse], "Just as they originate from the sun" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.31.15), and as it is said in the passage beginning, "Just as in the sky... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.31.16).

In the Fourth Canto, it is said: "He is beyond the darkness of the clouds and beyond light" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 4.31.17). And in the Tenth Canto, according to the words of Śrī Nārada: "One might think that He is enveloped by His own manifestations such as the vital breaths, just as the sun is obscured by clouds, frost, or eclipses. Even in this illustration, there is simply an inconceivability; it is exactly thus.

The activities such as the creation of the universe belong to the Lord alone, who is by his very nature changeless, through his power, which is indeed *māyā*; for there is no difference between power and the possessor of power. As it was said by the Lord:
"Nature (*prakṛti*) is whose material cause, and the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*) is whose support."
"Time is the manifestor of the existent; Brahman is that [existence]; but I am the triad.
Thus, having severed the doubt regarding the body of the Lord, that which was stated beginning with "by place, by time," and so forth, [is established].

With two and a half verses, [the author] cuts through even the doubt regarding the living being (jīva) as it pertains to the Lord (īśvara). That which consists of the wretchedness and other forms of helplessness of the living being—even though he is capable of experiencing the Lord’s own nature, knowledge, bliss, and so forth—and likewise the bondage of one who is already liberated: this is Māyā.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is a manifestation of *māyā*; the meaning is that this duality is based solely upon ignorance.

This is the point: you ask how the loss of knowledge occurs for the individual soul (*jīva*) through the Unborn (*ajā*); yet if that loss of knowledge were real, then even that Unborn, as the Lord’s own power (*svaśakti*), would have to be punished by the Lord.

It might be so; however, that is not at all true, just as a person, having forgotten a jeweled anklet even though it remains upon their heart, grieves thinking, "The anklet is not there. Or, just as one, under the influence of delusion, imagines, "I alone committed the theft," even though it was committed by another; and thereafter—
Just as that fruit of suffering given by the king's men is indeed experienced,

so too, due to the power of beginningless attachment to ignorance, the *jīva*— having forgotten its own knowledge and bliss and having attained identification with the body— suffers upon encountering bodily attributes such as misfortune and the like.

In that case, to whom should the fault be attributed? Here, because [the Lord] has lost His sovereignty through association with that [matter] and wanders in saṃsāra like a wretched wife, and so forth— given that some degree of sovereignty is still perceived—
the individual soul (jīva) is also referred to by the word "Lord" (īśvara).

Others, however, explain it thus: [the opponent] asks how that Supreme Self—the Self whose consciousness is undiminished in terms of space, time, and so forth, and who is of the nature of pure consciousness—is joined with ignorance;

and then, relying on the view of the opponent, he provides the answer to the opponent's question with the words "This very [ignorance] belongs to the Lord. This very [ignorance] belongs to the Lord...

It must be an illusion (māyā). The meaning is that such a question would not be possible without being deluded by illusion. For it contradicts logic (naya); he states this very contradiction of logic: if even the Lord, the Supreme Self, were a living soul (jīva) due to being deluded by illusion, then wretchedness and bondage would indeed [follow].

It is appropriate to say that the one and only pure consciousness, when deluded by *māyā*, is the *jīva*, and at that very same time, when undeluded, is the *paramātman*. For it is an extreme absurdity to claim that anyone can be simultaneously deluded and undeluded by their own *māyā*. Therefore, by those who...
Thus it is asked, and it is resolved through the creation of a difficult dilemma that those very people are to be known as deluded by *māyā*.

In reality, however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the individual self (*jīvātman*) are by their very nature mutually distinct, like the sun and its rays—two portions of consciousness (*caitanya*). They are like a shadow and a ray.

Just as from the sun itself there arise two rays equal to the sun, which are neither different from the sun nor non-different from it, even so the power of *māyā* and the power of the individual soul (*jīva*), though arisen from the Supreme Lord and beginningless, are indeed distinct by their very nature, despite being non-different [from Him]. And thus it is stated in the *Vaidyaka*: "The *prakṛti* belongs to the person..."

"It is eternally like the very shadow of the sun. And so says the Śruti: "Just as sparks fly forth from a fire" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20), in this very way [the individual soul arises] from the Self; thus the jīva is a power (śakti).
"This is the lower nature; but know that other than this is My higher nature..."
"O mighty-armed one, that which has become the life-force by which this world is sustained" (Gītā 7.5). Thus ends the ninth verse from the Śrī Gītāsūtra.
When, in the absence of an external object, a person’s misconception of the self is perceived by an observer as the cutting off of his own head and so forth; [that is the nature of error].

Śrīdhara: Here he provides an illustration: just as, for example, even without the actual severing of one's head or the like, a mere false misconception arises in the observer—the witness of the dream—that "my head has been severed," so it is in this case. ||10||

The Sequence of Composition: Furthermore, even though the individual soul (*jīva*) does not actually possess those various states, the perception of them occurs solely through the Lord’s *māyā*. He establishes this with an illustration: "That which, by means of that [māyā], even without an object... That is to say, although for the sake of that *māyā* there is no object, nevertheless... [the perception arises].

That object does not exist even in the three periods of time; nevertheless, there may be a misconception regarding the self (ātmaviparyaya)—namely, that form consisting of the conceit of "otherness" preceded by forgetfulness of the self, such as "I alone am the possessor of those attributes.
For in this way, the genitive case in the word *upadraṣṭuḥ* is used in the sense of the third case, referring to the individual soul (*jīva*).
In the state of dream, the individual soul (jīva) may even see such things as the cutting off of its own head; however,
it is the Māyā of the Lord that superimposes upon that [dreaming soul] an object of that form which is established elsewhere,
for "it is mere Māyā, because its true nature is entirely unmanifest" (Brahma Sūtra 3.2.3).
According to the *Nyāya* [system]:

Viśvanātha states that therein, by means of the beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*)— which is of the nature of darkness (*tamaḥ*) and stands behind the Blessed Lord— the individual souls (*jīvas*), who stand behind the Lord in the form of beginningless aversion, [are affected].
Regarding that knowledge which is obscured, its being a real entity (vastutva) is neither the cause nor is there any purpose for it;
rather, this is simply the nature of darkness (*tamas*) that it is obscured by the light of one whose brilliance has been diminished.

To this he says: "by which object" (*yad arthena*). That is to say, because [it is obscured] by an object (*artha*), which is to say, by a real entity (*vastu*), a cause (*kāraṇa*), and a purpose (*prayojana*).
Even without this person—the individual soul (jīva)—the perversion of the self (*ātmaviparyaya*), which is the loss of knowledge and bliss, is perceived.
Regarding the word *artha*: "The word *artha* is used for an object, wealth, a cause, and a thing;
it also denotes the meaning of words and the purpose [of an action] upon its cessation," according to the *Medinīkośa*.

Here is an illustration: for the seer who is the witness of the dream, even though the head exists nearby, the absence of the head is perceived in the state of dreaming, such that one thinks, "This head of mine has been cut off. In exactly the same way, although there is in reality no loss of knowledge, bliss, and so forth, such a loss is nevertheless perceived during the state of ignorance (avidyā).

Even by darkness, the luminosity of gold, silver, and the like is not destroyed, but is merely veiled; likewise, it should be understood that just as darkness is dispelled by a powerful light such as a ruby, so too is ignorance pierced by the living being who is devoted.

In the second interpretation, however, the very suspicion of bondage through ignorance regarding the Lord— the Supreme Self, who is perfect Being-Consciousness-Bliss, omniscient, and all-pervading— is itself a defect. Furthermore, the established doctrine that "He alone is the individual soul (jīvātman) when under ignorance, and He alone is the Supreme Self when ignorance has departed" is merely an outward-looking perspective.

However, he states that "by means of which object" (*yadarthena*) bondage belongs only to the individual soul (*jīva*), who is a distinct spark of consciousness born from the divine consciousness, who is not omniscient, and who is bound by ignorance through His *tāṭastha-śakti* (neutralizing power); and that this bondage is likewise unreal (*avastubhūta*). The explanation is exactly as before; it pertains only to this person, the *jīva*, and not to others.
"But [it belongs] to another, the Supreme Self, Hari, who has been experienced by us"—this is the meaning. ||10||
Just as the trembling and other qualities caused by that [water] are seen in the moon reflected in water,
though they do not exist [in the moon], so too the qualities of the non-self are seen by the observer, though they do not belong to the Self.

Śrīdhara: In that case, why would it not be perceived even for the Lord? To this he says: Just as the property of trembling and so forth, caused by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of water, is seen only in the moon reflected in water and not in the moon situated in the sky, so too, although the property of the non-self—the body and so forth—is unreal, it appears to the one who identifies with it.
The meaning is that [this applies] to the Self as the individual soul (jīva) who is the seer, and not to the Lord (īśvara). ||11||

The sequential arrangement: For this very reason, he establishes by means of another illustration that even for the soul (*jīva*), though it is pure, the acquisition of the attributes of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) occurs solely through its form conditioned by that adjunct—just as in the case of water.
Just as this attribute of trembling and so forth belongs only to the moon reflected in water, which is produced by the limiting adjunct consisting of the water.

It is seen, but not that which resides in space; likewise, although the attribute of the non-self— the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of *prakṛti*— does not belong to the pure self, yet through the illusion (*māyā*) of the identification "I am he," there occurs an identification with the limiting adjunct of *māyā*, whereby the state of egoity (*ahaṅkāra-bhāva*), which stands in the place of a reflection, [is perceived].
Although this [vision] might belong only to the seer who exists in internal or other such states,
the meaning is that because he perceives Him through the conceit of non-difference from that [pure state], it belongs to him alone. Nevertheless,
this was stated by the Blessed Lord in the Eleventh [Canto]:
"Seeing them dancing and singing, he likewise imitates them;
so too, seeing the qualities of the intellect (buddhi), though himself desireless, he is made to follow along.
Thus it has been said: "For the pure one perceives the impure agent. And here, the word *vi-* [in *vicaṣṭe*]...
The essential point is precisely that immersion (*āveśa*).

Therefore, because the Blessed One possesses an internal, great, and exceedingly powerful inconceivable nature, there is no creation by means of *māyā*, even though it is external, powerful, and inconceivable. However, for the individual soul (*jīva*), there is creation by that [māyā].

The established conclusion [is as follows]: ||11|| [Paramātma-sandarbha 92] Viśvanātha: Now, let it be granted that the individual soul (jīva) possesses the concealment of knowledge, bliss, and so forth; but from where did it acquire such qualities as passion, hatred, sorrow, delusion, and desire? To this, he says: "Just as... (yathā).

The meaning is this: although qualities such as grief and delusion belong only to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is non-self, they appear to belong to the witnessing self, the individual soul (*jīva*), even though they cannot truly exist there; they are perceived there due to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*). An illustration for the perception of the attributes of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) as residing in that which is so limited (*upahita*) is provided: as in water.

Thus, the trembling and so forth caused by that—produced by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of water—is perceived as belonging to the moon; however, in reality, it does not belong to the moon but to the water alone. This is the meaning: the moon that is seen in the water is merely a mass of rays from the lunar orb, and not the moon itself. For instance:
Although the rays of the moon, the sun, and so forth spread across water, land, trees, walls, stones, and the like, among these objects,
it is said by people to be a reflection only where there is clarity. For the moon is indeed perceived as being distinguished by its specific retinue,
such as a face, nose, hands, feet, ornaments, and vehicles.
It is experienced by the people there; for he is the very example of the Blessed One.

When pervaded by the mass of rays that constitute his own essential nature, he is experienced with varying degrees of distinctness by those situated somewhat near and those situated somewhat far, respectively.
The analogy of the supreme self (*paramātman*) and the analogy of Brahman are to be understood [in this way].
However, the mass of rays existing outside of that, which has the form of a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) in the shape of a mandala, is the analogy for the individual living beings (*jīva*).
As for the reflection of that which is seen in the water, it is perceived merely as a reflection, but not [as the original object].

In reality, even that reflection in the water is seen as nothing other than the actual mass of rays; therefore, just as that very [mass] is associated with the attributes of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of water, such as trembling and so forth,
so too is the *jīva* associated with the attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), such as grief, delusion, and so forth.
Due to superimposition upon that [Self], the rays spreading out from it in this and that direction should be understood as the illustrations for individual living beings. ||11||
Indeed, through the dharma of cessation, by the compassion of Vāsudeva,
and by the yoga of devotion to the Blessed One, he gradually disappears here.

Śrīdhara: He states the means for its cessation: "That indeed is a quality of the non-Self; by the dharma of cessation, and by Vāsudeva’s compassion, and through devotion (bhakti-yoga) toward Him, it becomes obscured and invisible. By the word "gradually" (śanaiḥ), it is meant that this occurs in accordance with the practice of the means. ||12||

The sequential composition: "That indeed" refers to that which, through the dharma of cessation—characterized by a desireless nature and the yoga of devotion—arises as the compassion of Vāsudeva; by that [compassion], and gradually according to the degrees of that compassion, [the veil] is withdrawn. ||12||

Viśvanātha: If that is so, how is the liberation of the individual soul (jīva) achieved? To this he says: "By the quality of the non-self" means by knowledge mixed with devotion (bhakti), which is produced by the dharma of cessation (nivṛtti-dharma).
Likewise, it is by the compassion of Vāsudeva arising through the mediation of His own devotee.

It is concealed by the yoga of devotion to the Blessed One. The meaning of the statement is that the means for its cessation must be either knowledge or [renunciation]. The word "gradually" (śanaiḥ) means according to the degree of the cessation of misfortune, in accordance with the practice of the means. ||12||
When the senses have ceased their activity and the seer dissolves into the Supreme Self, Hari,
then all afflictions vanish entirely, just as they do for one who is in deep sleep.
Madhva: Liberation is the human goal known as the cessation of the senses. ||13||

Śrīdhara: Then, in response to the expectation of when the cessation of all misfortunes occurs, he says: "When there is the cessation—that is, the immobility—of the senses; where? In the Seer, the Self in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin). Immediately thereafter, the illustration 'as for one who is fast asleep' refers merely to the dissolution of all afflictions (kleśa), and not [to the state] again."
In rising. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Then, in response to the expectation of when the cessation of all misfortunes occurs, he says: "When...
In that context, according to the view of knowledge (*jñāna*), the "cessation" (*uparama*) of the senses refers to their dissolution (*laya*) into the mental modifications (*manovṛtti*).

To exclude the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he says: "When the Lord Hari, the Supreme Brahman, the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) within the Self of the seer, is being experienced through devotion that is an auxiliary to knowledge"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The illustration concerns the mere dissolution of all afflictions; it is just as in the case of one who is fast asleep, having attained deep sleep.

The miseries arising from the loss of wealth, children, and so forth, dissolve. Then, when there is the cessation—that is, the immobility—of the senses, such as the eyes and ears, toward Hari, who is enchanting with His own beauty and other qualities, and who is related to the Blessed Lord; [this state arises] for one whose mind is fixed in devotion.

Their eyes, ears, nose, skin, tongue, and minds are entirely immersed in beauty, fragrance, delicacy, sweetness, and skill; they do not, however, desire to grasp the taste of ordinary forms, sounds, and so forth. In what manner is Hari the self of the seer?

The meaning is that they make their own devotee the object of their compassionate glance within the very nature of the Seer. Or, "in the Supreme" (pare) means in the Supreme Lord, who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). The illustration refers merely to the absence of afflictions;
it concerns one who is fast asleep, not one who is dreaming or one who has just awakened from sleep. As it is said of him:
The afflictions seen in dreams, such as the cutting off of one's own head and so forth, dissolve. ||13||
Hearing the recitation of the virtues of Murāri brings about the pacification of all afflictions without exception;
how much more so, then, [the sight of] his lotus-like feet?
Devoted to the service of others, she has attained her own self.

Śrīdhara: He shows the cessation of afflictions through the yoga of devotion in the verse beginning with "aśeṣa. "Recitation" refers to the recounting of the qualities, and "hearing" refers to listening to them. Since [afflictions] are removed when they have been attained within the self—that is, in the mind—through loving meditation that exceeds mere hearing and chanting, what need is there to mention the application of logical reasoning?

The sequential composition: "Aśeṣa... and so forth. Here, in the two verses beginning with "O Brahman" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.7.23), this is the intention of the first question. Regarding the prayer to the deities of the principles (*tattva*), you have expressed that by the power of devotion, the Blessed Lord engages in the pastimes consisting of the essence of *māyā* at the beginning of creation.

That too is untenable, because of the contradiction with the nature of reality and the contradiction of its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*). As for the two verses beginning with "deśataḥ" [BhāgP 3.7.56], they should be understood as further questions introduced by way of that context.
Now, the answer follows: the four-verse section consisting of the remaining knowledge to be taught.

It is precisely according to the meaning of the second verse. In that context, regarding the phrase "this very one" (*seyam*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—by the words "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavataḥ*) [BhāgP 3.7.9]—is that He alone possesses inconceivable power (*acintya-śaktitva*). Here, the capacity of the power known as devotion (*bhakti*) is also manifested; for, furthermore, he [the Lord] is indeed [attained] through the dharma of renunciation (*nivṛtti-dharma*).

By such passages as these, the secret doctrine along with its means has been taught; therein, how much more so, by the principle of "how much less" (*kaimutya*), the fruit of devotion to that service is not merely the pacification of all afflictions (*saṅkleśa*), but rather, according to the manner previously described—
And it is thus illuminated that this is indeed the subjugation of the illustrious Blessed One. ||14||

Viśvanātha: Now, between the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of devotion taught for the purpose of quelling ignorance, which of the two is superior? To that end, he says "Aśeṣa... and so forth, asserting that devotion alone is superior. The word *kiṃ vā* means "how much more so," or "furthermore. *Ratiḥ* in service means intense attachment. It is obtained by the Self.
By the phrase "attained by itself in itself," the fact that *rati* (devotional love) is unproduced is indicated through its self-luminous nature.

The sense is this: if even instrumental devotion (*sādhana-bhakti*) pacifies ignorance (*avidyā*), how much more so the *rati* which is its result? Thus, the primary fruit of *rati* is not merely the pacification of ignorance, but rather the subjugation of the Lord.
Vidura said:
"O Lord, my doubt has been severed by the well-spoken sword of your words;
yet, O Blessed One, my mind runs toward both sides."

Śrīdhara: Welcoming the reply, he reveals his own sense of fulfillment with six verses beginning with "sañchinna. "The doubt that I had—namely, 'Even though there is no difference in being of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), how is it that the Lord possesses the agency of creating the world and so forth, or how does the individual soul (jīva) undergo transmigratory existence?'—has been severed by your excellent statement."
The sword, which was indeed a blade with a logical justification, has been severed by him; therefore, my mind now runs toward and correctly enters into both [realms]:
the sovereign independence of the Lord and the dependence of the individual soul. Thus, how can there be bondage through ignorance for the Self, whose nature is unimpaired consciousness?
Or from what does its cessation arise? This is the doubt. "In both cases" means in both bondage and liberation. ||15||
The sequence of the composition: For this very reason, he says, "completely severed" (*sañchinna*). This refers to both [states]: in the Lord (*īśvara*) and in the individual soul (*jīva*).
Alternatively, it means in the love for knowledge consisting of theoretical and practical wisdom (*jñāna-vijñāna*), and in devotion (*bhakti*) which is the means to that [love].
It "rushes forward" (*saṃpradhāvati*), meaning it enters thoroughly. ||15||
Viśvanātha: That which is well-spoken by you to awaken me—yourself—is indeed the sword;
by means of it, one enters with discernment, rushing toward both [realms]: the Lord and the individual soul. ||15||
Well said, O learned one! This description of Hari’s self-māyā is not without purpose;
though it appears baseless, for that which is outside the root of the universe has no foundation.
That which has been uttered regarding the nature and capacity of Madhva is meaningless and baseless;

for that which appears as connected to the body does not exist outside of my knowledge of Brahman, the root of the universe. Therefore, it runs toward both [the internal and the external], and thus I am excluded from it.
Nevertheless, one should dispel that notion [of selfhood].
However, there is no falsehood in one who speaks of the absence of qualities in the Self;
for the *Vyāsasmṛti* states: "Even speaking of the absence of qualities to one who has not asked, when it is for the sake of self-restraint, leads indeed to spiritual merit."
"Even though he possesses direct experience, Vidura speaks otherwise:

'Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, the Pārthas, Bhīṣma, Vidura, and Sañjaya, as well as others there who were portions of the gods and possessed direct perception of reality'—thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. (1618)

Śrīdhara: Because you have spoken well. What is that? It is this—that which appears as misfortune and so forth—is the abode (*ayana*) of Hari’s power, namely his *ātmamāyā*, which is the *māyā* pertaining to the individual soul (*jīva*), and it has that as its support. For [this misfortune] is purposeless like the cutting off of one's own head; it is unreal and rootless.
And it is rootless; for its root—the root of the universe—is nothing other than one's own ignorance. ||16||

The sequential arrangement: he restates the very matter already determined as the cause for dispelling doubt with five verses beginning with "Sādhu. It has been rightly explained that the movement (*ayana*) of Hari’s inconceivable *māyā*, which is dependent upon the self, is indeed "good" (*sādhu*), because without [the self], it would be externally meaningless (*apārtha*).
Even for individual souls (jīvas), that ignorance which is non-substantial, rootless, the root of the universe, and the cause of superimposition does not exist. ||16||

Viśvanātha: But how have you understood my well-spoken words? To this he replies: "O Brahmin! You have spoken correctly; what is it that was said? This [universe] has its locus in that which is the external power of Hari, namely his own *māyā*. Even though the Blessed Lord is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)," [so it is said].

By those qualities, [the Lord] appears to possess excellence and to be the agent of creation and so forth. That this is "purposeless" (apārtha) means it is without motive, because He delights in His own Self (ātmārāma). That it is "rootless" (nirmūla) means it is without cause, because there is no other instigator for Him; thus, what has been spoken by you regarding the nature of the Lord is indeed inconceivable (atarkya). Likewise, this...
The bondage of ignorance for the individual soul (*jīva*), as well as the misfortune and other such states arising from it, are indeed the play of the Self’s own *māyā*.
It has been declared that what pertains to the *jīva* is purposeless, causeless, and unreal;
this statement by Vidura is made with double meaning (*tantra*). Furthermore, regarding that which is external—the universe which exists without [the intervention of] that *māyā* of the Self—

The sense is that since there is no fundamental cause [other than itself], the Lord’s possession of attributes and his agency as the creator of the universe are not established by his own essential nature. ||16||
He who is the most foolish in the world and he who has gone beyond the intellect—both of these prosper in happiness; the person situated between them suffers.
Śrīdhara says: "Because of my limited knowledge, a doubt previously arose in me"—thus he says, "And he who...

The meaning is that both he who is most deluded and attached to the body and so forth, and he who has attained the Lord who is beyond the intellect and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), thrive—that is, they live—in happiness, because of the absence of the affliction of doubt.

But he who, through the pursuit of suffering, desires to abandon conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), yet is unable to sustain it due to the absence of the experience of his own bliss—he, indeed, suffers; this is the meaning. ||17||
The sequence of composition: the most ignorant person, devoid of discrimination between the essential and the non-essential, prospers in ease;
the two [others] become free from doubt and affliction. The "interposed" (antarita) is the "doubtful" (saṃśayita). ||17||

Viśvanātha: He says that due to his limited knowledge, until this day he had remained submerged in the suffering of doubt—"I have reached the Lord who is beyond Prakṛti, whose intellect is attached to sense objects like a most deluded beast; may there be happiness for both of us."

Thus they prosper; because of the absence of the affliction of doubt, they increase through both the bliss of sense objects and the bliss of the Lord. But he who desires to abandon the phenomenal world through the contemplation of suffering, yet is unable to sustain that state due to the lack of attainment of devotion to the Blessed One—he is "intermediate," situated between the two, owing to the absence of both types of bliss.
Immersed in the ocean of doubt, one suffers. ||17||
Having ascertained the non-existence of objects, I shall dispel even that notion of a self which has been perceived,
by means of service to your feet.

Śrīdhara says: "But now I am one who has achieved his purpose, since my doubt has been severed by you; only the persistence of what was previously sublated remains, and even that will cease through your grace. Thus he says: "Not [of] the Self, but of the non-Self—the phenomenal world (prapañca)—there is the absence of reality, even though it is perceived; this is the meaning here."
It does not exist, but is a mere perception; by serving at your feet, I shall determine that and cast even that perception aside—the meaning being that I shall remove it. ||18||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, he says that even now a remnant of his suffering remains: [he perceives] the absence of reality (*arthābhāva*) in the self—that is, in the individual soul (*jīva*)—meaning the absence of actual misfortune and so forth.

Even though I have reached a firm conclusion through the doctrine uttered from your mouth, I shall not dispel—that is, I will not remove—that very non-perception of the non-existence of the object, even though it has been perceived. ||18||
By serving that Lord, the immutable enemy of Madhu,
there arises an intense and overflowing delight at His feet, which destroys all affliction.

Śrīdhara: The "Ratirāsa" at the feet of Madhudviṣ (the Enemy of Madhu) is an intense, irresistible, and natural festival of love. It is so called because it "torments," meaning it destroys or annihilates, the "vyasana"—that is, the cycle of worldly existence. 19.
The sequence of the composition: How much is required merely to dispel the perception of the phenomenal world?
For [it is said], "by whose service... and "the destroyer of addiction"—the meaning is that this is merely a secondary quality of Him.
Viśvanātha: He says "yat" (that) to show what is impossible for service to the Lord's devotees: "yat... [and so forth].

The Lord, who is immutable (*kūṭastha*), by virtue of being the Blessed One, pervades all time with a single form; for Amara states: "That which pervades time is called immutable. The *rāsa* dance of Madhudviṣ, the slayer of Madhu—performed with passion (*rati*) and the sentiment of devotion (*bhāva-bhakti*) at the feet of Madhusūdana, in order to destroy the worldly existence of his devotees as if it were the demon Madhu.

The collection of rasas such as the peaceful (śānta) and the servile (dāsya), arising from the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva) and so forth, is intense; by its own sweetness, it overwhelms all ordinary and extraordinary sweetness. Therefore, the objection regarding its lack of comprehension—namely, "How insignificant is this!"—is [set aside]; such is the meaning. ||19||
For those of meager austerity, service upon the paths to Vaikuṇṭha is indeed difficult to attain—
there, Janārdana, the God of gods, is eternally praised in song.

Śrīdhara says: "Aha! I have attained that which is difficult to obtain. He explains: *durāpā* means difficult to attain. It occurs on the great paths—that is, those things which serve as the way—to Vaikuṇṭha, Viṣṇu, or his world (*tal-loka*).
In these [paths], through service to the great, there arises the hearing of Hari’s stories; from that, love for Hari; and by that...
The intended meaning is that even the identification with the body and so forth ceases. ||20||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, he says that this very service to the Great One is exceedingly difficult to obtain: "For those of little austerity"—this is said according to worldly convention, because service to the Great One is obtainable solely through their grace and thus lacks the nature of being a fruit of austerity.

Having first created the Mahat-tattva and the other principles along with their modifications in due order, and having extracted the Virāṭ from them, the All-pervading Lord entered into it— He who is eternally present among His devotees who have become the pathways to Vaikuṇṭha during the state of practicing the means to that end.
"From the honey [of the Vedas], he created Virāj, the Brahman. "Viṣṇu, the thousand-eyed and thousand-footed, entered the Brahman," so it is said in the Brāhma [Purāṇa].
Having entered the Brahman, he likewise [created] the tenfold vital breath (prāṇa).
"Viṣṇu created the sense organs, the objects of the senses, and the social classes. Thus it is stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*. (21)

Śrīdhara: He restates what was said in order to ask about another point with three verses, beginning with "Having created... [He created] together with the modifications such as the senses. Having extracted those portions and created the Virāṭ, the sequence of events is as follows: having thus accomplished his purpose, out of delight, he [performed] the remainder of the pastimes previously heard.
He asks: "Having created... (verse 21).

Viśvanātha: Thus, having accomplished his purpose, he repeats what was said [by the Lord] in order to inquire with joy about the remaining characteristics previously heard: "Having created... (verse 21).
That which they call the Primal Person, with a thousand feet, thighs, and arms,
wherein all these worlds abide in full expansion.
Śrīdhara: He describes the form of [Viṣṇu] who has entered [the body] with the words "yam" (whom). He qualifies Virāj with the words "yatra" (wherein).
"Te ime viśve sarve lokāḥ" means all these worlds; "savikāśam" means without contraction. ||22||
The sequence of composition: [I bow to] Him who lies within the causal ocean and the waters of the womb. 22.
Viśvanātha: [He is] Viśvanātha, upon whom all rest while he lies in the causal ocean, because all the universes exist within the very pores of his body. (22)
In that [system] wherein the tenfold vital breath— consisting of the sense objects, the senses, and the threefold [prāṇa]—
is proclaimed by you, and from which the social classes (varṇas) arise, tell us of its manifestations.
Śrīdhara: [The breaths] are of ten kinds, namely the five beginning with prāṇa and the five beginning with nāga.

Furthermore, the repetition of the words "the senses" and "the objects and the senses" is for the purpose of indicating their presiding deities; thus, it is accompanied by them, because prāṇa is the nourisher of all.
That is their association. Thus, the threefold breath has been described by you as being triadic;
its manifestations, beginning with Brahmā, are denoted by the word "emission" (visarga). ||23||
The sequential arrangement: therein, he restates what was said there—"in which [form] Virāj... (23).

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, in that Virāj who is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*), there are the objects of the senses (*indriyārtha*) and the senses themselves, together with them. It is threefold (*trivṛt*) by way of *saha*, *ojas*, and *bala*. From it alone come the castes (*varṇa*), and from its specific manifestations alone come the Brahmins and the other classes. Now, [I shall describe] the glories (*vibhūti*) of that Supreme Lord.
The [sacrifices] beginning with that for Prajāpati, etc. ||23||
There, together with sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and kinsmen of the same lineage,
there were subjects of diverse forms by whom this world was pervaded.
Śrīdhara: In whom, in which [qualities], this universe is stretched out—that is, pervaded. ||24||
The sequential composition: "Since" refers to the grandsons, that is, the daughters' sons. ||24||
Viśvanātha: In that regard, among those manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*), by the grandsons and daughters' sons... [24]
He, the lord of the Prajāpatis, reflected upon which were the Prajāpatis,
as well as the primary creations and secondary creations, the Manus, and the lords of the Manvantaras;
he also considered their Vedas and the accounts of their lineages and deeds.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having been questioned in this manner in the past, the venerable Maitreya [BhāgP 3.1.1]—with which the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya is introduced as a response to the inquiry of Parīkṣit—therefore, he states those very questions posed by Vidura until the conclusion. [He was] the Lord of the Prajāpatis.

The connection [of the words] "Brahmā" and so forth is with the word "describe," which will be mentioned later. He "created" (cakre) means he fashioned; "ninefold creations" refers to the primary emanations, and "subsidiary creations" refers to their various subdivisions. ||25||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Because his heart was of the same nature [as Parīkṣit’s], Vidura also asks about the very same matters that were asked by Parīkṣit in the second book, continuing until the end of the chapter.
Brahmā, the Lord of the Prajāpatis, [created] the tenfold creations, the secondary creations, and their subdivisions. ||25||
O son of Mitrā, describe the configuration and the dimensions of those worlds that exist above and below the earth, as well as the measurements of the earthly realm (bhūrloka).
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: O son of Mitrā, "saṃsthām" means the arrangement or configuration. ||26||

The sequential arrangement has not been explained. Tell us the detailed classification of the creation of animals, humans, and gods; of reptiles and winged creatures; and of those born from the womb, from sweat, from eggs, and from sprouts.

Śrīdhara: "The arrangement and distribution of creations" refers to those born from the womb, those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and those born from sprouts. "Those born from the womb" (*gārbha*) are viviparous; "those born from sweat" (*sveda*) are those produced from two [moisture and heat]; and "those born from sprouts" (*udbhidaḥ*) are those [born from the earth].
Of these... [27]
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: *Saṃvyūha* means distribution. "Womb-born" refers to humans and others born from a womb;
"sweat-born" refers to those born from sweat and eggs, such as worms, gadflies, and so forth; and "egg-born" refers to birds.
"Udbhid" refers to trees, shrubs, and so forth; [the term refers] to them. ||27||
Describe the noble prowess of Śrīnivāsa, who, through the descents of his qualities, creates the universe as the locus for its creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [state that the Lord] creates the primary creations and so forth, as well as the locus [of the world].
The sequence of their arrangement has not been explained.
[He also creates] the divisions of caste and stage of life according to their form, character, and nature.
The births and deeds of the sages, and the extraction of the Veda.
The drawing out of the honey is its division. ||29||

Śrīdhara: "Form" (rūpa) means the physical mark; "conduct" (śīla) means behavior, which is one's inherent nature consisting of tranquility and so forth; from that [comes] "drawing away," meaning separation. ||29||
The sequence of composition: [He is] creating—that is, performing—the emanation and so forth, as well as their support and the form of Prajāpati and others. ||29||
Viśvanātha: Form is the physical mark; character is conduct, which is one's innate nature consisting of tranquility and so forth; by these, there is attraction and differentiation. ||29||
O Lord, [tell me] the expansion of sacrifice, the path of yoga,
and the system of both *naiṣkarmya* and *sāṅkhya*, as remembered by the Blessed One.

Śrīdhara: "Vitānāni" means expanses. And [he mentions] the paths (mārgān)—that is, the ways—of dispassion (naiṣkarmya), of knowledge (jñāna), and of Sāṅkhya which is its means, as well as the system (tantra). This is the meaning. ||30||
The sequential arrangement consists of seven [sections], beginning with the *varṇāśrama*. The tantra remembered by the Blessed One is known as the *Pañcarātra*. (30)

Viśvanātha: *Vitānāni* means expanses. He refers to the paths of the eightfold yoga (*yoga*), the paths of dispassion (*naiṣkarmya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), its means (*tadupāya*), and Sāṅkhya. The *tantra* remembered by the Blessed One is the *Nāradapañcarātra*. The particle *ca* (and) is used in the sense of "also. ||30||
The unevenness of the paths of heresy, dwelling in a state of perversion,
and all the various courses of the individual soul born of the qualities and their actions.
Śrīdhara: The path of the heretics is their engagement [in worldly activity]; that indeed is the imbalance. ||31||
The sequential arrangement: the placement and establishment of those born in the reverse order, such as the Sūta and others. ||31||

Viśvanātha: From the path of heresy—that is, for the reason of the heretical way—there is indeed the irregularity regarding the location and arrangement of those born in the inverse order, such as the Sūtas and others. ||31||
He [should teach] the means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa without mutual conflict,
as well as the distinct rules for commerce, the science of government, and sacred learning.
Śrīdhara: [He should employ] the causal signs and the means without mutual contradiction. ||32||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Causes (*nimittāni*) refer to the means (*upāyān*) for livelihood (*vārtā*), such as the treatises on agriculture, commerce, and so forth; [the means] for the science of polity (*daṇḍanīti*), that is, the science of statecraft (*arthaśāstra*); and for sacred learning (*śruta*).
Of the Vedic scripture. ||32||
O Brahmin, [tell me] the ritual for the *śrāddha* ceremony, the creation of the ancestors,
and the arrangement of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars according to the divisions of time.
Śrīdhara [describes] the arrangement of the planets and so forth within the Kālacakra. ||33||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding the duration of time—such as days, nights, months, and years—the stability or state of giving or austerity, and whatever fruit results from *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial rites and public works).
The duty of one who is living abroad, and that of a man in times of distress;
It has not been explained by anyone;
tell me, O sinless one, that by which Janārdana, the source of dharma, might be pleased, or by whom he is fully propitiated.
Śrīdhara: By whatever path one may be satisfied; "of whom" means of such persons as these. ||35||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thus, because it was said, "In this way, the vows of the higher and lower [deities] have been heard from the mouth of Vyāsa," although these have for the most part been understood, [the author speaks] for the sake of independence regarding the mere object to be known.

He asks about that by which one's own desired object is intended to be accomplished. The word "vā" (or) has the sense of "and"; the meaning is: "Janārdana is the source—that is, the cause—of all [desires], even while requesting the fulfillment of desires produced by a state of longing.
Alternatively, it means "afflicting those whose desires are produced by a pure state of being through the pain of remorse arising from love," according to the sequence [of the verses].
The meaning is: "What is the means for attaining grace toward Him, and what are the qualifications of those who are eligible for it? Tell me that. ||35||
O best of the twice-born, teachers who are compassionate toward the distressed may speak even without being asked to their disciples, sons, and those who follow the minor vows (anuvrata).

Śrīdhara: The sense is that even what has not been asked, yet is worthy of being told to me, should be spoken; this is the intent of the sequence of the composition, which has not been explained [by others]. Viśvanātha: Even though it is my own desire, I do not know what ought to be asked; therefore, you, honorable sirs...
Thus he spoke, saying, "Please tell me out of compassion": "O Blessed One, regarding those principles (tattvas) for the sake of those who follow them—of which kind is their dissolution?
And therein, who would attend to them, and who indeed would rest upon them?"

Śrīdhara: *Pratisaṅkrama* means dissolution (*pralaya*). In that dissolution, who are those who lie down after [the Lord], sleeping following Him as He lies down like a king followed by his fly-whisk bearers? [The answer is: "of the principles" (*tattvānām*). That is to say, among those dissolutions ending with *prakṛti*.
By this, the eternality of the attendants (*pārṣadas*) alone is intended. Thus it is said in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*:
"For his devotees do not fall away even in the great calamity of dissolution;
therefore, he alone is Acyuta (the Unfallen) in the entire world, the all-pervading and imperishable."
They lie dormant and remain latent. ||37||

Viśvanātha: Having asked about the devotion to the means (*sādhana-bhakti*), and setting aside the dispute regarding the eternality of the devotion to the goal (*sādhya-bhakti*), he asks about dissolution (*pralaya*) with the words "of the principles" (*tattvānām*). Dissolution is the process of re-absorption (*pratisaṅkrama*). In that dissolution, who would attend upon this Supreme Lord as He lies down, like those holding chowries for a king?
"Or what things lie down with one who lies down and sleep with one who sleeps?"—thus [it was said by] the venerable Śrīsvāmicaraṇa.

By this, the eternality of the Lord's attendants (*pārṣada*), their devotion, and that world is intended. For this very reason, it is well known: "And His devotees do not fall away even in the great calamity of dissolution."
This is a statement from the Kāśīkhaṇḍa. ||37||
The configuration or essential nature of the individual soul and of the Supreme,
as well as the knowledge derived from the Vedas— this is the purpose for both teacher and disciple.
Śrīdhara: The nature of the person (*puruṣa*) is the reality (*tattva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the essential form (*svarūpa*) of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
That by which there is oneness between the two, as well as knowledge [of this], is the scriptural [teaching] based on the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣada*). (38)

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: The constitution (*saṃsthāna*)—that is, the mode of existence or the essential nature (*tattva*)—of the person who worships; likewise, the true form (*svarūpa*) of the supreme Lord who is to be worshipped.

Likewise, regarding worship, there is the knowledge derived from the scriptures—that which is spoken in the Vedas—characterized by the thought: "May this disciple learn from me, his teacher, that which is for the purpose of both teacher and disciple; and may I, from the teacher, learn devotion. The causes for this are association with the virtuous and so forth. ||38||
And the signs for this have been proclaimed here by the faultless sages;
for how could men possess knowledge of themselves, or even devotion and dispassion?
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, explain those means for attaining that knowledge which have been proclaimed by the wise.
He says, "Not by itself," because this [knowledge] does not arise without a teacher. ||39||
The sequence of composition: "Of the person" (puruṣasya) and so on, for one and a half verses.

This refers to the configuration of the person who perceives primordial nature and the rest, in the form of "thousand-headed" and so forth; then, from that, the knowledge of the Supreme Lord Śrī Bhagavān in the form of inquiry—this constitutes the remaining half-verse. (39)
Viśvanātha: O sinless one, the wise (sūri), who possess faultless and discerning intellects, state that this does not occur without a guru; thus he says: "By itself" (svataḥ). ||39||
Out of friendship for me, who am ignorant and whose vision has been lost by Māyā, please answer these questions of mine as I ask them out of a desire to know the deeds of Hari.
Śrīdhara: Because of my friendship and affection for me, [you have asked]; thus, due to these different syntactical connections (*anvaya-bheda*), there is no tautology of the word "me" (*me*). ||40||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask, "In that case, how were so many various questions posed?
To this he says: "Out of a desire to know—that is, a desire for attainment—of the deeds of Hari, such as service and the like, [he asked] these..."

"Tell me my questions so that, when all that I desire to know is accomplished, my mind may become single-pointed and independent of anything else in the service of the Blessed One. The sense is that only when there is one-pointedness of mind is there attainment of Him; thus [He says] 'me' (for me), meaning 'in order to uplift me'."
The redundancy of the word *mitra* (friend) is not to be suspected; for the meaning is that since you are the son of Mitrā, you too are indeed a friend (*mitra*) to all the worlds. ||40||
O sinless one, all the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities,
and gifts do not equal even a fraction of the gift of safety to living beings.
Śrīdhara: [This refers to] the granting of fearlessness to living beings through the instruction of reality. ||41||
The sequence of the composition: the meaning is that [the Lord] grants fearlessness to living beings who are terrified here and there, and especially to those who are afraid of saṃsāra. ||41||
Viśvanātha: This is not only for the sake of my own deliverance, but also for the sake of your acquisition of merit and fame; thus he says—"All," etc. (41).
Śrī Śuka said: Thus questioned regarding the ancient lore by the foremost of the Kurus, that foremost of sages—
With his joy greatly increased by the discourse on the Blessed One, and being thus inspired, he spoke to him as if laughing.
Śrīdhara: That which is manifested (*prakāśate*) in the Purāṇa is the "Purāṇakalpa," the subject matter desired to be known;
this Purāṇakalpa was questioned by that preeminent sage. ||42||
The sequential arrangement: that in which the ancient ritual procedure is inquired about. ||42||

Viśvanātha: He is called *purāṇakalpa* because he is capable (*kalpate*)—that is, competent—to explain the Purāṇas and the essential meanings of the Purāṇas. He is thus "the one who is questioned and is a master of the Purāṇas. Regarding the phrase "as if laughing," the actual meaning is that he was distinguished by a smile arising from joy. ||42||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, perfectly concluded for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.

Thus, in the glorious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, in the commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*, in the collection pertaining to the state of the Supreme Swan (*pāramahaṃsya*) within the work of Vyāsa, in the third book,
in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
The Seventh Chapter.
Maitreya said: "Ah, how worthy of service is the lineage of Pūru!"
He who was a guardian of the world and the foremost of the Blessed Ones has now become one who constantly renews, at every step, the garland of unconquered fame here on earth.
Śrīdhara:
In the eighth [kalpa], Brahmā was born from the navel of the Lord reclining upon the waters;
not knowing him and fearing the water, he nourished that powerful one through austerity.
He greets the listener. He is worthy of being served by the virtuous. Oh, how wonderful!

For, since you, the protector of the world, Dharmarāja, were born—that is, you arose—in this lineage; what kind of person are you? One for whom the Blessed Lord himself is the primary object of devotion. The reason for this is stated: "by Ajita," and so forth.
At every moment you renew yourself; you make yourself ever new. ||1||

The sequential arrangement: Thus, at the end of the second book, having spoken this much of the text—which contains the essence of the greatness of the four verses intended to introduce the statement "Now hear the Pādma-kalpa"—he speaks of that very [kalpa] with the words beginning "So I... regarding the Bhāgavata.
The meaning is that it is a specific type of Bhāgavata [Purāṇa] composed by Saṃkarṣaṇa and others. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the eighth [chapter], the four-faced Brahmā, born from the lotus-navel of Śrī Hari,
ceased his searching and, having attained samādhi, gazed upon Him.

"O Vidura! 'And I shall cast that [ignorance] away through service at your feet,' and so forth; and with the words, 'Whence can men have knowledge by themselves? and so on, you pray for my association. But in my view, direct association with you is extremely difficult to attain; by what crest-jewel among the great virtuous could it be obtained?"
Praising Vidura and expressing his joy, he says: "Ah! How wonderful! By her, this birth has been made meaningful;
even the lineage of Pūru has been rendered worthy of being served by the virtuous, since you were born therein."

Of what nature is he? Among the three—the Brahman, the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān)—who are the objects of worship according to different philosophical views, he is one for whom the Blessed Lord alone is the primary one.
Furthermore, even among the worshippers of the Blessed Lord here, he is one who constantly, at every moment, [wears] a garland of the fame of the Unconquered (Ajitakīrti).

The sense is this: I merely string together this garland of fame with the needle of my own tongue; you, however, by placing it within the interior of your ears and mind—which are exceedingly affectionate and full of love—render it eternally fresh. Thus, your greatness is truly ineffable. ||1||
Therefore, for the sake of the minor happiness of men who have fallen into great suffering, and for the cessation of that suffering,
I shall set forth this Bhāgavata Purāṇa.
As the Blessed One himself said directly to the seers:
Śrīdhara: For those who have encountered great suffering for the sake of a small pleasure, I set forth—that is, I begin—this work for the cessation of that suffering. ||2||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha says: "Since the answers to all your questions are found in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, a Purāṇa, I shall simply inform you of that particular good fortune"—thus he speaks, referring to that which is well-known.

I am a disciple of Parāśara. For the sake of "trivial happiness"—that is, for the sake of the insignificant pleasure of sense-objects—and for the sake of that suffering such as hell and the like, people perform actions for the purpose of happiness. Regarding this matter, whatever is appropriate, may the Blessed One say; whether or not [this is so], this very point is also appropriate as an answer to your initial question.
It has been stated that it becomes superior. ||2||
To the primordial Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, the god of unimpeded being, seated upon the earth,
they approached with the desire to know the reality that lies beyond him.
The preeminent sages questioned the prince.

Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry—"Who is this Blessed One? To which sages did he speak? And how was it obtained by you?"—he says, "Seated... and so on, in seven verses. [He is seated] upon the earth, in the subterranean realm (pātāla), possessing unshakable strength and unimpeded knowledge; therefore, he is superior to Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Of the illustrious Vāsudeva. ||3||
The sequential arrangement: "Seated" constitutes a group of four [verses]. "Wearing a crown," etc., is an epithet of Saṃkarṣaṇa. ||3||

Viśvanātha: In response to the inquiry—"Who is this Blessed One? To which sages did he speak? And how was it obtained by you?"—he says, "Seated... and so on, in seven verses. On the earth—that is, in the subterranean realm (pātāla)—he sat with unimpeded being (*akuṇṭhasattva*), meaning his nature is pure goodness (*śuddhasattva*) or his knowledge is unobstructed. Therefore...
Of Śrī Vāsudeva, who is beyond Saṃkarṣaṇa. ||3||
When they speak of him who is named Vāsudeva— him who highly values his own very abode,
whose lotus-bud of eyes is slightly turned inward—
Opening [the eyes] for the arising of the wise.
Madhva: The term *ādhāra* denotes the support, the substratum, the seat, and the receptacle; such is the definition.

Śrīdhara: He qualifies that very [support]—[the Lord] who, having experienced His own seat, His own support known as Vāsudeva, which is of the nature of supreme bliss, upon the path of meditation, honors it highly.

He worships with supreme excellence; he slightly opens his lotus-bud eyes, which were previously turned inward and withdrawn, casting a glance of compassion for the sake of the exaltation of Sanatkumāra and others. ||4||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He further qualifies that very [object]: "honoring their own *dhiṣṇya*," meaning highly venerating their own foundational reality (*āśrayatattva*) with supreme excellence; what is that? To this he says: "that which... (*yad*).
"Drawn inward" means turned toward the interior;

the meaning is that this is for the sake of experiencing the bliss of the nature of Vāsudeva. Furthermore, "even slightly" is said for the sake of the spiritual advancement of the wise, such as Sanatkumāra and others. ||4||

The daughters of the serpent king worship that lotus which serves as a footrest for him, while they themselves perform ritual ablutions with the masses of their own matted locks, moistened by the waters of the celestial river.
Those seeking boons [worship] with various offerings accompanied by love.
Śrīdhara: [He provides] a qualification of the sages with a half-verse: "moistened by the waters of the celestial river.

The sense is that as they descend from Satyaloka to Pātāla for the purpose of hearing the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, they descend continuously right through the middle of the Gaṅgā. [The phrase] "in which lotus" refers to that upon which their feet are placed.
Touching it and bowing down, they worship that lotus with various offerings so that it may be accompanied by love; they do so seeking boons, desiring husbands. (5)

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: He qualifies the sages with [the following] one and a half verses. By the phrase "moistened by the waves of the celestial river," it is meant that as they descend continuously from Satyaloka to Pātāla for the purpose of hearing the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, [they are so drenched].
The sense is that they descended right into the middle of the Gaṅgā. "Upadhāna" means a pillow. "Varārthāḥ" means those desiring a husband. ||5||
Those who know him, repeatedly praising his deeds with words full of devotion and faltering steps,
[worship] that crown of a thousand excellent jewels.
Whose thousand fierce hoods were illuminated.
Śrīdhara: [They] sing of the deeds performed; by what? By speech in which the words falter due to passion. Those who know them are "knowers thereof" (*tajjñāḥ*). A "thousand" is *sāhasra*;
that which is illuminated by the finest gems—the most excellent jewels—within the thousand crowns (*kirīṭa*).
The connection with the preceding verse is: "They questioned him who possessed a thousand of wildly expanded hoods. ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [The devotees] recite the deeds performed. By what? By speech in which the words falter due to passion (*anurāga*). "Those who know them" (*tajjñāḥ*) refers to the feet of the Master (*svāmī*), according to the *Svāmicaraṇa*. [The deeds] performed...
A thousand pastimes indeed constitute a *sāhasra*; therein, by means of "maṇipravekaiḥ," that is, the foremost jewels—Amara states:
"The words *mukhya*, *varya*, *vareṇya*, *praveka*, *anuttama*, and *uttama* [all mean] 'foremost'. This connects with the preceding verse as "they asked. ||6||
This was indeed proclaimed by the Most Blessed One to Sanatkumāra,
who was devoted to the dharma of cessation;
and he, being questioned, spoke it.
O Sāṅkhyāyana, O you who uphold your vows!
Śrīdhara: It was taught by that Saṃkarṣaṇa to Sanatkumāra. ||7||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: By that Saṃkarṣaṇa [it was told] to Sanatkumāra; the suffix *tamap* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*) to mean "most venerable" (*bhagavattama*). Alternatively, it means "the most excellent among the venerable ones (*bhagavat*) who possess knowledge of the origin and so forth of the world. (7)
Sāṅkhyāyana, the foremost of the paramahaṃsas, desiring to speak of the Lord’s glories, spoke them to our teacher, who was well-prepared to receive them.
And then [the knowledge] of Parāśara and Bṛhaspati.

Śrīdhara: [He is] preeminent in the dharma of the paramahaṃsas. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in *vivakṣamāṇa* is used because the substitute root *vac*, which replaces *brū*, is conjugated in both voices (*ubhayapadin*). [The term] *anvitāya* means "to the one who has followed. ||8||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: [This is] for Bṛhaspati, from Bṛhaspati. ||8||
That compassionate sage, having been told by Pulastya in the past, related this primordial Purāṇa to me;
O child, I shall now relate it to you.
To one who is faithful and constantly devoted to his vows.

Śrīdhara states that regarding the phrase "spoken by Pulastya," there is this narrative: having heard that his father had been devoured by a Rākṣasa, Parāśara was about to engage in a sacrifice against the Rākṣasas, but he desisted at the word of Vasiṣṭha;
thereafter, Pulastya, pleased with him for protecting his own lineage, granted him a boon.
"You shall become a proclaimer of the Purāṇas. ||9||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding the statement that "that Parāśara was told [the story] by Pulastya," this is the narrative: having heard that his father had been devoured by a *rākṣasa*, Parāśara, following the words of Vasiṣṭha, engaged in a *rākṣasa-satra* (a sacrifice for the destruction of demons).
Then, having desisted from that [destruction], Pulastya, being pleased because his own lineage had been protected, granted him a boon, saying: "Be a narrator of the Purāṇas. (9)
Then this entire universe was submerged in water,
which the One, reclining upon the couch of the serpent king with eyes closed in sleep, caused to close.
Having found the opportune moment, he is free from desire, delighting in his own self.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having demonstrated the transmission of the tradition from Saṃkarṣaṇa, he speaks of the Lotus-born (Brahmā) in order to describe his manifestations: "When [the world] was submerged and immersed in the waters of the single ocean, then Śrī Nārāyaṇa, with eyes closed and his power of consciousness unobscured, [remained] in his eyes..."

The meaning is that he closed his eyes. Having abandoned the diversion of *māyā*, he took delight in his own self, having made a festival of the bliss of his true nature (*svarūpānanda*). For this very reason, he was *nirīha*, which is to say, inactive. ||10||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Having thus demonstrated the transmission of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* from Saṃkarṣaṇa, he begins that [narrative] which is difficult [to understand]: "At that time, it was submerged, that is, immersed in the waters of the single ocean (*ekārṇava*)."

It was so. When? At the time of the occasional dissolution (*naimittika-pralaya*), when Śrī Nārāyaṇa, lying within the cosmic egg (*garbhoda-śāyin*), whose vision was unblinking and whose power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) was unobscured, closed His eyes—this is the meaning.
The word *talpe* is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). "In dalliance" means during the act of sporting together with His own selves, that is, His inherent potencies (*svarūpa-śakti*).
Having celebrated the festival, he became free from worldly effort, having abandoned all expectation of gain. ||10||
Having placed the subtle elements within his body and activating the power whose nature is Time,
he dwelt in that water upon his own station.
Just as fire has its power obstructed within wood.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, the impelling of the power of time (kāla-śakti) is for the purpose of awakening [the Lord] at the occasion of creation. "In His own station" means in His own abode. The absence of external activity is illustrated by the example: "just as fire. ||11||

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, in order to describe his manifestations (*vibhūti*), he sets forth that very Purāṇa, beginning with the words "submerged in water" (*udāpluta*) and continuing with "the universe here [consists of] the three worlds, which is within him" (*viśvam atra lokatrayaṃ so'ntar iti*). Regarding the phrase "the subtle elements of the beings" (*bhūtasūkṣma*), [it refers to] those accompanied by the *tanmātra*s of the dissolved earthly portions of the living beings residing in the three worlds.

The subtle bodies (*liṅgaśarīra*) alone are to be known; they are precisely what is called the "collective subtle body" (*samaṣṭiliṅgaśarīra*), because water and other elements exist outside the three worlds. It is for the purpose of depositing these [elements] within the internal body that [the Lord], by means of the power of solidifying water—beginning with the phrase "consisting of time"—lies within the waters.

Because it is beyond the range of vision for those residing in Maharloka and other higher worlds situated outside, it has therefore emerged from that water whose mass of waves is tossed by the winds at the end of the Yuga; and since it will be stated later that "He rests upon the lotus," the analogy of fire should be understood as being applicable here as well. ||11||
Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask, what is the state of the living beings residing in the three worlds at that time?

To this he says: "He by whom the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣmāṇi*)—that is, the subtle bodies of gods, humans, and others throughout the three worlds—have been deposited within the body, specifically in the midst of the body of Śrī. In what manner?
Therefore, he says: impelling— that is, setting in motion— his own power which consists of time and has the form of time,

by the force of His will, at the very moment the dissolution begins, He destroys all the gross bodies of those residing in the three worlds and consigns their subtle bodies (liṅgaśarīra) into the internal body of the Lord.
The meaning is that these very [elements] are what they call the collective subtle body (*samaṣṭiliṅgaśarīra*).

Being thus situated in his own place—the netherworld (*pātālatala*), which is his own abode—he dwelt even though submerged in the waters of the single ocean, by virtue of his power to solidify water. And as for his being beyond the range of vision for those dwelling in Maharloka and the other higher worlds, there is this illustration:
Just as in the case of fire. ||11||

And for a thousand cycles of the four ages, sleeping within the waters, he brings the mechanism of karma under his control by means of his own power, which he himself has uttered and is known as Time.
He beheld all the worlds contained within his own body.
Śrīdhara: Accompanied by His own power of consciousness (cicchakti), He was sleeping in yogic slumber (yoganidrā).

Having been brought to or reached by His own power of time (kālaśakti), which had been previously appointed for the purpose of awakening Him, He beheld the collection of karmas (karmatantra)—the aggregate of activities—which were "drunk up," that is, dissolved. ||12||
The sequence of composition: he by whom the system of karma, which was obtained immediately after the dream, has been joined to living beings. ||12||

Viśvanātha: He states how long he rested in this manner with the words "four," etc. The meaning is that while awake along with his own active power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), he was as if sleeping; and while lying down along with his dormant power of illusion (*māyāśakti*), he was indeed asleep. Consequently, at the time of the conclusion of the dissolution (*pralaya*), by means of his own power called Time (*kāla*):

He is one by whom [the world] has been brought forth for the sake of enjoyments and so on, and joined to the individual souls residing within himself, each according to its own karma; and therefore, he beheld even the worlds— from Brahmā down to the stationary beings—
as having come into his own self in a subtle form, in order to cause them to move while remaining himself inactive.
Such is the intended meaning. ||12||
The object internalized by that one whose vision is intent upon subtle objects is extremely subtle;
it is pierced by the quality (guṇa) following after time.
Then the vital air burst forth from the region of the navel.
"Madhvaḥ": "The lotus, which had been dried up by the wind, became split open by the waters; thus [it was said] in the *Padma-purāṇa*.
Śrīdhara: "One whose vision is intent upon the subtle reality for the sake of the creation of the world;
being pierced—that is, agitated—by the quality of *rajas* conforming to time, [he perceives] the most minute, that is, extremely subtle, object."
The meaning is that he has emerged from the region of the navel, being about to be born, about to give birth, or about to arise. ||13||
The sequence of composition: "sūṣyan" means about to produce its own effect; "abhidyata" means manifested, that is, arisen and increased. ||13||
