Viśvanātha: Following the logic of the aforementioned support (*poṣanyāya*), he says: "Of that Nārāyaṇa, whose vision has entered into the subtle objects—that is, into all the *liṅga-dehas* (subtle bodies) of living beings—with the desire to extract [the soul], the object situated within that [vision] is a particular material entity (*prākṛtapadārthaviśeṣa*) that is exceedingly minute."

Though exceedingly subtle, he was pierced by the quality of passion (rajas) which follows time; thus agitated, and about to be born and to emerge, he burst forth from the region of the navel and ascended upwards.
That lotus bud suddenly rose up through the power of karma ripening in due time;
by its own radiance, it illuminated that vast expanse of water.
Illuminating like the sun, which is its own source.
The self of the honey is Viṣṇu; his source is this. ||14||

Śrīdhara: That extremely subtle object arose as a lotus bud, awakened by Time (*kāla*), which brings to fruition the actions (*karma*) of living beings through their unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). Its source (*yoni*) is the Self, Śrī Viṣṇu.
[Commentary on the sequence: This lotus bud was indeed born from something other than the navel-lotus of Nārāyaṇa.
Because it consists of ordinary meaning. ||14||

Viśvanātha: That object (the egg), having become a lotus bud over time, arose from the waters of the great ocean of dissolution and remained in the region above; it is called "like the sun" because the Self, Śrī Viṣṇu, is its source (yoni) and because He awakens the karmas—the unseen potencies (adṛṣṭa) of living beings.
The meaning is that since he shines by his own radiance alone, there is no need for another sun to illuminate him. ||14||
Viṣṇu himself entered that world-lotus, which illuminates all qualities;
within it, the Creator himself, consisting of the Vedas, [resided].
He became that one whom they call the Self-Existent (Svayambhū).
From Madhva, who resides in the lotus [of the heart] of Hari, the four-faced Brahmā was born there;
he is the manifestation of all qualities and has the earth as his essence,
for it is in the earth that all qualities such as sound and the rest are manifested.
"For the purpose of providing a seat for him, the earth is called a lotus," so it is said in the *Mokṣadharma*. (15)

Śrīdhara: That lotus, which consists of those worlds, illuminates all qualities and objects of enjoyment for living beings; thus it is so called. He from whom that [lotus] was born is indeed Viṣṇu. The syllable *u* is used as an address.
"He entered" (*prāvīviśat*) means that he, whose power is unimpaired, entered by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). Into that [lotus].

Upon the lotus presided over by Viṣṇu, the Creator Brahmā came into being. Of what nature was he? He was composed of the Vedas themselves, not one who had acquired the Vedas through study. Who was he? He is the one whom they call Svayambhū (the Self-Existent) because he has no seen father; at the end of the previous kalpa, he had become one with Nārāyaṇa through sleep.
And when he had awakened, he attained manifestation through the gateway of the lotus in that very Padma-kalpa; such is the meaning. ||15||
The sequence of the composition: "In that world," etc. He, being Viṣṇu himself reclining upon the waters of the cosmic egg (*garbhodaka*), is the Lord of the Universe (*viśvanātha*).

And therefore, "that world-lotus" means the Virāj, who is the self of the worlds. The particle *u* is used as an address. He alone, at the commencement of dissolution, is he whose very belly is the Vairāja.

He entered in a subtle form. And at the end of the dissolution, that very Vairāja Viṣṇu, who lies within the Garbhoda ocean, manifested in the form of a lotus and entered—that is, he entered as the inner controller (antaryāmin)—the word "entered" being used in its own sense with the suffix *nic*. Of what kind was the lotus? [It was] of all the qualities and the effects of those qualities.

In that lotus, where there is the manifestation—that is, the illumination—of the enjoyments of living beings such as heaven, hell, and so forth, was the Creator Brahmā. Who is he? He is the one whom they call Svayambhū because he has no visible progenitor;
at the end of the previous kalpa, he had become one with Nārāyaṇa through sleep. In that [lotus]...

When [the Self] is awakened—for this very reason, the meaning is that it is manifested through the door of the lotus—here one should understand the threefold nature of Brahman itself: as the gross Vairāja, the subtle Hiraṇyagarbha, and the four-faced creator of the world and so forth. ||15||
Remaining upon that lotus pericarp and not seeing the world,
he wandered about in the sky with his eyes turned upward.
He obtained four faces directed toward each of the cardinal directions.
Śrīdhara: And he says that in that kalpa he became the four-faced one (Brahmā)—"in her" (tasyām).
While circumambulating, remaining right there, he was one whose eyes were turned and moved for the purpose of looking at the world as he shook his neck. ||16||
The sequence of events: wandering and revolving in that very place, with eyes rolling and panting from the longing to see [him] simultaneously in the four directions, he obtained four faces. (16)

Viśvanātha: While still standing there, as he circumambulated and turned his neck to observe the world, he simultaneously cast his gaze into the four directions; because of the solitude of the sky, with his eyes turned toward the mere expanse of space, he directed his vision in the four quarters and thus obtained four faces. ||16||
Therefore, having resorted to the lotus that has emerged from the water whose waves are tossed by the winds at the end of the eon,
one perceives the true nature of the world.
The primordial god did not truly know himself.

Śrīdhara: In order to state that his status as the creator of the world arises from the power of knowledge and action manifested solely through the worship of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, and not by himself, [the author] first describes his delusion: "From that water, the lotus (*kañja*) emerged and rose up; even though he resorted to that lotus in its entirety..."
He did not directly perceive the reality of the world nor his own self. The word *u* expresses astonishment.

Of what nature was [the ocean]? It was one in which a circle of waves (*ūrmicakra*) arose from all sides, because it was tossed and shaken here and there by the wind at the end of the age (*yugāntaśvasana*), the wind of universal dissolution. ||17||
The sequential arrangement: "grown from the water. This is because even above the space where the illustrious Nārāyaṇa lies, it remains uncovered. ||17||

Viśvanātha: In order to make known among the worlds that the power of Brahmā for creation and so forth arises solely through the power granted by the Lord and not from himself, [the Lord] speaks of the delusion of Brahmā, even though he was already skilled in the arts of creation and so on practiced in previous lives. "Tasmāt salilāt" means resting upon the lotus that had sprouted and emerged from that water. "U" is an exclamation.
In the midst of the world's astonishment, he did not perceive the reality of the waters, nor the reality of the Self; from what kind of water?
From that which was like the end of a Yuga—the "Yugānta-śvasana," the wind of universal dissolution. ||17||
Who is this one who says "I am," seated upon the surface of the lotus?
And from where does this lotus come, which is not distinct from the waters?
For indeed, there is something here beneath it.
Wherever one dwells, one must surely be virtuous.
Regarding the word *madhvaḥ*: according to the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa], it signifies the primary [reality] as "one, non-dual, and absolute by itself.
It is with the existent Brahman; for the *Maitrāyaṇīya Śruti* states: "That Brahman reflected: 'From what source might there be a lotus for Brahmā? (18)
Śrīdhara: He describes the reflection of that ignorant being: "Who is this who am I upon the back of the lotus?
From where has this single, non-dual lotus arisen? Surely there must exist someone beneath it by whom this [lotus] is presided over. Thus he looked upward.
The connection is with what follows. And thus says the Śruti: "He saw [it] while standing upon the lotus-leaf;
he thought: 'There exists that upon which this rests. (18)
The sequential arrangement: "Who is this?"—this constitutes a pair of verses (yugmaka). ||18||
Viśvanātha states the reasoning of that ignorant one: "Who am I on the back of this lotus?
What is this, from where, or from what has this lotus arisen? It is non-dual and indeed one. Furthermore, there is certainly some substance here below upon which this lotus is situated."

Therefore, being one who ought to experience that which is to be experienced by a wise person (*sudhī*), I, the wise, the learned, the enlightened (as stated in the *Amara-kośa*: "a wise person, a scholar, an enlightened one"), having thus gazed upwards—this connects with what follows. And so says the Śruti: "He saw [it] while standing upon the lotus leaf; he thought: 'That exists in which this [universe] resides.'"
"He presides over," so it is said. ||18||
Having gazed upward in this manner, he entered into the water through the hollows of those lotus stalks;
yet he did not go further inward than the interior of that harsh lotus stalk.
Searching the navel, he found that which was ageless.

Śrīdhara: And he states that due to his outward-directed activity, even after a long time, that [state] was not attained—by means of two verses beginning with "saḥ" (he). "Of that lotus-stalk," meaning by the channels and internal cavities of its stalk;
"of that lotus-stalk," meaning the base or foundation of the stalk of that lotus.
Searching, even though he had gone as far as the lower limit, he did not find it then.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Demonstrating that without the will of the Blessed One, the effort of a person possessed of egoism would lead only to futility, he says—"He [by means of] *nālībhiḥ*, i.e., by the openings of the channels (*nāḍī*)."

Even though he had gone as far as the base—the very foundation—of the stalk of that lotus with a harsh stem, namely the lotus from the navel of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, he did not find it; that is, he did not reach it. The sense is that without devotion, its attainment is impossible. ||19||
In the shoreless darkness, as he searched for his own creation, there arose a vast wheel with three rims,
which stirs up fear in those who possess bodies.
The weapon of the Unborn consumes his lifespan.

Śrīdhara: O Vidura, "ātmasargam" means his own cause. "Triṇemiḥ" refers to Time (Kāla). "Hetiḥ" of the unborn Viṣṇu is the weapon in the form of the Sudarśana discus. By saying "inspiring fear in embodied beings," it is implied that [this period lasts] for a hundred years. ||20||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Ātmasvarga" means one's own cause; "trinemi" refers to Time (*kāla*). That Time, which impels—that is, announces—the fear of death and the proximity of the end of life for embodied beings, namely men. *Āyuḥ* (life).
"Parikṣiṇoti" means that which consists of a hundred years; "the weapon of Aja Viṣṇu" refers to the essential nature of a portion of the Sudarśana weapon. ||20||
Then, having turned back without having attained his desire, that god returned to his own abode; slowly, with his mind withdrawn through mastery over his breath, he remained there.
He sat down, having ascended to the practice of meditative absorption.
Śrīdhara: He describes how he beheld the Lord through inward-turned vision with two verses.

Thereupon, he desisted from his search. "By whom desire—the longing of the mind—was not attained. His own abode is the lotus. "He whose mind was restrained, having been turned back by conquered breath," therefore...

Having thus ascended—that is, having relied upon—the yoga of meditative absorption (samādhi), being in such a state, he sat down, that is, he took his seat; this is the sequence of the composition. The phrase "one who has ascended the yoga of meditative absorption" implies a general form of aspiration preceded by the hope: "May whatever object may be the cause of all things manifest within me."

In this context, the application of concentration (samādhi-yoga) should be understood as the state of functioning non-differently from that [object], due to the absence of knowledge regarding specific forms. ||21||

Viśvanātha: He describes the attainment [of the goal] by him who has abandoned self-conceit, through the Lord’s will and meditation upon Him—from that searching. With his mind withdrawn and his thoughts restrained, he sat down—that is, he settled—upon his own seat, the lotus. Samādhi is that which arises from meditation on the Blessed One.
One-pointedness of mind. ||21||
In time, through a full human lifespan spent in the practice of yoga, his awakening blossomed;
he himself beheld that which was shining within his own heart.
He saw what had never been seen before.

Śrīdhara: He is one whose awakening has grown—that is, arisen—by means of that yoga which was fully perfected over a period of a hundred years, the lifespan of a man. That which he had previously not seen even while investigating it, he now saw manifesting of its own accord within his own heart. 22.

Regarding the sequence of the composition: it should be understood that Śrī Maitreya speaks of "a hundred years" as the lifespan of a person with reference to the current Kali Yuga. In reality, however, in the tenth chapter of the subsequent text, following the words of the Blessed Lord, "Perform great austerity," and so forth, [the lifespan is different].

By the statement, "Viriñca likewise performed penance for a hundred divine years" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.10.4), this very point is to be understood. However, that which was stated in the second book, "for a thousand divine years" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.9.8) and so forth, is to be understood as pertaining to the Brāhma-kalpa. ||22||

Viśvanātha: It should be understood that Maitreya says "by a human lifespan," meaning by a period of time consisting of a hundred years, with reference to the current Kali Yuga. "By means of fully engaged yoga" means by meditation on the Lord which has reached the stage of maturation. "In meditation, he was shown to us"—that is, to his devotees.

As stated above, although he previously searched for that which is the presiding seat of his own lotus-feet and did not see it, he now saw it manifesting of its own accord within his own heart. ||22||
A single person was lying upon a couch formed by the coils of the serpent Śeṣa, white as a lotus stalk,
his head adorned with a thousand jewels that served as a parasol of hoods.
By days, the darkness was destroyed in the waters at the end of the age.

Śrīdhara: He describes what he saw with nine verses beginning with "mṛṇāla-". The phrase "he saw" is to be supplied to each of the nine [verses]. Upon that very couch, which was the body (*bhoga*)—the serpent Śeṣa—who was both fair-complexioned like a lotus stalk (*mṛṇāla*) and long; where situated? On the couch (*paryaṅka*).

Those whose heads are covered on all sides by ten thousand parasols formed by hoods, and whose crowns are set with jewels— the darkness was dispelled by the splendors of those gems amidst the waters at the end of the eon.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He describes that very subject with nine verses: "His hoods themselves are ten thousand parasols;
by the splendors—the radiance—of the crest-jewels, the gems situated upon their heads, the darkness is destroyed."
In the waters of universal dissolution. ||23||
Casting its gaze upon the mountain of green emerald, which has the twilight clouds for its lower garment and a vast golden summit,
and which possesses jewels, oceans, medicinal herbs, and fragrant flowers;
He whose feet are like the branches of bamboo trees, adorned with garlands of forest flowers.
Śrīdhara: Of what nature is the person? He is one who eclipses—the very splendor of a mountain of emerald stones, a peak composed of emerald rock—by means of his own extraordinary beauty;
he eclipses the beauty of one whose lower garment is the twilight cloud.
[He is] casting [light] with his yellow garment; with his own crowns upon that mountain which has many golden peaks and a broad golden summit;
he whose forest-garlands (*vanamālā*)—consisting of jewels, streams, medicinal herbs, and *saumanasya* flowers (or rather, clusters of flowers themselves)—are like flutes.
He whose arms are like branches (*bhūjā*) and whose feet are indeed like tree-stumps (*aṅghripā*), that is he; and of him [is this].
This is the meaning: if the jewels and so forth are situated upon him like garlands, and the bamboos are like his arms, and the trees are like his feet, then [one perceives] his splendor.
...as if casting away [the world] with his arms and feet, which were adorned with garlands of his own jewels, pearls, and *tulasī* flowers. ||24||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "dispelling the *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the mountain of emerald"—that is, the fancy that "Is this a mountain consisting of emerald gems?"—is itself a *utprekṣā*.
The meaning is that he surpasses even her by the excellence of his own beauty; that is, he is incomparable.

Of what nature is he? The meaning is that he casts aside the clouds of twilight—which are like a girdle (*nīvī*) upon his hips—with his own yellow garment (*pītāmbara*); this is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). On his heads are great golden crowns as if they were diadems.
"Of him whose [peaks]," meaning his own crowns; "of him who has forest-garlands," meaning forest-wreaths consisting of jewels, secondary gems, medicinal herbs,
and clusters of flowers (*saumanasya*), that is,
by means of his own jewel-necklaces, pearl necklaces, *tulasī* garlands, and flower garlands— the term "forest-garland" (*vanasrak*) being used here to denote these.

Because it is stated as merely a "garland" (*mālā*). Alternatively, in both cases—whether [the compound is] *ratnādibhir vanasrag yasya* ("one who has a forest-garland made of jewels, etc. or otherwise—it should be explained that there is only one forest-garland (*vanamālā*). According to the definition of a forest-garland as "a garland consisting of leaves and flowers reaching down to the feet," it should be understood that the mention of jewels, pearls, and so forth is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). The bamboo [flutes] are situated above.
"Of him whose lower parts are like arms and whose feet are like trees"—that is, by means of his own arms and feet. (24)
In length and breadth, according to his own measure,
he encompasses the three worlds with his body,
adorned with various divine ornaments and garments.
Whose body and attire were graced by the splendor of his royal office.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "by means of his own body as a measure" (*svamānadehena*) means that which measures by way of length (*āyāmataḥ*) and breadth (*vistarataḥ*). It is a "measure" (*māna*) because one is measured by it; it is a "comparison" (*amāna*) because it is beautiful and without comparison (*nirupama*), thus a "body that is a beautiful comparison. Alternatively, it is a "body that is perfectly immeasurable" (*suṣṭhu amānaḥ*), being unlimited. Or else, it is "by those two [length and breadth] through a proportionate measurement" (*svānurūpapramāṇena*).

For this very reason, the three worlds are contained within him; likewise, he is distinguished by that body which possesses a splendor (*śrī*) created all around by various, manifold, divine, and unprecedented ornaments and garments. Thus, although he is exceedingly beautiful by his very nature, he has adopted an external appearance.
He saw him whose body was adorned with ornaments; or rather, in response to the expectation "by what [did he see him]? the connection is that he saw him by means of such a body. ||25||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon. *Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, [he is] that which is measured by its own proportions—meaning having a measure corresponding to itself—in terms of length (*āyāma*) and breadth (*vistara*); and who, by virtue of being situated within the body, is distinguished by being well-measured through union (*śleṣa*), that is, immeasurable or unlimited.

By this, he clarifies his lack of limitation: by one who has created the splendor—the beauty—of various divine, supermundane ornaments and garments through the inclusion of the three worlds, which pervade the triple universe; likewise, by one whose effort—that is, his desire—is directed toward bestowing [them] upon others. As soon as [he saw] whom...
The meaning is that because his resolve is true, he obtains whatever form he desires at that very moment. ||25||
To those men who worship the lotus feet of the Wish-Fulfilling Tree by means of solitary paths for the sake of their own desires,
he compassionately reveals his moon-like nails.
Whose beautiful petals are the fingers parted by rays of light.
Madhva: Distinct, that is, different from others. ||26||

Śrīdhara: [He is] showing His lotus feet, which grant all desires to those men who worship Him through pure and solitary paths prescribed by the Vedas for the sake of their desired fruits; [showing them] while slightly raising and offering them. The nails themselves are moons; their rays are the beams of light, by which—
The fingers themselves are divided and joined; that which possesses beautiful petals [is the hand]. ||26||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "For his own desire" means for the fruit he himself desires; or rather, "his own" refers to the Lord (*bhagavān*) himself who is the desire, meaning for the sake of attaining the Lord alone; [or] for the desire of the Lord himself.

Or rather, [the purpose is] to gladden the Blessed One with services; by means of solitary paths— pure because they are unmixed with knowledge, ritual action, and so forth— or by means of paths consisting of the states of servitude, friendship, and so on, which are free from passion and the like, one serves the "wish-fulfilling cow" (kāmadugha), which fulfills the desires suitable for service.

He is shown raising and displaying one foot-lotus slightly from among his thousand foot-lotuses; for there, by the use of the singular number in the word "pādapadma" (foot-lotus) in the subsequent verse [beginning with] "mukhena," and by the stylistic indication within this very context through the three verses beginning with "puṃsām," [it is established].

The vision of the descent of Śrī Kṛṣṇa was indeed shown to Brahmā; regarding that, it is said in the Gopālatāpanī Upaniṣad (1.26): "That Brāhmaṇa, meditated upon and praised by me incessantly, became awakened at the end of a parārdha, and He appeared before me in the guise of a cowherd.
Thus says the Gopālatāpanī Śruti.

"And because of the vision of the narrative in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*. Some say this refers to the vision of the lifting of the lotus-foot of that very form of Madanagopāla, the Tribhaṅga-mūrti, whose feet are crossed, specifically his right foot. [The phrase] "the beautiful fingers, pierced and intermingled by the rays of the moon-like nails," is explained as follows:
"Of which the petals are such"—thus, the marvelous nature of this lotus is stated because it has been caused to blossom by the rays of the moon. ||26||
With a face that dispels the suffering of the world with its smile, adorned with shimmering earrings,
and made crimson by the luster of his bimba-fruit-like lower lip;
Honoring him with her beautiful nose and lovely eyebrows.

Śrīdhara: [He is] one who honors his worshippers with a smile that removes the suffering of the world, which is adorned by two shimmering earrings, by the luster of his bimba-like lower lip acting like a red hue,
and by a beautiful nose and lovely eyebrows.
One who honors and shows respect. ||27||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He is honoring those worshippers by returning their honors; since he does not personally appropriate their enjoyments or liberation, the meaning is that he is, as it were, clearing his debt of service to them through that very act.

That is merely the pain of longing to behold her, or the affliction of yearning for her who possesses beautiful eyebrows—a single eyebrow that reveals the secret state of love and is thus worthy of being honored; by this, it is indicated that she is indeed a special devotee. ||27||
O child, he is beautifully adorned with a garment as tawny as the filaments of the kadamba flower, with a girdle upon his hips,
and with a necklace of infinite value.
By him who cherishes the Śrīvatsa upon the surface of his chest.

Śrīdhara: [His body] is well-adorned at the waist by a garment that is tawny like the filaments of a *kadamba* flower and by a girdle. O child! The meaning is that his chest is well-adorned with a priceless necklace upon the breast, which is dear to the Śrīvatsa mark located there. ||28||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: O child! O Vidura! [By] the necklace, which is dear to that chest marked with the Śrīvatsa. (28)
The lord of the world-tree, whose thousand branches are his thousand arms adorned with supreme armlets and excellent jewels, whose root is the Unmanifest, and whose feet are the worlds.
Its branches were entwined by the coils of the lords of serpents.
"From that, the unmanifest, consisting of the three qualities, was produced, O best of the twice-born," thus it is said in the Mokṣadharma [of the Mahābhārata]. (29)

Śrīdhara: He qualifies Him with the metaphor of a great sandalwood tree. His thousand—meaning infinite—arms, which are like branches, are strewn over and pervaded by excellent (*parārdhya*) armlets (*keyūra*), bracelets (*aṅgada*), and the finest gems (*maṇipraveka*).
Even the sandalwood tree has its branches covered with fruits, flowers, and the like, which are comparable to armlets and other ornaments.

Its root—the unmanifest *pradhāna*—is its lower part; or rather, its root is the unmanifest Brahman, because it takes the form of the manifestation of Brahman. Even the root of a tree is not manifest.

The Lord of the feet (Viṣṇu), whose nature is the world, whose branches— meaning trunks or limbs— are encircled, entwined, or touched by the coils, hoods, or body-parts of Ananta, the Lord of Serpents;
for according to the Vedic revelation, "O Lord of the Forest, grow forth with a hundred branches" (Ṛgveda 3.8.4), he too is surrounded by serpents.
He becomes enveloped. ||29||

The sequential composition [of the commentary] begins with the phrase "having the unmanifest as its root" (*avyaktamūlam*). This means that its root is not manifested—that is, it is not described—by those learned in the scriptures; the sense is that, as the root of all, it is devoid of any other root.
Alternatively, it means that the Lord himself, being unmanifest, is its root, [just as he is the root] of the trees whose forms are the worlds.
Indra, the Lord. ||29||

Viśvanātha: Because he has perfumed the entire universe with the fragrance of his own glory, he is described by way of the metaphor of a great sandalwood tree; he qualifies that [tree] as follows: it is one whose thousand—meaning infinite—branches are its outstretched arms that pervade the universe. It is unmanifest...

Even by way of suggestion (*vyañjanayā*), it has not been stated by anyone that He has no root because He is beginningless; as it is said: "That Self is the support of His own support. This is clear in the case of the tree. Furthermore, He protects—that is, guards—the fourteen worlds with but a single foot, and He is also Indra, the possessor of sovereignty (*aiśvaryavān*).

The meaning is "the lord of the majesty of a single foot. Alternatively, among the worlds, those which are "feet" (aṅghripās)—of them he is the "Indra" (lord). He is one whose "branches" (valśāḥ), that is, trunks, are "enveloped" (adhivītāḥ)—touched—by the "coils" (bhogaiḥ) or hoods of the Lord of Serpents, Ananta; as it is said: "He grows with a hundred branches" (Ṛgveda 3.8.4).
From the scripture; in the alternative case, [the tree] has its trunk and branches entwined by many snakes. ||29||
O Blessed One, [I bow to] the mountain that is the abode of moving and unmoving beings,
the kinsman of the lord of serpents, embraced by the waters,
and possessing a thousand golden peaks like crowns.
Manifesting with the Kaustubha jewel within its breast.

Śrīdhara: In the phrase "casting down his gaze," although [the mountain] has already been described by means of the metaphor of a mountain, he describes it again with further qualifying attributes. The Blessed One himself is the mountain (*mahīdhra*);
he is the abode (*okaḥ*) or dwelling place of all moving and unmoving beings, and that [mountain] is likewise. He is the kinsman of the lord of serpents (*ahīndra*), and that too is likewise.
He is the kinsman of the lords of serpents. He is enveloped and covered by the waters. The mountain Maināka and others are likewise [so covered].

He whose golden peaks are indeed a thousand crowns—Meru and other mountains are likewise [so adorned]. Just as a jewel manifests somewhere within the womb of a mountain, so too does he manifest clearly.
One in whose womb—that is, within whose form—the Kaustubha jewel is seen. ||30||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Having described [the Lord] by means of the metaphor of a sandalwood tree, he now describes him by means of the metaphor of a sandalwood mountain (*candanaparvata*) in order to show that his own support is also himself; the Blessed One alone is the mountain.

Malayagiri— the abode and refuge of all moving and unmoving beings— is embraced by the serpent-king Ananta and other lords of serpents with the Garbhoda and Kṣīroda oceans; it is he whose thousand peaks are golden-hued,
for the peaks of the Malaya mountain are of a golden color.
He who has the Kaustubha jewel within his womb—that is, in the midst of his form—because Mount Malaya, being a mine of jewels, possesses the nature of a mountain. ||30||
[He saw] Hari, who wears as a forest garland his own fame— which possesses the beauty of the traditional Vedic honey-bees—
and who is unapproachable by the sun, moon, wind, or fire, yet is present through his three abodes.
It was difficult to approach because of the warriors moving about in their chariots.

Brahmā beheld Viṣṇu, who is composed of the three abodes, surrounded by the primary elements— such as Sūrya, Candra, Vāyu, Agni, and others— who had come forth, and by the liberated beings such as Vāyu and others.
"Because there was no other existence apart from that, he desired to create that [world] from it. Thus, in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. (31)

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he was "encircled by a forest garland," meaning covered by one hanging from his neck. The Vedas themselves are the honey-bees; she who possesses beauty (*śrī*) through them is [the goddess Śrī]. Thus, he saw Him in the form of a mountain and so forth, and realized, "This is Hari"—this is the meaning. He was "unapproachable" even by the sun and other celestial bodies.

The meaning is that [the Lord] cannot be encompassed by His own activities. Furthermore, [He is surrounded] by those whose splendor—that is, manifestation—pervades all three worlds; by the Prādhanikas (those belonging to the primary host), such as Sudarśana and others, who run about on all sides for the purpose of protection, having the great battle (*pradhana*) as their objective.
It is difficult to approach and hard to attain because of its being the cause [of all things]. ||31||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Nivītaṃ yuktaṃ hariṃ" means that, perceiving [the mountain] in the form of a mountain and so forth as being joined with Hari, he recognized, "This is Hari";
[he was able] to comprehend [him] through the sun and other [deities] by means of their own functions.

The meaning is that it is impossible. By the "three abodes"—those whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss—who wander about for the sake of protection, running on all sides; or by the "warriors," namely the Sudarśana discus and others, or the attendants such as Jaya and Vijaya, who sport in battle (pradhana), acting as the cause [of its destruction].
Difficult to approach by others, hard to attain. ||31||
At that very moment,
the Lord, the creator of the world, beheld within that lotus at his navel himself, as well as water, wind, and space.
Beyond this, there is no further vision of the creation of the world.

Śrīdhara: If he saw Hari at that very moment, then indeed, while observing the creation of the worlds, he beheld in his navel-lake a lotus, as well as the wind—the wind of dissolution—and the sky. ||32||
The sequence of composition: "Then" (tarhi) [is used]. Hereafter follows the instrument of creation. ||32||

Viśvanātha: At that very moment, he beheld in the lake of his navel a lotus; and in that lotus, he saw himself, as well as the triad of elements—air and space within the four directions. There was nothing beyond this, such as earth and so forth. He is one whose vision and desire for creation consist in the manifold creation of the worlds. (32)
Tainted by passion, desiring to create progeny, and perceiving only this much of the seed of karma,
he praised that worshipful one as he turned toward emission.
With his self absorbed in the path of the unmanifest.

Śrīdhara: The seed of karma is the cause of the creation of the world. Tinged by *rajas*, that is, endowed with the quality of *rajas*, he thus desired to create offspring; [he manifested] only this much—the pentad beginning with the navel-lotus—and even during the act of emission, his mind was directed toward it.
His mind was fixed upon the Blessed One on the path of the unmanifest. ||33||
The sequence of composition: "He" refers to him who, being joined with *rajas*, desired to create progeny.

Having perceived that this pentad beginning with the navel-lotus is indeed the cause of the creation of the worlds, although his mind was intent upon emission (*visarga*), he nevertheless offered praise while fixing his mind upon the Lord on the path of the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
The meaning. ||33||

Viśvanātha: The seed of karma is the cause of the creation of the world. Contemplating, "I shall take refuge only in the Lord, thinking, 'How can I perform this emission (visarga) consisting of just these five, beginning with the lotus? and thus abandoning attachment to emission, [he proceeds] upon the path of the unmanifest.
He whose self and mind are firmly fixed upon the illustrious Blessed One. ||33||
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the third book in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord; it is perfectly suited for the virtuous.

Thus ends the vision of the Blessed Lord, in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, within the *Pāramahaṃsya-saṃhitā* of the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya*, the commentary on the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatamahāpurāṇa* composed by Vyāsa, in the Third Book.
The Eighth Chapter.
Now begins the Ninth Chapter: The Hymn to Brahmā by Pādmodbhava.
Brahmā said:
You have been known by me today after a very long time; indeed, it is a reproach that the course of the Blessed One is not known by embodied beings.
O Blessed One, there is nothing else besides you; even that which appears as manifold through the interplay of the qualities of māyā is not pure.
The honey does not exist by itself; even that which exists dependent upon it is impure. And that diversity of its own nature also appears as non-existent due to the difference in location.
Though Hari is one, he is perceived as if manifold because of the diversity of his locations.
"There is no difference anywhere for Him, who is the inner controller of all"— thus says Śrīdhara in the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa*,
in the ninth [chapter], regarding the unborn [Brahmā] seeing Nārāyaṇa pleased by his austerity.
Sinking in the single ocean, he offered praise with the desire to create the worlds.

Manifesting his own fulfillment through the knowledge of the Blessed One and grieving for those who are ignorant, he says: "You are known. After a very long time, through worship over many years, you have been known by me today. Alas!
This is indeed a reproach, a fault of embodied beings. What is it? That [the truth] regarding the state of your, the Blessed One’s, nature...

"The reality is not known. To this he says: "Since you alone are fit to know it because of its being true, and nothing else because of its being untrue; there is nothing other than you (tvat). Even that which appears to exist is not pure reality. How can there be the perception of what is non-existent? To that he says: "That which..."
For it is from the agitation of the qualities of Māyā that you alone appear vast and manifold in form. ||1||

The sequence of the composition: "You are known. [An objection: What is the loss in not knowing? To that he says: "The body," etc. "Gait" (gati) refers to the state consisting of one's essential nature, powers, and so forth. [An objection: Is there not something else perceived besides such a gait? To that he says: "Other than such as you, there is no other reality" (tattva). Or alternatively:

It exists, yet even that is not pure; rather, the meaning is that you alone are the pure reality (*tattva*). The reason for both cases is "illusion" (*māyā*): by means of your own internal power consisting of infinite majesty, you, who are inherently pure, shine forth extensively in the form of the universe—that indeed is [the case].

The sense is that it appears only through the transformation—that is, the intermingling of the qualities—of the power of one's own substance known as Māyā, which is external and of the nature of Pradhāna; therefore, there is no purity therein. ||1||
Viśvanātha: In the ninth [chapter], Brahmā, having praised the Lord who lies within the Garbhodaka ocean— the inner controller within himself—
obtained the power for creation through a rain of His grace.

Demonstrating that it is only the knowledge of the Lord—which is obtained through His grace and is the sole cause for His direct realization—that can truly occur, he says: "You are known. The meaning is: "Today you have been known by me," that is, after a very long time, even though I have been meditating upon you for many ages. [This is so] because of such beauty as yours.

"Perhaps at some time, having known the Blessed One while in a state of meditation rather than through mere study, I shall meditate upon Him"—alas, alas! this pride of knowledge was made in vain. Likewise, the hope that "the Lord, appearing in the very form thus meditated upon, might grant me His vision" was also made in vain; such is the implied meaning, because...
The underlying suggestion (*anudhvani*) is this: "Not even a fraction of such beauty exists in great emeralds, blue lotuses, fresh clouds, and the like;
therefore, though you were meditated upon in that form, you have become manifest in this very form—how indescribable is the majesty of your grace!"
Having personally experienced the tasting of that sweetness, he grieves for others who have not experienced it.

For embodied beings—that is, living creatures—this alone is a reproach, a fault. What is it? That the nature of your reality, O Blessed One, is not known; such beauty, sweetness, and so forth are not experienced by those who possess bodies.
Thus, the very fruit of maintaining this body is the worship of You; for it is only through this that such a true nature can be experienced—this is the intended meaning.
Now, one might ask: in this diverse world, what other object of experience could possibly be so exceedingly sweet as this?

Is there nothing else, such that you declare this [knowledge] to be the faultless path for embodied beings? To this he replies: "There is nothing other than You which indeed ought to be adopted for the sake of knowledge"—this is the meaning. "O Blessed One" (bhagavan):
because of Your state of being blessed (bhagavattva), there is truly nothing else; for the word *bhaga* denotes all non-material attributes such as beauty, fame, and so forth.
The sense is that there is no object of enjoyment whatsoever without the eyes, ears, and so forth.
Now, one might object: "Is there not the very happiness of heaven that is to be enjoyed by all the senses? To this he replies: "Even that is not pure.
That too is impermanent due to its perishability and other such traits; it is insipid because of its subject to change, and it is limited.

The meaning is that even something extremely base is not pure or holy, nor is it fit to be tasted by a host of *kāminīs* (lustful women), whereas [the other] is visible even to a gathering of swans (*haṃsa*) who possess nothing.
Furthermore, because that too is the effect of your power of *māyā*, it is not other than you.

He said: "From the intermingling and transformation of the qualities of *māyā*, [the world] becomes vast, consisting of forms such as heaven, the state of Brahmā (*pārameṣṭhya*), and universal sovereignty (*sārvabhauma*). (1)

This form of yours, which was first assumed as the single seed of hundreds of incarnations for the sake of constant grace toward those from whom darkness has forever been dispelled by the dawning of the essence of awakening—
From which lotus-abode of my navel I have manifested.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: since I have emerged from the abode of the navel-lotus, and since I behold this nature of the Blessed One which consists of pure bliss, and since I am supported by it, there is nothing beyond this.
Therefore, that "it is not known" is a blemish (*avadya*) only in comparison to the Supreme; for that which has been grasped since beginningless time is indeed what is being grasped here.

"That divine form of Hari which dwells in the midst of the Ocean of Milk, consisting solely of knowledge and bliss—there is nothing superior to it anywhere. From that unmanifest, which is beginningless and eternal, the four-faced [Brahmā] was born. Thus it is said in the Adhyātma [Purāṇa].
It is the self of the elements and the senses, as indicated by the passage beginning with "that which it attains" (yad āpnoti). ||23||

Śrīdhara: But surely you too do not know correctly, for even this form which has been seen by you consists of the *guṇas* alone. Brahman alone, devoid of *guṇas*, is the reality. To this he says with two verses beginning with "rūpam": [it is] eternally—that is, always—withdrawn through the manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which arises from the emergence of the essence of awakening.

O Tamas, because this form of yours has been assumed and manifested by you alone out of your own autonomy for the sake of favoring virtuous devotees— being the single seed and root of the hundred incarnations whose nature consists of pure being— for the purpose of demonstrating that:
He shows that she is the seed for the manifestation of virtues: "From whose navel... (verse 2).
The sequence of composition: the pair beginning with "rūpam" (form). First, before the incarnations of the qualities (*guṇāvatāra*) and so forth;

"taken up" means acquired and brought forward for the sake of the virtuous, that is, manifested—because, as will be stated in the verse beginning with "aviśvam" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.3), if it were subject to creation, it would follow that the universe is included within it.

Because one whose qualities of all material nature (*prakṛti*) have eternally ceased through the arising of the essence of awakening cannot, like an individual soul (*jīva*), be subject to its grasping; for here "darkness" (*tamas*) refers to material nature, as in passages such as "Where am I? Darkness, Mahat, Ego... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.11), since darkness cuts off awakening on all sides.
Regarding the fact that there is but one seed for hundreds of incarnations, he provides an illustration based on his own experience, saying: "That which is not...
Because it was the first of all creations, it is described as such [by the word *ātman*].
(Bhagavatsandarbha 53) Viśvanātha: Now, even this form of mine is indeed of today; if it is of today...

Anticipating the objection that "it was only today that you were known to be truly impermanent here, so your own statement is itself the proof," he says "rūpam" (the form). Because of the emergence of that *avabodharasa*—the power of consciousness which constitutes your very nature—the darkness of *māyā* has eternally (*śaśvat*) ceased for you, who are thus the eternal one (*sanātana*). In this regard:

The venerable teacher [Vallabhācārya] states that because of the word "constantly" (*śaśvat*), the meaning is "taken up" (*gṛhīta*) and "manifested" (*āviṣkṛta*). The context is that it has been brought into the presence of the virtuous (*satām*). Some say that although there is non-difference, it is spoken of as if there were difference, just as in the expression "the qualities were taken up by Māyā. Others say it means "taken up by the agent who is the essence of awakening" (*avabodharasa*). ||2||
Beyond this, O Supreme One, I behold Your own nature— pure bliss, free from conceptual construction, of unimpeded luster—
the single creator of the universe, who is not the universe itself, within my very self.
I have taken refuge in that which consists of the elements and the senses.
Śrīdhara: O Supreme One! Your splendor is unpierced, meaning your light is unobstructed; therefore, it is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*) and devoid of differentiation (*nirbheda*).

For this very reason, it is pure bliss (*ānandamātra*). I do not perceive that which is your true nature as being separate or distinct from this form; rather, this very form is that. For this reason, [I offer my salutation] to you.

"I have resorted to this form of yours. He says "also because of its fitness": it is "one," the foremost among those worthy of worship; for it is the "creator of the universe" (*viśvasṛj*), since it creates the universe, and therefore it is "non-universal" (*aviśvam*), being other than the universe. Furthermore, it is the "self of the elements and the senses," the self of both the elements and the senses.
The meaning is "the cause. ||3||
The Sequence of Composition: Indeed, I do not perceive that which is your true nature hereafter—the form of the complete Bhagavat and so forth—but rather, I have resorted to this present form.
He qualifies that true nature: "Bliss alone; bliss is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.6.1).

And it has been stated that Brahman is His portion (*mātrā*), which is of the nature of non-differentiated consciousness (*nirviśeṣacidrūpa*). In Him, no diverse conceptualization (*vividha-kalpa*)—that is, the mental construction of creation and so forth—exists. This is because He who exists in Mahāvaikuṇṭha in the form of the Lord (*bhagavat*) and others remains indifferent toward the acts of creation and so forth; for in that state, it is the *puruṣa* alone [who is active].
Because it has come into operation. This has been stated: "But through the temporal function of Māyā" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.5.26), and so forth;

and also "The three forms of Viṣṇu," and so forth. "Unpierced by Māyā" means that His splendor (*varcas*), brilliance (*tejas*), and power (*śakti*) are not divided by her. He qualifies this form with the words "the creator of the universe," and so forth.

The meaning is that the Self is the essential nature called *pradhāna* of both the elements and the senses; it is by depending upon this very [Self] that even *pradhāna*, the cause of the universe, functions. ||3||

[Bhagavatsandarbha 53] Viśvanātha: Now, some explain that Brahman alone, devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), is the primordial source of all, and not Brahman with attributes (*saviśeṣa*). To this, he says: "Not from this," etc. O Supreme One! That which is Your essential nature...
Brahman is non-conceptual, without distinction, and pure bliss; I see nothing higher than that form.

However, the meaning is: "This alone is That," and not "That alone is this. O you of unpierced splendor! [The term] *aviddhavarcaḥ* means one whose splendor (*varcas*), or light (*tejas*), is unpierced (*aviddha*)—that is, undivided by time, space, and so forth—and is thus all-pervading.
The sense is that this very fire is that Brahman. As it was said by the Blessed One to Arjuna in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"That supreme, highest Brahman pervades the entire universe."
"O Bhārata, you should know that this dense splendor is mine alone. (Mahābhārata, Vanaparvan 2.114.12).

Now, even if there is identity between the two, where do you take delight? To this he says: "Not the universe, distinct from the universe, consisting of consciousness"—this is the meaning. But I am indeed the universe itself, because [I am composed] of the elements, the senses, and the self.
By whom? By that very body, senses, and mind through which one experiences pleasure; he who possesses intoxication and pride because of that—thus his own material nature is described. ||3||
Indeed, this auspiciousness of the world has been shown by You for the sake of our auspiciousness in meditation,
O Lord; we pay homage to You, the Blessed One, and shall follow after You.
He who is disregarded by those destined for hell due to their attachment to what is false.
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But even so, this [vision] is conditioned and merely recent. Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"That indeed is this very same thing. O Auspiciousness of the World! Because that was shown by you (*te*) for the welfare (*maṅgalāya*) of us, your worshippers (*upāsakānām*), during meditation (*dhyāne*). For it is not [possible] for those whose minds are intent upon the path of the unmanifest (*avyaktavartmābhiniveśitacittānām*).

The sense is that our view, which admits of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is logical. Therefore, we pay homage to you by means of *anuvidhāna*, that is, through devoted service. If so, why is it that some do not respect me?
To this he replies: "He who is disregarded... [by those] through false attachments consisting of the base sophistries of those who deny the Lord (*nirīśvara*). 4.
The Sequence of Composition: Now, one might object: "In that case, is this form not characterized by the qualities of *prakṛti*? He says "no":

"That indeed is this" (*tad vā idam*). The meaning is: "That very thing is this. Even though, according to the principle stated by Akrūra in the passage "[He who has many forms yet is of one form]" (*bhā.pu. 10.40.7*), He appears as distinct, [He remains that same reality].

Therefore, because there is no difference [between us], even though [the Lord] is supported by Pradhāna, He is not attached to it according to the principle stated in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.1.1: "By His own power, He has forever cast away all deceit. If that is so, how then are You perceived? To this he replies: "In meditation" (dhyāne). That is, in our devotion characterized by meditation.
Because it has been shown thus through its own independence. If so, what is the cause for perceiving this particular form?

To that he says: "For the sake of the worshippers. For those who perform such worship with the desire for creation, although they themselves possess desires, they are unable to provide a reciprocal favor because they contemplate such assistance [from the Lord].

"He simply bows down to him"—thus, having shown that he acts out of compassion even though his own desires are fulfilled, [the author] censures those who look outward from that state with the words "those who... Here, "unworthy ones" refers to those who, through excessive sophistry, conceive of things imagined by their respective forms of ignorance. (4)
[The Bhagavatsandarbha 53] Viśvanātha: Now, why do you not take refuge in the nature that is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣasvarūpa*)?
To this he replies: "This well-known nature, which is indeed certainly possessed of attributes (*saviśeṣa*)."
For the sake of the auspiciousness and welfare of all beings dwelling in the fourteen worlds— namely,

for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, which are themselves auspicious— it is only when there is worship of this form that dharma and the other goals become wholesome and meaningful; otherwise, they are in vain.
The meaning is that they come into being; the intention is that the nature devoid of distinctions does not exist in this way.
Likewise, for us as well, it is shown to be precisely this [nature] during meditation, and not that [devoid of distinctions];
therefore, there is also a superiority in His compassion. Consequently, to Him, whose nature possesses distinctions—
We offer only our salutations to You, who are an ocean of the qualities of consciousness;
the sense is: "What further service, indeed, am I able to perform?

Now, as for those who argue that this form is not composed of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), but rather consists of *māyā*— [The response follows: ...[the text continues with the refutation of that view]... [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly here].
"Do some people not actually respect me? To this he says: "He who is disregarded...

The meaning is that those who are destined for hell will surely fall into hell. Or, it refers to those who associate with the wicked and who maintain the fallacious view that "all this is unreal" or "merely false. ||4||
But those who smell the fragrance of the calyx of your lotus feet, carried by the breeze of the Vedas through the openings of their ears,
and who have grasped your feet with supreme devotion— of them [there is no rebirth].
O Lord, you do not depart from the lotus-heart of your own devotees.
"Madhva says: That form of Hari which is manifest in the heart is called 'fragrance' (gandha).
By the word 'excellent' (uttama), however, the entire form is expressed;
for no distinction whatsoever is admitted between fragrance and that which possesses fragrance. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmatarka*. 5.

Śrīdhara says: "Those who worship you with reverence have achieved their life's purpose," as expressed in the verse beginning with "ye tu. *Śruti* means the Veda; that itself is the wind (*vāta*), by which [the message] is brought or conveyed. *Nāpaiṣi* means "you do not depart.
Those who listen to your stories with great reverence—in their hearts you shine eternally. Thus [it is said].
The meaning [is as follows]. ||5||

The sequential arrangement: Establishing that very point—those who are pure devotees (śuddhabhakta), for them Your lotus feet alone shall be the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha), since You Yourself regard them as such. Thus He says: "But those who... Here, by the word "but" (tu), their status as the most highly esteemed is indicated.
It has been established. "You do not depart" means that you do not wish to go away. In this regard, the ultimate proof is provided by the verse beginning with "your own," and so forth. ||5||

Viśvanātha: In the scriptures, those who worship the formless (nirviśeṣa) nature are called the wise (jñānins), while those who worship the qualified (saviśeṣa) nature are called devotees (bhaktas). Among these two groups, he declares with two verses that the devotees alone are the ones who have achieved their purpose and are beloved—beginning with "But those... (ye tu)—where "Śruti" refers to the Veda.

Or, "hearing" (śravaṇa) is the wind; by that [wind], they were led—that is, brought there. Consequently, like bees greedy for the fragrance of his lotus-feet, they grasp his very lotus-feet as the supreme human goal; thus he says: "by supreme devotion," characterized by love.

"Do not depart"—just as they are greedy for your lotus feet and do not abandon them, so too you are greedy for their heart-lotuses, which are full of the sweetness of love, and do not abandon them; thus, a mutual subjugation is indicated. ||5||
So long does there exist fear caused by wealth, body, and friends;
so long does there exist sorrow, longing, humiliation, and vast greed; and so long does there exist the false grasping of "mine," which is the root of all affliction.
As long as the world does not choose your feet, which grant fearlessness.
Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says: "To that extent" (*tāvat*). While wealth and such are present, there is fear;

when they have gone, there is grief; and again, there is longing; from that, humiliation; and yet, there is vast greed (*lobha*) or thirst (*tṛṣṇā*); and when they are somehow obtained again, there is the false insistence of "mine-ness" (*mama-ity-asad-āgraha*). This is the root of affliction (*ārti*), being the source of fear, grief, and so forth.

The reason is this: one should not choose [other paths] nor should one rely upon them. The sense is: by merely taking refuge at your feet, fear and other such states cease; how much more so when you are revealed? ||6||

The sequence of the composition: Now, one might ask, "If fear and the like caused by wealth and other such things exist, how could there be such an attachment to the sweetness of the Self? To this, he says: *tāvat* (so long). He does not choose [them], nor would he resort to them merely as a refuge. ||6||
Viśvanātha: Now, if they too possess wives, sons, wealth, and so forth, they are indeed still transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*);
to this he says "no, no," and by way of the natural flow of the argument, he states a portion [of the meaning] with the word "for the time being" (*tāvat*).
The meaning is that *saṃsāra* is fear caused by attachment to wealth and the like. He provides an elaboration of that very point:
"Sorrow," and so forth, [continues] only until one chooses Your feet through the state of being the sovereign Lord and so on.
The sense is that when there is such a supreme choice, attachment to wealth and the like ceases due to attachment to You.
And even if some devotee were to remain attached to wealth and the like, even then [it would not be so].
He says "Cintā" (thought): "The false grasping at 'mine' is the root of suffering and the cause of saṃsāra for as long as [it persists].

Merely by choosing your feet as objects of service, the root of suffering—such as attachment to wealth and so forth—is eliminated, just like the bite of a snake whose fangs have been pulled out; this will be explained further on. For that long...

Regarding the statement that "passion and the like are thieves," this was explained by the force of the two readings of the word *tāvat* in the verse beginning with "O Kṛṣṇa, as long as those people [do not belong to you]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.36). And thus, by the phrase "but those who are yours," those possessed of devotion (*rati*) are indicated; by the half-verse "as long as there is fear," those possessed of the cessation of misfortune (*anartha-nivṛtti*) are indicated; and by the [subsequent] "as long as... [the cessation of rebirth is indicated].
By the half-verse beginning with "mama," it is stated that devotees who have not turned away from the three kinds of worldly objects are no longer subject to transmigratory existence:
"Those whose intellects are destroyed by fate, who through attachment to You have their senses turned away from all that is inauspicious..."
Wretched and their minds perpetually overcome by greed, they constantly perform unwholesome deeds for the sake of a mere tiny fragment of sensual pleasure.

Śrīdhara: It has been stated that those who, though being free from desire, do not honor You, are destined for hell. But those who, being averse to hearing Your stories and so forth, are intent on actions performed for the sake of desire—they are exceedingly dull-witted. Thus he says: "By fate their intellects are destroyed, their understanding lost. This is because of their attachment...
Those whose senses are turned away from hearing, chanting, and other such practices that remove all suffering; their faculties are unwholesome, meaning they bring about insecurity. //7//
Sanātana (Ha.bha.vi. 10.466) writes regarding the fault of aversion with two verses beginning with "By fate" (*daivena*).

Because it pacifies all inauspicious things, ill omens, or sufferings arising from incidental association—whether in the form of hearing and chanting or through discourse—it is so called. [Those who are] averse due to lack of faith...

Those whose sense faculties have ceased [their outward activity] are "those with withdrawn senses. This state of having liberated senses manifests either that fruit or its cause—meaning they bring it about. "Unwholesome" refers to actions that produce insecurity. (7)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, if this were so, then all wise people would become [liberated] and take refuge at my feet; in that case, who would remain in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)? To this he says—with destiny (*daiva*).

Due to the adverse karma arising from their transgression against you, they repeatedly afflict these beings with unwholesome actions— both those that are desired and those that are forbidden— as well as with hunger, thirst, and the three humors,
and with cold, heat, wind, rain, and mutual strife.
O Urukrama, as I behold this, my mind sinks down, burdened by the fire of desire and by anger that is exceedingly difficult to bear.

Śrīdhara: He demonstrates its very unwholesomeness. Hunger and thirst, as well as the three humors—wind, bile, and phlegm—with these [afflictions], and with this most difficult-to-bear, unbearable fire of desire, and with infallible wrath—that is, with uninterrupted anger—the minds of those who behold these creatures being tormented [are moved].
He sinks down. ||8||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "And as for those others who are like beasts and so forth, who do not know anything of their own benefit or harm, I truly pity them. Thus he says: "Hunger, thirst, and the three humors..."

The winds, the bile, and the phlegm; by these, these creatures are afflicted with one another—even toward their own sons, wives, and so forth—and are tormented by the fire of desire and by an unshakable, uninterrupted wrath.
The word "sudurbhareṇa" (by that which is very difficult to bear) is an adjective qualifying both [the fire and the wrath]. As I behold these creatures being thus afflicted, my mind [is pained].
He desponds; alas, alas! "How will there be a deliverance for these?"—thus he sinks into despair. (8)
O Lord of Men, as long as a person perceives this separation of the self from the objects of the senses as the power of Māyā belonging to the Blessed One,
so long will this cycle of worldly existence not cease.
Even though it is fruitless, an action directed toward an object brings forth a multitude of sufferings.
Madhva’s [explanation]: The power of *māyā* is the power of the Lord’s will. Knowability belongs even to that which is difficult to perceive;
it possesses a superior capacity for manifestation.
There is non-difference even from the Lord, and there is an intimate internal connection at the beginning of creation and so forth.
It is said that this Māyā is either the will or the power of Hari.

That which has dependence on the Blessed One as its nature, whose state is that of being his wife, and which is beautiful in form—that is called Māyā; however, Śrī is considered to be joined with defects and is insentient.
"Transformation, defects, and likewise consciousness belong to her; this Māyā, which consists of the bondage of the world, always envelops the Śaivalas. Thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*.
"I shall meditate, I shall think, I shall see, and I shall hear"—such is the state of differentiation.
"The enjoyments of the senses [occur] by the power of Hari's will residing in the individual soul. Thus it is said in the *Ṣāḍguṇya*.
For the sake of the enjoyment of the senses; though seemingly purposeless, they serve the purpose of rites such as sacrifice. (9)

Śrīdhara: But if such transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*) is ultimately unreal, why is despondency felt? To this he says: "As long as... This "separateness" of the self is its state as the body and so forth.
That which has its power—its superiority—derived from Your Māyā, which takes the form of the objects of the senses; not [otherwise].

It would not turn back nor cease; it brings about a mass of suffering. That in which action has its purpose and fruit—according to the reading "this is distinctness," as long as one views this body and so forth as "distinct from you," that [ignorance] does not cease, even though it is futile. ||9||
The sequential arrangement: And that [state] would belong to living beings only through the conceit of independence from you;
intending this, he says "as long as" (yāvat). As long as one perceives one's own separateness or independence from the Blessed Lord. ||9||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But since this transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*) is of such a nature as to be unreal, why do you despair because of it? To this he replies with the words "As long as... (*yāvad*). As long as one perceives—that is, experiences—this separateness of the self (*ātman*), the individual soul (*jīva*), namely its state as a body and so forth, [it is] the power of the Lord’s *māyā* in the form of sense-objects.

In that case, cyclic existence (saṃsṛti)—though futile and devoid of reality—would neither cease nor come to rest; for it is from this [existence] that the purpose and fruit of actions and deeds result, which bring about a multitude of sufferings. (9)

O Lord, even the sages— whose senses are exhausted by the day's labors, who lie down at night with minds full of various desires, whose sleep is shattered in an instant, and whose efforts to achieve their goals are thwarted by fate— are thus afflicted.
Averse to your company, they wander here in saṃsāra.
"Madhvaḥ": those whose instruments of action are brought forth by objects. Regarding this, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Ignorance is said to be night; knowledge is declared to be day. (10)

Śrīdhara: Let it be so for those lacking discrimination; but for the discriminating, they are already liberated, so what need have they for devotion? To this he says: "Those whose senses (karaṇāni)—meaning the organs—are occupied and engaged during the day with objects of suffering and affliction, and who possess not even a fragment of sensory pleasure at night, because [of the darkness] in the night..."

Lying down, their sleep was broken in an instant by the sight of dreams; struck by fate, they were thwarted on all sides, their plans for wealth and their efforts toward wealth being frustrated. ||10||

Sanātana (Ha.bha.vi. 10.304): He states that even those possessed of discrimination, if they lack devotion, always experience the miseries of saṃsāra and so forth—beginning with the words "ahnī" (by day). Those whose organs—the sense faculties—are occupied during the day and afflicted; nor is there even a fragment of happiness for them at night.

For they lie down with no confidence, their sleep shattered moment by moment by the sight of dreams; struck by fate and thwarted on all sides, their efforts toward the attainment of wealth have been frustrated. ||10||

The sequential composition: For this very reason, there is even disregard for the sages perfected in their respective paths; thus he says, "With their senses distressed by being occupied during the day," and so forth. By their very nature, worldly beings become averse to devotion toward you. What need is there to say more? Even the sages perfected in their respective paths [are likewise].

If those in this world were to turn away from devotion to you, they would wander in saṃsāra just like that; or rather, even sages, if they were turned away from you, would certainly continue to wander in saṃsāra. Being in what state do they wander? To this he says: "Having ascended with difficulty to the supreme station," beginning with the words *ahny āpṛta* and so forth.
As stated in such passages as Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.2.32, Śrī Yama has said:
"Neither the sages nor even the gods truly know the dharma directly promulgated by the Blessed Lord."
The Asuras, humans, Siddhas, and chief [beings] are not [present there], much less the Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, and others.
Svayambhū, Nārada, Śambhu, Kumāra, Kapila, Manu, Prahlāda, Janaka, Bhīṣma, Bali, and we ourselves— [are the knowers of this].
O warriors, we twelve recognize this Bhāgavata Dharma, which is secret, pure, and difficult to understand; by knowing which, one partakes of the immortal nectar.
"In this world, this alone is recorded as the supreme duty for men:
the yoga of devotion toward the Blessed One through the chanting of His names and other such means" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.1.19). And so forth.
The meaning is this: we indeed recognize these as the promulgators of the Dharma, yet we do not generally teach them in our own Smṛtis and other works.

For they are secret (*guhya*), meaning they are not to be disclosed; they are difficult to understand and impossible for others to grasp correctly. The reason for their secrecy is stated: "Having known which, one attains immortality" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.3.21).
For this very reason, it will be stated later: "Generally, this great personage knows this, but not this other one" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.3.25), and so forth.

Here, the meaning is that the "great personage" (mahājana) is someone distinct from the twelve [sages] and those who belong to the traditions they favor, even if he is endowed with great qualities. Therefore, it was rightly said: "Even during the day, he did not suffer from thirst," and so on.
The specific details regarding this should be seen in the *Śrī Bhakti-sandarbha* (verse 10) [Bhakti-sandarbha 113].
Viśvanātha: Nor should it be said that the cessation of transmigratory existence—which is imagined through ignorance—occurs through knowledge alone;
for even those possessing knowledge continue to transmigrate if they are devoid of devotion. Thus he says: "In the day... (etc.).
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: even wise sages, being averse to attachment to you, continue to transmigrate while remaining in such a state.

There is also a reading "munayaḥ" (sages). In what state are they? They are those whose senses (*karaṇāni*), meaning the organs, are occupied during the day with various activities and are thus afflicted; such they are by destiny.

Those for whom the composition of meaning—the presentations of objects of enjoyment—is struck down; and thus, by the verse beginning "And so by fate" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.7), the performers of ritual action (karmiṇaḥ) are indicated; by "Hunger and thirst" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.8) and so forth, the deluded (mūḍhāḥ); and by "Engaged during the day" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.10), the knowers (jñāninaḥ).
Those subject to transmigration have been described as being of three kinds. ||10||
O Lord, you indeed dwell within the lotus-heart of men purified by the yoga of devotion, your path being perceived through both scripture and direct vision;
for whatever they contemplate of you, O far-famed one, with their intellect, [that very thing you reveal].
You assume those various forms for the sake of bestowing constant grace.

Madhva [says]: "You bestow their respective forms; as the Lord is conceived, so does the individual soul become"—thus it is in the *Tantrasāra*. And Śrīdhara [cites]: "In whatever way one worships Him, that very thing one becomes.
Thus, having stated that for non-devotees there is no cessation of saṃsāra, [he speaks] regarding devotees...
He states the cessation of that [doubt] with the word "you": you reside (*āsse*) in the lotus of the heart purified by the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*).

You are one whose path has been beheld through sacred revelation (*śruta*), that is, through hearing (*śravaṇa*). Furthermore, even without hearing, whatever form or body of yours your devotees meditate upon according to their own will in their minds, that very thing [is manifested].
You bestow [your grace]; you manifest [itself] for the sake of favoring the virtuous, that is, the devotees. ||11||
The sequential composition: What more need be said than that you are indeed under the control of your devotees?
Thus he says: "Thou. Here, *bhaktiyoga* means love (*prema*). *Paribhāvitatva* means having been rendered fit (*yogyatām āpāditatvam*). [This] has been heard.
[This refers to] the hearing and reflection upon the Vedas and Vedic scriptures that establish the Blessed One.

If so, what is the cause for the manifestation of my specific form? To this he says: "Whatever [is attained] by the intellect"—that is, by a particular state of intelligence acquired through what has been heard. They are those previously mentioned who have seen the path of truth through revelation.
Whatever men contemplate, that very form You assume; "praṇayase" means You lead it forth with excellence, that is, You manifest it.
[An objection: "But I am the Lord; how could I be under their control? To this He says: "For the sake of bestowing grace."
The sense is that when they exist, your grace alone is the cause of their being under your control, and nothing else. Now, one might ask:

"How can there be knowledge of my many forms by mere hearing? And in the absence of that, how could there be devotion fixed upon any one of them? To this he says: "O Urugāya!"—by means of the Veda, you...
The meaning is that she may be praised in many ways, according to each person's own perspective. ||11||

Viśvanātha: It goes without saying that devotees cross over the cycle of existence even without knowledge, since by means of devotion they bring even You under their control; thus he says: "By the yoga of devotion, [the mind] is thoroughly (*pari*)—that is, in every way (*sarvatobhāvena*)—cultivated (*bhāvite*), meaning perfumed (*vāsita*); for the *Amara-kośa* states: 'The words *bhāvita* and *vāsita* have three meanings'. Or else:

"O You who are manifested through the cultivation of *bhakti-yoga*!"—the meaning is that You have been fully (*pari*) and from every side (*sarvato-bhāvena*) cultivated and made manifest by *bhakti-yoga* alone; thus, for You to become manifest, *bhakti-yoga* itself, when established with steadfastness (*niṣṭhayā*), shall be the sole cause. For this very reason, for them...

"You sit and remain seated within the lotus of the heart; you do not depart from there, nor do you go away, O Lord"—as stated previously in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (3.9.5). He is one by whom the path was first heard from the mouth of the Guru, and subsequently seen—that is, directly realized—by which path You have come to the lotus of the heart.
The implied meaning (*dhvani*) is that they thoroughly discern that path, which is the mode of devotion as a means; hence,
the secondary implication (*anudhvani*) is that whoever possesses the desire for your attainment should discern that very path from that [devotion] itself.

Furthermore, as the venerable teachers (Svāmicaraṇa) have stated: even without hearing [the scriptures], whatever form or body Your devotees meditate upon by their own will, You bestow—that is, You manifest—that very thing.
Or else, those practitioner-devotees (sādhakabhaktāḥ) contemplate with their intellect whatever accords with their respective natures; that very thing [You grant].
You lead their bodies to the state of perfected forms; you bring them forth with excellence. The sense is: "Oh, how you are subject to the power of your own devotees! ||11||
He does not become overly pleased even when propitiated with abundant services by hosts of gods whose hearts are bound by desire,
since he alone is unattainable through anything other than compassion for all beings.
Among various people, he is attentive; his inner self is a friend to all.

O Madhva, you who are worshipped with heartfelt devotion by the hosts of gods out of compassion for all beings, yet do not become overly pleased by people whose desires are bound and who offer elaborate services;
you who are propitiated by Brahmā and others through devotion, knowledge, compassion, and the like.
"What is the use of service rendered to him by those who are lustful? Thus it is said in the *Satyasaṃhitā*. 12.

Śrīdhara: He says that you are very easily accessible to those devotees who are free from desire, but not to others, with the words "not [to others]," etc. By means of accumulated and powerful services, such as offerings of flowers and so forth; and by that which is unattainable for the wicked and non-devotees—namely, compassion for all beings—which is the cause of grace. The word "one" (*eka*), etc., [indicates this].
The sequence of the composition: "Not so," etc. The word "you" (*bhavān*) is to be supplied as the subject.
And thus, since you, being propitiated even by ordinary people through compassion for all beings, become exceedingly gracious;
why is this? To this he says: "For you alone are the friend, the inner self, and the attentive witness within all diverse persons."

And thus: in what manner were they by the hosts of gods? The meaning is that because desire was bound within their hearts, they were possessed of rivalry and envy here and there. Therefore, the sense is that for the sake of pleasing you, devotion consisting solely of compassion for all beings must be practiced. ||12||

Viśvanātha: Even among those [devotees], he says that only those who are free from desire (*niṣkāma*) are most excellent, and not those with desire (*sakāma*). The ellipsis is "You do not become exceedingly gracious toward them. By indicating that the very absence of compassion toward all beings—due to their being intent on their own self-interest—is the cause for the lack of excessive grace in the case of those with desire, [he praises] those who are free from desire.
However, because he is devoted to the welfare of others, compassion for all beings is natural to him; thus, even his extreme favor is natural.

He says this: "Insofar as he is exceedingly gracious through compassion for all beings"—compassion that is unattainable for the wicked—the sole cause of this extreme favor is you alone, who have applied yourself and fixed your attention upon diverse people.
Since He is a well-wishing friend who seeks the welfare of others, one might ask:
"If this is so, why do You not Yourself, out of compassion, deliver them? To this He replies:
"You are their inner self; it is for the sake of Your own devotee Yaśodā that [You manifest] this power which delivers the world."

The meaning is that, having deposited His own power of compassion within them, He Himself maintains a state of indifference everywhere by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). And thus, by the two terms "friend" (*suhṛt*) and "inner self" (*antarātman*), the Supreme Lord’s faults of cruelty and partiality are respectively refuted, and His affection for His devotees is established.

This has been illuminated. Nor should it be argued that such a view entails the undesirable consequence of universal liberation; for in the phrase "through compassion for all beings," the word "all" is used in the sense of "abundance" alone—just as in the expression "the umbrella-bearers are going"—and thus the compassion of the devotees of the Blessed One is also generally [included].
Indeed, this is because we observe that it is not universal.

Or rather, although a devotee must certainly exercise compassion toward all beings, even that does not imply the liberation of everyone; for seeds, though sown everywhere, do not take root even in saline or alkaline soils.
