They "grow" because even in the case of Nārada and others, the fruitfulness of their compassion toward Dakṣa and the rest is observed. ||12||

Therefore, for men, the propitiation of you, O Blessed One, through various rituals such as sacrifices, by means of charity, fierce austerity, and service, is for the sake of performing virtuous deeds.
The Dharma is established there where it never dies.

Śrīdhara: Since you are not highly pleased with those who possess desires, therefore the attainment of desire is not the supreme fruit of ritual actions; rather, it is only your own propitiation [that is the goal].
He says, "Of men," indicating that the connection with desire is for the sake of providing encouragement through an intermediate result.

The propitiation of you, the Blessed One, is indeed that which is both a religious duty (*dharma*) and the highest fruit of action; this is the reason for its preeminence. For the *dharma* entrusted to you is never lost nor does it perish, whereas the *dharma* performed for the sake of desire perishes once that desire has been granted—this is the meaning. ||13||
The sequential arrangement: Let alone [the requirement of] being free from desire in worship and the like; even in various ritual acts, that very state is supreme.
Thus he says: "Of men" (puṃsām). "Worship" (ārādhana) means pleasing [the Lord]. The meaning is: one does not die, but rather remains forever bestowing love for You. ||13||

Viśvanātha: Since those who are free from desire (*niṣkāma*) are the best in devotion, he says "of men" (*puṃsām*) to show that even when one lacks the capacity for exclusive devotion, devotion consisting of the dedication of worldly and Vedic actions—which has become the primary element—must also be performed as being free from desire. [He does this] by means of various worldly actions such as sacrifices (*adhvara*) and the like.

The meaning is that the worship you perform with Vedic rites offered to You, as well as whatever you eat, is taught by the Blessed Lord (as stated in Gītā 9.27). Here, the offering of all actions—both worldly and Vedic—is subordinate to the Vedic alone, and not to the worldly alone; likewise for the worldly.
One should observe the distinction that hearing, chanting, and so forth are causes only when they are offered [to You].
That alone is the purpose of good deeds; why is it the fruit of virtuous actions? Because when dharma is offered unto You, it never dies nor perishes, but rather exists in the form of worship.
It transforms. The meaning is that the dharma which has sensual pleasure as its purpose perishes once it has bestowed that pleasure. ||13||
Salutations to the Supreme One, whose intellect is pure awareness, for whom the delusion of duality has been swallowed up by the very splendor of His eternal essential nature;
who manifests as the instrumental cause for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe through His divine play.
We offer this salutation to You, the Lord of the Rasa dance.

Madhva’s [doctrines are]: the knowledge of the Lord’s imperfection, the lordship of Viṣṇu over others, the distinction between His incarnations and the individual soul, as well as the lordship of the individual soul,
the individuality of the Lord, and even the non-difference between those two and the insentient world.
"The delusion of duality is so described; it never exists at any time in Hari.
In others, even among the virtuous, it gradually departs through His grace. Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. 14.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, he says "we bow to You alone" because You are one for whom the delusion of difference has been forever and at all times dispelled by the very consciousness of Your own nature (*svarūpacaitanya*). Furthermore, You are one whose intellect (*dhiṣaṇā*) is indeed awakening (*bodha*), that is, the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*). Alternatively, *dhiṣaṇam* means the locus (*āśraya*). For this very reason, You are "for the sake of others" (*parasmai*). In this context:
The cause—the Māyā which is the instrumental cause for the manifestation of the universe and so forth; the *rāsa* is the sport consisting of Her playful pastimes (*vilāsa*).
To You, whose [sport] is such, we have offered this salutation (*namaḥ*), that is, we have performed this act of bowing down. ||14||

The sequence of the composition: "Eternally" (śaśvat). To You, by whom—through the majesty of Your own nature (*svarūpamahasa*), that is, through the power of Your own nature (*svarūpaśaktyā*)—the delusion of difference from the individual souls (*jīva*) and others has been swallowed up and removed; for such a You, with whom no delusion of difference from them can possibly exist, [I bow]. By way of that distinction (*tad-vailakṣaṇyena*).

The meaning is: "to one determined to be distinct from them. For this very reason, it is said "to the intellect of awakening," meaning not to one who, like a living being (*jīva*), is sometimes even joined with non-awakening. ||14||

Viśvanātha: Having thus described the two-fold worship of devotees, he bows to the two forms of the worshipable object belonging to the *jñānī* and the devotee (*bhakta*), which possess the characteristics previously mentioned: "To Him by whom the ocean of delusion—consisting of duality—has been eternally swallowed up by His own essential consciousness, just as [the ocean was swallowed] by Agastya."
We offer salutations to Him whose intellect (*dhiṣaṇā*) is the cause of the experience of the essential nature of pure consciousness;

salutations to that one whose essential nature is without distinction. Likewise, we offer salutations to Him who, through His divine play, finds delight (*rāsa*)—that is, experiences union—in that very *māyā* which is the instrumental cause for the manifestation of the universe and so forth, and which consists of His glancing look.

To Him whose essential nature is endowed with specific attributes; or rather, to Him for whom there is a *rāsa*—a particular form of dance accompanied by the assembly of cowherd girls—manifested through His playful activity (*līlā*) as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), according to the scripture: "At the end of a supreme age (*parārdha*), He awoke and perceived that He had appeared before me in the guise of a cowherd. [And] to the lotus-foot of the wish-fulfilling tree.

By the phrase "showing [this]," and because of what was stated previously, it is made known that even among those whose essential natures possess distinctions, the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme perfection and the ultimate refuge, whose incarnations, qualities, and activities are mere imitations.
Those who, helpless at the departure of life, utter His names—
casting off instantly the impurities of many births—
they attain the unobstructed immortality; I take refuge in that Unborn One.
"Those who are overwhelmed by devotion to Madhava"—
meaning those who, being overwhelmed by devotion to Viṣṇu, are speakers of His name alone;
even they attain liberation quickly, how much more so those who constantly meditate upon Him— thus it is said in the Vyomasaṃhitā.

Śrīdhara: Revealing his sovereignty through the fact that he bestows liberation merely by the utterance of his name, he offers salutation with the words "of whom... Those [incarnations] in which there is a "simulation" (viḍambana)—that is, an imitation—of the descents and so forth;
among these, the simulations of the descents are "the delighter of Devakī" and so on, while the simulations of the qualities are...

[The names] such as "the omniscient one" (sarvajña) and "affectionate toward his devotees" (bhaktavatsala); [and the deeds] such as "the uplifter of Govardhana" (govardhanoddharaṇa) and "the enemy of Kaṃsa" (kaṃsārāti). Even when their life-breaths are departing, though they are helpless, they merely utter [these names]. Śamalam means sin (pāpa). Apāvṛtam means with the veil removed (nirastāvaraṇa). Ṛtam means Brahman.
They attain [it]. ||15||

*Sanātana* (Ha.bha.vi. 11.426): Those [works] in which there is a mimicry (*viḍambana*), imitation (*anukaraṇa*), or reliance (*avalambana*) upon the incarnations (*avatāra*) and so forth. Among these, examples of the mimicry of incarnations include [epithets such as] "Delighter of Devakī" (*devakīnandana*) and others;
examples of the mimicry of qualities (*guṇa*) include "Omniscient" (*sarvajña*) and "Affectionate toward devotees" (*bhaktavatsala*) and others; and examples of the mimicry of actions (*karman*)...

"Uplifter of Govardhana," "Slayer of Kaṃsa," and so forth. Even at the departure of life, though helpless, they merely chant [these names]. "Śamalam" means sin; "apāvṛtam" means with the veil removed;
"ṛtam" means Brahman. They attain it suddenly, that is, immediately. The meaning is that they become liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
The structural arrangement [of the verse] is as follows: "By whose descent... and "even at the departure of life...
indicate, respectively, their state of being mere subtle elements (*tanmātra*) at that time and their impure phonemic nature.
"Helpless" (*vivaśāḥ*) means by some other cause even without His will; for Amara states, "the root *vaś* means 'to desire'."

He states the reason for such power: "avatārādi" (incarnations, etc.). This means that they resemble those [incarnations] and possess powers equal to them. Among these, the "imitations of incarnations" include [names] such as Nṛsiṃha;
the "imitations of qualities" include [names] such as Bhaktavatsala; and the "imitations of actions" [include names such as... [Note: The source text appears to be truncated here].
"O upholder of Govardhana," and so forth. "Truth" (*ṛtam*) refers to the Blessed Lord Himself, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
This is because it has been stated: "The Blessed Lord showed His form to Brahmā for the sake of purifying the reality of the Self. (15)

Viśvanātha: Proclaiming his supreme sovereignty and compassion by bestowing his own state even upon people who are like beasts— merely through the appearance of his name, and without even a trace of the knowledge of the object of worship or the practice of meditation as previously defined— he accepts one's surrender only in his specific (saviśeṣa) form.
He makes this request: "Of whomsoever" means that [the forms] are similar to the incarnations (*avatāra*) and so forth, possessing powers equal to those; such is the context.

Alternatively, they are those by which there is a mimicry (*viḍambana*)—that is, an imitation—of the incarnations and so forth, as in the case of actors and the like. Or else, they are "mimicries of the incarnations and so forth" because they denote specific living beings such as one's own brothers, sons, and so on.

The meaning is that these names are inconsistent with His incarnations and so forth. In this regard, there are names such as "This is Kṛṣṇa," "This is Rāma," or "This is Nārāyaṇa," which are mere imitations of His incarnations;
and names such as "The Compassionate One," "The Friend of the Wretched," or "Dāmodara," which are imitations of His deeds.
Those people who, like Ajāmila and others, utter these names even when helpless at the moment of death—

They merely utter [the word]; they proclaim *ṛtam*—the Blessed One whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), from whom all impurity (*śamalam*) or sin has been removed and whose veil has been cast off—for the sake of purifying the reality of the self. This is because it was explained in that very same way in the passage: "Showing his form to Brahmā" (*brahmaṇe darśayan rūpam*).
Or rather, I, Giriśa, and the omnipresent Lord himself—
the three causes of the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of the world— having pierced our own root, have grown as a single tree with vast branches from that three-quartered foundation.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Tree of the World.

"The state of being Brahmā and others belongs to Viṣṇu, while His status as their controller remains; His nature as the Fish and other incarnations is likewise, and it is never otherwise intended. Thus it is said in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*.
And: "Hari, residing in Ananta, Āsana, Vaikuṇṭha, and the Ocean of Milk, is three-footed. (16)

Śrīdhara: There, demonstrating the activities of the incarnations of the qualities (guṇāvatāra), he offers salutation: "He who is indeed one, whose three parts (tripāt) are the three beginning with Brahmā as his feet (pāda) or branches (skandha); and who possesses vast outgrowths (praroha)—that is, secondary branches (śākhopaśākhā)—in the form of Marīci and others, as well as Manu and others. Being such as this...

He grew; salutations to that tree whose form is the universe! Having done what did he grow? Having pierced—that is, having divided—the very Self which is its own root and foundation, in the form of the three *guṇas*. You yourself have declared this in the *Tripād* [Upaniṣad]: "I am Brahmā, and I am Giriśa..."
The meaning is that he, having become three-footed—namely Svayambhū, Viṣṇu, and the Lord (Vibhu)—who are the causes of maintenance, creation, and dissolution, grew great. ||16||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Manifesting that it is not only I alone who take refuge [in You], but rather that since all things beginning with Mahat have arisen from You, taking refuge in You is indeed appropriate for everyone.

He pays homage. He who, being one and three-footed—having Brahmā and the others as his three feet (or branches), having Marīci and the Manvantaras as his thighs, and having [the lineage of] Śākha and Upaśākha as his sprouts—thus grew; having done what? Having pierced the Pradhāna, which has the Self as its root and the Self as its cause.

Having divided [the Lord] according to the three qualities (guṇas), he states that He indeed possesses three forms; the statement beginning with "I" and so forth is an indication according to what is appropriate, meaning that "I" and the others are the causes of maintenance and so on. Here, because the word "himself" (svayam) is used in relation to Viṣṇu in the phrase "the all-pervading Viṣṇu himself," there is no [distinction] for Viṣṇu as there is for Brahmā and Giriśa.

It has been made known that difference is inherently based on qualities (*guṇa*). Or rather, those very things such as the *ahaṃkāra* (ego) and so forth are themselves the root cause even of the Self (*ātman*). Likewise, having split itself and attained a difference produced by its own power (*svaśakti*), it first became three-footed in the form of the three worlds, and thereafter grew forth from its thighs.
"Having the form of the fourteen worlds, obeisance to that tree which has the appearance of the universe"—thus its universal form (*viśvarūpatva*) is described. ||16||
The world is devoted to evil deeds and negligent regarding wholesome action; yet, toward this very worship of you that you yourself have proclaimed,
there exists a powerful hope for life here.
It cuts [the fetters] instantly; let there be salutation to that one who is without blinking.
"By means of his eternal vision of knowledge, the Lord perceives even a *lava* of time eternally, as well as that which is momentary; therefore Hari is 'unblinking' (*animiṣa*).
And the 'unblinking' nature of time [is established] because of the eternal observation of the *lava* and other units. Thus it is stated in the *Tantrasāra*. (17)

Śrīdhara: Having thus described the imitation of the activities of the incarnations of the qualities (*guṇāvatāra*), he now bows down, showing that very form of His known as Time (*kāla*) and its activity, with two verses beginning with "In the world" (*loke*). [The verse describes one who is] "addicted to improper action" (*vikarmanirataḥ*), meaning intent on contrary actions; and regarding what is "wholesome and beneficial" (*kuśale hite*), namely that which is his own and proclaimed by You Yourself.
Regarding the action consisting of your own worship as explicitly stated, it is indeed said in the *Gītā*:
"Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give,
and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī— perform all that as an offering unto Me" (*Gītā* 9.27).
As long as one remains heedless and lacks focused attention toward that [reality], for so long does this world persist for the sake of the unblinking Time. ||17||

The sequential arrangement is as follows: *vikarman* is action directed away from the Lord. *Arcana* (worship) is that which is prescribed in the *Pañcarātra* and other such texts, for it is stated in the *Mokṣadharma* section of the *Mahābhārata*: "The Lord himself is the speaker of the entire *Pañcarātra*" (*Ma.bhā.* 12.337.62). ||17||

Viśvanātha: Having described his universal form (*viśvarūpatva*), he now bows to Viśvanimiṣa as the embodiment of Time. "The world"—meaning humans and others—"is negligent" (*pramatta*) regarding virtuous action, being lacking in focused attention. What is that virtuous action? To this he says: "in the worship of You."

Now, some explain that because of the statements, "having worshipped Him with one's own duty" and "the wise worship the embodiment of knowledge through the sacrifice of knowledge," the worship of the Lord must indeed occur through both the yoga of action and the yoga of knowledge; to this, he says: "This worship of mine is [performed] by You alone, according to what was spoken by You."

This is because it is stated directly: "Those means for the attainment of the Self which were indeed proclaimed by the Blessed One" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.34), as found in the Eleventh Book; and from the Mokṣadharma: "The Blessed One himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra" (Mahābhārata 12.337.62). Thus, the meaning is: "in one's own," that is, in what belongs to oneself and what is to be performed by oneself.
Thus, it is illuminated that the authority of Time (Kāla) extends only to those other than your devotees.
The meaning is: even the hope for the life of this non-devotee is [not granted], let alone the desire for enjoyments and the like;
[this is said] regarding the unblinking Time. ||17||
For even I, though seated upon a throne for two parārdhas and honored by all the worlds, was afraid of him when he performed austerities,
desiring to obtain many sacrifices.
Salutation to that Blessed One, to you who are intent upon sacrifice.

Śrīdhara: Let alone the talk of the world; for even though I have ascended to that abode or station which lasts for two *parārdhas*—originating from you who are called Time—I am afraid. And being afraid, desiring to obtain you, seeking to reach you, I have performed penance. In what state?

*Bahusava*: one for whom there are many *savas*, meaning sacrifices or years. The sense is that he has performed penance for many sacrifices or for many years. *Adhimakhāya*: to the presiding lord of sacrifice. ||18||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha states: He declares the limit of the aforementioned power of time—since from that time I, Brahmā, although occupying the abode, the station of Satyaloka, which lasts for two *parārdhas*.
I am likewise afraid while desiring to restrain [Time], wishing to bring Time under my control;
and being one who has performed many *sava*s—that is, many sacrifices—I have also practiced austerity.
The meaning is that I am afraid even of that.

[Objection: "But when you were engaged in many sacrifices for the purpose of bringing time under your control, what reasoning did you have at that time? To this he replies: "Salutations to You, the presiding deity of sacrifices (*makhānām adhiṣṭhātṛ*), for the sake of [controlling] sacrifice (*adhimakhāya*).
With the thought, 'May time come under my control through the very performance of sacrifices (*makha*) by You, who are the presiding deity of sacrifices,' [I offered them]."
The meaning is as follows: On the contrary, I have been brought under the sway of Time alone; even now I am afraid.
Therefore, the implication is: "Without pure devotion to You, Time cannot be conquered"—thus having realized the truth today, from now on I shall practice only pure devotion. ||18||

He who, though his objects of enjoyment were already dispelled, took delight by his own will among the wombs of living beings— such as animals, humans, and gods— in order to preserve the boundaries established by himself, even while his body remained confined.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Supreme Person.
Madhvaḥ: one whose delight is never cast aside, one who possesses eternal delight. ||19||

Śrīdhara: Now, demonstrating the activities of His various playful incarnations (līlāvatāra) occurring at those respective times, he says: Having voluntarily assumed forms among the species of living beings, such as animals and so forth, He sported out of a desire to maintain the boundaries of dharma established by Himself; in reality, however, it was solely through the experience of His own bliss.

Even though he has cast off the pleasure of sense objects, he remains the Supreme Person because he is untouched by the attributes of those various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). As it is said in the *Gītā*:
"Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable..."
"Therefore, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). [Gītā 15.18] ||19||

The sequence of the composition: Since the objects within the sphere of the individual soul and material things have been cast aside by Him, He has assumed a body by His own will out of a desire to protect His devotees, thus manifesting His form. (19)

Viśvanātha: Having thus offered salutation [to Śiva] both as the form of the universe and as its controller in the form of Time (Kāla), he now offers salutation to him as the supreme object of worship, whose essential nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda).
The ellipsis "descended by his own will among animals and so forth" is to be supplied. [He has descended] out of a desire to protect the boundaries established by himself.
He rejoices because he delights in the Self, even though he has renounced the pleasures of the senses—as it is said:
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—that offering of devotion from the self-restrained person, I accept. (Gītā 9.26)

He took delight only in those things—such as garlands, sandalwood paste, fragrant flowers, and beds—brought by His own devotees for His enjoyment, in order to maintain the boundaries He Himself had established;
for He said: "I do not desire myself without My holy devotees" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.4.64).

The sense is that even while delighting in the Self, He is as if His desires are not yet fulfilled. Although garlands and other such items are material objects (*prākṛta*), when they are employed for the sake of the Lord, they become non-material (*aprākṛta*) at that very moment; this will become clear in the Eleventh Book [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.25.27–29]. According to the view of Bhāguri, "one whose body is contained" (*avaruddhadehaḥ*).

The meaning is that, through the dissolution of the causal ignorance (*avetya-ākāra-lopa*), by virtue of his sovereign power (*vibhutva*), his body is unobstructed and consists solely of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
Alternatively, it refers to the limit (*maryādā*) consisting in his subjection to his own devotees, which constitutes the boundary established by himself.

His body is embraced by Śrī Yaśodā with the desire for Him in every respect and the longing for His attainment— as if she were Dāmnī— and likewise by other devotees through the cord of affection. Therefore, because He is superior to all,
including the creators of the great [universe] and the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the intended meaning is that this refers specifically to the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa.
As it has been said:
"Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)" [Gītā 15.18]. ||19||
He who, though untouched by ignorance, bore sleep through the fivefold state of existence, having made the affairs of the world his belly’s contents—
a sleep as pleasant as the touch of the serpent-couch within the waters.
Revealing happiness for people amidst that which is garlanded with terrifying waves.

Śrīdhara: Now he bows to the single form currently being perceived with the two verses beginning with "yo 'vidyayā. Although he was not overcome by that ignorance—which consists of the fivefold functions (the five *vṛttis*) and which is the cause of sleep—he bore the yogic sleep (*yoganidrā*). The connection with the following verse is: "Salutation to You, such as that. [The word] *jaṭharīkṛtāḥ* means placed within the belly.

Explaining that for an undiscriminating person sleeping within the waters where there are garlands of terrifying waves, the pleasure of sleep is such as this—he by whom the worldly course, the maintenance of the world, has been dissolved; whose bed is the serpent itself; and whose touch is pleasant—that sleep.
The meaning is "showing" or "mocking. For this very reason, there are qualifiers such as "within the water" and so forth.

Alternatively, it means revealing or expanding the bliss of rest for people exhausted by previous kalpas. This is intended to illuminate that, at such a time, one must endure even unbearable suffering oneself for the sake of helping others.
The qualifiers. ||20||

The sequence of the composition: He approves of the very visible pastime of that Supreme Person who has descended, [expressed by the verse beginning] "He who... By manifesting within himself that very bliss of sleep which belongs to ordinary people through his divine play, he reveals therein both the state of being a refuge inaccessible to others and the quality of having a bed of pleasant touch.
He states the reason for its ease with the words beginning "within the water" (antarjale). ||20||
Viśvanātha: Now, with two verses, he bows to his own chosen form as it is currently perceived.

Although he was not overcome by that ignorance—which consists of the fivefold functions (the five *vṛttis*) and serves as the cause of sleep—he nevertheless bore [the semblance of] sleep; therefore, this sleep of yours is composed solely of your own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
The state [of being]. He is one by whom the course of worldly life—the succession of the world—has been made his belly, that is, dissolved within his stomach.
She is she whose touch is pleasant, [even] upon a serpent-skin bed (*kaśipu*). [This applies even] to an ordinary person in the ocean of universal dissolution, garlanded with terrifying waves.

The sense is that, by explaining how there is happiness for one who lies upon a soft bed situated in the midst of water, you are merely acting out of sport (līlā), just like an ordinary person; or rather, even at the time of universal dissolution,
when the ocean strikes fear into all people, you sleep comfortably even upon a serpent-bed.
The intended meaning is that you alone—and no other—are fearless in all times, in all places, and amidst all attachments.
Explaining "happily," [it means] that even when a person is possessed by fear due to time, place, or attachment, one who is sleepy sleeps happily indeed. ||20||

Salutations to You, O Yoga, by whose grace I was born from the abode of the navel-lotus as the worshipful one who provides the means of sustenance for the three worlds, while You remain within my belly.
To him whose lotus-eyes were blossoming at the end of sleep.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, [I am he] from whom the lotus of whose navel is the very abode; for whom the three worlds are the instrument (upakaraṇa). Or rather, he who benefits the three worlds by means of their creation and so forth is such, and by his grace I existed; he in whose belly resides "bhava," the phenomenal world of saṃsāra.
His eyes were like slightly blossoming lotuses at the conclusion of his yogic sleep. ||21||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He whose instruments—the three worlds—were obedient to his command;
or rather, he who benefits the three worlds through the processes of creation and so forth. He is Bhava (Śiva) residing within the belly.

To him for whom the manifold proliferation of saṃsāra [has ceased]; to him whose eye is now blossoming like a lotus at the end of night following the conclusion of yogic sleep—to him, O my Lord, O ocean of compassion, wake up, wake up! The sense is: "I am your servant; let me perform the auspicious *rātrika* offering."
May this one Lord, the sole friend and Self of all worlds, who gladdens beings with His divine power through His goodness,
touch my vision with that very same power, so that I may—
"I shall create this as before; for he is fond of those who bow down to him."
"Keśava, the Supreme Person, performs his own activities together with Ramā through his own power; he himself performs some of these," so it is said in the *Nāradīya*.
"The primary meaning of the word 'Self' (ātman) is Viṣṇu alone, the eternal one."
Those whose bodies and minds are filled with doubt, as well as their intellects and vital breaths, are likewise [bound].
"Even Brahmā is secondary; for there is a gradual progression toward the state of Selfhood. Thus it is stated in the *Prakāśasaṃhitā*. 22.

Śrīdhara: Having thus offered praise, he makes this petition with the four verses beginning with "So 'yam": "If He, by means of His goodness (*sattva*), knowledge (*jñāna*), fortune (*bhaga*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), shall gladden (*mṛḍayate*) and bring happiness to the universe, may He touch my vision—that is, my wisdom—and unite it [with Him], so that I may become capable of creation; for..."

He is fond of those who bow to him, and I have bowed; there is no other to be petitioned, because he is the Blessed One. He alone is the friend of all the worlds, since he is the one pervasive Self, the inner controller, and the underlying thread of the entire sequence [of scripture].
This has not been explained [elsewhere].

Viśvanātha: Having thus offered praise, he prays with the four verses beginning with "so 'yam" (this very one). He is the friend and protector of all worlds—both material and spiritual—and the Self, the object of unconditional love. He is "one" because there exists no other such being. This is because, by virtue of his quality of *sattva*...

By means of his characteristic of protection (*pālana*), he gladdens (*mṛḍayate*) and brings happiness to all beings in the entire world who are of a natural (*prākṛta*) disposition; by means of his "fortune" (*bhaga*), that is, his own sixfold sovereignty (*ṣaḍaiśvarya*), he also gladdens those devotees who are not of a natural disposition (*aprākṛta*). Therefore, through even a mere fraction of that very essence (*sattva*) and through his fortune (*bhaga*), [grant] my vision—that is, my wisdom—which is currently natural.

"Because of his devotion, may he touch and protect even a portion of the non-material [nature]; for I shall know how to create material beings such as Marīci and others, and how to manifest non-material beings such as Nārada and others, since that Lord is dear even when merely prostrated before. ||22||
This bestower of boons upon those who have sought refuge, having assumed incarnations characterized by specific qualities, will delight [the world] through his own power;
even as he creates this display of his own prowess therein, let the mind [be fixed] upon him.
One should apply oneself [to yoga] so that one may abandon the defilement of karma.

Śrīdhara: Whatever action He shall perform by His own power together with Ramā, may that very Lord engage and impel my mind—even as I create this universe by His command—to manifest His own prowess, which is indeed the prowess and majesty of Viṣṇu Himself; [may He remove] attachment to action and its consequences.
And so that I may abandon—that is, cast off—impurity, which is the evil of disharmony and the like. ||23||

The sequential composition is as follows: "This one" refers to Him who has assumed incarnations characterized by qualities—not through the causal power of *māyā*, but by means of His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*) known as *Ramā*. He is one whose incarnations possess such qualities as affection for His devotees and so forth. "His own prowess" means that it consists of Your own prowess.
In this way, the universe would come to be; therefore, it is possible for me to bring that about through Your power alone.
Consequently, my prayer for that end is indeed appropriate—this is the intended meaning. ||23||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, fearing creation consisting of the quality of *rajas*, he prays for the elevation of his own devotion. The meaning is: "May you, O Lord, be the granter of this boon to me who have sought refuge.
[He prays] "with Ramā," meaning with her who is his very own essential nature (*svarūpa*), and not with *māyā*. Therefore...
He whose incarnations are devoid of [worldly] qualities—may my mind be engaged in, or directed toward, his work such as the lifting up of the earth. Of me, who am doing what?
Even while creating this universe, which is characterized by the prowess—the power—of my own Lord, that is, while creating through him.

The meaning is that my mind should not become attached [to anything else], but rather to the stories of His pastimes alone; I shall abandon the impurity of karma—the sin of inequality arising from the creation of the universe. ||23||
For that person of infinite power who exists here within the lake of the navel, I was the power of discernment (*vijñāna-śakti*);
this manifold form is the manifestation of him as he unfolds it through me.
May the utterance of the hymns of the Veda not cause you harm.

Śrīdhara: May the creative utterance (*visarga*)—the pronunciation—of the words that constitute the limbs of my Veda, which I am expanding, not cause harm; [the Veda] from whose navel-lake I arose while existing within the waters, and which belongs to the mind whose nature is the principle of *mahat* and whose power is consciousness, and which is the presiding deity of that [mind]. [The word "girām" ends in a consonant.]
The meaning is that, according to the principle "it is spiritual luster," let it not be omitted. ||24||

The sequence of the composition: May my Brahmanic splendor (*brahmatejas*), which consists of the recitation of the Veda, not be lost while I am creating this [universe] down to that which is characterized by the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). The meaning is that, unlike ordinary Brāhmaṇas, [my splendor] should not be diminished through negligence. Regarding the phrase "mā rīriṣīṣṭa," the root *riṣ* means "to injure."
The form [of the verb] with the *yaṅ* elided (*yaṅluk*) in the *liṭ* tense, when used in the sense of the agent as object (*karmakartṛ*), is Vedic.

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, O Blessed One, ocean of sovereignty, that I have gained even this mere drop of entry into you is surely due to the grace of Vedic study alone. For it has been said: "The Veda is your eye, O Lord"; yet now—

Because of my lack of resolve regarding the various activities for the purpose of creation, the forgetfulness of that Veda might occur; therefore, he prays, "May it not be so": "O Nābhi, from the lake of your navel while you were in the waters, I was born as the *vijñāna-śakti*, the person consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-puruṣa*)."

May this emission of the words that constitute the limbs of my Veda— which expands this universe as the form of the Supreme Lord, who is the collective soul (samaṣṭijīva) or the presiding deity of the principle of intellect (buddhitattva)—
not suffer excessive loss through forgetfulness caused by Māyā; may the manifold expansion of the divisions such as the Ṛgveda and others not be destroyed.

The meaning is "let it be. The form *kiṣ* is a Vedic usage in the *liṅ* (optative) mood of the *yaṅ-luk* (intensive without suffix) of the root *hiṃs* in the sense of "injury," used here with the reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*). ||24||
Thus that Blessed One, possessed of abundant compassion, rising with his lotus-eyes expanding in a smile of increasing love,
[spoke] to dispel our despondency regarding the conquest of the universe.
May the ancient Person remove [it] with his honeyed speech.

Śrīdhara: With a smile born of increased love, causing [the world] to blossom, He rose up for the victory and manifestation of the universe, and—by the force of the word "and"—for our grace as well. ||25||
Sanātana is one whose compassion is unfailing and who is exceedingly merciful; therefore, by means of that smile born of increased love, he unfolds, causes [the world] to blossom,
and causes it to open its eyes for the victory and emergence of the universe—
or else, for the subjugation of the universe through the propagation of his own devotion— or else, for the great festival of the world.

And by the word "ca" (and), it is meant "for the sake of special favor. May [the Lord] remove the despondency—the sorrow and suffering arising from the dissolution or from the lack of drinking the nectar of Your long-delayed arrival—of us, Your devotees, with His honey-sweet voice. This verse has been written here in accordance with the practice of the learned; however, there are others as well.
These may be recited as desired. [Haribhaktivilāsa 16.328] Kramasandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, it is solely through the Lord’s compassionate glance and the command of His grace that the servant [attains this].
Thinking, "May there be joy free from doubt," he prays for that very thing with the words "so'sau" (that is He).

May He, unfolding and causing [all things] to unfold, grant us victory everywhere in the universe—meaning the absence of defeat in creation and other activities—and by the force of the word "ca" (and), the fulfillment of the previously mentioned desires. Mādvhyā.
By the word consisting of sweetness, which contains the command "Create the universe," [the world was produced]. ||25||
Maitreya said:
Having thus perceived his own origin through austerity, knowledge, and meditative absorption,
and having praised him with words as far as his mind could reach, he ceased, appearing as if exhausted.

Śrīdhara: [He approached] Him from whom his own birth originated. Having perceived [Him] through austerity (tapaḥ)—meaning physical discipline—knowledge (vidyā)—meaning meditative worship—and concentration (samādhi)—meaning one-pointedness, and having praised Him according to his ability, he ceased as if exhausted. ||26||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "That from which one's own manifestation arises—[one should know that] austerity is bodily; through the form of the teacher and the shrine, he manifests his own state" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 11.29.6)—according to this principle.

Having attained the worship of that mantra through spontaneous inspiration, and having perceived [the deity] through meditation and one-pointed concentration of the mind, he praised [Him] according to his ability; then, as if dejected by the non-perception of a compassionate glance, he ceased [his recitation]. ||26||
Then, having perceived Brahmā’s intention, Madhusūdana [beheld him] whose mind was despondent because of that water resulting from the dissolution of the kalpa.
To him, who was weary of himself due to his knowledge of the world’s structure,
he spoke with profound words, as if to pacify his dejection.

Śrīdhara: The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the two verses is as follows: having perceived the intention of Brahmā, who was weary from his efforts to understand the structure of the world, [the Lord] spoke to him. By that water of dissolution, [Brahmā’s] mind became dejected (*viṣaṇṇacetasam*).
*Kaśmala* means delusion (*moha*). The word *iva* indicates that it is like the complete pacification of all delusion. (27–28)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [He was] dejected in mind because of the waters of the dissolution—the water that gathers at the time of universal destruction—and likewise for himself and for the worlds, such as the gods, animals, and so forth.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having perceived and understood the intention of Brahmā—who was weary regarding the cognition of that [creation], namely the sequence of establishing emanations through their appropriate nature and form—he spoke to him, as if pacifying his dejection and delusion (*kaśmala-moha*). ||28||
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Veda-garbha, do not yield to sloth; exert yourself in the work of creation.
For that which you now request of me was already ordained by me in the beginning."
Even the prayer for honey is indeed my own instigation. ||29||

Śrīdhara: O Vedagarbha! Do not fall into *tandrī*, that is, the laziness born of despondency. As for his prayer, "May [the Lord] touch my very sight with that [grace]," and so forth, that has already been accomplished previously. ||29||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: He shows that it pacifies all delusion. "Do not fall into *tandrī*—that is, ignorance. The implication is that for one who possesses the knowledge of all the Vedas, as [Vedagarbha] does, ignorance is not appropriate. Now, [an objection]:...

I am doubtful regarding my own capacity for creation. To this he says: "In the act of creation. One should not fear that one's effort will be fruitless; to this he says: "Consisting of that"—meaning, "May He touch my vision with that very [power]," as he entreats me. (29)
"Furthermore, O Brahmin, practice asceticism and acquire knowledge centered upon me; through these two, with your heart within, you shall behold the worlds unveiled."
And it is said: "The contemplation of the honey [of the Self] is called austerity (tapas), and steadfastness in knowledge is proclaimed as the goal. ||30||
Śrīdhara: If that is so, then why do I not know? To this he says: "Furthermore" (bhūyaḥ). ||30||
The sequence of composition: "Furthermore" [means] austerity, such as breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth. ||30||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But now, what will be gained by my exertion? Those worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, which are to be created by me, are not even seen. To this he says: "Furthermore... Penance (*tapas*) is one-pointedness of mind;
knowledge (*vidyā*) is the practice of mantras. Even though the worlds exist externally, [he perceives them] within the heart itself.
You shall see the worlds beginning with Bhūr and the beings therein, such as humans, as uncovered—that is, devoid of the veil of water.
Then, having seen those very things being shown by me exactly as they exist within your own heart, you will easily project them externally, like a scribe who has viewed his work in a mirror. ||30||
Then, endowed with devotion toward yourself and the world, and being composed in mind, O Brahmin, you shall see me pervading all; and within me, you shall see the worlds and yourself.
"Madhva says: 'In every body Hari resides; in him all the worlds are established.
Even though he is only the size of a thumb, he is the Supreme, for the Supreme Power is all-pervading. And:
'While I abide within the self... [31]

Śrīdhara: Being endowed with devotion and concentrated in mind, you shall see—indeed, you will behold—Me existing as the pervader within yourself and within the world, as well as the individual souls (jīvas) within yourself. ||31||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding that which was prayed for—that "even under the power of absorption in creation, I shall not forget you"—he says: "Therefore, even at the time of creation, being endowed with devotion and composed..."

You shall see Me within yourself, in your own mind, and in the external world; likewise, O Yaśodā, you shall see the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, as well as the individual souls, within Me during My pastime of eating clay. Or rather, in the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, through the cowherds, calves, and so forth, you shall see Me—the all-pervading—within Me, along with the worlds, the cosmic eggs.
Or rather, you shall see your own many forms as the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), each possessing four arms. ||31||
But when the world perceives me as abiding in all beings like fire within wood, then indeed it shall abandon its delusion.
Śrīdhara: He says that delusion ceases everywhere upon seeing Me with the words "But when... (*yadā tu*). "Praticakṣīta" means he would see. ||32||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha says: "That which was requested—that the impurity of karma (*karmaśamala*) might be [removed] as in the case of Vijayā—can indeed occur in such a state; thus he says: 'But when... [he] shall behold (*praticakṣīta*), that is, see.
*Kaśmala* means delusion (*moha*). ||32||
When one perceives the self as devoid of the elements, the senses, the qualities, and the latent impressions, and as endowed with its own true nature through me, it attains sovereign bliss.
The honey, by its very nature, is joined with me; for the form of the individual soul (jīva) residing in the heart becomes united with the Supreme Lord.
Having abandoned the identification with the body and so forth, [one realizes this] within the heart where the form of the individual soul resides.
And having seen that very body situated at the lotus feet of Hari.
"When one perceives [the Self] through direct intuition, then one attains liberation"—thus says Śrīdhara in the *Dattātreyayoga*.
And he states that "one is liberated upon the cessation of false knowledge" by using the word "then" (*yadā*). [He means:
the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the referent of the term "Pure Being" (*śuddhatva-padārtha*), perceives the Self as being essentially devoid of the elements and so forth.
Seeing that [Self] as unified with me, who have become its very essence—that is, endowed with that reality—one then attains self-sovereignty, which is liberation. ||33||

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] begins with the words "yadā" (when). Devoid of the elements and so forth, the individual soul (*jīva*) is joined—by its very nature—with me, who am the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) and the substratum of that soul's power; thus it attains its own sovereignty, such as equality in power (*sārṣṭya*) and the like. ||33||
Viśvanātha: In response to the expectation of at what stage one might attain you, he says:

when the self (ātman), being devoid of the elements (bhūta) and so forth, [remains] in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone—and not by abandoning its status as an individual soul (*jīvātmatva*)—it has "gone near" (*upa-ita*) to me, the Supreme Lord who is to be served, for the sake of service.

Seeing that [the goal] has been attained, he then shines together with his own Lord; thus he is a *svarāṭ* (self-ruling), and he attains or reaches *dāsya*—the state or activity of being a servant (*dāsa*) of Him. However, some [maintain that this is not so], because the praise of both the undifferentiated (*nirviśeṣa*) and differentiated (*saviśeṣa*) natures was already undertaken.

The wise devotees who worship that [deity] explain this verse by means of the *tantra* (the internal method) as revealing the final stage [of realization]. For instance, when the man of knowledge (*jñānī*), perceiving himself as the pure state (*śuddhatva*) united with— that is, one with— the "That-word" (*tat-pada*) which is the essential nature of the object, at that time...

When that occurs, one attains self-sovereignty, which is liberation. Likewise, the devotee—though fivefold as peaceful and so forth—is endowed with [the Lord's] own nature: as peaceful by virtue of being the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), as a servant by virtue of the nature of service, as a friend through friendship alone, as a father and so forth through affection (*vātsalya*), and as beloved through love alone.

The meaning is exactly as follows: one's own self is likewise endowed with the fivefold states of existence, and directly with the Supreme Brahman—the Lord—as well as with a friend, a son, and so forth, and with a beloved, each according to its respective nature. Sovereignty (*svārājyam*) is [attained] by means of one’s own form as pure consciousness, through one’s own Lord.
It shines together with a friend, a son, and so forth, as well as with a beloved; it attains, that is, reaches, the state or essence of being such. ||33||
As you desire to create many offspring through the vast expanse of various karmas, your own self does not falter; this is your most excellent favor toward me.
Śrīdhara: Because he is *varṣīyān*, meaning more aged; the sense is that he is exceedingly superior. ||34||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha says: Having thus taught the true nature of knowledge, devotion, and aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), he states—beginning with "nānā"—that his grace toward you is not merely for the present day, but is indeed eternal.
The older one is the elder. ||34||
The most wicked quality of passion (rajas) does not bind you, the primordial sage,
even as you create living beings, for your mind remains fixed upon me.
Śrīdhara: He speaks of grace itself through four verses beginning with "the sage" (ṛṣim). [He says this] because your mind is bound to me. ||35||
The sequence of the composition: regarding the word "the sage" (ṛṣim), it was stated previously in the Second Canto as follows:
"Adhere to this doctrine with supreme concentration;
you shall never be deluded amidst the various cycles of kalpas" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.9.36).
Therefore, even that which was spoken by Him Himself, such as "O dear one, my speech is not observed to be false" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.6.34), is established.
As for the fact that His possession by another is heard of in some instances, that indeed cannot be permanent;
thus it should be understood as merely a semblance thereof. Let it be granted that His delusion is heard of in the Tenth Canto. That—

But this is not due to passion; rather, it is through the vision of the specific majesty of the Lord and the desire to see those specific qualities, for it is heard in that very context in passages such as *ambhojanmajaniḥ* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.13.15). Likewise, in the Eleventh Canto, knowledge is taught to Sanaka and others by Him in the form of a swan (*haṃsa*).
The obscuration of the knowledge of Brahman should be understood as existing for the purpose of manifesting its own majesty. ||35||
Viśvanātha says: "Do not fear the quality of *rajas*," he says [to him] with the word "the sage" (*ṛṣim*).

In the tenth book, his distraction is not due to *rajas*, but rather solely by the power of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the fortune of beholding His charming majesty; this is explained in that very place. (35)
I have been known by you today, even though I am difficult for embodied beings to discern,
since you consider me to be distinct from the elements, the senses, the qualities, and the self.

And [it is said]: "One who perceives Madhava as the one joined to all things—be they the elements, the senses, the mind, the intellect, the three qualities, and so forth—in His capacity as their controller, knows Keśava. (36)

Śrīdhara: Because you consider it to be unjoined with the elements (bhūtas), the senses (indriyas), the qualities (guṇas) such as sattva and the rest, and the self (ātman), which is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). ||36||

Regarding the sequential arrangement: as for what was stated, "I am known," that should be understood in accordance with the five verses spoken by Brahmā beginning with "You are known" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.1). ||37||

Viśvanātha: Since you consider this form of mine— which, though possessed of form, is unjoined with the elements and so forth— to be such by virtue of the arising of the essence of consciousness, therefore, this form of mine consists neither of the elements such as earth and the rest, nor of the sense organs composed of light, nor of the *guṇa-māyā*, nor of the *ātman*.
The meaning is that you are not merely a living soul (jīva), but know yourself to be Brahman directly.

Therefore, the Lord’s intention should be understood as follows: the very contemplation of my form as being existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda) and as being beyond illusion (māyā) is the sign of whether one possesses knowledge of me or lacks it. ||36||
While you were in doubt about me, my very self was revealed to you from within,
like the root of a lotus being sought by one searching for it through the stalk in the water.

Śrīdhara: While you were searching for the root—the foundation—of the lotus in the water by means of its stalk as your path, there must have been doubt regarding my existence based on that support; yet it was not seen.
Thus, when the uncertainty arose as to whether I exist or do not exist, my self—my own true nature—was revealed by me within the heart, not outside.
It has been shown. ||37||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: Since my own form becomes visible through my own inconceivable will alone, and not because it is actually perceptible by the senses such as the eyes, you yourself are the proof of this.

He said: "In order to fulfill your purpose, my very self, whose form is Śrī, has been [placed] by me within my heart, both externally and internally. Or rather, it has also been shown externally—for according to scripture, 'the attire of a cowherd appeared before me'—since the vision of the Self is something to be bestowed; thus, there is also the inclusion of the action."

The fourth case ending (*caturthī*) is used here in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*), meaning "it should be done for me. When? The meaning is: while you were searching for the root of the *puṣkara* flower, and when there was a doubt regarding me—namely, the uncertainty as to whether or not I am present. Here, because neither austerity (*tapas*) nor meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is mentioned, those two are also [implied] as being subordinate to the sight of me.
In reality, it is not a cause, but rather my own will; thus, one should understand that he made this secret doctrine known even to Brahmā. ||37||
O dear one, that you have composed this hymn to me, marked by the excellence of my stories,
or that you are steadfast in asceticism— this indeed is my grace upon you.

Śrīdhara: O dear one, O Brahmin! You have performed [this]. My very narrative is the source of prosperity; it is marked by that. This absence of bondage—this steadfastness of the mind upon Me, this knowledge of Me, the vision of My form within the heart, the praise of Me, and devotion to austerity—if all this is present, it is entirely My grace.

The sequential arrangement: "And that which... Even in the state of being an animal or a human, such a thing as merely my narrative is a source of prosperity; therein, moreover, the distinction lies in the hymn being marked by that [narrative].
"This very one... means that all of this is of the nature of my grace. ||38||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, he says that even your hymns of praise and so forth came into being solely through my grace: "Whatever you have done—that is, what you performed—all that is this well-known, manifest grace of mine. The meaning is: "Understand that each of those [works] is the effect of this very [grace]. ||38||
I am pleased; may it be well with you, for out of a desire for the victory of the worlds, you have praised me by describing my qualities, even though I am devoid of qualities.
"Keśava is pleased with him who knows Hari as being endowed with qualities such as omniscience and devoid of qualities such as *sattva*"; thus it is said in the *Vyomasaṃhitā*. (39)
Śrīdhara: Even while describing that which appears to consist of qualities, [he] describes it as being indeed devoid of qualities. ||39||

The sequence of the composition is as follows: "I am pleased. Some praise [the Lord] as being endowed with material qualities (*prākṛtaguṇa*), while others praise Him as being devoid of them. The meaning is: "Having presented [Him] as consisting of qualities (*guṇamaya*)—distinguished by infinite non-material qualities—and then as being devoid of those [non-material qualities] and abounding in material qualities, you have praised Me."

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, he says "I am pleased" to show that he is exceedingly gratified by devotion arising solely from his own mercy, and thus one should observe his wondrous method: [he is pleased] with the desire for the victory of the worlds—that is, with the desire that the worlds being created by him may be endowed with victory—and with that which consists of the *guṇas*.

Since you have praised me—who am an ocean of auspiciousness, possessed of form, yet devoid of qualities and free from the attributes of ordinary beings such as *sattva*—I am pleased; may it be well with them. However, those who praise me, Śrī Nārāyaṇa, as consisting solely of qualities by virtue of my possessing the qualities of *sattva* and so forth, but not [as I truly am]—[may it be well with them too].
Because they are devoid of qualities, the sense is that "I am not pleased with them," and thus "may it not be well with them. ||39||
Whoever, being a man, should constantly worship me by praising me with this hymn,
to him I shall quickly become fully propitious, for I am the Lord who grants boons for all desires.
"Madhu is that which has surpassed the authority of the gods who hold specific offices;
for it always brings pleasure to Viṣṇu even more than devotion and other such qualities. Thus [it is said]. 40.
Śrīdhara: What need is there to say that he is pleased with you? He says: "He who... (verse 40).
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He says "He who... [verse 40] to show that there is no need to say anything more than "He is pleased with you."
The attainment of the supreme good for men through meritorious works, austerity, sacrifices, gifts, and the concentration of yoga is considered by those who know the truth to be my own gratification.
The supreme sovereignty of Madhva is liberation; even in liberation, my own affection is what brings delight.
For even for the liberated Hari, my affection is what causes him to rejoice in every respect—so it is stated in the Vāmana Purāṇa. (41)

Śrīdhara: And he says that there is nothing superior even to my own pleasure: "The fruit of supreme liberation (niḥśreyasa) accomplished through works of public utility (pūrta) and the like is indeed my own pleasure; such is the opinion of those who know the truth. (41)

Sanātana (Ha.bha.vi. 11.47): And he says that there is nothing superior to my pleasure—by means of the verse beginning with "pūrtena. The fruit of supreme beatitude (*niḥśreyasa*) which is accomplished (*rāddha*) or perfected through works of public utility (*pūrta*) and so forth, is indeed my own pleasure; such is the opinion of those who know the truth. ||41||

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Thus, having praised His own love for the devotee, He now praises the devotee’s love for Him as well, beginning with the words "by means of *pūrta*. That very love for Me, whether mediated through acts such as *pūrta* (public works) or direct, is itself the perfected fruit of liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), established through thorough inquiry.
Because that alone is what is accepted by those who know reality. ||41||

Viśvanātha: And he says that there is nothing superior to my pleasure: "That fruit of supreme liberation (niḥśreyasa) which is accomplished or achieved through works of public utility (pūrta) and so forth—that, according to the opinion of those who know the truth, is my very own pleasure. Without my pleasure, even an accomplished supreme liberation is not truly supreme; therefore [it is said]."

The meaning is this: those who know reality perform acts such as *pūrta* (public works) solely for the sake of pleasing Me; they desire only to bring joy to Me, and do not wish to make Me an object of their own personal pleasure.
Therefore, being pleased with them every day by virtue of that *sāttvika* devotion, I grant them liberation.

O Creator, I am the Self of all selves and the most beloved even among those things that are dear; therefore, one should fix one's love upon Me, for it is for My sake that the body and other such things are held dear.
"Indeed, the self is dearer than everything else; yet Hari brings about even that self's state of being dear.
Therefore, Hari is dearer even than one's own self. Thus it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta*. (42)

Śrīdhara: Here he states the reason: "I am" (aham). He is the Self (ātman) of the individual souls (jīvas), whose limiting adjunct (upādhi) is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). Therefore, being the most beloved (preṣṭha)—the dearest among even those things that are already dear (preyas)—He is irreproachable. "Yatkṛte" means for whose sake or for what purpose. ||42||

The sequential composition establishes this as follows: "I am the Self. This means that even for the selves—the pure individual souls—it is the very love that consists of the grace of the one who is supremely dear without qualification or limit that must be prayed for. ||42||

Viśvanātha: Revealing that for those possessing devotion to the qualityless (nirguṇa), I am the object of their love, and thus indicating that in reality I alone am fit to become the object of the love of all living beings, he establishes love for himself with the words "I am. I am the Self (ātman) of the selves (ātmanām), that is, of the individual souls (jīvas).
Because the Supreme Self is the cause for which the body and so forth are considered dear, there is affection for wives, children, and others through their connection with the body;
affection for the body through its connection with the individual self (*jīvātman*); and affection for the individual self through its connection with the Supreme Self.
Thus, affection for the individual self and the rest is ultimately rooted in the Supreme Self alone as its natural basis.
[The term] "figurative" (*aupacārikī*) refers to the gradual decrease in dearness toward those [objects].

But then, how can the sentence "one should cultivate passion for me" (*mayi ratiṃ kuryāt*) have the nature of an injunction (*vidhitva*), since passion is already established? For it has been said: "An injunction applies where there is absolute non-attainment [of the action]. It is replied: with respect to *māyā*...
Indeed, the scope of authority extends only as far as the individual soul (jīvātman) and not beyond that to the Supreme Self (paramātman);

thus, for humans and others who have fallen under the bondage of Māyā, experience proceeds only toward illusory objects, and even for the individual soul, there exists an imputed state of being illusory. Nevertheless...
However, although natural love exists for the Supreme Self, because there is an absence of direct experience,
there is an absence of love for it— just as a merchant who is unaware of his own vast wealth suffers from poverty; thus, the scripture enjoins love for it.

Furthermore, although the Supreme Self is in reality the most beloved and is directly experienced by the knowers of truth (*jñānins*), He does not become an object of love without *rati*; therefore, He becomes the most beloved for the devotees (*bhaktas*) alone, existing throughout all places and times,
but not for the knowers, just as [fire] is [the beloved] of those afflicted by cold and other such sufferings.

Even though the sun—which bestows the pleasure of light upon the eyes—is directly experienced, the reason why some people do not feel attachment toward it is simply the absence of a sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*). And the sun, though the provider of that pleasure, remains indifferent toward them. In the same way, those who possess knowledge indeed [remain indifferent] within the darkness of ignorance.

Because they lack a sense of "mine-ness" even toward Brahman, which bestows the bliss of one's own direct experience, they do not feel attachment to it; and Brahman, too, experiencing itself as indeed devoid of distinctions, remains indifferent toward them. And when a person devoted to the Sun—whether sighted or blind—has propitiated the Sun through devotion, [he perceives Him] right here as possessing hands, feet, and so forth.
Just as one perceives a horse, chariot, charioteer, and so forth, and brings them under the sway of one's own love,
even so the soul— whether liberated or bound— experiencing the Supreme Self with its specific attributes through devotion alone becomes enamored of Him,
and brings Him under the sway of its own love; therefore, [the Lord is] superior to everything else.

The state of being most dear belongs to devotees through devotion alone—whether as the sole factor or as the predominant one—and not to those possessing knowledge through devotion that has become subordinate. Therefore, it should be understood that the Supreme Self Himself has said, "Hence, one should cultivate attachment toward Me. Or else, for the reason stated regarding attachment, [He said] "toward Me."

One should cultivate delight. For one who, for the sake of such delight, feels no affection for the body and so forth—even from that [delight], the discerning person does not come to cherish the body and its like; the sense is that those who desire liberation would certainly not think that the perfection of devotion consists merely in service, chanting, and so on performed by means of the body, senses, and other such instruments. ||42||
"By means of this self of yours, which consists of all the Vedas and is born from yourself,
create subjects as they were before, as well as those that reside within me."

Śrīdhara: Therefore, you have already achieved your purpose; nevertheless, he says "all... [and so forth], meaning: "Create this triple world, which is yourself, as well as those creatures who abide within me.
By what? By yourself alone, independent of anything else. In this regard, he states that there is no need for an external means of knowledge:
"Consisting of all the Vedas" means that the Self (*ātman*) is the source or cause of this [knowledge];

this indicates the preeminence of the powers of knowledge and action. By the phrase "as before," it is stated that there is also the practice of *rāga* (attachment/delight). "They rest in me" means that for those already established [in that state], there is merely a manifestation [of what was previously latent].
By saying "it must be done," the absence of effort is expressed. ||43||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Regarding that which was prayed for—"May [the Lord] not cause harm to the Veda"—he says: "By him who consists of all the Vedas. The sense is: "The Veda must not be forgotten by you. This...
"Create beings by means of this very self, whose self is I alone as the source (yoni) and cause.

He causes [the Lord] to remember the creation of the previous day with the words, "they rest in me. By saying that only the manifestation of those already existing needs to be performed, the absence of effort is stated; this is indicated by the word "and" (ca).
And practice devotion. ||43||
Maitreya said: To that very creator of the universe, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa,
the Lotus-navelled One manifested this [universe] in His own form and then vanished.
Śrīdhara: Having manifested and revealed this creation, Padmanābha, in the form of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, withdrew and became invisible. ||44||

The sequence of composition: having manifested this world of creation (*sṛjya*) by means of his very own form as the Lotus-navelled One (*kañjanābha*), Viśvanātha vanished; that is, having revealed this world, he disappeared in his own form as Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
In this regard, [the text] is like the four verses from the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* beginning with "I alone existed here in the beginning" (*aham evāsam evāgre*).

In the *Sārārthadarśinī*, the commentary by Harṣiṇī for those whose hearts are devoted, some say that the Blessed One taught this four-verse section of the *Bhāgavata*— beginning with "When, in the Pādma Kalpa, in all the worlds," "when it was devoid [of duality]," "by means of the accumulated merit," and "I am the Self of selves"— during that time.
The ninth chapter of the third [part] is concluded, which is well-connected with the virtuous.

Thus ends the hymn to Brahmā, titled "The Birth of the Lotus," within the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, in the third book of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatamahāpurāṇa*, the commentary on the *Brahmasūtras*, the compendium of the Paramahaṃsas composed by Vyāsa.
Ninth Chapter;
Tenth Chapter:
The Sequence of the Arising of the Principles and Other Elements.
Vidura said:
When the Blessed One had vanished, how many kinds of progeny did the omnipresent Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, create— from his own body or from his mind?
Śrīdhara:

In the tenth [chapter], in order to state the attainment of the inquiry regarding time, the creation arising from that is described in ten ways according to its divisions into primary (prākṛta) and so forth. (1)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
The definition of time is stated generally in the tenth [chapter].
Thus, emanation is of ten kinds, distinguished as the primal (prākṛta) and so forth. ||1||
And those matters concerning you, O Blessed One, most wise one, which have been asked of me—
explain them in due order and sever all our doubts.
Śrīdhara says: "me" means by me; "vadasva" means speak, or it means shine forth. ||2||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Speak" means "speak," because [the Lord] knows everything in every way. ||2||
Sūta said: Thus urged by that Kṣatriya, O Bhārgava, the sage Kauṣāravi, being pleased, then answered those questions residing in his heart.
Śrīdhara: "Urged" means requested. The meaning is that he speaks of those very questions residing in his heart; they have not been forgotten by him. ||3||

The sequence of composition: the phrase "Sūta said" and so forth constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). This is established by Sūta himself; it is not a restatement made by Śrī Śuka. On the other hand, phrases such as "Maitreya said" are imitations of the words of Śrī Śuka. The readings "Śuka said" and "Bhagavat said" do not exist.
Highly esteemed by many. ||3||

Viśvanātha: By the words "O Bhārgava" and so forth, his capacity for knowledge is indicated. The phrase "residing in the heart" means that they were not forgotten by him because he was not distracted. ||3||
Maitreya said: Viriñca likewise performed divine penance for a hundred years,
having absorbed his self into the Self, just as the unborn Lord had instructed.
Having fixed the mind upon the Supreme Lord within oneself, [one should drink] the honey. ||4||
Śrīdhara: Having absorbed the self—the mind—into the Self, which is Śrī Nārāyaṇa. ||4||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Within the Self, Śrī Nārāyaṇa, [he places] the self, which is the mind. ||4||
Beholding that lotus and the water shaken by Kṛtavīrya at that moment, the Lotus-born One was presided over by the Wind-god.
For, by means of his increasing ascetic power and the knowledge established within himself,
he, whose strength of higher cognition had grown, brought down the wind along with the waters.

Śrīdhara: Brahmā, who is born from the lotus (*abjasaṃbhūta*), remained presiding over that [lotus]; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent. Having beheld that lotus and the water—of what nature were the lotus and the water?
It was shaken by that wind whose vigor was produced by the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*); thus he descended.
The connection is with what follows [in the subsequent verse]. ||5|| He whose consciousness and strength were increased; he drank and cast down everything. ||6||
The sequential arrangement: "That" refers to the pair [of verses]. The sense is that it grew as much as it had diminished during the dissolution (*pralaya*). 5–6.
Viśvanātha: [The word] *abjasaṃbhūtaḥ* means Brahmā, who was born from the lotus; the suffix *-kta* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), as in "he who presided over that lotus.

The connection with the following verse is: "Having seen that very lotus and the water shaken by the wind, he descended. By what kind of wind? By that which was produced at that time, the time of dissolution (*pralaya*).
The meaning is that he destroyed it with his vigor. It should be understood that at the time of dissolution, the water and the wind increased to exactly the same extent as they had grown. ||5||
Beholding that lotus which pervaded the sky and upon which she was seated, she thought: "By this [lotus], I have fashioned the worlds that were previously dissolved."
Śrīdhara: *Puṣkaram* means a lotus. [The phrase] "I have fashioned the three worlds that were previously dissolved" refers to the sequence of creation; it has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: And therefore, *puṣkaram* is the lotus, pervading the sky as far as Satyaloka.
Having prepared the raised [altar], I shall create it. ||7||
Then, impelled by the karma of the Blessed One, he entered the lotus calyx and split that single [lotus] in many ways— into three parts, which were to be further divided into fourteen.

Śrīdhara: Being thus urged and appointed by the Blessed One himself to perform the task, he then entered the lotus bud and divided—that single [lotus]—into three according to the form of the worlds (*lokarūpeṇa*). To the doubt as to how the creation of the three worlds could come from a single lotus bud, [he says:]...
To ward off the objection regarding his vastness, he says: "In fourteenfold form" (meaning as the fourteen worlds);

"in many ways" (meaning in even more diverse modes). It is "to be conceived," that is, capable of being brought into being. Therefore, the meaning is that it is not surprising for him to create the three worlds. ||8||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: And therefore, having entered—that is, having penetrated—the Lord appointed him to the task of creating the world; he divided that one [entity] alone threefold, in the form of the three worlds.

To dispel the impossibility of how the creation of the three worlds could proceed from a single lotus bud, he describes its vastness— it is capable of manifesting (*bhāvya*) itself in the form of the fourteen worlds (*dvisaptadhā*), in many ways (*urudhā*) even beyond that; therefore, the formation of the triple world by it is not impossible.
"It was wonderful," says the venerable master. First, he shattered it in three ways with the stalk and the lotus-bud;
then in fourteen ways; and then in many ways according to the divisions of the worlds such as those of the Sun, the Moon, and so forth.
Others say: "Of what kind? It was 'bhāvya'—to be meditated upon by the worshippers of Vairāja. (8)
This much has been gathered regarding the various states of the world of living beings;
for this supreme state is the ripening of dharma that is without external cause.
Madhva: [This refers to] that which is performed without motive, with the understanding that it is an offering to Brahman; for there is a scriptural text stating, "A is Brahman.

Śrīdhara: He states the reason for the division in the form of the three worlds: "This much"—namely, the distinction of the arrangement of the world of living beings (*jīvaloka*), which is the place of enjoyment for living beings (*jīvānām*) and is created every day—is the form of the three worlds.

A specific type of composition has been described. Now, one might ask: since the Parameṣṭhin is no different from other living beings (jīva) in that respect, why does the creation of the Brahma-world not occur every day? To this he says: "For" (hi), because this [creation] is the ripening—that is, the fruit—of the instrumental cause, which is desireless dharma. This is an illustrative indication (upalakṣaṇa).
The worlds beginning with Mahas and those dwelling therein, as well as the three worlds [below],

undergo birth and destruction at every kalpa because they are the fruits of desire-driven karma. This is because the worlds beginning with Mahas are the fruits of desireless dharma appropriate for meditative worship.
There is no destruction until the end of two parārdhas; the meaning is that for those residing there, liberation generally occurs after that point. ||9||

The sequence of the arrangement: this much extends up to the twenty-eight-fold [division]. But because Śrī Brahmā is distinguished above all, he is said to be their creator; thus it says, "of Dharma. The meaning is that it is performed by its own nature (*svabhāva*) as something causeless (*animitta*), and not even through various volitions (*saṅkalpa*) like those of a householder. This is the ripening (*vipāka*).
"Whose transformation has reached the ultimate limit. The word "this one" (asau) serves to distinguish Him from other Brahmas, for it is stated [in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 11.10.30]:
"Even Brahmā has fear of Me," and so forth. ||9||

Viśvanātha: The specific arrangement of the individual and collective structures (*vyaṣṭi-virāṭ-samūha*) of the world of living beings—the particular configuration of the locations suitable for their reflections—is thus described. Now, one might ask: "How can the creation of the structures for so many individual souls be accomplished by Brahman alone? To this, he says: "For (hi) because of this..."

The meaning is this: what is impossible through the power of austerity? For even dharma that is signless and free from desire—such as asceticism and knowledge—has its fruition as its very form of ripened manifestation. ||9||
Vidura said:
"O Brahmin, O Lord, as you have described the characteristics of Hari, who possesses manifold forms and performs wondrous deeds, please explain to us further that characteristic known as Time."
Madhva: "The definition (*lakṣaṇa*), the defined (*lakṣya*), the self (*ātman*), and the essential nature (*svarūpa*)—these are what are called [the aspects of time]," such is the statement.
Śrīdhara: Having heard that there is a difference in the creation of the world due to the difference in time, and desiring to know that very time, he asks:
"That which you have spoken of as the definition, the essential nature, and the self called 'time'—how is time?"
The meaning is: "Is it conceived? Or what is its subtle and gross form? Describe this as it truly is. ||10||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: [The phrase] "the system of karma manifested by what is called Time" means [He is joined] with the quality that follows Time; by Time;
by that Unborn One (Aja) who possesses a human lifespan; by the potency produced by that Time, and so forth.

Since dissolution, creation, and so forth, as well as human effort and the like, are accomplished by Time alone, he asks about Time, having forgotten it: "Please describe exactly as it is that characteristic and essential nature which you have called 'Time'. (10)
Maitreya said: The Puruṣa, whose form is the intermixture of the guṇas, who is without distinction and without support, created himself as that material cause for his own sport.
The honeyed [nectar] effects a transformation of the qualities; seeing that, it is not established elsewhere.

"In what, O Blessed One, is he established? "In his own majesty," says the Śruti. That material cause is the agent who effects the transformation of the qualities; for the sake of creation and so forth, that Person [is the cause].
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—these three forms were created by himself. ||11||
