Śrīdhara: Here, the general nature of time is stated; however, it will be explained in detail in the subsequent chapter. The "intermingling of the *guṇas*," which is the transformation into *mahat* and so forth, that very process by which it is brought about is what is meant by "time"—this is the sense. And it will be said in the eleventh [chapter]: "Time is the intermingling of the *guṇas*; it is *svabhāva*; it is the *sūtra*."

And thus [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.22.13]. But by itself, it is without distinction; "not established anywhere" means not terminating anywhere, being devoid of beginning and end. To demonstrate this very point, he says "the Person"—meaning that the Lord performs creation and so forth with that [Person] as the instrumental cause—as it is taken up [as material cause].

It is called *upādāna* because it is accepted as the material cause (*nimitta*). He created that very Self, in which time is the material cause and [time] is the instrumental cause, in the form of the universe; for there is nothing to be created apart from Himself. This is merely a statement of fact; the point is simply that He created by means of time as the instrumental cause.
This is what is intended to be expressed. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: He whose form—that is, knowledge of his own nature—arises solely from the "intermixture of qualities," meaning from the transformation of the great principle (*mahat*) and the rest; but by himself, he is without distinction and not established anywhere.

"Unending" means devoid of beginning and end. He says "Puruṣa" to indicate that Time is that which, acting as the efficient cause (*nimitta*), brings about creation and so forth. It is called "material cause" (*upādāna*) because it is taken up or accepted as the efficient cause; [the phrase refers to] that in which Time itself is the material cause, the efficient cause.
He created the universe, which is denoted by the word "Self," because it is the effect of the power of the Self. ||11||
The entire universe, consisting of nothing but Brahman, exists sustained by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu,
as delimited by the Lord whose form is unmanifest time.

The honey [madhvaḥ] has Brahman as its creator. By means of *māyā*, that is, by its power, that form there which is called the Lord of Destruction (*saṃhartṛ-īśvara*) is what is known as Time (*kāla*); for the root *kal* means "cutting" or "dividing. Now, the threefold Veda (*trayī*) is indeed the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; Nārāyaṇa beheld that.

They call you the "Person" (*puruṣa*), for you are established in nothing else; indeed, he is full. Run toward *sattva* for the sake of acquiring these qualities! Viṣṇu is indeed [the lord] of *sattva*, Rajas is named Brahmā-Īśāna, and he entered into Tamas. Brahmā is named the four-faced one.
The Lord named Īśāna has five faces; he who has entered into that Īśāna is indeed called Kāla—yes, they call him Kāla—so says the Saukarāyaṇa Śruti. ||12||

Śrīdhara: Demonstrating the absence of anything to be created apart from Himself, He shows that time is the instrumental cause of creation with the words "the universe" (*viśvam*). The entire universe—which is essentially the subtle elements of Brahman (*brahmatanmātra*) and exists as such—is withdrawn by the illusory power (*māyā*) of Viṣṇu. It is then delimited and distinguished [from its causal state] by the Lord as the agent and by time as the instrumental cause.
It has been explained. By the phrase "whose form and nature are unmanifest," its inherent lack of specific distinctions (*nirviśeṣatā*) is shown.

Now, the sequence of the composition describes Time: that which is a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), an indicator, consisting of action through the interplay of the *guṇas*—such as transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth—is brought about by the coordination of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) through various distinct forms.

The meaning is that whatever is perceived is "time. It means that [the world], which was merged with the Māyā— the power of creation and so forth— of Viṣṇu, the Lord, being established in identity within Viṣṇu-Brahman itself, has been delimited and separated by Time, which is the Lord in the form of His sovereign power.

Viśvanātha: He who delimits the universe is Time; thus he says, "the universe. This universe, which exists perfectly through the *māyā* or power of Viṣṇu, has as its cause Brahman-in-its-subtle-elements (*tanmātra*). It is delimited by the Lord, that is, by Time in the form of the Lord's sovereign power, such that it is defined as "this much."
"Whose unmanifest form is made the object of discernment"—by this, its inherent lack of distinctions is shown;
for as it is now, so it was before and so it will be hereafter.
[It is said: "The creation, the dissolution, the cycle of existence, and liberation itself are all Madhu."
The worlds beginning with the celestial sages, as well as the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
Existing from beginningless and endless time, this flow of the world is always of one and the same nature; it is real and is by no means illusory in any way whatsoever.
But those who would speak otherwise than this are indeed destroyers of all;
they are cursed by the gods, beginning with Brahmā, as well as by the sages, humans, and others.
Those who know all things as Brahman, yet do not know that the individual soul (jīva) is Brahman, go to the lowest darkness along with the Itihāsas and the Vedas.
"Those who recognize Viṣṇu as equal to others, and those who hate Viṣṇu—all go to a terrible darkness, and for them there is no emergence at any time. Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. (13)

Śrīdhara: To demonstrate its lack of foundation, he states the instability of the flow of the universe, which is its effect: "Just as it exists now, so it was in the past and will be in the future. (13)

The sequence of composition: "Just as" refers to half a verse. "Such a creation," meaning of the nature of dissolution and so forth in the manner previously described, is either *prākṛta* (primary) or *vaikṛta* (secondary). In this regard, some are primary, created by Īśvara, while others are secondary, created by Brahmā; however, there is also that which consists of both.
It will be explained [later]. ||13||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But since the universe is non-existent due to its lack of existence at the beginning and the end, how can the limitation of this unreal universe be logical? [Response: One should not say this; thus he says, "Just as...
Even previously, at the start of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), this universe certainly existed, and subsequently...
The intention is that since it will indeed exist even at the end of the subsequent dissolution, its nature is not one of falsity, but rather simply of perishability. ||13||
Its creation is ninefold, consisting of that which is primary (prākṛta) and that which is secondary (vaikṛta);
its dissolution is threefold, caused by time, substance, and quality.
In the case of a *tāmasa* entity, *sattva* is indeed the cause of its dissolution;
likewise, *tamas* is the cause of the dissolution of a *sāttvika* entity, and in some cases, *rajas* is the cause for the dissolution of both.
"This dissolution is declared to be by way of qualities (*guṇataḥ*), but by way of substance (*dravyataḥ*) it is through that which is opposed;
by way of time (*kālataḥ*), the dissolution of every entity is measured by time. Thus [it is stated] in the *Brahmataraka*. (14)

Śrīdhara: Having thus described time in general, he now describes it specifically, restating the very divisions of creation previously mentioned as its cause, beginning with the word "creation. That which is both primary (prākṛta) and secondary (vaikṛta) is the tenth; its cause is indeed the threefold dissolution (pralaya).

He said: Dissolution is eternal (nitya) by time alone; it is occasional (naimittika) through the substance [of fire] such as Saṃkarṣaṇa; and it is elemental (prākṛtika) through the qualities (guṇas) as they swallow up their respective effects. ||14||
The sequence of composition: In the phrase "But the first," the word "where" (*yatra*) is connected with what precedes as well.

Although there is no creation of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest in this Padma-kalpa because they were already established previously, nevertheless, "where"—that is, at the time of the creation of the Great Principle—the inequality of the qualities (*guṇa-vaiṣamya*) occurs for the self, namely the individual soul (*jīva*).
That enumeration is solely for the purpose of understanding the extremely subtle sequence. ||14||

Viśvanātha: Having thus defined time in general, and intending to define it specifically in the subsequent chapter, he summarizes—both what has been explained in detail regarding creation as its cause and what is yet to be explained—in ten categories for the sake of easy understanding, stating: "Creation," etc. As for that which...

The remainder is that [dissolution] is both natural (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*), making ten types in total. He describes the threefold dissolution caused by those very factors: the eternal dissolution is by time alone; the occasional (*naimittika*) is by means of substances such as Saṃkarṣaṇa and fire; and [the dissolution] by the qualities (*guṇas*) occurs as they swallow up their respective effects.
Natural. ||14||

The first creation is that of the Mahat from the Self through the imbalance of the qualities; the second, however, is that of the Ahaṃkāra, wherein there arises the emergence of substance, cognition, and action.
Of the *tamas* there is sweetness (*madhu*), while *rajas* is twice that; and *sattva* is likewise twice *rajas*.
Thus, by measure, these three qualities born of *prakṛti* exist.
In that state, there would be pure goodness (sattva), and even in passion (rajas) there would be more than a hundredfold [of goodness];
however, darkness (tamas) is proclaimed to be there as only a hundredth part of that passion.
In tamas there is likewise sattva, but ten times more tamas;
and rajas is one-tenth of that [tamas], for that which is rajas is rooted in tamas.
When sattva has dissolved by nine-tenths and tamas remains by one-tenth, it becomes mixed;
indeed, the wise know this state as equilibrium.
But when all that rajas is joined with tamas,
then they call it the principle of Mahat, which arises from four parts.
In that state, there is a threefold division: one part is rajas and likewise one part is tamas;
they call that the form of Brahman, known as the inequality of the qualities (guṇa-vaiṣamya).
That very same [element] becomes pure *sattva* in relation to the others;
Śrī is to be known as the fundamental *sattva*, while Bhū is said to be the fundamental *rajas*.
Tamas is the root, as are Durgā and Mahālakṣmī, who have women as their root;
he who has transcended the qualities (guṇas) and the root of the qualities is Janārdana.
The *rajas* that exists in the root-*rajas*, and the *rajas* that exists in the root-*tamas*,
as well as the *tamas* in the root-*tamas*— the *mahat-tattva* consists of those very elements.
In that [intellect], there are ten parts of *sattva* and one part of *rajas*;
the *tamas* should be known as one-tenth of that; the *ahaṃkāra* consists of those [qualities].
That Rudra is to be known as characterized by tamas only in comparison with Viriñca;
however, in comparison with others, he possesses sattva, and his [qualities] such as sattva and the rest are likewise [relative].
"From that [unmanifest], the sattvic portions are proclaimed as the mind and so forth;

the portion of rajas is the senses, and the portion of tamas is ether and the other elements. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Tattvaviveka*. He elaborates upon those very creations with the words beginning "the first," and so on.

This continues until the end of the chapter. The definition of *mahat* (the Great Principle) is that the qualities [of the intellect] derive their differentiation from Hari, the Self. Regarding *ahaṃ* (the ego), its definition is given by the words "wherein" (*yatra*). The three creations to be described—beginning with substance (*dravya*)—are the creation of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which is the creation of the gross elements (*bhūta-sarga*), and the creation of the subtle forms of the elements (*bhūta-sūkṣma-sarga*).
The meaning is: it possesses the power of substance and is the producer of the great elements. ||15||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He explains those very creations with the words beginning "The first" (*ādya*) up until the end of the chapter. The definition of the Great One (*mahat*) is that, from the Supreme Lord who is the Self, there arises the differentiation of the qualities (*guṇa-vaiṣamya*); this is the first [creation].

This is the ego (ahaṃkāra); its characteristic is as follows: "wherein... The elements (bhūta), the objects of knowledge (jñāna), the organs of knowledge (jñānendriya), the deities, the mind (manas), and the actions (kriyā)—the organs of action (karmendriya)—arise from that. That is the third creation, the elemental creation (bhūtasarga), which consists of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and possesses the power of substance (dravya).
The fourth creation is that of the senses (aindriya), which consists of both knowledge and action.
The Madhvas [say]: "The elements possess the power of substances because they flow into other elements;
likewise, they possess the power of the subtle elements because they consist of sound and the rest."

The organs of speech and so forth possess the power of action (kriyā-śakti), while the mind and the gods possess the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). Thus it is said. Furthermore, the gods are powers of knowledge.
Because it is the root of these, the ego (ahaṅkāra) possesses the three powers;
compared to humans, the gods are proclaimed to be characterized by sattva.
Even there, those belonging to the quality of sattva are said to be the deities of the ultimate reality;
even among them, Rudra is of the nature of sattva, and even among him, the Four-faced One (Brahmā) is so.
Brahmā and Rudra are changeless, though they arise from a differentiation of bodies;
Indra and the others possess modifications, and therefore they are considered to be "evolutes" (vaikārika).

Since these very [elements], when taking the form of the sense organs, become highly transformative and are intensified by the quality of pure cognition (jñāna), they are therefore designated as "taijasa" (fiery).
Since the capacity for change has indeed ceased in the sense-faculties,
even the name "changeability" does not apply to them.
Just as in a Brahmin family a fool is called "fool," so too a Śūdra, though being a fool,
is not called a fool because of his fitness for learning.
"For beings are indeed characterized by *tamas* because they are somewhat obstructed;
yet Hari himself possesses full knowledge, even though [the knowledge of others] may be well-accomplished. Thus it is said. (16)
Śrīdhara: The fourth consists of the organs of knowledge and action; the fifth is the *vaikārika* [ego], which comprises the deities presiding over the senses and the mind. (16)
The sequence of composition: *tanmātraḥ* means that in which the *mātrā*—the subtle state—of those elements (*bhūta*) exists.
As for the word *yas tu*: the particle *tu* is used for filling the verse; according to Amarasimha, "the words *tu*, *hi*, *ca*, *sma*, *eva*, and *vai* are used for filling the verse. ||16||

Viśvanātha: The "creation of elements" (bhūtasarga) consists of the subtle elements (tanmātra); it is that which possesses power within the substances, namely the gross elements (mahābhūta), meaning it has the capacity to manifest them. This is because it is the self, that is, the essential nature, of the organs of cognition and action. ||16||
The fifth is the divine creation of transformation, of which the mind is composed;
the sixth, however, O Lord, is the creation of darkness, which is characterized by a lack of discernment.
But as if unintentionally, through the Lord’s perception of Hari,
this fivefold ignorance appeared from the Great Soul, Madhva.

Of the thousand beings who possess the quality of *sattva*, there are a hundred parts of *rajas*; and of those characterized by *tamas*, there is one part that is all-knowing. That portion which consists of pure *tamas* is ignorance (*avidyā*), which has five branches.
The Daityas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas, who were aware of their suffering, [issued] from that body;
that which was composed of the quality of rajas became the constant source of birth for human beings.

The egg-born [creation] of Brahmā is concealed by the material *sattva* that is itself veiled by *rajas*, which is in turn enveloped by *tamas*; this applies to those who are stationary as well as those who move.
Even there, however, darkness is proclaimed to exist in a hundredth part of the form;
from that [darkness] Rudra is born, and from him follows the rebirth of Indra and the other gods.
When that sattva is concealed by the dust of the elements, humans [arise];
but these qualities of the gods remain established, pervading everything. || 17 ||

Śrīdhara: But the sixth [creation] belongs to *tamas*, the ignorance (*avidyā*) consisting of five sections. It is called "the creator of non-intelligence" (*abuddhikṛt*) because it produces both the obscuration and the projection of living beings; listen to that from me. (17)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "The *vaikārika* [creation] pertains to the *sāttvika-ahaṃkāra*. The creation of the gods, who are the presiding deities of the sense organs, and the creation of the mind (*manas*)—which consists of that [intellect]—is the third."

The meaning is as follows. These five types of creation have been described as belonging to *pradhāna*. He now describes the creation that is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*) with the words "the sixth, however" (*ṣaṣṭhas tu*).
The word "however" (*tu*) marks a new beginning. The creation of darkness—that is, of ignorance—is the sixth;
it was produced by the power of the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, which is non-intellect (*abuddhi*), the deluder of individual souls, and is known by the name *avidyā*.

This is the meaning: ignorance (avidyā), knowledge (vidyā), and illusion (māyā) are the three functions of Pradhāna. Among these, by means of Pradhāna, the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with Earth are created as truly real; it is by these alone that the collective and individual forms of the gross and subtle limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva) come into being.

But by the second ignorance (*avidyā*), which deludes the individual soul (*jīva*), there is created the fivefold darkness (*tamas*)— consisting of ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live— which is the unreal connection of the *jīva* with that [first] ignorance. Thus, this world, composed of both the real and the unreal, is created by both *pradhāna* and ignorance.
By the third knowledge, however, the knowledge that dispels the fivefold ignorance was produced; this will be explained in detail later on. ||17||
These six are the primary creations; now hear from me about the secondary ones as well.
This is the divine play of the Lord Harimedhas, who partakes of the quality of passion (rajas).
The form of Madhu is beyond the qualities (guṇātīta), consisting of bliss for Brahmā and the other gods;
it is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), wherein there exists the preeminence of sattva alone.
That which is superior is darkness, and that which is inferior is [light], by their very nature;
however, in the case of an embrace within that which is eternally composed of consciousness, there is no distinction whatsoever.

There is no distinction whatsoever between Prakṛti, which consists of the qualities (guṇas) and is the root cause, and the Supreme Reality, Vāsudeva; how much less so [is there any distinction] in Him?
All principles beginning with the Unmanifest (avyakta) and ending with earth (pṛthivī) are known as primordial natures (prakṛti).
The creation that has these as its material cause is recited as the "primordial" (prākṛta) creation.

The egg is to be known as the modified (vaikṛta); that which arises from it is called the secondary modification (vaikṛta). Furthermore, ignorance (avidyā) has five sections, [which were] created by Hari from the elements in the past.
Having been extracted and cast into Brahman, she emerged from him again;
because this was to demonstrate his power as a creator, she is therefore considered to be "Prakṛti" (the primordial nature).
"These qualities of Hari are always the objects of His independent sovereignty;
they are independent even of Prakṛti and of Brahmā, but among other deities, they are considered dependent, each in their respective order. Thus it is said. (18)

Śrīdhara states that [the Lord] should be heard without weariness: "The sport (*līlā*) of Hari—that whose object is wisdom (*medhā*) removes *saṃsāra*"; or else, "this" refers to the form of the creation beginning with Tamaḥ. "Of those possessing *rajas*" means "of Him whose nature is Brahman. In this interpretation, *abuddhikṛtaḥ* is in the nominative case.
The meaning is "produced through lack of attention. The primary creation (mukhya-sarga) was first made as if it were a dream.
[This refers to] the stationary beings (tasthuṣām), that is, the immobile things. ||18||

The sequence of the composition: the meaning is that [the Lord] does not [act] personally in the presence of those possessing *rajas*, but rather as Brahman conditioned by that [agency]. In the commentary, the phrase "beginning with *tamās*"—by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), the inclusion of the primary creation and so forth is to be understood. [The phrase] "caused by lack of attention" refers to Hari’s...
The meaning is that this is due to the independence of meditation, whereas for Brahman there is a deviation from that [independence]. ||18||

Viśvanātha: These six are "prākṛta" (derived from primordial nature) because they are born from *prakṛti*, the power of *māyā*. He explains that those who will be described as born from him (*me mattaḥ*)—the *vikṛti* (modification), the collective Virāṭ, and Brahmā—are "vaikṛta" (derived from modification). [He further specifies: Hari [is born] from the intellect (*medhā*) of him who is of the nature of Brahmā and partakes of the quality of *rajas*.
Of that. ||18||
The seventh is the primary creation of the stationary beings, which is sixfold:
trees, herbs, creepers, plants with inner bark, shrubs, and forest trees.
Śrīdhara explains the sixfold nature [of trees]: those that bear fruit without flowers are *vanaspati*s;
*oṣadhi*s are those whose life ends with the ripening of their fruit; *latā*s are those that require support to climb; *tvaksāra*s are bamboo and the like;
*vīrudh*s are creepers (*latā*) themselves that do not require support due to their rigidity; and those that bear fruit with flowers are *druma*s.
The sequential arrangement consists of seven and a half [chapters]. ||19||

Viśvanātha: [He is] the foremost (*mukhya*), meaning he who exists at the beginning (*mukhe*) because stationary beings (*sthāvara*) come first among the world consisting of both the stationary and the moving; that is, among those things that stand firm (*tasthūṣāṃ*). *Vanaspati*s are those that bear fruit without flowers. *Oṣadhi*s are those whose life ends with the ripening of their fruit. *Latā*s are those that require something to climb upon.

Bamboo and the like are *tvaksāra*. Creepers (*latā*) themselves, which require climbing due to their rigidity, are *vīrudhaḥ*. Trees (*drumāḥ*) are those that bear fruit by means of flowers alone. ||19||
They have an upward flow, consist mostly of darkness, possess internal contact, and are characterized by differentiation.
The movement of those who abide in the sweetness [of the teachings] is attained through the observance of the primary state;
because they generally act for the benefit of others, they are remembered as belonging to the primary stream.
Neither below nor above, but only among the horizontal beings (tiryag-yoni) does birth occur there;
and even without the utility of sacrifice or benefit to the virtuous, it occurs precisely there.
Therefore, they are called "those who flow horizontally" by the wise,
because for the most part their downward movement occurs without effort.
Those who flow downwards are proclaimed as human beings;
by means of self-restraint, those who go upwards are the sole partakers of the divine and of liberation.
"Therefore, they are proclaimed as 'those whose stream flows upwards' (ūrdhvasrotas). Thus it is said in the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa].
[This applies] to animals and immobile beings who act with prior intelligence, as well as to Asuras, Rakṣasas, and likewise Piśācas.
The "downward-streaming" (arvāk-srotas) is designated by rule for those such as the Asuras;
the meaning of this term "mukhya-srotas" (principal stream) is "upward-streaming" (utsrotas). That which is indeed called "highest" (uccatama) is precisely what is meant by "upward."

"Those who flow upwards from this [state] are indeed gods, but not those beyond them; for the word 'ut' (up) signifies merely the upward direction, and therefore it is applied to stationary beings as well. And: "The animals and the stationary beings are said to be 'those with internal touch' (antahsparśāḥ)."
"For that knowledge which arises in the heart through direct perception, inference, and scripture," so it is said in the Padma Purāṇa. (20)
Śrīdhara says: He states their common characteristic: those whose upward flow is the movement of food;
who consist mostly of *tamas* and possess unmanifest consciousness; who have internal contact, meaning they perceive only touch and nothing else, and even that only internally, not externally.
The qualifiers possess many distinctions, such as non-uniform transformation and so forth. ||20||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He states their common definition: those in whom the flow of food moves upward;
they are predominantly characterized by *tamas*, with unmanifest consciousness, and possess internal touch—that is, [their experience] is limited to the interior alone.
Experiencing distress, characterized by unstable transformations and many other such divisions,
the eighth creation of animals is considered to be of twenty-eight kinds.
They are ignorant, shrouded in dense darkness, perceiving through the sense of smell, and lacking heart-knowledge.
"Madhvaḥ": the meaning is that they know only that which is heart-pleasing without effort, and not through scripture or reasoning;
for he has been assisted in sacrifices by twenty-eight specific [deities].
This is how it is calculated for animals by those who know the lunar calendar. ||21||
Śrīdhara: He describes the creation of the animals (*tiryak-srotas*) with the words "of the animals" (*tiraścām*).
That [creation] consists of twenty-eight divisions. The definition of animals is as follows: *avidas* are those devoid of knowledge of the future and so forth;
*bhūritamasas* are those whose concern is limited solely to the knowledge of food and such; [and those who seek their desired object] by means of the sense of smell alone...
They know; though lacking conscious awareness in the heart, they possess long-term continuity and are not void.

And so says the Śruti: "Now, as for other animals, their cognition consists only of hunger and thirst; they do not speak what is known, they do not see what is known, they do not know the morrow, nor the worlds of light and darkness. (21)
The sequential arrangement is as follows: "cow," "goat"—this group of four should be understood as each individual member serving as an illustration for many. (21)

Viśvanātha: *Tiraścām* means of those with horizontal currents (*tiryaksrotas*). *Avidaḥ* means devoid of knowledge of their own offspring and so forth. *Bhūritamasaḥ* means those whose concern is limited solely to food and the like. *Ghrāṇajñāḥ* means they perceive the desired object through the sense of smell alone. *Hṛdyavedinaḥ* means devoid of long-term reflection and possessing only slight discernment. And thus:
The Śruti says: "Now, as for other animals, their cognition consists only of hunger and thirst;

they do not speak what is known, they do not see what is known, they know nothing of the morrow, nor of the worlds of light and darkness. Or rather, being enveloped in dense darkness, these many beings perceive with the sense of smell alone that which is dear to them within the heart.
In this way they find [them], and they take them for the sake of food, bedding, and so forth. ||21||
The cow, the goat, the buffalo, the black boar, the gayal, and the ruru deer—
these, O best of men, are the cloven-hoofed animals, as are the sheep and the camel.
The donkey, the horse, the mule, the gayal, the śarabha, and likewise the yak—these, O Kṣattṛ, are the single-hoofed animals; now hear of the five-nailed beasts.
Dog, jackal, wolf, tiger, cat, hare, porcupine,
lion, monkey, elephant, tortoise, monitor lizard, crocodile, and so forth.
Kites, vultures, cranes, hawks, eagles, bears, peacocks, swans, cranes, ruddy geese, crows, owls, and other such birds;
The honey-bee, the cow, the goat, the buffalo, the black boar, the gayal, the ruru deer,
the camel, the donkey, the horse, and likewise the mule and the ass.
The Gaura, the Śarabha, the Chamari, the dog and the jackal;
the wolf, the tiger, the cat, the lion, and the hare and the śalpa.
"The monkey, the elephant, the iguana and others, aquatic creatures, and likewise birds"— thus it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.
Although the tortoise is included among the "aquatic creatures" as the twenty-eighth [member], it is mentioned separately for the purpose of demonstrating its possession of five claws (*pañcanakha*).
The yogi who constantly meditates upon both the objects of creation, endowed with their respective forms, and the Creator himself,
is not born again.
Thus, according to the statement from the Skanda Purāṇa, this is said for the purpose of enjoining the recollection even of well-known animals such as those with cloven hooves.
It is said in the *Ṣāḍguṇya*: "The word of the treatise is traditionally held to be twofold: for the sake of recalling what is already well-known, and for the sake of making known what is unknown.
And in the *Abhidhāna*: "The *valgura* is called both a dancing bird and a *salaluka*."
There are twenty-eight principal species among animals;
whichever other [animal] is similar to any one of these should be included within that same category.

"The serpents dwelling within the water, as well as the species such as insects and so forth—their bodies are in every respect dominated by water. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Satyasaṃhitā*, stating exactly twenty-eight varieties: those with cloven hooves, beginning with cows and ending with camels.
There are nine types of cloven-hoofed animals. ||21||
The six single-hoofed animals beginning with the horse (*svara*) are as follows. He states the twenty-eight divisions:

the nine two-hoofed, cloven-hoofed animals beginning with the cow (*go*) and ending with the camel (*uṣṭra*); the twelve five-clawed animals beginning with the dog (*śva*) and ending with the monitor lizard (*godhā*). Thus, these land-dwellers number twenty-seven. Then there are the water-dwellers beginning with the crocodile (*makara*), and those beginning with the heron (*kaṅka*).
They are taken as being unified under the category of "well-gone" (svagā) by way of their status as forest-dwellers (*abhūcaratvena*). Thus, there are twenty-eight varieties.

Among these, the *kṛṣṇa*, *ruru*, and *gaura* are specific types of deer; furthermore, other animal beings (*tiryak-prāṇin*) are likewise included within these very categories as appropriate. ||2225||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: From the cow (*go*) to the camel (*uṣṭra*), there are nine animals with two hooves or two claws; *avi* means a sheep. From the donkey (*khara*) to the yak (*camarī*), there are six animals with one hoof. From the dog (*śva*) to the monitor lizard (*godhā*), these are the five-clawed animals.
Twelve. Thus, these land-dwellers total twenty-seven. The crocodiles (*makara*) and so forth are water-dwellers;

the *kaṅka* cranes and so forth are land-dwellers; the swans (*haṃsa*) and so forth, moreover, are water-dwellers; and the crows (*kāka*) and so forth, moreover, are land-dwellers. These [beings], beginning with the crocodiles, are taught as being of only one kind. Such is the case.

There are twenty-eight varieties, beginning with the cow; among these, the *ruru*, the black, and the white are specific types of deer. Other animal beings are likewise included within these categories as appropriate. ||2225||
But the ninth, O Kshattri, is the downward-streaming [creation], consisting of a single type of men;
they are characterized by passion (rajas), devoted to action, and regarding suffering as happiness.
"Those established in *rajas* and those established in *tamas* are known as the two types of *arvāk-srotas* (downward-streaming).
The *asuras* and others are established in *tamas*, while human beings have a predominance of *rajas*. Thus it is stated in the *Vyomasaṃhitā*.
Śrīdhara [comments]: "He whose movement of food is downward is *arvāk-srotas*. The shortening [of the vowel] is an archaic (*ārṣa*) usage."
The creation of men and the characteristics of men: those in whom rajas is predominant [are the men]. ||26||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Arvāksrotas" refers to one whose movement of food is downward (*arvāk*, i.e., below). The shortening [of the vowel] is an archaic (*ārṣa*) usage. This is the characteristic of humans, beginning with the word "rajas" (passion), etc. [2326]
O best of beings, these three alone constitute the Vaikṛta creation, as does the creation of the gods;
whereas that which is called the Vaikārika creation is the Kaumāra, which partakes of the nature of both.

Regarding the term *madhvaḥ*: the gods perceive happiness even in suffering, for it is stated that their intellect perceives all objects perversely and is characterized by the quality of *tamas*. However, the gods who possess a singular state of being focused on happiness do not act in this way, as stated in the *Ṣāḍguṇya* [chapter] regarding the Dānavas.
They call him *kaumāra* because he is the youth; he is the one born from within the gods.
Because he is the progenitor of the *vaikārika* [gods], he is both *prākṛta* (primary) and *vaikṛta* (secondary).
Among the others who are indeed *vaikārika*, he is so called because he is the cause of their slight experience of objects.

"Even the eight groups are said to be of a dual nature. And as for the phrase "and the creation of the gods," the meaning of the word "and" (ca) is that they are of a dual nature. However, the creation of the gods, being the *vaikārika* [sāttvika], has already been described as being of the nature of primordial matter (*prākṛta*). ||27||
Śrīdhara: These three are exclusively *vaikṛta* (evolved), not like the *kaumāra* [creation], which is of both natures (*ubhayātmaka*).

The phrase "and the divine creation is *vaikṛta*" is to be supplied [from the previous context]. However, the *vaikārika* divine creation was already mentioned among the *prākṛta* [creations] earlier. This [present one], however, being inferior to that, is *vaikṛta*; and because it is a divine creation, it is included within that [category].
And the creation of Sanatkumāra and others is both primary (prākṛta) and secondary (vaikṛta); the meaning is that they are created as deities and as humans. ||27||

The sequence of composition: That which is *vaikārika* (evolutive) consists of the forms of the principles (*tattva*) and their deities; because it is *prākṛta* (derived from primordial nature), it has been described previously, but the *vaikṛta* (modified) is not described here—this is the meaning. However, the *kaumāra* (the realm of Kumāra) is of both natures, because those [deities] have merely manifested within the mind of Brahmā.
This is intended to express that [the object] is included within the category of things to be created. ||27||

Viśvanātha: These three are indeed merely *vaikṛta* (evolved). And the creation of the gods (*devasarga*) is also *vaikṛta*. In response to the inquiry as to what constitutes the *prākṛta* (primary) creation, he says: "That which is *vaikārika*"; for the creation of the gods, who arise from the *vaikārika-ahaṅkāra*, is declared among the *prākṛta* creations, because they were created by Brahmā. Furthermore, [it is so called] because they are created by him alone.

And the *vaikṛta* [creation] is likewise the *kaumāra*; however, the creation of Sanatkumāra and others is of both natures (*ubhayātmaka*), because they were produced from the mind through meditation on the Lord, as stated in the subsequent passage:
"He created others from that [mind]," since they were produced by the Lord through meditation on the Lord.
And because it is produced from Brahman, the meaning is that it is both natural (prākṛta) and modified (vaikṛta). ||27||
The creation of the gods is eightfold: the wise ones (vibudhas), the ancestors (pitṛs), the asuras, the gandharvas and apsarases, the siddhas, the yakṣas, the rākṣasas, and the cāraṇas.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, vidyādharas, kinnaras,
and so forth— these ten are known as the creations (sargas) proclaimed by Viśvasṛj.
The eightfold classes of gods, including all the Vibudhas, have been declared;
here there are exactly one hundred Pitṛs and thirty Asuras.
Two hundred are proclaimed for the Gandharvas and Apsarases;
seventy for the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas; and thirty for the classes of Cāraṇas.
One hundred Siddhas are likewise found among the other seventy classes;
these indeed are the Ūrdhvasrotas, while others are known as the Arvāksrotas.
Among the gods who are products of the *vaikārika* [sattva] nature, these indeed are the primary enjoyers;
the other gods, however, are not enjoyers, and for that reason they are so designated.
They are omniscient and worthy of worship; they are devoted to them alone.
Likewise, they are performers of dance and song, as well as makers of vehicles and the like.
Those who speak of success and failure, and their spies here and there;
indeed, by these distinctions, they are considered to be of eight kinds as those who perform service.

"And others who are omniscient are proclaimed as the *vibudhas* (the enlightened ones); likewise, others have reached eight different internal divisions through various respective actions. Thus it is said in the *Tattvaviveka*.
"If gods and others were to be born with defects among humans and so forth..."
"Nevertheless, the gods, asuras, and so forth, are likewise certainly to be known [as such]. Thus [it is said]. (2829)

Śrīdhara: And the divine creation (*devasarga*) is eightfold. Among these, there are three divisions beginning with the *vibudhas* (gods). There is one for the *gandharvas* and *apsarases*; one for the *yakṣas* and *rakṣases*; one for *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*;
one for *siddhas*, *cāraṇas*, and *vidyādharas*; and one for the *kinnaras* and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the following are included]:...
These include the Kiṃpuruṣas, Aśvamukhas, and others; this will become clear in the twentieth chapter. ||2829||
The sequence of composition: "The creation of the gods" consists of one and a half [verses]. ||28||

Viśvanātha: The divine creation (*devasarga*), however, which is of a modified nature (*vaikṛta*), consists of eight divisions. Among these, there are three divisions beginning with the *vibudhas* (gods);

one division consisting of *gandharvas* and *apsarases*; one consisting of *yakṣas* and *rākṣasas*; one consisting of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*; one consisting of *siddhas*, *cāraṇas*, and *vidyādharas*; and one consisting of *kinnaras* and so forth—thus making eight divisions.
By the word "etcetera," [beings such as] the Kimpuruṣas and others are included; [the term] Viśvasṛj refers to the Supreme Lord and Brahmā. ||2829||
Henceforth I shall proclaim the genealogies and the Manvantaras;
thus, at the beginnings of the Kalpas, the self-born Hari, the Creator, becomes immersed in the quality of passion (rajas).
He whose resolve is unfailing creates himself from himself by means of himself.
"Madhva is Hari, eternally immersed in the qualities (guṇas), because he dwells in the midst of the qualities;
yet, due to his lack of ego-consciousness, there is indeed no contact with those qualities for him. And:
"Having created the bodies of the gods and others, He made Himself manifold."
"By being the controller of that [nature], he is the Self, distinct from nature through the differentiation of bodies"—thus in the *Nāradīya*.
"Hari himself is the agent, the instrument, and the action;
though the Selfs are manifold, nature possesses independence"—thus in the *Āgneya* [Purāṇa]. (30)
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that Hari himself became the Self-born (*ātmabhūḥ*). ||30||
Because the Lord possesses the power of illusion (*māyāvitva*),
they do not admit a sequence of before and after regarding this reversal of qualities in creation, just as in the case of a whirlpool in a river.
O Kṣattṛ, those who are celebrated as the gods, Asuras, and others by way of name and form in this Kalpa, were the very same in other Manvantaras.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: Well then, is there first creation or dissolution? To this he says: "guṇa... etc. In the case of creation, which is a transformation of the *guṇas*, one who is wandering—that is, whose nature is to wander—is a "wandering-wanderer" (*bhrāmyadbhrami*). Just as for one wandering in a river there is neither beginning nor end, so it is with creation and dissolution.
This is the meaning. He states the beginninglessness and uniformity of saṃsāra with the words "gods, asuras, and so forth. "Those very same" means they have those names and those forms. ||3132||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha*: not explained. Viśvanātha:
thus, in the *Sārārthadarśinī*, [this is] the *Harṣiṇī* for those whose hearts are devoted.
The tenth chapter of the third [section], which is well-connected with the virtuous, is concluded.

Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Sequence of the Origin of the Principles, etc. in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, within the third book of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*, a compendium of the state of the Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa) composed by Vyāsa.
The Tenth Chapter;
The Eleventh Chapter:
An Exposition on the Nature of Time.
Maitreya said:
That which is the ultimate limit of distinct entities, which is manifold and never conjoined,
should be known as the atom (paramāṇu), from which arises the delusion of unity among men.
In order to demonstrate the measure of time, [the text] shows the measure of substance by way of illustration.
Just as from a human being, the world also perceives through specific vision alone.
But they are unable to perceive the specific distinction between its parts and sub-parts.
The sages have declared that the ultimate limit of motion is directly perceived;
that should be known as the atom (paramāṇu), which Kaṇāda and others describe as being partless.

"Even though it possesses infinite parts, they call it [an atom] because of its appearance to a deluded vision; for even if the parts themselves possess infinitude, their state of being atoms is stated for the sake of distinction. Thus says the *Tattvaviveka*.
From many parts, on all sides. ||1||
Śrīdhara: Thereafter, in the eleventh [chapter], time— from the atom (*paramāṇu*) and so forth up to the *yugas*,
*manvantaras*, and beyond— is described, beginning with the *kalpa* and extending to the beginningless.

Thus, having generally described the tenfold intermixture of the *guṇas* as the defining characteristic of time, [the author] now defines the object delimited by that very time in order to describe its specific nature through two verses: "That which is the final, ultimate part of the existent effect, of which there is no further part... [and so forth].
It is "non-multiple" (aneka) because it has not reached the state of being an effect; it is "uncombined" (asaṃyuta) because it has not reached the state of a composite aggregate.
For this very reason, that atom is to be understood as existing even when the states of being an effect and a composite aggregate have always departed.
What is the proof for this? To this he says: "Because from those [atoms], when combined, for people who engage in worldly transactions..."

The illusion of unity is the cognition of a whole (*avayavin*). Thus, in the fifth chapter, during the refutation of the whole, he will say: "That specific quality which is produced by their collection. The sense is that [the whole] is postulated because the effect [otherwise] would be unaccounted for. ||1||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
Furthermore, in the eleventh [chapter], time is also characterized in its specific aspects.
From which the measure of months, years, yugas, and so forth is known.

Being unable to characterize the first, ultimate, subtle moment in its own nature, [the author] characterizes the object that is delimited by it: that which is the final part of the specific portions of existing effects such as earth, beyond which no further part is possible. Now, one might object: because of the singular form "final" (*carama*), [is this not a single thing?]

Is that [atom] only one, or is it many? Here, for the sake of knowing subtle time, although they are many, the singular number is employed because only one is useful. Now, one might ask: is it taken here as combined with others or uncombined? To this he says: the atom is to be understood as indeed uncombined (*asaṃyuta*).

But the meaning is that it is not actually seen. [Objection: If so, then what is the proof for its existence? To this he says: "From which"—that is, from those [particles] when combined, there arises the delusion that they are a single unity.
[This refers to] those extremely subtle particles moving through the aperture of a window-lattice joined with the rays of the sun.

The meaning is that [the object] becomes an object of cognition (*buddhi*). Its sixth part is the atom (*paramāṇu*), and the meaning is that it is indeed invisible. By the use of the word "some" (*keṣāṃcit*), it is suggested that for certain types of insects whose bodies are the size of motes (*trasareṇu*), something indeed becomes visible. ||1||
The absolute isolation of the very existent entity, abiding in its own essential nature, is the supreme Great One— the undifferentiated and uninterrupted.
The supreme greatness of Madhva—in terms of time, space, and qualities—belongs only to the Existent (sat), which is the Supreme Brahman itself.
Since the word "sat" is used figuratively for other things as well, [the author specifies] "of the category of reality" (padārthasya);
that is, of that which is the primary denotation of the term "sat."

"The primary intended meaning is the *artha*, while another is called the *vācya*; however, when applied to non-primary meanings, the word *artha* is used in a subordinate sense. Thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*.
If this is so, then by the passage beginning with "equal even to a gnat," it follows that there is also a state of having that [atomic] dimension for one situated elsewhere.

Therefore, regarding the phrase "of that which abides in its own nature": since its nature is that which veils the world, there is from that [nature] a certain greatness or smallness; hence, it is called *kaivalya*. Even therein, because it possesses many kinds of forms, it is called *aviśeṣa* (the undifferentiated). Because even that which is all-pervading exists as merely a span in measure, therefore—

"Without interval" (*nirantara*) refers to that which is the absolute state (*kevalabhāva*) of the Supreme Brahman. That which has entered within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) and so forth, which veils it, is merely another form of that very same [Brahman], such as the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) and so on; whereas that all-pervading form which exists without being a mere part (*ekadeśa*), a limited measure (*prādeśa*), or any specific dimension such as "measured by a span" (*prādeśamātra*) and the like—that alone is the "Supremely Great" (*paramamahat*).
The wise know that the absence of a limit of time is the infinity of time,
and likewise, the absence of a limit of space is the infinity of space.
Those who know reality understand that the immeasurability of qualities constitutes the infinity of the substance;
this threefold eternity and infinity belongs to Hari alone, and to no one else.
Although its infinity exists in all its essential forms and possesses three characteristics,
nevertheless, it is also subject to limitation in terms of space.
Limitation and likewise pervasion are both applicable even to that which is of a single nature;
this is due to its inconceivable and wondrous sovereignty, and is for the sake of conventional usage alone.
In reality, there is no limitation whatsoever, whether by quality or by time.
Although there is pervasiveness even spatially across all forms,
and not even an atom’s worth of difference or distinction exists among them,
nevertheless, due to the possession of sovereignty, there is a distinction of atomicity therein.
Therefore, for the sake of facilitating comprehension, its non-pervasiveness is also stated.
That which is its pervasive form, supreme and designated as Nārāyaṇa, they call the Void, the Brahman; and that which arises from it is the second, the Creator.
The one called the Supreme Person (Parama-puruṣa) is limited by space, though he is all-pervading;
the third, known as Vāsudeva, is limited and envelops the entire world.
"The world is pervaded in its entirety by the Fourth, named Viṣṇu," so it is said in the *Brahmatarka*.
Although there is an equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*) of the all-pervading form of Brahman by primordial matter (*prakṛti*) in the form of time and so forth,

[the term "abiding in his own nature"] is used because [Brahman] is included within the primary subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), whereas [primordial matter] abides in something other than that.
It has been said:
"Even though Brahman is all-pervading, it resides within the Goddess who embodies Time and the other [principles];
because she, like the Lord Hari himself, is supreme and does not go elsewhere."
"That which resides in the Great One (mahat) and so forth is superior to that which resides elsewhere," thus says the *Brāhma*.

"Inferred" (*anumita*) means known in accordance with scripture and worldly experience. They say that "inference" (*anumā*) is twofold, as it is designated as both [verbal] knowledge and that which is born from a logical mark (*liṅga*).
The time that a person dwelling in this world,
even one of great wisdom and keen intellect, could perceive— that is the duration of a single atom.
Nor would it be the case that [the world] is uninterrupted by creation and so forth, nor that it exists immediately thereafter;
likewise, it could not have the nature of specific entities such as atoms and the like.
"In the *Brahmatarka* it is said: 'That which is devoid of distinctions such as prior and posterior is Time, the supreme and great.
These qualifiers—'abiding in its own nature,' 'isolation,' 'without distinction,' and 'uninterrupted'—are stated here in sequence as attributes of Time, which is likewise supreme and great."
The infinity of Hari is threefold— by way of space, time, and substance—
but no other entity possesses such infinity, whether in terms of space or time, nor even primordial nature (prakṛti).
Likewise, there is no infinity of space for sound in terms of time;
for that very [sound], whose nature consists of both time and sound, always belongs to Hari.
Not even a fraction of her capacity exists even in the qualities of knowledge and bliss;
therefore, Vāyu is inferior to her, and Śeṣa, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Hara are inferior to him.
"Therefore, Indra and the others are inferior in all qualities; of this there is no doubt," so it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.

"Because he is the sustainer of the existence of atoms and so forth, and because he is the enjoyer, the Supreme Lord is designated as 'Time' (kāla), being expressible by such names as 'atom' and so on. And:
"That which is Time—the inner controller of time—is the very nature of the existent Brahman, devoid of distinctions; that alone is Brahman."
He enjoys it; and that Brahman is the supreme Great One, because even He lacks the threefold limitations.
Everything exists everywhere, and the enjoyer, too, is like a single enjoyer due to His lack of distinction.
Hari, whose nature is inconceivable, unborn, and all-pervading, abides by virtue of His own sovereignty—thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*.

Śrīdhara, having spoken of the subtle, speaks of the gross: "of the existent alone" (*sata eva*). For that very existent whose ultimate part is the atom, which is the mere effect, abiding in its own nature and not having reached another state of transformation—that which is its isolation (*kaivalya*), its oneness (*aikya*), is the supreme great (*paramamahān*). As for its being masculine [in gender], however...

Because it is the counter-correlate of the atom. Now, an objection is raised: "Since every category of object possesses various specificities (*viśeṣa*) and is mutually distinct, how can there be unity in it? To this he replies: "The non-specific (*aviśeṣa*) is that which is devoid of the intention to express specificities, and the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), when devoid of the intention to express distinctions and being continuous, is the supremely great (*paramamahat*)."
The meaning ||2||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Having stated the ultimate subtle [state], he also speaks of the ultimate subtle [state] itself—that very reality which consists of all effects, whose final part is an atom, and which abides in its own essential nature.
The isolation (*kaivalya*) and unity (*aikya*) of that which existed prior to dissolution and transformation is the "Supreme Great" (*paramamahān*);

however, its "masculinity" (*puṃstva*) is due to its being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of the atom. Now, [an objection is raised]: "If every category of object possesses various specificities (*viśeṣa*) and is mutually distinct, how can there be unity for it? To this, he says: "It is without specificities" (*aviśeṣa*).

The meaning is that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), when devoid of the intention to express particularity and devoid of the intention to express uninterrupted difference, is "supremely great" (*paramamahat*). ||2||
In this way, O best of men, time too is inferred in its subtlety and its grossness;
the Lord, who is unmanifest, all-pervading, and the consumer of the manifest, [is known] by means of the movement of his manifestation.

Śrīdhara: Just as this object is both subtle and gross, so too is time inferred [as such]. By the word "and" (ca), the intermediate state is included. "Configuration" (saṃsthāna) refers to the state of atoms and so forth; "enjoyment" (bhukti) is pervasion. By that [pervasion], the Lord is [described]; thus, Hari’s power, though inherently unmanifest, enjoys.
It is so called because it pervades and delimits; it is all-pervasive and skillful in its arising and other functions. ||3||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Just as this object is both subtle and gross, so too is time known through inference. In what manner? [It is known] by its configuration (*saṃsthāna*), which is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the atom and the infinitely great.

Because he is a portion (*bhāga*) of the Lord’s power through his enjoyment (*bhukti*) and pervasion (*vyāpti*), he is called *Bhāgavat*. Though himself unmanifest, he enjoys—that is, pervades and encompasses—the manifest entire phenomenal world (*sarvaprapañca*). He is all-pervasive (*vibhu*) for this very reason, or else he is skillful (*dakṣa*) in the acts of creation and so forth. ||3||
That time which experiences the state of an atom is indeed the atom;
but that time which experiences the non-differentiation of the existent is the supreme Great Time.

Śrīdhara explains this very point with the words beginning "He... and so forth: He who experiences the state of atoms—the atomic condition—of the existent phenomenal world (prapañca) is time as an atom (paramāṇu).
He who experiences its undifferentiated totality is the supremely great (paramamahat). This is [the distinction].

The meaning is as follows: regarding the solar revolution which will be described in the passage beginning with *graharkṣatārācakrastha* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.13), the time taken by the sun to traverse the space of a single atom (*paramāṇu*) is called a *paramāṇu*. And the time taken for [the sun to traverse] the entire [ecliptic] consisting of the twelve zodiacal signs...

It transcends the cosmic egg (bhuvanakośa); that time, consisting of the year, is the supreme great one. Through its revolution, it reaches its limit of two parārdhas by means of the sequence of yugas, manvantaras, and so forth. And thus, in the fifth [chapter], he will explain the division of time and so on solely through the motion of the sun. ||4||

The sequence of composition: He explains precisely what was stated [in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.10.3] with the words "That is time. Here, in the commentary, regarding the phrase "it traverses the space of an atom," it should be understood that this occurs by way of the celestial sphere consisting of the middle path. [It traverses] the entire cosmic egg.

In the phrase "it transcends," however, it should be understood that it transcends its own state. Furthermore, in the phrase "he who attains the state of an atom," the meaning is specifically that he transcends the spatial dimensions of an atom by means of the form of the sun. And it will be stated later that there is no difference between that time and the sun: "He who [projects] the power of the emanated manifoldly" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.15).

By this [it is meant]: Alternatively, that which enjoys—that is, pervades—the state of being an atom (*paramāṇutā*), like the object denoted by that term, is the "atom-time" (*paramāṇu*). That which enjoys the undifferentiated state of the existing manifold (*prapañca*) and pervades everything from its creation until its dissolution is "supremely great time" (*paramamahān*).
The meaning is that its form consists of two *parārdhas*. And so it will be stated: "This time begins with the atom (*paramāṇu*) and ends with two *parārdhas*" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.38). ||4||

Viśvanātha explains the meaning of the term "the enjoyer" (*sambhoktṛ*): that time which "enjoys"—that is, passes by in the form of the sun—the state of being an atom (*paramāṇutā*) of an existing effect, that is the atom.
According to the perspective of the passage to be cited later, *graharkṣa* [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.13], it is the duration of time by which...

The sun traverses the space of a single atom; the meaning is that such a duration of time is an *paramāṇu*. And he, in the form of the sun, experiences the entire manifold world without distinction through the cycles of years, yugas, and so forth; that time which begins from the creation of the manifold world is the supremely great.
The meaning is that the entire duration of time from [the beginning] up to the end of the dissolution (*saṃhāra*) is equally "supremely great" (*paramamahat*).
In that regard, the designations and measurements of the atoms (*paramāṇu*), subtle particles (*aṇu*), and minute particles (*trasareṇu*)—which are constituent parts of effects—are indeed equal;
likewise, the designation for the supremely great effect and for time is equal, as it is for those situated between them.
It should be understood that there is a difference between perception and the means of valid cognition. ||4||
Two atoms (paramāṇu) make one minute particle (aṇu), and three of those are traditionally said to constitute a mote (trasareṇu);
this mote is perceived when it enters the rays of the sun through a lattice window, moving along the very path of space.
"Madhvaḥ" means that [the honey] has come within the range of vision; the sense is that it has been perceived, due to the distinction between the two heaps. ||5||

Śrīdhara: Now, beginning with the definition of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, he describes its state during the intermediate period. Two atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute a dyad (*aṇu*). Three dyads constitute a triad (*trasareṇu*). He states that this [triad] is perceptible in the words "through the sunlight in a lattice" (*jālārka*); it is perceived in the rays of the sun entering through a window-lattice.

Who was he? He who, due to his extreme lightness, went—having gone—following after his own [shadow]; or according to another reading, following after his own [shadow], he was perceived, but not on the earth (gām). ||5||

The sequential arrangement: the verse beginning with "the atom and the two" is a general statement regarding both the categories of objects and time, and it functions as a single unit through the relationship between the illustration and the illustrated. 5.

Viśvanātha: Two atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute one *aṇu*; three *aṇus* constitute a *trasareṇu*, which is perceptible; thus he says, "by the sunbeam through the lattice. This is perceived by the eye as moving with extreme lightness through the very sky within the sunbeams entering through a window, but not [perceived] on the earth (*gāṃ*). It has not descended...

In this reading, the meaning is that such a thing moves. If it is asked what evidence there is for the existence of atoms (*aṇu*) and ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), the answer is the mote (*trasareṇu*) itself. For instance, when there is an abundance of grossness (*sthaulya*) among the parts, a whole (*avayavin*) must be postulated; however, the ultimate atoms are not [the cause], because they lack grossness, whereas grossness [is present in the mote].

The fact that [an object] is composed of multiple entities constitutes the grossness of the atom; since this would not be possible without a *paramāṇu*, the *paramāṇu* is established. Since the visibility of a *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust) would not be possible without the grossness of its constituent parts, the *aṇu* is established. Likewise, for the sake of the grossness of the *aṇu*, there must be at least two *paramāṇus*.
It is postulated [as three], but not as three-ness, four-ness, and so forth, according to the principle that when something is first presented, it serves as the governing factor (*tantra*).
Just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds," for the sake of abundance, only three-ness—even though it is minimal—is postulated;
such is the logic here. ||5||
The time it takes to swallow three *trasareṇus* is known as a *truṭi*.
A hundredth part of that is a *vedha*, and three of those are known as a *lava*.
Śrīdhara: That piercing [of the heart] in which there are a hundred parts in the form of *truṭis* (moments). ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "A triad of *trasareṇu*s. According to the *Sūryasiddhānta*, a *truṭi* consists of three *trasareṇu*s; it is said that a *truṭi* is the amount [of dust] that enters a lotus petal pierced by a needle. As much as...

The time in which a lotus petal is pierced by [a needle] is called a *truṭi*; this is the meaning. That piercing (*vedha*) which consists of a hundred such *truṭi*-parts is called "piercing by a hundred *truṭis*" (*truṭiśatena vedha*); this is the meaning.
Three of those [piercings] constitute a *lava*. ||6||
A *nimeṣa* should be known as three *lavas*; those three are traditionally taught to be one *kṣaṇa*.
Five *kṣaṇas* are known as a *kāṣṭhā*, and fifteen of those are a *laghu*.
Śrīdhara: Three of those *nimeṣas* are traditionally taught as one *kṣaṇa*. Fifteen *kāṣṭhās* constitute one *laghu*. (7)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: Three *nimeṣas* are traditionally taught as one *kṣaṇa*. Fifteen of those *kāṣṭhās* are said to constitute one *laghu*. (7)
Fifteen *nāḍikās* are indeed declared to be one *laghu*;
two of those make a *muhūrta*, and six or seven of those make a *prahara*, or *yāma*, for men.
Regarding the honey-mixture (*madhu*): it may be seven [verses] due to deficiency or excess. ||8||

Śrīdhara: A *prahara* consists of six or seven *nāḍikās*. That itself is a *yāma*, the fourth part of both day and night. There are six [nāḍikās] during decrease [of the day] and seven during increase. It should be understood that this excludes two *muhūrtas* belonging to the twilight (*saṃdhyāṃśa*). Furthermore, the word "or" (*vā*) is used there to indicate lack of fixed rule regarding those divisions every day.
Because they are impossible to count. ||8||
Regarding the sequence of arrangement: "six or seven. There, the word "or" (vā) includes all the intermediate possibilities. ||8||

Viśvanātha: A *nāḍikā* is a *daṇḍa*; two *nāḍikās* make one [unit]. Six or seven *nāḍikās* constitute a *prahara*, which is also called a *yāma*. It is a fourth part of the day or the night; it consists of six [units] during the period of decrease and seven when the increase begins. This should be understood as excluding the *ghaṭikās* of the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*). Even there—
The word "or" (vā) indicates that there is no fixed rule, because it is impossible to enumerate their specific varieties every day. ||8||
A vessel weighing six palas, with a hole made by four gold māṣas each measuring four aṅgulas in size, is that which takes as long to sink in a prastha of water as [the time specified].
Four *kākaṇikās* of honey are called a twentieth part;
they also call that a *kṛṣṇalā*, and four of those make a *māṣaka*.
When it has been made four finger-breadths long, the door is constructed with a circumference equal to that of the four-month period.
In a beautiful vessel of water shaped like a lotus with six petals and a capacity of one *prastha*,
if the weight exceeds [the capacity], it will be filled quickly even by a small amount of water.
In cases of extreme cold or physical blemish, fulfillment is achieved by means of Māgha alone;
therefore, during the spring season, it is fulfilled by the water situated at Prayāga.
"The examination of the purification of the channels would not be possible otherwise," so it is said in the *Pādma*.

"The purification of the *kali* [the central channel] should always be performed with pure, lukewarm water, like the rays of the sun, flowing in a continuous stream," so it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa*. (9)

Śrīdhara states the measurement of the *nāḍikā*: "Unmāna" is that by which something is measured; it is a vessel fashioned from six *pala* of copper. A *māṣa* consists of five *guñjās*. With four of these [māṣas], fashioned in the form of a rod four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, a base-opening is made; through that opening...

The time it takes for water measuring one *prastha* to enter [the vessel] and for it to become submerged and sink is one *nāḍikā*. Herein, the rule regarding the two *pala*-sized holes is that if they are larger, one would sink quickly, and if they are smaller, one would sink slowly. (9)

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: He states the measurement of the *nāḍīkā* vessel: "That by which something is measured is a 'measurement' (*unmāna*); it is a vessel fashioned from six *pala*s of copper, where one *pala* consists of sixty-four *māṣa*s."
Five *guñjās* make one *māṣa*. Four of these, fashioned in the form of sticks four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) long, are used to create a root-opening;

by means of that opening, as much water as measures one *prastha* enters, and the time it takes for [the vessel] to become submerged or sink because of that is a *nāḍikā*. Here, the *pala* and the opening are [the basis of calculation].

If there is an excess [of weight], it will sink quickly; if there is a deficiency, it will do so slowly—this is the rule for the *pala* and the probe. Furthermore, since a probe made of silver or similar materials might cause the hole to expand, gold is also prescribed as the material for the probe. ||9||
The Yāmas are four; there are four days for mortals, both of them;
a fortnight consists of fifteen days, O giver of honor, being the bright and the dark.
Regarding *madhvaḥ*: where there is a word expressing duality for both [sides], there the designation *ubha* is used even in the dual number. (10)
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [state]: "ahanī" means day and night. ||10||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained.
The conjunction of those two is a month; that [month] is a day and night for the ancestors.
Two of those [months] are a season (*ṛtu*); six [seasons] are a solstice (*ayana*), namely the southern and the northern, in heaven.
Śrīdhara: Six months constitute an *ayana*. [The word] "in heaven" (*divi*) connects with what follows. ||11||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Six months constitute an *ayana*. The word "in heaven" (*divi*) connects with what follows. (11)
They say that two solstices constitute a day and night; twelve such days are recorded as a year.
One hundred years is declared to be the maximum lifespan of the Nāgas.
Śrīdhara: They say that "in heaven" refers to a day and night of the gods; [twelve months constitute a year]. (12)

The sequence of the composition: The statement "the planets and stars," etc., is merely a description of the sun's motion; it does not intend to define the limits of time, because it is impossible for the year to possess such supreme magnitude. ||12||
Viśvanātha: His two solstices are the day and night of the gods in heaven; twelve months constitute a year.
Stationed within the wheel of planets, lunar mansions, and stars, the omnipresent, unblinking Lord traverses the universe—from the infinitesimal atom upwards—by means of the completion of the year.

Śrīdhara says: By this sequence, he explains that this Sun constantly consumes life-span—the planets (graha) such as the Moon and others, the lunar mansions (ṛkṣa) such as Aśvinī and others, the stars (tārā), which are other minute constellations;

the Lord (īśvara), the omnipresent master, the Sun, who is the soul of time (kāla-ātmā) and is unblinking, situated within that wheel of time (kālacakra) which is characterized by those [celestial bodies], [consumes] the world.
He traverses, that is, he wanders through, the cosmic egg consisting of the twelve zodiacal signs. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: And he says that the sun takes away the lifespan of men through its rising and setting—the planets (*graha*) being the moon and so forth, the lunar mansions (*ṛkṣa*) being Aśvinī and so forth, and the stars (*tārā*) being other constellations (*nakṣatra*). Of these...

"He stands in the circle of the wheel" means he resides in the wheel of light (*jyotiścakra*). "Unblinking" refers to his nature as Time (*kāla*). "The pervasive one" is a portion of the Lord (*īśvara*). He "moves around," meaning he revolves. ||13||
Saṃvatsara, Parivatsara, and likewise Iḍāvatsara,
Anuvatsara, and Vatsara— thus, O Vidura, it is declared.
Madhva is the year named Iḍāvatsara, situated in the twelfth lunar mansion;
he who is Hari in the twelvefold cycle of lunar days is Anuvatsara.
The year that is situated within three hundred and sixty days is the *vatsara*;
that which is situated in the twelfth part of the revolution of Jupiter is the *parivatsara*.
"The year, which is Hari, resides within the twelve months of the solar cycle;
thus, although he is named Time, the Supreme Lord resides within time. So it is said in the *Brahmatarka*.
Because he is seen at all times, the wise know him to be "unblinking" (*animiṣatva*).
"Or because of the constant movement of the Great Soul who abides in time," so it is said. ||14||

Śrīdhara: The division of the years and so forth should be understood through the distinctions of the solar, Bārhaspatya, Sāvana, Cāndra, and Nākṣatra months. Furthermore, some say as follows: when the *saṅkrānti* occurs on the first day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).

The simultaneous commencement of the solar and lunar months constitutes a year (*saṃvatsara*). Consequently, by solar measure six days increase in a year, while by lunar measure six days decrease in a year; thus, due to this twelve-day discrepancy, the two [calendars] become one ahead and the other behind.
Thus, five years pass according to the degree of such intervals; within that period, two intercalary months (malamāsa) occur. Then, the sixth year begins again. ||14||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha states: Since it was said that [the Lord] is situated within the wheel of planets, constellations, and stars, he now describes the different names of the year according to the movement of the sun and the movement of the planets and so forth—beginning with "the year" (*saṃvatsara*), which is based on the solar motion.
"Parivatsara" is according to the motion of Jupiter; "anuvatsara" is according to the motion of the moon.

Since the constellations (*ṛkṣas*) and stars (*tārās*) have no motion of their own, their motion is solely that of the celestial sphere (*cakra*). Even therein, for the constellations, a year consists of twelve months measured by twenty-seven days; for the stars—
It should be known as the *idāvatsara* year, consisting of thirty solar months (*sāvana*) by way of their numerical measure;
it is that variety of elemental being which, swelling the power of the emanated world through its own energy, courses in the sky for the sake of man's non-delusion.
To that five-year period of time, which expands through sacrifices the world composed of the gunas under the name of "Time," offer your tribute.
"Madhva is the dispeller of the delusion of non-existence through his sacrifices and his own insights;
for the sake of instructing beings on their seniority and juniority and for the performance of sacrifices and other rites,
Hari, abiding in time, exists while awakening the power of those to be created"— thus it is stated in the *Tantraprakāśikā*.
Śrīdhara: Being such as this, the Self of Time must be worshipped constantly by those who are vigilant; thus he says, "He who...

He runs through the sky, that is, in the atmosphere, repeatedly causing the potential power of seeds and other causes—which pertains to the objects to be produced, such as sprouts and so forth—to swell forth in many ways through his own power in the form of Time, thereby directing them toward their effects.

Who is he? He is a particular elemental manifestation, the sun, whose form is a sphere of fire. For what purpose does he run? For the sake of removing the delusion—the error or confusion—of the person;
that is to say, by causing the exhaustion of life-span and so forth, he turns them away from attachment to sense objects. But as for those possessed of desire...
Offer worship to him who initiates the five-year cycle, he who expands through sacrifices the fruit of heaven and other rewards consisting of virtuous qualities. 15.
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha asks: "For what purpose is this conception of different years?
He replies—"He who..."—stating that it is for the sake of accomplishing the religious duties (*dharma*) and so forth prescribed for each respective year, for those who are to be created.

Manifesting— that is, making manifest— the power or capacity of plants and other beings within their sprouts and so forth by means of his own power in the form of Time, in manifold ways, who is this particular being among the elements, a specific great element in the form of the solar orb, that runs in the sky or atmosphere? For what purpose does he run for the sake of the Person (puṃsaḥ)?
For the sake of a person’s freedom from delusion and for the cessation of confusion regarding the directions, the magnitude [of time],

and so forth— for those with desires, [it serves] to make known the results such as heaven consisting of the *guṇas*, and the times for performing rites prescribed for the year and so on through sacrifices to be undertaken; therefore, [he spoke] to that Kali, the initiator of the five-year cycle (*yuga*).
Offer the ritual gifts for worship, beginning with the arghya water. O righteous people! ||15||
Vidura said:
This lifespan of the ancestors, gods, and humans is traditionally held to be the maximum.
Tell me of the destination of those others who exist beyond the kalpa and are possessed of knowledge.

Śrīdhara: This measure of lifespan, calculated as one hundred years according to their own respective measures, is conceived and produced every day; thus, a *kalpa* is that which is outside of the three worlds (*trailokya*). "The wise" (*vidaḥ*) refers to those possessing knowledge. Regarding the sequence: this is the lifespan of the ancestors and others, and it is each according to its own [measure].

The meaning is that it consists of the calculation of time as previously stated. "A hundred," however, refers specifically to humans. For, having previously described the reckoning of time for humans, ancestors, and gods, it was determined that the maximum lifespan of humans is one hundred years. [This applies] to Indra and others who remain for the duration of a *manvantara*.
And there is the attainment of a greater measure for others, such as Brahmā, Sanaka, and so forth, who live beyond the kalpa—that is, outside the day of Brahmā. ||16||

Viśvanātha: This refers to the lifespan of those wise ones, such as Sanaka and others, as well as Bhṛgu and others, who remain beyond even the daily *kalpa* for a hundred years according to their own respective measures; [this verse describes] their destination and life-span. ||16||
Surely the Blessed One knows the course of time;
indeed, the wise perceive the universe with the eye perfected by yoga.
Śrīdhara: "By one perfected through yoga" means by one who has attained accomplishment through yoga. ||17||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: The Blessed Lord Bhavān [is one] who has attained success through yoga (yogarāddhena), that is, one who has achieved perfection in yoga. ||17||
Maitreya said:
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali— these constitute the cycle of four yugas,
which is carefully defined as lasting twelve divine years.

Śrīdhara: It should be understood from the force of the subsequent verse that [this lasts] for twelve thousand years. *Avadhānam* means that which is attended to; it consists of the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) along with its parts (*aṃśa*). ||18||
The sequential arrangement: the meaning of the words beginning with "kṛtam" is as follows—one hundred and eighty human years (360) constitute one year of the gods;
twelve thousand such [divine] years constitute their *caturyuga*. And that [period], for humans...
