The number of years amounts to four million three hundred and twenty thousand (4,320,000). That alone constitutes the cycle of the four ages beginning with the Kṛta (Satya) Yuga; for it is thus: the Kṛta (1,728,000), Tretā (1,296,000), Dvāpara (864,000), and Kali (432,000).
Two thousand yugas of the gods constitute one day and night of Brahmā; this amounts to eight padmas, or 800,000,640,000,000 years of human beings. ||18||

Viśvanātha: Since Bhṛgu and others have lifespans outside the current *kalpa* that are equal to the lifespan of Brahmā himself, he states the measurement of the *yugas* and so forth in order to describe the lifespan of Brahmā—beginning with "The Kṛta...
[verse 69]. By "years" (*varṣaiḥ*), he means thousands of years. "Measured" (*avadhīyata*) refers to the *avadhāna*, which consists of the *saṃdhyā* and *saṃdhyāṃśa*.
Accompanied by that. ||18||
In the Kṛta and subsequent ages, respectively, there are four, three, two, and one thousand years; these numbers are doubled for the hundreds as well.

Śrīdhara: In the Kṛta Yuga, there are four thousand [years] for the main period, and eight hundred for the two junctions (sandhyā) and their sub-junctions (sandhyāṃśa)—four hundred for each. This same calculation should be applied to the Tretā and subsequent ages as well. ||19||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "In due order" means that in the Kṛta Yuga there are four thousand [years]; for both the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) and the subsidiary twilight (*saṃdhyāṃśa*), there are four hundred each, totaling eight hundred. This is likewise for the Tretā and subsequent ages.
It should be applied. ||19||
The interval between two periods of one hundred [divine years] each, known as the dawn and the twilight,
is what those who know it call a *yuga*, wherein Dharma is ordained.

Śrīdhara: At the beginning of a *yuga* is the *sandhyā*, and at its end is the *sandhyāṃśa*. A *yuga* is that which lies between two periods consisting of hundreds [of years] as previously stated. He states its specific characteristic with the words "wherein":
the meaning is that it is where specific dharmas such as the immolation of cows (*gavālambha*) and so forth are prescribed. This refers to the common dharma.
But it certainly exists even during the two transitional periods (sandhyāṃśa). ||20||
The sequence of composition: regarding the phrase "between the twilight and the twilight-part," it means "at the end of the twilight and the twilight-part. ||20||

Viśvanātha: At the beginning of a Yuga is the Sandhyā (twilight), and at its end is the Sandhyāṃśa (the twilight-part). Of what nature are these two? They are those in which hundreds [of years] have been stated as their number; the period situated between them is called a Yuga. In that [Yuga], Dharma... [is present].

The specific dharma (*dharmaviśeṣa*) consists of meditation, sacrifice, service, and recitation; however, the common dharma (*sādhāraṇadharma*), being subordinate, exists in both the transitional periods (*saṃdhyāṃśa*) as well. Furthermore, it should be understood that whichever dharma belongs to a particular age (*yuga*), that very same dharma is the predominant one during its corresponding transitional periods and sub-periods.
Three hundred and sixty human years constitute one year of the gods.
Thus, forty-three lakh and twenty thousand human years are called a *caturyuga* by the term *yuga* in the scriptures. Among those, seventeen lakh and twenty-eight thousand [years]...
In truth, the Tretā age lasts for twelve hundred and ninety-six thousand years;
the Dvāpara age for eight hundred and sixty-four thousand years;
and the Kali age for four hundred and thirty-two thousand years. (20)
Dharma, consisting of four quarters, follows men in the Kṛta age;
in the other ages, it departs by one quarter through unrighteousness as that quarter increases.

Śrīdhara: [In the Kṛta age] it is complete with four quarters; in the Tretā and subsequent ages, it diminishes by one quarter at a time. This occurs due to unrighteousness (adharma) increasing quarter by quarter. And this is merely a description of its essential nature for the sake of generating detachment (vairāgya), not for the purpose of suggesting a literal contraction of dharma. ||21||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [The Dharma] is complete with four quarters (*catuṣpāt*). Targeting human beings, it passes away quarter by quarter through the cause of increasing—by one quarter at a time—through unrighteousness (*adharma*) in the other ages, such as the Tretā and so forth.
It diminishes. ||21||
A thousand yugas of the three worlds constitute a day for Brahmā;
his night is of equal duration, O dear one, during which the Creator of the universe closes his eyes.

Śrīdhara: Outside the three worlds, extending from Maharloka up to Brahmaloka, one thousand cycles of the four ages constitute a single day; it is during this time that Brahmā, the creator of the universe, closes his eyes and sleeps.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Outside the three worlds, extending from Maharloka up to Brahmaloka, one thousand cycles of four ages constitute a single day; at which time the creator of the universe, Brahmā, closes his eyes.

At that very time, he sleeps after the one lying within the Garbhodaka ocean. Thus, two thousand yugas constitute a day and night of Brahmā. During that period, there are eighty-four crores of years according to the reckoning of human beings.
At the end of the night, the world-cycle (kalpa) that has begun continues for as long as the day of the Lord, during which he sustains fourteen Manus.

Śrīdhara: Regarding that, he describes the duration of his stay there with four and a half verses beginning with "niśāvasāne" (at the end of the night). "Bhuñjan" means protecting; the sense is "pervading. ||23||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha says: Therein he describes the state during the day with four and a half verses beginning with "niśāvasāne" (at the end of night).
"Bhuñjan" means protecting or governing the fourteen Manus; the sense is that he pervades them. ||23||
Each Manu enjoys his own period for seventy-one and a quarter [kalpas].
During the Manvantaras, there are Manus, their descendants, sages, gods,
and the lords of the gods along with those who follow them, all existing simultaneously.
Madhva: The Lord residing in the day is the enjoyer.
Beyond seventy-one yugas, the enjoyment (bhukti) of a Manu consists of one hundred and eight and a half lakhs of years, plus an additional four thousand years.
Furthermore, there is a dissolution of one hundred and five [years];

in the first of the six [Manvantaras], it is proclaimed as two thousand years. Such is the duration of the interval of a Manu, and likewise for Indra and the others—thus it is stated in the *Mahāvārāha*. (24)

Śrīdhara: Slightly more than seventy-one yugas pass. The protectors of the earth belonging to the lineage of Manu appear in succession, whereas the Seven Sages and the others exist simultaneously at the same time. The lords of the gods are the Indras; those who follow them—
The Gandharvas and others are also [included therein]. ||24||
The sequential arrangement: "one's own, one's own," [is] half a verse. ||24||

Viśvanātha: A Manu, such as Svāyambhuva and the others, presides over a period spanning seventy-one *caturyugas* slightly more than that; in the divine reckoning (*devamāna*), this amounts to eight hundred and fifty-two thousand years, whereas in the human reckoning (*manuṣyamāna*), it is thirty crores of years.

Sixty-seven lakhs and twenty thousand. Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "O twice-born one, O great sage, they are calculated by number as thirty full crores, and likewise sixty-seven other hundred-thousands (niyutas)."
"O twice-born one, twenty thousand years, without any addition, is the reckoning of a *manvantara* in human years.
Thus, the lineage of Manu becomes the protector of the earth in succession; however, the Seven Sages and the others—
They arise simultaneously, at the very same time; the lords of the gods, the Indras, as well as those such as the Gandharvas and others, follow after them. ||24||
This is the daily creation of Brahmā, which sustains the three worlds,
wherein the birth of animals, humans, ancestors, and gods occurs through their respective karmas.
Śrīdhara: He is so called because he causes the three worlds to revolve. ||25||
The sequential arrangement: "simultaneously" means within their respective manvantaras. ||25||
Viśvanātha: He exists in the three worlds; thus, the meaning is that he is the creator of the three worlds. ||25||
In the Manvantaras, the Blessed One, manifesting his own nature through his forms,
protects this universe along with Manu and the others, his prowess having been awakened.

Śrīdhara: By means of His own forms—the incarnations during the Manvantaras such as Manu and others—who serve as gateways, He manifests His puruṣakāra (divine effort) and protects the universe. ||26||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By means of his own forms—his incarnations—he manifested his manly prowess; having assumed the form of a person, he withdrew his power by taking up the quality of darkness alone (tamas).
Having completed all his duties at the proper time, he remains silent at the close of day.
Śrīdhara: With five verses he describes the state during the night. *Tamaso mātram* means a mere trace or particle of darkness.
*Pratisaṃruddhavikramaḥ* refers to one by whom prowess has been restrained or withdrawn. *Anugata-aśeṣam yasmin* means that in which everything without exception has entered or followed along. ||27||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: He describes the state occurring at night—having assumed a particle (*mātrā*) of *tamas* as a trace for the sake of withdrawing the three worlds, he effects the withdrawal in the form of Kālāgnirudra.

His prowess is obstructed and enveloped by fire and other elements; he is one by whom the three worlds, beginning with the earth (bhūr), are pervaded—this is because it was previously stated that "prowess consists of bhūr, bhuvaḥ, and svar. Furthermore, he is one in whom the entire multitude of living beings residing in the three worlds has followed after and entered. [He remains] silent.
The meaning is that he has abandoned the playful diversions of illusory manifestation. ||27||
Into that very [ocean] the three worlds, beginning with Bhūḥ,
are absorbed when the night has set in and the moon and sun have been released.

Śrīdhara: He clarifies that very point with the words "tam eva" (that very [Self]). The expression "anv api dhīyante" is a usage in the reflexive passive (*karmakartari*). The meaning is: "they become concealed. How? Just as the moon and the sun become [concealed] when they are released or separated [from their light]. ||28||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He clarifies that very point with the words "tam eva" (that very [one]). The expression "anv api dhīyante" is a usage of the reflexive passive (*karmakartari*). The meaning is "they become concealed. How? [By] being liberated.
Just as the moon and the sun become [invisible] when they are devoid [of light]. ||28||
When the three worlds are being consumed by the power of the fire of Saṃkarṣaṇa,
Bhṛgu and the other sages, afflicted by its heat, depart from Maharloka for Janaloka.
Śrīdhara: Afflicted by the heat of that fire from the mouth of Saṃkarṣaṇa, which is the very form of the Lord’s power, they go to Janaloka. ||29||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha*: not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: In response to the expectation of "in what manner," he says: "In the three worlds" (verse 29).
Meanwhile, the oceans, swelling at the end of the eon, instantly inundate the three worlds with waves driven by fierce winds of violent fury.
Śrīdhara: The oceans—the seas—swollen at the end of the kalpa; they are both those whose agitation and turbulence are intense, and those impelled by fierce winds, as well as the mountains. (30)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Immediately" (*sadyaḥ*) means that while the three worlds have been burnt, [it occurs] without delay.
The burning, however, should be understood to last for a hundred years. And those who possess intense arrogance and agitation—those...
And those [oceans] have waves stirred by fierce winds. ||30||
Within that water sits Hari upon his infinite throne,
his eyes closed in yogic sleep, being praised by the inhabitants of the world.

Śrīdhara: Those whose abode is Janaloka, as well as others who have gone to Maharloka—by them [is there] a sequential arrangement; those whose waves are stirred by fierce winds with violent surges. ||31||
Viśvanātha: The fifth among the functions of the powers of consciousness (cicchakti), such as Vimalā and the others, is called Yoga;
at that time, it takes the form of sleep. With his eyes gladdened by that [power], he was surrounded by the sages dwelling in Janaloka, the abode of people. ||31||
By means of such days and nights, as characterized by the passage of time,
even his supreme lifespan of a hundred years appears as if diminished.
"Of this honeyed *brahman*, for it has been said that the day of *brahman* [is its measure].
No measurement of the lifespan of the Blessed One exists in any form whatsoever.
Because he is beginningless, without middle, and endless, he is immutable (*avyaya*). Thus says the *Harivaṃśa*. (32)

Śrīdhara: For the sake of generating detachment, he says: "By such days and nights, the hundred-year lifespan of all living beings—even that lifespan of this Brahmā which is the maximum for them—is as if diminished, as if exhausted; this is a common worldly expression. The meaning is that it has almost come to an end. ||32||

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: By the statement, "I am afraid of Time, because even the lifespan of this Brahmā is indicated to be exhausted, having almost reached its end" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.18), he speaks as one who fears Time.
Even Brahmā, having become detached from the enjoyment of sense objects, worships the Lord incessantly as a devotee.
Humans, however, possessing such limited lifespans, do not worship Him while indulging in sense objects—what kind of audacity is this?
Thus, it has been stated that the purpose of defining time is to demonstrate the necessity of exerting effort toward devotion and detachment.
Half of that lifespan is called a *parārdha*;
the first *parārdha* has indeed passed away, and the second is now proceeding.
Śrīdhara: "At the beginning of the previous *parārdha*"—this is merely a statement of the subject matter through three [verses].
The sequence of composition is: "That half," meaning in this present day. (33)
Viśvanātha says: He states that lifespan is divided into two parts with the words "that which... (verse 33).
At the beginning of the first half of the cosmic cycle, there occurred a great eon known as Brāhma,
during which Brahmā came into being— he whom they know as Śabdabrahman.
Śrīdhara: The reason for the state of being a lotus is "that which" (yad). ||34||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Of the preceding" refers to those [periods] mentioned in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* as the *pitṛkalpas*, such as the Śvetavarāha and others; by means of those thirty *kalpas* alone, [the days] from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapratipad*) up to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) [are accounted for].

Thirty days of those very *kalpas*, repeated again and again, constitute a month; twelve months make a year; and fifty years make one *parārdha*. Therein, at the beginning of the first [period], it is called "Brahma" because the Śvetavārāha [incarnation] itself is the lunar day (*tithi*) of Brahmā’s birth.

It is expressed by the word "Brāhma. And that lunar day (tithi) should be understood as the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, according to the statements of the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra). ||34||
At the end of that very [kalpa], there occurred the aeon which they call Pādma,
during which the lotus of the worlds arose from the lake of Hari’s navel.
Śrīdhara: But this [topic] was stated at the beginning of the second [chapter]. ||35||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The *Kalpa* is the *Pitṛkalpa*; they call this very last *Pitṛkalpa* of the *Parārdha* the *Pādma*. The reason for its being called *Pādma* is expressed by "yad" (which). Therefore, in all *Kalpas* indeed...
The lotus is not of the nature of the world; rather, the meaning is that it exists only here and there. ||35||
But this second eon, O Bhārata,
is also described as the one renowned as Vārāha, wherein Hari was a boar.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having stated the measure of the lifespan of created beings by means of time as the instrumental cause, he speaks of that reality which is devoid of temporal limitation with the five verses beginning with "This time. It is merely metaphorically designated [as time], for even by this sequence there is no calculation of lifespan for it; thus he says: "of the unmanifest" (avyākṛtasya).

For the Self of the universe, who is the cause of the world, who is devoid of the limiting adjuncts of effects, and who is therefore infinite and beginningless, there can be no sequential arrangement [of time].

Thus, by means of the conceptualization of Brahmā’s day, one should understand the conceptualization of the day of the one lying within the Garbhodaka ocean; for even he accepts yogic sleep at the end of that day.
He speaks thus regarding the conception of time for Him who reclines upon the ocean of causes: "This is Time.
For, according to the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "Taking as their support the duration of His single exhalation, the lords of the cosmic eggs born from the pores of His hair live [within it]. (36)

Viśvanātha: This means that it is the first day of the fifty-first year of the current second *parārdha*. Here, within the narrative of the *Pādma-kalpa*—which was introduced with the words "Now hear the *Pādma-kalpa*" and continues with "the universe was submerged in water," and so forth—[this occurs].

Because only a single lotus is heard of in the waters of the universal ocean (*ekārṇava*), and because only a single Brahmā arises there— as seen from such statements as "not seeing anything else there"— and because Sanaka and others, who possess the lifespan of a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*),
are not perceived there, some [maintain that] at the end of the first *parārdha*, [the worlds of] Mahar, Jana, Tapa, and Satya [dissolve].

Having described how even those who remain until the end of two *parārdhas*— without perishing— are likewise submerged by the flood of waters, and how all those there whose lifespan is a *kalpa* enter into Śrī Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Brahmā, [the text then describes] at the conclusion of the first *parārdha*, the beginning of the second *parārdha*.

They say that the Śvetavārāha [Purāṇa] is indeed the Pādma; and in the twelfth chapter, the manifestation of Sanaka and others, as well as Marīci and others, from Brahmā himself—just as in the Brāhma-kalpa—will be described.
Nor should it be said that this refers only to the narrative of the Brāhma-kalpa, because the narrative of the Pādma-kalpa is what has been introduced.

Therefore, regarding the phrase "and at its very end," the meaning is "at the end," that is, at the conclusion or completion. As for the word "this," the particle *tu* has the sense of *eva* (only/itself); thus, this very [kalpa] is known as the Pādma or the Vārāha. The reason for this is the phrase "wherein he was"; by the use of the particle *api* in the expression "of the second also," the first half of the Brahmā-cycle is indicated.
They explain that even a *kalpa* is called *pādma*. ||36||
This time, known as two parārdhas, is metaphorically designated as a single moment (nimeṣa) of the unmanifest,
infinite, beginningless, and world-souled [Brahman].

Śrīdhara says: Because time lacks the capacity to determine that [Self], he states: "This time, though it is the Lord (īśvara), is not at all capable (prabhu)—that is, not able—to rule over the 'Abundance' (bhūman), the Perfectly Full One; for it is the Lord only of those who pride themselves on their abode, namely, those who identify with the body and the home. (37)
The sequential arrangement: [it concerns] those who identify with the abodes, namely those who hold authority over Satyaloka and the other worlds. ||37||
Viśvanātha: Having thus described time in its subtle and gross forms, he now speaks of the ultimate gross form, the supremely great time—known as two *parārdhas*.
Although there is no possibility of an end to time, it is that very duration which is designated by this term in the scriptures due to its ultimate grossness.

That too is but a moment (nimeṣa) of the Supreme Lord, who is the Self of the universe. Now, one might ask: "In this way, is his lifespan also calculated by means of a sequence of moments and so forth? To this, he says "no, no" with a playful tone, stating a portion of the answer: "In some cases, it is figuratively called a 'moment' (nimeṣa). [This refers to] that which they live upon, taking as their support the duration of a single exhalation of His.

The statement in the *Brahmasaṃhitā* and other texts that "the lords of the cosmic egg are born from the hair-pores" is merely a figurative expression—such as calling [Brahmā] "Niśvāsa" (Breath) in certain places—and does not mean that there is actually even a moment's lapse. This is because the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) is devoid of modifications produced by time; the reason for this is that it is infinite and beginningless (*anādi*).
The meaning is "of that which has transcended the limitation of time," because [it belongs] to the Self of the World, the cause of the entire world including time and so forth. ||37||
This time, beginning with the atom and ending with the supreme limit of two parārdhas, is the Lord;
yet it is not capable of governing the Infinite One, for the Lord is the master of those who merely imagine themselves to possess abodes.

Śrīdhara: Elaborating upon what was stated by the word "of the Great" (*bhūmnaḥ*), he says: "Endowed with the sixteen modifications joined with the eight primal natures"—the meaning is that [the world] is accompanied by and originated from those. This connects with the subsequent clause: "this egg-shell, having entered which, appears like an atom."
Of what nature is it? It is fifty crores of yojanas in extent within, and on the outside, it is surrounded by the seven [spheres] beginning with earth, such as the Viśeṣa and so forth. ||38||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He clarifies once more the very meaning already suggested with the words "This is the time" (*kālo 'yam*). [It refers to] the abode of the Supreme Lord (*bhūman*), for those who consider themselves residents of the worlds of authority such as Satyaloka. (38)
Accompanied by the modifications and joined with the specific elements (viśeṣa) and so forth,
this external egg-shell extends for fifty crores [of yojanas].

The ten sense organs, together with the mind, which are contained within the egg, should be known as modifications (vikāra); the elements (bhūta) and the ego (ahaṃkāra) are beyond the Great One (mahat).
"They say that the earth is distinguished by the multiplicity of sound and the other [qualities].
Because of its subtlety, it envelops the cosmic egg; indeed, these [elements] increase tenfold, each being double the size of the preceding.
From the unmanifest (avāk) down to primordial nature (prakṛti), these eight are known as the eight primary natures (prakṛtis). Thus it is said.

"Due to the multiplicity of bodies, as well as because they are seen individually within the very same divine bodies throughout the past and the future, the multiplicity of cosmic eggs (aṇḍas) exists through the power of Viṣṇu and not otherwise. Thus it is stated in the Brahmatarka.

"Brahmā saw a single egg become manifold, each entering a hair-pore; likewise, he saw himself within those [pores] individually. Thus it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*. And in the *Mahābhārata*: "There was one great egg. (39)

Śrīdhara: Of what kind? By those in which each subsequent one is ten times greater than the preceding, starting from the measure of an eggshell (āṇḍakośa). Not only is this one [egg] so, but others are also observed. ||39||
The sequence of composition: the pair beginning with "by the modifications" [is as follows]. The modifications (*vikāra*) consist of the eleven organs and the five gross elements;

the primordial natures (*prakṛti*) consist of Nature (*prakṛti*), the Great One (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); and those beginning with the Great One (*mahad-ādi*) are both primordial natures and modifications (*prakṛti-vikṛti*).
According to the principle that "seven [are causes]," even Mahat and the others are considered *prakṛti* (primordial nature) with respect to their own respective effects;

thus Viśvanātha states that she is the delimiting factor of the entire universe, as implied by the term "O Soul of the World" (*jagadātman*), saying: "together with the sixteen transformations and the eight primordial natures."

The meaning is that it has begun from that [egg]. This egg-shell, having entered which [the world] is perceived like an atom—this is the connection with what follows. Of what nature is it? It is surrounded on the outside by the seven [elements], earth and so forth, beginning with "particularity" (viśeṣa). ||39||
Wherein, having entered like a single atom, one perceives millions of other cosmic eggs situated within, each increasing tenfold over the last.
Regarding this, they say: "The Imperishable (akṣara) is Brahman, the cause of all causes;
it is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, the Great Self, the Puruṣa himself."
The *madhvaḥ* are the bodies contained within; the *dhāma* (abode) is the house, the multitudes of cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*).
Yama is time for human beings, and his time is Sudarśana. Rudra is the time even for him, and Brahmā is the time for him as well; Durgā is likewise his [time].
At the dissolution of Brahmā, that Goddess exists in the form of the wheel;
she alone, abiding within Brahmā and the others, perpetually withdraws the worlds.
"Viṣṇu is her director; he is called the Supreme Time (paraḥ kālaḥ).
She herself is the one who presides over time (kālābhimāninī), but she is not the sovereign of the Lord of the Universe.
He alone is her lord, the Ruler, Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords. Thus it is said. ||40||
Śrīdhara: He is the cause of all causes; *dhāma* means His essential nature. ||40||

The sequential arrangement: others are also observed; thus, the covering of water and so forth is to be understood for all [elements] in this very manner, according to the reasoning previously stated. ||40||

Although, according to the manner previously described, even a Great Person (mahāpuruṣa) is certainly not subject to time, nevertheless, because his nature consists of the play of appearance and disappearance, he is not denoted by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable). Rather, his supreme essential form is the Lord himself, who is eternally manifest; therefore, that [Lord] alone is denoted by that term.

He said: "Regarding that, they say... They declare that very thing which is the supreme abode of the Great Soul Viṣṇu, known as Mahāviṣṇu—the reality that is his own essential nature as the supreme portion (*paramāṃśa*), self-established, imperishable, eternally manifest, Brahman, and the perfect state of the Blessed Lord (*bhagavattva*). For even the Puruṣa, who is the cause of all, [proceeds from it].
The cause. ||41||
Viśvanātha: By what kind [of worlds]? By those in which each succeeding one is ten times greater than the preceding, measured by the size of the cosmic egg (aṇḍakoṣa).

Not only this one alone, but others also are perceived as the abode—the body—of Viṣṇu while he lies upon the causal ocean (kāraṇārṇava). According to Amara, the words *dhāman* and *tviṭ* denote both an abode and a body.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, perfectly suited for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.

Thus, in the glorious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, in the commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*, in the *Pāramahaṃsya-saṃhitā* of Vyāsa’s collection, in the third book (*skandha*), within the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya,
[this is] the section titled "The Description of the Nature of Time."
The Eleventh Chapter. Om. Salutations to Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa.
The Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the second section of the third book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.
The Eleventh Chapter:
An Exposition on the Nature of Time.
Maitreya said:
That which is the ultimate limit of real particulars, being manifold and never conjoined,
is to be known as the atom (paramāṇu), from which arises the illusion of unity among men.
In order to demonstrate the measure of time for the *madhu*, [the text] shows the measure of substance by way of illustration:
"Even from a human being, the world is seen only through a specific [vision]."
But as for that specific distinction of being part and whole, they are unable to perceive it.
The sages have declared that the ultimate limit of motion is the atom; it should be understood as partless, according to Kaṇāda and others.

"Even though it possesses infinite parts, that which they call [an atom] is so due to erroneous perception; for even if its parts possess infinitude, their state of being atoms is stated for the sake of distinction. Thus ends the *Tattvaviveka*.
From many parts, on all sides. ||1||
Śrīdhara:
Thereafter, in the eleventh [chapter], time— from the atom (*paramāṇu*) and so forth up to the *yugas*, *manvantaras*, and beyond— is described as beginningless, culminating in the *kalpa*.

Thus, having generally described the tenfold interaction of the *guṇas* as a characteristic mark of time (*kāla*), he now defines the object to be delimited by that [time] in order to describe its specific nature through two verses: "That which is the final, ultimate part of the existent effect—the parts of which there is no further part... [and so forth].

It is "non-multiple" (aneka) because it has not reached the state of being an effect; it is "uncombined" (asaṃyuta) because it has not reached the state of being an aggregate. For this very reason, that atom must be understood as existing even when the states of being an effect and an aggregate have always departed.
What is the proof for this? To this he says: because from those [atoms] when combined, for people who engage in worldly transactions...
The notion of a whole is an illusion of unity. Thus, he will state in the fifth chapter during the refutation of the whole:
"That which is produced by the collection of those [parts] is the distinction. The sense is that it is postulated because the effect would otherwise be untenable. ||1||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha:
Furthermore, in the eleventh [chapter], time is also characterized in its specific aspects.
From which the measure of months, years, yugas, and so forth is known.

Being unable to characterize the first, ultimate, subtle moment by way of its own nature, [the author] characterizes the object that is delimited by it: that which is the final part of the specificities or portions of an existing effect such as earth, beyond which no further portion is possible. Now, one might object: because of the singular number in the word "final" (*carama*), [how can there be multiple parts?]

Is it only one? No, rather it is many. Here, for the sake of knowing subtle time, although they are many, the singular number is used because only one is functional. Now, one might ask: is it then taken here as combined with others or uncombined? To this he says: the atom is to be understood precisely as uncombined (*asaṃyuta*).

The meaning is that it is not, however, actually seen. [Objection: If so, what is the proof for its existence? To this he says: "From which"—that is, from those [atoms] combined together—the delusion arises that there is a unity of these [parts].
Just as in the case of the extremely subtle particles moving through a window-opening joined with the rays of the sun.

The meaning is that "intellect arises. A sixth part of that [intellect] is indeed an atom (*paramāṇu*), and its meaning is that it is truly invisible. By the expression "of these" (*eṣām*), it is implied that for certain specific types of insects whose bodies are the size of a *trasareṇu*, some [atom] is indeed visible. ||1||
The absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of that very reality which exists in its own essential nature— that which is supremely great, undifferentiated, and continuous— is [the state of liberation].
*Madhvaḥ*: The supreme greatness [of the honey] in terms of time, space, and qualities belongs only to *Sat*, the Supreme Brahman.
Since the word *sat* is used figuratively for other things as well, he specifies "of the thing" (*padārthasya*), meaning:
of that which is the primary denotation of the word *sat*.

"The primary intended meaning is the *artha*, while another is called the *vācya*; however, when applied to non-primary meanings, the word *artha* is used in a subordinate sense. Thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*.
If this is so, then by the passage beginning with "equal even to a gnat," it follows that there is also a state of having that [atomic] dimension for one situated elsewhere.

Therefore, [it is said] "of that which abides in its own nature. Since the nature of the world-obscuring [Self] possesses a certain degree of greatness and minuteness, there is "isolation" (*kaivalya*). Even therein, because it possesses many kinds of forms, there is "non-distinction" (*aviśeṣa*). Because even that which is all-pervading exists as merely a span in measure, therefore—

"Without interval" (*nirantara*) means that which is the absolute state (*kevalabhāva*) of the Supreme Brahman. That which has entered within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) and so forth, which veils it, and its other forms such as the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), constitute a single part; whereas that form which is all-pervading, excluding such specific measures as a "span" (*prādeśa*) or "the size of a span," is indeed the supremely great (*paramamahān*).
The wise know that the absence of a limit of time is the infinity of time,
and likewise, the absence of a limit of space is the infinity of space.
The knowers of reality understand that the immeasurability of qualities constitutes the infinity of the substance;
this threefold eternity belongs to Hari alone and to no other.
Although its infinity exists in all its essential forms and possesses three characteristics,
nevertheless, it is also subject to limitation in terms of space.
Thus, both delimitation and pervasion are applicable even to that which is of a single nature;
this is due to its inconceivable and marvelous sovereignty, and it is solely for the sake of conventional usage.
Furthermore, there is no delimitation whatsoever of it by way of qualities or by way of time.
Although pervasiveness exists even spatially in all forms,
and not even an atom’s worth of difference is found among them,
nevertheless, atomicity exists due to the possession of sovereign power.
Therefore, for the sake of facilitating comprehension, its non-pervasiveness is also stated.
That which is its all-pervading form, the supreme designated as Nārāyaṇa, they call the Void, the Brahman; and that which is the second, the creator from which [the world] arises.
The one called the Supreme Person (Parama Puruṣa) is limited by space, yet he is all-pervading;
the third, known as Vāsudeva, is limited and envelops the entire world.
"The world is pervaded in its entirety by the Fourth, named Viṣṇu"— thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*.
Although there is an equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*) of the omnipresent Brahman-form with primordial nature (*prakṛti*) in the form of time and so forth,
because [the Lord] is included within the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*) and does not abide elsewhere than that, He is said to be "abiding in His own essential nature" (*svarūpāvasthita*).
It has been said:
"Even though Brahman, which is all-pervading, resides within the Goddess who consists of Time and other such principles, it does not go elsewhere;
for she is like the self of the omnipresent Lord Hari."
"That which pertains to the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth is superior when it pertains to something else," thus it is stated in the *Brāhma*.

"Inferred" (*anumita*) means known in accordance with scripture and worldly experience. They say that "inference" (*anumā*) is twofold, as the designation [indicates]: "just as knowledge born from a sign (*liṅga*)."
As much as a person dwelling in the world might perceive,
that time— belonging to one of great wisdom who is devoted to the gods— is a single atom.
Nor would it be the case that [the world] is uninterrupted by creation and so forth, nor even that it follows immediately [thereafter];
likewise, it could not possess a specific nature consisting of atoms and the like.
"In the *Brahmatarka*: 'That which is devoid of distinctions such as prior and posterior is Time, the supreme and great.
These qualifiers—'abiding in its own nature,' 'isolation,' 'without distinction,' and 'uninterrupted'—are stated here in sequence as attributes even of the supreme and great Time."
In terms of space, time, and substance, Hari alone possesses infinity in these three ways;
no other entity possesses it, nor does primordial nature (prakṛti) in terms of space and time.
Likewise, the infinity of sound and time is not [limited] by time;
for that very [power] consists of both time and sound, and yet it belongs eternally to Hari.
Not even a fraction of her power exists in the qualities of knowledge and bliss;
therefore, Vāyu is inferior to her, as are Śeṣa, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Hara.
"Therefore, Indra and the others are inferior in all qualities; of this there is no doubt. Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
"Because he is the sustainer of the existence of atoms and so forth, and because he is the enjoyer, the Supreme Lord is called 'Time' (kāla), being designated by such names as 'atom' and so on. And:
"That which is Time—the inner controller of time—is the very nature of the existent Brahman, devoid of distinctions; that alone is Brahman."
He enjoys it; and that Brahman is also the supreme Great One, because it too lacks the threefold limitations.
Everything exists everywhere, and the enjoyer, being non-distinct [from all], is like a single enjoyer.
Hari, whose nature is inconceivable, unborn, and all-pervading, remains established by virtue of his own sovereignty—thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*.

Śrīdhara, having spoken of the subtle, speaks of the gross: "of the existent alone" (*sata eva*). For that very existent whose final part is the atom, which is the mere effect remaining in its own nature and not having attained another modification—that absolute oneness (*kaivalyam aikyam*) is the supreme great. But as for [the quality of] masculinity...

Because it has the atom as its counter-correlative. Now, an objection is raised: since every category of object possesses various specificities (*viśeṣa*) and is mutually distinct, how can there be unity in it? To this he replies: "The non-specific" (*aviśeṣaḥ*) means devoid of the intention to express specificities;
"the continuous" (*nirantaraḥ*) means devoid of the intention to express distinctions; thus, the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is the "Supremely Great" (*paramamahān*).
The meaning. ||2||

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Having stated the ultimate subtle [state], he also states the ultimate subtle [state] of that very same reality which consists of all effects and abides in its own nature, the last part of which is the atom.
The isolation (*kaivalya*) and unity (*aikya*) of that which existed prior to dissolution and transformation is the "Supreme Great" (*paramamahat*);

however, its "masculinity" (*puṃstva*) is due to its being the counter-correlative of the atom (*paramāṇu*). Now, an objection is raised: since every category of object possesses various specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) and is mutually distinct, how can there be unity for it? To this, he says: "It is without specific qualities" (*aviśeṣaḥ*).

The meaning is that the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), when devoid of the intention to express particularity and devoid of the intention to express differentiation, is "supremely great" (paramamahān). ||2||
Thus, O best of men, time as well is inferred in its subtlety and its grossness;
the Lord, though unmanifest, all-pervading, and the enjoyer of the manifest, [is known] through the movement of his manifestation.

Śrīdhara: Just as this object is both subtle and gross, so too is time inferred. By the word "and" (ca), the intermediate state is included. Its "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) refers to the state of atoms and so forth; its "enjoyment" (*bhukti*) is its pervasion (*vyāpti*). By that [pervasion], it is called "Bhagavān"; thus, the power of Hari, though unmanifest by nature, enjoys.
It is thus because it pervades and delimits; it is all-pervasive (vibhu) and skillful (dakṣa) in its arising and other functions. ||3||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Just as this object is both subtle and gross, so too is time known through inference. In what manner? [It is known] by its configuration (*saṃsthāna*), which is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the atom and the infinitely great.

Because he enjoys and pervades that [universe] by virtue of being the power of the Lord, he is "Bhāgavat" (the Possessor of Parts); though himself unmanifest (*avyakta*), he enjoys, pervades, and delimits the manifest (*vyakta*) entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*). He is "Vibhu" (all-pervading) for this very reason, or else he is "Vibhu" because he is skillful (*dakṣa*) in creation and the other cosmic functions. ||3||
That time which experiences the state of an atom is indeed the atom;
but that time which experiences the non-distinction of the existent is the supreme, great Time.

Śrīdhara explains this very point with the words beginning "He... and so forth: He who experiences the state of atoms—the atomic condition—of the existent phenomenal world (prapañca) is time as an atom (paramāṇu). He who experiences its undifferentiated totality is the supremely great (paramamahān). This is [the meaning].

The meaning is as follows: regarding that solar revolution which will be described in the passage beginning with *graharkṣatārācakrastha* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.13), the time taken by the sun to traverse the space of a single atom (*paramāṇu*) is called a *paramāṇu*. And the time taken to traverse the entire [path] consisting of the twelve zodiac signs...

It transcends the cosmic egg (bhuvanakośa); that time, consisting of the year, is the supreme great one. Through its revolution, it reaches its limit of two parārdhas by way of the sequence of yugas, manvantaras, and so forth. And thus, in the fifth [chapter], he will explain the division of time and so on precisely through the motion of the sun. ||4||

The sequence of composition: He explains precisely what was stated [in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.10.3] with the words "That is time. Here, in the commentary, regarding the phrase "it traverses the space of an atom," it should be understood that this occurs by means of the celestial sphere (*jyotiścakra*) consisting of the middle path. [It traverses] the entire cosmic egg (*bhuvanakoṣa*).

In the phrase "he transcends," however, it should be understood that he transcends his own state. And in the phrase "he who consumes atom-ness," the meaning is precisely that he transcends the spatial dimensions of atoms by means of the form of the sun. Furthermore, the non-difference of that time from the sun will be stated: "He who [projects] the power of the emanated manifoldly" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.15).

By this [it is meant]: Alternatively, that which enjoys—that is, pervades—the state of being an atom (*paramāṇutā*), like the object denoted by that term, namely the state of extreme subtlety, is the "atom" (*paramāṇu*) of time. That which enjoys the manifold world (*prapañca*) without distinction—that is, which pervades everything from its creation until its dissolution—is the "supremely great" (*paramamahat*) time.
The meaning is that its form consists of two *parārdhas*. And so it will be stated: "This time begins with the atom (*paramāṇu*) and ends with two *parārdhas*" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.38). ||4||

Viśvanātha explains the meaning of the term "the enjoyer" (*sambhoktṛ*): that time which "enjoys"—that is, passes by in the form of the sun—the state of being an atom (*paramāṇutā*) of an existing effect, that is, the very nature of an atom;
according to the perspective of the verse to be cited later, *graharkṣa* [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.13], it is by such a duration of time that...

The sun traverses the space of a single atom; the meaning is that such a duration of time is an *aṇu*. And he, as Time in the form of the sun, experiences the entirety of that very manifestation without distinction through the cycles of years, yugas, and so forth; from the commencement of creation until the end of the phenomenal world, that Time is supremely great.
The meaning is that the entire duration of time from [the beginning] up to the end of the dissolution (*saṃhāra*) is equally "supremely great" (*paramamahān*).
In that regard, the designations and measures of the atoms (*paramāṇu*), subtle particles (*aṇu*), and motes of dust (*trasareṇu*)—which are constituent parts of effects—are indeed equal;
likewise, the designation alone for the supremely great effect and for time is equal, as it is for those situated between them.
It should be understood that there is a difference between perception and the means of valid cognition. ||4||
Two atoms (aṇu) constitute one minute particle (paramāṇu), and three of those are said to be a mote of dust (trasareṇu);
this is perceived by the rays of the sun entering through a lattice window as it moves through the sky.
"Madhvaḥ" means that [the honey] has come within the range of vision; the sense is that it has been perceived due to the distinction between the two heaps. ||5||
Śrīdhara: Now, preceded by the definition of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, he describes its state during the intermediate period.

Two atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute a dyad (*aṇu*). Three dyads constitute a triad (*trasareṇu*). He states that this [triad] is perceptible: "By the sunlight through a lattice," etc. It is perceived in the rays of the sun entering through a window-lattice.

Who was he? He who, due to his extreme lightness, went—having gone—following after his own self; or according to another reading, he was understood as following after his own self, and not the earth (gām). ||5||

The sequential arrangement: the verse beginning with "the atom and the two" is a general statement regarding both the categories of objects and time, by virtue of the relationship between the illustration and the illustrated and their sharing a single name. ||5||

Viśvanātha: Two atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute one *aṇu*; three *aṇus* constitute a *trasareṇu*, which is perceptible; thus he says, "by the sun through the lattice. This refers to what is perceived by the eye as moving with extreme lightness through the very air within the rays of the sun entering through a window-lattice, and not the earth (*gāṃ*). It has gone deep... [text fragment].

In this reading, the meaning is that "it moves while being thus constituted. If it is asked what the proof is for the existence of atoms (*aṇu*) and subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is the mote (*trasareṇu*) itself. For instance, when there is an abundance of grossness in the parts, a whole (*avayavin*) must be postulated; however, the atoms [themselves] are not [the cause], because they lack grossness, whereas grossness [belongs to the whole].

The fact that [an object] is composed of multiple substances implies that the grossness of an atom could not exist without a *paramāṇu*; thus, the *paramāṇu* is established. The visibility of a *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust) could not exist without the grossness of its constituent parts;
thus, the *aṇu* is established. Likewise, for the sake of the grossness of an *aṇu*, there must be at least a duality of *paramāṇus*.
It is postulated [as three], but not as three or four and so on, according to the principle that when something is first presented, it serves as the basis for the rest;

just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds," although the word *tri* (three) is used in the sense of abundance, only the number three is postulated because of the reasoning involved. ||5||
The time it takes to consume three *trasareṇus* is known as a *truṭi*.
A hundredth part of that is a *vedha*, and three of those are known as a *lava*.
Śrīdhara: That piercing [of the heart] in which there are one hundred parts in the form of *truṭis*. ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "A triad of *trasareṇu*s. According to the *Sūryasiddhānta*, a *truṭi* consists of three *trasareṇu*s; it is said that a *truṭi* is the amount [of space] pierced by a needle in a lotus-petal. For as long as...

The time in which a lotus petal is pierced by a needle is the meaning of *truṭi*. That in which there are a hundred such parts in the form of *truṭis* is the piercing with a hundred *truṭis*; this is the meaning of "piercing with a hundred *truṭis*.
Three of those [piercings] constitute a *lava*. ||6||
A *nimeṣa* should be known as three *lava*s; those three have been declared by tradition to be one *kṣaṇa*.
Five *kṣaṇa*s are known as a *kāṣṭhā*, and fifteen of those are a *laghu*.
Śrīdhara: Three of those *nimeṣas* are traditionally taught as one *kṣaṇa*. Fifteen *kāṣṭhās* constitute one *laghu*. (7)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Three *nimeṣas* are traditionally taught as one *kṣaṇa*. Fifteen of those *kāṣṭhās* are said to constitute one *laghu*. (7)
Fifteen *nāḍikās* are indeed declared to be a *laghu*;
two of those are a *muhūrta*, and six or seven of those are a *prahara*, or a *yāma*, for men.
Regarding the honey-mixture (*madhu*): it may be seven [verses] due to deficiency or excess. ||8||

Śrīdhara: A *prahara* consists of six or seven *nāḍikās*. That itself is a *yāma*, the fourth part of both day and night. There are six [nāḍikās] during a decrease [of the day] and seven during an increase. It should be understood that this excludes two *muhūrtas* belonging to the twilight (*saṃdhyā*). Even there, the word "or" (*vā*) is for the sake of indicating lack of strict rule regarding those divisions every day.
Because it is impossible to calculate [them]. ||8||
Regarding the sequence of arrangement: "six or seven. There, the word "or" (vā) includes all the intermediate [numbers] as well. ||8||

Viśvanātha: A *nāḍikā* is a *daṇḍa*; two *nāḍikās* [make one *ghaṭikā*]. Six or seven *nāḍikās* constitute a *prahara*, which is also called a *yāma*. It is a fourth part of the day and the night. When [the day] decreases, there are six;
when the increase begins, there are seven. This should be understood as excluding the *ghaṭikās* of the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*). Even in that case—
The word "or" (vā) indicates uncertainty, because it is impossible to enumerate their specific varieties every single day. ||8||

It should weigh twelve half-palas, have a hole made with four gold māṣas each measuring four finger-breadths, and take as long to sink in one prastha of water [as it takes for the water to fill the vessel].
Four *kākaṇikās* of honey-liquor are called a twentieth part;
they also call that a *kṛṣṇalā*, and four of those make a *māṣaka*.
When it has been made four finger-breadths long, the door is prescribed to be as wide as its circumference for a period of four months.
In the case of a prastha-measure vessel with six petals filled with auspicious water,
even when overloaded by a bhāra of weight, it will quickly become full.
In cases of extreme cold or impurity, the fulfillment [of the rite] is indeed by means of the Māgha [waters];
therefore, during the spring season, it is by means of the water located at Prayāga.
"The examination of the purification of the channels would not be possible otherwise"—thus it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
"The purification of the *kali* [vessel] should always be performed with pure water, warm and flowing like the rays of the sun"—thus it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*. (9)

Śrīdhara: He states the measurement of the *nāḍikā*: "The measure (*unmāna*) is that by which something is measured; it is a vessel fashioned from six *pala*s of copper. A *māṣa* consists of five *guñjā*s; with four of these [māṣas], arranged in the form of a rod four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, a root-opening is made. By means of that opening..."

The time it takes for water measuring one *prastha* to enter [the vessel] and for it to become submerged and sink is one *nāḍikā*. Herein, the rule for the *pala* and the pin is that if the *palacchidra* is larger, it would sink quickly, whereas if it is smaller, it would do so slowly. (9)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: He states the measurement of the *nāḍīkā*—the term *unmāna* means that by which something is measured; it is a vessel made of six *pala*s of copper, where one *pala* consists of sixty-four *māṣa*s.

Five *guñjās* make one *māṣa*. When four of these are arranged in the form of a stick four finger-breadths long, a hole is made at its base. Through that hole, as much water as measures one *prastha* enters, and the time it takes for the vessel to become saturated and sink is a *nāḍikā*; here, the [measurement] is based on the *pala* and the hole.

If [the weight] is excessive, one would sink quickly; if it is deficient, one would sink slowly—this is the rule for the *pala* and the probe. Furthermore, since a probe made of silver or similar materials might cause the hole to expand, there is also a rule regarding the use of gold. ||9||
O giver of honor, there are four *yāmas*, and for mortals there are both days and nights;
a fortnight consists of fifteen days, namely the bright and the dark.
Regarding *madhvaḥ*: where there is a word expressing duality for both [the speaker and the listener], the term *ubha* is used even in the dual number. (10)
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: "ahanī" (the two days) means a day and night (ahorātra). ||10||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained.
—o)0(o— The conjunction of those two is a month; for the ancestors, that is a day and night.
Two of those seasons make an ayana, namely the southern and the northern, in the sky.
Śrīdhara: Six months constitute an *ayana*. This [term] connects with what follows "in heaven" (*divi*). ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Six months constitute an *ayana*. [The word] "in heaven" (*divi*) connects with what follows. ||11||
They say that a day consists of two solstices, and twelve such days are recorded as a year;
the maximum lifespan of nāgas is declared to be one hundred years.
Śrīdhara says: "In heaven" refers to the day and night of the gods; [this consists of] twelve months. 12.

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] is as follows: the phrase "planets and constellations" (*graharkṣa*) is a mere statement regarding the motion of the sun; it does not intend to define the limits of time, because it is impossible for a single year to possess such supreme magnitude. ||12||
Viśvanātha: Your two solstices are the day and night of the gods in heaven; twelve months constitute a year.
Abiding within the wheel of planets, constellations, and stars, [He creates] the universe through [the process beginning with] the atom.
At the end of the year, the all-pervading Lord, the unblinking one, returns.

Śrīdhara: By this sequence, he says that this Sun constantly consumes life: the planets (graha) are the Moon and so forth; the lunar mansions (ṛkṣa) are Aśvinī and so forth; the stars (tārā) are other minor constellations (nakṣatras). The wheel of time (kālacakra) is that which is characterized by these; situated therein, the unblinking, all-pervading Lord (vibhu īśvara), whose nature is Time, is the Sun who [governs] the world.
He traverses, that is, he wanders through, the cosmic egg consisting of the twelve zodiacal signs. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: And he says that the sun takes away the lifespan of men through its rising and setting—the planets (*graha*) being the moon and so forth, the lunar mansions (*ṛkṣa*) being Aśvinī and so forth, and the stars (*tārā*) being other constellations (*nakṣatra*). Of these...

"He stands in the circle of the wheel" means he resides within the wheel of light (*jyotiścakra*). "Unblinking" refers to his nature as Time (*kāla*). "The pervasive one" (*vibhu*) is a portion of the Lord (*īśvara*); he "wanders about," meaning he moves all around. ||13||
"O Vidura, it is thus declared that there are the Saṃvatsara, the Parivatsara, the Iḍāvatsara, the Anuvatsara, and the Vatsara."
Madhva is the year named *iḍāvatsara*, situated in the twelfth lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*);
he who is Hari, existing in the twelvefold cycle of lunar days (*tithi*), is the *anuvatsara*.
The year that is situated within three hundred and sixty days is the *vatsara*;
that which is situated in the twelfth part of the cycle of Jupiter is the *parivatsara*.
"In the month of Sauradvādaśaka, that year which is Hari resides; thus, although he is named Time, the Supreme Lord dwells within Time. Thus it is said in the Brahmatarka.
Because he is perceived at all times, the wise know him to be "unblinking" (animiṣa).
"Or because of the constant movement of the Great Soul who abides in time," so it is said. ||14||

Śrīdhara: The divisions of the year and so forth are to be understood through the distinctions of the solar, Bārhaspatya, Sāvana, Cāndra, and Nākṣatra months. Some, however, say as follows: when the *saṅkrānti* occurs on the first day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight...

The simultaneous commencement of the solar and lunar months constitutes a year (*saṃvatsara*). Consequently, by solar measurement six days increase in a year, while by lunar measurement six days decrease in a year; thus, due to this twelve-day discrepancy, one becomes either ahead of or behind the other.
Thus, five years pass according to the degree of such intervals; in their midst, two intercalary months (malamāsa) occur. Then, the sixth year begins again. ||14||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha states: Since it was said that [the Lord] resides in the wheel of planets, constellations, and stars, he now describes the different names of the year according to the movement of the sun and the movement of the planets and so forth—beginning with "Saṃvatsara," which refers to the solar movement.
"Parivatsara" is according to the motion of Jupiter; "anuvatsara" is according to the motion of the Moon.

Since the constellations (*ṛkṣas*) and stars (*tārās*) have no motion of their own, their motion is solely that of the celestial sphere (*cakra*). Even therein, for the constellations, a year consists of twelve months, each measuring twenty-seven days; as for the stars—
Due to the absence of [a separate] calculation, it should be understood that an *idāvatsara* consists of thirty solar months (*sāvana*) as its measure—
one who, by his own power, causes the creative energy (*sṛjya-śakti*) to expand extensively.
A manifestation of the elements courses through the sky to prevent the delusion of men;
spreading forth the qualities composed of the gunas by means of sacrifices under the name of Time— to that five-year cycle (yuga), offer your tribute!
"Madhva is the dispeller of the delusion regarding the distinction between the unreal and the real, through his sacrifices and his own wisdom;

for the sake of instructing beings on their seniority and juniority and for the performance of sacrifices and other rites, Hari, abiding in time, remains active while awakening the power of those to be created. Thus it is stated in the *Tantraprakāśikā*.

Śrīdhara: Being such as this, the Self of Time (kālātman) must always be worshipped by those who are vigilant; thus he says, "He who... He runs through the sky—that is, in the intermediate space—causing the potential power of seeds and other causes directed toward the effect to be manifested in many ways through his own power in the form of Time, thereby bringing the effects toward actualization. This refers to the sprout and so forth which are to be produced.

Who is he? He is a particular elemental division, a specific great element (*mahābhūta*), the Sun, whose form is a circle of fire. For what purpose does he run? For the sake of removing the delusion (*bhrama*) of the person—that is, for the cessation of confusion (*moha*).
The meaning is that he acts by turning away attachment to sense objects through the depletion of life-span and so forth. But as for those possessed of desire—
Worship him who causes the fruits of heaven and other realms, consisting of merit, to expand through sacrifices—he who set in motion the five-year cycle. 15.
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha asks: "For what purpose is this conceptualization of different years?
He replies—"It is for the sake of establishing the religious duties (*dharma*) and so forth prescribed for each respective year"—by the words "ya" (those) [referring] to those who are to be created.

Whirling in the sky—that is, in the atmosphere—he manifests and reveals in manifold ways the power and capacity of plants and other beings, such as sprouts, through his own power in the form of Time. Who is this particular being, this specific great element, the Sun whose form is a sphere of light? For what purpose does he whirl for the sake of the person (puṃsaḥ)?
For the sake of a person’s freedom from delusion and for the cessation of confusion regarding the directions, the magnitude [of time],

and so forth— for those with desires, [the Lord provides] the fruit consisting of heaven and other realms made of the *guṇas* through sacrifices to be performed at the times prescribed by the year and other measures; therefore, [he gave this knowledge] to him who set in motion the five-year cycle, Kali.
Offer the ritual gifts for worship, beginning with the water of honor (arghya). O righteous people! ||15||
Vidura said:
This is remembered as the maximum lifespan for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings.
Tell me of the destiny of others who may be knowers beyond this eon.

Śrīdhara: This measure of lifespan, calculated as one hundred years according to their own respective measures, is conceived and created every day; thus, a *kalpa* is that which is outside the three worlds (*trailokya*). "The wise" (*vidaḥ*) refers to those possessing knowledge.
The sequence of the connection [of the text] is: "This is the lifespan of the ancestors and so forth. This very thing is according to each [being's] own [measure].

The meaning is that it consists of the calculation of time as previously stated. "A hundred," however, refers specifically to humans. This is because, having previously described the reckoning of time for humans, ancestors, and gods, it was determined that the maximum lifespan of humans is one hundred years. [This applies to] Indra and others who remain for the duration of a Manvantara.
And there is the attainment of a greater measure for others—namely, Brahmā, Sanaka, and so forth—who live beyond the kalpa, that is, outside the day of Brahmā. ||16||

Viśvanātha: This refers to the lifespan—the destination and duration of life—of those wise ones such as Sanaka and others, as well as Bhṛgu and others, who, by their own measure, remain for a hundred years even beyond the daily *kalpa* and elsewhere. ||16||
The Blessed One indeed knows the course of time;
for the wise behold the universe with the eye perfected through yoga.
Śrīdhara: "By one perfected through yoga" means by one who has attained accomplishment through yoga. ||17||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "The Lord" refers to Bhavān; "accomplished through yoga" means perfected by yoga. ||17||
Maitreya said:
Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the cycle of four yugas.
It was carefully examined for twelve divine years.

Śrīdhara: It should be understood from the force of the subsequent verse that [this lasts] for twelve thousand years. *Avadhānam* means that which is attended to; it consists of the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) together with its constituent parts (*aṃśa*). ||18||
The sequence of the composition: the meaning of the words beginning with "kṛtam" is as follows—a year of the gods consists of three hundred and sixty (360) human years;
twelve thousand of those [divine years] constitute their four yugas. And that [period], for humans...
The number of years amounts to four million three hundred and twenty thousand (4,320,000). That alone constitutes the cycle of the four ages beginning with Kṛta. For it is thus:
Kṛta is 1,728,000; Tretā is 1,296,000; Dvāpara is 864,000; and Kali is 432,000. Thus...

Two thousand yugas of the gods constitute one day and night of Brahmā. That amount is equal to eight padmas, or four hundred and sixty-four quintillion (800,000,640,000,000,000), years of human beings. ||18||

Viśvanātha: Since Bhṛgu and others, whose lifespans extend beyond a kalpa, possess lifespans equal to that of Brahmā himself, he states the measurement of the yugas in order to describe the lifespan of Brahmā—beginning with "Kṛtam. By "years" (varṣaiḥ), he means thousands of years. "Avadhānam" refers to that which is determined; it consists of the *saṃdhyā* and the *saṃdhyāṃśa*.
Accompanied by that. ||18||
In the Kṛta and subsequent ages, respectively, there are four, three, two, and one thousand years; these numbers are doubled for the hundreds as well.

Śrīdhara: In the Kṛta Yuga, there are four thousand years; for both the twilight (saṃdhyā) and the subsidiary twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa), there are four hundred each, making eight hundred. This same calculation should be applied to the Tretā and subsequent ages as well. ||19||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "In due order" means that in the Kṛta Yuga there are four thousand [years]; for the two junctions (*saṃdhyā* and *saṃdhyāṃśa*), there are four hundred each, totaling eight hundred. The same applies to the Tretā and subsequent ages.
It should be applied. ||19||
The interval between two periods of one hundred [years] each— the twilight and the partial twilight—
is called a *yuga* by those who know it, wherein Dharma is ordained.

Śrīdhara: At the beginning of a *yuga* there is the *sandhyā*, and at the end there is the *aṃśa*; these two together constitute the *sandhyāṃśa*. The *yuga* is that which lies between those two, whose number has been stated as hundreds. He states its specific characteristic with the words "wherein":
the meaning is that it is wherein specific dharmas such as the immolation of cows (*gavālambha*) and so forth are prescribed. [This refers to] the common dharma.
But it certainly exists even during the two transitional periods (sandhyāṃśa). ||20||
The sequence of composition: regarding the phrase "between the twilight and the twilight-part," it means "at the end of the twilight and the twilight-part. ||20||

Viśvanātha: At the beginning of a *yuga* is the *sandhyā*, and at its end is the *sandhyāṃśa*. Of what nature are these two? They are those whose number consists of the stated hundreds; the period situated between them they call a *yuga*. In that [period], Dharma... [is as follows].

The specific dharma consists of the practice of meditation, sacrifice, and recitation; however, the common dharma is subordinate. This indeed exists even in the *sandhyāṃśa* periods. Furthermore, it should be understood that whichever dharma belongs to a particular *yuga*, that very same dharma becomes the primary one during both its *sandhyā* and *sandhyāṃśa* periods.
Three hundred and sixty human years constitute one year of the gods.
Thus, forty-three lakh and twenty thousand human years are referred to in the treatises by the term *yuga* as a *caturyuga*. Within that [cycle], seventeen lakh and twenty-eight thousand [years]...
In truth, the Tretā age lasts for twelve hundred and ninety-six thousand years;
the Dvāpara age for eight hundred and sixty-four thousand years;
and the Kali age for four hundred and thirty-two thousand years. (20)
Dharma, consisting of four quarters, follows after men;
it departs from others by one quarter through unrighteousness as that [unrighteousness] increases.

Śrīdhara: [In the Kṛta age] it is complete with four quarters; in the Tretā and subsequent ages, it diminishes quarter by quarter. This occurs due to adharma increasing quarter by quarter. And this is merely a description of its essential nature for the sake of generating detachment, not for the purpose of suggesting a contraction of dharma itself. ||21||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [The Dharma] is complete with four quarters (*catuṣpāt*). With respect to humans, in other ages such as the Tretā and so forth, it passes away, decreasing quarter by quarter due to the cause of unrighteousness (*adharma*) increasing quarter by quarter.
It diminishes. ||21||
A thousand yugas for the three worlds constitute a single day outside of Brahmā;
his night is of equal duration, my dear, during which the Creator of the universe closes his eyes.

Śrīdhara: Outside the three worlds, extending from Maharloka up to Brahmaloka, one thousand cycles of the four ages constitute a single day; it is during this time that Brahmā, the creator of the universe, closes his eyes and sleeps.

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Outside the three worlds, extending from Maharloka up to Brahmaloka, one thousand cycles of the four ages constitute a single day; at which time the Creator Brahmā closes his eyes.

At that very time, he sleeps after [the Lord] who lies within the Garbhodaka ocean. Thus, two thousand yugas constitute a day and night of Brahmā. During that period, there are eighty-four crores of years according to the calculation of human beings.
At the end of the night, the cosmic cycle (lokakalpa) begins,
lasting as long as a day of the Blessed One, during which he presides over fourteen Manus.
Śrīdhara: Regarding that, he describes his state during the day with four and a half verses beginning with "niśāvasāne. "Bhuñjan" means protecting; the sense is "pervading. ||23||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Therein, he describes the state during the day with four and a half verses beginning with "niśāvasāne" (at the end of night). "Bhuñjan" means protecting; that is to say, pervading the fourteen Manus. ||23||
Each Manu enjoys his own period for seventy-one [cycles] plus a quarter;
during the Manvantaras, there are Manus, their descendants, sages, and gods.
And they become lords of the gods simultaneously, as do those who follow them.
Madhva: The Lord residing in the day is the enjoyer.
Beyond seventy-one yugas, the enjoyment of a Manu consists of eighteen hundred and fifty thousand years, plus one thousand and four [additional years].
Furthermore, there is a dissolution of one hundred and five [years];

in the first of the six [Manvantaras], a period of two thousand years is proclaimed for the interval of a Manu, and it is the same for Indra and the others. Thus it is stated in the Mahāvārāha Purāṇa. 24.

Śrīdhara: Slightly more than seventy-one yugas pass. The protectors of the earth belonging to the lineage of Manu appear in succession, whereas the Seven Sages and the others appear simultaneously at the same time. The lords of the gods are the Indras; those who follow them are...
The Gandharvas and others are also [included therein]. ||24||
The sequential arrangement: "each its own," this constitutes one half-verse. ||24||

Viśvanātha: A Manu, such as Svāyambhuva and the others, presides over a period extending for seventy-one *caturyugas* slightly more than that; in the divine reckoning (*devamāna*), this amounts to eight hundred and fifty-two thousand years, whereas in the human reckoning (*manuṣyamāna*), it is thirty million years.
Sixty-seven lakhs and twenty thousand. Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "O twice-born one, O great sage, the number is calculated as exactly thirty crores, and another sixty-seven niyutas."
"O twice-born one, twenty thousand years, without any addition, is the reckoning of a *manvantara* in human years.
Thus, the lineage of Manu becomes the protector of the earth in succession; as for the Seven Sages (*saptarṣi*) and the others, however—
They come into being simultaneously and at the very same time; the lords of the gods, the Indras, as well as those such as the Gandharvas and others, follow after them. ||24||
This is the daily creation of Brahmā, which sustains the three worlds,
wherein the birth of animals, humans, ancestors, and gods occurs through their respective actions.
Śrīdhara: He is so called because he causes the three worlds to revolve. ||25||
The sequential arrangement: "simultaneously" means within their respective manvantaras. ||25||
Viśvanātha: He exists within the three worlds; thus, the meaning is that he is the creator of the three worlds. ||25||
In the various Manvantaras, the Blessed One, manifesting his own nature through his forms,
protects this entire universe with Manu and the others, his prowess having been awakened.

Śrīdhara: By means of His own forms—the incarnations during the Manvantaras such as Manu and others—who act as gateways, He manifests His puruṣakāra (human-like effort) and protects the universe. ||26||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: One whose manly prowess has arisen through his own forms—that is, through his incarnations—and who has manifested the form of a person (puruṣākāra).
Having taken recourse to the quality of darkness alone, his prowess suppressed and all his activities followed by Time, he remains silent at the end of the day.

Śrīdhara: With five verses he describes the state during the night. "A mere trace of darkness" means a slight remnant. "By whom valor has been completely restrained" means by whom it has been withdrawn. "In which everything without exception has entered" means that in which all things have followed after and merged. ||27||

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: He describes the state occurring at night—having assumed a portion (*mātrā*) of *tamas*, a mere fragment for the sake of dissolving the three worlds, in the form of Kālāgnirudra, he effects the dissolution.

His prowess is obstructed and enveloped by fire and other elements; he is one by whom the three worlds, beginning with Bhūḥ, are pervaded—this is because it was previously stated that "prowess consists of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ. Furthermore, he is one in whom the entire multitude of living beings residing in the three worlds has followed after and entered. [He remains] silent.
The meaning is that he has abandoned the playful diversion of illusory manifestation. ||27||
Even the three worlds, beginning with Bhūḥ,
follow after him alone when the night has set in and the moon and sun have been released [from his power].

Śrīdhara: He clarifies that very point with the words "tam eva" (that very [Self]). The expression "anv api dhīyante" is a usage in the reflexive passive (*karmakartari*). The meaning is: "they become concealed. How so? Just as the moon and the sun become free from, or devoid of, [their respective veils]. ||28||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He clarifies that very point with the words "tam eva" (that very [state]). The construction "anv api dhīyante" is a reflexive passive (*karmakartari*); the meaning is "they become concealed. How? Being released...
Just as the moon and the sun become [invisible] when deprived [of their light]. ||28||
When the three worlds are being consumed by the fire of Saṅkarṣaṇa through his Śakti,
Bhṛgu and the others, afflicted by its heat, depart from Maharloka for Janaloka.
Śrīdhara: Afflicted by the heat of that fire from the mouth of Saṅkarṣaṇa, which is of the nature of the Lord’s power, they go to Janaloka. ||29||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha, in response to the expectation of "in what manner," says: "In the three worlds" (verse 29).
At that moment, the oceans, swollen by the fires at the end of the aeon and driven by waves tossed by fierce winds of violent fury, instantly inundate the three worlds.
Śrīdhara: The oceans—the seas—swollen at the end of the kalpa; they are both those whose turbulence and agitation are fierce and who are driven by violent winds, and Maya as well. 30.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Immediately" (*sadyaḥ*) means that while the three worlds are being consumed, without delay;
however, the burning should be understood to last for a hundred years. And those whose agitation and turbulence are intense—they...
And those whose waves are tossed by fierce winds. ||30||
Within that water sits Hari, whose seat is infinite,
with eyes closed in yogic sleep, being praised by the inhabitants of the world.

Śrīdhara: Those whose abode is Janaloka, as well as others who have gone to Maharloka—by them, in their sequential arrangement, [the waves] are those whose billows are stirred by fierce winds of violent force. ||31||

Viśvanātha: The fifth among the functions of the powers of consciousness (cicchakti), such as Vimalā and the others, is called Yoga; at that time, it takes the form of sleep, and by means of it, his eyes are closed. [He is] with the sages residing in Janaloka, the abode of people. ||31||
By means of such days and nights, as characterized by the passage of time,
even his supreme lifespan of a hundred years seems as if it has already been diminished.
"Of this sweet [soma], of this sacred word (*brahman*)," because it has been stated that "the day belongs to *brahman*.
There exists no measure of the lifespan of the Blessed One in any form whatsoever;
for he is imperishable, being without beginning, without middle, and without end—thus says the *Harivaṃśa*. (32)

Śrīdhara says: For the sake of generating detachment, he states: "By such days and nights, the hundred-year lifespan of all living beings is [measured]; even that lifespan of this Brahmā, which is the maximum limit, is—as the worldly saying goes—as if diminished, as if exhausted. The meaning is that it is nearly gone. (32)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By the statement, "I am afraid of Time, because even the lifespan of this Brahmā is indicated to be exhausted, having almost reached its end" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.9.18), [the Lord speaks] while fearing Time.

Even Brahmā, having become detached from the enjoyment of sense objects, worships the Lord incessantly as a devotee; yet humans, possessing such limited lifespans, do not worship Him while indulging in sense objects—out of what audacity?
Thus, it has been stated that effort toward devotion and detachment is essential, which explains the purpose of defining time.
Half of that lifespan is called a *parārdha*;
the first *parārdha* has indeed passed away, and the second now proceeds.
