Śrīdhara: "At the beginning of the previous parārdha"—this is merely a statement of the subject matter through three [verses]. Regarding the sequence of composition: "that half" refers to this present day. ||33||
Viśvanātha says: He states that lifespan is divided into two parts with the words "That which... (verse 33).
At the beginning of the previous *parārdha*, there occurred a great eon (*kalpa*) named Brāhma,
in which Brahmā came into being— he whom they know as the "Brahman of Sound" (*śabdabrahman*).
Śrīdhara: The reason for [his] being Padma is that which [is expressed by] "yad" (verse 34).
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding the phrase "of the preceding," [it refers to] the thirty *kalpas* mentioned in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* by Śvetavarāha and others, which constitute the *pitṛkalpas*; by these very thirty *kalpas*, [the days] from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapratipad*) until the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) [are accounted for].
Thirty days of those very *kalpas*, repeated again and again, constitute a month;

twelve months make a year; and fifty years make one *parārdha*. Therein, at the beginning of the first [cycle], it is called "Brahma" because the White Varāha himself is the lunar day (*tithi*) of Brahmā’s birth.

It is expressed by the word "Brahma. And that lunar day (tithi) should be understood as the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, according to the statements of the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra). ||34||
At the very end of that [kalpa], there occurred the kalpa which they call the Pādma,
during which the world-lotus arose from the lake of Hari’s navel.
Śrīdhara: But this [topic] has been stated at the beginning of the second [chapter]. ||35||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha [comments]: "Kalpa" refers to the *Pitṛkalpa*. They call this very *Pitṛkalpa*, which is the final one of the *Parārdha*, the *Pādma*; the reason for its being called *Pādma* is given by the word "yat" (which). Therefore, in all the *kalpas* indeed...
The lotus is not composed of the entire world, but rather exists only here and there; such is the meaning. ||35||
But this second eon, O Bhārata,
is also described as the one renowned as Vārāha, wherein Hari was a boar.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having stated the measure of the lifespan of created beings by means of time as the instrumental cause, he speaks of that reality which is devoid of temporal limitation with five verses beginning with "This time. It is merely figuratively designated [as such], for even by this sequence there is no calculation of its lifespan; thus he says: "of the unmanifest" (avyākṛtasya).

Therefore, for the Self of the universe—the cause of the world—who is devoid of the limiting adjuncts of action (*kāryopādhi*), infinite, and beginningless, there is no sequential arrangement [of time]. Thus, by means of the conceptualization of Brahmā’s day, one should understand the conceptualization of the day of the one lying within the *garbhoda* ocean; for even he accepts yogic sleep at the end of that [day].
He speaks thus regarding the conception of time for Him who reclines upon the ocean of causes: "This is Time.
For the *Brahmasaṃhitā* states: "Taking as their support even the duration of a single exhalation of Him, the lords of the cosmic eggs born from the pores of His hair continue to live. (36)

Viśvanātha: This means that it is now the first day of the fifty-first year of the current second *parārdha*. Here, within the narrative of the *Pādma-kalpa*—which was introduced with the words "Now hear the *Pādma-kalpa*" and proceeds with "The universe was submerged in water," and so forth—[the following occurs].

Because only a single lotus is mentioned in the waters of the universal ocean (*ekārṇava*), and because only a single Brahmā is said to arise there— given the scriptural statement that "having looked there, he saw nothing else"— and because Sanaka and others, whose lifespans extend over a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*),
are not perceived there, some [maintain] that at the end of the first *parārdha*, the worlds of Mahas, Janas, Tapas, and Satya [dissolve].

Having described how even those who remain until the end of two *parārdhas*— without perishing— are submerged by the deluge of waters, and how all those there with a lifespan of a *kalpa* enter into Śrī Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Brahmā, [the text describes] at the conclusion of the first *parārdha*, the beginning of the second *parārdha*.

They say that the *Śvetavārāha* is indeed the *Pādma*. Furthermore, in the twelfth chapter, the manifestation of Sanaka and others, as well as Marīci and others, from Brahmā himself—as if in the *Brāhma-kalpa*—will be described;
nor should it be said that this refers exclusively to the narrative of the *Brāhma-kalpa*, because the narrative of the *Pādma-kalpa* is the one currently under discussion.

Therefore, regarding the phrase "and at its very end," the meaning of "end" (*anta*) here is "conclusion" or "completion. As for the word "this" (*ayam tu*), the particle *tu* has the sense of "only"; thus, this very [kalpa] is known as the Pādma or the Vārāha. The reason for this is the phrase "wherein he was," where the particle *api* in the expression "of the second also" implies that the first half [of the kalpa] begins with the Brāhma [kalpa].
They explain that even a *kalpa* is called *pādma*. ||36||
This time, known as two parārdhas, is metaphorically designated as a single *nimeṣa* of the unmanifest,
infinite, beginningless, and world-constituting Self.

Śrīdhara says: Because time lacks the capacity to determine that [the Self], he states: "This time, though it is the Lord, is not at all capable of ruling over the *bhūman*, the perfectly full one; for it is the lord only of those who take pride in their abode—that is, those who identify with the body and the home. (37)
The sequential arrangement: [it concerns] those who consider themselves established in the abodes, namely those who hold authority over Satyaloka and the other realms. ||37||
Viśvanātha: Having thus described time in its subtle and gross forms, he now speaks of the ultimate gross form, the supremely great time—known as two *parārdhas*.
Although there is no possibility of time coming to an end, it is that very [time] which is designated by that name in the scriptures due to its ultimate grossness.

That [period] is also but a moment (*nimeṣa*) of the Supreme Lord, who is the Self of the universe. Now, one might ask: "In this way, by the sequence of moments and so forth, is his lifespan also calculated? To this, he says "no, no" with a playful tone, stating a portion of the answer: "In some cases, it is metaphorically designated as a 'moment' (*nimeṣa*). For they live supported by the duration of even a single exhalation of His.
The statement in the *Brahmasaṃhitā* and other texts that "the lords of the cosmic egg are born from the hair-pores" is merely a figurative expression— using the term "breath" (*niśvāsa*)—
and does not mean that there is even a moment of actual time; for [the Lord] is the unmanifest,
devoid of modifications caused by time, and therein the reason is that He is infinite and beginningless.
The meaning is "of that which has transcended the limitation of time," because [it belongs] to the Self of the World, the cause of the entire world including time and so forth. ||37||
This time, beginning from the atom (paramāṇu) and ending with the supreme limit of two parārdhas, is the Lord;
yet the Lord is not able to rule over the Infinite One (bhūman), who is the true master of those who pride themselves on their abodes.

Śrīdhara: Elaborating upon what was stated as "by the Great One" (*bhūmnā*), he says: "endowed with the sixteen transformations joined with the eight primary natures (*prakṛti*)," meaning that [the world] is composed of those. This connects with the subsequent clause: "this cosmic egg (*āṇḍakośa*), having entered which, appears like an atom."
Of what nature is it? It is fifty crores of yojanas in extent within, and it is surrounded on the outside by the seven [spheres] beginning with Earth, such as Water and the rest. ||38||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He clarifies again the very meaning that has been suggested: "This is Time," etc. [It refers to] the abode of the Supreme Lord (*bhūman*), for those who consider themselves masters of the worlds such as Satyaloka and so forth. (38)
Accompanied by the transformations (vikāras), joined with the specific elements (viśeṣas), and so forth,
this external egg-shell (āṇḍakośa) extends for fifty crores [of yojanas].
The ten sense organs, together with the mind, which reside within the egg, are to be known as modifications; they are the elements, the ego, and that which is beyond the Great Principle (mahat).

"They say the earth is distinguished by the multiplicity of sound and the other qualities; because of its subtlety, it covers the cosmic egg. And: "The eight [elements] beginning with sound and ending with primordial nature (prakṛti) are known as the eight primary natures (prakṛtis), each being double the size of the preceding one. Thus it is said.
"Due to the multiplicity of bodies, as well as by those past and future,
and because they are seen individually within the very bodies of the gods,
the multiplicity of cosmic eggs (aṇḍas) exists through the power of Viṣṇu and not otherwise. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmatarka*.

"Brahmā saw a single cosmic egg become manifold, with each [egg] entering a single pore of Hari's body; likewise, he saw himself within them, each distinct from the others. Thus it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. And in the *Mahābhārata*: "There was one great cosmic egg. (39)

Śrīdhara: By what kind [of measures]? By those in which each subsequent one is ten times greater than the preceding, starting from the size of an egg-cavity (aṇḍakośa). Not only this one alone, but others also are perceived. ||39||
The sequence of composition: the pair beginning with "by the modifications" [is as follows]. The modifications (*vikāra*) consist of the eleven organs and the five gross elements;

the primordial natures (*prakṛti*) consist of Nature (*prakṛti*), the Great One (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); and those beginning with the Great One (*mahadādi*) are both primordial natures and modifications (*prakṛtivikṛti*).
According to the principle that "seven [are causes]," even Mahat and the others are considered *prakṛtis* (primordial causes) with respect to their own respective effects;

thus Viśvanātha states that she is the delimiting factor of the entire universe, as suggested by the term "O Soul of the World" (*jagadātman*), saying: "together with the sixteen transformations and the eight *prakṛtis*."

The meaning is that it has begun from that. This connection with what follows is: "this egg-shell, having entered which, appears like an atom. Of what nature is it? It is surrounded on the outside by the seven [elements], earth and so forth, beginning with their specific qualities. ||39||
Wherein, having entered like a single atom, there are perceived millions of other multitudes of cosmic eggs, each increasing tenfold over the preceding.
Regarding this, they say: "The Imperishable (akṣara) is Brahman, the cause of all causes;
it is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, the Great-Souled Puruṣa himself."
The Madhvas are the bodies contained within; the abodes are the houses, the multitudes of cosmic eggs.
Yama is time for human beings, and his time is Sudarśana. Even for him, Rudra is the time, and for him, Brahmā; and Durgā is the time even for him.
At the dissolution of Brahmā, that Goddess exists in the form of the Wheel;
she alone, abiding within Brahmā and the other gods, perpetually withdraws the worlds.

"Viṣṇu is her controller; he is called the supreme Time (kāla). She is the one who presides over time, yet she is not the sovereign of the Lord of the Universe. He alone, Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, is her master. Thus it is said. (40)
Śrīdhara: He is the cause of all causes; *dhāma* means his essential nature (*svarūpa*). ||40||

The sequential arrangement: others are also observed; thus, the enclosure of water and the rest is to be understood for all [the elements] in this very way, by means of the reasoning already stated. ||40||

Although, according to the manner previously described, even a Great Person (mahāpuruṣa) is certainly not subject to time, nevertheless, because his nature consists of the play of manifestation and concealment, he is not denoted by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable). Rather, his supreme essential form is the Lord Himself alone, who is eternally manifest; therefore, that [Lord] is what is denoted by that term.

He said: "Regarding that, they say... They declare that the very supreme abode of the Great Soul Viṣṇu—who is known as Mahāviṣṇu—which is directly manifest, self-established, and whose essential nature is the form of the Supreme Portion (paramāṃśa), is that very Imperishable (akṣara), eternally manifest Brahman, the perfect state of the Blessed Lord (bhagavattva). For even the Puruṣa, who is the cause of all, [is contained therein].
"The cause," thus [it is said]. ||41||

Viśvanātha: By what kind [of worlds]? By those in which each successive one is ten times greater than the measure of the preceding cosmic egg (aṇḍakoṣa). Not only this one alone, but others too are observed; "dhāma" refers to the body of Viṣṇu as he lies in the causal ocean (kāraṇārṇavaśāyin). According to Amara, the words *dhāman*, *gṛha*, *deha*, *tviṭ*, and *prabhāva* are synonyms.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, which is perfectly suited for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, the *Sārārthadarśinī*, [a commentary] for those whose hearts are devoted.

Thus ends the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya in the third book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Nature of Time.
Now begins the twelfth chapter, the Description of Creation.
Maitreya said:
Thus, O Kṣattṛ, has the majesty of the Supreme Self, known as Time, been described to you; now learn from me how he who contains the Vedas within himself brought forth creation.
Śrīdhara:
But in the twelfth [chapter], because the mental creation beginning with Kumāra has been fully developed,
the creation through sexual union (the progenic creation) is described by means of a twofold body.
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon. Viśvanātha states:
"He is the Creator who brings forth Sanaka and others, Marīci and others, and the Earth, Dharma, and Brahmā."
In the twelfth [manvantara], for the sake of increasing creation, he produced a couple from his own body.
Majesty is power. ||1||
In the beginning, the Primordial Creator emitted Andhatāmisra, then Tāmisra,
Mahāmoha, Mōha, and Tamas— these being the functions of ignorance.
"Sweetness is declared to be the darkness of night (*śārvara-tamas*), while delusion (*moha*) is its perversion (*viparyaya*).
Attachment to that is great delusion (*mahāmoha*), and anger is called the gloom (*tāmisra*).
Death is the blinding darkness (*andhatāmisra*); thus ignorance (*avidyā*) has five branches. So it is said in the *Mahābhārata*.
"In the *Harivaṃśa*, it is said: 'Darkness (*tamas*) is ignorance (*ajñāna*), perversion (*viparyāsa*), and delusion (*moha*); others, however, are the grasping at those [three]. (2)

Śrīdhara: Regarding the word "first" (*agra*): Brahmā first created the functions of ignorance (*avidyā*) within his own creation. Among these, *tamas* is the non-manifestation of one's true nature; *moha* is the notion of "I" with respect to the body and so forth; *mahāmoha* is the desire for enjoyment; *tāmisra* is anger upon the obstruction of that [desire]; and *andhatāmisra* is the thought "I" when that [desire] is destroyed.
Thus arises the notion, "I am dead. This very point is stated in the *Vaiṣṇava* [Purāṇa]: "Tamas is non-discrimination; delusion (*moha*) is the confusion of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
But great delusion (*mahāmoha*) should be understood as the longing for the pleasures of vulgar enjoyments."
"For death is indeed *andhatāmisra*, and *tāmisra* is said to be anger;
this fivefold ignorance has manifested from the Great Soul.
These very same [afflictions] are also stated in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra]: "Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the five afflictions (*kleśas*)."
Or as taught by Śrī Viṣṇusvāmī: ignorance, error, difference, fear, and sorrow. As it has been said:
"Error arising from one's own vision," and so forth. ||2||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The functions of ignorance (*avidyāvṛttayaḥ*) were already established; at the beginning of creation, they manifested from Brahman in the form of *tamas* and the rest. Thus he says: "He created" (*sasṛje*). In that context, what is called *tamas*...
The non-manifestation of the soul's true nature is *moha*. The superimposition of the notion of "I" upon the body and so forth is *mahāmoha*.

The superimposition of the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*) toward objects of enjoyment is *tāmisra*. Then, when there is an obstruction to enjoyment, the internalizing of anger—a quality of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—is *andhatāmisra*.

Death is indeed a state of fainting (mūrchā) consisting of the identification with anger. These states, though non-existent for the living soul, are created by ignorance (avidyā). As it is said in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa:
"Tamas is non-discrimination; delusion (moha) is the confusion of the internal organ."
Great delusion, however, should be understood as the longing for the pleasures of vulgar enjoyment.
"For death is indeed *andhatāmisra*, while *tāmisra* is said to be anger;
this fivefold ignorance has thus manifested from the Great Self.
These very same [afflictions] are also stated in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga-sūtra]: "Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the five afflictions (*kleśa*)."

Or as taught by Śrī Viṣṇusvāmī: ignorance, error, differentiation, fear, and sorrow. In reality, however, ignorance (avidyā) has only two attributes: concealment (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa). These two alone are expressed by the terms ignorance, egoism (asmitā), and the sense of self-existence (ātmabhāva), as well as by the terms error and misconception (viparyāsa).

It should be understood, however, that although attachment, aversion, and dogmatic adherence are indeed properties of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), they are described as manifestations of distraction (*vikṣepaprapañca*) because distraction is their predominant aspect. ||2||
Having seen that most wretched creation, he did not think highly of himself;
then, with a mind purified by meditation on the Blessed One, he created another.
Śrīdhara: He did not think much of it; he did not approve of it. ||3||

The sequential composition: "Having seen" constitutes a pair of verses. The meaning is that he created those very beings who had been produced during the Brahma-kalpa and manifested them there for the creation of the three worlds. ||3||

Viśvanātha: To make it known that only knowledge (*vidyā*) is the remover of ignorance (*avidyā*), he states—in the passage beginning with "having seen"—that even the functions of knowledge manifested from Him alone in the form of Sanaka and others;
[this refers to] when the Supreme Lord [appeared] at the end of the first *parārdha* while Brahmā and the other gods, whose lifespans last for a great kalpa, were still living.
He states that just as Brahmā was born from the lotus in the Pādma-kalpa, so too did Brahmā bring forth Sanaka and the others once again. ||3||
Then the Self-born [Brahmā] addressed the sages Sanaka, Sananda, Sanātana,
and Sanatkumāra, who were free from worldly activity and possessed sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas).

Śrīdhara: Although there is no creation of Sanaka and others in every kalpa, nevertheless, they are referred to here as belonging to the creation of Brahmā. In reality, however, it is only the primary creations and so forth that occur in every kalpa;
Sanaka and the others, having been created specifically in the kalpa of Brahmā, continue to exist [throughout subsequent cycles]. ||4||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "And Sanaka," etc. The four functions of knowledge (vidyā) are indeed Sāṅkhya, Yoga, dispassion (vairāgya), and austerity (tapas). It is these very [functions] that manifest in the form of the quartet beginning with Sanaka.

Furthermore, since knowledge is fruitless without devotion, even in the practices such as austerity that accompany it, devotion must remain as a subordinate quality; thus, even Sanaka and the others are seen to be possessed of devotion.
The manifestation of primary devotion, however, will be described later in the form of Nārada. ||4||
The Self-born spoke to those sons: "O dear sons, create progeny. But they, being devoted to the dharma of liberation and taking refuge in Vāsudeva, did not desire that.
Śrīdhara: Svabhū is Brahmā. ||5||

The sequence of the composition: The phrase "those [who]" provides the reason for their lack of desire [for worldly things], namely that they possess the nature of liberation (*mokṣadharmāṇaḥ*). Now, one might object:

even the Lords of Creatures (*prajāpati*) are seen to possess the nature of liberation. To this he replies: "They have Vāsudeva as their supreme goal. This is because [the scriptures speak] of [their devotion] toward the gods, sages, beings, ancestors, men, and so forth. (5)

Viśvanātha: By the statement "they did not desire that," it is indicated that the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) must indeed be the dispeller of the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) rooted in ignorance (*āvidyaka*). ||5||
Thus addressed by his sons who had rejected his instructions,
he strove to restrain the unbearable anger that had arisen within him.
Śrīdhara: "Avadhyāta" means disregarded. Those by whom the instruction was rejected—that is, not accepted—[are so described]. (6)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Neglected" (*avadhyātaḥ*) means disregarded. By saying "he proceeded to restrain [him]," the rajasic nature of Brahmā is made manifest. Thus, regarding the creation of Sanaka and the others from the darkness (*tamas*).
The arising of his tamasic and sāttvika states should first be understood. ||6||
Though being restrained by the intellect, from the middle of the eyebrows of Prajāpati,
there was immediately born that very Wrath as the blue-and-red youth (Kumāra).
Śrīdhara: He is that very one who is wrath; thus, "that wrath. (7)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: In order to demonstrate that just as knowledge is the remover of ignorance, so too ignorance may be the remover of knowledge, [he speaks] regarding Brahman, even when the arising of knowledge has occurred.

He describes the manifestation of anger—which is primarily a function of ignorance and is designated as *tāmisra*—in the form of Rudra, with the verse beginning "Dhiyā": "tanmanyuḥ" means the anger (*manyu*) of that Prajāpati; or alternatively, it refers to that very anger itself [as the deity].
Thus, even though he is anger, he is called Nīlalohita (the Blue-and-Red One) because his color is indeed that of anger. ||7||
That blessed Bhava, the first-born of the gods, wept:
'O Creator, O Teacher of the World, bestow names and stations upon me!'"
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha states his version of that pastime: "He, indeed... (verse 8).
"—o)0(o—" Hearing these words of his, the Blessed One Pādma, honoring them, spoke with auspicious speech: "Do not weep; I shall do that for you."
It has not been explained by anyone at all:
"O best of gods, why did you weep like an agitated child?"
Then the creatures will address you by the name Rudra.
Śrīdhara: Like a child. ||10||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— The heart, the senses, the vital breath, space, wind, fire, water, and earth;
The sun, the moon, and heat—these were established by you as the foremost positions.
Śrīdhara: [They were] already performed by me previously, at the outset. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding "in the heart" (*hṛdi*): because the heart and other organs are effects of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), Rudra, who presides over the ego, is appropriately situated in those respective locations. In the case of the Krodha [tradition], however, it refers to the wrath within the heart.

He is engaged in his very place of birth; he abides even in the eyes, hands, feet, and sense organs, indicated by their respective functions. Likewise, he is present in the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), indicated by the inhalation and exhalation through the nose.
Similarly, he is present in the external ether through the fierce and terrible sounds of lions and the like, and in air, fire, and water.

Because they possess the qualities of drying up, burning, and flooding the earth through their own transformations—such as thunderbolts and the like—and because they form a collective mass through lions, tigers, serpents, and so forth; and because the sun and moon possess the power to kill through heat and cold respectively, anger resides in them as well. Thus, "tapa" [means]...

This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) that includes Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and dispassion (vairāgya) as well; for even these, in the absence of being protected by devotion, are seen to be grounds for anger, according to such statements as "those whose fury is inflamed by asceticism" (tapodīpitamanyavaḥ). Therefore it has been said:
"Having with great difficulty ascended to the highest station, they then fall down below, disregarding [it]."
"Your feet [are the refuge]," as stated in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.2.32. ||11||
Manyu, Manu, Mahinasa, the great Śiva, the one whose banner is Truth (Ṛtadhvaja),
Ugraretas, Bhava, Kāla, Vāmadeva, and the observer of vows (Dhṛtavrata).
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: "Manyu" and the following eleven are the names of the Rudras. ||12||
Dhī, Dhṛti, Asalomā, Niyut, Sarpi, Ilāmbikā,
Irāvatī, Svadhā, and Dīkṣā— these Rudrāṇīs are your wives, O Rudra.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been commented upon in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: "Dhī" and so forth are the eleven names of Her powers (*tacchaktayaḥ*). ||13||
"— O you who are with your wife, take these names and stations! By means of these, create many offspring, for you are the lord of progeny."
Śrīdhara: Accompanied by Śrī, that is, together with your wife; endowed with these abodes and names, create progeny. 14.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon. Viśvanātha: Accompanied by a wife (*sayoṣaṇaḥ* means *sastrīkaḥ*). Being endowed with these locations and names, create progeny. (14)
Thus instructed by his own guru, the Blessed One Nīlalohita created beings equal to himself through the nature of the essence of sentient beings.

Śrīdhara: *Sattva* is strength; *ākṛti* is the state of being blue and red; *svabhāva* is intensity; by these, the arrangement of the sequence has not been explained. Viśvanātha: *Sattva* is strength; *ākṛti* is the state of being blue and red; *svabhāva* is intensity.
Beholding countless hosts of Rudras created by Rudra who were devouring the world on all sides, Prajāpati became apprehensive.
Śrīdhara: Having seen the hosts of Rudras. ||16||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The syntactical connection is "having seen the hosts of Rudras created by Rudra. (16)
"Enough with creating such subjects as these, O best of gods,
who burn the quarters of the sky with their fierce eyes along with me."
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
—o)0(o— Perform austerity; may prosperity be yours, which brings happiness to all beings.
Just as in the past, you were the creator of this entire universe through austerity alone.
Śrīdhara: The Creator will create. ||18||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Perform penance"—at the time of creation and maintenance, this is not Rudra’s auspicious play; rather, it is an instance of *viparītalakṣaṇā* (ironic indication), as he prompts him toward penance, saying "be a creator as before," though [the result] will not be auspicious.

The meaning is that just as you withdrew the universe at the end of previous kalpas, so too shall you be its withdrawer hereafter. Some maintain that in certain kalpas even Śiva created progeny just like Brahmā:
"I create the universe through austerity; I swallow it again through austerity."
I fear asceticism; my power is entirely rooted in asceticism that is difficult to overcome.
Others say that this was stated by the Blessed One because he is one with Śiva. 18.
By austerity alone does a person directly attain the supreme light, the Blessed Lord Adhokṣaja,
who dwells in the secret cave of all beings.
In terms of sweetness, as well as in time, power, knowledge, bliss, and all other qualities, Viṣṇu alone is supreme; Lakṣmī is inferior to him.
From Time, by an infinite fraction, the four-faced one [Brahmā] is inferior;
Vāyu is said to be equal to him by a large fraction.
By necessity, only Vāyu alone attains the state of Brahman, and no other;
therefore, although they are said to be equal, there is a slight deficiency in Vāyu’s status.
That period is ten years, after which there is the birth of their women as well;
the time beginning with bliss and so forth is a tenth part of that, occurring after a year.
As long as there is a subsequent birth, so long would it be imperishable if it were prior;
Brahmā and Vāyu are those two deities, and the portion of that region consists of happiness and the like.
The lifespan of Śeṣa and Garuḍa is also one thousand divine years;
Śeṣa and Rudra, as well as Brahmā and Vāyu, are likewise related to one another in this same manner.
The goddesses shall have one-tenth of that [share], and from them Indra and the others are considered [to derive their portions].
Thus it has been stated both previously and here; it is not intended otherwise anywhere. Wherever there might be a statement to the contrary, that will be for the purpose of delusion.
The reversal of prior and posterior occurs due to the cause of manifoldness.
Thus it is stated in the *Tattvaviveka* composed by Viṣṇu; and furthermore: "Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into bliss; among the gods and asuras, Maghavan is the foremost," and so forth.
Indra and the others, Sanaka and the others, Dakṣa and the others, and whoever else there may be—
The sages, the Manus, the gods, and whoever else are under his control.
Without a doubt, all others are inferior to Rāmā in every quality;
there has never been anyone equal to her in the past, nor will there be anyone such in the present or the future.

"Except for Hari, Brahmā, Vāyu, Śeṣa, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara together with their wives—it should be understood that anything else spoken [as supreme] is said for the purpose of delusion. Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇukṛtatattvaviveka*. (19)
Śrīdhara: This has not been commented upon in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.

Viśvanātha: According to the maxim, "Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people also do" (*Gītā* 3.21), the worldly folk will also cross over [the ocean of saṃsāra] by learning austerity from you.
He said: "By austerity alone. (19)
Maitreya said:
Thus instructed by the Self-born (Brahmā), he circumambulated the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati).
Having addressed him with "So be it," he entered the forest for the sake of asceticism.
Then, as he meditated upon creation, ten sons were born to him who was endowed with the power of the Lord, serving as the causes for the continuation of the worlds.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu;
Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, and Dakṣa, and Nārada was the tenth among them.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: He states that even *karmayoga* manifests in the form of Marīci and others—[beginning with the words] "Marīci.
The success of knowledge, detachment, austerity, yoga, and action occurs through devotion alone; likewise, he himself [attained it].

Since devotion alone, being independent, bestows all fruits and is itself the nature of the fruit, at the very end [the author] describes the manifestation of devotion in the form of Nārada, saying: "In the tenth... (22).
Nārada was born from the lap; Dakṣa from the thumb of Svayambhū;
Vasiṣṭha was born from the vital breath (prāṇa); Bhṛgu from the skin; and Kratu from the hand.
Pulaha was born from the navel, and the sage Pulastya from the ears; Aṅgiras was born from the mouth, Atri from the eyes, and Marīci arose from the mind.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been commented upon in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.

Viśvanātha: From the "lap" (*utsaṅga*), meaning from the place of affection; by way of pun (*śleṣa*), it means from "excellent association" (*utkṛṣṭāt saṅgāt*), that is, from the company of the virtuous (*sādhusaṅgāt*).
According to the view expressed in such passages as "The waters are called *nārāḥ*," the Supreme Lord is denoted by the word "man" (*nara*).

It is said: because it bestows upon a person—through the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "this belongs to him"—that which belongs to him, namely service, friendship, and so forth toward the Blessed One, the *nārada* is the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*). ||2324||
Dharma is on the right side of her breast where Nārāyaṇa himself resides;
Adharma is behind her, from whom comes Death, the terror of the world.
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: He states the origin of *dharma*, saying "Dharma," because the supreme *dharma* consists in the performance of enjoined *bhaktiyoga* and *karmayoga*. [The word] "from the breast" (*stanāt*).

From the most excellent place, even from the heart—the highest and most beloved part—he speaks of the arising of *adharma* (unrighteousness) through the non-performance of what is ordained as *dharma* and the performance of what is prohibited; thus he says, "unrighteousness. The word "behind" (*pṛṣṭhataḥ*) refers to an inferior location.
Because it is not very dear. ||25||
Lust is in the heart; anger is from the eyebrows; greed is from the lower lip;
speech is from the mouth; the oceans are from the penis; Nirṛti, the abode of evil, is from the anus.
Śrīdhara: From the lower lip, that is, from the lower lip (adharoṣṭha). ||26||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: [The author] states the origin of desire and the other [afflictions] which incite that [adharma], so that one might understand how adharma comes to be—"in the heart," that is, in the mind; because the mind is not dependent on the person (*puruṣa*), it resides there.

This indicates that the uprooting of desire is difficult to achieve. It should be understood that for anger and the other afflictions as well, which arise from the mind itself, the locus of their manifestation is simply the movement of the eyebrows.
Even while possessing desire, anger, and so forth, there may still exist the scholarship consisting of knowledge of the scriptures.
To demonstrate that very point, he states the origin of Sarasvatī with the words "from his mouth" (āsya). ||26||
From Chāyā was born Kardama, the lord and master, the husband of Devahūtī;
and from the mind and body of the Creator of the Universe, this world was born.
Śrīdhara; Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: To show that even for those who always possess tamasic and rājasic dispositions, there may occasionally arise some degree of sāttvika emotion, he says: "From the shadow of her loveliness" (27).
O Vidura, we have heard that the Self-born One desired his own slender daughter Vāc, who captivated his mind, even though she was without desire for him, while he was full of desire."
Śrīdhara: In order to describe the creation performed by means of another body, he states the cause for abandoning that [previous] body, beginning with the words "speech" (vācam) and so forth. ||28||

The sequential arrangement: The statement beginning with "Speech as a daughter" is intended to terrify those whose orientation is inward toward the body; for those whose orientation is outward, it serves to instruct the ignorant by means of that example, through such behavior, and by way of disregarding [the worldly]. ||28||
Viśvanātha: Since even those who are exceedingly learned and possessed of great discernment may not conquer their desire,
he says "the word" (*vācam*) in order to indicate that one should not dwell in secret with daughters, sisters, and so forth—
even though this was already heard by us (*naḥ śrutam*), he speaks thus for the sake of making that knowledge known, despite the impropriety.

It is indicated that one speaks only while fearing [error] and perceiving no fault; however, one should not be terrified by the thought that "if one perceives a fault, there will be a downfall like that of the sons of Marīci," for this has been heard by us.
Nor should it be thought that this might not have been seen even by some who exist in this eon.
The intention is that, by way of incidental discussion, this very karma belonging to a past kalpa has now been described;
for this was not heard immediately after receiving the instruction from the *Bhāgavata* consisting of four verses, as stated by the Blessed One:
"Abide by this doctrine with supreme concentration; you shall never be deluded amidst the various mental constructions of the world. Thus ends the *Jagadānanda*. In the *Mātsya*, however:
That most severe austerity which he performed for the sake of creation—
all of it went to ruin through his desire to approach his own daughter. (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 1.2.39)
Seeing that their father had set his mind upon unrighteousness,
the sages, headed by Marīci, gently awakened him out of confidence.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha: "From confidence" means from friendship arising from the relationship of progenitor and offspring, and not from anger arising from the perception of evil; or rather, even a transgression of great men does not cause harm.
Thus, by merely following out of trust and fearing what might be undesirable for the world, he awakened them;
this illuminates the absence of any fault on the part of Marīci and the others. ||29||
this was not done by those who came before you, nor will it be done by those who come after; for you,
though a lord, would go to your own daughter without restraining your passion."

Śrīdhara: Neither those who preceded you—Brahmā and others—or anyone else has created this; nor will those who follow you in the future ever create it. [It is] the offspring of the body, namely desire (kāma). ||30||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: By the "ancients" (*pūrvaiḥ*), meaning by the worlds belonging to previous kalpas, or by those such as Brahmā who existed before you; [he refers to] Kāma, the son of Aṅga. (30)
"O Teacher of the World, even for those who are most powerful, this is not easy to proclaim:
that by following the conduct which the world practices, it indeed attains security."
Śrīdhara: Even for those who are most brilliant—those of exceeding splendor—their conduct does not become "suślokya," that is, it does not bestow good fame, if [it is as described]. (31)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "Suślokya" means worthy of being celebrated; "vṛtta" means conduct or life-story. ||31||
Homage to that Blessed One who, by his own radiance,
has manifested this Dharma which abides within the self; he is worthy to protect it.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been commented upon in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.

Viśvanātha: Even though Brahmā was thus awakened, when he did not wake up, it was established as the conclusion that, without the grace of the Blessed One, desire cannot be pacified by any other means.
Having recollected the Blessed One, those sages took refuge in him alone; thus he says: "Therefore... (32).
Seeing his sons, the lords of progeny, speaking thus before him,
the Lord of Progeny (Brahmā), feeling ashamed, then cast off his body.
The quarters of the sky seized that terrible darkness which they know as mist.
"Madhva says: 'That which Brahmā, the Lord, abandoned is known as human speech;
they know that goddess Sarasvatī, his own wife, to be Speech (Vāc) itself. Thus it is said. (33)
Śrīdhara: [He made] his body slender. ||33||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By saying "he cast off his body," he made it known that for a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), the primary atonement is indeed death; [this occurred] during the interval of two *parārdhas* of his [life].

Because the abandonment of the body is possible [only through the abandonment of worldly existence], it is the abandonment of existence itself that is described as the "abandonment of the body. As for the directions, they too are even now enveloped by darkness. //33//
Once, as the Creator was meditating, the Vedas issued from his four faces:
"How shall I create the worlds assembled together just as before?"

Śrīdhara [comments]: For the Creator Brahmā, who was meditating, "How shall I create?", there emerged from his mouth four [beings] endowed with the number four—conjoined and well-united. As in the past, in the previous kalpa, so was the sequence of their arrangement; this has not been explained [here].

Viśvanātha: Based on such statements as, "The power of the most brilliant does not lead to fault, just as fire consumes everything" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.32), one should not suspect that even Brahmā—who followed his own daughter—is stained by impurity; thus, he describes Brahmā’s brilliance with the words beginning with "kadācit" (at one time).

The meaning is that by the passage ending with "strengthened by various powers," [it is shown that] while He was meditating, "As I created in the past, so shall I create now," the Vedas appeared; thus, since the entire manner of creation is contained within the Vedas, the intention is that He may create easily by virtue of the Lord's command.

The ritual system of the four officiating priests (*cāturhotra*), together with the auxiliary sciences (*upavedas*) and the methods of reasoning (*nayās*), as well as the four quarters of Dharma and the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-vṛttayas*), [are all contained herein].

Śrīdhara: The *cāturhotra* is the ritual procedure of the four officiating priests, beginning with the *hotṛ*. The *karmatantra* is the expansion of the sacrifice. Together with the *upavedas* and the systems of logic (*nyāya*), the stages of life (*āśrama*) and their respective duties existed;
however, the sequential arrangement has not been explained here.

Viśvanātha: The duties of the four officiating priests—the Hotṛ, Udgātṛ, Adhvaryu, and Brahman—constitute the *cāturhotra*. Along with the ritual systems, the expansion of sacrifices, the Upavedas, the Nayas, and the Nyāyas, there were also the stages of life (*āśrama*) and their respective modes of conduct. 35.
Vidura said:
He is indeed the Lord of the creators of the universe; he emitted the Vedas and other scriptures from his mouth.
O one rich in asceticism, tell me what the Lord created by means of each [means].
Madhu, presiding over speech, created the Vedas; and Brahmā, likewise presiding over all [the senses], fashioned the sacrifices and other rites through speech. (36)
Śrīdhara: From the mouth, that is, from the mouths [of the sages]. ||36||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: From the mouths [mukhataḥ means] from the faces (mukhebhyaḥ). ||36||
Maitreya said:
[He created] the Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan from his eastern and other faces.
He established the scriptures, sacrifice, hymns of praise, and expiation in their proper sequence.

Śrīdhara states the sequence of the creation of the four officiating priests (*cāturhotra*): *śastra* is the duty of the Hotṛ priest, consisting of recitations using unchanted mantras; *ijyā* is the duty of the Adhvaryu priest; and *stutistoma* refers to praise (*stuti*) and the chanted hymn (*stoma*), where "praise" is the congregational singing (*saṅgīta*), and "hymn" is that which is prescribed for its purpose, such as the collection of verses (*ṛksamūha*) beginning with "the Trivṛt Stoma comes into being."
The *ūda* is to be employed for the purpose; the *brāhma* is the expiation. 37.

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: He describes the creation of the *Caturhotṛ* [mantras]: *Śastra* is the recitation of a hymn without chanting (*apragīta*), the ritual act of the *Hotṛ*; *Ijyā* is the ritual act of the *Adhvaryu*; *Stutistoma* refers to praise, which is singing (*saṅgīta*).

The *stotra* is a collection of *ṛc*-verses intended for that purpose; the *trivṛt-stoma* and so forth are the duties prescribed for the *udgātṛ*; the *prāyaścitta* (expiatory rite) is the duty of the *brahman*. ||37||
He created Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda,
and the Veda of Architecture (Sthāpatya) from his mouths in order, starting with the eastern one.

Śrīdhara states the sequence of the Upavedas: "Āyurveda," etc. [He says] "by the mouths of the Self. *Sthāpatyam* is the science of Viśvakarman (architecture). The arrangement of the sequence has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: He describes the creation of the Upavedas with the words "Āyus" and so forth. *Sthāpatyam* is the work of an architect (*sthapati*), namely the science of Viśvakarman. (38)
The Lord, the all-seeing, created the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as the fifth Veda from all his mouths.
Madhva: "Having heard from the mouth of Hari himself the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, [one should know] those such as the Mahābhārata which were composed later by Hari and others. (39)
Śrīdhara: Not explained.
Kramasandarbha: The pair beginning with "itihāsa" [is as follows]. That which begins with "itihāsa" has been explained in the first book (Skandha). ||39||
Viśvanātha: "To all" means to all [the Purāṇas], because they consist of commentaries on the Vedas. ||39||
the Ṣoḍaśin and Uktha sacrifices from the eastern face; then the Purīṣya Agniṣṭut,
the Āptoryāma Atirātra, and the Vājapeya together with the Gosava.
Śrīdhara states the sequence of the ritual manual (*karmatantra*): "The *ṣoḍaśin* and the *uktha*," etc. The *purīṣī* is the piling (*cayana*).
The *agniṣṭut* is the *agniṣṭoma*. The arrangement of the sequence has not been explained.

Viśvanātha states the creation of the *karmatantra*: "The Ṣoḍaśin and the Uktha... The Pūriṣya-cayana, Agniṣṭut, and Agniṣṭoma—this sequence [of emanation] from the right face is to be understood everywhere in this manner. ||40||
He created knowledge, charity, austerity, and truth as the constituent parts of Dharma,
and he likewise established the stages of life (āśramas) along with their respective modes of livelihood in due order.

Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [interpret] "vidyā" as purity (*śauca*), based on the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "The supreme purification of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is considered to arise from the knowledge of the Lord. [They interpret] "dāna" as compassion (*dayā*), based on the statement: "Other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of fearlessness to living beings. And thus: austerity, purity, compassion, and truth.

There is no contradiction with the statement in the First Canto, *pādāḥ kṛte kṛtāḥ* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.17.24), because that refers to the sequence of the arrangement; it has not been explained [here].
The livelihoods in the household are indeed those of the Sāvitra, the Prājāpatya, the Brāhma, and likewise the Bṛhat, as well as Vārtā, Sañcaya, Śālīna, and Śiloñcha.

Regarding "madhvaḥ": "Brahmacarya pertaining to Prajāpati consists in having one wife and approaching her only during her season," according to the Smṛti of Vyāsa. Regarding "vārtā": "The Yāyāvara should be known [by this]; for you are indeed alone and possess no accumulation. (42)

Śrīdhara states that each of the stages of life (āśramas), beginning with studentship, is fourfold: *sāvitra* studentship lasts for three nights for one who studies the Gāyatrī starting from the initiation (*upanayana*);
*prājāpatya* studentship lasts for a year for one who performs the observances (*vrata*); and *brāhma* studentship lasts until the completion of the acquisition of the Vedas.
The *bṛhannaiṣṭhika* [is one who lives by] the great lifelong vow. *Vārtā* is the livelihood of agriculture and so forth, which is not prohibited.

*Saṃcaya* is the livelihood of officiating at sacrifices and so forth. *Śālīna* is the livelihood of not begging. *Śiloñcha* is the livelihood of gathering fallen ears of grain and single grains. The singular number is an archaism (*ārṣa*). These are the modes of livelihood for those living in the household.
Alternatively, "śiloñcha" is a locative case used for a singular compound; thus, the meaning is that they remain in the house despite such a difference in their mode of livelihood. ||42||

The sequential arrangement: "sāvitra" and so forth are the various types of student life (brahmacarya), as indicated by the term "vārtā. All these form a copulative compound (dvandva) which, according to the rule that such compounds may optionally be treated as singular, becomes a singular entity—just as in the rule "an *ac* vowel having the duration of *ū* is termed short, long, or protracted" (Pāṇini 1.2.27). ||42||

Viśvanātha: For one who studies the Gāyatrī beginning from the initiation ceremony (upanayana), there is the Sāvitra celibacy (brahmacarya) lasting for three nights; for one practicing the vows (vrata) for a period of one year, there is the Bṛhat celibacy—thus celibacy is of four kinds. Livelihood (vārtā) refers to occupations such as agriculture that are not prohibited. Accumulation (sañcaya).

Livelihood through officiating at sacrifices and the like; *śālīna* is livelihood by not begging; *śiloñchana* is livelihood by gathering fallen ears of grain and single grains. The term *śiloñcha* is a singular *dvandva* compound, similar to the rule *ūkālo’j hrasvadīrghaplutaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.27). The word "in the house" (*gṛhe*) is used because of the fourfold classification of means of subsistence.
The meaning is that the householder's stage of life (gārhasthya) is also of four kinds. ||42||
The Vaikhānasas, Vālakhilyas, Auḍumbaras, and Phenapas dwell in the forest;
among those who have renounced, there are first the Kuṭīcakas, then the Bahūdakas, the Haṃsas, and the Niṣkriyas.
"Those who subsist on honey are the Vaikhānasas; those who eat roots are the Mūlabhakṣas; those who eat fruits are the Uḍumbaras;
the Vālakhilyas eat all things; and the Phenapas and Vatsaphenapas subsist on foam. Thus it is said. 43.

Śrīdhara: There are four types of forest-dwellers (*vana-stha*). Among them, the *vaikhānasas* subsist on crops that ripen without being ploughed. The *vālakhilyas*, upon obtaining fresh food, renounce any food previously stored. The *audumbaras*, having risen at dawn, sustain themselves with fruits and other provisions gathered from whichever direction they first see.

Subsisting on foam and fruits that have fallen of their own accord, the *kuṭīcaka* is primarily devoted to the duties of his own stage of life (*āśrama*). The *bahūdaka*, having made action subordinate, is primarily devoted to knowledge.
The *haṃsa* is intent on the practice of knowledge. The *paramahaṃsa* is free from ritual action and has attained reality. And all of these—
Each subsequent one is superior. ||43||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The *vaikhānasas* are those whose livelihood consists of crops grown without plowing. The *vālakhilyas* are those who, upon obtaining fresh food, renounce previously stored food. The *ūḍumbaras*, having risen in the morning, [go] in whatever direction...
First, they subsist on what they find; then, they subsist on fruits and the like gathered [by others]; then, they subsist on foam;

and finally, they subsist on fruits and the like that have fallen of their own accord. Thus, due to these differences in livelihood or names, the forest-dweller stage (*vānaprasthāśrama*) is also fourfold. Regarding "renunciation" (*nyāsa*), the stage of the wandering mendicant (*saṃnyāsa*) is likewise fourfold.

Among them, the *kuṭīcaka* is primarily devoted to the duties of his own stage of life (*āśrama*); the *bahūdaka*, having made action subordinate, is primarily devoted to knowledge; the *haṃsa* is intent on the practice of knowledge; and the *niṣkriya* has attained reality. Thus, they are superior in successive order. ||43||
Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, Vārtā, and likewise Daṇḍanīti;
these were his utterances, for the Praṇava was his heart.
Madhva states: "The science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*) is a systematic discipline (*tantravidyā*), and it follows the Vedas.
That which was specifically proclaimed by Kapila is to be known as such; however, those [systems] spoken by Śiva and others are to be understood as being outside the Veda."
"The science of government (daṇḍanīti), the duties of kings (rājadharma), and the three Vedas are proclaimed [as branches of knowledge].
Agriculture, trade, and so forth constitute livelihood; endowed with these, life proceeds.
That which was created by Brahmā in ancient times is known by the name Ānvīkṣikī and the others. Thus it is said.

The *praṇava* issued from the eastern face; the *praṇava* and the [syllables] beginning with *bhūḥ* issued from the three faces. The Vedas and likewise the stages of life (*āśrama*) revolved clockwise. (44)

Śrīdhara states the origin of Nyāya and the other sciences in their order starting from the east: "Ānvīkṣikī," etc. Ānvīkṣikī and the others are the sciences of liberation, duty, pleasure, and wealth. The three [worlds] are separate as *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*; the fourth is the aggregate of them. As Āśvalāyana has said: "Thus the vyāhṛtis are declared."
"Separately or combined. Alternatively, "maha" is the fourth [vyāhṛti]. And thus says the Śruti:
"These three vyāhṛtis are indeed bhūr, bhuvaḥ, and suvaḥ; of these, Māhācamasya used to declare this fourth one as 'maha'. So it is said.
From the space of the heart, from the beginning. ||44||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He states the origin of Nyāya and the other sciences in the order starting from the East—namely, "Ānvīkṣikī" and so forth.
Ānvīkṣikī and the others are the sciences of liberation (*mokṣa*), duty (*dharma*), pleasure (*kāma*), and wealth (*artha*). [The worlds] Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar are mentioned separately.

There are three; the fourth is the aggregate—thus there are four *vyāhṛtis*. As Āśvalāyana has said: "Thus the *vyāhṛtis* are declared, both separately and also collectively. Or else, *mahaḥ* is the fourth. And so says the Śruti:
"These three utterances (vyāhṛtis) are indeed *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *suvar*. Of these, Māhācamasya used to declare this fourth one as 'Mahatī'. Thus [it is said].
"From the heart" means from the space within the heart (*hṛdayākāśāt*). If the reading is *dahṛtaḥ*, the meaning is the same. ||44||
The Uṣṇih was from the body hair of that Lord, and the Gāyatrī from his skin;
the Triṣṭubh arose from his flesh, and the Anuṣṭubh and Jagatī from the bones of Prajāpati.
Śrīdhara: He is "snuta" because he is produced from the sinews (snāyu), according to the Vedic revelation: "The Anuṣṭubh has sinews. ||45||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha says: He states the origin of the meters with the words "of that" (*tasya*). "From the flowing" (*snutaḥ*) means from the channel that covers all the limbs; this is because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "The *anuṣṭubh* consists of sinews. (45)
From the marrow, the *paṅkti* meter was produced; from the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the *bṛhatī* arose. Touch became its life-force (*jīva*), and the vowel is declared to be its body.
They say the *ūṣman* sounds are the senses, and the *antaḥstha* sounds are the strength of the Self;
through their distribution, the seven vowels became the Prajāpati.

"From his mouth arose the *madhya* (semivowels), from his life-force (*jīva*) the *svara* (vowels), from his body the *ūṣman* (sibilants), and from his strength the *antasthā* (laterals) were born by the Lord. And:
"Whichever limb a [phoneme] is produced from, it shall be designated by the name of that limb. ||4647||

Śrīdhara: Having stated that in the Mahākalpa Brahmā became the embodiment of Śabdabrahman, he now describes the origin of the phonemes (varṇas) by means of one and a half verses beginning with "sparśa. *Sparśa* refers to the five groups beginning with *ka*; *svara* refers to [the vowels] beginning with *a*; and *ūṣmāṇaḥ* refers to the group of four consisting of *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*.

The semi-vowels (*antasthā*) are *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*. The seven musical notes (*svara*) are *ṣaḍja* and the others. Regarding the phrase "by means of movement" (*vihāreṇa*), which refers to play (*krīḍayā*), the sequential arrangement has not been explained.
Viśvanātha states the origin of the phonemes (*varṇa*) with the verse beginning "the contact consonants" (*sparśa*), consisting of one and a half verses.

The five groups beginning with *ka* are the consonants (*sparśa*). The vowels (*svara*) begin with *a*. The sibilants (*ūṣman*) are the four: *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*. The semivowels (*antasthā*) are *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*. The seven musical notes (*svara*) are *ṣaḍja* and the rest. [This is] by means of wandering (*vihāra*), that is, by play (*krīḍā*).—o)0(o—
Beyond that [individual soul], which consists of the Word-Brahman and has both manifest and unmanifest aspects,
there shines forth the pervasive Brahman, augmented by manifold powers.
Madhva: Brahmā, whose essence is the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), is designated by all words;
for there is no object [of speech] apart from names such as Nārāyaṇa and the like.
"The manifest is said to be the universe, while the unmanifest consists of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest.
Because he pervades that [universe], Brahmā is always remembered as being of the nature of the manifest. Thus it is said. (48)

Śrīdhara: For this very reason, because Brahman consists of the subtle essence of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), he says that the Supreme Lord is eternally manifest: *vaikharī* is manifest, while the *praṇava* is unmanifest; from that [unmanifest] self, the Supreme Lord shines forth as the transcendent (*para*) of that Brahman. Of what nature is He? He is Brahman, the all-pervasive whole (*paripūrṇa*). In that regard, from the unmanifest self...
The pervasive form of Brahman shines forth; from that manifest self, it appears in various forms such as Indra and others, augmented by manifold devotions. ||48||
The sequential arrangement is as follows: "Śabdabrahman" refers to the manifest (vaikharī) and the unmanifest (praṇava).

From everything that consists of these two, it is the Supreme Lord alone who shines forth as the Vedānta; He alone is Brahman in His perfectly complete form. The reason for this is that, while His essential nature is undivided, His power is manifold.

Viśvanātha: He states that the brilliance of Brahman is indeed supreme solely through the manifestation of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara)—[referring to] one whose self (ātman) and body (deha) consist of nothing but the Śabdabrahman, which is the Veda. Since the manifest [speech] is Vaikharī and the unmanifest is the Praṇava, for him whose very essence is that, Brahman is the supreme object of worship.

The Supreme Lord shines forth and manifests perfectly; He who is Brahman as accessible through non-dual knowledge is the same as the Blessed One (Bhagavān) when accompanied by various powers as accessible through qualified pure knowledge. Therefore, it has been established that He possesses no impurity arising from following after a maiden.
Then, taking up another [form], he set his mind upon creation,
even though the creation of the sages of great power had not yet expanded.
"Of the honeyed [soma] of the seers of manifold power"—this is "the lion's glance.
Where the subsequent [words] are superior, there is "the lion's glance"; thus it is stated in the Brahmatarka. (49)

Śrīdhara: That [form] which was previously emitted became mist and darkness; thereafter, she assumed another body, one characterized by uncurbed desire and attachment. However, the body of the Śabda-Brahman exists eternally.
He states the reason for assuming this other body with the words beginning "of the sages" (ṛṣīṇām) and so forth. ||49||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: That which was previously emitted became mist and darkness; thereafter, [she assumed] another body, one attached to unrestrained desire. But the body of the Śabdabrahman (the Word-Brahman) exists eternally. [Objection: Surely by that...

Since in a previous creation Marīci and the others created the vast majority of beings, one might think that no further effort was required from him in this creation; therefore, he says: "Of the ṛṣis" (verse 49).
Having understood that, O Kaurava, he reflected further in his heart:
"Aha! This is a marvel to me, even though I am constantly occupied."
Śrīdhara says: He expresses his anxiety with the words "Alas! [and so forth]. "Of one who is occupied" means of one who is performing an activity. ||50||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Indeed, subjects do not prosper; surely fate is the obstacle here.
Thus, for him who had acted appropriately and was then observing fate, [the time arrived].
The body [is so called] because it is pervaded by honey (madhu). ||51||
Śrīdhara: "Yuktakṛtaḥ" means those who act appropriately, performing what is fitting. ||51||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Of one who acts appropriately—that is, one who does what is fitting. ||51||
Whose form was it that became twofold, which they call the body?
From those two divisions of form, a pair was produced.
Śrīdhara: For this very reason, out of wonder at how the form of which Brahman has become twofold, they even today point to his body [as a witness]. (52)

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: For a certain Brahmā who observes only his own destiny (*daiva*), his single form is twofold: one with a beard and another with two breasts; thus it is of two kinds.

It came to be that both [the body and the self] are denoted by the word "body" (kāya) because they are related to one another; according to the rule for the *naḍa*-class of words, the suffix *yat* is applied, and its elision (*lopa*) is a Vedic archaism. ||52||
The male who was there became the self-ruling Manu Svāyambhuva; the female who was there, known by the name Śatarūpā, became the queen of that high-souled one.
Śrīdhara: That woman was his queen. ||53||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
At that time, offspring indeed increased through the practice of sexual union.
And he, moreover, begot five offspring upon Śatarūpā.
Śrīdhara: *edhām* means they attained growth. He explains that very point with the words *sa cāpi*.
*Kramasandarbha*: this has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: And he is Svāyambhuva. ||54||
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, O Bhārata, and three daughters, O best of beings: Ākūti, Devahūti, and Prasūti.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
He gave Ākūti to Ruci, but the middle one to Kardama.
And from Dakṣa he gave Prasūti, from whom the world was filled.
Śrīdhara: Because [it arises] from their lineages. ||56||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Because of those [streams], by whose successions... ||56||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, appropriately concluded for the virtuous.
— o)0(o— Thus ends the third book in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsya, within the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*.
The twelfth chapter, titled "Description of Creation," from the Dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
In the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, concerning the lifting of the earth,
Śrī Śuka said: "O King, having heard the most meritorious words spoken by the sage..."
The descendant of Kuru, intent upon the stories of Vāsudeva, questioned him further.
Śrīdhara:
In the thirteenth [chapter], [he describes] the slayer of demons who arose from the Boar-form manifested to lift up the earth, which had been suddenly submerged during Manu’s desire to create.

The composition of the sequence: "ādṛta" means one who possesses regard (ādṛti), that is to say, one who is respectful; the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for the *arśa-ādi* group. ||1||
Viśvanātha:

In the thirteenth [incarnation], as Brahmā was meditating with his mind on the Word (Vāk), the Boar (Kroḍa) emerged from his nostril and went to the earth; praised by the twice-born, he lifted up the earth.

"Ādṛtaḥ" means one who has respect for this [story]; the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*, meaning "possessing respect," that is, "respectful. Alternatively, he is "respectful" in the sense that he desires Vidura to hear this through the very act of narration itself, thinking, "May this sweetness of mine become meaningful through its tasting by him [the listener]. Or again, he is "respectful toward the story" by both the speakers and the listeners.
This is the meaning. ||1||
Vidura said:
"He was indeed the universal sovereign Svāyambhuva, the beloved son of Svayambhū."
O Sage, what did he do after regaining his beloved wife?
Śrīdhara: [He is so called] because he is the son of Svayambhū, being a portion of his body. ||2||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
O best of men, [listen to] the life-story of that royal sage, the first king.
Speak to me, for I am full of faith; he indeed has Viṣvaksena as his refuge.
Śrīdhara: He whose refuge is Viṣvaksena, who is Hari himself.
[This is] Kramasandarbha; Viśvanātha has not commented upon it.
O Mukunda, for men who have labored long over sacred learning, the goal praised by the wise is indeed the direct hearing of Your various qualities.
Those whose hearts possess the lotus-feet [of the Lord].

Śrīdhara: Therefore, he says that his life story must be heard: "Indeed, this very purpose has been praised—that is, extolled as the primary meaning of the sacred learning (śruta) of those men for whom there is long-standing exertion.
[This applies] to those devotees (bhāgavatas) in whose hearts the lotus-feet of Mukunda reside, regarding the hearing of His qualities."
Thus [it is] that. ||4||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states that even for the learned, knowledge becomes fruitless without hearing the accounts of those who possess direct perception [of the truth]: "Of that [knowledge] which has been heard from the mouth of the Guru and for which there has been long labor..."
The meaning is: "the study of the scriptures and so forth. This very thing is the purpose (*prayojana*). "Praised" means lauded;

"other than that" means censured—this is the meaning. And who is that [person]? It means: for those in whose hearts the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa reside, for each of them, there is the hearing and chanting of His qualities, and so forth.
Śrī Śuka said:
To Vidura, who was speaking thus with humility—
With his hair standing on end as he was being led toward the discourse on the Blessed One, the sage, serving as a footstool for the thousand-headed one, spoke thus.

Śrīdhara: [The word] *sahasraśīrṣā* refers to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the meaning is that His feet are placed upon him, or that Śrī Kṛṣṇa affectionately extends His feet onto his lap. He addressed him—that is, he spoke to him—the sage Maitreya, who was being led by him.
Being set in motion. ||5||

The sequential arrangement: It is well known in the *Mahābhārata* that the pillow for the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the supreme form among thousands of infinite heads—is the *Śrī Bhagavat*. This is according to the rule *śīrṣaḥ śīrṣan chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.60).
The Blessed One Pāṇini.

Viśvanātha: To dispel Vidura’s doubts, the Lord assumed a form with a thousand heads and was held in his house; in the Mahābhārata, during the meal at Vidura’s house, the Blessed One served as a pillow for Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet, acting as a cushion upon his lap.
It is well known that [one] sleeps having placed [the feet] upon the feet; being led—that is, being set in motion—by him.
Maitreya said:
When Svāyambhuva Manu was born together with his own wife, he,
with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, addressed him who contains the Vedas within himself as follows:
Śrīdhara: [He created] Brahmā, who contains the Vedas within his womb. ||6||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— You alone are the father of all beings, their creator and provider of sustenance.
Nevertheless, by what means could there be service for you from us, your subjects?

Śrīdhara: You alone are the father of all, since you alone are the creator of birth, the provider of livelihood, and the nourisher. Therefore, although you have no need for others, please ordain by what action our service to you may be performed; this is the connection with the following verse. ||7||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Therefore, perform that [rite]; salutations to you, whose own power is to be praised in all ritual acts.
Having performed that which brings fame in this world and ensures a favorable rebirth in the next.

Śrīdhara: O worshipful one, among our own powers—that is, among the actions within our capacity—by which action might it be [achieved], please ordain that; tell us, "This is what must be done. Having performed which, and when it has been performed, [one attains it] everywhere—in the hereafter, in the next world. ||8||
Regarding the sequence of composition: in the phrase "having done which," the word "situated" (sthitasya) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. ||8||

Viśvanātha: O worshipful one, among our own powers—that is, among the tasks within our capability—by which action might your service be rendered? Please ordain that; the meaning is "command it. The words "of me," understood from the context, are to be supplied with "having performed which" (*yat kṛtvā*) while I remain [at your disposal]. ||8||
Brahmā said:
"I am pleased with you, my son; may it be well with both of you, O lord of the earth."
"Instruct me with a heart free from guile; I have surrendered myself to you."
Śrīdhara: May there be well-being and prosperity for you both! Since you have instructed me—meaning, you have taught me—and since this has been offered and presented by yourselves, I am pleased. (9)

The sequence of composition: *Matsara* is the hatred of the welfare of others. And since that [hatred] occurs here among those of the same class who act according to the Guru’s command while remaining solitary, it is said [in the verse], "by those whose *matsara* has departed. (9)
Viśvanātha says: "He is pleased with you"—this is a dative case (sampradāna), as in the expression "she lies down for her husband" (*patye śete*).

Therefore, may there be well-being (*svasti*) for both of you, the woman and the man. Since he has taught me—that is, instructed me—by himself, offering [the teaching] through his own self, the qualifying word is not explicitly stated.
The meaning is that everything, including the locus of the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) and the locus of the sense of "mine" (mamata), has been fully offered. ||9||
"O hero, sons must show such honor to their father;
they should respectfully receive him with diligence, free from envy, and according to their ability."

Śrīdhara: *Apacitiḥ* means worship. The word "ājñā" (command) is to be supplied as the object of *gṛhyeta* (should be accepted). Those from whom envy has departed—envy in the form of thinking, "Sanaka and the others do not perform [this]; why should we do it?"—[are those who accept the command]. ||10||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: *Apacitiḥ* (reverence) should be understood as service; the word "command" (*ājñā*) is to be supplied. [The phrase] "by those whose envy has departed"—meaning those from whom such envy has gone, namely: "Sanaka and the others do not perform it, so why should we not carry out the command?"—refers to them.
Therefore, having procreated offspring upon her who are equal to yourself in their qualities,
rule the earth according to dharma and worship Puruṣa with sacrifices.
Śrīdhara: "Gāṃ śāsa" means "instruct" or "protect"; [the object is] "puruṣam," namely Hari. ||11||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Gāṃ" means the earth; "śādhi" means protect or rule over it. ||11||
"O King, my supreme service would be through the protection of the subjects;
Lord Hṛṣīkeśa is pleased with you, the sustainer of the people."
Śrīdhara: He will be pleased with you, the protector of his subjects. ||12||

The sequence of the composition: "apārthāya" means for the sake of being purposeless. This is because, when the Self is not honored by itself, the Self is disregarded precisely on its own account through the disregard for the Supreme Self. ||12||
Viśvanātha: "For me" means for my sake, or "to please me. ||12||
But for those with whom the Blessed One Janārdana, whose emblem is the sacrifice, is not pleased,
their labor is indeed in vain, since they have not honored the Self itself.
Śrīdhara: "What fault is mine if the Lord, being indifferent, is not pleased? To this he says: "Of those... [and so on].

"Yajñaliṅga" means having sacrifice as His form. "From whom the purpose has departed" means that it leads only to exhaustion. Because the Self itself was not honored by them; when He is not pleased...
Because its own purpose is not established, and because it is the self of all. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He is "lingified" (known) by sacrifices—that is, by acts of worship such as honoring, hearing, and chanting—because the Self itself has not been honored; that is, because of a lack of reverence for the Supreme Self. By one's own [Self].
For, due to such disregard for the self, when that [self] is not satisfied, one's own purpose is simply not accomplished. ||13||
Śrī Manu said:
O destroyer of Mura, I shall abide by the command of the Blessed One.
O Lord, please grant me a place here for my subjects and for myself.
Śrīdhara: I shall abide—I will remain—O destroyer of afflictions, O destroyer of sins! Grant me permission;
give me leave to stay here. ||14||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: *varteya* means "I shall dwell. *Sthānam* means "the place of residence. *Anujānīhi* means "consider" or "permit. *Amīvasūdana* means "O destroyer of sins. ||14||
Since the earth, the abode of all beings, has sunk into the great waters,
O God, let an effort be made by you to raise her up for the sake of the Goddess."
Śrīdhara: If it is asked, "What is the earth? he says: that which is the *okaḥ* (abode) is the earth. O Lord, [this refers to] this Goddess.
Regarding the sequence of the composition: the passage beginning with "that which is the abode" (*yad okaḥ*) occurs in the context of the *Padma*.
Just as there is an indication of the discourse on Brahmā, it should be understood that there is also an indication of the story of the White Boar (*Śvetavarāha*) occurring in the present kalpa.
In this very context concerning Svāyambhuva Manu, there will also be the story of Cākṣuṣa Manu, consisting of the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa by the daughter of Dakṣa through the lineage of Pracetas.

But here, since he has appeared with a dark complexion, the author will later describe him as "dark-blue like a tamāla tree. "In the great waters" refers to the *garbhodaka* (the waters within the cosmic egg). ||15||

Viśvanātha: Now, if it is asked whether you know—or do not know—from having heard it, where the Manus together with their progeny were in each preceding Kalpa, he says "yad oka" (wherever was their abode), truly affirming: "I indeed know.
The illustrious Maitreya said: But Parameṣṭhin, seeing the earth thus submerged in the midst of the waters,
reflected for a long time with his intellect, wondering, "How shall I raise her up?"
Śrīdhara: Even though drinking was performed previously, I shall lift up—that is, I shall rescue—her who has become dejected and submerged in the midst of waters that have suddenly arisen. ||16||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
While I was creating [the world], the earth, being flooded by the waters, sank into the netherworld (*rasā*).
Now, what should be performed by us, who have been appointed to this creation?
May that Lord, from whose heart I arose, ordain it for me.
Śrīdhara says: He expresses his very anxiety: "Of the Being who was creating with words and waters; [the earth] went to Rasā, that is, Rasātala.
By those appointed by the Lord to the task of creation, let Him alone ordain and accomplish what is to be performed by me;
such is the sequence of the composition. "Gone to Rasā" means she remained submerged until that space [was filled].

"Of whom," [referring to] even *rasā* because it is a cavity of the earth; this is the meaning of the half-verse. From the heart, by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), Viśvanātha [creates]; "the netherworld" (*rasām*) means the *garbhoda* ocean, characterized by the netherworld (*rasātala*).
Since the netherworld is a cavity of the earth, it is impossible for the earth to sink there. "Let him ordain"—this is what must be performed.
Thus, there is an ellipsis (anuṣaṅga) from the preceding [sūtra]. ||17||
" While he was thus meditating, O sinless one,
a young boar the size of a thumb suddenly emerged from the opening of his nostril.

Śrīdhara: The "boar-child" (varāhatoka) is a subtle boar. Being situated in the sky (*khastha*), meaning remaining in space, the sequence of the composition states: "the boar-child emerged. By the absence of such a state [of physical form], it is made known that there is no conventional usage such as "son-ness" and so forth. In some places, however, he is described as being the size of a thumb (*aṅguṣṭhaparimāṇaka*).
The masters will write [it] first as being merely the size of the tip of a thumb. ||18||
Viśvanātha: Varāhatoka is the subtle Varāha. ||18||
O Bhārata, even as he was looking on, that [being], staying in the sky, reportedly grew to the size of an elephant in an instant; that was a great wonder.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: "Gajamātra" means measured by the body of an elephant. ||20||
Having seen that boar-form together with the young Marīci and other brahmins, as well as Manu, he reflected upon it in various ways.
Śrīdhara: "In various ways" means in many ways. ||20||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha states: "This has not been explained.
—o)0(o— What is this divine being that exists under the guise of a boar?
"Oh, how wonderful! This has emerged from my nose!"
It was not explained by anyone.
In an instant, what was seen as being only the size of the hair on a thumb became like a massive boulder.
Is it perhaps this sacrifice of mine that distresses the Blessed One’s mind?
Śrīdhara: Previously he was seen the size of a thumb-tip; now he is like a massive boulder. Viṣṇu is the sacrifice itself; by concealing his own form, he causes my mind distress. (22)
