The sequence of composition: distressing [the mind] by the manifestation of unperceived forms, and agitating the mind with doubts. ||22||
Viśvanātha: Yajña is the incarnation [of Viṣṇu] during the first Manvantara; "distressing" means agitating the mind with doubts through the manifestation of his unperceived form. ||22||
" While he was thus reflecting along with his sons,
the Blessed Lord Yajñapuruṣa, resembling the king of elephants, let out a roar.

Śrīdhara: While he was thus reflecting, there arose a roar. A sequence of words equal to the king of mountains roared, as if uttering a "huṃ" sound in assent; it was like a great mountain, the lord of peaks. (23)
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Hari gladdened Brahmā and those best of the twice-born.
The Lord made the quarters of the sky resound with his own roar.
Śrīdhara: By his own unique thundering. ||24||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Making the quarters—the directions—resound, that is, causing them to possess echoes.
Having heard that gurgling roar of the illusory boar, which was intended to exhaust his own fatigue,
those inhabitants of Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—
With three purifiers, the sages sang [the hymn].

Śrīdhara: *Ghargharitam* refers to a sound imitating that particular [animal’s] cry. *Aniścayena yaḥ svakhedaḥ* means that which destroys—that is, exhausts or causes the disappearance of—the distress caused by uncertainty. The repetition of the word *te* (you) is for the purpose of proclaiming their renown. With the three purifiers—the mantras of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas—they praised him.
They praised him. ||25||
The sequence of composition: here, *māyā* is indeed compassion. ||25||

Viśvanātha: [The term] *māyāmayasya* means "consisting of *māyā*," "consisting of compassion (*kṛpā*)," or "consisting of knowledge (*jñāna*"); or alternatively, it means "of him from whom even *māyā*—that is, ignorance (*avidyā*)—has its affliction (*āmaya*), i.e., its disease. *Ghargharitam* is the sound imitating that particular type [of noise]. It refers to the exhaustion resulting from their own uncertainty or from the failure to protect the earth.

Brahmā and the others praised—that is, extolled—Thee, who art the consumer, the destroyer, and the annihilator; likewise, the renowned sages such as Bhṛgu and others, the inhabitants of the celestial regions, praised Thee with the three purifiers, namely the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. This is to be explained by the double occurrence of the word "te" (Thee).
To those virtuous ones, Brahmā— the embodiment of the Vedic tradition— perceived their own qualities being extolled.
Having roared again for the sake of the emergence of the gods, he who possesses the gait of a lordly elephant entered the water.
Śrīdhara: He whose form is expanded and praised by the Vedas; for this very reason, he describes his own qualities accordingly.
Thus, having understood—that is, having ascertained—the Veda which is that Brahman uttered [by him]. (26)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He whose form is the expansion of the Vedas, consisting of all the Vedas, and not a material body;
for the Vedas are of the nature of the Lord’s own breath, and [this form arises] from the playful manifestation of that very breath of the Lord.

It should be understood that for one who has entered the nose of a Brahmin, there is the state of being a pig. Therefore, having ascertained—that is, having known—the Veda (brahman) as the very recounting of the qualities of those sages, namely the description of their own qualities composed by those sages themselves. ||26||
With its tail raised, the sky-ranger is fierce, shaking its mane, its skin covered in coarse hair.
With clouds struck by his hooves and white fangs bared, the Lord Mahīdhra shone like a vision of light.
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry, "In what state did he enter?", he explains by means of two verses.
[He was one] by whom the tail was tossed aloft; a sky-roamer (*khacara*), moving through the atmosphere; harsh (*kathora*), meaning hard;
[one whose] mane (*saṭā*) consists of hair on the shoulders; and one whose skin has rough (*khara*), that is, sharp, bristles.

By whom the clouds were struck with his hooves; he whose tusks were white—that is, exceedingly bright—and whose light was his very gaze, because at that time there was no other source of illumination; he shone, he was resplendent; he who is the upholder of the earth. ||27||
The composition of the sequence: that whose skin has rough hairs is [the subject]. ||27||

Viśvanātha: He describes the meditation on him as he enters the water: "He by whom the tail-hair was tossed upward. "Moving through the sky" (*khacara*) means that he descended into the three worlds from the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) solely by way of the path of space. "He whose skin is covered with coarse hair. His very glance is light.
He who is like the moon and the sun; a mountain-bearer (*mahīdhra*), meaning a supporter of the earth or one equal to a mountain— he,
sniffing the path of the earth with his sense of smell.
Under the pretext of play, he himself became a limb of the sacrifice;
though possessing formidable fangs, he entered into the Brahmins as they recited their prayers, looking upon them with eyes that were not terrifying.

Śrīdhara: Under the pretext of sport, he assumed the guise of a boar; thus, though himself the very limb of the sacrifice, he entered the water, sniffing with his snout like a beast, while looking upward at the Brahmins who were chanting hymns of praise. (28)

The sequence of composition: [This is] a pretext for play, a disguise as an ordinary boar; however, because he is a constituent part of the sacrifice (*adhvara*), his form is that of a non-ordinary boar—this is the meaning. He says "by the sense of smell" (*ghrāṇena*) to show that even his very nature is like that of a boar; yet, by his form, though he is fierce to others, he possesses a compassionate gaze toward his devotees.
He says "supremely delicate" and then [contrasts this by] saying "terrible. ||28||

Viśvanātha states his play (*līlā*) [of the Lord] with the words "by the sense of smell" (*ghrāṇena*). He explains that the sacrifice itself is the "sport" (*kroḍā*), while the "boar" (*varāha*) is merely its "disguise" (*apadeśa*). This is done through the poetic figure of *apahnuti* (concealment), as in the verse: "The tender golden creeper bears a pair of fruits under the guise of breasts."
The reality of being a boar (*kroḍatva*) alone is made known.
According to the definition: "That [figure] is *apahnuti* (concealment) wherein the subject at hand is denied and something else is established. Here, *kaṃ* means water. ||28||
That ocean, thundering as its belly was shattered by the force of the falling Vajrakūṭa peak, [roared].
As if with arms in the form of long, released waves, he cried out in distress: "O Lord of Sacrifice, protect me!"

Śrīdhara: He then describes the roar of the ocean at that time. That ocean, the *udanvat*, as if afflicted, thundering—that is, making a sound—cried out: "O Lord of Sacrifice, protect me! Save me! He expresses the similarity to one who is distressed: "The long waves were cast forth," meaning they were extended.

He is distinguished by those arms. The cause of his distress is as follows: the body of the Blessed One was like a mountain of diamond (*vajrakūṭa*), and by the force of its falling, his belly was shattered; this sequence [of events] has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: He imagines the sound of the ocean at that time. The ocean—whose belly was shattered by the force of the fall of the Lord’s body, which was like a mountain peak (*vajrakūṭa*) made of diamond—cried out in distress, as if fearing for its own life. O...!
"O Lord of Sacrifice, protect me! he cried out. ||29||
With his hooves like razor-edged arrows, he tore through those waters, reaching from this shore to the further shore across the three-fold Rasā.
There he saw the cow that he had himself placed there at the outset as the vessel of life for his intended sleep.

Śrīdhara: At that time, in Rasā, in the subterranean realm (rasātala), he beheld the earth (gāṃ pṛthvīm). Who? Triparuḥ—he whose three joints (parūṃṣi) consist of the three pressings (savana); the meaning is that he is the embodiment of sacrifice (yajñamūrti). What was he doing? Piercing the waters with hooves resembling arrows (kṣuraprāḥ) that have long points.

How? Just as there is a far shore—the limit and end—of waters that have reached the further bank, which are themselves empty of a further shore, so [He] rends [the universe]. Of what nature is He? At the beginning, at the time of dissolution, desiring to sleep—that is, wishing to rest—therein, within those waters, in whom the individual souls (jīvas) are supported.
He himself directly upheld—that which is the support of all living beings;
the meaning is that he held it within his own womb. By this, he demonstrates the absence of effort in its extraction. ||30||

The sequential arrangement: the half-verse beginning with "svadaṃṣṭrayā. Herein lies a specific detail from the *Viṣṇudharma*: "Having placed his two feet upon the mass of the coils of the Lord who dwells at the base of Pātāla, he supports the earth."
"May that Hari, for whom no comparison exists, be for the increase of my auspiciousness—He who is Acyuta.
Here, however, [the author] will later state: "having trodden with His own hooves upon the water. (30)

Viśvanātha: Then, as if with *kṣurapras*—specific types of weapons—he tore through the waters with his hooves; he tore through them in such a way that he reached the very limit, the end, of even those waters that were shoreless (*utpāra*). He whose joints (*parus*) consist of the three *savana*s (the three daily pressings of the Soma sacrifice)—that is to say, he whose form is the sacrifice.

"In Rasā" means in the subterranean realm (pātāla) characterized as Rasātala; that is to say, in Garbhoda. This is because Atala and the other six [realms] are considered part of the earth due to being cavities within the ground, and thus it is impossible for the earth to exist within Rasātala itself.
As it is stated in the Viṣṇudharma:
He who, having placed his feet upon the mass of enjoyments belonging to the Lord at the root of Pātāla, supports the earth— there was no one who could serve as a comparison for that Acyuta.
"May Hari be for the increase of my auspiciousness.

Here too, he will say, "trampling with his own hooves upon the water. He himself upheld the earth—the supporter of living beings (jīvadhānīm), so called because living beings (jīvāḥ) are supported within it—by lifting it up in the form of the Vedas.
This is the meaning. ||30||
Having lifted up with his own tusk the earth that had sunk down,
he rose from the netherworld (rasā) and shone forth brilliantly.
There too, his intense fury inflamed by the beautiful navel [of his discus], he struck the Daitya as he was rushing forward with a mace.
He struck down with ease that elephant of irresistible prowess as it charged, like a lion against an elephant in the water;
his temples and snout were stained with the mud of its blood.
Just as a lordly elephant, cleaving through the earth.
Madhva: But Hiraṇyākṣa, born of Brahmā, was the first to be killed by the tusk;
he himself, possessed by a *pārṣada*, was the second, killed by the striking of the ear.

"By that Hari, in the form of a boar, while lifting up the earth which had previously been submerged in the waters of dissolution and was being submerged for a second time," so it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. (32)

Śrīdhara: Having arisen from the netherworld (rasā), he shone forth; he appeared most beautiful. Even there, in that water, he [the Lord]—his prowess being unbearable, meaning incapable of being endured—[encountered] that Daitya Sunābha, who was approaching with his mace raised, obstructing and striking back; [the Lord], like a well-kindled discus, [overcame him].

He whose anger was intense; or rather, while I was present, why this insult? Thus incited by Sunābha, that Blessed One, like a lion, slew [the demon] with ease as if he were an elephant—this is the connection with the following verse. (31) The lordly elephant, tearing up the earth in play...
Just as one's cheeks and snout become reddened with red ochre, so too his very blood was the mud;
he was one whose cheeks and snout were marked by that [blood]. ||32||
The structural arrangement (*kramasandarbha*): Regarding the phrase "even there" (*tatrāpi*), it means "even in such a flood of confluence" (*tādṛśasamplavāmbhasi*).
Here, the particle *api* expresses wonder (*vismaye*). This statement regarding non-difference is not made merely because of the commonality of being a flood and so forth;

rather, in reality, this contingency applies specifically to the confluence of other visual perceptions (*cākṣuṣāntarasamplave*). For this very reason, [it does not apply] to the confluence of the *Svāyambhuva* and other [scriptures].
Because those residing in the three worlds have not yet appeared, and for the protection of those dwelling in Maharloka,

this [state] has been praised by the inhabitants of Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka alone; yet during the conquest of the quarters by Hiraṇyākṣa at the end of the Cākṣuṣa dissolution, the stability of the created beings was long-lasting.
Thus it is clear. Alternatively, the phrase "even there, in the Varāha incarnation" means "at any time whatsoever.
The examples of the king of beasts and so forth are merely a ladder for experiencing his prowess and other qualities. ||3132||

Viśvanātha: There too, even in such a flood of waters—*api* is used here in the sense of wonder—he slew the Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa. There is also a reading, *ādidaityam*. Of what sort was he? Approaching with a mace. And of what sort was he [Viṣṇu]? Inflamed by the discus with its beautiful nave (*sunābha*). Even while I was present...
He whose fury was kindled by the thought, "He is raising his mace against you," compared the Lord Varāha—

who, standing upon Mount Trikūṭa, was striking down that elephant-king who was wandering in all four directions to obstruct him who was obstructing him— to a lion that slays even lions, śarabhas, and other such creatures, and protects the earth situated there.
By tearing up the earth in play, he becomes one whose cheeks and snout are reddened with red chalk (gairika);
for Amara states that *jagatī* refers both to a specific meter and to the earth. ||3132||
O Lord, dark as the *tāla* tree, lifting the earth with the tip of your white tusk in the playful gait of an elephant!
With palms joined in reverence, Viriñci and the other foremost gods approached the Lord with hymns of praise.
"Sometimes, even by way of transposition, [the names] are spoken of without discrimination;
in various places, stories are told for the purpose of deluding the wicked. Thus it is said in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.

Regarding the phrase "without discrimination," the meaning is that they are not stated after having been carefully distinguished (*avivecya*); it does not mean a lack of discernment on the part of the author.

"How could there be ignorance in the omniscient Vyāsa of noble deeds? Śrīdhara [explains] this as being for the purpose of deluding the wicked; having perceived [this], they praised him with Vedic hymns (*anuvāka*) and similar verses. ||33||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Here, at the beginning of the Svāyambhuva Manvantara within the Śvetavarāha Kalpa, the Śvetavarāha manifested from the very nose of Brahmā and [lifted up] the earth alone.
Having lifted [the earth], he then vanished; later, during the sixth Manvantara, the Cākṣuṣa, he appeared again during a sudden dissolution to lift the earth as the Blue Boar and slew Hiraṇyākṣa—
thus Maitreya spoke here, having unified the two boar-līlās.
This is to be understood from the *Śrībhāgavata-mṛtakārikā*. And they [the verses] are as follows:

"He appeared twice in this kalpa, during the first interval of Manu Svāyambhuva: once from the nose of Brahmā for the sake of uplifting the earth, and once from the water during the period of Cākṣuṣa. (10)
To slay Hiraṇyākṣa during the lifting of the earth, that foremost of fanged beings became the glorious four-legged Varāha; he is sometimes regarded as the "human-boar" (Nṛvarāha).
Sometimes dark as a rain-cloud and sometimes white as the moon, this most ancient embodiment of sacrifice is remembered as possessing two colors. (12)
The creation from Dakṣa Prācetasa is heard of in the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara;
therefore, it is appropriate that the birth of Hiraṇyākṣa occurred at that very time, as he was the son of the Pracetasas belonging to the lineage of Uttānapāda. [Laṅkāvatāra-bhāṣya 1.3.1013]
Diti was the daughter of Dakṣa himself, and Hiraṇyākṣa was the son of Diti. ||15||
At the beginning of that kalpa, even for Manu there was no birth of a son; where was that Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, where was Diti, and where was the son of Diti? (16)
Therefore, Maitreya has recounted the deeds of Śrī Varāha, which occurred across two different times, all together in one place, in accordance with the questions of Kṣattṛ.
It is stated in some Purāṇas that this dissolution occurred in the midst of a Manvantara due to a sage’s curse directed against Manu. (18)
"This dissolution of Padmanābha occurred spontaneously during the interval of the Manu Cākṣuṣa; and in some places it is said that this was for the sake of his divine play (līlā).
[Laṅkāvatāra-bhāṣya 1.3.1519] Thus.
They praised him with Vedic hymns (*anuvāka*) and with verses similar to those *sūkta*s. ||33||
The sages said:
Victory, victory to you, O unconquered one, O creator of sacrifice!
Homage to you who shake off your own threefold body;
homage to you, the causal boar, in whose pores the mountains lay hidden.

Śrīdhara: "O Ajita! 'It has been conquered, it has been conquered by you'—this repetition (*vīpsā*) expresses excitement. 'That which is manifested or fashioned by sacrifices'—thus [is he described]. 'The Trayī,' consisting of the Vedas. 'They have vanished' means they have almost disappeared.
'For the sake of the boar' refers to the cause, namely, the lifting up of the earth. (34)
The sequential composition: To the Supreme Brahman as the cause, who is Śūkara by nature. ||34||

Viśvanātha: "Victory, victory has been achieved by you! O Unconquered One! The meaning is: "Conquer, conquer! You nourish the sacrifices; the meaning is: "O cause of all sacrifices! [You nourish] the Trayī, which consists of the Vedas;
O cause of the entire world! ||34||
"O God, this form of yours, which consists of the sacrificial ritual, is indeed difficult for those of evil nature to behold."
The Vedic hymns are upon his skin, the sacrificial grass is in his body hair, the clarified butter is in his sight, and the fourfold priestly office is in his feet.
Śrīdhara: Elaborating upon His nature as the sacrifice, they offer praise with the four verses beginning with "His form" (*rūpam*).

The *chandas* are the Gāyatrī and other meters. By way of restating the meters that constitute the limbs of the sacrifice, their status as parts of the Lord's body is enjoined. The absence of the long vowel in the word *barhiḥ* is an archaic (Vedic) usage. *Dṛśi* means in the eye.
The *cāturhotra* consists of the fourfold set of rites beginning with the *hotṛ*. ||35||
The sequence of composition: Therefore, he states with the four verses beginning with "rūpam" that the entire ritual procedure has that [Brahman] as its basis. ||35||
Viśvanātha: Expanding upon the nature of the sacrifice, they offer praise with the four verses beginning with "rūpam.

In the verse beginning with "tvaci chandāṃsi," the meaning should be understood as follows: the Vedas (*chandāṃsi*) and so forth have your skin and other limbs as their very cause. The absence of the long vowel in the word *barhiḥ* is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).
The fourfold rites beginning with the Cāturhotra. ||35||
The *sruc* was in his mouth, the *sruva* in his nostrils, the *iḍā* in his belly, and the *camasa* cups in the cavities of his ears.
The *prāśitra* is in your mouth, the cups (*graha*) are in your swallowing; O Blessed One, that which is your chewing is the *agnihotra*.

Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha explain: the *sruk* and *juhū* ladles are at the tip of the snout; the *sruva* spoon is at the two nostrils; the *iḍā* is the vessel for consuming the sacrificial food; the *camasas* and *grahas* are the vessels for Soma;
the *prāśitra* is the vessel for the portion of the Brahman priest; and the *grasana* is the cavity within the mouth, so called because it is "swallowed" (*grasyate*) by means of it.
Chewing is eating. ||36||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained. —
The initiatory birth and the attendant rites are the neck.
You have the Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya offerings as your tusks;
the Pravargya is your tongue; the head of the sacrifice is yours; the Āhavanīya fire is your truth; for the layers of the altar are indeed your vital breaths.

Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [explain]: *dīkṣā* is the initiation sacrifice (*dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi*). *Anujanma* is repeated manifestation. The *upasads* are three sacrifices. *Śirodhara* is the neck. The *prāyaṇīyā* is the sacrifice immediately following the initiation. The *udayanīyā* is the concluding sacrifice. He whose tusks are these very [sacrifices].
The *pravargya* rite, involving the *mahāvīra* vessel, is performed prior to each *upasad*. The *satya* is the fire devoid of oblations.

The *āvasathya* is the domestic (*aupāsana*) fire. The union of these two constitutes a pair. That is the head of you who are the embodiment of the sacrifice (*kratu*). The layers (*citayaḥ*), consisting of the piling of bricks, are the five vital breaths (*asavaḥ*). ||37||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —o)0(o— Soma, however, is the semen; the libations are its state of existence.
O God, the various structural divisions are your constituent elements;
you are all sacrificial sessions, the joints of the body, and the bond of all sacrifices and rituals.

Śrīdhara: The *prātaḥsavana* and other [pressings] are the *avasthiti*, which is the state of sitting (*āsana*), or the states of childhood and so forth. The seven varieties of ritual terminuses (*saṃsthā*)—namely, the Agniṣṭoma, Atirātra, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya, Atirātra, and Āptoryāma—are the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*), such as skin, flesh, and so on. The *satras* are the twelve-day sacrifices and others.

[The forms] consist of the aggregates of many sacrifices. Sacrifices (yajña) are those without Soma, while rituals (kratu) are those with Soma; you are of that nature. He whose bond is precisely that—namely, the *iṣṭi*, which is the performance of sacrifice—is [described as such]. ||38||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The *savanas* are the ritual times beginning with the morning; *avasthiti* is the sitting posture;
the distinctions of the *saṃsthās* are the Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya, and Atirātra.

The *āptoryāma* refers to the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*), such as skin, flesh, and so forth. The *satras*, such as the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) and others, consist of a collection of many rituals. Sacrifices (*yajña*) are rites without Soma, while *kratavaḥ* are those with Soma; You are the embodiment of both these forms.
*Iṣṭi* is the act of sacrificing, which is devotion to You that constitutes a limb of the sacrifice; You are he for whom that very devotion is the bond. (38)
Homage, homage to You, the deity of all mantras,
the substance of all sacrifices, the very soul of ritual action!
Salutations again and again to the teacher of knowledge, who has been realized through dispassion, devotion, and self-conquest.

Śrīdhara: Repeating exactly what was stated previously along with its supporting details, they offer salutation: "Obeisance, obeisance. [This is] to the one whose nature is action (*kriyātman*), who consists of all mantras and so forth, and who is the form of general activity (*sāmānyavyāpāra*). Furthermore, through action conjoined with detachment (*vairāgya*), there is purification of the mind (*sattvaśuddhi*); from that, devotion (*bhakti*); and from that, mastery over the self (*ātmajaya*).
To the one for whom there is stability of mind, and to the Guru who bestows such knowledge—that knowledge which is experienced and directly realized through that [stability]—[salutation]. ||39||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Praising the aforementioned meaning in brief, they prostrate themselves, saying "Salutations, salutations.
To the one whose nature is action (*kriyātmane*), that is, to the one whose form consists of activities such as sacrifice and the like; even though you are thus, through your divine play (*līlayā*).

Because you set the path of action in motion, you are the embodiment of all causes. Nevertheless, they say that your realization can only occur through devotion alone, free from longing for the fruits of action;
that is, devotion conjoined with *vairāgya*—the state of being devoid of desire for the fruits of actions, whether seen or unseen.

To him by whom knowledge concerning his own object has been manifested—that is, directly realized—through that very conquest of his own mind; therefore, to that teacher of wisdom (*vidyā-guru*). You alone are that knowledge which leads to you, as stated by you in [Gītā 10.10]: "I give that yoga of discernment (*buddhi-yoga*) by which they come unto Me."
The sense is: "You ought to give. ||39||
O Blessed One, O Supporter of the Earth, this earth together with its mountains shines resplendent, held by you with the very tip of the point of your tusk.
Just as a lotus plant with its leaves is crushed by the tusks of a lordly elephant emerging from the forest.
Śrīdhara: O Bhūdhara! Together with the mountains (*sabhūdharā*) means together with the peaks. Of the lordly elephant emerging from the water of the forest; by the tusk (*datā*). ||40||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Oh, how great is the fortune of the earth that you support her!

Thus he describes her with the verse beginning with *daṃṣṭrā*. O Supporter of the Earth (*bhūdhara*)! [The earth] together with the supporters of the earth—that is, along with the mountains—from the forest and from the water.
The phrase "a lotus pond with leaves" compares its buds, flower-buds, and so forth to high and low mountains;
and this form consisting of the three Vedas is that of a boar.
Moreover, with the circle of the earth offered and held by you,
it shines with the splendor of the great king of the Kulaparvatas when heavy clouds rest upon its peaks.

Śrīdhara: It was said that "the earth supported by you shines. Now they say that your form shines by means of the terrestrial globe—[expressed in the verse beginning with] "The Trayī... The word *atha* indicates a change of subject. This form of yours, which is the terrestrial globe held by your tusk (*danta*), shines—that is, it is beautiful—by means of that [tusk]. [The phrase] "that which is borne on the horn" refers to what is supported by the horn.
By that [laughter], there was a dense, exceedingly great, and vast display of graceful charm (*vibhrama-vilāsa*). ||41||

The sequential composition: therefore, even that which consists of the three Vedas shines forth as the very form of the Lord of the Kulācala mountains, through its playful manifestation, just like a dense cloud resting upon a peak that stands in the place of the earth's surface; such is the meaning. ||41||

Viśvanātha says: Just as the earth shines when supported by you, its Lord, so too do you shine when supported by the earth through her devotion; thus they say—"The Trayī... and so forth. The splendor (*vibhrama*) is the beauty produced by the cloud (*ghana*) borne—that is, supported—by the peak of the king of the Kulācala mountains, the great mountain.
As follows: ||41||
Establish her; she is the wife for the sake of the worlds, both those that move and those that stand, and you, O Father, are her mother.
And may we worship her with reverence along with you— she in whom you have deposited your own splendor, as one places fire within the kindling wood.

Śrīdhara: For the sake of the world, for the purpose of providing a dwelling place; [we offer] that wife, the mother of the worlds, since you are the father. This being so, remaining there with you as our father, we shall perform mental homage (*vidhema*)—that is, we shall bow down—to this mother, or rather, we shall serve her with prostration.

The ritualists have established the power to maintain their own splendor through mantra, just as one establishes fire in the two kindling woods (*araṇi*); the sequence of the composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha says: "If it is asked, 'What is your desired goal? That is the vow (*vrata*),' then [the answer follows]."

They said: "Establish her. For the sake of the world, for the purpose of a dwelling place, you are the father of this wife, the mother of the moving world; therefore, together with you as father, let us pay homage to this mother with reverence—we shall perform an act of salutation. You have sustained the power to maintain your own splendor.
Just as sacrificial priests maintain the fire within the kindling wood (araṇi), so [should one maintain it]. ||42||
"O Lord, who else could have faith in this,
that you uprooted the earth when it had sunk into the lower realm?"
There is no cause for wonder in you, O source of wonder to the entire universe, who by means of your illusory power (māyā) created this world of extreme amazement.

Śrīdhara: They say that this which you have done is extremely difficult to perform—“Who? meaning, O Lord, who other than you would believe in, or desire, this uprooting—that is, the lifting up—of the earth performed by you? For such wonder does not exist in you.

In whom all wonders reside—why so? Because you, O Lord, created this entire universe, which is most wonderful and marvelous; or rather, "most wonderful" is an adverbial modifier for the act of creation itself. ||43||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: They say, "O Lord, we shall sing of this sport of yours which is difficult for others to perform," beginning with the word *ka*. O All-pervading One! Who else other than You could be the uprooter of the earth—that is, the one whose agent is You, acting through You?
"One should have faith" means that one should desire to act and resolve [to do so]. ||43||
Shaking his own body composed of the Vedas, [he said:
"We are the inhabitants of Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka."
O Lord, we are thoroughly purified, being repeatedly wiped by the drops of auspicious water shaken from the matted locks of your hair.
Śrīdhara: Displaying amazement, they pray with two verses beginning with "vidhunvata" (shaking).
We have been sprinkled and purified by those auspicious droplets of water which were tossed upward and splashed from the tips—the ends—of his mane. 44.

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon. *Viśvanātha*: "The lifting up of the earth by you is no cause for wonder; rather, this alone is the true wonder—that under that very pretext, while appearing to fall into the great ocean, you were in fact overcome by compassion for us alone."

They said: "By you, through the nectars of the water used for washing your own limbs, which were directed ever upward, we sages have been made to achieve our purpose"—thus they spoke with the verse beginning *vidhunvata*. (44)
Alas! He whose mind has fallen away indeed seeks the further shore of actions, he who is himself incapable of performing action.
O Blessed One, bring peace to this entire universe which is deluded by its connection with the qualities of Your illusory power (māyā).
Śrīdhara: "He who beholds the further shore of your deeds" means he who desires to know them. He is endowed with that union which is joined with your *yogamāyā* and its qualities;
therefore, ordain the welfare and auspiciousness of the universe, so that, having known you as one of inconceivable and infinite power, [they may attain liberation].
The meaning is: "I worship [you]; thus, please favor me. ||45||

The sequential composition [of the words] is as follows: "sa vai" (he indeed). The form "eṣa te" belongs to the root *iṣ* (bhauvādika) meaning "to go," which is connected with the vowel *ṛ*. Consequently, because its primary sense is "motion," it is explained as "he perceives" (*avalokayati*) by virtue of its meaning being "to know. And since that [literal sense of motion] is impossible here, the actual meaning is simply "he desires to know" (*jñātum icchati*).

Viśvanātha: "Thus, how can we describe even a portion of His pastimes? Even though we are knowers of all the Vedas, we do not know even a single drop of that ocean of pastimes in its entirety; what then of others who are mere wretches?
Thus they say: *sa vai* and so forth. He who seeks the limit of Your activities—that is, one who thinks, "I know [it]"—[does not truly know].

The meaning is "he conceives [it as real]. The root *iṣ* belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa* (meaning "to go"). Now, one might object: "Granted that the individual soul (*jīva*) deluded by *māyā* may not know [the truth], surely Nārada and others who are Your devotees and have transcended *māyā* do indeed know it? To this they reply:

"O You, whose *yogamāyā* is a specific modification of the function of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), and whose *guṇayoga* consists of the conjunction of the *guṇas*, and who possesses *avidyā*..."

By those two, the entire universe—both the non-material (aprākṛta) and the material (prākṛta)—is deluded. Among them, those who are non-material and devoted to You are deluded by being immersed in the sweetness of Your pastimes through *yogamāyā*. And those other living beings who are material are deluded by *māyā* amidst the pleasures and pains of the senses.
The meaning is: "Who will know the further shore of your actions? Therefore, bestow peace so that we may understand;
the intention is that there should be no false pride [in thinking one knows]. ||45||
Maitreya said:
Thus was he attended by sages who were exponents of the Veda.
Treading upon the water with his own hooves, he supported the earth.
Śrīdhara: "Being approached" means being praised. "Treading with his own hooves" demonstrates the bestowal of the power of support even upon the water. "Avitā" means a protector. ||46||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Being approached" means being served with praise. "Upon the water, having trodden with his own hooves upon the water" shows the bestowal of the power of support even upon the water. [He is] the protector (*avitā*).
The protector. ||46||
Thus the Blessed One, Viṣvaksena, the Lord of Creatures,
Hari, having playfully cast the earth— which had been raised up from the netherworld (rasā)— back into the waters, departed.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [comment]: "He went to his own world"—this is the ellipsis. Or, "He vanished"—this is the sequence of the composition; "he went to his own world" is the ellipsis. ||47||
He who thus [listens to] this auspicious narrative of Hari, the one of beautiful intellect, who is skilled in narration—
One should listen with devotion or cause others to hear this; Janārdana quickly becomes gracious toward one who desires it in their heart.

Śrīdhara: [He is] one whose illusory and deceptive deeds are to be told. One should cause [others] to hear them (śravayeta/śrāvayeta); the shortening [of the vowel] is an archaic Vedic usage (ārṣa). "Uśatīm" means desirable. "It pleases in the heart" means it brings satisfaction within one's own mind. ||48||

The sequence of the composition: Thus, he will say "hiraṇyākṣam" and so forth. [He refers to] Hari-medhas, whose resolve is to remove the suffering of the world; [the one] endowed with that praiseworthy and laudable *māyā*, which is his grace (*kṛpā*).
He states its very praiseworthiness by saying: "Let him hear," etc. (48).
Viśvanātha: [He is] one in whom *medhā*—the intellect—is present, which carries away (*harantī*) and destroys the worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) of his devotees.

His *māyā*—whether it be the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), compassion (*kṛpā*), or the power of his own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*)—is to be told and described. One should cause [him] to hear that which is desirable (*uśatīm*, lovely). ||48||
When that Lord, the master of all blessings, is pleased,
what is difficult to obtain? What need is there for those blessings, which are but mere fragments?
To those who worship with undivided vision, the Supreme One, dwelling within the cave of the heart,
Himself bestows His own supreme state.
Śrīdhara: Although blessings are easily obtained, they should nevertheless not be prayed for; thus he says:

"Enough with those blessings," meaning those which are trivial and of the nature of fleeting particles (*lava*). Nor should one fear that devotion to the Lord would then be fruitless; thus he says: "without the perception of any other fruit apart from the worship of the Blessed One."
Knowing that devotion is causeless because it dwells within the secret cave of the heart, He Himself bestows the attainment of His own state upon those who worship Him. 49.
The sequential arrangement: even though His grace bestows all fruits, He states the supreme fruit [in the verse beginning] "In that"—*tasmin*.
"His own state" (*svagatim*) refers to knowledge in the form of His own manifestation (*svasphūrti*). ||49||

Viśvanātha: What thing is difficult to obtain? Indeed, everything is easily obtained. Even so, enough with those blessings! [The meaning is: by those which are of the nature of fragments, petty, and insignificant. Nor should one fear that worship at that time would be fruitless; thus he says: "ananyadṛṣṭā" (seen by none other).

The explanation of the venerable Svāmīcaraṇa is that [the Lord] knows that devotion—which is causeless because it resides in the cave of the heart—is free from the perception of any other fruit apart from the worship of the Blessed One. ||49||
who in this world is truly a knower of the essence of human goals who would prefer the nectar of stories concerning the Blessed One over ancient tales?
Alas, who other than a man would not become dispassionate after drinking from the ears with the cupped hands of devotion this teaching that destroys worldly existence?

Śrīdhara: Therefore, who indeed—save for one who is no better than a beast (naretara)—could ever become weary of or cease from drinking in, in some way or another, the ancient stories of past events? ||50||
The sequential composition: And thus, that very story becomes impossible for them to abandon, like a stream of nectar; he expresses this by way of contrast with the verse beginning "Who... (50).

Viśvanātha: One who knows that devotion alone is the great fruit of all human goals (puruṣārtha) is called a "knower of the essence. However, one who explains that devotion is merely a means to achieve human goals and is not itself the form of the fruit is indeed a beast; thus he says: "Who indeed... regarding the ancient stories.

"Among those who have lived before, who else but a non-human beast would feel detachment from that which destroys existence and annihilates saṃsāra? Oh, what a marvel! He is indeed a beast! Thus tormented repeatedly by the flow of tears born of longing, he slowly withdraws even that hook of the mind.
The state of being a bound soul (paśutva) has been indicated for the yogin whose characteristics will be described hereafter. ||50||
Thus ends the thirteenth [chapter] of the third [section], appropriately joined for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus ends the third book in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, which is the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the glorious Mahāpurāṇa, the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.
In the Dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Lifting of the Earth," ends here.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Śrī Śuka spoke regarding the impregnation of Devakī:
Having heard what was described by Kauṣārava, [Devakī...]
With palms joined in reverence, Vidura— steadfast in his vows and not yet satiated— again questioned him concerning the narrative of Hari, who had assumed the form of the causal Boar.
Śrīdhara:
In the fourteenth [chapter], the motive for his killing is stated;
it is said that at twilight, Diti’s conception of a child from Kaśyapa occurred out of desire.
Regarding the sequence of composition: "by that very same [means]" means by that very same means by which he upheld the earth in the Svāyambhuva and Cākṣuṣa manvantaras. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the fourteenth [chapter], Diti desired the sage at evening against his will;
she repented, thinking, "I have become the mother of wicked sons and the granddaughter of the virtuous."
The word "ca" has the sense of "eva" (only/indeed). ||1||
Vidura said:
O best of sages, by that very Hari, who is the embodiment of sacrifice, [the world was sustained].
We have heard that the primordial Daitya, Hiraṇyākṣa, has been slain.
Śrīdhara: We have heard from your own lips that very [hand] by which the earth was lifted up. (2)
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: It should be explained that by that very same Hari who lifted up the earth during the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara], Hiraṇyākṣa was slain during the Cākṣuṣa [Manvantara]. ||2||
And why, O Brahmin,
did a battle occur between him, who was lifting the earth with the tip of his own tusk as if in play,
and the king of the Daityas?
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: *mṛdha* means battle. ||3||
The sequence of composition: in the phrase "and of that" (*tasya ca*), the word *ca* has the sense of "again" (*punar*). ||3||
"O Sage, speak at length of his birth to me, who am faithful and devoted;
my mind is not yet satiated, for my curiosity is great."
It was not explained by anyone.
Maitreya said:
Excellent, O hero! You have asked well concerning the incarnations of Hari, which you inquire about as that which cuts through the noose of death for mortals.
Śrīdhara: The reason for his goodness is that you ask about the narrative of the incarnations of Hari;
thus, he is one who "shatters," that is, releases, the noose of death. ||5||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: O Hero! This question asked by you, who desire to hear the war-play of Hari, is excellent; for under the guise of this inquiry, you ask about the stories of the two incarnations, Varāha and Nṛsiṃha.
Because those two [the Lord and the Goddess] appear when the cause of enmity is mentioned, he says "of mortals" (martyānām) in order to fulfill the purposes of others as well. ||5||
When the boy Yayāti, son of Uttānapāda, was sung of by the sage,
he placed his foot upon the head of Death and ascended to the abode of Hari.

Śrīdhara: He demonstrates that very point. By means of which narration [is it told how] Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, while still a mere child, was addressed by the sage Nārada? Thinking that if a celestial chariot were brought for Dhruva by Sunanda and others at that time, he might expect to abandon his body, [Nārada] did not allow him to leave his body even when death was imminent.
He abandoned it; however, as if on a staircase, having placed his foot upon its summit, he ascended the celestial chariot and reached the abode of Viṣṇu. For it will be said:
"Having circumambulated and worshipped that foremost of dwellings, and having had the benediction performed for him by the twice-born..."
"He desired to preside over that, assuming a golden form" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.12.29); such is the sequence of the text.

By her, through whose power, even as a mere child, being ever-present, he ascended to the station of Hari at the time of death—even while casting off the body—as if placing his foot upon the very head of Death. However—

In this context, "childhood" (arbhakatva) should be understood as youth (kiśoratva). It is established by reasoning that the hearing [of the Veda] occurred after he had attained kingship, because one of an age suitable for kingship requires necessary [qualifications], and also because of the mention of the birth of sons and so forth. ||6||
Viśvanātha: Regarding the statement that "only the narration of Hari's deeds is the savior of the world," he provides the proof:

by means of which narration [the Lord stood] upon the head of Death. Having learned that it was Dhruva’s time of death, as soon as Death arrived, Sunanda and others brought a celestial chariot (vimāna); yet Dhruva was searching for a staircase to ascend it.

Seeing Death standing there, he thought, "This is a blessing," and placing his foot upon Death's very head, he ascended a celestial chariot without even leaving his body and went to the abode of Viṣṇu. ||6||
Now, in this regard, this ancient history has been heard by me as described formerly by Brahmā, the god of gods, to the gods who questioned him.
Śrīdhara: He introduces a historical narrative (itihāsa) to explain the cause of their conflict—beginning with "atha" [verse 1].
This history, described by Brahmā to the gods who were inquiring about it, has been heard by me. (7)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [This was spoken] by me in connection with the gods who were questioning me. ||7||
O steward! Diti, the daughter of Dakṣa, afflicted by desire and longing for offspring, took pleasure in Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, as her husband at the time of twilight."
Having worshipped the Lord of Yajus-mantras, Agni-jihva Puruṣa,
with milk while he sat composed in the fire-chamber as the sun was setting, [he attained his goal].

Śrīdhara: To introduce the inquiry of the gods, he first relates the context of the birth of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu, beginning with the words "Diti" and continuing until the end of the chapter. [He refers to] Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci. "Hṛcchaya" means desire; she was afflicted by that.

Therefore, she desired him during the twilight (*sandhyā*) alone. That too was in the *agnihotra* hall; even there, he was composed in meditation. He whose tongue is fire—the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*), Lord of the *yajus* sacrifices, Śrī Viṣṇu. This concludes the couplet concerning Diti. 8.

Viśvanātha: To introduce the inquiry of the gods, he first describes the occasion of the birth of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu, beginning with the words "Diti" and continuing until the end of the chapter. [He refers to] Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci. [She was] afflicted by a desire in her heart.

Afflicted by desire, she went there at twilight itself; even there, into the fire-sanctuary (*agnihotra-śālā*), and even there, to him who was concentrated—having performed his meditative absorption—at twilight, that is, precisely at the time when the sun sets.
[She approached] Viṣṇu, the Lord of the *yajus* sacrifices, whose tongue is fire. ||8||
Diti said:
"O learned one, for your sake this Kama stands before me with his bow drawn."
Having displayed his prowess, he torments the wretched woman as an elephant torments a plantain tree.
Śrīdhara: He will say, "the wretched one who speaks much" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.14.16).

In that context, her wretchedness (*kārpaṇya*) is described by the two verses beginning with "this [man] to me," and her excessive talking (*bahubhāṣaṇa*) is described by the four verses beginning with "O husband.
*Dunoti* means it torments or afflicts. *Vikramya* means having manifested valor. *Rambhām* means a plantain tree.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "This [man] is me"—when the husband has his eyes closed, both physical and visual [expressions] are entirely ineffective during the act of union;
likewise, among verbal expressions, those arising from words and those arising from meaning [are likewise ineffective].
They are suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*). Since they find no room at all in Kaśyapa, whose intellect is fixed upon the Supreme Lord,

even though it is not the natural disposition of noble women to express a desire for sexual enjoyment toward a man directly, nevertheless, Diti, maddened by the torment of the god of love, seemed to swallow her shame and apprehension.

She spoke aloud for the sake of breaking his concentration, meaning: "He appears as if seen directly before me. By saying "for your sake," she placed the blame on her husband himself, implying: "If I had remained alone, what would he have done to me? [The word *dahati*] means "it burns"; thus, how is it that you, my husband, do not [protect] me?
The sense is that she is a *rākṣasī* (demoness). Now, one might ask: "How could you suddenly cast aside your shame? To this he replies:
"Like Rambhā. The sense is: if even one's very life-breaths are perishing, then what is the use of shame? ||10||
Therefore, while my co-wives— who possess children— are being consumed by envy at their own prosperity, may you, may blessings be upon you, bestow your favor upon me.
Śrīdhara: "Āyuṅktām" means may he join [them] from all sides; "yunaktu" means may he perform it correctly. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: And it is not only I who, afflicted by desire, entreat for sexual union; rather, she says "that" (*tat*) to show that even one seeking a son [entreats]. Let him "unite" (*āyuñjītām*), meaning let him act in every way. ||11||
The fame of those women who possess great respect for their husbands enters the worlds;
indeed, it is through their offspring that a husband such as you is born.

Śrīdhara: For women who have attained great honor from their husbands, their fame pervades and fills the worlds through their progeny in the form of sons; for there is a Vedic revelation: "She becomes a wife (jāyā) because [the husband] is born again (jāyate) in her. (12)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "May I become illustrious and possessed of sons through your grace"—thus she says. "From the husband" means from the presence of the husband; [this refers to] women who have received great honor.

"Fame pervades the worlds through progeny in the form of sons; for according to the Vedic revelation, 'She is called a wife (jāyā) because she is born again (jāyate) from him. Or rather, the meaning is: since a husband such as you is himself born—that is, brought into being—by means of progeny, how could I not be one who possesses progeny? ||12||
In ancient times, our father, the venerable Dakṣa, who was deeply affectionate toward his daughters,
asked each of us individually, 'Dear children, whom do you choose as a husband?'"
Śrīdhara: Our father questioned us individually.
The implication is this: although the disposition toward you is equal among all thirteen of us, it is unbecoming of you to act with partiality. ||13||
The sequential arrangement: by repeating the word "sa" (he/that), the sense of the dative case and the sense of the genitive case are to be applied. ||13||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, she says "purā" (formerly), meaning: even before the marriage, I ought not to have been one whose words were rejected by you as being full of passion for another. Our father did not ask us. ||13||
Having understood the disposition of his daughters— who were cultivating their mental continuums—
he bestowed upon those thirteen of them who were devoted to virtuous conduct.
Śrīdhara: *Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that even though we were not uttering your name out of shame, he suddenly knew it through our gestures alone by means of another person; [he knows] those daughters.
The meaning is that, being among those thirteen, how can it be that I alone am childless? This disparity is improper. ||14||
Now, O lotus-eyed one, fulfill my auspicious desire;
for the approach of the distressed toward a Great Being, O Abundant One, is never in vain.
Śrīdhara: Indeed, it does not go in vain, for [this is] toward one as great as you, the most exalted. (15)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, [one might object]: "Since you strive to break my meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for the sake of your own pleasure in the evening, how can you be said to possess a disposition equal to mine? To this he replies: "By the affliction of the distressed" (*ārtopasarganam*). Is it not the case that I am currently distressed?
"I shall do it"—the sense is that you, being supremely compassionate, surely know the scriptural principle that "one who is distressed does not wait for the [proper] time. ||15||
"O hero! Thus did Mārīca address that miserable woman, who spoke much and was overwhelmed by the affliction of love,
consoling her with his words."
Śrīdhara: [He refers to her] whose delusion—that is, infatuation—has been intensified by the god of love. ||16||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "O hero! Just as there is no one like Kaśyapa who is a hero of righteousness (*dharmavīra*) such as you, he replies while merely conciliating him—and not threatening him with an angry sidelong glance—if...

The sense is that had she displayed even feigned anger, her internal torment of love would have been suppressed by fear. By the word "increased" (*pravṛddha*), the meaning is that one who is reeling from the god of love cannot endure conciliation. ||16||
O timid one, I shall fulfill for you whatever dear wish you desire;
for who would not grant her that wish, since from it comes success in the three aims of life?"
Śrīdhara: The praise of the wife for the purpose of evading the time of twilight—by means of these five verses beginning with "This one" (eṣa). From whom: from her presence. ||17||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon. *Viśvanātha*: "This I am yours. It should be understood that this composition of many words by Kaśyapa was merely for the purpose of passing the evening. ||17||
Having taken up all stages of life, one who possesses a wife through his own stage of life crosses over the ocean of calamities, just as one crosses the sea by means of watercrafts.
Śrīdhara: "Having taken up all the stages of life"—the meaning is that by delivering even those [others] from distress through the giving of food and so forth, he himself crosses over. ||18||

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] is as follows: "all stages of life" (*sarvāśramān*). Since even the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) arises from the householder alone, Viśvanātha explains: "all stages of life" means that by rescuing all four stages of life through the giving of food and so forth—even with difficulty—he himself crosses over. ||18||
O proud woman, they say that she is indeed half of one’s own self for a man who desires his own welfare;
by placing his burden upon her, a man moves about free from anxiety.

Śrīdhara: [She is] half of one’s own body, because both [husband and wife] have joint authority over ritual acts (*karma*). The connection with the word *yad* (which) is with the third verse, [ending in] *tāṃ tvām*.
"One's own burden" (*svadhuram*) refers to the weight of actions pertaining to the seen and the unseen. "Free from fever" (*vijvaraḥ*) means free from anxiety. ||19||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: That woman who is half of one's own body, according to the Vedic scripture stating, "This wife is indeed half of one's self";
[he entrusted] his own burden, the weight of actions pertaining to both the seen and the unseen worlds. ||19||
Relying upon which we may conquer, with ease, the enemies of the senses that are difficult for other stages of life to defeat,
just as a lord of a fortress conquers bandits.

Śrīdhara: "By playful movements" means by graceful sports. Regarding "we shall conquer": the sense is that the senses of [the Lord] together with His wife generally do not wander here and there. ||20||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "The lord of the fortress" (*durgapati*). For bandits indeed plunder people only by taking refuge in a fortress; the meaning is: how can they prevail there against one who is the lord of the fortress?

In this context, the "difficult path" (durga) refers specifically to the enjoyment of sensual objects. It is those who have fallen from the state of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth due to fate who fall away there, but not householders; for since their specific enjoyments are sanctioned by the scriptures, they do not produce adverse karmic results (*duradṛṣṭa*). ||20||
"O mistress of the house, neither we nor others who are greedy for virtues could possibly imitate you, even with our entire lifespans."

Śrīdhara: Even those like you are not capable—that is, not able—to fully reciprocate for you, who have performed so many acts of kindness, through their own counter-services; nor are others, even those who are greedy for virtues and lovers of merit, capable of doing so, even with a complete lifespan. This is because of the word "vā" (or/even).
It has been stated that there is no power [to act] even through other births. ||21||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Thus, by relying on a woman alone, even a householder enjoys sense objects with ease and does not fall into hell, whereas one who is dispassionate [does not]. Therefore, [I address] you, that well-known [woman].
We men are not capable of imitating the female sex or becoming like them through such acts of service; "even with the entirety of one's lifespan" means even with a full life;
and by the word "or," it is implied that this would hold true even over the course of other births, as well as for those other guests who are seekers of virtue.

He perceives their virtues; however, in this context, irony is suggested by the use of the singular "you" (*tvām*) alongside the plural "we" (*vayam*), as well as by the address "O long-lived one" (*āyuṣe*) and so forth. ||21||
Nevertheless, I shall gladly do this for you for the sake of progeny;
wait but a moment so that they may not outshine me.

Śrīdhara: Although it is impossible for you to imitate [me], [this is] for the sake of progeny, that is, for the birth of a son. They do not find it pleasing, nor do they censure it. Wait; bide your time. ||22||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thus, although imitation of you is impossible, let me first remain as I am and fulfill this desire for procreation—that is, for the birth of a son. Surely, enough with this verbal display; there is no need for delay.
Because of his endurance of suffering, he quickly entered the bedchamber; regarding this, it is said: "They do not exult, nor do they revile; wait, bide your time. (22)
This is the most terrible hour, fearsome to behold even for the terrible ones;
it is in this hour that the beings who follow the Lord of Beings roam about.

Śrīdhara: Frightening her who disregarded his own censure, he describes Śrī Rudra with seven verses beginning with "eṣā": "This is the hour of the terrible ones; and she herself is of terrible appearance. (23)

The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained. Viśvanātha, instilling fear in her who disregards censure, describes Śrī Rudra with seven verses beginning with "eṣā": she in whom the sight of the terrible ones exists, and for that very reason, she is most terrible (*ghoratamā*).
The phrase "of the terrible ones" (ghorāṇām) means "those whose master is Ghorā. He states who these terrible ones are with the words beginning with "they move" (caranti). ||23||
"O virtuous lady, during this twilight, the Blessed One, the creator of beings and king of spirits,
surrounded by a host of spirits, wanders about upon his bull."
Śrīdhara: "By the assemblies of spirits" means by the hosts of elemental beings. ||24||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Disregarding even the living beings, she speaks again: "In her... (24).
Grey with the dust and smoke from the winds of the cremation ground’s wheel,
his mass of matted locks is scattered with flickering flashes of light.
The god, whose stainless golden body is enveloped in ashes,
beholds you, O best of gods, with three eyes.

Śrīdhara: If it is argued that, in that case, one should merely avoid being directly in front of him, he says in response: "He whose mass of matted hair (*jaṭākalāpa*) is smoky (*dhūmra*), scattered (*vikīrṇa*), and radiant (*vidyota*) with the dust of the whirlwind (*cakrānila*) that is in the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*); [he who is] covered with ashes (*bhasmanāvaguṇṭhaḥ*)."
The god, whose stainless body is covered like gold, beholds with three eyes—the moon, the sun, and fire;

this [phrase] is to be supplied (anuṣaṅga) in the following three verses as well. Since the sons-in-law of one man are addressed to each other as "brothers," [the speaker says] "this is my brother" and "he is your husband's younger brother" for the sake of modesty.
It has been said: ||25||

The Sequence of Composition: Now, how can this [man] take pleasure in association with cremation grounds and the like? If he were to take pleasure in them, then even our own wicked conduct would become pleasing. Furthermore, if he is called a "brother-in-law" (devara), then since he is just like us, why should he be an object of such great respect? To this, he says: No.

Regarding the phrase "of him" (*yasya*): the sense is that because he possesses great majesty (*mahānubhāvatva*) and is the bestower of all prosperity upon us, any disregard for him would surely result in fault. Here, the conclusion is established by resorting to one of his occasional pastimes (*līlā*), namely, [the story of] her whose enjoyments were already experienced and who was cast away at his feet, intended as an instruction for the world. ||25||

Viśvanātha: If it is argued that, in that case, one should merely avoid being in his presence, he says in response: He is one whose mass of matted hair (*jaṭā*) is smoky, scattered, dispersed, and radiant, like a whirlwind (*vātamaṇḍalī*) of dust in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). He is covered with ashes (*bhasmanā avaguṇṭha*).

The meaning is: "He whose body is stainless like gold, being such as he is, that god sees with three eyes—the moon, the sun, and fire; this is the fruit of our offense, and he will surely give it to us immediately. And he says "devara" (brother-in-law) to show that he is neither unrelated to him nor even unknown to him.

Thus, the sons-in-law of one man are addressed to each other as "brothers. Therefore, the sense is: "How are you not ashamed that he is my brother and you are his brother-in-law (devara), or that you are mine? ||25||
He for whom there is no one in the world, whether kinsman or stranger, who is not highly esteemed, nor anyone who is to be censured.
Alas, we who through our vows hope for the unborn, yet have already experienced the enjoyments cast off by her feet!

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "Even so, he would surely forgive everything regarding his own kin, who are to be respected for their greatness. To this, he says: "For him, there is no 'own kin' and so forth, because of his equanimity, which is like that of the Lord.
He describes that very sovereignty: "By that foot with which [the world] was cast away, abandoned from afar like a used garland (*nirmālya*)."
Having worshipped Him through vows, we pray for that great grace—the manifestation consisting of Māyā, who is unborn and whose enjoyments have been experienced. 26.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, although I, being distressed, have indeed offered a libation of water out of shame and fear, you too should not be afraid in this matter; for you are my own kin, who ought to be honored for your greatness.
"May that Lord indeed forgive everything"—to this he says: "Of whom there is no...

The sense is that because of his lordship, he is equal toward all, and thus has no one as his own or as his kinsman. He describes that very sovereignty: by which foot the Unborn One (Ajā) was cast away, like a used garland, abandoned far off after her enjoyment had been exhausted.
We pray for that divine manifestation and great grace; even therein, by means of our vows, we remain desirous, meaning that we partake only of the food that is the remnant of that [grace]. ||26||
Whose blameless conduct the wise praise, desiring to pierce the veil of ignorance.
Although he had cast aside all equality and superiority, he himself practiced the conduct of a *piśāca*, for such is the way of the virtuous.

Śrīdhara: He says with two verses that one should not mock him by calling him a "piśāca" (demon) for renouncing pleasures that are not forbidden. [He describes] his conduct, which is blameless and free from attachment to sense objects; those who desire to break it are those wishing to destroy it. ||27||
The sequential arrangement: having demonstrated the loathsomeness of the body, it serves as an instruction for specific individuals that one must remain established in the Self. ||27||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But surely I know all the virtuous conduct of him as well—he who, being naked, always remains in union with a woman, and whose ornaments are funeral ashes and bones. To this, [the Lord says]: "O evil-minded Diti, listen from me to the truth regarding his conduct."

He said: "The conduct of one that is indeed irreproachable and beyond criticism—all that the wise praise with reverence; the meaning is that they thereby become liberated from saṃsāra. [The term] *nirasta* [is used] because of his identity with the Blessed One (*bhagavat*). Alternatively, it means that by virtue of his equality—that is, by possessing qualities of equality—the superiority [of others] has been cast aside.
Those unfortunate ones indeed laugh at the desired conduct of one who finds delight in his own self and is unaware [of worldly things].
By those very clothes, garlands, ornaments, and ointments with which the food of dogs was cherished as their own self.
Śrīdhara: "The desired" means the intended purpose, which consists of instructing the world. "The ignorant" refers to those who lack knowledge;

or alternatively, it means "of him from whom no other is wise," that is, of the Omniscient One. He speaks of the unfortunate ones with the words "by whom": "the food of dogs" means a body fit to be eaten by dogs. This [body] is regarded as one's own self.
[This is] by means of the cognition "this is the self. ||28||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* states: By means of the vision of non-difference from the Supreme Lord, [the author] speaks of Brahmā and the others as "incarnations of qualities" (*guṇāvatāra*).

Viśvanātha explains that the meaning is: "mocking" (*viḍambana*) refers to the imitation of future states of the body, which serves to awaken dispassion (*vairāgya*). Regarding those who revile [these incarnations], he says "they laugh" (*hasanti*), implying that they remain bound in *saṃsāra*.
"Unfortunate" means they are not objects of compassion for anyone. They are ignorant of the desired intention of one who is devoted to Śrī Kṛṣṇa within their own self; and that desire is as follows:
"Excellent perfumes, flowers, garments, ornaments, and so forth are worthy only of my Lord, the Blessed One."

Thinking, "Since these were given to him, I shall not enjoy them," those unfortunate ones have cherished their own bodies— which are but food for dogs, fit only to be eaten by dogs— with clothes and other things, under the delusion that "this very thing is the self. (28)
Brahmā and the others are the guardians of the boundaries established by Him;
for this entire universe is His cause and is indeed Māyā.
Even the practice of a Piśāca is obedient to his command;
oh, how the conduct of the All-pervading Lord is a mockery!
"Rudra performed the conduct of a Piśāca solely by the command of Viṣṇu;
Viṣṇu acted as a mimic for the sake of slaying the pregnant woman," so it is said in the Vārāha Purāṇa. (29)

Śrīdhara says: "Aha! His conduct is inconceivable. He explains: by whom Brahmā and the others were created, and who maintain their respective boundaries and offices; he who is the cause of all; by whom this universe was made; and whose very Māyā obeys his command—the mockery of such an All-pervading Supreme Lord is indeed inconceivable.
The meaning. ||29||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding that, he says—"Who are we wretched ones before Viśveśvara?"—referring to those who, even though created by Him, [observe] the boundaries (*setu*) consisting of the evening [rituals], women, all virtues, food, one's own offspring, renunciation, and so forth.

They protect [the world]. For that which is the cause of something, and upon which even its illusion depends—even for such a being, oh, how strange is this demon-like behavior! Therefore, every action of the all-pervasive Supreme Lord is merely a mockery, a mere imitation. ||29||
Maitreya said: Thus addressed by her husband, she, her senses agitated by the god of love, spoke.
She took the garment of the brahmin seer, shameless as a low-caste woman.
Śrīdhara: Even though it has been thus made known—that is, informed—by her husband Nirūpaka, she acts like a *vṛṣalī*, that is, like a prostitute. ||30||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Even though it has been thus made known or informed by the Lord; or rather, "by the Lord" being the cause, even though it has been thus informed, [she behaves] like a *vṛṣalī*, that is, like a prostitute.
Desire devours its own solitude, as has been shown by others;
in this matter, the authority is Brahman itself, which declares that for a man, women are [like] Diti. (30)
Having understood his wife's persistence in that improper act,
he bowed to destiny and sat down with her in private.
Śrīdhara: "In forbidden action" means in prohibited action. "To Diṣṭa" means to the Lord in the form of destiny (fate).
"He sat down near her" indicates sexual intercourse. ||31||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "Diṣṭāya" means for his own unseen destiny; "upaviveśa" means he took pleasure [in her]. ||31||
Then, having touched water, restrained his breath, and controlled his speech,
he meditated and recited the stainless Brahman, the eternal light.
Śrīdhara: Having sipped water and bathed, while meditating upon the eternal Brahman—the stainless light denoted by the word *bharga*—he recited the Gāyatrī, the Praṇava, or both. (32)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Having touched water—that is, having bathed and sipped water—he muttered the *praṇava* or the *gāyatrī*. ||32||
But Diti, O Bhārata, ashamed by that blameworthy deed,
approached the brahmin-sage and spoke with her face cast downwards.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: "By the fault of action" means by the defect of karma. ||33||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained. —
Diti said:
"O Brahmin, may the bull among beings, Rudra— the lord of creatures— to whom I have committed an offense, not destroy this embryo of mine."

Śrīdhara: "May he not disregard me; may he not kill me"—this is the meaning. He states the seed of the suspicion regarding his slaughter: "O Rudra. "Aṃhasam" means I have committed the offense of *aṃhas*. ||34||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "He did not strike" means "may he not kill. ||34||
Homage to Rudra, the great god, the fierce, the bountiful,
the auspicious one who has laid down his staff, yet who wields the staff of wrath.
Śrīdhara: He is Rudra because he causes that suffering (*rud*) to flow away (*drāvayati*);
to him, the fierce (*ugrāya*), who is not to be transgressed; to the bountiful (*mīḍhuṣe*), who pours forth fruits for those with desires;
to Śiva for those without desires; in reality, to him who has laid down the rod of punishment; and to the wrath (*manyave*) that wields the rod against the wicked at the time of dissolution.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: She bows down, full of remorse: "To Rudra, who will cause me to weep; or rather, by his grace, will my *rut*—my crying—be *drāvita*, that is, removed? For [he is] the Great God."
Is he to forgive my offense? Or is he fierce, and will he destroy this embryo of mine?

Or is he the Bountiful One, who will sprinkle the tree of my heart’s desire with the nectar of compassion, since he is auspicious and has cast aside his rod of punishment? Or is he one who wields the rod, and will he punish me, since he is wrathful?
To the one whose very nature is wrath. ||35||
May that Lord Bhāma, who bestows grace upon the entire world, be gracious to us;
for even toward women who are objects of compassion, the divine husband of Satī is merciful— even to a hunter.

Śrīdhara: *Bhāma* means the husband of a sister. He is one whose grace is vast (*uru-anugraha*), even toward a pitiless hunter. By the phrase "the husband of a virtuous wife" (*satī-pati*), he indicates that [the Lord] himself understands the nature of women. (36)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thus, while still in a state of doubt, she praises [the Lord], displaying her own wretchedness, and therefore prays for fearlessness from him. *Bhāma* means the husband of a sister (*bhaginīpati*). He is one whose grace (*anugraha*) is vast (*uru*).

This indicates that he himself knows the nature of women—that even for a woman whose husband is a pitiless hunter, he remains her "husband of a virtuous wife" (satīpati). Alternatively, the sense is: "Out of consideration for Satī, let him not punish me, her sister," or rather, "Let that Satī wipe away my offense. ||36||
Maitreya said: To her, who was trembling and seeking a blessing for her own creation that would be beneficial to the world, [he spoke].
Having completed his evening twilight rituals, Prajāpati said to his wife:
Śrīdhara: [He gave] the auspicious blessing for his own creation, that is, his own progeny, which is worthy of both worlds; he from whom the observance performed at twilight had ceased. ||37||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [She is] worthy of her own creation, that is, her own lineage, in both worlds (lokyaṃ). ||37||
Kaśyapa said:
"Because of the impurity of your own self, as well as because of these momentary faults..."
Through transgressing the commands of one's father and through extreme disrespect toward the gods.

Śrīdhara: Because of the impurity—that is, the lack of cleanliness—of their own minds; because of the momentary [nature] of the twilight; and furthermore, because of the transgression—that is, the violation—of my command, [the wrath of] the gods who are the followers of Rudra [is unleashed]. ||38||
The sequence of composition: the pair beginning with "due to impurity" [refers to the following]. A *muhūrta* is of the nature of the twilight; [the fault arises] from that occurring. (38)

Viśvanātha: Because of the impurity—that is, the lack of purity—of your own mind, you two are cruel-minded. You are "terrible" due to the nature of that hour, which is the Sandhyā; and because the Sandhyā consists of two *ghaṭikās*, you two are "twofold. [This is so] by the transgression—that is, the violation—of my instruction, my word of command.

And because they have broken the boundaries of dharma and have shown contempt for the gods, the Śrī Rudras, they are haters of the Blessed One. O inauspicious woman! The sense is that misfortunes shall surely befall you and your two sons.
O wicked woman, two most wretched sons shall be born to you;
O fierce one, they will repeatedly cause the three worlds, along with their guardians, to cry out in distress.
Śrīdhara: By these four reasons, the two sons are the lowest of the stomach-born and the basest of offspring. O Caṇḍī, O wrathful one! ||39||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "The two born from his belly" (*jāṭharau*) means those inferior sons produced from his abdomen; thus, [the world] from both individual and collective defects, etc. "O Caṇḍī," even in my words of dharma, that which was done by you—
"You have committed an act of extreme violence; enjoy its fruit!"—by saying "you are indeed a mine of lust and anger," Kaśyapa's wrath toward her was clearly manifested. (39)
When living beings are being slaughtered, when the wretched are innocent of any offense,
when women are being seized, and when the great-souled ones have been provoked to anger.
Śrīdhara: Of the virtuous beings who are being slain. ||40||

The sequence of the composition: "of living beings" constitutes a pair of verses. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when [the Lord] was about to cause the worlds to cry out, then, while living beings were being slain and women were being seized, and while the Great-Souled Ones were enraged—[this is the connection]. (40)
Viśvanātha: If one asks how long their lifespan is, he says, "Listen," beginning with the words "of living beings" (*prāṇinām*), which means "among living beings. ||40||
Then the Blessed Lord Viśveśvara, the creator of the worlds, being enraged,
will descend and slay him, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt strikes down mountains.
Śrīdhara, the wielder of the hundred-jointed [thunderbolt], the bearer of the vajra, Indra. ||41||
Kramasandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Like Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt who bears a hundred [cities] before him. ||41||
Diti said:
"O Blessed One, [grant] my death at the hands of you yourself, whose navel is beautiful and whose arms are noble."
O Lord, I pray that my two sons may not suffer from the wrath of this Brahmin.

Śrīdhara: He whose noble arm is adorned with a beautiful navel (the Śārṅga bow). Having been told, "On the earth, among those provoked by me," she, her heart filled with apprehension, makes this request so that [harm] may not come to the brahmins. ||42||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By him whose arm is noble with the beautiful-naved discus;
[the meaning is] "my two sons shall see that exceedingly beautiful arm of his being raised up"—thus, they are indeed fortunate.

"Two sons shall be born to me; and although death is inevitable, my liberation from all sins shall come through their hands. I hope—I desire—that they may deliver even me. Thus, as the mother of such sons, I too—during the course of my life—[shall be delivered].
"Even though I have not beheld the form of the Blessed One, through my connection with my son, I shall consider myself as one who has seen the Blessed One;

yet, I do not hope for death at the hands of an angry Brahmin. By your words, "When the Great-Souled Ones are provoked," my mind is filled with apprehension that my two sons will die from a Brahmin’s curse, and thus I am truly distressed.
The sense is: "Having heard that my death was now at the hands of the Blessed One, I have become steady-minded; [O] Ākhidya! ||42||
Neither for one consumed by the staff of Brahmā nor for one who causes fear to living beings do the denizens of hell show favor,
regardless of whatever womb that person may enter.
Śrīdhara: Likewise, even those in the hells do not favor him—that is, they do not show compassion—whichever womb he has entered while residing there. ||43||
The sequence of composition: they do not bestow grace, nor do they permit going near them and so forth. ||43||

Viśvanātha: Because [of the statement] beginning with "not Brahman," the two genitive endings are used in the sense of the accusative. Even a denizen of hell likewise—whichever womb he enters—he does not receive grace while remaining there. 43.
Kaśyapa said:
"By immediately reflecting upon the remorse for the grief already felt,"
Because of her great pride toward the Blessed One, and out of respect for me as well.
Śrīdhara: [The grief] arises from the offense committed; from that, sorrow; from that, remorse;
