and from "pratyavamarśana," which is the deliberation on what is appropriate and inappropriate, toward the Blessed Lord Hari and Bhava, Śrī Rudra—by these five causes. ||44||
The composition of the sequence: "it was done," [amounting to] one and a half [verses]. ||44||

Viśvanātha: [The state of being] "stained" (*eta*) arises from five causes: the offense committed, the grief resulting from it, the remorse resulting from that, and the subsequent reflection upon them. (44)
And there shall be one among the sons of that very son who is esteemed by the virtuous;
they shall sing his pure fame, which is equal to the fame of the Blessed One.

Śrīdhara: Among the sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s son, one will be esteemed by the virtuous. He describes that very person with five and a half verses beginning with "gāsyanti. *Samam* means together, along with, or similar. (45)
The sequential arrangement: "They shall sing"—this consists of three and a half [verses]. ||45||
Viśvanātha: Among the sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s son, one will be esteemed by the virtuous; indeed, the virtuous alone shall sing of him equally, together, or in a fitting manner. ||45||
Just as gold is purified by means of various treatments,
so shall the virtuous cultivate themselves through practices such as freedom from enmity, in order to conform to their own moral discipline.

Śrīdhara: Just as base gold is purified by means such as heating through various methods, so too will they cultivate and purify themselves through methods such as freedom from enmity in order to conform to, follow, and attain his character and nature.
The sequence of composition: He states the fruit of singing his glory with the words "by means of yogas. To follow means to pursue by way of approval. ||46||

Viśvanātha: Just as gold of inferior quality is purified through processes such as heating, so too will they cultivate and purify their own selves by means of practices such as freedom from enmity, in order to follow, conform to, and attain his character and nature. ||46||
He by whose grace this universe becomes serene and who is its very self—
that Blessed One, who perceives through his own vision, is pleased by one’s gaze that is free from any other object.

Śrīdhara: That which is the cause of universal grace is of such a nature that one’s own vision is its witness. By means of such a vision—one characterized by the thought "the Blessed Lord alone is the Truth"—He is pleased; that is, He will attain satisfaction. ||47||
The sequential composition: by means of that [consciousness] which is non-different [from it], consisting of its singular manifestation. ||47||

Viśvanātha: By whose grace—that is, by reason of the favor of that Lord—this entire universe becomes gracious toward Prahlāda. Of what nature is it? It is that very Self who is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*);
as such, in the form of the inner controller, he impels the worlds in such a way that even Indra and others, who were enemies of his father, [become well-disposed].

The meaning is that she is gracious toward Prahlāda. She is "svadṛk" (seeing her own), for she looks with affection only upon her own devotees. By such a vision—that is, by such an intellect—in which there is no other, it is meant that no one else is able to enter into her intellect. ||47||
He was indeed a great devotee of the Lord, a high-souled one of great majesty, the most eminent among the great.
For, having established this Vaikuṇṭha within his heart through the power of his fully matured devotion, he will abandon this world.

Śrīdhara: The reason for this is stated in the words "He indeed" (*sa vai*). He is the Great Soul (*mahātman*), whose vision is uninterrupted; he is of great majesty (*mahānubhāva*) and great power (*mahāprabhāva*).

Among even the great, he is the greatest (*mahiṣṭha*), being exceedingly great. Having established Hari, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, within a heart that has been purified and made manifest through ever-increasing devotion, [he abandons] the conceit of the body and so forth.
He will abandon it. ||48||

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] explains the state of being a great devotee (mahābhāgavatatva) itself, from the words "the high-souled one" (mahātman) up to "whose face is adorned with earrings" (kuṇḍalamaṇḍitānanam). ||48||

Viśvanātha: [He is] the Great Soul, possessed of great fortitude and great intelligence; or he is one in whom even great states such as paralysis (*stambha*) and perspiration (*sveda*) are the very manifestations of love (*premānubhāva*). The reason for this is that his heart (*āśaya*) or mind has been made manifest—that is, brought to the state of experiencing—the mere reality residing in Vaikuṇṭha through intensified devotion.
Having established this illusory world, he will abandon it. ||48||
Free from greed, upholding moral conduct, a mine of virtues,
rejoicing in the prosperity of others, and feeling compassion for those who suffer.
He was no enemy to the world, but a remover of its sorrow, like the king of stars [the moon] dispelling the heat of summer.
Śrīdhara says: He describes the state of being a great devotee (mahābhāgavata) with the words "free from greed" (alampaṭa). Śīladhara means one of good character.

An "ākara" of qualities such as fortitude and so forth means the place of their origin. "Delighted by the prosperity of others" means [joyful] when others are in a state of well-being. "One for whom no enemy has arisen" (na bhūtaḥ śatruḥ yasya). "Born in the summer heat" (nidāghe bhavam)—[refers to the heat of the summer season].
Just as the moon removes heat, so shall he become the remover of the world's sorrow. ||49||
The sequential composition: the pair of verses beginning with "alampaṭa" [is verse 49].

Viśvanātha says: He spoke of devotion to Him and the great qualities arising from devotion; now he says, "Listen also to His other natural qualities that are conducive to devotion"—beginning with "free from greed. He states that these qualities are indeed impossible to describe: "a mine of qualities" (*guṇānām ākaraḥ*). Regarding the prosperity and wealth of others... [toward] others.
Just as the moon removes the heat born of the summer season for suffering beings, so shall he become the remover of the world's sorrow. ||49||
Pure within and without, the lotus-eyed one,
whose form is sustained by the will of his own person.
Your grandson shall behold the face of the illustrious ornament of women, adorned with shimmering earrings.

Śrīdhara says: He describes the state of having unbounded vision with the word "within" (*antar*). [He is one] by whom forms are repeatedly assumed at will through his own powers (*puruṣas*). Śrī herself is the beautiful woman (*lalanā*); she is the ornament (*lalāma*) of that [vision]. The seer (*draṣṭā*) shall behold her. (50)

The sequence of events: He was high-minded and profound in intellect. Thinking, "There will be enmity even with him," and that through that very [enmity] they would both be destroyed by suffering, and because of the mutual destruction of those born in happiness, [he acted]. (50)

Viśvanātha: Within, by means of meditation in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and without, directly with his two eyes, the grandson Prahlāda—the beholder—will see [Him]. Śrī herself is the woman, the beloved; He is her *lalāma*, that which serves as her ornament. (50)
Maitreya said:
Having heard that her grandson was a devotee of the Lord, Diti rejoiced greatly.
And having learned from Kṛṣṇa of the slaughter of his two sons, the high-minded one was overcome with grief.
"Worlds [attain liberation] through the slaughter by Viṣṇu’s hand [of the demon] Madhu, but never for any other devotee;
nevertheless, for the sake of deluding the asuras, it was not disclosed clearly in some places or others"—thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
And: "Hiraṇyakaśipu also [fell into] darkness due to his reviling of the Blessed One."

"Those who are inherently destined for a good state may become the cause for others, such as sons and so forth; there may be fitness through beginningless devotion. But how can there be a [good] state for one who is unfit? Thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*. (51)
Śrīdhara: The noble-minded one was full of enthusiasm, thinking that through battle with Hari, if his two sons were to die, they would attain fame and a virtuous rebirth. ||51||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He rejoiced greatly, thinking, "Alas, alas! My evil deeds will result in a fruit that is rare even for the crest-jewels of virtuous deeds; oh, what great fortune is mine!"
"O Ānanda, my two sons are high-minded; their good reputation will lead them to fortunate rebirths," she thought with an enthusiastic heart. (51)
Thus ends the fourteenth [chapter], which is well-connected for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.

Thus ends the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya in the third book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
The fourteenth chapter, titled "The Conception of Diti.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter: "The Description of Vaikuṇṭha."
Maitreya said: Diti bore that energy of Prajāpati for a hundred years, which destroys the splendor of others, fearing the torment of the gods.
Śrīdhara:
In the fifteenth chapter, Brahmā, questioned by the gods whose splendor had been destroyed, explained the cause of that—
the Brahmin’s curse and so forth— concerning Viṣṇu and his two servants in Vaikuṇṭha.
Having thus stated the introduction to the dialogue between the gods and Brahmā, he now speaks in order to relate that dialogue:

"The splendor and vigor of Kaśyapa, the son of Prajāpati, destroys the splendor of others"—so it is said. This is a Vedic usage [of the future tense]. Because he will, through his two sons, effect the "ardana," that is, the affliction or torment, of the gods; for that reason...
While walking back and forth. ||1||

The sequence of the composition: "Śaṅkamānā" means [the mother] fearing that, once the child is born from her womb, he will surely slay the destroyers of the Asuras. Regarding the commentary, although one should have said *ārṣa* for *tejoghnam*, the usage *tejohanam* is an archaic (Vedic) form; for if the suffix *ṭak* were applied according to the rule *amanuṣyakartṛke ca*, the form would necessarily be *tejoghnam*. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
Questioned by the gods regarding the truth concerning the two sons of Diti,
Brahmā spoke of the curse upon the two attendants of Viṣṇu in the fifteenth [chapter].

Then, in response to the inquiry, "What is the news regarding Diti’s womb?", he says: *prājāpatyam* means belonging to Prajāpati Kaśyapa. It is so called because it destroys (*hanti*) the splendor (*tejaḥ*) of others; the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134. She was apprehensive because of the affliction or torment of the gods (*surāṇām ardanam*). Alternatively, [it refers to] Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the Asuras (*asurārdana*), from whose hand [the child would be born].
Because of hearing about death. ||1||
Because he had struck down the light in the world, the guardians of the quarters were deprived of their luster;
they reported the pervading darkness of the directions to the Creator of the Universe.
Śrīdhara: By that embryonic splendor, the light was destroyed; the radiance of the sun and other luminaries had ceased.
"Hataujasaḥ" means those whose power and influence were struck down. "Vyatikaraṃ" refers to a state of confusion or pervasion caused by darkness. ||2||
The sequence of composition: [he] underwent a conjunction, that is, a contact, with darkness. ||2||
Viśvanātha: *tena* means "by that"; *garbhatejasā* means "by the splendor of the womb. There is also the reading *āhataloke*.
*Vyatikaram* means "pervasion" (*vyāptim*). ||2||
The gods said:
"O All-pervading Lord, you know this darkness about which we are greatly distressed."
For nothing remains unmanifest to the Blessed One, whose path is untouched by time.

Śrīdhara: Do you know? Do you understand? What are you reflecting upon? Because of this, we are agitated and afraid. It is unmanifest and unknown; its path—the range of knowledge—is not touched. ||3||
The sequence of composition: In some places it says, "Here the gods spoke. With the words beginning with "This is that," they praise Brahmā through his non-difference from the Supreme Lord. ||3||
Viśvanātha: You surely know this, because you are the Blessed One, the omniscient one, whose path of knowledge has not been obscured by time. ||3||
O God of gods, Sustainer of the world, Crest-jewel of the lords of the world! You are the knower of the nature of all beings, both those that are higher and those that are lower.

Śrīdhara: Praising Brahmā as the Supreme Lord, they pray with seven verses beginning with "O God of gods. "O crest-jewel of the lords of the worlds": you are a knower of intentions (*bhāvavit*), meaning you know with what intention the embryo of Diti is growing. ||4||
The sequence of composition: Lokapāla is the sacred forest. ||4||
Viśvanātha: O crest-jewel of the world-protectors, Indra and the others! ||4||
Homage to you whose vigor is consciousness, who have entered this world through illusion;
homage to you, the source of the unmanifest, who has assumed the distinctions of qualities.

Śrīdhara: He whose wisdom, vigor, and strength [are such]. To him who has approached—that is, attained—this body of Brahman. By whom the distinction of qualities, namely the quality of *rajas*, has been grasped. Or: he whose source (*yoni*) of the manifest phenomenal world (*vyakta-prapañca*) is the cause; or, he whose source is not manifested—that is, not known by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The sequential composition: with the words beginning with "namaḥ," there is praise through non-difference from the Supreme Lord. (5)

Viśvanātha: To him who has approached—that is, attained—this body of Brahmā; to him whose cause (yoni) is the Unmanifested Supreme Lord himself, characterized by the differentiation of the qualities (guṇas), namely rajas. ||5||
But those who, with undivided devotion, meditate upon you as their own self,
[meditate] upon the Supreme, who is the soul of both the existent and the non-existent, and in whom the worlds are woven.
For those whose yoga is fully matured, who have conquered their breath, senses, and self,
and who have obtained your grace, there is no defeat from any quarter whatsoever.

Śrīdhara: Experiencing suffering at every moment due to having desires, those who praise the disinterested devotees say the following in two verses: "Those who meditate upon you with undivided, desireless devotion (*bhāva*);
[the word] *bhāvayanti* means they nourish the individual souls (*jīva*); [the word] *protāni* means woven or strung together within yourself."
"By whom the worlds [are pervaded]" means that he is the cause of the manifold expansion of the sentient and the insentient.
The reason for this is stated: "consisting of both being and non-being"—that is, having the nature of both effect and cause—and yet, in reality, transcending both. (6)
Those by whom the breath, the senses, the self, and the mind have been conquered are those whose yoga is fully matured; it is for them alone that your grace has been obtained. //7//

The sequence of composition (*kramasaṃdarbha*): The pair of verses beginning with "But those who... [states that] for those who have obtained your grace through exclusive devotion, there follows the mastery of breath and so forth by their own accord, due to having successfully accomplished the yoga of devotion; such is the sequence. ||67||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, those who are worshippers of Hiraṇyagarbha [do so] with a "non-different" (ananya) disposition—that is, a disposition that is non-distinct from the Supreme Lord; or else, they "cultivate" or meditate with a "non-different" disposition, meaning with desireless devotion (*bhakti*). He is so called because he "cultivates" or creates the individual souls (*jīva*) of the self, owing to his being the universal aggregate (*samaṣṭi*).

[He is] that by whom the worlds are woven and spread out within himself; therefore, he is that in whom exist both the virtuous and the non-virtuous—the living beings such as gods, asuras, and others who are themselves the self.
Salutations to You, the foremost one, by whose word all creatures are restrained like cows by a rope, and who, being their master, receive their tribute.

Śrīdhara: Others, however, say that [those who perform rituals] are perpetually afflicted by the toil of action—referring to the verse beginning with "yasya" (of whom). They are "dependent" (*āyattāḥ*), meaning under the control of the "cord" (*tanti*), which is the tethering-rope (*dāmanī*). Or, it may mean for the "Chief Controller" (*mukhya-niyantre*) in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Thus says the Śruti: "His speech is the cord; names are the tethers," and so forth. (8)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: By means of speech characterized as the Veda. And thus says the Śruti: "His speech is the warp; names are the threads," and so forth. (8)
Therefore, O Lord, bestow welfare upon those on earth whose religious rites have been eclipsed by darkness;
it behoves you to look upon those who have fallen into distress with a gaze of abundant compassion.

Śrīdhara: Those whose ritual duties have been lost due to *tamas*—that is, through the absence of the distinction between day and night—[protect] us who are afflicted, that is, fallen into calamity. (9)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By "darkness" (*tamasā*), he means the absence of the distinction between day and night; [he rescued] us who had fallen [into it] with abundant compassion—that is, with non-meager mercy. ||9||
"O Lord, this embryo of Diti, the vital energy deposited in Kaśyapa,
grows like fire in fuel, shrouding all the quarters in darkness."

Śrīdhara: They say that "āpad" (calamity) is the cause; this "garbhaḥ" (womb/embryo) is its qualifier. "Arpitaṃ" means deposited or placed; "kāśyapam ojaḥ" means the vital energy or seed of Kaśyapa. "Diśas timirayan" means making the quarters of the sky pervaded by darkness. ||10||

The sequence of composition: we ask precisely about the cause of the embryo. As for the statement that "darkness was born from the embryo," we already know this; thus he says—"this. In some places, the reading is *edhate* (it increases). ||10||
Viśvanātha: Now, as for the specific news, they say regarding that: "The seed, the vital energy and prowess, deposited by Kaśyapa, became the embryo of Diti. (10)
Maitreya said: O mighty-armed one, that Blessed One, who is beyond the range of sound, laughed and spoke.
The Self-born One, pleasing the gods with his melodious voice, replied to them.
Śrīdhara: Having understood Diti’s wicked conduct and smiling, he replied, becoming the object—that is, the focus—of the words of the gods, which were their petitions. ||11||

The sequential composition: As if laughing at the children, [the author], by indicating that Brahman is not within the common range of perception through the phrase "within the scope of mere sound," reveals its majesty. ||11||

Viśvanātha: Ah! The ignorant praise me alone—laughing at them as an old man might at children, thinking, "What am I, a wretched being, to protect one from such calamity? The word *śabda* refers to the petitions of the gods; it is within their range, that is, their domain. (11)
Brahmā said:
My mind-born sons, Sanaka and the others, were born before you.
Free from longing, they traveled through the worlds by way of the sky.
Śrīdhara: They were born before you. ||12||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha says: "First, hear this ancient and wonderful story concerning the cause of this calamity"—thus he speaks in the verse beginning with *mānasāḥ*. (12)
Once, they went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, which is honored by all the worlds, belonging to the Lord Vaikuṇṭha of stainless soul.
Śrīdhara: They went to the world named Vaikuṇṭha. ||13||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Because of him, the selves—the internal organs—become stainless, that is, pure.
There dwell all those men who, having Hari as their sole motive, worshiped Lord Hari through dharma performed without any other worldly purpose.
"By offering [the fruits of action] to Viṣṇu without any motive, those who are liberated and established in their authority go to the world of Vaikuṇṭha out of detachment.
While delusion may occur anywhere for those who are not liberated, it shall never occur for those who are liberated. Thus it is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
And it is said: "The mind-born [progeny] of those whose nature is dark (kṛṣṇātman) were established.

And: "Those who are horizontal (tiraścīna), as well as all stationary beings, go to the Imperishable (vikuṇṭha) through knowledge; even those not yet liberated attain liberation upon the exhaustion of their karma by means of disciplined practice. ||14||

Śrīdhara describes them with twelve verses beginning with "vasanti": those whose forms are like that of Vaikuṇṭha, Hari; [they worship] by means of dharma that is *niṣkāma* (free from desire), meaning that in which no motive or fruit acts as an impeller; they have worshipped him, having performed *ārādhana*. ||14||

The sequential composition: Those whose forms consist of eternal bliss, like that of Vaikuṇṭha itself, dwell there. Likewise, that in which the Supreme Lord Himself—He for whom no other instrumental cause exists—is both the instrumental cause and the fruit; by means of that dharma known as Bhāgavata, they [worship] Hari.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "and they, while propitiating Him, dwell wherever [He is]. This is because of what will be stated later, such as [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.20]: "by those who have seen the feet of Hari to an exceeding degree," and [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.5.23]: "wherein they do not go," and so forth. ||14||

Viśvanātha: The forms of Vaikuṇṭha are those possessing the same form as the Lord (bhagavat-sārūpya). "Without cause" means that the absence of any personal motive is itself the cause, the impelling factor; the meaning is "by means of disinterested, supreme dharma. "Worshiping" means they have worshiped [Him] previously. ||14||
And where the Primal Person, the Blessed One who is the object of the sacred word, dwells—
the Bull who, pervading the stainless *sattva*, bestows grace upon us, his own people.

Śrīdhara: "Where" means that which is within the range of words, yet known solely through the Vedānta. "Virajam" refers to the form of pure being (*sattva*). "Viṣṭabhya" means having supported or sustained. "Vṛṣaḥ" is the embodiment of Dharma. "Svānām" means for his own people. ||15||
The sequence of composition: Having assisted the quality of *sattva* through His presence, the Bull (the Lord) rains down all bliss. ||15||

Viśvanātha: Having supported—that is, sustained—the *viraja* (dustless) *sattva*, which is *śuddhasattva* (pure goodness), meaning that everything belonging to Him—His names, forms, qualities, pastimes, and so forth—is entirely *śuddhasattva*. He is the bull (*vṛṣa*) among His own, appearing directly as the supreme form of dharma. ||15||
There lay the forest named Naiḥśreyasa, shining with trees that grant all desires and with the splendors of every season, like liberation itself embodied.

Śrīdhara: He describes the forest located there with four verses beginning with "where" (yatra). [The phrase] "by those whose beauty consists in the abundance of flowers and so forth in all seasons" refers to those [trees]. ||16||
The sequential composition: Absolute liberation is pure bliss of devotion; that very same [bliss] has become as if embodied, because it consists of that one perfection alone. ||16||

Viśvanātha: By the phrase "as if intoxicated by the state of liberation" (kaivalya), it is stated that the grove of trees is eternally perfected, consists of the supreme bliss of undisturbed uniform flavor, and is desirable even to the birds who delight in themselves. ||16||
There, the Vaimānika gods, together with their consorts, constantly sing the deeds of the Lord which destroy all impurities.
Even those whose minds were disappointed by the fragrance of the honey-sweet mādhavī flowers, which do not bloom beneath the water, now cast their anger upon the wind.

Śrīdhara: *Caritāni* means deeds or exploits. *Bhartuḥ* means of the Lord. *Anuvikasantyaḥ* refers to creepers (*latāḥ*) belonging to spring (*mādhavyaḥ*), which are full of honey (*madhu*) or nectar (*makaranda*). Alternatively, it refers to the flowers (*sumanasaḥ*) of the spring season (*mādhavyaḥ*), which bloom (*anuvikasat*) and spread (*prasarat*) nectar; [the fragrance] is that of these flowers.

Even those whose intellects were shattered and obstructed sing while casting aside—that is, disregarding—the wind that carries that fragrance. By this, it is shown that even amidst unsurpassed sensual pleasures, the attendants of the Blessed One remain attached to the bliss of worshipping the Lord. ||17||
The sequential composition describes it precisely as such with the words beginning "the celestial beings" (*vaimānikāḥ*).

By the phrase "in the midst of the water," the splendor of various groves and so forth is suggested. Because [the water] is a manifestation of the Blessed Lord’s glory (*śrībhagavad-vibhūti*), it emulates His fragrance through its own scent.

Those whose intellects were shattered by him, who produced that particular recollection, attained a delusion of supreme bliss; yet, through their grasping at the multitude of the Lord's qualities, they cast aside even that wind which carried its fragrance. ||17||

Viśvanātha: "Śamala" refers to the removal of all impurities of the living beings existing within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), while for themselves, it serves to pacify the suffering of separation from that [state]. The celestial beings (vaimānikas), in order to manifest a particular melodic tone, descended from their celestial chariots into the waters within the lake.
The meaning is "with their necks submerged in water. Alternatively,

they were deprived [of their pride] by the fragrance of honeyed mādhavī flowers— which, though blooming within the water itself, were covered with their own leaves and so forth by women standing on the bank who had climbed the branches of trees reaching into the water.

The meaning is that even those whose intellects have been obstructed in their single-minded absorption in relishing the deeds of the Blessed One nevertheless continue to sing, and do not cease from singing. However, they are fanning the wind, [crying out]:
"O you, most gentle and cool breeze, swollen with the fragrance of *mādhavī* flowers! [Delight yourself] in the sweetness of the nectar of the Blessed One’s divine play!"
"Whose mental faculties and activities have been submerged? Why do you strive to draw them out?
Do you consider yourself sweeter even than they? Thus rebuking him as a fool, [the sages] regarded him as if he were Kaivalya incarnate;
for, as previously stated, although the fragrance of the flowers in that forest and so forth are of the nature of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), [he was distinct from them].
By this implication, it is shown that even the bliss of devotion is superior to the bliss of Brahman. ||17||
He who [is the refuge] of pigeons, cuckoos, cranes, ruddy geese, gallinules, swans, parrots, partridges, and peacocks;
The clamor subsided for a brief moment while the lord of bees sang loudly, as it were, the stories of Hari.

Śrīdhara: "Anyabhṛta" refers to cuckoos; "dātyūha" refers to the cataka bird. "For only a moment" means for a mere instant. By this, it is shown that even the birds dwelling there experience supreme bliss through hearing the narrations of Hari and so forth. (18)
The sequential composition: The *dātyūha* is a water-dweller that cries out "kva-kva" during the rains;

the lord of bees (*bhṛṅgādhipa*) is a certain preeminent bee who presides over the forest garland (*vanamālā*), for he is exceedingly dear to the Blessed One, and thus by his very nature, like Śrī Garuḍa.
In those [beings], it should be understood that singing—which consists of syllables and has sound as its essence—is indeed spoken by Hari;
the word "as if" (iva) indicates a similarity to the narrations of Hari performed by His attendants and others, just as in the case of the lute and so forth. ||18||
Viśvanātha: The birds there, like those traveling in celestial chariots (*vaimānika*), are also supremely devoted and free from envy;
thus he says—*pārāvatyaḥ* are female pigeons, *anyabhṛtāḥ* are cuckoos, and *dātyūhāḥ* are known as *ḍāhukas*. *Aciramātram* means very quickly. O, now the discourse on Hari proceeds!
"Let us all, for now, simply listen in silence"— with these words, the clamor subsided. Then,

when the lord of bees, who holds the Blessed One’s forest garland as his prerogative, was humming something that was like the very essence of Hari-kathā (stories of Hari), though appearing like the distress of Hari—
sounding "hari-hari" according to the maxim of the moth's letters— how long did it last?

The meaning is that they utter sounds that do not constitute their own [proper] speech. The intention is: "I do not know what kind of respect those birds would have for him while he is directly singing the stories of Hari. ||18||
Mandāraka, kunda, kurava, utpala, campaka, arjuna, punnāga, nāga, bakula, ambuja, and pārijāta.
When the fragrance is honored by the wearing of tulasī ornaments,
the gods highly esteem the austerity performed therein.
When the Lord has been worshipped by His devotees and has placed the Tulasī garland upon Himself, they highly esteem His austerity for the sake of its fragrance. ||19||

Śrīdhara: Mandāra and Pārijāta are specific types of celestial trees (*suratru*). Kurava is the *tilaka* tree. *Utpala* is that which blooms at night; *ambuja* is that which blooms by day. *Nāga* is the *nāgakeśara*.
These various kinds of flowers (*sumanas*), though fragrant, [are surpassed] by the *tulasī* used as an ornament by Śrī Hari. By means of the *tulasī*, [he surpasses them].

When the forest in which her fragrance was honored highly esteemed her asceticism; by this it is stated that those residing there were indeed appreciators of virtue, not envious ones. The connection with the preceding verse is: "to such a forest as that, they went to Vaikuṇṭha. (19)

The sequence of composition: In this context, it is said that even immobile beings possess knowledge and praise the qualities of pleasing the Lord belonging to others—this is expressed by the verse beginning with "mandāra... (1.19). Here, "arṇa" refers to a specific type of flower, and "sumanasas" should be understood as the deities presiding over those respective flowers.

Viśvanātha: He states that even the trees there, like birds, are devoid of rivalry, envy, and the like, and are instead supreme devotees—namely, the *mandāra* and *pārijāta*, which are specific types of celestial trees (*suratru*), the *kurava* (the *tilaka* tree), the *arṇa* (a specific flower), and the *nāga* (the *nāgakeśara*); these are the trees.

Even though her flowers were supremely fragrant, when the scent of that *tulasī* was honored and respected by Śrī Hari— who wore *tulasī* ornaments while wandering in the forest— at which time he said in that very forest,
"O, you are blessed, O *tulasī*! they highly esteemed the austerity of that *tulasī* alone, and not their own.
Therefore, the inner longing of those [residents] is implied: "Since we know what her austerity is, let us go from here to the land of Bhārata and practice that very same austerity.
And thus, even the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha desire birth in the land of Bhārata; therefore, [it is superior] even to Vaikuṇṭha.

The excellence of the land of Bhārata is being extolled; the meaning is that they hold it in high esteem rather than envying it. For they are *sumanasaḥ*, meaning pure-hearted, or in the alternative sense, flowering trees. By this, the three categories—viviparous (*jarāyuja*), oviparous (*aṇḍaja*), and soil-born (*udbhida*)—are indicated through terms such as *vaimānika* (celestial beings), *pārāvata* (pigeons), and *mandāra* (the celestial coral tree).
Those who worship Hari exist [in this way], but it should be understood that the fourth type, the sweat-born (svedaja), does not arise from caste (avarṇāt). ||19||
that [city] which was crowded with celestial chariots made of lapis lazuli, emerald, and gold, whose occupants gazed solely at the prostration before the feet of Hari;
Those whose broad hips and faces graced with smiles belonged to those whose very souls were Kṛṣṇa, did not instill passion through their laughter and other such charms.

Śrīdhara: He further qualifies Vaikuṇṭha itself as being "crowded" (saṅkulam), meaning pervaded. By what? By the celestial chariots (vimānas) of devotees—seen merely by the bowing and prostration at Hari’s feet—which are made of vaidūrya, emerald, and gold, rather than those obtained through ritual actions and the like.
Those whose hips were broad, and whose faces were radiant with smiles— even they, whose very souls were fixed on Kṛṣṇa, did not arouse passion through laughter, jesting, and the like. ||20||
The sequence of the composition: they did not take up the emerald dust—that is, the dust of Vaikuṇṭha—which is itself emerald;
rather, because they too were supreme devotees, it served only to kindle their devotion.
Viśvanātha: Having described the splendor of the gardens surrounding [the city], [he now describes] that which stands in the center.

He describes the splendor of the city of Vaikuṇṭha with the words "tat" and so on. The meaning is that [Vaikuṇṭha] is seen merely by the act of bowing at Hari’s feet—even by such limited worship—and not even by complete limbs such as knowledge, ritual action, and the like. Furthermore, there, among the worlds of people who are blissfully satisfied by the joy of worship...
By the reasoning stated previously, even the bliss of Brahman is not sufficient; how much less so the bliss of sense objects?

Thus he says: "Even those most beautiful women, as vast as the slopes of millions of mountains, [are surpassed] by the smiles and other gestures of those whose souls are Kṛṣṇa and whose minds are immersed in Kṛṣṇa."
By means of their natural activities—such as superior smiles, glances, movements, and conversation—the unborn [Lord] did not at all arouse desire, nor was he agitated by them. (20)
Śrī Rūpiṇī, having abandoned all faults, was playing her lotus-feet with a toy lotus in the abode of Hari.
It is perceived as if it were a wall of crystal overlaid with gold, since no further effort is required for its cleansing.

Śrīdhara: Śrī is Lakṣmī; she is beautiful, possessing a charming form, and is seen in that world as a virtuous woman performing the sweeping in the abode of Śrī Hari. She causes her lotus-feet to tinkle by making them sound with anklets, and she is one from whom faults and fickleness have been released. Or else:
With his arm extended and freed from defects—[he asks] in what kind of dwelling? In one whose walls are made of crystal, and which is endowed with gold here and there for the sake of beauty;
[it is said] so that Śrī might bestow her favor upon the acceptance of this [dwelling], for the sake of others such as Brahmā and the rest.

That is the effort. The meaning is this: although there is indeed no dust there, nevertheless, being reflected in many ways upon the portions of the wall partitioned by the golden plates, she appears as such through her modesty and devotion while twirling her toy lotus. ||21||

The structural arrangement: This [state] is eternally free from defects, just as it is said that "this Self is free from sin" (*apahatapāpmā*). Therefore, it is that very [state] which, by its devotion, acts as the cleanser through the sense of being utterly humble, that is indicated here, and not [the state of] the beloved (*preyasī*) as previously described. As it was stated during the pilgrimage to Kurukṣetra:
Śrī Kālindī says: "I am the sweeper of that house" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.83.11). In the phrase "with the trembling lotus," the instrumental case is used in a figurative sense (upalakṣaṇe). ||21||

Viśvanātha: What need is there to say that all are possessed of the bliss of worshipping Hari? He says this in two verses, stating that even Lakṣmī herself is always present there, worshipping Him—she who is personified, endowed with supreme beauty, and making her lotus-feet tinkle with anklets as she moves with a slow gait.

In the palace of Hari, within the crystal walls interspersed with gold for the sake of beauty, she who was free from fault appeared like a broom sweeping the clear walls; for her reflection was cast upon them as she extended her arm, holding a playful lotus, like a golden broomstick.
She appears as if performing a sweeping; here, the *līlāmbuja* (play-lotus) stands in the place of the broom.

Or rather, she is like another maidservant who is actually sweeping, as it was said during the pilgrimage to Kurukṣetra: "That house is being swept. In that case, she is "muktadoṣā," meaning free from fault.
In the phrase "by the play-lotus," the instrumental case is used in a figurative sense (upalakṣaṇe); nor should she be considered as one who possesses the greatness of the Sālva king.
To this he says: she is that very one for whose favor Śrī herself bestows her grace, and for this purpose there is the effort of others, such as Brahmā and the rest. ||21||
In his own grove, amidst ponds with coral banks and pure nectar-like waters, he worshipped the Lord with *tulasī* leaves, accompanied by his female attendants.
Beholding her own face with its prominent nose, Śrī worshipped it, thinking,
"O blessed one, this is the remains of the Lord's meal."
Śrīdhara: O friends, O gods, in which world Śrī thus reflected, thought, or considered?

What was she doing? In those ponds whose banks were made of coral and whose waters were stainless and like nectar—within her own grove, the Lakṣmī-vana—she was accompanied by her maidservants and by tulasī plants.

While she was worshipping Śrī Viṣṇu, she saw her own face reflected in that water— endowed with beautiful tresses and an exquisite nose— and thought, "The Blessed One has kissed me after partaking of the remnants. By this, it is shown that even Lakṣmī’s happiness of conjugal fortune arises solely through the grace of the Blessed One.
This has been illuminated. ||22||
The sequential arrangement [of the verses] begins with "in the ponds" (*vāpīṣu*). This is because the husband alone possesses the nature of the supreme deity;

therefore, with the intention that he alone should be worshipped for the sake of attaining good fortune (*saubhāgya*), [the verse speaks of him]. Furthermore, because his manifestation occurs there through meditation by the people, and because of the union of one's own form with the perception of one's own reflection therein.

The appearance of being kissed is also consistent [with this]. Alternatively, the meaning is that she thought [the food] was "leftover" (uccheṣita) because it had been consumed (upabhukta), as she remembered it through its successive transmission from one person to the next. ||22||

Viśvanātha: Having described the devotion of service (*paricaraṇabhakti*), he now speaks of the devotion of worship (*arcanabhakti*) for that [deity], as is the case for practitioner-devotees (*sādhaka-bhaktas*): "In the ponds and long lakes with water equal to nectar, in his own forest, in the Lakṣmīvana located in a portion of the Niḥśreyasavana, [one should worship] the Lord Śrī Nārāyaṇa with *tulasī* leaves."

Desiring to perform her morning bath for worship, she first sat upon the middle of the steps to wash her face; looking down at her own reflection in the water— possessing beautiful locks of hair and an excellent nose— she beheld it, [only to find] it had been defiled by the Blessed One.
He thought, "It has been made into leavings by the kissing and drinking of her lower lip.
Or rather, having seen his own reflection merged with the reflection of a blue lotus in that water, he perceived that the Blessed One had kissed her face; thus, an outburst of emotion arose. 22.

Those whose minds are fixed on other objects do not proceed to the destruction of their sins through the exposition and recitation [of scripture], but instead listen to wicked stories that destroy the intellect.
Alas, those very scriptures which were heard by men of ruined fortune— having had their essence extracted—
cast them instead into the darkness of those who have no refuge!
The praises of Madhva are restatements [of what has already been said]. ||23||

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, of what nature is that [Vaikuṇṭha]? It is that which those do not go to who listen to wicked stories. What are those? They are stories concerning other objects, such as wealth and desire, which differ from the recounting of the *racanā*—the creative play consisting of creation and so forth—of that Hari, the destroyer of evil (*aghabhit*).

They cause the loss of intelligence. The reason they do not proceed [to heaven] is this: those [doctrines], though true, when heard by men of ruined fortune, cast them through the ear into various hells—darknesses that are refugeless and without support.
Alas, what a pity! Of what nature are they? They are those by which the essential merit of the ears is seized.
Regarding the *kramasaṃdarbha*: in the verse, "The destroyer of sins, the slayer of the demon Aghāsura—

even Agha himself had his sins washed away by the touch of whom" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.12.38), having set aside the description of what is already well-known in that context, the subject here is a different arrangement belonging to another.
"Those whose [speech] consists of those stories" means that they never listen to the stories of the Blessed One.
"In darknesses" refers to the pits of saṃsāra which are like hells. "Essence" refers to discernment and so forth. ||23||

Viśvanātha: Regarding the inquiry as to who is qualified to go there [to that state], he first states those who are unqualified: "From the recitation"—that is, from the repetitive chanting—"of the narrative of his pastimes," which is the composition of the *Śṛṅkhala* that destroys sins; [conversely,] even narratives concerning other subjects, such as those dealing with the systems of Nyāya and other sciences, [are unqualified].

Those who hear wicked stories do not go to Vaikuṇṭha. If so, where do they go? To this he says: "Those wicked stories which were heard by those whose fortune was destroyed"—thus, only those whose fortune is destroyed are qualified for that destination. Therefore, it is by men whose fortune is destroyed alone that the essence has been consumed and grasped.
Those stories, whose greatness is conceived as something to be heard, for that very reason forcibly cast those unfortunate ones into various hells of darkness. ||23||
Those who, though entreated by us, have nevertheless entered upon the human state,
wherein they possess knowledge concerning reality along with its corresponding dharma;
Alas, deluded by his far-reaching māyā, they do not offer worship to that Blessed One.

Śrīdhara: In this context, they grieve for them. Although they have attained—that is, reached—the human condition (*nṛgati*), which even we, beginning with Brahmā, have entreated [them to attain], they do not perform the worship of Hari. Of what sort is that human condition? It is one in which [there exists] dharma.
Knowledge of reality arises [for her], because she is the means of accomplishing both of those.

Alas! They have indeed been deluded by the extensive *māyā* of that Blessed One. "Alas" (*bata*) expresses lamentation. And if this is the connection: it is not only they who do not proceed, but also those who do not perform the worship of the Blessed One.
They do so because they too are deluded by their own illusion. ||24||

The sequential arrangement: "Those who have requested" means those who have reached—that is, attained—that human birth in which there exists dharma culminating in the dharma of the Lord, and in which there is knowledge of the reality culminating in the dharma of the Lord. Even though they have attained that [birth], those who...

Those who do not offer worship to the Blessed One—the root of all dharmas and all forms of knowledge—do not perform it; they are utterly deluded. As it has been said: "Alas, those who do not take refuge in the mighty strides of the Wide-Strider (Urukrama)" [Bhāgavatapurāṇa 2.3.20], and so forth. Likewise, in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
Even having attained human birth— which is most difficult to obtain and desired even by the gods—
those who have not taken refuge in Govinda have long deceived their own selves.
Having wandered through eighty-four hundred thousand births among the various classes of living beings,
those persons eventually attain human birth through the cycle of rebirth.
"Even that [knowledge] became fruitless for those wretched people who possess self-conceit,
because they did not take refuge in the two feet of Govinda.
Or rather, [he spoke of] such [a place] where all knowledge regarding various objects and every dharma was born.
Even those who have entered the human condition—who, having reached it, were indistinguishable from animals—have now been turned away [from that state]. ||24||

Viśvanātha: Alas, alas! Although only those of human birth possess the qualification to go there, and not those of divine or other births, nevertheless, even among humans, there are some whose intellects have been led astray from the true purport of the scriptures due to a lack of devotion.

He grieves for them, thinking, "They have been deceived"—referring to those who, having attained human birth on the land of Bhārata, have reached this state of manhood which even we, beginning with Brahmā, have prayed for, and who, while worshipping Kṛṣṇa, might attain [liberation] in a mere moment. Alas! When will they do so? Thus he laments for those who have obtained this human condition.

If, in whatever [state], one possesses knowledge concerning reality— that is, regarding Brahman— accompanied by dharma, yet does not offer that even as worship to the Blessed Lord, nor performs it, such persons are deluded by His māyā; for without devotion, there is no attainment of the fruit even from dharma and knowledge.
This is the state of affairs. Or rather, those who perform knowledge accompanied by religious duty (*dharma*) but do not perform worship are deluded.
Or again, they perform worship of the Lord alone but do not offer it to the Lord, because their intent is directed toward [their own] pleasure.
They do not conceptualize; thus, they are those who possess desire for devotion. ||24||
And those who, following the lead of the Bull among Sages, go to the realm of the Unblinking One,
are indeed far above us, their character worthy of our aspiration.
Their limbs were made to bristle with joy by the faltering, tear-filled emotion of their mutual longing as they spoke of their illustrious husband.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, of what nature [is it]? And that which stands above us, they go toward it. Who?

Hari, the best (*ṛṣabha*) among the gods who do not blink (*animiṣa*), by following after whom Yama is far away for them. Or rather, those for whom the restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*) have been cast far away; according to another reading, the meaning is that their egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) has been cast far away.

Those whose virtuous conduct, beginning with compassion, is worthy of longing; moreover, those whose limbs are made to bristle with horripilation along with a flow of tears born from the agitation and helplessness caused by their mutual passion for recounting the glorious fame of their Lord Hari— or rather, as an adjective qualifying "those traveling above us."
The meaning is that because they are free from egoism, even those who are superior to us depart [from this world]. ||25||
The sequence of composition: the meaning is "of those who do not blink," that is, those who are independent of time. ||25||

The *Bhagavat-sandarbha* (71) states: "Vaikuṇṭha," which is situated above us and whose nature we desire; or, those for whom Yama is far away—meaning they have rendered the observances of *yama* and *niyama* distant through their perfection—or they go [there]. By the phrase "of the husband, the mutually renowned" (*bhartur mithaḥ suyaśasaḥ*), such a [state] is indicated.

The well-known fact that devotion sets aside even the bliss of liberation has been indicated [by the verse]: "O Lord, those who have taken refuge at Your feet do not value even the ultimate [liberation], for they are skilled in and relish Your stories,
whose fame is a sacred bathing place" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 3.15.48).
On account of the statement by Sanaka and others. ||25||

Viśvanātha: Now he speaks of those who are qualified (adhikārin)—"And those... and so forth. Hari is the bull (ṛṣabha) among the immortals; those for whom Yama is far off due to their following him—or rather, those for whom the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama) have been cast far away. In the reading "dūre'ham," it means those by whom egoism (ahaṅkāra) has been cast far away. They are superior to us, being even higher than we are.

They are those whose conduct is merely to be desired by us, but not something to be attained. What is that conduct? Regarding this, he states their authority: "Of the husband and the lord," meaning through mutual affectionate discourse, because of the perception of a particular aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*). In some places...
In the Purāṇas and other texts, it is occasionally heard that certain asuras also go there;

however, because they lack the experience of the bliss of the spiritual manifestations (*cid-vibhūti*) found there, their going is effectively equivalent to not going at all— just like being in royal palaces made of jewels, though they possess various qualities such as diverse fragrances and so forth.

Just as the entry of tigers, leopards, and other such animals occurs only by the command of the king— who, out of a particular curiosity, desires to show them to the various groups of his own attendants—
so too [is it for those] who dwell in their own extraordinary, eternal abode, when they [wish to show themselves] to their own kinsmen out of curiosity.

To demonstrate various types of beings— sometimes fierce *asuras*, sometimes virtuous ones such as Bhṛgu and others, and sometimes those who have transcended the three qualities (*guṇas*) such as Sanaka and others— the Blessed One himself leads them by his own will and, because they possess the appropriate fitness, quickly extracts them from there once again.

However, it should be understood that He brings those who have attained perfection through exclusive devotion to Vaikuṇṭha by means of His own attendants and celestial chariots, and causes them to dwell there forever; He causes them alone to taste the sweetness of His own abode and the sweetness of His pastimes and so forth. ||25||

That divine [splendor], presided over by the Teacher of the Universe, uniquely worthy of worship by all worlds, and possessing the luster of the most excellent celestial chariots of the various foremost gods;
Then, having reached that unprecedented Vaikuṇṭha by the power of yogic illusion, the sages attained supreme joy.

Śrīdhara: Then, having immediately reached that unprecedented Vaikuṇṭha, the sages attained supreme and most excellent joy. The reasons for its being unprecedented are as follows: it was presided over and occupied by Hari, the teacher of the universe; it is the sole object of worship for all the worlds; and it is divine.
It is transcendent (*alaukika*). It is that in which there is the splendor—the radiance—of the various celestial chariots (*vimāna*) of the foremost gods.

"By the power of *yogamāyā*" means having approached by means of the influence of the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*); however, in the case of the Supreme Lord, *yogamāyā* should be understood as the manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). (26)

The sequence of events: [This occurred] solely through the power of the Lord's energy, by means of the force of *yogamāyā*, and not by my own power; for it was said by the Blessed Lord: "This beholding of the worlds is the result of my own desired power. (26)

Viśvanātha: Now he describes the arrival of Sanaka and the others there— "Then, having approached that Vikuṇṭha by the power of the Lord's energy, namely Yogamāyā, which acts in accordance with the Lord's will, and not by their own power, they attained supreme joy through the grace of the Lord, in a manner that was unprecedented."

They attained [it]. Here, by the two words "supreme" (parām) and "unprecedented" (apūrvam), it is shown that the joy of Vaikuṇṭha is superior even to the joy of his experience of Brahman. Of what nature is Vaikuṇṭha?
It is "directly presided over by Hari himself, the teacher of the universe"; thus, the power of his māyā has no authority here.

This is the meaning. The fact that he summoned even the sages solely out of compassion to instruct them in his own devotion is the matter suggested by the title "Teacher of the Universe. It is a place where the splendor of the various celestial chariots of the foremost gods shines forth. (26)
Having passed through those six stages without attachment, the sages, who were of equal age, then reached the seventh.
The two gods appeared, grasping their maces, adorned with the finest armlets, earrings, and crowns that served as their towering headgear.

Śrīdhara: In that Vaikuṇṭha, there were six courtyards with gates and walls. Not being attached—meaning not forming an attachment to those various wonderful sights due to their intense longing for a vision of the Lord—they beheld two divine gatekeepers who were of equal age and who held clubs in their hands.
The two of them possessed a beautiful appearance, adorned with excellent armlets and other ornaments. ||27||
The sequential arrangement: "In that" constitutes a couplet (yugmaka). ||27||
Viśvanātha: Then, having passed through the six enclosures and the gates of that Vaikuṇṭha, they are "unattached" because, from birth, they have experienced Brahman;
thus, they lack attachment to the various objects such as beauty, fragrance, and loveliness found in those gates, walls, and so forth.
Not performing [it]. ||27||
He is girt with a forest garland of intoxicated bees,
and his four dark arms are arranged across his chest.
With their brows arched, their mouths revealing a clear exit, and with their slightly bloodshot eyes, they both assumed a hint of impetuosity.
Of the honey [of his speech], together with the brow situated at his mouth, which has emerged [from it]. ||28||
Śrīdhara: He describes those two [arms]. By that forest garland (*vanamālā*) in which intoxicated bees are present, the two [shoulders] are draped;

they are adorned by being placed around the neck. Among the four arms—those that are dark blue (*asita*) and black (*nīla*)—they are placed in the middle. And the face is slightly reddish-brown (*manāgrabhasa*).
[The two nostrils] possess agitated [breaths]; the two exits, the nostrils, are clearly blossomed, meaning their passages for the breath are fully opened. ||28||
The sequence of composition: the word "door" (*dvārī*) is the reason for a slight degree of impetuosity. ||28||

Viśvanātha: Now, in the seventh enclosure, he saw the two divine gatekeepers, Jaya and Vijaya, holding maces; even there, they possessed faces that were somewhat impetuous and slightly agitated by anger. In response to the inquiry as to by what characteristic [this was known], he says: "By the eyebrows," and so forth.

To the phrase "by means of the clear exit," the qualifying term "by means of the nose-breaths" (*nāsāśvāsābhyām*) must be supplied; [the demons] entered through the door of these two while they were blinking, without asking permission.
Just as the eastern gates were formerly made of gold and diamond, so too are you,
O sages, everywhere free from poison; for by your own vision you move unimpeded and devoid of fear.

Śrīdhara: While these two were looking on, disregarding them and without even asking for permission, they entered the first six gates; in that same manner, they also entered the seventh gate, which had panels adorned with gold and made of diamond. The reason for not asking permission was that [the same] was true everywhere.

They move about unhindered and unobstructed. The reason for their fearlessness is that they act according to their own vision without partiality; this sequence of composition has not been explained [by others].
Viśvanātha states the cause of their anger: "While these two were looking on, [the others] saw them..."

Without asking questions and disregarding the six previous gates—which were like city battlements equipped with diamond bolts and door-panels—they entered just as they had done before; they entered the seventh gate in the same manner. He states their very nature as the reason for their failure to ask questions: "In all places, they..."
They move about unhindered, incapable of being struck down by anyone. ||29||
Having beheld those four youths, clad in girdles of wind,
who were aged yet possessed of the vigor of the five senses, and who had realized the true nature of the self;
And those two, whose character was hostile to the Blessed One, mocked his splendor and caused those unworthy of it to stumble with a cane.

Śrīdhara: [They were] naked Vātaraśanas, appearing like five-year-old children even though they were old; and by the word "and" (ca), [it is implied] by command as well. "Askhalayatām" means they prevented [them]; that is, those who do not deserve such stumbling. "Aho, even here there is audacity"—such was their splendor.
Laughing: "Those two possess a disposition that is contrary to the Blessed One, the God who is the Protector of Brahman. (30)
The sequence of the composition: the meaning of the phrase "those whose character is hostile to the Blessed One" is as follows.

Since the Blessed One is the Supreme Lord in every respect by his very nature, he tolerates the transgression of his own sovereignty by Brahmins and others; however, his servants tolerate it all the more.

Since they are unable to tolerate any transgression against that portion [of the Lord] which has obtained the authority of protection through His appointment, those two, being of a nature contrary to the Blessed One's, cannot endure this.
The illustrative example, however, is to be understood as the very account of Citraketu, Śiva, and Śivā. (30)

Viśvanātha: Those whose garments, small bells, and all other clothing and ornaments were characterized by the wind; having seen those who possessed knowledge of Brahman—though aged and equal in age to Brahmā himself—appearing like five-year-old boys, [he struck them] with a cane.

By holding their cane-like arms crosswise and, by means of the word "and" (ca), with the verbal command "Let him not suddenly enter the inner assembly of the Blessed One," Jayavijaya obstructed and turned them back. Thinking, "They do not deserve such an obstruction," those two [then addressed] Jayavijaya: "Oh! Even there, due to their knowledge of Brahman, they display audacity through egoism."

Thus, having laughed at their arrogance, [the Lord] considered that even through his two servants, there would be no violation of his own devotion to Brahmanas, because those whose character conforms to the mind of the Master are not to be punished, but rather become virtuous; such is the underlying meaning. ||30||
Even those most worthy of heaven were forbidden by the two doorkeepers of Hari, who, while the others blinked, remained unblinking.
Their eyes suddenly overwhelmed by the slight influence of the god of love, they spoke, their desire to behold their dearest friend thwarted.
"Sometimes, due to a Brahmin’s curse, adversity arises for Madhva, as well as for Jaya and Vijaya, until the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa. Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa. (31)

Śrīdhara: Having arrived here in Vaikuṇṭha through great and exalted service to the Lord, and dwelling there as one whose nature conforms to His—among those who follow the path of the Lord and possess equal vision—what is this disparity in the disposition of you two? Why is it that some are permitted to enter while others are not?
[The opponent says: "He is indeed such [a person]. Surely, for the sake of protecting their master, this is the very nature and virtue of the two gatekeepers.

To this they reply: "In him... [and so on]. "Of the two deceivers" means of the two who are fraudulent. "Like oneself" means by way of one's own example; that is, just as we two are fraudulent, so too might someone else be fraudulent.

"He will enter. This is the meaning: for no one comes here except a devotee of the Lord; nor is there any apprehension of fear, since the Lord is perfectly tranquil and thus free from any potential for hostility.
Therefore, you two are merely rogues. ||31||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: While the "unblinking ones"—the gods of Vaikuṇṭha—were looking on, even those most worthy (*arhattama*), though highly entitled to approach the Lord, were being forbidden by Hari’s two gatekeepers.

They said: "When there was a frustration or obstruction of their desire to see Hari, their best friend, they were suddenly characterized by anger born of lust; those whose eyes were thus overwhelmed and pervaded [by that emotion]... (31)
The sages said:
Who is this that has come here to serve you, the Blessed Ones, so devotedly?
The nature of those who dwell there is inherently turbulent;
yet toward that man of tranquility who has abandoned all strife, what cause for suspicion could there be for you two deceivers, as if toward one's own self?

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: the meaning is that just as there is a state of contradictory natures between you two, so too what could possibly be suspected here concerning the Blessed Lord? Therefore, the prohibition is useless. ||32||

Śrīdhara: While the gods were looking on, those sages, being forbidden by the two gatekeepers of Hari, spoke these three verses beginning with "Who are you two? When there was an obstruction to the desire for a vision—that is, the wish to see—the most intimate friend Śrī Hari, the younger brother of Kāma (Cupid) became anger; by that [anger]...

Those whose eyes are suddenly and unexpectedly flooded with agitation—this indicates that even those who are most worthy of honor are not exempt from anger; thus, being an Arhat is not a sufficient reason for the absence of wrath. ||32||

The sequence of the composition: With three verses beginning with "Who indeed... (ko vā), he censures even the appropriate deliberations of those two gatekeepers regarding the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha—who possess varying degrees of proximity such as *sālokya* and *sāmīpya*—on account of their being colored by desire for Kṛṣṇa’s younger brother and according to their own respective natures. ||32||

Viśvanātha: Out of being colored by anger, they first revile him with the words "Who indeed... [and so forth]. Among those who possess his qualities—that is, those whose qualities are equal to the Lord's—even among them, for those dwelling right here in his presence, what is this "injustice" (viṣama), namely the prohibition "Brahmins must not enter," which stands as an obstacle to the very nature of the Lord?

[The opponent says: "It is their very nature. But surely even the Lord’s sages enter in the guise of Brahmins through deception; therefore, first the Brahmins themselves must be investigated, and only then allowed to enter. [The teacher replies:
"In that case, you two yourselves are deceivers in the guise of his devotees."

They say that while you two, being his haters, are engaged in the destruction of his great qualities—such as his devotion to Brahmanas, his tranquility, and his freedom from physical passion—no one else present here need be suspected of such intent; thus they say, "In him," and so forth. And by the maxim, "He regards the world as himself" (*ātmavat*), [he regards] both of you as himself.
The sense conveyed by the rhetorical question (*kāku*) "Who, even among the two deceivers, is to be suspected? is that you two alone are to be suspected—
for indeed, O Blessed One, there is no space here within your entire womb [for anyone else].

Where the wise perceive the self within the self, as space within space— even there, O you two who bear divine marks, what terrifying fear has been instilled by you that causes his very belly to burst?
When the Blessed One resides within the entire belly, there is indeed no division.

In this world, they perceive the form of the Blessed One situated within as being one with that which is situated outside, like the sky within the sky. Why have you two produced fear regarding the cause of the distinction between individual bellies?

The sense is that fear exists for one who is fearless because of being the inner controller of all; otherwise, why would there be a prohibition? "All those who perceive Brahman as distinct have fallen into ruin."
"Even everywhere there is fear for them, and for those who have died, only darkness. Thus it is stated in the *Tattvaviveka* (33).
Śrīdhara: And they say that the seed of fear and suspicion is duality (*bheda*), and that no such thing exists in Him;

thus they say, "Not indeed" (*na hi*). Within whose belly the entire universe resides, and in whom this world exists—in that Blessed One, the wise (*dhīra*) knowers do not perceive any internal difference (*antara*) from themselves; rather, they perceive the Self within this Supreme Self.

They perceive it as being contained within [the Supreme], just as the space within a jar is contained within the great space (mahākāśa). Just as another person, such as a king, experiences fear associated with the breaking of his belly, such was the fear of this Śrī Hari; for that reason, O Kārṣṇeya, you two who were wearing the guise of gods produced that fear in him specifically.
What? The meaning is: nothing at all. ||33||

The sequence of the composition: The wise ones, established in Brahman, [perceive] that differentiation which exists individually within the bellies—that is, the bodies characterized by them—and its fulfillment is the essence [of their state]. As for what was said regarding the cause of fear, Viśvanātha says:
"Listen, you two fools, listen!"—they say this with the words "Not indeed," and so forth; for [everything] is indeed complete.

The meaning is that those who might be suspected by you both also dwell within His very belly— He in whose belly the universe resides. Here, in Vaikuṇṭha, where the wise, the possessors of knowledge, do not perceive any internal difference— that is, any distinction— between the Self (the individual soul) and the Supreme Self, the Lord.
In the sky—that is, in the great space—there is a fear for this Supreme Lord, like the fear experienced by the space within a jar from two celestial beings bearing divine emblems.
This fear is that some enemy might come here in disguise and burst open the belly of this Lord; for what reason was that fear specifically produced? What is it?

"Speak first before us"—this is the meaning. Here, although the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*), which possesses the nature of limited knowledge, dependence, and so forth, is subordinate to the consciousness of the Lord (*īśvaracaitanya*)—which consists of infinite auspicious qualities such as omniscience and the like—and is thus governed by Him, just as heat is subordinate to the sun; [nevertheless...]
Even if it were differentiated by its very nature (*jāti*), even then, because the sages such as Sanaka and others are knowers (*jñānin*),

and because in the path of the knowers the grasping of universal consciousness (*citsāmānya*) alone is enjoined for the sake of attaining the nirvāṇa realized through non-dual knowledge (*advaitajñāna*), [this does not apply] to those who are particular instances of consciousness (*cidviśeṣa*).

Since the apprehension of the attributes of the Lord and the individual soul, as well as that of Māyā, has been prohibited, it should be understood that the analogy of the great ether for the Lord and the individual soul is not untenable. ||33||
Therefore, we of dull intellect resolve here to perform that which is most excellent for you both, on behalf of that Supreme Lord of Vaikuṇṭha.
For one departing from this world toward the intermediate state, these three are the most evil enemies where he finds himself.
The three enemies of the honey [of the Self] reside within the three bodies. ||34||

Śrīdhara: Therefore, since you two are servants of that Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, we shall deliberate upon what is appropriate to perform here in this offense—that which is most auspicious for Him. They say that very thing: by seeing the existence—the state of being—of internal division, from this...

"Depart from the world of Vaikuṇṭha—to those worlds where these three enemies mentioned in the Gītā, namely desire, anger, and greed, exist within this most sinful observer of internal states; or rather, depart from this Vaikuṇṭha to worlds more sinful than this. (34)
The sequence of the composition: May you two go to the sinful worlds, the multitudes of people; may you be born among them.
In that journey, these aforementioned worlds—the multitudes of Daityas, Rākṣasas, and Kṣatriyas—are the three enemies even of this Blessed One. (34)
Viśvanātha: Having thus reviled [Him], because they were not pacified, they again curse out of extreme anger.

Therefore, for you two dull-witted beings, we shall perform a meditation (*dhī*) to effect the supreme excellence (*prakṛṣṭa-prakarṣa*) of that Lord of Vikuṇṭha. In this regard, the perception of duality is particularly [to be avoided].
The warding off of the brāhmaṇa is a degradation for the God who is the benefactor of the brāhmaṇas; its absence alone is an elevation.

To bring that about, we ourselves must deliberate, as it is our immediate concern. Having remained silent for a moment, they said this very thing: "Depart from this Vaikuṇṭha to those worlds where there are the most sinful."

For people like you who belong to the class of offenders, these three enemies mentioned in the Gītā— desire, anger, and greed— arise through the perception of a sense of duality. Here, by the use of the word *ime* (these), which denotes something directly perceived, it is indicated that these [enemies] such as anger and the rest have now arisen from this very body.
The intended meaning is [that which is] approved by Sarasvatī. ||34||
Having both heard those words of theirs, he [perceived] that terrible Brahma-staff, which could not be warded off by multitudes of missiles.
Immediately, the two attendants of Hari, trembling violently and grasping his feet, fell down in extreme distress.
Śrīdhara: Having perceived their uttered speech, which was terrible;

having perceived that brahmadanda, the curse of the Brahmins; and having perceived that it was unavoidable even by all collections of weapons—the two attendants of Hari, out of extreme cowardice and fear, grasped his feet.
While performing [the act], they fell down like a staff. Of what nature was Hari?
He was one who conceived fear—greater even than that of those sages who were thus situated.
The sequence of the composition is as follows: by the phrase "having perceived that Brahma-staff," it is indicated that previously these two [had been] among them...
It is understood that he had no knowledge of his being a Brahmin, for he was greatly afraid of the Brahmins. (35)

Viśvanātha: "Alas, we have committed an offense in that the Brahmins have been provoked to anger"—thus he expresses their despondency with the words beginning with *teṣām*. They were first afraid of Hari; the form *bibhyatuḥ* involves the elision of the vowel *u*, which is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. And then, out of extreme timidity, they grasped the feet of those [Brahmins].
As they were doing so, they both fell down like a staff. ||35||
May that punishment which has been inflicted upon us sinners by your honors take away even our entire offense against the gods.
May there be no delusion for you two as you travel further and further downward, which, through a trace of regret, would destroy your remembrance of the Blessed One.
Even for one who has slighted a teacher, there is punishment for [the offense of] honey. ||36||
Śrīdhara: To those who were repenting, "Alas, we have committed an offense," the two replied:
"O sinners, that very punishment which was appropriate for you has been inflicted by the Blessed Ones.
There is no fault whatsoever on your part in this matter; therefore, let this [punishment] be for us two, who [committed] every slight against the gods."

May it remove the sin consisting of the transgression of the Lord’s command; yet, by even a fraction of that repentance born of Your grace, may there be no delusion obstructing the remembrance of the Blessed One as we descend deeper and deeper into the wombs of the ignorant, but rather, may even that delusion lead only to remembrance.
"May it flow forth"—this is the prayer. ||36||

The sequential composition: Having realized that they were born as enemies of themselves and having recognized their enmity, they pray for the mere remembrance of Him, saying, "May it be so. The syntactical connection here is: "In such an offense, may there be no delusion that destroys the remembrance of the Blessed One. (36)
Viśvanātha: Alas! It is we ourselves who have committed the offense, in that you two were cursed for being devotees of the Lord.
Alas, alas! What more can we do beyond this? Our lifelong pride—that anger and the other passions had been conquered—has been reduced to dust here in Vaikuṇṭha; thus he spoke to them with remorse.

Each spoke individually: "Whatever punishment you have inflicted upon me for my sins and offenses because of my devotion to the Blessed One, may that become a blessing; I perceive that very thing within myself as a benediction, not as a punishment. The reason for this is that they both spoke together once more: "Whoever..."
May this rod [of punishment] completely remove all our offenses arising from the slighting of the gods due to contempt for you,
from acting contrary to the will of the Blessed One, and from manifesting anger unbecoming of the realm of Vaikuṇṭha— namely,
every offense committed against you, the Blessed One, and the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.

We should not resort to that; rather, by even a single fraction—a mere trace—of this present remorse of yours which is born of compassion, may we two obtain exactly this: even as we fall lower and lower, may there be no delusion that destroys the remembrance of the Lord. For delusion is the adversary of the intent to serve the Lord.
It will surely come to pass; for since your curse cannot be otherwise [rendered ineffective], that too is a delusion.
May even that [delusion] lead only to memory, and not to forgetfulness—this is my prayer. (36)
Thus, at that very moment, the Blessed One, whose navel is like a lotus and who is dear to the hearts of the noble ones, became aware of the transgression committed by his own people.
Accompanied by Śrī, he proceeded to that place, causing the feet of the great sages who are supreme swans to be sought after to tremble.
For those who remain here in this state of sweetness, there shall be no further delusion as before. ||37||

Śrīdhara: Thus, having immediately perceived the transgression and offense of his own people toward those great ones, he went to that place where they were confined. "Dear to the hearts of the noble ones" means pleasing to them. "Setting his feet in motion"—the underlying sense is this: [he wished to prevent] the suffering born from the obstruction of seeing my feet.
Displaying anger and saying, "I shall subdue them," he went on foot under the pretext of haste;
for he wished to appease Śrīsāhitya by fulfilling his desires with riches, even though the latter were free from worldly longing. (37)

The sequence of composition: To show that the Blessed Lord arrived at that very place at that very moment, he says, "Thus, at that very time," and so forth, in fourteen verses. This is explained in order: "Thus" (evam). And the commentary:
"Thus, having immediately perceived the transgression—that is, the offense—of his own people against the great ones, at that very instant..."

He went to that place where Sanaka and the others were detained by Jaya and Vijaya. It was a region dear to the hearts of the noble ones (*ārya*). "Moving his feet"—the underlying intention is this: "By showing them my feet, I shall pacify the anger born from their obstruction of the sight of my feet."

Under the pretext of haste, he proceeded on foot; and having filled even those free from desire with his splendors through his glorious literary works (*śrīsāhitya*), he did so in order to ask their forgiveness.
In this regard, for the sake of bestowing bliss even upon those who delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*), by means of the sight of his feet—

It is the state of being a solid mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānandaghana*). By means of the word "Śrī" (Glorious One), it is intended to convey that even the play of His power (*śakti*) is not other than His own essential nature. The use of the plural form "of our own" (*svānām*) is either because the offense of both [the husband and wife] extends to all members of the retinue, or out of great respect for those two.
By using the word "his own" (*sva*), it is intended to show that the Munis do not possess such a sense of ownership as he does.

Alternatively, by saying "moving his feet," rather than "accepting even sandals," a special degree of reverence for the Munis is demonstrated. By saying "with Śrī," he shows that she too was not hidden from them.
Having thus indicated it, their very offense was made firm.
(Bhagavatsandarbha 85) Viśvanātha: In this way, by means of tears in the guise of mere droplets from the ocean of inner dejection born from the perception of each other's offenses—

When Sanaka and his brothers— Jayavijaya— had been purified of their faults as if bathed by the rays streaming outward, and when the true nature of both their Brahminhood and devotion was made manifest to the assembly members present,
devotion shone forth through the very act of self-reproach, and that [self-reproach] was illuminating.

Devotion draws the Lord toward this very purpose; as if taking this matter as authoritative, the Blessed One, the God of Brahman and the one who is affectionate toward his devotees, arrived right there at that time. Thus he says: "In this way.
He refers to the transgression of the good by his own people—that is, the violation of a Brāhmaṇa committed by his own devotees—and [the state] in the hearts of the noble ones.
The sense is that just as [the sun] appears, so too he (the Lord) appears even in their eyes.
In that region of the seventh door, [the two feet] are to be sought—that is, they are worthy of being sought—by the great sages;
likewise, after non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) must be required.
