Likewise, after experiencing the nature of Brahman, they are worthy of experiencing the nature of the Lord;

for this very reason, with the intention: "Moving my feet, I shall first cause them to experience the sweetness of My feet and then immerse them in the ocean of the wonder of supreme bliss," [He acts].

With the thought, "These [devotees] know that 'Sahaśrīḥ' refers only to my external power (bahir-aṅgā), and not to this Śrī who is my essential nature (svarūpa-bhūtā)," I cause them to experience even this power of bliss (āhlādinī-śakti). ||37||
But they pointed out to him— that object of his own vision, which was the fruit of their own meditative concentration— as he arrived, having been provided with the means [of access] by their own men.
From the two fans of Haṃsaśrī, there fell a spray of water like moonbeams from the white parasol, stirred by the auspicious breeze.
The filaments of the two moons are rays of honey. ||38||

Śrīdhara: There, he describes the god seen by them in five verses. "They saw him as he arrived" (*taṃ tv āgataṃ te'cakṣata apaśyan*); the verb *apaśyan* extends back to the fifth verse. He was one whose appropriate requisites for travel—such as an umbrella, sandals, and so forth—had been quickly brought back by his own men. How?

It is true: fortune is to be enjoyed through one's own meditative absorption; that very Brahman is the object of the senses. By the auspicious and favorable breeze from the two moving fans—resembling swans—that belong to those two [princes] who possess splendor, the white parasols, with their moon-like tassels, were made to tremble and sway.
That very white parasol, because of its resemblance to the moon, is the moon; its filaments are the hanging pearl necklaces, from which drops of water fall—
*sīkara* meaning a drop of water— in which [the moon] it is situated.

The sequential composition: "taṃ tu... constitutes a group of five verses. The connection is as follows: "Te" (they), namely Sanaka and the others, "acakṣata" (spoke of) "tam" (Him); and having gazed upon Him, "nemuḥ" (they bowed). [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.42]. Of what nature was He? "Svasamādhibhāgyam": that Brahman which is the fruit to be attained (*bhāgyam*) through one's own meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
That alone is the object of the senses; or rather, it is the fortune of the means consisting of one's own meditative absorption (samādhi),
which takes the form of the fruit, because that [fruit] is the object of the senses through its manifestation via all the cognitive faculties refined by the power of its own self-luminosity.
Now, being clearly experienced as it is, this establishes— as in the previous case—
that all its attributes, namely sound, touch, form, taste, and smell,
are essentially composed of the mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). Likewise, it is eternally so.
Having first experienced the manifold variety of sweetness that is ever-arising in such a manner,

they serve the Blessed One with a mass of supreme love and bliss; and being served by His own people who have brought various articles necessary for service, He is somehow, somewhere, and at some time [perceived].
Thus, at that time, by some rise of fortune born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he saw only [the Lord];

this demonstrates that the state of those most learned ones— who are objects of longing— is permeated by the playful manifestation of some power of the bliss of the Blessed One within the divine persons of Śrī Vaikuṇṭha.

Now, because they cause agitation to the mind by inflaming their longing for the Blessed One, he describes the similar nature of their attendants and so forth with three and a half verses beginning with "haṃsa": *keśarā* refers to long pendants made of pearls. Here, the parasol is treated as the moon, and the *keśarā* are treated as droplets of spray.
[This is] a metaphor (*rūpaka*). Because of their connection with the moon, the water-droplets acquire the nature of nectar (*amṛta*).
[Bhagavatsandarbha 85] Viśvanātha: Therein, he describes with five verses that sweetness which has been experienced by them.
In that regard, the sweetness of form is all-pervasive in the direct perception of the Blessed One;

as for the sweetness of sound and so forth, it should be understood that these are experienced by them through a certain degree of the power of attachment directed toward their respective objects, which has been bestowed by the Blessed One. But that—

There, they saw him who had arrived; they did not see him [clearly] because his necessary belongings had been taken away by their own men. "Oh, the feet of the Blessed Lord are now adorning the courtyard outside!"—with such a sudden surge of joy, they gazed upon him.
The meaning is that, out of extreme longing, the devotees residing in the city gates, the capital, celestial palaces,
and the groves came forth and prepared various jewels, garments, ornaments, fruits, perfumes, flowers, garlands, and *ārātrika* lamps.
He became an object of their senses, falling within the range of their perception.
[Objection: "In that case, does it not follow that he [the teacher] becomes an object [of perception]? To this, he replies with a roar and a threatening gesture of his eyebrows:

"For them, his own self-concentration (*svasamādhi*) is the very embodiment of fortune, even for the experience of the bliss of Brahman within the form of Brahman in their own hearts. Oh! By the mere sight of him, even our own self-concentration becomes fruitful.

They thought, "It has come into being"—the sense being: what deluded person could even imagine that those [fans] could have the status of objects for that form and so forth? Moving back and forth like swans, they were fanned by a favorable breeze from both sides of those two moving fans, and thus they were swaying and shifting.

[He entered] that [palanquin] from which sprays of water were dripping from those "filaments" (keśara)— the pearl necklaces hanging down— which were like the moon (śaśin) because the white parasol (ātapatra) was itself the moon, and whose filaments were the pearl necklaces hanging therefrom. Here,
by means of hyperbole (atiśayokti), the hanging pearls are identified as filaments, and thus the parasol [is likened to a lotus].

The form of a thousand-petaled lotus with its face turned downward is superimposed; by this, the coolness, fragrance, and softness of the parasol are manifested. Likewise, the spray-water, through its connection with the moon, possesses the nature of nectar. ||38||
With a countenance radiant with total serenity, he whose splendor is longed for touches the heart with a fraction of his affectionate gaze.
With his own splendor gracing his dark and broad chest,
he seemed to be beautifying his own abode with his crest-jewel.
The Kaustubha gem is the form of Brahmā, and the crest-jewel is likewise Prāṇa. ||39||
Śrīdhara: [He is] well-disposed through the grace of the entire host of sages who are the gatekeepers;

the abode and locus of all desirable qualities; touching the heart and gladdening it with a digit of affectionate gaze—that is, with a loving sidelong glance. In the interpretation where there is a desire to describe the three worlds:
Heaven extends as far as Satyaloka; his own abode, Vaikuṇṭha, stands like a crest-jewel, beautifying and adorning it.
The sequence of the composition is as follows: "kṛtsnaprasāda" refers to the complete and full grace bestowed upon the sages.

Therefore, he has a beautiful face with a charming countenance. However, the favor of the two attendants (*pārṣada*) is not explicitly stated here, because of the contradiction with what will be said later, beginning with "These two... (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.16.2). Alternatively, "sumukha" refers to the favor of the entire host of gatekeeping sages; he is the abode of all desirable qualities.

The term "place" (*sthāna*) demonstrates that those respective qualities possess such a nature. "Gaze of affection" refers to *vilāsa* (divine play). "Heaven" (*svaḥ*) refers to the places for the enjoyment of bliss, because they consist of eternal and infinite bliss; [the Lord is] the crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*) of them. "The abode of the Self" (*ātmadhiṣṇya*) is His own essential place, Śrī Vaikuṇṭha. Even in such a place...

By means of the Śrī (Goddess of Fortune) in the form of a line adorning his chest, he appears as if making himself auspicious, or as if placing a special ornament there. The word *iva* is used here as a poetic figure (*vākyālaṅkāra*). By this, the eternity and supreme excellence of Śrī-Vaikuntha are indicated. And it has been said: "That [Vaikuntha] is the teacher of the universe..."

In such passages as these, beginning with "They attained supreme joy" (*āpuḥ parāṃ mudam*), and as will be stated later, beginning with "Then those sages, having seen... (*atha te munayo dṛṣṭvā*) and ending with "the Vaiṣṇava splendor" (*vaiṣṇavīṃ śriyam*). (Bhagavatsandarbha 85)

Viśvanātha: While we, who have uttered curses against our own devotees, are submerged in an ocean of doubt as to whether the Blessed One is inwardly angry or not, he is "sumukha"—possessed of a gracious countenance—by means of his entire grace, both internal and external. For this very reason, alas! alas! toward us, on the contrary, there is only grace.

"Pūrṇa is perceived," thus it resounded within the hearts of the multitude of sages as they beheld with their eyes and other senses that abode of Pūrṇa—the locus of beauty, sweetness of voice, fragrance, delicacy, compassion, and magnanimity, all of which are objects of longing. Alas! Woe upon us two, consumed by the fire of Brahmā’s curse and falling downward!

Thinking, "Such sweetness of vision will never again be possible," Jayavijaya were submerged in an ocean of grief and wept; yet, by a mere fraction of His skillful glance of affection directed toward them—which touched the hearts of all the people there—how great is His tenderness for His devotees! Thus it is said.

Captivating the minds [of all], he beautified his own abode, Vaikuṇṭha— like a crest-jewel upon the crowns of the heavens reaching as far as Satyaloka— with a golden line situated on the left side of his body; for blessed is that Vaikuṇṭha where the inhabitants behold this golden line.
He makes her possess such good fortune that she gazes upon Lakṣmī on the chest of the Blessed One;

this same interpretation should also be applied to the "poison" (gara). Here, the sweetness consisting of compassion and the sweetness of form are to be known as experienced by her mind and eyes. (39)
Upon her broad hips clad in yellow garments, she shone with a girdle of many strings and a forest garland that seemed to hum with its bees.
With his beautiful bracelets upon his forearms, he placed one hand on the shoulder of the son of Vinatā and shook a lotus with the other.

Śrīdhara: [He is] upon that yellow garment (*pītāṃśuka*) which possesses a broad hip as its support; and he is joined with a forest-garland (*vanamālā*) resounding with bees. Alternatively, the phrase "making [himself] beautiful" (*subhagayantam*) may be connected with what precedes. He has bracelets on his lovely forearms (*prakoṣṭha*). [He is] upon the shoulder of Garuḍa.

By whom one hand is placed [on the hip], while with the other hand he is shaking—that is, brandishing—a lotus, a playful lily; and if the reading is *vinyasya*, then the words beginning with *valgu* are adjectives qualifying the hand. (40)

*Commentary on the Arrangement*: In the phrase "pītāṃśuke" (on the yellow garment), the instrumental case is used in the sense of a secondary attribute (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "with a girdle" and "with a forest garland.
[Bhagavatsandarbha 85] Viśvanātha: [It refers to] that upon which a broad hip exists as its locus.

The sound of the suffix *in* (implying possession) is suggested by the phrase "this hip is mine alone and not another's" through the yellow garment (*pītāṃśuka*), wherein her own ownership has been superimposed. Furthermore, by the phrase "with a girdle shining upon such a yellow garment," she remains having established her own ownership even over the yellow garment itself, which has become her own locus, by placing it above that [hip].

The meaning is as follows: likewise, having made that girdle his own abode, by means of the forest garland situated upon it—of what sort? "Resounding with bees"—having thus made even the forest garland his own abode, the quality of existence (*sattva*) was superimposed upon it by the bees; therefore, the sovereignty over everything belongs to the Lord through the bees alone.

The sense is that [the gift] has been given. The connection of the words ending in the third case—“his own abode” (ātmadhiṣṇyam) and “making auspicious” (subhagayantam)—is with the preceding [phrase]. "Valgu" means charming; "wherein there is a bracelet on the forearm" (valgu prakoṣṭhe valayam yatra). Thus, he has his left hand placed upon the shoulder of Garuḍa. In the reading "vinyasya," the word "valgu" [is understood].
The word "ādi" (beginning with) is an adjective qualifying the hand. With the other—the right hand—he is "whirling a lotus";

that is to say, under the pretext of whirling a play-lotus, he makes the heart-lotuses of the sages—though already firmly established in the taste of Brahman—unsteady by revealing his own sweetness. And by that, O sages!...

"Why do you now agitate the mind from that bliss whose nature is indistinguishable from the Self and which has been ascertained as the supreme of all? Why do you not steady it right there? Do not abandon your own steadfastness!"—thus is the jest expressed among the sages. 40.
His face, with its high cheeks worthy of adornment by makara-shaped earrings flashing like lightning, is crowned with a jeweled diadem.
With a most precious necklace held within the space between his staff-like arms, and with the Kaustubha gem resting upon his neck.
Śrīdhara: [He is] one whose face possesses a prominent nose and cheeks worthy of being adorned by those two fish-shaped earrings which surpass lightning with their own luster;
he who wears a crown set with jewels; and in the space between the cluster—that is, the multitude—of his staff-like arms.

By means of that necklace—standing in the center, captivating the mind, or causing one to sport; most precious and excellent—and resting upon the neck. The sequence of composition is as follows: "like lightning," captivating and enchanting. ||41||

Viśvanātha: He whose face has a prominent nose and whose two cheeks— worthy of being adorned by those two earrings shaped like crocodiles which surpass lightning with their own luster— are thus [described].

The meaning is that the multitude—that is, the collection—of his staff-like arms, by stealing—that is, robbing—the minds of the sages, enters the hollow of the arm precisely because of the fear caused by that very theft.
Here, the word *kaṃdhara* (neck), which has a value of ten million (*parārdha*), is used to denote the chest. Or alternatively:
The grammatical construction is as before: [He is adorned] by the Kaustubha gem, which has gone from the two shoulders through a golden thread and hangs down as far as the chest. ||41||
This is indeed a mockery," Indirā said with a smile, her mind conceiving that [the form] was fashioned by her own kin and replete with manifold beauty.
Whose eyes, never satiated with joy, did not bow in reverence upon beholding my body, which is worshipped by both Bhava and yourselves?

Madhva says: "Composition is said to be of two kinds: that which lacks an author and that which consists of existing memory; however, among those things already established, it is memory. Thus [says] Śrīdhara in the *Śabdanirṇaya*. What more need be said? I alone am the playful smile of Indirā.

The conceit that "He is a treasury of all beauty" has been eclipsed here by the splendor of the Lord's beauty; this was fashioned by the minds of His own devotees. The meaning is that the servants reflected thus within their own minds. Why? Because He is enriched with manifold excellence and beauty.

This is fitting. Furthermore, they beheld him manifesting his form—a body that serves both me, Bhava (Śiva), the Lord, and yourselves. Having seen him, with how many heads did they bow in joy? Their eyes were not particularly satiated. ||42||

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Having thus described the similar nature of even his [the Lord’s] attendants and so forth, he speaks again of that very same [Lord’s] supreme attractiveness: "In this regard, He is approached" (*atropasṛṣṭam*). *Indirāyā utsmitam* means the pride of Lakṣmī. Here, [He is] "approached" (*upasṛṣṭam*) by her toward the Blessed One. [This is said] regarding Him who possesses qualities such as supreme beauty.

It was conjectured by those [women] in their minds that, through the constant acquisition of their beloved, he had become eternally and exceedingly manifest; the reason for this is that he is enriched with great excellence and endowed with an infinite abundance of essential nature, beauty, and qualities.

Now, one might ask: "How can there be a manifestation of such a supreme reality, which is even for Lakṣmī herself a great secret treasure? To this, he says: "To me" (*mahyam*). [He is] one who accepts the limbs of Bhava and of you; that is, one who accepts our devotion as his own object.
The meaning is: "entering for the sake of accomplishing this or that effect.
Your nature of supreme ascetic power is a source of wonder that transcends the threefold boundaries and exceeds all measure.

"Even though You conceal Yourself through the power of Your *māyā*, some who possess no other state of being than Yours behold You incessantly. (Stotraratna, 13) Likewise, it is because of such scriptural passages as:
"Devotion alone leads to Him; devotion alone reveals Him," and so forth. That which...

Or rather, they spoke of him as being such; the meaning is that those whose sight was not yet satiated gazed with joy and bowed their heads even while looking on, wondering, "Who is this? [Bhagavatsandarbha 85].
Viśvanātha: What more need be said? I myself am the smile of Indirā among all beauties.
The thought "it is a treasure" refers to the ego-inflation that had been directed toward the beauty of the Blessed One;

this has now vanished, as conceived by the minds of his own devotees. This is what was reflected upon in their own hearts by the servants—thus says the Master’s own feet (the author). Through the attainment of her beloved, who possesses qualities such as supreme beauty, her...

The meaning of the context is that *utsmita* (smile) is that which has been produced or manifested with pride and superiority. Alternatively, it means that even by me— who am worshiped by Brahmā and others, and who am superior in every respect through my beauty, qualities, and sweetness— this [smile] has been rendered subordinate (*upasṛṣṭa*) to the Blessed One.
The meaning is that [the body] has become secondary. For this reason— and because of the word "ca" (and)—

it refers to one who possesses a body characterized by an excellence of smile from Indirā (Lakṣmī), which arises from joy at the thought, "I am blessed, for such a beloved is mine," and which is further endowed with appropriate garments, ornaments, and so forth, as well as with love.

The meaning is that he beautifies [his limbs], rather than disfiguring even his beautiful body with ashes and the like as Śambhu does; for the use of words such as "worship" (*pūjā*) is indeed observed even in reference to the adornment of one's own limbs, as in the phrase "a slight worship of the feet" found in works on physiognomy (*sāmudrika*) and so forth.

And that [body] is indeed through doors consisting of more than a thousand servants; thus he says: it was fashioned with great excellence by means of a subtle intellect alone—the intellect of his own personal attendants—which effects a constant distinction in the various ornaments such as garments and the like. Furthermore, of what nature is the body?

The meaning is that the "greatness" (mahaḥ) of Śambhu—which belongs to you, to those like us, and to me—is indeed to be worshipped through meditation in another realm with fragrances, flowers, and so forth; it is not, however, to be directly served in Vaikuṇṭha as it is for them. This refers to the root *maha* in the sense of worship (*pūjā*).
This is the form of a word ending in the *cur* class of suffixes. They described him as being thus;
then, having gazed upon him with particular intensity, their eyes remaining unsated, with how many heads did they bow? (42)
— the breeze from the lotus-pond of that lotus-eyed one, mingled with the filaments of his lotus-feet and the nectar of *tulasī*...
Entering through their own openings,
he caused agitation in both the minds and bodies of those who were devoted to the Imperishable.

Śrīdhara: He states that even for them, the bliss of worship (*bhajanānanda*) exceeds the bliss of their own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*). The wind, joined with the nectar (*makaranda*) of the *tulasī* flowers—which are mixed with the filaments (*kiñjalka*, *kesara*) of His lotus feet—[is inhaled] through one's own opening, namely the nostrils, by those who enjoy the imperishable (*akṣarajuṣām*), that is, those who partake in the bliss of Brahman.
Agitation in the mind, excessive joy, and horripilation in the body. ||43||

The sequence of composition: regarding the word "tasya" (of Him), it should be explained here as "the *tulasī* mixed with the filaments of the lotus. At that time, both the lotus and the *tulasī* should be understood as being situated within the forest garland (*vanamālā*).
Let it be so; [now consider] those primary and secondary limbs which constitute the very self of the Blessed One, and among them...
The meaning is that the capacity to cause agitation belongs to the wind associated with it as well. The rest [is explained] by them. ||43||

Furthermore, Viśvanātha says: Moreover, what more need be said? Those sweet nectars of the Lord’s limbs, having brought about a supreme wonder even greater than the bliss of Brahman, immersed them within themselves.

The wind, which is connected to an object related to even a single limb of Him, conquered them by causing agitation and displacing them from their own state; thus he says: "of him" (tasya). It refers to that which is connected to the nectar of the *tulasī* which is mixed with the filaments (*kiñjalka*) of his lotus-feet—that is, the nails possessing white and reddish luster.
The wind is within them, having entered into their internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as if to exercise its own authority there.
But surely, entering another’s inner apartments without permission— as Sanaka and others did— is suddenly improper.

If this is argued, he states the correct reasoning there: "By its own opening," that is, by the nostril; for the nostril is indeed the opening of the air itself—the sense being, whose permission would one need to obtain in order to enter it?

Having gone there, what did he do? To this he says: he caused agitation in both the mind and the body. First, having forcibly cast the mind into a state of blissful transformation (*sānandavivarta*), he agitated it; then he also agitated the body through trembling, tears, horripilation, perspiration, and so forth. For in the world, even another person [asserts] his own authority over the territory of another.
Desiring to act, he first seizes the governor of that region, plunders him, and agitates him; thereafter, he causes even that entire region to be crushed by his own army.
But surely, for those who enjoy the bliss of Brahman, their mind consists of nothing but the bliss of Brahman; how [then can they be so disturbed]?
"May the bliss of the Blessed One make that [state] consist of Himself? To this he replies: "Even for those who enjoy the Imperishable.
The sense is that its power is such precisely because of its superior sweetness. ||43||
Or rather, having gazed upon the dark lotus-bud of his face, with its most beautiful lower lip and jasmine-like smile;
Having received the blessing, they should again gaze upon his pair of feet, which serve as a support for the ruby-red jewels of his nails, and fix their minds thereon.

Śrīdhara: With two verses, he describes the agitation caused by joy. "Te vai" (they indeed)—this refers to the interior of his very mouth, which is the calyx of a black lotus (*asitapadma*). The phrase "the calyx of a black lotus" (*asitapadmakośam*) is a poetic figure of hyperbole (*abhūtopamā*). It refers to that [mouth] in which there is a smile like jasmine flowers upon his most beautiful, reddish lower lip. Ut... [text fragment].
Having looked upward and attained their heart's desire, those very nails— which are like red gems— became their refuge;
then, looking downward at the pair of feet which served as that support,
and gazing again and again in this manner, they were subsequently [struck with wonder] because of the inability to grasp the beauty of all his limbs simultaneously.
They would have placed [it], having meditated. ||44||
The sequence of composition: Having looked with an upward gaze at her face, which is like the slightly blossomed calyx of a blue lotus,
and having again looked with a downward gaze at the pair of her feet, [he gazes] repeatedly.

The meaning is: having seen the body from the glorious face down to the glorious feet; afterwards, with a sense of boldness, they closed their eyes out of agitation and fixed their gaze upon them—meaning that even internally they saw that very same thing.
Alternatively, the meaning is that due to the intensity of their devotion, they saw only the pair of feet afterwards.
Or rather, the meaning is that due to the intensity of their devotion, they saw only the pair of feet afterwards.
Regarding the term *nirvarṇanam*, Amara states: "Nidhyānam, darśanam, ālokanam, and īkṣaṇam [are synonyms]. This is from the lexicon (*koṣa*).

The inner portion is devoid of the external layer of petals. (44) [Bhagavat-sandarbha 85] Viśvanātha: Thus, for those whose vital breaths have been purified by the fragrance of *tulasī*, since the senses are dependent upon the vital breath, first, through the two eyes, there is the perception of the sweetness of form.

Because the beauty of their forms and the sweetness of their features possess an infinity of variety in every limb, [the author] describes the state of helplessness caused by the pressure of bliss when there is a simultaneous desire to grasp them all, brought about by the emotion of agitation (*āvega*), with the words "te vā" (those indeed).
The word "vai" expresses certainty: their face alone is the bud of a blue lotus.
The meaning is as follows: having observed that which is covered by an outer layer of coarse bark possesses an inner part of superior sweetness;

and beyond that, there is a sweetness of laughter and jesting that is most excellent. "Having received blessings" refers to those [blessings] granted for the sake of devotion by the father Brahmā and by his brother Nārada.

The meaning is that the blessings were given previously, and they were obtained through the attainment of their fruit. Having perceived only a slight sweetness in her face, wondering "Oh, what kind of beauty is this in her feet?", they remained unsatisfied and cast their eyes upon the sweetness of her feet; thus he says—"Again," [referring to] the nails.

Having again looked at their pair of feet—the refuge and support consisting of those very ruby-like jewels—in the lower part [of the body], they gazed slightly; the meaning is that having looked at the face once more, they beheld it in this manner again and again. "Nirvarṇana," however, means intense contemplation (nidhyāna).
The *Amara-kośa* states: "darśana, ālokana, and īkṣaṇa [all mean 'seeing'].

Thus, the venerable Svāmipādas say that because it is impossible to grasp the beauty of all limbs simultaneously, one should subsequently fix one's gaze upon them—that is, one should meditate [upon them] in this manner. Likewise, in this context, [the phrase] "having received the blessing" occurs later [in the text].

By these two verses beginning with "pitṛānuvarṇitarahāḥ," it is shown that although devotion arises in them through the Lord’s grace alone—which follows upon His compassion for their devotion—yet because the Lord’s grace is so preponderant, they are designated by that [grace] according to the maxim: "Designations are made according to what is most abundant.
Thus, the devotion of Sanaka and the others arises solely through the Lord’s grace, and by means of that very devotion, theirs...
This is well known as the experience of its sweetness. ||44||
for men seeking the ultimate goal here through the paths of yoga,
this is the highly esteemed abode of meditation, delightful to the eye.
They praised him, who was manifesting a manly form and endowed with eight innate and natural enjoyments that could not be achieved by others.
Śrīdhara: [He is] the object of meditation for those men seeking the goal through the paths of yoga;

highly esteemed and a locus of great reverence, or rather, approved by many who perceive the truth (*tattvadṛś*). He displays a human form (*pauṃsnaṃ vapuḥ*), characterized by innate qualities uncommon to others and not achieved through effort.
They praised him fully, extolling him as endowed with the eight eternal sovereign powers, beginning with *aṇiman*. ||45||

The sequence of the composition: "Of men" (puṃsām). It is highly esteemed even by Brahmā because it is a dense manifestation of light, and thus a fit object for supreme reverence. "Displaying His male form" (pauṃsnaṃ vapur darśayānam): His own body is non-different from that male form known as Śrī Viṣṇu, which is the form of the descent of the qualities (guṇāvatāra) belonging to the Puruṣa dwelling within the Garbhodaka ocean.

The meaning is that he manifests [himself], but not in a manner of transformation (*anyathātva*) like Brahmā and others. "By the non-different" (*ananyena*) means by his own [powers] which are established as his very nature (*svarūpa*). For this very reason, they are "innate" (*autpattikaiḥ*), meaning they are established as beginningless just like him. He is endowed with the eightfold sovereignty (*aṣṭaiśvarya*) beginning with *aṇiman*—that is, he is distinguished; not...

This is indicated by the word *tūpa*. By means of this, through its function as a qualifying attribute of the basis for their praise, it is suggested that they possess such a nature, being endowed with all divine perfections (*bhaga*) characterized by sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). ||45||

Viśvanātha: However, since even those seeking liberation lack pure devotion, they do not desire to grasp its sweetness; yet, for them too, there is no liberation without meditation upon Him. Thus he says: "Of men... regarding their goal.

The meaning is that since the state of meditative absorption (*dhyānāspada*)— which is highly esteemed through reasoning and the paths of yoga consisting of the eightfold limbs— is necessarily to be meditated upon in its qualified form, the very nature of Nārāyaṇa is what is agreed upon by many;
thus, [the Lord] is shown "displaying his body related to the Puruṣa" (*pauṃsnaṃ vapur*).
It is implied that even apart from forms such as Mohinī, there exists within him a vast multitude of aspects denoted by the term "Bhagavat.

By the word "by another," the meaning is "by his own [aspects] which are established as being identical with his essential nature. For this very reason, they are described as "eightfold, innate, and eternal."

Because they are enjoyed— that is, tasted— with devotion through the objects of enjoyment consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, smell, compassion, action, and sovereignty, as well as through various kinds of devotees, they are called "enjoyments" (*bhoga*). Among these,
[the first are] sound and so forth.

The seven forms of sweetness (*mādhurya*)— denoted by the words *sauśvarya*, *saukumārya*, *saundarya*, *mādhurya*, *saurabhya*, *vātsalya*, and *līlā*— are objects of enjoyment for the six senses of the love of devotees; the eighth,
denoted by the word *bhagavat*, is the hexad of majesty (*aiśvarya*), which is enjoyed by devotees, seekers of liberation, and liberated souls alike.
It should be understood that [the fruit] is to be tasted according to one's capacity. By the "eight enjoyments" is meant the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā*. Thus it is said.
The Kumāras said:
O Infinite One, You who were hidden even though You had entered the hearts of the wicked, have this very day been attained by us at the very root of our eyes;
for as soon as You entered the cave of our ears through the opening of our ears.
The secret described by my father, who was born from you.

Śrīdhara said: "It is not surprising that You manifest eternally in the form of Brahman; however, that You are now visible in person in this most auspicious and pure essence-form (śrīmūrti)—oh, how great is our good fortune! Thus they spoke. O Infinite One, You who, though residing within the hearts of the wicked, remain hidden from them—

You do not shimmer; you have not become hidden from us. You have been attained and reached at this very moment, right before our eyes. The reason for your lack of invisibility is that as soon as our father—by whom you were born—described your secret and instructed us in the mystery, at that very instant, for us...
"Having entered through the path of the ear, you have reached the cave of the intellect; you have arrived," [he said]. ||46||

The Structural Arrangement (*Krama-sandarbha*): Now, since the Blessed Lord is of such a nature, [the author] establishes His own form—which manifests that very nature—by means of a hymn of praise uttered by them alone to express their own inner heart, beginning with "Śrī-kumārā ūcuḥ" (The venerable Kumāras said). He states the hymn with five verses beginning with "yaḥ" (He who...). Here, even for those who abide in the Imperishable (*akṣara*),...
Following this, the passage is explained as follows:
It is not surprising that You shine eternally in the form of Brahman;

however, You are now directly perceived through a form whose essence is identical with the Supreme Reality of dense light, manifested by a particular function of Your own essential power characterized by pure *sattva*.

"Oh, what fortune is ours! they said: "O Infinite One! You, who remain hidden even while dwelling within the hearts of the wicked as their inner controller (antaryāmin)—meaning You do not manifest—do not remain hidden from us.
The reason for this is that whenever [the world] arises from You, ours..."

The secret described by our father, the mystery known as love and devotion taught in the *Catuḥślokī*, has at that very moment entered the cavity of my ear and, taking on that very form, shines within; thus, it reaches the root of my eyes.

"You alone have prepared this; you have attained it. By the excellence of his compassion, he has at that very moment entered the right eye; the meaning is that he has manifested there. The word *raha* is sometimes seen ending in a short vowel, as in such passages as: "His mothers, whose love was rooted in secrecy (*raharūḍhabhāvāḥ*), worshipped him" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.55.40).
It is seen [in the text]. Regarding the phrase "not even today," the reading "so'dyaiva" (thus even today) followed by "kva" (where? is not supported by the *Ṭīkā*.
In some places, it reads "no'dyaiva" (not even today). ||46||

Viśvanātha: "Oh! How boundless is the greatness of great compassion, since we have been made to experience such bliss of direct realization by the Blessed One! Oh, how fortunate we are! Thus they said:
"O Infinite One! O Ocean of boundless sweetness and sovereignty! You, who, though dwelling within the hearts of the wicked..."
Not only have you, who had vanished, today been restored and reached the range of our vision, but you were so even before.
[The sages ask: "When indeed was I seen thus? To this, they respond with affection: "At the time when... You do not remember.

"Even as soon as you, whose secret was described by our father Brahmā at his own birth, entered and reached the cave through the path of our ears"— this is the meaning: O son of mine who has realized Brahman, for one who has experienced Brahman, the direct perception of the Lord is even more [significant] than the direct perception of Brahman.
May he too grant you joy multiplied ten millionfold— he, the Blessed One, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with four full and long arms,
adorned with bracelets, armlets, earrings, and other ornaments, moon-faced, and resplendent in Vaikuṇṭha.

As soon as we heard the words of blessing and grace from our father, a devotee of the Lord, that "it is attained through devotion," we realized that since the cause has been obtained, the attainment of its fruit is inevitable;
thus, even this present vision of the Lord was, in effect, simultaneous with the grace of His devotee.

By the phrase "we are those who know," [the Lord implies]: "Alas, O Blessed One, you are not independent; you show mercy to us only because you are dependent upon your devotees. Thus, the majesty of the compassion shown by His devotees is truly ineffable. ||46||
O Blessed One, may we know you as that supreme reality of the Self, who now bestows delight upon these beings through your very being.
That which the dispassionate sages, their knots untied, know within their hearts through the yoga of firm devotion made known by repentance.

Śrīdhara: [Objection] "But the reality of the Self taught by your father is of one kind—something unseen—whereas I am surely something else, because I am visible. [Reply] "It is not so; for through the recognition of 'I' (asmad-pratyabhijñā), difference is refuted," they say, with the word "Him" (tam). O Blessed One, You are indeed the Supreme Reality of the Self.

We know; we understand; we recognize. [Objection: But how can such sovereignty belong to the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (nirupādhi)? To this they reply: "By means of Sattva"—that is, by means of the form of pure Sattva—for these devotees. It creates "perfectly" at every moment, right now, "delight," meaning affection.

They say that the reality of the Self alone is [the goal]. Through repentance and compassion, and by means of firm yogas of devotion—such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—which have been realized and known, the sages know that which is in the heart. Of what nature are they? They are free from the knots [of worldly ties], devoid of ego-inflation, and for that very reason, free from passion.

The sequential composition: they determine that very reality as the supreme through direct experience—expressed by the words "to You. O Blessed One! To You, who have been instructed in the secret by Your father, we offer salutation as the Supreme, characterized as the Blessed Lord—that Reality of the Self which is Brahman, for it is said: "I am indeed the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27).

In accordance with the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā, we know—that is, we recognize—that very same Supreme Brahman, which is well-known from the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa and other sources as "the auspicious refuge of the all-pervading Self who is endowed with consciousness" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.5). How so? To this they say: "Now," that is, at present.

The meaning is: "Due to our limited being (*sattva*), we did not recognize the manifestation of this form for so long; however, now we have ascertained it through direct experience. They say this to show that it is not merely a matter of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*): "Even for us, who are experiencers of Brahman, [there is] delight..."

The implication is that even Rati would not have felt passion for you had you acted otherwise. Alternatively, it means "inspiring love in us," referring to these of ours who are experiencers of Brahman, at this present time of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). This [state] is supreme.

They manifest You through their internal experience as those who delight in the Self—with the words "that You. Those who are detached, renowned for such a state as it is said: "The mind touched by the bliss of Brahman never rises again" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.15.35)—even such sages, though free from bonds and devoid of egoism, [speak thus].
By those means— namely, the knowledge of the supreme reality of the Self made known through Your grace, as stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 4.30.32: "May there be devotion to You in me"—

which are obtained solely through Your grace, like the earth and other elements— and by means of steadfast yogas of devotion that are unshakable according to the principle of *sālokya*, *sārṣṭi*, and so forth (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.29.13).
"It is known," as it has been said: "And the sages who delight in the Self" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.7.10), and so forth.
[Bhagavatsandarbha 85] Viśvanātha: What need is there to speak of the direct perception of You? Even when You are out of sight...

They say that even the bliss of narrating and glorifying your stories is superior to the bliss of Brahman: they do not count, nor do they value, even the ultimate liberation known as *sāyujya* (union) as being your grace; how much less so any other status, such as that of Indra and the rest? They [aspire] to the heights of heaven.
That in which fear is offered—that is, deposited—by those who have blossomed [with pride]. Who are they?
To this they say: "Those who... The meaning is that only those who know the essence of the story are skillful; others are unskillful.
Of what kind of story? One whose glories, being worthy of praise due to their purifying nature, are like sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Or rather, it is a qualification of this [term] "bhavataḥ" (of you). ||48||
They do not even reckon your favor as absolute, much less anything else that inspires fear through the raising of your eyebrows.
O dear one, those who have taken refuge at your feet are skilled in and connoisseurs of the rasa of your narrative, whose fame is a sacred bathing place worthy of being celebrated.
Madhva:
Therefore, for those who have no other dependence, there is an abundance of bliss beyond those seeking liberation;
through the maturation of that state, they attain liberation by means of the vision of Brahman prior [to the final end].
Liberation is solely devotion; even in liberation, one shall be happy. ||48||
Śrīdhara: Even they themselves, in order to pray for devotion, speak of the supreme happiness of the devotees:

they do not reckon with, nor do they value, even that ultimate liberation known as *mokṣa* which is granted by Your grace; how much less so any other station, such as that of Indra? They [value] only that which is bestowed by the upward-raising and blossoming of Your eyebrows.
That in which fear is laid to rest—by whom?
O dear one, by those who are connoisseurs of the flavor of Your discourse. Of what nature are You?
One whose fame is a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) worthy of being celebrated for its beauty and sanctity.

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, although they previously possessed a realization of non-duality, their minds have now been diversified by the playful manifestations of the power of the bliss of one's own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*). Thus, in order to once again pray for devotion characterized by duality, [the author] speaks of the supreme happiness of the devotees, beginning with the words "not ultimate" (*nātyantikam*). "Ultimate" (*ātyantikam*)...
Even the clarity characterized by liberation, let alone any other state such as that of Indra and the rest. ||48||

[The Bhagavatsandarbha 85] Viśvanātha: What need is there to speak of the direct perception of You? Even in Your absence, the bliss of chanting and glorifying Your stories is greater than the bliss of Brahman; thus they say—"the ultimate..."

They do not even count or respect that grace known as liberation (mokṣa)—even union (sāyujya)—as being due to Your grace; how much less so any other status, such as that of Indra and the rest? They are those in whom fear has been cast and placed by the raising and expansion of Your eyebrows. Who indeed are they?

Regarding this, they say: "Those who [know] the limbs... This means that only those who understand the essence of the narrative are truly skilled; others are unskilled. Of what kind of narrative? It is one whose glories are worthy of being proclaimed and are like sacred fords (*tīrtha*) because of their purifying nature.
Alternatively, this may be an epithet of "your" (*bhavataḥ*). ||48||
Granted that existence may lead us to the hells by our own misdeeds, yet if only our mind would delight at your feet like a bee!
If the beauty of Your feet were as pleasing to our speech as the tulasī plant,
and if the cavities of our ears were filled by the multitude of Your virtues;
Madhva:
To the extent that intense suffering is experienced by those who are supremely devoted, to that same extent there is an abundance of bliss in liberation; if that is so, then devotion increases. (49)

Śrīdhara: Now, manifesting their own offense, they pray for devotion with the words "Kāmam" and so forth. O Blessed One, prior to this, no sin (*vṛjina*) existed for us; now, however, all [sins] have arisen, because we have been cursed regarding Your devotion. Therefore, by those sins of our own, [we shall fall] into the hells.
Granted that our birth might come to pass— *nu* here denotes deliberation— if, however, Your mind should delight in our feet, just as a bee delights in flowers even while being pricked by thorns,
so too if it should take pleasure therein, disregarding all obstacles; [Your] feet possess such beauty, just like the *tulasī*.

If Your feet were not beautiful even without regard for their qualities, then our words would likewise not shine; and if [the ears] were filled by the multitude of Your qualities, they would merely fill a small cavity like the ear-holes—thus they pray in the manner of beggars. But this is the hidden intention.
Because the auditory canal is of the nature of space (*ākāśa*) and because the multitude of qualities (*guṇagaṇa*) is formless (*amūrta*), there can never be a filling of it;
therefore, hearing will always bear fruit.
This is the sequence of the composition: "Kāmam" [is used] with reference to the fact that upon the attainment of that [knowledge], the subsequent and prior portions [of karma]...

By the principle stated in *Brahmasūtra* 4.1.13, "The two [bondage and destruction] exist because of the designation of them," Hari possesses such qualities as being able to forgive even those who, though possessing the knowledge of Brahman, have committed sins that cause them to fall into many hells— sins for which [normally] neither union with nor destruction of the self would be possible.

As in [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.7.10], this indicates His state of being the most wonderful and supreme of all. "Aha! Even the hells would surely exist; yet even that is not sufficient [to deter us]. We have no fear even of them.
Here, however, the root cause of the evil fruit is indeed our turning away from the Blessed Lord; may He [protect] us from that."
"May it be so," they pray with a tone of longing; "nu" is used here in the sense of deliberation.

If, however, your mind should delight in our feet—even there, like a bee, solely out of regard for the taste of their sweetness, and not out of regard for the experience of Brahman—so too [should you delight] in our words, and so forth. Herein lies the offense of the devotee.

It should be understood that the Blessed One’s forbearance consists in the fact that their anger is produced merely by his will, and thus their offense is only apparent. In these two verses, because it is not in contradiction with our desire for nothing other than devotion to you— even in hell— devotion alone is better.
"Obtained through its own inherent force.
[Bhagavatsandarbha 85] Viśvanātha: Now, it may be objected: "Indeed, my devotees are truly such that they do not even reckon liberation.
What is your present resolve—regarding pure devotion or regarding liberation? Speak of that clearly."
Thinking that this is sufficient by way of its literal expression, they say: "May there be existence (*bhava*) for us alone, but not liberation (*mokṣa*).

Even in that case, [they ask] regarding the hells—that is, even among the wombs of the denizens of hell—what greater gain is there than that, or what indeed is the loss in liberation? He states that [thought]: "The mind..."

Just as a bee delights in flowers even when pricked by thorns, so too, if one should delight [in devotion] while disregarding obstacles—thus is love (prema) manifested. By the word "yadi" (if), there is obtained a blessing and a longing that even in a hellish womb, for one devoted to Him, even hell is superior to liberation. [This refers to] the luster of His feet.
"Those whose beauty is such"— just as the *tulasī* plant does not remain elsewhere due to the absence of its own natural splendor,
but shines only at [Viṣṇu’s] feet, even so may our words also shine only in the description of the qualities and names of Your foot-form, and nowhere else. "May it be fulfilled."

In that regard, let no other news enter; or rather, since this fills even the small cavity of the ear, hearing, chanting, and remembering must be practiced constantly. Thus, the threefold bliss does not exist at all in liberation (*mukti*), though it may possibly occur in worldly existence (*bhava*); therefore, even an inferior state, namely worldly existence itself, has been prayed for.

Liberation. "In this very way, O Lord, among thousands of wombs"—whether as insects, birds, or wild animals—such a prayer is the very nature of those whose devotion is free from desire. That this brings about both the bliss of uninterrupted worship and the destruction of worldly existence, even when unintended, is the very nature of the Blessed One as well.
It should be understood in all cases. ||49||
O Much-invoked Lord, since You have manifested this form,
our eyes have attained complete satisfaction by it.
Therefore, let us offer this homage to the Blessed One,
who is known as the Blessed One whose arising is difficult for those lacking self-mastery.
Śrīdhara: "Today we have attained our purpose," they said. O Puruhūta, of vast renown!

That which you have made manifest—your vision for those who are not self-possessed, whose senses are unsubdued, and who find you difficult to perceive even when you are unmanifest; to You who are thus realized... [they say].
To you, we offer this homage. ||50||

The sequential composition: Nevertheless, they say that our attainment of this state of having fulfilled our purpose is most wonderful—beginning with the word "prāduḥ" (manifest). To You, who, though unmanifest to those devoid of exclusive devotion to Your Self, have thus become perceived by us; to You, we offer this salutation.
This is what is meant here: these are the teachers even of those supreme and subordinate gurus who have attained perfection through the knowledge of Brahman.
For this very reason, it is said: "of the great sages who are Paramahaṃsas" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.37).
To You, that mass of knowledge, my own nature...

"In the beginning of the words of the venerable Aṃśumat, it is said: 'It is to be contemplated in the heart by Sanandana and others, whose delusions regarding the distinctions of the qualities of Māyā have been utterly destroyed. It is therein that the sages correctly proclaimed the reality of the Self."
It is well known from such passages as "He declared to him [the Self]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.7.5) at the beginning of the discourse on Brahman, and from the Śruti:

"To him whose impurities had been washed away, the Blessed Sanatkumāra showed the shore beyond darkness" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2), and so forth. However, the powers such as *aṇimā* belong only to one who has already attained experience.

Even an obstacle is to be contemplated, but not so the experience of one who has attained perfection; for as the venerable Kapiladeva stated: "One who has ascended the yoga of samādhi along with its manifold details, having realized the reality, does not again partake in that which is like a dream" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.28.38).

For this very reason, it has been explained by them as well that even their anger and other such emotions arose solely through the will of the Blessed Lord—which brings about even the most difficult of occurrences—for those whose delusion regarding the distinctions of the qualities of *māyā* had been utterly destroyed. Thus, it is established that they are perpetually immersed in the bliss of Brahman. That...

It has been stated: "even for those who resort to the Imperishable" (BhāgP 3.15.43), and "he who has disappeared" (BhāgP 3.15.46), and so forth. Furthermore, elsewhere it is heard that those who resort to Brahman possess undistracted minds.
Likewise, in the seventh [canto], there is the speech of Śrī Nārada:
"The mind that is unpierced by desire and the like, whose all functions have been stilled, and which has touched the bliss of Brahman, shall never arise again at any time. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.15.35]

Nevertheless, their state of having their minds drawn by the bliss of the Blessed One is described. Similarly, such a state is heard of others who delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*) in passages such as: "Though his mind was intent on his own happiness and he had cast aside all other worldly existence, his very essence was still drawn by the charming pastimes of the Unconquered One" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.12.68). Thus it is said.

Now, is this process of devotion on their part for the sake of gathering the world, or is it due to the force of ancient impressions? It is not so; for in both cases, as in the verse, "Just as one who is blinded by the intoxication of liquor [BhP 3.28.37]," such absorption is impossible. Indeed, a lack of absorption is observed elsewhere—

"Sanaka and my other mind-born sons, your ancestors, wandered through the worlds by way of the sky, free from longing" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.12). From this statement, there is absorption in the Blessed One; [He whose feet are to be sought after by the great sages who are paramahaṃsas] (Bhāgavata Purāṇa...).

In this passage [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.37], there is the statement that [the Lord] is to be sought after by those who are opposed to arbitrariness; whereas in the fifth book, in the prose passage [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.3.11]: "Of the sages who delight in the Self, whose every impurity has been shaken off by the fire of sharp, unattached knowledge, and who incessantly recite the multitude of Your qualities... (pañcame tu...).
Devotion to Him alone has also been stated in the verse: "The essence [of their hearts] was drawn by the unconquered and charming pastimes" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.12.69).

Furthermore, in this very context, His quality of bestowing happiness is explicitly stated in such passages as: "O Lord, our eyes have attained complete cessation [of worldly perception] through You" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.50). In this regard—

Furthermore, one should not explain this by suggesting that because of the previously mentioned reasons, because of the consequence of finding fault with what was praised, and because of the direct statement, "touching the heart with a fraction of a loving glance" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.15.39), only the eyes experienced happiness and thus detachment alone was implied. Therefore, for those who delight in the Self...

Because it is the locus of delight, the very reality of the Self (ātman-vastu) called Brahman is indeed the Blessed Lord (Śrī Bhagavān). Even there, as it is heard [in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.15.43]: "He caused agitation in their minds and bodies, even though they were devoted to the Imperishable (akṣara)," he is therefore of even denser radiance than that. Such is he.

Furthermore, a manifold variety of bliss is perceived arising from the focused observation of the diverse major and minor limbs and other features of the Blessed Lord; and since this cannot be accounted for otherwise, it must indeed be a manifestation of the play of His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
Now, one might object: let it be that due to their abundance of bliss, [the devotees] possess only that very bliss of the undifferentiated essential nature (*nirviśeṣa-svarūpa-ānanda*) within Him.

It is a state of dense luminosity due to the specific qualification of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). For that very Brahman which flashes forth within a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) produced by pure being (*viśuddhasattva*), flashes forth as superimposed upon the Blessed Lord, who consists of dense, indivisible, and pure being.

When she has attained oneness with that [Supreme], she manifests with particular clarity. For this very reason, even the scriptural statements regarding the non-difference between the Śrī-vigraha (the divine form) and the Supreme Brahman are based solely upon their absolute identity (*atyanta-tādātmya*). Therefore, in each respective limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there is indeed only one [reality].

The supreme bliss of non-differentiation is directly perceived, yet not even a trace of the form of particularity is found therein; rather, the requirement for various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is based solely on the curiosity arising from the attainment of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) on that bliss at each successive stage.
Therefore, how could this means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establish that even those various limiting adjuncts possess the nature of the Supreme Reality?

If it is argued that [it] is established [as such], it is replied: In your view, that which is the manifestation of the Supreme Brahman within the pure mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) manifests correctly indeed;
for it is accepted that something possesses the nature of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) only when even a trace of the aspect of duality has been abandoned. As for incorrect knowledge...

Because you do not accept [the existence of] the principles (tattvas) and because liberation (kaivalya) would be impossible for that reason, it is not logical to accept the manifestation of a qualified form (adhikāvirbhāva) in the case of the venerable form (śrīvigraha) and so forth. Furthermore, what is your intention in saying that forms consisting of pure being (viśuddhasattvamaya) are distinct limiting adjuncts (vilakṣaṇopādhi)? Do they consist of its transformations (pariṇāma)?

Or is it that they are abundant in that [rajas]? Not the first, for it has already been stated that transformation is impossible due to the non-existence of rajas. Nor the second; for if one resorts to *arthāpatti* (presumption) on the grounds that those bodies and so forth in which that abundance exists are the effects of mixed *sattva*, then you would have to rely upon pure *sattva* for their maintenance (*sthiti*). [Bhāgavata Purāṇa]
In the collection of statements beginning with [10.2.34], it has already been stated that the term "pure" (viśuddha) would be redundant.
Alternatively, even if there were a state of being mixed, the very capacity for the manifestation of Brahman would not be possible in such a case;
how much less so in a specific instance? Furthermore, there would be a forgetting of the intended object (uddeśya).
Now, if it is argued that they too are described as being of that very nature by virtue of having the undivided, pure *sattva* as their substratum,
and that consequently they experience that Brahman within those [states] where the undivided, pure *sattva* has been experienced—

this is incorrect, because it involves the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). For they [the yogis] perceive that which is beyond the range of the senses and is the fortunate fruit of their own meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Because it is stated that [the Lord] is directly perceived (*sākṣād eva gocarīkṛta*), and because this contradicts the notion of being seen through a lineage of tradition (*paramparādṛṣṭatva*), his being composed of *prakṛti* is indeed refuted. Therefore, those [entities] are not transformations of material *sattva*, nor...

They abound in that [impurity], yet it has already been clearly stated that they are illuminated by pure *sattva* characterized by self-luminosity; for this very reason, once their status as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is refuted, the manifold variety of the bliss of those respective experiences is achieved. In the same way, that very [Self]—thus...
The statement that they "described it as being thus" would be meaningful only as a description of the beauty of various objects, since it serves the purpose at hand;
for the intended goal is accomplished merely by stating that [the world] consists of indivisible, pure *sattva*. Therefore:
And by the phrase "even after gazing, their eyes were not satiated" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.42), it is stated that the lack of satiety is caused by the form itself, because it pertains to the eyes;
and likewise, by the word "even" (ca), the state of being unable to transcend the syllable [of the name] is indicated.
The specific characteristic consisting of the wind whose fragrance is that of the lotus feet has thus been shown.

Otherwise, if the bliss of Brahman were perceived as devoid of distinction in both cases alike, then the phrase "even for those who possess knowledge" would refer primarily to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). It is precisely the pair of adjuncts [that is meant].

Because of the attainment of mutual rivalry; by this statement regarding the superiority of the bliss of experiencing the Imperishable (akṣara), even the notion that "this is merely a semblance of absorption, like the grief for a son experienced by Vaiśiṣṭha and others" is refuted.
For this very reason, it was stated by the venerable Svāmin as well: "Even more than the bliss of their own essential nature (svarūpānanda)..."
He states that there is a superiority in the bliss of devotion:

"Therefore, there is also diversity. For this very reason, even they have prayed with such diversity—as in [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.49]: "O, if only my mind would delight in Your feet like a bee," and so forth.

According to the maxim, "If one finds honey nearby, why should one go to the mountain?", there is no point in searching for other teachers; furthermore, they lack any curiosity to seek out such a teacher.
Moreover, no experience of non-difference from them is observed; on the contrary, having looked at them, [the disciples] bowed down.
In passages such as "Whose eyes are not satiated with joy? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.42) and "May Bhava, by our own sins, lead us to the hells as he pleases" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.49),
one perceives only the bliss of devotion characterized by duality, such as prostrations and other acts directed toward Him as its counter-positive.

Therefore, because it is devoid of illusory adjuncts (*māyikopādhi*) and because it appears as that which is to be abandoned (*heyāṃśa*), it is not possible for that [state] to produce a pleasure of a different kind; thus, these are indeed the manifestations of the very power of its own nature (*svarūpaśakti*), established through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*).
Moreover— let it be granted for now that in the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), according to their view,

there exists a direct identity with the Blessed Lord, who is Brahman itself reflected through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of knowledge; yet, even in the state of final liberation where all adjuncts are completely removed, such a direct identity with the intensely luminous Brahman remains.

Thus, as clearly stated in passages such as, "They do not even reckon Your grace as ultimate" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.48), there is no need for concern regarding the presence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). By the phrase "in Your narration" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.48), this very diversity is explicitly accepted as existing beyond the state of being the unconditioned Brahman.

Therefore, by the authority of the experience of the wise, it is determined that the Blessed One, whose inner majesty is infinite, is of the singular nature of bliss; and even while being of that nature, He possesses a density of light even greater than Brahman, as well as a manifold variety arising from the play of the powers of His own essential nature.

In this regard, even the liberated ones, assuming forms through their divine play (*līlā*), worship Him. As it is stated in the Śruti: "Him whom all the gods, those seeking liberation, and the exponents of Brahman honor," and here too are the teachers of the Advaita doctrine.
And in the Mahābhārata: "Kṛṣṇa is worshipped by the liberated who are free from delusion."
Having become Brahman, serene in soul, he neither grieves nor desires;
he is the same toward all beings.

"He attains supreme devotion to Me" (Gītā 18.54), thus it is stated in the Śrī Bhagavadgītā Upaniṣads. Furthermore, in the *Bhāratatātparya*, it is established by scripture that even for the liberated, devotion is indeed of the nature of eternal bliss; likewise, this is seen in the passage: "Until the final departure, for there too it is observed."
The *Sauparṇa-śruti*, authenticated by the *Madhva-bhāṣya*, states: "One should worship Him at all times until liberation;
for it is said that they worship Him. It is precisely with this in mind—referring to the connection with great devotees such as Śrī Prahlāda and Bali—that [the Lord acts].
It is also stated in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "Even for one who is liberated, no pleasure arises in Pātāla.
A specific detail regarding this should be understood from the *Śrī Bhagavat-sandarbha*.
(50) [Bhagavat-sandarbha 85] Viśvanātha: Thus, due to the desire for the threefold bliss arising from hearing Your glories and so forth...

"Even worldly existence, which is far removed from you, is prayed for; yet by you, even we who have committed offenses against your devotees have been made to drink the nectar of your own direct realization. Oh, such is the limit of your forgiveness, and such is your boundless compassion!"—thus they say with the word "prādurbhūta" (manifested). "Puru" means as much as possible, or by many people.

The meaning is: "O Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Govinda! You who were called upon by devotees saying, 'By Your grace, grant us Your vision'—by You, who manifested Your own form while being completely overcome by compassion arising from that call of Your own devotees, even we have been made successful. The word *dṛśaḥ* refers to eyes or the functions of the intellect; [the phrase] "this obeisance" (*idaṃ namaḥ*) [is directed toward You].
They display their joined palms held upon their heads.

"It" means "thus. Alternatively, "it" (id) is an adjective for "the Name" (nama), meaning that which goes toward the glorious lotus-feet. You are the Self of those who do not possess a self—that is, those for whom the [ordinary] self does not exist as an object of service.

The sense is that their emergence through attachment is difficult; they are "difficult to arise" (durudaya) because they lack self-control and are empty of self, being as good as dead. The meaning is that he is certainly as difficult to behold as the sun is to owls, for he is well-known [as such].
Here, [he is compared] to those crest-jewels who delight solely in the Self.

For Sanaka and others— who are well-known from such scriptural passages as "To him whose impurities have been wiped away, the Blessed Lord Sanatkumāra shows the further shore of darkness"— who have attained uninterrupted experience of Brahman even through hearing, the very sign of such a prayer in their devotion [indicates] that [their longing] is even greater than for the bliss of Brahman.

When the superiority of the bliss of devotion (*bhajanānanda*) is understood, it follows by itself that the forms, names, qualities, paraphernalia, and the abodes of the devotees of the Lord are composed of pure consciousness (*cidghana*); for,
as will be explained later in the *Kāpileya*, devotion cannot be established without such being the case.

Furthermore, its qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) will be explained. And there is the Śruti cited as authoritative in the *Bhāratatātparya*: "For even for the liberated, devotion has the nature of eternal bliss. Also, regarding the passage "Until death, for that too is seen," there is the *Sauparṇa-śruti* cited as authoritative in the *Mādhvabhāṣya*: "One should worship Him at all times."

"Indeed, it has been said that one should worship this [Lord] until liberation. For this very reason, with reference to the connection with great devotees such as Prahlāda and Bali, it is also stated in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "In Pātāla, who would not feel delight, even one who is liberated?"
Thus, in this *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
the fifteenth [chapter] has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous.
Thus ends the third book in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, in the Vaiyāsikī collection pertaining to the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
The fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Vaikuṇṭha," from the Dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
The Fall of Jaya and Vijaya.
Brahmā said:
While those sages, who were devoted to the practice of yoga, were thus chanting that [prayer],...
Having greeted him with joy, the all-pervading Lord whose abode is Vikuṇṭha spoke this:
Śrīdhara says:
When the sixteen [thousand] brahmins were consoled by Hari and felt remorse,
their favor was extended even while they remained in the state of asuras.

Having thus welcomed those words of theirs as they were speaking, he spoke this with eleven verses in a sequential composition. Having thus rebuked them for their self-centeredness, he praises them for their status as Brahmins with four verses beginning with "yasya" (of whom). *Kīrti* is the fame mentioned previously. Although they are lords of the world (*lokeśvarāḥ*),...
They are indeed far inferior to those two; nevertheless, it was explained in that manner in the commentary solely for the purpose of concealing obscenities. ||1||
Viśvanātha:

Hari, perceiving that those who knew their own kinship toward his servants and their devotion toward himself were now manifesting [their true nature] in the sixteenth [year], consented to their curse alone.
Thus was that speech of theirs as they spoke and offered praise. ||1||
The Blessed Lord said:
These two attendants of mine are Jaya and Vijaya.
Since you have disregarded me and committed this great transgression against my command.
O sages, that very punishment which has been imposed upon these two by you, who are devoted to me, is likewise approved by us for their contempt of the gods.

Śrīdhara: Since they, having treated me with contempt—that is, having rendered me insignificant—have committed a great transgression against you, therefore that very punishment has been accepted. ||2–3||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He says, "You should not fear out of apprehension of some offense," with these eleven verses beginning with "These two. "To me" means to my [self]. Because, having treated me with contempt—that is, having made me insignificant—he [acted] much... [the rest of the sentence follows].

"Your transgression against me—who am established in my own nature and whose nature is eternal—has been committed. To act contrary to my will is indeed a slight; therefore, the punishment you have inflicted upon yourselves must certainly be carried out by me," he said, using the word "those who. This refers to those for whom their vows are directed toward me, because of their contempt for me, the God.
The sense is that, in reality, this offense of these two pertains only to me. ||23||
Therefore, I seek to propitiate you today, for the Brahman is my supreme deity; indeed,
I consider that act of mine to have been committed against myself, since I have treated those who are truly men with disrespect.

Śrīdhara: For indeed, because the Brāhmaṇas alone are my supreme deity (daivata), therefore today I propitiate you. If it is asked, "What offense have I committed?", he says in response: "For that [which was done] by my men"—namely, that they were ill-treated and insulted—that was done by myself alone.
I think. ||4||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, he says "that [is] yours" (*tad vaḥ*) to show that the fault was mine alone toward you.
But how could there be a fault on your part? To this he says "for that... (*tad dhi*). [This refers to the case where] Jayavijaya...
The sense is: "If my two servants were not [present], or if I myself were not pleased with that, then no offense would be mine. ||4||
Whatever names the world utters when a servant has committed an offense,
that ill-repute destroys his reputation, just as a disease destroys the skin.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he says that these two have done what is undesirable for me alone: "The fame of that master whose names [they bear]... Here, *āmaya* refers to white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*). (5)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, how can there be an offense against you, the Supreme Lord? Even if there were an offense, who would be the punisher? Why do you shrink back from this? Let there be no punisher in that case, but ill-repute will surely follow.

Thus he says: the names of whichever master [are used]—thinking "this servant of such-and-such a person is a doer of evil deeds"—destroy the very reputation of that master. Just as the disease *śvitra* destroys the skin, yet at the same time produces the censure "this man is a leper" directed at the one who possesses that skin; this is the meaning. ||5||
He whose nectar-like, stainless fame purifies the world instantly upon being heard, reaching even as far as the dog-cookers (the lowest of outcastes), is Vikuṇṭha.
Thus, having received from you the renown of being one who has found the true path, I would cut off even my own arm if it were to act in opposition to you.
"Of Madhva: 'The unmentioned qualities of Viṣṇu have been stated, but his defects have not;
the perception of defects arises from ignorance, while the knowledge of qualities arises from the reality of the Self. Thus says the Paiṅgi Śruti.
Śrīdhara: 'In whose stainless glory, which is of the nature of nectar, there is immersion—that is, entry—by means of hearing...'"

He purifies the entire world, including even the outcaste (śvapaca), instantly—that is, at that very moment. Such as I am, having obtained (upalabdha) and attained (prāpta) from you, who have become the cause, a most beautiful (su-śobhanā) and sacred (tīrtha-bhūtā) fame; I could slay even the Lord of the World (Lokeśvara) who stands in the place of my own arm—what need is there to mention anyone else?
The meaning is this: the description of one's own qualities is solely for the purpose of exalting the Brāhmaṇas. ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, if it is argued that "your ill-repute arises from our transgression, and your fame arises from our favor;
therefore, the living beings such as ourselves, who are created by you, are even more supreme than you, O Supreme Lord," [then we reply:]...

If you ask, "How could we have become superior? he says—"Of whom... [referring to the verse]. I am that Vikuṇṭha, by whom fame in the form of a supreme holy place (sutīrtha) was obtained from you who served as the cause;
what then can be said of Jayavijaya, the objects of my possessiveness (mamatā), when even my own arm—the locus of my ego (ahaṃtā)—was cut off?
The sense is: "I might even cut [myself], yet being incapable of that, I am simply guilty before you. ||6||
By whose service the dust of his lotus feet, which instantly destroys all impurities and restores one's virtuous character, [is attained].
Fortune does not abandon me even though I am detached— she for whose sake others observe religious vows merely for the sake of a glimpse of her.
Madhva, though the supreme among all, speaks of attaining qualities from the worship of devotees such as Brahmins,
even while remaining eternally perfect.

And others might say somewhere: "But that [wealth] is acquired through the essence of the dust from their feet; and the best people also take it up for the sake of deluding the worlds. Thus it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Fortune does not [abandon] one whose character has been attained through service to the pure dust of the lotus-feet of the Brahmins."
That which abandons is "yat. ||7||

Śrīdhara: [He is] one by whom the pure dust situated upon the two lotus-feet has destroyed—that is, dispelled—the impurity of the entire world. Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "one in whom the pure dust adhering to the lotus-feet is present," and "one by whom all impurity has been destroyed. Thus it is obtained.

By whom this moral conduct has been attained; through whose service these virtues are mine, for that very reason Fortune does not abandon me even for the sake of a mere glance—a tiny fraction of her look. As for others, such as Brahmā and the rest:
"I shall cut off your hostile behavior"—this is to be connected with the preceding verse. (7)
The sequence of the composition: To the question, "How do you possess such a nature [of devotion] toward us? he replies with the words "by whose service" (*yatsevayā*).
The meaning is this: according to what will be stated later—that for Brahmins, who are gods among gods, the Blessed Lord is their own deity—it is by the very nature of those Brahmins that...

By the very service and association with you who are devoted to the meditation on Brahman characterized by [the state of] a *malla*, I have become one whose power is manifested by the pure dust residing upon your lotus feet;
thus, all impurity has been destroyed, since even toward those who worship me, there is indifference arising from my delight in the Self (*ātmarāmatva*).

Such a person has been born. Furthermore, he has become one who possesses the state of happiness consisting of affection for his devotees and so forth, having acquired moral conduct (*śīla*); and it is said that even though such a person as I am is detached, Śrī—the presiding deity of the entire universe—does not abandon nor forsake him. And thus:
The greatness of her has indeed become great through the service of others as well; thus he says, "Of whom...

The others are the world-protectors and so forth. Therefore, the intention is that what was said by him—"I am such a one to you," and so on—is truly well-said. In that regard, even that which is performed by you, such as salutation and the like, is also [of great merit].
It is only for fear of transgressing your will that [the objection] is not refuted. ||7||
Viśvanātha: [Objection] "But surely this very result of our coming to Vaikuṇṭha has occurred;
since you, who are our desired deity, speak thus even to us, what is there that you say which is contrary? To this he replies: "By service to whom my two lotus feet became established there..."

Even the dust particles purify the world; all impurities such as desire and the like have been destroyed by me, as well as by others for my sake. I have acquired virtues of good character, and even the goddess Lakṣmī—whose boundless wealth others, including Brahmā and the rest, undergo religious observances merely to obtain even a fraction of her glance—does not abandon me.
