The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: "I shall even cut off my own arm if those very people by whose service [you] all practice austerities and so forth should act in opposition to you. ||7||
I do not eat in that manner the sacrificial oblation, dripping with ghee and soaked in clarified butter, within the ritual enclosure, through the mouth of the consumer of the burnt offering.
That which comes from the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa as he moves about, eating his morsels of food with contentment while focused upon me through the ripening of his own past deeds.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, [the Lord] says, "I am not," meaning that the Brāhmaṇa is indeed my most excellent mouth; therefore, by your contempt for him, you have committed an insult against my very mouth. Thus he says: "I am not... Even though I am eating—that is, consuming—the sacrificial oblations such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offered by the sacrificer at the *vitāna* sacrifice through the mouth of Agni, the consumer of the oblation (*hutabhuj*), I am not [that Agni]. So it is said.

I neither eat nor do I consume. Whatever—such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like—is soaked and stirred with dripping, flowing clarified butter (*ghṛta*), I eat from the mouth of the wise Brāhmaṇa who partakes of it, tasting its flavor at every morsel; [that is, I eat] from the mouth of one who is satisfied by the fruits of actions offered unto me.
The meaning is "of one who is free from desire. ||8||

The sequence of the composition: Therefore, he says "Not by me... [verse 8], meaning that my own internal satisfaction shall likewise arise only through the satisfaction of the Brahmins, for they have been fixed upon me with great affection and have surrendered everything to me alone.

Viśvanātha says: "In this way, I serve only the Brāhmaṇas; and those who, through my vision, serve the Brāhmaṇas, they alone are my servants, because I eat only through the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa. Thus he says: "Not I... [The meaning is: the sacrificial oblation of the patron—such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*—is consumed by the fire, which is the eater (*hutabhuj*). By that [fire],...

Even though not eating or consuming with my own mouth, I do not eat in that way; rather, I eat from the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa, mouth to mouth, as he eats, taking every morsel and breath, drenched and pervaded by dripping clarified butter—
this should also be understood here in the case of one who acts or eats, through the fruits of actions dedicated to me.

By the word "of one who is satisfied" (*tuṣṭasya*), and by the subsequent statement, "Thus, for the Brahmins, the gods of gods, the Blessed One is their own deity" (*tathā viprāṇāṃ devadevānāṃ bhagavān ātmadaivataṃ*), having established that a Brahmin is unworthy of worship in the absence of devotion— just as one would not look upon a dog-eater— it is said: "In this world, one should not look upon a Brahmin who is not a Vaiṣṇava," and so forth.

The contradiction in the statement has been resolved. In that context, the meaning should be understood as "one who is not a Vaiṣṇava" and "one who hates Vaiṣṇavas. Thus, it is only a Brāhmaṇa who possesses his own dharma mixed with devotion who truly becomes a Vaiṣṇava, such as Vasiṣṭha and others. When devotion is predominant for the sake of liberation (kaivalya), even one who is a Brāhmaṇa by birth is a Vaiṣṇava.
Thus it is said; one should discern that this refers to those such as the venerable Nārada and others. ||8||
I bear upon my crowns the stainless dust from the feet of those who possess unbroken and unshakable yoga-māyā and divine opulence.
Who indeed would not revere the Brahmins, since the water used for their worship instantly purifies even the worlds of those who bear the moon as their crest-ornament?
Janārdana is the honey for the sages, for his devotees, and for other people as well;
he is likewise the source of Brahmā, of Śaṅkara, and of the cosmic eggs of the deities.

"He might even speak, utterly deluding [the listener], about the dearness and the venerability of himself and his own prosperity as being exceedingly improper"—thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. (9)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, who else would not resent even those who wrong the Brahmins, upon whose stainless dust I bear [my head] with my crowns? Of what nature am I?
I am one whose opulence consists of the play of *yogamāyā*, which is unbroken, uninterrupted, and unimpeded.

He is such that the water used for his worship—the water from his feet—immediately purifies the worlds together with the Lord who has the moon as his crest-ornament. Thus, although the Supreme Lord is himself supremely purifying, he thinks, "I am the one who bears [this water]. (9)
The sequence of composition: "Because it is thus, therefore [it is said] 'of those who... (9).

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, even an offense committed by a Brahmin must simply be endured and not retaliated against; thus he says, "Of those who... Who would not endure even those who wrong the Brahmins?
Indeed, everyone would. When the desire arises to know the reason for this, [the Lord], pointing to his own crown with his forefinger, says:

He said: "By those whose dust from the feet I bear upon my crown, and by the grace of supporting whom I attained the perfection of unimpeded *yogamāyā*; likewise, by Him whose water of worship—the water from His feet—immediately purifies the worlds along with Mahādeva, the moon-crested one—"
One should know that the dust from the feet of such a person is worn upon the head, and the nectar of his feet alone is to be received, and not that of anyone else. ||9||
Those who, with a sense of duality, regard my own bodies as the best of the twice-born, as the elements that nourish them, and as beings who have found no refuge;
For those whose vision is impaired by sin and who are arrogant with pride shall behold them;
then the vultures will angrily tear at them as they lie under the rod of my supreme punishment.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, what are my bodies that serve as my substrata? What are they? They are the "excellent twice-born" (dvijavarān), meaning cows that yield milk (*dogdhrīḥ*). Even if the reading were *duhituḥ* ("daughters"), it would still refer to cows, because they are born from Sūrya, who is a form of Viṣṇu, according to the scriptural statement: "Cows are the daughters of Sūrya. [These bodies] have found no refuge.
Those who, with a sense of division, shall look upon my domain as being devoid of protectors;
those whose vision is destroyed and ruined by sin;
those who are the vulture-shaped messengers of Yama, my appointed leader and punisher; and those whose wrath is like a serpent, [driven] by rage.
In their anger, they scratch with their beaks and tear [the flesh]. ||10||

The sequential arrangement: Therefore, he says—"Those who [disregard] my forms"—meaning those bodies which, because they lack distinguishing attributes, are the objects of my ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which are "mine" (*madīyā*) as the objects of my possessiveness (*mamatā*), and which, having found no refuge, are the objects of my compassion. He further states that if [the Brahmins and others] do not likewise form this very understanding regarding those who seek refuge in me among the Brahmins and the rest, they shall incur punishment.
By means of the cognition of difference, that is, by means of the cognition of "this" and "otherness" regarding each respective thing. ||10||

Viśvanātha: What need is there to speak of those who cannot endure the transgressions committed against Brahmins? He says that only those who perceive a difference between themselves and Brahmins are destined for hell: "Those people who milk my bodies"—meaning cows in the form of my own body; in the reading *duhitèḥ*, it refers to the cows themselves.
Because they are born from the Sun, who is the form of Viṣṇu, and because of the scriptural statement that "cows are the daughters of the Sun," those who—
being without refuge and protector, and with bodies intoxicated by the notion of duality—
shall look upon them with a sense of separateness, [I shall deliver] them to Yama, my appointed leader of punishment.
Those messengers who have the form of vultures, possessing the pride of serpents, scratch with rage and anger, and tear at the eyes and other parts with their beaks. ||10||
Those brahmins, whose hearts were satisfied as they honored me while I was casting [the challenge] with my intellect, their lotus-like faces moistened by the nectar of smiles;
Addressing me as "I" with a voice full of affection, like that of a son, they have brought me here.
Śrīdhara: He says that those who have become such as these bring me under their control: "Those who, even while speaking, awaken the men who revile them;
who, possessing the intellect directed toward Me, worship with the vision of Vāsudeva; and who are satisfied in heart, meaning their minds are filled with joy; [and who offer] a smile."
I [was addressed] by them— those whose faces were like lotuses, sprinkled and moistened as it were with nectar,
and who praised me with words possessing a trace of affection or the beauty of love, just as a tender father addresses an angry son,
or as sons address their father, or as Bhṛgu addressed me, or as I [addressed] you. By them, I...
"Upahṛtaḥ" means brought under control. ||11||
The sequential arrangement: Furthermore, he speaks specifically regarding the devotion of ordinary Brāhmaṇas with the words "He who...
The meaning is that the intellect which resides in me, characterized by devotion to Brahmā, follows precisely that [devotion]. ||11||

Viśvanātha: He says, "I alone am under the control of those who, even when Brahmins have committed transgressions, do not retaliate but rather treat them with greater courtesy"— those who, with that intellect directed toward Me,
which views all as the Blessed Lord, honor the Brahmins even while speaking to a man who insults them.

With hearts satisfied even by harsh words, they praise this Person, saying: "Like good sons addressing an angry father with speech full of affectionate artistry and the essence of love, you do not speak thus; rather, you rain down the nectar of compassion, which is supremely beneficial. Thus they offer their praise.

They awaken [him] and please him with tender addresses such as "O Lords! and "O Oceans of Compassion!"; they say, "Just as I am, so too are you; by them, Bhṛgu was brought near to me and subdued. ||11||
Not perceiving my husband’s resolve, and having immediately understood the course of your transgression, [they...]
Since they have come back to me once more, let it be my favor that their exile may soon come to an end.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, because they did not perceive—that is, were unaware of—my intention, let them both immediately attain the state appropriate for your offense and come into my presence. "That" refers to my favor toward them. He states that very thing: that their separation, once they have been supported, shall be brief—meaning swift.
"May it be fulfilled; may it be accomplished; may it be completed," [he said]. ||12||
The sequence of events: By the grace of the Blessed One, let those two come into my presence; however, please arrange for these two servants to be dismissed quickly.
That which is done for me by you is indeed a form of favor; otherwise, I would face punishment.
The sense is that there would be no happiness. ||12||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, the sense is this: "May these two, failing to perceive—that is, not seeing by fate—the intention or purpose of my own master, and immediately attaining the state appropriate for your offense, return once more to my presence; such is my prayer."

"O Lord, you yourself have stated with your own lips that those who transgress against a brāhmaṇa are indeed my offenders. Therefore, how can you again show affection toward those very two? To this, he spoke out of his own complete subjection [to them], saying: "Their grace is mine. This is because their grace toward Jayavijaya is my own grace.
Thus, it is not a matter of punishment; for the meaning is that one's inherent nature (*svābhāvika-dharma*) cannot be abandoned.

Therefore, let a "separation" (*vivāsa*)—meaning a distinguished dwelling together with me—of the two supported ones (*bhṛtayoḥ*, i.e., the two dependents) be arranged immediately; let them become capable [of this]. ||12||
Brahmā said: Then, to that goddess Uśatī, the Ṛṣikulyā Sarasvatī—
Even their own selves were not satisfied by tasting the blood of those who were bitten by wrath.
Madhvaḥ: the goddess who shines; Ṛṣikulyām: she who is devoted to the praise of the lineage of sages. ||13||
Śrīdhara: Having tasted Sarasvatī— the speech that is *uśatī* (desirable), the beloved goddess who shines forth, who is the *ṛṣikulyā* (the stream of the seers,
meaning she whose form is the flow of mantras, or one suitable for the lineage of seers)—
they shall become intoxicated by it, even those who have been bitten by a venomous serpent-like fury (*manyu*).

For the minds of those pervaded by the poison of anger cannot endure even pleasant speech due to the absence of any experience of aesthetic flavor; yet their own souls were not satisfied, nor did they think, "Enough. ||13||
The sequential arrangement: [he meditates on] the Goddess endowed with sovereign power. ||13||

Viśvanātha: [He beheld] Sarasvatī—the goddess of speech and the river—desirable and lovely (in one sense), and pure (in the other); playing with the intellect of sages, which consists of various conjectures and the like (in one sense), and with the venerable [goddess] (in the other);
beneficial to the lineage of seers (in one sense) and a stream or reservoir for the sages (in the other)—having tasted her sweetness.

Having experienced [this], their minds—bitten by a fury like a serpent and pervaded by the poison of anger—could not endure even pleasant speech because of the absence of any experience of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); indeed, neither their self, nor their intellect, nor their mind found satisfaction, and they did not think, "Enough. In that state, although there was great anguish for them...
The fact that the poison of the serpent of anger does not depart makes it known that the offense committed against a devotee is indeed difficult to overcome.
Nevertheless, even when such an offense by a devotee exists,
that experience of the sweetness of the fragrance of the Lord’s feet, the *tulasī*, and so forth—
The compassion felt by Jaya and Vijaya toward those [demons] immediately after their transgression against the Brahmins—
compassion which followed from the Lord’s own compassion— serves to demonstrate the very power of that divine grace;
therefore, had there not been this offense against the devotees on their part, then for these [demons], who have become vessels of the compassion of both the devotees and the Lord...
Pure love for servitude alone would have arisen; however, because of the presence of offenses, they remained merely peaceful devotees. As it has been said:
"Even a state of being reaches non-existence through offense against those most dear to Kṛṣṇa."
"...and its state of being a mere semblance, even its inferiority in kind" (Bhartṛhari,
VP 1.3.54)— thus, while opening their mouths, they listen to that which is trivial yet contains the depths of profound meaning.
Having plunged into that which is unfathomably deep, they do not understand his intended purpose.
Śrīdhara: "Satīm" means excellent. "Vyādāya" means having opened wide or extended; the sense is that he has applied his ear.

"Laghvīm" means concise in its syllables. "Gurubhir arthair gahvarām" means difficult to enter due to its weighty meanings—that is, unfathomable in its intention and profound in its substance. Even after plunging into it and investigating it, does he welcome us?
Do they censure him? Or do they mitigate the punishment we have imposed? They do not know. ||14||

The composition of the sequence: *satīm* means sincere and guileless; *gurvarthagahvarām* means that in which the purpose or goal is like a thicket, being difficult to penetrate; because it is *agādhagambhīrām*, meaning unfathomable in its depth—unfathomable in terms of its inner essence (*bhāva*) as it has no bottom, and profound in terms of its meaning (*artha*) as it is difficult to fathom. Therefore, having plunged into it to the best of one's ability, [one attains] satisfaction.

The meaning is that they do not know His desired activity therein, characterized by pastimes such as battle; thus says Viśvanātha: [He speaks] to those who listen with their ears opened wide—[to them He speaks] that which is *satī* (true, real, and beautiful), *laghvī* (concise in syllables), yet *gurubhir arthair gahvarām* (profound and difficult to enter due to its weighty meanings), and *agādhām* (bottomless).

With the intention of approaching her who was unapproachable, having plunged into and reflected upon her profound speech—whose internal and external meanings were difficult for outsiders to understand—he considered:

"Does she welcome us or reproach us? Does she impose a penalty for what we have done, or does she mitigate it, or does she dismiss it? Or does she charge us with an offense, or does she treat us as mere servants?"
"Because of their excessive devotion," they did not understand what He intended to do. Regarding this, the position of praise has already been explained.

As for the position of censure, although it was not intended by the Blessed One, it must be explained in this way because the sages, being afraid, imagined it within themselves, and because Sarasvatī had granted them the opportunity.

For instance, by introducing even the omniscient sages with the words, "These two attendants are mine," he implied: "O fools! You have cursed even my attendants; do you possess such power as this? Since you have overstepped so much, having treated me with contempt.

Regarding the phrase "transgression" (*atikramam*), because there was no prior mistreatment of the Blessed One by Sanaka and the others, this elliptical expression (*vakrokti*) of the Blessed One toward them is intended solely to manifest his anger. In reality, however, through the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) of the dative case, he implies: "First my own mistreatment was committed [by you], and then the transgression against you."
"Thus, the Blessed One has employed a reversal of the temporal sequence between cause and effect;

that very point is approved by us. Had our approval been given [earlier], then even the punishment inflicted by you would not have struck him, for though capable through the power of Brahmanic luster, he did not wish to strike with his hand; yet, it was my will."
Because it was spoken by the foremost;

and thus, the sense is that it is my very devotion to Brahmanas that maddens you, such that you would have become worth only half the price of a young boy. "I consider that [suffering] to be self-inflicted"—thus [says] Jaya and Vijaya.

Because of accepting [the Munis] as one's own self, there is an abundance of love; yet, thinking "I have attained fame through the holy sites from you," there is merely respect toward the Munis. Furthermore, the thought "I would even cut off my own arm" indicates that they alone are the objects of love, while the thought "by serving whom? indicates respect once more toward the Munis.
He too is merely an outsider; for what reason was the dust of his feet purified by the service of Brahmins alone?
By that service alone, were all his impurities destroyed? And by that alone, why does Lakṣmī not desert him?
Since there is no such cause, he says at the outset, "I am not like that," implying, "O Brahmins, you are lovers of food."
"Only those who are worthy of being fed," he said. "It is through the mouth of the Brahmin that I eat"—thus has his fame been spread throughout the worlds.
By the double meaning (*śleṣa*) "he grazes upon fodder," it is implied that the Brahmin is indeed to be honored like a cow;
because of his animal-like intellect, he rejoices in the respect shown by me, but not by you.
Thinking that some service to me might exist for the sake of my own pleasure,

he wears the dust from the feet of Brahmins upon his crowns; and because of that very act of bearing it, my sovereign power through *yogamāyā* is such that, for that same reason, the water from my feet is held in such high esteem as the Gaṅgā, which purifies the entire world.

The mockery itself has borne fruit. [Thinking] "they are my cows," there is no distinction between cows and Brahmins, for both are my body; thus, there was laughter once more. As for those who [speak of] Brahmins—anger is indeed the innate nature (*autpattika*) of Brahmins, and both I and my devotees [know] that.

"Even while laughing, they said, 'Forbearance is nectar; it has been granted by me only to my devotees. It was by that very quality that I was won over. Since forbearance has now ceased to arise in Jayavijaya, I have become indifferent toward them; therefore, the curse has taken effect upon you. Otherwise, it would never have prevailed."

For this very reason, because I was not indifferent toward Ambarīṣa, even the matted hair cast off by Durvāsas in his anger was rendered fruitless; on the contrary, the distress caused by my own discus was actually instigated by me, out of my devotion to Brahmins, resulting in acts such as Ambarīṣa’s falling at my feet.
"O Lord, whether you ordain punishment for these two or their means of livelihood,
we accept that without guile; or rather, let that penalty which is appropriate for us be maintained, since we,
though innocent, have been joined with guilt"— by observing this first statement, this interpretation as a form of censure is explained.
With palms joined in reverence, the brāhmaṇas, overjoyed and their hair standing on end, spoke to Him whose supreme sovereignty had been fully manifested through His yogic power (yogamāyā).
Madhva says: "The expansion of her eyebrows is the abode of Parameṣṭhin"—thus it has been stated. ||15||
Śrīdhara: Then, perceiving that [the Lord] was rejoicing, they, being overjoyed, spoke.

Their skin was agitated and their hair stood on end (*romāñcita*). In the reading *kūpita*, the state of having hair standing on end is expressed by the mention of the appearance of the pores of the body (*romakūpa*). The supreme sovereignty (*pārameṣṭhya*) had been commenced—that is, manifested.
"Mahodaya" means that which possesses supreme excellence; having manifested his status as sovereign lord, he honors the Brāhmaṇas for the sake of instructing kings—this is the meaning. ||15||

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary]: For them as well, qualities such as being "open-palmed" (prāñjali) are the cause of great devotion. Regarding the word "yoga," it refers to *yogamāyā*, which is the power of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*). Regarding the reading "kupita," it refers to skin in which there are sunken areas resembling wells that have formed in the intervals between the hair roots due to their swelling. ||15||

Viśvanātha: But how can there be an offense against you, the Supreme Lord? Even if there were an offense, why do you shrink from the thought of who would be the punisher? To this he replies: "Let there be no punisher; however, ill-repute will surely arise"—namely, that for such a master, this servant of so-and-so has committed an evil deed.

It destroys the very reputation of its owner. The meaning is that while the disease *śvitra* destroys the skin, it nevertheless produces censure for the person who possesses that skin, such that he is regarded as a leper (*kuṣṭhin*).
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, O God, we do not know what you intend to do,
even though you, the Overseer, declare, 'I have bestowed my grace upon him.'"
Śrīdhara: Since you, as the presiding Lord of all, have said, "I consider that [suffering] to be self-inflicted," implying,
"I have committed an offense," and since you speak of "your grace toward me" and so forth,
we do not know what it is that you intend to do.

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] begins with "Not we," etc. This is the meaning: for these two servants of Vaikuṇṭha, contempt for Brāhmaṇas is impossible. Furthermore, for us who are established in Brahman, anger is generally impossible, and especially so toward the attendants (pārṣadas) who have arrived here due to their devotion to the Lord.
We do not know what it is you intend to do, by which all those seemingly impossible things have been brought about.

The reason for this is that you are the presiding Lord both within and without, capable of making everything otherwise by virtue of being the Sovereign of All. Or perhaps it is our own fault, and not your intended purpose.

"Therefore, you yourself, as our presiding witness, should have previously restrained the internal organs of these two and of ourselves from their various forms of arrogance. And having intended for yourself the very accomplishment of your own desired goal, you say: 'For you have bestowed grace upon me.'"

Viśvanātha: Thus, although they have already understood the truth, they speak again with a question in order to hear his intention directly from his own mouth, saying: "We [do not know]," etc. The meaning is: whether it be the grace (*anugraha*) or the restraint (*nigraha*) he intends to perform; for since the Overseer (*adhyakṣa*), being the Lord of all, [acts] toward us...

When you say, "Have you not shown me favor by you? you first mock us out of a desire to deceive us, because such a thing is impossible; or else, out of devotion to Brahmins, you mock us while actually desiring to favor us for the sake of promoting the dharma you yourself have established—or is it indeed the truth?
The implication is: "Praise [the Buddha], for you are unable to know our intentions; let us, who are ignorant, understand your own purpose. (16)
O Lord, for one devoted to Brahman, the Brāhmaṇas are indeed the supreme deity;
for the Brāhmaṇas, who are gods among gods, the Blessed One is their own tutelary deity."
Śrīdhara: With the word "kila" (it is said), they state the ultimate truth indicated for the sake of instructing the world: "Of the brahmins...
You, O Blessed One, are the Self and the deity even of the gods of gods, those who are themselves worthy of worship by the gods. ||17||
The sequence of the composition: Regarding what was stated beginning with "of whom [the world says] 'he is immortal,'" they say: "of the Brahmin.

The particle *kila* indeed implies untruth; that is a misrepresentation. And since that [misrepresentation] here is solely for the purpose of instructing the world, it has been explained by them in that manner. And in that context, although the term "of the Brahmin" refers primarily to his virtuous character (*sauśīlya*),...

The sense is that although you possess such qualities, it is nevertheless appropriate [for you to act thus] for the sake of instructing the world. Therefore, it is intended to show that our status as deities is established solely through our devotion to Brahman, whereas your status as deities exists by your very nature. ||17||

Viśvanātha: Elaborating upon the difficulty of understanding the words from the mouth of Śrī [Kṛṣṇa], they say: "Because you are devoted to the Brahmins (*brahmaṇya*), the Brahmin is your deity (*daivata*). Thus, your own divinity is real, whereas that of the Brahmins is not; furthermore, through wordplay (*śleṣa*), since the Self (*ātman*) is the deity, apart from you, they are as if dead.
The sense is: "What indeed is that which you say, beginning with 'Even that [is attained] by service to the pure dust of the lotus feet' (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.16.7)? ||17||
From you, the eternal Dharma is protected by your incarnations;
you are considered the supreme secret of Dharma, the changeless one.
Madhva: Even Dharma is difficult to understand. ||18||

Śrīdhara: The elaboration on the purpose of teaching the world consists of eight verses beginning with "From you" (*tvattaḥ*). Dharma arises from you alone and is protected by your incarnations (*avatāra*s). It is therefore supreme, consisting of the fruit [of liberation], secret, and worthy of being offered. Furthermore, you are not subject to modification like the fruits of heaven and so forth; rather, you are changeless (*nirvikāra*).
Therefore, the sense is that for you who are such as this, this [action] is merely for the purpose of instructing the world. ||18||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, by means of dharma alone when it is being practiced, the worlds become worthy of worship. That dharma is characterized solely by devotion to Him (*tadbhakti*), not by adherence to the system of castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*). And that dharma...

They say that because only those devoted to Him promote [the truth], Your devotees are superior even to the Brahmins: "The eternal Dharma, characterized by devotion, has manifested from You; it is protected by Your forms—the devotees—through vision (dṛṣṭyā), for the vision of the virtuous is established in the sight of those whose bodies have been offered. Thus, it is guarded by Your forms, the devotees.
The meaning is "because it operates everywhere. And that Dharma is the supreme form of the fruit;
it is not subject to modification like the fruits of heaven and so forth, but is considered to be You Yourself, who are changeless.
The meaning is that the attainment of You alone is the fruit of devotion to You. In that regard:
No dharma other than these two—the eternal and the changeless—is explained. ||18||
"Indeed,
by whose grace yogins, having turned away from the world, cross over death directly— what is it that you, sir, might be favored with by others?"

Śrīdhara says: They say this is contrary [to reason]—namely, "they cross over. How could it be that you, by whose very grace yogis, having become detached and turned away [from worldly life], cross over death, would yourself be favored by others?
The meaning is: "not at all. (19)
The sequential composition [of the commentary] begins with the words "They cross over. The meaning is: that which would be favored—what indeed is that?
It is beyond the reach of logic (tarkātīta). ||19||
Viśvanātha: Among those Brāhmaṇas as well, those who have renounced the world (nivṛtta) are superior to those devoted to worldly activity (pravṛtti-niṣṭha).
Even among them, the yogis are superior; they are those by whose grace others cross over death.
Therefore, the question is: "Who are you, who would be graced by others?"—that is, what kind of person are you?
Due to an excess of wonder. ||19||
Indeed, that very prosperity which others, seeking wealth, approach at every moment while bearing the dust of his feet upon their own heads;
Longing for the world of Him whose splendor is like a fresh garland of tulasī offered at His feet by Dhanya, as if she were longing for the realm of the Lord of Bees (Kṛṣṇa).

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: [it refers to] the Lord of those who follow the honey-bee (the devotees), the Lord of those who grasp the essence. Śrīdhara says that the world of Tulasī, which dwells at His feet, desires to dwell upon His chest as if out of rivalry, even though it has already found a place there.
And as for what was said: "By whose service the pure dust of the lotus-feet immediately..."

"His entire [past] has been destroyed; he has fully regained his character," and so forth—this they say is utterly impossible, as expressed in two verses: "He whom the divine power Lakṣmī attends at every moment, on every occasion, she whose foot-dust is worn by the fortunate."

As if desiring the world— the abode and station— of that Lord of Bees, the chief of bumblebees, whose very place is the fresh garland of Tulasī offered at his feet by those of virtuous deeds, [the creeper] clings to his feet. 20.
The sequential arrangement: "Him" (yam). And here, as before, Lakṣmī is the presiding deity over the world (*jagad-adhikāriṇī*), and not the beloved consort of Vaikuṇṭha herself.
Because she is the crest-jewel of the supreme devotees (*parama-bhāgavata-śiromaṇitva*), he approaches her—that is, he worships her. "Loka" means the sphere of objects.

By stating that she desired even the sovereignty of a particular insect in Vaikuṇṭha, her extreme inferiority compared to the Lakṣmī of Vaikuṇṭha is demonstrated. Furthermore, by the word "as if" (iva), her lack of detachment even toward her own domain, the world, is shown. ||20||
Viśvanātha: As for that which was said—
that by service to him, one immediately acquires a character whose every impurity is destroyed by the pure dust of his lotus feet;

Regarding the statement, "Prosperity does not abandon me even though I am detached" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.16.7), they say that this too is difficult to understand because it is improbable; they explain this in two verses: "To You, whom prosperity—Lakṣmī, in the form of wealth—approaches and serves at every moment, on every occasion..."
She whose foot-dust is held [by the fortunate]—

your beloved, as if desiring the world (the feet) of that lord of bees, the chief of bumblebees, whose glory resides right there in the fresh garland of *tulasī* offered at his feet by blessed devotees— even she, through her devotion to you...
The meaning is "it is so. ||20||
He,
who was devoted to the highest bhakti, did not show great respect for her as she followed a life of solitary conduct.
Purified by the dust of merit from following in the footsteps of the twice-born, O you who bear the Śrīvatsa mark, why have you gone, you who are a vessel for fortune?
Madhva: [He was] exceedingly devoted to her because of his supreme devotion to the Bhagavat, and not out of lust.
Devotion to Hari, affection for Hari, and qualities such as knowledge and bliss—these belong to Brahmā, Vāyu, and their wives, both in their state of office and in liberation.
And for Śeṣa, Vāsava, Indra, Hara, and their wives beginning with Vāsava, they should be understood in their respective order; however, on the earth, it is otherwise due to the causal basis.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the body on earth may differ;
however, the characteristic of the body remains eternally the same throughout the sequence beginning with Brahmā.

"All virtues whatsoever are superior to Śrī, and by rule they all belong to Viṣṇu—both those explicitly mentioned and those not mentioned; of this there is no doubt. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Tattvanirṇaya*. [She who is] being attended by those of pure conduct through their secluded and purified services...

He who did not show great respect even while she was serving him—such a person are you. This is the meaning: Lakṣmī serves you indeed with such excessive greed. How so? For she thought thus: "This man is a seeker of the essence, yet he is as fickle as a bee; and he [the bee] is toward that which has come to his feet..."
He delights in Tulasī along with his retinue, remaining motionless; therefore, the beauty of His feet must be exceedingly great.

Consequently, even though I am situated upon His chest, I shall—enduring the rivalry of the many hosts of His attendants such as the yogis, and despite the co-wifely status with Tulasī—serve His two feet. Thus it is.
Even though she follows you with great eagerness, you do not pay her much heed;

for you possess the most excellent association only with the supreme devotees of the Lord, and thus you are a treasure-house of supreme good fortune. Therefore, because it is an attainment of what was previously unobtainable, [you think]: "By the grace of the Brahmins, Śrī does not abandon me."

The explanation is not correct. Furthermore, you yourself are the vessel for those qualities worthy of veneration and are supremely pure; yet how much more so do that holy dust which clings to you at every step along the path of the twice-born, as well as the Śrīvatsa mark, purify?

What do they purify? And for what purpose did you accept both those cows as ornaments? Therefore, statements such as "by whose service the dust of the lotus feet is purified" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.16.7) are intended merely for the sake of gathering the world (lokasaṅgraha). ||21||

The sequence of composition: Therefore, although she was being attended by those of pure conduct, he did not show her great respect, because he did not take anything from that world and because he repeatedly established himself in the world as one who is supremely free from desire (*niṣkāma*). In this commentary, the single word *kim* (what) would appear to be joined in both ways in both places, even though it is but one.
According to the maxim "like the word *brahman*. ||21||

Viśvanātha: [The Lord] did not pay excessive regard—did not hold him in too high esteem—due to his solitary conduct and pure services. Here, by the word "excessive" (ati), it is meant that he was not regarded merely as a wife; rather, he was indeed regarded as a devotee, since his association and attachment were directed solely toward the supreme devotees.

He: The sense is this: although you have always been seeking Fortune (Lakṣmī), and even though you were indifferent toward her, that you say, "By the very grace of the Brāhmaṇas, Fortune does not abandon me"—is that so?
Likewise, there is the merit attached to every step along the path of the twice-born (dvijas).

Likewise, why did you obtain the Śrīvatsa mark, and for what reason did you become a vessel of fortune, possessing the sixfold sovereignty? Furthermore, how is it that those very two—the dust of merit and the Śrīvatsa mark—purify you? All of this is difficult to comprehend.
"What indeed?"—this is the meaning. ||21||
O Blessed One, you who appear in three ages, this world of moving and non-moving beings has been sustained for the sake of the twice-born and the gods by your own three steps of Dharma.
Surely that accumulated passion and darkness, which cause obstruction,
have been dispelled by you through your boon-granting form of pure goodness.
"Because he holds the honey [of immortality], the Blessed One is called Dharma; because he restrains, he is called Yama," according to the *Śabdanirṇaya*.
By means of the three abodes—Anantāsana, Vaikuṇṭha, and the Ocean of Milk—...
The Blessed One Kapila provides protection by increasing the strength of sentient beings.
"Though devoid of *sattva*, having cast off both *rajas* and *tamas*," thus it is said regarding the distinctions of liberation;
and also, "He is called Kapila, Varada, and Vikala. Therefore, the body of Kapila, the Bestower of Boons (*Varada*), consists merely of the causality of *sattva*. (22)
Śrīdhara says: "And this is indeed appropriate for you, the embodiment of Dharma," thus they say with the three verses beginning with "Of Dharma.
He appears in only three ages, hence he is called *triyuga*. Alternatively, the three pairs (*yugāni*) of ages are the *triyugas*;
since he possesses these six qualities denoted by the word *bhaga*, he is *triyuga*. O *triyuga*!

O You whose nature is Dharma, [the world] has been sustained—that is, protected—by Your own three unique feet, namely austerity (*tapas*), purity (*śauca*), and compassion (*dayā*). It is said "by three" because these continue to exist even during the Kali age, despite the collapse of Dharma. Having done what? Having bestowed upon us, *naḥ*, the granting of boons (*varadā*).

By means of his subtle body, he struck that [demon] with his own being-form; having cast away and dispelled the *rajas* and *tamas* which were the strikers of those feet, it was surely sustained for the sake of the twice-born and the deities—or rather, the form *nirasya* is used here with the elision of the prefix *vi*. It is our... [tanu].
The meaning is "turn back. ||22||

The sequential composition: Now, out of despondency regarding their residence in Bhāratavarṣa, they speak with humility through three verses beginning with "Of Dharma," expressing their common status as Brahmins who have been affected by the inherent nature of each respective Yuga. The term "padbhiḥ" (by feet) is a dvandva compound with *ekaśeṣa* [retaining only one member]; it refers to each individual foot [of the verse].

The meaning is "by three parts each. Because there are three ages (yugas), in the Kali age—due to the absence of their manifestation—only a fourth part of each remains. Consequently, even as they gradually perish over time, they are repeatedly replenished by their very manifestation.

It has been said that [the world] consists of three; therefore, by means of this form of Yours which bestows desired objects—through its very appearance and its essential nature (sattva)—please dispel for us those three states consisting of *rajas* and *tamas*. By means of these qualities, we are set in motion toward the restraint or favoring of Your attendants; please withdraw those qualities Yourself by the splendor of Your own body.
The meaning is: "Make them such that they do not arise again. ||22||
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, they say, "O Brahmins, we have never before suffered defeat at your hands," and thus they speak: "Of Dharma... O Triyuga! You manifest in only three ages;
or rather, you are one in whom the three ages—the six qualities denoted by the word *Bhagavat*—reside.

He is the one who exists through the three ages (*triyuga*). By his own three unique qualities—asceticism, purity, and compassion—this entire universe is sustained and protected. It is said that he exists "through the three" because he persists even in the Kali age, despite the subversion of truth and dharma. He exists solely for the sake of the twice-born and the gods (*dvijadevatārtham*), that is, for the purpose of the twice-born and the deities.

Surely it has been filled. Having done what? Having cast out—that is, having dispelled—the dust and the darkness that strike those feet by means of the quality of *sattva*, through our own body which bestows boons upon us. ||22||
O best of the twice-born, if you do not protect your own family, then the bull [Dharma] will no longer be their protector, even with his own due honor and truthful speech.
At that very moment, O Lord, your auspicious path would have perished,
for the world would have accepted the authority of Ṛṣabha.
"Madhvaḥ": that whose very self is its own protector is "ātmagopa. ||23||

Śrīdhara: "The lineage of the best of the twice-born, which must be protected by you alone—[the one] who guards himself (ātmagopam)—if indeed you are not its protector or its guardian. [Note: Because the word *goptṛ* ends in the suffix *tṛn*, the genitive case is not employed. O Lord! The path—the way of the Vedas—will perish; it will go to destruction."
Of the most excellent Ṛṣabha; for he would have accepted that unworthy and false [offering]. As it is said in the Gītā:
"Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people also do."
"Whatever standard he sets, the world follows it. (Gītā 3.21) ||23||
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] should be understood as follows: "considering that to be the authority. ||23||

Viśvanātha says: Having determined that even now this is surely Your grace toward us and not Your punishment, we take heart and say: "The lineage of the best of the twice-born, which protects itself, must be protected by You alone;
for if You had not clearly protected it, O Bull (the embodiment of Dharma), it would not have been protected."
Or if [he] were the best, then, O Lord! the path—the way of the Vedas—would perish, would come to ruin. As it is said in the Gītā:
"Whatever a great man does, that very thing other people do."
"Whatever standard he sets, the world follows it" (Gītā 3.21). ||23||

Therefore, the intention is that such statements as "even though it is impossible for us [to attain it] through service" and so forth are intended solely for the purpose of instructing the world. ||23||
That [destruction] was as if undesired by You, the treasury of goodness, who desire the welfare of people and have uprooted all enemies by Your own powers.
By this much, alas, the splendor of you, the Lord of the Three Worlds and Sustainer of the Universe, is not diminished; rather, that very act of bowing down is your source of diversion.
"Even for the Asuras, who are hostile, there is eternal bliss, unlike that of worldly beings;
for what is considered 'unpleasant' by Hari is merely an object of the intellect's negation. Thus it is said.
Therefore, it is as if undesirable [only from a limited perspective]. (24)

Śrīdhara: If it is argued that [the world] should perish, they say in response: "That would be the destruction of the path of the Vedas"—this is a common worldly expression. Because You are a treasury of goodness (*sattva*), You desire to ordain welfare and peace for the people; for this very reason, by Your own powers, You have uprooted the adversaries of Dharma, such as kings and others. Therefore, for You...

It is indeed fitting that you bow before the family of Brahmā. But surely, for one of great majesty, bowing before others causes a loss of splendor? To this they reply: Your splendor and power have not been diminished or exhausted by bowing—that is, by performing this prostration—for the purpose of protecting Dharma; rather, that act of bowing and so forth is merely your sport.
The sequence of the composition: [He is] the one who is a treasure-trove, a storehouse of *sattva*;
the reason for the inviolability of his splendor is "the sustainer of the universe," the sense being that his splendor is immeasurable.
The reason for such a being’s bowing down and so forth is "for diversion," meaning consisting of bliss.
The meaning is: "because it is a treasure-trove for sentient beings. ||24||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "Let the path perish"—to this they reply. "The destruction of the Vedic path" is a common worldly expression. In the phrase *janāya*, it is either a dative of purpose (*sampradāna*) because the rule "the mention of an action must also include its object" applies, or it is a dative used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhy-arthe caturthī*). For this very reason, in the world, by means of his own powers—such as kings and others—...
[This applies] to one for whom the counteractive factors to the Dharma have been uprooted.
But is it not the case that even for one who is supremely exalted, bowing down before those who are base causes a loss of majesty?
To this they reply: "It is not merely that. For one who bows down for the purpose of protecting the Dharma, however, [there is no such loss].

The splendor and power of you who have performed this prostration are neither diminished nor exhausted; for that act of bowing and the like is merely your diversion, a particular source of delight. (24)
Or rather, O Lord, whatever discipline you ordain for these two, or indeed whatever livelihood you provide, we shall accept it without guile.
Or rather, let that punishment which is deserved be borne by us, we who, though innocent, have been joined with guilt.
Śrīdhara: Setting aside their refusal of the curse, they inform you: "Whatever punishment you shall ordain, whether it be our means of livelihood or even our very lives, we accept all of that;
for we, who were themselves innocent, have indeed joined these two with the guilt of this curse. (25)
The sequence of composition: Here, having determined that the very cause is something the Blessed Lord intends to do, they say: "In us... (25).

Viśvanātha: In truth, they say this to you, whose intentions are difficult to fathom: "Bowing down with body, mind, and speech, we make this representation to you"—whatever restraint (*dama*) or punishment (*daṇḍa*) you ordain because of our devotion to sacred knowledge (*brahmaṇyatva*), or likewise because of your affection for your devotees (*bhaktavatsalatva*), or whatever superior livelihood (*adhika-vṛtti*) you provide.
"We grant you all permission; O Lord, do as you please.

The meaning is that the curse bestowed by us shall go to the netherworld (rasātala). Again, trembling with fear and tears, they said: "Upon us... referring to those of us who, though innocent, have been [struck] by this sin.
"By means of a curse, we have joined [them together]; we have united them. ||25||
The Blessed Lord said: These two, having immediately attained the state of non-gods, [shall fall].

O brahmins, know this: the two of you, whose yoga is bound by a concentration sustained through intense fervor, shall soon return to my presence; for it was by me alone that the curse upon you was ordained.
The followers of Madhu, such as Hiraṇyakaśipu and others, were devoted within but angry toward Hari externally;
likewise, those such as Śambara and others were entirely angry, being under the sway of internal wrath. (26)

Śrīdhara says: Consoling them by saying, "Since this curse was caused by me, there is no fault on your part," he declares: "These two, having immediately entered the womb of an asura, shall again quickly come into my presence.
"Samādhi" refers to one-pointed concentration that has been gathered—that is, fully developed—by means of *saṃrambha*, which is the onset of anger.
O Brahmins! Know this: that curse which was cast by you has been followed through and made firm by me; that very curse was actually fashioned and created by me alone. ||26||

The sequence of composition: regarding their and those two’s absorption in the mind, he states the very cause for his own desire to act with the words "these two. "Gait" means movement, that is to say, imitation. First there was concentration through intense effort, and afterwards the yoga—the natural yoga of devotion—which belongs to them.
"Into their presence" means into the vicinity; it should be understood that this occurs immediately after attaining union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa and following His disappearance. ||26||

Viśvanātha: Consoling her with the words "Do not fear," he says, "These two... Those two by whom my yoga—which is conjoined with a concentration (*samādhi*) accumulated through the intensity of the onset of anger, and which is bound to that ripening of my meditation and practiced at every moment—is their union with me. O Brahmins!
That curse of yours was ordained by me alone;

for the sake of bringing about the demoniac nature of these two who are supremely devoted to Me, I brought you to Vaikuṇṭha and made these two gatekeepers, though they are of the nature of pure goodness (*śuddhasattva*), merely devoted brahmins.

The sense is: even by acting against you and provoking the anger of you who are the crest-jewels of those who delight in the Self, the curse was produced by me alone; for there was no offense whatsoever on the part of my two attendants, nor on your part.

"Is it not the case that, even though you are affectionate toward your devotees, what was the cause for your engagement in inflicting such suffering upon these two devotees? To this he says: "O Brahmins, understand that cause! The sense is: "Having reflected upon it, realize it through my omniscience; enough with [further] explanations by me. And that [cause] is:
The cause for both Jaya and Vijaya is simply a certain desire arising from the expansion of their affection. However,

O Lord of Lords, God of Gods, Master of Vaikuṇṭha, because they possess little power elsewhere and because there is no hostility toward us there, if Your Honor does not find the pleasure of desiring to fight there, then—
"By whatever means possible, please act so as to make us both adverse [to you], and thus experience the joy of battle with them"—

this is the request of your two servants, who cannot endure even an atom’s worth of deficiency in our being filled with all your bliss; yet this insistence is itself a manifestation of Your quality of affection for Your devotees.

It should be understood that this arises from the context of discerning the Lord’s fulfillment of all aesthetic sentiments (rasas), such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and others, as revealed by scriptural passages such as "Let it be produced by making [it] light," "That indeed is rasa," "Consisting of bliss," and "This is the inquiry into that which consists of bliss."

And thus, from the statement, "I perform various activities for the amusement of My devotees, who are composed of My own will" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.2), it follows that even the Lord's own will arose toward accomplishing those modes;
this is an explicit statement of a secret, which— alas— is a great offense even against Vaikuṇṭha.

Even for those who have attained supreme perfection, a fall to lower states may occur; how much more so for us, who are mere semblances of practitioners in the world of mortals? This [statement] is to be understood as intended to make practitioners and devotees cautious regarding great transgressions. (26)
Brahmā said:
Then those sages, having beheld him who was the vessel of delight for their eyes, [beheld him].
Vaikuṇṭha is its abode, and Vikuṇṭha is self-luminous.
Having circumambulated the Blessed One, prostrated before him, and taken leave of him,
they departed filled with joy, extolling the splendor of Viṣṇu.
Madhu’s wife is Svarūpaśrī; thus, Śrī is considered to be of two kinds for Hari. 28.
Śrīdhara: Hari, who produces a festival for the eyes, and his abode, the world of Vaikuṇṭha;
[he is] self-luminous, independent of any other light, because he is a transformation of pure goodness (sattva). ||27||
Having obtained permission and having taken leave; having circumambulated and performed a clockwise circumambulation; [he beheld] the Vaiṣṇavī Śrī described in Vaikuṇṭha. ||28||

The sequence of composition: Now, the pair of verses beginning with "atha. It is self-luminous (*svayamprabham*), meaning self-manifesting, because like the Blessed One, it consists of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). ||27||
Viśvanātha: Having honored and obtained permission from Hari, who is Vikuṇṭha, and his abode Vaikuṇṭha, which is self-luminous and self-manifesting because it consists of pure *sattva*. —o)0(o)—
The Blessed One said to the two Anugas: "Go; do not fear; may there be peace!
Although I am capable of destroying the power of Brahmā, I do not wish to do so; this is my resolve."
Śrīdhara: My own view, however, is the accepted one. This is the truth here:
although anger is not possible for Sanaka and the others, nor hostility toward Brahmins on the part of the Lord’s attendants, nor neglect of His own devotee by the Lord, and so forth—
Although there is no rebirth for those who have gone to Vaikuṇṭha, nevertheless, just as the Lord sometimes has the desire to create and so forth, He once developed a desire to fight.
At that time, because others were of little strength, and because even though His own attendants were equal in strength,
it was impossible for them to act as adversaries, He set these two [Nara and Nārāyaṇa] to prevent the Brāhmaṇas and directed His anger toward them.

It was resolved by the Blessed One himself that, by means of that curse as a pretext, the two adversaries should be brought together so that the spectacle of battle might be accomplished; therefore, everything is consistent. Thus it was said: "The curse was instigated by me alone," "Do not fear," "Let there be peace," and "I do not wish to kill you, but this is my resolve."
And [the passage] beginning with "me" and so forth. ||29||

The sequential composition clarifies that very state of desiring to act [upon the world]: "The Blessed One," and so forth. The sense is this: the appearance of even an *āsura* (demoniac) disposition in the two of you—who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)—is merely a semblance, like the possession of a body by actors, or like their imitation of various roles; it is not real.
For they will indeed explain it in that very way in the seventh [chapter], at the verse beginning "viṣṇucakrahatāṃhasau" (those whose sins were destroyed by Viṣṇu’s discus).
According to them, only the sins (*aṃhas*) of those two were destroyed, but not the two themselves.
This very point is [discussed] in the introduction to the seventh sentence within the sixth section, and in some places as the power of divine play (*līlā-śakti*).
The passage beginning with "evam" and ending with "ity eva" explains that, in reality, because he spoke in such a manner, there was no cause for anger or the like. To illustrate:
in some instances, his own power of divine play (*līlā-śakti*) manifests even toward those who are adverse, solely to nourish the sweetness of that very play.

Having projected such power upon favorable objects and personal implements, He likewise produces the appearance of immersion in sense-objects even for those dear ones; as in the description of Pūtanā: "Captivating the mind with her charming smiles and side-long glances..."

Regarding the phrase "of the inhabitants of Vraja" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.16.6), it is stated by the learned that she "captivates the mind" (*manoharām*) with the intention of expressing her being a mere semblance [of the Supreme], as if she were acting like one who captivates the mind (*manoharā ivācarantīm*). Furthermore, the fact that she has been granted power by Him is indicated in that very same passage:

For it is said: "Indeed, even the female demons (*yātudhānyas*) do not perform acts such as hearing [the Lord's names], which destroy Rākṣasas in their own rites, against the Lord of the Sātvatas. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.6.3).
In this very way it is fitting:
"The cowherd women thought that their lotus-handed Lord had come as if to behold Śrī in embodied form" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.6.6).

The meaning is: "Śrī" refers to the presiding deity of ordinary prosperity, and "pati" (husband) refers to anyone who possesses the appropriate prior merit; she was just as [described] before, with that sharp mind mentioned in passages such as Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.6.9, and while she was being gazed upon, her mother was indeed overwhelmed by her radiance.
It has been stated: "They did not remain [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.6.9].

In this very way, one should understand that in certain instances there is even the appearance of being overcome by *māyā* on the part of such [devotees]. As in passages such as: "Generally, let the *māyā* of my Lord be [powerful], for no other deluder exists even for me" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.13.37], and so forth.

[This applies] to Śrī Baladeva and others, as well as to Jayavijaya at the time of their birth as Daityas. In this regard, the distinction is that for the former [Baladeva and others], there was only a slight semblance of that [divine nature], whereas for the latter [Jayavijaya], it was complete; this is due to the absence of obscuration and the presence of obscuration, respectively, regarding their love and other qualities.
In that case, if those two were to fall into a state of enmity, it could not indeed be due to the agency of the Sage (Nārada), for in the verse "This is my view" (*bhā.pu.* 3.16.29),
the will of the Blessed One is established as the cause thereof.
Nor does that [will] result in their state of enmity, since He is composed of His own self-will (*bhā.pu.* 10.14.2).

This is evident from such passages as: "O Śakra, our Lord ordains for a person the cessation of the exhaustion caused by the three goals of life" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.11.23), and so forth; and because the point is established even more forcefully through the principle of *kaimutya* (the argument from the lesser). Therefore it has been said:
"In that way, O Mādhava, those who are yours and have bound their affection to You never fall away from the path."
Thus it is said in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (10.2.33). Nor should it be argued that even for those two, such a desire arose merely for the sake of quickly escaping the experience of their own offense;
for such supreme devotees do not accept even *sālokya* and other forms of liberation without devotion.

Since even hell is accepted when that [devotion] exists, as seen in passages such as "They do not take even the ultimate [suffering] into account" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.48) and "O Father, let our existence in hells be at will through our own sins" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.49).
For this very reason, they both made a similar request:
"May no delusion, which destroys the remembrance of the Lord, arise here for us as we descend lower and lower through a trace of remorse" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.36).

Nor should it be said that if there were no actual state of enmity between those two, there would be happiness even for other devotees; for that would contradict the very nature of devotion, which is characterized by affection for fellow devotees. Therefore, while their state of enmity is merely apparent, [the Lord’s attitude] toward them and toward His other devotees as well—[remains as it is].
It is established that there shall be the arising of aesthetic flavor (*rasodaya*). Therefore,
for the sake of accomplishing the battle, the curiosity of the Śrī-Bhagavān, and so forth— which grant happiness to all devotees—
[the Lord] assumes the illusory adjunct (*māyikopādhi*) consisting of enmity by means of his innate supernatural powers (*siddhi*), such as *aṇimā*.

Having entered by means of their own forms composed of pure sattva and having rendered [the beings] conscious through their presence, they remain there even while the latent impression of devotion has dissolved; yet, by the power of that very impression, they remain as if unpossessed. Therefore, both [conditions] are met: the state of enmity has departed due to the recollection arising from the state of enmity.
This applies even to external objects. With this very intention, the venerable Vaikuṇṭha also said: "Go; do not fear;
may there be well-being" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.16.29).
Likewise, in the battle with Hiraṇyākṣa, it is stated in the verse beginning with "pārṣṇigrāham" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.18.9).

And the commentary says: "The state of having fierce anger and the like, as well as the insults and so forth, are merely a simulation for the purpose of removing the fear of the gods who were terrified by the words of the Daityas; in reality, since he did not speak in that way, there is an absence of any cause for anger and the rest"—this is the [meaning].

Regarding "the splendor of Brahman" (*brahmateja*): as long as there was the presence of those whose devotion was conditioned by their status as Brahmins, the quality of devotion to Brahmins (*brāhmaṇyatā*) alone was predominant. Now, however, in the presence of the qualities of pure devotees, it is only the affection for pure devotees (*śuddhabhaktavātsalya*). This occurs only upon attaining a specific kind of devotion.
The meaning is: "because of the manifestation of His specific qualities.
This was already indicated previously: "When I had retired, she entered at the door, but was turned away by the enraged Ramā" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.16.30).
This verse, though considered controversial, is seen everywhere; however, in the Gujarati region, there exists a commentary by Viśvanātha.
At that very moment, seeing the two attendants, Jaya and Vijaya, standing nearby, He said:
"Go from here and proceed to the mortal world. Then, seeing them distressed by separation, crying out and weeping, [He spoke].
Again, he whose heart was like fresh butter moist with compassion said: "Do not fear; may there be peace and well-being for you both.

Do not go from here; remain right here in Vaikuṇṭha, serving me forever. The word *mā* ("do not") is connected to both parts of the sentence. Then, seeing them delighted, he spoke to destroy the curse of Brahmā:
"Though I am capable, I do not desire my own [power] for myself,
because I myself established the boundary that the curse of a Brahmin is unfailing; therefore,
just as Garuḍa gave up one portion of his wings to preserve the unfailing nature of the thunderbolt,"

In the same way, while they were proceeding toward the state of Asuras with one portion— that is, by means of each individual manifestation— and yet remaining in their own true nature even in Vaikuṇṭha, for this reason, in the account of Vāmana [it is said]:
"O King, seeing those hosts of the sons of Diti rushing toward them..."
Laughing, the followers of Viṣṇu, with weapons raised, repelled them.
"Nanda, Sunanda, Jaya, Vijaya, Prabala, Bala,
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Viṣvaksena, and Patattrirāṭ"—
among these and other attendants (*pārṣada*) of the Lord who were fighting, even among Jaya and Vijaya...

This is heard in the *Ullekha*. And since their status as attendants (*pārṣada*) and as Asuras cannot otherwise be accounted for immediately after [their births as] Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu, it must necessarily be explained in this way. ||29||
This was previously indicated by the enraged Ramā when she was formerly barred at the door while entering as I lay resting.

Śrīdhara: When I had retired and entered into yogic sleep, and you two were previously turned away by me as you were entering the door, then this which has now been spoken by the brahmins was already foretold by the enraged Ramā. ||30||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Although this verse beginning with "atrai tat purā" is seen everywhere, it has not been explained because it does not belong to the traditional lineage (asāmpradāyikatvāt). ||30||
"O you two, having discharged this offense against a Brahmin through the application of my wrath,
you shall return to my presence again in no very long time."

The devotees of Madhva were internally devoted but externally hostile; they were considered followers of Hari [by others], yet through their devotion they became purified, while those filled with hatred fell into states of affliction.
"Those Asuras who were born of Brahmā attained the status of Viṣṇu’s attendants;
however, those such as Kāliya and others, harboring hatred for Hari within, fell into darkness. Thus it is said.
Therefore, agitation is said to yield little fruit; indeed, it is bhakti-yoga alone [that is fruitful].
He is the deliverer from the sin of slaying a Brahmin. ||31||
Śrīdhara: You two will return; you [plural] will return. *Nikāśam* means "near" or "in the vicinity. ||31||

The sequential arrangement: In order to maintain the established order by restating the semblance of suffering resulting from the semblance of his offense, he says, "In me... The meaning is: by means of the semblance of the result of his agitation through yoga. ||31||

Viśvanātha: Nor should you worry even if you possess a portion of the nature of an Asura; for I too, through three incarnations, shall experience the joy of battle filled with the sentiment of heroism along with you both.
Thus, even in the state of being an Asura, you two will be performing service unto me.

But he says, "In my third birth, I shall accept you both directly": "In me" (mayi)—by means of that union or meditation which is the application (*saṃyoga*) in battles through *saṃrambha*, that is, through the onset of anger; by that, you two shall be received (*pratyeṣyataṃ*), meaning you shall come into my presence (*nikāśam*). [31]
Having instructed the two gatekeepers, the Blessed One entered his own celestial abode, which was adorned with rows of palaces and endowed with a splendor that surpassed all others.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
But those two bulls among the gods [lifted him] from the earth-world, which is difficult to cross.
Their prosperity destroyed by the Brahmin's curse, they became devoid of pride.

Śrīdhara: The ellipsis is "falling from the world of Hari" due to the insurmountable curse of Brahmā; or rather, they became bereft of their splendor precisely because of that world of Hari. "Devoid of pride" means their arrogance was destroyed.
As for the sequence of the construction: [they were] "bereft of splendor" (hataśriyau) due to a cause that was "insurmountable" (dustarāt), meaning impossible to abandon, and with difficulty...
They both became withered and devoid of smiles; the meaning is that this occurred by the will of the Blessed One alone, targeting the curse of Brahmā. ||33||
Viśvanātha: The words "falling from the realm of Hari" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Devoid of pride" means their bliss had vanished.
Then, as they were falling from the abode of Viṣṇu (Vikuṇṭha)...
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the foremost celestial chariots, O dear sons.
Śrīdhara: From the abode of Vikuṇṭha; "O sons," O gods. ||34||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: From the abode of Vikuṇṭha, that is, from his station; "upon the foremost of celestial chariots" (vimānāgreṣu) means upon the best of the celestial chariots situated in the worlds of Satya and the others; "O sons," O gods. ||34||
For those two very same foremost attendants of Hari have now arrived;
they are the fierce splendor of Kaśyapa that had entered the womb of Diti.
Śrīdhara: They have attained the splendor and vigor of Kāśyapa. ||35||

The sequence of composition: "tāv eva" (those two alone). Being those very ones in the form of attendants, they attained and entered [the state] through the supernatural power known as *aṇimā*. ||35||
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that they attained the splendor of Kaśyapa and the virility of Kaśyapa, having accepted them as their own bodies. ||35||
"O you, by the splendor of those two Asuras, the twin Yamās, your own energy has been eclipsed today;
the Blessed One now intends to restore it."
Śrīdhara: The two twins entered the womb together; by their splendor, your splendor was eclipsed and cast aside.
No remedy for this is possible, because now, at this very moment, the Blessed One Himself desires to ordain it thus. (36)

The sequence of the composition: in the commentary on the phrase "of those two," the meaning of the word "that" (tat) is precisely "in order to accomplish that very thing. Furthermore, it will always bring about only welfare for us, his devotees. ||36||

Viśvanātha: [The Lord said: "Since they are twins, equal to the God of Death (Antaka) because of their remaining portion, if you ask, 'Then perform some pacification,' who are we, wretched as we are, in that matter? We have no power even over the two attendants of the Blessed One who have fallen by his curse. Thus he says: "That pacification, indeed, only the Blessed One himself can ordain."
He desires. ||36||
He who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, whose yoga and māyā are difficult to overcome even by the masters of yoga; he is the primordial one.
That Blessed One, the Lord of the Three Worlds, will provide for our security;
what purpose, then, is there here for our deliberation?

Śrīdhara: If it is asked, "Even so, let some means be considered," he says in response: "Of the universe... He alone is the Lord of the three *guṇas*; at a time when *sattva* prevails, he will provide for our welfare (*kṣema*).
[This is] by means of reflection (*vimarśena*), that is, through deliberation. (37)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, if it is asked, "We are dying at this very moment; when will he bring about our cessation?"—let your honors die or live; his will alone is the cause, but...
He says "of the universe" (*viśvasya*) to show that he will indeed protect [it] at the present time of protection.
He says "by the lords of yoga" (*yogeśvaraiḥ*) to show that we do not know the manner in which this occurs;
the sense is that even for the omniscient ones, there is no knowledge [of it]. [Objection: But surely, even that [manner] is present here in the case of calamity...

Thinking, "Might he reflect upon something for our consolation," he says therein: "To what extent is there any purpose served by our reflection (vimarśa)? The underlying sense is that he might act otherwise even while being reflected upon by us. Thus it is stated in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for the hearts of devotees.
The sixteenth chapter of the third [book] is concluded, which is well-connected with the virtuous.

Thus ends the conversation between Vidura and Maitreya in the Third Canto of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, contained in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā dedicated to the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
The sixteenth chapter, titled "The Fall of Jaya and Vijaya."
The Seventeenth Chapter: The Origin of the Primordial Daityas during Hiraṇyākṣa’s World Conquest.
Maitreya said:
Having heard what was sung by the Self-born One, they were freed from their doubts regarding the cause;
thereupon, all the dwellers of heaven returned to the celestial realm.
Śrīdhara: Then, in the seventeenth chapter, their birth— which was terrifying to the world—
and the wonderful power of Hiraṇyākṣa during his conquest of the quarters are described.
Immediately after the word of Brahmā, "He will provide security," they were abandoned by suspicion. ||1||
The sequence of composition: the cause [is explained] as the reason for the arising of that affliction and for its remedy;
by "suspicion," [it is meant] by doubt. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
At their birth, portents clearly appeared in the seventeenth year;
and Hiraṇyākṣa, the conqueror of the quarters, mocked Pracetas.
The sense is that she has abandoned all doubt through her trust in the Blessed Lady alone. ||1||
But Diti, fearing for her offspring at her husband’s command,
gave birth after a full hundred years to twin sons, O virtuous lady.

Śrīdhara: According to the statement, "O Caṇḍī, by the command of her husband, she will repeatedly cause the three worlds along with their guardians to cry out" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.14.39), she was apprehensive on account of her two children, fearing an affliction from the gods. ||2||

The sequence of the composition: "Apprehensive of offspring" (apatyapariśaṅkinī). Because it was previously stated, "She was apprehensive of the Destroyer of the Asuras" (surārdanāt), she was therefore filled with fear in that regard. ||2||

Viśvanātha: Fearing that, according to the words of her husband—that he would cause the worlds to weep—there would be an affliction of all the worlds by their offspring, or that her offspring might meet its death at the hand of Viṣṇu, [she spoke]. ||2||
As they were being born, many portents fell there—
in the heavens, on the earth, and in the intermediate space— boding great misfortune for the world.
Śrīdhara: "There, at that time, they fell and they arose. The sequence of the composition is: "they brought great fear from all sides"; this has not been explained [by others].
Viśvanātha: "They fell and they arose" ||3||
The earth, together with its mountains, shook; all the quarters blazed;
thunderbolts fell along with meteors, and comets appeared as omens of distress.
Śrīdhara: The regions of the earth, together with the mountains; the banners raised them up—this is the ellipsis. ||4||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained. Viśvanātha: The words "and the comets rose" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. ||4||
A wind, most unpleasant to the touch, blew forth repeatedly emitting whistling sounds;
a host of tempests, bearing dust as its banner, uprooted the lords of the mountains.

"Madhvaḥ," "phaṭkāraḥ," "phutkārāḥ," as well as "kilakilā" and so forth—these are to be understood as imitative sounds (*anukāraśabda*), as well as any others considered to be of that nature. Thus is the definition. (5)
Śrīdhara: "Phūtkārān" is an imitation of the sound of a violent wind. "Nagapatīn" refers to great trees. He whose army consists of whirlwinds alone; he whose banner is dust alone. ||5||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Phūtkārān" is an imitation of the sound of a violent wind; he is one whose army (*anīkam*) or host consists of whirlwinds (*vātyā*). ||5||
When the host of stars had perished due to the mass of clouds resembling upturned lightning,
and darkness had entered the sky, no path could be discerned.

Śrīdhara: In which [clouds], the multitude of stars—the collection of the splendors of the sun and other luminaries—was lost by the mass, that is, the collection, of those clouds in which the lightning bolts seemed to laugh loudly; not even a slight trace of their position or location could be seen. ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: In that sky where the multitude of stars—the radiance of the sun and other luminaries—has been eclipsed by the mass of clouds, which seem as if they are laughing loudly with their lightning, he found his place. (6)
The ocean, its belly agitated and its waves surging, cried out in dejection;
and the rivers, along with their wells, were stirred up, their lotuses withered.

Śrīdhara: The ocean (*vārdhi*) is like one dejected; from it waves have surged forth, and within it the crocodiles and other creatures dwelling in its depths are agitated. It is accompanied by wells, ponds, pits, and the like, and in it the lotuses are withered. (7)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Vārdhi means the ocean; sodapānāḥ means together with wells. ||7||
Again and again, encircling halos appeared around both the moon and the sun;
and thunderclaps, sounding like the rattling of chariots, issued forth from the hollows of the sky.

Śrīdhara: *Paridhayaḥ* means halos or encircling rings. *Sarāhvoḥ* refers to the two [planets] seized by Rāhu. *Nirghātāḥ* are thunders from a cloudless sky. *Rathanirhrādatulyāḥ* are sounds resembling the rattling of chariots. *Vivarebhyaḥ* means from mountain caves. ||8||
Kramasandarbha: Not commented upon. Viśvanātha: *Nirghātāḥ* refers to thunders without clouds; *dhvanayaḥ* are sounds resembling the rattling of chariots;
*vivarebhyaḥ* means from mountain caves. (8)
In the villages, jackals vomited fierce fire from their mouths and howled inauspiciously with the shrieks of jackals and owls.
The word *madhvaḥ* refers to the sound of a chisel; it is also an imitative sound (*anukāraśabda*). The term *śṛgālāḥ* there refers to males.
The particle *api* is used in the senses of possibility, inquiry, reproach, doubt, and conjunction.
In that context, the destruction of jackals (*śṛgālāḥ*) and female jackals (*śivāḥ*) occurs when their voices are otherwise [than auspicious]. Thus it is stated in the *Āgneya-purāṇa*. 9.
Śrīdhara: Along with the howling sounds of jackals and owls, there were jackals (śivāḥ). ||9||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: Together with the sounds of *ṭaṅkāra* (cracking noises), the jackal-wives are auspicious (*śivā*). ||9||
Like singers and like weepers, raising their necks,
the village dogs then and there let out various cries.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: dogs are the lions of the village. ||10||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained. —
And the donkeys, O Kṣattṛ, striking the surface of the earth with their harsh hooves, [ran about].
Uttering loud cries of "khār," they rushed about in groups, intoxicated with fury.
The sound "khārkāra" is also an imitative word (*ānukāra-śabda*) for honey. ||11||

Śrīdhara: [They struck] with harsh and sharp [weapons]. O Kṣattṛ! Those who possess *rabhasa*—that is, agitation—at the sound of *svārkāra*, which is the braying of the donkey species; [they struck] *varūthaśaḥ*, that is, in groups. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: O Kṣattar! "Khārkāra" is an imitation of the sound of a donkey; those whose impetuosity—that is, their joy—is caused by that very sound [are so described]. (11)
Terrified by the donkeys, the birds flew up from their nests crying out;
and in the cow-pens and the forest, the animals voided dung and urine.
Śrīdhara: Terrified by the sound of the donkey, they cried out on all sides. ||12||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Terrified by the donkey—that is, by the word "donkey" (gardabha). ||12||
