The cows stopped lowing and yielded blood instead of milk; the clouds rained down pus; the divine images wept; and the trees fell even without a wind.
Śrīdhara: The cows were terrified and fled; they yielded blood instead of milk. The emblems of the gods wept; that is to say, tears flowed from the images. ||13||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: *Asṛgdohāḥ* means those who milk blood; *devaliṅgāni* means images of the gods. —o)0(o)—
Other most auspicious planets and even the luminous lunar mansions surpassed one another with retrograde motion and fought against each other.

Śrīdhara: The most meritorious celestial bodies, such as Jupiter and Mercury, as well as many other stars and the cruel planets beginning with Mars, overpassed him—having bypassed him—they moved by retrograde motion, turned back, and fought against him. (14)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Having bypassed the most meritorious ones such as Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and others, the other cruel planets, Maṅgala and the rest, moved by retrograde motion (*vakragati*), turned back and fought. ||14||
Seeing other great portents as well, the people— who did not know the true reality—
were terrified and believed that the dissolution of the universe was at hand, with the exception of the sons of Brahmā.
Śrīdhara: "Except for the sons of Brahmā," meaning without them, because they possessed knowledge of his own curse and so forth. ||15||

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] begins with the word "having seen. With the exception of the sons of Brahmā, such as Sanaka and others—who were created by Brahmā—all living beings, being ignorant of the true reality (*tattva*), were afraid and considered it to be the dissolution of the universe. However, the gods, because of the words of Brahmā, were knowers of the true reality and remained unafraid; they did not consider it to be the dissolution of the universe.
The meaning. ||15||
Viśvanātha: [He spoke to] Sanaka and the others, the sons of Brahmā, because of their knowledge of his own curse and so forth. ||15||
Then those two foremost Daityas, their own prowess suddenly manifesting,
grew with bodies as hard as stone like two lords of mountains.

Śrīdhara [comments]: "Those two" refers to those in whom one's own prowess—manifested as previously established personal power—is sequentially arranged. Here, the commentary supports the view that these two remain hidden by means of powers such as *aṇimā* (atomicity). ||16||

Viśvanātha: Even in the face of the curse of Brahmā, this was done to demonstrate that devotees of the Lord possess supreme excellence; for by the unperformed yet highly meritorious deeds of those two, [they attained] sovereignty over the three worlds, strength, majesty, enjoyments, yoga, lordship, and so forth—despite these being achieved through many performed [deeds].
And in order to state that there is not even a trace of the scent of the torments of hell due to evil deeds, he says: "Those two" (tāv). ||16||
Their arms, adorned with shimmering armlets, reached toward the sky, their crowns touching the heavens as their tips were joined together.
Making the earth tremble with their feet at every step,
they stood having surpassed the sun with their beautiful golden waistbands.

Śrīdhara: [The two] by whom the quarters and directions have been obstructed and pervaded; those whose arms possess throbbing armlets (*aṅgada*); the word *aṅgadā* here ends in the feminine suffix *-ā*, which is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*); [the two] with a waist possessed of a beautiful girdle (*kāñcī*). //17//
The sequential composition: just as there is the word *somapa*, so too might there be the word *aṅgada*. ||17||
Viśvanātha: He states that they became thus even at the age of five or six days with the verse beginning "In heaven" (divi).
*Kāṣṭhā* means the directions. The form *aṅgadā* ending in the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). ||17||
Prajāpati gave them a name, which was born before their own bodies from the two Yamas.
The subjects indeed know him as Hiraṇyakaśipu, whom she first gave birth to as Hiraṇyākṣa.

Śrīdhara: The meaning is that he gave him a name according to how they know the elder of the two twins born first from her own body—as Hiraṇyakaśipu—and how they know the one whom Diti first gave birth to—as Hiraṇyākṣa. This is the intention: for when...

At the time of conception, the semen entering the uterine flower enters divided into two parts by way of front and rear; then twins are born. And for those two, the birth from the mother occurs in the reverse order of the sequence of entry from the father.

"When the seed, having become twofold, enters the flower while it is discharging [its essence], then two embryos come into being; birth occurs through the reversal of the entry. This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) in the *Piṇḍasiddhi*.
Therefore, Diti first gave the name Hiraṇyakaśipu to the one born before her own body, and she gave the name Hiraṇyākṣa to the one whom she had previously brought forth. ||18||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained.

Viśvanātha states regarding the naming ceremony on the tenth day: Prajāpati Kaśyapa, between the twins, [gave] that one who was first born from his own body the name Hiraṇyakaśipu, as they know it. She...

He gave them names according to how they were known: he named the one whom Diti first gave birth to Hiraṇyākṣa, just as [he was] known. The connection [of the sentence] is made by supplying the words *yathātathayoḥ* (of the two, as they truly were).
When the seed, having split into two, enters and the flower discharges [its essence].
"Then two embryos come into being due to a reversal of birth and entry," according to the *Piṇḍasiddhi*.
By the paternal lineage, Hiraṇyakaśipu is the elder, because he was placed first by his father Kaśyapa.

Likewise, according to the order of their mothers, Hiraṇyākṣa is the elder, because he was born first of all from his mother Diti. Thus, although both are elders by virtue of this sequence, Hiraṇyakaśipu alone is designated as the elder due to the predominance of the father. ||18||
Hiraṇyakaśipu, arrogant and fearing death from no quarter, brought the three worlds along with their guardians under his control by means of his two arms and a boon from Brahmā.
Śrīdhara: Raised up by his two arms, he is free from death from any quarter due to the boon of Brahmā. ||19||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: "By the two arms" means by the strength of his arms alone. Regarding the phrase "and by the boon of Brahmā," the word "and" (ca) implies that the boon of Brahmā was also an assistant there. ||19||
His younger brother Hiraṇyākṣa, who was dear to him and brought him daily delight,
went to heaven with mace in hand, seeking battle and desiring to fight.
Śrīdhara: *raṇam* means battle. ||20||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Beholding him, whose speed was unbearable and who wore tinkling golden anklets...
He was adorned with the Vaijayantī garland, and a great mace rested upon his shoulder.
Intoxicated by the excellence of his mental vigor, unassailable and fearless from any quarter,
the gods hid themselves in terror, like serpents terrified by Tārkṣya.

"O gods, protectors of creatures, there is no conqueror of the boon [of immortality] except for one who possesses power or knowledge; nor is there such a boon without the Lord of all, as long as that very body has not entered another form. Thus it is stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya*.
Śrīdharaḥ: He whose speed and momentum are difficult to endure; he whose golden anklets are jingling;
he by whom a great mace is placed upon his shoulder. (21)
Arrogant and proud on account of their mental resolve, heroism, valor, strength, and excellence; merciless and unrestrained—they hid themselves away, becoming concealed. ||22||

The composition of the sequence: that pair [of verses] beginning with "tam. Viśvanātha: "Utsiktam" means arrogant due to the excellence of mental vigor—that is, the powers of the mind, the body, and the deities; "asṛṇyam" means unrestrained. (22)
Having seen them thus vanished by his own splendor, the king of the Daityas,
no longer beholding the hosts of gods including Indra, who were now intoxicated, roared loudly.

Śrīdhara: Having seen them obscured by their own splendor—that is, by their brilliance—and having realized they were intoxicated or drunk (kṣība), he did not perceive them; in the reading "klībān," it means those devoid of manliness. ||23||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Not seeing"—being intoxicated (kṣība), that is, being drunk; in the reading *klībān*, it means those devoid of manliness.

Then, turning back from his play, the Great Being plunged into the deep ocean with its terrifying roar,
like an elephant in rut.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.
Viśvanātha: Having seen no opponent at all in any of the ten directions, and being tormented by the heat of his own great power, he might somehow remain somewhere in the midst of the ocean.
Or, out of a desire to fight with him, he plunged into the ocean.
When he had entered there, Varuṇa’s soldiers, the hosts of aquatic creatures, became alert in mind and filled with trepidation.
Though not being struck, they were overwhelmed by his splendor and fled to a great distance.
Śrīdhara: Those whose intellects were dejected and dispirited; being overcome and eclipsed by his splendor and majesty. ||25||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
That one of great strength [remained] in the ocean for many series of years.
Treading repeatedly upon the great waves stirred by the wind,
O dear one, he struck the night with his mace as he approached the city of Varuṇa.

Śrīdhara: He struck the great waves with a *maurva* [bow], meaning made of black iron (*kārṣṇāyasa*) that kills by means of its string (*maurvī*). Alternatively, *mūrvā* is a specific kind of grass; the meaning is "with a rope made from it," firmly bound. He attained—that is, reached—the name "Vibhāvarī" (Night). ||26||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Having pervaded many years—that is, a multitude of years—he struck [the demon] with his mace, which was like a great wave.
Moving restlessly, he used a mace made of *maurva* iron—either black iron (*kārṣṇāyasa*) or consisting of *mūrva*, a specific kind of grass.
"Aha! There is some city in the midst of the water; therefore, I shall enter it"—thus he attained the name Vibhāvarī. (26)
There he beheld Pracetas, the protector of the world of the Asuras and the bull among the hosts of Yādavas.
Smiling and bowing down like a lowly person to mock me, he said: "O sovereign, grant me battle!"
Śrīdhara: Pātāla is the world of the asuras; [he went] to that protector. Having prostrated, he did so in order to mock or deride him. ||27||

The sequence of the composition: "The worlds of the Asuras are inhabited mostly by Dānavas; having seized him, the Asura servant brought him into the presence of Varuṇa" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.28.2)—thus from the Tenth Canto. ||27||
Viśvanātha: [He approached] the protector of the world of the Asuras and of Pātāla, having prostrated himself in order to mock or deride him. ||27||
"You are a world-protector and sovereign of great renown, who strips away the prowess of those arrogant heroes intoxicated by pride."
O Lord, having conquered all the Daityas and Dānavas in the world, he formerly performed the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Śrīdhara: Because you performed the Rājasūya sacrifice. ||28||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "You have performed the sacrifice" (*ayajad bhavān*) is a separate sentence; "having conquered" (*vijitya*) is an instance of indirect indication (*viparītalakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, since the Daityas were no longer present at that time, the Rājasūya could be performed by everyone.

The implication is that you must now defeat me and perform the Rājasūya sacrifice once again; or rather, even if the Rājasūya has already been performed by you, it will only then be truly accomplished for you if you conquer me. ||28||
Thus deeply provoked by his enemy, who was arrogant with pride, the Blessed Lord, the Master of Waters, [acted].
Quelling the rising anger with his own intellect, he said:
"We have attained the complete pacification of our limbs."
Śrīdhara: "Upaśama" means cessation from the curiosity for battle and other such activities. ||29||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "Pacifying by his own intellect" means by the reflection that "here my anger will not bear fruit. We have now attained tranquility.

The meaning is: "We have become old. The implication is that had I attained you during my youth, I would have conquered even a thousand like you. Alternatively, *upaśama* refers to renunciation (*sannyāsa*).
The implication is that had I not practiced renunciation, I would still be able to conquer you even now. ||29||
— I see no one other than the Ancient Puruṣa who [could oppose] you, who are skilled in the ways of battle, in this conflict.
The wise among the foremost of the Asuras will propitiate him whom those like you praise when he sings.
Śrīdhara: Go to him who will satisfy you, for you are skilled in the ways of war;
they praise [the one] who speaks. ||30||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "In that case, how shall I be delivered from this itching for battle? To this he says: "Behold!
Therefore, O bull among Asuras, go! For the wise heroes [grant boons] to the one who praises them.
They praise [him] for his quality of removing the itching of battle. ||30||
Approaching that hero from nearby, you shall lie in death upon the hero’s bed, surrounded by dogs, filled with wonder.
He who assumes various forms out of a desire to favor the virtuous, for the sake of subduing the wicked such as you.
Śrīdhara: *Ārāt* means quickly. *Vismayaḥ* refers to the destruction of pride. *Vīraśaye* means on the field of battle. *Rūpāṇi* refers to the incarnations such as the Boar and others. ||31||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, [the question] "In how many days shall I obtain him? is addressed there with the words "him" (*tam*). The meaning is: "from nearby, in exactly five days. Being free from pride (*vismaya* = *vigatagarva*), you shall lie down.

The sense is this: at present, however, you do not remain [at home] because you are afflicted by the disease of pride and are agitated by the itch for battle. The meaning is that the battlefield—where heroes lie—is a fitting bed for you. At that time, even the attendants who would have constrained your limbs, such as your feet, will be [your servants].

He says, "There will be many," referring to the dogs. [The opponent asks: "If that is so, then reveal his form, so that I may search both inside and outside this very universe right now, extract him, and fight with him; how could he possibly kill me?"

"You shall see"—thus he says there with the word "ya" (who). The meaning is: "I know in general that [He] assumes forms such as the Boar and the Man-Lion for the sake of pacification—that is, for destruction—but I do not know the specific detail of in what form He will slay You. ||31||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, which is well-composed for the virtuous, in this *Harṣiṇī*, the *Sārārthadarśinī*, intended for those whose hearts are devoted.

Thus ends the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya in the third book of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*, the compendium of the Pāramahaṃsyas composed by Vyāsa.
In the *Hiraṇyākṣadigvijaya*, the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Primordial Daityas," and the eighteenth chapter.
The Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa.
Maitreya said:
Having thus heard the words spoken by the Lord of the Waters, [he spoke].
O dear one, having reflected upon that and having learned from Nārada the fate of Hari, the haughty and arrogant Mahāmanas entered Rāsatāla with great haste.
Śrīdhara:
In the eighteenth [chapter], the great battle between Hiraṇyākṣa and the Boar, the upholder of the earth, which was indistinguishable [in intensity] and agitated the gods, is described.
Having heard that there was an opponent, you said, "I shall lie down," having disregarded—that is, not taking into account—that fact; for you are intoxicated with pride. (1)
The sequence of composition: having specifically reckoned—that is, having calculated and agreed upon.
Viśvanātha:
even after the dialogue between the Asura and Varāha.
In the eighteenth [chapter], the battle with the mace and this fear of Brahmā are described.

Having heard of his adversary, the high-minded one, with a heart full of enthusiasm, said, "You shall lie down" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.17.31) for the sake of pacification; this was indeed spoken because he disregarded— that is, failed to take into account— the certainty that his own death was impossible, and while searching for him, thinking "Where shall I find him?", he saw him before him by divine providence.
Having learned from Nārada, who had been questioned, about the destination and departure of Hari, he entered the Garbhoda ocean within Rasātala. ||1||
There he beheld Mount Abhijit, the upholder of the earth,
who was lifting the world aloft with his foremost tusk.
Stealing away the natural luster of his eyes with its own ruddy splendor, the forest-dwelling deer laughed aloud.

Śrīdhara: [He is] Śrīdhara; [he is] Abhijit because he conquers on all sides—that Śrī Hari by whom the earth was raised up with pre-eminence. With his foremost tusk—the tip of his tusk—he steals away the splendors of Hiraṇyākṣa’s own radiance with an eye endowed with a crimson luster. He steals it away with that eye.
Disregarding him, he thought: "Oh, how strange! A deer that roams the forest and a boar that dwells in the water [have come here]. ||2||

The sequential composition: [In the phrase] "aruṇaśriyā," there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "akṣṇaḥ" (of the eye), and the masculine form [is applied] because it has been previously stated as having a masculine counterpart (*bhāṣitapuṃskatvāt*). 2.

Viśvanātha: Since the play of battle (*yuddhalīlā*) was not specifically explained in the previously mentioned account of Varāha’s deeds, he speaks the following—beginning with "He beheld"—in order to explain it. *Abhijit* means "conquering on all sides" (*abhitaḥ jayati*), or else it refers to the presiding deity of the constellation Abhijit. It is that by which the earth was being raised up pre-eminently.

With his foremost tusk—the tip of which possesses its own luster—he steals away, or eclipses, the golden splendors of [the sun's] rays with that eye endowed with ruddy beauty; oh, how wonderful! A forest-dwelling deer and a water-dwelling boar! ||2||
"—O you ignorant one! Come here; release this earth of ours, which was entrusted to you by the Creator of the world, the dwellers of the nether regions."
O lowest of gods, you who have assumed the form of a boar, you shall not go in safety while I am looking on!
Śrīdhara: "Come, come! [This means] she has been entrusted to us, the inhabitants of Rasātala, the dwellers of Pātāla;
the implication is that otherwise her descent to Pātāla would not be possible.
Although these words were uttered by Hiraṇyākṣa for the purpose of insult, they actually praise the Blessed One.
For instance: Śrī Nārāyaṇa, who roams the forest and reclines upon the water, is sought after by yogis;

or, he is called *mṛga* because he hunts (*mṛgayate*) the wicked to slay them. The meaning of *ajña* is that there is no one more wise than him, thus he is "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*). Since the gods are inferior to him, O Supreme among Gods! even as I am looking at you, [do not disregard] me.

Even if you disregard her and continue to dwell with her, you will attain—indeed, you shall obtain—all our well-being, auspiciousness, and sovereignty; there is no doubt in this matter. Nevertheless, the meaning is: "Release her out of compassion for us.
By whom? By Him who has effortlessly assumed, or taken up, the form of a boar. ||3||

The sequence of composition: By means of his futile words, he makes it known that the state of being a Daitya is a mere appearance—this is indicated by the three verses beginning with "He said. Regarding the phrase "of the inhabitants of Rasā," it is understood that since heaven has now been conquered, the residence of these two has become in heaven itself; for even Rasā is merely a cavity within the earth.
Regarding the word *svasti*, there are two explanations because two *s* sounds are established here by both [Pāṇini 8.4.47] *anaci ca* and [Pāṇini 8.3.36] *vā śari*.
Viśvanātha: "Come," [meaning] arrive. She has been entrusted to us, the inhabitants of Rasātala, the dwellers of the netherworld;
the implication is that otherwise her descent to Pātāla would not have been possible.
Although these words were uttered by Hiraṇyākṣa for the purpose of insult, they actually constitute a praise of the Blessed Lord.
For instance: Śrī Nārāyaṇa, who roams the forest and reclines upon the waters, is sought after by yogis;

or, He is called *mṛga* because He hunts (*mṛgayati*) the wicked to slay them. *Ajña* means that there is no one wiser (*jña*) than Him, thus "the All-Knowing One" (*sarvajña*). O Supreme among Gods (*surottama*), even as I am looking at You, [You disregard] me... [who am the lowest among gods].

Even if you disregard her and continue to dwell with her, you will attain—indeed, reach—all our well-being and auspicious sovereignty; there is no doubt in this matter. Nevertheless, the meaning is: "Release her out of compassion for us.
By whom? By Him who has effortlessly assumed, or taken up, the form of a boar. ||3||
Why have you been maintained by us for our non-existence through rivals, you who slay the Asuras by means of illusion and conquer them out of sight?"
O fool, having established you— who possess the power of illusory yoga yet little true prowess— I shall wipe away the sorrows of my friends.

Śrīdhara: *Abhavāya* means for destruction; *bhṛtaḥ* means nourished. But in reality, the meaning is that he is supported, maintained, and taken refuge in for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*). You, who conquer through indirect means—that is, by stealth; but in reality, you conquer while remaining at a distance. *Saṃsthāpya* means having struck down; but in reality...

He whose power consists of inconceivable *yogamāyā* (the illusory energy of yoga), from whom all human effort is diminished—having properly established You, meaning having made You firm in the heart through devotion; O *mūḍhapra*, so called because You nourish (*prāti*) the deluded (*mūḍhān*), according to the verbal root *prā* in the sense of filling; [You who remove] the sorrows of Your friends.
I wipe away—that is, I destroy—the sufferings of saṃsāra; for you liberate even the kinsmen of the one who remembers [you]. This is the underlying sense.
Regarding the sequence of the composition: it is directed toward those who are deluded regarding the ultimate reality but are rendered helpless by devotion. Thus it is.
Viśvanātha: You have become the destroyer for our ruin—that is, for our destruction—at the hands of rival gods;
for you strike by means of *māyā* alone, and thus you conquer indirectly rather than directly.
Having established that very You, whose power is solely *yogamāyā* and not physical strength, and having slain [the enemy], [we shall remove] the grief of our friends.
I wipe away the tears of grief. Alternatively, "bhṛtaḥ" means supported, maintained, or taken refuge in for the sake of non-existence—that is, for liberation.

However, by His *māyā*—meaning by His grace (*kṛpā*)—He who slays even the *asuras* brings about their ultimate good destiny through that very act of being slain by Him. Therefore, precisely because of His abundance of compassion, He is perceived by all, even though He is otherwise beyond the senses.

The meaning is this: although You have become manifest, You are victorious over other deities who have become manifest with far fewer means; and although You have not become manifest, You exist in a state of superiority over all of them, even those who have become manifest with much greater means. [This is due to] Your inconceivable power in the form of *yogamāyā*.

The meaning is: having properly established You—You whose human effort (*pauruṣa*), such as the creation of the universe and so forth, is "small" (insignificant) for a person who is the creator of the great, and thus "inappropriate"—having made You firm through devotion within the temple of one's own heart; [O Lord] who [protects] those who are utterly deluded!
It is so called because it removes [suffering] even by the gift of one's own devotion; "prā" means completion.
The sense is: "I wipe away—that is, I destroy—the sorrows of my friends," meaning the miseries of saṃsāra, since You liberate even the kinsmen of those who remember You. ||4||
When you were struck down by the mace hurled from my arm, your head shattered, along with those who were yours;
The sages and all the gods who themselves offer oblations will cease to exist, being rendered rootless.
Śrīdhara: While you remain thus, with your head unshattered even by the mace hurled from my arm,
all those who now offer you tribute—
both the new devotees and the former devotees, the sages and the gods— are themselves rendered rootless without any effort on their part.
They will not perish; rather, the meaning is that they shall become firmly rooted. ||5||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: When he has passed away—that is, when he is dead—they will no longer exist; or rather, when he whose head has not been shattered by the mace, even through the skill of our arms, has passed away, those who...

Now they bring offerings unto you; the meaning is that both the new devotees and those former devotees—the sages and the gods—all shall, by their very own selves and without effort, become not rootless but rather possess firm roots. ||5||
Being pierced by the lances of his enemies’ harsh words,
he perceived that the Earth, resting upon the tips of his tusks, was terrified.
Having deceived everyone, he emerged from the midst of the waters like an elephant struck by a crocodile, yet accompanied by his herd.
Śrīdhara: That Hari, being pierced and tormented by the enemy’s very ill-spoken words—which were like *tomara* spears—beheld the Earth terrified as she was held upon the tips of his fangs;
enduring and bearing that piercing pain caused by the insults, he emerged. *Kareṇu* means a female elephant. In reality, however—
The meaning is that he was being pierced by the lances of his enemies' harsh words, which served as the instrumental cause;
specifically, he was being tormented by compassion upon seeing the suffering of Brahmā and others who grasp the literal meaning of what they have heard.
This is also the very meaning of the phrase "suffering the piercing. (6)
The sequence of composition: "sa tudyamāna... (He, being pierced...). Here, by the literal meaning, it is clearly admitted that those two possess the hidden state of being devotees. ||6||

Viśvanātha: That Hari, being struck by the javelins of the wicked speech of his enemy, the Asura; or, in another sense, being struck by the gods themselves—acting as the instrumental cause—due to the wicked speech of their enemies;
that is, being afflicted by compassion upon seeing the distress of Brahmā and the other gods who grasp the literal meaning [of the Veda].
This is the meaning. "Enduring the prick" means enduring the pain of occasional ill-spoken words;

that is, bearing them through the attainment of the happiness of occasional well-spoken words. For this very reason, he is like a female elephant (*hastinī*) who is both struck by a male elephant (*grāha*) and yet remains unharmed. //6//
As he was emerging from the water, a golden-haired fish pursued him like a great fish chasing an elephant.
Karāladaṃṣṭra, whose voice was like a thunderbolt, said:
"What is reprehensible for the wicked is not shameful for those devoid of modesty."

Śrīdhara: Following him as he emerged from the water—[he saw] that Daitya whose hair was tawny like gold, who had a shark-like (jhaṣa) face, whose fangs were formidable and prominent, and whose roar was like a thunderbolt. What indeed is censurable in shameless and wicked beings?

The meaning is that even fleeing is not censurable because there is no fear of reproach. Alternatively, thinking that running after [the enemy] while lifting up the earth for the benefit of the world is improper, he censures himself through the voice of the demons: "What [is the use] of us wicked ones, who are shameless and solely intent on our own self-interest?"
There is no counting [this] as a reproach; rather, it simply does not exist. The meaning of the phrase "He said, 'Fie upon us!

is the arrangement of the sequence: "him. In this regard, by means of a *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument, the true reality of both Śrī Varāhadeva and Hiraṇyākṣa is established through their respective knowledge.
It is understood that the conclusion lies precisely in praise. ||7||

Viśvanātha: Pursuing that Blessed One—running after him—what is censurable for the wicked who are devoid of shame (*gatahrī*), being shameless and lacking in heroism? On the contrary, there is no reproach at all. The meaning is that fleeing upon seeing an opponent is not improper.

In this sense, for those compassionate ones who have attained a sense of shame (*hrī*), such an act is censurable; however, because of their compassion, even a slight retreat for the sake of protecting the earth resting upon their fangs is not to be condemned—this is the meaning. Alternatively, for the Blessed One, who uplifts the earth for the benefit of the world, running after it would be inappropriate.

Thinking thus, the Daitya reproaches himself: "Is there any counting of our censurable deeds among us who are shameless, devoted solely to our own interests, and wicked? On the contrary, there is none at all; fie upon us!"—this is the meaning of what he said. ||7||
Having placed that cow in the region above the waters within its range, he deposited his own vital essence (*sattva*) into her.
He was praised with flowers by the Creator of the universe and filled with joy by the gods, even as his enemy looked on.

Śrīdhara: That Blessed One, praised by the Creator of the Universe and showered with flowers by the gods— or, according to another reading, praised by the gods with the flowers of the creators of the universe—
having placed the earth (gām) upon the water in a region accessible to worldly activity, [established himself] upon it.
He deposited his own being as the foundational power, even as Atri looked on. ||8||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "This earth is afraid"—thinking that a battle between himself and the Asura would not be right while accompanied by this [fear], the Blessed One [placed] the earth (*gāṃ*, *pṛthvīm*) above the surface of the water, within his range of vision.

Having placed and deposited her in a region within the range of his own eyes—that is, upon that cow—he bestowed his own being and his own power, so that she might not sink into the water; this is the meaning. In the reading *viśvasṛjām*, [the cow] was being filled with flowers showered by the Prajāpatis and the gods. While he was looking on...
Disregarding the enemy who was looking on. ||8||
A great medicinal herb, attached to a cord, fashioned like refined gold, with a variegated golden casing.
Laughing, he who was of fierce wrath addressed him who was repeatedly piercing his vital spots with harsh words.

Śrīdhara: *Parāparāk* means closely following behind. *Tapanīyopakalpam* refers to golden ornaments. He [saw] that Daitya who possessed a variegated armor (*daṃśa*) made of gold. The fierce anger and the insults and so forth were merely a simulation on the part of those terrified by the Daitya’s words.
This is for the sake of removing the fear of the gods; in reality, because he did not speak in that manner, there is no cause for anger or the like. ||9||

The sequence of composition: "connected with the Supreme" (*parānuṣaktā*)—here too it is the same as there. Also in the subsequent chapter, beginning with "Karālā" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.19.8), and likewise in the seventh book, that which was spoken by Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira regarding the censure of those ill-spoken words, and by Śrī Nārada concerning the Blessed Lord...
It should be understood that its establishment as untouchable was based merely on a figurative imitation [of such status] due to external conditions (aupādhika). ||9||

Viśvanātha: "Parā" refers to [the goddess] who has her back turned toward the one attached to or clinging to golden ornaments—that is, golden jewelry—and armor, but not through well-spoken words; this is the sense.
Therefore, she is one whose wrath is fierce due to hearing ill-spoken words, and this is her response to hearing well-spoken words.
Since it must necessarily be taken into account, a second meaning is also explained for the words of the Blessed One. ||9||
The Blessed One said:
"It is true, O forest-dwelling deer!"
I seek village-lions such as you;
O hero, O ill-omened one, those who are already bound by the nooses of death do not heed your boasting.
Śrīdhara [explains]: "village-lions" refers to dogs; "of one who is released" means of one who was bound; "boasting" refers to praise. ||10||

The sequential arrangement: The words of the Blessed Lord beginning with "It is true," etc., are spoken from the perspective of mere limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); though they may appear to be intended as a jest, they also convey the ultimate reality.
In that context, "roaming the forest" should be understood as dwelling in solitude. Nevertheless, out of compassion...

We search for, that is, we seek to liberate, those like you who are foremost among those attached to vulgar objects of sense. [Objection: But how can you show compassion toward us, who are so ill-behaved? To this he replies: "Not by the nooses of death," and so forth. (10)

Viśvanātha [explains]: "The village lions" refers to dogs. "Heroes" refers to those like us. Regarding the term "one who has been released," in one sense it means one who was bound; in another sense, it refers to forest-dwellers—devotees who have abandoned the enjoyment of sense-objects—who are visible only through compassion. Even so, they see the "village lions"—those dwelling in villages who are attached to sense-objects.
I seek even those who speak from his mouth to grant me their own place.

To the objection—"How can you show compassion toward such ill-behaved, self-praising men?"—he replies: "O heroes like us, heroes of compassion, do not take your boastfulness as a fault; for this very reason, yours..."
Of what nature is he? He is one who has been cast down by the nooses of death, having been excessively abandoned;
for Death has no jurisdiction over one toward whom compassion has been shown. O you who are not auspicious! For from you, nothing auspicious exists. (10)
We, these embezzlers of the treasures of the denizens of Rasātala, have lost our shame and have been driven away by your mace."
"Or else, let us somehow remain in the fray; for having provoked enmity with one who is stronger, where can we go?"

Śrīdhara: Those who seize deposits are those who steal entrusted property. "Driven away" means they were made to flee. "Even so, we remain," even though we are incapable; what for? Because we must indeed remain.
Why so? He says: "Where shall we go? because there is no place to which we must go. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He mocks with an ironic intonation (*kākūkti*): "Those who steal deposits—that is, those who steal entrusted goods—have been driven away, made to flee; yet they remain incompetent. Now, why this trouble? One may simply do as one pleases."
"Flee!"—to this he replies: "One must certainly remain," because [of the following], starting with "where... and so on.

In this context, even for the *rasaukasas* (the demons), those who seize deposits—that is, those who accept the offerings of worship dedicated through devotion—are devoid of shame; yet, it is precisely for the reason of their affection for devotees that they do not [act thus].

The meaning is: "We feel ashamed. For [the mace] has been made to flee—that is, its mind has been put to flight—by your words of praise; [this is derived from the root] *gad* with the suffix *aṅ* because it belongs to the *bhidādi* group. Nevertheless, we still stand even in battle (*ājau*) against you—the meaning is that we manifest the excellence of our own strength. Regarding the manifestation...
This is the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Now, one might object: "O lords, having gone to Vaikuṇṭha, you may shine in happiness; what is the use of the hardship of battle?
To this he replies: "One must remain [here]," meaning that by means of Sanaka and others, enmity was generated through a curse.
For the sake of the joy of battle, we must certainly remain in combat with you, the powerful one; where else shall we go? (11)
You are indeed the leader of the hosts of foot-soldiers; therefore, act without hesitation for our well-being this very moment!
Having established us here, wipe away the tears of your own kin—
that unrefined man who does not fulfill his own promise.

Śrīdhara: [He is] the lord (*adhipa*) of those who are leaders (*yūthapa*) among the chariot-warriors and the infantry; that is to say, the chief. "For the sake of ill-fortune" means for the sake of defeat. "Exert yourself quickly" means strive. "Irreproachable" (*anūha*) means free from censure. He who does not satisfy (*atipiparti*), nor fill, nor protect—such a person is "unfit for assembly" (*asabhya*), meaning unworthy of the assembly hall.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: O leader of the hosts of foot-soldiers (*padratha*), strive and exert yourself quickly for my ill fortune—that is, for the sake of my defeat. *Anūha* means "without deliberation. He who does not protect excessively.
This unrefined person, being unworthy, does not fulfill his role in the assembly;

alternatively, out of love for you alone, he has accepted the nature of an *asura* by pledging to produce the pleasure of battle with me. Therefore, [the verse begins] "He who his own... and so forth; for this very reason, [it says] "you" and so forth, referring to us (*naḥ*).

Strive to bring happiness [to them]. The dative case is used here according to the rule *kriyārthopapadasya* and so forth. For the sake of the life-breaths (*asūnām*), that is, for the purpose of sacrificing your own life—having done what? Having established [them] in your heart, having made them perfectly firm—wipe away the tears belonging to which joys of your own. 12.
Maitreya said:
Thus insulted and severely rebuked by the Blessed One with indignation, he—
He gave vent to an intense rage, like a king of serpents being toyed with.

Śrīdhara: He was insulted by the verse beginning with "satyaṃ vayam" (We are indeed truthful); he was provoked to anger and mocked by the two verses beginning with "ete vayam" (These are we). Thus, being made to play, he was like a great serpent, the king of snakes. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He was insulted; by the verse beginning with "Truly, we [are those]," he was provoked to anger and mocked; by the two verses beginning with "We are these," the King of Serpents, the great snake, was made to play.

In the alternative sense, he was "cast down" (adhikṣiptaḥ), meaning expelled from his office characterized by being a courtier; for that very reason, he was also "intensely seized" (prakarṣeṇa labdhaḥ) by the agent of wrath.
Thus, even though he was composed of pure *sattva*, he fell under the power of the curse of Brahmā, which was instigated by the will of the Blessed One.
The meaning is that he became composed of darkness (tamas). But then, at the time of battle, he took up—that is, seized—an intense and exceedingly heightened anger in an improper manner. ||13||
Breathing heavily in indignation, his senses agitated by wrath,
the Daitya approached with speed and struck Hari with his mace.
Śrīdhara: One whose senses are set in motion—that is, agitated—by anger. ||14||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
But the Blessed One [perceived] the force of the mace discharged by the enemy against his chest.
Moving obliquely, he deceived Death, as one skilled in yoga might deceive an approaching end.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: "Antakam" means death. ||15||
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] has not been explained. —
Again, [he saw him] repeatedly brandishing his own mace.
Enraged, Hari rushed forward, his lips bitten in fury.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
And then the Lord struck the enemy with his mace on the right eyebrow.
But he, O gentle one, being skilled, struck her back with his mace and slew her.
Śrīdhara: O gentle Vidura, he struck that mace even before it had reached him. ||17||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: That demon, however, struck down that mace of the Blessed One even before it had reached him. ||17||
Thus, with their two heavy maces, Haryakṣa and Hari,
both intensely enraged by their desire for victory, struck one another.
Śrīdhara, Viśvanātha; Haryakṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa. ||18||
The sequential composition [of the commentary] has not been explained. —
Of those two rivals, whose limbs were struck by sharp maces...
As the two, whose anger was increased by the scent of blood from their wounds,
moved along various paths with a desire for victory,
their conflict shone like that of two powerful bulls over a cow.
Viṣṇu, though unimpaired, manifests as if impaired; likewise, though peerless, he manifests as if equal.
Though unconquered, he manifests as if conquered; and though omniscient, he manifests as if ignorant.
Although infinite, he appears in all forms, and even Brahmā and the others abide within his mind.
"If they speak and act in accordance [with his instructions], he shall not experience suffering. Thus it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. 19.
Śrīdhara: *Spṛdhoḥ* means of the two contending [warriors]. Their limbs were struck by sharp clubs;

from their wounds flowed blood (*kṣatāsrava*), and the smelling (*ghrāṇa*) of that [blood]—that is, its inhalation—increased the fury (*manyu*) of both. *Vicitrān mārgān* refers to various maneuvers, the different types of whirling and striking in club-fighting.
*Ilā* means a cow; with her as the cause, [there are] two powerful, intoxicated bulls.
Even though *ilā* refers to the earth, it is for her sake. For indeed, these two bulls have for many days had blood flowing from their bodies, torn by the joy of locking their high horns together.
It is well known that the two leaders of the elephant herds, intent on crushing one another with fierce impetuosity and causing wonder, remain engaged in combat. ||19||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Of the two contending rivals, whose wrath was increased by the smelling of the blood (*kṣatāsra*) of their opponent; who were both intoxicated (*śuṣmin*) with pride regarding the cow (*ilā*), that is, the female elephant (*vāsitā*).

Like two powerful bulls upon the earth, the land of *ilā*, the two tigers among men, Hari and Haryaśva, shone resplendently amidst their enemies. For the Amarakośa states: "The words *bhū*, *go*, and *vāk* are synonyms for *iḍā* (the earth). (19)
of that high-souled Daitya, who was a limb of the sacrifice and had assumed the illusory body of a boar.
O Kauravya, the self-ruling Lord, surrounded by sages, came to the earth desiring to witness the crushing of the two enemies.
Śrīdhara: He whose very limbs are sacrifices; desiring to witness such a crushing battle between two enemies for the sake of the earth, Brahmā, the self-ruling lord, came there. (20)
The sequence of the composition: "Of the Daitya" means that [the world] was taken hold of through *māyā*—that is, through grace—and brought back toward the manifest universe (*prapañca*). ||20||

Viśvanātha: The meaning is "of the Boar (Varāha), the lord of Māyā," whose boar-form was assumed through *māyā*—that is, accepted as his own by virtue of his sovereignty. The context is that being "assumed through *māyā*" means having been brought back toward the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by grace (*kṛpā*). *Svarāṭ* refers to Brahmā. ||20||
Approaching with boldness, free from fear, having provided for his protection, and possessing invincible prowess;
Perceiving the Daitya, the Blessed One, the Thousand-eyed One,
spoke to Nārāyaṇa, the primordial Boar.
Madhvaḥ: He is the leader of a thousand because he is the progenitor of many kalpas. ||21||

Śrīdhara: Having arrived, he said to Nārāyaṇa—having done what? Having observed the Daitya. In what state was he? One by whom heroic prowess or pride had been attained; from whom fear had departed; by whom a counter-measure had been taken; and whose valor was unassailable and beyond remedy.
He is the leader of thousands, the guide of thousands of seers.
Kramasaṃdarbha: "Eṣa" (this one) refers to a pair [of verses].
Viśvanātha: He by whom heroic prowess or intoxication has been attained and brought near;
the leader of thousands of sages is Sahasraṇīḥ, that is, Brahmā. (21)
Brahmā said:
"O God, this is for you [the fruit] of those gods who have approached the soles of your feet."
Of Brahmins, of cows, and even of innocent living beings.
An offender, a creator of fear, an evildoer, and an Asura who has surpassed us—
this thorn, an unrivaled warrior, wanders through the worlds seeking [us].

Śrīdhara: O Lord! This demon is a wrongdoer who falsely imputes offenses against the gods and others who have come to the base of Your feet; he causes fear to those engaged in efforts to avoid such [accusations]; and having recognized them as terrified, he is an evildoer who seizes their wealth, life, and so forth. He has been subdued by us.
He by whom the boon was obtained; seeking a rival charioteer while looking about, he is without a rival charioteer, being devoid of any adversary. ||23||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: O Lord! An *āgaskṛt* is one who falsely imputes offenses;
a *bhayakṛt* is one who, upon seeing those engaged in efforts to avert such [imputations], causes them fear; and a *duṣkṛt* is one who seizes wealth, life, and so forth. ||23||
"O Lord, do not toy with this deceitful, arrogant, unrestrained,
and most wicked man like a child, for he is like a venomous serpent that has risen up."
Śrīdhara: Since this [being] is of such a nature, therefore do not play with him, do not make him sport.
O Lord! Just as a child plays with a venomous serpent that has arisen and become agitated by pulling its tail and so forth, so it is here. (24)
The sequential arrangement: "Do not [fear] him," etc., is the speech of the venerable Brahmā.

This is because his sense of majesty has contracted due to a particular kind of love characterized by immersion in such divine pastimes of the Lord's war. This is because the commentary explains [the phrase] as "since" (yat = yasmāt).
The reading is indeed "yad āśīviṣam" (when [it is] a venomous snake). Since this is the case everywhere, the word "yathā" (as) must be supplied and has thus been explained. ||24||

Viśvanātha: "Do not play with him like a child," meaning that he is himself the crest-jewel of the wise, though appearing ignorant; just as [one would treat] a venomous serpent that has risen up—[the subject is] Garuḍa, it is implied—or rather, because I consider this [creature] to be a venomous serpent that has arisen, it is implied. ||24||
Before this cruel one grows, having reached its own time,
O Lord, employ Your own divine power and abandon this evil, O Acyuta!
Śrīdhara: "Your own" refers to the demoniac (*āsuri*). O Lord! "Your own" refers to Your *māyā*. "Agha" means that which is of the nature of sin. ||25||
The sequence of composition: having resorted to, that is, having manifested, the power of Māyā. ||25||

Viśvanātha: "At his own time, which was demonic. O Lord! "By means of his own *māyā*, even You, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), will not be able to slay him when his strength has increased during that demonic hour"—from this it should be understood that even Brahmā, though possessed of sovereignty and knowledge, suspects what is undesirable solely out of affection.
As in the statement: "Though Vasudeva and Devakī were full of sovereignty and knowledge, my mind was unsteady with fear on account of you from Kaṃsa" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.3.29). ||25||
"— O Lord, this most terrible twilight, which brings confusion to the world,
approaches, O Soul of All; bring victory to the gods."
One should know that *madhvaḥ* means "respect" and *sumukham* means "favorable countenance"; however, *śambaṭkāraḥ* is a term for "eating. ||26||

Śrīdhara says: He states the very time [of its occurrence] with the words "this" (eṣā). It is the destroyer, the annihilator, of the worlds. The indeclinable *chambaṭ* is used in the sense of destruction. ||26||
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary]: "This" [refers to her] because of the manifestation of proximity due to fear. ||26||
Viśvanātha: *Chadmaṭkarī*; *chadmaḍ* is an indeclinable word signifying destruction. ||26||
Now this auspicious moment called Abhijit has arrived;
for our welfare, O friend, quickly cross over that which is difficult to cross."
"Madhvaḥ: Midday is said to be Abhijit, as well as the latter part of Āṣāḍhā;
the first half of Śravaṇā is also [Abhijit], and Abhijit is traditionally known as the Viṣuvat. Thus it is said. (27)

Śrīdhara: It is midday at the Abhijit asterism; that very moment is an auspicious conjunction (*muhūrtika-yoga*). The *muhūrta*—the time that bestows good fortune—is almost gone. Therefore, as long as there remains even a fraction of a *muhūrta*, cross over this [ocean] which is so difficult to traverse; destroy it! (27)
The sequence of composition: A *mauhūrtika* conjunction is a specific time occurring within a *muhūrta*. ||27||

Viśvanātha: *Abhijit* is the midday *muhūrta*; it is so called because it exists within the *muhūrta* itself. It has "gone," meaning it is almost passed. Therefore, the sense is: "As long as a portion of it remains, quickly cross over this difficult [period]; abandon it. (27)
By good fortune, this one who was ordained as your death has himself come before you;
having attacked and slain him in battle, establish the worlds in security.
Śrīdhara: You have encountered death, which was ordained and fashioned by you yourself at the time of [bestowing] curse or grace. Set it aside—place it in *śarman*, that is, in happiness. ||28||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained. Viśvanātha: "Tvā" means you; "vihitam" means created by you yourself at the time of [bestowing] a curse or a favor—this is the meaning. ||28||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, perfectly suited for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted. *||*

Thus ends the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya in the third book of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is the commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras* and constitutes the collection of the Paramahaṃsas, composed by Vyāsa.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa.
The nineteenth chapter: The Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
Maitreya said:
Having attentively received the sincere and nectar-like words of Viriñca,
he smiled and accepted them with a sidelong glance full of love.
Śrīdhara:
In the nineteenth [chapter], the praiseworthy slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa by the Boar, at the request of Viriñci and others during a great battle, is described.
It was both sincere and nectar-like; according to another reading, it was both guileless in intention and truthful.
"Even for me, who am Time itself, it teaches the power of the moment," he said, laughing and accepting it with a sidelong glance. ||1||

The sequence of composition: "Nirvyalīkam" means without guile and without deceit; it is immortal and dear because it consists solely of love. In an alternative reading, "ṛtam" means that which is also free from falsehood in its actual meaning. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
Hari slew that incompetent one who had created illusions in battle;
having struck him down with his own weapon, he killed him with his own hand in the nineteenth [chapter].

"O best of our kinsmen, this asura is sincere and without guile"—because such words were filled with love, thinking "before he grows too large," and so forth, they were like nectar; thus the Blessed One also tasted them with great respect, which is why the author says "smiling. "Oh, the power of my love! he thought.
With a sidelong glance imbued with affection, she accepted [the challenge], as if teaching even me—the very soul of Time—my own power for a mere moment, saying, "It is true;
acting exactly as you direct, I shall kill him this very instant. However, let there be the joy of the desire to fight between me and him."
The meaning is that he made it known [to him]: "Let this [bow] be filled today; I shall kill him tonight. ||1||
Then Akṣaja, leaping up, struck the enemy Asura— who was moving fearlessly right in front of him— with his mace upon the jaw.
Śrīdhara: "From the mouth" means facing forward; "on the jaw" means on the lower part of the cheek; "born from the eye" means manifested from the sense of smell of Brahmā. ||2||
The sequential composition: he who, though beyond the senses (*adhokṣaja*), is born of the senses (*akṣaja*); the meaning is that he has now become manifest in the eyes and other faculties. ||2||
Viśvanātha: "Mukhataḥ" means directly in front. "Hanau" refers to the lower part of the cheek. "Akṣajaḥ" means manifested from the sense of smell of Brahmā. ||2||
Struck by that mace from the hand of the Blessed One, she was shattered;
reeling, she fell and shone as if it were a marvel.
Śrīdhara: She was struck by him with his own discus;

then, being struck, she fell down, reeling, and shone. That was her falling from the hand of the Blessed One. Alternatively, by repeating the word "tat" (that), there is also a connection with the verb "reje" (shone): "that prowess of the demon shone."

The sequence of composition: The falling [of the arrow] from the Lord’s hand was as if wonderful; thus, the word "as if" (iva) indicates that because of the Lord’s will, such things are possible, and therefore it is not wonderful in reality. ||3||
Viśvanātha: That mace of Hari, struck by that asura, fell down after being displaced and whirled about; and it shone brightly. That falling was due to the power of the Blessed One. ||3||
Although he had then found his opportunity, he did not strike the unarmed one,
honoring the dharma established by Samṛddhi while provoking Viṣvaksena to anger.

Madhva states: "Dharma is truth," and Śrīdhara, citing the *Brahma-purāṇa*, says: "And Dharma is dear to Hari. Because of the difference in the phrasing of these two statements—specifically, that [the demon] did not cause harm nor strike [the sage] because he was honoring him—the word "sa" (he) does not constitute a redundancy. ||4||
The sequential arrangement: that dharma which exists among people when they are prosperous and engaged in battle. ||4||

Viśvanātha: Although he had found an opening (labdhatīrtha)—that is, although he had found a vulnerable spot—he did not strike. The reason for this is expressed by the words "honoring" (mānayan). And [the phrase] "provoking him" (prakopayan) implies: "O, do you think that even me I have become agitated and my mace has fallen down solely because of the strength of your arms, such that you consider yourself righteous?"
"You strike me without even showing yourself! Look, look here! In a mere moment, I shall take away your very life-breaths!"—this is the meaning: the Blessed One became enraged. ||4||
When the mace had been hurled away and a cry of "Alas!
Alas! had arisen, the Lord honored that dharma and remembered the Sunābha [discus].
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.
Kramasandarbha: By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the beautiful-navelled [discus]," it is understood that he also recalled his mace (*gadā*) previously. ||5||

Viśvanātha: Regarding her being "cast down" or fallen, this should not be suspected as the opinion of another school—like the falling of the Sārṅga bow during the battle with Śālva—because Hiraṇyākṣa was a *pārṣada*, and a *pārṣada* possesses strength equal to that of the Blessed Lord; and since their strengths are equal...

Because there is no absence of the possibility of the mace falling, and because the joy of battle cannot arise without an equality of strength, this falling of the mace is indeed an ornament rather than a defect, as it increases the enthusiasm of the Blessed One. [This was done] by the Blessed One, who is an ocean of love, in the place of the devotee.

The phrase "through the mouth of his own attendant" in the following verse should be understood as indicating the sense that he had already accepted his own defeat hundreds of times. Regarding the words "and the beautiful-naved [discus]," it is understood from the word "and" (ca) that he likewise first remembered his mace. ||5||
That discus, being engaged by the lowest of the sons of Diti, his own chief attendant, with its rim whirling wildly;
There, the sky-dwellers who did not know that [truth] uttered various words, saying, "May it be well with you; slay this one!"

Śrīdhara: [He is] one whose discus is ever-active and full of zeal. Toward those who are "clinging"—that is, those attaining a special degree of attachment—and who are "unaware of that," meaning ignorant of its power, [the Lord's glances] were directed from all sides.

The sequence of composition: externally by the lowest of the sons of Diti, but internally by his own chief attendant—this is the meaning. Regarding the reading "ditijābhidhena," it means [acting] in that form merely by name. ||6||

Viśvanātha: [He is] "vyagram," meaning filled with agitation; "hanta hanta," [expressing joy at the thought] "Alas, alas! The Blessed One has remembered me!"—[referring to him] by whom the discus was grasped in the hand [of the Lord] upon his own arrival. Here, there are three readings for the term *ditiputra*: *ditiputrābhidhena*, *ditiputrādhamena*, and *viṣajjamānam*.
The word "having seen" (vīkṣya) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. ||6||
Having observed him standing before him with his chariot-parts held back, his eyes like lotus petals, he— (o)0(o— ) — sa taṃ niśāmyāttarathāṅgam agrato vyavasthitaṃ padmapalāśalocanam |
Beholding this, his senses overwhelmed with indignation, he bit his lip in rage while breathing heavily.
Śrīdhara: Having perceived—that is, having seen—that Daitya standing before him with the discus raised, he, whose senses were overwhelmed—that is, agitated—by indignation and anger, bit [him]. ||7||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon. *Viśvanātha*: Having first observed the horse's harness and then seeing it standing again before him; [he looked at] the lip, that is, the lower lip. ||7||
Karāladaṃṣṭra, glaring with his eyes as if burning them,
lunged forward and struck Hari with his mace, crying, "You are slain!"

Śrīdhara: "Beholding as if burning with his two eyes" means looking [at him] as if incinerating him. By the word "as if," he indicates the actual absence of anger—the real meaning being: "You are slain! You are known! ||8||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Beholding" means seeing; [the meaning is] "you are slain. In the alternative sense, it means "you are known. (8)
O virtuous one, with his left foot, the Blessed Lord in the form of the Sacrificial Boar playfully struck that [demon],
who possessed the speed of the wind, while his enemy looked on.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: [she who has] the speed of the wind, possessing the velocity of the wind. (9) Kramasandarbha: not explained.
And he said: "Take up your weapon; strive, for you wish to conquer.
Thus addressed, he then struck again and roared loudly.
Śrīdhara: Exert yourself; make an effort, for you desire to conquer. (10)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Beholding her as she was approaching, the Blessed One stood firm.
He seized her as she approached him with ease, just as Garuḍa seizes a female serpent.

"Whatever one desires, whether by mind or even by body, all weapons and the like can be created at will; this is merely the play (*līlā*) of His infinite power. Thus it is said in the *Varāha-purāṇa*. (11)
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Kramasaṃdarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "That mace" (tāṃ gadām) ||11||
His own prowess thwarted and his pride destroyed, the great Asura,
shorn of his luster, did not wish for the mace being offered by Hari.
Śrīdhara: He whose pride and arrogance have been destroyed. ||12||
The sequence of the composition: "Offered" (arpitam) means thrown by the great warrior of the Daityas, Hiraṇyākṣa.
The word "cast" (kṣiptam) intends only the aspect of being released by the wings of Tārkṣya;
it does not intend the aspect that it was accomplished by his mere will as well. ||12||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
—o)0(o— He seized a trident with three points, flickering like blazing fire.
Just as one performing a malevolent rite against a Brahmin who has assumed the form of a sacrifice.

Śrīdhara: Just as a blazing fire is voracious and intent on devouring, so too [is he] greedy and eager for consumption; having observed Viṣṇu for the sake of sacrifice. An illustration regarding the performance of an improper act: just as one performing a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) directed against a Brahmin. 13.
The sequential arrangement: "For the sacrifice" (yajñāya). Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; the meaning is "having made him the objective.
Just as one performing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) takes up the sacrificial substance intended for a Brahmin, directed toward that Brahmin, so it is here. ||13||

Viśvanātha: [The demon] was like blazing fire (jvalana) possessed of flickering flames; likewise, he was greedy and intent on devouring, as if to kill a sacrifice personified for the sake of a ritual. This is an example of extreme impropriety: "to kill a Brahmin. ||13||
Then, by its own splendor, that [discus], emitting intense rays, shone within the sky as it was hurled by the great warrior of the Daityas.
With his sharp-edged discus, he cut it off,
just as Hari severed the outstretched wing of Tārkṣya.
Śrīdhara: [The sword] shining—manifesting—within its own interior, in the midst of space;

that which possesses a raised and fierce radiance or luster; with a sharpened edge like a whetstone; just as Hari, Indra, severed the cast-off wing of Tārkṣya; having utterly conquered the gods, [he seized] the jar of nectar.

The intention is as follows: while Garuḍa was carrying him away, he sacrificed one of his feathers in order to humble the unfailing thunderbolt hurled by Indra; just as Indra cut it off, and once severed, it shone brilliantly on its own, so too does [the Buddha] shine forth. //14//
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: That which has shining, blazing light within; likewise, that whose rays have risen up and extended even outside into the sky (*kha*). Or else, those rays shining within the sky, in the midst of space.
That [chariot] whose rays were blazing; with its sharp-edged, whetted rim, Hari— Indra— cut off the wing, that is,
the feather, which had been abandoned [by the enemy], just as he cut the wing of Tārkṣya, Garuḍa,
when Garuḍa, having conquered the gods, was carrying away the jar of nectar.
For the sake of providing unfailing protection against the vajra hurled by Indra, one feather was sacrificed.
Just as Indra cut off the crest and it shone in the sky, so too does it shine—this is the connection [of the verse]. ||14||
When his own trident had been cut to pieces by Hari’s wielder of many weapons, he returned to the broad, majestic chest of Hari.
His rage having intensified, that Asura, roaring, struck him with a hard fist and vanished from sight.

Śrīdhara: Since it has spokes, it is a wheel (*ari-cakra*); when that [wheel] was cut and shattered in many ways by him, having returned—that is, having come forward facing him—he struck Hari’s chest, his breast. ||15||

The sequence of composition: In passages such as "vṛkṇa" (cut), and so forth, there is an intensification of anger as in the preceding cases, yet it is merely a semblance of it; and [the description of] the striking and so forth occurs only after having recognized the great intensity [of the emotion]. 15.
Viśvanātha: When Vṛka was cut down, [Bhīma], having struck his own chest and perceived the direct absence of his own prowess in battle, vanished while intending to create illusions. ||15||
O Steward, though struck here by the Blessed One in the form of the Primeval Boar,
he did not tremble in the least, like an elephant struck by a garland.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [explain]: *manāk* means even slightly; *kvāpi* means in some part. ||16||

The sequential arrangement: immediately after that, he says "Thus by him" (tenettham). This refers to the one who is both the primordial cause (*paramakāraṇa*) and possesses the form of a boar (*śūkarākṛti*). ||16||
Then,
while Hari— the Lord of the power of yoga— was creating his own illusory energy (*māyā*), the demons unleashed their own *māyā*;
beholding which, the terrified creatures thought it was the end of the world.
Śrīdhara: [The dissolution] of this world; "upasaṃyamam" means the dissolution (pralaya). ||17||
The sequential arrangement: "subjects" refers to the sons of Brahmā and others. ||17||
Viśvanātha: Having first observed him who had taken up his chariot-weapon, and then beholding him again stationed before him, [he bit] his lip—the lower lip. ||17||
Fierce winds began to blow, driving forth darkness and dust;
from all directions stones fell, as if hurled by catapults.
Śrīdhara: And they propelled the darkness created from dust by means of catapults and machines. ||18||

The sequential composition: here, "stanayitnu" refers to what is called the lightning within the clouds. Viśvanātha [explains] that because it is used in the active sense, it means "by means of projectiles" or "mechanical devices. (18)
The sky, filled with masses of clouds accompanied by lightning and thunder,
rained down repeatedly upon the earth: putrid hair, blood, feces, urine, and bones.

Śrīdhara: "Naṣṭabhagaṇā" means that in which the *bhagaṇa*—the collection of constellations (*nakṣatra*)—has disappeared. By this, it is understood that due to the excessive strength of the Daityas, the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) granted by Brahmā was bypassed; for constellations are impossible during the day. (19)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By the phrase "whose [stellar] cycles have perished," it is understood that the Lord, eager for battle, bypassed the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) granted by Brahmā. ||19||
O sinless one, mountains were seen discharging various weapons;
there were naked female demons (yātudhānīs) bearing tridents with their hair disheveled.
Śrīdhara: [The phrase] "releasing various weapons" refers to those who were seen; likewise, the *yātudhānyas* (female demons) were also seen. The sequence of the composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Various weapons and *yātudhānyas* were seen. ||20||
By many yakṣas and rākṣasas, as well as by foot-soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants—
all acting as assassins— cruel and most murderous words were uttered.
Śrīdhara: "From the violent one, words such as 'cut! and 'pierce!'—words that are exceedingly cruel and most fierce—were uttered"; the sentence concludes right here. ||21||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Extremely cruel and exceedingly fierce words were uttered—that is, they were released. ||21||
Destroying the manifested illusions of the Asuras,
the Blessed One, the Three-legged One, discharged his beloved Sudarśana weapon.

Śrīdhara: [The phrase] "of those made manifest" means that she destroys manifest Māyā. In the reading "vināśanam," the genitive case is used exactly as heard [in the text]. He whose feet are the three *savana*s; the meaning is that he is the embodiment of sacrifice (*yajñamūrti*), according to the Vedic scripture: "Three are his feet. (22)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: In the reading "vināśanam," "vināśakam," and "vināśayan," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the accusative.
He whose three feet are austerity and so forth is "tripāt," the embodiment of Dharma. Or else, three...
The *savana*s are his feet; for according to the Vedic revelation, "He has three feet. The meaning is that he is the embodiment of sacrifice (*yajñamūrti*). ||22||
Then, as she remembered her husband’s command, a sudden trembling arose in Diti’s heart, and blood flowed from her breast.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: [The messenger delivered] such a command from her husband as that "your two sons shall be killed by the Blessed One. ||23||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —
When her own illusions had vanished, she approached Keśava once again.
Embracing him with anger, he beheld him standing outside.
Śrīdhara: Embracing her, placing his arms between her [shoulders], and pressing them together. ||24||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Having placed [the hand] between his arms and intending to massage him, even while embracing him, he saw that he was situated outside of himself. ||24||
As he was striking him with fists as hard as adamant, Adhokṣaja struck him at the root of the ear with his hand, just as the Lord of the Maruts struck the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Śrīdhara: He slew, he struck down; Vṛtra, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ; Indra, the lord of the Maruts. ||25||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: And therefore, Indra, the lord of the Maruts, [slew] that Asura Vṛtra, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ. ||25||
Struck by that Viśvajit with contempt,
his limbs reeled and his eyes rolled upward.
With his arms, feet, and hair scattered about, he fell like a great mountain shattered by the wind.

Śrīdhara: One whose body has its limbs whirling about; one whose eyes have been cast out or protruded; one whose arms and other members are shattered; a lordly tree, a great tree; "lulita" means uprooted; [this was done] by the wind, the mover of the atmosphere. ||26||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Nagendra is a great tree; lulita means uprooted. ||26||
Him lying upon the earth, possessed of unimpeded luster,
with formidable fangs biting his lip;
Having seen him, goats and other animals approached and praised him, saying, "Oh! Who indeed could attain such a state as this?"
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [interpret] *saṃsthiti* as death. ||27||
The sequence of composition: "Aja and the others," because they are accompanied by sages. ||27||
That which yogins meditate upon in solitude through the samādhi of yoga, desiring liberation from the unreal sign (liṅga).
Struck by his foot, that bull among the Daityas cast off his body while gazing at his face.

Śrīdhara: Because he desired to release [the demon] from the superimposed signs—that is, from the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra)—and because the boar’s forefeet themselves functioned as hands, it is not contradictory to say both that "he struck with his hand" and that "he struck with his foot. ||28||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [The phrase] "struck with his foot" (padāhata) is not contradictory to the statement "he struck with his trunk" (kareṇāhan), because for the Boar, only his two forefeet function as hands. ||28||
These two attendants of his, having fallen into an evil state due to his curse,
will regain their station after several more births."
Śrīdhara: Not explained.

Kramasaṃdarbha: "The gods said"—the gods are Indra and the others. To Him whose form is the essence of awakened sattva manifested at the time of maintenance, that is, to the one in the form of Śrī Viṣṇu. (29)
Viśvanātha: It is clear that [this] was due to the curse of the sages. ||29||
The gods said:
"Obeisance, obeisance to You, the thread of all sacrifices!"

O Lord, by good fortune this tormentor of the worlds has been slain; through devotion to Your feet, we have attained peace, having taken refuge in Your stainless essence-form during Your state of stability.
Śrīdhara: For the sake of the thread—that is, for the expansion or the cause—of all sacrifices. Aruntuda means one who pierces the vital points (marmas). ||30||
The *kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained.
Viśrīvanātha: [The term] *tantave* means for the sake of expansion (*vistāraka*) or for the sake of *kāya*. *Aruntuda* means one who pierces the vital points (*marmabhedin*).
Maitreya said: Having thus destroyed Hiraṇyākṣa of unbearable prowess, Hari, the primordial Boar, [departed].
He went to his own world, where the festivities were unceasing,
being praised by Brahmā and the other gods seated upon lotuses.
Śrīdhara: "Having caused to perish" means having slain. He was praised by Brahmā and others, beginning with Puṣkaraviṣṭara. ||31||
The sequential arrangement: [he saw] his own boar-form indeed. ||31||
Viśrīvanātha: Puṣkara means a lotus; viṣṭara means a seat. With those [words] beginning with "BAA tadā"—[this section marked by o)0(o)—I have spoken to you, O Hare, exactly as it was recited by me.
O Sumitrā, the deeds of him who has entered [this world] are such that Hiraṇyākṣa, though possessed of noble prowess,
was cast out like a mere plaything in the great battle.
Śrīdhara: I have spoken to you as it was told, without transgressing the words of the Guru; O good friend! "yathā" means in whatever manner. ||32||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "According to what was stated" means without transgressing the instruction of the Guru (*gurūkti*). [In the *Yogavāsiṣṭha* (YV),] the sense "as stated by the Guru" is obtained through the context. Thus, immediately thereafter (*tathānu*), it was told (*avādi*) to you (*te*); O good friend (*sumitra*)!
In what manner did that very activity come about? To this he says: "yena yena prakāreṇa" (in whatever manner). ||32||
Sūta said:
Having thus heard this discourse concerning the Blessed One as narrated by Kauṣārava, [the sages asked:]
O twice-born one, the highly fortunate Kṣattṛ attained supreme bliss.
Śrīdhara: O twice-born Śaunaka! ||33||

Regarding the "sequence of composition" (*kramasaṃdarbha*), it is understood from the words of Śrī Śuka beginning with "Kauṣārava," that this is the speech of Sūta, which is additional [to what was previously stated]. ||33||
Viśvanātha: Not explained. —o)0(o— Of other virtuous men of meritorious fame and exalted renown...
If there would be joy upon merely hearing [of it], how much more so for one who bears the Śrīvatsa mark?
Śrīdhara: Having heard what? ||34||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: He is the one renowned as Yudhiṣṭhira, the one of meritorious fame. ||34||
He who swiftly liberated the lordly elephant, who was seized by a great fish and meditating on his lotus feet, from his distress while the female elephants were crying out.

Śrīdhara: [He says] with two verses beginning with "yaḥ": "If He is easily accessible even to animals through mere devotion, yet otherwise difficult to attain even for the gods, who would not feel joy upon hearing His story? *Jhaṣa* means a crocodile.
By the words "while they were crying out," His compassion is expressed; He rescued them from the peril.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: What need is there to say that he delivers human beings merely by the hearing of his story?
For he delivers even animals by mere remembrance; thus he says—"He who... *Jhaṣa* means a crocodile.

What need is there to mention [rescue] from a fish? [He rescues one] even from the difficult cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). He is the Lord (*pati*) for those who are upright, who have no other refuge, and who seek Him as easily attainable for their own happiness.
What grateful person would not serve one who is difficult for the wicked to propitiate?

Śrīdhara: Not explained. Kramasaṃdarbha: "Him" (tam). By those who are straightforward (*ṛju*), meaning not crooked, and therefore having no other refuge; and by others, meaning those who are not so [virtuous]. "Grateful" (*kṛtajña*): one who recognizes that He is easily propitiated by the mere act of seeking refuge.
Because it bestows the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*), who would not serve it? The meaning is that, since this is so, one should desire nothing else by abandoning service to it alone. ||36||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, he states that it is always appropriate to worship Him—referring to the word "Him" (tam). He is the Knower (Kajñaḥ), skilled in protecting those who have come for refuge; [He is distinct] from the wicked, the crooked, and those who seek refuge elsewhere. ||36||
Whoever [hears] this most wonderful account of the slaughter of Hiraṇyākṣa, the divine play of the Lord who took the form of the causal boar;
O twice-born ones, he who hears it, sings it, or rejoices in it is instantly liberated even from the murder of a Brahmin.
Śrīdhara: [This refers] to Hari in the form of a boar, by reason of his lifting up of the earth and so forth. ||37||
The sequential composition: that very reality which is the cause of all—that is the very self whose body has the form of a boar. ||37||
Viśvanātha: [The Lord] impels even those possessed of desire toward listening to the narrative—“He who... (verse 37).
This [teaching] is of great merit, sufficient for purification, auspicious, and glorious; it is the ground of longevity and blessings.
O dear one, for those who hear it, this [account] increases the heroism of the vital breaths and senses in battle; Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate refuge.
Śrīdhara: For those who hear this playful sport of Hari at its conclusion, Śrī Nārāyaṇa becomes their refuge.

It is of great merit, bestowing heaven and other rewards; it is supremely purifying and exceedingly sanctifying; it is auspicious, bringing wealth; it is glorious, producing fame; and it is the ground for long life and blessings.
It is the abode, the protection, and the very ground for the life-breaths and the senses; this is so, my dear Vidura. (38)
The sequential arrangement: "This," [he says]. O dear Śaunaka! ||38||
Viśvanātha: Not explained. —o)0(o— Thus ends [the commentary] in the *Sārārthadarśinī*, the *Harṣiṇī*, for those whose minds are devoted.
In the third [chapter], the nineteenth [section] is joined, repeatedly joined with the virtuous.

Thus ends the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya in the third book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa.
The twentieth chapter,
titled "The Creation of the World," in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
Śaunaka said: O Sauti,
having established himself upon the earth as his foundation, what means did Svāyambhuva Manu employ for the path of those born of later descent?
Śrīdhara:
In the twentieth [chapter], because of the interruption caused by the birth of Varāha and other events,
the creation is recalled from the beginning in order to state the lineage of Manu which is now under discussion.
