"Pratiṣṭhām" means a place of support; "adhyasya" means having reached. O Sauti, son of Romaharṣaṇa, what doors did he create for the path—the way out—for those who were merged in the Lord during their later, more recent births? The meaning is: by what means did he create later-born living beings?
The sequence of the composition: Having heard the incidental account of the Varāha-līlā, he asks about the subject at hand with the words "the earth" (mahīm) ||1||
Viśvanātha:
That very emission which was previously described in brief is now explained in detail in the twentieth [chapter], with the intention of describing the lineage of Svāyambhuva.
O Sauti, son of Romaharṣaṇa! For what purpose did he create the supports and the abode?

For which gateways did he provide the path for the exit of those living beings of later birth—those souls merged in the Lord who were born after Sanaka and the others? By what means did he create these more recent creatures?
This is the meaning. ||1||
The steward Vidura was a great devotee of Kṛṣṇa and His exclusive well-wisher;
he abandoned his elder brother, along with his children, because he considered him a sinner toward Kṛṣṇa.
The son born of his body was not inferior to Dvaipāyana in greatness;
with his whole being he took refuge in Kṛṣṇa and was devotedly intent upon those who were dedicated to him.
Having approached Maitreya, the foremost knower of reality, as he sat at Kuśāvarta, what did those free from passion ask him regarding his service to sacred fords?

Śrīdhara: [Thinking] that this will be understood through the very dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, he speaks in order to inquire about that same dialogue with five verses beginning with "O Kṣattṛ. The reason for Śrī Kṛṣṇa's friendship is indicated by the word "yaḥ" (who).
The sinful one, having committed an offense against his elder brother Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was accompanied by his sons such as Duryodhana and others...

For this reason, he who abandoned [the path] out of disregard for the mantras spoken by Śrī Kṛṣṇa; [he was] "anavaraḥ," meaning not inferior. Regarding "mahitve," it means in greatness. "Kuśāvarte" refers to the current of the Gaṅgā. ||2-4||

The sequence of the composition: Thus, considering it inappropriate to pose an independent question when there is a desire to hear the narrative consisting of Vidura’s questions, he asks that very same question with five verses beginning with "O Kṣattṛ. And therein, if at any point...

He says, by means of three and a quarter verses beginning with "virajās tīrthasevayā," that even now, one should close those very doors and set them in motion again from the beginning. First, by serving sacred fords (*tīrtha*), one becomes *virajaḥ*—free from evil company and suffering—and thereafter approaches [the goal]. ||4||

Viśvanātha: With the intention of stating that the answer to this question is indeed given through the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, he says, "O Kṣattṛ," etc. "With his offspring" means accompanied by sons such as Duryodhana and others. "Anavaraḥ" means not inferior;
"virajaḥ" means one from whom *rajas* (passion/dust) has departed. This is because the phrase "by service to sacred fords" (*tīrthasevayā*) provides the reason.
And by proximity, the meaning is that the dust and impurity of the sacred fords themselves have been removed; [this occurred] at Kuśāvarta and Gaṅgādvāra. ||24||
O Sūta, as the two of them conversed, pure discourses indeed proceeded,
like the waters of the Gaṅgā that destroy sins by taking refuge in the lotus feet of Hari.
Śrīdhara: If it is asked, "What did they say? in response to "Tell me whatever you have asked," he says: "Of those two...
[verse 5]: "Surely conversations that destroy sins (aghaghnīḥ) took place."
The sequence of composition: by the words "have begun" and so forth, the desire to hear from the very beginning is once again made clear. ||5||

Viśvanātha: "Pure stories"—because those two [the cowherd and the cowherdess] were devotees, and because devotees are devoid of talk other than about Kṛṣṇa; "in the Gaṅgā," *gāṅgyaḥ* means the waters (*āpaḥ*) that destroy sin (*aghaghnīḥ*). ||5||

—o)0(o— Recite those [deeds] for us; may prosperity be yours! For who that knows the true essence would ever be satiated while drinking the nectar of Hari’s pastimes, the noble deeds worthy of being celebrated?
Śrīdhara: He is Hari, whose noble deeds are worthy of being proclaimed and are themselves praiseworthy. ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: "May it be well with you" (*bhadraṃ te*) is a benediction expressed with eagerness. [The phrase] "in which [the stories] or whose [deeds]" refers either to the narrative or to Hari, [describing it as one] in which there are noble deeds worthy of being celebrated. ||6||
Thus questioned by the sages dwelling in Naimiṣa, Ugraśravas,
whose inner self was dedicated to the Blessed One, said to them, "Listen!"
Śrīdhara: "Thus" refers to the words of Vyāsa. Ugraśravas is the son of Romaharṣaṇa.
Those for whom Naimiṣa was the *ayana*, meaning their place of resort. By him, the mind was fixed upon the supreme self (*adhyātma*). (7)
The sequential arrangement [of the text] begins with the words "by the sages" (ṛṣibhiḥ), because all of them, approving of the inquiry of Śrī Śaunaka, repeated it. ||7||
Viśvanātha: Internally, it is the mind. ||7||
Sūta said:
Of Hari, who by his own māyā had assumed the body of a boar—
Having heard of the lifting of the earth from the netherworld and the effortless slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa,
the descendant of Bharata was filled with joy and spoke to the sage.
Śrīdhara: Having heard of the lifting of the earth as a pastime and Hiraṇyākṣa being slain with contempt, Vidura, the descendant of Bharata, [was moved]. ||8||

The Sequence of Narration: Śrī Sūta, however, [anticipating the question], "Why should the sequence of Śrī Vidura be interrupted when it follows the sequence of the Blessed One? offers this answer, which is imbued with praise for him: "Of Hari...
It is understood that this very statement, originally spoken by Śrī Śuka, was merely repeated by this Sūta. Therefore...

Following this very sequence, he narrates everything; that is to say, having heard of the pastime consisting of the lifting of the earth, and having heard that Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by Him with contempt in that very same [pastime]. ||8||

Viśvanātha: Of that Hari—whose boar-form (*kroḍatanu*) was well-sustained (*suṣṭhu dhṛtā*) without deceit (*amāyayā*), meaning eternally established—the word *dhṛta* is a form of the root *dhṛ* belonging to the *tudādi* class, meaning "to stand. *Goḥ* means of the earth (*pṛthivī*). *Bhārataḥ* refers to Vidura. ||8||
Vidura said:
Having created the Prajāpatis for the sake of the creation of progeny, the Lord of the Prajāpatis [proceeded].
O Brahmin, you who know the path of the unmanifest, tell me: what did he undertake?
"In the creation and dissolution of Madhva, the gradation among the gods is clearly known;
it is held that the primary purport [of scripture] lies in the thorough knowledge of this gradation.
Therefore, that has been stated many times, and this other [work] is its illuminator. Thus it is said in the Vāmana Purāṇa. 9.
Śrīdhara: Because you are a knower of the path of the unmanifest; or else, it is an epithet of Brahmā. (9)
The composition of the sequence: one who knows the path of the unmanifest, a knower of the reality that is beyond the reach of those such as ourselves. ||9||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
—o)0(o— Those sages beginning with Marīci, and he who is Manu Svāyambhuva;
How indeed did they bring this about at the command of Brahmā?
Śrīdhara: [They] brought forth this world, contemplating it [in their minds]. ||10||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: They brought this world into being, that is, they produced it. ||10||
Did they create [the world] accompanied by a second, or were they independent in their actions? Or rather, did they all together fashion this universe?
Madhu and Kaiṭabha, along with Brahmā and Vāyu, and their respective wives, are the presiding deities (abhimānins).
From Ahaṃkāra arise Śeṣa and Viṣṇu, Rudra and Indra, and the women born of desire.
But for the mind, Aniruddha and Candra [are the presiding deities], as well as others as previously stated;
such is the sequence, though there is a reversal according to the distinction between the subtle and the gross.
"This sequence applies to creation, to the qualities (guṇas), to knowledge and so forth, or even to that which abides in liberation.
Any statement to the contrary is intended for the delusion of those born as asuras," so it is said in the Vārāha Purāṇa. (11)

Śrīdhara: "With a companion" means accompanied by wives. "Independent" means not depending on their wives. "In actions" refers to the creation of progeny and so forth. "United" means mutually dependent. This is the world. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: "Accompanied by a second" means having wives; "independent in rites" such as creation and so forth means not depending on others; "united" means requiring the assembly of many more. (11)
Maitreya said: By fate, which is inconceivable, supreme, and unblinking...
From the agitation of the Blessed One’s three qualities, there arose a great [manifestation].

Śrīdhara: In order to provide the answer to the question "What did Brahmā begin?"—namely, that he created the Yakṣas and others—he recalls the previously mentioned creation in seven verses beginning with "By fate" (*daivena*). As for the questions of Manu and the others, their answers will come later, after the commencement of the subsequent chapter. [He began] by means of that which is difficult to conceive.

By means of *daiva* (the unseen merit and demerit of living beings), by the Supreme Person (*mahāpuruṣa*) who is the presiding controller of *prakṛti*, and by *kāla* (time) which is the unblinking cause, there arose from the Lord—who is free from modification—the *mahat* (the Great Principle). This *mahat* consists of the three *guṇas* of *pradhāna* once they have become agitated. As it is stated in the *Tantra*:
"Moreover, they know that Viṣṇu has three forms designated as Puruṣa:
the first is the creator of the Mahat; the second resides within the cosmic egg; the third dwells within all beings. By knowing these, one is liberated. (12)

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): In order to introduce the account of the *pādma* creation, he recalls the preceding account of the *brāhma* creation for the sake of coherence, beginning with the words "by the divine power" (*daivena*) and so forth. From the Blessed One, the ultimate cause, the Great Principle (*mahat*) arose; and that [arose] not directly from Him, but rather from His power (*tacchakti*).

Precisely from that state called *pradhāna*, where the qualities (*guṇas*) are in equilibrium; from what kind? From that which has been disturbed by causes such as destiny (*daiva*), and therein by time (*kāla*), which is "unblinking" and even superior to destiny. ||12||

Viśvanātha: To answer the question "What did he begin?", he briefly restates everything that has already been said regarding the first part [of the narrative], for the sake of the elegance of the story, while about to describe the expansion of the emission (*visarga*). [He says: "By destiny" (*daivena*); by the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings; of what kind? "Inconceivable" (*durvitarkya*), meaning its root is difficult to understand; "supreme" (*pareṇa*).
From Pradhāna, which at the proper time experienced agitation due to the three guṇas, the Mahat arose; that is to say, from the Blessed One who was consecrated by the Blessed One. ||12||

From the Mahat, which is dominated by rajas and impelled by destiny, the Bhūtādi (Ahaṃkāra), possessing three genders, was born; it then produced the five elements, beginning with space, five by five.

Śrīdhara: "From the Mahat is born the Ahaṅkāra, the origin of the elements, possessing three characteristics and three qualities. The meaning is that although the Mahat is primarily characterized by *sattva*, at the time of the production of the Ahaṅkāra, it becomes dominated by *rajas* in accordance with its effect, because [the Ahaṅkāra] arises from the Mahat when *rajas* is predominant. "Fivefold" refers to the subtle elements (*tanmātras*).
The meaning is that he created the five great elements, the organs of cognition, the organs of action, and their respective deities. ||13||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: The meaning is that although the Great Principle (mahat) is predominantly characterized by *sattva*, at the time of the production of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), it becomes known as the "Thread" (*sūtra*) when it is predominantly characterized by *rajas*.

The meaning is that the ego (ahaṅkāra)— which possesses three genders and consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), being the source of the elements (bhūtādi)— created the five gross elements beginning with space, the five subtle elements, the organs of cognition, the organs of action, and their respective deities, five of each. ||13||
And being individually unable to create the elemental [world], they,
through the conjunction of destiny, united together and emitted a golden egg.
Śrīdhara: Being individually incapable of creating each material golden egg, they created them by combining together. ||14||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By the conjunction of destiny—that is, by the conjunction of the power of the Lord—having come together and met. ||14||
That soulless cosmic egg lay within the waters of the ocean;
the Lord dwelt within it for more than a thousand years.
Śrīdhara: *anvavātsīt* means he occupied or presided over. ||15||

The sequential composition: The "non-egg" (anḍakoṣa) is indeed the egg-shell itself, or the Virāṭ situated within it. Its state of being without a self (nirātmakatva) is due to the fact that even at that time, the individual souls (jīvas) have not yet awakened. The Lord (Īśvara), the creator of the Mahat, exists in the form of the second Puruṣa. ||15||
Viśvanātha: It is without self; there, no self is manifested. ||15||
From his navel there arose a lotus, radiant with the intense light of a thousand suns,
the abode of all classes of living beings, wherein he himself became the self-ruling lord.
Śrīdhara: That whose vast radiance is like that of a thousand suns; the lotus is the abode, the dwelling place, of all classes of living beings. Svarāṭ is Brahmā. (16)
The sequence of events: He who thus created [the world] in the Brāhma Kalpa, having entered [into it], a lotus arose from the navel during the Pādma Kalpa. (16)
Viśvanātha: In the lotus originating from the navel, Svarāṭ Brahmā resides. ||16||
Being thus entreated by the Blessed One, he who was reclining in the bed of the waters fashioned the structure of the worlds as before, according to his own established order.
"Madhvaḥ": by means of her own established state, that is, through the power of her abiding as the Blessed One. ||17||

Śrīdhara: He who lies within the interior of the embryonic waters (garbhodaka) in the reservoir of water; presided over and occupied by that Blessed Lord, he is the self-ruling sovereign (svarāṭ). By his own arrangement, through the sequence of names, forms, and so forth. ||17||
The sequence of manifestation: by its own state, through the process of manifesting various names, forms, and so forth within itself. ||17||

Viśvanātha: That Brahmā was presided over (adhiṣṭhita) by the Blessed Lord; who indeed is that Blessed Lord? To this he says: "He who... And thus, that Brahmā, being impelled by the Blessed Lord, [created] the structure of the world (lokasaṃsthā)—the arrangement of the world—by his own structure, namely the sequence of names, forms, and so forth. ||17||
He created ignorance through his shadow before him, consisting of five sections:
tāmisra, andhatāmisra, tamaḥ, moha, and mahātamaḥ.

Śrīdhara: *Chāyā* is the counterpart of *prabhā* (light); the meaning is "by that [darkness] he did not perceive. This is because it has been stated: "But that which is produced by the lack of intelligence of the Lord. *Mahātamaḥ* means *mahāmoha* (great delusion).
The use of the nominative case in *mohaḥ* is intended merely to indicate its essential nature. ||18||
The sequence of composition is shown as follows: "He created," [verse 18].

Viśvanātha: Since the egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) of living beings cannot arise within the bodies of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, gods, humans, and so forth—which are to be created by Brahmā—without ignorance (*avidyā*), Brahmā first brought those functions of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*) into manifestation through himself via the medium of Brahman; thus, as the form of *Tamās* (the quality of darkness), Brahmā created them.
He said: "It projects. By "shadow" (chāyayā) is meant by means of a shadow-like body; the meaning is "by darkness" (tamasā).

Here, ignorance (ajñāna), egoism (asmitā), attachment (rāga), aversion (dveṣa), and clinging to life (abhiniveśa) are to be understood respectively as darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and utter gloom (andhatāmisra). ||18||
He cast off his own body, composed of darkness, without taking pleasure in it;
the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas seized that night arising from hunger and thirst.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having restated the previously mentioned common creation, he describes the uncommon creation through a specific distinction, from the words "He emitted" (*visasarja*) until the end of the passage. The Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, born from that very [source], took possession of that emitted body which was of the nature of night.

[He entered] that [body] in which hunger and thirst arise. And in this regard, the Vedic scripture should be considered: "That body of his which was there, he cast off; it became the night," and so forth. (19)

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Not rejoicing in that body which was of the nature of shadow, and lamenting, "Alas, alas! At the beginning of creation, I became enveloped by darkness alone," he abandoned it; and that body discarded by him became night.
And immediately thereafter, at that very moment, the *yakṣas* and *rakṣasas* seized and took possession of her;

this is intended to mean that ignorance (*avidyā*) and its concomitant factors (*dharma*), namely the obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) and the distractions (*vikṣepa*), are the most predominant qualities of *yakṣas* and *rakṣasas*. Of what sort was she? She was one in whom the arising of hunger and thirst had occurred. In this context, "that which belongs to him" refers to that [ignorance].

The Vedic scripture beginning with "There was a body; he cast it away; that became darkness" should be reflected upon here. In this context, what is intended by the "abandonment of the body" of Brahmā, whose lifespan is two *parārdhas*, is simply the abandonment of his mental state (*bhāva*).
Consequently, a tamasic state such as anger manifested within the mind of Brahmā. From that...

The Yakṣas and Rākṣasas came into being; that state of darkness became night, and the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas alone took possession of it—this is the full extent of the meaning. Even though, for the sake of creation, he assumes and relinquishes separate bodies through the power of yoga, his lifespan remains two parārdhas.
Some also say that [the power] is obstructed even for the sake of enjoying sense objects, because it is observed that even gods such as Indra assume and abandon various forms. ||19||
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they rushed toward him to devour him;
tormented by hunger and thirst, they cried out, "Protect him! Eat him!"

Śrīdhara: "Upasṛṣṭāḥ" means overcome. "Jagdhum" means to eat, to consume. Since we are afflicted by hunger and thirst, some say, "He is our father; protect him out of compassion. Others, however, say, "Eat him! (*jakṣadhvam*); for the verbal root *jakṣ* signifies both eating and laughing.

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "Afflicted" means tormented; they [approached] that Brahmā in order to devour (*jagdhum*) him. Among them, some said, "He is our father," and out of compassion cried, "Do not kill him!"—[the root] *jakṣ* is used in the sense of eating (*bhakṣa*).
From the root *bhakṣa-hasana* (to eat and to laugh). ||20||
The gods, filled with agitation, said to them: "Do not devour me! Protect me!
Alas! You have become the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas who prey upon my progeny."
Śrīdhara: The god Brahmā, being agitated and afraid, said, "Do not devour me, do not eat me;

rather, protect me! O Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, you have become my offspring, my sons—you have been born. The meaning is that thus the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas were born with such a fierce nature. Among them, those who...
Those who said, "Eat! are to be known as Yakṣas; those who said, "Protect me! are to be known as Rākṣasas.
This is also an illustration that includes association with animals and other beings of a tamasic nature. ||21||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: The "deity" is Brahmā. [He says: "Do not devour me, but protect me! Oh, what a marvel, O Yakṣas and Rākṣasas! (21)
Whichever deities he emitted from his front, shining with splendor,
those seekers of the divine seized that radiance which was released as the day.

Śrīdhara: *Prabhayā dīvyan* means shining or radiant. Whatever deities were luminous and characterized by *sattva*, those he created as the foremost, that is, as the principal ones. Regarding the word "those" (*te*), although the deities (*devatāḥ*) were designated in the feminine, they are referred to here in the masculine (*taḥ*) because the intention is to express only their essential nature (*arthamātra*).
This is the detailed explanation. It should be understood that the same applies here to the phrase "yakṣas and rākṣasas.

Thus, they—desiring the gods (*devayantaḥ*) and sporting about (*krīḍayantaḥ*)—seized (*ahārṣuḥ*) the radiance (*prabhām*) emitted and abandoned by him, which was of the nature of day (*ahaḥ*). ||22||
The sequential composition: "devayantaḥ" (those seeking the gods). From the root *div* in the sense of "to injure," belonging to the curādigaṇa, the meaning is "one who is entreating. ||22||
Viśvanātha: Shining—that is, radiant—with a body consisting of *sattva* in the form of splendor;

he who created whichever deities as principal ones, that is, primarily. Here, the reference "whichever" (*yā*) should be understood as referring back to "those" (*tāḥ*) by way of the sense alone. [He created] those who were manifested...

The gods took—that is, they seized—that radiance which had been abandoned by him, his body in the form of the day. For what purpose? Desiring to sport, they did so for the sake of play; just as the night remains with the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, so too the day sports with the gods—this is the meaning. Thus it is said.
The context: Here, a state of grace—a sattvic disposition—manifested within the mind of Brahmā;
from that [grace] the gods were born, and that grace became the day. And they indeed took possession of that;
such is the meaning of this passage. ||22||
The god created gods from his hindquarters who were exceedingly lustful;
they, out of that lustfulness, approached him for sexual union.
Śrīdhara: The word division is *adevān* (not gods). According to the Śruti, "He created the Asuras from his buttocks.
[They were] excessively greedy and addicted to women. *Abhipedire* means they reached [him]. ||23||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: And thus, that desire (*kāma*), which was of a passionate nature (*rājasabhāva*), arose in his mind; from that, the Asuras were born. That state (*bhāva*) became Sandhyā, and the Asuras seized her; so he says—"O God..."

Thus [it is said], for according to the Śruti: "From his lower part he created the Asuras who were not gods. He states that from desire arises great misfortune, beginning with the words "He [created] him," etc. (23).
Then, laughing, that Blessed One, pursued with speed by the shameless asuras, fled away both enraged and terrified.
Śrīdhara: He fled, he ran away. ||24||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: *parāpatat* means she fled. ||24||
Approaching Hari, the giver of boons who removes the distress of those who seek refuge, he beheld the Self manifested in a form corresponding to his own devotion, out of grace for His devotees.
Śrīdhara: [He is so called] because he reveals himself in accordance with the desires of his devotees; having approached him in that manner, the sequence of the verses has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "Having approached" means having reached him by means of the mind alone; "he offered [himself]" is the ellipsis to be supplied. ||25||
"—O Supreme Self! Protect me! By Your command I created these creatures;
yet, O Lord, these wicked beings now seek to violate me."

Śrīdhara: He requested with two verses beginning with "pahī" (flee). Regarding the sequence of events for "yabhitum" (to copulate), that is, to violate [her] through sexual intercourse, Viśvanātha has not provided an explanation.
"You alone, it is said, are the destroyer of the afflictions for those worlds who are afflicted;
you alone are the bestower of afflictions upon them who do not draw near to you."

Śrīdhara: For those people of the world who have not approached and have not taken refuge at your feet, the sequence of your [teachings] brings about affliction; this is to be understood as intended to turn them toward himself. ||27||

Viśvanātha: [It is understood that] for those who have not approached Your feet—that is, for non-devotees who have not taken refuge at Your feet—You are the giver of suffering; whereas for those devotees who have taken refuge at Your feet, even though they are themselves afflicted by suffering, You are the destroyer of their suffering. Such a one, known as "the Sole One," is a certain being who is affectionately disposed toward His devotees.

The sense is that [He] does not exist [as an independent agent]. For those who have not taken refuge at Your feet, You alone—manifesting as time, karma, the planets, and so forth—are the sole bestower of affliction. Yet, for those very same people when they suddenly take refuge at Your feet, You Yourself directly become the destroyer of each and every one of those afflictions; for among Your devotees, time, karma, and the rest have no jurisdiction.
The intention [of the Lord] is as follows: your freedom from partiality, however, is illustrated by the example of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa). ||27||
" Having perceived his wretchedness, he who possessed the vision of the pure inner self said,
"Cast off this terrible body," and being thus addressed, he indeed cast it off.
O Madhva, even though he is omniscient and capable, Brahmā— being dear to Hari—
performs his actions as if ignorant and powerless, even while knowing [the truth].
"He cast off his former external body as if it were impure, but not his own [inner] self;
and Brahmā attained that state of being Hara and the rest, the foremost deity among the gods. Thus it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*. (29)

Śrīdhara: Hari, whose vision of the supreme self (*adhyātma-darśana*) was solitary and free from doubt—that is, who possessed knowledge of the minds of others—said, "Cast off your own body, which is terrible and defiled by passion. The word "said" is to be supplied [to the verb *vimuñca*].
Having been thus addressed, Brahmā cast off that body. Everywhere, "casting off the body" (*tanu-tyāga*) means the abandonment of that [body].
The abandonment of the mental state is what is intended; and its "grasping" should be understood as the attainment of that very state. ||28||

Regarding the sequence of the composition: in the commentary on the phrase "he should grasp that," the state known as *bhāva* (emotional absorption) should be understood as immersion in the object of creation.
And its duration is non-reflective thought (*amanana*), because it lasts for two *parārdhas*. ||28||
Viśvanātha: He is one whose vision of the supreme self (*adhyātmadarśana*)—that is, knowledge of the minds of others—is distinct and free from doubt.
The words "he said, 'Release [it]'" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. And because he spoke thus, Brahmā cast off his body. (28)
Her lotus-feet were tinkling with sound, her eyes were unsteady with intoxication,
and her hips were covered by a silken garment shimmering with a girdle of bells.

Śrīdhara: According to the scripture, "The junction of day and night occurred"; that body emitted by him became the evening twilight (*sāyantanī saṃdhyā*). And that is the time when passion (*kāma*) intensifies. Furthermore, because the Asuras possess a *rājasa* nature, they are lustful for women; therefore, having fashioned that very twilight into a woman, they...

He says that they have fallen into a state of delusion with three verses beginning with "her" (tām). She is one whose lotus-feet jingle with anklets; she is one whose eyes are unsteady with intoxication; she is one whose hips and waist-region are covered by a shimmering silk garment and a girdle of bells. ||29||

The sequence of composition: "tām" refers to the triad [of the three goddesses]. "Anyonya" (mutual) implies that even *śleṣa* (punning connection), like the lines [of a drawing], is accepted as a primary element. Alternatively, the substitution of "ya" occurs according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* [Pāṇini 7.1.39]. ||29||

Viśvanātha: Considering that she was a woman according to the subsequent statement, "thinking her to be a woman," and imagining that very twilight to be a woman, he says—"tāṃ kvaṇat..."—that the demons, being lustful for women, were deluded.
Here, [he describes] those who had flown into the sky with their own sounds in order to go toward their respective nests.

They fashioned anklets and girdles from the *caṭaka* birds, cranes, and the like; they fashioned feet, eyes, hips, and breasts from fragments of clouds possessing those very shapes. For this reason alone, in one place, the word *payodhara* (cloud/breast) is employed through a pun (*śleṣa*). The twilight’s own ruddiness was the red silk garment (*aruṇadukūla*). The bank...

"Kaṭitaṭam," meaning "the region of the hips"; the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied after the root *śliṣ* (to embrace) with the prefix *āṅ*, etc. Even though the suffix is marked with *ṅ*, the *guṇa* vowel change is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).
[She is] one whose high breasts are closely pressed against each other.
She possessed a beautiful nose and lovely teeth, and her playful glances were accompanied by a gentle smile.
Śrīdhara: She whose high, closely-set breasts are joined together by the pressure [of their proximity];
she who has beautiful teeth; she whose smile is tender and whose glances are playful. (30)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By the very reason of mutual interlocking (*śleṣa*) and compression (*upamarda*), she is one whose breasts (*payodharau*) are lofty (*uttuṅgau*), continuous (*nirantarau*), and without interval (*avyavadhānau*); [the dual ending] *-au* is replaced by the feminine suffix *-ām* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* etc.
Or rather, there is a substitution of *yā*. The light of the sun emerging from within [the clouds] is indeed the laughter and the glance;

sometimes, its disappearance behind a fragment of cloud is the concealment out of shame; and the long, dark fragments of cloud fallen from above down to the surface are indeed [the locks of hair]. (30)
Seeing that woman who was hiding herself out of modesty, her dark tresses forming a thick veil,
all the asuras were utterly bewildered by her beauty.

Śrīdhara: [He saw] one concealing herself by covering [her body] with a moving garment; she who possessed a mass (*varūtha*) or multitude of dark tresses. O Vidura, knower of dharma, having perceived—that is, having recognized—that woman...
(31). *Kramasaṃdarbha*: not explained.
Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "nīlālakavarūtham" [is explained as follows]. O Dharma! O Vidura! Having perceived—that is, having recognized—that woman... ||31||
—o)0(o— Oh, what beauty! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, her fresh youth!
In the midst of those filled with desire, she moves about as if devoid of passion.
Śrīdhara: He describes the sequence of contemplation for those who are utterly deluded, beginning with "Aho! (Verse 32).
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha says: He states their delirious outcries of lust and delusion, beginning with "Aho! (verse 32).
Reflecting in many ways upon that twilight figure in the form of a woman, those dull-witted men approached her with confidence and questioned her.
Śrīdhara: Having honored and paid respect to her, out of confidence and affection, those of evil intellect questioned her. (33)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Is she devoted only to us, or to another? Is she a goddess or a human woman?
Is she lustful or a celibate student?"—thus they reflected. *Abhisambhāvya* means having honored [her].
"Who are you, whose daughter are you, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks? What is your purpose here, O beautiful one?
With your beauty as your merchandise, you afflict us who are ill-fated."

Śrīdhara: [He asks] with three verses, beginning with "Who are you? Who are you by birth? Or whose daughter are you? O *bhāminī*—O angry woman! Beauty itself is wealth, an object of priceless value; that very beauty is the commodity (*paṇya*) fit for purchase. By not surrendering it, you distress us. (34)

The sequence of the composition: the cause of the affliction. Viśvanātha says: "O unfortunate ones," meaning those devoid of the wealth that is its price; "form alone is the priceless object, that very thing is the commodity fit for sale"—by means of that [commodity], you afflict us, the unfortunate ones who are unworthy even of your service, by the very act of embracing your bride.
Or rather, [the meaning is]: "You wish to seize me, or you harass me, yet you do not buy me; fie upon us unfortunate ones!
— Or else, O frail one, whoever you may be, it is by good fortune that we have beheld you.
You captivate the minds of those who gaze upon you with your play of the ball.

Śrīdhara: What is the use of inquiring about your caste, family, and so forth? Be who you may! By good fortune, this auspicious event has occurred, namely, the sight of you. However, you alone agitate and disturb our minds. [The sequence of the commentary is not explained.]
Viśvanātha: "You toss" means you churn. By means of the game of ball, the sun itself—tossing as it sets—is imagined as a reddish ball. ||35||
O graceful lady, your lotus-foot does not remain in one place as you repeatedly strike the falling bee with the palm of your hand.
The waist sinks down, oppressed by the weight of her large breasts;
her pure gaze is as if stilled, and the mass of her fine locks is motionless.

Śrīdhara: The speech of those with agitated minds does not remain in one place. O *śālinī* (praiseworthy lady), it does not prevail—that is, it does not become stable—in one place; or rather, it prevails—that is, it exists with supreme excellence—among the various playful movements in many places. [It describes] the falling sun and the leaping ball.
Your slender waist, terrified by the weight of your large breasts, sinks down and grows weary;
it spreads out slowly like a spent firebrand. Your beautiful mass of hair (*suśikhāsamūha*)—that is, your lovely tresses—is [falling].
In an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*), "a multitude of beautiful locks (*suśikhāḥ*)" refers to the collection of lovely hair being scattered. Herein...

The setting sun itself is the falling bird; the dispersal of clouds is the depression in the middle; the vision consists of the forms of stars; and darkness itself is the hair—such things are to be inferred. ||36||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: They describe the game of ball-play: "O graceful one! O praiseworthy one!
It does not conquer, that is, it does not remain steady in one place—the falling *pataṅga*, the ball moving downward; in the alternative sense, the setting [sun]."

The sun is moving; it languishes due to its thinness. The gaze is pure, as if free from desire; however, the meaning is that in reality it is full of longing within. It is weary, manifesting the exhaustion of playing with a ball. Therefore, bind the beautiful tresses—the lovely locks of hair—as they are being loosened; [O you who possess] a mass of beautiful tresses.
In this reading—"sv" is an indeclinable used as a separate word; consequently, the meaning is "a beautiful mass of crests. ||36||
Thus, the Asuras, being of deluded intellect, seized the evening twilight as it stretched out, thinking it to be a woman who was enticing them."
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha, thinking her to be a woman acting like a young girl, took hold of her. ||37||
Regarding the phrase "kramasaṃdarbhaḥ": thus [it is said]. For the twilight (saṃdhyā) indeed produces the manifestation of a woman in those who are desirous.

Consequently, it should be understood that the woman manifesting before them is perceived by them as non-different from her [the twilight], and in accordance with that perception, she has been described by the Lord of Sages (Śiva) as well. ||37||
Laughing with profound emotion and smelling his own self with his own self,
the Blessed One created by his splendor the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.

Śrīdhara: [The phrase] "laughing while smelling herself with herself" refers to her radiance and beauty. The laughing and the self-smelling are transformations resulting from the skillful manifestation of her beauty. (38)

The sequential composition: With a profound state of being (*bhāva*) characterized by pride in her own beauty— such that her gaze was not directed elsewhere— and having laughed in such a way, she herself smelled her own self with an excess of love and an experience of an excess of fragrance through her own splendor (*kānti*).
With a slender body full of luster. ||38||

Viśvanātha: When the beauty of Brahmā became manifest to his memory, then from him the Gandharvas and others were born, and that beauty became moonlight; he says "smiling" (prahasya) to indicate how they received it—that [beauty] by what kind of luster? One that is profound with emotion and reveals its own application.
Having laughed in such a way, he goes away smelling himself; this is because of the metaphorical identification of the light with that which possesses the light.
Thus, laughing, smelling, and so forth are signs of his relishing his own beauty. (38)
He indeed cast off that beloved, radiant body as moonlight;
and Viśvāvasu and the others joyfully took it up with affection.
Śrīdhara: *Jyotsnām* means in the form of moonlight. *Ta eva* refers to those very groups of Gandharvas and others.
*Viśvāvasupurogamāḥ* means those in whom Viśvāvasu is the leader or the foremost. (39)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Having created the *bhūtas* and *piśācas* through his own exertion, the Blessed One...
Seeing those naked ones with disheveled hair, he closed his eyes.
Śrīdhara: Due to his own *tandri*, which is laziness; and seeing them with their hair disheveled, he closed his eyes. ||40||

The sequence of composition: By means of a body characterized by "ātmatandriṇā"—that is, possessed of lassitude (*tandrā*)—this is also an elliptical expression for yawning, sleep, and intoxication, since these constitute the very process of its activity. Regarding them, Viśvanātha says: "At one time Brahmā became lazy, and from that [lassitude] arose the *bhūtas*, *piśācas*, and so forth."

That inertia became manifest in the form of yawning, sleep, and so forth; and those very [beings] seized it—thus he says: "Having created... That which has *tandrā* (lassitude) as its effect is *tandrin*, meaning *ālasya* (inertia); by that—o)0(o)—.
They seized that body of the Lord which he had emitted, known as Jṛmbhaṇā,
by which sleep and the moisture of the senses are seen among living beings; and they called that [body] Unmāda, by which they overwhelm those who are impure.

Śrīdhara: They call that sleep "the moisture" (vikleda) or "flow" (srāva) of the senses. By reason of this moisture of the senses, they overpower those who are present—rendering them defiled and bewildered—and they call that host of spirits and so forth "insanity" (unmāda).
The fourfold nature of the *bhūtas* and other subtle elements has been stated on account of their being the causes of drowsiness, yawning, closing the eyes, and madness. ||41||

The sequential composition [of the commentary] on the verse beginning with "jagṛhuḥ" consists of one and a half verses. For this very reason, he states it non-differently as "the sleep called jṛmbhaṇa. Furthermore, because he intends to emphasize the primary nature of the attribute (*dharma*) itself, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) has not been employed here.
In that state, which is the moistening of the senses and which they call "madness" (*unmāda*), there is indeed madness.
The meaning is that [the words] indicate that [object] as well by way of its non-difference from that [subject], saying "it exists. ||41||

Viśvanātha: That sleep by which there is a moistening (*vikleda*) of the senses—the mouth and so forth—in beings such as humans, and by which moistening they cause those who are already defiled (*ucchiṣṭa*) to be assailed (*dharṣayanti*), that assault is called insanity (*unmāda*). For this very reason, people assailed by spirits, ghosts, and the like, become insane.
They are called [thus]. ||41||
Considering himself to be full of vigor,
the unborn and powerful Lord created the hosts of Sādhyas and the hosts of Pitṛs in his absence.
Śrīdhara: *Ūrjasvantam* means powerful; *parokṣeṇa* means by an invisible form. ||42||

The sequence of the composition: Viśvanātha [explains that] Viṣṇu, endowed with *sattva* characterized by energy (*ūrjasvat*) through the granting of boons and so forth, once contemplated his own supreme power and transcendence;
and from those two [powers], the *Sādhyas* and the *Pitṛs* came into being, and they became the recipients of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings.

He said: "By two [qualities]: by being full of vigor and full of *sattva*; and by that *sattva*, [he conquers] the groups of *sādhyas* indirectly (*parokṣeṇa*) and the groups of *pitṛs* through their absence (*pārokṣyeṇa*). ||42||
The ancestors attained that body which is their own creation,
which the seers extend for both the Sādhyas and the Pitṛs.

Śrīdhara: From whom the creation of the self proceeds; for what purpose—that is, by means of which motive for being the recipient (saṃpradāna); "the poets" refers to those skilled in ritual action; "to the ancestors to be accomplished" means to one's own ancestors in their forms as such; "they extend" means they offer *havya* and *kavya* through the performance of *śrāddha* and other rites. ||43||

The sequence of composition: "Those" refers to the fact that, having known [them] as being truly endowed with that, they give to them; this is by means of which very specific characteristic, namely, the body itself, as the cause. ||43||
Viśvanātha: They are the *sādhya*s and they are the ancestors; the meaning is that they are suitable for that body.

For this reason—that is, because they extend the *havya*, the sacrificial food, to the *sādhya*s, and the *kavya*, the ancestral food, to the ancestors by means of the *śrāddha* and other rites—this is the sense. ||43||
He created the Siddhas and Vidyādharas by means of invisibility,
and he bestowed upon them that wonderful self known as the power of disappearance.
Śrīdhara: By means of concealment—that is, by the power of disappearance—even while remaining visible. ||44||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: At one time he brought about his own disappearance;
from that, perfected *vidyādharas* came into being—thus he says, "the perfected ones" (*siddhān*). ||44||
The Lord created the Kinnaras and Kimpuruṣas from his own self,
honoring himself by beholding the reflection of his own self.
Śrīdhara: "By means of the individual self" (pratyātmyena) means by means of a reflection (*pratibimba*). A reflection is an appearance of the self; it is the self-measuring of the self by the self.
For one who perceives such a reflection—such as a handsome person—the activity consists of gestures like nodding the head.
Precisely for this reason, there is a constant state of union through mutual honoring among those created from that [reflection]. (45)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He caused his own reflection to appear; and from that, Kinnaras and Kiṃpuruṣas were born—thus he says: "He, who... [referring to] *pratyātmanā*, meaning by means of the reflection.
Thinking "I am handsome," one honors oneself by means of the self alone, as if honoring the reflection of the self in a mirror. ||45||
They accepted that form which had been cast off by the Supreme Lord;
becoming a couple, they sang of Him alone at dawn through their ritual acts.
Śrīdhara: That is in the form of a reflection. It has not been explained by Krama-sandarbha through descriptions of his deeds and exploits.
Viśvanātha: That became the form of mutual gazing between the man and woman within each individual self.
Therefore, he says "But they... to show that they too accepted that very same thing. ||46||
Indeed, while lying down with his body possessed of enjoyments and filled with much anxiety,
he cast off that body out of anger because creation had not increased.

Śrīdhara: *Bhoga* means expansion (*ābhoga*), that is, extension such as the stretching out of the feet; [the Lord moves] with a body possessing that quality. *Anupacite* means not having attained growth. That [body] is endowed with enjoyment, anger, and so forth. ||47||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He abandoned his body while it was still lying there by means of the mind alone; and that [body] became the form of a snake or similar creature—thus he says, "the body," etc. "Bhoga" means expansion or extension, characterized by the spreading out of the feet and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: When the creation was not accomplished due to excessive reflection—thinking with such a mental disposition, "How shall my creation be perfected?"—there arose therein, in the midst of that very reflection, a certain lack of discernment, from which great anger ensued.
Immediately after that anger, he cast off his body. ||47||
Those hairs which were removed from here, O dear one, were born as serpents;
they became cruel crawling snakes and *nāgas* with massive coils and necks."

Śrīdhara: From this body, those hairs which were shed—that is, fell away—became snakes (*ahi*). From this [body] as it moved forward by the contraction of its feet, etc., [the creatures] became serpents (*sarpa*). For this very reason, they are called *nāga* because they do not go (*na gacchanti*); the meaning is that they possess extreme speed. Because they were born from the *bhoga* (the coiled body), [they are called *bhogin*].
Those whose necks are broad and large due to their hoods, and all of whom are cruel because of their association with that wrath;
the internal classification of their species is well known in the *Sarpasiddhānta*. ||48||

The sequence of composition: "Those which... Viśvanātha explains: "Even the falling out of his hair should be understood as consisting of his very being (*bhāvamaya*). From that body—referring to "from that" (*amutaḥ*)—those hairs which fell away or were shed became serpents.
From that [body] which was moving, crawling, and shifting due to the contraction of its feet and other limbs, those hands, feet, and so forth...
Those who have fallen away are the *sarpas*; and those such as the *muṇḍakandhara*s and others are the *nāgas*. Of what kind are they?

Because they are born from the *bhoga* (the body), they are those whose necks (*kandharā*) are broad (*uru*) due to the *bhoga* (hood). And all of them are cruel due to their association with anger. The internal classification of their species is found in the *Sarpasiddhānta*.
It is well-known. ||48||
Thinking himself to have accomplished his purpose,
that Self-born One then created, by means of his mind, the Manus who bring forth the worlds at the end [of the previous cycle].
Śrīdhara: When he became conceited, then he created the Manus. ||49||

The sequential composition: Regarding the phrase "as if having accomplished his task," the word *iva* (as if) implies that his previous duty has been fulfilled. [He created] *manu*s, who are human beings and the "shapers of the worlds" (*lokabhāvana*), being the causes for the emergence of all worlds through their actions; therefore, from Manu, progeny will come into being. ||49||

Viśvanātha: When, immediately after his reflection, Viśvanātha desired to create a couple so that his creation might be fully accomplished, joy arose within him. Then, from that [joy], the Manus came into being, and they assumed a male form consisting of the fulfillment of creation; thus he says in two verses beginning with "He [beheld] himself."
Regarding the phrase "the Manus": at that time, Svāyambhuva Manu was manifest and visible to all among them;

it should be understood that the others were visible according to their respective times. Because of the employment of the word "resides" (*atrāste*) here, this creation of Manu should be known as the very last. For this very reason, even that which will be described immediately following it—

This creation of the sages (*ṛṣisarga*) is to be understood as having occurred previously. Here, regarding the creations described in the tenth, twelfth, and twentieth chapters—which are stated sometimes in sequential order and sometimes by skipping steps according to the logic of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) or the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*)—this sequence should be known: first is the creation of ignorance (*avidyā*) consisting of five sections.
Then follows the creation of the forest trees and other vegetation; then the creation of serpents and the like;

(then the creation of cows, buffaloes, and so forth; then the creation of yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, kinnaras, kiṃpuruṣas, and the like; then the creation of Sanaka and others, as well as Marīci and the rest; then the creation of human beings, at the very end of all.
Then, from those [beings], even those previously created increased in the form of male and female;
from them, that self-possessed one created his own city, the Puruṣa.
Having seen them, those who had been created previously praised Prajāpati.
Regarding the word *madhvaḥ*: those gods who were created in the beginning; for it is said that upon seeing the creation of Puruṣa, the gods declared, "Well done! (sukṛtam). ||50||
Śrīdhara: To them he sent forth—that is, gave—his own *puruṣa*, a city (*pura*) in the form of a person (*puruṣākāra*), namely those Manus. (50)
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] is as follows: "from them" means being self-possessed (*ātmavān*), that is, being the supreme refuge (*paramāśraya*).
The reading *ātmanaḥ* is, however, commonly seen; in that case, the meaning is "the city of the supreme Self," that is, the locus of light (*prakāśasthāna*). ||50||
Viśvanātha: He created—that is, bestowed—his own city, which is his body in the form of a person. ||50||
—o)0(o— Aha! O Creator of the world, how well indeed has this been done by you, in whom all ritual actions are established; together with that, may we eat food, O Lord!

Śrīdhara: That which was performed by you is well-done; they call it a "good deed" (*sukṛta*). In this creation of Manu, there are rites such as the *agnihotra* and others. Therefore, O Brahman, let us all together eat the food—the sacrificial oblation consisting of *bhṛṅga* and so forth—in this [creation]. ||51||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: O Creator of the World! By "you" (*te*) is meant that when a particular creation by Manu (*manusarge*) occurs, ritual acts such as the *agnihotra* and others become established; the sense is that this is due to protection by those Manus.
"Saṃkaṃ" means together; "vayaṃ sarve" means we all; "annaṃ havir bhāgādi" means food, sacrificial oblations, portions, and so forth; "adāma" means we ate;
"he" is a separate word [used as an exclamation]. ||51||
Endowed with austerity, sacred knowledge, yoga, and perfect concentration,
the Rishi Hṛṣīkeśa created the Ṛṣis and his desired offspring.
Madhva: Even when the name of Hari is employed elsewhere, it is then understood as being internal to Hari, and not otherwise.

"And due to His sovereignty, even the inferiority of the Supreme is attributed [to Him], just as victory and defeat belong to a king even though he remains [stationary] among his own people. Thus it is said in the *Pādma*.
Therefore, Hṛṣīkeśa is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of Brahmā. (52)

Śrīdhara: Having described the creation of the body, he speaks of the creation of the sages (ṛṣis) with the words "by austerity" and so forth. Vidyā refers to meditative worship (upāsanā). Yoga here refers to posture and the like. Susamādhi is a state of absorption endowed with dispassion, lordly powers, and so on; he was joined with that.
Being Hṛṣīkeśa—one who has his senses under his own control—he, as Brahmā the Ṛṣi, created the Ṛṣis, the progeny.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Then he describes the human creation of Brahmā, who is endowed with *vidyā* (knowledge): "By austerity...
*Vidyā* is worship (*upāsanā*), *yoga* is the eight-limbed [path], *susamādhi* (perfect concentration), knowledge, dispassion (*vairāgya*), and *hṛṣīkeśa* (the Lord of the senses).
Having his senses under his own control, [he approached] the sages, Sanaka and the others. ||52||
And to each of them individually, the Unborn One gave a portion of his own body,
which was endowed with the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), yoga, austerity (*tapas*), knowledge, and detachment.

Śrīdhara: To the question, "What is that body of which he gave a portion? he says: "That which... That [body] in which concentration (samādhi), yoga, supernatural power (ṛddhi), sovereignty (aiśvarya), austerity (tapas), knowledge (vidyā), and dispassion (virakti) are found. ||53||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha asks: "What is that body from which he granted a portion? To this he replies: "Samādhi, knowledge, yoga, supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) consisting of the sovereignty of the *aṇimā* and other qualities, austerity (*tapas*), learning (*vidyā*), and dispassion (*virakti*) are found [in that body]."
In that [chapter]; immediately following this, the origin of Rudra and thereafter the creation of Marīci and others are to be known from the twelfth chapter. ||53||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, appropriately joined to the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus ends the third book in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā, which is the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
The twentieth chapter, titled "The Creation of the World," from the Dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa.
The Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. Now begins the third section of the third book of the Bhāgavata: The Discourse of Kapila.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter:
The Dialogue between Manu and Kardama within the conversation between Vidura and Maitreya.
Vidura said:
O Blessed One, let it be told where the highly esteemed portion of Svāyambhuva Manu was, wherein progeny were propagated through sexual union.
Śrīdhara:
In the twenty-first [chapter], it is described how Viṣṇu, pleased by his asceticism and learning,
arranged the marriage of Kardama with the daughter of Manu.
They prospered; they have prospered. ||1||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
In the twenty-first [chapter], Hari, pleased by his asceticism, was praised by Kardama.
Manu spoke regarding the arrangement of the marriage, and he arrived there.
They prospered; they have prospered. ||1||
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were indeed the two sons of Svāyambhuva;
they protected the earth, consisting of seven continents, according to righteousness.
Śrīdhara: The connection with the third verse is as follows: "Tell me how they both protected—how they cherished and guarded—the Dharma and the earth. ||2||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The connection with the third [verse] is as follows: "Tell me how they two protected [the world] without transgressing their duties (*dharma*). (2)
O Brahmin, his daughter, renowned as Devahūti,
was indeed declared by you to be the wife of the Prajāpati Kardama, O sinless one.
Śrīdhara: [This refers] to that Manu. ||3||
The sequence of composition: in some places, the reading is "Devahūti. ||3||
Viśvanātha: "Devahūtī" means Devahūti. ||3||
When she was thus united with him according to the characteristics of yoga, how many times did that great yogi emit his seed? Tell this to me, for I am eager to hear it.
Śrīdhara: [The word] "yuktāyām" means endowed with the characteristics of yoga, such as the restraints (yamas) and so forth. "How many kinds of virility did he create?
means how many sons did he procreate? ||4||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By means of the characteristics of yoga, such as the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), how many kinds of vigor did he create? The meaning is: how many offspring did he procreate? ||4||
O Brahman, tell me how the illustrious Ruci, or Dakṣa the son of Brahmā,
created living beings after obtaining his wife, the daughter of Manu.
Śrīdhara: The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that [the Lord] told how, having obtained Mānavī—the daughter of Manu—and Ākūti and Prasūti as his wives, he created all beings. ||5||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [He married] Mānavī, the daughter of Manu, as well as Ākūti and Prasūti. ||5||
Maitreya said:
Commanded by Brahmā to "create progeny," the venerable Kardama performed austerities on the Sarasvatī for ten thousand years.

Śrīdhara: "Ten thousand years" means ten thousand years; this is the intended sequence. Regarding the word *prajā* (offspring): if it were "ten thousand of ten years," then, since a relationship must depend on two relata, the form "of thousands" (*sahasrāṇām*) and so forth would also have been used; such is the sense.
The plural form for "thousands" is an archaic Vedic usage.
Viśvanātha: "Equal years" means ten thousand years. ||6||
Then, through the practice of yoga joined with meditative concentration,
Kardama approached Hari with devotion— the bestower of boons upon those who have sought refuge.

Śrīdhara: Then, during that austerity, he practiced—that is, he performed—worship by means of *kriyā-yoga*, the method of ritual service. He approached the Lord who grants boons to those who have taken refuge [in Him]. ||7||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Then," meaning after performing penance, yet even with that much penance, having failed to obtain a vision [of the deity]; "samādhi" is one-pointedness of mind, [attained] through *kriyāyoga*, that is, by way of ritual worship.
To the one who grants boons to those devotees who have approached him for refuge. ||7||
O Kshattri, when the Krita Yuga had begun, the lotus-eyed Blessed One, being pleased,
revealed himself to him, assuming a form that embodied the Word-Brahman.
Madhva: Brahman is the object of the word. 8.
Śrīdhara: Assuming a body composed of that Brahman which is knowable solely through sound (śabda), he revealed himself to him. ||8||
The sequential composition (*kramasaṃdarbha*): "For so long" (*tāvat*) means for as much time as it took until he had correctly attained [it].
Bearing—that is, manifesting—the nature of that Supreme Brahman which is to be realized through the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*). ||8||

Viśvanātha: By the word "tāvat" (meanwhile), it is indicated that as long as the worship is being performed, there is no delay in obtaining his grace. Śrī Svāmīcaraṇa explains: "Assuming a body consisting of that Brahman which is verbal—that is, knowable solely through words. This means assuming a form composed of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
Manifesting his devotion through offerings of fragrant paste, garlands, food, and other services, he addressed him as "Pūṣan"; or else,
[he beheld] that Viraja, who shone like the sun, wearing a garland of white lotuses and blue water-lilies,
with a face like a lotus surrounded by a mass of glossy dark locks, and clad in stainless garments.
Śrīdhara: Kardama, seeing Him situated upon his own head, prostrated himself on the ground;
he praised Him with words—this is the connection for the following four verses. *Padma* and *utpala* refer to the blossoming of day and night respectively.
He who possesses a garland (*srak*) of white lotuses (*padma*) and blue water-lilies (*utpala*). His locks of hair (*alaka*) are glossy and dark blue.
The multitude of them [rests] upon whose lotus-like face. ||9||
The sequence of composition: "sa tam" and so forth is a group of four [words]. He is one whose lotus-face possesses a mass of locks that are both glossy and dark blue. ||10||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
[He is] crowned, adorned with earrings, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
playing with a white lotus, his glance is a smile that touches the mind.
Śrīdhara: He whose plaything is the white lotus; him whose glance and smile touch the mind—that is, produce joy within the heart. (10)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Having stated that he holds the conch, discus, and mace, he says "white" (*śveta*) to indicate that in his fourth hand, in the place where the lotus would normally be, he holds a white water-lily (*utpala*) for the sake of play.
Having seen him stationed in the sky— with his lotus-feet placed upon the shoulders of Garuḍa, his smile and gaze producing joy in the mind of the beholder,
the Goddess Śrī resting upon his chest, and the Kaustubha gem upon his neck— [he was filled with devotion].
Śrīdhara: He whose chest bears Śrī; he who has the Kaustubha gem upon his neck. ||11||
The sequential arrangement: "He was placed" (vinyasta). By this, Garuḍa’s status as merely the son of Vinatā is set aside, because at that time there was no birth of Vinatā. ||11||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
With joy arisen and his desire attained, he fell upon the ground with his head;
then, his soul moved by natural affection, he praised [the Lord] with words while joining his palms in reverence.
Śrīdhara: He whose self (ātman)—that is, his mind—is of such a nature that its very essence is love, a quality established by itself; [he says]:
"Fie upon any other suitor for a bride than you, who are supreme bliss!"
Nevertheless, please show favor to me, who am wretched, by granting a boon.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He whose very nature is love, a quality established by itself. ||12||
The sage said:
"Ah! By the sight of you today, the perfection of our eyes has been attained for the entire multitude of living beings."
That vision which the virtuous praise through many births, and which yogins of perfected yoga aspire to attain.

Śrīdhara: "Batā" expresses joy. O Praiseworthy One! By the sight of you, the treasury of all beings, we have today attained the fulfillment and fruitfulness of our eyes; that is, we have enjoyed their perfection. He establishes that the sight of you alone bears great fruit: for you, whose sight is [sought] higher and higher by the virtuous...
Even those by whom yoga has been firmly established and grown through births that have reached the highest excellence. ||13||
The sequence of composition: In the commentary, he briefly states the meaning of the group of verses by Kardama, beginning with "You" and "Grant your grace.
The meaning of "grant your grace" is that, having granted a boon for the sake of destroying the fault of wretchedness (*kārpaṇya*), he should thereafter bestow his favor;
this is because [Kardama] has been described as one whose very nature is love. By the phrase "the boat for the ocean of worldly existence,"...
It is indicated that toward such a benefactor of the worlds, affection alone is appropriate. ||13||
Viśvanātha says: "Oh, what the height of my good fortune and the Lord’s compassion!
That I have obtained a vision [of You] so very soon," he says with the words "juṣṭam" (graced). "Batā" expresses wonder.
By Your vision, the perfection of our eyes has been achieved; my two eyes have this very day become truly perfected.
The sense is: "Now that it has become fruitful, let it be granted that even before this, though [the eyes] were accomplished, they were indeed not-eyes.
Of what sort are you? The meaning is: of one who is the very lowest among all sentient beings (*akhila-sattva*).
"Of a mass" means of one whose nature is a mass. "This is not fitting, and I have performed the practice"—this is the thought.

He said: "That which... O Worshipful One! Even those by whom yoga has been mastered through many births that are progressively superior to one another still merely aspire to it; they do not, however, attain it. ||13||
Those of dull intellect who, through illusion, worship Your lotus feet— the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence— for the sake of a mere fragment of desire, [are lost].
Even those desires that exist in hell, the Lord of the Zodiac grants them.

Śrīdhara, censuring those whose devotion is motivated by desire, says: "Those who... O Lord! Those whose intellects have been destroyed by Your māyā and who [seek] even a mere fraction of those desires that exist even in hell—they alone worship You;
yet You grant them even those very desires. ||14||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Alas, alas! That people worship you—who are thus an ocean of compassion—with selfish desire; oh, what ignorance on the part of the world! Thus he says: "Those whose intellects are destroyed by your *māyā*..."
They are indeed such, and none other; they worship only for the sake of a fragment of desire, to obtain a mere fragment of desire.

But you heap upon them many desires, even those they did not desire. Otherwise, being unacquainted with the bliss of devotion, they would not have delayed even for a moment in abandoning their devotion to you.
The intention is this: you give with the hope that, provided they do not abandon devotion, even they will eventually become free from desire;
however, your primary aim is not merely the act of giving itself. For those desires—consisting of wife, sons, family, power, and so forth—might even exist in hell, or even in a hellish womb.

However, since it is a rule that heaven and hell are produced by karma, whereas the enjoyments granted by you— even those of such a nature— lack the quality of being produced by karma and thus lack the power to bind, they are not [heaven or hell] in reality.
It should be understood that even the designation of the words "heaven" and "hell" is used in that way because they are similar to them.
Likewise, desiring to marry a wife of similar character— a cow for the household—
I approached the root that is the root of all things.
One of evil intent [is far] from the wish-fulfilling tree of the Lord.
Śrīdhara: He says "so it is" (tathā), meaning: "I too am just like those whom I censure for having desires.

Desiring to marry—that is, to wed—a wife who is like a cow yielding the three aims of life (trivarga) within the household—the stage of the householder—he [seeks] you, the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma).

I have approached the root, the foot; I have come to it. Should not something else be worshipped for the sake of desire and other goals? No, because this alone is the root of every human purpose (puruṣārtha). ||15||

The sequential arrangement [of the verses] is as follows: "It is the root of all"—meaning, "For men, the worship of His feet is the root of heaven and liberation, of all prosperities on this earth of nectar, and of all supernatural powers. (15)

Viśvanātha: He says "likewise" (tathā) to show that he who censures those with desires is himself the foremost among those with desires. Desiring to marry a wife—who, like a cow, milks the three aims of life (trivarga)—in the state of a householder (gṛhamedha), that is, the stage of the householder; by the word "cow," his own lack of intelligence is indicated, while her status as a "bull" (vṛṣatva) is implied.

It has been said. Furthermore, even among those possessed of desire, I am one of evil intent (*durāśaya*); the meaning is that I am devoid of wisdom because of my wicked purpose, since I have approached the foot—the root—of you, the wish-fulfilling tree (*kāmadugha*), solely desiring to marry [you]. That which has all things without exception as its root...
This is because of the statement beginning with "for men [it leads] to heaven and liberation," and so forth. ||15||
O Lord, by the word of Prajāpati and by the string of his lute,
this world is indeed bound and struck by desire;
and I, following the world, carry it along.
And this offering is for you, the white-eyed one who does not blink.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "In that case, why do you not worship Him solely for the sake of liberation? [Reply: Because of a lack of qualification. To this he says: "O Sovereign! This world, struck by desire, is bound like a beast by the tether of Your word, You who are the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati). And I too, O Śukla—O embodiment of pure Dharma!"
It is said that you follow the ways of the world; therefore, I bring an offering to you and obey your command, which consists of ritual action.

"To the one with unblinking eyes, the soul of time"—the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is: "For that purpose, I desire a wife. Not only do I bring an offering following the ways of the world, but furthermore—
"It is said that [this is] for the sake of repaying the three debts. (16)
The sequential arrangement: If that is so, why do you worship with mere affection alone? To this he says: "Prajā" (the progeny).

The sense is that even Prajāpati—who is subject to you, as stated in the Śrī Gītā (3.10) and elsewhere—speaks in such a manner only in accordance with your command. Now, one might object: "But [he is] struck by desire and bound..."
Let it be granted that you are not overcome by desire; how then do you not transgress that [dharma], like Nārada and others?
To this he replies: "Following the ways of the world. The meaning is: desiring to find a firm footing in those worlds.
The implication is that the abandonment of such social standing is difficult to achieve. Therefore, [he acts] for the sake of the Unblinking One (Animiṣa), because He is the essence of Time.
The sense is: "I bring and offer this oblation and gift of worship to you, the Impeller of all;
may such evil tendencies be turned back even when an evil fruit has been obtained in the future. This is the thought.
Although he, by virtue of his stainless nature, [remains] through mere restraint from the world of the heavy...

One accepts even such personal suffering, yet not out of a desire for status and the like; nevertheless, it should be understood that Viśvanātha, the crest-jewel of the most wonderful beings, perceives those very things within himself as defects.
[Objection: If such discernment exists, then why is he not entirely free from desire?
To the question "Do you worship [him]? he says: "By your word, 'Create offspring,' O Prajāpati Brahmā, the world consisting of Marīci and others was stretched out.
Having created the creatures along with sacrifice, Prajāpati spoke in the beginning."
And because of the statement in the Gītā: "By this you shall procreate; let this be the cow of plenty for your desired objects" (Gītā 3.10), even he speaks only in accordance with your command;
thus, there is no fault in him either—this is the resonance of your feet.

[Objection: Granted that the world may be bound by being overcome by desire; but you, being yourself free from desire, why do you not transcend it like Sanaka and others? To this he replies: "And I am one who follows the world, with a mind that conforms to it; the meaning is that I am not capable of becoming like Nārada and others."

Therefore, bound by the cord like a bull, I carry the burden; I follow your command consisting of ritual action (*karma*), and for that purpose I desire one wife—this is the meaning. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the implication is: "I also practice devotion to you for the sake of attaining you in the future. O Śukla! [This is] for the sake of the Unblinking One (*Animiṣa*).
The meaning is: "in order to propitiate you, who are Time itself. ||16||
Having abandoned the worlds and the creatures who follow after them, they have taken refuge in the parasol of your feet;
for one another, they drink the nectar of the discourse on your virtues.
Those whose bodily functions were discharged as nectar.

Śrīdhara: By the words "to the one who does not blink" (*animiṣāya*), it is stated that I perform this action out of fear of you, whose nature is time. With the following two verses, he states that such fear does not exist for your devotees. [He refers to] those worlds overcome by desire and the animals that follow them; even though they possess discernment, they are once again rendered inert by ritual action (*karma*).
Having abandoned and disregarded those like me, he speaks of those who have taken refuge in the parasol in the form of your feet:

the discourse on your qualities is itself the *sīdhu* wine, because it causes one to forget the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*); it is nectar (*pīyūṣa*) because it is pleasing to the taste. By that [wine], they are nourished and delighted.
The bodily conditions such as hunger, thirst, and so forth—by which [these are characterized]; the connection with "of these" is with what follows. ||17||

The sequential arrangement: For pure devotees, even attachment to desires and the like—which is caused by the contraction of worldly perception—is destroyed; he says the same thing in this regard with the words, "and the worlds" (verse 17).

Viśvanātha: But surely the world consists of fathers and the like who follow their commands, and sons, brothers, and others who are seen to be famous and happy both according to worldly custom and according to *dharma*.
Why do you censure them because they possess desires? [This applies] to those devoted ones free from desire who cause suffering to their fathers and others.
"What happiness or what fame belongs to those who possess nothing, such that you revile them?

To this he replies with two verses, beginning with "the worlds. By saying "animals," the sense is that because they are like animals, there is no fault in their renunciation. Alternatively, it refers to those "worlds" who are experts in the Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and other scriptures, as well as those who follow them.

Both of these groups—those who trust in the instructional words [of the teachers] while being ignorant of the scriptures, and those who lack devotion—are equally like animals, because they are devoid of devotion. The sense is that those who have resorted to the sandals themselves as a parasol are "without parasols" (nirātapatra), whereas the animals, by contrast, are truly ablaze. Furthermore, their happiness is inferior...

He said: "The discourse on your virtues is indeed *sīdhu* (liquor) because it causes one to forget the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), and it is *pīyūṣa* (nectar) because it removes death and is exceedingly sweet. By that very drinking of it, those who have cast off the bodily conditions such as childhood and youth, or hunger and thirst, become [liberated]."
The connection is with the action. ||17||
Their lifespan is not subject to the wandering of the decay of the senses;
it consists of thirteen spokes, three hundred and sixty joints,
six rims, infinite coverings, and three naves.
The world, having been torn away by the fierce current, runs on.
*Madhvaḥ*: [He is] one whose covering is infinite and whose limbs are infinite; this is the third excellence, according to the *Mahāvyākaraṇa*.
And because of such statements as "He was born from Mithilā through churning" (*mathanāt*), and so forth. ||18||

Śrīdhara: Your three-naved wheel of time (*kālacakra*), though it runs about cutting away and dragging along the world, does not run about cutting away the lifespan of these devotees of yours. Of what nature is it? It is the rotation (*bhrami*)—that is, the revolving—in the form of the imperishable (*akṣa*), the undecaying Brahman. Thus, "revolving" (*bhramat*).
Because it has the nature of revolving excessively where it ought to be spoken [of as "revolving"], the term *bhrami* (revolution) is used as a metaphorical designation for non-difference.

It is that whose spokes (*arāḥ*) are thirteen months, including the intercalary month; whose joints (*parvāṇi*) are three hundred and sixty days and nights—the elision of the case-ending in the word *śata* is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*); and whose rims (*nemayaḥ*) are the six seasons.
It is that which possesses infinite petals—moments, instants, and so forth—as well as streams in the form of leaves;

it has the three four-month periods as its naves, serving as its supporting rings; and it has a formidable current of intense velocity. By these very qualifiers, the wheel whose nature is the year is described.
It should be observed. ||18||

Regarding the sequence of the text: in the commentary, the word *triguṇā* appears as an addition here, since the term *trinābhi* must be etymologically derived in a different manner; however, in an authentic manuscript, the reading is indeed *trinābhi*. (18)

Viśvanātha: Only they conquer Time, not others; thus he says, "Not them" (*na te*). The construction is as follows: even though that three-naved wheel of time (*kālacakra*) runs along, having cut off and withdrawn the world, it does not run along cutting off the lifespan of these devotees of Yours. Of what nature [is that wheel]? The undecaying Brahman.

In that form consisting of syllables, there is a "whirl" (*bhrami*). Although one should say "whirling" (*bhramat*), the term "whirl" (*bhrami*) is used as a non-differentiated designation by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), because of its nature of excessive whirling. That [wheel] has thirteen months—counted by means of the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*)—as its spokes (*ara*). The absence of the case-ending (*aluk*) in the word "hundred" (*śata*) is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). It has the six seasons as its rims (*nemi*).
It is that which possesses infinite petals—moments, instants, and so forth—as well as streams in the form of leaves;
it has the three four-month periods as its supporting hubs and rings; and it has a formidable current with intense velocity. By these very adjectives, the wheel consisting of the year is described.
It should be observed. ||18||
Being one alone, out of a desire to create the world, you project through your own inherent power of yoga-māyā a second [form] within yourself;
thus you create this universe, protect it, and will again swallow it up.
Just as a spider, O Blessed One, [acts] by means of its own powers.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But why do you beg me, who am without attributes and indifferent? Nevertheless, since you alone are the agent of the creation and so forth of the universe through *māyā*, you yourself are the one to be entreated.
