To this he says: "Although You Yourself are indeed One, by means of the *yogamāyā* presiding over Your own self—which serves as the cause—those powers have been assumed."
The [powers] beginning with *sattva*—by means of those. "This" refers to the universe. The illustration regarding the lack of dependence on any means external to itself is: "just as," etc. ||19||

The sequential composition: With the intention that even those possessed of desire must pray to You alone, the Self of all, he says, "One. By means of the Yoga-māyā presided over by Himself for the purpose of creation, and by His own powers presided over by that [māyā], He is everywhere non-dual.
The change of case endings occurs for the sake of the sense; "bhavān" is a reading found in some places. ||19||

Viśvanātha: Well then, you praise only those who are free from desire as blessed, yet you yourself are unable to become free from desire. In that case, why do you not accomplish your own desire through another deity who grants results more swiftly? For in this world, there is no one other than you [who can grant such results].

"I do not see [anything else]," he says; for although he is himself alone, there is no second [entity] other than his own will, [and thus he acts] with a desire to create that is non-dual. Alternatively, the meaning is that your desire to create is indeed the very desire of Brahmā and others to create, and is not dependent upon anything else. This is "attained" (adhigata) within the self (ātmani), having reached it through the application of vision (īkṣaṇa).

By means of that *māyā* which possesses yoga, you perform the creation and so forth of the universe; or rather, by means of *yogamāyā*—the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) presiding over the self—as the cause, those powers such as *sattva* and the rest which have been assumed, by them this entire world [is manifested]. This serves as an illustration of its independence from external instruments distinct from itself; therefore, it is different from that.
The sense is: since there is no other deity, even though I am possessed of desire, you alone are to be served by me. ||19||
O Lord of the Unmanifest, this subtle element of the beings which You manifest for us through Your Māyā is surely not Your desired state;
yet even when You grant grace, You do so indeed by means of Your Māyā.
The Blessed One was observed by Lakṣmaṇa.

Śrīdhara: Although, because of its illusory nature (*māyikatva*), You do not wish to grant the pleasure of sense objects to Your devotees, nevertheless, in accordance with our own intention, please bring that about; thus he says: "Not this" (*naitat*).
O Lord (*adhīśa*)! To us who worship You, the state consisting of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣmarūpa*)—namely, the pleasure of sense objects such as sound and so forth—[is not desired].

"You expand" means you spread out through *māyā*. Even if this [expansion] of yours is not desired by You, may it nevertheless serve for our grace; the meaning is that it should lead to liberation immediately after the three debts have been discharged.
"When"—that is, because of which—[it occurs], through the *tulasī* which shines as if limited by *māyā*.
"You are endowed [with merit] and yet appear dejected; the meaning is that the sight of you in such a state bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||20||
The sequence of the argument: Therefore, because I am possessed of desire, one like me is indeed turned away from You;

yet You are supremely compassionate even toward that [state]. Thus he says: "This is not so. That object consisting of sound and the rest which You bestow upon us—this would not be Your own desire. How then do I bestow it?

To this he replies: "By means of *māyā*, that is, by a mere pretext, through his affectionate elder brother, for the sake of increasing his own affection for him"—the meaning is that, like giving a piece of sugar-candy to a younger brother, it was done under that guise solely to increase affection for himself; therefore, that gift was given.
But it may be for the sake of bestowing grace.

In this regard, the indicative mark is as follows: whenever you were seen by means of your illusory power (*māyā*) acting as the cause through compassion at the time of granting a boon, even then, there was the supremely blissful Tulasi, shining forth within the vision of the devotees.
"He is joined," [meaning] "the Blessed One. Regarding the reading *tanuvā* here, the meaning is "with such a tulasī-leaf as a body";
the intention is that even by means of indirectness (*pārōkṣyeṇa*), the granting of a boon may indeed occur. ||20||

Viśvanātha: If this is so, then [the sage] spoke with prostration to the Blessed One, who was granting him a boon, saying, "By my grace, may your wife, children, enjoyments, and sovereignty become most excellent," with the two verses beginning with "Not this" (naitat). O Lord! This state—that object desired by me—is yours.

The sense is this: it is understood from your statement that "the best of physicians does not give what is desired even to a sick person who craves unwholesome food," that one who acts solely for the benefit of his own devotees does not grant what is wished for.
How, then, do you give? To this he says: because [you grant] to us the subtle element of being (*bhūtasūkṣma*).
You manifest—that is, you grant—the pleasure of sense objects, such as sound and the rest, which are to be enjoyed by the senses; indeed, that is done through *māyā* alone, and not without *māyā*.

The meaning is: "This devotee is ignorant; otherwise he would become despondent," and thus [you grant it] solely out of consideration for me. This pleasure of sense objects, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), resides within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Thus, the meaning of that verbal root is: "you expand that very [power] by means of granting a boon.
Now, if this is so, does it mean you do not give at all? To that he says: "Let this be given for the sake of grace; however, even for the sake of grace, alas! alas! let it be given by me alone."

The meaning is: "This devotee has been cast into blind darkness by the excellence of sensual pleasures; therefore, let me uplift him"—this is for the sake of obtaining Your grace in the future as well.
The indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this is that at the time of granting the boon, You were now specifically observed (*vilakṣita*).
If it is asked, "Was He seen?", then [the answer is] yes;

for it is said that He was seen with a glance characterized by a smile and a touch of the mind through His grace. Even there, He was seen with a side-glance of grace illuminated by a smile, and moreover, with the Tulasī, which bestows supreme bliss when offered by devotees during service.

"Upalakṣitā cit" (consciousness characterized by) is from the *Amara-kośa*. To be "endowed with that body which consists of consciousness" is the very sign that the body is non-deceptive (*amāyika*), for it is precisely what must be attended to by devotees.
The granting of the vision of such a non-deceptive body is itself the sign of [divine] compassion. The term "Bhagavān" also applies here.
The recitation. ||20||
I bow repeatedly to You, whose feet are worthy of adoration, who by Your own creative power sustain the system of the worlds, and for whom all activity has ceased through direct realization.
A lotus that showers desires even more abundantly than it is small.

Śrīdhara: I bow to You, who bestow both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). The reason for Your granting of liberation is that in You, the purpose of ritual action—the experience of the fruits of karma—has ceased through realization (*anubhūti*) or knowledge. The reason for Your granting of enjoyment is that by means of Your own *māyā*, You cause the machinery of the world (*lokatantra*), the instrument of the universe, to revolve. Therefore...

He whose lotus-feet are to be bowed to by both those with desires and those free from desires; and among them, he who showers desires upon that person who possesses few desires and who practices devotion—him [I praise]. (21)

The sequence of the composition: The reason why that [Lord] is the giver of supreme delight is that, through His own experience, He has rendered the enjoyment of the fruits of karma powerless for His devotees; whereas for others, it remains in its natural form, such as "one's own" and so forth.
Therefore, the lotus feet of the Great Ones are by their very nature worthy of salutation, while [the ego] is exceedingly insignificant.
"Shining forth by means of raining down desires. ||21||

Viśvanātha: But this is not impossible for you; thus he says: "When, through your grace, you grant that experience of your own sweetness from which all purposeful activity and the enjoyment of the fruits of action have ceased—that very moment the desire for enjoyment will vanish of its own accord."

The meaning is as follows: He is one by whom the "tantra"—the system of worldly beings such as gods, animals, and so forth, which consists of the connection between actions and their fruits, namely pleasure and pain—is set in motion or produced through his own *māyā*, that is, by the impulsion of his own power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*).
The sense is that as long as you impel ignorance (*avidyā*), there will necessarily arise the desire for enjoyment (*bhoga*).
"Therefore, desiring now to increase creation, you make us filled with desire;

thus, even though we possess discernment, we are unable to abandon desires. Thus he spoke to Him: "You rain down desires even upon a person like me, who is so insignificant and utterly degraded" (21).
The sage said:
Thus addressed with sincere praise, the lotus-navelled Lord spoke to him with the nectar of his words.
Shining above the wings of Garuḍa,
with eyebrows dancing as he gazes with a smile of love.
Śrīdhara: With nectar that brings happiness; whose brow is dancing with His eyes, which are filled with love and smiles. ||22||
The sequential composition: that smile preceded by love, and that gaze preceded by it;
he whose eyebrows playfully dance to manifest His benevolence toward Garuḍa and others—He is Viśvanātha. "Avyalīkam" means without guile, sincere. ||22||
The Blessed One said:
"Having known your intention long ago,
I have already prepared that for which you yourself have worshipped me with self-restraints."
Śrīdhara: The caitya is the state of being within the heart; it was joined together—that is, constructed—by me.
That very thing for which I have been worshipped is this. ||23||
The sequence of composition: Even though he followed worldly convention in constructing the shrine (*caitya*), knowing that your inner heart was solely intent on pleasing me, he acted appropriately;
for in the end, it was as if he himself had become my son. Therefore, even though he possessed desire, [it was not a fault].
The meaning is that because of your single-minded devotion to pleasing Me, I have been properly worshipped by you alone, and not even by others who are free from desire. ||23||

Viśvanātha: "Caittyam" means the intention of the mind (*citta*). The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the base itself after words ending in *diś* and so forth (Pāṇini 4.3.54). "By me" means by me; it was composed (*samayoji*) or assembled (*saṅghaṭitam*). "By you alone, and no other. ||23||
O Overseer of Creatures, my honoring you could never truly be in vain;
for those whose souls are fully absorbed in me, it is all the more so when directed toward one such as you.

Śrīdhara: For those by whom the self—the mind—is "saṅgṛbhita," meaning grasped, held, and made one-pointed upon Me, whatever honor is due to Me would not be entirely in vain or fruitless, especially when offered to those such as you. Regarding that, the reason is given by way of *kaimutya* (a fortiori): "na vā" (it certainly would not be so). It bestows truth.

According to the principle expressed in "Whatever is requested of men when they have requested" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.19.27), my mere acceptance of worship should not be in vain—that is, yielding only a trivial result—but rather it should also yield the supreme goal for them;
this is especially true in the case of those like you among those who have fixed their souls upon Me. This is the meaning.
Viśvanātha: Nor does my worship perish merely after granting a desired object; rather, it bestows even my own state.
Thus he says, "Be comforted," according to the principle expressed in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 5.19.27: "When entreated by men, he truly grants what is requested.
By this logic, the mere honoring of me is not in vain.
It would not yield a fruitless result; rather, in the end, it would surely grant my own state.

Moreover, among those devotees who have gathered their selves in me and fixed their minds upon me, it is especially so for those like you—this is the meaning. [The form] *bhaktānām* is derived from *bhaj*, where the substitution of *bha* occurs according to the rule *hṛgṛahor bhaś chandasī*; the short vowel [in *bhaktānām*] follows the same rule.
The Vedic [tradition]. ||24||
The son of Prajāpati, the sovereign Manu, renowned for his auspiciousness,
residing in Brahmāvarta, rules over the earth bounded by the seven oceans.
Śrīdhara: [The term] *vikhyātam* means auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), characterized by prosperity (*abhyudaya*) such as right conduct (*sadācāra*) and so forth;

[it refers to] the sequence of its composition. Regarding the phrase "the seven oceans" (*saptārṇavām*): this is a metaphorical treatment of what is yet to be as if it were already accomplished, because those [oceans] will result from the ruts of Priyavrata’s chariot. ||25||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
And here, O Brahmin, that royal sage, skilled in dharma, together with his queen Śatarūpā, will come on the day after tomorrow desiring to see you.
Śrīdhara: O Brahmin! Together with the queen. ||26||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: O Brahmin! ||26||
O Lord, he will give his own daughter— dark-eyed, endowed with youth, character, and virtue—
who is seeking a husband, to you, her worthy match.
Śrīdhara: O Lord! O You who are endowed with the disposition of devotion to my worship! ||27||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [To one] who is suitable by virtue of age, character, and so forth. ||27||
Your heart has been concentrated for all these years;
therefore, O Brahmin, that royal bride will soon attend to you according to her desire.
Śrīdhara: *Yatra* means in whichever wife; *samāhitam* means established through intentional focus;
*nṛpavadhū* means a princess. ||28||

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] is as follows: throughout these years, that concentrated heart of yours which has been offered to me—wherever that exists, in her alone does there exist a heart worthy of being a partner in dharma (sadharmacāriṇī), equal to your own heart; this is the meaning. And it will be stated by the venerable Manu:
"In every way, she is worthy of you" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.22.11). ||28||
Viśvanātha: In whom—on whom—your heart is fixed and attached; [she is] a princess, a daughter of a king. ||28||
That vigor which is inherent in you shall produce offspring ninefold;
upon your own vigor, the sages shall directly bestow their own selves.

Śrīdhara: She who shall give birth to that virility held and maintained within herself will enjoy it—that is, [the virility] produced from that virility in the daughters. They will easily bestow sons upon themselves [their husbands]. 29.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Their semen (*vīrya*) has been borne—that is, held—within themselves in nine ways, meaning in the form of nine offspring. They will directly deposit their own semen into the daughters born of that semen.
And you, having correctly carried out my command as my most devoted servant,
and having dedicated all your actions and purposes to me as a sacred ford, shall attain me.
Śrīdhara: *Nideśam* means an order or command. *Uśattamaḥ* means one of pure being (*śuddhasattva*). *Tīrtha* means a worthy recipient;
by this, the act of giving is indicated. The meaning is: "one who has surrendered the fruits of all actions unto me. (30)

The sequence of composition: Since I am a worthy recipient (*pātra*), I am a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); therefore, whatever is offered into me is also called a "ford" with the intention of expressing the excellence of its inclusion within me—this is the underlying meaning. ||30||

Viśvanātha: Regarding that which was requested in the words "for the sake of your grace," he says in two verses beginning with "And you... Here, "tīrtha" means a worthy recipient; by this, the act of giving is indicated. The meaning is: "I am one to whom the fruits of all actions have been surrendered. (30)
Having shown compassion toward living beings and having granted them fearlessness, you, being self-possessed,
shall behold the Self together with the world within Me, and Me also within the Self.
Śrīdhara: By practicing compassion through the life of a householder and granting fearlessness through renunciation, you shall behold yourself and the entire world merged as one within Me. 31.

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary]: "In me, the supreme refuge, you shall see the Self; and in the Self, which is its substrate, you shall likewise see Me along with that world, and indeed the world itself"—this is the meaning. ||31||

Viśvanātha: By showing compassion toward living beings through the giving of food, clothing, and so forth in the state of a householder; and specifically by granting fearlessness through the instruction in devotion—this is the meaning. That which you now know through the vision of the scriptures—that the entire world, together with the self, exists within me, the Supreme Lord, who is the foundational reality—that...

In that way, you will then see Me directly; first, you will see Me as the Original Person (Ādipuruṣa) reclining upon the causal ocean, in the form characterized by a thousand heads and so forth. Then, within the pores of My very skin, you will see infinite millions of cosmic eggs together with their respective selves directly—this is the meaning. Likewise:
You already know Me now as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) dwelling within yourself; however, at that time—
you [will see] some [who perceive] a Person the size of a span (prādeśamātra) dwelling in the space within the heart of their own bodies.

"By means of *dhāraṇā*, they remember me alone— the four-armed Lord of the Milk Ocean, the third person (*puruṣa*) mentioned in the Second Book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa], who holds the lotus, the discus, the conch, and the mace. Thus, it is me whom they directly perceive.
The realized meaning is: "I shall show you every object that is to be seen";
or rather, "O Śrī Yaśodeva, when I have become your son, you will see the world and yourself together with me."

Likewise, as for myself, I am like one of the illustrious gopīs; having drawn him into my heart through the aperture of my eye and closing it, I embrace him with my limbs bristling with joy, like a yogī immersed in bliss. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.8)
"In this manner, as has been stated, you shall see," [he said]. ||31||
Therefore, O great sage, by means of a portion of my own self and through your power,
I shall bring forth the compendium of reality into your field, Devahūtī.
Śrīdhara: "By your power, having descended into Devahūtī"—this is the ellipsis. ||32||
The sequence of the composition: "By that vigor" (vīrya) means by its power; the ellipsis is "having become manifest along with it.
The meaning is: "Upon my manifestation, the power of your austerity will become manifest. And this will be stated by Prajāpati: "The white one, spreading my glory" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.24.4). ||32||
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, he says "Listen to some other news of bliss"—"Together with me," etc.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "I have manifested together with your virya (semen) and your multitude of daughters and offspring. (32)
Maitreya said:
Having thus addressed him, the Blessed One, whose perception is born of direct intuition, departed from the Bindu-saras lake, which is surrounded by the Sarasvatī river.
Śrīdhara: It is "born from the internal senses" (*pratyag-akṣaja*) because it arises—that is, becomes manifest—within the internal senses.
[It is located] from that which is surrounded, or encompassed, by the river Sarasvatī. ||33||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He is so called because he is born—that is, becomes manifest—within the senses that have become turned inward (*pratyagbhūta*). [He is born] from that which is surrounded, or encompassed, by the river Sarasvatī. ||33||
As he gazed on, the path of the perfected ones, praised by the lords of the Siddhas, passed away entirely,
while he listened to the songs of the lords of birds with their wings.
The hymn has been recited; the Sāman has been chanted aloud.

Śrīdhara: He whose path to Vaikuṇṭha—the way of the perfected ones—is praised by all the lords who have attained perfection through austerity, mantras, and so forth; or alternatively, he whose path is praised by all the lords of the perfected and is sought after by the perfected ones (siddhas)—he went [there]. Patrarathendra is Garuḍa; of him...
Hearing the *sāman* raised and manifested by the wings— according to the scripture, "The *bṛhat* and *rathantara* are the two wings"—
and hearing the *stoma* uttered, which is the collection of *ṛc*s that serve as the substratum for the *sāman*—
according to the scripture, "The *stoma* is the self. In the compound reading, the *stoma* uttered is the collection of hymns (*stotrīya*).
"Of which sāman... (34)

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon. *Viśvanātha*: While that Kardama was looking on, he [the Lord] was praised by all the lords of the Siddhas; he whose path is the path of the Siddhas, that is, the path to Vaikuṇṭha.
Garuda, the lord of winged creatures, hears the hymn—the collection of *ṛc* verses—uttered by his wings.

Of what nature is it? It is that which has the character of the *sāman* that has been raised up, i.e., manifested. In the compound reading, it refers to that raised-up *sāman* which possesses a hymn (*stoma*), meaning a collection of *stotrīya* verses, thus uttered.
"The Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are the two wings," according to the Śruti. ||34||
Then, after Śukla had departed, the venerable seer Kardama remained at Bindusaras, waiting for that time.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: Waiting for that time which is said to be "the day after tomorrow. ||35||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. Manu, having mounted a chariot adorned with gold and having placed his daughter upon it, wandered the earth together with his wife.
On that very day, O Sudhanvan, the Blessed One went to the hermitage of the sage Śāntavrata, just as he had commanded.

Śrīdhara: Having mounted that chariot which had golden (śātakaumbha) trappings, and having caused his daughter to ascend it as well, he wandered about in search of suitors. (36) O Sudhanvan Vidura, on that day... (37)
The sequence of composition: "Manu" constitutes a pair [of verses]. 36.
Viśvanātha: The grammatical construction is as follows: "On that day which the Blessed One commanded, while wandering over the earth, he arrived at the sage's hermitage. O Sudhanvan! O Vidura!
[It was] on that day when drops of tears fell from the eyes of the Blessed One.
Completely overcome by compassion, it was intensely directed toward those who had sought refuge.

Śrīdhara: In order to show that he attained supreme bliss merely by entering it, he describes the hermitage with these seven verses beginning with "yasmin... [and ending with] "prapanne kardame" (38).

The sequence of composition: "In which" refers to the group of seven verses. "Upon his having arrived" means as soon as he had arrived; "with [the mind] offered" means with it dedicated solely to him. The meaning is that in that very place, that mass of teardrops became the lake named Bindusaras. ||38||
Viśvanātha describes the hermitage with seven verses beginning with "yasmin": [he entered] into the mud where he had sought refuge. ||38||
That lake, indeed named Bindusaras, is overflowed by the Sarasvatī;
it is meritorious, filled with the auspicious water of immortality, and frequented by hosts of great seers.
Śrīdhara: [That place] in which the water is auspicious, health-giving, and as sweet as nectar. ||39||

The structural arrangement: In the commentary, the phrase "śivam ārogyam" (auspiciousness and health) means that which produces health, just as in the expression "āyur ghṛtam" (clarified butter is life). In some places, it appears as "arogam" (health). ||39||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained [previously].

[It was] endowed with the beauty of forest groves, rich in fruits and flowers of all seasons, and filled with networks of meritorious trees and creepers, and with the warbling of virtuous deer and birds.
Śrīdhara: [It is] endowed with networks—that is, clusters—of meritorious trees and creepers, in which the birds and deer warble auspiciously. ||40||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Enveloped by networks of creepers. (40)
Resounding with flocks of intoxicated birds, possessing the grace of drunken bees, displaying the prideful dance of intoxicated peacocks, and summoning the cries of intoxicated cuckoos.
Śrīdhara: *Ghuṣṭam* means resonant. It is that in which there is the playful sport (*vibhrama*) of intoxicated bees;
in which there is the grand display (*āṭopa*), the flurry of dancing, of peacocks acting as dancers who are themselves intoxicated; and in which intoxicated cuckoos call out to one another. (41)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Ghuṣṭam" means resounded. It is that [place] in which there is the *āṭopa*—the frantic movement of the dance—of intoxicated peacocks who act as dancers; and it is that in which intoxicated cuckoos are calling out to one another.
It was adorned with kadamba, campaka, aśoka, karañja, bakula, and āsana trees, as well as with kunda, mandāra, kuṭaja, and young mango saplings.
Śrīdhara: Adorned with *kadamba* and other trees. ||42||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
[The lake was] filled with the beautiful warbling of *kāraṇḍava* ducks, water-fowls, swans, ospreys, water-hens, cranes, ruddy geese, and *cakora* birds.
Śrīdhara: The birds, who were proponents of the theory of causality, warbled beautifully, as it were. ||43||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Having described the trees there, he speaks of the birds, beginning with "by *kāraṇḍava* ducks," and likewise: "by deer, boars, porcupines, *gavaya* oxen, and elephants."
It was surrounded by ox-tailed monkeys, lions, leopards, mongooses, and cobras.
Śrīdhara: [The forest] is surrounded by deer and other animals. Among them, *kroḍa* is the boar; *śvāvit* is the porcupine;
*marka* is the monkey; its specific variety is the cow-tailed monkey (*gopuccha*); *hari* is the ape or the lion; and *nābhi* is the musk-deer. ||44||
The sequence of composition: "Having entered," etc., consists of three and a half verses. "Not" (nā) means "not at all" (naiva). ||44||

Viśvanātha says to the deer: "It is even so. *Kroḍa* means a boar; *śvāvit* means a porcupine; *marka* means a monkey; *gopuccha* is a specific type of that [monkey]; *hari* means a lion; and *nābhi* means the musk-deer. ||44||
Having entered that best of sacred fords, the first king, together with his son,
beheld the sage seated there, into whom the sacrificial oblations had been offered.
Śrīdhara: [He is] one by whom the sacrificial fire has been offered, making him fit for the life of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*).
Viśvanātha: The connection of the sequence has not been explained.
His body shines with splendor, having long been engaged in fierce asceticism (*tapas*).
The Blessed One was not excessively emaciated, owing to his glances from the corners of his eyes which were moist with compassion.
And by hearing the nectar-drops of the nectar-like utterances of Him;

Śrīdhara [explains]: "By that body which is radiant with a formidable yoga"—the utterance (vyāhṛta) of that Blessed One, His very speech, is itself a digit (kalā) of nectar, like a digit of the moon composed of nectar.
By hearing his nectar, he is not overly emaciated; though lean from asceticism, he is not truly thin.
[The] sequence of composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: By that [asceticism] in which there is a fierce application (*ugrā yukti*) even in the midst of penance (*tapasi*); yet even that is not...
"Extremely slender yet not emaciated"—in this regard, two reasons are stated for that description: "by the corner of her compassionate eye" and "by the hearing of that.
By the latter, namely "by the hearing of the nectar-portion of the moon," its status as the primary nectar-portion is expressed. (46)
Having approached him— who was tall, with eyes like lotus petals, wearing matted hair and bark garments, soiled, and lacking any refinement— he offered him hospitality as was fitting.

Śrīdhara: "Pāṃśum unnatam" means having approached—that is, having gone near—he saw it as soiled; this refers back to the same verb [from the previous verse]. "Arhaṇa" is that by which one is honored, namely a great jewel; just as that appears soiled when it is unrefined (*asaṃskṛta*) and unpurified (*anirṇikta*), so too [is he seen].
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Having approached—that is, having gone near—the tall one, whose body measured eight spans (*vitasti*), he saw him who was soiled; the verb "saw" (*dadarśa*) is the same action as before. That by which one is honored is "honor" (*arhaṇa*).
That great jewel is unconditioned; it is just as if it were seen to be stained. ||47||
Then, as the god among men approached the hermitage and bowed before him,
he received him with hospitality, greeting him with a fitting welcome.
Śrīdhara: Having reached the leaf-hut (uṭaja), he welcomed him who was prostrated before his feet with blessings, and received him with hospitality—that is, with worship—honoring him. ||48||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [He saw him] who had reached the *uṭaja*, the leaf-hut; who was prostrating before his feet;
and who was again grasping his feet, accompanied by a fitting hospitality appropriate for a guest.

He received him with both arms, raised him up, and embraced him. Having done what? Having greeted him by saying, "O King, today you are seen to be the very personification of the divine power that protects the universe," he congratulated the king, who was rejoicing at having directly perceived the splendor consisting of ascetic power (tapas) in embodied form, thinking, "I have achieved my life's purpose."
The meaning is "having been praised in return. ||48||
When the sage had accepted the offerings and was seated, being self-controlled,
the other sage, remembering the command of the Blessed One, spoke with gentle words to please him.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been explained in the *Kramasaṃdarbha*.

Viśvanātha: [He is] one whose feet have been washed, who is seated upon a suitable seat of darbha grass and other materials, by whom the offerings (*arhaṇa*)—namely flowers, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, leaves, fruits, and so forth—have been taken up; and who is restrained, remaining silent.
It remains. ||49||
Surely, O Lord, this walking about of yours is for the protection of the virtuous and the destruction of the wicked,
for you are indeed the protective power of Hari.
Śrīdhara: *caṅkramaṇam* means wandering; *hi* is because. ||50||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: O Lord! "Whose wandering... and so forth; you alone are that very power of Hari for protection. (50)
Salutations to you, the Radiant One, who assume the forms of the sun, moon, fire, Indra, Vāyu, Yama, Dharma,
and Varuṇa within your own abode.

"Madhva states: 'Svāyambhuva Manu, Pṛthu, the two Arjunas, Brahmā, Śeṣa, the lords [of the worlds], Rudra, Indra, the sages, and so forth—all these are permeated by the entrance of Viṣṇu (viṣṇvāveśayuta), but they do not possess the very nature of Viṣṇu (na tu viṣṇusvarūpakāḥ). Thus it is stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya*."
Śrīdhara: He bows to Viṣṇu residing in Manu with the words "He who... [and so on]. "Sthāne" means at the time for those respective duties; "śuklāya" means to Viṣṇu. ||51||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: You truly and perfectly assume the forms of the sun and the others in their respective places;
therein, by your majesty you are the sun, by your fame you are the moon, and by your invincibility you are fire.

Indra by his sovereignty; Vāyu by his capacity to enter everywhere; and Pracetas by his subduing of the wicked. Therefore, salutations to you, the white one (Śukla), my chosen deity, who have once again come to my hut in your form! 51.
When he, having mounted his victorious chariot inlaid with clusters of gems,
terrified the wicked with his rattling, fierce bow.
Trembling the circle of the earth, trampled by the feet of your own army,
you wander about leading a vast host like the sun.
At that very time, O King, all the bridges established by the Blessed One— the foundations of the social classes and stages of life— would surely be destroyed by bandits.

Śrīdhara: The meaning of the five verses beginning with "na yadā" is as follows: although it is possible that you have come even by chance while wandering everywhere for the sake of protecting the Dharma, nevertheless, if there is some special purpose, let it be told. [The word] *jaitram* means victory-bestowing; [the word] *maṇigaṇā*...

The grammatical connection of the three [verses] is as follows: "When you, having mounted that chariot upon which [the world] is entrusted, do not traverse the circle of the earth, then the bridges would break. He whose fierce bow (*kodaṇḍa*) emits a thundering roar; by whom the binding of the social classes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) is maintained—alas!

The *Kramasaṃdarbha* [comments on] the three and a half verses beginning with "na yadā": "by chariot" means merely by the presence of the chariot. [It refers to the ground] trampled and churned by the feet of one's own army.
Viśvanātha [says]: "O King! Why have you come?"—how can we ask you this, since...

"I certainly know the reason for that," he says by way of contrast: "When you do not travel around the circle of the earth... The connection of the three [verses] is as follows: "then the embankments would break. He describes that [chariot] upon which the arraying of multitudes of jewels was placed as "victorious" (jaitra), meaning characterized by victory. He explains its very nature of victory: "by means of the chariot..."
By the mere proximity of the chariot, he [subdues] the wicked evildoers. ||5254||
And unrighteousness will flourish through men who are greedy and unrestrained;
while you lie prostrate, this world, seized by robbers, will perish.
Śrīdhara: By unrestrained men acting as the instrumental cause; while he was lying down, free from anxiety. ||55||

The sequential composition: "While lying down" constitutes half a verse. The protection and destruction of merit and demerit would be properly accomplished only through Your glance; likewise, the warding off of thieves would occur merely by Your attentive observation. ||55||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
Nevertheless, O Hero, I ask you: for what purpose have you come here?
That we shall fulfill with a sincere heart.
Śrīdhara: With sincerity and joy, we accept; we take it upon ourselves. ||56||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Nevertheless, even though I know it in general, I shall ask; I ask:
"Is it for this purpose that you wander here in my leaf-hut?"—it is certainly not for the sake of suppressing the wicked.
The sense is that it bears fruit within my leaf-hut. We accept or take it to heart with a sincere, guileless, or joyful heart. ||56||
Thus ends the twenty-first [chapter] of the third [book], which is well-joined for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya, in the Paramahaṃsa-saṃhitā of the Vaiyāsikī collection, in the third book,
within the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, [this is] the section titled "The Dialogue between Manu and Kardama."
The twenty-first chapter.
Maitreya said:
Thus, having manifested the full emergence of his qualities and deeds, [the Lord addressed] the sage.
As if feeling ashamed, the emperor spoke to him who had now ceased speaking.
Śrīdhara:
In the twenty-second [chapter], it is described how Manu gave his daughter Hūti to Kardama, exactly as directed by Viṣṇu, O Lord.
Thus revealed and praised, Manu— the sovereign whose excellence and preeminence consist of all virtues and deeds—
spoke to that sage who was withdrawn and devoted to renunciation, as if feeling bashful upon hearing his own fame, or out of apprehension regarding a refusal. (1)
The sequential arrangement: it is stated that Brahmā, in his form as Virāj, [proceeded] from his own mouth; this is said with reference to the mere class [of being]. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
It is related that in the twenty-second [chapter], the king Priyabhāṣī, having given his own daughter to Kardama who had realized the truth, returned to his own abode.

He is one in whom the manifestation and excellence of all virtues and actions have been revealed. [The sage] is one who has desisted from speech or is devoted to renunciation; [the poet says he acts] "as if with shame" because of hearing his own fame, since that sage is intent upon the ultimate truth and thus there is no occasion for worldly discourse to be addressed to him. ||1||
Manu said:
Brahmā created you from his own mouth out of a desire for self-preservation—
consisting of the Vedic meters, endowed with austerity and knowledge, disciplined in yoga, and free from worldly attachment.
For his protection, the thousand-footed one created us from his thousand arms;
for his heart is indeed called Brahman, and his limbs Kṣatra.

Śrīdhara: Intending to inform [him], "My daughter is to be married by you," he says with two and a half verses beginning with *brahma*, that the relationship between you and me was indeed established by the Lord long ago. "By the desire to protect himself" means by the wish to preserve himself; [the protection] of the Self consisting of the Vedas (*chandomaya*).

Paryāpti is protection and the propagation of the Vedas by His will. "You" refers to the Brāhmaṇas. "For their protection" means for the protection of the Brāhmaṇas. Brahma is the Brāhmaṇa caste; Kṣatra is the Kṣatriya caste. ||23||

The sequence of composition: thus, from the phrase "from the thousand arms," the heart [mantra] is [assigned] because of the predominance of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), while the limb [mantra] is [assigned] because of the predominance of the power of action (kriyā-śakti). ||23||

Viśvanātha: Fearing that he might suddenly be refused when the occasion for giving his daughter arises, [the Lord] first describes a certain relationship between a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya as being based on sound reasoning in two and a half verses beginning with "Brahma": "Of my own self, consisting of the Vedas... and so forth. Of myself, who am composed of the Vedic meters...
Out of a desire to protect, that is, with the wish to preserve through the promulgation of the Vedas, he created you Brahmins;
"paryāpti" here means protection. ||2||

To the question, "Who would protect the Brahmins? he says: "That" (tat). [The phrase] "from the thousand arms" refers to his identity with the Supreme Lord. Now, one might ask: "Who would protect the Kṣatriyas as well? To that he says:
"Brahma" means a Brahmin; "aṅga" means an arm. This is the meaning: for in this world, when a blow falls upon the heart...

The protection of the heart by means of the two arms is observed. When a blow falls upon the arm, one contracts the body and protects the arm right within the center of the heart; thus, the arm is the protector of the heart, and the heart is the protector of the arm. (3)
For this reason, the Brahmin and the Kshatriya protect each other;
thus the immutable God, who is the essence of both the existent and the non-existent, protects them.
Śrīdhara: Thus, that very Lord protected him. Who was he? He who consists of both the existent and the non-existent, who is the self of all; yet he is likewise imperishable and changeless. ||4||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Thus, by the power of austerity, the Brahmin protects the Kṣatriya;
by physical strength, the Kṣatriya [protects] the Brahmin. In reality, however, it is God.
The Supreme Lord alone protects both; He is the essence of both the existent and the non-existent, and yet He is imperishable and changeless.
By the mere sight of You, all my doubts have been severed, since the Blessed One has out of affection declared the dharma to me who desired to protect it.
Śrīdhara: He welcomes the sight of him and so forth, precisely in order to inform him [of his arrival], with the three verses beginning "Of you" (tava). ||5||
The sequential arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): The phrase "this is even more [significant]" is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*) following "that which the Blessed One himself has declared as Dharma.

Alternatively, it means that because of this very vision—and for the reason that it constitutes my own fitness—he himself has spoken even of Dharma; here, the cause of doubt is the impurity of the mind (*cittamala*). ||5||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, he says "of you," meaning, "I have come to you as my protector, and by your very sight I am protected. "By good fortune, the Lord—who is difficult for those of unrefined self to behold—has been seen by me, a Kṣatriya desiring to protect."
By good fortune, the auspicious dust of your feet has touched my head.
Śrīdhara: "Of those with unrefined selves" means those whose minds have not been brought under control. ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: For those of unrefined self, that is, for those of little merit. ||6||
By good fortune I have been instructed by you, and a great favor has been bestowed upon me;
for by a stroke of luck, auspicious words have reached my ears through my open ear-cavities.
Śrīdhara: Grace consists precisely in forms such as instruction and the like. *Uśatīḥ* means "the longing ones. ||7||

The sequential arrangement: Grace (*anugraha*)—consisting of compassionate vision and the like—is the cause for the capacity to receive one's own instruction. It is "uncovered" (*apāvṛtta*), meaning it is not obscured by defects such as a lack of attention to what is to be accomplished;
it is "many" (*bahutva*) because it manifests in manifold ways through longing. ||7||
Viśvanātha: "uśatīḥ" means "the longing ones. ||7||
O Sage, you ought to listen with compassion to what is being told by me, who am distressed by affection for my daughter and now despondent.
Śrīdhara says: He makes his request with seven verses beginning with "sa bhavān. His soul is distressed by affection for his daughter; thus, his petition has been made known. (8)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "And thus, by the sight of you, all my afflictions have indeed departed; however, one single affliction remains unassailable within my heart. Granting me consolation through your grace, [I shall describe] even that."
Thinking, "I shall reveal [the truth] while free from fear," he says: "He is the renowned ocean of compassion"—this is the meaning.
"Afflicted" means: "This affliction of mine does not depart even through discernment"—such is the sense. ||8||
"This is my sister, the daughter of Priyavrata and Uttānapāda;
she seeks a husband who is well-matched in age, character, virtues, and other qualities."
Śrīdhara: The suspicion that she was made a "putrikā" (appointed daughter) for the sake of Priyavrata and Uttānapāda is dispelled;
by saying "she is my daughter," it is shown that this Kṣatriya girl is suitable for you. (9)
The sequence of composition: the investigation of the present day and its narration are such that they are primarily intended as an aid to dharma; therefore, there is no cause for shame. //9//
Viśvanātha: The suspicion that she might be a daughter appointed as a son (*putrikā*) through the marriage of Priyavrata and Uttānapāda is dispelled.
The meaning is that, being a Kṣatriya maiden, she is indeed suitable for you as my daughter. ||9||
But when she heard from Nārada of your virtues— your moral conduct, learning, beauty, age, and character— she became firmly resolved upon you.
Śrīdhara: This is Devahūtī. (10)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been explained. Therefore,
O best of the twice-born, accept this [work] offered by me with faith,
which is entirely suited to you in your duties as a householder.
Śrīdhara: Accept; take it as your own. ||11||
Kramasaṃdarbha, Viśvanātha: [This] has not been explained.
For a counter-argument against desire that has already arisen is not praised;
how much less so for one who is attached to desire, even if he is otherwise free from worldly attachment?
Śrīdhara: [This refers to] an object that has arisen spontaneously or is already attained; "prativāda" means a refutation or rejection. ||12||

The sequence of composition: [This refers to one] for whom the acquisition of objects is solely for the sake of dharma—by the Creator himself brought forth as he rose [to action], who is free from attachment, and whose mind is devoid of clinging to the thought that such acquisition is merely for the purpose of dharma. ||12||
Viśvanātha: Nor should it be said, "I am an ascetic detached from the world; how can I accept your daughter?

To this he says: "The rejection or refusal of an object that has arisen spontaneously and is already attained applies only to one who is impassioned by desire. Thus, having perceived the desire within you, I [act accordingly].
The sense is: "I have come here; therefore, desire toward me must not be disregarded. ||12||
He who disregards one who has extended his hand and begs from a miser finds his great fame diminished and his pride destroyed by that contempt.
Śrīdhara: *Kīnāśa* means a miser. *Avajñayā* means by means of contempt or the insulting of others. ||13||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: In this regard, he states the worldly convention with the words "He who... Having disregarded [the donor] out of deference to his status and having rejected him out of shame, he [the recipient] again [approaches] even a wretched person who does not give.
The meaning is that he begs for that very desire, because by means of that very desire, which soon becomes powerful, both shame and self-respect are swallowed up; thus, pride is destroyed.
Therefore, a wise person who perceives the ultimate consequence should, while remaining within his own mind, [regard] even the present particular state [as such].

The implied meaning (*dhvani*) is that, having inferred through reasoning that he was about to be devoured by passion, one must accept even an unbidden object that has arrived first of all by chance, provided it is not forbidden. ||13||
"I have heard, O learned one, that you are prepared for marriage;
therefore, as a student (*upakurvāṇa*), accept from me this maiden who has been given in marriage."
Śrīdhara: He whose studenthood (*brahmacarya*) has a fixed limit is an *upakurvāṇa*. "To me" means to one given by me. ||14||
The sequence of composition: by means of contempt and the insults inflicted by others. ||14||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But by what characteristic did you recognize Kāma, who resides within my mind? What talk can there be of knowledge in that matter; I have not even heard of him. To this he says: "I, however...
(*ahaṃ tu*). "I heard you" (*tvā... aśṛṇavam*)—this hearing refers to the Lord who has attained manifestation.
Thus it should be understood that [the term] refers primarily to the former. He whose studentship (*brahmacarya*) has a fixed limit is the *upakurvāṇa*.
"Bestowed" means given by me. ||14||
The sage said:
"Certainly; I am desirous of marrying, and your daughter is unmarried. Since he is a suitable match for us both, this is the primary rite of marriage."

Śrīdhara: "And one who is not given away" means that because she has made her resolve in me alone, she has not been promised to anyone else. "The first" means the primary [wife], because there was no marriage prior to that; or it means the principal [wife]. ||15||
The sequence of arrangement: "Certainly. Although Ruci was given [in marriage] first, it is said that she was the "first" because the wedding ceremony itself was commenced right here. ||15||
Viśvanātha: "Unbestowed" (aprattā) means not promised to anyone; this is because there has been no marriage prior to that time. ||15||
O god among men, your desire for this daughter is great and well-known in the tradition of the Vedas;
who indeed would not honor your offspring?
As if casting down the Goddess Śrī by her very radiance.
She stood like Śrī, who, by her own radiance, surpasses all others—just as [the word] *madhvaḥ* [implies]. ||16||

Śrīdhara: *Bhūyāt* means "may he be. He is *pratīta*, meaning well-known through such Vedic mantras as, "I grasp your hand for the sake of good fortune, with me as your husband" (Ṛgveda 10.85.36). By the very luster of his own limbs, he possesses *śrī*, which refers to the splendor of ornaments and the like. ||16||

The sequence of composition: the meaning of the triad beginning with "May that desire come to pass" is as follows: "She, such as she is, even solicits me, though I am a mere ascetic; therefore, how could I abandon her who is a pure devotee?
And this will be stated by the verses beginning with "Having set out with my parents. [The word] *śriyam* refers to the Fortune of the world (*jagallakṣmī*).

Viśvanātha: May her desire be fulfilled. Her conviction lies in the marriage rites as correctly prescribed in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), well-known through such mantras as: "I take your hand for the sake of good fortune; with me as your husband, may you reach old age" (*Ṛgveda* 10.85.36). [This is accomplished] by the very luster of her own limbs.
Prosperity, which is the splendor of ornaments and the like. ||16||
Viśvāvasu fell from his own celestial chariot upon seeing her playing on the palace roof, her beauty enhanced by the tinkling of her anklets, her eyes distracted by the ball.
Having beheld this, his mind became utterly bewildered and deluded.
Śrīdhara: Beholding her, he fell [to the ground]. His mind was bewildered and agitated by delusion. She whose beauty rested upon her two feet, which were like two tinkling bells. ||17||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By means of the poetic figure of contrast (*vyatirekālaṅkāra*) in the phrase "as if casting aside Śrī," he describes her beauty, excellence, and so forth as being beyond compare, and then speaks of her natural power as well—in [the verse beginning with] "yām."

Thus: she, whose beauty was enhanced by her two tinkling feet, fell completely from the celestial chariot onto the surface of the earth; seeing this, she fainted. Even there, having become like one dead while still fully conscious, she immediately experienced the fruit of the great offense of having gazed [at him] with such intense passion.
The meaning is as follows: Now, because of the use of the suffix *ktvā* in the word "having looked" (*vilokya*), it would follow that Viśvāvasu had already seen her; therefore, [the poet] says:
"her, whom he had not seen, though she was seeking him—the ornament of women—by those whose feet have not been served by Fortune."
What wise person would not approve of Vatsa approaching Manor’s sister, who occupies such a high station?

Śrīdhara: [He saw her] who was the crest-jewel among women, the very ornament [of the world]; whom those who have not served the feet of Śrī are unable even to see, being unworthy of such a sight; who had come from the high station of Uttānapāda, having arrived there of her own accord. ||18||

The sequential arrangement: the pair beginning with "yām" [refers to this]. Because both were perceived by everyone as having their minds overcome by passion, it caused no shame; yet, because Priyavrata had then departed after becoming detached, it is called "the high station. (18)

Viśvanātha: Regarding this, he says "not at all, not at all"—the feet of my beloved deity, the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, have never been seen by people who have not served the glorious feet [of the Goddess]; they have been served by me alone.
Therefore, the likeness would belong to me alone and not to anyone else; such is the meaning. And by that [likeness], he who moves through the sky...

It follows that Viśvāvasu beheld her radiance alone, but not her person. He speaks of the excellence even of her noble birth: "your daughter, the object of your affection. [She is the daughter] of Uttānapāda, who occupies a high station; Priyavrata is not mentioned because he had already departed from there at that time. Even there—
That which comes of its own accord to those who have gone forth to meet it. ||18||
Therefore, I shall devotedly practice the virtuous discipline so that my own vital energy may be sustained;
from this, I shall fulfill the duties foremost among those of the Paramahaṃsa.
I hold in high regard those who speak of purity and are non-violent.

Śrīdhara: "I shall worship" means I shall accept. The agreement or covenant is: "The state of householdership lasts as long as there is the procreation of offspring; after that, renunciation. He states that very point: "as long as my own *tejas* (vital energy) bears the embryo," or else, "my own *tejas*, that is, the seed (*vīrya*), fallen from my body."

"One should maintain [these]. Beyond this, I consider that knowledge pertaining to the state of a paramahaṃsa consists of those primary qualities—non-violence, freedom from injury, tranquility, and so forth—which were directly and preeminently taught by Viṣṇu in his white form, and which should be practiced as extensively as possible. ||19||
The sequence of composition: May the splendor known as Kapila, belonging to the Self who is the Supreme Self, sustain it from me for as long as it may endure. ||19||

Viśvanātha: "By agreement" (*samayena*) means by an agreement consisting of a verbal contract (*bhāṣābandha*), such as: "As long as there is the production of offspring, one remains in the householder stage; thereafter, one enters renunciation" (*sannyāsa*). Alternatively, it means: "I shall serve [you] for as long as you maintain the splendor (*tejas*) that has descended from my own body"; even in that case, it is by agreement.
The meaning is: "at the very time when I obtain an opportunity immediately after the completion of the remainder of my ascetic penance.

Here, the literal sense of the matter (*vastvartha*) should also be understood as: "my own self" and "the splendor of my beloved deity," which is known by the name Kapiladeva. Following this, [he chose] those who are foremost among the Paramahaṃsas; or alternatively—

I consider those [teachings] to be superior even to the knowledge of the state of a paramahaṃsa, consisting primarily of devotion characterized by non-possessiveness, directly and preeminently proclaimed by the pure Viṣṇu himself; they are non-violent, free from injury, and should be practiced as extensively as possible. ||19||
From whom this diverse universe arose,
in whom it shall be dissolved, and in whom it abides—
he, the Lord of the Lords of Creatures, [is for me].
The Blessed One Ananta is the supreme authority.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely the command of your father Prajāpati applies only to creation, not to renunciation (saṃnyāsa). To this he says: "Since... He will "conclude," that is, go to dissolution. The word *vāva* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed). The meaning is that after the three debts have been discharged, renunciation alone has been taught by the Blessed One for those like me.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding this matter, he says "since... because for both you and me, the Blessed One alone is established in our memory as the authority. Alternatively: [Objection] But surely your father Prajāpati’s command applies only to creation, not...
Regarding this specific point, he says: "Since... (yataḥ). The sense is "it will be established" or "it will go to dissolution.
He is the Lord even of the Prajāpatis, such as my own father and others; therefore, he alone is the supreme authority.
The intention is that his command alone must be obeyed by me, and not merely that of my father. ||20||
Maitreya said: O Ugradhanvan, he spoke only this much regarding the one whose navel is a lotus, and then became silent.
Grasping it with his intellect, his heart was captivated by Devahūti’s face, which was beautified by a smile.
Śrīdhara: O Ugradhanvan Vidura! He was enticed by the mouth of the sage, and he himself is being tempted;
or rather, he has enticed [him] with his mouth. 21.

The sequential composition: She was captivated by that face which was graced—meaning it had attained a particular splendor—by a smile consisting of the grace born from the experience of Him whose navel is a lotus. She felt a longing, thinking, "This very one is a highly fortunate person, worthy of being my husband. ||21||

Viśvanātha: "O Ugradhanvan!"—the sense is that just as you, a hero, have turned back for battle, so too has he [turned away] from the path of devotion to the Lord (bhagavad-dharma) which was his own preference. Consequently, Kardama’s heart was captivated by the face of Devahūti, which was graced with a smile.

His mind became greedy for her; and by this, it is suggested that there was no remorse on the part of Manu and Śatarūpā, thinking, "Alas, alas! She has been bestowed upon one who is utterly dispassionate. (21)
Having clearly understood the resolve of his daughter and the queen,
he, filled with great joy, gave her to that man who was richly endowed with a multitude of virtues— a match for her.
Śrīdhara: He is Manu. "Afterwards" means immediately following. And having learned the resolve—the firm determination—of the queen. ||22||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: He is Manu; *anv* means immediately thereafter; [he learned] the resolve, that is, the intention, of his daughter Devahūtī, who was his queen, and of her mother. ||22||
The great queen Śatarūpā, out of affection, bestowed upon the couple costly wedding gifts, including ornaments, garments, and household requisites.
Śrīdhara: "Pāribarhān" refers to those things to be given at the time of marriage; "bhūṣāḥ" means ornaments, "vāsāṃsi" means garments, and "paricchadān" means household utensils. ||23||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: *Pāribarhān* means those to be given at a wedding; *anarghyān* means those whose values are great, that is to say, priceless. ||23||
Having given his daughter in marriage to a worthy suitor, the emperor was free from anxiety;
yet, embracing her with both arms, his heart was overwhelmed by longing.

Śrīdhara: *Prattām* means given. *Sadṛkṣāya* means to one who is similar. *Gatavyathaḥ* refers to one whose pain or anxiety has departed. *Autkaṇṭhyenonmathitāśayaḥ* refers to one whose heart is agitated by intense longing. ||24||
The sequential arrangement: "prattām" constitutes a couplet (yugmaka). ||24||
Viśvanātha: "Prattām" means "given away. ||24||
Unable to endure that separation and repeatedly shedding drops of tears, he sprinkled his daughter’s locks with the water of his eyes, crying out, "O Mother! O Child!"
Śrīdhara: Saying, "O Mother! O Child!", [he spoke] in order to endure her separation—this is an archaic (ārṣa) sandhi. He sprinkled water upon his locks of hair. ||25||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Speaking thus, "O child! ||25||
Having taken leave of that best of sages and being granted permission, the king, accompanied by his followers,
mounted his chariot with his wife and set out for his own city.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not commented [on this]. Kramasandarbha: "Having addressed" constitutes a *yugmaka* (couplet). [It refers to] both banks of the Ṛṣikulyā, that is, the Sarasvatī.
Beholding the perfections of the hermitages of the tranquil seers.
Śrīdhara: Of the two beautiful banks, which are for the welfare of the lineage of sages. ||27||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: [The river] of the sages (*ṛṣikulyā*), meaning the stream of the seers, or that which is beneficial to the lineage of the sages. "Of both" refers to the two beautiful banks (*surodhas*), meaning the lovely shores. (27)
Perceiving that he was approaching, the subjects from Brahmāvarta went out to meet their lord with songs,
hymns, and musical instruments, filled with great joy.
Śrīdhara: Having understood—that is, having learned—the intention, the subjects set out from the land of Brahmāvarta to meet their lord. ||28||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: *pratyudīyuḥ* means they went out to meet them. ||28||
There was a city named Barhiṣmatī, endowed with every prosperity,
where the hairs of the sacrificial horse fell as it shook its limbs during the sacrifice.

"From the hairs of this [Lord], whose nature is the bliss of knowledge, the *kuśa* grasses and other [sacred plants] arose as He shook them at Prayāga while in the form of a boar; those hairs became thousands of forms of the God. Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa.
In that very place there was a seat for them; [this is known] from the sūtra: "The first [vow] among the seven. ||2930||

Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry, "What is this Brahmāvarta?", he says: "Where the city named Barhiṣmatī [is located]. And where is that? "Where the hairs of the Sacrifice—the Sacrificial Boar—fell.
The word "where" (yatra) is to be connected with every clause. ||29||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been explained.
Viśvanātha, in response to the inquiry "What is this Brahmāvarta?", says: "Wherein lies the city named Barhiṣmatī. And where is that? "Wherein fell the hairs of the Sacrifice, [that is] Yajñavarāha."
Thus; the word "where" is connected to every instance [of the following]. ||29||
The kuśa and kāśa grasses were always of a verdant luster;
by means of them, the sages, having overcome the sacrificial-spoilers, performed their sacrifices.

Śrīdhara: By providing the etymology of the name Barhiṣmatī, he describes the excellence of that region through two verses. Kuśas and Kāśas were present—those whose luster and color were perpetually green.
Having brought about the defeat of the sacrificial-spoilers, such as Rākṣasas, [he established] the sacrifice, which is Viṣṇu. (30)
The sequential arrangement: "Kuśa and kāśa grasses" refers to those very things, possessing that very form. ||30||
Viśvanātha: He etymologically explains the name Barhiṣmatī: "The very hairs were the *kuśa* grasses"—this is the grammatical connection. (30)
Having spread sacrificial grass made of *kuśa* and *kāśa*, the Blessed Manu worshipped the Lord of Sacrifice, from whom he had obtained his station on earth.
Śrīdhara: [He went] to where he sacrificed to Viṣṇu, the Sacrificial Person (*yajñapuruṣa*). "Bhuvaṃ" means the place.

"Labdha-" ends in the suffix *tṛn*; the meaning is "having obtained. Or, it may mean "the Sacrificial Person from whom he obtained [it]. By this, it is shown that even compared to heaven, the earth is superior, and within that [earth], it is [that specific place].
It is said that this is the most excellent place. The sequential arrangement has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: By the word "outside" (*bahiḥ*), both [the earth and the body] are indicated as being composed of *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass; [it refers to] the earth in its form as the world (*bhūrūpa*).
"Having seized a place" (*sthānaṃ labdhvā*) ends with the suffix *tṛn*.
The Lord entered the city named Barhiṣmatī, where he took up residence;
there he entered a palace that destroys the threefold suffering.

Śrīdhara: He states the subject at hand: "The city named Barhiṣmatī which he inhabited"—the grammatical connection is that having entered the palace after resting in that city where he had previously dwelt, he enjoyed pleasures. ||32||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: He speaks of the subject at hand: "Having first entered my own abode, in which [abode] I formerly dwelt, [I shall enter] that which encompasses me. (32)
Together with his wife and progeny, he enjoyed all desires without conflict,
while his noble fame was sung by celestial musicians accompanied by women;
at dawn, he listened to the stories of Hari with an attentive heart.

Śrīdhara: Without contradicting other duties such as dharma and the like, his excellent fame was sung at every dawn; nevertheless, he himself listened to the stories of Hari alone while enjoying worldly pleasures.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: "Together with his wife" means [the phrase] is accompanied by a half-verse.

*Viśvanātha*: Without contradicting any other duty (*dharma*). At dawn (*pratyūṣeṣu*), meaning from the break of dawn onwards. With a heart captivated and permeated by the very sweetness of her speech.
Even the enjoyments were unable to cause the downfall of that sage, the son of Svayambhū, who was skilled in the powers of yoga and devoted to the Blessed One.

Śrīdhara: "In the yogic powers" (yogamāyāsu) means in the creation of desired enjoyments. "Because of which" (yataḥ) means because of that [power] which is capable of causing even the slightest fall—that is, of causing a slight decline or of overcoming [him]. ||34||
The sequence of composition: "niṣṇātam" constitutes a pair of verses (yugmaka). ||34||

Viśvanātha: By means of yoga—that is, through the very practice of the eightfold yoga—one becomes *niṣṇāta*, one who has reached the further shore, regarding *māyās*, which is to say, regarding illusory cognitions. Thus, he knows how to enjoy sense objects in such a way that, even when fully enjoyed, those objects are unable to produce attachment within him; this is the meaning. ||34||
His watches of the night were not spent in vain as he passed his time,
for they were filled with listening to, meditating upon, performing the rites of, and speaking the stories of Viṣṇu.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: it means that which has lost its essence (*gatasāra*) or is stale (*yātayāma*). As stated in the *Nāradīya*: "In this context, 'essence' (*yāma*) refers to the vital strength (*sāra*). (35)
Śrīdhara: Therefore, that cooked food whose *yāma* (watch of the day) has passed becomes "spent" (*gatasāra*).

Anything else that is spent is also called *yātayāma*. [The ancestors] were *ayātayāma*, meaning their essence was not spent. Those *yāmās*—the divisions of time—are so called because they cause one's own interval, namely the *manvantara*, to pass or elapse.
of one who acts and composes [the work] by means of his own words. ||35||

The sequence of composition: *ayātayāmāḥ* means not stale, not decayed, and not wasted; or alternatively, "untasted by others. According to Amara, *yātayāma* refers to both that which is decayed and that which has been used. The terms beginning with *śṛṇvataḥ* (of those hearing) should be understood in their respective order [with the following verbs]. [This applies to] *dhyāyataḥ* (of those meditating).
For one who remembers it with its specific distinctions, performs it, composes treatises concerning it, speaks of them, and teaches them. ||35||
Viśvanātha: At that time, his watches (yāmas) were not spent (ayātayāma), meaning they were not fruitless.

According to Amara, "that which is lived through and that which is consumed are both called *yātayāma*. Of what nature were they? They were those that caused him to pass his own internal *manvantara*. [This was] by means of his own words as he acted.
For one who composes in the form of poetry that is both visible and audible. ||35||
Thus he passed seventy-one yugas within himself,
having surpassed the three states of existence through his devotion to Vāsudeva.
Śrīdhara: [He is] one by whom the three states—waking and so forth, or those characterized by sattva and so forth—have been transcended. ||36||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: The three states of movement are waking and so forth, or existence and so forth; or they are the threefold suffering. ||36||
How do physical, mental, divine, human,
and elemental afflictions fail to distress one who takes refuge in Hari?
Madhvaḥ: Even while remaining in a human state during his final incarnation. ||37||
Śrīdhara: [The afflictions] are divine, atmospheric, human, arising from enemies, and elemental, arising from cold, heat, and so forth. O Vidura, son of Vyāsa! 37.
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha says: "In that regard, devotion alone is the cause," and states: "From the body... [This refers to: divine [afflictions] arising from the atmosphere; human [afflictions] arising from enemies; and elemental [afflictions] arising from cold, heat, and so forth.
At dawn, O Vidura! ||37||
He who, when questioned by the sages, proclaimed various auspicious dharmas for men of all castes and stages of life, being ever devoted to the welfare of all beings;
Śrīdhara says: He describes his extraordinary knowledge with the words "He who... [referring to verse 38], which concerns the common duties of men.
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
This wondrous life-story of Manu, the first king, has been described;
now hear of the birth of his offspring, who are worthy of description.
Śrīdhara: His offspring was Devahūti; [the commentary on] her birth and power has not been explained. Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Udayam" means power (prabhāvam). ||39||
Thus ends the twenty-second [chapter], which is perfectly suited to the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus, in the glorious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, in the commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*, in the *Pāramahaṃsya-saṃhitā* by Vyāsa, in the third book (*skandha*),
within the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, [this is the chapter] titled "The Bestowal of Devahūtī."
The Twenty-second Chapter.
Now begins the Twenty-third Chapter:
Devahūti’s Remorse, in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
Maitreya said:
When her parents had departed, that virtuous woman, skilled in discerning gestures,
constantly attended upon her husband with affection, just as Bhavānī attends upon Lord Bhava.
O sir, by means of trust, personal purity, reverence, self-restraint,
service, friendship, and sweet speech.
Śrīdhara: Then, in the twenty-third [chapter], the delight of Citrāṅgadā in a celestial chariot (vimāna) that moves at will, fashioned through yoga and endowed with every prosperity, is described.
When he had set out, that is, when the departure had been made. ||1||
The sequence of composition: "With confidence," etc., is a *yugmaka* (a pair of verses). ||1||
Viśvanātha: In the twenty-third [chapter], Rati is described as being created for Kardama by the Lord, who desired her as a bride because she possessed divine excellence.
Having cast aside desire, hypocrisy, hatred, greed, sin, and pride, she,
ever vigilant and diligent, gratified him who was more powerful than the powerful.
Śrīdhara: *Dambham* means hypocrisy or deceit; *agham* means the performance of forbidden acts; *tejīyāṃsam* means exceedingly brilliant. ||3||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Agha means offense or transgression. ||3||
That best of divine sages [beheld] her, the daughter of Manu, who was devoted to him and who,
by virtue of destiny, was seeking great blessings from her husband, who was superior even to the gods.
After a long time, seeing her emaciated and weakened by her observance of vows,
he, overcome with compassion, spoke with a voice faltering with love:

Śrīdhara: "From one who is more powerful than destiny" means from one capable of even altering destiny. "Emaciated by the performance of vows" means extremely lean due to a long period of time; such is the sequence of the composition. "He indeed" (sa vai) constitutes a *yugmaka* [couplet]. "Of great splendor" (*mahaśis*).

Such is the conclusion of that lineage. In some places it is said that Kardama spoke to her—her who was emaciated, whose strength was exhausted, who was wasted away, and whose body had been made thin. ||4-5||

Viśvanātha: [She was] by fate—that which is weightier than fate, even more powerful than fate, capable of making even fate otherwise. Or rather, having abandoned her desires, she was later, after some time, by fate—under the influence of the Supreme Lord’s impulsion—desiring great blessings, that is, her desires.
Afflicted by compassion for her who was desiring [him], he was tormented by the sight of her emaciation. ||45||
Kardama said:
"O Mānavī, bestower of honor, I am pleased today with your supreme service and your transcendent devotion."
This body, which is the most intimate friend of embodied beings,
is not fit to be sacrificed for my sake.

Śrīdhara: "A friend and beloved"—meaning that although he was worthy and praiseworthy, he was disregarded and not even counted for my sake; the sense is that he was neglected by one who is devoted to my service. ||6||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "That body was not taken into account" means it was not considered whether it should remain or perish;
[he says] "this is indeed appropriate for you, a supreme devoted wife," regarding the body...
He specifies: "It is appropriate to exhaust— that is, to bring to an end— for my sake, that is, solely for the purpose of service to Me,
those blessings of the Blessed One which were won by Me through My own dharma, and through austerity, meditative absorption, knowledge, and the yoga of the Self."
I grant you those very same [realms], which have been secured through your service to me— realms free from fear and free from sorrow, where you may behold the vision.

Śrīdhara: Penance, meditative concentration, knowledge, and worship—in these, the self-yoga which is one-pointedness of mind has conquered and attained divine enjoyments through the grace of the Blessed One; behold those very same enjoyments now secured by you and brought under your control. I grant you divine vision.
Just as you shall see with your vision. ||7||

The sequential arrangement is as follows: "Those who [worship] Me"—first their own duty (*svadharma*), then worship centered on that, then austerity (*tapas*), then meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which is one-pointedness, then the experience of knowledge (*vidyānubhava*), and then union (*yoga*) or conjunction with the Self, the Lord Śukla; by these, they are "conquered," meaning even through their own duties and so forth, by being intent upon Him.
The action is understood. ||7||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, for the sake of discharging this debt, nothing else is suitable to be given to you; rather, he says "those who" to show that this alone is the most difficult thing to attain. *Samādhi* is the ripening of meditation (*dhyāna*), and *vidyā* is worship (*upāsanā*); these two are indeed the union with the Self (*ātmayoga*).

The meaning is that those who were conquered by them, obtained, and secured—though they have now been brought under your control and acquired through righteous means—you shall behold with divine vision which I bestow upon you; by that vision, you will see them directly even now. Or rather, behold them clearly through my grace; enough of this.

The sense is "out of shame. Here, with the intention that through the grace of the Lord—which arises from one's own duty, austerity, meditation on the Lord, and so forth—both enjoyment and liberation would indeed be unimpeded, he says: "fearless and free from sorrow" (7).
Others, however, having their compositions of meaning shattered by the mere twitching of the Blessed One’s eyebrows—what need is there to mention the strides of the Wide-Strider?
You have attained perfection; enjoy the riches yielded by your own dharma.
Divine [powers], difficult for men to attain through the transformations of kings.
Śrīdhara: But what are other enjoyments? Nothing at all; the meaning is that they are utterly trivial.

The reason for this is: those [enjoyments] in which the arrangement of objects—that is, the desires—is destroyed by the "unfurling," namely the curving, of the eyebrow of the Lord Urukrama. By one's own duty...

"Those who are milked through devotion to their husbands"—thus [he refers to] them. "Difficult to attain" means difficult to reach. "The transformations of those kings"—those various distortions of enjoyment arising from the thought "we are kings";
by means of these, [he refers to] the sequence of the kings' transformations through the means of conciliation and the rest. (8)

Viśvanātha: He says "others" (*anye*) to show that even the enjoyments of heaven, though being experienced by others through [the power of] *ścy* and so forth, are indeed permeated by fear and grief—"nothing at all" (*kiṃ na*) means nothing whatsoever, because they are trivial, and so on.
Or, [it refers to those] who are being oppressed by their own duty, namely *pātivratya* (chastity), thinking, "I am a king," or "I am a queen."
By those modifications, they are difficult to approach; the meaning is that they are hard to attain. ||8||
Seeing him speaking thus, she who was expert in all yogic powers and sciences became free from anxiety;
with a voice overwhelmed by humility and affection, she spoke softly.
With her face graced by a smile and a bashful glance, she said:

Śrīdhara: Having observed her husband speaking thus—one who is expert and proficient in all forms of *yogamāyā*, sciences, and their respective modes of worship—she became free from anxiety and relieved of her cares. Overwhelmed by *saṃpraśraya* (humility) and *praṇaya* (affection), she spoke with a voice faltering with emotion.
She whose face was radiant with a smile and blossomed with laughter through a glance accompanied by a slight bashfulness spoke; she said. ||9||
The sequence of composition: here, in the word "evam" (thus), the term "īṣat" (slightly) is also a qualifier of "hasita" (laughter). ||9||

Viśvanātha: [She thought: "Yogamāyā, the manifestations arising from yoga, the sciences, and the modes of worship—my husband is discerning regarding these; he will grant me my post-mortem riches of enjoyment and liberation, but not those pertaining to this world. Thus reflecting in her mind, she was full of humility, modesty, and affection.

She spoke to her husband—she whose face was graced by a playful smile, and whose very glance was imbued with a slight bashfulness; she who, through a song that moved with such intensity as to leave one utterly overwhelmed, proceeded toward the mud (or toward Kardama). [The form "vihvalayā" is explained like the word "somapā. She said this to her husband.
Because an explicit expression of desire for sexual enjoyment constitutes a semblance of aesthetic flavor (*rasābhāsa*),

and because Devahūtī is like the crest-jewel of the finest women, it was impossible to express [the sentiment] directly through the two verses beginning with "rāddham"; therefore, her face was merely a glance veiled by a bashful smile intended for that recitation.
