She acted; there, her modesty and affection being manifested, caused her voice to become faltering in such a way that the two verses beginning with "rāddham" became clearly uttered. But as for her face, the meaning is that she remained silent at that time. ||9||
Devahūti said:
"O bull among the twice-born, O Lord of unfailing yoga and māyā, O all-pervading Master, I realize that this has indeed been accomplished by You."
The agreement you made with me— that there shall be a single physical union—
is a virtue for women of noble birth, resulting in a most exalted offspring.
Śrīdhara: "Batā" expresses joy. O bull among the twice-born! O best of the twice-born! O Lord!
all this has been accomplished and is already perfected in you; that I understand and know. However, let that agreement which was declared by you stand firm. "Sakṛt" means once.

The meaning is: "up to the mere occurrence of conception. For, when the husband is the most venerable—that is, the best—acting as the cause, the offspring of women is a great quality, a great gain. In the compound reading, since the husband is most venerable, from him there arises for virtuous women the "birth of qualities," that is, the expansion of virtues. Therefore...
The sense is: "Once the expansion of my virtues has occurred through the birth of a son, let everything you have said come to pass thereafter. ||10||

The sequence of composition: By the phrase "contact with the limbs," she wards off the agitation arising from the manifestation of passion that would otherwise have been occasioned; for [her love] is more profound. ||10||
Viśvanātha says: "Devahūti spoke"—the remainder [of the sense] being "by a sign of her eyes. O bull among the twice-born!
O best of Brahmins! I alone know and understand that this matter is already accomplished and established in you;
however, let that agreement which was declared by you be fulfilled once.

The meaning is that physical contact [with a husband] extends only as far as the conception of a fetus. For, when a most excellent offspring—the best of children—is the cause [of a woman's status], the virtue of virtuous women is indeed procreation, the birth of offspring;
for in its absence, there is only censure among women, such as "this woman is barren. This is the intended sense. [This applies to the reading without the visarga.]

In the compound "guṇānāṃ prasavaḥ" (the birth of virtues), under the guise of offspring, it is the husband's very virtues that are procreated by them; thus, the intention is: "May you have virtuous children through me. ||10||
In this matter, train yourself in what must be done according to the instruction,
so that this emaciated body of mine,
which yearns intensely for you, may be restored for you who have been overcome by the god of love.
O Lord, look upon that wretched abode of mine and see what is fitting for it.

Śrīdhara: [She] says, "O Lord, first perform the preliminary duties for the sake of physical union"—that is, "in that regard, concerning the physical union, learn the procedure, the means, according to the instruction and in accordance with the *kāmaśāstra*; understand it. The meaning is: "prepare it," by which—

Through the means of massage, food, drink, and so forth, may this wretched body of mine, emaciated by the intense desire to take pleasure, be perfected—that is, become capable of sexual enjoyment. Of what sort [of a woman]? Of one who has been overcome by that Mind-born One (the God of Love) who was stirred up by you alone. Therefore, for that reason, it is appropriate.
"Contemplate" means reflect; that is to say, deliberate. ||11||
The sequential composition: In that regard, instruct the woman desiring the birth of a virtuous son on what must be done.

By means of that performance which accords with your instruction and is consistent with the teaching, and by reason of that duty to be performed, may this body of mine—which has been overcome by desire—be purified through asceticism and other such means.

"Exceedingly emaciated and dejected, yet desiring pleasure, he would succeed; he would be fit for that. Immediately thereafter, Viśvanātha said: "Well then, enter the leaf-hut; I shall fulfill your desire.
[The other replied: "No, for with a body such as this—soiled and emaciated—it is not fitting for such a leaf-hut."

He says "therein" to show that [the goal] cannot be accomplished with such limited equipment. Here, regarding "contact with the limbs," one should train in the practice—the means of accomplishment—without transgressing the instruction of the treatises of Vātsyāyana and others, according to their teaching.
One should know this from oneself alone, because the methods of love are to be understood through personal experience; having known them...
The meaning is: "And please properly provide the various appropriate objects that stimulate aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), such as massages, food, and drink, so that this self—
the body— being emaciated and agitated by excessive passion, may attain success and become capable of sexual union."

Of what sort am I, who have been overcome by that mind-born god (Kāma) produced by you yourself through your very appearance and so forth? I am now truly wretched and destitute. Therefore, O Lord, you who are capable of creating everything through the power of yoga, please look for a suitable dwelling place befitting my passion.
Reflect upon this. ||11||
Maitreya said: O Vidura,
seeking to do what was pleasing to his beloved, Kardama then employed his yogic power and immediately manifested a celestial chariot that travels at will.
Śrīdhara: Then, at that very moment, he brought it forth; it became manifest. ||12||
The sequential arrangement: "Of the beloved," etc., constitutes the twelfth decade.

Viśvanātha: By the mere glance of her eyes from Devahūti, who remained silent, Kardama likewise remained silent; yet at that very moment, he performed all of that which had been expressed [by her]. He states that he did not give a verbal reply by beginning with the words "of his beloved" (priyāyāḥ) and so forth. ||12||
It was divine, yielding all desires, endowed with every kind of jewel,
resulting in an increase of all supernatural powers, and adorned with pillars of precious gems.

Śrīdhara: He qualifies that very [palace] with nine [epithets], beginning with "the cow of plenty for all desires" (sarvakāmadugha). It is endowed with all [precious things] such as gems. It is that in which there is an *udarka*—that is, a progressive increase (*uttarottarābhivṛddhi*)—of the accumulation of all prosperities and all riches. It is "adorned" (*upaskṛta*), meaning beautified. ||13||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Nor is it composed of incomplete happiness like that created by gods, humans, and so forth;
thus he says, "all" (*sarva*). Nor is it subject to gradual deterioration over successive periods of time, as is the case with ordinary celestial palaces (*vimāna*).

"Udarka" refers to that which possesses progressively superior results. "Upaskaraṇa" means equipment; he says "sarvakāla" (at all times) to indicate that it is not accompanied by the suffering associated with heat, cold, and so forth. It is endowed with divine implements and brings happiness at all times.
It was adorned with various colorful bands and banners.
Śrīdhara: *Upakaraṇa* means equipment or retinue. *Paṭṭikā* refers to specific types of narrow, broad-clothed strips; *patākā* means banners, [decorated] with those.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: [The temple was adorned] with ribbons, small banners, and large flags;
with garlands that were exceedingly thick and long, hanging from the eaves; and with those [ribbons] in which various flower-garlands of red, yellow, and other colors were strung between them. ||14||
It was adorned with various garlands and wonderful flower wreaths, where bees hummed melodiously,
and it shone with garments of fine linen, silk, and various other cloths.
Śrīdhara: [She is adorned] with those garlands (*sraj*) which possess wonderful flower-wreaths (*mālya*), and in which six-legged bees are warbling and humming in a charming manner. ||15||

The sequence of composition: Although *dukūla* and *kṣauma* are identical in being produced from *atasī* fibers, their internal distinctions must be understood; as Amara states: "The words *dukūla* and *kṣauma* are neuter. (15)

Viśvanātha: With *dukūla*—silk cloths produced from the cocoons of small insects; with *kṣauma*, fabrics made from flax fibers; with *kauśeya*, silks produced from large worms; with various *āṅkara* garments; and with cotton (*kārpāsa*)—these serve as the coverings for the four-cornered altar-platform (*catuṣkikā-vedi*). ||15||
In the dwellings arranged one above the other,
it was made lovely by separate couches, pillows, fans, and seats that were laid out.

Śrīdhara: [It is] "in houses constructed one above another"; "charming" means beautiful by means of *kaśipus*, that is, beds, and also charming by means of couches (*paryaṅka*) and so forth. The sequential arrangement has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: With *kaśipu*s, that is, with beds. ||16||
It was adorned here and there with various arts and crafts placed in their respective locations,
graced by great emerald plateaus and coral altars.
It was not described by anyone at all.
At its two gates, the thresholds of coral shone like diamond door-panels;
upon its sapphire peaks, it was adorned with golden water-jars.
Madhvaḥ: A door-bolt at the threshold. ||18||

Śrīdhara: At the doors—that is, at the gateways—the threshold (udumbara) was fashioned from coral; by this it shone, being adorned. It was equipped with door-panels inlaid with diamonds. On the peaks—that is, on the uppermost parts of the palaces—which were made of sapphire... ||18||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: [The palace] shines with thresholds made of coral; at its doors it possesses diamond panels—that is, it is equipped with door-panels of *hīraka* diamonds—and on its peaks, that is, on the summits of the highest parts of the palace. (18)
It was graced with walls of diamond set with the finest ruby eyes,
and adorned with various costly canopies and golden archways.

Śrīdhara: [The phrase] "by those which are like those possessing eyes" refers to the finest rubies (*padmarāga*). Or rather, it means "like those possessing eyes. By what? By the finest rubies. "By variegated canopies" means by collections of *vitāna* (canopies). The sequential arrangement has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: [He saw it] with sacrificial canopies that, by means of excellent fragments of rubies set into diamond walls, appeared as if possessed of eyes; and with golden arches renowned as "garlands of praise. ||19||
Flocks of swans and pigeons warbled here and there,
repeatedly alighting upon what they took to be their own kind, though those were artificial.
"Madhvaḥ" refers to artificial [ornaments] made for the sake of beauty. ||20||
Śrīdhara: Even artificial swans and other birds, thinking them to be their own kindred, have repeatedly perched upon them here and there and uttered their cries. 20.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thinking even artificial swans and other such creatures to be their own kin, they mount them here and there among their own flocks and cry out with full abandon. This is the place of recreation (*vihārasthāna*).
With pleasure-grounds, resting places, sleeping chambers, and inner bedrooms for enjoyment; with courtyards, open squares,
and pavilions arranged according to his delight, it was as if a marvel to himself.

Śrīdhara: A *vihāra* is a place for recreation or a playground; *viśrāma* is a bedchamber; *saṃviśa* is a place of enjoyment; a *prāṅgaṇa* is outside the house; an *ajira* is outside the enclosure wall;
"according to one's pleasure" (*yathopajoṣam*) means according to one's own comfort; and even though it is not subject to illusion, it is as if it causes wonder to oneself.
The sequence of composition: "of the self" [is used]. The phrase "even of the celestial chariot, as if it were a cause for amazement" is merely a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). ||21||

Viśvanātha: *Prāṅgaṇa* is the area outside the house; *ajira* is the area outside the enclosure wall. *Yathopajoṣam* means according to one's own pleasure or comfort. Even regarding the mud, the word *iva* is used because it was fashioned by himself;
thus, in reality, it does not cause him any surprise. ||21||
As she was looking upon that house with a mind not entirely joyful,
Kardama himself, who knows the inner disposition of all beings, spoke to her.
Śrīdhara: [He was] not very pleased because of his soiled body and the absence of female attendants. ||22||

The sequence of composition: because his feelings were not ignited due to the impurity of his body and so forth, he was not overly joyful; thus, in the phrase "by himself," some read "his beloved" (*priyām*) instead. ||22||
Viśvanātha: [The meaning is that he is] not overly pleased because of her soiled body and lack of female attendants.
"O timid one, having bathed in this lake, ascend this celestial chariot;
this is a sacred site (tīrtha) established by Śukra, which bestows blessings upon men."

Śrīdhara: In this lake, Bindusaras; ascend, climb up. It was made by Śukla Viṣṇu through the falling of the drops of bliss (ānandabindu). It is that which removes [impurity] and brings about attainment. ||23||

The sequence of composition teaches what is to be done: "Having immersed... and so forth, in a pair of verses. In some versions, it reads: "having [immersed] one's own hair, which has become matted like a braid (veṇī). (23)
Viśvanātha: [He is] the one who causes [the soul] to traverse and reach the Bindu-lake in the lake. ||23||
Accepting those words of her husband,
that lotus-eyed woman wore a garment of lotus fibers and bore her hair in a single braid.
Śrīdhara: *Samādāya* means having taken up or brought. *Sarajam* means soiled. *Veṇībhūtān* means those that have become matted locks. ||24||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Having taken up, that is, having brought [it]. ||24||
And with her limbs covered in mud and her breasts mottled,
she entered the lake of Sarasvatī, a reservoir of auspicious waters.

Śrīdhara: That [place] in which the two breasts are variegated and discolored; or, that in which the auspicious waters of Sarasvatī rest, or alternatively, that in which there are auspicious reservoirs of water and aquatic creatures. This is the sequential composition. Viśvanātha: Not explained.
Within the palace on the lake, he beheld one thousand maidens,
all of them in the bloom of youth and possessing the fragrance of lotuses.

Śrīdhara: Having plunged into it there, she beheld a wonder. She spoke to him with ten verses beginning with "Within the lake" (sāntaḥ sarasi). [The word] *utpalagandhayaḥ* means having the fragrance of lotuses (*kamala*). (26)
The sequential arrangement: "With an interval" constitutes a pair [of verses]. ||26||
Viśvanātha: [This portion] has not been explained.
Having seen her, the women rose up suddenly and said with palms joined in reverence: "We are your servants; command us, what shall we do?"
Śrīdhara: "We are your maidservants and attendants; command us," the women said to him. ||27||

*Commentary on the Composition:* Viśvanātha explains the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) as follows: "Instruct us, your maidservants; what shall we do for you? Alternatively, it means: "Instruct us—that is, command us—to serve you. (27)
Having bathed that high-minded woman with a most precious bath,
those givers of honor presented her with two spotless, new silk garments.
Śrīdhara: And then, by means of bathing—namely, with oil and other substances suitable for bathing. ||28||
The sequential arrangement: "By bathing," etc., forms a couplet. ||28||
Viśvanātha: By means of bathing—referring to the oil and other substances suitable for bathing—they gave them ornaments and such to wear;
and they gave food and drink for them to eat. ||28||
Excellently precious, most excellent, and radiant ornaments;
food endowed with every quality, and drink like the nectar of immortality.

Śrīdhara: "Parardhyāni" means most excellent; "varīyāṃsi" means those things dear to him; "dyumanti" means radiant or luminous. "Pānam" means that which is to be drunk; "amṛtam" means sweet; "āsavam" means intoxicating. ||29||
Regarding the sequence of composition: in many places, the reading is "parārdhyāni" (the most excellent). ||29||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
Now, [he saw] his own self in the mirror, wearing a garland and stainless garments, free from passion, having had rites for auspiciousness performed, and being highly honored by maidens.
Madhva saw [him] in a mirror. ||30||

Śrīdhara: The ellipsis is "he saw his own self in the mirror. He qualifies the self with four attributes. "Kṛtasvastyayana" means one for whom auspicious rites have been performed. The masculine gender [of the compound] is due to its grammatical coordination with the word *ātman*. (30)
The sequence of composition: now, the group of four beginning with "In the mirror" (athādarśe). ||30||
Viśvanātha: The ellipsis "he saw his own self" is to be supplied. ||30||
Having bathed and performed the ritual head-bath, he was adorned with all ornaments:
his neck graced by a golden coin-necklace, his arms encircled by bracelets, and his feet with tinkling golden anklets.

Śrīdhara: This is an elaboration of the word "viraja" (free from dust). "Snātam" means having bathed and washed after anointing the body with unguents. "Kṛtaśiraḥsnāna-abhyaṅgaḥ" refers to one by whom the head-bath and the oil massage have been performed. "Bhūṣita" (adorned) is explained here as follows: "niṣkaṃ" means a golden ornament; he who has a necklace (*padaka*) upon his neck. ||31||
The sequential arrangement: having performed the head-bath, one performs a bath of all the limbs with oil and other substances, beginning from the head downwards. ||31||
Viśvanātha: Some Western women do not bathe their heads; in order to prevent this, he says: "having performed the head-bath" (kṛtaśiraḥsnāna). ||31||
It was adorned with a golden girdle set with many jewels resting upon her hips, as well as with a highly precious necklace and armlets.

Śrīdhara: [She is] with that [city] which possesses many jewels; [and] with *rucaka*, an auspicious substance such as saffron and the like. This is stated in the Viśvaprakāśa: "The word *rucaka* refers to an auspicious substance, a neck ornament, or a tooth."
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: With a girdle (*kāñcī*) placed upon the hips—that is, fastened above—and with a *rucaka*, which is an auspicious object (the *Viśvakośa* states: "A *rucaka* is an auspicious object, a neck ornament, or a tooth"); [with these she shines].
Her face shone with beautiful teeth, lovely eyebrows, and eyes with smooth,
glistening outer corners that rivaled the sheaths of lotuses, while dark locks of hair graced it.

Śrīdhara: The words *sudatā*, *subhruvā*, and *cakṣuṣā* are used in the singular because they denote species (*jāti*). His face shines with these [features]. With what kind of eye? One whose outer corner (*apāṅga*), that is, the edge of the eye, is smooth, charming, and glossy. It rivals the calyx of a lotus.
Therefore, he touched the calyx of the lotus. ||33||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "By the eyes of the fair-browed one with beautiful teeth"—the singulars are used for the genus (*jāti*). "Smooth" means charming. "With that [eye] which has a glossy outer corner (*apāṅga*). It competes with the lotus bud.
Therefore, he touches the calyx of the lotus. ||33||
When she remembered Ṛṣabha, the beloved husband of the ṛṣis,
she went to where that Prajāpati dwelt together with his women.
Śrīdhara: And when he saw his husband, he then remembered that very place where he himself was also staying. ||34||
The sequence of composition: And therefore, he says "when" (yadā) to show that existence has arisen. ||34||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
Having then perceived herself before her husband surrounded by a thousand women, she fell into doubt regarding that yogic power.

Śrīdhara: Having perceived—that is, having seen—himself, and having seen her and his yogic course, that is, his yogic power, he felt doubt, [wondering] "What is this?", which is to say, amazement. ||35||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: But [he did not say] "going from the lake by means of the function of his feet"; rather, his movement through yoga is indeed marvelous. *Niśāmya* means having seen; that is, having seen his very movement through yoga and his yogic power.
Doubt—that is, the wonder of how this could have come to pass. ||35||
He beheld her, who had performed her cleansing bath, shining as never before,
bearing her own natural beauty with her lovely breasts veiled.
Śrīdhara: That sage [beheld her] wearing that very same form she had possessed prior to her marriage;
she whose beautiful breasts were covered and veiled. In an alternative reading, however, it is a specific description of her form.

As for the sequence of the composition: "He [beheld] her"—this constitutes a *yugmaka* (couplet). The reason for her being unprecedented [in appearance] is indicated by the word "ātmanaḥ" (of herself).

In the commentary, the phrase "prior to marriage" and so forth is understood through the natural force of the suffix *vat* in the word *apūrvavat*. For its "novelty" (*apūrvatva*) is indeed in relation solely to the state consisting of austerity (*tapomaya*). (36)

Viśvanātha: The meaning is that the sage was beholding her bearing exactly the same form as his own had been prior to the wedding. She was one whose beautiful breasts were covered and veiled. In the neuter reading, this is an adjective qualifying "form" (rūpa). ||36||
Attended by a thousand Vidyādharīs and beautifully dressed, the slayer of enemies, his heart filled with devotion, caused her to ascend that celestial chariot.
Śrīdhara: She whose two garments are beautiful; he in whom the emotion of love has arisen; O slayer of enemies, O conqueror of desire! (37)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: O slayer of enemies, O conqueror of desire! ||37||
In that celestial chariot, his majesty unimpaired, devoted to his beloved and with his body attended by Vidyadhara women,
he shone like a lake filled with clusters of blooming white water-lilies.
Like the lord of stars situated in the sky, surrounded by the stars.
Madhvaḥ: He who has raised up the waves; he who is not to be surpassed; he who is endowed with the supreme wave of nectar. ||38||

Śrīdhara: In that celestial chariot (vimāna), the sage shone, his majesty and sovereignty unimpaired, his body well-nourished and served. Like a full moon, the sage was as radiant and exceedingly beautiful as a cluster of blooming white water-lilies; the chariot was like the sky, and [the attendants] were like stars.
Those women are to be understood as having eyes like white water-lilies. ||38||

The sequential composition: "the lord of the stars" (uḍupatiḥ)—here *uḍu* refers to Rohiṇī, and she is to be understood as occupying the position of the beloved; the word "beloved" (*priyā*) itself is implied in both instances. ||38||

Viśvanātha: In that celestial chariot (*vimāna*), the sage shone forth; he was one whose body had been attended to and served. He was as lovely and exceedingly beautiful as a cluster of blooming white water-lilies (*kumuda*). The sage was like the full moon, the celestial chariot like the sky, those women like the stars, and their eyes like the white water-lilies.
This is to be known. ||38||
Therefore, in the valleys of the lords of the kulaparvatas— the abodes of the eight world-guardians— which possess the charm of breezes that are friends to the god of love,
and which resound with the auspicious sound of falling celestial rivers, he was praised by the perfected ones (siddhas).
Surrounded by a multitude of excellent women, he sported for a long time like Kubera, the lord of wealth.

Śrīdhara: By that celestial chariot; on the ridges—that is, in the caves—of Meru, the king of the principal mountains, which is the playground of the eight world-protectors; in those [ridges] whose loveliness and beauty are enhanced by the breeze that is the friend of the bodiless god of love—a wind that is cool and fragrant; while being praised and extolled by the Siddhas.
Accompanied by a multitude of beautiful women— a collection of the finest jewels— he took delight in those waters where the auspicious sound arose from the falling of the celestial Gaṅgā.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: With that celestial chariot (vimāna), he took delight. Meru, the king of the Kulācala mountains, is the "bearer of heaven" (dyudhru); on those [mountains] where the sound of Śiva arose from the falling of the Gaṅgā from above, he was accompanied by a multitude of women (lalanā). ||39||
In Vaiśraṃbhaka, Surasana, Nandana, Puṣpabhadraka,
Mānasa, and Caitrarathya, he took delight, joined in pleasure with Rāmā.
Śrīdhara: [He was] sporting in the divine gardens such as Vaiśrambhaka and in the Mānasa lake; the sequence of the composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: In the divine gardens such as Vaiśrambhaka and in the Mānasa lake. ||40||
Moving through the worlds in a radiant, vast celestial chariot that went wherever he desired, he surpassed the inhabitants of the heavens, like the wind.
Śrīdhara: "Atyaśeta" means having transcended and remained beyond. ||41||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: *atyaśeta* means he surpassed or exceeded [him]. ||41||
What is difficult for those men of unrestrained minds to achieve,
by whom the feet of the Lord of the Tīrthas— the refuge that transcends all calamity— have been taken as their support?
Śrīdhara: [This refers to] the wise ones of unrestrained mind. "Vyasanam" means saṃsāra; "atyaya" is that from which there is transcendence.

Regarding the sequence of the composition: "kim" (what) [is it]? For those of unrestrained mind, because their minds are not bound by other expectations, they have attained steadfastness (*dhairya*) in their own refuge. Or rather, it refers to those whose minds are free from dullness in all respects.
The terms "one whose feet are the ford" (*tīrthapada*) and "one who has transcended calamity" (*vyasanātyaya*) serve to exclude the possibility of difficulty in accomplishment;
for what is intended is the attainment of all things preceded by the removal of all obstacles. (42)
Viśvanātha: [This refers to] those of unrestrained minds whose thoughts are not bound to anything other than his feet. ||42||
Having surveyed the entire sphere of the earth according to its own configuration,
the great yogi, filled with many wonders, returned to his hermitage.

Śrīdhara: *prekṣayitvā* means having shown or displayed. *Gola* means a sphere or circle. *Svasaṃsthayā* means by its own configuration, that is, by the arrangement of the continents, regions (*varṣa*), and so forth; [he saw it] for as large as it is. *Bahūny āścaryāṇi yasmin tam* (that which contains many wonders)—the sequence of these words has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "Gola" means a sphere. To whatever extent it exists by its own configuration—that is, by the arrangement of continents, regions, and so forth—to that same extent [it is described]. ||43||
Having divided himself ninefold, he took delight for many series of years as if they were a single moment, sporting with the human woman Rāmā, who was eager for sexual union.
Śrīdhara: Having divided himself ninefold, he made himself into nine distinct parts. ||44||

The sequential arrangement: Viśvanātha, through the predominance of various qualities in the birth of each respective offspring, becomes ninefold; having divided himself into nine distinct forms, he exists in nine ways. (44)
Reclining upon that excellent, pleasure-inducing couch in the celestial chariot,
she did not perceive the passage of time while united with her beloved husband.
Regarding the term *madhvaḥ*: others have not explained the designation that one who has reached sixteen years of age is called *āvīcya*.
Thus, through the power of yoga, while the couple were sporting together...
A hundred autumns passed by for those two who were slightly languid with desire.
Śrīdhara: The autumns—that is, the years—passed by as if only slightly. ||46||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: They passed by slightly, as it were. ||46||
The all-pervading Lord, the knower of the self, who knows all intentions, having divided his own form into nine parts, impregnated her with seed while contemplating her through his own being.

Śrīdhara: Contemplating with great affection by means of himself, in the form of half of his own body; for when that is so, there will be virtuous offspring. "Nodhā" means ninefold. "The knower of all intentions" (sarvasaṃkalpavit) means knowing her intention to have many children. And "Vibhu" means capable of acting accordingly.

And the meaning of the phrase "a knower of the Self" is that he is unattached even to her; for it is stated in the Smṛti: "A male is born when the male seed is in excess, and a female when the female seed is in excess. ||47||

The sequential composition: "In her" means one who knows that resolve of all—the Lord Brahmā and the Prajāpatis such as Marīci—arising from the desire for creation; likewise, one who knows both himself and the Blessed Lord, his own teacher; and she [the goddess] who will bring forth ninefold the seed that is her own self.
"O great sage, the sages will readily place their own selves within your vigor.
Together with my own partial portion, through your vigor, O great sage, I shall bring forth the compendium of principles (Tattvasaṃhitā) in your field, Devahūtī. Such indeed was his instruction.

Even though this is so, nevertheless, because he had not yet completed that [task], it is understood that [the Lord] anticipated a further request for that very thing from him as he was about to renounce the world. However, in the case of Śrī Devahūti, no specific meaning is perceived in the phrase "as long as you shall maintain my own splendor. (47)
Viśvanātha: "Meditating upon that woman" means that at the time of conception, by meditating on a woman, a female child will be born; thus, he knows her desire for a female offspring.
"By himself, through his intellect, [he is] a knower of the Self and dispassionate" means that because of his lack of passion, his semen is scanty; for this reason also—
A female offspring would be born. As it has been said—"When the male seed is in excess, a male is born;

when the female seed is in excess, a female is born"—the meaning is that he knows her intention for many offspring, being one who knows all intentions in nine ways (or ten ways); "vibhu" means capable in every respect. ||47||
Therefore, Devahūti immediately gave birth to female offspring;
they were all beautiful in every limb and possessed the fragrance of red lotuses.
Śrīdhara: Immediately after this; "sadyaḥ" means on that very same day. [They are those] whose all limbs are beautiful. ||48||
The sequential composition: "the husband" constitutes a pair of verses (yugmaka). ||48||
Viśvanātha: Always on the very same day. ||48||
Perceiving that her husband was about to go forth into homelessness, she, weeping and standing outside,
smiled with a heart distressed and consumed by grief.

Śrīdhara: Having observed [him] as he was about to renounce the world, and having reflected, she spoke with a smile on her face; however, the sequence of the composition is that she spoke with a heart that was inwardly distressed, agitated, pained, and tormented—this much has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: "Smayamāna" (smiling) [is used] because it is natural for her to smile upon seeing her husband; however, in reality, the meaning is that she was with a mind that was distressed (*viklava*), agitated (*vyākula*), and tormented (*vidūyamāna*). ||49||
Drawing lines upon the ground with her toe, which possessed the luster of a jeweled nail,
she spoke these gentle words while slowly suppressing her flow of tears.
Śrīdhara: Her feet, which possess beauty (*śrī*) through the jewels that are her very nails, scratch the earth; this indicates the characteristic of her distressing anxiety. (50)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Devahūti said:
"The Blessed One has fulfilled everything that he promised to me."
Moreover, you ought to grant safety to me who have sought refuge in you.
Śrīdhara: *Upovāha* means he has accomplished or brought about. "Fearlessness" (*abhayam*) means: "remove that fear which arises from future wretchedness and from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). ||51||
The sequence of composition: Now, in some places it is said that "the illustrious Devahūti spoke"; furthermore, "fearlessness" takes the form of a prayer for forgiveness. (51)
Viśvanātha: He brought about, that is, accomplished. ||51||
O Brahmin, let husbands worthy of you be sought by your sisters;
perhaps there may be someone for my sake to end my grief when you have departed for the forest.

Śrīdhara: In this regard, he expresses his wretchedness. He has fallen into a state of wretchedness, thinking, "Your daughters must themselves seek husbands who are their own equals and worthy. Accepting the fear of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), he says: "Someone... for the purpose of imparting knowledge that removes sorrow (*viśoka*). [He is burdened] by debts through women.
The meaning is: "By your remaining here for some time, might there perhaps be some son who knows Brahman? (52)
The sequence of the composition: He expresses his very prayer with the words "O Brahman. "To you" means by you;
"equal to your daughters" means suitable for them. (52)

Viśvanātha: The sense is that since they are to be sought by you yourself, I have no concern even for their marriage. For the sake of dispelling my grief—that is, for the removal of sorrow—I pray that you remain for a few days out of compassion, so that I might obtain from you some worthy son as well. ||52||
O Lord, enough of this time that has passed for me,
who, through attachment to the objects of the senses, have abandoned my higher self.

Śrīdhara: If it is argued, "Enjoy the objects of the senses; what is the use of the knowledge of Brahman?", he says in response: "Let this much suffice for her who has abandoned the Supreme Self"—that is, for me. (53)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might ask, "Why do you speak in this manner as if you still desire the pleasure of sense-objects from me?
To this, he says with shame: "In all this time, that addiction to the objects of the senses..."
Therefore, enough; for by her, through whom the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord, has been abandoned, such a vast period of time of mine has passed in utter futility—this is the sense. ||53||
Though I was attached to the objects of the senses, I have directed my devotion toward you;
although I did not know your supreme nature, may this nonetheless lead to my fearlessness.
Śrīdhara says: Lamenting his own actions, he speaks with these four verses beginning with "indriyārtheṣu. "Me" means by me.
"Paraṃ bhāvam" means you, who know the Supreme Brahman. ||54||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "O great devotee, by even a momentary association with you, people are liberated;
yet for me, despite [your presence] lasting for so many years, no deliverance has occurred. In this matter, these two factors alone are the cause."

She said: "Regarding 'the objects of the senses'—the meaning is that your supreme state, your great distinction, and your high status as a great devotee (mahā-bhāgavata) are such that you have set out to renounce every object of possessiveness in a mere moment. "Nevertheless"—even so, please show compassion toward me, who am an offender.
The state of being. ||54||
That very attachment which, when directed toward the wicked by means of a deluded intellect, is the cause of worldly existence,
becomes conducive to freedom from attachment when directed toward the virtuous.

Śrīdhara: He explains how there can be attachment even toward Abhayā with the words "attachment" (*saṅga*). [The verse says: "By those of poor intellect, the eternal... (*adhiyājñānena sanātanaḥ*, *Ha. Bha. Vi.* 10.261). By people of poor intellect (*adhiyā*), meaning those devoid of discrimination, that which is produced among the wicked—which is the cause of saṃsāra, consisting of attachment, the enjoyment of sense objects, and so forth—is meant. The word "even" (*api*) is used in the sense of "also" (*eva*).
If that [mind] is directed toward the virtuous, then it becomes capable—meaning it is empowered—for detachment and for the destruction of saṃsāra. ||55||

The sequence of composition: "Saṅga" (association). Viśvanātha explains: "That very [association], even that which is preceded by [the influence of] the limbs [of poetry]"—this is the meaning. Furthermore, since the power of the object does not depend upon the intellect, he says "saṅga" (association), implying that association with a virtuous person such as yourself ought not to be fruitless under any circumstances.
Thus; "even by means of *adhiyā*, that is, through ignorance"—this connects with both instances. ||55||
He whose action here does not conduce to dharma, nor to dispassion,
nor to service at the feet of the Tīrthaṅkara— he is indeed dead even while living.

Śrīdhara: For one whose action proceeds from innate nature (*svabhāva*), it does not conduce to the goal of *dharma*, nor does it become oriented toward *dharma*; even in that case, it does not conduce to detachment (*virāga*) by means of the *dharma* of desirelessness (*niṣkāma-dharma*). And by that means, it would not culminate in service to Hari, the Lord whose feet are the sacred ford (*tīrthapada*). Thus...
The meaning. ||56||
The sequence of composition: "The holy ones (sādhu) are those whose feet are sacred sites (tīrtha)," because of the statement beginning with, "They make even [ordinary] places into sacred sites. (56)

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But why are you thus disenchanted? You possess such great wealth; therefore, enjoy the objects of the senses. To this, he says: "Not so" (na hi). For one whose activity—the functioning of the body, senses, and so forth—is not for the sake of dharma and the other goals [of life]... ||56||
Surely I have been firmly deceived by the illusory power of the Blessed One,
since, having encountered you who grant liberation, I did not seek release from bondage.
Śrīdhara: I am not one who desires liberation; I have not formed the wish to be released. ||57||

The sequence of the composition: "Even though she has somehow attained association with the Blessed One, I am yet deceived by even a fraction of ignorance regarding His majesty; therefore, the Blessed One’s own māyā is the cause here"—this is the meaning.
Viśvanātha provides an illustration for that: "I myself say: 'Though living, I am dead; I do not desire liberation.'"
"I have not even formed the mere desire to leave you," she said with tears and a faltering voice. ||57||
Thus ends the twenty-third [chapter], which is well-connected for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord.

Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Repentance of Devahūtī" in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, within the Third Book of the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsya, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa Śrīmad Bhāgavatam.
The Twenty-third Chapter.
Now begins the Twenty-fourth Chapter:
The Renunciation of Kardama in the Dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
Maitreya said: To his daughter Manu, who was thus speaking words of despondency, the compassionate sage spoke, remembering the words uttered by Śukla.
Madhvā is called Mālinī, Śālinī, Mālyā, Āryā, and Bhāryā. ||1||
Śrīdhara:
Then, in the twenty-fourth [chapter], he describes the birth of Kapila and his father’s renunciation after obtaining his son's permission for the sake of liberation from the three debts.
The praiseworthy Śālinī [verse]: "It was spoken by the White One (Śukla), together with me, through a portion of my own self," and so forth. ||1||
The sequence of composition: Regarding the word *śālinīm*, from the root *śāḍ* meaning "to praise," *śāla* means "praising"; that which possesses this is *śālinī*.
[The phrase] "remembering what was uttered by Śuklā" is used because of his one-pointed meditation upon her. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the twenty-fourth [chapter], the birth of Kapila is proclaimed according to the word of Brahmā;
the marriage of Kardama’s daughter, his renunciation, and the hymn follow immediately after.
The praiseworthy Śālinī [meter]. It was proclaimed by Śukla, beginning with "together with me, through a portion of my own self," and so forth. ||1||
The sage said:
"Do not distress yourself thus, O blameless princess;
the Blessed One, the Imperishable, will soon enter your womb."
Śrīdhara: Thus, do not grieve; do not feel distress toward yourself, thinking, "I am unfortunate. [It will happen] from nearby, that is, soon. ||2||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: O blameless one! Do not grieve in this way; do not cause yourself distress. (2)
You are firm in your vows; may prosperity be yours through self-restraint and discipline.
Worship the Lord with austerity, wealth, charity, and faith.
Śrīdhara: By *dama*, meaning the restraint of the senses; by *niyama*, meaning one’s own duty (*svadharma*); and by *tapāṃsi*, meaning the giving of wealth—by these. (5)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: And she says that you are not like any other ordinary woman who has failed to perform meritorious deeds—"In your previous birth you were one who maintained her vows, having performed the observances of vows and so forth; therefore, even in this birth, prosperity shall be yours."
That pure one, who spreads my glory, has been propitiated by you;
he, compassionate and devoted to Brahman, shall sever the knot of your heart.

Śrīdhara: Being the son of Audarya, he will cut—meaning sever—the knot of the heart, which consists of consciousness and insentience and is characterized by egoism, that is, the bondage; for he is so called because he "causes Brahman to be eaten," meaning he teaches it. ||4||
The sequence of the composition: "He by you" means he who is never able to forget that [truth]. Brahman is the reality of the Blessed Lord. ||4||
Viśvanātha: Being "audarya," born from the belly [as a son], he untied the "hṛdayagranthi," the bond characterized by egoism; being a "brahmabhāvana," he was a teacher of Brahman. ||4||
Maitreya said: Devahūti, having fully accepted with faith the instruction of the Prajāpati out of reverence, devoted herself to the Supreme Person, the immutable Guru.
Śrīdhara: Having placed his trust and having become convinced. ||5||
The sequence of composition: the message, the instruction, and the Guru, who is to be contemplated as the Guru. ||5||
Viśvanātha: [He is] the messenger, the instructor; him who, having been a son, will become a teacher. ||5||
After a long period of time had passed, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana,
having entered the seed of Kardama, was born from her like fire from wood.
Even in his descents as Madhva and others, the body of Hari arises from [the womb of] Śukla and so forth;
nevertheless, while residing in Śukla, he enters the body of the mother.

"Having dissolved the white [element] right there, the Lord Viṣṇu, whose nature is absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna), arises in due time, deluding the world. Thus it is said in the *Mahāvārāha-purāṇa*.
"Like fire in wood"—this is the illustration for its state as the mother residing within the individual (vyaktisthānamātṛtva). (6)
Śrīdhara: When a great many, indeed a vast amount, of time has elapsed. "Kārdama" means related to *kardama* (mud).
Krama-sandarbha: "Bahutithaḥ" refers to a time that completes many [units].

*Bahupūgagaṇasaṅghasya tithuk* (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.52) is a rule from Pāṇini’s section on ordinal numbers. *Vīrya* means the power of devotion; "attained by that" (*tadāpanna*) means brought under its control (*vaśībhūta*). ||6||
Viśvanātha: "Bahutitha" means when a great length of time—filling many [periods]—has elapsed.
This is according to the rule *tithug* (Pāṇini 5.2.52), which applies to words such as *bahu*, *pūga*, *gaṇa*, and *saṅgha*.
"Kārdama vīrya" refers to the power of devotion belonging to Kardama; he has been brought under control by that [power].
The meaning is as follows: just as fire exists within wood, he who dwells within her in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) manifested in the form of a son; this is the meaning. ||6||
Then the clouds played musical instruments in the sky;
the Gandharvas sang his praises, and the Apsarases danced with joy.
Śrīdhara: "Ghanāghanā" is a single word meaning raining clouds. They sang and they danced. (7)
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Ghanaghana" refers to thundering clouds; the meaning is "the gods.
Amara states: "Ghanāghana" means rain-bearing clouds. ||7||
Divine flowers fell from the sky, offered by those who move through the air;
all the quarters became serene, as did the waters and the minds.
Śrīdhara: "Apavarjitāḥ" means liberated. ||8||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "Avarjitāḥ" means sent forth. ||8||
The Self-Existent One, together with the sages Marīci and the others, went to that hermitage of Kardama, which was surrounded by the Sarasvatī river.
Śrīdhara: "Pariśritam" means surrounded. ||9||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: *Pariśritam* means surrounded or encircled. ||9||

O slayer of enemies, the wise and unborn self-sovereign [Brahmā], through his portion of being, was born from the Blessed One— the Supreme Brahman— in order to communicate the enumeration of the principles of reality.
Honoring his intended action with a pure mind,
and with his vital breaths rejoicing, he addressed Kardama as follows:
Śrīdhara: Having arrived, what did he do? He says [the answer] in two verses beginning with "the Blessed One" (*bhagavantam*).

For the purpose of specifically making known (*vijñaptyai*) the Sāṅkhya—that which contains the enumeration of the principles (*tattva*)—the unborn Brahmā, the self-ruling one whose knowledge is established by itself, knowing the Blessed One to have been born...

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the two verses is as follows: praising and honoring his intended action, characterized by vital breaths and senses that were greatly rejoicing, he addressed Kardama— and by the use of the word "and" (*ca*),
Devahūtī as well.
The sequence of composition: "To the Blessed One" constitutes a pair [of verses]. ||10||

Viśvanātha: By "sattva," the meaning is by means of a portion consisting of pure *sattva*, and not by his complete nature. For the sake of the specific knowledge (*vijñapti*) of that which possesses the enumeration (*saṃkhyāna*) of the principles—that is, for the sake of making it known in detail—he was born, manifested; [the author] knowing this, honors and worships him.
With his vital breaths and senses greatly rejoicing, he was observed to have made mud and to have called out "Devahūti."
Brahmā said:
"O dear one, you have rendered me honor with complete sincerity,
since you, O giver of respect, have accepted my words with due reverence."
Śrīdhara: In that regard, with five verses beginning with "by you," he speaks to Kardama: *apacitiḥ* means worship was performed;
*yat* means because; *nirvyalīkataḥ* means without guile, [you] accepted it properly. ||12||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: *Apacitiḥ* means service was rendered. ||12||
Only this much service should be performed by sons toward their father;
they should assent to the words of the guru with reverence, saying, "So be it."
Śrīdhara: [The word] "anumanyeta" (he should permit) is used only for this much. ||13||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: By "sons" (putrakaiḥ) is meant good sons. "Certainly" (bāḍham) means: "I shall do exactly as you command. ||13||
"O child, these true daughters of yours, slender-waisted,
shall multiply this creation manifold through their own powers."
Śrīdhara: "In manifold ways, through their powers and lineages, they will cause [the world] to flourish and increase.
The sequence of the composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Even if your sons had been born, even then this creation would not have increased in this manner.
He says "these" to explain how the creation will be expanded by those daughters: "by means of their powers," that is, by means of portions (aṃśaiḥ) possessing power. ||14||
Therefore, bestow your daughters today upon the foremost of sages according to their character and according to their preference; spread your fame throughout the earth.
Śrīdhara [explains]: "To the foremost sages, such as Marīci and others. (15)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. [Śukadeva says:
"O Sage, I know that primordial Person who has descended through his own *māyā*, bearing a body as a treasure-trove for all beings—that one known as Kapila."
Śrīdhara says: "But the son is the Lord himself," as he states in the verse beginning with "I know. [He knows] the treasure, the storehouse that grants all desires. (16)
The sequential arrangement: within oneself, there is *māyā* and compassion; by means of that [compassion]. ||16||

Viśvanātha: By His own *māyā* alone, He bears [Himself] as a treasure-trove and storehouse for all beings, bestowing all desired objects and granting sattvic knowledge and other virtues; the meaning is that, in reality, He who possesses an eternal body has thus descended. ||16||
Uprooting the tangles of karmic actions through the yoga of primordial wisdom and discerning consciousness,
he has golden hair, lotus-eyes, and lotus-feet marked with the lotus seal.
O Mānavī, this slayer of Kaiṭabha has entered your womb;
having severed the knot of ignorance and doubt, he shall roam the earth.
In the *Kāpileya*, it is stated: "But right knowledge is Sāṅkhya; that is also called Yoga. [1718]

Śrīdhara says: He speaks to Devahūti in three verses. *Vijñāna* is the direct realization taught in the scriptures of knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*), and *yoga* is the means; by that [yoga], he will "uproot"—that is, tear out—the "tangles" or roots of actions, which are the latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
His lotus-feet are joined with the *padma-mudrā*. (17) O daughter of Manu!
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the lack of knowledge of one's true nature; doubt and false knowledge are likewise [forms of ignorance]. This constitutes the "knot of your heart" (*hṛdayagranthi*).
The sequence of the composition should be understood as follows: [the Lord] cuts through ignorance and the other [afflictions] of others.
Because the place of the Lord’s manifestation consists of pure goodness (*śuddhasattva*), such things are not possible there.
However, it should be discerned that instructions and the like are given for the sake of the world's welfare, as was the case with Uddhava and others. ||18||

Viśvanātha says: He speaks in response to Devahūti—"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is indirect (*parokṣa*), while "realization" (*vijñāna*) is direct (*aparokṣa*); these two constitute *yoga*, meaning the means. By that [means], one should "uproot"—that is, pull out—the "matted locks," which is to say the roots or latent impressions (*vāsanās*) of actions.
"Ignorance" (*avidyā*) consists of ignorance of one's true nature, doubts, and false cognitions; [the world] is composed of that.
The knot of the heart. ||1718||
This lord of the hosts of Siddhas, highly esteemed by the teachers of Sāṅkhya, shall go by the name Kapila in the world; he is the increaser of your fame.
Śrīdhara: Being highly esteemed and well-honored, he will go—that is, he will attain [his goal]. ||19||

The sequential arrangement is as follows: "This [is it]. However, there is another distinction: Kapila, the author of the system, is not well-regarded because he contradicts the Vedas regarding the doctrine of God; for indeed, the author of the commentary has cited a statement from the *Padma Purāṇa* to that effect:
Kapila, known as Vāsudeva, proclaimed the Sāṅkhya system of reality to the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as to Bhṛgu and others;
likewise, he taught it to Āsuri, augmented by the meaning of all the Vedas.
And Kapila, as well as others, proclaimed the Sāṅkhya system—which is contrary to all the Vedas and bolstered by fallacious reasoning—to Āsuri and another. (19)

Viśvanātha: This [Kapila] is highly esteemed; however, another perfected being (siddha), the author of the system Kapila, is not well-regarded because his doctrine of non-divinity contradicts the Vedas. Indeed, the commentator has cited a statement from the *Padma Purāṇa* to this effect: "Kapila, known as Vāsudeva, is the reality..."
He indeed proclaimed Sāṅkhya to Brahmā and the other gods, as well as to Bhṛgu and the others;

likewise, he taught it to Āsuri, augmented by the meanings of all the Vedas. But another Kapila proclaimed a different Sāṅkhya to another Āsuri, one augmented by fallacious reasoning and contrary to all the Vedas.
Maitreya said:
Having comforted them, the Creator of the World, together with Nārada and the Kumāras,
traveled by means of his swan-vehicle to the supreme abode of the three-fold light.
Śrīdhara: The word "with the Kumāras" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. And "together with Nārada" means accompanied by Nārada.

Having stationed Marīci and the others for the sake of the wedding, Haṃsa—Brahmā—went forth together with these five lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika). "Tridhāma" refers to the third abode, heaven; its "parāṃ kāṣṭhām" is the highest limit.
To the world of truth (Satyaloka). ||20||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The words "with the Kumāras" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. Having established Marīci and the others for the sake of marriage, Haṃsa—Brahmā—together with these five lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*), went to the third abode (*tridhāma*).
From that [heaven], he goes to Satyaloka, which is even higher. ||20||
When Śatadhṛti had departed, O Kṣattṛ, Kardama, urged by him,
then gave his daughter to the creators of the universe (the Prajāpatis) exactly as he had been instructed.
Śrīdhara: [The term] "śatadhṛti" refers to Brahmā. ||21||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: To the creators of the universe (viśvasṛjām), that is, from the creators of the universe (viśvasṛgbhyaḥ), [he spoke] as declared—that is, without transgressing what is declared in the scriptures—unto Śatadhṛti, that is, Brahmā. ||21||
He gave Kalā to Marīci, and then Anasūyā to Atri;
he bestowed Śraddhā upon Aṅgiras, and Havirbhū upon Pulastya.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not provided a commentary.
Kramasandarbha: All [principles], beginning with *kalā*, are to be understood as being the powers (*śakti*) of the Blessed Lord. ||22||
He bestowed upon Pulaha a wife named Gati who was endowed with yoga, and upon Kratu a virtuous wife named Kriyā; he gave Khyāti to Bhṛgu, and Arundhatī to Vasiṣṭha.
Śrīdhara: "Yuktām" means suitable; "ayacchat" means he gave. ||23||

The sequential arrangement: Arundhatī is to be understood as the power of wifely devotion (pātivratya-śakti), for she is so named because she performs the fulfillment of her husband's wishes; thus, the terms "yuktām" (the disciplined one) and "satīm" (the virtuous one) are to be applied everywhere. ||23||
Viśvanātha: "Yuktām" means appropriate or fitting. ||23||
He gave to Atharvan the peace (śānti) by which the sacrifice is extended;
he welcomed the eminent brahmins who had performed their marriages along with their wives.
Śrīdhara: *Vitanyate* means it is expanded or made prosperous; the meaning is "the deity presiding over peace. *Samalālayat* means he gratified or satisfied [her]. ||24||
The sequential arrangement is thus: "And likewise, 'yayā' (by which). ||24||
Viśvanātha: "By this" (yayā) means that through peace alone, penance, sacrifice, knowledge-sacrifice, and so forth, become expanded and fruitful. ||24||
Then, O Kṣattṛ, those ṛṣis, having invited him after he had taken a wife,
departed for their respective hermitage circles, filled with joy.
Śrīdhara: Having invited and questioned [them], they attained joy (*nandi*), that is, gladness. ||25||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Having invited and questioned Nandin, [he asked about] joy (*harṣa*). ||25||
And he, perceiving that the Bull among the Gods had descended as the one who appears in the three ages,
approached him in a secluded place, bowed down, and addressed him.
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*, it is stated: "He is called 'Triyuga' because he descends [as an incarnation] during three of the four ages. (26)
Śrīdhara: And that sage [saw] Viṣṇu, who appears in three ages, in a secluded place, in private. ||26||
Kramasaṃdarbha: not explained.
Viśvanātha: And he is the Sage (Muni). ||26||
Ah! For those who are being tormented in hell by their own inauspicious deeds, the deities surely become gracious here after a long period of time.
Śrīdhara: Of those being tormented—that is, intensely burned—in hell, which is to say, in saṃsāra, by their own inauspicious sins. ||27||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [The Lord] says with three verses beginning with "Aho" that when You appeared in my house, Your unconditional grace alone was the cause, and that there is no quality whatsoever in me: "In this world, people are of three kinds... [and so forth].

Worshippers of other deities, worshippers of Brahman, and worshippers of the Blessed One are seen. Among them, he shows the state of the fruit of the worship of the first [group]: "Of those being cooked in hell and being scorched intensely in saṃsāra—even if they should find favor in even a single birth, that too..."
After a much longer period of time, and not immediately; and consequently, they also bestow the various fruits desired by each individual. ||27||
Ascetics strive to behold that state in empty dwellings through right yogic concentration, which has ripened over many births.
That very Blessed One, disregarding our offense today,
has been born in the homes of commoners— he who nourishes the side of his own kin.

Śrīdhara: Why? Because it is known that all the deities are pleased; he says this in two verses because of the attainment of what was unattainable. Through "well-perfected" [practice] matured over many births; through "proper yoga," which is the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), and through "concentration" (*samādhi*), which is one-pointedness of mind; in "empty houses," that is, in secluded places.
Of you, whose [it is] the state. ||28||

"Without taking into account—that is, disregarding—insult, contempt, or insignificance, he says: 'This is indeed appropriate for you,' because you are one who nourishes the side of your own devotees; such is he. (29)

The sequence of composition: [The author] says with a pair of verses beginning with "bahv" that although even common deities become pleased after a long time, You are not like them. Therein, he states Your uniqueness with the first [verse], which describes the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) as being subject solely to the relationship with Your own devotees; with the second [verse], [he speaks] of Your own people.
He sides with the faction of pure devotees. ||28||

Viśvanātha: He says "many" because for those of the second [category], perfection is possible only through many births. Since you, O Lord, have made your own state—the undifferentiated essential nature—directly perceptible to the seer through the yoga of perfect samādhi, we are among those of the third [category].

Extremely slow-witted, he says that even that greatness of His compassion is indeed boundless: "He Himself... Having disregarded—that is, not counting—the slighting by the world, which is a lack of respect for Him and a sense of His own insignificance, He says: "This is Your very nature:
You cause even those who practice devotion toward Me to excel. This refers to You, who take the side of Your own devotees.
"‘You nourish’ means you recognize them as your own; such is the sense. ||2829||
"You have descended into my house to make your own word true,
O Blessed One, the increaser of human beings, desiring to bestow knowledge upon your devotees."

Śrīdhara: He elaborates on this in two verses. You have descended of your own accord in order to make true your own statement, "I shall become your son," while desiring to bring forth knowledge and the means of knowledge, namely Sāṅkhya. (30)
The sequential arrangement [of the text] is the reason for its being such a statement; [it applies] even to Brahmā and others who are the objects of refuge for devotees such as ourselves. ||30||

Viśvanātha: He elaborates on this very point with two verses. Desiring to compose the Sāṅkhya, which is knowledge and the means to knowledge, he [the Lord] increases the honor and respect for devotees even over those who possess knowledge, because knowledge devoid of devotion is ineffective.
The meaning is: "because of establishing [it]. ||30||
O Blessed One, those very forms of yours are beautiful—
whatever forms please your own people, even though you are formless.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: Whatever forms, such as those of Brahmā and others, are pleasing to one's own people, those very forms are suitable for you to manifest; for it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* that "Hari becomes manifest there in whatever place is established as the Truth. (31)
Śrīdhara: Those forms of yours which are extraordinary, such as the four-armed form and others, are indeed your beautiful and appropriate forms.
And those forms resembling human beings which are pleasing to your own kin—those too are pleasing to you; this is the meaning. "Of the formless" means of one who is devoid of a material form. ||31||

The sequential arrangement [of the meaning] is as follows: whatever forms are pleasing to Your own kin, those alone are Your beautiful and appropriate forms, and no others; this is the sense. Furthermore, other forms—such as the loathsome form manifested for Rantideva—are to be understood as being of that same nature.
For it is precisely its illusory nature (*māyikatva*) that is stated there: "The lords of the three worlds appeared to those desiring fruit as the bestowers of fruit;
they were the Māyā fashioned by Viṣṇu"—so says the commentary (*ṭīkā*).

The lords of the three worlds, such as Brahmā and others, were first sent by Māyā in the forms of outcastes and the like for the purpose of testing His fortitude; this is the reason for their lack of beauty. Regarding the term "formless" (*arūpiṇaḥ*), the commentary explains it as being devoid of material form (*prākṛtarūparahita*), which implies His transcendence of the material realm (*aprākṛtatva*).
The sense is that it is not the case that such a form is unfit because it is impossible for it to be contemptible or because it is pleasing to one's own kin. ||31||

Viśvanātha: Those very forms of yours, who are eternally being-consciousness-bliss (*nitya-saccidānanda*), are "beautiful" (*abhirūpa*); that is to say, they are appropriate and consist of the density of being, consciousness, and bliss. These are the ones that please your own people; other forms, which do not please them, are in reality not your true forms.

They do exist, but they are merely illusory; for the revered teacher’s (Svāmīcaraṇa) commentary states that he is "formless," meaning devoid of a material form. Even though the form of Vairāja is pleasing as an object of meditation for certain devotees in the initial stage, it is not pleasing in the long run; therefore, even that [form] is [illusory].
Because form is ordinary, it is not the Blessed One's own form; such is the intention. ||31||
Truly, you are one whose footstool is always worthy of salutation by the wise who desire to know the ultimate reality;
you are the embodiment of sovereignty, detachment, fame, and awakening.
I take refuge in Pūrṇa, who is endowed with the glory of vigor.
Śrīdhara: One whose footstool is worthy of salutation; "filled" (pūrta) means complete with sovereignty and other qualities.
The sequence of words has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: While stating the characteristics of one who is beautiful and pleasing to the devotees...

He qualifies Śrī Kapiladeva with the word "you" (tvām): [he is] the great reservoir filled with the six qualities denoted by the word *bhaga*—consisting of sovereignty and so forth—which are of the nature of consciousness;
by means of that [reservoir], his essential form, which is full of the sixfold sovereignty, becomes the object of the devotees' salutations, worship, service, and so forth.
Thus it is illuminated that your form is indeed extraordinary. ||32||
The supreme Pradhāna, the Puruṣa, the Great One, Time, the Seer, the threefold one, the guardian of the worlds—
whose manifold expansion is followed by the experience of the Self.
I take refuge in Kapila, the power of Svachanda.
Madhva: Because he is encompassed by the Vedas, the Blessed Lord is called "Trivṛt" (the Threefold) by the wise.

Śrīdhara: Explaining [his] sovereignty and other attributes, he says: "The Supreme," meaning the Supreme Lord. The reason for this is that his powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are "self-willed," meaning they are under his own control. He states those very powers: "Pradhāna," which is in the form of *prakṛti* (primordial nature).
The Person is their presiding lord; the Great One is the form of the *mahat*-tattva; Time is their agitator;

the threefold is the form of the *ahaṃkāra*; and that which consists of the worlds is the protector. Thus, having described [the Self] through Māyā as having the nature of Pradhāna and so forth, [the text now describes its] state beyond phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*) by means of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
He said: [He is] one by whom the phenomenal world (prapañca), followed by the power of consciousness (cicchakti) through self-experience, has been dissolved into himself;
[he is] the "Seer" (kavi), meaning the omniscient witness of the manifestation and dissolution of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the rest. ||33||
The sequential arrangement: the poet is the individual soul (jīva). ||33||
Viśvanātha, while manifesting his sovereignty, says even something unconventional:
"But I take refuge in You alone, Kapila—even in that which is other than You, external in form, such as Pradhāna and the rest;
that Pradhāna which is the nature of Prakṛti, the Puruṣa who is the individual soul (jīva), the Mahat which is the form of the principle of Mahat-tattva, and Time."
Their agitator is the Poet (Kavi), whose form is the essence of the Sūtra, who is threefold, whose nature is the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra),

and who consists of the world-protectors such as Indra and the rest. Furthermore, because he is the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of the phenomenal world (prapañca), he is said to have the form of the phenomenal world— even though, by virtue of his own self-experience and conscious power (cicchakti), he stands outside the phenomenal world.

[He is] that by whom the manifold world (*prapañca*) has been followed and entered. Furthermore, because He is the cause of the manifold world, [the text] states that He is of the nature of the manifold world: "He whose powers, beginning with *māyā*, are independent and self-dependent.
This is because, by Your will alone, the entire manifold world has *māyā* and the other powers as its instrumental cause.

Since Māyā and the rest are non-different from that [Brahman] by virtue of being its powers (śakti), and since their effects are also non-different from it, the meaning is: "all this illusory form belongs to you alone, and it is unseemly. ||33||
Today I take leave of you, the lord of creatures; having had my debt discharged by you and my desires fulfilled,
I am now established upon the path of the wandering mendicant.
I shall wander, free from sorrow, joining you within my heart.

Śrīdhara: He requests permission for renunciation (*sannyāsa*). "I ask you" means that I ask whatever I have to ask. Since my debts—consisting of those toward the gods and others—which were incurred in the form of a son, have been discharged, I am one whose desires are fulfilled (*āptakāma*); therefore, [I seek] the path of those who wander forth, the renunciants (*sannyāsins*).
Resorting to the path, I shall wander about, yoking myself and remaining mindful of you. ||34||
The sequence of composition: here, "debt" consists of the fulfillment of the father's command. ||34||

Viśvanātha: The word *smābhiḥ* is used for the purpose of filling the meter. *Āpṛcche* means that I now, at this very moment, request permission for the sake of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). By you as the cause, I have descended; he whose debt consists of his father’s command in the form of "Create progeny" has been discharged. Furthermore, I am one whose desires are attained and whose heart's wish is fulfilled.
"Adopting the path of wandering mendicants and renunciants, I shall wander here and there, fixing my mind upon you and remembering you. Here, Śrī Kardama reflected thus in his mind:
"In my Lord, the one named Śukla, who is Śrī Nārāyaṇa himself, I have possessed a firm devotion to servitude since birth."
He dwells [therein]. Now that he has become my son, an irresistible affection will surely arise;
thus, the coexistence of servitude and parental affection is not conducive to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Furthermore, this Lord is entirely independent;
having plunged me into an ocean of grief, he will soon depart for the forest life. Therefore—

"Why should I not be the first to renounce? It is no fault of mine that I am departing, leaving behind the Lord who has descended into my home; for according to our Vaiṣṇava doctrine, the Lord to be worshipped is indeed dependent upon worship, and it is therefore more appropriate to exert great effort in the act of worship than even toward the object of worship itself."
Thinking, "I wish to provide him with a vessel that remains for eight watches in a secluded forest, free from obstacles," the Blessed Lord said:
"For what I have spoken is the authority for the world regarding both the mundane and the supramundane."
Then, O Sage, that which I spoke to you was born as the Truth.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: in the context of the world of truth, it refers to the object of knowledge as it truly is (*yathārthajñāna*). "Appearance" (*ābhāsa*) is synonymous with "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "light" (*āloka*), as well as being called the "appearance of the world" (*lokābhāsa*); such is the definition. ||35||

Śrīdhara: I have descended into your house specifically for the purpose of imparting knowledge; therefore, liberation is easily attained even while dwelling in your home. Yet, with the intention that you should go while constantly remembering Me—even if there is a persistent insistence that you must certainly depart—he says "by Me" in six verses. [This applies] to the true, worldly, and Vedic [realms].

And regarding worldly affairs, he demonstrates the authority of his own words: "Since I said to you, 'I shall become your son,' for that very reason, that has become *ṛta*—that is, the truth—just as it is; thus was my birth accepted. (35)

The sequence of the composition: "Whatever has been spoken by me is authoritative everywhere; therefore, for this very reason, I was born in your house. He demonstrates the cause of that [birth]: "That which I told you has also been accomplished. Otherwise, the authority of what I have spoken would be subject to deviation.
This is the state of affairs. And since there is validity [in my teaching], the intended meaning is: "Accept my instruction alone. ||35||
Viśvanātha: "O great sage! You desire to do exactly what I intend, because I have declared that everything must be abandoned and that my worship alone is to be performed by me. Thus he says:
"Indeed, that which has been definitely declared by me is: 'Having renounced all duties... (18.66).

That alone is the authority for the world through the *Ādigītā*, the *Upaniṣads*, and so forth—provided that there exists something truly transcendental (*alaukika*), supreme over all, and beyond the worldly. This is the meaning: "worldly" (*laukika*) refers to that which pertains to the world, namely the dharma characterized by the attainment of the three aims of life (*trivarga*); regarding that, even Manu and others have declared it to be the authority for the world.

The authority: When that dharma exists—which is extraordinary, distinct from the worldly, and characterized by the attainment of Me—it is precisely what has been spoken by Me that serves as the authority for the world regarding the supreme Bhāgavata dharma.
As it has been said: "Those very means for the attainment of the Self which have been proclaimed by the Blessed One... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.33).

Therefore, you have rightly reflected that you must depart, having renounced everything; this is the sense. He demonstrates the authority of his own words: "And for this very reason, that which I said—that I would become your son—has come to pass; that is indeed *ṛtam*, the truth. (35)
This is my birth in this world for the purpose of enumerating the principles for those seeking liberation from evil intent, so that they may attain the realization of the Self.
This path of the Self is unmanifest and has been lost for a long time;
know that this body has been assumed by me in order to set it forth again.

Śrīdhara: [The word] "know" (viddhi) is to be supplied from the subsequent verse [to complete the sense]: "Know that for the discernment of the principles (tattva-prasaṃkhyāna), which is esteemed by sages seeking liberation, [and which arises] from the signs of those with evil intentions. (36) Now, one might object:
this path of self-knowledge is already established from of old; it need not now be set forth as something new.
Regarding this, he says: "This [is]... The unmanifest is subtle. ||37||
The sequence of composition: "bhṛtam" means made manifest. ||37||

Viśvanātha states that [the Lord] makes known the purpose of His own incarnation: "Know" (viddhi)—this is the connection with the subsequent verse—for the sake of the discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) of the principles (*tattva*) which is conducive to the vision of the Self for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), [discerning them] from those of evil intent (*durāśaya*), that is, from those possessing a wicked subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). [The principles are: the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), the Subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the Lord (*īśvara*).

Even though there is no distinction between the embodied self and the body, the statement "the body has been sustained by me" is made according to worldly convention, following the principle that the divine intellect produces a sense of difference even where there is no difference.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities (guṇas) of the one devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Just as [the world] is grasped by the Māyā of the All-pervading Lord during its maintenance, creation, and destruction, so too should it be understood. //37//
Go as you wish, even though unbidden by me who have renounced all action;
having conquered death, which is so difficult to defeat, attain me for the sake of immortality.

Śrīdhara: "Kāmam" means according to your wish. "Āpṛṣṭaḥ" means permitted. Alternatively, the meaning is that just as you asked me for permission to go, so too have I asked you for permission to remain here.
By renouncing [action] in Me—that is, by the action surrendered to Me—one crosses over death through ignorance and attains immortality through knowledge.
For it is so stated in the Śruti: "He attains [it]. ||38||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: This has not been explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Having asked me"—the meaning is that just as you have asked me for permission to go, so too have I asked you for permission to remain here. How was it that I said, "Go"?

The sense is that even though you remain here, what you desire shall surely be accomplished; yet, if your mind still wishes to go, then by all means go. Devote yourself to immortality—for according to the Vedic scripture, "Having crossed over death through ignorance, one attains immortality through knowledge"—or rather, for the sake of immortality.

The sense is: although you have attained the status of my attendant—just as [the Lord] took birth as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others for the sake of being free from death—nevertheless, by virtue of your association with me, your birth will indeed come to pass. ||38||
Having perceived yourself as Me— the self-luminous one dwelling in the heart-cave of all beings—
by means of the Self within the very Self, you shall attain freedom from sorrow and fear.
Śrīdhara: And therefore, by perceiving Me, the Supreme, the Supreme Self, within yourself by means of your own self, you shall attain fearlessness, which is liberation. ||39||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Some [meditate on] the Self as a person the size of a span dwelling within the space of one's own heart, with four arms, in the manner described in such passages as Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.2.8.
[He saw] the Inner Controller, your chosen deity, as white, within himself by means of his own self, that is, by means of his intellect. ||39||
I shall bestow this internal knowledge which pacifies all karmas,
by means of which he shall also transcend fear.

Madhva says: But for one of universal wisdom, such [worldly existence] is essence-less; therefore, by realizing the Lord, the affliction—the calamity consisting of suffering, ignorance, and so forth—is destroyed. ||40||

Śrīdhara: [The Lord gave] this to his mother Devahūtī. "Śamanīm" means the uprooter. "He will cross over fear exceedingly," and "he will attain supreme bliss"—this is the meaning of the word "ca" (and). ||40||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He says "to the mother" (*mātre*) [in verse 40] to indicate that no anxiety should be felt on account of his son’s lordship or for the sake of his wife Devahūtī.
Maitreya said: Thus addressed by Kapila, the Prajāpati,
having circumambulated him with joy, departed for the forest itself.
Śrīdhara: "Samuditaḥ" means having been properly addressed; [then] having circumambulated him.
Kramasandarbha: not explained. Viśvanātha: "Samyag uktaḥ" means properly addressed; [then] having circumambulated him. ||41||
Observing a vow of silence, the sage took refuge in the Self alone;
free from attachment, he wandered the earth without a sacred fire and without a fixed dwelling.
Śrīdhara: This silence of the sages is a vow characterized by non-violence. ||42||

The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon [here]. One who yokes the mind to Brahman— that which is beyond both being and non-being, devoid of qualities (*viguṇa*) yet manifested through the appearance of qualities (*guṇāvabhāsa*)— should do so with single-minded devotion.
Śrīdhara: In that Brahman which is beyond both the existent and the non-existent; in that qualityless [Brahman] which illuminates the qualities;
when it has been experienced—that is, made directly perceptible—by means of single-minded, unwavering devotion. ||43||

The sequence of the composition: "the mind" constitutes a pentad. He states its preeminence even by way of the sequence of the stages of ascent: "the mind is Brahman.
