[This occurs] when it is made manifest through unswerving devotion characterized as a means—that is, when it is continuously and directly realized; without that [devotion], [it is not so].
Because no object whatsoever is established. ||43||

Viśvanātha: One who yokes that mind—which transcends all conventional objects, whether existent or non-existent, auspicious or inauspicious—to Brahman; in what kind [of Brahman]? In that wherein there is the manifestation, the radiance, of the qualities consisting of beauty, sweetness, sovereignty, and so forth, which are composed of consciousness (cinmaya).

In Him, who is devoid of qualities—that is, free from the material qualities—and who is manifested solely by unswerving single-minded devotion, brought within the range of experience of all the senses, such as the eyes and so forth. ||43||

Free from egoism and possessiveness, beyond dualities, possessing equal vision and self-knowledge, his intellect is inward-turned and tranquil; he is steadfast like an ocean whose waves have subsided.
In the *Mātsya Purāṇa*, it is stated: "Hari is called 'Sva' because his power is not dependent on anything else.
He is "Pratyagra" because he delights in the inner self (*pratyag-rati*).
And as the "Womb of Beings" (*bhūta-garbha*), he dwells within all beings; thus, he possesses these two forms and is truly full.
Therefore, they call him "Ātman" (the Self), because he is always endowed with the quality of attainment.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, he is free from the sense of "I" (ahaṃkāra) and so forth regarding the body and other such things. For this very reason, he is beyond the pairs of opposites (nirdvandva), undisturbed by cold, heat, and the like. He is one who sees with equanimity (samadṛk), not perceiving duality; rather, he is self-seeing (svadṛk), beholding only himself. His intellect (dhī) is turned inward, peaceful, and free from distraction.

The sequential composition: Precisely because of being free from ego (*nirahaṅkṛta*), one is free from "mine-ness" (*nirmama*). Due to the absence of that duality, the non-existence of the mind (*manas*) and the other faculties is established. One who possesses equal vision (*samadṛk*) does not perceive difference; one who possesses self-vision (*svadṛk*) perceives only Brahman itself through its identity with one's own true nature; such a person is inward-turned (*pratyak*), introverted (*antarmukhī*), and profoundly tranquil (*praśāntā*).
He whose intellect is free from distraction is one who possesses knowledge. ||44||
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, regarding all objects of worldly transaction, he is "devoid of egoism" (nirahaṅkṛti), and so forth.
He is one whose vision (*dṛk*)—that is, his perception (*dṛṣṭi*)—regards how much devotion there has been, is, or will be toward himself alone.
His intellect (*dhī*) is inward-turned, being devoid of outward activity; for that very reason, it is perfectly tranquil (*praśāntā*). ||44||
Having attained the Self through supreme devotion toward the Blessed Vāsudeva— the omniscient inner Self— he was liberated from all bonds.

Śrīdhara: Having thus described the cessation of the imagined limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he speaks of the attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord with three verses beginning with "Vāsudeva. One by whom the mind has found its self within the Self of the inner witness (*pratīc*), the individual soul (*jīva*); one from whom the bond of ignorance has been released. (45)

The Sequence of Composition: Thus, although the experience of Brahman has arisen through the power of the means of devotion mixed with the knowledge of Brahman, [the author] describes the subsequent experience of the Blessed Lord—which arises from the force of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of devotion and the resulting love—and so forth, in the verse beginning with "Vāsudeva. [This occurs] within the inner self (*pratyagātman*) of all.

By means of that knowledge of Brahman— by which egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and the rest, having obtained their self through its very power and becoming identical with it, exist as the supreme substratum characterized by love and devotion—
their manifestation occurs immediately after the dissolution of the natural (*prākṛta*) egoism and the rest.
The meaning is that he has attained those things consisting of pure *sattva*, whose nature is the bliss of love;
however, it does not mean that they themselves should return. Or rather, might these also become causes of bondage as before?
No, for it says: "His bonds are released" and "There is no return, according to the scripture" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). ||45||

Viśvanātha: To the question of how such a marvelous nature suddenly came to belong to him, he says: "Vāsudeva. By means of the supreme, most excellent love (*preman*) arising from the state of devotion (*bhakti-bhāva*) toward the Self—the inner witness, the individual soul (*jīva*)—the subtle body (*liṅga-deha*), although destroyed, [arises] again.

He is one by whom the self, mind, intellect, and so forth have been attained as non-material (aprākṛta). But surely, as before, these too become causes of bondage? To this he replies: "released from bonds," according to the principle [of the Vedānta-sūtras]: "There is no returning, on account of the scriptural word" (BS 4.4.22). ||45||
He saw the Blessed One abiding as the Self within all beings,
and he likewise saw all beings within the Blessed One and within himself.
Śrīdhara: He states the very attainment of the self-nature [of the Lord] in the words "the Self" (ātmānam). ||46||
The sequence of composition: This demonstrates that he has indeed attained his true self through the excellence of devotion.

Regarding the word "the Self" (ātmānam): here, "Self" refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman); the meaning of the sentence is that the Blessed Lord alone manifested Himself in every way to him. ||46||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, he states that he attained direct vision of the Blessed One: "He saw himself as the inner controller of all, the third person—the meaning being the one reclining upon the Ocean of Milk;
he saw that very Blessed One, his own chosen deity, white and four-armed. Likewise, within himself...

While remaining right here, he beheld with his eye born of yoga all living beings situated within hundreds of millions of cosmic eggs contained in the pores of the hair of the Primordial Person, who lies upon the causal ocean as the inner controller of Prakṛti. Thus, from the perspective of the yogi described in the second book, the sequence has been stated.

His superiority has been described. For he, desiring to see all things situated within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), goes from place to place after casting off his gross body. This one, however, remains right here and perceives the Lord reclining upon the causal ocean outside the entire cosmic egg, as well as all beings within the pores of His hair.

Even while free from desire, he beheld [the Lord]; and within the Blessed One as well, he beheld that very Self, his own chosen deity, the white-complexioned Blessed One. Within Him too, he beheld all beings within Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
thus, in Śrī Kardama, who was a worshiper of divine majesty, there occurred such a vision of majesty.
It should be understood that this is indeed appropriate. ||46||
By one who is free from desire and aversion, whose mind is equal toward all,
and who is endowed with devotion to the Blessed One, the state of a Bhāgavata has been attained.
Śrīdhara: Thus, in this way, he attained the state of a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavatī gati). According to another reading, it means that he himself attained that very state. ||47||

The sequential arrangement: Then he states the attainment of that very state directly with the word "icchet" (one should desire). Thus, the goal of the devotees (*bhāgavatī gati*) is attained when one is free from desire and aversion toward anything else because of its worthlessness; for that very reason, one should be even-minded toward everything. As it has been said: "All are devoted to Nārāyaṇa," and so forth. That which...
Alternatively, from the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*—where it is stated that he "dwells with Lakṣmī" (*sama*)—the phrase "with the mind fixed on the Blessed One" (*bhagavaccetasā*) is understood;

thus, in the reading "he attained the state of a Bhāgavata," it is Kardama himself who attained that state. In this context, "by means of the yoga of devotion to the Blessed One" (*bhagavadbhaktiyogena*) is the specific predicate. Thus...
Thus it is said in the Śrī Bhagavad-upaniṣad:
"Endowed with a purified intellect and having restrained the self with fortitude,
having abandoned objects such as sound and the like, and having cast off attachment and aversion..."
Frequenting solitary places, eating sparingly, with speech, body, and mind restrained,
he is constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation and has fully taken recourse to dispassion.
Having abandoned egoism, power, arrogance, desire, anger, and possessiveness,
one who is free from the sense of "mine" and tranquil is fit for becoming Brahman.
Having become Brahman, serene in self, he neither grieves nor desires;
equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to Me.
"Through devotion he comes to know Me in truth, both who I am and what I am;
then, having known Me in truth, he enters Me immediately thereafter" (Gītā 18.55).
Here, the root *viś* has the sense of "meeting," as in the case of [Duryodhana] abandoning Yudhiṣṭhira and [joining] Duryodhana.
"This king has entered" (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.29.38); thus it was explained by Śrī Svāmī himself that Vaikuṇṭha was seen by the gopas immediately after their attainment of Brahman. ||47||

Viśvanātha: Because [the state of being a householder] is to be abandoned everywhere in the world, Kardama—being free from desire and aversion and for that very reason possessed of an even mind (*samacetas*)—attained the goal of the Bhāgavatas; thus, in this reading, Kardama is joined with an even mind. ||47||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth [chapter] of the third [book], which is well-connected for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus, in the glorious Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā pertaining to the Paramahaṃsas, in the third book,
in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, [this is] the chapter titled "The Renunciation of Kardama."
The Twenty-fourth Chapter.
Now begins the Twenty-fifth Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
The Lord Kapila, the enumerator of the principles,
though himself unborn, was born by his own divine power (māyā) for the sake of instructing men regarding the Self.
Śrīdhara: In the twenty-fifth [chapter], having been asked by his mother regarding liberation from bondage,
the son Kapila first explains the supreme characteristic of devotion.
The casket of the jewels of yoga, entrusted by Kapila to his mother and constrained by her secret intent, is now clearly being opened.

Having first restated what has been said, he asks about the Yoga of Kapila with three verses, beginning with "Kapila. He is the "enumerator" (*saṃkhyātā*) of the principles (*tattva*); the meaning is that he is the founder of Sāṅkhya. For this very reason, he is "self-born" (*svayamjāta*).
[He appeared] for the sake of designating the Self—that is, for the purpose of making known the reality of the Self. ||1||
The sequence of composition: although he is himself unborn, by means of that *māyā*—which is compassion directed toward his devotees—he was born directly, becoming manifest. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
Questioned by his mother, Kapila, in the twenty-fifth chapter, spoke of that devotion—
its characteristics, its power, and its excellence in every respect.

He who is reckoned as the *Tattva*, the author of the enumeration of the *Tattvas*, and the founder of Sāṅkhya; though himself unborn, he has appeared by means of his own *māyā*—the meaning being that he has manifested the play of a non-material birth through the power of his inconceivable *yogamāyā*. "Both my birth and my action are divine."
Thus, because of the Lord’s statement, "He who knows this in truth" (Gītā 4.9), it is impossible to explain that the birth of the Lord is illusory (māyika). ||1||
Indeed, my vital breaths are not fully satiated by the fame of Śrutadeva, whose stature is the greatest among all men and yogis.

Śrīdhara: Among men, "of the *varṣman*" means of the most excellent or the eldest; among all yogins, "of the *variman*"—*variman* being the state of being excellent (*vara*)—this designation emphasizes the possessor of that quality. It means "of the most eminent" (*variṣṭha*), or alternatively, "because of being more excellent" (*varīyas*). They are renowned.

In the *Kīrti* [hymn]: "The vital breaths (*asavaḥ*), that is, the senses, are not satiated enough; he who plays with or shines through learning—that is, through hearing—is such. Alternatively, the connection is: "Even for him by whom the god has been heard many times (*bhūriśrutaḥ*), my vital breaths... ||2||
The sequence of the composition: *varimā* (vastness), which is the state of the chest (*uraḥ*), has the underlying purport of being the substratum.
While it should have been stated that [the senses] enter through the ear alone, there is a plurality [expressed] because the vital breaths (*asavaḥ*) are not satisfied;
this is because the eyes and other senses also enter into that speaker. Alternatively, by means of the ear, [there is the entry] even into such forms of the Lord as they appear.
It has been pointed out that the manifestation of the ear itself consists of the eye and the other [senses]. ||2||

Viśvanātha: Among men such as Kṣīrodaśāyin (Viṣṇu) and others, as well as among all yogins such as Dattātreya and the rest, my vital breaths— or my senses, such as hearing— have become renowned for the excellence and preeminence of this body, which has the form of Kapila.

They are not satiated even with much; for what kind of person am I, that they should play—that is, shine—by means of hearing (śruta), that is, by listening? Or rather, [it refers to one] by whom the Lord has been heard many times (bhūri-śruta). ||2||
Whatever the Blessed One, whose nature is independent, ordains through his own creative power (māyā),
recount those deeds to me, who am full of faith, for they are worthy of being celebrated.
Śrīdhara: He whose body (ātman) is subject to the will (chanda) or desire of his own people;
proclaim those deeds which he performs, for they are worthy of being celebrated. 3.
The sequential composition: "Therefore, whatever... means "whatever this is and whatever else.
By his own *māyā*, that is, by his own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa [created all this]. (3)

Viśvanātha: He whose self—meaning his body—is independent (*svacchanda*), self-governed, and not subject to karma like that of an ordinary living being (*jīva*); or alternatively, he whose self—meaning his body and its manifestation—is according to the will (*chanda*) of his own [desire].
Whatever action he performs by means of his own *māyā*, that is, through *yogamāyā*, and not by means of external *māyā*.

Because of the statement, "My birth and action are divine" (Gītā 4.9), although the word *yad-yad* refers to a single entity, through the use of repetition (*vīpsā*) to indicate multiplicity, it is connected with the plural-ended pronoun *tāni*.
They are *kīrtanyāni*, meaning worthy of being celebrated. ||3||
Sūta said:
Thus the venerable Maitreya, the friend of Dvaipāyana,
being pleased and prompted by [the inquiry into] Ānvīkṣikī, spoke this to Vidura.
Śrīdhara: Being thus impelled by you, just as you have urged me, so shall I [speak] accordingly, following those questions, regarding *ānvīkṣikī*, the science of the self. ||4||
The sequential arrangement: "O Dvaipāyana," and so forth; thus, according to the method of the purport of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||4||
Viśvanātha: "Thus" (evam) means in the manner that you are questioning me. In *ānvīkṣikī*, which is the science of the self (*ātmavidyā*). ||4||
Maitreya said: When his father had departed for the forest, the Blessed Lord Kapila, desiring to do what was pleasing to his mother, dwelt indeed at that Bindusaras.
Śrīdhara: At Bindusaras, in the lake Bindusaras. ||5||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "Thus" (evam) means in the manner that you are questioning me; [this refers to] in Ānvīkṣikī, which is the science of the self (ātmavidyā). ||5||
To her own son, who was sitting inactive and perceiving the highest path of reality, Devahūti spoke, recollecting the words of the Creator.

Śrīdhara: He is thus [called] because he shows the summit, the further shore, of the path of reality. "O Mānavī, this slayer of Kaiṭabha has entered your womb," and so forth—such are the words of the Creator. (6)
The sequential composition: "his own son"—even while observing his sovereignty, an excess of affection is manifested. ||6||

Viśvanātha: He is so called because he shows the summit, the further shore, of the path of reality (*tattvamārga*). This refers to the words of the Creator (Brahmā): "O Mā, this slayer of Kaiṭabha has indeed entered your womb," and so forth. (6)
Devahūti said:
O Infinite One, I am utterly despondent because of the thirst for unreal sense objects,
by which, when indulged in, one falls into blinding darkness, O Lord.

Śrīdhara: I am weary and exhausted from the thirsting—that is, the longing for sense objects—of these wicked senses; [I am weary] by that which, when anticipated and fulfilled, [only leads to further craving]. (7)
Regarding the sequence of composition: in some places, the phrase "Nirviṇṇā" (disenchanted) is preceded by "Devahūtir uvāca" (Devahūti said). ||7||
Viśvanātha: [She is] "disgusted" (nirviṇṇā) because of "thirsting" (tarṣaṇāt), that is, because of the longing for sense-objects;
she has attained a sense of revulsion toward that very thirsting which, when properly cultivated and practiced throughout this entire duration of time, leads to the "blind darkness" of saṃsāra. ||7||
Today, through your grace, I have obtained at the end of my births that true eye which reaches the further shore of this blind darkness so difficult to cross.

Śrīdhara said: "You alone are the supreme eye that leads one to the further shore; it has been obtained by me now, since at the end of my births, through your grace, [liberation] is to come to pass. (8)
The sequential composition: The true eye is not common; rather, it is independent of anything else because it illuminates all things, like the sun. ||8||
Viśvanātha: [He is] "pāraga" because he causes one to go to the further shore; therefore, he is "saccakṣuḥ," an eye that overcomes darkness. (8)
You are indeed the primordial Lord of men;
you have arisen like the sun, an eye for this world blinded by darkness.
Śrīdhara explains this in detail: "That Blessed Lord has arisen as the eye and as form, just like the sun. (9)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He says "He who" (*yaḥ*) to show that this [vision] belongs not only to me, but to everyone;
like the sun, he is the destroyer of all darkness. (9)
Therefore, O Lord, you ought to dispel my delusion—
this obstruction consisting of "I" and "mine" which has been applied by you.

Śrīdhara: "To draw away" means to remove. What is this delusion? He explains it: it is that persistent attachment—the insistence on "I" and "mine"—which you yourself have applied to this body and so forth. The second word "iti" is intended to include its effects, such as passion and the like. ||10||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, therefore, in order to first draw away—that is, to remove—the darkness of my delusion; for that very delusion is a drought, an obstacle to the rain of the nectar of devotion.

"What kind of thing is this 'I' and 'mine' regarding this house of the body and so forth?"—here the first word *iti* marks the end of the thought, while the second *iti* indicates the manner. The meaning is: "It is of such a nature as 'I am happy' or 'my house is prosperous. Because it is fashioned by Your Māyā, it has been joined by You alone. (10)
I have come for refuge to you, the worthy protector,
who are the axe that fells the tree of worldly existence for your own servants; I have come out of a desire to know the nature of Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
I pay homage to the most excellent among those who know the true Dharma.
Madhva says: Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Vāyu, Indra, Śreṣṭha, Hara, as well as Kāma, Śakra, Guru, Dakṣa, Manu and others, and the Bhāskaras and so forth.
"All living beings are successively designated by the name 'puruṣa.
The binding power of these two wives consists of all women as well as the cosmic egg (ajāṇḍa).
These are called by the term 'prakṛti' in due order; through knowledge of that, one is liberated. Thus it is said in the Dattātreyayoga.

Śrīdhara: The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Having gone to you for refuge out of a desire to know both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, I bow. *Kuṭhāram* means "the cutter" (of ignorance). ||11||

The sequential composition [is as follows]: for those servants of one's own devotees who are to be supported even by means of wages—for them too, it is the axe for the tree of *saṃsāra*, the sole instrument for the cutting performed by devotion.
And here, by the word *saṃsāra*, [it is meant] because it consists of a thicket of thorns in the form of base lineages that are alluring.

The state of being a binder is known to belong to primordial nature (prakṛti), which is illusion (māyā), through the inquiry into the Supreme Lord as the Person (puruṣa); for once primordial nature is known, it is possible to follow the Person by abandoning that [nature]. ||11||

Viśvanātha: [He approaches] you with the desire to know both Prakṛti and Puruṣa—that is, with the wish to understand who indeed is the Puruṣa who is subject to transmigratory existence, and what is Prakṛti from which his transmigration arises. And he says that there is no one else to be questioned in this matter: "the dharma of the virtuous."
Among those who know Him, he is the best, being one whose nature is devotion that turns back such worldly existence. ||11||
Maitreya said:
Having thus heard his mother’s faultless desire, which increases the liberation of men, [he replied].
With his face graced by a gentle smile, he spoke, the refuge of the wise and the virtuous, who are to be celebrated by the intellect.
Śrīdhara: [He is] one whose face is adorned with a slight smile, which increases liberation (apavarga) and generates delight in mokṣa. ||12||

The sequence of the composition: regarding the word "iti," the intended meaning of the smile is this: "I shall grant to these common men not only the increase of liberation, but even the supreme bliss known as devotion to Me. Alternatively, [the smile signifies] that for them too there shall be the increase of the yoga of devotion known as liberation, since [the Lord] is the refuge of the virtuous.
The meaning is: "by connection with that. How much more so for her own mother? ||12||

Viśvanātha: It is that which increases (*vardhana*) liberation (*apavarga*), that is, *mokṣa*—or, by punning, it is that which cuts down (*chedana*) the inferior group, namely the three aims of life (*trivarga*). He is the Self (*ātman*), that very Kapila, who exists as the object of service for those virtuous ones, those devotees; he is the goal (*gati*) for them. [And] "with a slight smile" (*īṣatsmita*) is mine.

The sense is: "You are the mother of the Supreme Lord; what worldly existence could there be for you? Nevertheless, with you as my object, I shall impart some instruction in order to uplift the worlds. (12)
The Blessed Lord said:
Yoga, which is spiritual in nature, is considered by Me to lead men to the supreme good— that state wherein there is the absolute cessation of both suffering and happiness.
Madhva says: That which pertains to the inner self within the body, such as the Supreme Self and so forth, is called *adhyātma*;
likewise, pleasure is that which is to be enjoyed through the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), while everything else is suffering.
"In liberation, [the world] goes to dissolution, but eternal bliss is enjoyed"—so it is said. ||13||
Śrīdhara: "Spiritual" (ādhyātmika) means centered on the Self (ātmaniṣṭha). "Wherein" (yatra) means in which [state]. ||13||
The sequential arrangement: therein, first of all, he states the means for liberation alone—namely, "yoga.
It is spiritual (ādhyātmika), being centered on the Supreme Self (paramātmaniṣṭha). ||13||
Viśvanātha: Spiritual yoga (*ādhyātmiko yogaḥ*), which is grounded in the individual self (*jīvātmaniṣṭhaḥ*), is the means for the sake of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasārtham*).

That [yoga] should be stated as being threefold: devotion (*bhakti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and [ascetic] discipline (*yoga*). Among these, in the case of the path of devotion, the supreme good is to be understood as the intended fruit. When that yoga exists, for one who is subject to worldly existence (*sāṃsārika*)...
The uprooting of both suffering and happiness. ||13||
O sinless one, I shall now declare to you this very yoga, which I previously spoke of when the seers desired to hear about the skillfulness of all its constituent parts.
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.
Kramasandarbha: The reading "yogam urvaṅganaipuṇyam" is supported by the statement regarding the connection; however, "sarvāṅga... was written by Svāmī. ||14||
Viśvanātha: [The place] where the sages—Nārada and others—are present, and where their vast limbs, that is, their skills and the dexterity in their performance, reside. 14.
Indeed, it is the mind that is considered by him to be the cause of both bondage and liberation for the self:
when attached to the qualities (guṇas), it leads to bondage; when delighted in the Puruṣa, it leads to liberation.

Śrīdhara: Demonstrating therein that proficiency in all limbs [of yoga] is dependent upon the restraint of the mind, he says: "The mind... [and so forth]. "In the qualities" means in the objects; "in the Person" means in the Supreme Lord.
The word *vā* (or) has the sense of the word *tu* (but). ||15||
The sequence of composition: it has attained mere delight (ratimātra), being established in the Supreme Self, the Puruṣa. ||15||

Viśvanātha: Indeed, it is the mind alone that binds and liberates the individual soul (jīvātman) through evil association and virtuous association; thus he says, "The mind. Attached—that is, intensely clinging—to the *guṇas*, which are the primary means of its own bondage;
this is the principle stated regarding bondage. [But when attached] to the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), who is devoid of *guṇas* (*nirguṇa*)...

The logical principle is that [devotion] is "delighting" (ratimat) because it is intent upon the destruction of the bondage of the qualities (guṇas), and it is "liberation" (mocaṇe). The word *vā* has the sense of the word *tu*. Here, the cause of the delight directed toward the illustrious Puruṣottama is indeed devotion alone;
it is neither knowledge nor yoga. As the means of liberation, devotion alone should be understood as appropriate.
In this regard, the verse numbered 4.29.80, beginning with "The mind alone," should be consulted:
"When the mind is free from the impurities such as desire and greed arising from the conceits of 'I' and 'mine,' it becomes pure, equal, and devoid of both suffering and pleasure."
"Because of non-attachment to external pleasure, there is no pleasure; because of the avoidance of suffering, there is no suffering.
When the mind, through devotion to Hari alone, becomes eternally blissful, it then beholds the Supreme Self by means of the clarity of the self. Thus it is said in the Kāpileya.
Because there is no difference in his own incarnations, he is described as being continuous;
because there is no difference in his qualities, body, and senses, he is therefore both distinct and similar.
"Because my power is unbroken and complete, I am always considered to be one;
the binding power called Prakṛti is separated from the power of Viṣṇu. Thus [it is said]. (1618)

Śrīdhara: He demonstrates how the accomplishment of the goal of human existence occurs through the restraint of the mind with three verses beginning with "I am. When the mind becomes pure, being free from—that is, devoid of—impurities. He states the indicator of the purity of the mind as follows: "free from suffering" (aduḥkham) ||16||
The sequential arrangement: "I" is the triad. ||16||

Viśvanātha: He states that even knowledge (*jñāna*) and yoga (*yoga*) possess the power of liberation only through the assistance of devotion (*bhakti*), by means of three verses beginning with "I am" (*aham*). The word *vītam* means "devoid of. The absence of impurities such as desire in the mind occurs through tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth, as well as through the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*); thus, the ancillaries (*aṅga*) of both knowledge and yoga are indicated. This is for the sake of purification.
He states the reason for this: "It would be free from suffering," and so forth; the word "it would be" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. ||16||
Then the person perceives himself as solitary, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti),
continuous, self-luminous, subtle, and indivisible.
Śrīdhara: "Nirantaram" means without interval; "nirbhedam" means without division. "Aṇimānā" means subtle; "akhaṇḍitam" means undivided. ||17||
The composition of the sequence: because it is continuous and eternal, it is unbroken, meaning free from interruption or division;
because it is subtle (*aṇimāna*), it is difficult to perceive—this is the meaning. ||17||

Viśvanātha: Then the person—the living soul (jīva)—perceives himself as distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti) and ignorance (avidyā), as continuous and devoid of the separation of the two bodies; therefore, he is self-luminous with unobstructed light. He perceives himself as atomic (aṇimānam), subtle, and even among the subtlest, "I am the living soul."
The meaning is that the statement of the Blessed One is of the supreme atomic measure by its very nature;
[it is] unbroken by the latent impressions of sense objects. ||17||
With a self endowed with knowledge and dispassion, and joined with devotion,
he beholds the indifferent [Self] and Prakṛti with its power destroyed.
Śrīdhara: "Hataujasam" means one whose vigor is destroyed and whose strength is diminished. ||18||

The sequential composition: Knowledge is discernment (*viveka*). That, along with detachment (*vairāgya*), has been established as being free from notions such as "I" and "mine. Devotion is devotion to the Lord (*bhāgavatī*); for without it, no goal whatsoever is accomplished.
"Deprived of vigor" means incapable of performing even the slightest action within oneself. (18)
Viśvanātha: [He is attained] by the self—that is, by the mind—endowed with specific knowledge and joined with devotion;

and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that devotion itself provides assistance therein, for without it, knowledge is incapable of producing its own fruit. [One attains Him] while remaining indifferent (*udāsīnam*), meaning unattached, toward *prakṛti*, which is one's own ignorance (*svāvidyā*).
Deprived of vitality, she was unable to perform even the slightest action within herself. ||18||
There is no path as auspicious as devotion directed toward the Blessed One, the soul of all,
for yogis seeking the realization of Brahman.

Śrīdhara says: "And for the purification of the mind, devotion alone is the internal means. Sanātana says: "No" (Ha.bha.vi. 11.564). [The meaning is: even for yogins, for the attainment of Brahman—that is, for the manifestation of the reality of the Self and for liberation—there is nothing as auspicious as devotion.
There is no path that is free from obstacles or of an auspicious nature. ||19||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Among the three, he states that devotion alone (*bhakti*) is superior, consisting of bliss and supremely auspicious, with the words "not [the others]," etc. By the phrase "by one who is engaged," it is meant that devotion alone is what is truly joined to the Blessed Lord.
The meaning is that she becomes "properly suited" (*samucitā*). This is because of the subsequent statement: "There is a certain devotion toward you that is appropriate.

For yogins who possess the means, when the Supreme Lord as Brahman has become their object, there is "accomplishment" (*siddhi*), which is the perfection of service, friendship, and so forth; for that [accomplishment]... ||19||
The wise know that attachment is an unaging bond for the self;
yet that very same attachment, when directed toward the virtuous, becomes an open door to liberation.
Śrīdhara: He states that the root of all this is association with the virtuous (*satsaṅga*), saying "association" (*prasaṅgam*).
"Uncovered" (*apāvṛtam*) means free from obstruction. ||20||
Sanātana (Ha.bha.vi. 10.261): *prasaṅga* means excessive attachment; *apāvṛtam* means unobstructed. ||20||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states with supporting arguments that the very root of that devotion is association with the virtuous (*sādhusaṅga*), saying "the occasion" (*prasaṅgam*). [He further describes it as] the door to liberation—such as *sālokya* and the rest—which is "unbarred," meaning free from obstruction.
It has been stated thus: even for those whose devotion is single-minded, liberation occurs as a result not intentionally sought through that devotion. ||20||
Patient, compassionate, friends to all embodied beings,
having no enemies, tranquil, virtuous, and adorned by goodness.
Those who practice firm devotion toward me with undivided intent,
having renounced their actions for my sake and abandoned their own kin and relatives;
They listen to and relate polished discourses concerning me;
various afflictions do not torment these whose minds are absorbed in me.
These are the virtuous ones, O virtuous lady, who are free from all attachments;
you should seek association with them, for they remove the defects of attachment.

And as it is said: "If the kind of devotion one has toward Me does not exist toward anyone else, then through this very exclusive devotion, by its intensity, one shall cross over the stream of worldly existence. Furthermore:
"Hari alone is the Full; there is no other. All others are considered to be under His control."
"That knowledge which is steady is called the knowledge of identity with the One (aikātmya-jñāna). Thus it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. ||23||

Śrīdhara: He describes the characteristics of the virtuous (sādhūs) with the four verses beginning with "titikṣavaḥ. The virtuous are those who follow the scriptures; they are those for whom goodness and excellent character are themselves their ornament. These devotees, possessing the aforementioned characteristics, are not scorched—that is, they are not afflicted—by the miseries, such as the internal (ādhyātmika) and so forth.
Why? Because their minds are fixed on me; the meaning is that those who are not overcome by afflictions are the virtuous (sādhu). ||2124||
Sanātana Gosvāmī (*Haribhaktivilāsa* 10.16): Those who are patient and forgiving by nature;
friends who benefit others without ulterior motive; peaceful—meaning free from anger and the like, or endowed with humility and other virtues;
those for whom good character alone is their ornament, or who possess such noble materials as garlands of *tulasī*; they [are the ones].

The term *sādhu*s means those who are devotees of the Blessed Lord (*bhagavad-bhakta*s). Having begun with the words, "I am dependent upon My devotees" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 9.4.63), the Blessed Lord concludes by saying, "The *sādhu*s are My heart" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 9.4.68), and so forth; thus, by the Blessed Lord Himself, it is established that *sādhu*s alone are indeed devotees.
Because of its manifestation: in this way, by the word *mahat* as well, primarily only a devotee of the Blessed Lord is denoted;

for this is understood from reflecting on the meaning of such statements as Śrī Prahlāda’s words: "How could there be great qualities in one who is not a devotee of Hari? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.18.12). Likewise, by the word *sat* as well, a devotee of the Blessed Lord [is denoted].
Thus:
"By devotion to the playful grace of the petals of whose lotus feet, the virtuous untie the knotted accumulation of karma" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.22.39).
This is the general direction [of the argument], following the meaning of such statements as these. //21//

Sanātana Gosvāmī (*Haribhaktivilāsa* 10.73): The meaning is "by that pure disposition (*bhāva*) in which there is no pursuit of results and so forth. *Bhāvena* means by love (*prema*). Therefore, [one attains] devotion in the form of hearing and so forth, which has reached a firm state of supreme steadfastness.

The connection with the following verse is that those who perform various acts consisting solely of the chanting of My names are "the virtuous" (sādhu). For this very reason, they have renounced actions performed for My sake—that is, with Me as the motive—or rather, for the purpose of attaining Me, or else for My pleasure. These are the actions they have abandoned.

Those by whom all obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*) and so forth have been thus abandoned; likewise, those by whom their own kin, relatives, kinsmen, and connections have been renounced—this should be understood as the external characteristic of being established in love. Previously, it was simply the abandonment of attachment that was mentioned, and from that, the mere absence of affection was stated. Here, however—
In every respect, the complete abandonment [of worldly ties] along with their roots has been demonstrated. Thus, its superiority has been established relative to each preceding stage.

In this manner, starting from devotion to vows (*vrata*) up to devotion to love (*prema*), one should infer the progressive superiority of each subsequent stage, as well as the superiority of each respective intermediate level. Therefore, in all respects—

Because this is the most excellent of all, its writing is placed at the very end. Thus, it has been stated by the venerable Hariyogeśvara as well: "He emits... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.55). This is the general direction. ||22||

Sanātana Gosvāmī (*Haribhaktivilāsa* 10.42): These [devotees], by listening to or speaking my stories, are not scorched—that is, they are not afflicted—by the miseries such as those pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*). Why?
Because their minds are fixed on me through the stories themselves; or rather, those who are not overcome by miseries [are the ones who listen and speak].
In the word "sādhu," the meaning [of "not burning"] is to be understood here, because the characteristics of a *sādhū* have been stated elsewhere.

Consequently, the fourfold definition has been stated as follows: the triad of hearing and so forth, and being overcome by the afflictions (*tāpa*). Alternatively, in the phrase "those whose minds are fixed on Me" (*madgatacetasaḥ*), it means that for those who are intent on remembering Me, the afflictions do not burn.
This is the meaning. In this manner, the greatness of those devoted to hearing, chanting, and remembering [the Name] should be understood in sequence.
As for the phrase "they are the virtuous" (*sādhavaḥ*): because they fall within the definition of the virtuous, it follows by itself. ||23||

Sanātan Gosvāmī (*Haribhaktivilāsa* 10.66): They are specifically devoid of and free from all external and internal attachments as well as attachment to anything else; this demonstrates the characteristic of an *ekāntin*. Therefore, you should yourself pray for association with them alone.

Because it is the supreme human goal and is exceedingly difficult to attain, it is to be desired even by the mind; what need is there to mention that it must be directly realized? This is the meaning. Alternatively, [an objection might be raised: "In that case, why do you not form an association with them? To this he replies: "Association with them should be sought by you from them alone."

The word "atha" (then) has this meaning: their association [with the Lord] may be obtained through compassion alone and through one's own devotion, but not otherwise. Now, it might be argued that even passion and hatred could somehow arise from such association. To this he says: "In that association, those who..."

They are "so" because they take away those defects; or rather, the meaning is that they will take them away by the mere sight of them. Or else, the meaning is that those ascetics are "detached" (niḥsaṅga) because attachment itself constitutes their defect; they are "so" because they attract even such people toward themselves by means of their own virtues. Therefore, for them...
The meaning is that, being drawn by his very greatness, she will herself abandon everything and depart. Enough with excessive detail. ||24||

The sequential arrangement: those who are peaceful, endowed with the fourfold means such as tranquility and self-control, and possessed of knowledge, are called "sādhus. And it will be said [in the Gītā] by the words, "Those great ones are even-minded and tranquil," etc.
By the words beginning with "enduring" (*titikṣavaḥ*), he describes their incidental qualities—even those who are themselves sādhus.

They adorn and honor other virtuous people, or rather, they for whom the virtuous themselves are their ornaments and attendants. Furthermore, by way of incidental discussion, he mentions specific types of virtuous persons with the verse beginning "In me" (12.13).
He concludes with the words "Therefore they do not suffer" (12.15)—referring to those who are "devoid of all attachments."
They are devoid of attachment to the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*). The word "attachment" (*saṅga*) constitutes half a verse.
The word "hi" (for) serves as a reason for the subsequent sentence as well. [2324]

Viśvanātha: He describes the characteristics of the saintly (sādhu) in four verses. Here, he states their incidental definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) with the words "enduring" (*titikṣavaḥ*). "Peaceful" (*śāntāḥ*) means gracious; "saintly" (*sādhavaḥ*) means straightforward. They are so called because they adorn and honor the saintly; or else, they are those for whom the saintly themselves are dear like ornaments.

He states the definition of its essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) with the word "mayi" (in me). Because words such as "other" (*anya*) convey a similar meaning, [the text says: "by that state"—namely, by servitude (*dāsya*), friendship (*sakhya*), and so forth—[a state] in which there exists no other object of worship like me, such as Brahmā, Rudra, or others; and for this very reason, because it has only a single object, it is "firm. [It is performed] for my sake.

Those who have renounced all dharmas according to my teaching beginning with "Abandoning all duties for the sake of attaining Me" (Gītā 18.66); those who have abandoned their actions according to my teaching beginning with "Having abandoned wife, home, and so forth" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.4.65), saying "How could I venture to abandon them?"; and those who have abandoned their own kin and others—these are the savory, pure, and guileless ones.

The miseries, such as those pertaining to the self (ādhyātmika) and so forth, do not scorch—that is, they do not afflict—those devotees. If they are not overcome by these miseries, they should be known as those whose minds are absorbed in Me and who possess firmness in remembrance.
They are free from all attachments and devoid of clinging to the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha). ||2124||
Through association with the virtuous, discourses that bring nectar to my heart and ears arise from the realization of my own spiritual power;
by delighting in them, one quickly enters the path to liberation.
Faith, delight, and devotion will follow in succession.

Śrīdhara: He establishes the status of association with the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) as a limb of devotion (*bhakti*) by saying "of the virtuous" (*satām*). Those [words] in which there is a perfect knowledge of the heroic power (*vīrya*) are "knowledge of the heroic power" (*vīryasaṃvidaḥ*). They are elixirs for the heart and ears, providing pleasure. From their enjoyment—that is, from their service—there arises liberation (*apavarga*), which is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), on the path to which [they lead].
In that Hari, first there will be faith, then delight, and then devotion; "will follow in succession" means it will come about gradually. ||25||

*Sanātana* (Ha.bha.vi. 10.273): Those [words] in which there is a correct understanding (*saṃvit*) of heroic power (*vīrya*) are "vīryasaṃvidaḥ. For this very reason, they are elixirs for the heart and ears, providing bliss. Through their *joṣaṇa*—that is, through their cultivation or service—in that Hari, who is the path to *apavarga*, which is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) or liberation (*mokṣa*).

First comes faith, then delight, and then devotion will follow; the meaning is that it will arise in this sequence. Delight (*rati*) is the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) known as *rati*, and devotion (*bhakti*) is characterized by love (*prema*). An explanation of these has been provided by the venerable Mahānubhāvas themselves in the *Rasārṇava*.
It certainly exists. ||25||

The sequence of development for the virtuous is as follows: first, there arises an interest (*rucis*) due to [the scripture] being like an elixir (*rasāyana*); even therein, through hearing accounts such as the extraction of the [alchemical] essence (*pattoddharaṇa*), there arises faith (*śraddhā*), which is to say conviction; from that, there arise love (*rati*) and devotion (*bhakti*).
These two are the prior and subsequent stages of devotion. (25)

Viśvanātha: [The author] states the sequence by which the mind develops devotion for the Lord solely through association with the saintly (sādhu-saṅga) in the verse beginning with "of the virtuous" (satām). Since it was previously stated that "association is to be sought," first there is faith;
then, from the excellent association with the virtuous, the narrations of My deeds arise—whereas from inferior association, they do not.

It is merely the act of worship, not the discourses themselves. From that superior association, discourses that bring about the cessation of misfortune arise. Then, those very discourses, producing steadfastness, result in *saṃvit*—the correct knowledge (*samyag-vedana*) of my power, that is, of my majesty.
They become such that they generate delight, serving as a nectar for the heart and ears. Then,
through the relishing of those stories with joy and savoring them, there arises faith, attachment, passion, devotion, and love for that Blessed One upon whose very path liberation lies.
"It will proceed" means it will come about in due order; the sense is that the devotion now being set in motion by me shall thus circulate in the world in this sequence. ||25||
Through devotion, a person who has developed detachment from the sensory objects seen and heard, by reflecting upon my words,
becomes disciplined in the restraint of the mind and engaged in yoga.
He will strive by means of the straight paths of yoga.

Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says: "By devotion" (bhaktyā). Through that devotion which arises from reflecting upon my creative play—the sport of creation and so forth—one becomes detached from sense-born pleasure.
[Detached] from what is seen or heard, whether pertaining to this world or the next; then, being diligent therein, one applies oneself to the restraint of the mind.
He will strive by means that are straightforward and effortless, because they are characterized primarily by devotion. ||26||

The sequential arrangement: therein, those who are attached [to the Lord] are of two kinds—those whose vision is common to the virtuous (sādhu) in terms of knowledge and so forth, and those whose vision is superior even to them. Among these, in order to subsequently describe the primary devotion of the latter group with its specific excellence, following the mother’s longing:

He points out the secondary [qualification] for those with common views by means of two verses beginning with "by devotion" (bhaktyā). Devotion alone constitutes the specific qualifications of the seeker: dispassion, application, and fitness for yoga. ||26||
Viśvanātha: Having described pure devotion (*bhakti*), he speaks of yoga with the words "by devotion" (*bhaktyā*).

Even one who is engaged in yoga through constant reflection upon my words and my divine sports (*līlā*)—whether seen or heard, pertaining to this world or the next—and who is diligent (*yatta*) in the restraint of the mind, that is, in bringing it under his own control, [is successful] by means of the straightforward [paths].
The meaning is that the person who will be born hereafter shall strive by means of the paths of yoga made easy through being permeated with devotion, which I am about to set forth;
[this applies] to one who has not practiced the qualities of *prakṛti*.
Through knowledge manifested by dispassion,
through yoga, and through devotion offered to me,
one attains me, the inner self, in this very life.
Śrīdhara: Thus, by not serving the qualities of material nature and through knowledge and other means, this individual soul attains and reaches Me alone even here in this very body. ||27||
The sequential arrangement: through non-association, through inquiry into what is to be abandoned, and through knowledge, one attains the reality that is the meaning of the term *tat*.

Then, by means of yoga with its eight limbs—manifested by detachment from sense objects and determined through the investigation of the meaning of the term *tvam*—and by means of devotion directed toward Me alone, with no other object, offered to Me, one [attains] Me.

Viśvanātha attains the inner Self, which is the referent of the word *tat*, by means of identity with the referent of the word *tvam*; having spoken of yoga, he now speaks of knowledge: "by non-attachment" (*asevayā*). That knowledge which arises from the non-attachment to the qualities of *prakṛti*—that is, to sense objects—which is obtainable through desireless action (*niṣkāma-karma*), by that [knowledge] one [attains] Me.

One attains or reaches the inner self, which is the referent of the word "That," through yoga; for since practices such as *yama* are limbs of knowledge (*jñāna*), the phrase "through devotion" (*bhaktyā*) is used because knowledge devoid of devotion is fruitless. ||27||
Devahūti said:
What kind of devotion is appropriate for you, and of what nature is it within my reach,
by which I may easily attain your state of liberation?

Śrīdhara: "Kācit" means "who indeed? "Ucitā" means "suitable" or "fitting. Even there, what kind [of suitability] do I have as a woman? "Gocarā" means "accessible" or "fitting. "Nirvāṇam" refers to your state or essential nature, which consists of liberation;
"anvāśnavai" means that immediately thereafter, I shall attain it with my whole being. In the reading "ajñāsā tu," [the meaning is] "I..."
The word "tu" (but) indicates the connection [to the following]. ||28||

The Structural Arrangement (*krama-sandarbha*): Now, having understood that devotion alone, as previously described, constitutes the state of being a living soul (*sarva-jīvatva*), they inquire about that very thing. Furthermore, considering themselves everywhere to be devoid of qualification due to their wretchedness, she asks about its specific nature with the words beginning "A certain [woman]... and so forth: "What indeed is this called 'devotion'?"
The meaning is: "What are its characteristics? And within that class of devotion, some form of devotion toward you might be possible for me to perceive as being appropriate. ||28||

Viśvanātha: "Kācit" means "who indeed? "Ucitā" means "is appropriate for you. By the phrase "na yujyamānayā" (not by one who is [merely] joined), since the excellence of devotion when it is being practiced is heard, the meaning is: "What kind of state is within the scope of me, a woman—capable of both knowing and practicing it? *Padam*.

Your lotus-feet are *nirvāṇa*, the very nature of liberation (*nirvṛti*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *nirvāṇa* is used for setting (the sun), for liberation, for the bathing of an elephant, for union, and for final release (*apavarga*). Alternatively, I shall easily attain (*anvāśnavai*) them directly (*añjasā*), so that they may be *nirvāṇa*, meaning free from all thorns (*niṣkaṇṭaka*). I shall obtain them through my own effort (*svāśnavā*).
In this reading, the connection is "I am not," thus. ||28||
O Blessed One, regarding that yoga consisting of liberation which was taught by you:
what is its nature, how many are its limbs, and from what does the awakening to reality arise?
Śrīdhara: The meaning is that he is one whose arrow is directed toward the Blessed One;
[this occurs] from which yoga. ||29||
Kramasaṃdarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: Although my desire to know and my wish to act concern only that devotion which is approved by you, nevertheless, for one who desires to know, it is said by the wise that "one's own doctrine must be known, as well as the doctrines of others"; thus there is a constant necessity [to study others' views].

And he says, "My knowledge is to be sought," meaning "that which is yoga. The sense is that the arrow [of inquiry] is cast at the Blessed One, like an arrow aimed at a target, so as to take the Blessed One as its mark. It has nirvāṇa as its purpose, having liberation as its goal. Likewise, it is that from which comes the awakening to the principles (tattvas), and that knowledge itself.
Of what kind? ||29||
Therefore, O Hari, please grant me this understanding so that, though slow-witted, I—
a woman— may easily comprehend through your grace that which is difficult to understand.
Śrīdhara: Understand; that is, make known specifically. "Sukham" means without effort. ||30||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Therefore (tat), for that reason, know (vijānīhi) this [truth] concerning me (mām); inform me of it. ||30||
Maitreya said:
Having thus understood his mother's purpose, Kapila, whose affection was directed toward that body in which he was born, spoke.
He indeed proclaimed the Sāṅkhya, which they call the tradition of reality, as well as the yoga of the expansion of devotion.

"Madhva says: 'The birth of others is from the white [seed], but that of Hari is from his own body; for one whose body is eternally manifest knowledge, how could there be birth from a white [seed]? Thus it is said in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa. (31)

Śrīdhara: Having thus understood the mother’s purpose and motive—the reason for his having developed affection—he spoke that which they call Sāṅkhya, in which the principles (tattvas) are enumerated and set forth in sequence; he proclaimed that expansion of devotion, which is itself an expansion.
And yoga. ||31||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon. *Viśvanātha*: That in which the purpose (*artha*)—the motive of affection—is the cause; wherein the principles (*tattva*) are manifested by means of the body (*tanu*) and are recited or enumerated; what is that? It is that which they call Sāṅkhya.
He taught the canopy of devotion and yoga. ||31||

The Blessed Lord said: That which is the natural activity of the mind fixed solely in *sattva*— the gods who are characterized by the qualities [of *sattva*] and whose actions are based on revealed scripture— is indeed [the state of goodness].
Signless devotion to the Lord is superior to spiritual perfection;
it quickly consumes the sheath of the self, just as fire digests what has been swallowed.

Regarding the term *madhva*: "He who does not transgress what is declared in the Śruti is one whose ritual action is to be proclaimed" (Bhaviṣya Parvan). Regarding the term *sattva*: "Because he is always endowed with all qualities, Viṣṇu is designated as *sattva*" (Kāpila).
"But for one whose devotion is incomplete, happiness will not reach fulfillment in liberation; therefore, complete devotion is superior even to such liberation. Thus it is said. (3233)

Śrīdhara: He characterizes *uttamā bhakti* (the highest devotion) as being asked by [the Goddess] what kind of devotion toward You is appropriate: "In *sattva*, that is, in Hari who is the embodiment of *sattva*, [there is devotion] toward those gods—the senses characterized by luminosity, or rather their presiding deities—by whom qualities (*guṇa*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are embraced and known."
The connection with what follows is this: that very disposition (*vṛtti*) which is devotion (*bhakti*) is weightier even than spiritual perfection (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*).

Of what nature is it? It is *animittā*, meaning free from desire. It is *svābhāvikī*, meaning spontaneously accomplished without effort. He states the cause for such a disposition in those [devotees]: "That which is heard following the utterance of the Guru" is *anuśrava*, namely the Veda; that...

That very action which is prescribed by the revealed scriptures belongs to those [sages]; for this very reason, the mind of that person of pure being (śuddhasattva) is single, uniform, and unmodified—this is the meaning. ||32||

And liberation indeed occurs as a necessary consequence; thus he says: "That devotion which digests—that is, exhausts—the sheath, the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra). An illustration for its accomplishment even without one's own effort is: just as the internal fire (jāṭhara) digests the food that has been swallowed and eaten. ||33||

*Sanātana* (Ha.bha.vi. 11.614): Devotion (*bhakti*) is that disposition (*vṛtti*) which exists within the *sattva*—that is, within the Lord Śrī Bhagavān, who is the very embodiment of *sattva*—of the gods, who are the luminous senses or their presiding deities. Thus, since the characteristics such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth have been specifically indicated, this is the general definition.
Those by which [the self] is characterized as having qualities beyond the senses are shown to be always fixed upon sense objects.
He states the cause for their functioning in such a manner: that which is heard following the recitation of the Guru is the *āmnāya*, i.e., the Veda;
that which is prescribed by it is the *ānuśravika*. Those whose [practice] consists of that very thing are [the performers of ritual action]. For this very reason, it is one.

The meaning is that of that man of pure being (*śuddhasattva*) whose mind is uniform and unchanging; or else, whose mind is fixed on the Blessed One alone. Or, this word may be connected with what follows: "and that devotion to the Blessed One belonging to the Blessed One belongs to one of single-minded intent."

The construction is as follows: being a virtuous wife (*satī*) of a man; for that very reason, being without cause and free from desire (*niṣkāmā*); and for that very reason, being natural and accomplished without effort (*svābhāvikī ayatnasiddhā*), she is even more weighty than liberation (*siddhi*).
Having thus stated the general definition at the beginning, her excellence is stated afterwards. A certain [woman] is suitable for you.

Because the supreme devotion was inquired about by Śrī Devahūti in the verse beginning with "bhaktiḥ" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.28), Sanātana [in Hari-bhakti-vilāsa 11.576] states: "Devotion that is causeless and desireless is weightier even than perfection or liberation;
and liberation indeed becomes a secondary consequence. He says this regarding that devotion which [opens] the treasure-house...

It digests and consumes the *liṅga-śarīra*. An illustration for this accomplishment occurring without effort is as follows: just as the digestive fire (*jāṭharo 'gniḥ*) digests the food that has been swallowed and eaten. The verse beginning with "Of the gods who have qualities as their marks" (*bhā.pu. 3.25.32*) and so forth is not included here. In that regard...

Furthermore, the preeminence of devotion is established by the description of its characteristics. Regarding devotion, it has been stated in that very same work (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa*) in five verses beginning with: "Those who do not desire identity with Him" (3.25.34).
Since that is not relevant here, it has not been included. Other such matters should likewise be inferred. ||33||

The sequential arrangement: the pair beginning with "of the gods" (devānām). Desiring to demonstrate that specific excellence of devotion appropriate for them through compassion toward them, he defines primary devotion itself with the half-verse beginning "of the gods. Faith, attachment, and devotion will follow in sequence [Bhāgavata Purāṇa].
Thus it has been said. Here, although both *rati* (pleasure) and *bhakti* (devotion)—

which differ merely in degree— are indeed nothing but *prīti* (affection), nevertheless, since that [affection] becomes most manifest in the devotion called *prema*, which is characterized by an intensification of *prīti*, she [the author] refers to it by the term "devotion" (*bhakti*).
He characterizes [them] by taking [these qualities] as the basis. And this is the meaning: regarding the qualities and marks, which are conditioned by the three *guṇas*;
those whose practiced actions (*karmācarita*) are "traditionally heard" (*ānuśravika*), meaning they are accessible through the *Śrutis*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth—they are thus described.
Among those gods—Śrī Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva—it is by the mere presence of *sattva*...

In Śrī Viṣṇu, who is characterized by the qualities of goodness (*sattva*), who is beneficent, and whose essential nature consists of the function of the power of pure *sattva*; and this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), meaning that [this applies] even to a single manifestation among the infinite manifestations of the Blessed Lord and others. By the word "only" (*eva*), it is meant that this does not apply elsewhere, nor even there [in other cases].

The specific form of knowledge that consists of a state of mind conforming to the disposition of a single-minded person is [defined as follows]: it is "without cause," meaning free from any desire for rewards; it is "natural," meaning arising spontaneously and effortlessly due to the inherent beauty of the object, rather than being produced by force; that devotion to the Lord (bhāgavatī bhakti) is love (prīti).
This is the meaning. Precisely because of its connection with *prīti* (joy), devotion (*bhakti*)—which is non-different from it—must be considered natural (*svābhāvika*).

Therefore, in this context, *prīti* alone should be understood as the primary sense by the word "function" (*vṛtti*). And that [devotion] is weightier than *siddhi*, which is liberation (*mokṣa*), because of scriptural statements such as *sālokya-sārṣṭi* [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.29.35]. Hence...

Thus, because it is well known that even that which is to be accomplished through knowledge may be disregarded, and because the purpose is established as the disregard of mere knowledge, the explanation "from knowledge" (*jñānāt*) is inappropriate. In this context, the state of having transcended the qualities (*guṇātītatva*) belongs to that mental state (*vṛtti*) by virtue of its being more weighty than liberation; even more so [than that].

The state of being intense supreme bliss, its arising in the mind solely through the special grace of the Blessed Lord, and its being designated as a mental modification (vṛtti) precisely by virtue of identity with that [grace] have been shown.
(32) He states a secondary quality of that [bliss] in the half-verse beginning with "it digests": (33)

[Prītisaṃdarbha 61] Viśvanātha: In that regard, in order to speak of the canopy of devotion (*bhaktivitāna*), he characterizes that certain devotion which is appropriate for You— the devotion toward the Blessed One which is fitting, supreme, and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇā*)— with the words "Of the gods" (*devānām*).

Of that person whose mind—possessing the nature of the intellect intent upon serving [Hara] as the one and only form, desiring to adopt your form, names, and so forth—is fixed on Śiva alone, who is the embodiment of pure being (*śuddhasattva*), and not on any other deity;
and whose mind does not, like that of yogis and others, desire to abandon it in the future; of such a person, thus...
For that man whose mind is fixed on the One alone, and not on knowledge, action,

and so forth— when the *sattva* (the state of being) of the senses, which "play" (*divyatām*) because they sport, or rather of those deities who preside over the senses and by whom the objects are "signified" (*liṅgyante*), i.e., made known— their objects, such as sound and the rest, become real objects.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: that function (*vṛtti*), which consists of the apprehension of His [the Lord's] words and so forth, and which is unrestrained and directed toward Him alone—that is devotion to the Blessed One (*bhāgavatī bhakti*).
In this context, the phrase "in the state of goodness alone with a one-pointed mind" means that the function of the senses occurs in the state of goodness alone.

It is connected to both [sides] by way of the maxim of the crow’s eye. Here, one should not suspect that the term *sattve* refers to those possessing the quality of *sattva*, such as Brahmā and Rudra; for this is excluded by the term *bhāgavatī*. Alternatively, *satya-bhāva* is *sattva*, meaning Vaiṣṇava-nature; [the compound means] "those whose minds are fixed on that."
For one whose mind is single-mindedly fixed on Vaiṣṇava as the auspicious goal, that activity of the senses directed toward Vaiṣṇavahood alone is *bhakti*.

Nor is their activity *bhakti* when proceeding according to one's own whims; rather, it belongs to those who practice in accordance with the mantra taught by the venerable Guru. Thus, the Guru speaks of "recitation" (*uccāraṇa*).

"Anuśrava" means that which is heard traditionally; it refers to the mantra. For those for whom that very action prescribed by you is the "ānuśravika" (scripturally revealed) and the constant duty (*nityakṛtya*), furthermore—so that there may be composure of mind through the elimination of impurities such as feces and urine.
Therefore, the anus and the generative organ are the means for propitiating him.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Viṣṇurahasya*, even the functions of the anus and the generative organ are designated as "devotion" (*bhakti*) through their connection with devotion; this defines the scriptural (*vaidhī*) means-devotion (*sādhanabhakti*).

Now, by separating it with the particle *tu*, [the author] indicates the devotion consisting of the internal state (*bhāvabhakti*) which is to be accomplished by that [means], namely that called *rāgānugā*.
The natural functioning of those who have become such is inherently superior even to perfection and liberation;
thus, the meaning obtained is that even this natural functioning is weightier and more excellent than liberation.
Furthermore, natural functioning is of two kinds: for some, it occurs solely through the instruction of the scriptures.
For one who has engaged in pure devotion as instructed by the Śrī Guru, through the repeated practice of worship,
there arises a natural inclination of the senses toward Hari for one who has ascended to the stages of steadfastness, relish, and attachment—
just as worldly people naturally possess such inclinations toward their husbands, sons, and others.
Furthermore, that disposition toward Hari which— by virtue of extraordinary impressions produced through the grace of great souls,
whether ancient or modern— arises naturally from the instruction of a guru, either before or immediately after it, even without the formal discipline of the scriptures,
and which consists precisely in the practice prescribed by the scriptures of devotion; that too [is a form of devotion].
The natural form of devotion is to be understood as superior by its very nature to the previous, rule-bound devotion (*vaidhabhakti*), as evidenced by authoritative means.

An example of this is to be known from the four verses beginning with *naikātmatām* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.34). As for the other, the path of attachment (*rāgānugā*), its superiority is innate; and no example of it need ever be cited.

Thus ends the verse. However, that which is non-natural suffers inferiority in terms of both its means of proof (*pramāṇa*) and its genus (*jāti*) when compared with those that are natural. An illustration of this is the pair of verses beginning with "This world as well as that one" (*imaṃ lokaṃ tathāmuṃ*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.39).
Since both types of this devotion are free from desire (*niṣkāma*), the intended fruit is that very devotion itself;

however, the unintended fruit is liberation (*mokṣa*). He speaks of that [liberation] with the words "it wears away" (*jarayati*). That devotion which wears away—that is, exhausts—the sheath, the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*); and furthermore, [it leads] him to liberation, which has knowledge as its cause.

He states the distinction [of liberation] by means of an illustration: "Just as the internal fire (analas) digests what has been swallowed and eaten, such as food. For that internal fire, since it is not possible for it to have any purpose other than nourishing the body, digests only the non-essential portion of the consumed food and so forth; however, by means of the essential portion, it sustains the vital breaths, the sense organs, and so on.
He nourishes the seven constituents [of the body], by which very [means] the body becomes possessed of vigor, fortitude, and strength; likewise,
his devotion consumes only the insubstantial portions of illusory objects such as sound, as well as their instruments and agents,
but not the substantial portions consisting of non-material sounds and so forth related to the Blessed Lord.
It also causes the decay of the senses and so forth, according to the Vedic revelation: "The eye of the eye, and the ear of the ear," and so on.
By these very [powers], the bodies of devotees become perfected; for this reason, [the ordinary body] is merely an insubstantial portion of *māyā*.

The *liṅgakośa* is referred to in the scriptures by such terms as "body" (*deha*), "senses" (*indriya*), and so forth; for example: "of those dwelling in the city of Vikuṇṭha, who are devoid of body, senses, and life-breath," and so on. Furthermore, just as the digestive fire (*jāṭharo 'gni*) digests the food and other substances consumed even without human effort, [the text explains] the manner in which it performs that digestion.

And yet, a person does not realize that devotion liberates from *saṃsāra* even one who makes no effort for the sake of liberation, but who constantly performs such acts as hearing and chanting while intoxicated by the relish of its sweetness. But how, and when, will the devotee [attain it]? Me—?
One does not reflect that "liberation has occurred," as it will be said: "By the great boat of Your feet, they cross the ocean of existence as easily as a cow's footprint" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.2.30).
Just as a person walking on a path does not reflect upon having stepped over a cow's footprint, so it is in this case.
Even though devotees may lack knowledge of the threefold Brahman,
this Self is not attained by instruction,
nor by intellect, nor by much hearing.
"Whomever He chooses, by him He is attained;
to him this Self reveals His own form"—
from this Śruti, [it follows that it occurs] through devotion arising from the Lord’s compassion.
Liberation arises solely from the knowledge that consists in the experience of His form, qualities, pastimes, sovereignty, and sweetness;

for even in the Śruti, "Only by knowing Him does one go beyond death," the word "only" (eva) indicates that such knowledge alone is the cause of liberation, and that knowledge is precisely of the kind described above in every respect.
But the knowledge of its true nature is as follows: "From which words turn back, unable to reach it along with the mind" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4);
"He by whom it is not thought, by him it is thought; he who thinks he knows it does not know it" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3);
"Only those who have attained heaven have not reached the inner limit because of its infinity" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.87.41).
This is certainly impossible for anyone, according to the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* scriptures.

Furthermore, it will be explained later that liberation in the form of the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman must be abandoned by devotees. Moreover, the digestive fire (*jāṭharānala*) begins to digest the food and other items consumed at the very moment of eating.
Just as even when begun, [the digestive fire] digests [food] properly only after three or four watches (yāmas), so too,
although devotion has set out to destroy the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)— which consists of grief, delusion, and the like— during the stage of practice (*bhajanadaśā*),
it destroys it properly only after some lapse of time; therefore, during the stage of practice...
It should be understood that even when sorrow, delusion, and the like have not yet departed, one must not perceive this worldly existence as real among those who are devoted.
Thus, [devotion] is that which possesses the mantra taught by the Guru and follows the procedures prescribed in the scriptures on devotion.

Devotion (*bhakti*) is the functioning of the sense organs, such as hearing, toward the Blessed One, which is devoid of desire for anything else and free from [the pursuit of] knowledge, ritual action, and so forth. When that devotion is of limited measure, it is "devotion as a means" (*sādhanabhakti*), which is non-natural (*asvābhāvikī*).
That same devotion, when it has reached full measure, becomes "devotion as the goal" (*sādhyabhakti*), which is natural (*svābhāvikī*) and constitutes "devotion as being" (*bhāvabhakti*).

That very same devotion, though small in measure, if it is natural (*svābhāvikī*) due to its excellence by birth alone and is named *rāgānugā*, is the *sādhana-bhakti*. Furthermore, when that [same devotion] becomes full in both birth and measure, it becomes *bhāva-bhakti* of the *rāgānugā* type;
this distinction is to be understood from the *Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu*. ||3233||
Some who are devoted to my service and whose efforts are directed toward me do not desire oneness with me;
they are devotees who remain attached to one another.
They celebrate my heroic deeds.
"Even if Hari does not desire to grant union (*sāyujya*) as a fruit, yet being satisfied by devotion, He grants it; they accept it solely as His command.
For such [devotees], there will be an even greater abundance of happiness in liberation. (34)
Śrīdhara: Devotion establishes its own superiority, not oneness; [this is shown] by five verses.

"Oneness" means liberation through union (*sāyujya-mokṣa*). "Those whose efforts are for my sake. "Having become attached," meaning having formed an attachment. "Manly deeds" refers to heroic exploits. (34)

Sanātana (Ha.bha.vi. 10.440) establishes that devotion is indeed superior even to liberation: "not [seeking] oneness with the Self. Oneness with the Self refers to the liberation of *sāyujya*; by means of service to His feet, he speaks of the very reality: "my efforts" (*madīhā*) means efforts solely for His sake, namely the activities of the ears, the faculty of speech, and so forth.

Regarding those [people]: he clarifies this very point with the word "ye" (those who). Having become deeply attached, they celebrate human heroic deeds—that is, they honor them through hearing, chanting, and so forth. By the word "prasajya" (having become attached), the natural excellence of flavor inherent in the celebration of heroic deeds, which serves as the cause for mutual affection, is shown.
Therefore, its status as the most venerable is established; such is the direction [of the argument]. ||34||

The Sequence of Composition: Now, an objection is raised: "Previously, liberation was stated to be the fruit; how then can it be said to be surpassed by this [devotion]? To this, he says: "Not oneness with the Self," and so forth. Some are connoisseurs of the unique rasa of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*). *Īhā* means longing or desire. Therefore, that [liberation] is merely a semblance of devotion (*bhakty-ābhāsa*).
The meaning is that it arises for those who came before. ||34||

Viśvanātha: Having stated the definition, he provides an illustration. Speaking first among those seven, he clarifies with reasons the verse beginning with "animitta" by means of four [verses], starting with "na": "Not for the sake of oneness with the Self—that is, for liberation in the form of identity with Brahman—"

The word "spṛhayanti" (they long for) establishes their superiority over [the state of] perfection. Now, one might ask: "Filled as they are with what happiness do they not find pleasure in the bliss of Brahman? To this he replies: [Their longing is] for the service of my feet alone by means of all the senses, and not for knowledge and so forth; they are *abhiratāḥ*, meaning intensely attached, being directed toward me (*abhi*) through the scriptures (*śāstra*).

By this, it is stated that devotion has the Blessed Lord as its object, consists of the activity of all the senses, is devoid of ritual action, knowledge, and so forth, conforms to the scriptures, and is innate. "Those whose effort and desire (*īhā-vāñchā*) are directed toward Me alone—that is, toward the relishing of My beauty, sweetness, and other qualities... [is the meaning].
Being devoid of desire for anything else, they repeatedly engage in and savor with praise the nectar-like pastimes of the Supreme Person, such as the lifting of Govardhana;
because of that, there is an absence of the bliss of serving His feet and an absence of the experience of His beauty, fragrance, and so forth.

And because of the absence of tasting the nectar of divine play (līlā), one does not take pleasure in the bliss of Brahman; thus, three reasons have been stated for the lack of desire for liberation. ||34||
O Mother, those virtuous ones behold my radiant,
divine forms, which bestow boons and possess serene faces with reddish eyes.
Together they utter a desirable speech.
Śrīdhara: With those forms of mine whose eyes are gracious; "together with" (sākam) means along with them.
The sense is that the bliss of experiencing the Supreme Lord is constant, and it is even greater in devotion. ||35||

The sequential composition: "the forms" means together with the various distinctions of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and their manifestations (*prasaṅga*). The meaning is that they have merged with one another. ||35||

Viśvanātha: Since they are devoid of longing for fruits ending with *sāyujya* (union), he says in two verses that they obtain this from me. "They see" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), implying that they also hear, smell, taste, and so forth. "Forms" (*rūpāṇi*) is also an elliptical expression.

And [they experience] sounds, fragrances, tastes, touches, and so forth—divine, non-material, bestowing boons, and granting the service of their desired objects.
