Or else, O devotees! they speak together with me, saying, "Choose a boon," and so forth. [The devotee replies: "I desire nothing other than service at Your feet."

"O Lord, a boon sought by those who possess nothing is better," they say; "neither the station of Brahmā nor the abode of Mahendra," and so forth. By the mere desire to hear their words, which are themselves desirable, it is said, "Choose a boon from me," and not otherwise.

The sense is that I too desire to grant them every boon. The venerable Svāmicaraṇas maintain that the bliss of experiencing the Supreme Lord is eternal and even greater than [the fruits] of devotion. ||35||
By those lovely limbs, by their noble grace, smiles, glances, and charming speech,
their hearts were captivated and their very lives taken; thus, devotion [arose].
It impels my subtle movement even against my will.

Śrīdhara says: "But the bliss of the Self will necessarily arise," and thus he states: "by them" (*taih*). [He refers to those] whose limbs—the face, eyes, and so forth—are beautiful and captivating; whose self—that is, their mind—is captivated;
and who have had their life-breaths—that is, their senses—drawn away. He describes those who worship them even against their will, that is, even though they are devoid of desire.

She impels—that is, she causes one to attain—the subtle goal, which is liberation. By what means? Through the noble qualities of the one whose self is absorbed [in her], such as *vilāsa* and others. Among these, *vilāsa* is playful charm; *vāma* is that which is captivating;
and *sūkta* is sweet speech. (36)

The sequential composition [of the commentary] begins with the words "designated as the fruit of one's own karma," and so forth; thus, due to his wretchedness and his desire for pure devotion alone, even though he did not wish for it, [he attained] that which is minute and subtle, difficult to perceive because it transcends material nature, characterized by the status of being an attendant [of the Lord]. ||36||

Viśvanātha says: "By the very sweetness of beholding me, which is experienced with aesthetic wonder (*sacamatkāram*), a lack of relish for *brahmasāyujya* (union with Brahman) is produced. He states this with the word "by them" (*taiḥ*). "By those limbs"—the beautiful and most enchanting parts, such as the limbs of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others—"sublime" (*udārāḥ*).

In those [deities] such as Vilāsa and others who grant the desired objects of their devotees, devotion—because it is the very life-breath of the mind—drives the devotee toward even the slightest state [of liberation], even against his will. O devotees!
It merely prompts you to accept liberation, which is of the singular nature of Brahman; it does not, however, bestow it.

He finds no opportunity; for through the Lord’s playful charms, smiles, glances, and sweet speech, their very selves have been stolen away, and thus there is an absence of anything to offer—this is the intended meaning.
Now, if this is so, then how can supreme devotion exist toward those who are unwilling? How could it be so?
Why does he employ this? It is said:
Someone who is indeed a giver of great jewels such as the cintāmaṇi, diamonds, and rubies may show even gold to supplicants, [thinking] otherwise that the giver has no gold at all.

Just as those of dull intellect who seek only gold might cause a foundationless structure to be built, so too devotion— acting for the sake of repelling the crowd of those who consider themselves knowers (jñānin) while seeking only liberation— employs even its own devotees in that manner; it should be understood,
however, that it does not intend to grant them liberation itself.

Or rather, devotion itself impels those people whose minds are absorbed in it toward the subtle goal; the meaning is that it does not seek nor desire the subtle goal—that is, it acts as the motivator for the absence of desire.
This is just as in the case of the two expressions "he impels one who is acting" (*kurvantam prayuṅkte*) and "he causes to act" (*kārayati*).

The meaning of the sentence containing the *ṇic* suffix is exactly the same as that of the *ṇij*-derived [causative] form itself. To illustrate: just as one might say "he causes him to cook" (*pācayati*) when it must be said that "he employs one who is cooking," and thus he is called "the instigator of the cooking" (*pacana-prayojaka*), in the very same way, devotion leads the devotees to the subtle goal (*aṇvīṃ gatim*).

While it should have been said that "he does not desire," it is stated that "he employs [the body] without desiring even the subtle movement. Alternatively, because he desires only devotion out of wretchedness— in the manner of [the verse beginning] "Whatever womb I enter, ordained by the fruit of my own karma"— even though he does not desire it, [he enters it] because of its being beyond nature (*prakṛti*) in a subtle way.
The context is that [the Lord] employs and causes one to attain the state known as being an attendant (*pārṣada*), which is difficult to understand.

Śrī Rūpagosvāmī’s venerable feet explain that He captivates the minds and lives of people who do not desire even the subtle state (*aṇvīṃ gatim*), by means of His playful charms (*vilāsa*) and so forth. Thus, even those who are "without desire" (*anicchataḥ*), meaning devoid of longing, [are drawn].

The venerable Śrīsvāmicaraṇa explains that [the root *yuj*] means "to employ" and "to cause to reach. This interpretation is also not entirely inconsistent, because the experience of all happiness by devotees through the various doors of the senses will be explained further on. And thus, devotion is devoid of [ordinary] desire.
Even if He were to forcibly lead them to liberation so that they might experience the bliss of Brahman—

bringing them to the lake of Brahman, where they would sink, and then, according to the manner described as "they were rescued by Kṛṣṇa," leading them out from there and appointing them as His own associates in the abode of the Lord, [He does so] so that they may always be filled with the bliss of devotion.
Some say that the intended meaning of "he causes to immerse" is to be understood from plunging into the meaning of the subsequent verse;
furthermore, [the Lord says: "Behold now that manifestation of mine, the wielder of *māyā*, that sovereign power consisting of the eightfold *aiśvarya* which has come forth."
They do not even desire the auspicious fortune of a devotee of the Lord;
rather, they attain it for themselves in this world.

Śrīdhara: He states that there is also an abundance of *vibhūti* (manifest power) and so forth therein: "Then (*atho*), immediately after the cessation of ignorance, although the attainment of *vibhūti*—the perfection of enjoyments located in Satyaloka and other realms, as well as the eightfold sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā*—has followed along with devotion and has been obtained spontaneously of its own accord..."

They do not long for the fortune of the Bhāgavatas, the prosperity residing in Vaikuṇṭha; although the meaning is that they do not desire it, nevertheless, in the world of Vaikuṇṭha, they surely attain it.
This is the sequence of the composition. He shows that very point with two verses beginning with "atho. Now, atho...

Immediately after the cessation of ignorance, through my *māyā*—that is, by virtue of compassion directed toward my devotees—I manifest my divine power (*vibhūti*) for their sake. This includes the abundance of enjoyments as well as the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*) beginning with *aṇimā*, which proceed spontaneously as established by my very nature; likewise, that which pertains to the *bhāgavatas*.

They do not even desire *śrī*— the prosperity known as *sārṣṭi*, which is directly related to the Lord— desiring only the bliss of devotion. Although the meaning is that they do not long for those [attainments], nevertheless, they surely attain (*aśnuvate*) them in my world called Vaikuṇṭha.
His particular affection for his own was demonstrated, as in the case of Sudāman, the excellent garland-maker:
he too chose unwavering devotion to that very Self of all,
as well as friendship toward His devotees and supreme compassion for all living beings.
"Thus, having granted him boons and Śrī, who increases his lineage... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.41.52).

By this, their lack of attachment there is illuminated. And by the words "after the cessation of ignorance" and "requested through my grace," the fact that those [boons] are of the nature of misfortune is refuted. Or rather, [requested] through Māyā.

By the phrase "even the prosperity attained in the world of Brahmā and so forth," it is shown that they possess mastery over all things, but not the enjoyment thereof; for because such [worldly] enjoyment is utterly trivial, it is unworthy of them. And there is a scriptural text on this point: "Just as here the world won by action perishes, even so there the world won by merit perishes."

Immediately following this, [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6] says: "Now, those who depart from here after having discovered the Self and these [deities] whose desires are true—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds. (37)

[The Essence of the Blessed One 65] Viśvanātha: Furthermore, since the practices of karma-yoga, jñāna-yoga, and so forth are established as being inseparable from devotion (*bhakti*), and because devotion— even when not accompanied by those specific practices— bestows their respective fruits, that which is [attained] through ritual actions...

Because [the word] "by austerity" and so forth is heard at the beginning [of the verse], even heaven and other such things are in reality the fruits of devotion alone. He says that those possessed of pure devotion dwell in my world itself and experience all forms of happiness that are not included within my worship— [this occurs] immediately after the cessation of ignorance (avidyā), by means of Māyā.

The vast majesty consisting of all the pleasures found within the entire universe— of which there is also the reading *māyinas tāni*— and the bliss of the eightfold yogic powers such as *aṇimā*, which has spontaneously arisen following devotion (*anupravṛttam*), as well as the divine fortune (*bhāgavatīm śriyam*) residing in Vaikuṇṭha, known as the attainment of equality with the Lord (*sārṣṭi-saṃjñām saṃpattim*).
The word "and" (ca) implies that they certainly do not long for even the bliss of Brahman;
the meaning is that although they have no desire for those [other states] because their self, mind, and life-breath are captivated by my smile, glance,
and so forth, nevertheless, they enjoy them in my world, Vaikuṇṭha, which belongs to me, the Supreme Lord.
"Indeed they attain [it]"—thus his particular affection for them is shown. ||37||
Those who are devoted to Me shall never perish, even in the form of peace; My unblinking weapon does not lick them up, for to them I am the beloved Self and a son.
A friend, a teacher, well-wishers, and one's chosen deity.
The Self [is the agent], because it is the agent of the taking up and so forth of the honey. 38.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: If that is so, then, like heaven and other such realms, the world—due to its lack of distinction—might at some point suffer the destruction of both enjoyers and objects of enjoyment. To this he replies: O You of peaceful form! Or rather, in Vaikuṇṭha, whose nature is that peaceful and pure *sattva*, those who are devoted to Me shall never perish.

They do not become deprived of enjoyments. My unblinking weapon and my Wheel of Time (Kālacakra) do not lick them—that is, they do not devour them. The reason for this is: "Of those who... [they are] like a son, an object of affection; like a friend, a locus of trust;
like a teacher, an instructor; like a well-wisher, one who acts for their benefit; and like a beloved deity.
He is to be worshipped. Thus, the meaning is that Kālacakra, who belongs to me, does not devour those who worship me with their whole being. ||38||

*Sanātanaḥ* (Ha.bha.vi. 10.183): O You who are the embodiment of the scriptures! [Those who take refuge in You] never perish, nor do they become deprived of enjoyment. The reason for this is: *animiṣo me hetiḥ*—my weapon, the Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*), does not lick them; it does not swallow them. Or rather, it does not even touch them with the tip of its tongue.
The reason for this is given in the words "of those who": they are an object of affection like a son; a locus of trust like a friend;

an instructor like a guru; one who acts for their welfare like a well-wisher; and worthy of worship like a beloved deity. The meaning is that the Wheel of Time belonging to Me does not devour those who thus worship Me with their whole being.
Alternatively, the meaning is that they will not perish; even while enjoying various objects of the senses and so forth, they do not fall away from their own path.

Or else, the meaning is that they do not become invisible to me. Therefore, the Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*) is unable to lick or, in any way, even touch it with its tongue. The word "and" (*ca*) here [indicates this].

Because, among those categories, everything is established by [considering them as] being just one or the other. Alternatively, there are those for whom I am directly in the form of a beloved and so forth. In that context, a "beloved" (*priya*) is an object of affection due to such things as receiving assistance;
the "self" (*ātman*) is beloved by its very nature; and "friends" (*suhṛd*) are all kinsmen and relatives.
The beloved deity; the Lord who bestows his very self—among these, the increasing difficulty of attainment should be inferred in successive order.
For example, he is the beloved husband to the sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, and he himself is the very Self to the cowherd women.
Thus, in this context, due to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of describing the greatness of the devotees, the sequential order is not required. (38)

The sequential arrangement: Now, if that is so, since there is no difference in their being "worlds" (*loka*), might the enjoyers and the objects of enjoyment therein ever perish, as is the case with heaven and the like? To this he says: In Vaikuṇṭha—that which possesses a peaceful, unchanging form (*śāntarūpe*)—the worlds inhabited by those devoted to Me (*matparās*) never at any time [perish].

Those who are devoid of objects of enjoyment will perish; they do not exist. My weapon, the unblinking Kālacakra, does not lick them—it does not swallow them—according to the Vedic revelation: "He does not return again" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1).
"O Arjuna, all worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return;
but having attained Me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth again"—thus from the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣad. It is also stated in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*: "Supreme" means most excellent.

It is the *parāyaṇa* because it is the place of going, the state that is free from the fear of returning. In the masculine gender, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. He says "of whom" (*yeṣām*) to show that their greatness is not merely this much:
they are dear to Lakṣmī and the others, and they should be meditated upon as such. Thus, the Self is the Supreme Self (*paramātmā*).
He is the son of Sanaka and others; the grandson of Bhava and others; the friend of Śrī Śrīdāma and others; the teacher of Śrī Pradyumna and others;
and like the Pāṇḍavas and others, he alone is their friend in various forms—such as being the brother of one, the nephew of another, or the son-in-law of yet another—and is their beloved deity.
It is as in the case of Uddhava and others;

or rather, it was said thus with reference to Goloka and other realms, for there the Śrīgopas exist eternally in such a state, such that there is no one else who is a recipient of their love except Me.

The meaning is as follows. Alternatively, what kind of state do those people attain in that world immediately after the cessation of ignorance? To this he says: "Of those who..."—referring to any of those groups of sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, as shown in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa, who possess the latent impressions [of their devotion] and [call out], "My dear Lord! regarding me.

The meaning is that whoever meditates upon Me— whether they be Sanaka and others who possess latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and meditate on Me as "This very Self is indeed Brahman," or others who do so in any other way— they alone attain [Me]. The plural number in the word *suhṛdaḥ* ("friends") is used for the sake of generality.
This is said with reference to the various distinctions within friendship. Thus, in the fourth book of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, in the words of Śrī Nārada:
"Those who are peaceful, impartial, pure, and pleasing to all beings, being dear kinsmen of Acyuta, go directly to the abode of Acyuta" (Bhā.Pu. 4.12.37).

Therefore, it has been shown that devotion in the form of affection for a son is appropriate for you, since you are not born from me; and her ultimate conclusion was likewise: "Even though she had realized the truth, she remained as affectionate as a cow when her calf is lost" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 3.3.21). [Bhagavatsandarbha 65]

Viśvanātha: [Objection: But if that is so, then since there is no difference in their being worlds (*lokatva*), the enjoyers and objects of enjoyment might at some time perish, just as in the case of heaven and other such realms. To this he says: In my world, which is peaceful—that is, whose nature is unchanging—the worlds dwelling therein, being devoted to me, shall never perish, nor shall they be deprived of objects of enjoyment.
[They] exist. "My unblinking weapon, the Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*), does not lick them,
nor does it swallow them"— for according to the Vedic revelation,
"O Arjuna, all worlds up to the realm of Brahmā are subject to return."
"But having come to Me, O Kaunteya, rebirth does not exist"—thus it is stated in the Gītā-Upaniṣads.

Furthermore, in the *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*, the word *parāyaṇa* is explained as "the supreme, most excellent goal or abode, free from any suspicion of returning. This refers to those for whom I am dear (*yeṣām ahaṃ priyaḥ*).
[He is] the beloved for those possessing the mood of the lover; the Self for those of peaceful devotion; the son for those possessing the mood of parental affection;

the friend for those possessing the mood of friendship; the teacher for those possessing a specific mood of servitude; the well-wisher (in the plural)—the plural form being a Vedic archaism—for those possessing various types of friendship; and the cherished deity for those possessing the mood of servitude. And so it has been said:

In the *Nārāyaṇavyūhastava*: "Salutations again and again to those who, ever-exerting themselves, meditate upon Hari as they would a husband, a son, a friend, a brother, or a father, and with the same affection as toward a friend."

Regarding the scriptural statement, "He is attainable only by whomsoever He chooses," the meaning should be understood as follows: he is attainable by one whom He chooses out of affection—as a father, a brother, a friend, or as a son, servant, and so forth. This is an illustration of natural devotion (*svābhāvikī bhakti*) characterized by attachment (*rāgānugā*).
This is to be known. ||38||
This world and likewise that one, the self that moves between both;
and those who follow the self here—wealth, cattle, and homes.
Having abandoned all others, those who worship me alone, who am thus facing in all directions, with undivided devotion— I carry them across beyond death.

Śrīdhara: He says, "I grant such liberation as this to those who are exclusively devoted," in two verses beginning with "imaṃ. "Ubhayāyinam" means that which goes to both worlds—the self with its limiting adjuncts (sopādhika). "Anu" refers to those [relatives] such as sons and wives, as well as animals and so forth. "Rāyaḥ" means wealth. And others... [39]... and others.
From grasping, from death, and from saṃsāra, I shall cause you to cross over, to go beyond. ||40||
The sequential composition: He concludes in the same manner with the following two verses beginning with "imaṃ" (this).

Thus, in such ways as being dear and so forth; "viśvatomukham" means having infinite manifestations according to various states; "ananyayā" means by that which is unmixed with any other state. ||39-40||
Viśvanātha: With two verses, he provides an illustration of instrumental devotion (*sādhanabhakti*), which is not innate.

"Having cast off attachment to this [world] characterized by attachment to visible enjoyments, to that [heaven] characterized by attachment to invisible enjoyments, to the one who goes to both—that is, to the self which moves between both—and likewise attachment to the enjoyer, the locus of the sense of 'I' (*ahantā*)," just as...

Attachment to enjoyments and the like is understood from the praise of enjoyments and so forth; likewise, the abandonment of attachment to those very things is understood from their censure. As it has been said: "And while enjoying those desires, he censured them as resulting in suffering" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.20.28). Similarly, those [desires] which have the self as their object...

"Sons, wife, and so forth," as well as "wealth" such as riches and the like—meaning that in whichever direction these things go, I remain facing right toward them. "With undivided [devotion]" means devoid of devotion to other deities, as well as devoid of knowledge, ritual action, and so on. [From] death...

The meaning is: "Even though they do not desire to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra because they only long for devotion, I shall carry them across—that is, I shall cause them to reach the further shore—even without having commanded them thus. As it has been said: "She who quickly consumes the sheath," and so forth. (3940)
Nowhere else but from me, the Blessed One, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa,
the Self of all beings, does intense fear cease.

Śrīdhara: He states that for non-devotees, however, there is no liberation by any means at all—with the words "not" (na). "Other than My Lord" (mad-bhagavato 'nyatra) means other than Me, the Lord; "the Self of all beings" (sarva-bhūtānām ātmanaḥ).
By these three qualifying attributes of the Lord—beginning with "Lord"—His power, independence, and beneficence [are indicated].
And it has been said: ||41||

The sequential arrangement: As for what was stated by you in your inquiry regarding primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), that is simply nothing at all; thus he says: "Not elsewhere" (na-anyatra). ||41||

Viśvanātha: He says that there is no liberation at all without devotion to Me—"other than Me" meaning "without Me," which is to say, without devotion to Me. Although My own nature is infinite as the object of devotion, by means of the three qualifiers, the preceding ones are primary.
He indicates some of the forms that are to be served: first, the Lord is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, who is complete;

then Śrī Rāma, the Lord of the Primal Person (Puruṣa) and the Master of the Supreme Abode (Paravyoman); and then the Self (Ātman), who is the inner controller of material nature (prakṛti) and the inner controller of the cosmic aggregate—these constitute the triad of Persons (puruṣatraya). These are the incarnations of the Person (puruṣāvatāra).
The Fish, the Tortoise, and others are also to be known [as such]. ||41||
Out of fear of me this wind blows; out of fear of me the sun shines;
Indra sends rain, fire burns, and death moves about—all out of fear of me.
Śrīdhara clarifies His sovereignty with the words "out of fear of Me. And the Śruti says: "Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises;
out of fear of Him Agni and Candra, and Death as the fifth, run forth" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1).
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, you have stated that [liberation comes] "by unswerving devotion"; therefore, one might ask with some arrogance: "Do other gods, when not propitiated, ever cause suffering to your devotee? To this [he replies]:
He said: "Me. And the Śruti says:
"Out of fear of him the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises;
out of fear of him Agni and Candra, and Death as the fifth, run on" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1).
The sense is this: if they should ever cause even a single devotee of mine suffering, then I shall not delay at all in casting them down from their respective positions of authority. ||42||
Through the yoga of devotion joined with knowledge and dispassion, yogis enter the soles of my feet for their ultimate security— a state free from all fear.
Śrīdhara: Regarding the point that liberation comes only from worshiping Me, he cites the conduct of the virtuous as proof—"Knowledge," etc.
[This is] a sequence of verses; it has not been commented upon [here].
Viśvanātha: Having described pure devotion, he speaks of devotion mixed with knowledge and so forth—"Knowledge," etc.
In this world, the emergence of the highest good for men is precisely this:
that the mind, through the intense yoga of devotion, is firmly fixed upon Me.
Śrīdhara: He concludes with the words "this much. That the mind, when offered unto Me, becomes steady—this alone is the extent [of the means]. ||44||
The sequence of the composition: as in the verse beginning with "Of the gods," he states his own view with the words "This much" (*etāvān*).

The meaning is: by means of that which is intense, firm, unbreakable through yoga, ritual action, and so forth—in other words, by that which is pure. That which is offered by that very [means] becomes "existent" (*sat*), meaning stable; this alone is the [means to] the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
The manifestation of the supreme human goal. ||44||
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, he states that his own devotion alone is the most excellent of all—“*etāvān*” (so much).

The sense is that there is nothing whatsoever for the arising of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) superior to this; rather, everything else is indeed inferior to it. [This occurs] through intense, firm, and unbreakable [devotion], not through knowledge, ritual action, and so forth.
The meaning is "by means of the pure"; it is the arising of *niḥśreyasa*, the supreme human goal. ||44||
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
this twenty-fifth chapter has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous.
Thus, in the glorious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, in the commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*,
in the *Pāramahaṃsya-saṃhitā* of Vyāsa’s compilation, in the third book (*Skandha*), in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
The twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Devotion," in the *Kāpileya*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
In the *Kāpileya-tattvasamāmnāya*,
the Blessed Lord said:
"Now I shall explain to you the characteristics of the principles (tattvas) individually."
Having known which, a person may be liberated from the qualities of material nature.
Śrīdhara:
In the twenty-sixth [chapter], for the sake of distinguishing between the Spirit (puṃs) and Primordial Matter (prakṛti),
[the nature of] all entities is described according to Sāṅkhya by way of the difference in their characteristics of birth.

The Knower of Reality has declared here the Sāṅkhya doctrine concerning the self, which was taught by Dhātar to his son, by Mitrā’s son to the Kṣatriya, and by [Vasiṣṭha] to his mother, according to its primary significance.

Regarding the statement, "That which they call the tradition of reality is Sāṅkhya," three things are introduced here: Sāṅkhya, devotion (bhakti), and yoga. Having spoken of devotion, he now states Sāṅkhya with the words "Now" (atha). ||1||

The sequence of composition: Having thus fulfilled [the purpose], he describes even the paths such as Sāṅkhya-knowledge and Yoga for the sake of discernment alone, until the conclusion—beginning with the word "yathā" (as follows). ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the twenty-sixth [chapter], the characteristic origin of the Mahat and the other principles is described;
likewise, by means of those [principles], the Virāṭ is explained, and his consciousness [is established] through the entry of the Self.

When Mātrā was questioned regarding the paths of devotion (*bhakti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), she spoke of devotion; yet, even after she had fulfilled her mother’s purpose by that very means, she taught that because results such as heaven and liberation cannot be granted through the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*) or the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*) without devotion, devotion is the sovereign goddess (*mahādevī*) presiding over all of them.

Since even the followers of that sovereign lady (Sāmrājyavatī) ought, out of curiosity, to desire to know her karma, knowledge, and so forth, he says "Now" (atha) in order to speak of her knowledge at this point. ||1||
I shall describe to you that knowledge which they say leads to the supreme good for a person— the vision of the Self— which severs the knot of the heart.

Śrīdhara: Regarding "knowledge": I shall describe to you that knowledge consisting of the vision of the Self, which for that very reason severs the knot of the heart, removes egoism, and is said to have the supreme good as its purpose. It is from the knowledge of the characteristics of reality alone that the knowledge of the distinct Self arises.
That which comes into being is "bhāva" (existence). ||2||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Now, one might ask: "What will come of knowing the definitions of the principles (*tattva*)? To this he says: "Knowledge" (*jñāna*).
The sense is that from the very knowledge of the definitions of the principles, the knowledge of the isolated Self (*viviktātman*) arises. (2)
The Self is beginningless, the Person, devoid of qualities, beyond primordial nature;
it is the inward abode, self-luminous, by whom the universe is pervaded.
It is well known that the Madhva [scriptures] declare: "He is supreme; He is neither born nor does He die.
For even the *jīva*, which has assumed the attributes of the limiting adjuncts such as the body, is born and dies through delusion (*bhrānti*), just like in a dream.
What need is there to mention the case of identifying with the body, since that too is a delusion?

"Īśvara is endowed with distinctions such as omniscience and sovereignty; how much more so for the independent [Supreme Being]? Birth, death, and so forth would belong to another [limited being], since even for the *jīva* there is a connection with birth, death, and so on due to delusion. Thus it is stated in the Mahākaurma Purāṇa. (3)

Śrīdhara: Therein, he defines the Puruṣa as "without beginning" (anādi). The Puruṣa is the Self alone. What is this Self? It is that whose abode is consciousness (sphūrti) directed inward toward each object of perception. He rules out the position of momentariness by saying "without beginning. He rules out the position of being a transmigrating being by saying "beyond Prakṛti."
"Other" means unattached. He precludes [the Lord] having qualities such as knowledge by saying "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇaḥ).

He precludes being an object of knowledge as held by the Mīmāṃsakas and others by saying "self-luminous" (svayaṃjyotiḥ). By this very term, the manifestation [of the Self] as the substratum of knowledge, as maintained by the Prābhākaras, is also refuted.
The reason for its being self-luminous is that the universe is permeated by it—the word "shines" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
By these very reasons, the transcendence of this Puruṣa over Prakṛti is also established. ||3||

The sequential composition: "beginningless" means that the Self is indeed the Supreme Self, the Person devoid of qualities (*puruṣo nirguṇaḥ*), free from the qualities of primordial nature (*prākṛta*). By the phrase "by whom the universe is pervaded," His status as the cause of all is indicated.
Through this, His possession of infinite powers (*anantaśaktitva*) is shown by virtue of being the illuminator of manifold variety. (3)

Viśvanātha: Therein, he defines Puruṣa: the Puruṣa is the Self, beginningless and eternal; indeed, he is the Supreme Self (Paramātman) himself, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), meaning free from the qualities of Prakṛti. For he is beyond Prakṛti. He is the inward-facing abode inaccessible to all the senses, and he is the ocean of causes. Therefore, he is self-luminous (svayaṃjyotiḥ).
Self-luminosity is the reason for its being self-effulgent; the ellipsis is "by which the universe, being pervaded, shines forth. ||3||
The all-pervading Lord, as if in sport, accepted that subtle divine Prakṛti, composed of the Guṇas, which had approached him of its own accord.
Of the honeyed [drink]: "upāgatām" means situated nearby. ||4||

Śrīdhara: Here, *prakṛti* is twofold due to the distinction between the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) and the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*). Among these, by the power of concealment, that very [prakṛti] is *avidyā*, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*). By the power of projection, that very [prakṛti] is *māyā*, belonging to the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī*). And the *puruṣa* is twofold, in the form of the individual soul and the Lord. Of these, that which...

That individual soul (*jīva*) transmigrates due to non-discrimination from *prakṛti*; however, he who, having brought *prakṛti* under control, performs the creation of the universe and so forth, is the Lord (*īśvara*). In this regard, [the author] describes the manner of the soul's transmigration through non-discrimination from *prakṛti* with five verses beginning with "He, this very one. [He perceives] the subtle, unmanifest, divine...
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) and the arrangement of the sequence is as follows: "He attained the power of the god Viṣṇu, which had come forth through sport, by mere chance" (*yadṛcchayā*).

This very Supreme Self, by "mere chance"—that is, by his own free will—which is his "sport" (*līlā*), "attained," meaning he willed. As stated in the *Brahma Sūtra*: "But as in the case of worldly beings, his sport alone [is the cause]" (2.1.33).
This follows from logic, as well as from the Vedic scripture: "He thought" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.5). ||4||

Viśvanātha: This Supreme Self, by His own will—that is, by His own independence—due to His inherent power, at the very moment of His desire to emanate the world bound by karma, spontaneously assumed the form of the individual soul-power (*jīva-śakti*) as a sport; the meaning is that, bestowing His virility (*vīrya*) upon her, He "reflected" (*aikṣata*). ||4||
Beholding Prakṛti creating offspring of various qualities and identical forms, he was instantly bewildered here by the concealment of his knowledge.
"Madhvaḥ" means he bewildered, that is, he caused delusion. Understand this from me—as in the expression "having performed the marriage," and so forth. ||5||

Śrīdhara says: He describes her *līlā* with the words "by the qualities" (*guṇaiḥ*). She is called *jñānagūhā* because she conceals or veils knowledge (*jñānam gūhayati āvṛṇoti*). And so says the Śruti:
"The unborn, one, red, white, and black..."

"Producing many offspring of similar form, the unborn one lies beside her, taking delight in her; yet another unborn one leaves her once she has been enjoyed. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5) Thus it is said.
He became bewildered and forgot his own self. ||5||
The sequential composition: Next, he describes the state of another person with the words "by the qualities" (*guṇaiḥ*).

And [he describes her] as creating that [world] by means of a single part. Here in this body, that well-known person called the *jīva* became deluded by the very *prakṛti*, through its function known as ignorance (*avidyā*), which is a secret of knowledge. In this context, the word "beholding" (*vilokya*)...

By the words "by this," "he was deluded," and "by the concealment of knowledge," it is understood that the knowledge which is inward-turned (pratyagbhūta) in contrast to the outward-turned (parāgbhūtā) primordial nature (prakṛti) and the ignorance produced by it, must be His very own power of essential nature (svarūpa-śakti). And likewise in the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣad: "Knowledge is covered by ignorance; by that..."
"Living beings are deluded" (Gītā 5.15). ||5||

Viśvanātha: Regarding that, he describes the delusion of the individual soul (*jīva*): "Beholding *prakṛti*, that individual soul, situated here in this *prakṛti*, immediately—at the very moment of contact with *prakṛti*—becoming joined with the very *prakṛti* through its function called ignorance (*avidyā*), which is a cave of knowledge, became deluded; he forgot his own true nature, due to primordial ignorance (*anādyavidyā*) that is ever-present."

The meaning is that just as the individual soul (*jīva*), even when engaged [in activity], perceives its own true nature somewhat during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), so too, prior to creation, even during dissolution (*pralaya*), it remained perceiving its own nature; however, at the commencement of creation, it forgot that [nature]. Of what kind? [It refers to] subjects (*prajāḥ*) diverse through the qualities (*guṇaḥ*), such as *sattva* and the others.
[She is] creating; and thus says the Śruti:
"The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form."
"For one unborn soul, being attached, lies along with her; another unborn soul, having experienced enjoyment, leaves her.
Thus, through meditation upon the Supreme, the person [attains] agency from Prakṛti.
While actions are being performed by the qualities, one imagines them within the self.
"Where one causes [another] to act, there the agency is said to belong primarily to the one who is entirely independent;
for instance, it is taught that even one who knows Brahman partakes in saṃsāra [only as a subordinate agent]. Likewise:
'Whether in dissolution or in creation, [the Lord acts] while remaining untainted at any time.'"

"Brahman remains at all times devoid of primordial nature (prakṛti). Thus it is said in the Kāpileya. Likewise, through the contemplation of the Supreme and by the will of the Supreme Self, the individual soul (jīva) imagines within itself that primordial nature is the agent. (6)

Śrīdhara: "Parābhidhyāna" means superimposition upon primordial nature (prakṛti); by that [superimposition], while actions are being performed by the qualities of nature, one imagines agency in the self. ||6||

The sequence of the composition: Through the contemplation of the Supreme (parābhidhyāna) and the immersion into primordial nature (prakṛti), by means of the thought "I am indeed nature," one imagines oneself to be the agent in actions performed by the qualities of nature.
In this state, because the contemplation of the Supreme is impossible for one devoid of ego-sense (nirahaṃbhāva), there arises the ego-identification born from the immersion into the Supreme.
Because it does not cause concealment, there certainly exists within that [state] another specific form of the "I-sense" (ahaṃbhāva);
and since that rests solely upon one's own pure nature, it is clear that it is not a cause of saṃsāra.
This very point is stated: when these two types of egoism are dormant in the group of senses and in the "I," one is the immutable (kūṭastha).
The absence of recollection of that [state] in the absence of latent disposition (*āśaya*) has been shown in the passage *āśayam ṛte tadanusmṛtir naḥ* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.3.39).

This is because the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which consists of the conceit of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi-abhimāna*), remains dormant; and by the phrase "there is no recollection of that," it is shown that there is a reflective awareness of the self alone in the form "I slept happily. For this very reason:

Even in this reflection, "I did not know myself," there is an absence of recollection for one who identifies with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), whereas for another, there is recollection by virtue of being the witness of ignorance; such is the direction of the argument. //6//

[Paramātma-sandarbha 30] Viśvanātha: "Just as one who watches another dancing or singing imitates them" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.22.53)— according to this principle, through the contemplation of the Supreme and the superimposition of material nature (*prakṛti-adhyāsa*), that *prakṛti* becomes the body.

Thus, by the thought "I am indeed the body," one imagines oneself to be the agent in actions performed by the qualities of *prakṛti* and in the perceptions of form and so forth. In that state, since the absence of egoism (*nirahaṃbhāva*) makes higher contemplation (*parābhidhyāna*) impossible, and because the egoism born from the penetration of the Supreme acts as a veil, [the obscuration] certainly exists.

In that state, there is a specific form of the "I-am-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*) directed toward another. And it is clear that because this [state] rests solely upon one's own pure essential nature (*śuddhasvarūpa*), it is not a cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). It should be discerned that when a Brahmin youth, while still possessing egoity (*sāhaṅkāra*), is possessed by a spirit, he says, "I am a spirit. (6)
[In this regard, one should consult the Brahma-sūtra 3.2.5: "But because of the meditation on the Supreme, [the nature] is concealed; for from that arises his bondage and its opposite.
Thus, his transmigratory existence, bondage, and dependence are caused by that.
It belongs to the Lord who is a non-doer, a witness, and one whose self is liberated.
"O Madhva, Viṣṇu, and the Gurus, the independence of the individual soul (jīva) is eternal;
however, that state of dependence upon another which it possesses ceases through knowledge. And:
"It is an agent neither because of being a non-doer nor because of being powerless; rather, it is a non-agent because of being unafflicted, or else because of not being an effect."

Śrīdhara: "That" refers precisely to the conceit of agency. Although this person is in reality a non-agent due to being a mere witness, there is bondage through actions. For the Lord, who is independent and whose self is fulfilled, there is dependence regarding experience caused by the bondage of karma.

The meaning is that this entire cycle of transmigration—the continuous flow of birth and death—belongs to that which is essentially of the nature of happiness; all of this occurs due to the non-discrimination of primordial nature (prakṛti). ||7||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: That [bondage] belongs to this individual soul (*jīva*) precisely because of its conceit of agency; for although it is in reality nothing but a witness and thus a non-agent, it is bound by actions. Just as [the property] of a king...

A person is called a king; likewise, even for the Lord—who is denoted by the word "Īśa" and whose nature is the power of Īśvara—there is dependence on experience caused by the bondage of karma. Even for one whose self is fulfilled and whose very nature is bliss, there is saṃsṛti, the continuous flow of birth and death. ||7||
They know Prakṛti to be the cause in the agency of action and its instruments;
they know Puruṣa, who is beyond Prakṛti, to be the experiencer of pleasures and pains.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: "This [Lord] is the agent; he is not created, and he is the cause and the Lord of the universe," so it is said in the *Mahābhārata*. "By means of the power of Śrī Viṣṇu, the eternal Viṣṇu himself is the creator of the world through Brahmā and others, and the bestower of pleasure and pain."
"Lord Hari alone personally effects the agency regarding pleasures and pains;
the state of being the enjoyer and the cause thereof resides in the individual soul (jīva) and nowhere else. Thus says Śrīdhara in the Bhaviṣyat Parva.
Now, [an objection may be raised]: since agency and so forth are perceived as being in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with consciousness itself...
Let that [agency] be accepted as belonging to the self alone; to this he says "no. The effect is the body; the cause is the sense organs;
the agent is the group of deities. They know Nature (prakṛti) to be the cause for the person's attainment of those states, because there is no modification in the immutable one (kūṭastha) by itself.
The meaning is that agency and so forth are produced solely by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) which is a transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
As for the statement, "But they know the Puruṣa to be the cause in regard to being the enjoyer," its intended sense is this:
although agency and so forth, as well as the state of being an enjoyer, reside only in the ego-sense, nevertheless, [the Puruṣa is the cause] of the modification...

Because it terminates in the insentient, experience has the substrate as its primary element; because it terminates in consciousness, that which is superimposed [upon consciousness] has the primary element. ||8||
The sequence of composition: that which functions through the predominance of its limiting adjunct (upādhi) is designated as having the attributes of that adjunct;

thus he says, "the effect," etc. Here, in such passages as "they know Nature (prakṛti) to be the cause of the agency of cause and effect," [the agency] functions through the predominance of the Supreme Self and is therefore indeed without limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika).
As it is said:
"The one who acts without attachment is considered *sāttvika*; the one blinded by passion is known as *rājasa*;
the one whose memory is lost is *tāmasa*; and the one devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) takes refuge in me. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.25.26).

Now, he says "bhoktṛtve" (regarding the state of being an enjoyer) to show that the state of being an enjoyer, by virtue of its nature as consciousness (*saṃvedana*), ultimately culminates in that very same conscious form (*cidrūpa*). The phrase "they know the cause" is to be construed with what precedes it.
Here, according to the commentary (*ṭīkā*), the analogy of a reflection is to be understood; for in this case, [qualities such as] trembling and so forth belong to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
Dharma [is the cause] of that which is superimposed, whereas illumination belongs to the substrate itself. However, even in our own system, that too is not accepted;
for since even action is impossible without consciousness, there is a disparity between the example and the case at hand. ||8||

Viśvanātha: Bondage for the individual soul (*jīva*) arises solely through its actions (*karman*), and for those actions, both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* are respectively the causes in their accomplishment and in the experience of their fruits; thus he says—"the effect," etc.
Since the accomplishment of action occurs precisely through the elements (*bhūta*), the senses (*indriya*), and the deities (*devatā*), [he speaks of] those elements, senses, and deities.

Regarding the agency of cause and effect, they know *prakṛti* alone to be the cause; for since their state as such is produced by *prakṛti* itself, the meaning is that the soul’s (*jīva*) agency in action is dependent upon *māyā*. Furthermore, since the Supreme Lord alone is the bestower of the fruits of action, the soul is the experiencer of the fruits of its actions.

He says that [the soul's state] is indeed dependent on the Lord: "They know the agency of the person (puruṣa) to be the cause for the individual soul's (jīva) experience of the fruits of its actions"—this is the grammatical connection. ||8||
Devahūti said: O Supreme Person, please describe the characteristics of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa— the two causes of this world— and that which constitutes their nature as being and non-being.
Madhva [states] that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless. ||9||

Śrīdhara: Thus, having understood the transmigrating person and its cause, *prakṛti*, he now asks about the Lord (*īśvara*), the cause of the world, and His *prakṛti*—beginning with the words "Of *prakṛti*. Of this universe; that which consists of both the real (*sat*) and the unreal (*asat*), namely the effects in their gross and subtle forms. Of those two...
Of primordial nature and the person. ||9||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: And therefore, desiring to know those two—the *prakṛti* and the *puruṣa*—in particular, he says: "Of *prakṛti*... Of this universe, that which is both existent (*sat*) and non-existent (*asat*), both gross and subtle.
Whatever the nature of the effect may be. ||9||
The Blessed Lord said:

That which is composed of the three qualities (guṇas), unmanifest, eternal, and consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, is called Pradhāna and Prakṛti; it is without distinction, yet appears as if possessed of distinctions.
One should know that which consists of the manifest and the unmanifest, and which is of the nature of both being and non-being.
When it is devoid of creation, it is purely manifest; when desiring to create, it possesses the nature of both.

"Nature (prakṛti), which is manifest in the form of effects, is considered to be threefold. Because it is the primary cause of all effects, it is proclaimed as 'Pradhāna' (the Primary). Due to its lack of differentiation and its non-derivativeness from other causes, and because she rests upon the illustrious Viṣṇu, she is so called. Thus it is stated in the *Harivaṃśa*.
"The specific effect is indicated by the specific [cause], since it is from the specific that the effect is seen," as stated in the *Pādma*. (10)

Śrīdhara: Therein, he defines *prakṛti*. That which is *pradhāna* is precisely what they call *prakṛti*. What is that *pradhāna*? It is, by its own nature, devoid of distinctions (*aviśeṣa*), yet it possesses distinctions (*viśeṣavat*) and is the substratum of the specific manifestations (*viśeṣa*). If so, is it Brahman? No, for it consists of the three *guṇas*. Is it the principle of *mahat* and so forth? No, it is the unmanifest (*avyakta*), not an effect (*akārya*).
Is it time and so forth? No; it consists of both the existent and the non-existent, in the form of cause and effect. Is it the individual soul or primordial nature? No; it is eternal. ||10||
The Sequential Composition: Now, he states the definition of *pradhāna*, which is the constituent part that serves as the material cause (*upādāna*), beginning with the words "That which...

That which is indeed composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*)—the aggregate of the three qualities, *sattva* and so forth—is precisely what they call the *avyakta*, the *pradhāna*, and the *prakṛti*. The reason for its designation as *avyakta* (the unmanifest) is its lack of differentiation (*aviśeṣa*).

Because it consists of the equilibrium of the three *guṇas*, its specific distinctions are unmanifest; for this very reason, it is understood to be designated as "the Undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*). The reason for its designation as "Primal Matter" (*pradhāna*) is that it possesses distinctions. By virtue of being the substratum for the specific effects of its own parts—namely, the *mahat* and so forth—it is superior to them. Regarding its designation as "Nature" (*prakṛti*): [The text continues: ...because it is the source from which all things proceed. The reason for its designation as "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) is that it is not perceived by the senses. It is called "the Unperceived" (*aliṅga*) because it is devoid of the marks (*liṅga*) of the manifest world. It is called "the Cause" (*kāraṇa*) because it is the cause of the entire universe. It is called "the Root" (*mūla*) because it is the root of all existence. It is called "the Indestructible" (*akṣara*) because it is imperishable. It is called "the Eternal" (*nitya*) because it is constant. It is called "the Immutable" (*avyaya*) because it does not undergo transformation. It is called "the Sovereign" (*īśvara*) because it rules over all. It is called "the Self-sufficient" (*svatantra*) because it is independent. It is called "the Unborn" (*aja*) because it is not produced. It is called "the Unborn One" (*ajā*) because she gives birth to the world. It is called "the Unborn Mother" (*ajām ekām*) because she is one and unborn. It is called "the Unborn Source" (*ajām ekām lohita-śukla-kṛṣṇām*) because she is the source of the three *guṇas*. It is called "the Unborn Origin" (*ajām ekām bhūta-bhāvinyām*) because she brings about the existence of all beings. It is called "the Unborn Originator" (*ajām ekām bhūta-bhāvanīm*) because she causes all beings to come into being. It is called "the Unborn Originator of All" (*ajām ekām sarva-bhūtānām*) because she is the originator of all beings. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the Past and Future" (*ajām ekām bhūta-bhavyasya*) because she is the originator of both past and future. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the Present" (*ajām ekām bhūta-bhavyasya*) because she is the originator of the present. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the Three Times" (*ajām ekām bhūta-bhavyasya*) because she is the originator of the three times. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the Entire Universe" (*ajām ekām sarvasya jagataḥ*) because she is the originator of the entire universe. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the Manifest and Unmanifest" (*ajām ekām vyakta-avyaktasya*) because she is the originator of both the manifest and the unmanifest. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the Perceptible and Imperceptible" (*ajām ekām dṛśyādṛśyasya*) because she is the originator of both the perceptible and the imperceptible. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the Known and Unknown" (*ajām ekām jñeyājñeyasya*) because she is the originator of both the known and the unknown. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the Attainable and Unattainable" (*ajām ekām prāpyāprāpyasya*) because she is the originator of both the attainable and the unattainable. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the Finite and Infinite" (*ajām ekām parāparasya*) because she is the originator of both the finite and the infinite. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the High and Low" (*ajām ekām uccanīcasya*) because she is the originator of both the high and the low. It is called "the Unborn Originator of the Superior and Inferior" (*ajām ekām śreyas-pāpīyasoḥ*) because she is the originator of

The cause (*hetu*). It is that whose nature (*svarūpa*) is an underlying essence (*anugata ātmā*) consisting of both being and non-being (*sadasadātmaka*), because it persists as the causality within the effects and causes—such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth—which are themselves of the nature of being and non-being. Nevertheless, it is eternal, because during the dissolution (*pralaya*) it exists as the mere causal self, and during creation and maintenance it exists with all its constituent parts.

The phrase "of which the essential nature is unmodified" means that its nature is such that it has not undergone modification by way of the fivefold non-quintuplication (*apañcīkṛta*); thus, both its status as Brahman and its form as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth are excluded. This is because Brahman is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), whereas the Great Principle and the rest are effects (*kārya*) in relation to the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Alternatively, because it is impossible to define [it] due to its being a source of wonder in every respect, it is expressed by the words "that which" (yat-tat). For this very reason, those learned in the Vedas (śrauta) and those following the Smṛtis call that substance, which is renowned by the term "Pradhāna" because it is the most excellent of all, "Prakṛti. Its nature as a source of wonder is precisely what is meant.

He demonstrates this: although the unmanifest (avyakta) consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), it remains unmanifest; whereas the manifest (vyakta), being possessed of qualities, necessarily becomes manifest. Likewise, while the effect is existent and the cause is non-existent, both are eternal because they consist of that very essence, unlike clay and other such materials. Similarly, although [the unmanifest] possesses distinctions through the qualities of sattva and so forth, it is undifferentiated in its state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmyarūpatva); no other entity is like this.

Thus, when the meaning of the complete sentence has been established in this way, over-pervasions (*ativyāpti*) are to be avoided as appropriate by means of attributes such as oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth. [Paramātmasandarbha 55] Viśvanātha: Therein, he defines *prakṛti*: that which indeed possesses the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
The combination of the three qualities (guṇas), beginning with *sattva*, is precisely what they call the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), Primal Matter (*pradhāna*), and Nature (*prakṛti*).

Regarding the reason for its designation as "Unmanifest": it is because it lacks specific differentiation, being a state of equilibrium among the three qualities, and thus its particularities are not manifested. Regarding the reason for its designation as "Primal Matter" (*pradhāna*): it is because it possesses the potential for specific differentiation.

It is superior to those [evolutes] such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, which consist of its own parts and effects, because it serves as their substratum. The reason for its designation as *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is that it is "of the nature of both being and non-being. This means that its essence (*ātman*) or intrinsic form is that which persists as the cause throughout the entities—from the Great Principle onwards—which exist in the forms of both cause and effect.

It is eternal because it exists even during the dissolution of the universe in the form of its cause alone. Alternatively, that which is indefinable and is called *pradhāna* (the primary) because of its excellence, they call *prakṛti*. He explains this very indefinability: although the unmanifest (*avyakta*) consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), it indeed becomes manifest as possessing qualities (*saguṇa*). Just as: [example follows].

The effect exists [in the cause], the cause is non-existent [as an effect], and that which consists of those [causes] is eternal; yet clay and the like, being of such a nature, are indeed observed to be impermanent. In the same way, a substance possessing specific qualities such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth is indeed observed to be of one form, whereas that other form, the non-specific (aviśeṣa), is not observed. ||10||
The wise know this group of twenty-four principles to consist of five, five, four, and ten Brahmans.
Śrīdhara: In order to state the definitions of the other principles (*tattvas*), he enumerates them with the words "by five," and so forth.
By this numerical distinction, this group of twenty-four—in which there are these twenty-four—he, the wise, know as the *prādhānika* group, consisting of the effects of *pradhāna*. (11)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: In order to state the definitions of the other principles (*tattva*s), he enumerates them—beginning with "by five," and so forth:
that group which consists of five, likewise five, four, and ten.

The wise know that the group of principles arising from Pradhāna—which is wonderful—is Brahman, and they worship that group as Brahman. Of what nature is this group? It is that in which these twenty-four [principles] exist, beginning with the great elements:
namely, the five great elements—earth, water, fire, wind, and ether.
And I consider the subtle elements (tanmātras) to be of that same number as the [gross] objects, such as odor and the rest.
Śrīdhara explains this with three verses beginning with "the great elements": there are exactly five of them. ||12||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha*: not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: He explains those [five] with three [verses]. They are exactly five. ||12||
The ten sense organs are the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose;
speech, the two hands, the two feet, the generative organ, and the anus is said to be the tenth.
It has not been explained by anyone [else]:
"The mind, the intellect, the ego, and the consciousness—this is the internal self;
its fourfold distinction is characterized by its functional modes."
"Madhu said: 'The intellect (buddhi) creates doubt for the sake of determination;
the mind (manas) is indeed egoism (ahaṅkāra); and the heart (citta) is the cause of memory. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. ||14||

Śrīdhara: "Antarātmaka" refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). It has not been explained [here] as a sequential arrangement by means of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that serves to differentiate.
Viśvanātha: "Antarātmaka" refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). By means of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that serves to differentiate...
By means of function. ||14||
Thus far has this arrangement of the conditioned Brahman been described by me in its entirety; that which is the twenty-fifth principle is Time.

"Madhva [says]: Hari is the Brahman devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), while Śrī is remembered as the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa*). The principles (*tattvas*) are born from her limbs; therefore, it is said that they are of His form. Thus, in the *Harivaṃśa*.
"The Supreme Person dwelling in the heart is Hari, who is Time and all-pervading."
"Or rather, Hari residing within the body of Rudra is called Kāla. Thus [it is stated] in the Brāhma [Purāṇa]. 15.

Śrīdhara: "As much as has been declared by me, just so much has been reckoned and calculated by those who know the truth. Regarding time, however, he states two views: 'That which is time is the twenty-fifth [principle]. The suffix *ka* is used here in the sense of 'slight' (or 'mere'). The meaning is that it is merely a particular state of *prakṛti*. (15)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: [This refers to] the expansion of the quality of *sattva*, beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*). Regarding time, he states two views:
"That which is time is the twenty-fifth" means that it is simply a particular state of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) itself.
Some say that power and human effort are [the cause], while others say it is time, from which fear arises for the agent who is deluded by egoism and has fallen under the sway of material nature.

*Madhvaḥ*: The human power (*pauruṣa-prabhāvam*) is the state of the Person (*puruṣasya*), His pervasive form manifested through excellence. "Some" refers to those possessing perfect knowledge, who are non-material (*aprākṛta*). ||16||

Śrīdhara: Some, however, say that "pauruṣam" refers to the power (*prabhāvam*), the majesty (*vikramam*), or the time of the Person, the Lord. He characterizes that very time in two ways, from which fear arises.
Of whom? Of one who has gone to, or reached, *prakṛti*. For this very reason, it is for one who is deluded by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) within the body.
Of the agent, the individual soul (jīva). By this, he is characterized as the one who effects withdrawal. ||16||

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Some, however, say that "pauruṣa" refers to the power and prowess of Puruṣa, that is, Īśvara; they maintain that Time is indicated here as the agitator of the individual soul (jīva), since fear arises for the agent—the jīva—from it.
O Mānavī, that from which the activity of Prakṛti— whose qualities are in equilibrium and who is devoid of distinctions—
proceeds, is designated as the Blessed Lord Kāla (Time).
Śrīdhara defines [the Lord] by way of being the cause of creation: "Of Prakṛti," etc. (17).
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha characterizes him as the agitator of *prakṛti* as well: "of *prakṛti*," etc. (17).
The Blessed One, who exists internally in the form of the Puruṣa and externally in the form of Time, pervades all beings by means of his own creative power (māyā).
Madhva states: "The divine form consisting of Nārāyaṇa is the agitator of Prakṛti;
He is considered the Supreme Puruṣa, the creator of Mahat within Prakṛti."
That very [principle] called Vāsudeva is the regulator of the principle of Mahat;
while Hari, known as Saṃkarṣaṇa, is the controller of the subtle ego (ahaṃkāra).
Viṣṇu, known by the name Pradyumna, is the regulator of the gross ego;
the Lord Hari, as Aniruddha, is the regulator of the principle of the mind.
"The principles beginning with Mahat and the individual souls (jīvas) are likewise born from the limbs of Brahman;
through the distinction between the subtle and the gross, Aniruddha is born of desire. Thus it is stated in the Kāpileya [Purāṇa]. 1819.

Śrīdhara: Who is this Blessed One? He says "within" (antaḥ) regarding him: he who exists within all living beings as the Puruṣa, as the inner controller, and as the Equal One—meaning he remains perfectly permeated, entirely free from modification—and externally he is this Blessed One in the form of Time. Or rather, he who is the Puruṣa.
That which is well-known as time is the twenty-fifth principle. However, some say that time is the power (*prabhāva*) of the Person (*puruṣa*).
The reason for this is that it is the very characteristic of power. The reason why the Person alone is time is stated as "of primordial nature" (*prakṛteḥ*).
The reason for intending both [the Person and primordial nature] is given as "within. The rest is the same. Thus, in this way...

There are twenty-four divisions of Prakṛti; by intending the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), there are twenty-five principles (tattvas); and by intending their difference, they become twenty-six. ||18||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: For this very reason, internally, in the form of the Puruṣa, as the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), He governs; He is perfectly pervasive, remaining permeated [through all things] while Himself free from those modifications; and externally, He exists in the form of Time.

The controller of all beings and all living creatures; thus, this primary group consists of twenty-four in number. Together with Time and the individual soul (jīva), these two, along with the two—primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa)—constitute the twenty-eight principles (tattvas). ||18||
By destiny, the Supreme Person deposited His seed in His own womb, which was subject to agitation; she gave birth to the Great Principle (mahat-tattva), which is golden in nature.

Śrīdhara: Now, by means of the text beginning with "From fate" (*daivāt*) and ending before "these, without being combined" (*etāny asaṃhatya*), he states the definitions of the principles (*tattva*) preceded by their origin.

Among those, he states the definition of the mind (*citta*) preceded by its origin in four [verses]. [The first is: "From fate," meaning from the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*).

She, in whom the qualities (guṇas) are agitated, brought forth the Great Principle (mahat-tattva)—that Prakṛti having produced its potency, which is the power of consciousness (cic-chakti), within the womb, that is, the place of manifestation, namely Prakṛti itself. He describes the nature of the Great Principle: it is golden, meaning it abounds in light. ||19||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, while the *tattvas* (principles) are to be defined, he first states the definition of the mind (*citta*), preceded by its origin: "The qualities (*guṇas*), which are the attributes, are agitated by destiny (*daiva*) and time (*kāla*)."
In that womb, which is the locus of manifestation, the seed—consciousness known as the power of cit—brought forth Prakṛti, the principle of Mahat; it was golden, meaning it abounded in light. ||19||
Manifesting the entire universe within himself, the immutable sprout of the world drank up with his own splendor the intense darkness that causes the self’s slumber.
"Because Keśava, the sprout of the universe, delights [the soul] in the lap of Madhu;
he who created the great living being and swallowed the deluding darkness. Thus it is said. (20)

Śrīdhara: [The Lord], manifesting the universe—the expansion consisting of the ego and so forth—which resides within Himself in a subtle form, drank up the intense darkness of the time of dissolution.
He is *kūṭastha*, meaning devoid of dissolution or distraction. Of what nature was that darkness? It causes the Self to fall into deep sleep.

"He covers" (pracchādayati) means "he conceals"; that is to say, he who previously, at the time of dissolution, caused the Great Principle (mahat) to dissolve back into primordial nature (prakṛti). ||20||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Manifesting—that is, making evident—the universe (*viśva*), which consists of the expansion of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth, residing within the Self and existing in a subtle form within Himself; [the term] "Great" (*mahān*) is used everywhere in the masculine gender by omitting the word *tattva*.

Because this very [Self] has been made the subject of the description: "The immutable one (kūṭastha)—the Self free from the dissolution and distraction of the mind—causes itself to sleep"; the meaning is that He caused that darkness which, at the time of the previous dissolution, had dissolved the Great Principle (mahat) into primordial nature (prakṛti), to fall asleep. ||20||
That which is the quality of purity, clear and tranquil— the state of the Blessed One—
which they call Vāsudeva, that mind is of the nature of the Great Principle (mahat).
Regarding *madhvaḥ*: from that form of the Blessed One known as Vāsudeva, the mind (*citta*) consisting of *mahat* arises;
and by the word *sattva*, qualities such as perfect bliss (*pūrṇānanda*) and so forth are expressed. (21)
Śrīdhara: In this context, he describes the worship of the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) with the words "That which...
He states that it is well-known in all the scriptures: "clear" means transparent; "tranquil" means free from passion and other afflictions;
and it is the "abode" (*pada*) of the Blessed One, the place of his realization. For this very reason, they call it by the name Vāsudeva. This...

The meaning is as follows: in its form as the *adhibhūta* (the objective element), that very principle is designated as "Mahat" (the Great); in its form as the *adhyātma* (the subjective element), it is "citta" (the mind);

and in its form as the object of worship (*upāsya*), it is Vāsudeva. Its presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) is Kṣetrajña. Likewise, in the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), Saṃkarṣaṇa is the object of worship, and Rudra is the presiding deity; in the mind (*manas*), Aniruddha is the object of worship.
It should be understood that Candra is the presiding deity, Pradyumna is the object of worship within the intellect (*buddhi*), and Brahmā is the presiding deity;
this sequence of the composition has not been explained [elsewhere].
Viśvanātha: That which is well-known as the mind (*citta*) is of the nature of the Great One (*mahat*), the principle of Mahat (*mahattattva*).

The meaning is that it thus abides within the body in the form of the mind (*citta*). The pure, stainless, peaceful state of the Blessed One—devoid of passion and the like—is the seat of worship (*upāsanā-pīṭha*); it is that which they call the Blessed One known as Vāsudeva, [abiding] sequentially within the mind, ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and the internal organ (*manas*).

Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are the deities to be worshipped; they are to be known for the sake of purifying the mind and so forth. Viṣṇu, Rudra, Brahmā, and Candra, however, are the presiding deities. ||21||
Clarity, immutability, and tranquility are declared to be the characteristics of the mind through its modes of activity, just as the supreme nature of water is defined by its qualities.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: "That Hari, known by the name Vāsudeva, who resides within the principle of Mahat (*mahattattva*), is said to be the generator of the mind (*citta*) for each and every living being. And:
"Clarity and other such qualities of the mind are called its distinct attributes," beginning with "clarity" (*svacchatvam*).

In the *Tattvaviveka*, it is stated that "the disposition (*avakāra*) of the mind and so forth, which is like still water, is a slight modification. In the *Śabdanirṇaya*, it is said that "function (*vṛtti*), nature (*svabhāva*), conduct (*vṛtta*), and stability (*sthiti*) are synonymous. Thus, the meaning is that the definition is declared by means of functions; that is to say, it is the natural definition. ||22||

Śrīdhara: Transparency (*svacchatva*) is the capacity to receive the reflection of the Lord. Unchangeability (*avikāritva*) is the state of being free from dissolution and distraction. The primordial nature of water (*apām prakṛtiḥ*) is its state prior to foam, waves, and so forth. The meaning is that it is just like that [primordial state], which is sweet, transparent, and tranquil before contact with the earth.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the qualities such as clarity (*svacchatva*) are not perceived in the mind (*citta*) residing within the body? To this he replies: "Clarity is the capacity to receive the reflection of the Lord; immutability..."
The definition of the mind— that is, of *citta*— is stated to be freedom from lethargy and distraction, tranquility, and freedom from passion and the like,
by means of its very own natural fluctuations (*vṛtti*). Just as the supreme nature—
the most excellent inherent character— of water is such that, by virtue of it, water is clear and free from foam, waves, and the like.

They become sweet and tranquil. Just as [water] becomes turbid and so forth through contact with the earth and other elements, in the very same way, the mind also becomes turbid through contact with consciousness when it is attached to an improper object; this is the meaning. ||22||
From the principle of Mahat, undergoing transformation and arising from the potency of the Lord,
the ego (ahaṅkāra), which is the power of action, became threefold.
From which arise the Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Tāmasa [evolutes]— namely,
the mind, the senses, and even the great elements.
He is the very one whom they call the thousand-headed Ananta,
the Puruṣa known as Saṃkarṣaṇa, who consists of the elements, the senses, and the mind.
"Madhva says: 'The Great Principle (Mahat) is primarily characterized by knowledge, while the Ego (Ahaṅkāra) is predominant in action;
nevertheless, in comparison with the [subsequent] spokes [of the wheel], that [Ego] is also said to be predominant in knowledge. And:
"That which is presided over by a deity is traditionally known as *adhidaiva*. And: "The *Vaikārika* [ego] is *adhidaiva*."

The phrase "and so forth" indicates the sense of the ablative case. Regarding the locative case, the *Śabdanirṇaya* states: "Where independence is intended to be expressed, that [locus] takes the first [nominative] case.
Agency belongs to the form of the mind (*manas*), while being the object of action belongs to the form of the body.
And the status of the ego as an instrument is due to its being the essence of the sense faculties.
Since the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva) arises through the mind, the mind is known as the agent;
for it is the proximate limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the soul that is the agent by its very nature.
Since the senses are the instruments for action and knowledge, they are the means;
the body is designated as the effect, because it is produced again and again.
The father of the gods (Brahmā) is peaceful in form, while [the father] of the *karana*-beings has a mouth of blood;
as long as knowledge does not shine forth, he is considered the deluded father of the elements (*bhūta*).
This ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is of three forms; they know him thus as Śeṣa. Thus [it is stated] in the *Tattvaviveka*.
Śrīdhara: Indicating that such continued devotion arises solely through grace, and demonstrating His compassion even toward those who have done Him harm, he says:
"Oh, how wonderful is the nature of His compassion! For even though she desired to kill Him, Bakī—the wicked Pūtanā—He made her drink the Kālakūṭa poison gathered in Her breasts."

Even though she was wicked, Yaśodā attained the state appropriate for a nurse; the meaning is that he granted a noble destiny even to one merely through the guise of devotion. Who else, then, should we worship? ||23||

Is it not well known that the Blessed One favors only the devotees? True; yet I consider even the demons to be devotees, for like the devotees, they too perceive the Blessed One directly through their intense absorption in meditation upon Him. Thus he says: "With fury... (Saṃrambhaḥ).
Those whose minds were possessed by an onset of fury and were thus intent upon that path— precisely because of this,

they beheld [saw] him in battle, whose enemy was Sunābhāyudha (the one with the discus-weapon), who had Tārkṣya Kaśyapa’s son Garuḍa upon his shoulder; therefore, it is fitting to show favor even toward them.
This is the meaning. And he will say: "Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.1.28). ||24||

Now, in order to explain the manner of his concealment, he relates his life story briefly from the beginning: He was born to the wife of Vasudeva; while Kaṃsa, the lord of the Bhojas, was in his prison, [Kṛṣṇa], desiring to personally bring about the welfare and happiness of this earth, by means of Aja...
And having been entreated by Brahmā. ||25||
The composition of the sequence: he is one who possesses the power (*śakti*) for the production of mental states (*manas*) and so forth in ritual actions (*kriyā*). ||23||
The mention of "by the mind" is an elliptical expression; it should be understood here that [the process applies] to the gods as well, to all beings, and even to the great ones.
Furthermore, the intermediate sequence beginning with the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) is to be understood. ||24||

The meaning is that they declare the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) to be "directly infinite" (*sākṣād anantaṃ*), seeing the attainment of identity between the object of worship and its substratum, and thus speak of it as being equal to that [Brahman]. According to Amara, *sākṣāt* refers to both "directly" and "equal to perception. He qualifies the ego with the word "bhūta"—[meaning] infinite.
He distinguishes [the Lord] by means of the three words beginning with "thousand-headed": therein, the meaning of "the first person" is the person named Saṃkarṣaṇa. ||25||
Viśvanātha states the definition of *ahaṅkāra* (ego) preceded by its origin: "From the principle of *mahat*" (*mahattattvāt*).
The mention of "the power of action" (*kriyāśakti*) is illustrative, because it also possesses the powers of knowledge, action, and substance.
For from those—the *vaikārika*, *taijasa*, and *tāmasa* [forms of *ahaṅkāra*]—the mind, the senses, and the elements arise respectively.
"Bhava" means origination. Regarding that, he states the deity to be meditated upon: "Sahasra... [and so on]. By the maxim of "the beds cry out," the meaning is "that which resides in Him. ||2325||
The definition of the ego (ahaṅkāra) is its nature as agent, instrument, and object; or alternatively, it may be characterized by the qualities of the tranquil, the terrible, and the deluded.
