Śrīdhara states the definition: "agency" (kartṛtva) means [the state of being] in the form of deities and so forth; "instrumentality" (karaṇatva) means [the state of being] in the form of the senses; "effect-ness" (kāryatva) means [the state of being] in the form of the elements; while "quiescence" and the rest mean [the state of being] in the form of the three qualities (guṇas) of their respective causes.
The sequential arrangement: agency. ||26||

Viśvanātha: Agency exists in the form of the deity; instrumentality in the form of the senses; and the state of being an effect in the form of the elements; while qualities such as tranquility and so forth exist through the nature of the three *guṇas*. ||26||
From the transforming Vaikārika [ahaṃkāra], the principle of mind (manas) was born;
from its functions of volition (saṃkalpa) and doubt (vikalpa), the origin of desire proceeds.
Śrīdhara: He states the definition of the mind (*manas*) preceded by its origin in two verses beginning with "From the vaikārika...
*Saṃkalpa* is thought; *vikalpa* is specific thought. That mind for which the arising of desire occurs through *saṃkalpa* and *vikalpa* has a function (*vṛtti*) consisting of desire.

It is described as having the nature of a characteristic (lakṣaṇa), but not as the origin of the Pradyumna-vyūha, because that [Pradyumna] lacks the status of being an effect of volition (saṃkalpa) and so forth, and because it is Aniruddha who is stated to be the vyūha to be meditated upon. ||27||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: That from which [arises] the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—the general desire to grasp an object—and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is the specific desire to grasp that same general object through various forms of resolve.
From those two, the arising of desire—that is, the longing of the mind—occurs. ||27||
For they know him who is called Aniruddha, the supreme lord of the senses,
dark as an autumnal blue lotus, and who is to be gradually propitiated by yogis.

Śrīdhara: "Śārada" refers to the blue lotus (indīvara) of the autumn season; [the Lord] is dark like that, because He is to be gradually propitiated—that is, fit to be brought under control—due to His being difficult to grasp. (28)
The sequential arrangement: "That which they know" is as before. ||28||
Viśvanātha: Whatever is situated in whatever [is its locus]. ||28||
From the Taijasa principle, as it undergoes transformation, the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva) arose;
it is the cognition of the manifestation of objects and the faculty that favors the sense organs.
Madhva: It is that specific cognition which occurs upon the manifestation of an object. (29)
Śrīdhara: With two verses beginning with "taijasāt," he states the definition of the intellect (buddhi) preceded by its origin.
O Sati! The phrase "consciousness whose nature is the manifestation of objects" is stated for the purpose of excluding the mind (citta).
The phrase "the favoring of the senses" refers to determinate knowledge (savikalpajñāna). As for the phrase "the sovereign of the organs (hṛṣīka)"...
That, however, has already been explained in the case of non-conceptual cognition. ||29||
The sequence of composition: the pair beginning with "from the taijasa" [is as follows]. The function of the *citta* is mere apprehension;
that of the *buddhi*, however, is cognition (*vijñāna*) consisting of the manifestation of objects;
that of the *manas* is mere reflection. And this [process] results in the recollection "this is that," which occurs immediately after determinate knowledge (*savikalpajñāna*).
Viśvanātha: [The statement] "Vijñāna is the nature of the manifestation of objects" is intended to distinguish it from the *citta*;

however, it should be understood that *vijñāna* in the sense of consciousness is actually a property (*dharma*) of the *citta*. Regarding "the favoring of the senses," the meaning is that the five senses are not able to function without the *buddhi*. Although...

The mind (*citta*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the internal organ (*manas*) are also auxiliaries to the senses; however, the specific manner in which they assist them should be understood through the intellect (*buddhi*). For instance, in the cognition "I hear a sound," first a mere volition is established by the *citta*; then, by the *buddhi*, there arises the manifestation "this is a sound"; and finally, by the *manas*...
The desire to grasp sound is through the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), wherein one’s own self-conceit is projected; such is the distinction. ||29||
Doubt, error, certainty, memory,
and sleep— these are said to be the distinct characteristics of the intellect (buddhi) according to its functions.
"Madhva says: 'The common [cognition] is born of the mind (mānasa), while that which arises from specific [perception] is born of the intellect (buddhija).

Unwavering doubt is of the intellect; wavering [doubt] is said to be mental (mānasa). Memory is flickering when it is of the intellect, whereas memory born of the mind (citta) is indeed stable. Thus it is said.

"That by which an object is known is called its characteristic (lakṣaṇa); the wise know that it is twofold: its own nature (svarūpa) and its distinctness (pṛthaktva). Thus [it is stated] in the Kāpileya. 30.

Śrīdhara: Doubt and the rest are merely the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) of substance (*dravya*). Error is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Certainty is valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*). Sleep is slumber (*nidrā*), according to the statement of Patañjali: "Valid cognition, error, conceptualization, sleep, and memory [are the five functions of the mind]. (YS 1.6) ||30||

The sequential arrangement: the distinction regarding *buddhi* is that it consists of the contemplation of various specific qualities following the cognition of doubt and so forth. Here, however, Brahmā is the presiding deity to be worshipped within *buddhi*, while Pradyumna is the object of knowledge; as before, non-difference is stated for the purpose of worship. ||30||

Viśvanātha: The manifestation of substance itself is the world-appearance (*prapañca*); error (*viparyāsa*) is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), while certainty (*niścaya*) is valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*); sleep (*svāpa*) is slumber.
This is according to the statement of Patañjali: "Valid cognition, error, conceptualization, sleep, and memory [are the five mental modifications]. (YS 1.6) ||30||
The sense organs are indeed composed of light (taijasa), distinguished by their functions as either action or cognition;
for the power of action belongs to the vital breath (prāṇa), while the power of cognition belongs to the intellect (buddhi).
Śrīdhara: He states the origin of the senses: "taijasāni" means they are born from the *taijasa* (fiery) *ahaṅkāra*.

The word "eva" (only/alone) is used to dispel the doubt that the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) might be of the *vaikārika* (pure) nature. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that both types of senses are indeed *taijasa*. The reason for this is given by the words "prāṇasya," for (*hi*) because...

The power of action belongs to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the power of cognition belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, because the vital breath is of the nature of *taijasa* (fiery/active), the sense organs—which possess that power of action—are also of the nature of *taijasa*. Likewise, because the intellect is of the nature of *taijasa*, the sense organs—which possess its power of cognition—are also of the nature of *taijasa*; this is the meaning.

The sequential arrangement: The sense organs (*jñānendriya*) are also of the nature of *taijasa* (fiery), because they consist predominantly of *rajas* due to their being determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*). ||31||
Viśvanātha: The sense organs are indeed *taijasa* (fiery), having been produced from the *taijasa-ahaṅkāra*.

The word "indeed" (*eva*) is used precisely to dispel the doubt that the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) might be *vaikārika* (pure). The reason why both types of organs are *taijasa* is stated as "of the vital breath" (*prāṇasya*). For (*hi*), because... of the vital breath.

Therefore, because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) possesses the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), it is fiery (*taijasa*); likewise, the sense organs, which possess that power of action, are also fiery. Similarly, the intellect (*buddhi*) possesses the power of cognition (*vijñāna-śakti*);
thus, because the intellect functions through conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna-vṛtti*) and is consequently abounding in *rajas*, it is fiery by nature.
The sense organs, which possess the power of cognition belonging to that [self], are also composed of light (taijasa). ||31||

And from the tamasic principle undergoing transformation, impelled by the potency of the Lord, there arose the subtle element of sound; from that came the ether, and the sense of hearing is the perceiver of sound.
"Madhva [says]: 'The primary wind, the Sūtrātman, is born together with Mahat;
and from Tejas, Ṛju, Sparśa, and so forth—these are remembered as his sons. Thus [it is said]. (32)

Śrīdhara: Having first described the origin of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), he explains the origin of the gross elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*) and their characteristics in fifteen verses starting with "From the *tāmasa* [aspect]... As for the verses beginning with "The ear, however, is the perceiver of sound," the mere relationship between the sense organs and their objects is stated after the origin of the objects; their actual origin is not described there.
Because it has already arisen previously; it goes to or reaches the sound, thus it is "sound-going" (śabdagam). ||32||
The sequential arrangement: the potency of the Lord is the form of time, and its power is that sound is apprehended by the ear;

by this, the extrinsic definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) is indicated. That which is graspable by the ear is "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*). Other [explanations] are merely further elaborations; the same applies to what follows. ||32||
Viśvanātha: The potency of the Lord is the form of Time; by its power, that sound is impelled.

In response to the inquiry as to who perceives that sound, he says: the ear—the sense organ of hearing—is the product of the *taijasa* (fiery) *ahaṅkāra*; it "goes to" or reaches the sound, which is the agent [of perception]. ||32||
Sages know that the definition of sound is its being the substratum of meaning, its serving as a mark for the observer,
and its being nothing more than space itself.
The state of being based on an object for the honeyed [words] means having an object as their domain. ||33||

Śrīdhara states the definition of sound: its nature consists in being dependent upon an object and being expressive of that object. Its being a "mark" (liṅga) for the observer means it serves as an indicator of a speaker who is concealed by a wall. As it has been said: "The mark [is established] between the observer and the observed. The fact that sound is merely the dimension of space (nabhasas tanmātratva) refers to its subtlety.
The connection [of the words] is "the definition" (lakṣaṇam). ||33||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Poets state the definition of *śabda* (the word). What is that? It is being the locus of meaning (*arthāśrayatva*), being the designator of meaning (*arthavācakatva*), and being the mark for the observer (*draṣṭṛliṅgatva*).

It is the state of being a knower by Vyāsa, Śuka, and others who witnessed the divine sports (līlā) of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth; or else, it is the state of being a communicator even for a speaker concealed behind a wall, as well as the state of being merely that [subtle element], namely the subtle form of space (ākāśa). ||33||
The characteristic function of space is to provide openings for living beings both externally and internally,
and to serve as the locus for the vital breaths, the senses, and the self.

Śrīdhara states the definition of space (*nabhas*): "Of beings," etc. Its nature as a giver of apertures (*chidra*) means its nature as a giver of room (*avakāśa*). It is the locus for external and internal activity. The "self" (*ātman*) here refers to the mind (*manas*).

Its being the "abode" (*dhiṣṇya*) of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth means its being their support in the form of apertures such as the channels (*nāḍī*). "Function" (*vṛtti*) means its effect (*kārya*).

Such is the definition of the function-characteristic (*vṛttilakṣaṇa*). Likewise, in what follows, one should understand that by means of one verse the arising of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross elements (*mahābhūta*) is shown; by the second, the definition of the subtle elements; and by the third, the definition of the gross elements. ||34||

The sequential arrangement [of the definition] is as follows: being the substratum of sound is the definition of the specific substance [ether], and its being a mark (liṅga) for the perceiver is also mentioned.

However, the definition of its essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is "consisting of that alone" (*tanmātratva*), namely, being ether itself; and this definition is intended precisely with the desire to express non-difference. In reality, however, sounds and the like are of two kinds [external and internal], belonging to substances such as ether.

There are two states: the subtle state and the state of the qualities (guṇa). Among these, the former consists of the subtle elements (tanmātra), while the others consist of objects such as sound and so forth. ||34||

Viśvanātha states the definition of space (ākāśa): its nature consists in being the giver of apertures—that is, the giver of room—and being the locus for the conventional usage of "outer" and "inner. Its nature is also defined by its functions and qualities, such as being the abode of the vital breaths, the senses, and the mind, serving as their support in the form of channels and other cavities. (34)
From the sound-tanmātra of space, undergoing transformation through the movement of time, touch arose;
from that came air, and the skin is the receptacle of touch.
Since it is known by the word *madhvaḥ* alone, that is its mark of Hari;
because of the absence of touch and the other [sensory qualities], it is proclaimed as the subtle element (*tanmātra*) of space.
And the others, such as touch and the rest, are merely subtle elements (tanmātra) due to their prior arrangement;
one quality alone persists in each of the five gross elements.
Sound consists of phonemes and is eternal; it is resonance born from space.
Space itself, when subtle, is designated as "resonance" (dhvani).
When that very [sound] is manifested, it becomes perceptible solely by the ear;
from the subtle element of sound within space, the mere quality of sound came into being.
"Touch and the other qualities are also proclaimed to be the subtle states of air and the rest;
the subtle senses indeed exist, while the gross ones arise from the ego (ahaṅkāra).
Furthermore, they are accumulated from the elements, and again from the body of Brahmā. Thus it is said. [3537]
Śrīdhara: What is this "tvak"? It is that by which there is the *saṅgraha*—the complete grasping—of touch (*sparśa*).

The word "masculinity" (*puṃstvam*) is used because of its fixed gender. Alternatively, the ellipsis is: "from that [tvak], the grasping of touch arises. This was stated for the purpose of showing the successive connection of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), beginning with the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*). ||35||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: From the ether (*nabhas*) which consists of that alone—namely, sound itself—from that [ether], by means of that through which [it] is properly grasped (*saṃgṛhyate*); the suffix *ap* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). The skin is the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*).
The meaning is that it is the instrument for the apprehension of touch. ||35||
Softness, hardness, coldness, and heat—this is the tactile quality of touch; such is the subtle essence (tanmātra) of the wind.

Śrīdhara states the definition of touch: "Softness," etc. The meaning is that the nature of touch (*sparśatva*) is its essential characteristic (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, this constitutes the state of being a subtle element (*tanmātratva*) of the wind (*nabhasvat*). ||36||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states the definition of touch (*sparśa*): the meaning is that "touch-ness" (*sparśatva*) is its essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*). The state of being a subtle element (*tanmātratva*) belongs to the wind (*nabhasvat*), which is air. ||36||

Shaking, expansion, reaching, and leading—these are the characteristic actions of air with respect to substances and sounds; its nature as the self of all the sense organs is likewise its defining mark.

Śrīdhara: *Cālana* is the shaking of tree branches and the like; *vyūhana* is the gathering together of grass and the like; *prāpti* is the conjunction of a fragrant substance with the sense of smell, as well as the contact of that which possesses coldness and so forth with the sense of touch;
it is the leading of sound toward the ear; and it is the selfhood of all the senses.
The state of being a corroborator (*upodbalakatva*). It is characterized by the action, which is the effect; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
However, if one analyzes the compound as "the action itself is the characteristic" (*karmaivābhilakṣaṇam*), then the suffix is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). ||37||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states the definition of air (*vāyu*): shaking of tree branches and the like; pushing together (*vyūhana*) is the clumping of grass and the like; reaching (*prāpti*) is conjunction with any material object; [the quality] of substance and sound [is the conjunction] of a substance.
Odor acts toward the sense of smell; coldness and other qualities act toward the skin; and sound acts as a conductor toward the ear. Here, "attainment" (*prāpti*) is indeed conjunction (*saṃyoga*);
it should be understood that movement, expansion, and conducting are specific types of conjunction. Furthermore, wind possesses the nature of all the senses or the quality of enlivening them.

Karma alone is the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) in every respect; it is called a "characteristic" because one is characterized by it—the suffix *lyuṭ* being used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). ||37||
And from the subtle element of touch belonging to air, impelled by the gods, form arose;
from that, fire emerged, which is the eye for the perception of form.
Vāyu attains everything from Hari himself;
therefore, they call Vāyu, the lord of beings and the master, "Prāpti" (the Attainer).
Since the primary Vāyu is eternally present within all others, for that reason [he is so named].
"Their qualities are said to reside in them, yet there is no lowness in him because of that act. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*.
Even its own nature is called "action" because it is an object; thus it is said in the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "It is split [or analyzed] due to being an object. (38)
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.
Kramasaṃdarbha: The meaning is that "the luminosity of light" refers to its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*), and thus it is that which makes [light] known.
For the uniqueness of light is understood precisely through its form (*rūpa*), as it possesses a unique form.
Substance is fire. ||38||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
"Substantiality," "formality," "quality-ness," "individuality," "configuration-ness," and "luminosity"—O virtuous lady, these are the functions of light consisting of form alone.

Madhva: Manifestation is its state of being established through manifestation. Its quality is luminosity (*prakāśatva*). It is designated by the term "light" (*āloka*) precisely because it is a quality and is called "illumination" (*prakāśa*). Furthermore, it is also designated by the terms "fiery nature" (*tejastva*), "fierceness" (*ugratva*), and "cruelty" (*kraurya*). ||39||

Śrīdhara: Being the form of a substance (*dravyākṛtitva*) means being that which imparts the configuration to a substance. Being a quality (*guṇatā*) means being perceived as subordinate to a substance. However, sound is perceived quite independently. Even for touch and so forth belonging to an imperceptible substance, there is perception quite independently; but this is not the case for color.

"It is not so"—this specific distinction regarding it has been stated. "Abiding in the individual" (vyakti-saṃsthātva) means that its configuration (saṃsthā)—that is, its arrangement—is the very configuration of the individual substance; the meaning is that it is perceived as a transformation (pariṇāma). The "fiery nature" (tejas-tva) of fire is its uniqueness (asādhāraṇatva). ||39||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He states the definition of *rūpa* (form): it is the state of being the configuration (*ākṛti*) of a substance, that is, the imparting of form.
*Guṇatā* (the state of being a quality) is the cognition [of it] as subordinate to a substance; however, for a word, there is cognition through its own independence alone.

A substance that is not perceptible [by other senses] is cognized independently through touch alone; however, this is not the case for color. "The state of having the configuration of an individual" means that its very nature is the configuration—the specific arrangement—of the individual substance, which exists precisely by virtue of the substance's own dimension.
The meaning is: that which is the cognition of its own dimension. The "fiery nature" of fire is its state of being a mere subtle element (tanmātra); its functions are visible. ||39||
Illumination, cooking, drinking, eating, and the subduing of cold—
these are the functions of fire, as well as drying, hunger, and thirst.

Śrīdhara: Illumination is making manifest; cooking is the preparation of rice and the like. Hunger and thirst are eating and drinking, and by means of those [terms], eating and drinking are also indicated. (40)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states the definition of fire (*tejas*): illumination is making manifest; cooking is the ripening of rice and the like. Hunger is the state of being hungry; thirst is the state of being thirsty. Through these, [fire performs] eating and cooking. (40)
From the transformation of mere form, impelled by fate, fire arose;
from that, the subtle element of taste was produced, and from it came water, while the tongue became the perceiver of taste.

Śrīdhara: The tongue is the organ of taste (*rasanendriya*). It is called *rasagraha* because the taste is apprehended by it; or rather, the sense is that the apprehension of taste arises from it. ||41||

The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon. "Astringent, sweet, bitter, pungent, and sour—in many ways, the single taste is differentiated through the transformation of the elemental constituents (*bhautika*)."

Śrīdhara: Among the astringent and other tastes, the salty taste should also be understood [to be included]. The meaning is that "rasa" refers to that which, though being originally one—namely sweet—becomes divided in this way into many varieties among material substances that possess the quality of conjunction.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha* states the definition of rasa: "Astringent," etc. Among the [six] material qualities, salt (*lavaṇa*) should also be understood [to be included]. Of the elemental substances that are conjoined, that which is solely sweet is one...
The meaning is that this *rasa* is divided into many kinds. ||42||
Moistening, coagulating, satisfying, vitalizing, nourishing, and the removal of heat— these, moreover, are the functions of water.
The term *madhvaḥ* refers to the state of being a drop (*bindubhāvaḥ*); its flowing and trickling are recorded in the lexicon as *syandanaṃ* and *sravaṇam*.
In relation to earth and fire, there is a preponderance [of water] in the body. (43)

Śrīdhara: *Kledanam* means moistening. *Piṇḍanam* is the forming of a lump, such as clay and so forth. *Tṛptiḥ* is the quality of providing satisfaction. *Prāṇanam* is life; for there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "prāṇa consists of water. *Āpyāyanam* is the removal of the distress of thirst. *Undanam* is softening. [The variant] *ondanam* is the same.
The meaning is the same even in the reading [of the commentary]. "Abundance" (*bhūyastvam*) refers to the repeated emergence of that which has been drawn up from a well or similar source. ||43||
The sequential arrangement [is established] by the abundance [of qualities], as in the case of the ocean and so forth through the sight of the moon and other [celestial bodies]. ||43||

Viśvanātha: He states the definition of water (*ambhas*): *kledana* is the act of moistening; *piṇḍana* is the forming of lumps, such as clay; *tṛpti* is the quality of providing satisfaction; *prāṇana* is life, according to the Vedic scripture, "Life is composed of water" (*āpomayaḥ prāṇaḥ*); *āpyāyana* is the removal of the distress of thirst; and *udana* is...
"Softening. Even when the reading is "undana," the meaning is the same. "Abundance" refers to the repeated emergence [of water] even after it has been drawn from a well or similar source. ||43||

From water, which undergoes transformation through its mere quality of taste when impelled by destiny, the mere quality of smell arose; from that [smell] came earth, and the sense of smell, which perceives smell.
Śrīdhara: One who possesses fragrance attains fragrance. ||44||

The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. "Due to the distinct differences among the constituent parts of substances— such as *karambha*, putridity, fragrance, tranquility, intensity, sourness, and so forth— a single odor is divided [into many]."

Śrīdhara: *Karambha* is a mixed fragrance, such as that of side dishes (*vyañjana*) and the like when seasoned with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and so forth. *Pūti* is a foul odor. *Saurabhya* is the fragrance of camphor and the like. *Śānta* is the scent of the *śatapatra* flower and the like. *Ugra* is the pungent smell of garlic and the like. *Amla* is the sourness of the tamarind fruit (*tintiṇī*) and the like. [These belong to] things that are composite.
The meaning is that odor is that which is distinguished in this way due to the inequality of the constituent parts of a substance. ||45||

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: He states the definition of odor (gandha)—*karambha* is a mixed odor, as in the case of condiments and the like when prepared with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and so forth; *pūti* is a foul odor. ||45||
Cultivation is the station of Brahman; retention is its true qualification. The manifestation of the qualities of all beings is the characteristic function of the earth.

*Madhvaḥ* means the state of being a producer (*bhāvanam utpādakatvam*). Regarding the station of Brahman, the *Kāpileya* states: "The earth is the station of Brahman because Brahman is perceived within the body. Manifestation (*vyaktatvam*) occurs through the particularity of existence (*sad-viśeṣeṇa*). According to the *Brāhma*: "That which is unmanifest is called 'non-existent' (*asat*), while that which is manifest is called 'existent' (*sat*). It is the differentiation of all the qualities of sentient beings within the body.
For indeed, the qualities of all living beings are manifested during the state of worldly existence.
The body is to be known as composed of earth; the sense organs are of water;
the fire residing within the stomach is of fire; and the cavities originate from space.
"All vital breaths consist of air, and each of them is further fivefold," so it is stated in the Kāpileya. 46.
Śrīdhara: *Bhāvanā* is the bringing about of Brahman’s manifestation through the assumption of form, such as that of an image.

*Sthāna* is its abiding, characterized by being distinct from water and other elements, without dependence on any other substratum. *Dhāraṇa* is the state of being the support for water and the rest. For the existent things (*satām*), such as ether and so forth, it is the *viśeṣaṇa*, meaning the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of all [things].
The manifestation of sentient beings, living creatures, and their qualities such as masculinity and so forth, is their disclosure through specific transformations. ||46||

The sequential composition: "Meditation" (*bhāvanam*). Meditation upon that Supreme Lord, Brahman—meaning its being the cause for recollection by means of analogies such as the form of sapphire and so forth—is not perfect when applied to water and the like, because of the absence of fragrance and other qualities therein. Alternatively, it refers to meditation upon Him in the form of the Virāṭ.
The state of being a limiting adjunct of meditative cultivation. ||46||

Viśvanātha states the definition of earth: *bhāvana* is its being the cause for the creation of images by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord; *sthāna* is its existence independently, distinguished from water and the other elements;
*dhāraṇa* is its being the support for water and the rest; and *satya* is a qualification of ether and the others.
The meaning is that the "qualifying cause" (viśeṣaṇahetu) is that from which such cognitions as "the sky is soiled" or "the wind is grey" arise.

The "manifestation" (udbheda) of all beings—that is, living creatures—and of their qualities, such as masculinity and so forth, refers to their being made manifest through specific transformations (pariṇāmaviśeṣaiḥ). ||46||
That whose object is a specific quality of space is called the sense of hearing;
they know that whose object is a specific quality of air to be the sense of touch.
Śrīdhara: It has been stated that the ears and other [senses] have the capacity to grasp sound and so forth; and their definition is precisely that.
Thus he says with five half-verses: "Sound is the specific quality of space, whose object—that is, its sphere—is sound. (47)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha states: It has been stated that the ears and other senses are the perceivers of sound and so forth; and since their definition is precisely that, he says: "A specific quality of space (*nabhas*) whose object—that is, its domain—is sound, is the ear."
That whose object is a specific quality of fire is called the eye;
that whose object is a specific quality of water they know as the tongue;
and that whose object is a specific quality of earth is called the nose.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
Kramasandarbha: "Of the fiery [element]" and so forth, for one and a half verses. ||48||
For the property of one thing is indeed seen in another due to its inherence therein;
therefore, the distinction between entities is perceived only on the level of the elements.
Śrīdhara: He shows what is excluded by the term "specific quality" (guṇaviśeṣa) with the words "of the Supreme" (parasya).

A quality of the Supreme Cause, such as sound and so forth, is observed in the subordinate effect, such as air and so forth, due to the persistence of the cause. Therefore, every specific quality of entities such as space and the rest, including sound and so forth, [is found] in earth.
Thus it is perceived, because of the concomitance (anvaya) of four [elements] therein; as in the case of water and so forth, it is only according to that specific concomitance and not all [elements].
But in space (ākāśa), because there is no concomitance with anything else, it is only one. ||49||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, he states that among the five elements, there is an increase in qualities in successive order:
the quality of the supreme cause [space], such as sound, [is present] in the subsequent effect, such as air.
It is observed through the continuity of its causes. In that regard, in space (*ākāśa*), because there is no continuity with anything else, there is only sound. In air (*vāyu*), there are two:
sound and touch. In fire (*tejas*), there are three: sound, touch, and form. In water (*jala*), there are four:
sound, touch, form, and taste. ||49||
When these seven principles, beginning with the Great One (mahat), were indeed not yet combined,
the Source of the World, endowed with time, action, and the qualities (guṇas), entered them.
Śrīdhara: Having thus explained the arising of the cause, he describes the arising of the effect with three and a half verses.
When these [elements] existed without being combined—that is, not yet joined—then the Lord, the origin of the world, entered them.
The mention of "seven" is stated with the intention of highlighting their predominance; however, it is indeed intended that He entered all of them.
The sequence of composition: "These," etc. Now it should be understood that [the Lord] is endowed with specific qualities such as time and so forth.

Viśvanātha: Having thus described the origin of the cause, he speaks of the origin of the effect—"When these principles remained uncombined and unmixed, then the Lord, the source of the universe, entered [them]."

First, he entered by means of the power (*śakti*) that effects integration, for the purpose of unifying all the *tattvas*. Then, at the end of a thousand years, it should be understood that he entered as their inner controller (*antaryāmin*). Time (*kāla*), the agitator; action (*karma*), the unseen merit/demerit of living beings (*jīva-adṛṣṭa*); and the qualities (*guṇa*), which is primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—he is accompanied by these. And "seven" [refers to these].
This was stated with the intention of emphasizing the primary [factor]; however, entry is intended to apply to all as well. ||50||
Then, from those [elements] interpenetrated and joined by that [Pradhāna], an insentient egg arose,
from which this Virāṭ Puruṣa emerged.
Śrīdhara: From these [elements], which were pierced and agitated, this Virāṭ Puruṣa arose from this egg. ||51||

The sequential composition: That which had arisen, the Virāṭ Puruṣa consisting of Hiraṇyagarbha—the collective individual soul—arose; having transcended as if from deep sleep, he became conscious. ||51||
Viśvanātha: By that entry, from the principles (tattvas) which were first agitated and then immediately joined and united with it, the Egg (aṇḍa) arose— that is, was produced—
from which the Virāṭ Puruṣa, whose nature is Hiraṇyagarbha, the collective individual soul (samaṣṭijīva), emerged from sleep.
Having transcended [the senses] as it were, he became fully conscious. ||51||

This egg, known as the "particular" (viśeṣa), is surrounded by the elements beginning with water, each increasing tenfold over the preceding, and is further enveloped on the outside by Pradhāna; therein lies this expansion of the worlds, which is the form of the Blessed Lord Hari.
Śrīdhara: "The form of the Blessed One" is said with the intention of [showing] non-difference from the Puruṣa. ||52||

The sequential composition: Although they had risen and attained union with their respective seats, they entered into the effort—that is, they exerted themselves—in raising up this Virāj and in accomplishing his external activities. ||52||
Viśvanātha: "The Egg" (aṇḍam). That which has the designation or name "the particular" (viśeṣa).
It is surrounded by successive outer coverings of *prakṛti*, each ten times greater than the preceding one. Its form is illusory (*māyika*). ||52||
Rising from the golden egg-shell that rested upon the waters,
Mahādeva entered it and divided the ether in many ways.

"Since Brahmā was clearly born from that egg which was insentient like honey (madhu), therefore they call it the 'Brahmāṇḍa' (the Egg of Brahmā); and Virāj is called Brahmā because of his manifestation. Thus [it is said]. (53)

Śrīdhara: In that regard, he explains the division into the internal self (*adhyātma*) and so forth with nine verses beginning with "From the golden one" (*hiraṇmayāt*). "Having arisen" means having abandoned indifference; "having entered him" means having presided over him. He is both "great" (*mahān*) and "divine" (*devaḥ*). "Space" (*kham*) refers to the cavity. ||53||

The sequential composition: Viśvanātha divided the void (kha), which is space, manifoldly, having separated it part by part. Regarding that, he explains the division into the internal self (*adhyātma*) and so forth, beginning with "from the golden" (*hiraṇmayāt*). Having entered—that is, having presided over—it, the Great God divided the manifold void, which is the cavity.
He made them separate, one by one. ||53||
His first mouth was split open, and from it speech arose;
from speech came fire, and then the nostrils were formed, from which breath and smell emerged.

Śrīdhara: Fire came into being with Speech; he entered [it]. The two nostrils were split open. Being woven (*ūta*) by Prāṇa, that is, sewn together (*syūta*), he became the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) within these two nostrils—this is to be supplied as the grammatical connection. ||54||
The sequential arrangement: Speech, too, is indeed the causal portion of the individual mouths. 54.

Viśvanātha: Vahni (Fire) came into being with Vāṇī (Speech); he entered [the body]. From the nose, the two nostrils were split open; from the breath (*prāṇa*), he became the breath (*prāṇa*), being woven together by the breath. The phrase "he came into being in these two nostrils" is to be supplied as a grammatical connection (*anuṣaṅga*).
The qualification "from the breath" (*prāṇataḥ*) is to be understood as applying to all the sense organs through a change of gender (*liṅgavipariṇāma*). ||54||
From the nose the wind was split apart; from these two, the eyes and sight emerged.
From that, the sun was split apart; from the ears, hearing and then the quarters of space arose.

Śrīdhara: After the sense of smell, the wind [arose]. The qualification "as breath" (prāṇa) should be understood to apply to all the senses as well. Regarding the two readings *nyabhidyetām* and *anvabhidyetām*, the meaning is the same. Then they entered the quarters. 55.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: After the nose, the wind entered. In the same way, for the subsequent [terms] ending in the fifth case, the explanation should be understood as "immediately after that. The sun was split open.
There are two readings: "nyabhidyetām" and [the other]. ||55||
Then the skin, the body hair, and the beard and so forth were manifested;
from that, the plants came into being; thereafter, the male organ was manifested.
Śrīdhara: By the word "etcetera," hair is meant.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Herbs and waters are those presided over by their respective deities.

Viśvanātha: This has not been explained. From that [semen], water came into being; indeed, the anus was pierced open. From the anus came the apāna breath, and from the apāna came Death, the terrifier of the worlds.
It was not explained by anyone at all.
Then his two hands were manifested, and from them came Balarāma, the self-ruling lord;
and his two feet were manifested, and from them came Hari, whose movement is swift.

"Madhva—the deity named Yajña—is also to be known as the presiding deity (pādadevatā) of the feet. Hari, eternally possessed by him, they call that [deity] the presiding deity of the feet. How could he, whose self is complete and pure, possess the status of being the presiding deity of the senses? Thus it is said. (58)
Śrīdhara: Svarāṭ is Indra; Hari is Viṣṇu. ||58||
The sequence of composition: Hari is a specific deity who is an incarnation through immersion in that [state]. ||58||
Viśvanātha: Svarāṭ is Indra; Hari is a particular deity possessed by Hari—such is the context. ||58||
His veins burst forth, and from them blood was brought;
from that the rivers came into being. Then his belly burst forth.
Śrīdhara: It has been brought forth; it is born. ||59||

The sequential arrangement: "the channels" constitutes half a verse. Viśvanātha: "Lohitam" refers to the sense organ that circulates blood and so forth; it has been brought forth, i.e., produced. (59)
From that, hunger and thirst arose; the ocean became their source.
Then his heart was split open, and from the heart, the mind emerged.
It has not been explained by whom:
"From the mind (manas) the moon was born; from the intellect (buddhi) the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati);
from that, Rudra as the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); and from that, the consciousness (citta) and the object of consciousness (caitya) came into being."

The Lord Viṣṇu, who is the inner controller even of the Lord of the Caitya (Brahmā), manifested himself by his own will from the four-faced one; therefore, he is remembered as being born of Brahmā. ||61||
Śrīdhara: Among the intellect and the other faculties, the heart alone is the locus. The Lord of Speech is Brahmā. Caittya is the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). ||61||

The sequential arrangement: "I" (aham). Here, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), who is the Lord (*īśvara*) existing in the state of Hiraṇyagarbha and the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), is to be understood as this Pradyumna-form. This is because the individual soul (*jīva*), being an agent, lacks the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) and lacks the status of a deity (*devatā*); therefore, it exists only as residing within the Supreme Person (*īśvarapuruṣa*).
And by means of questions and answers, his supreme capacity will be demonstrated through the passage beginning with "by the mind" (cittena) and so forth. ||61||
Viśvanātha: The heart alone is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), beginning with the mind (*manas*).

The Lord of Speech (*girāṃ patiḥ*) is Brahmā. The "Caittya" is Vāsudeva, the presiding deity of the intellect (*citta*); he alone is the deity to be worshipped within the *citta*. He is also [the deity] of Hiraṇyagarbha, the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*).

As Pradyumna, He is the inner controller; it should be understood from the *Bhāgavatāmṛta* that He alone is the inner controller of individual souls (*vyaṣṭi-jīvas*) as Aniruddha. However, one should not say that the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) or the individual soul (*jīva*) is the presiding deity of the mind (*cittādhiṣṭhātā*), because its lack of agency, instrumentality, and so forth has been established everywhere.
In passages such as "He reveals his own state through the form of the preceptor and the caitya" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.29.6),

it should be understood that by the word *caitya*, the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) is meant precisely because he has the mind as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and not because he is the presiding controller of the mind. ||61||
For these gods, though they had risen up, were unable to rouse him;
they entered their respective abodes again in order to awaken him step by step.
Agni entered the mouth by means of speech, yet then the Virāj did not arise;
Vāyu entered the nostrils by means of the sense of smell, yet then the Virāj did not arise.
Through the eye, the sun did not arise from the Virāj;
through the ear, the quarters did not arise from the Virāj.
Then the Virāj rose up with skin and hair, but the waters did not rise up with the seed;
then the Virāj rose up.
Then Death did not raise the anus by means of the *apāna* breath; then the Virāj did not arise.
Then Indra did not raise the two hands by means of strength alone; then the Virāj did not arise.
Because of Viṣṇu’s departure, the Virāj did not rise up with his feet;
because of the rivers of the channels being filled with blood, the Virāj did not rise up then.
Then the Virāj did not rise up from hunger and thirst, for his belly was the ocean;
then the Virāj did not rise up from the heart, for his mind was the moon.
Then even Brahmā, through his intellect, could not rouse the heart of the Virāj;
then Rudra, through his ego, could not rouse the heart of the Virāj.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, Hari Janārdana, though capable, did not raise Madhva from his own feet;
rather, he remained there to ascertain the strength of Brahmā and Vāyu.
Then the Lord, entering the body of Brahmā, raised him up.

Brahmā is Bṛhaspati; for there is a Vedic text stating, "In which king Brahmā goes before. Furthermore, Bṛhaspati is the domestic priest (purodhāḥ) and the Brahman-priest; thus he is designated as "the Lord of the Brahman" (brahmaṇaḥ patiḥ). ||69||

Śrīdhara: With nine verses beginning with "These," he describes the re-entry of all [the elements] in order to distinguish the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) through both positive and negative concomitance. ||6270||

The sequential composition: Although they had arisen and attained union with their respective seats, they entered into—meaning they exerted effort toward—the raising up and the accomplishment of external movement of this Virāj. ||62||

Viśvanātha: In order to demonstrate, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) alone possesses all powers, he restates the aforementioned entry of all [beings] with the words beginning "these":
"When the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the mind, entered the heart as the object of thought (*caitya*)."
At that very moment, the Puruṣa Virāṭ arose from the waters.
Just as Brahmā emerged from a portion of Madhu,
so too did the Lord of the Universe depart from his own body along with Vāyu and Viṣṇu.
The gods, gathered together, were unable to raise him up except for those three of great strength; therefore, three of them entered into them.
Then, by the power of those [sages], and especially by the power of Hari, the Lord of Śrī, the body of Brahmā arose.
The one who identifies with the mind is indeed Brahman; the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is Hari residing therein.
He is called the vital breath (prāṇavāyu), and Hari himself is the Lord of those two.
Śrīdhara: Not explained.

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: "By the mind" (*cittena*). He entered [the body] and, for the sake of accomplishing external activity, he himself made a fresh effort to arouse everything; he arose and performed activity even externally.
He attained it. ||70||

Viśvanātha: Caittya is Vāsudeva; he alone is the *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field), the inner controller (*antaryāmī*). This is because of the statement in the *Gītā*: "And know me also as the *kṣetrajña* situated in all fields" [Gītā 13.2]. ||70||
Just as the vital breath, the senses, the mind, and the intellect are unable to rouse a sleeping man by their own power without that [self], so too [is it with the body].
Śrīdhara: By means of two verses beginning with "yathā," he states the purpose of the Sāṅkhya exposition, showing the individual body as an illustration for the cosmic body (virāḍdeha). ||71||

The sequential arrangement is as follows: the connection [of the verses] is by means of the two couplets beginning with "yathā" and the two beginning with "tam," [showing] how the Virāṭ did not arise without that; [the phrase] "pratyagātmānam" refers to the inner controller (antaryāmin). ||71||

Viśvanātha: He provides an illustration of the individual body (*vyaṣṭideha*) by means of the collective cosmic body (*samaṣṭivirāḍdeha*), using the word "just as" (*yathā*). Just as they are unable to awaken the individual [body] while it is asleep without that Supreme Lord who presides over the mind, so too is the collective cosmic body [unable to function] without Him.
"He did not rise" is to be connected with what precedes. ||71||
One should contemplate that inner Self within oneself, having discerned it through the intellect engaged in yoga, by means of devotion, dispassion, and knowledge.

Śrīdhara: First, devotion to the Supreme Lord; then, detachment from other things; then, the intellect engaged in yoga; then, one-pointedness of mind; and then, that knowledge by which one should contemplate the inner self, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), having discriminated it from this self, which is the aggregate of causes and effects. ||72||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha states the purpose of restating the number: "That [Self], which is the inner self (*pratyagātmā*) accessible through inward knowledge, [is to be sought] in this aggregate of cause and effect, in the self, that is, in the body, specifically in the individual self (*jīvātman*)."
Or one should reflect [upon this]. ||72||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, appropriately joined for the virtuous, in this third book of the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.

Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya, in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā pertaining to the Pāramahaṃsyas, in the tenth book, in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, [this is] the section concerning Kapila.
The twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Principles" (Tattvasamāmnāya).
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter,
"The Discrimination of Nature" (Prakṛtiviveka), within the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya concerning the teachings of Kapila.
The Blessed Lord said: Even though the person (puruṣa) resides in primordial nature (prakṛti), he is not tainted by the qualities of nature,
because he is changeless, non-doing, and devoid of qualities, like the sun reflected in water.
Śrīdhara:
Then, in the twenty-seventh [chapter], the method of liberation through the correct discernment of the person and primordial nature by means of many practices is described.

In order to establish that liberation is attained through discriminative knowledge, [the Lord] recalls the previously mentioned cycle of worldly existence—which arises from the non-discrimination of the pure *puruṣa* from *prakṛti*—in three verses beginning with "Though situated in *prakṛti*": "Though situated in the body, he is not tainted; he is not smeared by the qualities (*guṇas*) and their effects."
Because of pleasure, pain, and so forth; due to being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva), there is non-agency (akartṛtva), and from that, immutability (avikāritva). ||1||

The Sequential Composition: Now, he distinguishes the person known as the individual soul (*jīva*) from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), beginning with the words "Even though situated in nature" (*prakṛtistho’pi*). The meaning is that just as the sun, though seen in water, is not defiled by it, so too is this person. ||1||
Viśvanātha:

In the twenty-seventh [chapter], which extensively details the means of knowledge mixed with devotion, and through the discrimination between the Puruṣa and Prakṛti, the method of liberation is proclaimed.
In order to establish liberation through discriminative knowledge, he shows the individual self (jīvātman) as distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti):

although the person, the living self, resides within nature, it is a non-agent because it is devoid of qualities during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution; consequently, it is changeless, and for that reason, it is not stained—just as the sun reflected in water remains distinct from the water.

Like the rays of the solar orb, it is not in reality overcome by the properties of water. For when the trembling of water is caused by the wind, then there would also be a trembling of the reflection of the sun in that water. As it has been said: "Just as this light [is reflected] in water and on earth..."

"It is perceived as following the force of the wind" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.1.43). For this very reason, when the mind is thoroughly purified, the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha) is also purified;
for scripture states: "The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings" (Brahmabindu Upaniṣad 2). ||1||
When this very [self] becomes intensely attached to the qualities of Prakṛti, its nature deluded by the sense of "I," it conceives the false notion: "I am the doer."
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.

Kramasaṃdarbha: However, here, by way of the analogy of water and the sun, the analogy of the face and the mirror is intended; therefore, just as one's own face appears as if stained by the defects of the mirror, so too [is it] by being stained by that.
He says "he" to show that he falsely forms this conceit; [the means by which he does so is] "by the yoga of devotion. ||2||

Viśvanātha: He states, with two verses beginning with "sa eva," that saṃsāra is indeed based solely on the conceit [of identification] with that [body]. "When" refers to the states of waking and dreaming. ||2||
By means of that, one helplessly enters the path of saṃsāra,
remaining unextinguished due to incidental defects of karma within births mixed with the good and the bad.

Śrīdhara: Being unliberated, through incidental [births] produced by attachment to material nature, he attains the path of transmigratory existence within wombs that are mixed with the good and the bad—among gods, animals, humans, and so forth. ||3||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: By means of incidental [topics] arising from the context of the subject matter. ||3||
For even when an object does not exist, the cycle of worldly existence does not cease for one who dwells upon sense-objects,
just as one experiences the acquisition of misfortune in a dream.

Madhva [states]: "Ignorance is what is expressed by the word 'sleep,' and dream is indeed error. Śrīdhara [comments]: "But if that is so, since transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*) is unreal, what is the use of the effort to cease it?
To this he replies: "For regarding the object," etc. (Verse 4).
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, since that individual soul (*jīva*) lacks agency, causality, and so forth, how can there be bondage through actions performed by the body even when, in reality, there is an absence of action? To this he says: "In the object... (*arthe*).

Even though the object in the form of karma does not exist in reality, for one who meditates on sense-objects through the conceit of agency, there is an illustration: indeed, even the attainment of misfortune in a dream occurs solely from the ripening of meditation on objects accompanied by such conceit; this is the meaning. ||4||
Therefore, one should gradually bring the mind— which has become attached to the path of the unwholesome—
under control through intense yoga of devotion and dispassion.

Śrīdhara: Since meditation on sense-objects is the cause of worldly attachment, he says "for this very reason" that the mind must be restrained. [The mind should be restrained] on the path of the wicked senses, that is, on the path of sense-objects; by means of intense—that is, firm—[discipline], and by means of intense detachment. (5)
The sequential composition: having stated its status as a means, its deceptive nature is revealed because it has another result as its true intent. ||5||

Viśvanātha: Since meditation on sense objects is the cause of misfortune, he says "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) that the mind must be restrained. *Bhakti* and *yoga*—the singular compound of these two—and by means of that which is *tīvra*, meaning most powerful. ||5||
Practicing through the paths of yoga such as the restraints (yama) and so forth, endowed with faith,
with devotion toward me, with truthfulness, and by listening to my stories.

Śrīdhara: Describing the causes for the intensity of devotion and detachment, he explains the manner of liberation through knowledge in six verses. By practicing the path of yoga through the restraints (yamas) and so forth, repeatedly making the mind one-pointed and perceiving the Self—the non-dual Supreme Self that permeates all—one [attains liberation].

"Pratipadyate" (he practices) is to be connected with the sixth [verse]. "By truth" means by being free from deceit. "By disposition" means by love; this is the sequence of the composition. For this very reason, he states that there is a mixture of knowledge and action in the six verses beginning with "yama-". "By disposition" means by devotion. "By truth" means by conduct in accordance with reality. Thus, it is established regarding the individual soul (*jīva*).
The knowledge of purity connects [the practitioner] with the object perceived by the Lord. ||6||

Viśvanātha: Elaborating upon the meaning already stated, he describes the manner of liberation through knowledge: by practicing the paths of yoga beginning with *yama*, and thereby making the mind one-pointed through practice, the individual soul (*jīvātman*), having perceived the Supreme Soul (*paramātman*), attains that which is non-dual and pervades all things.

The connection is with the sixth [word]. "By a true disposition toward me" means by that true disposition—that is, the cultivation of the reality—regarding my form, name, pastimes, and so forth, through the vision of their reality;
it does not mean by a vision of me as Brahman mixed with *māyā*, nor by a cultivation of unreality toward me in the future. This is the meaning.
In that case—
because [the truth] is not established in you, those of impure intellect,
having with great difficulty ascended to the supreme state from there, [fall back].
"Those who disregard Your feet fall downward" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.2.32);
"Even freedom from action, if devoid of devotion to Acyuta... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.12.50); "The deluded despise Me when I have assumed a human form" (Gītā 9.11); they do not worship and they despise.
From such statements as "Falling from their station, they fall downward" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.5.33),

it is understood that even for the wise, liberation does not occur due to the lack of devotion characterized by the contemplation of the Lord’s form and so forth as being distinct from consciousness and bliss. ||6||
Through equanimity toward all beings, through freedom from enmity,
through non-attachment, through celibacy, through silence, and through one's own powerful duty.
Śrīdhara: By abandoning attachment through non-attachment; by that which is powerful and offered to the Lord. ||7||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By the stronger [power] offered to the Lord. ||7||
Content with whatever is obtained by chance, eating moderately, a silent sage,
dwelling in seclusion, peaceful, friendly, compassionate, and self-possessed.
Śrīdhara: One who has found refuge in solitude is a dweller in seclusion. ||8||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon. Viśvanātha: "One whose refuge is secluded" means a dweller in solitude; "possessed of self" means endowed with fortitude. ||9||
And while this body still persists with its continuations, one who does not harbor false attachments,
having perceived through knowledge the true nature of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, [is liberated].

Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [explain]: "By that knowledge" means by that knowledge through which the reality of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa has been perceived; [it refers to] the stubborn adherence to the unreal, namely the sense of "I" and "mine. ||9||
The sequential arrangement has not been explained.
Established in the state of withdrawn intellect, with the vision of other things distanced,
the seer of the Self perceives the Self by means of the Self, as one sees the sun with the eye.
Madhva: For sleep and so forth are indeed states of the intellect (buddhi). ||10||

Śrīdhara: He is one whose states of consciousness, such as waking and so forth, have ceased; for this very reason, he is one from whom other perceptions have become distant. Having perceived the pure Self by means of the self limited by the ego (ahaṅkāra), [the author] provides an illustration for the same single entity being both the instrument and the object through its states of being delimited and undelimited.
He said: "With the eye—that is, with the sun delimited by the eye—one sees the sun situated in the sky; in the same way, one who possesses self-vision sees the pure Self. (10)

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] is as follows: by the verse beginning with "upalabhya" (having perceived) and consisting of one and a half verses; for when the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is non-existent, it is by means of the Self itself, which is conditioned by that very [ego-sense] acting as a gateway. ||10||

Viśvanātha: He is one whose states of consciousness, such as waking and so forth, have ceased. Therefore, the knower, having experienced the Supreme Self through devotion by means of the pure individual self (*jīvātman*) alone, attains that very Self; thus he says: "having perceived" (*upalabhya*). By means of the self—the pure individual self, which is a spark of consciousness—he [perceives] the Self.

Having perceived the Supreme Self, the treasury of perfect consciousness, and having experienced it through devotion— just as one perceives the sun, the treasury of light, with a spark of light from an eye free from defects such as redness— the knower, possessing the vision of the Self,
attains and reaches it. In this context, even by means of an eye free from defects such as redness...
Just as an owl and the like do not see the sun, whereas humans and others who are different from them do indeed see it,

so too a knower (*jñānin*) who is devoid of devotion does not experience the Supreme Self even with a pure individual soul (*jīvātman*), whereas only one possessed of devotion experiences Him. "By devotion alone am I to be grasped."
"Thus, [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.14.21];
'By devotion one comes to know Me as I am in truth—both who I am and how great I am;
then, having known Me in truth, one enters into Me immediately thereafter' [Gītā 11.55]."
Because it was spoken by the Blessed One. ||10||
Free from all marks, ever-shining, it perceives itself as non-existent;
it is the bond of the existent, the eye of the non-existent, the all-pervading, and non-dual.

Śrīdhara: He attains Brahman, which is free from limiting adjuncts (*muktaliṅga*), unconditioned (*nirupādhika*), and which, while the unreal ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is non-existent, appears as "Being" (*sadābhāsa*), manifesting in the form of existence. He states the distinction [of this state] from the nature of the pure individual soul (*jīva*): it is the kinsman—that is, the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—of "Being," the causal primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and of "Non-being."
It is the illuminator of the effect, like the eye; it is woven through all causes and effects;
it is non-dual and perfectly complete. ||11||
The sequential composition: Having perceived the Self— which is free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), devoid of contact with conditions,

and therefore perfectly manifest as the nature of Being— one then realizes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) which, while remaining in that very same [Self], serves as the support for its manifestation and so forth.

He knows it; he further qualifies that very [knowledge]: the eye of those others who are non-existent (asat) is also its illuminator, which is pervasive everywhere, whether [the object] exists or does not exist. For this very reason it is non-dual; therefore, because of its primacy, the vision of the pure Self has that [eye] alone as its perceived object—this is the sense. And this is according to the maxim: "The reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is for the sake of another."

Viśvanātha: Of what nature is He? By the phrase "He who is embraced [and known] by the liberated," it is stated that He has become the object of experiential knowledge (*anubhava-jñāna*). He is "Him" because in this perishable world, only the Existent (*sat*) shines forth as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). He is the friend and lord of the Existent cause, and of the non-existent (*asat*).

By means of these five qualifiers— being the illuminator of the effects such as Mahat and the rest, being woven through all causes and effects, being pervasive, non-dual, and one— it is made known that, prior to the stage of realized experience,
it becomes the object of knowledge arising from the scriptures. ||11||
Just as a reflection situated in water is perceived by one standing on dry land,
so too is the sun situated in the sky perceived by its own reflection situated in the water.

Thus, the threefold ego is characterized by its own manifestations consisting of the elements, the senses, and the mind; by this, the seer of reality is always characterized by the manifestation of existence.
"The gods are reflections of the remainder of Madhu; Śeṣa is [the reflection] of Brahmā;
and he, in turn, is [the reflection] of the Supreme Brahman, and they reveal their own original archetypes (svabimba).
Therefore, through the door of one's own archetype, there is the manifestation of the Supreme Self. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmatarka*. 13.

Śrīdhara: With an illustration, he explains the realization of pure Brahman by means of the adjunct of the ego (ahaṅkāra)—"Just as," etc. When the reflection situated in water—the reflection of the sun—shines upon a wall inside a house, then by persons standing in the corners of that house...

Just as, by means of the reflection of the sun situated on a surface such as a wall, the reflection residing in the water is first perceived or observed—since it is impossible for the reflection of that which resides in the sky to appear within the interior of a house—the word "tathā" (thus) has the sense of "and" (ca); that is, "and just as. And just as...
The sun situated in the sky is perceived by one standing in the water. ||12||

Thus, the threefold *ahaṅkāra*— consisting of the elements, the senses, and the mind— is characterized by its form as that in which there is the reflection (*ābhāsa*) of the existent Brahman, [appearing] through the body, senses, and mind which are themselves limited reflections of the Self (*ātmapratibimba*). This is because the reflection of objects cannot arise without the reflection residing within the *ahaṅkāra*.
The meaning is that by this ego-sense, which always possesses a semblance [of reality], the Self—whose nature is the perception of truth and the realization of the ultimate—is characterized. ||13||

The sequence of composition: Thus, by means of a series of dreams, he provides an illustration for the perception of the root [reality] with the pair of verses beginning with "Just as" (yathā). ||12||

He concludes with the word "thus" (evam). [The Self] is characterized by those [entities] which consist of the elements and so forth, which have the aggregate as their limiting adjunct (upādhi), and whose manifestations are its own reflections;

that is, by those persons who stand in the place of men situated in the corner of a house, and in whom there exists the manifestation of the Self—which has the ego (ahaṅkāra) as its limiting adjunct—by means of the threefold ego as a limiting adjunct. From that...

And by this [process], in due order—by means of that which has the ego as its limiting adjunct (ahaṅkāropādhika), which serves as an indirect door, and likewise by that which is ever-manifest and pure, which serves as a direct door—the Supreme Self (paramātman) who perceives reality is also indicated; such is the meaning. ||13||

Viśvanātha: First, he states—with an illustration—the manner in which the individual soul (jīvātman) alone is to be known, and how, by means of that, the Supreme Self (paramātman) is then known: "Just as," etc. When the reflection situated in water, having the form of a mirror-image, is the motionless light of the sun...

When it shines upon a place such as a clear wall within a house, then the people standing in the corners of the house first perceive the reflection situated on that place; subsequently, as they reflect upon where this light comes from,
[they realize] by means of that reflection situated on the place— which is like the beautiful light of the sun— [the nature of the source].

The reflection situated in the water is seen and perceived as motionless; furthermore, as to where this reflection comes from, in that very same manner, by means of that very reflection situated in the water—a beautiful manifestation—the sun situated in the sky is perceived. In this very way, first by the discerning...
The elements, the senses, and the mind are seen to possess the light of the Supreme Self because they possess consciousness.
Therefore, one might ask: how can this light of the Supreme Self exist within these insentient things? [The answer is:
by means of the self-manifestations residing in the elements, senses, and mind—which are themselves composed of the elements, senses, and mind—[the light of the Self shines forth].

The individual self (jīvātman), in which the threefold ego-sense (trivṛd-ahaṅkāra) exists as a limiting adjunct (upādhi), is characterized as a ray produced from the light of the Supreme Self (paramātman). And thus, by means of this individual self—
which is ever-shining, existent, and full of devotion— the Seer of Truth (satyadṛk), who is truth-knowledge-bliss (satya-jñāna-ānanda), [is perceived].
The Supreme Self is characterized and perceived. ||1213||
When the subtle elements, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and so forth have dissolved here through sleep,
he who remains therein awake and free from egoism is the Self.
Then, considering himself to be that [ego], though unperished, he falsely imagines himself perished;
when the ego-sense has vanished, the seer becomes distressed like one who has lost his wealth.
Reflecting thus, he realizes himself as that which is the persistence and sustenance of the substance endowed with egoity.

Madhva says: In the absence of dissolution (*pralaya*), he who is wakeful is the seer of truth (*satyadṛk*). He who is "unperished" (*anaṣṭa*) yet appears as if perished, thinking "I did not perceive," is the afflicted individual soul (*jīva*), the seer. The individual soul (*jīva*) is the substance accompanied by ego (*ahaṅkāra*); its abiding state and its sustainer is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). ||1416||

Śrīdhara: Now, he shows through three verses the realization of the pure Self by means of experiencing it as the witness of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). When the elements and so forth—which are unreal, equivalent to non-existence, and unmanifest—have dissolved into sleep, one realizes that Self which is then awake and free from egoity (*nirahaṅkriya*).
The connection is with the third [member]. ||14||

Now, if he is indeed awake at that time, why does he not appear clearly, as in the states of waking and dreaming? To this he replies: previously, he was the perceiver, and thus he was clearly perceived through his state of being a perceiver characterized by conceptualization (*savikalpa*). But in deep sleep, because the objects of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), such as the elements and so forth, have dissolved, that [perception]...

When the ego, which is the object [of identification], has perished, one who—though himself not yet destroyed—considers himself as if destroyed out of delusion; for when one thing is destroyed, another becomes equivalent to being destroyed. An illustration of this is: like one whose wealth is lost, he becomes distressed and helpless, meaning he acts as if he were destroyed. ||15||

[Objection: But surely nothing is experienced in deep sleep; [Response: Not so, for one says, "I slept happily, I was not aware of anything," because there is a recollection (*pratisandhāna*) of the pure Self alone, even without specific cognition (*viśeṣajñāna*).
Thus he says: "In this way. [Objection: But since the recollection occurs with the notion of "I" (*sāhaṅkāra*), how can this be?
He states the absence of egoity (*nirahaṅkriyatva*) therein: [the Self] is the benefactor, the illuminator, and the sustainer of the substance accompanied by egoity—the aggregate of cause and effect.
Furthermore, because egoity is also an object of perception as a qualifier of that substance, the Self, as its perceiver, is distinct from it.
The syntactical connection is: "that self. ||16||

The sequence of composition: the triad beginning with "bhūtasūkṣma" [refers to] the unmanifest (avyākṛta), which is other than the pure individual soul (śuddhajīva) and exists within that which is non-existent [in relation to the manifest]. ||14||
Since there is the recognition immediately following deep sleep— expressed as "While possessing egoity, I did not know myself"—
that [recognition] occurs by way of qualifying that specific substance characterized as the aggregate of subtle elements and so forth, denoted by the word "mine" (mama).

Since even the ego (ahaṅkāra) would at other times become an object of perception, that which is expressed by the word "I" must be the self as the seer; the meaning is that it is the illuminator and the substratum distinct from that [ego]. ||16||

Viśvanātha: Indeed, we acknowledge it as true that the Supreme Self is experienced by the self of the devotee and the knower, just as the sun is perceived by the eye; however, in response to the expectation that He be shown directly—as one might see the individual soul (jīvātman) distinct from the triple-fold ego (trivṛd-ahaṅkāra), just as one perceives the eyes, ears, and so forth—[the Lord says:]...

He says [the answer] with three verses beginning with "bhūta-": when the elements and so forth have dissolved into the *pradhāna*—which, being unmanifest, is equivalent to non-existence—and have merged therein through sleep, the world then attains and experiences that Self, the individual soul (*jīva*), which at that time is free from sleep and devoid of egoism; this is the connection with the third verse. ||14||

[Objection: "In that case, enough with the practice of yoga! For when the dissolution of the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth occurs, it is sleep itself that brings about that experience of the absolute Self (kevalātman) which is the fruit of yogic practice.

To this, he replies with the word "thinking" (*manyamāna*). At that time, because of the dissolution of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and its effects, such as the elements and so forth, [the state is not one of mere sleep].

When the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) has perished, the living being (*jīva*), who is the seer, finds that because of the absence of objects to be seen, vision itself has perished; thus, although the Self is not itself destroyed, the living being—possessing ignorance—falsely imagines himself as if destroyed, just like one whose wealth has been lost, yet unlike one who still clings to the loss of that wealth. This is the meaning.

The meaning is this: it is only when there is the absolute dissolution of the principles that constitute the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva) through the practice of yoga that the soul becomes composed of its own essential form and bliss; this does not occur during occasional states such as deep sleep or cosmic dissolution. Just as, when one's wealth is lost, the happiness of being free from possessions does not arise.

But when attachment to wealth alone has perished, even so, for the individual soul (jīva), there is no attainment of its true nature (svarūpa) despite the destruction of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) during deep sleep or cosmic dissolution, nor does the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) occur without devotion and knowledge; thus, [this applies] to deep sleep and to ignorance (avidyā) along with its latent impressions (saṃskāra).
Because [the self] exists [as such], even the experience of the isolated self (kevalātmānubhava) is ineffective. ||15||

[Objection: Is it not the case that nothing at all is experienced in deep sleep? [Reply: Not so; for one has the recollection of the pure Self alone, in the form of the specific cognition, "I slept happily, I was not aware of anything. Thus he says: "In this way. Furthermore, [this applies] to the substance consisting of the aggregate of the elements, the senses, and so forth, which is accompanied by the ego (ahaṅkāra).

The meaning is that the body’s state of existence is its substratum—that very individual soul (jīvātman) depending upon which egoism and the other factors proceed toward objects of enjoyment. Likewise, that very individual soul is the recipient of grace; the meaning is that he is to be favored by the bestowal of the attribute characterized by his own status as an enjoyer. ||16||
Devahūti said:
O Brahman, Prakṛti never releases the Puruṣa,
O Lord, because of their mutual dependence and because of their eternity.

Śrīdhara: He asks, "Even though there is discrimination (*viveka*) through devotion and detachment (*bhakti-virakti*), since there is no mutual abandonment between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, how can there be liberation?"—with these four verses beginning with "the *puruṣa*.
Because *prakṛti* cannot attain its own nature apart from the *puruṣa*, and [the *puruṣa* cannot exist] apart from *prakṛti*...
Because there is no manifestation of the Puruṣa, and because they are mutually dependent and [the Puruṣa is] eternal, Nature (prakṛti) never abandons the Puruṣa; this is the meaning. ||17||

The sequential arrangement: even if there is mutual dependence, one might argue that if one [of the two] were perishable, the other could indeed be released from that [dependence]; but he says "because of its eternity" (nityatvāt) to show that this is not so. ||17||

Viśvanātha: Now, [the author] states the reasoning for the fact that even for devotees, liberation is indeed difficult to attain through means such as knowledge and exposition—namely, "the Puruṣa... and so on. Regarding the word "mutually" (*anyonya*): because he possesses power (*śaktimat*), the Puruṣa also resorts to his own power, which is *Prakṛti*, for the sake of the play (*līlā*) of creating the universe and so forth. *Prakṛti* also...

The meaning is that, by virtue of being a power (*śakti*), it necessarily relies upon its own possessor (*puruṣa*). One might indeed argue that either of the two could be perishable; however, he says "because of eternality" (*nityatvāt*) to show that this is not so. ||17||
Just as there is no existence of fragrance apart from the earth,
and just as there is none of taste apart from water, so it is with the intellect and the Supreme.

Śrīdhara: The example is given merely to show the absence of a negative concomitance (vyatireka)—just as there is no existence (bhāva), that is, no being (sattā), apart from it. Because the decay of fragrance is sometimes observed, another example is provided: "of water" (apām).
[This refers to] the intellect (buddhi), primordial nature (prakṛti), and the supreme person (puruṣa). ||18||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Existence (*bhāva*) as presence (*sattā*) does not exist [in the case of smell], because a decrease of smell is observed at some time; another example is that of water, [which serves as a counter-example] for the intellect (*buddhi*) which is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Of the person. ||18||
Since this bondage of action belongs to the person who is not the agent,
how can there be liberation for Prakṛti when the guṇas still exist?

"The one who possesses eternal vision is the Supreme Self; that living soul who knows nothing at all like one who is dead—that is to be known as the Supreme Self, and its support is the [individual] self. Thus it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*. (19)

Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says: "Of the non-agent" (akartuḥ). He whose support consists of those qualities—that is, while the qualities of *prakṛti* exist—how can there be liberation (*kaivalya*) for the *puruṣa*? (19)
The sequence of composition: "of the non-agent" (akartuḥ); therefore, for the reason stated previously. ||19||
