Viśvanātha: What follows from that? To this he says: "of the non-agent" (*akartuḥ*). That which has the qualities as its substratum—that is, while those qualities of *prakṛti* exist, for what reason could there be liberation (*kaivalya*) for the *puruṣa*, the individual soul (*jīva*), precisely because of that [very fact]? ||19||
In some cases, although intense fear has ceased through the contemplation of reality,
it arises again because its underlying cause has not been eliminated.
Śrīdhara: For this very reason, he says "in some cases" (kvacid) to show that even when the fear of saṃsāra has almost ceased, its resurgence is sometimes observed. ||20||

Regarding the sequence of the composition: even if [the Self] has another locus, the fact that the Puruṣa remains untouched by others like space means that the discernment of reality (*tattvaviveka*) must be performed; yet [the opponent's objection] is also ineffective, as he says: "In some places" (*kvacit*).
This very reading is accepted by all. ||20||
Viśvanātha: For this very reason, he says "in some cases" (kvacid) [in verse 20], indicating that even when the fear of saṃsāra has almost ceased, its emergence is still observed.
The Blessed Lord said:
By means of a motiveless motive— one's own stainless duty—
and by intense devotion toward Me, long cultivated through what has been heard.
By means of knowledge through which reality is seen, by powerful dispassion,
by yoga joined with austerity, and by intense self-concentration;
In this world, Prakṛti, though being burned day and night by Puruṣa,
gradually becomes invisible, like the fire-drill wood when the fire has been extracted from it.
Śrīdhara: Merely having a connection with *prakṛti* is not the cause of bondage; rather, it is attachment to it through the intellect (*buddhi*) consisting of the *guṇas*.

When that [attachment] ceases, liberation is possible. Anticipating that occasional emergence [of bondage] might be due to a deficiency in the means, he offers a rebuttal by describing the excellence of the means.

By three [means]: the cause is the fruit. That which is not the cause of its own arising is the dharma through which one acts with desirelessness. With an immaculate self—that is, with a stainless mind—and with that which is accumulated and nourished by learning, namely, by hearing the sacred narratives. ||21||
Being consumed and overwhelmed, it becomes concealed. ||23||

The Sequence of Composition: Here it is said: if that very non-discrimination is the previously mentioned cause, then in that case, mere reflection upon reality (*tattvāvamarśa*) would be sufficient; however, previously there was indeed aversion to the Lord (*īśvaravaimukhya*), as in such statements as "fear arises from attachment to a second. Therefore...

He determines through six [verses] that even what has been taught is that, in all cases, it is precisely the preliminary worship of Īśvara that is required. Here, the triad beginning with *animitta* is as follows: *jñāna* is inquiry; *darśana* is ascertainment; *tapas* is tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth; and *yoga* is the meditation upon the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*). Yoga.

Regarding the terms *saṃhanana*, *upāya*, *dhyāna*, *saṅgati*, and *yukti* from the section on various meanings: meditation (*dhyāna*) itself, when devoid of the distinction between the meditator and the object of meditation, is *samādhi*. Just as when a fire is intense, for the purpose of extinguishing it, the fire-stick (*araṇi*)—which is the cause of its manifestation—is used by people, [so too is this].
It is rendered internalized; likewise, that illusion (*māyā*) also becomes a tree from its own part.

Here, by stating that "the worship of His feet is the root of all accomplishments (*siddhi*s)," the mention of those [other practices] as being like limbs—while devotion is the principal factor—is intended to show that they are viewed there as merely other means among many.
For this very reason, their fruit is liberation alone. ||21||

Thus, by the phrase "of the Lord who resides in His own majesty—the cause of majesty—within a portion of the Blessed One’s power, while His power-possessorhood is manifest," the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) as being the power of His essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*) is demonstrated; this is shown by the passage beginning with "He [who] in the Unconquered" (*sa yad ajayām*). (23)

Viśvanātha: O Mother, nature (*prakṛti*) is not the cause of the individual soul’s bondage; rather, it is the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of its qualities, and that is produced solely by ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, liberation is possible only upon the cessation of ignorance.
Any occasional arising of fear, however, is due to a deficiency in spiritual means (*sādhana*); this is the intended meaning.

He offers a rebuttal by describing the excellence of the means (*sādhana*): "By that [means] through which the stainless and pure self—the internal organ—becomes active; wherein the sign (*nimitta*) is the fruit, and its absence is the 'signless' (*animitta*) itself, which is the motivator;
and [by that means] which is intense, naturally radiant in every respect, and accumulated through sacred learning."

Through being nourished by listening to my teachings, the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), which is the material nature (*prakṛti*) of the Person (*puruṣa*), is consumed and disappears by these means. Regarding the word "of fire": *araṇi* is wood.
Just as fire, having arisen from wood itself, consumes that very wood, even so does knowledge, having arisen from the subtle body, [consume it].
Thus it burns. ||2123||
Having enjoyed her pleasures and having constantly perceived their defects, she was renounced;
yet she does not bring any impurity upon the Lord who remains established in his own majesty.

Śrīdhara: This being so, he says that there is no further rebirth: "She whose enjoyment has been enjoyed"; "she whose fault is constantly and always seen"; therefore, having been abandoned by the Lord—who is not dependent on another, who abides in His own glory, and who has attained His own bliss. (24)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, even though the remaining *prakṛti*, which consists of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), is like a burning forest, if it remains in such a state, it will surely not cease to cause harm; thus he says: "Enjoyment has been experienced in many ways."
That [nature] from which heaven, hell, and so forth arise, and which for that very reason has been discarded by the discerning as if it had been chewed;

yet, even if it should happen to fall upon one by chance, it is that in which faults are perceived. This is because the Lord is eternally capable of discriminating between the good and the bad, and of both enjoying and abandoning [the former], as well as perceiving the faults [of the latter], while remaining established in His own glory—His own greatness.
On the path of the virtuous as taught by the guru. ||24||
For just as sleep brings many evils to one who has not awakened,
that very same sleep does not lead to delusion for one who has awakened.

Śrīdhara: [The author] states, with an illustration, that even though it is a cause of misfortune during the state of non-discrimination, it does not remain so after discrimination—using two verses beginning with "Just as" (yathā). Dream-sleep (*prasvāpa*) maintains and nourishes many misfortunes, even though it manifests for one who has awakened due to the force of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). ||25||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: That which is the cause of misfortune in the state of non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is indeed not so when discrimination (*viveka*) exists; thus he says with two verses beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*). *Prasvāpa* means dream, [which brings] many misfortunes.
It bears the bites of tigers, snakes, and the like; for one who has awakened, they may still manifest by the force of latent impressions (saṃskāra). //25//
Thus, for one who has realized the truth and finds delight in the Self, nature never causes any harm to the mind as it is engaged in Me.
It has not been explained by anyone [else].
When, thus delighting in the internal through time over many births,
the sage has become detached from everything up to the world of Brahmā;
Śrīdhara concludes with three verses beginning with "yadaiva": "In whatever time there is a sequence of many births" refers to the triad beginning with "yadaiva. ||27||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained [previously].
My devotee, having realized the truth through my abundant grace, attains the supreme good, which is his own abiding state, known as Kaivalya, and centered in me.

Śrīdhara: One who has awakened to the truth is one who has known the reality of the Self. His own state, called liberation (kaivalya)—the essential nature distinct from the body and so forth—is my refuge, the supreme good, and unsurpassed bliss. ||28||

The sequential composition: He says "my devotee" (mad-bhakta) to show that my devotee attains the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) directly through my grace alone. The meaning is: if one becomes my devotee through association with my devotees, then at that very moment. "By a greater [devotion]" means by a more powerful one in every respect. I...
That which has this as its support is described in the *Gītā*, beginning with "He who [worships me] with unswerving devotion" and ending with "For I am the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27). ||28||
Viśvanātha: "Sva-saṃsthānam" refers to one's own true nature, which is distinct from the body and so forth, and is known as liberation (kaivalya), namely Brahman.
That of which I am the very support—that is what is meant. As it has been said: "For I am the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27). ||28||
The wise man, whose doubts have been severed by his own vision, attains here directly that state from which,
once departed from the subtle body (liṅga), the yogi does not return.

Śrīdhara: One whose doubts and false cognitions have been severed by his own vision—that is, by self-knowledge—[attains this] upon the departure from the *liṅga*, meaning when the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) has perished. ||29||

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "By his own vision" means by the knowledge of the pure Self; "upon emerging from the *liṅga*" means when the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) has perished. ||29||
When, O dear one, the mind of the perfected one no longer clings to those illusions accumulated through yoga,
then my course shall be toward that which has no other cause.
Wherein there is no laughter at death for eternity.

Śrīdhara: At that time, however, the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) such as *aṇimā* become obstacles. When those [powers] have been accumulated and perfected through yoga—having no cause other than yoga—if the mind of the accomplished one (*siddha*) does not become attached to them, then, O dear mother, I am one who has transcended the ultimate limit.

Connected with that: in which state of existence there is no laughter of Death. The meaning is that when two [enemies] are separated, even one who has attained perfection thinks, "I have brought him under my control," and thus the laughter of Death—that is, pride—arises. ||30||
The sequential arrangement: when there is grace from me. ||30||
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, various enjoyments ranging from the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) to others are of the nature of obstacles;

[the author] says that the yogi should not become attached to them: when the mind of the perfected one (*siddha*) does not become attached to the various objects of enjoyment—the accumulated and flourishing manifestations of *māyā*—then [attainment] is absolute.
Liberation would be the goal. Among what kind of illusions? Those for which there is no cause other than yoga.

In which [goal], when attained, there is no laughter from Death (mṛtyu). The meaning is that when one is attached to sense objects, even if one is a perfected being (*siddha*), Death laughs out of pride, thinking, "I have brought him under my control. ||30||
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
the twenty-seventh [chapter] of the third [section] has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous.

Thus ends the chapter titled "The Discrimination of Nature" within the Kāpileya section of the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, in the Third Book of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, the compendium of the Pāramahaṃsyas composed by Vyāsa.
Chapter Twenty-Seven | Chapter Twenty-Eight | The Practice of the Means in the Kāpileya [Purāṇa]
The Blessed Lord said:
O daughter of a king, I shall describe the characteristics of yoga with seed (sabīja-yoga),
by which method the mind attains clarity and proceeds upon the true path.
"Madhva’s yoga is indeed *sabīja* (with seed), being Vaiṣṇava; the *nirbīja* (seedless) belongs to other deities.
For Viṣṇu is the seed of the world, while the other deities are the branches and so forth. Thus it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*. 1.
Śrīdhara:
Then, in the twenty-eighth [chapter], by means of the eightfold yoga adorned with meditation,
the knowledge of one's own true nature, liberated from all limiting adjuncts, is described.
Having briefly explained devotion and having described Sāṃkhya in detail,
Hari, in the form of Kapila, then taught the Vaiṣṇava yoga consisting of eight limbs.
Of that which possesses seeds and possesses an object; being serene. ||1||
The sequential arrangement: the syntactical connection is that by whatever rule or method [it is established], such is the definition of that specific type. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
Meditation on the eight limbs of yoga is described in detail [in this chapter],
because by means of it, the yogi may attain liberation effortlessly in the twenty-eighth [chapter].
Having thus instructed him in self-devotion and spoken of Sāṅkhya together with its adjuncts, the Lord,
whose body is the universe, began to explain the eightfold yoga combined with that [Sāṅkhya].
Of that which possesses seeds and that which possesses an object. ||1||
The practice of one’s own duty according to one's ability, desisting from unrighteousness,
contentment with what is obtained by fate, and worship of the feet of those who know the Self.
The cessation of vulgar conduct, delight in the dharma of liberation, constant eating of moderate and pure food, and frequenting solitary and secure places.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, possession of only as much as is necessary,
celibacy, austerity, purity, self-study, and worship of the Supreme Person.
Silence, mastery of posture, steadiness, and gradual conquest of the vital breath;
and the withdrawal of the senses from their objects into the heart by means of the mind.
The concentration of the mind upon a single part of one's own seat,
the contemplation of the pastimes of Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise the absorption of the self— this is called *samādhi*.
By these and other paths, one who has conquered the vital breaths and is free from sloth should gradually employ the intellect to yoke the wicked mind away from the path of untruth.
And Madhva says: "Samādhi is the state of the mind remaining steady without effort. (7)

Śrīdhara: Therein, he describes the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) in three verses, each consisting of two syllables more [than the previous]. Performing one's own duty according to one's capacity; abstaining from the worldly duty pertaining to the three aims of life (*traivargika*); and eating that which is measured, pure, and clean. In this context, "measured" means:
"One should fill two parts with food and fill one part with water;
one should leave the fourth part remaining for the movement of air"—this is well-known from the Smṛtis.
"Resorting to a secluded, solitary, secure, and unobstructed place" means [staying] there for as long as necessary.
The purpose [of yoga] is, for its part, the mastery of that much. He describes the limbs, beginning with posture, by means of three [sūtras].

Through the conquest of posture, there is steadiness. *Dhāraṇā* (concentration) is the fixing of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) together with the mind upon a single location among one's own stations (*svadhiṣṇya*), such as the *mūlādhāra* and others. [This pertains to] the self’s mind.
Concentration (*samādhāna*) is the state of having the Self as one's form. The sequential arrangement [of the path] by means of other ways, such as vows, gifts, and so forth, has not been explained.
Viśvanātha says: therein, he states the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) in three verses with two additional syllables each.

In that context, non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, non-possessiveness, celibacy, and silence are the *yamas*. Other practices, such as the performance of one’s own duty (*svadharma*), are the *niyamas*. The worldly dharma pertaining to the three aims of life (*traivargika*) consists of eating measured and pure food; therein, "measured" means:
"One should fill two parts with food and fill one part with water;
one should leave the fourth part remaining for the movement of air"—this is well-known from the *Smṛti*.
"Secluded" means a place that is solitary, secure, and free from fear; staying there [is what is intended]. For as long as...
The purpose is the attainment of that specific goal alone, and not the grasping of any further object.
He describes the limbs, beginning with posture (*āsana*), by means of three [verses]: through mastery of the existing posture, there is steadiness;
and by means of the mind, [one focuses] upon a single location among one's own seats (*svadhiṣṇya*), which are the stations of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) such as the *mūlādhāra* and others.

Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is the holding together with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Concentration (*samādhi*) is the stabilization of the mind within the self, which is the state of having the form of the self. By other paths as well—such as vows, giving, and so forth—one should "yoke," that is, apply oneself, to meditation. ||27||
Having established his seat in a clean place and mastered his posture,
he should sit comfortably upon it with an upright body and practice meditation.

Śrīdhara: He elaborates upon the seat and so forth, up until the word "pure" (śucau). Having established the seat with kusha grass, deerskin, and a cloth on top, or else comfortably in the svastika posture; the ellipsis is "one should practice the breath" (samabhyaset prāṇam).
"Placing the thighs within the space between the shanks and the tips of the feet between the knees—the wise know that the posture of the yogin is called *svastika*. (8)

Regarding the sequence of composition: in the phrase "seated in the *svastika*," the expression "according to one's comfort" (*yathāsukham*) is not appropriate; rather, the reading "seated in the *svastika*" (*svastisamāsīna*) is supported by the intended connection. However, here the reading "by means of the *svastika* posture" (*svastikāsanena*) is also appropriate, as it conveys the same meaning. [This is so] because of the word *svastika*.

The intended meaning is that the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) applies precisely there. Furthermore, if one explains it as "that in which a beautiful state (*sthiti*) exists," then even when explaining it as "according to one's pleasure" (*yathāsukham*), the term *svastika* remains consistent. ||8||
Viśvanātha explains the seat and other requirements: the seat (*āsana*) consists of *kuśa* grass, a deerskin, and a cloth placed on top;
seated upon that in such a way that it is truly auspicious (*svasti*), or rather, the meaning is "seated in the *svastika* posture. And as follows:
"Placing the thighs within the space between the shanks and the tips of the feet between the knees—wise men know that the posture of the yogin is called *svastika*. (8)
"One should practice the breath"—this is the ellipsis. ||8||
One should purify the path of the vital breath through inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka),
or by means of the contrary method, so that the mind becomes steady and unwavering.
Śrīdhara: Inhalation is the entry of external air into the interior; retention is the holding of the air once it has entered;

exhalation is the expulsion of the held air to the exterior. Or [one may practice] by means of the reverse order of exhalation, retention, and inhalation; or else, filling through the *iḍā* and exhaling through the *piṅgalā*.
Filling by means of the *piṅgalā* and exhaling by means of the *iḍā*—thus [one practices] in the reverse order. The word "vā" (or) has the sense of "and.
One should purify [the breath] so that, having become steady, it does not become unsteady again. ||9||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Inhalation through the left nostril of the external air is *pūraka* (inhalation).
The retention of the inhaled [air] is *kumbhaka* (retention). Exhalation through the right nostril is *recaka* (exhalation).
By means of the contrary [practices]—exhalation, retention, and inhalation—even the unstable mind becomes as unsteady as it was before. ||9||
The mind of a yogi who has conquered his breath shall soon become free from passion,
just as iron heated by wind and fire indeed casts off its impurity.
Śrīdhara: "Dhmātam" means heated. Just as iron or gold casts off its impurity, so too the mind becomes free from passion (*viraja*); the sense is that thereafter it will no longer be restless. ||10||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Loha means gold; dhmāta means heated. ||10||
One should burn away defects by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and sins by means of concentration (dhāraṇā);
one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna).
Śrīdhara states that the functions of *prāṇāyāma* and the other [limbs] serve as gateways to *samādhi*: "By means of *prāṇāyāmas*," etc.
"Defects" (*doṣān*) refers to wind, phlegm, and so forth. "Associations" (*saṃsargān*) refers to associations with sense objects. "Non-masters" (*anīśvarān*) refers to passion and the like.
*Dhāraṇā* is the stabilization of the mind together with the vital air (*vāyu*); for that which is stabilized, it is the continuous flow of mental modifications (*vṛtti*).
The distinction is that meditation (dhyāna) is the cessation of mental fluctuations (vṛttinirodha), which is concentration (samādhi). ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states their effects with the words "by means of breath-restraints" (*prāṇāyāmaiḥ*). [One purifies] defects such as wind and phlegm, sins which are evil deeds, attachments which are attachments to sense objects, and non-mastership which consists of passion, hatred, and so forth. ||11||
When one's own mind has become stainless and well-composed through yoga,
one should meditate on the supreme state of the Blessed One while gazing at the tip of one's own nose.
Śrīdhara: [The mind] has become well-composed and steady. "Kāṣṭhām" means a digit; the meaning is a form.
He whose gaze is fixed upon the tip of his own nose—this is for the sake of avoiding both lethargy (laya) and distraction (vikṣepa). ||12||
The sequential arrangement [of the terms]: "limit," "direction," and "boundary" mean, in short, the supreme essential nature. ||12||

Viśvanātha: Through yoga—consisting of the restraints (yama) and so forth—he is composed and steady; he beholds the tip of his own nose in order to avoid dissolution and distraction, having reached the ultimate state, which is his own supreme nature. ||12||
With a serene lotus-face and eyes as reddish as the interior of a lotus,
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace.

Madhva [comments]: "When one is unable to remember everything, one should focus on a single limb," because it has been stated, "as long as the mind does not waver. And Śrīdhara says: "Being unable to remember everything, the wise man should contemplate a single limb.
With seven verses, he describes Hari, the object of meditation, whose lotus-face is serene.
"He should meditate upon him"—this is the connection with the sixth [verse]. He whose eyes are reddish like the interior of a lotus, and who is dark-complexioned like the petal of a blue lotus. (13)

The sequence of composition: "prasannā" and so forth constitute a group of six verses. [The Lord is] ever anxious to favor His servants, for He is never satisfied even when bestowing the bliss of His own supreme devotion upon them. (13)
Viśvanātha:
Even among the nine-fold devotion, the great ones call him the third, the essence of the goals of human existence.
That meditation of Hari became the seventh [limb],
and here, the eightfold yoga serves for the attainment of liberation.

In this context, he describes the nature of the object of meditation for devotees and yogis, beginning with the word "prasanna. Regarding the term "śaṅkha," the fourth lotus should also be understood there. He refers to Him whose neck—that is, the throat—is adorned, bound, and encircled by the shining Kaustubha gem and its golden thread.
By her, whose voice was soft and sweet like that of intoxicated bees;
who possessed hips (the loins) shimmering with a girdle-string;
who had as his seat (viṣṭara) the very lotus-heart of his devotees; and whose scripture was not harsh.
"Apīvyam" means exceedingly beautiful. "Nityasthitam" means eternally abiding in the age of youth (kaiśora), that is, at fifteen years of age.
He is one whose fame is worthy of being celebrated and who is the very embodiment of a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha). ||1318||
Clad in yellow silk garments like the filaments of a blooming lotus,
with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest and the radiant Kaustubha gem resting upon his unbound neck.
Śrīdhara: He whose two garments are yellow like the filaments of a blooming lotus;
he who has the Śrīvatsa as his mark upon his chest; and he whose neck is adorned with the shining Kaustubha gem, never separated from it.
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: See the commentary on verse 13.
[He is adorned] with a forest garland pervaded by the resonance of intoxicated bees.
Adorned with a supreme necklace, bracelets, a crown, armlets, and anklets.

Śrīdhara: [It is] surrounded (parītam), that is, pervaded, by that [forest] which possesses a soft and sweet sound from intoxicated bees; [it is] one whose necklaces and other ornaments are supreme (parārdhya), meaning priceless. ||15||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: See the commentary on verse 13.
[He whose] hips shine with the girdle of the city of Kāñcī, and who sits upon the lotus of the heart as his seat—
Most beautiful to behold, peaceful, and increasing the delight of the mind and eyes.

Śrīdhara: He whose hips shine with the girdle of the city of Kāñcī; he whose seat is the lotus-heart of his devotees; and who thus causes the minds and eyes of his devotees to flourish—that is, to rejoice. (16)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: see the commentary on verse 13.
"Of lovely appearance, eternal, and honored by all the worlds."
He was tranquil in his youth, yet eager to bestow favor upon his servants.

Śrīdhara: Whose vision is directed toward His devotees and is *apīcya*—that is, exceedingly beautiful; who remains in the age of *kaiśora*, which is youth; and who is *kātara*—meaning intensely eager—in bestowing grace upon His servants. ||17||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: see the commentary on verse 13.
[He] whose fame is a sacred ford worthy of praise, who brings glory to those of meritorious renown.
One should meditate on the deity with all limbs complete, as long as the mind does not waver.

Śrīdhara: One whose fame is *kīrtanya*—worthy of being celebrated—and who is a *tīrtha* (a sacred ford) of glory; who brings renown to those of virtuous fame (*puṇyaśloka*), such as Bali and others; in whom all limbs are complete; and who neither falls away, nor departs, nor wanders astray. 18.
The sequence of the composition: One should meditate upon the deity with all limbs complete for as long as the mind does not waver.
When the mind has wavered, one should meditate by means of another method; this is stated by the words beginning with "sthitam" (established), etc.—see Viśvanātha’s commentary on verse 13.
Whether he is standing, walking, sitting, or lying down— dwelling in the cave of the heart— one should meditate upon him whose purpose is worthy of being beheld, with a mind of pure disposition.
Śrīdhara: He whose desired sport is to be beheld. ||19||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: In this context, he describes by way of a general rule (*tantra*) the pastimes to be meditated upon even by devotees who follow the path of passionate attachment (*rāgānugā-bhakti*):
[Kṛṣṇa] is situated in Vaikuṇṭha and at the foot of the desire-tree (*kalpataru*) in Vṛndāvana; and as He is walking...
From Vaikuṇṭha and from the cow-pasture to the forest; seated upon the jeweled lion-throne and on the peak of Govardhana;

reclining on the couch of Śeṣa and within the cave of Govardhana—the mind, possessing pure devotion, then beheld that which was worthy of being seen through the lattice-windows, even while standing outside, as He performed His desired pastimes.
That which is his activity. ||19||
Once the mind has found its footing there, pervading all the limbs,
the sage should perceive it and then concentrate it upon a single part of the Blessed One’s body.

Śrīdhara: Having thus described meditation on the whole [body], he speaks of meditation on each individual limb: "Having observed that mind by which the state attained therein has been established, having specifically focused upon it"—that is to say, upon each single limb one at a time. ||20||
The sequential arrangement: having observed and ascertained. ||20||
Viśvanātha: Having described the meditation on the whole [form], he now describes the meditation on each individual limb—“in that divine body” (20).
One should contemplate the lotus-feet of the Blessed One,
enriched with the emblems of the vajra, the goad, the banner, and the lotus,
and possessing a circle of lofty, radiant, red nails.
By means of its moonlight, it strikes away the great darkness of the heart.
Śrīdhara: He describes that very [lotus] in thirteen verses, beginning with the feet. One should contemplate it thoroughly.

It is "endowed" (āḍhyam) with the marks consisting of lines on the soles of the feet, such as the thunderbolt and others. By the moonlight of the circle (cakravālam), that is, the orb, of the high, red, and shining nails—

By him the darkness of the hearts of the great meditators has been struck down; and all this is stated as a qualification of the object to be adopted, precisely because it is that which is to be meditated upon. (21)

The Sequence of Meditation: Viśvanātha describes the meditation on each individual limb in successive order, beginning with the feet, to dispel the darkness of incapacity from the hearts of great meditators—starting with the word "Vajra.
This refers to the meditation on the sole of the right foot while he stands at the root of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru).

Since Kṛṣṇa, who is graceful in the *tribhaṅga* posture, is visible to his devotees, one should meditate on a goad (*aṅkuśa*) on the surface of the little toe of his right foot. On the surface of the goad is a thunderbolt (*vajra*), on the surface of the ring toe is a lotus (*saroruha*), and on the surface of the lotus is a banner (*dhvaja*). In this manner, the barley-corn (*yava*), discus (*cakra*), and so forth are to be known on the surface of the big toe. By these...
Rich with marks and signs; "darkness" means sin. ||21||
By the water of the preeminent river issuing from his purification, which was applied as a sacred tirtha upon his head, Śiva became auspicious;
[that water] was like a thunderbolt hurled at the mountain of the meditator’s mental impurities.
One should meditate for a long time upon the lotus feet of the Blessed One.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, by whose purification—that is, by whose washing—the water of the Gaṅgā, the foremost of rivers, which has issued forth, became auspicious even for Śiva; that is to say, he attained supreme bliss. This refers to Him who dwells in the mind of the meditator.

Like a thunderbolt hurled—that is, cast—upon the mountain of impurity, which is the mountain of sin; or rather, that by which a thunderbolt in the form of its own mark was hurled upon the mountain of impurity. ||22||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Having described the sweetness of the lotus-feet, he speaks of their majesty: by the water of that most excellent river, the Gaṅgā, which issued forth through the washing (*śauca*) [of those feet], [the world is purified] upon its head with abundance.

The meaning is that by the act [of wearing him]—or rather, by the authority (adhikāra) obtained through the power to bear him upon his head—he who was Śiva became Śiva even today; he thought, "I have become Śiva. Thus, the mental impurities of the meditating person, such as passion and hatred, were cast away upon those very mountains.
That which possesses the vajra as its own characteristic mark; likewise, my lotus feet serve as a goad to lead the elephant of the mind of the devoted meditator onto the right path,
as a lotus to adorn the lake of the mind, and as a banner to bestow upon the mind the sovereignty of supreme excellence.

It should also be understood that he holds a barley grain to bestow the most excellent fame; an umbrella to pacify the threefold affliction; and a wheel and other symbols for the sake of protection from all sides. ||22||
That [lotus] which the lotus-eyed mother Lakṣmī, who is adored by all the gods, placed upon the two knees of the Creator as he rested them upon her own thighs,
with the radiance of her sprout-like hands—
One should place that which has been cherished in the heart of the Lord Abhava.

Śrīdhara: The two knees and the two shanks extending up to them of the All-pervading One—the Creator of the entire universe—were fondly caressed and served by Lakṣmī, the Mother of Brahmā, through the skill of her touch.
He says "of the Unborn One" (abhavasya) to ward off the notion that he might appear as an ordinary transmigrating being. One should place him in one's heart; that is, one should meditate upon him.
The arrangement of the sequence: the two knees constitute the *trika*. ||23||

Viśvanātha: It has been stated that one should meditate on Him as reclining; therefore, one should place the two knees and the two shanks extending to them of the Lord reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa within the heart—those [limbs] which indeed belong to the all-creating Brahmā and are attended by the skillful massaging of His mother, Lakṣmī.
"Adorned with the radiance"—meaning beautified by the redness and yellowness—of her sprout-like hands;
"by the lotus-eyed one" means that their loveliness was undoubtedly tasted by her two eyes.
This very sweetness and majesty of the shanks and knees should be understood in the same way for what follows as well.
Since there is no existence for that which is non-existent, [existence does not exist for it]. ||23||
His thighs, resting upon the arms of the Suparṇa,
are resplendent and storehouses of vital energy, possessing the luster of *atasī* flowers, and are encircled by a long, hanging, excellent yellow garment.
The orb of her hips is embraced by a girdle of many strings.

Śrīdhara: [He is] upon the arms and shoulders of Suparṇa; the two repositories, the supports, of *ojas* (vital energy) and *bala* (strength); shining with a luster like the flower of the *atasī* plant;
and that which resides in the yellow garment (*pītāmbara*) which hangs down as far as the ankles.

The construction of the sequence is as follows: "One should place in one's heart that orb of the Lord's hips, which possesses an embrace—that is, a close contact—consisting of a girdle-belt"; this connects with what precedes it.
[Furthermore,] the pair of breasts is the location for entering the cave.
The area below the chest characterized by that [chest].

Viśvanātha: It has been stated that one should meditate on Him as He goes; therefore, one should place in the heart the two thighs of Hari, who is mounted upon Garuḍa and going to grant boons to Pṛthu, Dhruva, and others. [Above] the two arms...
The meaning is "above the two shoulders. *Nitambabimba* refers to the orb of the hips. ||24||
The navel-lake, situated within the hollow belly of the cave that is the vessel of the universe, wherein the lotus of all worlds— the source of the Self— is established,
is borne upon the two breasts of this [Lord], which are like emerald bulls.
One should meditate upon the pair, white as the rays of a pure pearl necklace.

Śrīdhara: One should meditate upon this navel-lake of Hari. Of what nature is it? It is situated within that belly which serves as the secret abode for the treasury—that is, the collection—of the worlds. In that navel-lake is the lotus, the seat (*dhiṣṇya*) of Brahmā, the Self-born, which consists of all the worlds.

"Arrayed" means raised up. Likewise, one should meditate on the pair of breasts which are like two excellent emerald gems (*harinmaṇi*). [The breasts] are fair—meaning white—due to the rays of the pure necklaces.
The sequence of the composition has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: One should meditate upon the lake of the navel of Him who lies within the Garbhoda ocean. It is situated in that belly which is the cave—the foundational abode—of the collection of worlds (*bhuvana-kośa*).
Therein, the lotus, which is the abode of the Self-born (*ātma-yoni*) and consists of all the worlds, is spread out and risen.

Likewise, her two breasts were shaped like *cakrikā* (circular ornaments) and resembled two excellent emeralds (*harinmaṇi-vṛṣau*). Alternatively, it may mean that her breasts were such that the bull (*vṛṣa*)—representing Dharma—possessed the color of an emerald (*hariṇmaṇi-varṇa*), since the right breast is traditionally associated with Dharma. [She was adorned] by the rays of bright pearl necklaces.

It should be understood that by the words "fair" and "white," it is also indicated that one should meditate upon a white Śrīvatsa mark on the upper part of the right breast, which spirals to the right and possesses a luster like that of a pearl necklace. ||25||
The chest, which is the dwelling place of the Greatly Prosperous One who is like a bull, bestows bliss upon the minds and eyes of men;
and the neck, for the sake of further ornamenting the Kaustubha jewel—
One should direct [this] in the mind toward him who is honored by all the worlds.
Śrīdhara: One should meditate upon the chest and the throat of the preeminent Ṛṣabha, the abode of great majesty and the dwelling place of Mahālakṣmī. Of what nature is the throat?
It is that which serves as the supreme ornament for the Kaustubha gem worn there for the sake of adornment.
The meaning is: for whom this is the purpose; that is, he who adorns himself with the Kaustubha gem alone.
"Bestowing satisfaction upon the minds and eyes of men and of those who remember [him]" is a qualifier for both [the Lord and the jewel]. ||26||

The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] is as follows: regarding the term "adhivāsa," Viśvanātha has shown that it refers to its supreme allure. He explains that one should contemplate the chest [of the Lord], where the dwelling (*vāsa*) of Mahālakṣmī—who possesses great majesty—is superior (*adhi*) [even to the Kaustubha], situated on the left side; it is an ornament even more excellent than the Kaustubha gem.
The meaning is: "and that neck for which even the Kaustubha gem would serve as its purpose, and by which [the gem] would be adorned. ||26||
And one should contemplate the thousand-spoked [wheel] of unbearable splendor, whose arm-rings have been polished by the turning of Mount Mandara, and which stands above the world-protectors.
And that conch, which was the royal swan for his lotus-like hand.
Śrīdhara: Those [hands] upon which the armlets—bracelets—are cleansed and made radiant;

those upon which the world-protectors (lokapālas) have taken their seat; [those possessing] a wheel with a thousand spokes; and whose splendor is unbearable, like a royal swan upon a lotus-hand. ||27||
The sequence of composition: "Of Mount Mandara," etc. The intention lies solely in its majesty (śauṭīrya), not in its cleansing, because its state of being cleansed is eternally established.

Therefore, this is a case of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*), which is apprehended through poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). [This is] the transformation.
And this should be understood here for the sake of establishing [the point] well. ||27||

Viśvanātha: One should meditate upon the arms of Hari as he churns the ocean—arms upon which the armlets and other ornaments are polished and made radiant—and from whom the world-protectors (Lokapālas) have become authorized devotees; [the arms] of the Lord Vaikuṇṭhanātha, in his four [hands].

"One should meditate upon the four weapons, beginning with the discus, in his hands, as well as the garland and the Kaustubha gem"—this he states with the verse beginning "one should contemplate" (sañcintayet). The discus has a thousand spokes. ||27||
One should remember the Kaumodakī, the beloved mace of the Blessed One, smeared with the mire of the blood of hostile warriors,
and garlanded with a swarm of bees humming with their song.
The stainless reality of the caitya is the jewel upon its neck.

"Madhu is Brahmā through the conceit of the mind (*citta*); Hari is the *caitya* (the object of that mind) due to its regulation by Him; and that Brahmā shines as the Kaustubha gem upon the throat of Hari. Thus it is stated in the Bhāgavata-tantra. (28)
Śrīdhara: One should meditate upon the garland and the jewel on his neck—smeared and anointed with the mire that is the blood of those enemies who are warriors and fighters;
it is resonant and proclaimed by the swarms of honey-bees; it is the reality of the Caittya-jīva. That...

It is stated in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa: "The Blessed Lord Hari bears his own self— the stainless, quality-less, and untainted soul of this world— in the form of the Kaustubha gem" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.22.68).

The sequential arrangement: "digdhām" (smeared). As before, because of the repeated state of being smeared, the reality of the *jīva*—which is of the nature of the great aggregate (*mahāsamaṣṭi*)—is the locus for its manifestation;
the meaning is that it is a specific manifestation of the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*) himself. It is stainless (*amalam*), transcending the qualities (*guṇātītam*). Thus it has been said:
In the *Vaiṣṇava-purāṇa*: "The Lord Hari bears himself, untainted and pure beyond the qualities (*aguṇa*), as the very nature of the Kaustubha gem for this world" (ViP 1.22.68).
Thus, since his ornaments as well are the Supreme Brahman, the excellence of their substratum is established by the principle of "how much more so" (kaimutya). ||28||

Viśvanātha: *Digdhām* means smeared. *Upaghuṣṭām* means resounded. Although the term *caitya*—derived from the sense that "it exists" (*bhavati*) or "manifests" (*āvirbhavati*) within the mind (*citte*)—refers everywhere exclusively to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), here it refers instead to the individual self (*jīvātman*), because it is the power (*śakti*) of that [Supreme Self]. [This refers to] the *caitya*, which is the individual self, the power of the individual self.
This is the reality. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"The Lord Hari bears his own self, which is untainted, free from qualities, and stainless, in the form of the Kaustubha gem" (ViP 1.22.68).
The meaning is that the infinite rays of the Kaustubha gem itself are the individual souls (jīvas). ||28||
One should contemplate the lotus-face of the Blessed One, who has assumed a physical form here out of compassion for his servants,
[a face] which is graced by the swaying of shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings.
With its stainless cheeks illuminated and its noble nose.
Śrīdhara: Of him whose form was assumed by that intellect which had shown compassion—that is, had exercised mercy—toward his servants;
in whom the two stainless cheeks were illuminated by the quivering, that is, the movement, of his shimmering dolphin-shaped earrings; and in whom the nose was noble, that is, prominent.

The sequence of the composition: [He is] one by whom the forms have been taken—that is, drawn from and brought here to this world—by means of that intellect which is filled with compassion for those devotees who, being contemplative, have assumed the forms of their respective desired deities. ||29||

Viśvanātha: She is "Anukampitā" because compassion has arisen toward her; the suffix *it* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *tāraka*. Alternatively, *anukampita* means compassion or mercy; she whose form (*mūrti*) was assumed for the sake of her own dwelling by that intellect (*dhī*) which consists of or is identical with such compassion—O you who are the very essence of my own nature and power!

"Out of compassion, take whichever form among my manifestations you desire in this mortal world for the sake of dwelling within it as you please," he said; and having spoken thus, she distinguished [the forms], for the swaying of the shark-shaped earrings was indeed caused by the movement of the fly-whisks being waved by the attendants stationed on both sides.

It may be understood either by a nod of the head or by a movement of the neck intended to express the excellence of the tasting of the dancing, singing, instrumental music, rhythmic clapping, and lute-playing of her circle of female companions. By the word "spotless" (*amala*), the two cheeks are indicated as being like mirrors for the finest jewels.

With the reflections of his pair of swaying shark-shaped earrings, his two eyes—resembling wagtails—becoming dancing masters, seem to make the four sharks that have come to the surface of his chest dance;
this is the suggested poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). "With a noble nose" means having a prominent nose; "noble" (*udāra*) refers to one who is generous or great.

Because of this designation, that [lotus]— which is the abode of Śrī, which is fit to be tasted by the nose, which bestows its own entire essence, which is served by bees, and which is endowed with its own splendor and possessed of a mass of curved filaments— is worthy of being offered as one's all.
One should meditate with unwearied mind upon the lotus-eyed one, who possesses shimmering eyebrows and casts a glance that upbraids the pair of fish [of the god of love].
Madhu is Śrī herself, who is the very form of Hari; Indirā, however, is that which rests upon him. 30.

Śrīdhara: One should meditate on that which exists surpassing the lotus—the abode of Śrī—which is itself attended by its own splendor and beauty as well as by bees, and which serves as the refuge for a pair of fish.
In this regard, there is a surpassing of the bees by the locks of hair, and of the pair of fish by the two eyes.
It should be observed that "in which the eyes are like lotuses" is another simile; "in which the eyebrows are shimmering"; and "consisting of mind" means appearing within the mind. (30)

The sequence of composition: One should meditate upon that eye which has the form of a lotus and which surpasses the interior of the most excellent lotus that is the abode of Śrī (Lakṣmī). Alternatively, in the word *abja*, the suffix *suluk* is used according to the rule "supāṃ suluk...
etc., for metrical reasons; its qualifier is *śrīniketam*, [referring to] the pair of fish.
And here, it should be understood that the two eyebrows are intended as a comparison for the lotus, by means of which the face surpasses the lotus.

In this context, regarding the eye being like a lotus, it is explained in this way precisely because it nourishes a particular excellence of beauty. It is composed of mind (*manomaya*), indicating the various playful manifestations of compassion within the Blessed Lord.
Or [it is] Śrī Bhakti, who is possessed by the various playful manifestations of devotion within her. ||30||

Viśvanātha: And that lotus-face, the abode of Śrī, which, though attended by bees and though being the refuge of the pair of fish (the eyes), surpasses other lotuses—meaning, it eclipses them with its own splendor—that one should meditate upon; such is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). In that regard:

The suggestion (*ākṣepa*) of bees by means of the mass of her curly locks; the suggestion of a pair of fish by means of her eyes, which resemble lotus petals. The meaning is that she has attained a mental identity with [the Lord] through her own mind, as it were, due to the excellence of her relish (*svāda*). Her two eyebrows are radiant, manifesting compassion toward her devotees.
Where that [is]. ||30||
His gaze, released from his eyes with abundant compassion to pacify the most terrible threefold suffering,
was accompanied by a gentle smile and possessed vast grace.
One should meditate for a long time in a cave with expansive contemplation.
Śrīdhara: [The word] *kṛpayā* means excessively or exceedingly. *Akṣibhyāṃ nisṛṣṭam* means emitted or directed from the eyes.

*Snigdhasmitenānuguṇitam* means joined or accompanied by a gentle smile. That in which there is abundant grace (*vipula-prasāda*). Regarding the sequence of the composition within the cave of the heart: by that smile which is gentle—that is, which manifests an excess of affection—[it is accompanied].

Repeatedly multiplied without interval and thus expanded; for this very reason, or because of that, he whose grace (prasāda) is vast—or in whom such [grace] exists—[resides] there, in the cave of the heart, which takes the form of the abode of the supreme secret. ||31||

Viśvanātha: One should meditate upon the glance of that Hari. It is that very affectionate smile—which was emitted and fashioned from his two eyes for the sake of pacifying the most terrible threefold suffering (tāpatraya) of the meditator—that is [the object of meditation]. First, there is the sweetness characterized by that smile, which is then followed by...
That in which [the merit] is multiplied by ten million times ten million through the sequence beginning with threefold multiplication. ||31||
The exceedingly noble smile of Hari, which dries up the ocean of intense tears of grief for all the worlds bowed down before him,
was fashioned by his own *māyā* for the purpose of enchanting them.
The circle of her eyebrows was fashioned by the Sage for the sake of the Fish-bannered God.

Śrīdhara: One should meditate upon that smile of Hari, which dries up the ocean of tears shed by all the worlds who have bowed down in intense grief; and one should meditate upon His exceedingly noble circle of eyebrows. Of what nature is it? It is for the purpose of enchanting even the god of love (Makaradhvaja) through His own illusory power (māyā).
It was composed by a sage for the benefit of sages; that is to say, in order to delude Kāma himself, who had set out to delude the sages. ||32||

The structural arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): By means of the qualification of the ocean of tears born of intense grief, the fact that laughter increases the ocean of tears of supreme bliss is suggested (*dhvanyate*). Consequently, even though it possesses the nature of the moon, its novelty is established, because it differs from the well-known moon in that it increases a salt-water ocean.

He describes the auspiciousness of the sequence with the words "for the sake of infatuation" (*sammohanāya*). This should be understood as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*); for by means of intonation (*kāku*), violence is suggested. ||32||

Viśvanātha: One should meditate on the smile of Hari. It is that [smile] which specifically dries up the ocean of tears born of intense grief arising from separation for all those devotees who have bowed down and possess moods such as servitude and friendship;
it is "most noble" because it lifts one out of the ocean of grief and places one in the ocean of bliss.

The meaning is "giving a plunge" [into bliss]. Alternatively, by means of the drying up of the ocean of tears consisting of the intense sufferings and sorrows of saṃsāra, there is suggested the swelling of the ocean of tears consisting of the love and bliss that transcends saṃsāra. By this—
Even in his state as the moon, there is a sense of wonder, for it is well known that the moon causes both the Ocean of Milk and the salt ocean to swell.
One should meditate upon his circle of eyebrows, which, through its own illusory power (*māyā*), acts by means of a deceptive casting forth.
It has been composed and presented for the purpose of completely enchanting even the fish-bannered god of love (Kāma).

Now, one might ask: how could it possibly delude the fish-bannered god? To this he replies: "For the sake of the sages"—that is, out of sheer anger at the thought that this [poem] might disturb even those sages who subsist on leaves and water while practicing austerities; such is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). ||32||

One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who has settled within the cavity of one's own body, whose smile is the vehicle for meditation, whose thick lower lip shines with a reddish glow, and whose row of slender teeth resembles a line of jasmine buds.
With a mind offered through moist devotion, one should not desire to see [anything] as separate.
The meaning is: "One should not desire to see him as separate from the honey; one should desire to see him alone. ||33||

Śrīdhara, having described the meditation on the gentle smile (*mandahāsa*), speaks of the meditation on the loud laugh (*sphuṭahāsa*): one should meditate upon the loud laughter of Viṣṇu, his boisterous laugh. Of what nature is it? It is the "object of meditation" (*dhyānāyana*), meaning that due to its extreme beauty, it becomes the object of meditation effortlessly. This refers to its beauty.

Thus he says: [the face] in which a row of the very fine (tanavaḥ) and subtle (sūkṣmāḥ) teeth—which have become reddened by the abundant (bahulayā) and superior (adhikayā) luster (bhāsā) or radiance of the lower lip—is shimmering;
[and which is] situated within the cavity of the body, in the space of the heart, being known through devotion moistened by the essence of love for Him.
Having thus fixed his mind, he should not wish to see anything separate or distinct from that; the meaning is that he should not cause the mind to waver. ||33||
The sequential arrangement: with devotion and respect. ||33||

Viśvanātha: It has been stated that one should meditate on the desired object of contemplation; therefore, [this refers to] a certain bee who, while perched upon a bed of flowers in some secluded spot, did not leave the vicinity of the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, and other features of his beloved out of an intense longing for her fragrance.

Terrified by the humming sound, she was constantly fidgeting—lifting her garments as she ate, and turning her neck and eyes about—saying with a plaintive tone: "O crest-jewel of connoisseurs! I fall at your feet; drive this away so that I may see you."

One should meditate upon the loud laughter—the smiling laugh—of the Blessed One as he speaks, saying: "O Lord of Bees, listen as you look! Do not abandon her today; enjoy her! This laughter becomes the object of meditation spontaneously, without effort, and therein lies its sweetness.
He said: "In which [face], the rows of jasmine buds—the very fine, delicate teeth that have become ruddy by the abundant luster of the lower lip—are shimmering;
one should not desire to see it as something separate from the Self (nāsmāt) residing within the cavity of one's own heart, that is, perceived in the space of the heart."
And because one would not even wish to know [it], since there is no other superior reality than the essence of the goal of human life (puruṣārtha),
the sense is that for devotees, this very delusion consisting of the bliss of tasting [this] is the supreme samādhi. Thus ends the third limb of nine-limbed devotion.
Even this meditation, which is preeminent in the sweetness of the Lord’s incarnations, qualities, and pastimes,

was indeed described in the context of the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga) for the very purpose of drawing even those yogis who have entered the great abyss of yoga and immersing them in the nectar-ocean of the mellows of devotion (bhakti-rasa). And it is observed that—

"O royal sage, although he was already perfected in the state beyond qualities (nirguṇa), his heart was captivated by the pastimes of the One of Excellent Fame (uttamaśloka), such that he studied this narrative. Thus it is said.
These [pastimes] are to be worshipped by those who travel the path of non-duality (advaita).
Having received initiation at the lion-throne of our own bliss,
we have been forcibly enslaved by some rogue— a lecher after the cowherd girls.

Thus, by these various statements, it is clear that even great yogis such as Bilvamaṅgala, the son of Vyāsa, and others, through the power of the Great Lord’s grace, are indeed immersed solely in the aesthetic flavor of devotion (bhaktirasa). ||33||
Thus, having attained devotion toward the Blessed Lord Hari, his heart melting with love and his hair standing on end from joy,
he was repeatedly overwhelmed by a stream of tears born of intense longing.
And he gradually withdraws that hook of the mind as well.
Śrīdhara explains *samādhi* with two verses beginning with "evam": Yoga is of two kinds, namely *nirbīja* (seedless) and *sabīja* (with seed). Among these, regarding *nirbīja-yoga*:
"From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away..."
"Then, having restrained this from here and there, one should bring it under control within the Self alone" (Gītā 6.26).

Thus, as stated in the Gītā and other texts, *samādhi* performed by an unworthy person is difficult to achieve; however, it is easy when practiced with a seed (*sabīja*). For in that state, while meditating upon Hari, who is the embodiment of supreme bliss, [the mind becomes steady] without effort.

The cessation of the mind occurs. As it has been said: "Devotion to Me bestows upon those whose self and life-breath have been captivated a subtle goal, even against their will" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.36).
Therefore, having introduced that very [devotion], I shall state the definition of yoga with its seed; that indeed is the state of being accomplished without effort.
He demonstrates this: one by whom such devotion (bhāva)—that is, love (prema)—has been attained toward Hari through the path of meditation;
likewise, one whose heart melts through devotion, whose hair stands on end out of joy, and who is repeatedly overwhelmed by a flood of bliss with a stream of tears flowing from intense longing.

While attempting to seize the Blessed One who is difficult to grasp, even the mind—which serves as a means like a fishhook for catching a fish—becomes detached from the object of meditation; that is to say, one's effort in maintaining that concentration becomes slack. ||34||
The sequential arrangement: "Thus, in Hari. Thus, by the practice of the previously mentioned devotion mixed with yoga, one becomes one who has attained *bhāva* toward Hari.
In that regard, the sign is "by devotion," and so forth. By devotion, such as remembrance (*smaraṇa*) and the like. Even so; and that—

By virtue of the sweetness of the object of meditation, his mind attains such a state that it gradually detaches itself and becomes liberated. The sense is that for one by whom devotion has been practiced as a limb of yoga, [the mind is freed] precisely from the fault of hypocrisy regarding the desire for isolation (*kaivalya*). As it has been said: "Dharma is cast aside..."

In the passage, "Deceit (*kaitava*) is supreme here" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 1.1.2), the word "supreme" (*para*) indicates that even the desire for liberation (*mokṣābhisandhi*) is a form of deceit. For this very reason, by the word "hook" (*baḍiśa*), there is implied hardness, a lack of aesthetic savor (*arasavittva*), hypocrisy (*dāmbhikatva*), and the pursuit of one's own self-interest alone. But those who are pure devotees (*śuddhabhakta*) are not...
Sometimes they abandon that object of meditation in such a manner as was said by the King:
"O Kṛṣṇa, a person whose soul is purified does not leave the soles of Your feet,
just as a traveler who has been freed from all afflictions does not leave his own shelter" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.8.6).
And by the illustrious Nārada:
"O dear one, a person who serves Mukunda should never, under any circumstances, undergo the cycle of worldly existence like an ordinary man."
"Remembering the embrace of Mukunda’s feet, a person who has grasped the aesthetic essence (rasa) would not wish to abandon it again" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.19).
By the statement "he who has grasped the rasa does not abandon it," the similarity of others to iron, stone, and so forth is implied.
This has been indicated; indeed, the Blessed One would not act otherwise than that. As it was said by the venerable Brahmā:
"O Lord, having accepted the feet of Your own people with supreme devotion, You do not depart from the lotus-heart of those men. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.5]
"And he releases his heart through the *hotṛ* priest, for whose [heart] it is not manifest" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.55).
For this very reason, in the preceding passage, there is the qualification "of one's own men" (*svapuṃsām*), where *sva-* is used as a specific attribute.
Or rather, even that which consists of the state of having attained devotion toward the Blessed One is a hook for His mind.

By the word "api" (also/even), the meaning is that one separates from or abandons even the Blessed One through the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of isolation (*kaivalya*), because [the Blessed One] is manifested as an entity and so forth. And by the word "hook" (*baḍiśa*), this is implied:
[one abandons him] by means of the mind, which stands in the place of a hook, [casting it out] from the Blessed One, who stands in the place of a great sacred ford such as the Gaṅgā.

Because the object of apprehension— standing in the place of the fish— is perceived as the partless Brahman manifested through its homogeneity within that aspect of the "laughter" (*hāsa*), which is self-luminous and of the nature of bliss, the seeker who has abandoned the pursuit [of the world] due to the realization of what was already established attains only the state of a fisherman, and not [the state of the fish].

The state of being a virtuous person (*sādhulokatva*) arises merely from the pleasure derived from immersing oneself in that [worldly existence]. Consequently, by way of its similarity to the livelihood of a fisherman with a hook (*baḍiśajīvika*), its inferiority is indicated; however, this is not so in passages such as *svasukhanibhṛta* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.12.62), where the word *rucira* is used.
He praises the captivating pastimes of the son of Śrī Vyāsa; in his speech, the excellence of one such as he is demonstrated. As it is said:
"Seeking the propitiation of the Blessed One, they were free from desires."

"But those men who do not desire even the supreme goal are skilled in their own self-interest" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.18.74). Regarding these two types of qualified practitioners, it should be understood that the ultimate cause for their distinct final goals is precisely the difference in their association with the Great One (mahat-saṅga), which is the root of everything everywhere. By them...

In passages such as "with beautiful limbs" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.36), and so forth; however, verses beginning with "whose soul was stolen" (hṛtātmanaḥ) are not cited here. Since that [verse] is read within the section concerning pure devotees starting from "his state of being the one Self" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.34), its explanation is exactly as it has been demonstrated.

This is logical. This very statement of Śrī Kapiladeva, along with its examples, such as "A person who has developed detachment through devotion... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.26), should also be understood.
For it is said previously: "In this regard, faith, attachment, and devotion will follow in succession" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.25).
Only devotion has been shown. Later, when its definition is asked for, he states that definition, saying:
"Devotion is weightier than perfection" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.32), and "Some do not desire oneness with Me" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.34); thus, it is characterized by being independent of liberation.

The status of being the primary subject matter has been stated. Furthermore, in the verse "She who quickly consumes the storehouse" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.35.33), the destruction of the storehouse of *māyā* is described as a secondary quality (*ānuṣaṅgika-guṇa*) of that devotion.
In passages such as "By means of such devotion, a person... and so forth, even for that kind of devotion, [the result is attained] only through the assistance of knowledge and the like.
Having stated that [devotion] is the sole means of achieving liberation, its secondary designation was mentioned. Therefore, even here, only a semblance of that devotion is first shown—as follows:
"Seeing him upon the earth, everyone was overwhelmed by the joy of his gaze."
"O King, they fell like a staff, and rising slowly, they offered praise" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.9.3).

Here too, one should cite as an example the semblance of devotion (*bhaktyābhāsatva*) on the part of the gods, whose intent was merely the destruction of their enemy named Vṛtra and the attainment of sovereignty. [Prītisandarbha 73]
Viśvanātha: But that yogī who, being extremely dull-witted and lacking the grace of the Great Lord, even after experiencing this sweetness of meditation,
fails to find its true savor and seeks to abandon it— he, though having reached the goal of yoga,
is the most inferior among yogīs and is utterly deprived of the nectar of devotion.
It is said that through devotion alone one attains liberation consisting of the experience of the inner self (pratyagātman), preceded by the destruction of the twenty-one kinds of suffering;
however, one does not attain liberation consisting of the experience of Brahman. Thus he says, beginning with "In this way," and so forth.

The conclusion of the chapter: Regarding the phrase "in Hari, the Blessed One," because He is captivating and possesses the sixfold opulences (*bhaga*), He is filled with sweetness, sovereignty, and nectar; yet, although He has attained a state of being (*pratilabdhabhāvaḥ*), that state is obtained through *śleṣa* (punning association) as a mere semblance (*pratirūpatayā*) and not as a true correspondence (*anurūpatayā*). In this regard, indeed—

The word "api" (even/also) applies to every [term]. Even one who has attained such a state, even one whose heart melts, even one with hair standing on end, and even one being repeatedly tormented by a stream of tears caused by intense longing—
even he, from that very state, separates or causes to be separated the "fishhook of the mind," as well as [ordinary] knowledge.
The meaning is that because there is no injunction for renunciation through devotion (*bhakti-saṃnyāsa*)— unlike the various [injunctions] such as "one should renounce into me"— and because,

on the contrary, there exists a prohibitive injunction stating "one whose mind is offered with a heart moistened by devotion should not desire to see [the Lord] separately," this dull-witted person separates [the devotee] from Him solely by his own will. [The word used is] *viyuñjyāt*.

Because of the application of the piercing [hook]: since his mind is a hook, even though he is of such a nature, it causes him to be separated from that very essence consisting of sweetness. For the purpose of removing the longing for the taste of sense-objects, the mind is cast into the sweetness of the Lord; therefore, even that longing for His sweetness—

The meaning is that for the sake of cessation, one should withdraw that mind even from that [object]; "gradually" means that when the mind is properly engaged, disengaging it is indeed difficult; therefore, while the engagement is not yet perfect, one should do so slowly through practice—perhaps two or three times, or four or five times.
Within seven or eight days, it certainly causes [the object] to be separated; for the hook is indeed made of iron.
Therefore, unlike gold, silver, and so forth, it does not melt like butter and the like;
rather, due to the intensity of the heat of the fire, it becomes slightly liquid and immediately thereafter hardens again.

Therefore, it is said that "the heart melts" (*dravaddhṛdaya*), but not that "the heart has melted" (*drutahṛdaya*). Just as a fishhook, despite being constantly immersed in the waters of holy fords such as the Gaṅgā, remains crooked and devoid of taste; and just as a lure for fish is hypocritical because its mouth is covered with a piece of desirable flour-paste.
In the same way, even the mind of one whose yoga is contested— though purified by sacred sites— is hard, crooked,
and hypocritical because its mouth is covered by meditation and devotion that merely attract the Lord;
as stated by the venerable Svāmīcaraṇa in the passage, "Dharma is free from deceit" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.1.2).
By the word "pra," even the aspiration for liberation (mokṣābhisandhi) is explained as being deceitful;

precisely because of the defect of deceit regarding the desire for isolation (kaivalya), the Goddess Śrī Bhakti—who is the most excellent of all and who takes the form of meditation—was worshipped by him as a limb of yoga, yet was later abandoned. Of that [person]:
The touch of the yogic mind-hook is indeed painful even for the Blessed One; therefore, upon its separation,

it is the Blessed One alone who grants liberation— consisting of the experience of the inner self preceded by the cessation of the twenty-one kinds of suffering— to that fisherman of yogis who has lost such a mind-hook.

He grants [liberation], but not liberation in the form of the experience of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). However, those who delight in the Bhāgavata tradition say that to one who is seen as a practitioner of the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) as described in the *Bhagavadgītā*, and who does not abandon meditation on the Lord, He grants even liberation in the form of the experience of the Supreme Self; for he—
At no time can he bear to be separated from the sweet form of the Blessed One. As it was said by the King:
"O Kṛṣṇa, a person whose soul is purified does not leave the soles of Your feet."
"Like a traveler who has abandoned all afflictions and reached his own refuge," so it is said.
And by Uddhava:
"To You, the Lord and Beloved of the Self of all, who are the refuge of those who have taken shelter..."
"Who indeed would abandon that which bestows all goals and is created by one's own efforts?
And by Śrī Nārada:
"Remembering again the embrace of Mukunda’s feet..."
"One should not desire to abandon [the world], for people grasp at its flavors" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.19).
By the term "grasping at flavors," even among yogis, only those such as Śrī Śuka and others are truly commended.
In this very preceding verse, it is stated: "With a mind moistened by devotion, one should offer everything to Him and not desire to see anything else."

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāgavata*, "one whose mind is offered" (*arpitamanā*), once the mind has been offered to Him, since there is no sense of ownership over that mind, how could one separate it from Him? Or how could one be considered a "stealer of what was given"? If such were the case, censure would be unavoidable. Furthermore, the Lord would reside only in the hearts of devotees and not in those of yogis. As it is said:
By Brahmā:
"O Lord, because Your feet have been grasped by them with supreme devotion, You do not depart from the lotus-hearts of Your own people. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.54) Thus it is said.
And by Āvirhotra: "He whose heart does not release [the Lord]," etc. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.55). ||34||
When the mind— freed from its support, devoid of objects, and dispassionate— suddenly attains nirvana like a flame,
the person perceives therein the one Self, unobstructed.
He reflects, having turned back the flow of the qualities.

The honey—the individual consciousness of one's own mind, which has abandoned its support and is directed toward Viṣṇu—attains that Nirvāṇa; it abandons the identification with the body through the identification with its own consciousness. ||35||

Śrīdhara: When, at that very moment, [the mind] is thus devoid of objects—and for that very reason, devoid of support—since it is impossible for the meditator to remain without a connection to an object of meditation; nor can there be an object such as sound and so forth as previously described, because [the mind] is detached from those through the experience of supreme bliss. Therefore...

It attains dissolution in *nirvāṇa*. The meaning is that, having abandoned the state of being a mental modification (*vṛtti*), it transforms into the form of Brahman. Just as a flame, when its support and object have ceased, transforms into the form of the light of the great elements; in this state, there is no interval, and it is one, devoid of the distinction between the meditator and the object of meditation.
He perceives the Self as undivided and pervasive. The reason for this is that the flow of qualities—the limiting adjuncts such as the body and so forth—has ceased and departed from him. (35)
The sequential arrangement: In order to apply the method of renunciation, he says "muktāśrayam" and so forth;

this is to be seen in the introduction to the fourth sentence of the sixth section, as follows: even while living, there arises the direct realization of Brahman—which has attained identity with the direct realization of one's own nature as the witness (jīva)—that serves as the indicator of the falsity of the connection with the effects of Māyā imagined through ignorance.

The meaning is that this is a specific type of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). This very definition of liberation is shown in the *Śrī Kāpilīya* in the four verses beginning with "the support of the liberated" (*muktāśrayam*). For there, one whose flow of the qualities (*guṇa*) has ceased beholds the Self as the Supreme Self. ||35||

Viśvanātha: Anticipating the question, "What would be the state of the mind when the nature of the Lord is abandoned as taught in the path of the most inferior yogis? he says: "Muktā... (liberated). Thus, when the mind is without an object [other than] the Lord, then it would have liberation as its support, since it is devoid of any connection with an object of meditation.

Because it is impossible for [the mind] to remain in the meditator, nor could there be, as before, an object such as sound that is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), since [the mind] is detached from that through the experience of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). Nor would it again take as its object that which is of the very nature of supreme bliss. This is indicated by the word "gradually" (*śanaiḥ*) in the phrase "it gradually detaches."
Furthermore, because it is to be separated from that [body], it therefore attains, that is, reaches, *nirvāṇa*.

The meaning is that just as the flame of a lamp goes out when separated from its oil and wick; in this state, when the mind has dissolved, the person—the individual soul—[attains liberation] due to the destruction of the covering in the form of the subtle body (*liṅga*).

He beholds the one, pure Self, the inner self (pratyag-ātman), without any intervention; and because of that, he does not transmigrate—as it is said: "he whose flow of the qualities (guṇa-pravāha) has turned back, [that is,] whose limiting adjuncts such as the body and so forth have ceased. (35)
He too, by this final cessation of the mind,
has come to rest in that majesty which is beyond pleasure and pain—
even that causality of the two sufferings which exists when there is no agent.
Having reached the ultimate limit of perceiving the self of others, one establishes it within one's own self.
"In the *Śabdanirṇaya*, it is said: 'The one who makes honey [sweet] is the individual soul (*jīva*), while the Supreme Lord is the maker.

Since their respective suffering and happiness are known to be difficult to endure, the Supreme Viṣṇu is the bestower; therefore, He bears names such as 'Dukha' (Suffering) and so forth. Thus it is stated in the *Harivaṃśa*. (36)

Śrīdhara: Nor does he transmigrate again as if having merely woken from sleep; thus he says: "He too—that very same person—is established (*avasita*) in that majesty which is the nature of Brahman, having attained its finality (*avasāna*) or culmination. By what means? By the ultimate withdrawal of the mind, which is free from ignorance. This is the distinction from deep sleep (*suṣupta*); for in that state...
Ignorance exists, but not now. The reason for this is that it has been eliminated by the practice of yoga; such is the meaning.
[Objection: Even so, if pleasure and pain are attributes of the self (*ātman-dharma*), how can there be identity with Brahman?
To this he says: that which was previously the causality and the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) with respect to the two sufferings—namely, pleasure and pain—[no longer exists].

Even that [action], though unreal, he performs through the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) created by ignorance; the meaning is that he perceives it as being grounded in that [Self] alone. For the sequence of stages—beginning with one who has realized the supreme Self and culminating in one who has directly realized the reality of the Self—has not been explained.

Viśvanātha says: "And he is that dissolution of limiting adjuncts (upādhilaya), as in the state of deep sleep. He explains: "He, that person—the individual soul (jīva)—by reason of the cessation of the mind, attains that majesty; for that majesty of his own which was previously forcibly carried away by the mind has now been reached through the destruction of the mind."

He has come to rest, that is, he has attained the final goal, in the essential nature of knowledge-bliss (*jñānānanda*). By what kind of mental withdrawal? By that which is "final," meaning devoid of ignorance; this is the distinction from deep sleep (*suṣupti*), for in that state ignorance exists, whereas it does not now. The reason for this is: "by this [withdrawal] produced through the practice of yoga"—this is the meaning. In that state...

In what kind of greatness [is this]? It is observed that pleasure and pain are indeed attributes of the self (ātman). Therefore, how can the self be something external to them? To this, he says: when the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)—the agent produced by ignorance—is absent, there is no causality for pleasure and pain.

The state of being the agent of actions that cause pleasure and pain arises from identification with those [states].
