However, this person— having reached the pinnacle of the Supreme Self, having directly realized the reality of the Self, and being the pure Puruṣa— establishes within that very [Self] all that agency and enjoyership which previously existed in his own self, once that [identification] has ceased.
The meaning is that he perceives [the world] as being fixed solely in That (Brahman), because of the absence of egoism within himself. ||36||
The perfected one, having realized his own true nature, does not regard that body— whether standing or risen— as real;
he sees it as something arrived by chance or departed by the power of fate.
Like one blinded by the intoxication of wine who has dressed himself in fine garments.

Śrīdhara: He has understood the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman according to their reality. He describes his liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) with two verses beginning with "the body" (*deham ca*): the perfected one (*siddha*), characterized as described above, does not even perceive the body; how much less pleasure and pain? Having risen from his seat and remaining right there...

One does not perceive that which has departed from its place, or even that which has returned there again by the power of destiny, because one has attained one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). Or rather, it refers to that body from which one attained one's true nature. An illustration for the non-recognition of something that still exists is provided: "a garment wrapped around," meaning encircled at the waist.
Whether standing or moving, one blinded by the intoxication of liquor does not see. ||37||

The sequential arrangement: having come to rest and attained finality within the majesty that constitutes his own true nature, he has realized the ultimate limit of the Supreme Self; thus it is said in the passage beginning with "he too, by this... and so forth. (37)

Viśvanātha: He describes his liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) with two verses beginning with "the body" (*deham ca*). "The final one" (*caramaḥ*) means one who has reached the final state; a perfected being (*siddha*) does not perceive the body, for how could there be pleasure or pain? "He attained" (*adhyagamat*) means he reached [that state]. "Set aside" (*parihṛtam*) means cast off; having risen from his seat, he rose up and remained right there.
Just as one blinded by the intoxication of liquor does not perceive whether something is standing still or moving. ||37||
Indeed, even the body, subject to destiny, remains with its life-breath as long as it observes its own originating karma;
one who has ascended to the yoga of samādhi perceives that [body] along with its manifold expansion.
But one who has awakened to reality no longer experiences the dream.

Śrīdhara: "Thus, one for whom the reality has been realized" refers to the passage beginning with "the body also," and so forth. Therefore, his experience of the mere *prārabdha* karma occurs precisely through non-attachment.
Thus it has been said: "What delusion, what grief can there be for one who perceives oneness? But then, [one might object]: [The text continues: ...If that is so, then...

How do the body's engagement in activity, its withdrawal from it, or even its continued life occur? To this he says: "The body too... *Daiva* refers to prior latent impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*). Under their influence, as long as the karma that initiated the body remains, it continues to persist—that is, it lives. "With breath" means possessing the senses. [Objection: But then, in that case, regarding that [body] once again...

Regarding the possibility of attachment there, he says: He does not again resort to that body—which is like a dream-body and so forth, accompanied by the phenomenal world (saprapañca) and including sons and others—and does not identify with it as "I" or "mine. This is because he has ascended to, or attained, yoga culminating in samādhi; therefore, he is one who has awakened to reality.
He by whom the reality of the self [is known]. ||38||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Now, one might ask: "In that case, how can his body remain alive? To this he says: "The body too...
By the power of *daiva*, which is prior latent impression (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), it moves; as long as it continues to perceive, it lives.
Thus [he is] with his vital breaths and his senses. But would there not be attachment to that once again?

To this he says: he does not resort again to that body along with its manifold extensions (prapañca) and accompanied by sons and so forth, because he does not identify with it as "I" or "mine," since it is like a dream-body and the like. The reason for this is: he has ascended [to a higher state].
He is one by whom yoga has reached its culmination in meditative absorption; therefore, he is one by whom the awakened reality, the true nature of the self, has been realized. ||38||
Just as a mortal is perceived as distinct from both his son and his wealth,
so too is the Person (puruṣa) distinct from the body and other such things, even though they are regarded as one's own self.

Śrīdhara says: He describes the manner of awakening through six verses, beginning with "yathā" (just as). [This occurs] even from a son or others who are regarded as one's own self due to the power of excessive affection. "Martya" refers to a father or similar relative; "puruṣa" refers to the witness of the body and so forth.
This sequence of composition is entirely appropriate for those who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), because:
He states that the referent of the word "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha) is exactly like that: "And as from a son... (verse 39).

Viśvanātha says: "For the sake of awakening, those seeking liberation should always contemplate in this way," and he explains this with three verses beginning with *yathā*. Just as a mortal father and so forth are perceived as distinct even from a son and others who are regarded as one's own self due to excessive affection, in that very same way is the individual soul (*puruṣa* or *jīva*). (39)

Just as fire is distinct from a firebrand, from a spark, or even from smoke— all of which are its own products and are themselves regarded as being of the nature of fire— so too is it distinct from that which is conceived as the self.
From the elements, the senses, the internal organ, and from that which is called the individual soul (jīva),
the Lord known as Brahman is likewise seen to be distinct as the Self.

Śrīdhara: Even though there is no separate existence [of the smoke], he states the distinction along with an illustration: "Just as from a firebrand, that is, from wood currently burning; 'from its own source,' meaning from the fire produced from it; and even from that which is considered to be the very nature of the fire, that is, its essential form—for one who is utterly lacking in discrimination has the misconception of fire even in the smoke."
Even from a fire-brand that has already been established, the fire which burns it and illuminates it is indeed distinct. ||40||

The meaning of the sequence of the text is as follows: the Seer is distinct from the elements (bhūta) and so forth; likewise, that which is designated as Brahman is distinct even from that which is designated as the individual soul (jīva); and similarly, the Blessed Lord who impels them is distinct even from primordial matter (pradhāna). He says "just as" because the referent of the word *tat* (That) is even more [distinct] than that. Now, regarding its...

He clarifies that the effect of the power of *māyā* and its distinctness from the individual souls (*jīvas*) is like sparks and smoke from a firebrand, by means of the two verses beginning with "Just as from a firebrand. This is the meaning: from a firebrand—which is its own source and material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), conditioned by a handful of wood—as the cause of fire, there arise both the sparks and the smoke.

Therefore, just as fire is distinct from its respective fuel, and just as that fuel is distinct from the fire-brand (ulmuka), so too is this fire distinct from that triad— however it may be conceived—
even from that which is regarded as its very self, since fire exists as a constituent part within the smoke by virtue of its nature as a burner.
Also from what is already known. ||40||

Likewise, from the individual soul (jīva) designated as the "spark," from the *pradhāna* which stands in the place of the firebrand— that is, from the splendor of the Lord conditioned by the *pradhāna*— and from the *bhūtādi* (the origin of the elements) which stands in the place of the smoke,
the Lord, who is the material cause of all, exists separately. He is that very Self who, by means of His own portion...

As the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of each respective thing, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) manifests in some qualified person as pure, undifferentiated consciousness (*nirviśeṣa-cinmātra*), and is designated as Brahman; for this very reason, He is the Seer who witnesses their initial, middle, and final states. In this regard, [the analogy of] the firebrand and so forth applies.

One must discern that within the fire, which has entered the fuel as its own constituent part, there is the quality of illumination belonging to its own essence and the quality of burning belonging to the portion that is the fuel. [Paramātmasandarbha 68] Viśvanātha: Now, just as a mortal exists as something distinct from his son, wealth, and so forth—

The individual self (jīvātman) is not perceived in that same way as being distinct from the body, the senses, and so forth. To the question of how the Supreme Self (paramātman) is to be understood as distinct from the individual self, he says: "Just as [the fire is distinct] from a firebrand.
Even though there is no separate spatial location, [the Supreme Self] is distinct from both Māyā and its effects, and from the individual self.

Regarding the point that the Supreme Self is indeed distinct [from the individual self], here is the illustration: it should be explained in this way because of the tautology between the words *yathā* and *ulmuka*. Just as fire becomes distinct from the burning wood (*ulmuka*), and just as it is distinct from the *ulmuka*, so too is the Supreme Self distinct.

Likewise, [it is] separate from the spark; and just as it is separate from the spark, so too it is separate from its own effect, the smoke. For by one who lacks discrimination, even that which is intended to be the nature of fire—by way of its being the self (ātmatva) or the essential form of fire—is conceived of as such: "This is a firebrand, this is a spark, and this is smoke; all these are fire. That which...

Or, the meaning of the second occurrence of the word *yathā* is "accordingly" (*yathāvat*). Regarding "from the second firebrand" (*dvitīyolmukāt*), the term "firebrand-eater" (*ulmukād*) is an epithet for fire, meaning that which consumes or causes to blaze. He applies this to the illustrative case (*dārṣṭāntika*): from the primary cause (*pradhāna*), which stands in the place of the firebrand, there arises that which is designated as the individual soul (*jīva-saṃjñita*), namely, that which is known by the name "individual soul" (*jīva-rūpaḥ saṃjñitaḥ*), [producing] consciousness (*saṃjñām cetanām*).

Therefore, from that which consists of the elements, the senses, and the internal organ— which stand in the place of sparks— the Self, who is the Supreme Self, stands apart like fire; for he is the Seer,
and as such he is indeed distinct from the seen, remaining unattached even while dwelling together with it, since the Blessed Lord possesses inconceivable sovereignty.
The meaning is that the Blessed One alone has attained the designation "Brahman," and he appears as non-differentiated pure consciousness to a certain qualified person. ||4041||
One should perceive oneself in all beings and all beings in oneself,
through a state of non-duality, just as one perceives the identity of those beings with that [Self].
*Madhvaḥ*: [This refers to] through non-dual devotion (*ananyabhāvena*) and the non-distinction (*abhedena*) from those forms;
[it denotes] her state of being that very self (*tadātmatām*) and her agency as the giver of gifts (*dānādikartṛtvam*) regarding the realm of beings (*bhūtaviṣaye*). ||42||
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.

Kramasaṃdarbha: Regarding that, he says—in three verses beginning with "all"—that the man of knowledge (jñānī) should perceive the referent of the word *tat* (the Supreme Reality) as non-different from the referent of the word *tvam* (the individual self). ||42||

Viśvanātha: Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self as distinct from all [else], one should perceive His state as the cause and the locus of dissolution of all things; thus he says, "In all beings.
The meaning is that the cause itself assumes the nature of the effect, since the effects also have their locus of dissolution therein.
He states that [it] has the nature of being a cause with the words "all," etc. "That nature" means the nature of the great elements. ||42||
Just as a single light is perceived as manifold within its various sources due to the inequality of the qualities of those sources, so too does the Self abide within primordial nature (prakṛti).
Śrīdhara:
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: The perception of multiplicity arises because the Supreme Self resides within each individual body.

And he says that the cognition of "auspicious," "inauspicious," and so forth is not real: "Just as fire, which is light, [appears] in its own sources, the pieces of wood, due to an inequality of qualities—through distinctions such as length, shortness, curvature, straightness, smell, color, and so on—so too does the Self, the Supreme Self, appear in the body, which is primordial matter (prakṛti). (43)
Therefore, having overcome this divine nature of his own, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent and is difficult to discern, he abides in his true form.

Śrīdhara: Having overcome the divine power (*daivī śakti*) of the Lord Viṣṇu—which is the cause of bondage for the individual soul (*jīva*), who is His own partial manifestation (*aṃśa*)—and having conquered it solely by His grace, he abides in his true nature as Brahman. The sequence of the composition is as follows: "he abides" means he is absorbed into Brahman. ||44||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, since it is Prakṛti alone that causes harm by manifesting multiplicity, one should conquer her; thus he says—"one's own," meaning one's own adjunct (upādhi). "Divine" means consisting of karma. Or else, having overcome the power of the Lord Viṣṇu, which is difficult to conceive and difficult to transcend.
"Indeed, this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the *guṇas*, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion.
By means of these very words of the Blessed One, having conquered [the illusion], one abides in one's own nature as the form of unobscured consciousness.
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
the twenty-seventh [chapter] of the third [section], which is perfectly suited to the virtuous, has been completed.
Thus, in the glorious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, in the commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*, in the *Pāramahaṃsyasaṃhitā* of Vyāsa’s collection, in the third book (*skandha*),
within the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya concerning Kapila.
The twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Performance of the Sadhana.
The twenty-ninth chapter.
In the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, concerning the son of Kapila, Devahūti spoke regarding the characteristics of the Mahat-tattva and the others, as well as of Prakṛti and Puruṣa:
"Devahūti said: [Tell me] the characteristics of the Mahat and the rest, of Prakṛti, and of Puruṣa."
That by which their true nature is characterized is the ultimate reality.
O Lord, tell me in detail the path of the yoga of devotion, which you declare to be the root as it is taught among the Sāṅkhyas.
Madhva: It has been explained in the same manner as it is established among the Sāṅkhyas; that which is the root of Sāṅkhya, they declare to be its defining characteristic. (2)
Śrīdhara:
In the twenty-ninth [chapter], the yoga of devotion is indeed described in many ways;
furthermore, the power of time and the terrible cycle of worldly existence are taught for the sake of detachment.
Having first restated what has been said, he asks about the divisions of the path of devotion (bhakti-mārga) with two verses:

"The definition of the mahat-tattva and the others has been told just as it is in the Sāṅkhya systems. By which definition? The meaning is that it is ultimately real and mutually distinct. That which is the root of bhakti-yoga...
That which is the root of whatever has a purpose has been stated. Tell me in detail the path—that is, the method—of that yoga of devotion. ||12||
The sequence of composition: the definition consists of this pair of verses. That [definition] is the exposition of the principles beginning with Mahat;
they declare it to be such that devotion (bhaktiyoga) alone is its root and its intended goal. ||12||
Viśvanātha:
In the twenty-ninth [chapter], the manifestation of states—both with and without qualities—is observed;
therein lies the sequence of honor accorded to living beings and the power of time.

Having heard of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, and wishing to hear again— after first restating what has already been said— the Yoga of Bhakti with its divisions as something to be personally practiced, she asks: "The characteristics of Mahat and the other principles have been explained in the Sāṅkhyas, that is, in the Sāṅkhya scriptures, according to their respective definitions."

The true nature (*svarūpa*) of these [principles], beginning with Mahat, is indicated—that is, known—as being established. Of what kind? It means it is ultimately real and mutually distinct. That knowledge of their true nature is said to be the root, that is, the cause; for without it, their nature remains unknown even if it has been intellectually grasped.
The meaning is that it becomes thus. Tell me the path—that is, the method—of that application of the verb *bhavati*. ||12||
O Blessed One, tell me of that dispassion by which a person may become free from everything,
and explain to me the various transmigrations of the world of living beings.
Śrīdhara: By which narrative of the cycles of existence one may become free from passion. ||3||
The sequential arrangement: "detachment" constitutes a pair of verses. ||3||

Viśvanātha: Since some degree of detachment (*vairāgya*) is required for entry into the practice of the state of being (*bhāvakṛti*), he asks about that [detachment] with the words "dispassion" (*virāga*). Explain those cycles of transmigration (*saṃsṛti*) by means of this narrative of transmigration. ||3||
Alas, for the sake of which people perform wholesome deeds, you cause Time— whose form is that of the Lord— and others who are supreme, to assume their true nature.

Śrīdhara: [It refers to] you, who possess the form of the Lord, who are of great power, and who are identical with the self; because of whom—that is, out of fear of whom—people perform wholesome, meritorious deeds. ||4||
The sequence of composition: explain the essential nature of time. ||4||
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, describe the true nature of Time, which is Your own form; for it is because of that, out of fear of Time, [that You have come]. ||5||
For the world, which possesses false conceptions, lacks the eye of wisdom, has long been asleep in darkness without refuge,
and is exhausted by a mind permeated by karmic actions—
You indeed appeared as the sun of yoga.

Śrīdhara: [For the sake] of the world which is sightless and ignorant; therefore, whose self-conceit (*ahaṅkāra*) consists of attachment to the body and so forth which are illusory; therefore, exhausted by an intellect (*dhiyā*) permeated by attachment toward ritual acts (*karmasu*); and for that very reason, long asleep in the shoreless darkness of *saṃsāra* which offers no refuge—you [are here] for its awakening.
You have indeed manifested as Bhāskara, the illuminator of yoga. ||5||
The composition of the sequence: the meaning is that he is the sun of yoga, the supreme illuminator. ||5||

Viśvanātha: [He is the Lord] for the sake of removing the dullness of pride born from the world's false conceit; for the sake of bestowing the eye upon the sightless; for the sake of destroying the darkness of sleep in the world for one who is slumbering in *saṃsāra*;
and for the sake of drying up the puddle of fatigue for one exhausted by a mind attached to ritual actions (*karma*).
Yogabhāskara is the sun that illuminates the lotus of the yoga of devotion, action, and knowledge. ||5||
Maitreya said:
Having thus welcomed his mother’s gentle words, the great sage,
O best of the Kurus, being pleased yet moved by compassion, spoke to her.
Śrīdhara: "Ślakṣṇam" means beautiful. ||6||

The sequence of composition: [He] rejoices, being pleased by the excellence of the question because it arises from the knowledge of the greatness of devotion; however, compassion arises from [the devotee's] wretchedness. 6.
Viśvanātha: [This has] not been explained. The Blessed Lord said:
"O beautiful lady, the yoga of devotion is cultivated in many ways through various paths."
The disposition of men is differentiated by way of their inherent nature, qualities, and conduct.

Śrīdhara: By "ways" (mārgaiḥ), he means specific modes. He explains those very ways: by the way of the qualities (guṇas) that constitute one's own nature, that is, through the distinction of their functioning (vṛtti). "State" (bhāvaḥ) means intention (abhiprāyaḥ). The meaning is that there is a distinction in devotion (bhakti-bheda) due to the distinction in the mental resolve regarding the fruit.

The structural arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Devotion (*bhakti*), which has no other cause and is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇā*), is nevertheless manifold due to its different modes of activity (*vṛttibheda*). Thus he says: "by means of paths," that is, by specific types of ways; for it is through the path of one's own *bhaktiyoga* itself, by means of its different modes of activity such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, that there arises the state of being (*bhāva*), which is to say, self-identification (*abhimāna*). Through that differentiation...

Indeed, by means of qualities such as servitude and so forth, and by distinctions such as the darkness (tamas) and other modes, as well as through acts like violence, the disposition—that is, the intention—of persons is differentiated. A specific detail regarding this is to be seen in the *Bhaktisandarbha*.
[In this regard, the *Muktāphala-ṭīkā* states: "This is ultimate, because beyond it there is no other mode."]

This very [path] is designated as *bhaktiyoga*. This is because the word *bhakti* has its primary meaning here alone; such devotion (*anurāga*) is directed toward other fruits, but not toward Viṣṇu when there is an absence of fruit, for that would result in the abandonment of devotion. And in the *Śrīgopālatāpanī-śruti*: "Devotion (*bhakti*) is his worship (*bhajana*)."
Thus, here, the mental construction of that [Self] as being free from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) pertaining to this world and the next is itself "niṣkarmya" (freedom from action). Regarding this,
the distinction between the path of one's own nature and the path of existence arises for the wise through incidental application, as stated in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.25.
This has been shown by the passage beginning with "ity ādinā" and ending with "yeṣām ahaṃ priya ātmā" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.38).

Here, the term *bhāvinī* means a person endowed with *bhāva*. [From the Bhaktisandarbha, Viśvanātha: By the verse "devānāṃ guṇaliṅgānāṃ" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.32), [the state of being] beyond the modes (*nirguṇā*)...]
Since the nature of devotion (*bhāva-kṛti*) has already been mentioned, [the author] here first states [the verse] to define devotion with attributes (*saguṇa-bhāva-kṛti*):

"O beautiful lady, *bhakti-yoga* alone is *bhāva*, meaning intention; in a person possessing that [intention], it is manifested, contemplated, and known in many ways through various paths or specific modes. And that—

The state [of devotion] is differentiated— that is, it becomes manifold and possessed of various distinctions— by way of the path, which is the specific mode of activity of those qualities such as darkness (*tamas*) that have become its very nature. Although devotion is by its essential nature devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), when it is colored by the innate qualities such as darkness belonging to persons, it becomes "with qualities" (*saguṇa*) through names such as "darkness" and so forth.
The state of being. ||7||
For he who, with intent toward violence, hypocrisy, or even envy, being impulsive and possessed of divided vision, directs his disposition toward me— he is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).

Śrīdhara: "Abhisandhāya" means having formed a resolve. "Saṃrambhī" means prone to anger. "Bhinnadṛk" means one who perceives duality. Whoever performs devotion (bhāva) [with these traits], even if it be of three kinds, is characterized by tamas. ||8||

The Sequential Composition (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, those who have established themselves in their own essential nature alone (*kevalasvarūpasiddhāḥ*) are illustrated. Among them, the one with desire (*sakāmā*) and the one desiring liberation (*kaivalyakāmā*) are figuratively designated as possessing various qualities according to the qualities of the devotee’s resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

Therein, the one with desire is of two kinds: *tāmasī* (of the nature of darkness) and *rājasī* (of the nature of passion). Of these, for the former, [the path is] by way of the path of qualities (*guṇamārga*).
He states the distinction with three verses beginning with "abhi": having formed an intention (*abhisandhāya*) or made a resolve, one who is full of agitation (*saṃrambhī*), meaning full of anger;

one whose vision is divided (*bhinnadṛk*), meaning one who perceives pleasure and pain everywhere as if they were his own; and one who is merciless (*niranukampa*)—this is the implied meaning. Here, the term "full of agitation" (*saṃrambhī*) should be understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for greed and the other [afflictions]. ||8||

Viśvanātha: First, defining the tamasic mode of mental activity (*bhāvakṛti*), and considering the impropriety of stating that "the tamasic mental activity would be [the agent]," he says: "The person possessing that [activity] is indeed designated by terms such as 'tamasic' and so forth.
[He explains: "Having intended—that is, having formed a resolve; being *saṃraṃbhī*, meaning full of anger; and having a divided vision (*bhinnadṛk*)."
One who perceives duality does not see that pleasure and pain are the same in others as they are in oneself;

thus, the meaning is that such a person is devoid of compassion. Whoever would direct a state of being—that is, an attitude—toward Me is of three kinds and is characterized by *tamas*. The threefold nature of this *tāmasa* state of being has been clearly stated.
In the *Bṛhannāradīya*:
"O protector of the former distinction, he who worships Hari with faith for the sake of destroying another becomes the lowest among those characterized by tamas, like a fruit-bearing [tree]."
She who worships Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, with a deceitful mind— just as an unchaste woman treats her own husband— is a mediocre person of tamasic nature.
"O protector of the earth, hear now: when one sees those devoted to the worship of other gods and worships Hari out of rivalry, that devotion is the highest form of *tāmasa*.
Thus, the threefold nature of the performance of devotion—whether *rājasa* or *sāttvika*—should be understood. [Nārada Purāṇa 1.15.1402] ||8||
He who, with a sense of duality, worships me in an image or other such forms while aiming for sense objects, fame, or power, possesses a rajasic disposition.
Madhva: The distinctness of those forms. ||9||
Śrīdhara: "Pṛthagbhāva" means one who perceives difference. ||9||

The sequence of composition: "As for the latter [verse], it is as follows: 'viṣayān... Viśvanātha has shown that this indicates the cause of rajasic nature (rājasattva), namely: "He whose disposition (bhāva)—that is, longing (spṛhā)—is directed separately from me toward objects and the like, and not toward me. He whose disposition is elsewhere, apart from me, specifically toward objects and so forth.
Whether performed with a view toward the accomplishment of karma, or its dedication to another,
or with the thought "one should sacrifice," such a sense of separateness is sattvic.
"Non-separation from the Madhu [the Lord] is that which is characterized by *sattva*.

An ignorant person should worship in the form of the divine image; otherwise, he becomes possessed of fault. But one who knows, while worshipping, remains endowed with virtue and does not become possessed of fault. Thus it is stated in the *Kāpileya*. (10)
Śrīdhara: *Karmanirhāram* means the destruction of evil. *Parasmin* refers to the Supreme Lord.

*Tadarpaṇam* means the dedication of action; the meaning is "with the aim of pleasing the Blessed One. *Yaṣṭavyam* means with the aim of fulfilling the injunction; the meaning is "one must sacrifice. The perception of duality and the worship of an image and so forth [are prohibited] in all three cases.
The same applies to the other types as well. Thus, there are three sub-divisions each within the *tāmasī* and other forms of devotion;

among these, each subsequent type is superior. In this way, each of the nine practices—such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), chanting (*kīrtana*), and so forth—possesses nine further subdivisions. Consequently, qualified (*saguṇā*) devotion consists of eighty-one varieties. ||10||
The sequential arrangement: Now, she who desires isolation (*kaivalya*) is indeed of the *sāttvika* nature.

As it is said: "With a view toward the removal of karma"—that is, aiming for liberation (*mokṣa*). She is either one who offers all actions to the Supreme Lord, or one who [realizes] that He is the one to be worshipped by all.

One who worships the Supreme Lord with the thought that "this worship must certainly be performed because it is established as a daily obligation," rather than through the knowledge of the true nature of devotion— precisely for this reason, as before, there remains a state of separation; such a person conceives of liberation alone as the human goal, distinct from devotion.
He is called *sāttvika*. The intention of the subsequent [verse] is also that the purpose should be solely the exhaustion of karma (*karmanirhāra*).

And it has been said: "The *sāttvika* agent is unattached" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.25.25), "Isolation (*kaivalya*) is *sāttvika* knowledge" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.25.23), and "*Sāttvika* happiness arises from the Self."
[From Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.25.28] Thus, both the means and the goal achieved thereby possess qualities (*saguṇatva*).
The illustrative example here is the latter half of the verse alone: "one should sacrifice.
[Bhaktisandarbha 233] Viśvanātha: He who would sacrifice with the aim of *karmanirhāra*, that is, the destruction of karma, by means of which devotion...
The meaning is that the sole purpose is indeed the exhaustion of karma. "Offering that to the Supreme Lord" means the offering of that action;

the sense is that one should perform sacrifice in such a way that it becomes an offering of one's own duty—that is, one should practice devotion consisting primarily of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth.
It must be sacrificed to by all, for it is necessarily to be performed because it is established as a constant injunction (*nityavidhi*),

just like the duties of one's own stage of life (*svāśramakarma*). Therefore, he who sacrifices with the very understanding that "this sacrifice is [like] the performance of the duties of one's own stage of life," [performs it] as a separate state— that is, as something distinct from devotion.

One whose disposition or intention is directed toward liberation is [a *sakāma* devotee]. Thus, this ninefold devotion with desire (*sakāmā*) should be understood according to its progressive superiority. Among these, *sāttvikī* devotion generates knowledge in someone; even there, depending on whether knowledge is subordinate or primary, it is designated as "peace" (*śānti*) or "joy" (*rati*).

It produces [devotion] that is indeed devoid of qualities (*nirguṇā*). When knowledge is predominant, devotion— which is itself a subordinate limb of that knowledge— leads only to liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*) for someone who offers fruitful actions such as the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), and not to liberation through co-residence (*sālokya-mokṣa*) consisting of pleasure and sovereignty, which consists of the offering of ritual action.
However, the peace found in the surrender of fruitless action belongs to that devotion which is *rājasa* or *tāmasa*;
when the attainment of the [expected] fruit occurs, yet there is an absence of true devotion, generally that very fruit is the result,
though through the majesty of devotion it may be slightly superior even when the fruit is attained by someone.

However, regarding the reality of devotion, one should understand that even she (the Goddess) becomes devoid of qualities (nirguṇā) in due time, according to such scriptural views as: "When entreated by men, She truly grants their desired object" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.19.28). ||10||
Merely by hearing of my qualities, the movement of the mind toward me, who dwell in the secret cave of all, becomes uninterrupted, just as the waters of the Gaṅgā flow unceasingly into the ocean.
The characteristic of devotion-yoga that is beyond the gunas has indeed been declared:
it is that devotion to the Supreme Person which is causeless and uninterrupted.

Śrīdhara: Devotion devoid of qualities (*nirguṇā bhakti*) is indeed of only one kind; he describes it with these two verses beginning with "merely by hearing of My qualities. That devotion which consists of the mind's orientation toward Me, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), merely by hearing of My qualities—that is the yoga of devotion devoid of qualities.

The connection [of the words] is "the characteristic. "Uninterrupted" means continuous. "Characteristic" means essential nature (*svarūpa*). "Causeless" means devoid of seeking a result. And "unimpeded" means free from the perception of duality. ||1112||

The Sequential Arrangement: Now, that very [form of devotion] for the sake of which these various types of devotion were described in order to understand its excellence—that which is free from desire (*niṣkāma*), devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), absolute (*kevala*), established in its own nature (*svarūpasiddhā*)—is now being described. This alone was previously mentioned as being at the summit of all, under the name "possessing nothing" (*akiñcana*). That [devotion]...

He says [the answer] with the pair of verses beginning with "By the mere hearing of my qualities" (*madguṇa*): not, however, with the intention of establishing another subject therein. He who lies within the cave—the cave being the state beyond the reach of all the instruments composed of material qualities (*prākṛta*)—dwells there in secrecy and in immobility.
In that [state], my mental movement—which is uninterrupted and impossible to be checked by another object—is what is meant.

Regarding its uninterruptedness, "as" serves as the illustration. The word "movement" (gati) is drawn over from the preceding [verse], because it is required there. "Characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) means the essential nature (svarūpa).

But what is to be made of that scriptural mention of its qualities? For it cannot be designated in either of two ways: because there is no other object to be aimed at (*uddeśya*), and because it lacks the nature of a mental modification (*manogati*). To this he says: "causeless" (*ahaitukī*), meaning devoid of any expectation of fruit;

"uninterrupted" (*avyavahitā*), meaning directly manifest by virtue of being established as one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-siddhatva*), and not established through superimposition (*āropa-siddhatva*).

It is of the nature of separation. Such devotion is merely service by means of the ears and other senses, and that is its essential form—this is the meaning. By the word "merely" (*mātra*) and by the phrase "uninterrupted," it is established that the movement of the mind is causeless and so forth; therefore, there is no need for a separate application [of effort], as it is unfit for such. The agent is *sāttvika* and unattached.

In passages such as these, by statements like "I am devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and have me as my refuge" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.25.25), the quality-less nature of the activities and other attributes dependent upon Him is established:
"All the qualities worship Me, who am devoid of qualities and independent."

And because it is heard in this passage—“Friendliness, love for the self, equanimity, non-attachment, and so forth are not qualities [of the material world]” (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.13.40)—that even those qualities are non-material (*aprākṛta*). ||1112||

Viśvanātha: Having already defined "disinterested devotion" (*nirguṇā bhakti*) in the passage, "Of the gods whose marks are the qualities" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.25.32), he defines it once more for the sake of easy understanding:
"Merely by hearing of my qualities, in Me alone who dwells in the secret cave of all..."

Because it abides within the entire internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the movement of the mind becomes uninterrupted toward the form of Śrī Puruṣottama, which is easy to meditate upon; just as the flow of the Gaṅgā’s waters is uninterrupted in the ocean,
this is the established meaning for which the definition of *bhaktiyoga* has been set forth.
Just as water, even when turned back by its own waves by the ocean, has its course only toward the ocean,

so too, even though one is enticed by fruits such as *pārameṣṭhya*, *sārṣṭi*, and *sālokya*, their course is toward me alone. And thus, for those whose minds are devoted, there is this analogy with the water of the Gaṅgā.

The qualities of swiftness, coolness, purity, being worshiped by the world, and so forth have been mentioned. In response to the inquiry as to what the definition of that very [devotion] is, he says: "It is causeless"—that is, devoid of a cause, which is to say, devoid of any expectation of a further fruit; and because it is self-luminous and its own nature is the fruit itself, it is not like the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*) and the like.

This is the intended meaning. However, because the love for the company of the saintly (*sādhusaṅgaprema*) belongs to the first and twelfth stages (*bhūmi*), its status as cause and effect does not exist in reality; this has already been explained in the First Book (*Prathama-skandha*). The meaning is that devotion (*bhakti*) which is "uninterrupted"—that is, devoid of the intervention of knowledge, ritual action, and so forth—is itself "beyond the qualities" (*nirguṇā*). Of devotion...

That even the happiness of dwelling in the abode of faith and so forth is devoid of the modes of nature is to be understood from the Eleventh Canto of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, which states: "My refuge is devoid of the modes" (11.25.25), "But in service to Me, one is devoid of the modes" (11.25.27), and "My refuge is devoid of the modes" (11.25.29).
People do not accept even the granting of residence in the same world (sālokya), equal power (sārṣṭi), proximity (sāmīpya), similarity of form (sārūpya), or oneness (ekatva), without my service.

Śrīdhara: By the logic of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so"), he states the desirelessness of devotees: *sālokya* is dwelling with me in the same world; *sārṣṭi* is equal sovereignty; *sāmīpya* is being in close proximity;
*sārūpya* is having an identical form; and *ekatva* is *sāyujya* (union). Even these, though being offered, [they do not desire].

They do not accept it; what then is the point of my desire? This is the meaning. Regarding the sequence of the composition: he specifically demonstrates its causeless nature with the words "sālokya" and so on. People who belong to me do not accept even *sālokya* and other such states, nor indeed even when they are being offered, rather they accept service to me (*matsevana*).
He disciplines them. If they do indeed accept [the teaching], then they accept it solely for the sake of serving me, and not for its own sake;

this is the meaning. *Sārṣṭi* means equal sovereignty. *Ekātva* means union with the Blessed One (*bhagavat-sāyujya*) and union with Brahman (*brahma-sāyujya*). Because these two consist in being absorbed into that [Brahman], they lack the purpose of serving it.
The intended meaning is that non-apprehension itself is necessary. ||13||

Viśvanātha: Clarifying the meaning suggested by the analogy—that the Ganges water finds its course in the ocean—he states, by way of the principle of *kaimutya* (the "how much more so" argument), the selflessness of people who possess devotion as defined above: *sālokyam*, which means dwelling with me in the same world; *sārṣṭim*.
*Samānaiśvarya* is equality in sovereignty; *sāmīpya* is proximity; *sārūpya* is similarity of form;

*ekatva* is union (*sāyujya*). The sense is: "Even when these are being offered, they do not accept them—how much less could there be a desire for them? Some say that if they were to accept them, it would be solely for the purpose of my service (*matsevārtha*), provided they do not [otherwise] engage in my service.
The meaning is "they grasp. ||13||
That very yoga, called the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga), is declared to be ultimate;
by means of it, having transcended the three qualities (guṇas), one attains to My own state of being.
Śrīdhara: Why, then, do they worship [Him]? He says, "He alone," because devotion itself is the supreme fruit.
Now, it is well known that the attainment of Brahman, having abandoned the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), is the supreme fruit.
True; however, that is merely incidental to devotion. Thus he says: "by which yoga of devotion."
For my state, for the state of Brahman. ||14||

The sequential arrangement: therefore, that very state, by virtue of being the ultimate fruit, constitutes liberation (*apavarga*); this is the meaning. This is because of such passages as "They do not reckon it as ultimate" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.48), and because it is well-known as the ultimate dissolution.
Regarding this, the *Muktāphala-ṭīkā* states: "This [state] is absolute, because there is no other mode beyond it.

This alone is designated as *bhaktiyoga*. For the word *bhakti* has its primary meaning precisely here, in accordance with its etymological sense (*anvartha*); whereas in other cases, there is attachment only to the fruit, and not to Viṣṇu upon the attainment of that fruit."
This is [the meaning of] "through the renunciation of attachment.

And in the *Śrīgopālatāpanī-śruti*: "Devotion (bhakti) is the worship of Him; it is the fixing of the mind upon Him alone, through a state of detachment from the conditions of this world and the next. This indeed is freedom from ritual action (*naiṣkarmya*)."

Thus [it is said in] the *Goṭā-u.* (1.14). In the *Śatapatha-śruti*: "Yājñavalkya said: 'Therefore, a person should worship Hari with love for the sake of his own welfare. The meaning is: "with love" means with the desire for mere affection; that which is for one's own welfare—for that purpose.

If it is argued that liberation (*apavarga*) is indeed the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Lord preceded by the transcendence of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), [the author] replies with the words "by which" (*yena*), because even for that [realization], such a nature is established by its very essence.
"By which" means by that which is never to be abandoned; "for my being" (*bhāvāya*) means for my existence, that is, for the sake of direct realization.

One becomes capable and attains success; as stated in the fifth [chapter], "Just as there is the prescription of colors and liberation" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.19.19), and "He who [is devoted] to the Blessed One" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.19.20),
and so forth— this is characterized by the yoga of devotion that has no other cause.
"...the knot of ignorance regarding the signs of various states of existence, by means of the door of blindness" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.19.20), up to that point.
Therefore, although she is devoid of qualities (nirguṇā), she must be understood as being manifold. This has been stated at the beginning of this section:

"O beautiful lady, the yoga of devotion is cultivated in many ways through various paths; the disposition of men differs according to the path of their own inherent nature and qualities. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.29.7).
Here, "path" refers to specific modes. Therefore, one should proceed by the path of one's own particular yoga of devotion.

The meaning is that by means of the different modes of activity—such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—the disposition (*bhāva*) characterized by self-identification [with the Lord] is differentiated; by that differentiation, through [modes such as] servitude and so forth, the qualities such as *tamas* and the rest are differentiated; and by that further differentiation, through acts such as violence and so forth, the dispositions or intentions (*abhiprāya*) of men become manifold.
[Bhaktisandarbha 234]

Viśvanātha: Why, then, do they worship? He says "that very [state]" because devotion itself is the supreme fruit. "Ātyantika" means that which exists at the absolute end (atyanta), at the conclusion of all things. Now, one might ask: is not the word "ātyantika" used to denote *sāyujya* (union)? To this he replies: "Named bhaktiyoga"—this is called bhaktiyoga, and it is even superior to that.

The meaning is "an additional fruit. For this very reason, this is sometimes expressed by the word *apavarga* (liberation) and sometimes by the word *nirvāṇa* with respect to Brahman. As it is said in the fifth [skandha]: "And liberation also occurs... which consists of the yoga of devotion directed toward the Blessed One alone, having no other cause" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.19.21].

Thus [it is said]. And in the seventh [book], in the passage beginning with "The attainment of Adhokṣaja here," it says: "The wise know that to be the bliss of the liberation of Brahman" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.7.37), and in another Purāṇa: "The wise say that exclusive devotion to Hari is liberation. Devotion (*bhakti*) is the act of worshipping Him (*asya bhajanam*). That...

The mental construction of that [Self] occurs precisely through the absence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) pertaining to this world or the next; and the Gopālatāpanī Śruti also states: "This alone is freedom from action" (Goṭā.U.
1.14). Now, it may be argued that liberation from bondage consisting of the three guṇas is universally recognized as the supreme fruit. True.
But he says that this [crossing] is incidental to devotion (bhakti): "by which yoga of devotion," meaning by having transcended, surpassed, or gone beyond;
for when the ocean of saṃsāra consisting of the three guṇas becomes like a cow's footprint merely by taking refuge in My feet, its crossing occurs.

The meaning is that [this] occurs even without formal inquiry. By means of one's own great dharma, practiced as a causeless [duty] for the sake of attaining my nature— that is, for love directed toward me—
and by means of the highly praised *kriyā-yoga*, which is perpetually free from excessive violence.

Śrīdhara: He states the means for such devotion with five [verses]. "By that which is well-cultivated" means by that which is properly performed. "By self-duty without motive" means by the obligatory and occasional duties. "By the most exalted" means by that endowed with faith and other qualities. "By the yoga of action" means by the mode of worship described in the *Pañcarātra* and other scriptures.
By one who is praised and free from desire. ||15||
The sequential arrangement: an example of the mixture of action and knowledge is the pentad beginning with "by that which is practiced.
By one's own duty (*svadharma*) which is practiced—that is, properly performed—and which is motiveless (*animitta*), being free from desire;
by that which is most exalted and endowed with faith and other virtues; by the yoga of action (*kriyāyoga*).

By means of the Vaiṣṇava practice prescribed in the *Pañcarātra* and other scriptures; which is "praiseworthy," meaning it possesses an excellent place, time, and so forth, and is performed without desire; and which is "not excessively harmful," meaning it is devoid of extreme violence. The word "excessive" (*ati*) refers to the avoidance of injury to life-force and the like, while the inclusion of leaves and such for the sake of obtaining fruit implies the acceptance of parts of living beings. (15)

Viśvanātha: He states the limbs of this "creation of bhāva" (bhāvakṛti): "And that which has been practiced, being of a causeless nature"—thereby, one's own dharma (svadharma) is that which has been practiced and accepted by those who preceded him through their pure creations of bhāva.

The meaning is "by that. And that [purification] should be understood as consisting solely of the procedures for purifying substances such as the body, clothing, and vessels by means of earth, water, and so forth, as prescribed by the authorities of the Smṛti scriptures, and being devoid of mantras;
for it is excellent because it is suitable for the performance of acts such as worship (*arcanā*) and the like. According to another interpretation: "for my sake."

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Lord’s own statements, such as "those who have abandoned their duties" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.22) and "having abandoned even their own [duties] as enjoined by Me" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.11.32), as well as the futility of the term "niṣevita-pada" (the state of being served/attained) in this context, [if it were not attained] through *kriyā-yoga*.
By means of the method of worship taught in the *Pañcarātra* and other scriptures; by that which is "praiseworthy," meaning possessing an excellent location and so forth;

and by that which is "not excessively harmful," meaning free from extreme violence—the word "excessively" (*ati*) here refers to [the avoidance of] cleaning and plastering the temple of the Blessed One for such purposes.

It was made known that there is no fault even in the subtle injury to living beings— which is extremely difficult to prevent and difficult to perceive— occurring during the performance of rituals such as the offering of various *naivedya* foods on the *nāḍī* lines,
nor even in the plucking of vegetable leaves, roots, fruits, and the like; this was taught through the quality of goodness (*sattva*).

Through fortitude, non-attachment, and the abandonment of harmful association; and by hearing of the defects and virtues of the internal state of the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), one must necessarily listen to its defects and virtues in order to direct the inner organ toward the performance of virtuous states— [specifically] regarding the defect of the teeth and so forth within one's own inner organ.

And this is also for the purpose that, once there is knowledge of its present existence, people might engage in the performance of duties prescribed in injunctions such as "one should conquer the great [ego] through worship," thinking, "for a person whose duty is precisely the hearing, chanting, and so forth concerning Me, that very dharma is to be practiced. For such a person, the dharma consisting of hearing, glorifying, and so on regarding Me alone is what must be performed.

The mind is the substratum. The meaning is that [the soul] attains the state of being one whose nature is endowed with the yoga of devotion—the goal characterized as described above—by the mere hearing of my qualities, according to the thought: "He approaches me, who possesses the quality of having heard [my teachings]. ||1519||
Through beholding, touching, worshipping, praising, and saluting my abodes;
through the contemplation of me within all beings; and through goodness and non-attachment.

Śrīdhara: [One should worship] my abode, such as my image and so forth, through seeing it and other such acts, with goodness (*sattva*), with fortitude (*dhairya*), and with non-attachment (*asaṅgama*), that is, with dispassion (*vairāgya*). ||16||
*The Sequence of Arrangement*: "My abode, my image, and so forth" (Bhaktisandarbha 229).
Viśvanātha: The commentary on the fifteenth verse of the *Sāṅkhyaka-śloka* should be consulted.
Through great respect for the great, compassion for the wretched,
and friendliness toward those equal to oneself, as well as through self-restraint and observance of rules;
Śrīdhara: Not explained.
Kramasaṃdarbha: Non-violence, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*.
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the *niyamas*. (17)
Viśvanātha: The commentary on the fifteenth verse of the Sāṅkhya should be consulted.
Through internal listening, through the chanting of my name,
as well as through straightforwardness, association with the noble ones, and likewise through the absence of egoism.
Śrīdhara: By "ārjava" is meant "akauṭilya," that is, by straightforwardness and the absence of crookedness. ||18||

The sequence of composition: the spiritual self, the scripture for the discernment of the self, through *nirahaṅkriyā*, that is, by means of freedom from pride. [Bhaktisandarbha 229] Viśvanātha: The commentary on the *Sāṅkhyakārikā* should be consulted.
A person whose disposition is completely purified by these qualities of my dharma quickly attains me, whose nature is known through mere hearing.

Śrīdhara: The disposition—that is, the mind—of a person who follows my dharma, one who practices the dharma of the Blessed Lord; the sequential arrangement: "the disposition of a person who follows my dharma, who practices my dharma.
"He approaches me directly, possessing only the quality of having heard [of me]" means that by the mere hearing of my qualities, he approaches me [Bhāgavata Purāṇa].
The meaning is that one attains *dhruvānusmṛti*, characterized by the descriptions beginning with [3.29.11].

Here, there is also a mixture with knowledge (*jñāna*) through internal hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth. Although pure devotion (*śuddhabhakti*) is the goal (*sādhya*) here, the reason for its presentation as a means consisting of devotion mixed with knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-miśra-bhakti*) is as follows: [the following is the root of that].

They declare thus, in accordance with the questions of Śrī Devahūtī. [Although devotion is the goal to be accomplished, it is shown that its means consist precisely of devotion mixed with knowledge and action; moreover, that which was asked by her in that manner is also indicated as being rooted in devotion. As for their own view, however, it is that of the virtuous.

In the context beginning with *prasaṅgāt* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.25), this very means for attaining pure devotion has been demonstrated. However, it should be understood that she asked thus because of an extraordinary eagerness to hear the path of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). (19) [Bhaktisandarbha 229]
Viśvanātha: See the commentary on the fifteenth verse of the Sāṅkhyakārikā.
Just as the wind-vehicle carries away the scent from its source to the nose,
so does the mind devoted to yoga reach the immutable Self.

Śrīdhara: An illustration of attainment without effort is given: "the wind is the vehicle that carries the fragrance. From its source—that is, from its location—it "appropriates" it, making it one with itself. That mind which is unchanging and equanimous. 20.
The sequential composition: "Just as" (yathā) refers to the statement of the relationship, namely that it imitates me, the Self, the Supreme Self. ||20||

Viśvanātha: An illustration of attainment without effort. The wind is the vehicle that carries the fragrance; from its own abode or location, it reaches and pervades the nose. In the same way, the mind—when joined with devotion, action, and yoga—reaches the Self, which is the Supreme Self. Just as...

Just as the wind carries the fragrance residing in a lotus pond to the nose, so too this aggregate of the limbs of bhakti leads the mind—intent on yoga and established in the yoga of bhakti—to the Supreme Lord; such is the meaning. ||20||
I am always established as the self of all beings within all beings;
disregarding Me, a mortal performs a mockery of worship.

Śrīdhara: To state that purity of mind arises only through the vision of the Self in all beings, he speaks in seven verses beginning with "I am," censuring exclusive devotion to images and the like. *Arca* means a mockery or imitation; or, it refers to the mockery of worship within the context of an image. [This leads to] contempt and neglect.
The censures regarding dress are refuted in sequence by four [verses]. ||21||

The sequential arrangement: Śrī Kapiladeva has censured even contempt and the like toward ordinary living beings, how much more so toward those devoted to the Lord. For instance—in the verse beginning with "I"—starting from the individual soul (*jīva*) among living beings, according to the manner to be described.

The *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) within all beings, down to those whose selves and lives are dedicated to the Blessed One. The meaning is: "having disregarded me by disregarding them"—that is, having shown contempt for me, who am the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) over them.
Then, he who makes an *arcā*, an image of me, after having done that [disregard], performs a mockery of it.
The meaning is that you are indeed showing contempt.

[Bhaktisandarbha 106] To state that purity of mind arises only through the vision of the Self in all beings, he speaks in seven verses beginning with "I am," censuring exclusive devotion to images and the like: "Arcaiva... (Worship alone...).

"Viḍambana" means imitation; or, in the context of worship, it means a mockery of worship. Disrespect, neglect, hatred, and censure are prohibited respectively by the [following] four [verses]. ||21||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, even such devotion as this is contracted by offense alone; and that offense is generally rooted in great contempt. Since those who are "great" exist in the world in great numbers, though they are difficult to perceive, one should therefore [offer salutations] to all beings for the sake of avoiding such offenses.

Thinking that [the devotees] should be honored with the understanding that they are presided over by one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), and stating that even the service to the form of the Blessed Lord does not yield its fruit properly in their absence, He— as if out of affection for His own devotee who, due to his lordship, fails to show honor to living beings— appears as though He were angry because of that failure to act for their benefit.

Śrī Kapiladeva spoke with six verses beginning with "I am... and so forth. Therein, contempt, indifference, hatred, and slander are respectively prohibited by the first four [verses]. "Arcā" means my image; to perform worship toward it is merely to mock me. (21)
He who, out of delusion, abandons me— the Self and Lord dwelling within all beings— and worships an image instead, offers his oblation into ashes alone.
Śrīdhara: Having abandoned, that is, having disregarded. ||22||

The sequential arrangement [of the verses] is as follows; he states that very point: "He who, out of delusion... etc. Out of delusion—that is, due to a foolish intellect thinking, "This is some image made of stone or wood"—he who, having abandoned me, the Supreme Self and Lord, who dwells within all beings, fails to perceive my identity with that [image], [worships] my own worshipful form (arcā).
One worships the image and, from the perspective of mere worldly custom, offers water and other offerings to it.
As stated in the *Agni Purāṇa* regarding the lamentation of the ascetic King Daśaratha, whose son had been slain:
"Did I perhaps conceive the notion that the image of Hari was made of stone?"
What [is the merit] of one who has ever seen on the road a devotee of Viṣṇu?
"I showed no respect in my mind toward one whose body was marked with that mudrā;
by the ripening of that karma, I have such grief for my son.
As it has been said:
To perceive a stone in Viṣṇu who is worthy of worship; to perceive an ordinary man in one's gurus; to perceive caste-consciousness in a Vaiṣṇava;
or to perceive mere water in the water at the foot of Viṣṇu or the Vaiṣṇavas—which washes away the impurities of the Kali age;
and to perceive a mere common sound in the pure mantra of His name, which destroys all defilement—[these are the five great sins].
Or he who possesses an equal regard for Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, as for anyone else—that person is a denizen of hell.
Thus, because that fool lacks my vision, he also comes to despise all beings;

consequently, due to that fault, just as someone might offer oblations into ashes, there is an absence of fruit for that person who lacks faith—this is the meaning. As for those who, having cast aside the injunctions of the scriptures, perform sacrifices while endowed with faith...

In accordance with the manner stated in such passages as *Gītā* 17.1, whatever arises merely from worldly tradition—even if there is some degree of faith—is simply the state of being a "lowest" devotee (*kaniṣṭha-bhāgavata*). As it is said:
"He who strives with faith for the worship of Hari in the form of an image alone..."

"Nor among others who are devoted to Him; such a devotee is considered ordinary (prākṛta). Because of such statements as these, although devotion performed in whatever way necessarily culminates in its fruit, nevertheless, that fruit does not arise immediately.
Thus, its fruitfulness has been stated and will be stated further by such passages as: "One should worship in the image and so forth" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.29.25).
[From the *Bhakti-sandarbha*] Viśvanātha: By His sovereignty, He says "He offers oblations into ashes alone" in order to instruct His own devotees.

This is a statement of reproach. Likewise, even the Blessed Lord himself, having stated in the verse "He who perceives a self in a corpse" (*yasyātmabuddhiḥ kuṇape*) that "his intellect is fixed on the earth" (*bhaumaijyadhīḥ*), then issues a rebuke by saying "he is indeed a donkey among cows" (*sa eva gokharaḥ*).
In the same way, even contemporary true gurus [reprove] their own dear disciple...

They reproach [the devotee], saying: "Even though you are devoted to your own service, as soon as you see even a mere trace of an offense against the devotees of Hari elsewhere, you perform service to me; you reduce me to ashes, making me experience nothing but suffering. But in reality, the sages never speak in such a manner—as for example: * *śrīmadbhāgavate (10.29.34)*: "O Lord, those who are devoted to You do not even look upon the faults of others; how much less would they ever commit an offense against You? * *śrīmadbhāgavate (7.5.31)*: "O Supreme Person, those who are Your devotees do not find fault with others; how could they ever commit an offense against You, the source of all auspiciousness? * *śrīmadbhāgavate (11.2.42)*: "O Lord, the wise ones who are devoted to You do not see the faults of others; how could they ever commit an offense against You, the embodiment of all virtues? In truth, the sages never speak in such a way. For instance: * *śrīmadbhāgavate (6.3.21)*: "O Lord, those who are devoted to You do not find fault with others; how could they ever commit an offense against You, the source of all auspiciousness? * *śrīmadbhāgavate (10.29.34)*: "O Lord, those who are devoted to You do not even look upon the faults of others; how much less would they ever commit an offense against You? * *śrīmadbhāgavate (11.2.42)*: "O Lord, the wise ones who are devoted to You do not see the faults of others; how could they ever commit an offense against You, the embodiment of all virtues? Thus, the sages never speak in such a manner. As it is said: * *śrīmadbhāgavate (10.29.34)*: "O Lord, those who are devoted to You do not even look upon the faults of others; how much less would they ever commit an offense against You? * *śrīmadbhāgavate (7.5.31)*: "O Supreme Person, those who are Your devotees do not find fault with others; how could they ever commit an offense against You, the source of all auspiciousness? * *śrīmadbhāgavate (11.2.42)*: "O Lord, the wise ones who are devoted to You do not see the faults of others; how could they ever commit an offense against You, the embodiment of all virtues? In truth, the sages never speak in such a way. For instance: * *śrīmadbhāgavate (6.3.21)*: "O Lord, those who are devoted to You do not find fault with others; how could they ever commit an offense against You, the source of all auspiciousness? * *śrīmadbhāgavate (10.29.34)*: "O Lord, those who are devoted to You do not even look upon the faults of others; how much less would they ever commit an offense against You? * *śrīmadbhāgavate (11.2.42)*: "O Lord, the wise ones who are devoted to You do not see the faults of others; how could they ever commit an offense against You, the embodiment of all virtues? In truth, the sages never speak in such a manner. As it is said: * *śrīmadbhāgavate (10.29.34)*: "O Lord, those who are devoted to You do not even look upon the faults of others; how much less would they ever commit an offense against You? * *śrīmadbhāgavate (7.5.31)*: "O Supreme Person, those who are Your devotees do not find fault with others; how could they ever commit an offense against You, the source of all auspiciousness? * *śrīmadbhāgavate (11.2.42)*: "O Lord, the wise ones who are devoted to You do not see the faults of others

"He who strives with faith for worship of Hari only in the consecrated image (arcā), and not toward His other devotees—he is considered a *prākṛta* (materialistic) devotee. And the commentary of the venerable Svāmicaraṇas states: "Not even toward His devotees, and certainly not toward others."

He performs [it]. *Prākṛta* means the original nature or the beginning. The meaning is that one whose devotion has only just begun will gradually become supreme; such is the sense here. On this point also, it will be said later: "One should first worship in the image and so forth" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.29.25), and so on. ||22||
The mind of one who hates another’s body, who is conceited, who perceives things as distinct,
and who harbors enmity toward living beings, does not attain peace.
Śrīdhara: Not explained.

Kramasaṃdarbha: Since even mere contempt is of such a nature, all the more so—"toward one who hates" (dviṣataḥ)—meaning one who perceives with division, who lacks the vision of the single inner controller everywhere, and for that very reason, one who is conceited; therefore...
Thus it is for one who harbors enmity. And so it is stated in the Mahābhārata:
"Hṛṣīkeśa quickly becomes gracious toward that pure person who, compassionate like a father to his son, does not cause distress to others. (23)
Viśvanātha: Those who perceive with partiality do not realize that the suffering of another is equal to their own suffering. ||23||
O sinless one, even when worshipped with various kinds of materials and ritual actions, I am not at all pleased by the worship of one who treats the assembly of living beings with contempt.
Śrīdhara: [This refers to] action produced by material substances; [it applies] to one who insults the assembly of beings and reviles them. ||24||

The sequence of composition: Furthermore, [the thought] "I am [insulted]"—for one who is insulted, even the censure of the reviler is equal to hatred. Or rather, a man pierced by arrows that strike his vital organs does not suffer as much [as he does from such insults].

Thinking that this [verse] is not out of order because it is superior to what was stated in the manner of Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.23.3— "For the harsh arrows of the wicked pierce the vital spots"— it was not recited before the verse concerning hatred. 24.

Viśvanātha: A man pierced by arrows that strike his vital organs does not suffer so much as he is tormented by the harsh words of the wicked, which pierce the very vitals of those who treat him with contempt and revile him. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.23.3)
Thus, they say that according to the manner described, censure is even greater than hatred. ||24||
One who performs their own duties should worship me, the Lord, in an image and so forth,
only so long as they do not know me abiding within their own heart and in all beings.
Śrīdhara: In that case, is worship of an image and so forth entirely useless? No, he says: "In an image and so forth.

As long as one does not know Me, who resides in all beings, within one's own heart—performing one's own duties according to opportunity without conflict with [prescribed] action. By this, it is shown that even for one established in action (*karmaniṣṭhā*), that very same limit applies.
This has been stated. ||25||

The sequential arrangement of the argument: Thus, the fault of one who lacks faith in devotion due to the absence of knowledge of the Lord has been stated. Now, while teaching that the very worship of Him—conjoined with one's own duty—is the cause of that knowledge which is the basis for such faith, He also acknowledges that such worship is not fruitless.

Regarding the phrase "in the image, etc.": one should worship in the image and so forth while performing one's own duties only so long as one does not know—that is, does not realize—the Lord, who am I, abiding in all beings.
In this context, there is the state of being assisted by one's own duties; for one who has not yet developed faith lacks the qualification for pure devotion. Therefore...

It will be established [later] by the passage beginning with "having developed faith in my teachings" (*jātaśraddho matkathāsu*). Therefore, it follows that one who has developed faith after the knowledge of the Blessed One (*bhagavajjñāna*) should not worship while performing his own worldly duties;
rather, he should perform only pure worship and so forth. And that will be established: "first, the ritual actions" (*tāvat karmāṇi*).
By the passage beginning with "one should perform" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.20.9), the meaning is that one must not abandon the image;
an installed image is not to be discarded, but should be worshipped as long as one lives.
Better is the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of the head.
Thus, because it contradicts the Śrī Hayaśīrṣa Pañcarātra. ||25||

Viśvanātha: For those possessing pure devotion, contempt for living beings generally does not occur because their internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is inherently pure. However, for those whose devotion is mixed with ritual action (*karma-miśra-bhakti*), such contempt certainly may arise. As long as there is impurity of the internal organ, it persists; but when that purity is attained, it ceases.

He says that one should not remain [in that state] and therefore should not perform action either—in the words "in the image, etc. One who performs their own duty is practicing sattvic devotion mixed with action. The phrase "as long as" means that as long as the state of perceiving the Self in all beings has not arisen, one does not [cease action] because of the qualification for ritual action.
"One who performs his own duty"; however, the meaning is that one should worship Me in the image while practicing devotion mixed with knowledge. ||25||
For one who creates a division between himself and another,
death brings intense fear to that person of divided vision.

The "honey" (madhvaḥ) is Brahman, which has split open the interior of the belly; for one who does not perceive a difference between the Brahman residing within oneself and the Brahman residing in another—according to the Śruti: "The belly is Brahman. ||26||

Śrīdhara: *Antarā* means "between," that is, "a distinction. *Ut* means "even. *Aram* means "slight. The meaning is: "I, who am Death, create fear for him who perceives even the slightest distinction. Alternatively, *antarā* means "in the middle"; *udara* means "the body. I, as Death, produce fear for him [who perceives a distinction within the body]. ||26||

The Sequence of Composition: Now, he says "of oneself" (*ātmanaḥ*) because worship preceded by one's own ritual action does not succeed without compassion for all beings. [One] creates a division within the belly by piercing the abdomen, but does not view it as equal to oneself on account of being the locus of the ego. And therefore—
The meaning is that even upon seeing those who are hungry and so forth, he maintains only his own belly and such;
for him, whose vision is divided, I—in the form of death—am the terrible fear of saṃsāra. ||26||

Viśvanātha: He who makes a distinction between his own belly and the belly of another—that person is none other than I, the very embodiment of death. Indeed, knowing that the belly is possessed by the flames of the digestive fire equally for oneself as for another, one should feed a living being afflicted by hunger just as one would oneself.
The meaning is that otherwise, one does not cross over the fear of death. ||26||
Then, one should honor me— who have made my abode as the self of all beings within all beings—
with gifts and respect, and with an eye undivided by friendliness.

Śrīdhara: Now, therefore, [he sees] Him who has made His abode, who has taken up residence, in all beings. The reason for this is that He is the Self of beings, the Inner Controller (antaryāmin). [He sees Him] with an undivided eye, that is, with equal vision. ||27||

The sequential arrangement: He concludes with the word *atha*. Now, for this reason, one should act as is appropriate—by giving according to one's capacity, or in its absence, by honoring—and with an undivided eye, as previously stated regarding Sanaka and the others by the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha: "Those who milk my forms [as] the best of the twice-born..."
"And my beings, having found no refuge, [perceive me] with a sense of duality" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.16.10), and so forth.
This introduction was intended beforehand as that which was stated in "whatever violence... and so on;
it is pointed out as being for the purpose of nourishing each of those [beings]. ||27||

Viśvanātha: Now, one might object: "Since there are indeed infinite living beings afflicted by hunger who constitute the primary objects [of compassion] in the previous [verse], and they surely come into the presence of the provider upon hearing of him, who indeed possesses the fortitude to feed them like King Ratnideva? To this, he says: "Or rather, for their sake..."

"Even when one lacks the capacity to give as much as desired, one should honor [the recipient] with gifts and other such offerings. Furthermore, according to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The particles *atha* and *ataḥ* may occur in the senses of doubt (*saṃśaya*), eligibility (*adhikāra*), auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), alternative (*vikalpa*), immediate sequence (*anantara*), inquiry (*praśna*), entirety (*kārtsnya*), commencement (*ārambha*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*)."
Furthermore, even when those seekers of enjoyment treat him with contempt by insulting him and so forth, he should not offer any counter-contempt;

rather, he should honor them with respect through praise and other means, regarding them as superior even to himself. As it was said by the Blessed One: "They [should be honored] with the thought that they are my very self."
"Even as they cast [stones] at him, their hearts were satisfied, their lotus-like faces moistened with the nectar of smiles," and so forth.

[He regards them] as equal to himself, with a friendliness that is undivided and unbroken—that is to say, straightforward. Thus, even through the conduct of one free from deceit, although they may be angry, the Lord remains situated within them.
The meaning is that he should not become angry at all. ||27||
Living beings are indeed superior to non-living things; from among them, O auspicious one, those who possess breath are superior;
from among them, those with consciousness are preeminent; and from among them, those possessing the functions of the senses are superior.
The Madhvas are those who possess breath and are endowed with movement. ||28||

Śrīdhara: To state that even therein, one should apply an increasing degree of honor and so forth according to the subsequent [categories], he describes the gradation with six and a half verses beginning with "The living beings" (*jīvā*). "Non-living" (*ajīvānām*) means from the insentient. Then, among those [living beings] as well, "possessors of breath" (*prāṇabhṛtaḥ*) are those who possess the function of vital breath. "Conscious" (*sacittāḥ*) means possessing knowledge.
In these [trees], there are functions of the sense organs. Subtle functions of the sense organs indeed exist even in trees;

for thus it is recorded in the Mokṣadharma section of the Mahābhārata: "Therefore trees see, therefore trees smell," and so forth. However, the function of the sense organ of touch is well known [in their case].

The sequential arrangement: therein, because [the merit] accrues equally to all, he specifies [the recipients] with six and a half verses. "Non-living things" (*ajīva*) refers to withered crops and the like; "living things" (*jīva*) refers to living crops and the like.
Furthermore, among those, "sentient beings" (*prāṇabhṛt*) are identified by such signs as drawing up water from the earth and vomiting it out again.

Living stones and the like possess consciousness because they were previously endowed with vital functions such as flying upward, but were later paralyzed by Indra’s thunderbolt; for it is heard that mountains possess internal cognition through the activity of their senses,
just like sight and other faculties, even from a distance through the activity of touch.

Trees and other such beings, who possess knowledge of the space from which they themselves arise, exhibit an increasing degree of excellence as one proceeds from each preceding stage to the succeeding one, by virtue of possessing one additional quality at each step.

Viśvanātha: And unlike one possessing isolated knowledge (*kevalajñānī*), my devotee does not regard all things with an equal vision; rather, he should honor them according to their relative gradations. He demonstrates that gradation in six and a half verses. [He states: "Living beings (*jīva*) [are superior] to non-living things (*ajīva*), such as withered grass and the like."
Those that do not digest grass and so forth are superior; from them come the living beings.

Living stones and the like exist by sustaining the functions of life through signs such as drawing up water from the earth and exuding it. From them come those with consciousness, for previously they exhibited activities such as flying, and later they were paralyzed by Indra’s thunderbolt.
