According to the treatise, the mountains possess internal consciousness. Among them, those that perceive touch are superior; among those, the perceivers of taste are more excellent;
among those, the perceivers of smell are better; and from them, the perceivers of sound are the most eminent.
According to Madhva: Jīvas alone exist by their own nature, distinguished as animals, trees, and so forth;
in saṃsāra there is a perversion of these, while in liberation they possess their respective true forms.
Among those, the immobile are inferior to the liberated beings who possess mobility;
the human-liberated are superior to them, and the fully liberated (vipramukta) are even greater than those.
Then, from those who know the Vedas and understand their meaning— who are liberated by mere instruction— the sages [received it], and from them the gods, who sever all doubts.
"Then Indra is one whose dharma is complete; then Garuḍa is free from attachment.
Whether in liberation or in transmigratory existence, these qualities are truly beneficial for them. Thus it is said in the Kāpileya. 29.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, compared to those who perceive touch, fish and others who perceive taste are superior; bees and others who perceive smell are superior; and snakes and others who perceive sound are superior. ||29||

The sequential arrangement: therefore, compared to those who perceive touch, those who perceive taste—such as ants and fish, who through the tasting of flavors know their own respective food whether it be edible earth or inedible—are superior; superior to them are those who perceive smell, such as bees; and superior to them are those who perceive sound, such as serpents.
In that regard, some are even experts in the terminology concerning the causes for joining together, fleeing, and so forth. ||29||

Viśvanātha: Even among those, compared to the trees and such that perceive only touch, there are earthworms and others who perceive taste and possess knowledge of what is edible and inedible for themselves;
there are minute insects on flowers such as the *bakula* who perceive smell; and there are those who perceive sound, fleeing upon hearing a noise.
Some are water-insects. ||29||

Among those who know the distinctions of form therein, and among those with two rows of teeth, those with many feet are superior; among them, four-footed beings are superior, and among them, two-footed beings.

Śrīdhara: [The term refers to] crows and others who know the differences in forms. Those who have teeth on both [jaws]; from those with many feet as opposed to footless beings, [the meaning is] those with four feet; from them, the two-footed human. ||30||

The sequential arrangement [of categories] is as follows: from those previously mentioned, the crows and others are known for their distinct forms. Those with teeth on both sides and many feet, such as the *carmacāṭī* and others, possess teeth on both sides because they have the capacity to cut fruits and the like. Quadrupeds are the animals; birds are those whose means of locomotion are their two wings.
And "two-footed" means a human being. Although others possess four feet, two feet, and so forth, they are inferior because they lack such specific qualities.

However, for these [humans], the state of being footless is a mark (*liṅga*)—despite their excellence in having consciousness and so on, and despite their possession of hands and other limbs—indicating an excellence of intellect; thus, [they are superior] to the former.

It consists of an excellence of qualities (*guṇotkarṣamaya*). There is a progressive superiority from each preceding stage to each succeeding one, due to the addition of one quality at a time. Thus, in other cases as well, the gradation should be understood through the increase or decrease of superior qualities, such as by means of divine empowerment (*devatādhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth.
There is supreme excellence in the Himalayas and other such places, in the Tulasī plant and others, and in cows and the like. ||30||

Viśvanātha: Those who know the distinctions of form include crows and the like; those with teeth on both sides include snakes and the like—the fact that they have teeth on both sides is to be known by the mark of their cutting through wood such as *puṣpa* with many feet. Quadrupeds are animals; bipeds are humans. Among these, each subsequent group [is more numerous] than each preceding one.
In general, superiority [of merit] arises from a preponderance of qualities.

When considering the superiority of specific qualities such as divine presiding presence and so forth, there is a greater degree of worthiness for worship everywhere— in places such as Śrī Govardhana and Veṅkaṭācala, as well as in sacred plants like the tulasī— due to the absolute preponderance of such qualities.
That which is established by those who know the treatises is indeed what should be known. ||30||
From that [arose] the four castes, among whom the Brāhmaṇa is the highest;
even among the Brāhmaṇas, he who knows the Veda and understands its meaning is superior to the others.
Śrīdhara: Thereafter, the castes arise among them. ||31||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Then, among those [three]. ||31||

One who knows the meaning and can dispel doubts is superior to him; one who performs his own duty is superior to him; one who is free from attachment is greater than him; and one who does not milk [exploit] his own dharma for personal gain is even greater.

Śrīdhara: A *mīmāṃsaka* is one who cuts through doubt. Furthermore, he is a performer of his own duty (*svakarmakṛt*) even beyond that. He is characterized by freedom from attachment; the meaning is that he is desireless, not milking [the cow] for his own personal merit (*ātmano dharma*). ||32||
The sequence of composition: one who milks dharma is a performer of action free from desire. ||32||

Viśvanātha: Even compared to such a person who does not properly perform his own duty, the one who performs his own duty is superior; among those, the best is the knower (jñānī) who is free from attachment, because he is a non-milkman—that is, one who does not grasp the fruit of his own duty performed in a previous state. ||32||
Therefore, for one who has offered all actions, objects, and the self to me without interruption—
for that person whose self is offered to me, who has renounced action in me,
and who is a non-doer through equal vision— I see no higher being.

Śrīdhara: He by whom all actions, their objects, their fruits, the self, and the body have been offered; for that very reason, he is "uninterrupted," meaning unimpeded. [He offers this] to the "non-doer," who is devoid of the conceit of agency. ||33||

The sequential arrangement: "Therefore" constitutes half a verse. "Uninterrupted" means devotion that is not separated from knowledge and the other [perfections]. Regarding the non-agent—one who, by having offered his very self, does not depend on actions such as maintaining himself—when devotion is performed toward the Blessed Lord, even in that case...
[This is said] by one who, knowing his own dependence on the Blessed One and being free from pride regarding that [dependence], possesses equal vision; and because,

through the equality of being presided over by the Blessed One, he desires the welfare of others just as he does for himself— since the distinction is intended here [in the verse] by such statements as "living beings are indeed superior to non-living things," therefore [it is said] "among My devotees."

Thus, one should perform [the practice] with an abundance of reverence and so forth; however, in other cases, it should be done as it occurs or according to one's capacity—this is the intended meaning. ||34||

Viśvanātha: From him [the Lord] as well, he is one by whom all activities—such as the operations of hearing, seeing, and so forth—and all objects and riches, as well as the self consisting of the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*), the locus of "mineness" (*mamatā*), and the mind, intellect, and other faculties, have been offered into me, within my names, forms, and so on; he is thus "uninterrupted" (*nirantara*).

It is free from the intervention of karma, knowledge, and so forth; it belongs to one who has renounced action—that is, one who has abandoned the duties of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*)—as stated previously: "one who has renounced actions for my sake. Even when performing acts of devotion to Me, he is a non-doer, because he possesses the realization that "it is Bhagavān alone who causes me to perform this act of devotion."

From a state of equanimous vision that is free from the conceit of agency through its own autonomy, one perceives everything—including pleasure, pain, and so forth—as being exactly the same for oneself. As it was said by the Blessed One:
"O Arjuna, he who, by comparison with himself, sees the same everywhere..."
"Whether in happiness or in suffering, that yogi is considered supreme" (Gītā 6.32).
And:
"In a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, and in an elephant... [Gītā 5.18].

"The wise see the same in a dog and even in an outcaste" (Gītā 5.18)— this "seeing with equanimity" mentioned there must be explained [in a specific sense], because otherwise it would contradict the previously introduced statement that "living beings are superior to non-living things," and so forth. ||33||
With the mind, one should bow down to these beings with great reverence, thinking:
"The Blessed Lord has entered [them] as a portion of the individual soul."
Madhva: Together with a portion of the individual soul (jīvakalā), one should honor all beings and bow to the Lord as their abode. ||34||

Śrīdhara: The meaning is that He has entered by way of His perspective as the inner controller (antaryāmin), through the act of measuring [the world] with a portion of Himself, which is to say, through His presence within the individual souls (jīvas). ||34||

The sequential arrangement: "By the mind these... means by the portion of the individual soul (jīva-kalā), that is, by its presiding presence within them. In this regard, one should also remember the verse from the Śrī Gītā beginning with "I am equal toward all" (Gītā 9.29). Thus, for those who are beginners in worship...

However, for practitioners endowed with faith, reverence toward all beings is established within the Lord Himself, through the manifestation of the Lord’s omnipresent majesty. As it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
O hunter, these virtues of yours, such as non-violence and the like, are indeed not extraordinary;
for those who are engaged in devotion to Hari cannot be scorched by others.
In the manner to be described, this state of pure kinship and so forth arises for practitioners as well,
in accordance with the character of the residents of Śrī Gokula— whose kinship is already established—
and in accordance with such qualities of the Lord. For those in whom this state has arisen, however, there is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).
And cessation is indeed one's own inherent nature. As it is said: "Wherein the wise, having suddenly cast aside the delusion of attachment to the body and so forth, [become devoted]."
"They attain that ultimate state of the paramahaṃsas, in which non-violence is indeed their supreme own-duty" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.18.22).
Beyond that, one should perceive the nature of the Blessed Lord within all beings as being one's own self among those who have attained the highest perfection.

In accordance with such passages as [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.45], that [the worship of the tree] is indeed established. As for the fact that in those contexts for practitioners— such as in [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.31.14], "Just as by watering the root of a tree"—
one perceives a redundancy regarding other forms of worship, that is merely...
[This applies] only to those forms of worship based on the independent view [of the deity].

Here, however, only the worship of the Lord as presiding over each respective [object] is enjoined. And the necessity of devotion toward that [Lord] is accomplished precisely through that connection—which elsewhere is immediate.
It should be understood that this is for the purpose of separating oneself from attachment and aversion.

For this very reason, Bharata incurred an obstacle because he abandoned the worship of the Blessed Lord out of mere compassion for living beings; conversely, Rantideva and others achieved their goal through the vision of the Supreme Self.
Therefore, the claim that devotion to the Blessed One consists primarily of compassion toward living beings rather than ritual worship is refuted;

likewise, this is established by the word "api" (also) in the passage: "by the auspicious yoga of action, which is not excessively harmful, performed constantly," as a means for attaining the devotion to the attributeless [Brahman] immediately prior [to the realization of the Self].

In the practice of *kriyā-yoga* characterized by the worship of the Pāñcarātrikas, even a slight act of injury—such as the gathering of leaves and flowers—is prescribed. Therefore, one should not show disregard toward others; rather, one should show respect and so forth because of their connection to the Blessed One (*bhagavat*). However, independent worship [is not permitted].
It is censured. It was indeed well said: "He who is free from pride and whose desires are fulfilled" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.9.21), and so forth.
This very context was intended previously when it was stated: "Whatever injury... and so on.

He is designated as such by way of nourishing that [body]; the meaning is: by means of a portion of the individual soul (jīva-kalā), by means of that [divine] portion, and by way of being its inner controller (antaryāmin). ||34||
Viśvanātha: Together with that digit (kalā) which is of the nature of the individual soul (jīva). ||34||
O descendant of Manu, both bhaktiyoga and [jñāna]yoga have been proclaimed by me;
by either one of these two, a person may go to the Supreme Person.
Regarding honey: because one is necessarily determined by the existence of the other, it is [designated] by means of either one alone. ||35||

Śrīdhara: He concludes the discussion on *bhaktiyoga* together with the previously mentioned eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*), saying "and *bhaktiyoga*. O Mānavī! [This refers to] the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣa. (35)

The sequence of composition: Regarding the word "bhakti" (devotion), since yoga also possesses a seed (*sabīja*) and is thus mixed with devotion, it is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). However, between these two most effective means, one is distinguished by being effortless while the other is characterized by effort; from this distinction, their relative strength and weakness are understood respectively.
Even in the case of the person who is the object of attainment, a gradation should be understood by way of the differences in manifestation. ||35||

Viśvanātha: He concludes the previously mentioned *bhaktiyoga* together with the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) by saying "bhakti... and so forth. One shall go to the Puruṣa; that is, one shall attain Me, the Supreme Lord. Through *bhaktiyoga*, there is the direct perception of My glorious form, which is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*). And through the eight-limbed yoga...

Because the direct realization of the nature that is non-different from the Self is what is expressed in the scriptures by the term "attaining Me" for both [the jīvanmukta and the videhamukta]. ||35||
This is the form of the Blessed One, of Brahmā, the Supreme Self—
the supreme, primary Puruṣa, the divine, whose activity is governed by karma.
The divine substratum of the differentiation of forms is designated as "Time" (kāla),
from which fear arises for beings such as Mahat and the rest, who perceive through fragmented vision.

Śrīdhara: Regarding that which was asked further—"explain the transmigrations of the individual soul (jīva) and the true nature of time"—he says this in one and a half verses beginning with "etat. This is the form of the Lord which governs everything.
Of what nature is it? It consists of both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, and yet it is also supreme (*para*), being distinct from them. This alone is the divine (*daiva*).

Thus it is said. Of what nature is it? It is that from which arises the manifold activity of karma, characterized by various cycles of rebirth (*saṃsṛti*). The meaning is that the diverse transmigrations are produced by karma impelled by destiny (*daiva*). ||36||

This very form of the Blessed One is also designated as "Time" (*kāla*). Of what nature is it? It is the locus, the substratum, and the cause of the differentiation of forms—that is, the alteration of things. For it has been said: "From Time comes the transformation of the *guṇas*"; and it will be stated later: "Time is the transformation of the *guṇas*. This is the divine [nature].

It possesses a marvelous power. He states this very point with the words "of beings" up until the end [of the verse]: that is, of the individual souls who preside over the principles beginning with Mahat. ||37||
The sequential arrangement: He demonstrates this very point with the verse beginning "This" (etad).

This reality called Puruṣa, which is accessible through the two-fold yoga of devotion and so forth, is indeed the form—the essential nature—of the Lord Brahmā and the Supreme Self; it is the triad of forms designated as Bhagavat and the rest, and not anything other than that.

The meaning is "divided. For it has been stated here [in the Bhagavad-gītā 1.2.11]: "Those who know reality say that the Person is indeed non-dual knowledge. This is because of the Vedic revelation: "I was already here before," which explains the nature of the Person (puruṣatva). In this context, although there is no difference between the form and the possessor of the form, [the distinction is made].
The intention to express distinction is like [the statement] "the body of a stone statue";

that reality is supreme and indeed without adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). It is the differentiation of various manifestations of that single reality through the manifestation and non-manifestation of specific attributes (*svarūpadharma*) of its own nature.
This is the state (*bhāva*).
Thus, having described the three pure forms primarily, he describes the other triad.
This very [triad] is "the primary *puruṣa*," meaning the form of *puruṣa* characterized by the primary limiting adjunct (*pradhānopādhika*). In the city (*puri*)...

According to the *nirukti* (etymological derivation), it is called "puruṣa" because he "lies" (*śete*). Although the reading "pradhāna" appears in many places, it is not accepted by Svāmī. Here, the distinction is maintained that the Supreme Self possesses the status of a witness (*sākṣitva*), whereas this [puruṣa] possesses agency (*kartṛtva*). Furthermore, the difference between Bhagavān and Brahmā has already been explained. And this very point...

The reality previously described—consisting of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and the person (*puruṣa*)—is designated as "fate" (*daiva*) and "time" (*kāla*) through the differentiation of the Lord’s functions. Among these, the definition of fate is that from which the activity of karma proceeds; the definition of time is "form" (*rūpa*). Alternatively, it is that by which one identifies things as "that," "this," or "the present."
This is its specific qualification; the meaning is "the substratum of those respective forms. The reason for this is: "divine," which means possessing inconceivable power. ||36||
Viśvanātha: [Objection: But you say that by either of those two, a person should go to the Puruṣa;
you do not say that "the Puruṣa should come to me. Therefore, who is that Puruṣa? To this, touching his own chest with his index finger, he says: "This" (etad). This is the meaning: he who...
Indeed, among those who have realized the true state, among the devotees, the wise, and the practitioners of Brahman-yoga, the Supreme Self resides;
that which is His supreme, non-material form is this very one. The meaning is: "I am indeed Your son, O Supreme Lord.
Not only this much, but [He is also] the primordial nature, the person, the individual soul, unseen destiny, time, and so forth.

He says, "This form of mine is indeed such": *pradhānam* (primordial matter) and *tatpravartakaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the person who impels it)—these two are a compound treated as a singular. *Daivam* (fate) is the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings; it is of various kinds because it arises from actions consisting of both merit and demerit.

Likewise, that which is designated as "time" (kāla) is also my own divine nature of wondrous power; it is the locus, the support, and the cause of the differentiation of forms—that is, the transformation of entities.
For it has been said: "From time arises the interplay of the qualities. She asked about this time.

He says that the characteristic has been stated because from Him comes the fear of all— of the insentient principles beginning with Mahat, of the individual souls who identify with them, and of all ignorant ones who perceive diversity, throughout the states of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. (37)

He who, having entered within, devours all beings by means of those very beings, he who is the refuge of all— He is that one named Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of sacrifice, Time, the Lord of all who ordain.
Śrīdhara says: He states the cause of fear with the words "He who... He devours—that is, he withdraws—the elements by means of the elements themselves.
He is the presiding deity of sacrifice (*adhiyajña*), the giver of the fruits of sacrifice. [The phrase] "of those who measure" refers to those who bring others under their control. (38)
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] has not been explained.
Viśvanātha says: He describes the manner of fear with the words "He who... He devours—that is, withdraws—the very elements by means of the elements.
He is the presiding deity of sacrifice (*adhiyajña*), meaning he is the bestower of the fruits thereof by virtue of his authority over sacrifice. For those who contemplate...
And even for those who exercise control [over others]. ||38||
To him, no one is dear, nor anyone is hateful, nor anyone is a kinsman;
undistracted himself, he, the bringer of the end, enters into people who are distracted.

Regarding the term *madhvaḥ*, Śrīdhara, in the *Kramasaṃdarbha* of the *Kāpileya*, states: "Neither is he hateful nor dear to Hari beyond what is appropriate. Viśvanātha has not provided a commentary on this.
Out of fear of whom this wind blows, and out of fear of whom the sun shines;
Out of fear of whom the god rains, and out of fear of whom the host of stars shines;

Śrīdhara: His terrifying nature, well-known from such scriptural passages as "From fear of him the wind blows," is also due solely to his form as Time; thus he says with the six verses beginning with "That... From fear of whom—that is, by whose impulsion—the wind blows, moving with smallness or greatness and in various directions; [the sun] shines somewhere.
Sometimes it manifests preceded by heat, because it possesses both rising and setting; thus does it appear. ||40||
Kramasandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Because [it arises] from that which is called Viṣṇu. ||40||
That the trees, along with the creepers and the medicinal herbs,
each in their own season, produce flowers and fruits.
Śrīdhara: From which [cause] they are afraid. ||41||
*Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
Because of him, the rivers flow in fear, yet the ocean does not overflow;
because of his dread, the fire burns along with the mountains, and the earth does not sink.
Śrīdhara: From whom the rivers flow in fear; by whom the earth, together with the mountains, is kindled—that is, set ablaze. 42.

Regarding the sequence of composition: according to the maxim, "In the Kali age, the Gaṅgā flows only in certain places," it follows that at times she may not flow at all; Viśvanātha states that she "shines" (indhe) in some place at some time, even if she remains unmanifest.
She "shines" (indhe), meaning she blazes—that fire—along with the mountains upon the earth.
Even under the weight of a man full of many sins, she does not sink; rather, even in hardship, she maintains her fortitude.
Indeed, in the extreme distress at the end of the Dvāpara age, she revealed her true nature to Brahmā in the form of a cow. ||42||
Because of his restraint, the Great One gives space to those who breathe— that which is the sky— and expands his own body as the world enveloped by the seven [elements].

Śrīdhara: By whose command and through whose restraint this sky exists, the Great One (Mahat) expands—that is, spreads out—his own body, which is the principle of Mahat (mahattattva) in the form of a sprout, as the world. ||43||

The sequential composition [of the verse] is as follows: this corporeal ether provides space for the vital breaths of living bodies—that is, it grants room for the activity of breathing—but it does not provide such space for those who are dead; the meaning is that it no longer serves as their abode. ||43||

Viśvanātha: By the regulation and by the direction of this sky (*nabhas*), it grants space—that is, room—for those who breathe, for living beings possessed of the activity of respiration, but not for the dead; [it is] Mahat, the Great Principle, Brahmā, who [transforms] his own body, the Vairāja world, into the worlds beginning with Bhūr.
He causes it to expand. ||43||

Out of fear of him, the gods, who take pride in their qualities, act during the creation and other cosmic phases throughout the ages; under whose control this entire world of moving and non-moving beings exists.

Śrīdhara: The gods, beginning with Brahmā, who possess pride in their qualities and are the controllers of those qualities, proceed with the creation and other activities of this universe; "anuyugam" means again and again, at every age. ||44||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Those who take pride in their qualities are Brahmā, Dharma, Rudra, and others; "in every age" means in every kalpa. ||44||
He is the infinite one who brings an end, Time itself, without beginning and the original creator, imperishable;
producing beings through beings, he destroys the end-maker, Death, by means of death.

Śrīdhara: Being the progenitor (*janayann*) of people—such as sons and others—by means of people—such as fathers and others—he is the "First Creator" (*ādikṛt*). By means of death, he also slays the "End-maker" (Death itself), and thus he is the "Bringer of the End" (*antakara*). Yet he himself is without beginning (*anādi*), infinite (*ananta*), and imperishable (*avyaya*).
[The *Kramasaṃdarbha* has not commented on this.]
Viśvanātha: Being the progenitor through people such as his father and others, he is the "First Creator" (Ādikṛt). ||45||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter of the third [book] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord, composed for the benefit of the virtuous.

Thus ends the chapter titled "The Yoga of Devotion" in the Kāpileya section of the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, within the Third Book of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, the compendium of the Pāramahaṃsa school composed by Vyāsa.
Chapter Twenty-nine.
Chapter Thirty:
The Ripening of Karma concerning Kāpileya, in the Dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
Kapila said:
"Surely this person does not know the vast prowess of that [Brahman],
even though he is being driven away by it, like a mass of clouds by a powerful wind."
Śrīdhara:

But in the thirtieth [chapter], the downward course resulting from sin— the *tāmasī* state of lustful persons whose minds are agitated by the pampering of their bodies, beauty, and so forth— is proclaimed.

Having first described the power of Time (*kāla*), he elaborates upon the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*)—brought about by diverse karmas—for the sake of dispassion (*vairāgya*) over three chapters. Of this very powerful Time (or, according to another reading, *baline*); though being driven or shaken, like a row of clouds [does not overcome] the prowess of the wind.
The Veda. ||1||
Regarding the sequence of composition: in the reading "balinā," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "by that very time. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
Hari revealed to his mother, through five chapters, devotion both devoid of attributes and endowed with attributes, as well as the two forms of knowledge-yoga characterized by goodness (sattva).
Then, indeed, by means of three chapters, he sequentially demonstrated the dark, the passionate, and the pure (sāttvika) destinies resulting from actions.
In the thirtieth [chapter], he describes the aging of youth and the torments of hell for those bound by worldly existence, whose minds are distracted by wives, sons, and the like.

Now, with three chapters, he elaborates upon the worldly suffering experienced by those who perform various actions without devotion to Hari. Regarding the reading "tasya kālasya balino balineti," [it means]: whatever object one pursues with great effort for the sake of happiness, [it results in suffering].
The Blessed One, the Supreme Person, shakes off each and every thing for the sake of which one grieves.

Śrīdhara explains *vikrama* (valor/effort) itself: whatever object one acquires or brings about with difficulty and exertion, that very object Lord Time (*kāla*) shakes off and destroys; "for the sake of which" means for the purpose of which. ||2||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: The Blessed Time (bhagavān kālaḥ). ||2||
That fool who, out of delusion, considers the house, field, and wealth— which belong to this transient body along with its attachments— to be permanent.

Śrīdhara: The cause for grief is as follows: because the houses and so forth belong to the body together with its attachments, such as wife and other relations; "vasu" means wealth; and the particle "ca" (and) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. ||3||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: What is the cause for this grief? Because, O living being (*jantu*), in this worldly existence (*bhava*) accompanied by its attachments (*sānubandha*)—that is, together with wife and other kin—whatever womb (*yoni*) one may follow; [in that very womb one must return].
In each and every one of those, he finds satisfaction and does not become dispassionate.
Śrīdhara: Demonstrating the state of being foolish, he elaborates upon suffering with fourteen verses beginning with "The living being" (jantuḥ). ||4||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha points out the state of being dull-witted [of the opponent] with the words "the living being" (*jantu*). ||4||
Even while dwelling in hell, a person does not wish to abandon the body,
for he is deluded by the divine illusion (devamāyā) despite the existence of infernal bliss.
Śrīdhara: [It occurs] in the hellish [state], which is produced by the consumption of hellish food and so forth. ||5||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: In Nārakī, which is produced by [experiences such as] eating in hell and sexual union with women. ||5||
With his heart deeply rooted in self, wife, children, home, cattle, wealth, and kinsmen, he holds himself in high esteem.
Śrīdhara: One whose heart has taken firm root and whose desires have spread abroad; he esteems himself highly and exults, thinking, "I have achieved my purpose. (6)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He whose heart has such a root that is firmly established. ||6||
With all his limbs burning from the burden of maintaining them,
this fool of evil intent incessantly commits misdeeds.
Śrīdhara: [He is] by means of the anxiety for nourishment caused by the burden of supporting [others]. ||7||
The sequence of composition: in some places the reading is *sandadhyāt*. This is not approved by Puṇyāraṇya.
Viśvanātha: [He is burdened] with the anxiety of marriage, such as protection, nourishment, pleasing [the wife], giving her away in marriage, and so forth. (7)
His mind and senses were captivated by the deceptions of unchaste women through conversations held in private,
and by the sweet, lisping chatter of young children.
In houses characterized by deceptive practices and governed by the machinery of suffering, the householder remains unwearied; while applying remedies for suffering, he regards them as happiness.

Śrīdhara: He describes the state of having evil intentions: "He whose self and senses are captivated. By what means? By that which is fashioned in secret even with unchaste women (*puṃścalī*), consisting of sexual union and the like;
and by the chatter of sweet-talking children. This connects with the subsequent phrase, "he considers it to be happiness."
8. "Deceits" refers to those dharmas, which are dominated by suffering, that abound in financial hypocrisy and the like. 9.
The sequence of composition: "ākṣiptātmā" constitutes a pair of verses (yugmaka). ||8||

Viśvanātha: "Kūṭas" refers to those doctrines in which there is an abundance of deceit regarding wealth and other such faults, and which consist primarily of suffering within the systems of suffering. ||9||
For he who, by means of wealth acquired through grave violence,
nourishes those whose support causes him— who eats only the remnants— to sink downward himself.

Śrīdhara: He nourishes those by whose nourishment he himself sinks downward; thus, even enjoyment is difficult for him to obtain—this is the meaning of the term "Śeṣabhuj" (the consumer of the remnants). ||10||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "One who eats the remnants" means one who eats what remains after [others] have eaten; thus, the meaning is that even the enjoyment of food is difficult for him to obtain. ||10||
When his livelihood is being destroyed despite repeated efforts to restore it,
the weak man, overcome by greed, develops a longing for the wealth of others.
Śrīdhara: *Vārtā* means livelihood. *Niḥsattvaḥ* means powerless. Regarding *parārthe parasve*, the sequence of words has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: *Vārtā* means livelihood. ||11||
Incapable of supporting his family, unfortunate, and of futile effort,
the fool— deprived of fortune and wretched— sighs while lost in anxious thought.
Śrīdhara: "Akalpa" means incapable or incompetent. ||12||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Meditating on the means for the livelihood of his sons and others. ||12||
In this way, when he is no longer able to support himself, his wife and others no longer respect him as they did before, just as farmers treat an old ox.
A *madhvaḥ* is considered a *kīnāśa*, that is, a cultivator. ||13||
Śrīdhara: They do not show the same respect as they did before. *Kīnāśāḥ* means miserly farmers; *gojaram* means an old bull. (13)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: *Kīnāśa* refers to farmers; *gojara* refers to an old bull. ||13||
There too, without having yet conceived world-weariness, he is supported by those who support him;
having acquired deformity through old age, he faces death within his home.

He remains as if disregarding what is offered, like a house-guardian taking his food; he is like one afflicted by illness, with a non-blazing digestive fire, eating little and exerting himself little.
Śrīdhara: "Being nourished" means being sustained. (14) "Having disregarded" means having cast aside with contempt; "placed near" means thrown close by.
"House-guardian" refers to a dog. "Taking" means eating. "Afflicted with disease" means sick. (15)
The sequential arrangement: "In that case also," etc., [consists of] one and a half verses. ||14||

Viśvanātha: Previously supported by his sons and others who were maintained by him, he now describes the manner of their maintenance: "Disregarding them with contempt, eating like a house-dog that has been thrown [food] before it, he becomes afflicted with disease. (1415)
As the breath departs with great difficulty due to the channels being obstructed by phlegm,
the patient suffers from cough, labored breathing, and exhaustion, and makes a gurgling sound in the throat.
One should know that *madhvaḥ* means "upward movement" or "rising. ||16||

Śrīdhara: *Uttāra* means with eyes protruding outward; one whose channels, which serve as the pathways [for breath], are obstructed by phlegm; one who has exerted himself through coughing and labored breathing; and one who makes a wheezing sound (*ghuraghura*). ||16||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By the cause of the upward-moving wind—which rises upwards with an excess of *kāśa* and so forth, and by means of the channels of the *nāḍīs* obstructed by phlegm—the pupil (*tārā*) of the eye is turned upward (*udvartitā*).
He who makes the sound "ghuraghura. ||16||
Lying down, surrounded by his own kinsmen who are lamenting,
though being addressed, he says nothing, having fallen under the power of the noose of Time.
Śrīdhara: "Parivīta" means surrounded or encircled. Viśvanātha: [This term] is not explained.
Thus, one whose mind is occupied with the maintenance of the family and who has not conquered his senses...
He dies while his own kinsmen weep, his mind afflicted by intense pain.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [explain]: *astadhīḥ* means one whose intellect is lost. ||18||
The sequence of composition has not been explained.
Then the two terrifying messengers of Yama, with eyes like those of a *sarabha*, arrived;
seeing them, his heart was struck with fear and he discharged excrement and urine.

Śrīdhara: For one who has died, there are two destinies according to their merit and demerit. Among these, he describes the destiny of the sinful with the words beginning "the messengers of Yama" until the end of the verse. Having seen those two, whose gaze was impetuous and full of wrath... (19)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He describes the destiny of the deceased, the sinful soul—[with the words] "the two messengers of Yama. As he is dying, [they] envelop him in a body of torment, bind him with nooses, and [seize him] by the neck with force.
Just as royal officers punish one who has traveled a long distance [to evade them], so too [should one punish] according to the duration [of the offense].
Śrīdhara: Having turned back, that is, having restrained [the mind]. ||20||
The sequence of composition: having enveloped him in a body of torment and entered it, they "confine" him; this is the meaning.
The words "they lead those two" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. ||20||

Viśvanātha: Having extracted him from the gross body and having caused him to enter a body consisting of torment, they lead him—meaning they cause him to reach—the two [destinies], having surrounded and restrained him. ||20||
With his heart pierced by those two, trembling from their threats, he was devoured by dogs on the road; afflicted, he recollected his own past sin.
Overcome by hunger and thirst, scorched on the path of hot sand by the sun, forest fires,
and winds, he was beaten with a whip upon his back with great difficulty.
Even one who is powerless moves about in water that has no resting place.

Śrīdhara: Whose heart was pierced by their threats; he, being distressed, wandered about—this is the connection with the second [verse]. (21) Enveloped and pervaded by hunger and thirst; in which [desert] the sand was heated; from which the hermitage—a place of rest—and water had departed. (22)
The sequential arrangement: "of those two" constitutes a couplet. ||21||
Viśvanātha: [The king], remembering his own sin through their threats—that "this is the fruit of that very sin"—[traveled] on a path devoid of resting places and water. ||21||
Falling here and there, exhausted and fainting, he rose again only to be swiftly led by the evil path to the abode of Yama.
Śrīdhara: He is led to the abode of Yama. ||23||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Having traveled ninety-nine thousand yojanas along the path in either three or two *muhūrtas*, one is led to undergo the torments of hell.
Śrīdhara says: He states a specific detail regarding that very point: "Having been led by two [messengers] for ninety-nine thousand yojanas belonging to the path, when there is an excess of sin. (24)
The sequence of arrangement: "of the leagues" constitutes a group of four [verses]. ||24||
Viśvanātha: [He was led] ninety thousand yojanas—ninety thousand plus [something]—belonging to the path; having been led there in just two muhūrtas due to an excess of sin. ||24||
Setting one's own limbs on fire by wrapping them with flaming torches and the like,
or the eating of one's own flesh, whether cut by oneself or provided by another.

Śrīdhara: He shows the torments briefly in four [verses]. "Incineration" means reaching a state of blazing. "Consuming one's own flesh"—the meaning is that one eats one's own flesh, whether cut by oneself or cut by another. (25)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states the very tortures—“ādīpana” (setting on fire), “prajvalana” (blazing), and so forth—with the connection being “he undergoes these. [The body] is cut or severed by oneself, in front, or by another. ||25||
While still alive, there shall be the extraction of his entrails by dogs and vultures in the abode of Yama,
and he shall suffer self-destruction through being bitten by snakes, scorpions, gadflies, and other such creatures.
Śrīdhara: "Ātmano vaiśasam" means the suffering of oneself. ||26||

The sequence of composition: "uddhāram" is the accepted reading. By connecting it with "prāpnoti" (he attains), the word "pīḍām" (suffering) may also be explained as being in the accusative case, since this is the general rule. ||26||
Viśvanātha: "Vaiśasam" means suffering or affliction. ||26||
Cutting them limb from limb, causing elephants and others to be split apart,
felling them from mountain peaks, and confining them in waters or pits.
Śrīdhara: *Bhidāpanam* means causing the attainment of division. ||27||
The sequence of composition: *kṛntana* means cutting (*kartana*). ||27||
Viśvanātha: *Bhidāyāḥ* means of splitting or tearing apart; *āpannam* means reaching or attaining. ||27||
The tortures such as Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Raurava, and the rest,
which are fashioned through mutual union— whether a man or a woman experiences them.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not commented [on this].
Kramasaṃdarbha: "And he experiences those torments. Regarding the phrase "through mutual association":
because of the context of the most wicked householder, it follows that both the man and the woman would become most wicked.
Mutual attachment is the cause of an excess of evil. ||28||
In this very place, O Mother, they declare that there is both hell and heaven;
for those very torments that belong to hell are indeed observed here as well.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: the word *eva* in the phrase *atraiva* signifies proximity—the *Śabdanirṇaya* states that "the word *eva* is restrictive in the sense of proximity as well as in the sense of primacy"—thus the meaning here is "it exists even here. ||29||
Śrīdhara: Nor is this impossible, for it is observed even here; thus he says, "Therefore indeed," which refers to the sequence of the composition [of the text]. It has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Nor is this impossible, for even here, in the case of royal punishment, there are some...

Because both the tortures such as being cut limb from limb and the enjoyment of pleasures such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and ointments are seen [in this very world], he says: "Right here," and so forth:
"Thus, while maintaining a family, or even merely filling his own belly..."
Having abandoned both in this world, after death one experiences such a fruit as that.
Śrīdhara: Both [mean] one's own family and one's own body. ||30||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Both [mean] "family" and "belly. *Pretya* means having died. ||30||
Alone one enters the darkness, leaving behind this body of one's own,
with the provisions for the journey consisting of merit and its opposite— provisions that were acquired through harm done to living beings.

Śrīdhara: Many enjoy wealth acquired through sin, yet the doer alone goes to hell; thus he says, "The one. Having abandoned right here in this world his gross physical body—which was nourished by injury to living beings—he possesses as his travel-provisions (pātheya) only that which is other than merit, namely sin, to be experienced [in the hereafter]. (31)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He for whom the only provisions (*pātheya*) for the journey of death are "other than virtue," that is, sin alone;
having abandoned that gross physical body which was nourished by injury to living beings.
A man suffers in hell for the impurity acquired through fate by supporting his family, like one who is distressed after having lost his wealth.
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But let him go, having abandoned even his sin. To this he says: "By destiny," etc.
He experiences the impurity—the sin—of that maintenance of his family, which was brought about by destiny, that is, by the Lord. ||32||

The sequence of the argument: Even though it is said that [the world] is "by fate" (daiva), this does not imply the cruelty of the Lord (īśvara); for according to the maxim, "The Lord is to be viewed like the rain-cloud," [he is impartial]. ||32||
Viśvanātha: He alone experiences the stain—the impurity—brought upon that sinful sustainer of his family by fate, like one whose wealth has been stolen, even while separated from his family. ||32||
For the living being who, eager to maintain a household, relies solely on unrighteousness, goes to Andhatāmisra, the final abode of darkness.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely the maintenance of one's family is indeed enjoined; to this he replies with the words "by means of what is solely... The "final station" of darkness refers to the place of hell. ||33||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: The place or abode of *tamas*, which is hell. ||33||
Having traversed in due order all the various torments and states of suffering existing below the world of men, he would return here again, purified.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he describes the manner of attaining a human body:

having sequentially experienced all those torments that exist prior to—that is, below—the attainment of the human world, namely the human body—and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the wombs of dogs, pigs, and so forth—all of these having been undergone through experience.
The meaning is that, having become pure with his sins exhausted, he attains human status once again in this world. ||34||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "As many torments as there are"—by the word "as many," those births such as dogs, pigs, and so forth are meant;
having reached them in succession and having his sins exhausted through experience, being purified, he shall again attain the state of a human being.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, appropriately joined to the virtuous, in this *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord.

Thus ends the chapter titled "The Ripening of Karma" within the Kāpileya section of the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, in the Third Book of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, the compendium of the Pāramahaṃsa school composed by Vyāsa.
Chapter Thirty. Chapter Thirty-one:
The Course of the Soul in the Discourse between Vidura and Maitreya concerning the Son of Kapila.
The Blessed Lord said:
Driven by past action and guided by destiny, the living being,
taking refuge in a drop of the male's semen, enters the womb of a woman for the sake of obtaining a body.
Śrīdhara:
In the thirty-first [chapter], the royal path (rājasī gati) is described, wherein the attainment of human birth in this world through a mixture of merit and demerit occurs in the intermediate state.
It was stated previously that "he may return here again" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.30.34); this very point is now shown in detail.
By means of action performed in the past, he enters into that which has the Divine—the Lord—as its very eye, its leader, and its impeller. ||1||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha:
In the thirty-first [chapter], [the topics are] the sufferings of the womb, birth, childhood, and youth.
By speaking in this very way, devotion to the Jīva is shown even while in the womb.

Regarding the statement, "He may return here again" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.30.34), he shows the manner of that: by means of past action (*karman*), which has the divine Lord (*īśvara*) as its very guide—that is, its leader and impeller—he enters [into the womb]. ||1||
In one night it becomes the *kalala*; in five nights, the *budbuda*;
in ten days, the *karkandhū*; and after that, the *peśī* or the *aṇḍa*.
"Madhva says: The various types of fetal development will arise from the differentiation of karma;
therefore, various configurations of the fetus are described in the treatise. Thus [ends the section] on the six qualities. 2.

Śrīdhara: The *kalala* is the mixture of semen and blood; the *budbuda* is globular in shape; the *karkandhu* is the fruit of the jujube tree, which is firm and shaped like it; the *peśī* has the form of a lump of flesh;
or the *aṇḍa* occurs within the womb.
The sequential arrangement: "the *kalala*. Here, the etymological explanation (*nirukta*) should be cited. ||2||

Viśvanātha: *Kalala* is the mixture of semen and blood. *Budbuda* is shaped like a bubble. *Karkandhu* is the shape of a jujube fruit (*badarī*). *Kaṭhina* is the *peśī*, a mass of flesh that is the material cause of the placenta (*jarāyu*). *Aṇḍa* refers to the egg-form found in the wombs of birds and other such creatures. ||2||
In one month, however, the head is formed; in two months, the body with its limbs such as arms and feet;
and in three months, the nails, hair, bones, skin, and the emergence of the genitals and apertures.
Śrīdhara: The "body" (vigraha) is the division of the limbs, such as the arms and feet; and the "signs" (liṅga) are the apertures, along with their origin. ||3||
Kramasaṃdarbha: not explained. Viśvanātha: The division (*vigraha*) by two months is the analysis (*vibhāga*). ||3||
By four [elements] the seven constituents arise; by five, hunger and thirst;
by six, enveloped by the fetal membrane, it wanders in the right side of the womb.
Śrīdhara: Enveloped, that is, covered by the *jarāyu*, the membrane surrounding the embryo. ||4||

The sequence of arrangement: "In the right side, in the womb. Because this was stated with reference to a male, it is well known that a male fetus is in the right [side] and a female fetus is in the left. ||4||

Viśvanātha: "Enveloped by the *jarāyu*," meaning covered by the fetal membrane. "In the right side of the womb" is stated because the subject under discussion is the male; it is well known that a male fetus is in the right and a female fetus is in the left. ||4||
Nourished by the food, drink, and other substances consumed by his mother,
that creature lies within the pit of feces and urine in the birthplace of living beings, without the mother's consent.

Śrīdhara: He whose bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*) increase through the food, drink, and so forth consumed and eaten by his mother; he lies in that disagreeable pit which is the source of living beings (*jantūnām saṃbhavaḥ*). And so it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
A channel named Āpyāyinī is attached to his navel;
likewise, it becomes connected within the cavity of the intestines of women.
In this way, what has been eaten and drunk by women passes into the womb;
indeed, the living being, its body nourished by those [nutrients], attains growth. Thus [ends verse 5].
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Regarding the root *edh* [in the term *edhaddhātu*]: "The channel named Āpyāyanī is fastened to it at the navel."
Likewise, in women, it arises bound within the cavity of the intestines.

"Thus, according to the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: 'The food and drink consumed by women circulate likewise within the womb; and when his body has been nourished therein, that creature attains consciousness. [Furthermore:
'With all his limbs torn by worms, due to his extreme delicacy, at every moment...'"
He suffers great affliction and repeatedly falls into a swoon due to those hungry beings there.
Śrīdhara: Whose entire body was wounded by the worms dwelling there as they fed upon him, due to his extreme delicacy and tenderness. (6)

The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon [here]. [The fetus] is afflicted by all the pains arising from every limb when touched by the pungent, sharp, hot, salty, dry, sour, and other intense substances consumed by the mother.
Enveloped by the fetal membrane and surrounded on the outside by the intestines,
he remains with his head tucked toward his belly, his back, head, and neck bent,
unable to move his own limbs like a bird in a cage.
Śrīdhara: [He is] with intense, unbearable [pains]; he whose pain has arisen in all his limbs. "He remains" is the connection with what follows.
By the *ulba*, that is, the *jarāyu* (chorion). He whose back and neck (*śirodharā*) are bent, that is, become crooked.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: By "ulbaṇaiḥ" is meant "unbearable. By "ulbena" is meant "by the placenta (jarāyu).
He remains with his back and neck curved. "Śakunta" means a bird. ||78||
In that state, having regained mindfulness by chance and remembering the karma produced over hundreds of births,
what happiness indeed can one find while breathing this long, final breath?
Śrīdhara: By fate—that is, by the force of previous karma—he was one who had regained his memory. Remaining there, he stayed for a long time, in a state of distress and without drawing breath. ||9||
The sequential composition: remembering for a long time, extending over a prolonged duration, in such a way that it is without interruption of breath. ||9||
Viśvanātha: By fate—that is, by the power of past karma—he remembers [it] for a long time, extending over a great duration, in such a way that there is no pause in his recollection. ||9||
Having attained consciousness from the seventh month onward, though trembling,
he does not remain in one place due to the winds of birth, like a brother born of excrement.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [comment]: "He is shaken by winds that cause birth; he is a 'co-uterine' one, born from the same womb, a worm produced from excrement. (10)
The sequence of events: Trembling and shaken, unable to remain still in one place,
the terrified seer Saptavadhri, with palms joined in reverence,
praised with faltering words that Lord by whom he had been cast into his belly.

Regarding the word *madhvaḥ*: Śrīdhara states in the *Śabdanirṇaya* that "the senses (*indriyāṇi*) are called *vadhrayaḥ*, and they are also termed *hṛṣīkāṇi*. [The term] *nāthamānaḥ* means "begging" or "suffering"; the seer (*ṛṣiḥ*) here is one who perceives the body as the self. He is "afraid" (*bhītaḥ*) of dwelling again in a womb. [The word *saptavadhrayaḥ* refers to] one whose seven *vadhrayaḥ* are the constituent elements (*dhātavaḥ*) that act as bonds.
He, with a distressed and agitated [mind]. ||11||

The sequential arrangement is as follows: "nāthamāna" (seeking protection). The intended meaning is this: it has already been illustrated by the words of Śrī Śaunaka that even a single instance of worship makes the entirety of one's life fruitful, as stated in the passage beginning with "āyur harati vai puṃsām" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.3.17). This applies even through a semblance of devotion.
The power of devotion to destroy sin is seen in the case of Ajāmila and others;

likewise, it is heard in scripture that devotion is the cause for attaining the supreme goal through the destruction of all karma and other obstacles with very little effort. As stated in the *Laghu-bhāgavatam*:
"Whatever sin is present, whatever has passed, and whatever is yet to come—
all that is quickly consumed by the chanting of the name of Govinda.
Likewise, in that context, there is the causal efficacy of a connection with devotion to Him in any manner whatsoever.
It is seen [in scripture]. In the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"That God, when propitiated, shall grant liberation in whatever manner;
even if he does not intend it, O twice-born, the consumer of oblations (fire) burns when touched."
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara: "By the mere initiation [into the worship] of Kṛṣṇa, men indeed attain liberation;
how much more so those men who always worship Acyuta with devotion? Thus it is said.
In the *Bṛhannāradīya*: "Even those who perform the worship of Viṣṇu even once, though unintentionally, for them the bondage of worldly existence never arises. (*Nāradīya Purāṇa* 36.58)
In the *Pādme Devadyutistuti*:
"He who, unwearied, should utter the name of Nārāyaṇa even once, having become pure in his inner self, attains liberation. Thus it is said.
In the *Itihāsasamuccaya*, in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Puṇḍarīka:
"Even those who are cruel, of wicked conduct, and always devoted to sinful behavior,
go to the supreme abode if they take refuge at the feet of Nārāyaṇa."
"Vaiṣṇavas, whose impurities have been removed, are not tainted by sin;
they purify all worlds like the risen thousand-rayed sun.
For this very reason, there is the statement of the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"Whoever has surrendered but once and entreats, saying 'I am yours,' to him I grant fearlessness at all times; this is the vow of Hari.
Thus says Śrī Rāmacandra in the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa.
"Even if one has taken refuge only once and pleads, 'I am yours,' I grant fearlessness to all beings; this is the vow of Hari.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*:

"The life of one devoted to Viṣṇu for even five days is indeed superior to a thousand kalpas of one devoid of devotion to Keśava. And: "When one, fallen into terrible worldly existence, involuntarily utters His name... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.1.14).
The words of Śaunaka and others state: "O Blessed One, this is indeed not impossible" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.16.44).
Furthermore, there are the words of Citraketu and others.
Therefore, as for the praise of the Lord that is heard here regarding the living being situated within the womb, it belongs to that very [being].

Samsara is also described therein; it is stated that this description is made in the singular because of the unity of the genus (*jāti*). In reality, however, only a certain fortunate individual praises [the Lord] and he alone crosses over. Knowledge of the Blessed One does not arise for everyone. And likewise, according to the etymological school (*nairukta*), there are three types.

People are found—some remember only their successive previous births; some practice Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and so forth; but others [remember] the Supreme Person. As it is stated in that very same work, after reading: "In the ninth month, he becomes complete in all his limbs" (Nirukta 13.19), [it says] regarding one who has died...

And again I am born, and again I am dead; such is the alternative recitation for that meditation: "The creature, being afflicted and facing downwards, should practice Sāṅkhya-yoga, or [meditate upon] the Puruṣa as the twenty-fifth principle."
And so it is said: "Then, in the tenth month, he is born," and so forth.
Here, by the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or a person," it is understood that the knowledge of the Blessed One belongs only to some [devotees].
Furthermore, the efficacy of devotion throughout all stages of life has been described.

Description as a unity despite plurality is seen elsewhere as well; for example, in the third [chapter], even while describing the creation of the *pādakalpa*, there is a description of the creation of Sanaka and others who were created during the *brāhmakalpa*. And in the *Ṭīkā*:
This statement is joined [to the context] by identifying it with the similarity of merely describing the creation performed by Brahmā;

and it is also like the account of the Śrī Varāha incarnation. Therein, at the beginning of the first Manvantara, when the earth was submerged, the Śrī Varāha descended from the nose of Brahmā, and while lifting her up, he engaged in battle with Hiraṇyākṣa.

It is described that he did so; and Hiraṇyākṣa was born of Diti, the daughter of Dakṣa of the Pracetas lineage, at the conclusion of the sixth Manvantara. Therefore, such a description [is appropriate].
This is logically consistent only with the intention to express identity through the mere act of descending, just as [the sun's reflection] is identical to its mere immersion in water;
likewise, it must be understood here that one individual soul merely praises while another transmigrates.
In this regard, as before, devotion is seen to be the indirect cause for attaining the supreme goal.
In the *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*, within the section on the greatness of hoisting the flag (*dhvajāropaṇa-māhātmya*), it is stated:
"By those devoted to the service of ascetics who are devotees of Viṣṇu..."
"Even those who have merely looked upon him attain the supreme goal, even if they are sinners.
Thus it is said in the *Śrī Viṣṇudharma*:
"A hundred future generations and likewise a hundred past generations of one's lineage [are saved]."
Causing the temple of the Blessed One to be built, he leads [himself] to the state of the world of Acyuta.
"Those men who shall be born and those who have passed away in this lineage throughout the duration of the kalpa—
he delivers them all by establishing an image of Lord Hari.
This is the command of Yama to his messengers:
"By that devotion to the Blessed One through which the image of Vāsudeva was commissioned,
nine times ten thousand born in his lineage have transgressed your command.
Thus he spoke.
"O sinless one, you have been purified by twenty-one ancestors together with your forefathers,
since you, O virtuous one, were born into this family as its very purifier. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.10.18) "By twenty-one ancestors belonging to his previous births from former kalpas."

However, in this present birth, Hiraṇyakaśipu, Kaśyapa, Marīci, and Brahmā alone are his fathers. [At the beginning of the introduction, there is an additional reading in some manuscripts: "In the same way here too, it should be inferred that one individual soul praises while another transmigrates."]
The suffix *liṅ* in the word *stuvīta* expresses possibility (*sambhāvanā*).

Consequently, the meaning is as follows: there might be some sage there; if, by virtue of fortune produced through an accidental association with a great soul of the past, he should become a beholder of the Blessed Lord, then...

"He also praises" (stauty api). For this very reason, referring specifically to one past individual soul endowed with such fortune, there is the designation using both the singular number and the perfect tense suffix (*liṭ*) in the expression "the soul said" (*jīva uvāca*).
However, if one intended to express the soul in its general temporal state, the form "the soul speaks" (*jīvo vadati*) alone would be appropriate. ||11||

Viśvanātha: The seer, who perceives the Self, being afraid of worldly existence, addresses the Lord while praying for a blessing upon himself, saying, "May the grace of the Blessed One be upon me," and noting that the seven gates are the very bonds.

"He who [possesses] the elements (dhātavaḥ) is he. "He should praise him with a distressed (viklavayā), that is, agitated mind," because there is no possibility of piercing [the fetus] and so forth while in the womb; thus, the optative (liṅ) is used in the sense of the result according to the rule *hetuhetumator liṅ*. Consequently, the meaning is: "Whoever would worship the Blessed One, he should praise Him even in the womb," whereas another living being, however, would not praise Him.
It is obtained. For this very living being, transmigration will be described and has been described in its true state, but not even for one who praises the Blessed Lord.
"Even those who perform the worship of Viṣṇu but once, even without desire..."

"For them, the bondage of existence never arises at any time" [Nā.pa. 36.58]. And: "To him who, having approached but once, entreats, 'I am yours,' I grant him fearlessness forever; this is the vow of Hari," and so forth.

Because it would contradict thousands of other scriptural statements, for this very reason, the present tense was not employed in the manner of "the soul dwelling for ten months praises Hari"— as one might say "he sleeps in a pit of feces and urine," "he falls into a swoon," or "he sits having placed his head"— but rather, it is said, "the soul spoke" (*jīva uvāca*).
This is indeed a usage in the past tense. By this, it is indicated that some devotee living in a previous birth was thus praising Hari while in the womb, but not everyone;
for this very reason, the etymologists also recite: "In the ninth month, he becomes complete in all his limbs" (Nirukta 13.19).
Having recited thus, there is another reading for that meditation: "I have died and been born again; I have been born and died again," and so forth:
"The creature, being afflicted, is indeed joined [to suffering] with its face turned downward."
One should thoroughly practice Sāṅkhya-yoga, or [meditate upon] the Puruṣa consisting of twenty-five principles.
And thus: "Then, in the tenth month, he is born," and so forth.

Regarding the statement from the *Garuḍopaniṣad*, "Or a man," by the force of the word "or" (*vā*), one who is a performer of ritual action (*karmī*) remembers only his previous births, such as "I, the living being, having died, am born again. Another [remembers]...

A knower of the Sāṅkhya system [meditates on] Sāṅkhya, a certain yogi [meditates on] Yoga, and a devotee [meditates on] the Supreme Lord as the twenty-fifth Puruṣa beyond the twenty-fourfold Pradhāna; for it is a logical principle that what has been practiced in previous lives manifests even within the womb. ||11||
Jantu said:
"The lotus-foot of Him who, desiring to protect the world that had approached Him, assumed various bodies on earth, moves upon the ground."
Therefore, I go for refuge to Him who is fearless from all sides, by whom such a destiny, befitting the wicked, has been shown to me.

Śrīdhara: I, such as I am, take refuge in the lotus feet of the Blessed One—which are fearless from any quarter and which He assumed through His own will in various forms to protect the world that has approached Him for shelter. [The phrase] "moving upon the earth" is intended to refer to the incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. By whom [this grace was shown], even to one like me who is unworthy and unfit for such a state.
The state characterized by dwelling in the womb has been shown for him. ||12||

The sequence of the composition: "Moving upon the earth. Indeed, at that time, due to the incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there is here a sign of one who has assumed various bodies; for he alone is the source of all incarnations. And this statement of Śrī Kapila refers to his incarnation during a previous kalpa, concerning those who were non-existent [in the present sense] and perishing through supreme calamities.

By whom such a state—characterized by his own spontaneous manifestation and capable of uprooting [my suffering]—was seen, that is, revealed, as befitting me; or rather, such a state consisting of suffering was made the object of his compassionate gaze as befitting me, a wicked person. Otherwise, this manifestation of his would not have occurred.
The sense is that it must indeed be so. ||12||

Viśvanātha: The phrase "moving upon the earth" is intended to refer to the incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; this is the view of the venerable teacher (Svāmīcaraṇa). The indicative mark (*liṅga*) here is the expression "having assumed various bodies," because he alone is the source of all incarnations. Furthermore, this statement by Kapila refers to that particular incarnation belonging to a previous *kalpa*; such is the context. It is of this nature...
The state characterized by dwelling in the ocean of suffering within the womb was indeed appropriate for me, an unrighteous person, and it has been shown;

or rather, it has been "seen" (adarśi) in the sense that it has become the object of his compassionate gaze, for otherwise such a manifestation of him toward one as most sinful as I would not be possible—this is the intended meaning. ||12||
But he who here remains as if bound, his self veiled by karmas, having resorted to the illusion (*māyā*) consisting of the elements, senses, and the subconscious (*āśaya*),
[yet abides in that which is] pure, changeless, and indivisible consciousness— [he is the liberated one].
I bow to that which has taken its abode within the heart being scorched by heat.

Śrīdhara: Now, in response to the inquiry—"Who is this one whom you go for refuge? Or what is the distinction between you and him, by virtue of which there exists the relationship of served and server?"—he says: "In this context, having taken recourse to, that is, having relied upon, Māyā—which consists of the elements, the senses, and the internal organ (āśaya), and which has transformed into the form of a body—within the mother’s body, by means of karmas..."

I am he who remains as if his true nature were veiled and as if bound; yet I bow to him who remains right here [in this very state]. To the question "In what manner? he shows the distinction indicated by the word "tu" (but): though situated and perceived within the heart that is being scorched, he is thus unchanging. Why? Because he is pure.
It is without limiting adjuncts. Why is that? Because it is one whose consciousness is undivided. ||13||
The sequence of the composition: Even though He resides within one's own heart while it is being heated [by spiritual practice], He does not manifest;

[the author] shows that very sudden manifestation with the words "But he who... Here, because He co-exists with the individual soul (jīva) within a body such as mine, He is as if bound by its karmas. Because He does not manifest within that [body], [He is affected] by them.
The meaning of the word "tu" (but) is that he remains as if his self were veiled, but unlike me, he is not actually bound.

Having done what? Having resorted to and set in motion *māyā*. Therefore, for him who is the initiator of *māyā*, there is no bondage of karma and so forth; rather, the point is that this is merely a defect of perception belonging to those lacking discrimination.

In reality, however, "pure" and so forth means that which has been concluded or experienced. Alternatively, "here" (atra) means "abundantly" (bhūri), because he imitates [the world] in various ways at the time of his descent. As it is said: "Know him to be Kṛṣṇa" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.55], and so on. ||13||

Viśvanātha, remembering the marvelous pastimes and compassion of his own Lord, said with wonder: "Does He indeed abide here within the very bodies of miserable creatures like us, which consist of manifold sufferings, for the sake of protecting us? Or rather,"
The sense is: "We do not know [how this occurs] by way of His spontaneous play. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "I bow to Him.

He says: "While I am experiencing the fruit of my own evil deeds, it is entirely fitting that I remain here bound by karma; but how is it that He remains even as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) here in this foul-smelling great hell?"

As if bound by karmas, yet not actually bound; because my lotus feet move upon the ground of Vṛndāvana, I am as one whose self is covered, and likewise as one whose true nature is covered by the body, yet not actually covered. By the very reasoning already stated, having done what? [Having overcome] Māyā, which consists of the elements and so forth.
"Having relied upon its own power, it sets [the world] in motion.
Now, one might object: "In that case, since it relies on *māyā*, would not impurity and transformation follow as logical consequences?
To this he says: "It is pure and changeless. The reason for this is: "It is undivided consciousness, like my own knowledge."
The meaning is that his knowledge cannot be shattered by illusion (*māyā*).

Now, one might ask: "How is this understood by you? To this he replies: "Since he, remaining within this heart that is being tormented on all sides, has bestowed such knowledge even upon me—how could his knowledge be shattered?"
It may be so. ||13||
I am that conscious Self, distinct from the body composed of the five elements, which is covered by the objects and qualities of the senses;
by that [Self], I [realize] that very Seer whose greatness is unimpeded.
I bow to the Supreme Person, who is beyond both primordial nature and the individual soul.

Śrīdhara: But surely you too are in reality pure, according to such scriptural texts as, "For this person is unattached. So how is there this distinction between the two of you? To that he says: He who is concealed—falsely and not in reality—within the body composed of the five elements; for by that [concealment]...

I bow to Him who is devoid of a body, unattached, and whose nature consists of the senses, the qualities, the objects, and consciousness—meaning He whose essence is composed of the senses, the qualities, the objects, and the reflection of consciousness—and whose majesty remains unobscured by that very body. How so? "Unobscured" (avikuṇṭha) means not covered (avaguṇṭha).

The meaning is: he whose greatness has its covering or veil dissolved by recitation (*pāṭha*). The reason for this is that he is the supreme controller of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Why? Because he is the *ṛṣi*, which means the omniscient one;
the sense is that he possesses the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*). The implication is that the distinction between them is created by knowledge and ignorance (*vidyā-avidyā*). ||14||
The sequential arrangement: Thus, he connects [the text] regarding bondage, non-bondage, and so forth with the word "he" (*yaḥ*).

Just as I am concealed within the body, so too, because of his entry into it by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), he is concealed therein yet remains detached, devoid of contact with it. The reason for his own lack of contact with it is stated: "by the senses," etc.
He states the distinction [between them] by virtue of his not being touched by that [matter], using the word "by him" (*tena*).

Because he is untouched by the body, senses, and so forth, he is "unobstructed" (*avikuṇṭha*) and so on. The sense is: "of us two," because of the difference in the essential natures of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, which are respectively fit to be touched by ignorance (*avidyā*) and unfit to be so touched.

Or rather: that which consists of the senses, qualities, objects, and consciousness, whose nature is consciousness superimposed upon the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), and which was thus concealed and covered within the body composed of the five elements by that very manner— namely, through its own ignorance of the Lord and so forth— I am that same [self], now devoid of that aforementioned Lord.
Therefore, I bow to Him who has attained the state of being turned away from [the world], yet who suddenly manifests within my mind;

I praise Him because He consists of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). In this regard, he demonstrates his own unworthiness in extolling His majesty with the words beginning "unobstructed" (*avikuṇṭha*). [He praises Him as] the Sage (*ṛṣi*), the teacher even of Brahmā and others, and [beyond] primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
And the supreme ultimate reality of that Great Person who perceives it is that self-existent Blessed One named Śrī Kṛṣṇa in human form; this is the meaning. ||14||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But if this is so, how could He remain here in this body? To this He says: I am that Self whose very nature (svarūpa) is such that it is devoid of the body here, and whose consciousness (cit-caitanya) resides in those very things—the senses, the qualities, and the objects—even as I remain hidden within this body.

Likewise, the meaning is that he who stands here devoid [of attributes] is as if not standing at all. For that reason, his majesty (*mahiman*) is not "dulled" (*kuṇṭha*) by any particular distinction. According to the reading *avaguṇṭha*, following the opinion of Bhāguri, the elision of the vowel *a* occurs in this compound; thus, it means one whose majesty is "unveiled" (*avaguṇṭha*), that is, whose sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is unobscured.
Beyond primordial nature (prakṛti) and its witness, the Great Person (mahāpuruṣa), is the supreme reality beyond both of them—the Supreme Being, Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||14||
While wandering on this worldly path, which is bound by the qualities and actions of Māyā, he— having lost his memory through the exhaustion of that journey— might once again choose the world.
By what reasoning, and without the great favor [of the teacher]?
Śrīdhara: [Objection: Surely this bondage will be removed by knowledge; what is the use of saluting the Supreme Lord?

To this he says: "By whose Māyā, having lost his memory, this individual soul (jīva), wandering on the path connected with worldly existence through the exhaustion caused by it—that is, through the suffering produced by it—is [bound] from the Great..."

Without the grace of that very Lord, by what reasoning could one again choose—that is, resort to—the world as one's own true nature? He characterizes the path as being one where vast actions caused by the qualities (guṇas) are intense fetters; [this is so] without the favor of the Lord.
The meaning is that, due to the absence of knowledge, he alone is to be served. ||15||

The sequence of the composition: having raised the doubt that one might depart without being connected [to the Lord] and thus perform worship, he speaks of its rarity, beginning with "That which... (yad). The meaning is as follows: for that world [of the Lord], who is your own refuge—as expressed in the words "by whose grace" (*yasya mañjayā*) and so forth—the cause of attaining it again is, first of all, the great grace [of the Lord] alone, and that is difficult to obtain.

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But how was such devotion obtained by you? To this, he says that the cause for obtaining such devotion is indeed the great grace [of the Lord], beginning with the words "yad" (when). "By that"—meaning by the cause of the exhaustion from wandering upon His path—"this person," one such as myself, has lost his memory.

Without a great favor, by what logic could one choose the world of the Blessed One as one's desired boon? Indeed, by no means at all. Therefore, this is surely the manifestation of the grace of my own guru, who was a devotee of Kṛṣṇa in a previous birth.
The meaning is: "Devotion to Kṛṣṇa. ||15||
Which god was it that bestowed this knowledge which persists throughout the three times among all things stable and moving?
Following the path of the karma of Jīvaka, [we seek] him.
May we worship [Him] for the sake of pacifying the threefold suffering.
Of the sweet things, which is the most pleasant? ||16||

Śrīdhara, establishing that the Lord alone is the giver of knowledge, says: "As for this knowledge which has the three periods of time as its object, who other than Him could have bestowed it upon me? None at all.
