But He is the God, the Lord Himself. [An objection: "Could not some other eminent living being (jīva) bestow it? [He replies: "No," saying: "In the form of a living being..."

The meaning is that we follow the path of karma; therefore, apart from that, no one else is capable [of such a task]. Having stated the impossibility of anyone else in this regard, he speaks of its possibility: "One should worship Him by whom the internal controller (antaryāmin) has been followed as a portion within both the immobile and the mobile. (16)

The sequence of the composition: Therefore, he says "knowledge" (jñānam), meaning that out of reverence for the great grace of the ancient [sages], we have now taken refuge in Him alone—who has manifested self-knowledge—in order not to forget Him; the plural number is used because of the existence of other individual souls (jīvas) common to ourselves, and He is eternal in nature throughout the three periods of time. ||16||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do you know that Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) whom you worship? [Reply: He says it is by inference (*anumāna*) alone—"That knowledge which He bestowed even upon me, the lowly"—that is to say, He held it for me and bestowed it. Who could that God be? Among the gods, who indeed...?
He by whom [the self] is inferred through the very impossibility of explaining knowledge otherwise as being primary—

that part which exists as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), shining throughout the three times (past, future, and present) and persisting among all moving and stationary beings; [he knows] the path of karma belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*).
Fallen into a pit of blood, feces, and urine within the cavity of another body, with your frame intensely scorched by the digestive fire,
you count your months while desiring to escape from here.
O Blessed One, when indeed will this one of wretched intellect attain final liberation?

Śrīdhara, making known his own suffering, says: "O Dehi! [The word *dehin* is used here. One who has fallen into that well of blood, feces, and urine within the cavity of the mother’s womb—the interior of another body—and whose body is intensely tormented there by the digestive fire; for this very reason, one whose intellect is miserable desires to emerge from that cavity.
Desiring to depart, he counts his own months, wondering: "Ah, when indeed will this sequence of steps lead me outside? This has not been explained [by others].
Viśvanātha says: "O Lord! My suffering and my happiness consist in the attainment of Your feet."

Thinking, "All this is under your control; therefore, out of extreme childhood and extreme youth, I ask something," he addressed the Blessed One with this very intention: "I am an embodied being (*dehī*) within the cavity of another body, in the hollow of my mother's womb; desiring to emerge—that is, to become separated—from this cavity, [I shall spend] my months..."

Counting thus, "This is the eighth, this is the tenth," this person of wretched intellect and perverted mind— whose vision is fixed upon his own misery and pleasure— will at some point be led out, expelled by you from here; for him, there is no capacity to endure that hardship.
The underlying sense is: "Since it is impossible [to reach you], I shall worship you from the outside. ||17||
O Lord,
may that protector of the distressed be satisfied by his own deed alone— that he was led to such a state by one as compassionate as you for ten months.
Who indeed would not join their palms in reverence toward him?

Śrīdhara: Remembering that favor rendered, he says: "By whom [such a state of knowledge was given]"—meaning by one such as you, who is incomparable. "May he himself be satisfied by his own deed alone.
The meaning is: who could possibly repay the favor done by him except through the mere joining of palms?

The sequence of the composition: "Such a state"—that is, a condition characterized by devotion to You. By the ellipsis of the word *bhavatā* (by You), it is suggested that [the Lord] is incomparable, as He acts like Himself (*bhavat-tulyena*). May He be satisfied by His own act alone. If this most wretched person is once graced by me, then how [could he not be saved]?
The meaning is: "one should abandon," having reflected upon this. ||18||
Viśvanātha: [Objection: "In that case, when will you be released? Having said this to me, why do you now instill such cruelty by saying, 'Drive you out from here even while I am still present'?
To this, she replies with shame, apprehension, a sweet tone, a portion of her body, and self-reproach: 'By whom [I was made] such as this by the gods...'"

"Even while staying in the womb for ten months, I have been made to attain a state characterized by devotion to you— a state otherwise difficult to reach— by one as exceedingly compassionate as you. By this elliptical expression (*ākṣepalabdha*) derived from the epithet "one like you," it is understood that you alone are compassionate, being similar to [the Great Compassionate One], and no other.
The figure of speech *ananvaya* (the non-comparison) has been illustrated. He says: "Even with a lifespan equal to that of Brahmā, it would be impossible for me to create a replica of this;
let him be satisfied with his own work alone. Who indeed could provide a remedy for that, other than by means of mere salutation? Who could possibly be able to do so for you? (18)
Indeed, this one who has sevenfold power beholds with his intellect that ancient Puruṣa within his own body— the one who is embodied yet bodiless, and by whose creation I have come into being.
Behold it both outside and within the heart, as if it were a well-known shrine.
Regarding *madhvaḥ*: Just as the Supreme Self is bodiless, even the body of the Supreme Self is [so considered] because it is subject to His control.

However, the knowledge of reality will arise for the gods while they are still in the womb; or else, for the most excellent sages and others, it occurs after many births. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. (19)

Śrīdhara: By the words "such a state," it is said that he has attained a knowledge distinct from other births; he describes that very distinction with the word "sees. This other [being], the seven-gated living soul (jīva), such as an animal and so forth, [perceives] pleasure and pain within its own body, that which arises in the physical frame (śārīraka).

Indeed, he alone sees [the truth]. I, however, by means of the intellect created by Him and through the knowledge bestowed by Him, became one whose body was disciplined— *dama* being an indicative term for one possessed of a body endowed with tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth— and that very same ancient, beginningless [Lord].
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "I see the Person, full both externally and within the heart. How so?
Like a mental concept (*caitya*) perceived as something not beyond the senses; the meaning is: like the enjoyer who is the locus of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
This is the sequence of the composition: by the verse beginning with "such a state" (*bhā.pu. 3.31.19*), [it is shown that this occurs] in the human species.

It has been stated that he has attained a cognition distinct from others. He clarifies that very distinction by saying, "he sees. This one, having entered the human species as Saptavadhri, while still a living embryo, [perceives] everything there through the intellect (dhiṣaṇā) produced therein.

In the existence of bodies traversed through many births, one perceives only pleasure and pain; yet another, some fortunate person, becomes a "dama-body" (one whose body is disciplined), possessing a body endowed with yoga as characterized by that [discipline]. I, however, am that very one who—though indistinguishable from those various living beings—is [defined] by the intellect bestowed [by Him].

I see that as well; and therein the etymological explanation (*nirukta*) is shown immediately after the statement concerning its cultivation, beginning with: "I have died and been born again, and having been born, I have died again" (Nirukta 13.19), followed by: "One should thoroughly practice Sāṅkhya and Yoga, or [meditate upon] the Puruṣa consisting of twenty-five principles. Regarding this, the commentators also [state]:
Furthermore, by the words "I, moreover," Viśvanātha— who is thus recognized as distinct even among the human species—
declares his own excellence through the Lord’s extraordinary grace and his distinction from others: "He sees," meaning this one who has entered the human species is the seven-gated [body].

The living being within the womb perceives only pleasure and pain through the intellect (*dhiṣaṇā*) during the formation of the body, as described in the *Śārīraka*. Yet, there is another, more fortunate one who, while remaining in his own body, becomes a wise man possessing self-control. But I am that well-known sinner, by whose creation—

Through that intellect which has been bestowed upon me, I see— I behold— that Ancient Person, the Supreme Person, the object of meditation, the presiding deity of the mind, the Lord who is to be served even by the mind, who is recognized both externally and within the heart,
and whom I perceive as if already attained through direct intuition; and here, according to the Nirukta, by the word "vā" (or).

The threefold nature of living beings has been shown immediately after the statement regarding that contemplation: "I have died and was born again; I have been born and shall die again" (Nirukta 13.19). One should practice Sāṅkhya and Yoga, or [meditate upon] the Puruṣa consisting of twenty-five principles. ||19||
Thus, O Lord, though dwelling within this dark well of a womb— a residence of manifold sufferings— I have no desire to emerge outside,
for there the divine illusion (devamāyā) assails whatever comes near.
It is because of false cognition that this wheel of saṃsāra revolves.

Śrīdhara: Expressing the agitation caused by worldly existence through the lack of discernment, he resolves upon the very path to liberation with the two verses beginning with "So, I... O All-pervading Lord! Just as [worldly life] is an abode of manifold sufferings, even while dwelling in the womb, I—who am that same person—do not wish to emerge from the womb.

The reason for this is as follows: in that place which is like a blind well, the *māyā* of you, O Lord, approaches and pervades every living being who has come forth and entered it. Following that *māyā*, false cognition—the notion of "I" regarding the body—and the wheel of worldly existence (*saṃsṛticakra*) involving relations with wife, children, and so forth, approach [the individual].
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Now, you speak thus to me out of devotion alone;
why then do you distress yourself with sorrow here, since you will inform me when you shall attain liberation?

"Right now, I shall cause [the soul] to emerge from this womb"—to this he replies, "No, no, I am not that. Wherever a living being has come forth externally, your divine Māyā approaches and pervades him;
following which, and following her, arises the false notion of "I" regarding the body, and from that, the wheel of saṃsāra. ||20||
Therefore, free from despondency, I shall quickly rescue myself from this darkness by my own effort alone,
so that this calamity with its many openings may never occur again.
May it not be that I have failed to pay homage to the feet of Viṣṇu.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, remaining right here, free from dejection and undisturbed, I shall, by means of my own friend—the intellect in the form of a charioteer—extricate myself from this darkness of saṃsāra.
May this calamity of suffering, which has many openings in the form of various wombs, not befall me.
It will be so, and it will not be so; what is your method of proof in this matter?
To that he says: "By me, those two feet of Viṣṇu have been brought near—that is, they have been made to reach my heart. (21)

The sequence of the composition: Since I have been made such a vessel of grace, therefore, by the Supreme Self Himself, our well-wisher, who has brought near—that is, caused to be present—the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who has descended there in part, as it is famously said: "Proclaim to us the heroic deeds of Him known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.1.2).
"Wherever my own feet, which are the form of Viṣṇu, [are placed], there I shall likewise uplift myself, so that [it may not happen] again," and so forth. ||21||

Viśvanātha: What, then, do you conclude? To this he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt). Remaining in that very state, even through suffering, free from dejection—that is, undisturbed—I shall, by means of this very intellect (*buddhi*) given by You which acts as my friend and charioteer, deliver myself from darkness, that is, from *saṃsāra*, just as [in the following example].
This calamity—characterized by this gross body with its many apertures and nine gates—shall not befall me;
it will not come to pass. What means do you possess for this? To that he replies:
"By whom [the feet] have been resorted to"—that is, by whom Your feet, O Viṣṇu, have been taken refuge in through remembrance, chanting, and so forth.
Kapila said:
Thus, with his mind fixed on this while still in the womb for ten months, the sage, offering praise,
is suddenly cast headlong by the winds of birth for the sake of delivery.
Śrīdhara: [The term] *daśamāsya* means one for whom ten months are the defining limit; this is an indication of the moment immediately preceding birth.
*Ṛṣi* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*). *Sadyas* means at that very instant. *Avācīna* means facing downwards. The wind is the cause of delivery. It "throws" or pushes [the soul] out. (22)

The Structural Arrangement: In this context, the phrase "the Blessed Lord said" appears in some places. That seer who perceives the Blessed Lord—such as a certain Śrī Śukadeva described in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* according to the manner previously stated—becomes one whose mind is perfected and who possesses complete knowledge of the Blessed Lord while still in the tenth month of gestation, offering praise.

Therefore, the sense is that since its greatness has already been described as a mere incidental consequence, its appearance in various worldly states such as birth and so forth need not be further described. However, regarding the "difficult-to-live" state that is now under discussion, he says—"Immediately," etc.—to indicate that one should hear again of its miserable condition: "going downwards," meaning descending into the path of saṃsāra.
The meaning is "continuing [in the womb]. When that [embryo] has reached ten months, the vital wind (*māruta*) which is the cause of birth casts it out immediately.

However, one who—like Śukadeva—is filled with the knowledge of the Blessed One, he manifests by his own independence alone; this is the meaning. But as for the individual souls (*jīvas*) situated in the intermediate state...

The intended meaning is that a gradation [of intensity] is to be understood. It should be noted here that, since there is syntactic unity (ekavākyatva), even in the first half [of the verse], only words ending in the accusative case would have been employed. ||22||

Viśvanātha: Having acted thus, one whose mind is resolved that "I shall worship Kṛṣṇa even while dwelling within the womb"—the grammatical connection being that such a person, while offering praise, becomes a seer (ṛṣi) indeed. The implication is that for him, once he has emerged from the womb, there is no further cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). As for the subject under discussion, it is precisely as stated previously.
"The soul has departed; hear now of its miserable state," he says—"at once" (*sadyas*).

The wind that causes birth, moving downward toward the lower regions of worldly existence, casts out [the soul] at once—that is, at the very moment of the tenth-month [conception]. By that [wind], even one who might be a seer (*ṛṣi*) through his own praise—[is cast out].

The meaning obtained is that [the soul] emerges from the womb even without being impelled by the winds of labor. In this context, if only a single *jīva* were intended, then in the first half-verse as well, words ending in the accusative case—such as *kṛtamatiṃ*—would have been employed; such is the structure of the composition. ||22||
Released by him, he suddenly turns head-downward in distress and emerges with great difficulty,
breathless and deprived of consciousness.
Śrīdhara: "Avasṛṣṭaḥ" means having been cast down. ||23||
The sequential composition: he whose memory—characterized by the recollection of each preceding birth—has been destroyed. ||23||

Viśvanātha: He is one whose memory has been destroyed—meaning he possesses the characteristic of not recollecting his successive previous births, such as [thinking], "I have been killed," "I am dead," or "I am born again," and so forth. ||23||

The sequence is as follows: suddenly impelled by that wind of birth and cast downward, with his head turned down and facing below, he emerges outside with great difficulty and much suffering— being distressed, helpless, breathless, and fainted, his memory destroyed, meaning his previously mentioned consciousness has perished.
He comes. ||23||
Fallen upon the earth and smeared with blood, he writhes like one born of excrement;
when his knowledge has departed, having reached a perverted state, he cries out piteously.
Śrīdhara: [The root *ru*] expresses crying out repeatedly as *rorūyati* and *rorūyate*. ||24||

The sequential arrangement: "fallen" constitutes a triad. Like a worm in excrement and urine—that is, in a place of feces—the meaning is that when one has forgotten the great sufferings of previous births regarding the objects of pleasure and pain experienced over many lifetimes, one becomes miserable through even a present minor suffering alone. ||24||

Viśvanātha: Viṣṭhābhū cries out repeatedly like a worm; when ancient knowledge has departed, he cries out repeatedly in a contrary state characterized by ignorance. Even for the soul of a devotee, due to the very nature of things, knowledge remains mostly obscured from childhood onwards. Therefore, only a slight [remnant of it remains].
It should be understood that for one whose former latent impressions have been awakened through association with the virtuous, the attainment of the Blessed One occurs through devotion.
He, being nourished by people who do not know his supreme will,
has fallen into an undesirable situation and is unable to refuse it.

Śrīdhara: [This refers to] one who, not knowing the intention or desire of another, provides what is unintended—such as administering a drink of neem juice under the pretext of stomach pain when the other is crying for the sake of milk, or providing milk when the other is crying due to actual stomach pain, and so forth. ||25||

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: By a person such as a mother, who does not understand the intention (*abhiprāya*) of another’s speech, and who, imagining stomach pain when there is crying for the sake of milk, or hunger when there is crying, causes that person to drink milk.
Laid upon an impure couch defiled by sweat-born vermin,
the creature is powerless to scratch its limbs or even to move from its seat.
Śrīdhara: "Being powerless even in the acts of sitting, rising, and moving, he cries out repeatedly"—this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*).
Krama-sandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "Not *īśaḥ*, meaning not capable. "He cries out repeatedly"—this is the syntactical connection. ||25||
Gnats, mosquitoes, bedbugs,
and the like bite the raw skin of one who is weeping and devoid of wisdom, just as worms devour a worm.

Śrīdhara: [He refers to] that whose skin is fresh and tender. Viśvanātha: [He refers to] that whose knowledge was produced while still in the womb; the sequence of the composition has not been explained.
[Viśvanātha continues: [He refers to] that whose skin is fresh and tender. *Kṛmikam* means a tiny worm. (27)
Thus, having experienced the suffering of childhood and likewise of youth, he failed to obtain his desired object; through lack of knowledge, his anger was kindled, and he was overwhelmed by grief.
Possessed by desire, together with his body, pride, and increasing wrath, he engages in conflict with those who desire, leading to his own destruction.
Śrīdhara: Childhood lasts for five years; after that comes the stage of *paugaṇḍa*, which precedes youth.

In that stage, there is the suffering of study and so forth. He describes the suffering of youth with three and a half verses. "Overwhelmed by grief" means pervaded by sorrow due to not obtaining what one desires; "whose anger is kindled by ignorance" means whose wrath is inflamed by lack of knowledge.
He, along with his body, creates conflict and opposition through increasing pride and anger,
leading to his own end and destruction.
The sequential arrangement: "Thus" refers to the pair of verses [28].
Viśvanātha: With kindled fury— that is, with blazing anger— and afflicted by grief— that is, pervaded by sorrow—
the ignorant embodied being, repeatedly within this body composed of the five elements,
possesses the false grasp of "I" and "mine," and thus the one of poor intellect forms such a notion.
Śrīdhara: He elaborates upon ignorance. In a body composed of the elements, one harbors the false attachment of the notion "I" and "mine. (30)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: He demonstrates ignorance. Since the body is composed of the five elements, its distinctness from the self (*ātman*) is quite evident. Yet, even so, one forms the notion of "I" and "mine" with respect to it.
A false apprehension grasps only a non-existent object, and not an existent one. //30//
For that purpose, one performs action by which, being bound, one enters the cycle of existence;
thus, fettered by ignorance and karma, one follows along while inflicting suffering.

Śrīdhara: "For that purpose" means for the sake of the body. That body by which one is bound through action is what follows—meaning it comes again and again, or persists. Why? Because one is bound by ignorance and action; thus it is so. ||31||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Artha" means for the sake of the body (*deha*). That by which one is bound through action; that body which follows along in order to give—i.e., to bestow—suffering such as the pain of hell and so forth upon the living being (*jīva*) due to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since he is bound by karma, it is folly to think that the very body which causes suffering is nourished even by sinful deeds. ||31||
If a living being again delights in following the path of the wicked, who exert themselves for the sake of the genitals and the belly, he enters into darkness as before.

Śrīdhara: If he has resorted to—that is, remained established in—the path of the wicked, or if, even while established on the path of the virtuous, he delights with the wicked, then he enters the darkness of hell in the manner previously described, such as by returning in a body of torment. ||32||

The sequence of composition: Having stated the fault of attachment to common desires, he speaks of the fault of attachment born of sin—beginning with "yadi" (if). By "asadbhiḥ" (by the wicked) is meant by the most sinful. ||32||

Viśvanātha: "As before" means that by the method previously described—namely, by the phrase "if [associated] with the wicked"—the body of torment returns and enters hell. However, if [the being] stands upon the path followed by the virtuous who are intent on the service of Kṛṣṇa and rejoices therein, he attains Kṛṣṇa, just as before.
And thus it is obtained [in scripture]: "In this regard, 'as before' means as in the case of the previously mentioned living devotees.
Truth, purity, compassion, silence, intelligence, fortune, modesty, fame, forgiveness, tranquility, self-restraint, and majesty—all these go to destruction through association with him.
One should not form an attachment to those who are unpeaceful, deluded, self-destructive, and wicked,
nor to those pitiable ones who are like playthings for women.

Madhva [in the verses beginning with] "asat-saṅgam" censures association with the wicked through three verses. Intellect (*buddhi*) has the Supreme Person as its object; prosperity (*śrī*) consists of wealth and grain; modesty (*hrī*) is shame;
fame (*yaśas*) is renown; forbearance (*kṣamā*) is endurance; tranquility (*śama*) is the restraint of the external senses; self-control (*dama*)...
Restraint of the mind; "bhaga" is exaltation; "from the association with whom"—that is, from the association with those who are wicked. ||33||
Among those who maintain a fragmented self and those who possess knowledge only of the mere individual soul (jīva). || 34 ||
Śrīdhara: In this context, "dayā" (compassion) is sometimes read as "tapaḥ" (austerity); this [place] is esteemed as a sacred forest. ||33||

[This applies] to those whose selves are fragmented by the notion that the body is the self, and who are as dependent as play-animals for women. Just as bondage arises from association with those attached to women, it would not arise from association with others.
Regarding the sequence of composition: in some places "tapa" (austerity) appears where "dayā" (compassion) is expected; this is the view of the Puṇyāraṇya school.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), the meaning is that just as one should not act toward those wicked people, so too one should not act toward women, who are like playthings for deer. ||3334||

Viśvanātha: With three verses beginning with "Truth," he characterizes those who are truly non-existent (asat) and prohibits association with them. The meaning is that they are "self-destroyers" (*ātmaghātinaḥ*) because they cause their own downfall.
[The verse states: "In this way, his delusion would not arise, nor would there be bondage through attachment to others."
Just as [defilement arises] for a man from association with a woman, and just as it does from association with one who is attached to her.
"Among virtuous men as well as among women, attachment does not bring about fault;
for virtues, according to their fitness, do not produce defect in living beings who have seen [the truth]. Thus it is said in the Vārāha Purāṇa. (35)
Śrīdhara:

In the *Kramasaṃdarbha*, he demonstrates that very fault with the words "not so. Here, "attachment" (*saṅga*) consists of various worldly concerns and the like, arising from their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*). ||35||
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, the word "and" (ca) should be supplied here [in the verse] as "and by associating with those who associate with him. ||35||
[In this regard, verse 11.14.30 should be consulted.
Having seen his own daughter, Prajāpati was overcome by her beauty;
assuming the form of a bear, he shamelessly pursued her as she had become a deer.

Śrīdhara: He elaborates upon how association with women is a cause of calamity through seven verses beginning with "Prajāpati. Having assumed the form of a bear (*ṛkṣarūpī*), that is, taking the shape of a deer, he [assaulted] her who had become a *rohit* deer, meaning she was in the form of a doe;
he was devoid of shame, being utterly brazen (*hatatrapa*). ||36||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* does not provide an explanation.

Viśvanātha says: Nor should it be argued that a woman is unable to cause the intellect of great beings—who possess discriminative knowledge and other such qualities—to falter; thus he says that Prajāpati Brahmā [fell for] her who had become a deer (*rohid*).
While she was in the form of a doe, he, assuming the form of a rishi, took the shape of a deer. ||36||

In this world, who indeed is a man of unimpaired intellect— other than the Sage Nārāyaṇa— who could remain so amidst those created by those who were themselves created by Him, while this world is composed of the illusory power (māyā) consisting of woman?
In the *Ṣāḍguṇya*, Śrīdhara states: "Madhu is declared to be the primary [form of] fear, and Māyā is said to be under his control.
Created by that Brahmā were Marīci and others; created by them were Kaśyapa and others;
and created by them as well were gods, humans, and so forth. Among these, what man indeed could have an unimpaired intellect and an unattracted mind?

The sequence of the composition: Although he has been brought into another creation by him, Śrī Nārāyaṇa’s composure remains entirely unshaken; thus [the author] says "the sage. Alternatively, the meaning is: who indeed could there be such a person as one who is inseparable from Nārāyaṇa yet remains unattached to him? ||37||
Viśvanātha: By that Brahmā, Marīci and others were created; by them, Kaśyapa and others were created;

and by those Kaśyapas and others, gods, humans, and so forth were created. Among those beings who have come into existence, while they exist without Nārāyaṇa—that is, apart from Nārāyaṇa—and while they do not worship Nārāyaṇa...
This is the meaning. Among them, one must not explain [the text] as "except for Nārāyaṇa," because that would entail the undesirable consequence of Nārāyaṇa being created by Brahmā. ||37||
[In this regard, the verse at 11.26.15, which contains a corresponding meaning, should be consulted:
"Behold the power of my illusory form consisting of women, which conquers the quarters; she brings even those who have trampled her feet under control by a mere movement of her eyebrows."
Śrīdhara: [He conquered] even the heroes who were conquerors of the quarters. ||38||

*Kramasaṃdarbha*: According to the *Amarakośa*, "kevalam" is an indeclinable meaning "only. It functions as an adjective for "the knitting of the eyebrows" (*bhrūvijṛmbha*). Therefore, the meaning is "by the knitting of the eyebrows alone," according to Viśvanātha. [He describes those] who, having conquered all directions—the conquerors of the quarters—had returned to their own inner apartments.

Even toward universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), that proud class of women first tramples them with her feet, humbling them with kicks, by means of a frown made crooked with anger—expressing: "Fie on you! Having abandoned me, why do you go on a world-conquest to enjoy the women of other lands? Thus she makes them the first to be overcome by her foot-strikes.
It is simply settled; the sense is that no further reasoning need be sought here. According to Amara, *kevalam* is used in the sense of "settled" (*nirṇīta*). ||38||

One who desires to ascend to the supreme further shore of yoga should never form an attachment to women; having attained the realization of the Self through service to Me, one should remain steadfast.
They say that this is the gateway to hell for him.
Śrīdhara: One by whom the gain consisting of the nature of the Self has been obtained. For this seeker of liberation, those women whom yogis call the gateway to hell— [39]
The sequence of composition: even toward one's own women; "niraya" means saṃsāra. ||39||

Viśvanātha: A knower who desires to ascend to the supreme shore and a devotee who has attained self-realization should not form an attachment even toward their own wives; for by the maxim that "one who is lying down does not fall downward," it follows that even a ritualist (*karmī*) who engages in sexual union with women is not defiled. This...
Of the mere male. ||39||
[In this regard, verses 11.14.29 and 11.26.24 should be consulted. When a woman who is a deceptive illusion created by the gods approaches slowly,
one should look upon her as one's own death, like a well concealed by grass.
Śrīdhara: One should regard that Māyā in the form of a woman—who approaches slowly under the pretext of service and the like—as death itself, which is adverse. ||40||

The sequential connection [of the commentary] is as follows: "Her" (tām). Just as one looks upon another animal under one's protection falling toward a well covered with grass—which is death itself—so too does he look upon her, who is concealed by her womanhood, as his own form of death; this is the meaning. ||40||

Viśvanātha: He says that even she who, perceiving a man to be dispassionate, approaches him under the pretext of service and so forth while manifesting her own lack of desire, is likewise a bringer of misfortune—“she who approaches” (yopayāti). “He should look” (īkṣet) means he should observe.
In this regard, because there is no intention on the part of someone [like a woman] to think, “May a person fall into me like a well covered by grass,” [the result is different].

It is implied that a woman who does not come even when called from the side, or who is indifferent in every respect, or who possesses devotion, knowledge, dispassion, and so forth, or who is unconscious due to madness, or asleep, or even dead, is to be abandoned from afar in every way. ||40||
Out of delusion, she considers him her husband as he approaches like a bull;
through association with women, she has attained this female state which bestows wealth, offspring, and a home.
One should recognize that [world] as consisting of husband, children, and home—
a death brought about by fate— just like the song of a hunter.
Śrīdhara: With these two verses beginning with "yāṃ manyate," he speaks thus regarding a woman who desires liberation:

"That illusion (māyā) of mine which, acting like a man (ṛṣabhāyatīm), she considers to be a husband who bestows wealth and so forth—then one should know that male-formed illusion to be death. This is the connection with the subsequent verse.
For, in a previous birth, this living being (jīva), though himself a man, became a woman at the time of death due to attachment to women and through the meditation upon a woman. ||41||
One should recognize that [the sound] takes the form of death as one's husband and so forth; just as the singing of a hunter (mṛgayu), though perceived as favorable, is the death of the deer. ||42||
The sequence of composition: "yām" constitutes a pair of verses (yugmaka). ||4142||

Viśvanātha: Just as a woman is the cause of misfortune for men who possess devotion and knowledge, so too is a man the cause of misfortune for women who possess devotion and knowledge; thus he says in two verses beginning with "yām.
He considers my *māyā*, who acts like a man (*ṛṣabhāyatīm*), to be a husband who bestows wealth and other such things.
Due to association with women, at the time of death, the living being attains womanhood through the meditation upon a woman. ||41||
One should recognize that illusion (māyā) as death in the form of a husband and so forth; just as a deer, though the song of a hunter brings pleasure, recognizes it as death. ||42||
Moving from world to world with the body as his living soul,
a person performs actions incessantly while still experiencing their fruits.
Of the honey: by that which has become the individual soul, [that is] by that which has become the karma of the individual soul. ||43||

Śrīdhara: Thus, the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (*jīva*) has been explained in detail. In that context, its movement from one world to another and its birth and death under the influence of karma have been described. Regarding this, the following doubt may arise: "But how can there be movement from one world to another for that which is all-pervading? And how [can there be birth and death] for that which is eternal?"
Regarding birth and death: when karma is exhausted through experience, birth and death are no longer admitted;

so how could there be a further arising of karma for him? To this, he says—"by means of the body"—to show that both the transition to another world and karma are possible. [This occurs] by means of the element (bhūta) that has arisen as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva).
Following to another world by means of the subtle body (liṅgadeha), one performs actions without ceasing; thus, the non-termination of actions is stated. ||43||

The sequential composition: Now, even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is inherently devoid of volition and so forth, he explains its departure to other worlds and such through four verses beginning with "By the body" (43).

Viśvanātha: Thus, the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) has been elaborated. Regarding this, an objection is raised: "Now, what is the logic in this? When the soul performs auspicious or inauspicious karma with a certain body, it abandons that body and experiences its fruit—such as heaven—in another body; what is the reasoning behind this? In that regard, by which...

"One performs action with the body and experiences its result with that very same body"—thus he says. By means of the "body" which has become the living self (*jīvabhūta*), that is, the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), one follows after the worlds—from the mortal world to the world of heaven, hell, and so forth.
It is precisely through the movement of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that one performs action; for the movement of the living self (*jīva*) as conditioned by that adjunct is likewise possible.

In that state, even while experiencing enjoyment, without yet having fully attained it, one returns again to the mortal world and performs actions; therefore, it has been said that one performs and experiences [the fruits of] action solely by means of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*). ||43||
For the body, composed of the elements, the senses, and the mind, follows this living soul;
its cessation is death, while its manifestation is birth.

Śrīdhara says: He describes the occurrence of birth and death—the *jīva* is the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), which is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of this Self and follows it. The body, composed of the elements (*bhūta*), the senses (*indriya*), and the mind (*manas*), is a modification of the gross elements and so forth; it is the locus of experience for those two [the Self and the *jīva*]. Their cessation is the state of being unfit for activity; that is the death of this *jīva*.
It is said: manifestation is occurrence; birth is called "arising" (janman). ||44||
The sequential arrangement is subordinate and dependent upon karma. ||44||

Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask: "In that case, why is there the perception of death and birth, such that after dying from this world of mortals one enjoys heaven, and having returned from heaven, one is born again? To this he says:
The *jīva* is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul; likewise, the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) follows this self, as does the gross body, which is the locus of experience.

Having merged together, they become a single body composed of the elements, the senses, and the mind. The non-restraint of this [body]—its incapacity for action—is the death of this living being (jīva). And that occurs upon the departure of the gross body, at the time immediately preceding the acquisition of another gross body. However, in states such as deep sleep (suṣupti) and the like, although it does not perform its own functions, [it is not dead].

The capacity for action certainly exists even when deep sleep has been broken, because that respective capacity is observed immediately thereafter. Manifestation (*āvirbhāva*), however, is the state of becoming visible;
it is birth (*sambhava*), and that occurs at the time of emerging from the womb upon the departure of the body—the seat of experience—and the attainment of another gross body.
It would be so. ||44||

When the locus of the perception of substance possesses the fitness for the observation of substance, that is its fivefold state; from the conceit of "I" (ahaṃkāra), there arises the vision of substance.
Just as when the eyes lack the capacity to perceive the constituent parts of a substance, at that very same time, the seer lacks the capacity to see through those two eyes.
Therefore, one should not feel terror, nor miserliness, nor agitation;
having understood the course of the living being, the wise man should wander here free from attachment.
The capacity of the eyes to see, which constitutes the seer's status as a seer, [arises] from the presence of honey. ||46||

Śrīdhara: He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration. When there is an incapacity—due to defects such as cataracts or jaundice—in the eyeball and other sites of the perception of substances for the seeing of color and so forth during the observation of a substance, at that very time, [the same applies] to the sense organ of the eye.

Unfitness: when there is unfitness of these two—the locus and the eye—it is precisely then that the living soul (*jīva*), the seer, lacks the fitness to see. Thus, the meaning is that when there is a deficiency in the gross body (*sthūladeha*), there is a deficiency of the subtle body (*liṅga*); that alone is the death of the soul, not [death] in its own right. In some places, one additional verse is recited.

In this context, the meaning is as follows: when there is an incapacity for the perception of substance regarding the gross body—the locus for the apprehension of substance—that is "fivefoldness" (pañcatva), which is death. The manifestation of the gross body as a substance through the conceit (*abhimāna*) "I am this very thing" or "this is I" is birth. [This occurs] in the two eyeballs...
The unsuitability for perceiving the form and other qualities of the constituent parts of a substance [is established]; the rest is the same.

Since, in reality, there is no birth, death, or the like for the soul (*jīva*), therefore one should not feel terror at death, nor should one practice wretchedness or dejection regarding life, nor agitation in the effort to remain alive. ||4547||
The sequential arrangement: the pair beginning with "the perception of substances" [is explained] in verses 45–46;
[this refers to] these two, the gross and subtle bodies.
Viśvanātha: He states again the characteristics of death and birth more clearly, beginning with "substances" (*dravya*).

Here, "substances" refers to all material objects situated in the mortal world (having seen the example). And although these are perceived only by means of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), nevertheless...

When the gross body, which is the locus for the perception of substance, is subject to decay, that very incapacity for the observation of substance at any given time is what constitutes the state of "fivefoldness" (pañcatva). When the gross body is fragile, the subtle body likewise becomes incapable of perceiving substance; this alone is not the death of the living being (jīva).

The meaning is "from itself. Birth (*janma*) is the entry of the conceit (*abhimāna*) "this very thing is I" into the gross [body] due to ego-inflation (*ahaṃmāna*). The meaning is that the perception of a substance—that is, of any object whatsoever residing in the mortal world—is the cause of perception. Here, the illustration is as follows: just as in the case of the two eyes, the eyeballs (*netragolaka*).
The unfitness for perceiving the constituent parts of substances may arise in the form of defects such as cataracts or jaundice, or through fragility;

that very thing constitutes the unfitness of the sense organ, the eye. When there is unfitness in both these—the location and the eye—then at that very moment, there is also unfitness for the seeing of the person who is the seer. And that is unfitness.

Since it is established that [the soul] can arise only in the world of mortals and not in heaven or hell— this being the interpretation obtained for the illustrative case as well— the conventional usage of "birth" and "death" does not apply to the arising and destruction of the gross bodies belonging to those in heaven or hell; rather, the destruction of the gross body alone constitutes the destruction of the subtle living being (*jīva*).
It is metaphorically designated as such, and so too is its arising; because, in reality, there is no birth, death, or the like for the self. ||4547||
With a mind endowed with right vision and joined with yoga and dispassion,
one should move through this world fashioned by Māyā, having cast off the physical body.

Madhva: The knowledge of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) is the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). For the individual soul (*jīva*), which is unattached to the body and its like, there are no resulting pleasures, pains, and so forth; how much less so for the body, given its insentience? ||47||

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But if one is entirely free from attachment, how can there be life? To this he says: with that intellect (*buddhi*) which is "right vision" (*samyag-darśana*), because it sees and discriminates correctly; having cast down the body—that is, having deposited it—in this world fashioned by *māyā*; the meaning is that one should wander about after abandoning attachment to it.
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Having deposited the body there, that is, having abandoned attachment to it. ||48||
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
this thirty-first chapter, which is perfectly consistent with the virtuous, has been concluded.
Thus, in the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, in the commentary on the *Brahmasūtras*, in the *Pāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā* by Vyāsa, in the third book (*Skandha*),
within the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, [this is] the chapter titled "The Course of the Soul" in the teachings of Kapila.
Chapter Thirty-one;
Chapter Thirty-two:
The Ripening of Karma concerning Kāpileya, in the Dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
Kapila said:
Now, he who dwells at home performing the duties of a householder milks his own wealth and dharma, and further replenishes them.
"One who has even a slight devotion to the Blessed One will go to heaven by means of good deeds;
one without devotion goes to hell, while even one with good deeds goes to heaven. Thus it is said in the Vāmana Purāṇa. (1)
Śrīdhara:
In the thirty-second [chapter], the upward ascent through the qualities of sattva is proclaimed;
however, for one devoid of the knowledge of reality, there is a return from that state once again.

Thus, the destiny of one who performs sinful actions has been described; now, with four verses beginning with "atha," he describes the destiny of one who performs actions for the sake of desire (*kāmyakarman*). He who, while dwelling in the household itself, milks his own duties—stating what is to be milked: desire and wealth—he fills them again, that is, fulfills and practices those duties once they have been milked. ||1||
The sequential composition: [He] milks the fruits, which stand in the place of milk, from the dharmas, which stand in the place of a cow-pen.
In some places, the reading is "his own dharmas" (svān dharmān). ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the thirty-second [chapter], having declared the return and non-return for those who perform ritual actions with desire and those without desire, he censured those who are not devotees.

Having thus described the destiny of unenjoined sinful action, he speaks of the destiny of enjoined action performed with desire, beginning with the word "atha" (now). Dwelling only in the house—that is, in the very home—he milks the dharmas. He states what is to be milked: desire, wealth, and dharma. Furthermore, he fills those dharmas again and again.
He fulfills and practices [the vow]. Just as, having grazed the cows, one milks them, and then grazes them again with the hope of obtaining milk once more. ||1||
And he, deluded by desire and turned away from the Dharma of the Blessed One,
performs sacrifices to the gods and the ancestors, being endowed with faith.
Śrīdhara: He too, being averse to dharma in the form of worshiping the Blessed One, sacrifices even to the worldly gods and the ancestors. (2)

The sequence of the composition: "And he too" (*sa cāpi*). The word *ca* (and) has the sense of a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*), meaning that just as the previously mentioned person of sinful deeds is averse to the dharma of the Lord, so too is "he.
The word *api* (even/though) means: even though he is a performer of Vedic rites, nevertheless. From him, who grants all desires...
The cause for being turned away from the Dharma of the Blessed One and likewise for being oriented toward that which is other than it is:
one who is deluded by desire, that is, devoid of discernment. ||2||
Viśvanātha: Although he has performed the prescribed rites, he is still a censurable candidate; thus [the author] says: "And he too... (2).
A man whose mind is overcome by faith in that, who is devoted to his ancestors and gods,
and who drinks the soma juice, shall return again to the lunar world.
Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says: one whose mind (*mati*) is "overcome," that is, pervaded, by faith in them;

one for whom there is a vow (*vrata*), meaning a religious observance (*niyama*), for the sake of the ancestors and the gods; and a "drinker of Soma" (*somapā*), which means having drunk the Soma juice therein. ||3||

Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: There, the Soma-drinkers, having drunk the Soma, shall return; they shall fall back down again when Hari, seated upon Ananta, reclines upon the couch of the Lord of Serpents.
These very worlds go to destruction for those householders.

Śrīdhara: Having stated that even while remaining in the world, one falls due to the exhaustion of merit, he now speaks of the dissolution of the worlds as well: "And when [there is] daily dissolution" (4).
The sequential composition [of the verse] means: he lies within the three worlds; that is, he does not pay attention. ||4||

Viśvanātha: What need is there to speak of their falling downward? Even the worlds they are to attain fall downward every day along with Brahmā; thus he says: "And when [there is] the daily dissolution" (yadā cāharahaḥ pralaye). ||4||
Those wise ones who do not violate their own duties for the sake of desire or wealth,
having laid aside worldly actions, are tranquil and pure in heart.
Devoted to the dharma of cessation, free from possessiveness and free from egoism,
they possess a mind that is completely purified by the goodness attained through their own dharma.
Śrīdhara: With three verses, he describes the attainment of Him alone as the goal for those who are steadfast in the dharma of the Blessed One.

But those who, for the sake of desire and wealth, do not harm—that is, do not neglect—their own duties; who are free from attachment (*niḥsaṅga*), being unattached; and by whom actions have been surrendered, having been offered to the Lord. (56)

The sequential arrangement: "Those who [perform] their own duties," etc., is a triad. "Tranquil" means exceedingly peaceful; "with their intellects fixed on the Blessed One" is a direct instruction for his worship. ||56||

Viśvanātha: Having stated that those who perform actions with desire undergo repeated return, he now declares the non-return of those who perform actions without desire, beginning with the word "ye" (those). "They do not harm" means they do not cause pain, nor do they desire the fruits of dharma such as heaven and the like. "Detached" means free from attachment. "Having renounced actions" [means they have surrendered the sense of agency].
Those who have offered the fruits of their actions to the Lord. ||56||
By way of the sun, they go to the Person who faces in all directions,
the Lord of the high and the low, whose nature is the contemplation of the origin and end of this world.
Śrīdhara: They go to the Puruṣa, who faces all directions and is perfectly full.
And so says the Śruti: "Through the gate of the sun, those free from passion (viraja) proceed to where the immortal Puruṣa, whose nature is imperishable, resides.
Primordial matter (prakṛti) is the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa). That which exists within the process of origination is the instrumental cause (nimitta-kāraṇa).

The sequential arrangement: "Sūrya," etc. In the Śruti, the mention of attaining that [state] is by way of indicating the attainment of its location; here, however, it is direct, and thus there is identity of meaning through that intended sense. And so, their very oneness of self is perceived. This should be understood elsewhere as well. There, in the Śruti...

The meaning of the words is that "dustless" (virajaḥ) means free from contact with material nature (prakṛti). By this, the non-material nature of that world is indicated; and by the phrase "wherein the Person is immortal," its eternity is likewise made known. ||7||
Viśvanātha: Having attained knowledge, they go to—that is, they reach—the Person who faces all directions and is perfectly full;

the meaning is that they become liberated. And so says the Śruti: "Through the gate of the sun, those free from passion proceed; there indeed dwells the immortal Person, whose nature is imperishable. Of this world...
Prakṛti is the material cause (upādānakāraṇa), while that which exists at the end of production is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa). ||7||
Those who contemplate the Supreme remain in the world of the Supreme for as long as the dissolution of Brahmā occurs at the end of two parārdhas.

Śrīdhara: With the view that they belong to the Supreme Lord, he describes the gradual attainment of that state even by those who worship Hiraṇyagarbha in three verses beginning with "at the end of two parārdhas. "Of the Supreme" means of Hiraṇyagarbha.
"Those who contemplate the Supreme" are those who worship Hiraṇyagarbha while viewing him through the perspective of the Supreme Lord. (8)
The sequential arrangement: "tāvat" means having reached its first part. ||8||

Viśvanātha: Since Brahmā is indeed a partial incarnation (*guṇāvatāra*) of the Supreme Lord, even for those who worship Hiraṇyagarbha from the perspective of the Supreme Lord, liberation together with Brahmā will certainly occur in due course through knowledge mixed with devotion.
"For when the time of reabsorption arrives, they all, together with Brahmā,
at the end of the Supreme, enter the supreme state of the Paramātman"— thus says the Śruti.
However, as for those who are worshippers of Hiraṇyagarbha alone, there is no liberation for them even upon the liberation of Brahmā.

He said—[the answer] is given in three verses beginning with "at the end of two parārdhas. "The world" refers to Satyaloka; those who contemplate the Supreme Brahman are intent on the meditation of Vairāja. (8)

When He, whose nature consists of the three *guṇas*, desires to withdraw [the universe] and enters the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), which is enveloped by earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, the senses, their objects, the primary elements (*bhūta*), and so forth, that is Time (*kāla*).
Having experienced that which is called "the other," the Supreme Self-existent One [is realized].

Śrīdhara: Desiring to withdraw the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa)— which is surrounded and joined by the five great elements beginning with earth, as well as the mind, the sense organs, the objects such as sound, the ego (ahaṅkāra) consisting of the elements and so forth—
he [enters] the unmanifest Lord known as the Supreme (parākhya).
The period characterized by two parārdhas. ||9||

The sequence of the composition: Puṇyāraṇya explains that "desirous of withdrawing" (pratisañjihīrṣuḥ) means desiring to abandon, while "desirous of grasping" (jighṛkṣuḥ) refers to [the Lord]. Viśvanātha states that "consisting of the three qualities" (guṇatrayātmā) means having attained identity with primordial nature (prakṛti). Furthermore, he says that when the great dissolution occurs, Brahmā is liberated, using the word "earth" (kṣmā) as an illustration.
Desiring to withdraw his own body— the Vairāja form— enveloped by the earth and other elements, and wishing to abandon it, he,

though composed of the three qualities and characterized by the quality of rajas, enters the Unmanifest Supreme Lord, the inner controller of primordial nature; having realized that time called "Supreme," which consists of two *parārdhas*.
Thus, having departed and entered after the Blessed One,
those yogins who have conquered their vital breaths and minds, being free from passion,
[attain] together with him the ancient Person, the Immortal.
Those who have abandoned egoism attain Brahman, which is the primary source.

Śrīdhara: Having gone far away—that is, having departed—the yogins who have entered into the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha go together with that very *amṛta*, which is of the nature of supreme bliss, the primary matter (*pradhāna*), the exalted Brahman; they do not [go] previously. This is because they have abandoned the conceit of "I" regarding that [state]. And thus says the Smṛti:
"When the time for reabsorption has arrived, at the end of the supreme [Brahmā], all those of perfected self enter the supreme state together with Brahmā. (10)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thus he says "in this way" (*evam*) to show that even upon the liberation of Brahman, those who worship him are not liberated due to the absence of devotion. Having departed, they cast off their bodies in the world of Brahmā itself.

Those yogins who have entered into the Lord Brahmā, together with that very Brahmā, approach and enter the ancient Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord, the Pradhāna, the most excellent Brahman; they do so while still possessing the conceit that "we are the worshippers of Hiraṇyagarbha. By that [conceit]...
The sense is that their dissolution is not absolute in the Supreme Lord, but rather merely natural; therefore, upon the creation of the world again, their creation will also take place. ||10||
Therefore, O beautiful lady, go with devotion for refuge to Him whose majesty has been heard, who has made His abode in the heart-lotuses of all beings.
Śrīdhara: However, the devotees of the Blessed One attain Him directly and not through a gradual process;
therefore, He says "Now, therefore" (*atha tasmāt*) [in verse 10], instructing you to worship Him directly with *bhāva*, that is, with love (*premṇā*). ||11||

The sequential arrangement: Now, regarding the word "atha" (now): according to the manner stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.25.38, "By my nature, I am their beloved, their very self, and their son," they possess a singular identification with being beloved and so forth.
Furthermore, since this is already established for them, he says "bhāvinī" (the future one) to indicate that it is specifically through the state of being a son. ||11||

Viśvanātha: Regarding the word "atha" (now/therefore): since no one can cross over [the ocean of worldly existence] without devotion, you should therefore seek refuge in that very Lord. O noble lady! The sense is that, since you already possess the feeling of being a mother toward me, the Supreme Lord, instruction in devotion for you would be like grinding what has already been ground.
He who is the first among all moving and stationary beings, the womb of the Vedas, together with the ṛṣis,
the lords of yoga such as Kumāra and others, and the perfected ones (siddhas) who promote yoga.

Śrīdhara: Thus far, it has been stated that for those devoted to the Blessed Lord, attainment of Him occurs without interruption through non-difference from Him; however, for those who worship Hiraṇyagarbha, it occurs gradually.
But regarding worship through difference, he says—"The first [even]..."—to show that even Brahmā and the others return, let alone others.

With four [verses]: the connection with the third verse is that he who is the "womb of the Vedas" (*vedagarbha*), even when the transformation of the qualities (*guṇavyatikara*) has occurred, being authorized to the station of Brahmā, is born just as before. It is not only he alone, but together with the sages such as Marīci and others, and with the lords of yoga (*yogeśvara*) and others. ||12||

The sequence of the composition: "the first" refers to the group of four. By the "vision of duality," that is, by seeing [the self] as distinct from the Supreme Lord; and by the "vision of Hiraṇyagarbha," meaning through the conceit (abhimāna) that "I am indeed Hiraṇyagarbha. The meaning is: "from that agency and state of being a worshiper. For worship (upāsanā) indeed...

It is free from decay. [Objection: But surely another powerful karma might cause a different birth; to this he says: "by means of non-attachment" (*niḥsaṅgena*). Here too, it should be construed as "because of agency" (*kartṛtvāt*), though the meaning is "because of being the producer of the action. In that regard, having distinguished the creation of the great seers (*maharṣi*) and others—
He shows [this] by saying "sovereignty. As before, it is produced through action, dharma, and yoga;

thus Viśvanātha [is the cause]. Now, one might ask: how do we understand that Brahmā could be liberated and yet not desire to liberate his own devotees? To this, [the Lord says]: "Those who take refuge in me alone cross over this māyā."
Because of the hearing of the Lord’s declaration in [Gītā 7.15], he says: even Brahmā transmigrates without devotion;
how much more so others, those wretched ones? He is the "first" because he is the creator of all moving and stationary beings;
thus, although he is the causal form and the "womb of the Vedas," being the knower of all the Vedas, even together with the seers such as Marīci and other yogis, [he is subject to bondage].
What need is there to mention that it is together with practitioners, even with the lords of yoga who have attained perfection? ||12||
Due to the perception of duality and the conceit of agency, even through action performed without attachment,
the Supreme Person, the Bull among Men, appears as Brahman with attributes because of his state as an agent.
Śrīdhara: There are two causes for rebirth: through the perception of difference and through the conceit of agency;
and as there was a cause for the previous state, namely, "by means of action performed without attachment and without desire. (13)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The conceit that arises from a perspective of duality toward the Blessed One, thinking, "Just as Rudra destroys and Viṣṇu protects, so too do I, as Brahmā, create."

Therefore, that which is the agency [of the world]— the Great Brahma, who is endowed with qualities (*saguṇa*) and composed of auspicious attributes (*kalyāṇaguṇamaya*), the creator— having entered into Him at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), is born again as before when, in due course, the agitation of the *guṇas* occurs and the principle of Mahat and the rest arise. He is Brahmā.

This is the meaning: even those great sages and others who are attached to them, having enjoyed the powers such as *maṇitva* (the power of becoming minute) produced through the yoga of action and knowledge during the previous Mahākalpa, return and revolve again at the commencement of a new Mahākalpa. ||13||
Having transmigrated again in time through the form of the Lord,
when there is a transformation of the qualities (guṇas), he is born just as before.
Through the intoxication of full knowledge (*madhvaḥ*), having entered the Supreme Lord in the abode of union,
one is born again as before, arising in states of high and low.
When there is no longer the intermixture of the *guṇas*, this emerges externally in two ways.
Even in the absence of the intermixture of qualities (guṇas), the distinctions of high, low, and so forth remain as before.
"And for Viṣṇu and for those who are liberated, it never occurs. Thus [it is said] in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa. 14.

Śrīdhara: Having done what is it produced here? First, having enjoyed the sovereignty of Brahmā (pārameṣṭhya), and afterwards, at the time of dissolution, having approached—that is, attained—the Puruṣa who possesses qualities (saguṇa) and presides over the qualities (guṇādhiṣṭhātṛ), who is the form of the first incarnation; those [beings], headed by the sages, [attain] the sovereignty fashioned by their own karma.
The grammatical connection is as follows: having served the Puruṣa and having transmigrated according to their respective offices as before, they return once again. ||14||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask: how can there be a perception of difference or egoistic pride among the Lords of Yoga such as Sanatkumāra and other perfected beings (siddhas), as well as among other teachers who are omniscient due to their initiation into yoga?
If those two were established [as separate], how could there be the state of being a Lord of Yoga (yogeśvara) and so forth? It is said:

for those who are free from ego-inflation, there certainly exists the contemplation of non-dual Brahman; however, upon the removal of duality, even regarding the Blessed One, because of the notion that He is Brahman variegated by *māyā*, He is regarded like any other *māyic* object.
Likewise, the perception of duality and the conceit that "we, as experiencers of Brahman, are negating the formalized form"—
from these two very defects arises the agency and the qualification for ritual action; from that,
there is rebirth— this is also [the case].

This was stated because certain Brahmās, Brāhmaṇas, yogis, jñānis, kumāras, and others residing within this particular universe are not devotees; however, for all others residing in other universes, such as Brahmā and the rest,
there is the attainment of states such as devotion, love for liberation, devotion, and service to the Lord.
They are to be understood according to their respective degrees of devotion. ||14||
Having enjoyed even that sovereignty and the state of Brahmā produced by dharma,
they return once again when there is a transformation of the qualities (guṇas).

Madhva: In the absence of any modification of qualities, when the dissolution has arrived, they return again to the Supreme Lord. Brahmā, the divine one, surrounded [by his attendants], having entered the Supreme Lord during the dissolution, [remains] in heaven; then this world proceeds forth again in a twofold manner.
Having enjoyed there, within the abode, the enjoyments that are the fruit of the dharma of knowledge,
one enters into Nārāyaṇa, wherein knowledge is manifest as one's own innate bliss.
In this very manner, for them, association and separation occur within the kalpa;
there is eternal constancy and eternal happiness, and likewise, the most excellent enjoyments are created.

"Just as formerly there was a difference in status between Hari and others due to their respective qualities, so too it was between Brahmā and the others, and among yet others, according to their circumstances. Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. 15.

It has not been explained by others through three [other means]. But those here whose minds are unattached to actions, being endowed with faith, perform entirely all the non-prohibited obligatory rites.
Those whose minds are dulled by passion, who are driven by desire and have unconquered senses,
daily perform sacrifices with wealth, their hearts finding delight in domestic life.

Śrīdhara: Since even those who worship Brahman are thus subject to rebirth due to their perception of duality and their conceit, what need is there to speak of those who perform actions for the sake of desired fruits? Thus, censuring them, he speaks in six verses:
"But those here whose minds are attached to actions, performing unprohibited rites—whether optional or obligatory..."

They perform all their duties; they go by the southern path of Aryaman, via the path of smoke, to the world of the ancestors—this is the connection with the fifth [section]. In between, there is a censure of that [path]. ||16||
The sequential arrangement: "Those who," etc., is the group of five [verses]. ||16||

Viśvanātha: Since even those beginning with Brahmā undergo such rebirth when there is an absence of devotion, in what category could those who perform actions for the sake of desire (kāmyakarmin) possibly stand? Thus, censuring them, he says in six verses, beginning with "But those here... They perform all actions, including both the obligatory (nitya) and the optional (kāmya), provided they are not prohibited.

Even they are censured, let alone those who perform improper actions while engaged in ritual acts; such is the sense. [This applies] to one whose intellect carries away the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). ||1618||
Those men devoted to the three aims of life are averse to the discourse concerning the enemy of Madhu, whose heroic exploits are so worthy of being told.
Surely they are struck down by fate who, having abandoned the nectar of the stories of Acyuta,
listen instead to the tales of the wicked, just as those who eat excrement consume feces.

Śrīdhara: Śrīdhara is he whose intellect removes the cycle of worldly existence. Those seekers of the three aims of life who are averse to the stories of that enemy of Madhu, whose vast exploits are worthy of being told;
and those who, having abandoned the nectar of Acyuta’s stories, listen instead to the tales of the wicked—they are surely [possessed] by fate.
The grammatical connection is "are prescribed" (vihitāḥ). ||1819||

The sequence of the composition: By the word "by fate" (daivena), the meaning is that there is no deliverance from hell for them at all, and thus they are not to be described; by the phrase "the story of Acyuta," it is made known that all other stories are indeed worthless. Just as those who eat excrement abandon rice-cakes and the like to seek only filth, so it is here.
The meaning. ||19||

Viśvanātha: The nectar is the story of Acyuta alone; having abandoned that, all other songs are merely false verses. Indeed, who would not enjoy nectar once it has been obtained? To this he replies: "Like excrement.
The meaning is that those who eat feces abandon milk, sugar-candy, and the like, and seek out only excrement.
By the southern path they go to the world of the ancestors belonging to Aryaman;
having performed the funeral rites at the cemetery, they are born again according to their offspring.
Śrīdhara: From the world of the ancestors, they are born again among their offspring, such as their own sons and so forth.

They have performed the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and ending at the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). The meaning is that they are those who act according to what has been prescribed. ||20||
The sequence of composition: the meaning is that they performed the rites ending with the cremation ground and attained those [results]. ||20||
Viśvanātha: From the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*), they are born again among their offspring, such as their own sons and so forth.

This means that they have performed the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and ending at the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), being performers of the actions prescribed by the scriptures. ||20||
Then, when their merit is exhausted, they fall helplessly back into this world,
their prosperity suddenly snatched away by the gods.
Śrīdhara: How are they born? To this he says: "Then they fall again toward this world," meaning those whose means of enjoyment have been deprived of their rising prosperity. (21)
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: How are they born? To this he says: "Then they fall again toward this world," for those whose [means of] rising are the instruments of enjoyment. (21)
Therefore, with your whole being, worship the Supreme Lord,
whose lotus feet are worthy of worship, through devotion that takes refuge in His qualities.
Śrīdhara: [He worships] the Supreme Lord, the Parameṣṭhin, with all his being—that is, with extreme affection—and with that devotion which takes refuge in His qualities. (22)

The sequence of composition: "With all one's being" means with one's entire self; "with devotion" means with love. One might ask, "How could that [devotion] arise? To this he says: its very basis and cause for engagement is his qualities themselves. For when one reflects upon him in the manner described in passages such as *Aho bakīyam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.23), that devotion indeed arises.
The state [of being]. When it is said "the lotus feet of the one worthy of worship," then even his beauty and other qualities shine forth.
The meaning is that this will cause one to delight in that worship of him constantly. Thus, in this way, any other human goal (puruṣārtha) there is also excluded. ||22||

Viśvanātha: Just as he spoke thus at the end for those devoted to *nivṛtti-karma* (renunciation) in the verse beginning with "Then, take refuge in Him... (*atha tam... śaraṇaṃ vraja bhāvena bhāvini*), where His majesty is heard from the scripture;
likewise, he spoke also at the end for those devoted to *pravṛtti-karma* (active engagement): "Therefore, you... (*tasmāt tvam...*); by that [he means the following].

The sense is: "Do not perform action that is either withdrawn from worldly life (nivṛtta) or engaged in it (pravṛtta). Worship Hari with devotion through every state of being and with your whole self. [An objection: But how can that very devotion arise? To this he says: worship Him with that devotion for which His very qualities are the refuge and the cause of its engagement.
"Fit for worship" means: the thought is that to which lotus would not be pleasing to a honey-bee?
Devotion-yoga (bhaktiyoga) directed toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva quickly produces dispassion (vairāgya) and the knowledge that is the vision of Brahman.
Śrīdhara: He states that through devotion, both knowledge and dispassion arise spontaneously: "Vāsudeva... (23).

The sequential arrangement: even one who desires knowledge and so forth should practice that very same thing; thus he says—"Vāsudeva," [meaning] Viśvanātha. Even one who desires knowledge and so forth should practice devotion alone; thus he says—"Vāsudeva.
The vision of Brahman is the direct experience of Brahman. (23)
When his mind does not grasp at inequality—whether as pleasant or unpleasant—among objects through the activities of the senses, even though those objects are equal; |||

Śrīdhara: He establishes that very point: when the mind of this devotee, being fixed immovably upon Him alone through attachment to the Lord's qualities, does not perceive discordance among sense-objects by means of the activities of the senses. (24)
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] should be understood according to the maxim: "And that hook of the mind, too, one gradually detaches. ||24||
Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask: by what characteristics are knowledge and dispassion, which are born of devotion, to be recognized?

In response to this expectation, he says: when the mind of this devotee, through its attachment to the qualities of the Lord, becomes fixed upon Him alone and remains unmoved even by the functions of the senses toward all material objects.

The meaning is that although objects such as the visible, the audible, and the tangible are in fact equal insofar as they are all perceivable by the senses, one does not perceive the disparity of thinking, "This audible object and so forth is dear to me," or "This is unpleasant, such as the inaudible and so forth";
rather, one should maintain an even-mindedness toward praise and blame, clods of earth and gold, and the like.

At that very moment, he perceives himself by means of the self as free from attachment, possessing equal vision, devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted, and having ascended to the supreme state.
"The forms of Viṣṇu as the Fish, the Tortoise, and so forth, consist solely of pure knowledge;
yet those who consider them to be material go to the lowest darkness. Thus it is said in the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa]. (25)

Śrīdhara: At that very moment, he perceives the Self by means of the self as self-luminous. Of what nature is that perception? It is "equal" (*sama*). Why is that? Because it is "free from attachment" (*niḥsaṅga*); for from attachment, indeed, inequality arises.
The reason for being free from attachment is that it is "devoid of the rejectable and the acceptable" (*heyopādeyarahita*). Why is that? Because it is the "established state" (*padaṃ vyavasitam*).
"Ascended" means having attained the certainty that "I am supreme bliss. ||25||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: That very self, by means of the intellect, [perceives] its own individual soul (*jīva*) as having ascended, or nearly ascended, to the state (*pada*) which is the nature of Brahman, on account of reasons such as being free from attachment.
He beholds; he experiences. ||25||
The Supreme Brahman, the Paramātman, the Lord, and the Person are mere consciousness;
though the Blessed One is one, he is perceived as distinct through various states such as the visible object and so forth.
Śrīdhara: It was stated that [they are] "equal in all objects"; he now demonstrates that very equality.

Pure consciousness alone is well-known by such terms as "Supreme Brahman" and so forth; yet, through the forms of the seen, the seer, and the instrument, it is perceived as distinct. Because it is equal in being pure consciousness alone—thus [is the meaning].
The meaning. ||26||
The sequential arrangement: he connects it in the same way with the words "mere knowledge" (*jñānamātram*). The Seer is knowledge; the state of being is contemplation (*bhāvanā*).

Through various separate modes of contemplation, such as the yoga of knowledge and so forth, the one Lord alone—who is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman and the like—is perceived. Thus, the status of being a constituent part (*aṃśitva*) accrues to the Lord himself; however, in another interpretation:

Since the intended meaning is established by the word *mātra* alone, the inclusion of the single word [“only”] and the mention of masculinity (*puṃstva*) would be inappropriate. In that regard, it should be discerned that through the yoga of knowledge, the Supreme Brahman is attained; specifically, the one possessing the eightfold yoga is the Paramātman, whereas through purity and devotion, it is the Bhagavān himself. And therein, regarding Brahman—

The definition is "mere knowledge. The meaning is that while the Supreme Self is the Lord (Īśvara) and the Person (Puruṣa), who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti) and its inner controller (antaryāmī), the Blessed One (Bhagavat), however, is indeed the Blessed One himself—the Lord of Great Vaikuṇṭha, endowed with the six perfections in their entirety. This is as follows:
It should be understood that this is also an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the manifestation of that infinite [state]. [Bhaktisandarbha, Viśvanātha:

And thus, as stated in the chapter on the yoga of devotion, they behold my beautiful [forms] in the abode of the Lord (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.35)—that is, the state of being a beloved attendant in the divine realm. Likewise...]

The fruit of knowledge is oneness with Brahman, as stated in the chapter on the yoga of knowledge: "The supreme good, which is one's own abiding state, called liberation (kaivalya), has me as its refuge" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.27.28).
Likewise, that which is taught in the chapter on the eightfold yoga is liberation (nirvāṇa), which is free from support, devoid of objects, and dispassionate.

Through such passages as "He attains" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.28.35), even the fruit of yoga—liberation itself—is understood to result from the cultivation of specific forms of knowledge. However, now, by means of the verses beginning with "Therefore, you...
(Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.32.22) and "O Vāsudeva... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.32.23), all of that [is further elucidated].
