It is stated that the fruit of the yoga of devotion and knowledge is accomplished by devotion alone:

"Whether free from desire, possessing all desires, or desiring liberation, one of noble intellect should worship the Supreme Person with intense yoga of devotion" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.3.10). Thus it is said.

And as in the passage beginning, "Whatever is attained by rituals and whatever by austerity" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.20.32), [it is said]: "A devotee of mine attains everything directly through the yoga of devotion to me."
"If one somehow desires heaven, liberation, or my own abode" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.20.33).
Thus it will be said. In response to the inquiry, "What is the means for that?", he says: "mere knowledge" (*jñānamātra*).
The one Lord, Vaikuṇṭhanātha, who is full of the sixfold opulences, is indeed the Seer (*dṛśi*), which is knowledge, through the objects of sight and so forth.

By means of such instruments as those, by practitioners who possess distinct meditations upon distinct entities, the Supreme Brahman is approached (*īyate*)—or, according to another reading, it is caused to be approached (*īryate*). Alternatively, [it is approached] through visible forms, invisible forms, and forms that are both visible and invisible. In that regard, of the Supreme Brahman...
The characteristic is "mere knowledge. The characteristic of the Supreme Self (paramātman) is that He is the Lord (īśvara) and the Person (pumān).

Therefore, since the Blessed One alone is both Brahman and the Supreme Self, by means of devotion (bhakti) itself—which is the means for attaining Him—one achieves one's own goal: the status of being a beloved attendant (pārṣada), as well as union (sāyujya), which is the goal achieved through the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga).

It is accomplished; yet, in that same way, the status of being a beloved attendant is not accomplished through the means of Brahman, namely knowledge, nor through the means of the Supreme Self, namely yoga, precisely because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*). In this regard, because Brahman is formless (*nirākāra*), its essential nature is invisible; and because the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is also formless, [its nature is likewise invisible].
Invisible:
some [perceive] a person the size of a span dwelling within the space of their own heart.
According to the view of some, based on passages such as *caturbhujaṃ* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.2.8) and the Śruti text *sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*, the Lord is visible because He possesses a form; however,
because the Blessed One is Brahman and the Supreme Self, He is invisible at the time of His descent (*avatāra*).
The visible is at other times both visible and invisible. As it is stated in the first book of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"The primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu, whose form is Brahman; here, this Lord of the World exists both in an unmanifest form and in a manifest form."

"Viṣṇu himself is established in the form of Brahman" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.2.55–56). The meaning of this is as follows: "inferior" refers to that which is of a material and unmanifest nature; therefore, he exists in his manifest form in the supreme, non-material abode. ||26||
By means of this complete yoga alone, the yogin is joined with his desired goal in this world: namely, total non-attachment.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: Since knowledge alone is the very nature of the Self, it is already eternally attained; why then is it to be attained through yoga, which is accomplished by numerous means? To this he says: "This much... It is "joined" (yujyate), meaning it is attained. The meaning is that the fruit of yoga is precisely the elimination of attachment to the phenomenal world (prapañca). ||27||

The sequence of the composition: In all these cases, devotion alone is the root; however, through the yoga of knowledge and so forth, there is merely the removal of the phenomenal world (prapañca). Thus he says: "This much," etc. (27).

Viśvanātha: He states a certain common means for the three types of practitioners to achieve the fruit of dharma, beginning with "This much alone": by means of yoga—namely, that which is called devotion (bhakti), that which is called knowledge (jñāna), and that which is called [eightfold] yoga (yoga)—[he describes] what belongs to the yogin, the devotee, the man of knowledge, and the practitioner of the eight-limbed yoga.

Complete non-attachment toward the objects of the senses is non-attachment; this alone is the "desired object" because it accomplishes what is desired. The meaning is that one is applied to, joined with, or made fit for it.
The sense is that by means of complete non-attachment alone, one attains the object of one's own desire, whether it be worldly affection or liberation.
The single, attributeless Brahman appears through the outward-turned senses as an object possessing qualities such as sound and the like, due to delusion.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But how can the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is perceived through perception and other means of knowledge, be refuted? For such perception is an error. To this he says: "Knowledge" (*jñāna*). [The world appears] as an object-form (*artharūpeṇa*) characterized by qualities such as sound and so forth, which are directed outward (*parācīnaiḥ*) or turned away; whereas [true] knowledge is devoid of such qualities (*nirguṇa*).
The meaning is that Brahman alone shines forth, and no object exists separately from it. ||28||

The Structural Arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, even if Brahman consists of consciousness alone, how can the phenomenal world—which eternally has that [consciousness] as its substratum—be dispelled by consciousness alone? And if it remains, how could there not be a lack of "Lordliness" (*bhagavattā*)? It is said in reply: although both [the world and Lordliness] have that [consciousness] as their substratum, [they differ].

Because the state of being the Blessed One is eternally established by its own essential nature and power, and because it constitutes the supreme human goal for those who delight in the Self just like the Self itself, it cannot be discarded, nor is it intended to be discarded. Furthermore, Brahman is indeed within the range of words for living beings, but not within the range of [ordinary] experience; rather, it is that which belongs to the Upaniṣads.
Because of the Vedic revelation, "I ask about the Person," and because of the logical principle, "Since [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*),
the connection between that [Brahman] and its effect, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), is negated by the scripture itself—
through such passages as "Brahman is one only, without a second," and "Always with its own splendor. Therefore, in that regard:
The effort of living beings at logical reasoning achieves nothing; rather, it is the conscious reality (*cidvastu*) itself that constitutes the true nature of the living being (*jīva*),
which is experienced by the living beings during the states of waking and dreaming as the illuminator of the inert object of illumination,
and in deep sleep as the very form that shines forth by itself, because of which [one experiences] "I am happy."

"I slept," and so forth, is subsequently connected [to the waking state]. This being the case, regarding this twofold body which appears to living beings as consisting of both conscious and insentient natures:

therein, the conscious portion is the essential nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), while the insentient portion is the effect of *pradhāna*. However, the conscious portion becomes manifold only through its connection with various insentient entities.

Whatever shines forth becomes the cause of saṃsāra. Therefore, intending to show that this conscious element (cidaṃśa) shines forth as distinct from the insentient, he describes it as such with two verses beginning with "Knowledge" (jñānam).
It is one, pure, and because it is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), it is knowledge in the form of consciousness (cidrūpa), belonging to Brahman who occupies the position of the sun.
Being non-different from Brahman, [the Self] stands in the place of the atoms of rays;

yet, through that very delusion produced by the external sense organs which are turned away from it, it appears in the form of objects such as the ether within the body— possessing attributes like sound— and is perceived as having attained identity with them.
Therefore, the meaning is that discrimination must indeed be practiced for the purpose of eliminating that [misconception]. ||28||

Viśvanātha: Now, devotion is what we desire to perform and has been understood from scripture; likewise, knowledge and yoga are also what we wish to investigate and have been understood from scripture. However, the non-dual knowledge therein has not been correctly understood;
therefore, please explain it briefly. Consequently, [the following is] the knowledge accepted by the proponents of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavādins*).

He said: That which is knowledge, the one non-dual Brahman, is itself perceived through the causes—the outward-turned, averse senses such as hearing—which arise from the power of *māyā*; it is apprehended in the form of objects possessing attributes such as sound, as in:
"this drum has sound," "this woman has form," or "this has taste."

The milk appears as "it has been tasted" and so forth through the delusion of the living being; the meaning is that in the absence of all the sense organs, since there is no differentiation of cognition, that single cognition is non-dual Brahman itself.

[Objection: In that case, would it not follow that this entire universe is false, just as the object perceived in an error is false? [Reply: Not so. In the cognition "this is silver," because there is no cognition of it as mother-of-pearl, the status of silver in the mother-of-pearl is indeed false; however, in the case of the statement "one sees only color with the eye,"...

The experience indeed occurs as "this is a cognition whose instrument is the eye, whose agent is [the self], and whose object is form," wherein Brahman, as pure consciousness, appears as the substantive;

however, the agent, instrument, and object are merely qualifiers that differentiate the referent of the word "cognition" and are projected by *māyā*, the external power (*bahiraṅga-śakti*). Thus, it is not [a case of Brahman being differentiated].

Their falsity is to be known. Having created [the world] through its own function of ignorance (*avidyā*), the individual soul (*jīva*) is caused to wander from innate knowledge and is cast into infinite varieties of cognition characterized by the distinctions of creator and so forth that it itself has fashioned. This very [process] constitutes the soul's delusion regarding the manifold cognitions that take the form of objects.

Activity is like that of cows, donkeys, and the like: even when pure Gaṅgā water is present, their activity toward thirst is directed only toward water in various dug-out channels and such, due to delusion alone, and not so for humans whose intellects are free from delusion. Here, by the qualification "turned away" (*parāṅmukhaiḥ*) applied to the senses, [it is implied that they do not perceive the truth].
However, when the senses are not turned away, not directed outward, but rather turned toward the Blessed One,

the differentiation of knowledge— such as "this flute of the Blessed One possesses sweet sound" or "this body of the Blessed One is Śyāmasundara"— which is grounded in the conscious reality (cidvastu), is not cut off, precisely because that [consciousness] is Brahman itself.
The Bhāgavatas say: ||28||
Just as the Great One is of the nature of the ego, threefold, fivefold, and self-ruling, so too is he elevenfold; from him comes the cosmic egg, which is his body and the world.
Madhva is the Lord Indra, the destroyer of cities, who consists of the eleven senses as well as the five elements; he is the sovereign ruler and the one who presides over all.
"The wise know this entire egg-like world to be the body of Śakra;
Rudra is its lord and possesses three qualities, and from him come Brahmā and then Hari"—thus it is stated in the Vāmana Purāṇa (29).
Śrīdhara: He demonstrates the very nature of the object by providing an illustration, beginning with "yathā" (as follows).

The ego-form is the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense). And that is threefold, consisting of the three *guṇas*. Furthermore, it is fivefold in the form of the elements (*bhūta*), and elevenfold in the form of the sense organs (*indriya*). The self-ruling (*svarāj*) is the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). Of that—

The body of the individual soul (*jīva*) is the cosmic egg and the universe; from which [egg], through the principles beginning with *mahat*, such a sequential arrangement appears. Thus, when discrimination has arisen, this individual soul (*jīva*), though appearing as a distinct form (*vyaṣṭi-rūpa*), appears in the same manner as the collective form (*samaṣṭi-rūpa*): namely, as a self-ruler (*svarāṭ*) and self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) by virtue of its predominance in knowledge.

The meaning is that he shines as one who is truly existent. In what manner does this individual soul (*jīva*), in its collective form, shine as a self-ruling lord (*svarāṭ*)? To this, he says with the words beginning "the Great One" (*mahān*).
The meaning is: even though he has attained identity with the collective *mahat* and so forth. Of that self-ruling soul...
He demonstrates the very nature of being a collective totality with the words "of that," because from it the world—the entire multitude of moving and non-moving beings—comes into existence. ||29||

Viśvanātha: It has been stated that [the world] appears in the form of objects; therefore, he shows that every illusory entity is indeed included within the category of objects—beginning with "Just as... The Great One is the mind (*citta*);
the ego-form is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and is fivefold.

Furthermore, it exists in eleven forms: as sound and so forth, as ether and so forth, and as the sense organs. It is the self-ruling totality (*samaṣṭi*), the individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*), the cosmic form (*virāṭ*), and the body of the pure individual soul (*śuddhajīva*), as well as the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*).
From these—Mahat and the rest—this entire illusory universe arises; such is the nature of these principles beginning with Mahat.
Because it is an object of the intellect, it possesses the nature of an object. ||29||
Indeed, with faith, devotion, and constant practice of yoga,
one whose self is composed and who is free from attachment perceives this through dispassion.
"Like honey": just as they perceive these [objects], so too do the ignorant perceive my forms as consisting of knowledge, such as the Fish incarnation and others. ||30||
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But then, why does a person not understand it in this way? To that he says: "This is Brahman. (30)

The sequential composition: And this reality of consciousness (cidvastu) one perceives by means of that very practice of yoga previously described— which is characterized by devotion preceded by faith in the worship of the Lord and performed constantly with its seed— as one whose self is composed, and so forth.
The meaning is that the Sāṅkhya who denies a Lord does not see [the truth] merely through discrimination, without devotion and so forth. ||30||
Viśvanātha: He states the qualified person for this knowledge: "This Brahman is of the nature of knowledge. (30)
Thus, O venerable lady, has been told this knowledge, which is the vision of Brahman,
by means of which the reality of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa is realized.
Śrīdhara: He restates in brief the very meaning already explained for the sake of easy comprehension—namely, "iti" (thus). O Gurvi, O venerable one! ||31||

The "sequence of arrangement" (*kramasaṃdarbha*): this refers to the aforementioned type of knowledge. What is the vision of that Brahman—which is knowable through the scriptures alone—and what is the gateway to that knowledge? He restates its nature as being of the aforementioned type with the words "by which": [the vision] of *prakṛti*, that is, *pradhāna*, and of the *puruṣa*.
Of the living being. ||31||
Viśvanātha: He restates the very meaning already expressed in brief for the sake of easy understanding: "O Gurvi! O Mother! (31)
The yoga of knowledge centered on Me, which is beyond the gunas and characterized by devotion—
though there are two [paths], their single meaning is that which is defined by the word "Bhagavat."
O Madhva: without knowledge and devotion, liberation does not exist for anyone;
nor can both be attained by either one of these two without the grace of Viṣṇu.

"Even so, although these two exist as one, since [the result] is not fixed, liberation may certainly be attained by even one; however, the other is a means for that purpose. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Harivaṃśa*. And by this yoga of knowledge, it is the Blessed One alone who is to be attained, just as...

He says "by the yoga of devotion" (bhaktiyogena): the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga) which is beyond the qualities (nairguṇya), and the yoga characterized by devotion (bhakti) which is centered on Me—of these two, there is but one single purpose or goal. What is that?
It is that for which the word "Bhagavat" is the defining characteristic or indicator. This has been stated in the Gītā: "They attain... [15.4].
"Devoted solely to Me, they find delight in the welfare of all beings" (Gītā 12.4). ||32||

The sequential arrangement: Having stated "mere knowledge" (*jñānamātra*) here, he demonstrates that the entire purport [of the scripture] lies in the Blessed One alone, clearly making this understood through the two verses beginning with "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Both "established in Me" (*manniṣṭhaḥ*) and "beyond the qualities" (*nairguṇyaḥ*) are qualifiers for both [the devotee and the Lord]. In that regard, although liberation (*kaivalya*) is characterized by *sattva*,...

Although the state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) is not possible according to the Lord’s statement, "Knowledge is remembered as firmly established and devoid of qualities" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.25.24), it is nevertheless called "devoid of qualities" in view of the qualitylessness of its fruit, which is liberation (*kaivalya*). This very point he states: "Of both, one..."
"Thus is the meaning.
[Bhagavatsandarbha 93] Viśvanātha: Since yoga results in knowledge in the future, there are only two means mentioned in this section—knowledge and devotion—for those two goals to be accomplished.

Although there is a duality between attaining Brahman and attaining the Blessed Lord, since the Blessed Lord alone is Brahman according to the logic already stated, the attainment of the Blessed Lord would be the only single fruit; thus he says: "By knowledge...
The sense is that "one who is established in Me" is so because I alone am Brahman. He is "nairguṇya," meaning devoid of the qualities (nirguṇa).

And that yoga which has devotion as its characteristic—the purpose and goal of these two is one and the same. What is this? It is the word "Bhagavat," which is the characteristic—that is, the indicator—of it. This was stated in the *Gītā*: "They, devoted to the welfare of all beings, attain Me alone" (*Gītā* 12.4); for I am the foundation of Brahman.
Because of the statement, "And of the imperishable nectar" (Gītā 14.27), the attainment of both union (*sāyujya*) and love (*preman*) is established through the Lord alone. ||32||

Just as a single object, which is the locus of many qualities, cannot be brought [to perception] by the senses through their separate doors, so too the Blessed One cannot be fully grasped by the various paths of the scriptures.

Śrīdhara: Now, an objection may be raised: it is understood from the scriptures that the fruit of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) is the attainment of the Self (*ātman*), whereas the fruit of the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) is the attainment of the Lord who is the object of devotion. How, then, can these two have the same purpose?
Anticipating this doubt, he establishes the point by means of an illustration: "Just as [there is one substrate] for many qualities such as form, taste, and so forth..."
A single object, such as molasses or milk, is perceived in various ways by the senses engaged through different channels:
as "white" by the eye, as "sweet" by the tongue, as "cold" by the sense of touch, and so forth; likewise, the Blessed One, though truly one, is apprehended in those various forms. (33)

The sequential arrangement: that which cannot be led by the senses is grasped in its entirety by the mind alone. Therefore, because it brings about the realization of all aspects, the yoga of devotion to the Blessed One should be understood as standing in the place of the mind. For this reason, it alone is declared to be the primary limb (*aṅgin*). In the phrase "by means of dispositions" (*bhāvaiḥ*), [the word] "by means of desires" (*kāmaiḥ*) [is intended].
"Sometimes he is not perceived," thus says Puṇyāraṇya.
Viśvanātha comments: The Lord is not only accessible through knowledge and devotion;
rather, because He possesses infinite power (*ananta-śakti*), He is accessible through every means of attainment. To illustrate this, he provides an example, beginning with "Just as... (yathā).

A single substance such as milk, which is the substratum for many qualities like color, taste, and so forth, is perceived in various ways by the sense organs operating through distinct doors and separate channels: it is perceived as "white" by the eye,
as "sweet" by the tongue, as "cold" by the skin, as "fragrant" by the nose, and [as "sound"] by the ear.

Thus, each individual object—such as that which is designated "milk"—is experienced as possessing its own specific property, rather than being grasped through various properties; therefore, it is not an object whose nature is "milk" [in a composite sense].
However, by means of the mind, which is the king of the senses, this [object] bestows pleasure and brings satisfaction.
This object, designated as "white, sweet, cool, fragrant milk," is perceived as being endowed with all those respective qualities; likewise, by means of the paths of the scriptures—
such as ritual action and knowledge— it bestows heaven, because it takes the form of heaven, liberation, and so forth.

The Lord (Īśvara) is the Self who bestows liberation; He is experienced as the one part that is Brahman. However, through devotion as the primary means, the Blessed One—who has become the object of love and who bestows all fruits such as heaven and liberation—is denoted by terms such as "Lord" (Īśvara).

"It is experienced in every way"—this is the commentary seen in the *Bhāgavatāmṛta*. For instance: "Just as a single object, such as milk, which is the locus of qualities like color and taste, is known by many senses."
The Blessed One is perceived as white by the eye and sweet by the tongue;
likewise, though he is one, he is apprehended in many ways through various modes of worship.
Just as sweetness is to be grasped by the tongue alone and not by other [senses],
so too do the eyes and the other [faculties] each grasp their own respective objects.
Likewise, all other forms of worship reside in the external organs,
whereas devotion resides in the mind, since it attains all those various goals.
Thus, in the *Pravara-śāstras*, the superiority of Kṛṣṇa is declared on account of his being the very nature of Brahman and his preeminence in qualities such as sweetness. [La.Bha.
1.5.2015] Thus, by means of ritual action, sacrifices, gifts, austerity, Vedic study, and self-restraint...
Through mastery over the self and the senses, and by means of the renunciation of actions.

Śrīdhara: He elaborates upon the very path of the scriptures with three verses beginning with "by action" (kriyayā). By "action" is meant action in the form of *pūrta* (charitable works); by "sacrifices" (*kratubhiḥ*) is meant ritual offerings; "reflection" (*marśanam*) is *mīmāṃsā* (philosophical inquiry); and "victory over self and senses" is the avoidance of what is prohibited. ||34||

The sequential arrangement: therein, while enumerating *bhaktiyoga* as the cause for the complete vision (*pūrṇadarśana*) and ritual action (*kriyā*) and so forth as the causes for the partial vision (*khaṇḍadarśana*), he demonstrates the various distinctions of their manifestation by means of the three verses beginning with "by ritual action" (*kriyayā*). The triad beginning with "by ritual action" is as follows:

The duty of the householder; austerity for the forest-dweller; and the study and contemplation of the Vedas for the student—having thus described the path of the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) with the words "the self" and "the two," he now describes the paths of the section on meditation (*upāsanākāṇḍa*) with the words "by yoga": by means of various limbs and diverse distinctions.

He speaks of the paths of the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*) with the words "by the yoga of devotion" (*bhaktiyogena*) and "by the realization of the reality of the Self" (*ātmatattvāvabodhena*); the meaning is: by love and by the experience of Brahman. In that regard, he states the specific practice that serves as the gateway to devotion with the word "by dharma" (*dharmeṇa*); the meaning is: by the dharma pertaining to the Blessed Lord. He demonstrates that very point with the word "both" (*ubhayam*).

"By that which has its mark therein"—this very phrase clarifies the state of possessing both marks: namely, that dharma which is *pravṛtti* (active engagement) toward the Blessed Lord and *nivṛtti* (withdrawal) elsewhere; thus it possesses both. He states the gateway to the second path:
"and by means of dispassion (*vairāgya*) consisting solely of withdrawal (*nivṛtti*)," is the meaning. Here, that which is to be accomplished is also...

It should be understood that [the goal] is included herein; he now states the distinctions regarding the manifestation of what is to be attained: the *saguṇa* [Brahman], in the form of heaven and so forth, is attained through the path of ritual action (*karma*); the *nirguṇa* [Brahman], in the form of Brahman, is attained through the experience of Brahman;
the Lord, who perceives all by His own nature as the Self, is attained through the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*); and [the goal] is attained through the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅga-yoga*).

The meaning is that, in accordance with the accomplishment of the two limbs of that [state], it leads to the attainment of those two; in some cases, it leads to the attainment of the qualified (saguṇa) state which consists of the respective specific accomplishments. ||34||
Viśvanātha: He elaborates upon the paths of the scriptures with three verses beginning with "by action" (kriyayā).
The triad of action and the rest is the duty of the householder; austerity is that of the forest-dweller;

and reflection (*marśana*)—meaning inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*)—along with self-study (*svādhyāya*) and reflection, is that of the student (*brahmacārin*); and the dyad beginning with "the Self" (*ātman*) is that of the mendicant (*bhikṣu*).

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "by the yoga of devotion indeed" (*bhaktiyogena caiva hi*), he makes known that [the other means] are mixed with devotion— since one must apply it everywhere as "by action and by the yoga of devotion," "by sacrifices and by the yoga of devotion," and "by gifts and by the yoga of devotion"— it follows that without this mixing with the yoga of devotion, [liberation does not occur].

It makes known the incapacity of ritual actions and the like to accomplish their own respective fruits. Furthermore, by means of the two words "eva" (only) and "hi" (indeed), which express restriction and certainty, it makes known that the reality to be accomplished through ritual action and so forth is determined to be attainable solely through the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*). Therefore, [it establishes] the [supremacy] of the yoga of devotion.
The state of being the foremost of all should be understood as being like the essential nature of the Blessed One himself. ||34||
Indeed, by means of yoga with its various limbs and by the yoga of devotion,
and through dharma characterized by both marks, he who follows both the path of active engagement and the path of withdrawal [attains the goal].
Śrīdhara: By the "dual mark," meaning by the characteristics of both having desires and being free from desires. He explains that very point with the words "He who...
The sense is that even heaven and the like, which are attainable through dharmas involving desire, are indeed the qualified nature (saguṇa-svarūpa) of the Blessed Lord himself. ||35||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: By the two marks characterized as "with desire" (*sakāma*) and "without desire" (*niṣkāma*). He clarifies this very point: "That dharma which possesses engagement and withdrawal. (35)
Through the realization of the reality of the Self and through firm dispassion,
the Lord— who is both with attributes and without attributes, and who is self-luminous— is attained by these means.
Śrīdhara: By these paths; "self-seeing" means self-luminous. ||36||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "With qualities" (*saguṇa*) means having the form of heaven and so forth, which is attainable through ritual actions and sacrifices;
"without qualities" (*nirguṇa*) means having the nature of Brahman, the Supreme Self, and so forth, which is attainable through renunciation, yoga, and so forth.

The term *svadṛk* means that he perceives only his own devotees who are devoted to no other with undivided attachment; thus, the meaning is that the form of the Lord is attainable through the yoga of pure devotion. ||36||
I have described to you the fourfold nature of the yoga of devotion,
as well as Time, whose unmanifest course runs within all living beings.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having concluded the discussion on the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) and having stated its identity of purpose with the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), he concludes the section on the yoga of devotion and so forth with two verses beginning with "I have declared" (*prāvocam*).
[The path] is fourfold, distinguished by the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and the qualityless (*nirguṇa*). It moves within [the heart], [encompassing] birth, dissolution, and so forth.
He performs it. ||37||

The sequential arrangement: therein, he reiterates the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga) as the primary subject with the pair of verses beginning "I have spoken. That by which its own essential nature is defined is its fourfold characteristic. And for that very purpose, time and the other factors were described; thus he says: "Of time... (37).

Viśvanātha: Thus, having concluded the discussion on the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) and having demonstrated that its ultimate steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) lies in the Blessed Lord alone— who is attained through the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*)— and having established by means of an appropriate illustration that the Blessed Lord alone is the goal of all paths such as ritual action (*karma*), [the author] now [turns to] the yoga of devotion and so forth.

He concludes with two verses beginning with "I have declared": "The fourfold transmigrations of the individual soul, produced by ignorance and karma and distinguished by the three qualities and the qualityless state— O dear one, entering into these, the self does not know its own destination."
Śrīdhara: My dear mother! ||38||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. Indeed,
one should never teach this to the wicked, nor ever to the undisciplined, nor to the arrogant, nor to the divisive, nor to those who merely display the banner of righteousness.
One should not teach this to one who is greedy, nor to one whose mind is fixed on the household life;
never to one who lacks devotion to Me, nor even to those who hate My devotees.

Śrīdhara: With two verses beginning with "Not this," he shows those who are ineligible for instruction: one who brings distress to others for his own sake; one who is divided [in mind] and of evil conduct; and one who is a hypocrite, bearing the banner of righteousness (dharmadhvaja). ||3940||

The structural arrangement [of the commentary] on this pair of verses is as follows: "Not so" [is the response]. A "wicked person" (*khala*) is one who has entered [the assembly] with the desire to find fault, even if he belongs to an opposing faction; an "undisciplined person" (*avinīta*) is one devoid of the decorum expected of a disciple; an "obstinate person" (*stabdha*) is one who is arrogant;

a "divided person" (*bhinna*) is one who has reached a state of schism due to a different philosophical view; and a "mere banner of righteousness" (*dharmadhvaja*) is one who holds up the banner of dharma for the sake of mere livelihood.
One who manifests such a state is: one who is greedy; one who, though free from various faults, has lost his fortitude through greed;

one whose mind is fixed on the household, being excessively attached to children, wife, and so forth; one who is devoid of devotion (abhakta), possessing latent impressions (saṃskāra) opposed to my devotion despite being endowed with qualities contrary to those [of the devotee]; and one who hates the devotees.
Even though there may be a semblance of the refinement of devotion, they possess the great defect of being opposed to true devotion;
the sense is that among such various types, not even one is to be accepted. ||3940||

Viśvanātha: He shows those who are ineligible for this instruction with the words "Not this" (*naitat*). A *khala* (wicked person) is one who desires to learn [this] merely through feigned devotion for the sake of finding fault. An *avinīta* (undisciplined person) is one devoid of the boundaries of conduct prescribed by the learned; a *stabdha* (arrogant person) is one possessed of excessive pride; and a *bhinna* (divisive person) is one who creates schism through another's doctrine.
One who has attained [the status of a practitioner] but whose banner of Dharma is merely for the sake of gain, prestige, and so forth, while being devoted to the Dharma only nominally;

one who is greedy, meaning one who is excessively covetous of sense-objects even though free from those various other faults; one whose mind is fixed on the household, meaning one who, though not excessively covetous of sense-objects, is deeply attached to children, wife, wealth, and the like; and one who is without devotion.

Even if one is free from all faults— whether mentioned or unmentioned— if they are devoid of devotion to me; moreover, even if by mistake or negligence they should occasionally teach these [truths] to others, they should never, under any circumstances,
teach them to those who hate my devotees, as indicated by the use of the genitive case (*mad-bhakta-dviṣām*) which refers to their very associates.
How much less, then, could it be from them? ||3940||
To one who is faithful, devoted, humble, and free from malice;
to one who has cultivated friendliness toward all beings and is intent upon service.
Let it be given to one who has produced dispassion toward external things, whose mind is tranquil,
who is free from envy, and who is pure— to him for whom I am the dearest among his beloveds.
Śrīdhara: He states the qualified person by means of two verses beginning with "śraddadhānāya" (to the faithful one). ||41||
The sequential arrangement: He speaks of those who are the opposite [of the aforementioned] as qualified [disciples] with the following pair of verses, beginning with "śraddadhānaḥ":

one who is faithful (*śraddadhānaḥ*) is one who possesses conviction in my devotee-guru and in the scripture taught by me; one who is devoted (*bhaktaḥ*) is one endowed with the latent impressions of devotion; one who is humble (*vinītaḥ*) is one who observes the proper conduct of a disciple; and one who is free from malice (*anasūyuḥ*).
When one observes that respect for the guru increases due to the preceptor’s superior qualities—whether they share the same lineage (*satīrtha*) or otherwise—one becomes, on the contrary, happy;

one forms friendships and is endowed with compassion. One is devoted to service and tireless in attending upon the guru. Regarding the word "externally" (*bahiḥ*), the meaning is that just as one is detached externally, so too is one internally. One is free from envy (*nirmatsara*).

Desiring all that is auspicious, pure, and sanctified both internally and externally; the causal relationship between these qualities may be analyzed as desired. By the phrase "of whom I am [the disciple]," the definition of the teacher is also stated through the grammatical connection that "it is given by such a teacher. Alternatively, he states the result for such a disciple with the words "of whom... (yasya).
The meaning is: "of one who has become such that I shall be exceedingly dear to him.

Although the previous defects may have been abandoned here, it should be understood that their mention is for the purpose of separately identifying the positive qualities (vyatireka). Furthermore, these qualities should be understood as being present collectively.
However, regarding the deficiency of those respective limbs, there is a lack of qualification; thus, with reference to those very qualities, he says: "Pure," etc. (41).
Viśvanātha states the qualified candidate with two verses beginning with "śraddadhānāya": [he is] one who is detached from external objects. ||4142||
O Mother, that person who hears this even once with faith,
or whoever recites it with their mind fixed on Me, indeed attains My state.

Śrīdhara: He states that even for one devoted to hearing and chanting this [text], the attainment of My state alone is the fruit—beginning with "He who... The particle *ca* (api) is used in the sense of "even. Such a person also attains My state; *hi* signifies certainty.
This sequence of composition determines the purport of the multitude of His own instructions through the declaration of the fruit.
"Ya idam" means the path of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*). ||43||

Viśvanātha: What need is there to speak of the fortune of those who perform this [practice]? Listen as he describes the fortune resulting from merely hearing and chanting it: "He who... and so forth. Being one whose mind is fixed on Me (*maccitta*), he attains My state (*matpadavī*), which is the place where My feet are set down. ||43||

Thus ends the thirty-second [chapter], appropriately joined to the third, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Blessed One, and which is well-suited for the virtuous.

Thus ends the section titled "The Ripening of Karma" within the Kāpileya narrative of the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya, in the Third Book of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, a compendium of the Pāramahaṃsya tradition composed by Vyāsa.
Chapter Thirty-two | Chapter Thirty-three:
The Narrative of Kapila in the Dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya.
Maitreya said: Having thus heard these words of Kapila, his mother Devahūti, the beloved wife of Kardama, indeed [acted].
With the veil of delusion cast aside, she bowed down to him and praised him, the ground of perfected accomplishment marked by the domain of reality.
Śrīdhara:
In the thirty-third [chapter], however, the liberation while living (jīvanmukti) of that very [Kapila’s] mother through the arising of knowledge by means of Kapila’s instruction is proclaimed.
She is one from whom the film of the nature of delusion has fallen away—that is, the veil [has been removed]. The principles (tattvas) themselves are the object;
the accomplishment marked by that is the knowledge of Sāṅkhya, and she is the ground, the field, and the instigator of that. ||1||

The sequence of composition (*kramasaṃdarbha*): The meaning is that it is the ground, the support, and the instigator of that perfection—the manifestation of the Supreme Self—which is marked or characterized by those principles (*tattva*) that are the objects of inquiry into reality (*tattvavicāra*). The same applies elsewhere. The reading here is *etad* (this), referring to the Puṇyāraṇya; hence [the term] *siddha*.
Therefore, there is the statement of the relationship. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
Praised by Devahūtī in the thirty-third [chapter], Śrī Kapila departed for the forest;
she too followed him by the very path he had instructed.

Janitrī means the progenitor. She is the one from whom the veil of delusion—the mass of ignorance concerning devotion, knowledge, and so forth—has fallen away. She is marked with respect to the principles (tattva), that is, with respect to the principles of devotion, the principles of Sāṅkhya-knowledge, the principles of Yoga, and so on.

He who, through supreme proficiency, had produced lines in the calculation of his finger-joints (aṅkagaṇanā), and who was one from whom the perfected stages (siddhabhūmayaḥ) and the people dwelling on the earth (bhūtalasthajanāḥ) proceeded; him [he saluted]. ||1||
Devahūti said:
Moreover, that unborn body of yours, composed of the elements, the senses, and their objects, was lying within the waters.
He, who was born from the lotus in his own belly, meditated upon that stream of qualities which contains all seeds in their entirety.

"Madhva" means that which consists of the elements, the senses, their objects, and the self; from these, the Pradhāna (primordial matter) arises. You are composed of that Pradhāna, yet you are superior even to the gods who are themselves predominant [over it], as stated in the Vārāha Purāṇa. ||2||
Śrīdhara: The word "atha" marks a new sentence. Although he is unborn (*aja*), he meditated upon your form alone;
he did not see it [directly]. And he himself was born from the lotus of your own abdomen;
you alone ordain the creation and so forth of the universe, for there is no one who is the creator of your creation and so forth. He...
The connection of the three [verses] is as follows: "How was you, being such as this, held by me within my womb?
Of what nature was that body? It was manifest (*sat*). The reason for this is: "lying within the waters.
Of what kind [was it]? It consisted of the elements (*bhūta*), the senses (*indriya*), the objects of the senses (*artha*) such as sound and so forth, the self (*ātman*), and the mind (*manas*).
The meaning is that it is pervaded by these. Why? Because it is that in which there is a flow of the qualities (guṇas). Why?
Because it is the seed, the cause, of the entire aggregate of effects and causes. ||2||

The sequential arrangement (*kramasaṃdarbha*): Now, the word "atha" (now/then) constitutes a triad. Alternatively, it marks the beginning of another statement. Although Brahmā is well known as "the unborn" (*aja*), he was born from Your belly; he meditated upon Your form—that is, he performed worship—in order to achieve his own preeminence. What is that form?

Regarding this, he says: "In the water. The meaning is: "lying in the waters of the cosmic womb" (*garbhodaka*). And what is the nature of that [water]? In what manner did He meditate? To this he says: "Being" (*sat*). He meditated upon the seed of all things as having the very nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). The meaning is that He contemplated it as the imperishable seed. Because...
The meaning is that which is the self, the cause, and the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of the elements and so forth, consisting of that and possessing its power.
For this very reason, from the belly of Him from whom such a flow of the *guṇas* proceeds, He alone—who is thus—brings about creation and the rest, not those [elements] and so forth. ||2||
Viśvanātha says: "That you rescue me from the cycle of worldly existence by imparting this truth is not surprising.

What is truly surprising is this: that you, O Supreme Lord, who have within your womb infinite millions of cosmic eggs, were born from my very womb—I, a lowly human being. Thus he speaks with the words, "Now... (atha).

At the beginning of the sentence: although he was unborn, even Brahmā meditated only upon your form lying within the waters—the waters situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa)—specifically your form as the one reclining in the embryonic ocean (garbhoda-śāyin); the sense is that he did not see it at the very outset. Of what kind? [That form which consists of] the elements (bhūta), the senses (indriya), and their objects (artha).

That which consists of the Self, consisting of its own nature, and is indeed of the form of consciousness and bliss, and not a modification of primordial matter (prakṛti)—that which carries forth excellently the qualities such as affection for devotees; that which is real, the truth, and the seed, the cause of the entire universe. ||2||
You alone, whose power is distributed through the flow of the qualities (guṇas), ordain the creation and so forth of the universe;
you are free from desire and your resolve is unfailing.
The Lord of the self, possessing inconceivable and thousandfold powers.

Śrīdhara: In what manner do you perform the creation and so forth? He is one by whom power (*vīrya*, i.e., *śakti*) is divided in the form of a flow of the *guṇas*. The meaning is that he performs [creation] through the medium of power, not directly. Since he is desireless (*anīha*), that is, inactive (*niṣkriya*), how then can there be creation and so forth even through the medium of power?

What does He ordain? To this he says: He whose intention is unfailing is one whose resolve is true. For what purpose does He ordain it? He is the Lord of *ātman*s, that is, of the individual souls (*jīva*s). The meaning is: for the sake of the experience of the individual souls. But how can a single being ordain such diverse experiences? To this he says: "Inconceivable are His thousands."
He whose powers are immeasurable. ||3||

The sequence of composition: the reason for this is that he is one by whom power (*vīrya*), which is his own capacity (*svaśakti*), has been divided and bestowed upon Brahmā and the others, being differentiated through the flow of qualities (*guṇa*) and the distinctions in their successive manifestations (*vṛtti-paramparā*). And because of that, he is unstained; thus he says: "He is effortless (*anīha*) and of unerring intention (*avitathābhisandhi*). Regarding his effortlessness (*anīhatva*) therein:

The reason [for this] is: "The Self is the supreme witness. The subsequent reason is: "The Lord has His own free will. Regarding that, he states the reason for the lack of contradiction: "not by reasoning" (*atarkya*). The meaning is that there is no cause for wonder on account of this much regarding Him who possesses inconceivable and infinite power; rather, there is yet another aspect of His infinity, according to the Śruti.
The meaning is that [the Veda is authoritative] because it has the Word as its source (śabdamūlatvāt). ||3||

Viśvanātha: He is one by whom power—the capacity for creation and so forth—has been distributed and bestowed through the flow of qualities, that is, through the succession of the *rajas* and other *guṇas*. He is one whose intention is unfailing, meaning his resolve is true. ||3||
O Lord, you who were nourished within my womb— how indeed could it be that this universe once lay within your belly alone upon a single banyan leaf at the end of an eon?
The illusory infant lay down, drinking from his mother's breast.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, how could You—who contained this entire universe within Your belly during the dissolution—be held by me in my own stomach? Surely, why say such a thing while I am but an infant? To this he replies: "Like a drop on a banyan leaf" (*baṭapatra*). One who drinks from the foot is *aṅghripāna*; this refers to the big toe of the foot. This...
The sense is that even childhood is likewise merely an illusion (māyā). ||4||

The sequential composition [of the verse] is as follows: "But you... If it is argued that [the child's behavior] was for the sake of childhood play by my will, then that [play] would have occurred spontaneously; thus he says: "On the leaf of the *baṭa* tree... Māyā is the inconceivable power (*śakti*), and the child is one whose primary nature is that [power]. ||4||

Viśvanātha: The sense is: "How were you, such as you are, borne in the womb by me, a mere human woman? You yourself must tell the cause of this wonder. [The Lord says: "But how can you speak thus to me, your own child?
To that he replies truthfully: "At the end of the age, at the time of dissolution, in a single banyan tree..."

"You were lying on a leaf. For what purpose? [The meaning is: "As a compassionate child-form, I am a deceptive infant so that even worldly people, accustomed to fondling children, may be able to meditate upon me.
In that regard, he describes the appropriate and sweet pastimes: "drinking from his feet."

The meaning is this: having abandoned all other pleasure, all wise men immerse themselves solely in the sweetness of My feet; it is with the thought that "this very [sweetness] must also be tasted and experienced by me" that they do so. ||4||
O Lord, you have assumed this physical body for the sake of pacifying evils and for the prosperity of those who follow your commands,
just as your incarnations as the boar and others were.
In the same way, this [person] also acts for the sake of attaining the path of the self.
*Madhvaḥ*: *dehatantraḥ* means the expansion of the body; for it is stated in the *Tantramālā*: "The term *tantra* denotes expansion (*tati*), light (*prakāśa*), and extension (*vistāra*). (5)

Śrīdhara: Alternatively, he says that you were not carried in my womb like another offspring, but rather have appeared by your own will, as in the case of the boar and other incarnations: "You are dependent on a body, possessed of a body, one who has assumed a form. [This refers to] the wicked, the sinful, those who follow your commands.
For the prosperity and abundance of those who follow his command, for the discovery of their own path, and for the revelation of the way of knowledge. ||5||
The sequence of the composition: To the question "For what purpose is such a manifestation? he says "Thou" (tvam).

Therein, having connected the purpose in general with the half-verse beginning with "Thou," he states it specifically with the words "Just as" (yathā); the word "therefore" (tasmāt) is to be supplied as the remainder. ||5||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, this is indeed your very nature—that you descend in this manner solely out of compassion; thus he says: "You are dependent on a body. Just as another child who has entered his mother's womb is dependent on the mother's body, so too are you, by way of divine play (*līlā*), dependent on the body of my mother. Or rather, [the word *dehatantra* refers to] the body...

He is one whose [attendants] possess vehicles, garments, ornaments, and equipment. For what purpose? For the pacification of the sins of those who behold him, and for the prosperity—meaning the perfection of devotion, knowledge, and so forth—of those who receive his commands and follow your instructions. This too is an incarnation as Kapila.
For the sake of attaining the path of devotion and knowledge pertaining to oneself. ||5||
By hearing and reciting his name, by bowing down to him, or even by remembering him at any time,
even a dog-eater immediately becomes fit for the sacrificial bath.
How much less, O Blessed One, could it be from seeing you?
Śrīdhara: Therefore, he speaks by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument, saying, "I have achieved my life's purpose through the sight of you.
From the mere hearing and chanting of whose name—even at some time or place—a *śvapaca* (one who eats dogs)—that is, a dog-cooker—is even fit (*kalpate*) for the *savana*, the Soma sacrifice.
It exists. By this, its state of being worthy of worship is indicated. ||6||

The sequential arrangement: [the author] states, in two verses, that even at some time or place, there is the power to destroy even those sins already set in motion (*prārabdha-pāpa*). The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is simply "due to the cause of hearing the name," etc., because of the requirement of what follows and because the word "even" (*api*) would otherwise be incoherent. Here, the term "doghood" (*śvādatva*) refers specifically to being a particular species of dog-eater.

Because of the etymological derivation "one who eats dogs" (*śvānam atti*), which employs the present tense, it follows that he possesses that habit, just like a carnivore (*kravyāda*). However, if one intended to prescribe an expiation for an occasional act of eating, the past tense would have been used. Furthermore, according to the maxim that "conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) supersedes etymological meaning (*yoga*"), that [habitual sense] prevails.
This is contradictory; therefore, the commentators [refer to him] as a *śvapaca* (outcaste). It is said: "He is fit for immediate sacrifice"—just as it is said:
"By whomsoever the two syllables 'Ha-ri' are uttered even once, by him the girdle is fastened for the journey toward liberation."

In this regard, the meaning is that one becomes one who has attained the commencement [of practice] within that very capacity. The intention is that, having attained the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*) in the very next birth, one would then be eligible for that [practice] and so forth. ||6||

Viśvanātha: By the logic of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so"), he says "that which... [in verse 17], meaning that by the mere sight of you, the world becomes one who has achieved its purpose. *Prahvaṇam* means prostration. "Even at some time" (*kvacid*) means even from an occasional remembrance.
Even a dog-eater (*śvāda*), that is, even a *caṇḍāla*, immediately—that very moment—becomes fit for the *savana*, the Soma sacrifice.

He becomes fit; like a Brāhmaṇa who performs the Soma sacrifice, he becomes worthy of worship. Thus, the destruction of the sins of the prārabdha-karma that originate from a low birth is indicated. As it was said by the venerable Śrī Rūpa Gosvāmī:
"Indeed, it is considered that low birth alone is the cause for being unfit for the *savana* (sacrificial bath).
Whatever sin constitutes the origin of that low birth, that very sin is what has already been set in motion (*prārabdha*).
[Bhāravi, Sarasvatī: O Blessed One! In some cases, by merely hearing or reciting one's name..."*]

First is the hearing of Your name, O Blessed One; thereafter is its chanting. From bowing—that is, from prostrating one's head before You—and from remembering—that is, through the remembrance of You, the Blessed One—even one born of the lowest of the low, the outcaste Śvapaca, [is purified].

Immediately, at that very moment, he becomes fit—that is, capable—for the *savana*, the Soma sacrifice, through the sight of you; furthermore, why indeed [should he do more]? "I have achieved my purpose"—this is the meaning. ||6||
Oh, how much greater even than an outcaste is he on whose tongue-tip your name resides!
The noble ones have performed austerities, offered oblations, and bathed in sacred waters for his sake.
The Brahmins spoke, uttering his name.

Śrīdhara: He establishes that point: "Aho bata! Oh, what a wonder! Even a dog-eater (śvapaca) is more venerable than this very person for the reason that Your name resides on the tip of his tongue; or rather, 'ataḥ' means 'because it resides [on his tongue]'. Why so? To this he says: they alone have performed penance (*tapas*) and offered oblations (*juhuvuḥ*)."

They have performed [these acts]; they have bathed, having bathed in sacred fords (*tīrtha*). They alone are noble (*ārya*), meaning those of virtuous conduct. They have recited the *brahman*, that is, the Veda; since the praise of your name contains within it the essence of austerity (*tapas*), the meaning is that they are most meritorious. Alternatively, in another birth, all these things—sacrifices and so forth—were performed by them.
The meaning is that this is understood through the arising of great fortune from the chanting of your name. ||7||

Regarding the sequence of arguments: as for what was stated—that "therefore, one is fit for the immediate performance of the *savana* sacrifice"—that too is of no consequence, because [in that case] everything such as austerity (*tapas*) and so forth would be subsumed within the mere utterance of His name;
and for this very reason, the one who utters His name is superior to those who perform austerity and the like.
Intending to say "it might even be so," he says: "Alas, indeed! However, the explanation should be understood exactly as it appears in the first alternative (*pakṣa*) of the *Ṭīkā*. ||7||

Viśvanātha: Regarding what was said—that he is fit for the sacrifice immediately even now—that too is nothing [extraordinary], because his fruitfulness would actually be superior even to that of the performers of the Soma sacrifice. Thus he says, "Aho bata!
which means: this is a marvel even among marvels. [This applies to] that outcaste (śvapaca) at whose tip of the tongue...
The meaning is that it was uttered incorrectly, in that it was [pronounced] only at the tip of the tongue and not on the whole of it;
"it exists" but "has not occurred" means it was uttered incompletely;
"name" is singular, meaning there is not a plurality of names; [whereas] on the whole of the tongue, they were uttered completely.
The sense is: "What need is there to mention many names? Or rather, it means "in order to please you.

Therefore, that outcaste (śvapaca) becomes most venerable (garīyān), meaning he possesses the fitness to instruct others even in the mantras consisting of [divine] names; this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: "In that case, let that outcaste (śvapaca) perform sacrifices, study, austerities, and so forth. To this, he says: "They have performed" (*tepuḥ*). What can be said of him alone? The restriction is understood that even others who merely utter your name—they alone have performed [the penance]. This is because in others, austerity is not seen to be complete or possessed of all its constituent parts. Thus...

Since no distinction was specified, they performed *tapas* (asceticism) of every kind; they offered oblations at all sacred fords (*tīrtha*); those very ones were the noble ones (*ārya*), and none others; and those very ones recited—that is, studied—the *brahman*, the Veda.

According to Amara: "An *anūcāna* is one who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*) from a teacher. This applies here in the verses beginning with "they performed penance" (*tepuḥ*).

Because of the use of the past tense (*bhūta-nirdeśāt*) and because of the use of the present tense in the word "they recite" (*gṛṇanti*), as soon as Your names are being grasped, all [other duties] such as austerity and sacrifice become as if already performed. They are neither being performed nor yet to be performed;
therefore, how could they perform those [other rites] again? For this very reason, regarding the actions of devotees—

It should also be understood that they lack the qualification [to perform such acts]. By using a verb in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, which speaks of something out of sight, the sense is that those very things are already established even by means of asceticism (*tapas*) and so forth, yet they do not know them; how much less, then, would they undertake the labor of their accomplishment?
Here, by the use of the present tense in the word *gṛṇanti* ("they proclaim"), it is implied that there is indeed no interruption in the recitation of their names.
But it should not be explained as "it would be so at that very time," for it is a wonder that one who has long since departed might now take up a name and then abandon what was bound.

Because in such statements as, "By hearing [this] even once, even a Pukkaśa is liberated from saṃsāra," the use of the word "once" (sakṛt) would be contradicted [if liberation were not achieved immediately]. ||7||

Sarasvatī: He upon whose tip of the tongue—that is, at the edge of his palate—resides your name, O Goddess, is therefore more venerable and superior even if he be a *śvapaca* (outcaste) born of a low family such as a dog-eater or a leather-worker, because of his designation as a consecrated sage (*daikṣavipra*). Oh, how wonderful! Those who chant your name...
They uttered [sacred sounds]; they practiced austerities—meaning those ascetics performed them with excellence;

they offered oblations, having performed the *homa*; they bathed in all the sacred fords (*tīrthas*); and being noble ones of virtuous conduct, they recited—that is, they studied—the Veda along with its auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*).
I perceive you as that Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, who is to be realized within the self through the inward-flowing stream [of consciousness],
and whose flow of the guṇas has been destroyed by his own splendor.
I bow to Viṣṇu, who is Kapila and the womb of the Vedas.
Śrīdhara: When the mind has been withdrawn into the Self within the inward-flowing stream, that which is to be contemplated—that which is to be meditated upon—is He whose womb is the Vedas. ||8||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Therefore, being ignorant, I am not at all able to praise you; thus I simply bow to him—with the words "to him" (*tam*). When the mind has been withdrawn into the inward current (*pratyak-srotas*). ||8||
Maitreya said: Thus praised with faltering words, the Supreme Person known as Kapila, who is affectionate toward his mother, spoke to his mother.
Śrīdhara: [spoke] with a voice that was unhurried and profound. ||9||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Because he is devoted to his mother, [he speaks] with faltering and stammering [words]. ||9||
Kapila said:
"O Mother, by following this path which I have described to you as so easy to practice,
you will before long attain the supreme goal."

Śrīdhara: By that [path] which is easy to practice (*susevya*), which is spoken by me, and which has been undertaken and performed, you will reach—meaning attain—the supreme limit, which is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). This is because it was stated that it is "easy to practice" due to its being the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*). (10)

Viśvanātha: The meaning is "by means of the yoga of devotion that is well-practiced. By being established in it—that is, by its performance—you will reach the supreme limit, the perfection of love (*prema-siddhi*). Although you already possess the eternally perfected state of motherhood, such a statement should be understood as being solely for the purpose of instructing the world. ||10||
Have faith in this teaching of mine, which is cherished by those who discourse on Brahman;
through it you shall attain fearlessness from me, whereas those who do not know it encounter death.
Śrīdhara: "Yāyāḥ" means "you will go. "Atadvidaḥ" means those who do not know my thought; that is, the ignorant. ||11||
*Kramasaṃdarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "To me" means to my [self]. "Yāyāḥ" means you will go. ||11||
Maitreya said:
Having thus demonstrated that true path of his own, the Blessed One,
Kapila, being permitted by his mother, who was a knower of Brahman, departed.
Śrīdhara: "Anumata" means permitted or authorized. ||12||
Regarding the sequence of composition: in the verse beginning with "uśatīm," some read "satīṃ tām" instead. ||12||
Viśvanātha: The reason for this consent is the reflection: "I declare and know that even this son of mine is indeed Brahman; therefore, how can I possibly keep him at home by my own will? ||12||
And she too, disciplined in yoga according to the instruction on yoga given by her son,
remained composed in that hermitage at the confluence of the Sarasvatī.
Śrīdhara: [She] was concentrated at Bindusaras, which was like a floral crest (*āpīḍa*) for Sarasvatī; or, according to the reading "Sarasvatyā," it was as if encircled by a crown. ||13||

The sequence of composition: "And she" forms a couplet (yugmaka). In the reading "by Sarasvatī," the meaning is that she was adorned by her [the goddess] at that Bindusaras lake; the instrumental case is used according to the rule exemplified by the expression *prakṛtyābhirūpaḥ* ("naturally handsome"). ||13||
Viśvanātha: [He is] upon the crest-ornament (*āpīḍa*) of Sarasvatī, which is like a flower-crown (*puṣpamukuṭa*). ||13||
With matted hair and curly locks, she was brownish from frequent immersion [in water];
wearing rags and emaciated, she sustained herself through fierce asceticism.

Śrīdhara: In what state was she while being composed? To this he says: She was one who bore locks of hair that were repeatedly turned tawny (kapiśa) and reddish-brown (piśaṅga) by bathing three times a day (trisavana), as well as her own body, which was naturally curly, clad in bark garments, and emaciated. ||14||
Regarding the sequence of composition: in the phrase "abhīkṣṇāvagāha," the reading "abhīkṣṇagāha" is the opinion of Svāmī and Puṇyāraṇya. (14)
Viśvanātha: Constantly bathing three times a day; wearing matted locks instead of curled hair; and clothing oneself in rags rather than a body [adorned with finery]. ||14||
The incomparable state of householdership of Prajāpati Kardama, brought forth by the power of his asceticism and yoga, is to be desired even by the inhabitants of celestial chariots.

Śrīdhara: The syntactical connection with the sixth verse is as follows: having abandoned her own exceptional state of household life—which had flourished through the asceticism and yoga of Prajāpati Kardama—she, distressed by the separation from her son-like Lord, made her face somewhat indescribable and overwhelmed with grief. ||15||
The sequential arrangement: "Of Prajāpati" constitutes a group of six. "Vibudhānucarāḥ" (the attendants of the gods) refers to the female attendants of the gods (*vibudhānucaryaḥ*);

[it denotes] something indescribable (*kiñcit*), just as in the expression "extremely impure" and so forth. The reason for this is stated by Viśvanātha: "of Prajāpati" and so on; the speaking (*vadana*) of these [beings] is something indescribable.
The connection with the sixth [verse] is that she "made [him] agitated by grief. ||15||
His couches were like the foam of milk, made of ivory and adorned with gold;
his seats were made of gold, as were his highly pleasant coverlets.

Śrīdhara: In that state of household life (*gārhasthya*), there appear beds and coverlets as white and soft as the foam of milk, as well as couches fashioned from ivory; there are golden side-stands, seats such as stools and the like, and upon them are covers of exquisite touch. (16)
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
In walls of clear crystal and great emeralds,
jewel-lamps shine, as do women endowed with jewels.
It was not explained by whom:
"The house-garden is delightful with many blossoming celestial trees,
filled with pairs of warbling birds and singing, intoxicated bees."
Śrīdhara: Delightful with many celestial trees. ||18||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. [It says:
"Where the followers of the gods sang of themselves having entered a lotus-scented pond and being fondled by the mud."
Śrīdhara: [He saw] himself having entered that garden where Devahūtī was. ||19||
Kramasaṃdarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [He saw] Devahūtī, who had entered her own self. ||19||
Abandoning even that which is most desired by the wives of Indra, she,
distressed by the separation from her son, made her face appear somewhat altered.

Śrīdhara: Even for those women who are most desired by Ākhaṇḍala—Indra—that [state] is the most cherished object of their longing; having abandoned that, and having relinquished attachment to it. ||20||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
When her husband had departed for the forest, she, distressed by the separation from her offspring,
though she had realized the ultimate truth, became like a cow longing for her calf when it is lost.
Śrīdhara: He describes the unbearable nature of separation from a friend with the verse beginning "The forest" (vanaṃ). She became like a cow longing for her calf when it is lost. ||21||

The sequence of the composition: He states that the love known as *vātsalya* (parental affection) belonging to the Blessed One surpasses all other [forms of love]—in the verse beginning with "the forest. Even though she has realized the ultimate reality (*tattva*), because her internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is pure, at the very moment of hearing [the teaching], she manifests the various attainments to be accomplished through those respective means. ||21||

Viśvanātha: The Blessed One states that the affection known as *vātsalya* (parental love) overcomes all other [affections]—in the verse beginning with "The forest. Even though her husband Kardama had gone to the forest, she remained alive while gazing upon her offspring;
yet, she was distressed by the separation from him as well—alas! Where are they, and who are they? Let them see their offspring!
"Turn back at once, sirs! Otherwise I shall not live!"—thus lamenting like a cow, she has, as it were, suddenly forgotten her entire knowledge of reality; such is the sense. ||21||
Meditating upon that very god, the golden-hued Hari, who is the offspring [of the gods],
she soon became free from desire for such a household, O dear one.

Śrīdhara: He states the fruit of meditation performed during separation: "free from desire" (niḥspṛhā) means "devoid of latent impressions" (nirvāsanā). [In the commentary on] the four and a half verses beginning with "that very one" (tam eva), he says "that" (tam) because even the previously described abandonment of the home occurred in that same manner—[he went] to Hari, Kapila.
The meaning is: meditating upon him who had appeared in the form of Kapila, and remembering him as her own child, she meditated upon him specifically in his capacity as her offspring. ||22||
Viśvanātha: He states the fruit of meditation arising from separation [from the beloved] in the verse beginning with "tam eva" (that very one). ||22||
Meditating on the form of the Blessed One, which he described as the object of meditation,
the son [meditated] upon it with a serene countenance, through both collective and individual reflection.
By means of the flow of devotion, by powerful dispassion,
and by the knowledge born of disciplined practice which has Brahman as its cause.
Then, by means of the pure self, he [perceives] himself as facing in all directions,
with the specific qualities of Māyā concealed through his own direct experience.
With his mind established in Brahman, the Blessed One who is the refuge of the self.

Śrīdhara: Then, as his son Kapila spoke, he meditated upon that form of the Blessed One and meditated upon himself as facing in all directions and omnipresent; thus, with his mind established in Brahman, he became [as described]—this is the connection with what precedes. By means of what did he meditate?
With a pure self and mind. ||23||

He states the causes for purification: by means of knowledge born from yoga in the form of a continuous flow of devotion, from dispassion, and from disciplined practice; and as for disciplined practice, it is described in the Gītā:
"For one whose food and recreation are regulated, whose exertion in actions is regulated..."
"For one whose sleep and awakening are disciplined, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering" (Gītā 6.17).
By means of Brahman—that which brings about the state of being Brahman—[he attains it]. ||24||
The reason for its being "facing in all directions" (viśvatomukha) is stated: it is concealed by its own experience, that is, by the manifestation of its own nature;
it is that whose qualification or limitation is caused by the qualities of *māyā*. ||25||
In what kind of Brahman? In the Blessed One, who is the refuge of the selves, that is, the individual souls. ||26||
The sequence of the composition: How, or in what manner, did she come to know the reality?

To this he says with three and a half verses beginning with "dhyāyantī" (meditating). At the time of the discourse on knowledge, her mind was fixed upon Brahman; at the time of the discourse on devotion, her mind was fixed upon the Blessed Lord.

It came to pass; however, it should be understood that even the knowledge of Brahman there served only to strengthen the knowledge of the Lord, for in accordance with the *Gītā* and other texts such as "Having become Brahman, the self becomes serene" (*Gītā* 18.54), he describes the Lord in that very same way: "For I am the foundation of Brahman, which rests within the Self. (*Gītā* 14.27)

According to the Śrī Gītā (14.26), "the auspicious refuge," and according to the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa, "the support of the mind, of the all-pervading, and likewise of the Self"; it is a qualification of this [Self] that it is the cause of abiding in Brahman,
and it is called the "cause of Brahman" because it arises from the collection of properly performed practices and the collection of causes for attaining Brahman.

The meaning is "by means of the cause for the manifestation of Brahman. This refers to what was previously stated as "by means of detachment from the means" (*sādhanavairāgya*) and "by the pure one" (*viśuddhena*), and so forth. One should contemplate the self—the pure individual soul (*jīva*)—specifically through the Self, which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), by way of identity (*tādātmya*) with that [Supreme Self], being itself pure and entirely devoid of even the possibility of contact with ignorance (*avidyā*).

He describes the manner in which the individual self (*jīvātman*) attains purity by stating, "meditating on [the Lord] who faces all directions and is omnipresent," using the phrase "by means of one's own experience. The reason for abiding in the Blessed One is "through the yoga of the continuous flow of devotion"—
that is, through the constant movement of the mind set in motion by love, in the manner described by the words "merely by hearing of my qualities" and so forth.

This is the meaning. Having first reflected upon the means for that [attainment] through both collective and individual considerations, preceded by an investigation into positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), his son, with a serene countenance, described the form of the Blessed One as the object of meditation—he taught it as the sphere of *dhyāna*. "Meditating upon that" refers to that very [form].

The meaning is this: that which is taught as having knowledge (*jñāna*) as its fruit according to one's particular latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is indeed performed as having love (*prema*) as its fruit according to one's own latent impressions. Nevertheless, it should be understood that even the causality for knowledge occurs as a secondary consequence (*ānuṣaṅgika*) of that very same devotion. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa... casting aside the path of devotion, which is the way to the highest good (*śreyas*).
[This is from] 10.14.4, etc.
He describes that state at that time with three and a half verses. Among them, "nivṛttā" constitutes one and a half.
"Jīvāpatti" is the superimposition of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra).

Viśvanātha: Then she thought: "Alas, alas! O Blessed One, my mind, distressed by separation, does not abandon its state of being a son toward you; therefore, having sat for a moment in solitude, I shall cast off this state of being a son, fix my mind, and practice that very meditation which was described. Thus she meditated.
He said: "She meditates. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: meditating upon the form of the Blessed One, her mind was established in the Blessed Brahman.
By means of that collection of practices which is appropriate and joined with yoga in the form of a continuous flow of devotion; or rather, as it is stated in the *Gītā*:
"For one who is disciplined in diet and conduct, disciplined in actions,
disciplined in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering" (Gītā 6.17).
Therefore, through disciplined practice, and through the dispassion and knowledge born therefrom which have Brahman as their cause—

The meaning is: "by means of the cause that is pure devotion arising [within him]," and not by means of the knowledge of the reality of identity with the form of Brahman. For this very reason, because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), he [beheld] that Self—the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that Blessed Lord—purified throughout the ten directions.

The remainder [of the sentence] is: they see that which has such a face—that is, which has attained manifestation—by means of their own experience, their own realization; and they see it in such a way that the specific qualities of Māyā have become concealed therein; [they see it] in the Blessed One, the Brahman, the supreme self who is the refuge of the selves, the individual souls.

It is that state in which the intellect of the wise, the devotees, and the yogins is established in the ultimate reality— the perfect, all-encompassing essential nature. Therefore, by the phrase "through the yoga of the continuous flow of devotion," it is indicated that *bhāvabhakti* (emotional devotion),
characterized as being [awakened] by the mere hearing of My qualities, is what is meant by the word "flow."

It was indeed so for her. Likewise, that knowledge of the referent of the term *tvam* (the individual self) and the referent of the term *tat* (the Supreme Self), which is inseparable from the third stage (*bhūmikā*) for the wise, is certainly useful in the system of devotion (*bhaktimata*) as the knowledge of the devotee and the Lord—the worshiper and the object of worship.
As it has been said regarding those two specific types of knowledge:

Because it is useful for entering into devotion, that which is the seventh stage— meditation (*dhyāna*)— for those practicing the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*), is indeed the third limb of ninefold devotion (*navāṅgabhakti*) and is supremely useful; thus Devahūti, having grasped that knowledge of the wise and the meditation of the yogis according to the maxim "like a bee that consumes only the essence," [proceeded].

It is included within devotion (bhakti) as that which is to be personally practiced; for this very reason it was said, "by means of knowledge, which has Brahman as its cause," and as he said, "O son, [it is] the object of meditation. ||2326||
Because the state of being a living soul had ceased, she had attained nirvāṇa through the destruction of the afflictions;
because she was eternally established in samādhi, the delusion regarding the qualities had been overturned. She did not then remember her own self, like one who has awakened from a dream.

"Madhva [says]: 'For all embodied beings, until liberation, the adjuncts of the individual soul (jīvopādhi) and so forth exist by necessity; however, their non-existence is proclaimed because it would be fruitless. Thus [it is stated] in the Varāha[-purāṇa]. (27)

Śrīdhara: [Objection: Even so, since the *guṇas* still exist, how can there be no recollection? To this he says: because of her state (*bhāva*), that is, her essential nature (*tattva*), which consists in a concentration (*samādhi*) that is eternally ascended and firmly established;
